title: Networking
text:
Networking
Learn networking from first principles to NetOps by designing, building, breaking, and verifying networks. Containerlab and netlab support labs using freely available images, including FRR, Arista cEOS, and Nokia SR Linux.

title: Networking
text:
Learning path

Lab platform and a first topology.
Networking foundations and packet capture.
Layer 2 switching, VLANs, loops, and aggregation.
IP routing and services: static routes, DNS, DHCP, NAT, redundancy, and MTU.
Dynamic routing: OSPF, BGP, policy, and convergence.
Security, operations, and automation.
Tunnels, overlays, and fabrics.
Optional advanced tracks: routing security, transport and applications, and forensics.
Projects and the multi-NOS lab workbook.
Command references.

Use the workbook guide and learning paths to choose exercises and prerequisites. Use each diagram to predict the path, build the lab, verify the control and data planes, then introduce a failure and explain what changed. The workbook includes optional cEOS exercises that require an independently obtained image; consult the image provider for access and licensing. The workbook complements the core chapters: choose labs that match your topic and available images. Cisco and Juniper labs may be added as optional tracks later.
Every serious lab should include a topology and addressing plan, verification, and a failure scenario. Topology diagrams follow the shared illustrated light and dark SVG standard; conceptual diagrams explain the behavior being tested.

text: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try

title: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
text:
Learning goals

Read a Netplan YAML file as a declaration of devices, addresses and routes, not as a list of ip commands.
Choose a renderer (networkd or NetworkManager) that actually runs on the host, and know what happens if you pick the wrong one.
Write working fragments for ethernet, 802.3ad bonds, VLAN subinterfaces, bridges, static routes and source-based routing-policy.
Know the difference between netplan generate, netplan apply and netplan try, including the 120-second rollback window.

Version note: Netplan was not installed on the writing host (Linux 6.12.94+, 2026-11-12), and netplan generate / apply / try were not run (no root, no installs). The YAML and CLI behaviour below are taken from the current Netplan documentation (stable YAML reference, design page, and the generate / apply / try manual pages). Verify them on an Ubuntu or Debian lab host before you trust a change on a machine you can only reach over the network you are editing.

title: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
text:
What Netplan is
On Debian/Ubuntu-style hosts, the network configuration you edit is a set of YAML files under /etc/netplan/. A generator reads every *.yaml in that directory, merges them, and writes backend configuration under /run for the renderer you selected. The renderer — systemd-networkd or NetworkManager — is what actually brings links up, runs DHCP, and installs routes.
  /etc/netplan/*.yaml
           │  netplan generate
           ▼
     /run/systemd/network/*.network   or   NetworkManager keyfiles
           │  renderer
           ▼
        kernel links, addresses, routes
You almost never edit the generated files. If a setting is missing from the YAML, it does not belong in /run.
The on-disk format is version 2. That is the only supported value; if you omit version, it defaults to 2.

title: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
text:
Renderers
The renderer key may appear on network:, on a device type (ethernets:, bonds:, …), or on a single device. The default, if you say nothing, is networkd.








Renderer
Typical home
Notes




networkd
Headless servers, most lab VMs
Lightweight. DHCP overrides, accept-ra, optional: and most routing-policy features are first-class here.


NetworkManager
Desktops, some appliance images (Raspberry Pi OS with NetworkManager, Ubuntu Desktop)
Better Wi-Fi and modem support. A few networkd-only keys are ignored or not implemented.



The failure mode that takes a lab host off the network is simple: the YAML says nothing, so Netplan defaults to networkd, but the image is only running NetworkManager (or the other way around). The generator writes units or keyfiles that nobody is applying. The link stays down or has only a link-local address. If you are writing a network-config for cloud-init or Pi OS, set renderer: explicitly to the daemon that image actually starts.
You can mix renderers on one host — for example NetworkManager on wlan0 and networkd on a bonded pair — but keep the lab path boring: one renderer, named at the top of the file.

title: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
text:
Worked examples
These listings are documentation examples, not the output of netplan apply.

A lab NIC with DHCP
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    enp1s0:
      dhcp4: true
      optional: true
optional: true tells networkd not to stall boot waiting for this link. Use it on ports that are often unplugged. Leave it off for the uplink you need before SSH comes back.


Static address and a default route
gateway4 and gateway6 are deprecated. Write a default route:
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    enp1s0:
      addresses:
        - 192.0.2.10/24
        - "2001:db8:1::10/64"
      nameservers:
        addresses: [192.0.2.53, "2001:db8:1::53"]
        search: [lab.example]
      routes:
        - to: default
          via: 192.0.2.1
        - to: default
          via: "2001:db8:1::1"
to: default is the documented spelling of 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0. If the gateway is not on-link according to the prefix, add on-link: true.
To accept a DHCP address but not the DHCP default route (so a static default on another NIC wins):
      dhcp4: true
      dhcp4-overrides:
        use-routes: false
use-routes and route-metric work on both renderers; most other DHCP overrides are networkd only. If both dhcp4 and dhcp6 are true, networkd requires the two override maps to be identical.


Bond, VLAN and bridge
A pattern you will use on a lab hypervisor: two physical ports in an LACP bond, a VLAN on the bond for the lab uplink, and a bridge that VMs or Containerlab management can attach to.
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    enp1s0: {}
    enp2s0: {}
  bonds:
    bond0:
      interfaces: [enp1s0, enp2s0]
      parameters:
        mode: 802.3ad
        lacp-rate: fast
        mii-monitor-interval: 100
        transmit-hash-policy: layer3+4
  vlans:
    bond0-100:
      id: 100
      link: bond0
  bridges:
    br-lab:
      interfaces: [bond0-100]
      addresses: [192.0.2.1/24]
      nameservers:
        addresses: [192.0.2.53]
      routes:
        - to: default
          via: 192.0.2.254
      parameters:
        stp: false
Empty ethernets entries are enough when the IDs already match the kernel names and the addresses live on the bond, VLAN or bridge. Bond modes you will actually use: 802.3ad (LACP), active-backup (two uplinks, one active), and sometimes balance-xor. lacp-rate: fast is only meaningful in 802.3ad.
STP on a Linux bridge defaults to on in Netplan (parameters.stp defaults to true). That surprises people who expected a dumb hypervisor bridge. For a two-port lab bridge with no loops, set stp: false. For a real looped L2 domain, leave it on and set priorities deliberately.


Source routing
Two uplinks, two default routes, traffic from a service address forced out the second path:
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    enp1s0:
      addresses: [192.0.2.10/24]
      routes:
        - to: default
          via: 192.0.2.1
          metric: 100
    enp2s0:
      addresses: [198.51.100.10/24]
      routes:
        - to: default
          via: 198.51.100.1
          metric: 200
          table: 100
      routing-policy:
        - from: 198.51.100.10
          table: 100
          priority: 100
table: on the route and on the policy must agree. Give every policy rule a unique priority (mandatory on the NetworkManager backend, a good habit everywhere). This is the same idea as ip rule / ip route show table in the policy-routing chapter: Netplan is how a Debian/Ubuntu host persists it.

title: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
text:
generate, apply and try
Three commands, three jobs.
netplan generate parses every /etc/netplan/*.yaml (and any extra file you pass), validates the merged tree, and writes backend files under /run. It does not change the running network. You will not normally run it yourself: apply and try call it. It is the right tool when you want “is this YAML legal?” without touching links.
netplan apply generates, then asks the renderer to bring the configuration up. If devices were renamed, it may unbind and rebind them so udev can run, then invoke the renderer again. There is no automatic rollback. A typo in via: or the wrong renderer can drop the management address and leave you on the wrong side of a locked door.
netplan try is the remote-safe variant. It applies the configuration and waits 120 seconds by default (--timeout). If you do not confirm — interactively, or by sending SIGUSR1 — it rolls back. SIGINT rejects immediately. Use --config-file to try a file that is not already in /etc/netplan/.
Two caveats from the manual, both worth treating as real:

Some designs (STP is the documented example) may take more than a minute to settle. If you try a bridged topology with the default timeout, you can roll back a correct config that had not finished converging. Raise --timeout.
If try times out or is cancelled, verify that the previous configuration actually came back. The documented advice is: check the running addresses and routes, and check that the YAML on disk is the YAML you think it is, before you reboot.

Other useful subcommands, all still documentation-only here: netplan get / netplan set for a single key, netplan status for a human view of what is configured, netplan info for feature flags.

title: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
text:
Gotchas

Match by MAC when you set mtu:, macaddress:, or offloads and the renderer is networkd. Matching on the current interface name races udev renaming.
Do not use gateway4 / gateway6. Write routes: with to: default.
link-local: defaults to IPv6 only. link-local: [] disables IPv4 and IPv6 link-local addresses on that device.
accept-ra and dhcp6 interact with SLAAC. Setting dhcp6: true is how you ask the client to honour M/O flags in Router Advertisements; accept-ra alone does not start DHCPv6.
Empty member lists are legal: a bridge or bond can come up with no ports, which is useful while you are wiring VMs, and useless if you expected traffic.
Open vSwitch: if any device carries an openvswitch: mapping and OVS is not installed, Netplan treats that as an error and will not apply the file.
Permissions: keep /etc/netplan/ root-owned and not world-readable if a file contains Wi-Fi or 802.1X secrets.

title: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
text:
Common mistakes

Leaving renderer unset on an image that does not run systemd-networkd.
Running netplan apply over SSH on the only uplink, instead of netplan try.
Putting addresses on the physical NICs and on the bond or bridge they belong to.
Forgetting to declare the parent ethernet of a VLAN, or the members of a bond.
Expecting netplan generate to change the running system.
Assuming a successful try timeout always restored the previous configuration, without looking.

title: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
text:
Boring rule
Edit YAML, not /run. On any host you can reach only through the interface you are changing, use netplan try, wait until you can still ping, then confirm. Never apply first and hope.

title: Netplan: YAML, Renderers, Bonds, VLANs, Bridges and try
text:
Try this

On an Ubuntu VM you can get a console on, write a DHCP ethernet file, run netplan generate, and read the unit it wrote under /run/systemd/network/. Then netplan try the same file.
Deliberately set renderer: networkd on a NetworkManager-only image (or the reverse) and record what ip addr shows after apply. Restore with the console.
Build the bond + VLAN + bridge example with stp: true, then with stp: false. Time how long the bridge takes to forward, and set --timeout accordingly.
Add a second default route in table: 100 and a routing-policy from: rule. Confirm with ip rule and ip route get <addr> from <src>.
Take a working file, change gateway4: to a routes: default, generate, and diff the emitted backend config.

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Containerlab Fundamentals
Containerlab turns a YAML topology into runnable network labs: create nodes, wire virtual links, attach a management network, and destroy everything cleanly. This chapter is the operator’s manual for the rest of the book’s labs.

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Read and write a minimal *.clab.yml topology

Deploy, inspect, connect, and destroy labs

Choose free node kinds (FRR, Linux, etc.)

Understand management network vs data-plane links

Export a graph and use consistent naming

Recover from partial deploys and leftover state

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Prerequisites

Linux host or VM with nested virt as needed (Docker or podman per Containerlab docs)

containerlab installed (install guide)

Permission to run privileged containers / sudo as required

Images pullable from public registries for free kinds

Check:
containerlab version
docker version   # or podman

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
How Containerlab fits together
topology.clab.yml
       │
       ▼
 containerlab deploy
       │
       ├─ create containers (nodes)
       ├─ create veth/links between interfaces
       ├─ attach management network (SSH/mgmt IPs)
       └─ optional startup configs / binds
Destroy reverses the graph. Source of truth is the YAML (plus mounted configs), not hand edits inside nodes.



Triangle lab

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Minimal topology: two Linux nodes
name: twoping

topology:
  nodes:
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20

  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "h2:eth1"]
Save as twoping.clab.yml.
sudo containerlab deploy -t twoping.clab.yml
sudo containerlab inspect -t twoping.clab.yml
Address the link and test (interfaces may need addressing—Alpine is raw):
# Names often: clab-twoping-h1
docker exec -it clab-twoping-h1 sh
# inside:
ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev eth1
ip link set eth1 up
# on h2:
# ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev eth1 && ip link set eth1 up
# ping 10.0.0.1
For real labs you bake addressing into startup scripts or use NOS images that apply configs. Pattern: deploy → configure via files → verify.

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
section: Triangle of FRR routers (book default pattern)
text:
Triangle of FRR routers (book default pattern)
FRR containers give you a real control plane without licenses.
name: triangle

topology:
  nodes:
    r1:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/r1:/etc/frr
    r2:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/r2:/etc/frr
    r3:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/r3:/etc/frr

  links:
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth1", "r2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r2:eth2", "r3:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r3:eth2", "r1:eth2"]
Note: Pin image tags deliberately (example tag may differ—check current FRR container tags). Each node mounts its own ./config/rN to /etc/frr.

Startup config sketch (config/r1/daemons + frr.conf)
FRR images expect daemons enabled. Example frr.conf ideas (interface names must match):
frr version 10.2.1
frr defaults traditional
hostname r1
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.0.12.1/24
!
interface eth2
 ip address 10.0.13.1/24
!
ip route 0.0.0.0/0 10.0.12.2
!
line vty
Exact FRR container entrypoint behavior evolves—follow the image README. The topology pattern (binds + links) is the durable skill.


Lifecycle
sudo containerlab deploy -t triangle.clab.yml
sudo containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml   # if supported in your version
sudo containerlab inspect -t triangle.clab.yml
docker exec -it clab-triangle-r1 vtysh
sudo containerlab destroy -t triangle.clab.yml --cleanup

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Topology YAML anatomy



Key
Purpose




name
Lab name prefix for containers/namespaces


topology.nodes
Node inventory


topology.links
Point-to-point (or multipoint via extras)

How Containerlab treats the node

Container image

Commands after start (use sparingly; prefer files)

Publish container ports to host (mgmt tools)

Static management address (optional)




Kinds you will actually use



Kind / image pattern
Role




linux + Alpine/Debian
Hosts, simple routers with FRR image


FRR container on linux kind
OSPF/BGP labs


srl (SR Linux community)
Modern NOS practice (free image path)


VyOS / SONiC images
Optional diversity



Always confirm license-free use for the image you pull. This book never requires paid virtual NOS licenses.

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Links and endpoints
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth1", "r2:eth1"]
Rules of thumb:

Interface names must match what the NOS expects or what you configure

Point-to-point links are veth pairs under the hood

Do not reuse the same interface name twice on one node

Leave eth0 for management if the kind uses it for mgmt


Multipoint / LAN segments
Patterns include attaching multiple nodes via a bridge node or kind-specific multipoint links. Early labs stick to point-to-point for clarity; L2 chapters introduce switch nodes.

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Management network
Containerlab creates a management network so you can SSH/API to nodes without using data-plane links.
sudo containerlab inspect -t triangle.clab.yml
# Note mgmt IPv4 addresses
ssh admin@<mgmt-ip>   # credentials depend on image
Predict: Breaking a data-plane link does not remove SSH via mgmt (unless you broke the host docker network). That separation mirrors production OOB vs in-band—use it.

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Inspect, exec, save
# Table of nodes and mgmt IPs
sudo containerlab inspect -t triangle.clab.yml

# Shell
docker exec -it clab-triangle-r1 bash

# FRR
docker exec -it clab-triangle-r1 vtysh -c 'show interface brief'

# Destroy
sudo containerlab destroy -t triangle.clab.yml --cleanup
--cleanup removes lab containers and lab-specific wiring; use it to avoid ghost interfaces.

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Lab directory layout (recommended)
labs/triangle/
  triangle.clab.yml
  README.md
  addressing.md
  verify.sh
  config/
    r1/
    r2/
    r3/
  captures/
cd labs/triangle
sudo containerlab deploy -t triangle.clab.yml
./verify.sh

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Graph and documentation
sudo containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml
Import diagrams into your journal. Combine with a hand-drawn addressing plan—graph alone lacks subnets.

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Partial failure recovery
If deploy dies halfway:
sudo containerlab destroy -t triangle.clab.yml --cleanup
docker ps -a | grep clab
# remove stragglers if needed
sudo containerlab deploy -t triangle.clab.yml
Also check:
docker images | head
df -h          # disk full breaks pulls
ip link | wc -l  # too many leftover veths

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Predict → observe → fix lab

Setup
Deploy twoping with addresses applied via exec for speed (acceptable for learning; later prefer binds):
name: twoping

topology:
  nodes:
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "h2:eth1"]
Note: exec timing can race interface creation on some versions—if eth1 missing, retry commands or use a small sleep in a script bind.


Predict

ping 10.0.0.2 from h1 succeeds

ip neigh shows REACHABLE for peer



Observe
docker exec clab-twoping-h1 ping -c 3 10.0.0.2
docker exec clab-twoping-h1 ip neigh
docker exec clab-twoping-h1 ip -br a


Fix inject
docker exec clab-twoping-h2 ip link set eth1 down
docker exec clab-twoping-h1 ping -c 2 10.0.0.2  # fail
docker exec clab-twoping-h2 ip link set eth1 up


Harden
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
docker exec clab-twoping-h1 ping -c 2 -W 1 10.0.0.2
echo OK
Re-deploy from clean destroy and ensure verify.sh still passes.

Mistake
Symptom

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Version awareness (mid-2026)
Containerlab releases steadily. Skills that stay:

Topology as code

kinds + images + links + binds

deploy / inspect / destroy lifecycle

Syntax extras (stages, components, interfaces block style) may appear in newer docs—read containerlab.dev for your installed version when YAML fails validation.
containerlab version
containerlab help deploy

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Security and shared hosts

Labs often run privileged networking—isolate lab hosts

Do not expose mgmt SSH to the internet

Pull images from trusted registries; pin digests for CI later

title: Containerlab Fundamentals
text:
Summary

Containerlab materializes YAML into namespaces, containers, and links

Master deploy → inspect → exec → destroy –cleanup

Prefer binds/startup configs over irreproducible exec-only hacks

Keep per-lab directories with verify scripts

FRR + Linux free images cover most of this book’s spine

Next: Netlab Fundamentals—how to layer a declarative intent compiler on top of Containerlab to automate IP addressing, protocol configurations, and validation suites.

title: Netlab Fundamentals
text:
Netlab Fundamentals
While Containerlab excels at spinning up containers and wiring virtual Ethernet pairs, running real multi-node routing topologies requires hundreds of lines of boilerplate device configurations, IP address spreadsheets, and manual routing daemon setup.
Netlab (developed by Ivan Pepelnjak) solves this problem by providing a declarative network intent and configuration compiler. Rather than replacing Containerlab, Netlab uses Containerlab as its primary virtualization provider (provider: clab). You describe what you want in a high-level YAML topology; Netlab automatically plans IP subnets, assigns loopback and transit addresses, generates vendor-specific configurations (FRR, Arista cEOS, Nokia SR Linux, Cisco XRd), and instructs Containerlab to deploy the lab.

title: Netlab Fundamentals
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Articulate the distinction between the orchestration layer (Containerlab) and the intent/configuration layer (Netlab).
Install and configure Netlab with Containerlab on a Linux system.
Write concise declarative topology files (topology.yml) with automated module activation (OSPF, BGP, BFD, VLANs).
Inspect compiled artifacts (netlab create) to understand the underlying Containerlab topology and generated NOS configuration files.
Operate the full lifecycle: netlab up, netlab connect, netlab inspect, and netlab down.
Run automated verification test suites using netlab validate.
Inject realistic network impairments (latency, jitter, packet loss) using netlab tc.
Swap network operating systems (e.g., FRR to Arista cEOS or Nokia SR Linux) with a single configuration parameter.

title: Netlab Fundamentals
section: The Dual-Engine Model: Why Both Tools Matter
text:
The Dual-Engine Model: Why Both Tools Matter
When learning networking from scratch, choosing between Containerlab and Netlab is not an either/or dilemma. They serve distinct, complementary purposes across your learning journey:








Capability
Containerlab Direct (*.clab.yml)
Netlab with Containerlab (topology.yml)




Mental Model
Physical / Virtual link plumbing (veth pairs & namespaces)
Network architecture & protocol intent


IP Addressing
Completely manual; you must assign every IP on every interface
Fully automated IPAM; computes /30, /31, or /24 transit and /32 loopbacks


Protocol Config
Manual; you author and mount /etc/frr/frr.conf or vendor configs
Automated; Jinja2 templates render native NOS configs from modules


Ideal For
L1/L2 mechanics, raw ARP, custom bridges, packet crafts
OSPF, BGP, EVPN-VXLAN, multi-area fabrics, failure drills


Validation
Manual CLI checks and docker exec commands
Automated testing assertions with netlab validate


NOS Portability
Low; changing NOS requires rewriting all config files
High; change device: frr to device: eos or device: srlinux



Curriculum Rule of Thumb:
Use raw Containerlab for visceral wire-level understanding in early foundation chapters (inspecting ARP frames, Linux bridges, MTU fragmentation). Transition to Netlab when studying dynamic routing protocols, transit policies, and data center fabrics to eliminate syntax fatigue and focus on architectural principles.

title: Netlab Fundamentals
text:
Installation & Setup
Netlab is distributed as a Python package (network-lab) that interacts directly with Docker and Containerlab.

Prerequisites
Netlab requires Python 3.9+, Docker (or Podman), and Containerlab. On Ubuntu/Debian:
# Ensure Python virtual environment tools and Ansible core are installed
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y python3-pip python3-venv git

# Create a dedicated virtual environment or install via pipx / pip
python3 -m pip install --upgrade network-lab


Automated Platform Provisioning
Netlab includes a self-bootstrapping command that verifies system requirements, installs Containerlab, configures Docker, and sets the required user groups (docker and clab_admins):
# Verify installation prerequisites and dependencies
netlab check

# Automatically install or update Containerlab and dependencies
sudo netlab install containerlab
Verify your active environment:
netlab test clab
This command deploys a two-node lightweight container lab, validates bidirectional connectivity over a virtual link, and tears down the lab cleanly.

title: Netlab Fundamentals
section: The Anatomy of a Netlab Topology
text:
The Anatomy of a Netlab Topology
A Netlab topology is saved by default as topology.yml in your working directory.

Minimal Triangle Topology with OSPF
Here is the exact equivalent of the three-router OSPF triangle that required three separate configuration files and complex volume binds in raw Containerlab:
# topology.yml
---
provider: clab
defaults.device: frr

module: [ ospf ]

nodes:
  r1:
  r2:
  r3:

links:
  - r1:
    r2:
  - r2:
    r3:
  - r3:
    r1:


What Happens Behind the Scenes?
When you run netlab up, the Netlab compiler executes a multi-step pipeline:
topology.yml
    │
    ▼
1. Topology Transformation (Assign IP subnets, loopbacks, router IDs, interface names)
    │
    ▼
2. Jinja2 Config Generation (Render /etc/frr/frr.conf and daemons for r1, r2, r3)
    │
    ▼
3. Containerlab File Generation (Emit clab.yml with nodes, kinds, mounts, and links)
    │
    ▼
4. Containerlab Orchestration (sudo containerlab deploy -t clab.yml)
    │
    ▼
5. Initial Configuration Push (Mount configs or apply via daemon sockets)
To see the compiled Containerlab YAML without starting containers, run:
netlab create
Inspect the generated artifacts in the current directory: - clab.yml: The generated Containerlab topology. - hosts.yml / ansible.cfg: Automation inventory for Ansible and Python scripts. - config/: The auto-generated initial configurations for each device (e.g., config/r1/frr.conf).

title: Netlab Fundamentals
text:
Operating Netlab Labs
Netlab abstracts away container naming conventions (clab-<labname>-<nodename>) and provides uniform commands across any operating system.

1. Starting and Stopping Labs
# Create configuration, deploy containers, and configure devices in one step
netlab up

# Inspect running nodes, interfaces, and IPv4/IPv6 address assignments
netlab inspect

# Cleanly stop and destroy containers, veth pairs, and management links
netlab down


2. Connecting to Devices
You do not need to run docker exec -it clab-... vtysh. Netlab connects directly to the device CLI:
# Open an interactive CLI session on router r1 (starts vtysh on FRR)
netlab connect r1

# Run a non-interactive show command across a node
netlab connect r1 vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"


3. Graphing Topologies
Netlab can automatically render visual diagrams of your topology in SVG or ASCII format:
# Generate a graphical visualization of the lab topology
netlab graph -o topology.png

title: Netlab Fundamentals
text:
Automated Verification with netlab validate
In enterprise NetOps, verifying that a network functions according to specification is done through automated tests rather than manual pings. Netlab provides an automated validation engine built directly into the topology file.
You can declare expected states under the validate key:
# topology.yml with validation rules
---
provider: clab
defaults.device: frr
module: [ ospf ]

nodes:
  r1:
  r2:
  r3:

links:
  - r1:
    r2:
  - r2:
    r3:
  - r3:
    r1:

validate:
  ospf_neighbors:
    description: "Verify all routers reach Full OSPF adjacency"
    nodes: [ r1, r2, r3 ]
    plugin: ospf_neighbor(count=2, state='Full')

  loopback_reachability:
    description: "Verify end-to-end routing between loopbacks"
    nodes: [ r1 ]
    exec:
      r1: ping -c 2 10.0.0.2
      r1_to_r3: ping -c 2 10.0.0.3
Execute the test suite with a single command:
netlab validate
If an adjacency is stuck in ExStart due to an MTU mismatch or a broken link, netlab validate reports a red failure with actionable diagnostic outputs.

title: Netlab Fundamentals
section: Simulating Real-World Links with netlab tc
text:
Simulating Real-World Links with netlab tc
Production networks suffer from latency, jitter, packet reordering, and drop rates. Netlab integrates Linux Traffic Control (tc / netem) directly into links.
You can define impairments declaratively in topology.yml:
links:
  - r1:
    r2:
    # Emulate an intercontinental WAN link
    bandwidth: 100mbps
    latency: 45ms
    jitter: 5ms
    loss: 0.5%
Or inject impairments dynamically during a live lab drill using the netlab tc CLI tool:
# Add 50ms latency to the link between r1 and r2
netlab tc set r1 eth1 --delay 50ms

# Inject 10% packet drop to observe BFD or OSPF dead timer behavior
netlab tc set r2 eth1 --loss 10%

# Clear all impairments
netlab tc clear r1 eth1

title: Netlab Fundamentals
section: Multi-NOS Portability: The Ultimate Learning Superpower
text:
Multi-NOS Portability: The Ultimate Learning Superpower
One of the greatest advantages of Netlab is device abstraction. Dynamic routing protocols are vendor-agnostic standards, but vendor CLIs differ dramatically.
In Netlab, changing your entire lab from FRR to Arista EOS, Cisco IOS-XR, or Nokia SR Linux requires modifying one line:
# Change default device from FRR to Arista cEOS
defaults.device: eos
Or mixing different operating systems in the same topology:
nodes:
  r1:
    device: frr       # Linux FRR routing daemon
  r2:
    device: eos       # Arista cEOS
  r3:
    device: srlinux   # Nokia SR Linux
When you execute netlab up, Netlab applies standard OSPF configurations across all three distinct operating systems automatically. This enables you to focus on protocol interoperability, RFC compliance, and packet behavior without getting derailed by syntax differences.

title: Netlab Fundamentals
text:
Summary & What Comes Next

Containerlab is your runtime foundation: it wires containers, creates Linux bridges, and provisions network namespaces.
Netlab is your network compiler: it automates IP addressing, configures routing protocols, conducts automated testing, and simulates link conditions.
Throughout this book:

Early chapters (Ethernet, ARP, VLANs, static routes) use raw Containerlab and Linux containers so you understand the raw kernel plumbing.
Advanced routing chapters (OSPF, BGP, EVPN-VXLAN, Clos fabrics) provide Netlab topologies as the primary recipe, alongside the compiled Containerlab configurations for complete architectural clarity.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
Containerized network labs are designed for ephemerality, but real-world engineering requires persistence. When you deploy a network topology using Containerlab, configure BGP sessions across five routers, and execute containerlab destroy, where does that configuration go? If you redeploy the lab, do your routers boot with their factory defaults or with the complex routing policies you spent three hours building?
Understanding how state persists across lab lifecycles is the difference between a reliable network simulation platform and a frustrating source of lost work. Containerlab provides a structured mechanism for handling state, but it relies on an explicit hierarchy of precedence. If you do not understand how Containerlab handles lab directories, startup-config declarations, and host volume binds, you will eventually face silent configuration overrides or data loss.
This chapter details the exact mechanics of state persistence in Containerlab. We examine the three distinct layers of state, walk through the state lifecycle step-by-step, explore versioned backups with containerlab save --copy, highlight critical operational traps, and establish operational rules for reproducible lab design.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
Learning goals

Differentiate between the three state persistence layers: lab directory artifacts, topology startup-config definitions, and host-to-container volume binds.
Trace the lifecycle of running configurations through deploy, runtime modification, containerlab save, standard destroy, and subsequent deploy.
Configure versioned configuration backups using containerlab save --copy and restore them using template magic variables (__clabLabName__ and __clabNodeName__).
Identify and prevent state traps, including lab directory precedence collisions, read-only volume bind failures, and non-persisted linux container filesystems.
Construct topology files that guarantee consistent state behavior across team environments.

Version note. Containerlab was not installed and was not run on the writing host (2026-11-13, Linux 6.12.94+). No containerlab deploy, save, or destroy commands were executed. All command listings, terminal outputs, and file tree structures in this chapter are written from the official containerlab.dev documentation and are illustrative.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
The Three Layers of Persistence
To manage state effectively, you must separate state into three distinct architectural layers. Each layer operates at a different scope and has a different lifecycle.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| LAYER 1: Lab Directory Artifacts (Auto-generated & Runtime Managed)               |
| Path: ./clab-<lab-name>/                                                          |
| Contains: Node runtime dirs, generated TLS certs, auto-saved NOS configs          |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                          |
                                          v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| LAYER 2: Topology Startup-Config (Declarative Base)                               |
| Path: Defined in topology YAML (local path, inline YAML, or remote URL)           |
| Role: Initial seed configuration for clean deployments                            |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                          |
                                          v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| LAYER 3: Host Volume Binds (Explicit Filesystem Passthrough)                      |
| Path: Defined under node `binds:` section in docker volume syntax                 |
| Role: Direct mount of host files/directories into target NOS/Linux container path |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Layer 1: Lab Directory Artifacts
When you deploy a topology (for example, a file named spine-leaf.clab.yml with name: demo), Containerlab automatically creates a directory named clab-demo in the working directory of the lab file (or under CLAB_LABDIR_BASE if set).
This lab directory acts as the operational state store for the active topology. It typically contains:

Root CA and Node Certificates: TLS certificates auto-generated by Containerlab for gNMI, eAPI, or HTTPS services.
Per-Node Working Directories: Subdirectories dedicated to individual nodes (e.g., clab-demo/leaf1/).
Persisted NOS Configurations: Files saved by Network Operating Systems (NOS) when executing containerlab save or issued directly inside the NOS CLI (e.g., clab-demo/leaf1/config/startup-config).

Nodes using the linux kind typically do not receive a dedicated per-node directory inside the lab directory unless a feature requires one. State inside a standard linux container lives in the ephemeral container filesystem unless you mount it with a Layer 3 bind.


Layer 2: Topology startup-config
The startup-config attribute in the topology file specifies the baseline configuration a node should load when it boots for the first time. Containerlab supports three formats for startup-config:

Relative or Absolute File Path: Points to a file on the host filesystem (e.g., startup-config: configs/leaf1.cfg).
Embedded YAML Literal: Multiline string embedded directly in the topology YAML file.
HTTP/HTTPS URL: Remote configuration fetched by Containerlab during deployment.

startup-config acts as a seed configuration. As detailed later in this chapter, Layer 1 lab directory contents will override Layer 2 startup-config during redeployment unless explicitly forced otherwise.


Layer 3: Host Volume Binds
Host volume binds map files or directories from the host filesystem directly into the container’s filesystem using Docker volume syntax (host_path:container_path[:mode]).
nodes:
  spine1:
    kind: ceos
    image: ceos:4.32.0F
    binds:
      - configs/spine1-custom.cfg:/mnt/flash/startup-config:ro
      - /etc/timezone:/etc/timezone:ro
Volume binds bypass Containerlab’s automated artifact handling. However, a bind will not automatically persist an NOS running configuration simply because it exists. A volume bind only persists state if it maps to the exact internal path where the specific NOS writes its startup or running configuration upon executing a save operation.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
State Precedence & The Startup Lifecycle
The most common point of confusion in Containerlab state management is understanding which configuration source takes effect when a node boots.

The Precedence Rule
When Containerlab boots a node, it evaluates configuration sources in the following strict order of precedence:

Existing Lab Directory File (Layer 1): If a configuration file exists in clab-<lab_name>/<node_name>/ from a previous run, Containerlab uses this file.
Topology startup-config (Layer 2): Used only if no existing configuration is found in the lab directory, or if enforce-startup-config: true is set, or if deployment is run with --reconfigure.
Empty / Default State: Used if neither Layer 1 nor Layer 2 configuration is present.

                          [ Node Boot Initiated ]
                                     |
                                     v
                  /-------------------------------------\
                 < Is 'enforce-startup-config: true' or  >--- YES ---> [ Load Layer 2: ]
                 <      'deploy --reconfigure' set?      >             [ startup-config ]
                  \-------------------------------------/                      ^
                                     |                                         |
                                     NO                                        |
                                     v                                         |
                  /-------------------------------------\                      |
                 < Config file exists in Lab Directory  >--- YES -> [ Load Layer 1: ]
                 <   (clab-<lab_name>/<node_name>/)?    >           [ Lab Dir Config]
                  \-------------------------------------/                      |
                                     |                                         |
                                     NO ---------------------------------------+


The Standard State Lifecycle
The diagram below illustrates how configuration state changes across a complete lifecycle of deployment, runtime edits, saving, destruction, and redeployment.
 [ Host: configs/leaf1.cfg ] 
           |
           | 1. containerlab deploy
           v
 [ Active Container: leaf1 ] ---> 2. Operator applies runtime CLI changes (e.g., IP addresses)
           |
           | 3. containerlab save
           v
 [ Lab Dir: clab-demo/leaf1/flash/startup-config ]
           |
           | 4. containerlab destroy (WITHOUT --cleanup)
           v
 [ Container Destroyed | Lab Dir clab-demo/ PRESERVED on Host ]
           |
           | 5. containerlab deploy
           v
 [ Recreated Container: leaf1 ] <--- Loads from clab-demo/leaf1/flash/startup-config
                                     (Runtime edits PRESERVED; configs/leaf1.cfg IGNORED)
To demonstrate this lifecycle, consider the following sequence of commands (illustrative):
# Illustrative command sequence based on containerlab.dev documentation

# 1. Initial deployment (loads startup-config from topology)
containerlab deploy -t spine-leaf.clab.yml

# 2. Operator connects to node and alters running state
docker exec -it clab-demo-leaf1 Cli -c "configure; interface Ethernet1; ip address 10.0.0.1/30; end; write memory"

# 3. Save state across the lab
containerlab save -t spine-leaf.clab.yml

# 4. Destroy the lab without cleanup flag
containerlab destroy -t spine-leaf.clab.yml

# 5. Redeploy the lab
containerlab deploy -t spine-leaf.clab.yml
At step 5, leaf1 boots with 10.0.0.1/30 intact on Ethernet1. Containerlab saw that clab-demo/leaf1/flash/startup-config existed in the lab directory and mounted it into the new container, ignoring the original configs/leaf1.cfg specified in the topology file.


Overriding Lab Directory Precedence
If you want to discard runtime changes and force nodes to re-initialize from their original Layer 2 startup-config, you have three options:

Deploy with --reconfigure:
# Illustrative command written from containerlab.dev docs
containerlab deploy -t spine-leaf.clab.yml --reconfigure
This wipes the existing clab-<lab_name> directory before deploying, forcing Containerlab to read the topology’s startup-config.
Destroy with --cleanup:
# Illustrative command written from containerlab.dev docs
containerlab destroy -t spine-leaf.clab.yml --cleanup
containerlab deploy -t spine-leaf.clab.yml
Passing --cleanup removes the clab-<lab_name> directory upon destruction.
Set enforce-startup-config: true in Topology:
topology:
  defaults:
    enforce-startup-config: true
  nodes:
    leaf1:
      kind: ceos
      startup-config: configs/leaf1.cfg
When set to true, Containerlab forces the node to load configs/leaf1.cfg on every deployment, even if a saved configuration exists in the lab directory.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
Detailed Mechanics of containerlab save
Executing containerlab save instructs Containerlab to issue kind-specific save commands to running nodes and update their persisted artifacts in the lab directory.

Kind-Specific Save Commands & Paths
Because different Network Operating Systems handle configuration persistence differently, Containerlab maps each kind to its native CLI save command and destination path inside the node’s lab directory:








Kind
Native CLI Save Command Executed
Destination Path in Lab Directory




srl (Nokia SR Linux)
sr_cli -d tools system configuration save
clab-<lab>/<node>/config/config.json


sros (Nokia SR OS)
NETCONF copy-config
clab-<lab>/<node>/config/cf3/config.cfg


ceos (Arista cEOS)
Cli -p 15 -c wr
clab-<lab>/<node>/flash/startup-config


csrx (Juniper cSRX)
cli show conf
clab-<lab>/<node>/config/juniper.conf


cisco_iol (Cisco IOL)
write memory
not listed in the --copy path table



Kinds that do not report a saved config path are silently skipped by save --copy. Standard linux nodes have no save routine. Cisco IOL is in the save command table (write memory) but is not in the --copy path table; do not assume a timestamped copy was written unless the kind is listed.


Node Filtering
You can restrict the save operation to specific nodes using the --node-filter flag:
# Illustrative command written from containerlab.dev docs
containerlab save -t spine-leaf.clab.yml --node-filter leaf1,leaf2
This is useful when performing targeted maintenance or testing configuration changes on a subset of routers without overwriting saved states for the entire lab.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
Versioned Configuration Backups: save --copy
While standard containerlab save overwrites the primary config file in the lab directory, containerlab save --copy creates timestamped configuration snapshots.

How save --copy Works
--copy takes a destination directory, resolved relative to the current working directory unless it is absolute. Containerlab copies each kind’s saved file to that destination, not into a second copy inside the lab directory. The official layout is:
<copy-path>/clab-<labname>/<node-name>/<config>-<YYMMDD_HHMMSS>.<ext>   # timestamped copy
<copy-path>/clab-<labname>/<node-name>/<config>.<ext>                    # symlink to latest
An illustrative listing, from the containerlab.dev save page (their example used config-260207_091500.json for SR Linux):
# containerlab save -t srl02.clab.yml --copy ./startup-configs
# illustrative — from containerlab.dev, not run here
./startup-configs/clab-srl02/srl1/config-260207_091500.json
./startup-configs/clab-srl02/srl1/config.json                 # symlink -> latest
./startup-configs/clab-srl02/srl2/config-260207_091500.json
./startup-configs/clab-srl02/srl2/config.json
The destination is created if it is missing. Running save --copy again to the same directory keeps earlier timestamps and moves the symlink. For cEOS the copied file is flash/startup-config; for SR OS, /config/cf3/config.cfg; for cSRX, config/juniper.conf. Kinds that do not report a path are skipped.


Dynamic Restoration with Magic Variables
You can reference timestamped configuration files or lab directory paths directly inside your topology file using Containerlab magic variables. Containerlab expands these variables dynamically during template parsing:

__clabLabName__: Evaluates to the current lab name.
__clabNodeName__: Evaluates to the current node name.


Example: Dynamic Bind to Versioned Artifacts
The usual pattern, from the official save --copy documentation, points startup-config at the copy destination (here startup-configs/), using __clabLabName__ and __clabNodeName__ so one topology works for every node. For SR Linux the symlink is named config.json; for cEOS it is startup-config. Illustrative SR Linux wiring:
# after: containerlab save --copy startup-configs -t mylab.clab.yml
name: mylab
topology:
  nodes:
    node1:
      kind: srl
      startup-config: startup-configs/__clabLabName__/__clabNodeName__/config.json
    node2:
      kind: srl
      startup-config: startup-configs/__clabLabName__/__clabNodeName__/config.json
Do not confuse that directory with ./clab-<lab>/, which is the live lab directory and is what destroy --cleanup and deploy --reconfigure delete.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
Zero Touch Provisioning (ZTP) & suppress-startup-config
In automated lab environments, you may want nodes to boot completely unconfigured so they can obtain their configurations dynamically via DHCP/ZTP (Zero Touch Provisioning).
However, if Containerlab detects a startup-config definition or auto-generates default artifacts, it may pass parameters that interfere with the NOS ZTP process.
To prevent Containerlab from applying any initial startup configuration, set suppress-startup-config: true:
name: ztp-lab

topology:
  nodes:
    leaf1:
      kind: srl
      image: ghcr.io/nokia/srlinux:24.3.1
      suppress-startup-config: true
When suppress-startup-config is enabled: - Containerlab will not generate or mount an initial startup configuration file. - The NOS boots into its default factory state, triggering native DHCP discover and ZTP workflows.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
section: Annotated Topology & Host File Tree Walkthrough
text:
Annotated Topology & Host File Tree Walkthrough
To see all three persistence layers working together, consider an enterprise lab topology with an Arista cEOS leaf switch, a Nokia SR Linux spine router, and an Ubuntu Linux host.

Complete Annotated Topology File
# Illustrative topology file: production-lab.clab.yml
name: prod-ref

topology:
  defaults:
    kind: ceos

  nodes:
    # --- NODE 1: Arista cEOS (Uses Layer 1 + Layer 2) ---
    leaf1:
      kind: ceos
      image: ceos:4.32.0F
      # Layer 2: Baseline config seed
      startup-config: configs/leaf1.cfg

    # --- NODE 2: Nokia SR Linux (Uses Layer 1 + Layer 3) ---
    spine1:
      kind: srl
      image: ghcr.io/nokia/srlinux:24.3.1
      # Layer 2: Baseline config seed
      startup-config: configs/spine1.json
      # Layer 3: Direct bind for custom licensing and logging
      binds:
        - /etc/srl/license.key:/opt/srlinux/etc/license.key:ro
        - ./logs/spine1:/var/log/srlinux:rw

    # --- NODE 3: Linux Host (Uses Layer 3 exclusively for state) ---
    client1:
      kind: linux
      image: ubuntu:24.04
      # Layer 3: Linux containers do NOT persist state in lab dir automatically
      binds:
        - ./host-data/client1/etc-netplan:/etc/netplan:rw
        - ./host-data/client1/home:/home/ubuntu:rw
      exec:
        - ip addr add 192.168.10.10/24 dev eth1


Host Filesystem Tree Structure
Below is the corresponding directory structure on the host system after deploying the lab, making runtime modifications, and executing containerlab save --copy:
.
├── configs/                             # LAYER 2: Seed Configs (Version Controlled)
│   ├── leaf1.cfg
│   └── spine1.json
├── host-data/                            # LAYER 3: Explicit Host Binds
│   └── client1/
│       ├── etc-netplan/
│       │   └── 01-netcfg.yaml
│       └── home/
├── logs/
│   └── spine1/                          # Mount destination for SR Linux logs
├── production-lab.clab.yml              # Topology Definition File
└── clab-prod-ref/                       # LAYER 1: Auto-generated Lab Directory
    ├── .tls/                            # TLS material (docs: .tls, not a ca/ folder)
    ├── leaf1/                           # Node directory for cEOS
    │   └── flash/
    │       └── startup-config               # cEOS saved running-config (lab dir)
├── startup-configs/                     # LAYER 1b: save --copy destination (not the lab dir)
│   └── clab-prod-ref/
│       └── leaf1/
│           ├── startup-config-260113_003000   # timestamped copy (illustrative name)
│           └── startup-config -> startup-config-260113_003000
    └── spine1/                          # Node directory for SR Linux
        └── config/
            └── config.json              # Saved SR Linux configuration JSON

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
Critical Traps and Operational Hazards

Trap 1: Leftover Lab Directory Silently Wins Over New startup-config

Symptom: You update configs/leaf1.cfg on the host, run containerlab deploy, but the switch boots with your old configuration.
Cause: A clab-<lab_name>/leaf1/ directory already exists from a previous run. Containerlab gives Layer 1 precedence over Layer 2.
Resolution: Run containerlab deploy --reconfigure or containerlab destroy --cleanup.



Trap 2: Read-Only Volume Binds (:ro) Block containerlab save

Symptom: containerlab save fails or reports permission errors when attempting to write node configurations.
Cause: You mounted the target configuration file or directory using the :ro (read-only) flag in Layer 3 binds.
Resolution: Ensure paths where the NOS writes its runtime state are mounted as :rw (read-write), or rely on Layer 1 auto-generated mounts instead of manual binds.



Trap 3: Binding the Wrong Configuration Path

Symptom: You create a host bind - ./my-leaf.cfg:/etc/frr/frr.conf for a container kind whose internal management agent actually reads /etc/frr/frr.conf.sav. The router boots with factory defaults.
Cause: Different NOS images store startup configurations in different paths.
Resolution: Verify internal NOS target paths in the official containerlab.dev node documentation before configuring Layer 3 binds.



Trap 4: Assuming linux Kinds Persist Like NOS Kinds

Symptom: You install packages (apt-get install iperf3) inside an Ubuntu container, destroy the lab, redeploy, and iperf3 is missing.
Cause: Containerlab does not execute save routines for linux kinds. The container root filesystem is entirely ephemeral.
Resolution: Custom binaries or packages must be baked into a custom Docker image, installed via exec hooks during deployment, or mounted via Layer 3 volume binds.



Trap 5: Editing Files Inside Container Workdirs Directly

Symptom: You edit clab-demo/leaf1/flash/startup-config while the lab is running, but changes are lost or overwritten.
Cause: Many NOS containers buffer running configurations in memory and flush them to disk upon shutdown or save, overwriting your manual edits.
Resolution: Apply CLI changes through docker exec, gNMI, or SSH, then run containerlab save. If editing files directly on the host, do so while the lab is stopped (containerlab destroy without --cleanup).




Trap 6: World-readable secrets in the lab directory
The lab directory holds TLS keys, licenses, and saved configs. It often ends up mode 0777 or owned by root on a shared lab host. Treat clab-<lab>/ as sensitive: tighten modes, keep it out of git, and do not copy it onto a world-readable share.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
Companion Tools: netlab Integration Pointer
Tools like netlab (https://netlab.tools) build on top of Containerlab as an abstraction and orchestration layer.
When using netlab, configuration templates are rendered dynamically into an intermediate directory (typically netlab.snapshot.yml and associated rendered files). netlab manages the creation of Containerlab topology files and orchestrates startup-config generation.
While netlab abstracts topology creation, the underlying persistence layers remain identical: Containerlab still creates clab-<lab_name> directories and enforces the exact same precedence rules described in this chapter.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
Boring Rule
Treat Layer 2 startup-config files in your repository as the baseline you can regenerate. Do not treat an uncommitted clab-<lab>/ directory as the long-term store. After a session you care about, run containerlab save (and save --copy if you want a timestamped backup), inspect what landed on the host, and copy the bits you want to keep into version-controlled configs/ before containerlab destroy --cleanup.

title: Persistent State in Containerlab Labs
text:
Try This (Operational Exercises)

Exercise 1: Trace Precedence Collision

Create a minimal topology single-switch.clab.yml with a single cEOS or SR Linux switch and a startup-config pointing to configs/switch1.cfg containing host name SW-BASELINE.
Deploy the lab (containerlab deploy -t single-switch.clab.yml). Verify host name is SW-BASELINE.
Connect to the switch CLI and change the host name to SW-MODIFIED.
Run containerlab save -t single-switch.clab.yml.
Destroy the lab without --cleanup (containerlab destroy -t single-switch.clab.yml).
Update configs/switch1.cfg on the host to set host name SW-NEW-SEED.
Redeploy the lab (containerlab deploy -t single-switch.clab.yml).
Check the switch host name. Observe that it boots as SW-MODIFIED (Layer 1 won over Layer 2).
Redeploy with --reconfigure (containerlab deploy -t single-switch.clab.yml --reconfigure). Observe that it now boots as SW-NEW-SEED.



Exercise 2: Versioned State Snapshotting

Using the switch topology from Exercise 1, execute containerlab save -t single-switch.clab.yml --copy ./startup-configs.
Inspect ./startup-configs/clab-<lab>/<node>/, not only clab-<lab>/<node>/.
Confirm a timestamped file (<config>-<YYMMDD_HHMMSS>.<ext>) and a symlink with the original filename pointing at the latest copy.

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
text: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
text:
Learning goals

Use containerlab inspect as the inventory of a running lab: table, --wide, JSON and CSV, and --all across labs.
Graph a topology four ways (HTML server, drawio, Mermaid, Graphviz dot), including --offline when nothing is running.
Log in with the generated SSH config and know where Ansible and Nornir inventories are written.
Run the same command on many nodes with containerlab exec, and know when exec cannot reach a VM-based kind.

Version note: Containerlab was not installed on the writing host, and no lab was deployed (no root, no installs, no Docker). Commands, default paths and example tables below are taken from the current containerlab.dev documentation (inspect, graph, exec, inventory / SSH config, and the nodes manual). Run them on your lab host and treat the tables here as the documented shape, not as a capture from this machine.
This chapter goes deeper than the short inspect/graph sketches in Containerlab Fundamentals. It does not repeat topology YAML, kinds, or deploy/destroy.

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
text:
Inspect: what is actually running
containerlab inspect is how you answer “which nodes, which image, which management address, is it up?” without walking docker ps.
# this lab, from a topology file
containerlab inspect -t triangle.clab.yml

# the same lab, by name
containerlab inspect --name triangle

# every lab on the host (first row of each lab also shows the topo path)
containerlab inspect --all

# add owner (the user who started the lab; sudo is unwrapped)
containerlab inspect --all --wide
Default output is a table: name, container ID, image, kind, state, management IPv4 and IPv6. --wide adds topo path, lab name and owner. --format json and --format csv emit one object or row per container, with fields including lab_name, labPath, absLabPath, name, container_id, image, kind, state, status, ipv4_address, ipv6_address and owner. JSON is the format you pipe into scripts; CSV is the format you paste into a sheet; the table is what you read on the terminal.
--details is the other extreme: it is essentially docker inspect for every lab container. Use it when you need labels, mounts or networks, not as the default.
If you started the lab with sudo, inspect still reports the original user as owner. That matters on a shared lab host when two people have labs up at once: inspect --all --wide is how you see who owns the leftover triangle.
With --runtime c9s (clabernetes), inspect reads Kubernetes Topology objects instead of local Docker containers. inspect --all then lists topologies across namespaces; JSON grows namespace, pod, and load_balancer_address. That runtime is a later chapter; the command names stay the same.

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
section: Graph: four renderings of the same YAML
text:
Graph: four renderings of the same YAML
containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml starts an HTML server (default :50080) and draws the topology with the NeXt UI. If the lab is running, the graph includes management addresses from inspect. --offline forces the topology file only — no cluster or Docker access required for the mermaid, dot, drawio and offline-HTML paths.
# interactive HTML, running lab if present
containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml

# different port
containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml --srv ":3002"

# custom HTML template plus static assets
containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml --template my-graph.html --static-dir ./static

# files you can commit or paste
containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml --drawio
containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml --drawio --drawio-args="--layout horizontal"
containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml --mermaid --mermaid-direction LR
containerlab graph -t triangle.clab.yml --dot
--node-filter r1,r2 graphs a subset of nodes and only the links among them. The documented default HTML auto-layout uses the node group: property (spine, leaf, border-leaf, server, or a numeric tier). Set group: in the topology if you want the HTML view to look like a Clos instead of a hairball.
Caveats from the manual, all worth honouring:

The Graphviz --dot path is brittle when node names contain dashes or unusual characters. Prefer HTML or drawio.
--drawio runs the clab-io-draw container on the local host, even if the lab itself was scheduled elsewhere. --drawio-version pins that image; the default is latest.
--offline (and mermaid/dot/drawio) work from the YAML alone. The default HTML mode that reads running containers, and --node-filter, are rejected on the c9s runtime unless you stay offline.

A graph is not an addressing plan. Export it, then keep subnets and VNIs in the lab README.

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
section: SSH config, generated for each lab
text:
SSH config, generated for each lab
On deploy, Containerlab writes a per-lab SSH client config, documented as:
/etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/clab-<lab-name>.conf
The documented shape is:
# Containerlab SSH Config for the srl lab

Host clab-srl-srl
  User admin
  StrictHostKeyChecking=no
  UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null
After that, ssh clab-srl-srl uses the kind’s default username and does not prompt you to trust a host key that will change on the next destroy/deploy. That is convenient in a lab and wrong for production: UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null and StrictHostKeyChecking=no disable TOFU on purpose because lab nodes are disposable. Do not copy this snippet onto a machine that reaches real routers.
As of Containerlab 0.77, a topology credentials.identity-file (at defaults, kind, group or node level) is rendered as an IdentityFile directive in that same config. Relative paths resolve against the topology file’s directory; ~ is expanded. You should not need ssh -i once that is set.
Older lab notes sometimes recommend a catch-all in ~/.ssh/config:
Host clab-*
  User root
  StrictHostKeyChecking no
  UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null
Prefer the generated per-lab file: the username is kind-aware (admin on SR Linux, not always root), and you do not blanket-disable host-key checking for every future host whose name happens to start with clab-.
Management SSH is independent of the data plane. If you shut a veth to drill a failure and SSH dies, you broke the management network (or the host Docker bridge), not the experiment you meant to run.

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
text:
Inventories and topology-data.json
Every deploy also writes, in the lab directory:







File
Role




ansible-inventory.yml
Ansible inventory, nodes grouped by kind, with ansible_host set to the management address and, for some kinds, ansible_user / ansible_password / ansible_network_os


nornir-simple-inventory.yml
Nornir simple inventory (hostname, username, password, platform)


topology-data.json
Machine-readable topology: names, management addresses, links, labels



Ansible groups follow kinds by default. A node label ansible-group: spine adds an extra group. The label ansible-no-host-var: "true" (defaults, kind or node) omits ansible_host, which some connection plugins require. Nornir groups come from labels that start with nornir-group. CLAB_NORNIR_PLATFORM_NAME_SCHEMA=scrapli or napalm changes the platform field; the default is the kind name.
topology-data.json is filled from a Go template (auto.tmpl by default). --export-template can point at full.tmpl or a custom file. The full template may include TLS private keys — do not commit it.
These files are how a Makefile or a CI job talks to a lab without scraping inspect tables.

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
text:
exec: one command, many nodes
containerlab exec -t triangle.clab.yml --cmd 'ip -4 addr show'
containerlab exec -t triangle.clab.yml --label clab-node-kind=linux --cmd 'ip -br link'
containerlab exec -t triangle.clab.yml --cmd 'vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"' -f json
--cmd is a single string; quote it. --label key=value narrows the node set (labels are on the container; docker inspect will show them). Output is plain by default, or json with -f json.
exec is docker exec with a topology filter. For VM-based (vrnetlab) kinds, that container is the QEMU launcher, not the guest NOS. A guest command then fails with executable file not found in $PATH. SSH to the management address (or the kind’s native CLI) instead. The same warning applies to the node-level exec: list in the topology: those commands also run in the container namespace.
Environment-variable flags exist for almost every option (CLAB_INSPECT_ALL=1, CLAB_TOPO=...). Useful in CI; easy to forget locally when a flag and an environment variable disagree (the flag wins).

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
text:
Common mistakes

Graphing a running lab, shipping the PNG, and never writing down the prefixes.
Copying the generated SSH config’s StrictHostKeyChecking=no into a production ~/.ssh/config.
Using containerlab exec against a vrnetlab kind and debugging the guest image when you only reached qemu.
Parsing table output in a script instead of --format json.
Forgetting --offline when you want a mermaid file from YAML on a machine that cannot see Docker.

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
text:
Boring rule
inspect is the source of truth for “is it up and what is its management address?”. The generated SSH config and inventories are how humans and tools use that address. Graph is for the journal, not for the addressing plan.

title: Containerlab Inspect, Graph, SSH and Inventory
text:
Try this

Deploy the book’s FRR triangle, then capture inspect --all --wide, inspect -f json and inspect -f csv for the same lab. Diff what each one makes easy.
Run graph --offline --mermaid and graph --drawio from the YAML without the lab up. Then run default graph with the lab running and compare addresses.
SSH to a node using only the generated Host name, with no -i and no user@.
Point a one-play Ansible ping at ansible-inventory.yml. Add ansible-group: spine to two nodes and confirm the extra group.
On a linux kind, exec --cmd 'ip -br link'. If you have a VM-based kind, run the same exec, record the error, and repeat over SSH.

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
text: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
text:
Learning goals

List the configuration modules netlab can deploy, and attach them at topology, node, link and interface scope without fighting the merge rules.
Treat netlab up as a pipeline (create → start provider → initial → module configs), and know when to use netlab config, netlab collect and netlab down instead of editing generated files.
Write validate: tests that fail closed on a missing adjacency, and run them as a single command.

Version note: netlab was not installed on the writing host, and no provider, container or VM was started (no root, no installs). Module names, merge behaviour and command roles are taken from the current netlab.tools documentation (optional configuration modules, the module reference, and the command descriptions on the project front page). Confirm with netlab show modules on a machine that has the tool.
Netlab Fundamentals already walks a first topology, netlab up / down / connect, a first validate: example, and netlab tc. This chapter is the catalog and the provisioning lifecycle, not a second hello-world.

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
section: Modules are how protocols get configured
text:
Modules are how protocols get configured
A netlab topology describes nodes and links. Modules are the optional plugins that turn that graph into OSPF, BGP, IS-IS, VLAN, VRF, EVPN, and so on. The documented list shipped with netlab is:







Module
What it configures




bfd
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection


bgp
BGP sessions, originations, address families


dhcp
DHCP clients and servers


eigrp
EIGRP (vendor-specific; use only when the lab needs it)


evpn
Ethernet VPN control plane


gateway
First-hop gateways (VRRP, anycast)


isis
IS-IS


lag
IEEE 802.3ad link aggregation, including MLAG where supported


mpls
LDP, BGP-LU, MPLS/VPN


ospf
OSPFv2 / OSPFv3


ripv2
RIPv2 / RIPng


routing
Generic routing: statics, prefix lists, route maps, redistribution


sr
Segment Routing (MPLS)


srv6
Segment Routing over IPv6


stp
Spanning Tree


vlan
VLANs


vrf
VRF tables


vxlan
VXLAN data plane


network services
Additional services documented alongside the modules



Device support is not uniform. The source of truth on a installed box is:
netlab show modules
netlab show module-support
netlab show modules -m isis
Those commands were not run here. Run them before you assume FRR, SR Linux or cEOS implements the feature you just added to the YAML.

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
section: Where a module parameter is allowed
text:
Where a module parameter is allowed

The topology-level module: list is inherited by router, bridge and daemon nodes, not by hosts. A host that should run a module needs its own module: list.
A node-level module: replaces the inherited list; it is not merged. module: [] means “configure no modules on this node.”
Module-named dictionaries (ospf:, bgp:, isis:) can sit on the topology, on a node, on a link, or on a node-within-a-link (an interface). Global values merge into node values; link values merge into interface data; a few node attributes (OSPF area is the documented example) are copied onto interfaces.

The documented merge example is worth keeping in your head:
defaults:
  device: frr
  ospf:
    area: 0.0.0.0
    process: 2
  bgp:
    as: 65000

module: [ ospf ]
ospf:
  process: 1

nodes:
  r1:
    ospf:
      router_id: 10.0.0.17
      area: 0.0.0.1
  r2:
    module: [ bgp, bfd ]
After expansion, the topology uses ospf, bgp and bfd. r1 keeps area 0.0.0.1 and router-id, and inherits process 1 (the topology value wins over the default 2). r2 runs BGP and BFD only — its node module: dropped OSPF — and inherits bgp.as: 65000.
Set a protocol off on one interface with module: false on that interface (the documented exception to “everything is a dictionary”).

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
section: A multi-module lab, still just YAML
text:
A multi-module lab, still just YAML
defaults.device: frr
provider: clab
module: [ ospf, bgp ]
ospf:
  area: 0.0.0.0
bgp:
  as: 65000

nodes:
  r1:
    bgp.as: 65001
  r2:
  r3:
    module: [ ospf ]

links:
  - r1-r2
  - r2-r3
  - r1:
    r3:
    ospf.cost: 20
r1 and r2 run OSPF and BGP; r3 is OSPF-only. The r1–r3 link has a higher OSPF cost. Addressing, router-ids, interface names and the rendered FRR config are netlab’s job.

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
text:
Provisioning is a pipeline
netlab up is not a single opaque “boot.” Documented stages are:

Build an addressing plan and a routing design from the topology.
Write provider files (containerlab or Vagrant) and an Ansible inventory.
Start the lab with the provider.
netlab initial — deploy interface addresses, users, and the baseline device config.
Deploy module configuration snippets from netsim/ansible/templates/<module>/<device>.j2.

Useful commands once that pipeline is clear:







Command
Role




netlab up
The whole pipeline


netlab down
Destroy the provider lab


netlab initial
Replay baseline config (addresses, users)


netlab config
Push an extra configuration snippet you wrote


netlab collect
Save running config back from the devices, before you tear the lab down


netlab connect / netlab exec
Interactive or one-shot CLI


netlab capture
Packet capture on a VM or container interface


netlab graph
Topology picture


netlab validate
The tests you declared in YAML



The standing trap from the first BGP lab still applies: do not edit generated files and then rerun netlab up. Your edits vanish. Change the topology (or a documented extra-config hook), or netlab collect the running config into a file you own, then decide whether it belongs in YAML or in a netlab config snippet.
netlab down does not collect for you. If the lab taught you something, collect first.

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
section: Validation that can fail the lab
text:
Validation that can fail the lab
netlab validate runs tests declared under validate: in the topology. A test can call a plugin or an exec: command. A failing assertion should be a non-zero exit — that is what you want in a Makefile or a CI job.
defaults.device: frr
provider: clab
module: [ ospf, bgp ]

nodes:
  r1:
    bgp.as: 65001
  r2:
    bgp.as: 65002

links:
  - r1-r2

validate:
  ospf_full:
    description: "r1 has a Full OSPF neighbor"
    nodes: [ r1 ]
    plugin: ospf_neighbor(count=1, state='Full')
  bgp_up:
    description: "r1 has one established BGP session"
    nodes: [ r1 ]
    plugin: bgp_neighbor(count=1, state='Established')
  ping_loopback:
    description: "r1 can reach r2's loopback"
    nodes: [ r1 ]
    exec:
      r1: ping -c 2 10.0.0.2
Plugin names and arguments are those supported by your netlab version — check the docs or netlab validate --help on the lab host rather than assuming the spellings above still match. The idea is stable: declare the intended state next to the topology, do not keep a one-off verify.sh as the only memory of what “working” meant.
When a test fails, fix the topology or the network, not the test, unless the test was wrong. An adjacency stuck in ExStart is usually MTU or a mismatched network type; a missing BGP prefix is usually origin or policy. Validation tells you that it broke; the protocol chapter tells you why.

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
text:
Common mistakes

Setting node module: [ bgp ] and wondering why OSPF vanished (replacement, not merge).
Expecting a Linux host node to inherit topology module: [ ospf ].
Editing clab or FRR files under the working directory and rerunning up.
Running down before collect after a successful drill.
Writing validate tests that only ping, and never check the control plane.
Assuming every module runs on every device kind without netlab show module-support.

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
text:
Boring rule
The YAML is the lab. Modules, addresses and tests live there. Generated files are a cache. If you cannot rebuild from YAML and pass netlab validate, you do not have a lab yet — you have a snowflake.

title: netlab Modules, Provisioning and Validation
text:
Try this

On a machine with netlab, run netlab show modules and netlab show modules -m evpn. Note which of the free images in this book actually support EVPN.
Take the OSPF triangle from Fundamentals, add module: [ ospf, bgp ] and a different ASN on one node. Predict sessions before up.
Override module: [] on one triangle node and watch validate fail. Restore the module list, not the generated config.
Make a change in vtysh, netlab collect, netlab down, netlab up, and confirm whether the change survived (it should not, unless you also changed the YAML or a config hook).
Add a validate: plugin for neighbors and an exec: ping. Break a link with netlab tc or by shutting an interface, and keep the test output.
