title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
Containerlab runs a topology on one machine. That machine’s memory is the ceiling: the lab host in this book fits two cEOS nodes and one SR Linux node before it starts swapping. Clabernetes, or c9s, takes the same topology file and schedules it across the workers of a Kubernetes cluster, one pod per network node, with the links stretched between pods. Since Containerlab 0.80 you drive it with the same containerlab command and a different runtime: --runtime c9s.
This chapter is for the day a lab outgrows the host, or several people need labs on shared hardware. It explains what c9s builds, what it needs from the cluster, which Containerlab habits carry over and which do not, and how to run, inspect, capture and tear down a lab on it.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain how a Containerlab topology becomes c9s Topology, Node, Link and NodeProfile resources and one pod per network node
Check that a cluster meets c9s’s requirements before you install anything
Validate a topology for c9s and emit its manifests without touching a cluster
Deploy, inspect, exec, capture, stop, start, save and destroy a lab with containerlab --runtime c9s
Predict which topology features c9s rejects, and what happens to saved device state on destroy

Version note. Nothing in this chapter was run on the writing host. It has no Kubernetes cluster, no Docker, and no Containerlab, and nothing could be installed. Every command and behaviour is taken from the Containerlab c9s runtime documentation (containerlab.dev, describing Containerlab 0.80 and later) and the c9s documentation at c9s.run, read on 2026-11-13. The c9s runtime needs a Clabernetes release with Node run state and the clabwire capture contract, which the Containerlab docs give as 0.11 or newer; the direct-runtime API it relies on arrived in c9s 0.9. Older guides that mention launcher pods, nested Docker, LauncherProfile or clabverter describe the incompatible pre-0.9 design. Do not follow them.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
What c9s builds
 topo.clab.yml ──containerlab --runtime c9s deploy──> Topology (c9s.run/v1alpha1)
                                                         │  compiled by the c9s manager
                          ┌──────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐
                          v                              v                         v
                    NodeProfile                     Node  (one per node)       Link (one per wire)
              (expose, resources,                        │
               scheduling, probes)                       v
                                               Deployment ─> Pod
                                               ├─ device container (the NOS image itself)
                                               ├─ clabwire connectivity sidecar (links, mgmt)
                                               └─ planner init container (file staging)







Resource
Holds




Topology
The rendered Containerlab definition, stored in the cluster


Node
One network node: kind, image, run state, readiness, management address


Link
One point-to-point wire between two node interfaces


NodeProfile
Reusable Kubernetes policy: how nodes are exposed, resources, scheduling, probes, management subnets



Three design choices explain most of c9s’s behaviour:

The NOS runs as an ordinary container in an ordinary pod. There is no Docker inside the pod and no launcher. kubectl exec and kubectl logs against the device pod reach the network OS directly.
A connectivity sidecar wires the links. Each pod runs clabwire, which builds the lab links as veth interfaces inside the pod and carries each wire to the far pod as plain UDP between sidecars. That is why a link can join nodes on different workers with no special CNI.
Management is routed, not bridged. Every node still gets a management address from the topology’s mgmt subnet, but the shared management network is a routed mesh between pods (VXLAN inside the pods, with proxy ARP and IPv6 neighbour discovery), not one L2 segment. From outside the cluster you reach nodes through Kubernetes Services, a LoadBalancer by default.

By default containerlab deploy creates a Topology and lets the c9s manager compile it. With --no-topology-cr, Containerlab compiles client-side and creates the NodeProfile, Link and Node resources itself. Both produce the same lab. The second suits GitOps pipelines that apply generated manifests.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
What the cluster must provide
Check these before installing. Each one is a requirement stated in the c9s installation and runtime documentation.







Requirement
Why




Kubernetes 1.31 or newer
c9s relies on restartable init containers (native sidecars) and server-side field selectors


Privileged pods allowed in lab namespaces
Every device pod runs a privileged connectivity init-sidecar. With Pod Security Admission, label lab namespaces pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged


VXLAN and nftables in the worker kernel
The management mesh is kernel VXLAN inside pods; management translation uses an nftables table in each pod’s namespace


Pod-to-pod UDP 14789 and 14790, kubelet to TCP 14791
Management mesh, link wires, and the sidecar readiness probe. NetworkPolicies must allow them


/dev/kvm on workers
Only for VM-backed (vrnetlab) kinds


A default dynamically provisioned storage class
Per-node persistent volumes for saved device state (unless you deploy with --no-persistence)


A LoadBalancer implementation (MetalLB on bare metal)
To reach node management from outside the cluster


Registry access
Private images use ordinary imagePullSecrets; mirrors are configured on the workers’ container runtime



The licensing rule from the image matrix still applies: a vendor image you imported on your lab host must be pushed to a private registry the cluster can pull from, and only if your licence allows it.

Installing c9s
From the c9s documentation, with Helm, into an existing cluster:
helm upgrade --install --create-namespace --namespace c9s \
    clabernetes oci://ghcr.io/clabernetes/clabernetes/clabernetes
kubectl -n c9s get pods     # manager pods must be Running
The chart also installs two ClusterRoles for lab users, clabernetes-lab-viewer and clabernetes-lab-editor. To try c9s without a cluster, the clabernetes repository’s make try-c9s target builds a disposable single-node KinD cluster with MetalLB and a sample SR Linux plus Network Multitool lab. The c9s quickstart says 8 GB of RAM and 4 CPUs should be enough, which the lab host has.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
The workflow
Selecting the runtime is one flag or one environment variable:
containerlab --runtime c9s deploy -t topo.clab.yml
# or
export CLAB_RUNTIME=c9s
containerlab deploy -t topo.clab.yml
Containerlab picks the cluster from CLAB_KUBECONFIG if set, otherwise from the normal kubeconfig rules, and the context from CLAB_KUBE_CONTEXT.

1. Validate and look before you deploy
These commands use the same compiler as deploy:
containerlab --runtime c9s validate -t topo.clab.yml
containerlab --runtime c9s deploy --emit-crs -t topo.clab.yml > topo-crs.yaml
containerlab --runtime c9s deploy --dry-run -t topo.clab.yml

validate reports whether c9s can represent the topology. It never contacts the cluster and works without a usable kubeconfig, so it belongs in CI (see Containerlab in CI). Compilation is fail-closed: every construct c9s cannot preserve is reported with its field and line, all in one pass.
deploy --emit-crs prints the Namespace, ConfigMaps and Topology (or NodeProfile/Link/Node with --no-topology-cr) as YAML, without contacting the cluster. Read it once. It is the clearest picture of what c9s will create.
deploy --dry-run does contact the cluster and prints the exact create, update and delete plan. An empty change list means the lab already matches the file.



2. Deploy
containerlab --runtime c9s deploy -t topo.clab.yml
Containerlab stages local files (startup configs, licences, bind sources) into per-node ConfigMaps, creates the resources, and waits until every node is ready, streaming each node’s phase: planning, file preparation, image pull, connectivity, container start-up. The default wait is ten minutes because large NOS images take time; change it with the global --timeout. Each lab lands in its own namespace, c9s-<lab-name>, unless you pass --namespace (which must already exist).
Two things differ from local Containerlab:

Readiness is process-level by default. A node is ready when its containers run and pass any healthcheck the image defines. A NOS that is still booting services can be “ready”. Use an image healthcheck or a c9s TCP/SSH probe if your checks need application-level readiness, or poll protocol state as the CI chapter does.
Staged files are snapshots. Editing a startup config on your laptop changes nothing until you deploy again. Each staged file is limited to 950 KB.



3. Inspect and reach nodes
containerlab --runtime c9s inspect -t topo.clab.yml
containerlab --runtime c9s inspect --all
containerlab --runtime c9s inspect -t topo.clab.yml --format json
The address inspect prints is the node’s LoadBalancer address when one exists, otherwise its allocated management address. JSON output adds namespace, pod, container, node_uid, exposed_ports and load_balancer_address, and container_id becomes <namespace>/<lab>/<node>, for example c9s-clos/clos/srl1. Scripts that used Docker container names should switch to these fields.
containerlab --runtime c9s exec -t topo.clab.yml --cmd 'ip addr'
containerlab --runtime c9s logs -t topo.clab.yml -n srl1 --tail 100
exec uses Kubernetes pod exec into the device container. The machine running containerlab does not need Docker at all, only cluster access. docker ps on that machine shows nothing for a c9s lab, and that is normal. The cluster is the source of truth:
kubectl -n c9s-<lab> get node.c9s.run,link.c9s.run,nodeprofile.c9s.run,deploy,pod,svc,cm,pvc \
  -l c9s.run/topologyOwner=<lab>


4. Capture
containerlab -r c9s capture -t topo.clab.yml \
  --target srl1:e1-1 --target srl2:e1-1 --duration 30s -w srl.pcapng
containerlab -r c9s capture --name clos --target srl1:e1-1 -w - | wireshark -k -i -
containerlab -r c9s capture --name clos --list
Capture runs inside each target pod’s clabwire sidecar and merges the streams into one pcapng file, one interface block per node:interface. Interface names are the names inside the node, or the topology’s alias (e1-1 or ethernet-1/1 on SR Linux). The management interface cannot be captured. This replaces the host-side ip netns exec ... tcpdump habit, which has no equivalent here because the lab’s namespaces are on cluster workers.


5. Stop, start, restart, save
containerlab --runtime c9s stop -t topo.clab.yml -n srl1
containerlab --runtime c9s start -t topo.clab.yml -n srl1
containerlab --runtime c9s save -t topo.clab.yml --copy ./startup-configs
Stop and start patch the node’s spec.runState; they never touch Deployments directly. A stopped node keeps its Node, Services, links and saved state. Its links go carrier-down on every peer, like an unplugged cable, which makes stop a clean way to run a link-failure drill. save --copy runs each kind’s normal save inside the device and copies the result back to your machine in the usual Containerlab layout.


6. Destroy, and where saved state lives
By default deploy gives every node a PersistentVolumeClaim with reclaim policy Retain. Saved device configuration lives there, so a pod restart or eviction never reverts saved work.







Command
Persistent claims




destroy
Kept, with the c9s-<lab> namespace; the next deploy boots from them


destroy --cleanup
Deleted, then the namespace


redeploy
Kept


redeploy --cleanup, deploy --reconfigure
Deleted before redeploying



This is the c9s equivalent of the lab directory that Persistent State in Containerlab Labs discusses: a plain destroy does not give you a clean slate. Use --cleanup when you want one. Deploy with --no-persistence for labs that should factory-reset on every pod replacement.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
Names, namespaces and RBAC
Kubernetes object names are lowercase DNS labels. Containerlab rewrites names that do not fit instead of rejecting them: lower-case, every character outside a-z, 0-9 and - becomes -, a leading digit gets a clab- prefix, and long names are truncated with a hash. R1 becomes r1 and PE_1 becomes pe-1. The original name is kept in a c9s.run/originalNodeName label. Two nodes that differ only by such characters (R1 and r1) are an error. The lab name must fit in 59 characters so that c9s-<lab> stays within 63.
For shared clusters, bind the shipped roles per namespace instead of handing out cluster-admin:
kubectl create rolebinding alice-lab-editor -n team-a \
  --clusterrole clabernetes-lab-editor --user alice
containerlab --runtime c9s --namespace team-a deploy -t topo.clab.yml
clabernetes-lab-editor covers creating and changing lab resources, exec, port-forward and deleting the lab’s claims. It does not include creating namespaces, which is why the example deploys into a pre-created team-a. inspect, events and logs work with clabernetes-lab-viewer.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
What does not carry over
The c9s runtime rejects, with a named error and before creating anything, every field it cannot preserve. The ones you are most likely to hit:







Local Containerlab feature
Under c9s




bridge, ovs-bridge, host, ext-container pseudo-nodes
Rejected


mgmt-net: and macvlan link endpoints
Rejected


stages (boot ordering between nodes)
Rejected; startup-delay per node is honoured


cpu-set, per-node runtime, auto-remove
Rejected; cpu and memory become Kubernetes limits


deploy --node-filter, destroy --node-filter
Rejected; deploy the whole lab, then use filters on start, stop, exec, save


deploy --graph, --export-template, --restore
Rejected


containerlab tools ...
Rejected


graph reading running containers
Rejected; graph --mermaid, --dot, --drawio from the file still work


Host-side tc/netem on lab links
Not available the same way; the links live on cluster workers


mgmt.network, mgmt.bridge, mgmt.mtu, mgmt.external-access
Accepted with a warning; they have no Kubernetes meaning


Pinned host ports such as 8080:80
The node-side port is kept, the host half is dropped, with a warning


Point-to-point links at any MTU, startup configs, exec, save, inspect
Supported as on local Containerlab



The practical consequence for this book’s labs: the point-to-point FRR, SR Linux and cEOS topologies carry over unchanged. Labs that hang hosts off a Linux bridge node, or rely on tc netem from the host (as the DSCP and delay chapter does), need rework: replace the bridge with a switch NOS node, and run netem inside a Linux node instead of on the host.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
section: Lab: one topology, two runtimes (not run on the writing host)
text:
Lab: one topology, two runtimes (not run on the writing host)
This lab uses the KinD quickstart cluster on the lab host, so it costs nothing beyond memory. It was not run on the writing host.

Build the cluster. In a clone of github.com/clabernetes/clabernetes, run make try-c9s. Predict: the run ends by printing SSH, gNMI and NETCONF addresses for an SR Linux node. Ping 192.0.2.1 from SR Linux as the quickstart describes, then keep the cluster.
Validate a book lab. Take the single-node topology from Reading SR Linux with gNMI, or any point-to-point lab from the lab host track. Run containerlab --runtime c9s validate -t <file>. Predict: it passes. Now add a bridge node and validate again. Predict: a named error for the bridge, with its line.
Read the manifests. Remove the bridge and run deploy --emit-crs. Find the Topology, the c9s.run/topologyOwner label, and the ConfigMap holding the startup config.
Deploy, inspect, compare. Deploy with --runtime c9s. Run inspect --format json and note pod, namespace and container_id. Run docker ps on the lab host and explain why the NOS containers are not there (they run under KinD’s container runtime inside the KinD node).
Link failure drill. Start a capture --target <node>:<intf> on one end of a link. stop the node at the other end. Predict: the interface goes lower-layer-down on the peer, containerlab --runtime c9s events reports it, and routing on the surviving node withdraws the peer’s routes. start the node and watch it recover.
Destroy twice. Save a config change, destroy, deploy again. Predict: the change is still there, from the retained claim. Then destroy --cleanup and deploy. Predict: back to the startup config.
Clean up with make try-c9s-clean.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
Gotchas

Old guides. Anything mentioning launcher pods, nested Docker, LauncherProfile, clabverter or disableExpose is pre-0.9 and incompatible.
docker ps is empty. Expected. Use containerlab --runtime c9s inspect or kubectl.
destroy keeps saved state. Use destroy --cleanup for a clean slate.
Pod Security Admission blocks the privileged sidecar unless lab namespaces are labelled privileged.
NetworkPolicies must allow UDP 14789/14790 between device pods and TCP 14791 from the kubelet, or links never come up and nodes never go ready.
Ready is not converged. Without an image healthcheck or probe, ready means the processes run. Check protocol state before you trust a lab.
Name rewriting. PE_1 becomes pe-1 in everything Containerlab reports. Scripts that match on the original name should use the c9s.run/originalNodeName label.
Vendor images and registries. Push licensed images only to private registries, and give the cluster pull credentials through imagePullSecrets.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
Boring rule
Validate and read the emitted manifests before you deploy, treat the cluster as the source of truth, and destroy with --cleanup unless you mean to keep the lab’s saved state.

title: Clabernetes (c9s): Running Containerlab Topologies on Kubernetes
text:
Try this

Write a topology with nodes named R1, PE_1 and 9core, and predict the c9s names before running deploy --emit-crs. Expected: r1, pe-1 and a clab- prefixed name.
Add stages to one node and run validate. Expected: a fail-closed error naming the field; startup-delay instead is accepted.
Deploy the same lab twice with different --namespace values. Expected: two independent labs, as long as both namespaces already exist; Containerlab does not create or delete namespaces you name explicitly.
Run containerlab --runtime c9s inspect --format json and write a one-line jq filter that prints name and load_balancer_address for every node.
Bind clabernetes-lab-viewer to a test user in one namespace and try deploy as that user. Expected: refused. inspect and logs work.

text:

The main path of this book uses open-source and freely available lab images only. No paid virtual NOS license is required to finish the curriculum. This chapter catalogs practical choices (as of mid-2026 practice) and how to size a lab host.

title: Free Image Matrix & Resources
text:
FRR as the workhorse
FRRouting implements OSPF, BGP, IS-IS, statics, and more with a Cisco-like vtysh. Container images are the fastest path:
# Example — check quay for current stable tags
docker pull quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
Strengths: control-plane labs, policy, dual-stack
Limits: not a full merchant silicon simulator; L2 features depend on how you combine Linux bridging
Lab pattern:
# snippet
r1:
  kind: linux
  image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
  binds:
    - ./config/r1:/etc/frr
Enable only needed daemons (bgpd=yes, ospfd=yes) in daemons file to save RAM.

title: Free Image Matrix & Resources
text:
Linux endpoints
Alpine is small and fast:
h1:
  kind: linux
  image: alpine:3.20
  exec:
    - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils busybox-extras
Debian if you need a richer package set:
h1:
  kind: linux
  image: debian:bookworm-slim
  exec:
    - apt-get update && apt-get install -y iproute2 iputils-ping tcpdump iperf3 mtr-tiny
Tip: bake a personal lab image with tools preinstalled to save time:
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils tcpdump iperf3 mtr bind-tools
docker build -t local/lab-endpoint:1.0 .
Use local/lab-endpoint:1.0 in topologies.

title: Free Image Matrix & Resources

SR Linux community (optional track)
Nokia SR Linux community images are commonly used with Containerlab for modern streaming telemetry and CLI/model exposure—without classic paid chassis IOS requirements. Follow current Containerlab kind: srl documentation for image names and credentials.
Use SR Linux when you want:

Do not block L2/L3 fundamentals waiting for SR Linux. FRR+Linux is enough for competence.

title: Linux Networking for Lab Hosts
text:
Linux Networking for Lab Hosts
Containerlab sits on Linux networking primitives: namespaces, veth pairs, bridges, routes, and basic filtering. If you only drive YAML without understanding the host, debugging feels like magic. This chapter builds the host-side intuition you need before (and during) Containerlab work.

title: Linux Networking for Lab Hosts
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain how network namespaces isolate stacks

Create veth pairs and bridges by hand

Add addresses and routes; verify with ip route get

Use tcpdump inside a namespace

Map Containerlab links to veth/bridge concepts

Apply minimal filter awareness (nft/iptables, rp_filter)

title: Linux Networking for Lab Hosts
text:
Learning goals in practice
You will build a two-namespace router lab without Containerlab, then tear it down. That is the same physics Containerlab orchestrates for you.

title: Linux Networking for Lab Hosts
text:
Core objects







Object
Role




Interface
L2 endpoint (physical, veth, bridge, vlan subint)


Network namespace
Isolated network stack (interfaces, routes, sockets)


veth pair
Virtual cable: two ends, often in different namespaces


Bridge
Software switch in the kernel


Route
FIB entry: destination → device / next hop


Rule
Policy routing (advanced; optional here)



ip -br link
ip -br addr
ip netns list
ip route

title: Linux Networking for Lab Hosts
text:
Network namespaces
A namespace process sees the root namespace. Lab nodes (containers) each get a namespace.
# Create two namespaces
sudo ip netns add ns1
sudo ip netns add ns2
ip netns list

# Run a command inside
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip link
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ping -c1 127.0.0.1
Loopback exists per namespace; bring it up if you care about local sockets:
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip link set lo up

title: Linux Networking for Lab Hosts
text:
veth pairs: virtual cables
# Create pair veth-a <-> veth-b
sudo ip link add veth-a type veth peer name veth-b

# Move ends into namespaces
sudo ip link set veth-a netns ns1
sudo ip link set veth-b netns ns2

# Name + address inside each ns
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip link set veth-a name eth0
sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip link set veth-b name eth0

sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev eth0
sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev eth0

sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip link set eth0 up
sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip link set eth0 up

# Test L3 on-link
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ping -c 2 10.0.0.2
Predict: ARP resolves; ICMP works; no router required because same subnet.
Observe:
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip neigh
sudo ip netns exec ns1 tcpdump -ni eth0 -c 10 arp or icmp &
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ping -c 2 10.0.0.2

title: Linux Networking for Lab Hosts
text:
Bridges: software switches
Connect multiple endpoints as if on a switch:
sudo ip netns add h1
sudo ip netns add h2
sudo ip netns add h3

sudo ip link add br0 type bridge
sudo ip link set br0 up

# veth for each host: host side in ns, peer on host attached to bridge
for n in 1 2 3; do
  sudo ip link add veth-h$n type veth peer name veth-b$n
  sudo ip link set veth-h$n netns h$n
  sudo ip netns exec h$n ip link set veth-h$n name eth0
  sudo ip netns exec h$n ip addr add 10.10.0.$n/24 dev eth0
  sudo ip netns exec h$n ip link set eth0 up
  sudo ip netns exec h$n ip link set lo up
  sudo ip link set veth-b$n master br0
  sudo ip link set veth-b$n up
done

sudo ip netns exec h1 ping -c 2 10.10.0.2
sudo ip netns exec h1 ping -c 2 10.10.0.3
Bridge FDB (MAC table):
bridge fdb show br br0
# or
ip neigh  # not the same; FDB is L2 forward database
bridge link show
After pings, you should see learned MACs on the bridge ports.

title: Linux Networking for Lab Hosts
text:
Routing between namespaces
Classic: two LANs and a router namespace.
h1 (10.1.0.10/24) -- veth -- r (10.1.0.1 + 10.2.0.1) -- veth -- h2 (10.2.0.10/24)
sudo ip netns add h1
sudo ip netns add h2
sudo ip netns add r

# h1 <-> r
sudo ip link add v1 type veth peer name r1
sudo ip link set v1 netns h1
sudo ip link set r1 netns r
sudo ip netns exec h1 ip link set v1 name eth0
sudo ip netns exec r  ip link set r1 name eth1
sudo ip netns exec h1 ip addr add 10.1.0.10/24 dev eth0
sudo ip netns exec r  ip addr add 10.1.0.1/24  dev eth1
sudo ip netns exec h1 ip link set eth0 up
sudo ip netns exec r  ip link set eth1 up
sudo ip netns exec h1 ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec r  ip link set lo up

# h2 <-> r
sudo ip link add v2 type veth peer name r2
sudo ip link set v2 netns h2
sudo ip link set r2 netns r
sudo ip netns exec h2 ip link set v2 name eth0
sudo ip netns exec r  ip link set r2 name eth2
sudo ip netns exec h2 ip addr add 10.2.0.10/24 dev eth0
sudo ip netns exec r  ip addr add 10.2.0.1/24  dev eth2
sudo ip netns exec h2 ip link set eth0 up
sudo ip netns exec r  ip link set eth2 up
sudo ip netns exec h2 ip link set lo up

# Enable forwarding on router ns
sudo ip netns exec r sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

# Default routes on hosts
sudo ip netns exec h1 ip route add default via 10.1.0.1
sudo ip netns exec h2 ip route add default via 10.2.0.1

# Test
sudo ip netns exec h1 ping -c 3 10.2.0.10
sudo ip netns exec h1 traceroute -n 10.2.0.10

sudo ip netns exec h1 ip route get 10.2.0.10
sudo ip netns exec r  ip route get 10.2.0.10 from 10.1.0.10 iif eth1
sudo ip netns exec r  ip -s link show eth1

sudo ip netns exec r sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0
sudo ip netns exec h1 ping -c 2 10.2.0.10   # expect fail
sudo ip netns exec r sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

If the “router” only had a connected route on one side (misconfigured static elsewhere), one-way traffic appears. With connected routes on both interfaces above, both directions work. Later static chapters amplify return-path bugs.

title: What Is Networking?
text:
What Is Networking?
A network moves data between endpoints over links, using protocols—agreed rules for format, addressing, and behavior. Everything later in this book (VLANs, OSPF, VXLAN) is a specialization of that idea.

title: What Is Networking?
text:
Learning goals

Distinguish local delivery (same L2 domain) from routed delivery (across networks)

Explain why we use layered protocols instead of one monolithic format

Tie lab tools (Containerlab, ip, captures) to those ideas

title: What Is Networking?
text:
What problem networking solves
Without a network, processes on different machines cannot cooperate. Networking provides:

Reachability — a path exists (or is reported as unreachable)

Naming / addressing — who is who (MAC, IP, names via DNS)

Multiplexing — many conversations share links (ports, VLANs, queues)

Reliability options — best-effort (UDP/IP) vs recovered streams (TCP)

Policy — who may talk to whom, with what priority

title: What Is Networking?
text:
Switching vs routing (first cut)
Same subnet / VLAN          Different subnets
─────────────────          ─────────────────
  Host A ──switch── Host B    Host A → gateway → … → Host B
  Frame uses MAC             Packet uses IP; each hop rewrites L2

Switching (L2): deliver a frame inside one broadcast domain; learn MACs; flood unknown unicasts.

Routing (L3): deliver a packet across networks; each router decrements TTL and chooses a next hop.

You will refine both in the Layer 2 and Layer 3 parts. Foundations give vocabulary and host-level truth.

title: What Is Networking?
text:
Protocols as contracts
A protocol answers:

What bits mean (headers, fields)

Who may send what next (state machines)

How errors are signaled (ICMP, TCP RST, DHCP NAK)

Vendors invent CLIs; RFCs and open implementations define the contracts this book cares about.

title: What Is Networking?
text:

Networks fail in partial, asymmetric, and time-dependent ways. A Containerlab topology lets you:

Reset and try again

title: What Is Networking?
section: A network as a chain of decisions
text:
A network as a chain of decisions
A network is a collection of links and forwarding systems that carry data between endpoints. A host does not need a complete map of the Internet: it needs a destination address, a usable route, and a way to send to the next hop. Each router repeats a local forwarding decision. That division of work scales, but it also means one wrong decision anywhere on the path can prevent delivery.
Consider a browser contacting a server on another subnet. The host obtains an IP address for the name, selects a source address and route, resolves the local next-hop address to a link-layer address, and sends a frame. A switch forwards that frame within its VLAN. The router removes the incoming link header, selects an outgoing route, and sends a new frame. The server processes the IP packet, delivers its transport payload to a socket, and responds along a route of its own. The return path need not be identical to the forward path.

Delay, capacity, and loss
Bandwidth is a link’s transmission capacity; throughput is the useful data delivered per unit time. Latency includes serialization (putting bits on a link), propagation, processing, and queueing. On a 100 Mb/s link, transmitting a 1,500-byte IP packet alone takes roughly 120 microseconds, excluding link overhead; propagation and queues add more. A 10 ms round trip is not the time to transmit every packet: several packets can be in flight simultaneously.
Buffers absorb bursts but cannot fix a sustained arrival rate above service capacity. When a queue fills, packets are dropped; before it fills, queueing delay increases. A link can therefore have high latency or loss without being physically broken. Distinguish availability (can it work?), correctness (does it reach the intended destination?), and performance (does it work within the required time and capacity?).






Tip



Before changing a device, write down the source, destination, expected path, and observable proof at each hop. A successful ping proves a particular ICMP exchange, not that every application or packet size works.

title: TCP/IP and the Layered Stack
section: What a layer promises—and what it cannot promise
text:
What a layer promises—and what it cannot promise
A layer describes a service and the information needed to use it. Ethernet provides delivery across a local link; IP provides best-effort delivery between IP addresses across networks; TCP supplies an ordered byte stream between endpoints. None of these guarantees that the application is healthy. Ethernet delivery to a router is not end-to-end delivery to a server, and a TCP handshake is not proof that a database query succeeds.
Headers are not a physical nesting of independent machines. They are bytes in one transmission, interpreted by successive components according to protocol identifiers: Ethernet EtherType selects an L3 protocol; the IPv4 Protocol or IPv6 Next Header identifies the next header; TCP/UDP ports help identify a socket. IPv6 may have extension headers between the base header and transport header. Layering explains common responsibilities, but real systems have interactions across boundaries: a tunnel consumes MTU, while a firewall may inspect transport headers.

The planes are different questions
The data plane forwards an actual packet. The control plane builds or changes forwarding information, for example when OSPF exchanges routes. The management plane lets an operator observe and configure a device. A router can have an established routing adjacency while a data interface drops traffic; conversely it may continue forwarding with installed routes while a management session is unavailable. Test both the decision and the actual traffic.

title: Packets, Frames, Encapsulation

Packets, Frames, Encapsulation
Data is wrapped in headers as it descends the stack and unwrapped on the way up. Clear names prevent confusion in captures and design talks.

title: Packets, Frames, Encapsulation

Learning goals

+------------------+

+------------------+

Reverse order: FCS check → MAC → Ethertype → IP → protocol → ports → app.

title: Packets, Frames, Encapsulation
text:
Maximum sizes and MTU

MTU: max IP packet size a link will accept (commonly 1500 on Ethernet)

Oversized IPv4 packets may be fragmented if allowed, or dropped with fragmentation-needed feedback; IPv6 routers return Packet Too Big rather than fragmenting.

Tunnel encapsulation consumes underlay capacity; a VLAN tag increases frame size and does not necessarily reduce IP MTU when the link supports tagged frames.

Details and labs: Layer 3 ICMP/PMTU chapter later; foundations need the idea.

text:
Worked packet walk: local and remote destinations
Assume host A is 192.0.2.10/24, its gateway is 192.0.2.1, and host B is 198.51.100.20. A chooses the gateway because B is outside the connected prefix. It resolves 192.0.2.1, not B, with ARP. Its Ethernet frame has A’s source MAC and the gateway’s destination MAC, while the IP header still has A and B as source and destination. At the router the incoming frame is removed and a new outgoing frame is constructed. The IP source and destination normally stay unchanged, but TTL decreases; NAT or tunneling can change the observed headers.
If B were 192.0.2.20, A would normally resolve B directly and send a frame to B’s MAC. A frame’s destination MAC is a next-hop address on one link; it is not a globally meaningful end-to-end address. Switches forward the existing frame within a broadcast domain, while routers create a new link-layer frame for the next link.

Size arithmetic and capture caveats
With an IPv4 MTU of 1500 and no IPv4 or TCP options, at most 1460 bytes remain for TCP data in one IP packet: 1500 − 20 IPv4 − 20 TCP = 1460. IPv6’s base header is 40 bytes, so the equivalent is 1440 before extension headers or TCP options. Ethernet headers and FCS are outside that IP MTU. A VLAN tag increases Ethernet frame overhead; whether it reduces available IP MTU depends on the link’s supported frame size. Tunnels add outer headers, so their inner MTU must fit the underlay.
IPv4 routers may fragment when allowed, but a packet with Don’t Fragment set must instead be dropped if too large, normally with an ICMP fragmentation-needed message. IPv6 routers do not fragment packets; the source uses Packet Too Big feedback and may fragment at the source. Blocking that feedback can create a path-MTU black hole. See RFC 8200 and RFC 8900.
A host capture may show packets before segmentation or after receive aggregation because of offloads, and apparent checksum errors can occur before hardware completes a checksum. Ethernet FCS is often not supplied to the capture at all. Capture at both endpoints or on an intermediate link before assuming the capture is a literal wire image.

title: Link Layer and Ethernet
text:
Ethernet delivery and MAC learning
An Ethernet address is 48 bits, conventionally written as six hexadecimal octets. A unicast destination identifies one interface; a broadcast destination (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff) is delivered to the broadcast domain; multicast identifies a group. A switch learns a source MAC against the ingress port and VLAN when it receives a frame. For a known unicast destination it selects the learned port; for an unknown destination it floods within the VLAN, excluding ingress. Broadcast and relevant multicast also have VLAN-scoped handling. Entries age out, so learning is dynamic rather than a permanent inventory.
A switch’s forwarding decision uses the destination MAC and VLAN, not the destination IP route. A router makes an IP forwarding decision between networks. An access port associates untagged frames with a VLAN; a trunk can carry several VLANs, usually using 802.1Q tags. A VLAN is a logical L2 broadcast domain, not an IP subnet, though a simple design commonly maps one subnet to one VLAN.
A frame check sequence detects corruption; it does not repair the frame or prove that the sender is trustworthy. In full-duplex switched Ethernet, endpoints transmit and receive concurrently; collisions are not the normal explanation for a modern full-duplex link’s packet loss. Inspect interface errors, drops, link negotiation, and switch counters in context.

title: Physical Ethernet: Media, Optics, PoE and Fault Isolation
text:
Physical Ethernet: Media, Optics, PoE and Fault Isolation
A routing protocol cannot repair a damaged fiber, an incompatible transceiver or a powered device that never starts. Conversely, a physical link can be up while a VLAN or route is wrong. Diagnose from measured symptoms at both ends and keep physical status separate from forwarding and application reachability.

title: Physical Ethernet: Media, Optics, PoE and Fault Isolation
text:
Choose a compatible link
Twisted-pair copper carries electrical signals over balanced pairs. Fiber carries light and offers electrical isolation; single-mode and multimode are different fiber systems with different optical characteristics. A connector that fits does not prove that the transceivers, wavelengths, fiber type, strand count, polarity, reach and host port modes match. A multimode optic and a single-mode optic cannot be treated as interchangeable merely because they have the same nominal line rate. Some optics use two fibers, others use wavelength multiplexing or multiple lanes; follow the exact transceiver specifications and cable plant documentation.
Copper link distance and supported speed depend on the Ethernet PHY, cable category, installation and channel quality. Do not assume every copper Ethernet link supports the same speed or 100-meter reach. Terminations, patch panels, pair integrity and interference matter as well as patch-cord length. A cable that lights a link at a lower speed may still fail the required channel test at the intended speed.
At both ends compare the configured and operational speed, duplex, supported and advertised modes, autonegotiation, link status and error counters. Some media and speeds require particular negotiation behavior; do not force settings blindly or assume all devices behave alike. A duplex mismatch on a link capable of half-duplex can cause poor performance and errors even when link is up. Modern full-duplex switched links do not normally experience classic shared-medium collisions.

title: Physical Ethernet: Media, Optics, PoE and Fault Isolation
section: Read counters as a time series
text:
Read counters as a time series
Collect interface and transceiver state at both ends, note time and traffic load, and compare deltas over a known interval. Counters may reset on reboot, interface reset or hardware rollover; names and meanings are platform-specific. Correlation is a lead, not proof of a particular cable defect.







Observation
Candidate causes and next evidence




No physical link
Administrative state, remote power, cable, optic type, polarity, mode or negotiation


Link up but CRC/FCS errors rise
Corruption on the receive path: inspect both ends, cable, optics and test results


Link flaps
Power, cable movement, optical levels, transceiver, negotiation or hardware logs


Drops without physical errors
Queue congestion, policing, buffer pressure or software processing; inspect drop reason and direction


Link healthy but no service
VLAN, STP, aggregation, addressing, filtering and return path



A receive error on one end does not uniquely identify the bad component: the transmitter, channel or receiver can all contribute. Compare both directions and change one component at a time. Corrected forward-error-correction (FEC) counters can reveal margin degradation before uncorrectable errors, but FEC reporting and thresholds depend on the PHY and device. A rising corrected count is not itself proof of packet loss. Match FEC configuration and supported modes on both ends where required.



One direction of an optical link budget

title: Physical Ethernet: Media, Optics, PoE and Fault Isolation
text:
Optical power and loss budget
Optical power is commonly shown in dBm, an absolute logarithmic power level; loss and margin are differences in dB. Suppose, for one direction and wavelength, the measured transmitter output is -2 dBm and the far-end receiver reports -8 dBm. The approximate measured difference is -2 - (-8) = 6 dB. If that receiver’s specified minimum sensitivity is -10 dBm, its received level is 2 dB above that lower limit. This is a simplified reading, not a certification: verify the receiver’s upper and lower allowed power limits, wavelength, calibration, measurement method, connector and splice loss, and the transceiver’s specified operating range. Too much received power can also be a problem.
Repeat in the opposite direction; each direction has its own transmitter, receive level and fiber path. Use the correct optical power meter, source and reference procedure when certifying a link. Module digital diagnostics are useful operational clues but can have tolerance and reporting limits. Never look into a fiber end or optical port; follow the site’s optical safety and inspection procedures. Clean and inspect connectors using appropriate equipment and approved procedures.

title: Physical Ethernet: Media, Optics, PoE and Fault Isolation
text:
Power over Ethernet
Power sourcing equipment (PSE), such as a switch port or compatible injector, supplies power to a powered device (PD), such as an access point or phone. Standards-based PoE performs detection and classification before supplying operating power. Check the endpoint’s required power and supported standard or mode against the port’s capabilities, the switch’s remaining power budget, cabling and any injector in the path. PSE power and delivered PD power are not identical because cable loss consumes power. LLDP power negotiation may affect an implementation’s allocation, but support and behavior vary.
A device can power on with limited function, reboot under load, or negotiate a lower operating mode when power is insufficient. A data-link LED does not prove that the powered device has its requested budget, and a powered endpoint does not prove the data VLAN is correct. Do not assume a passive injector provides standards-based detection; use equipment and procedures approved for the endpoint.

title: Physical Ethernet: Media, Optics, PoE and Fault Isolation
text:
Worked fault-isolation exercise
Use a spare, authorized link and record device models, port names, optics/cable labels, speed, duplex, counters, transceiver diagnostics and timestamps at both ends. Hardware behavior and commands vary; this exercise is a procedure and has not been run on a specific physical switch.

Baseline: establish bidirectional traffic between known test endpoints. Record counters before and after a fixed interval. Confirm the application and both paths work; a link LED alone is insufficient.
Cable path: using a known-good compatible patch cable on a spare link, change one cable at a time. Record which counters rise, whether link speed changes, and the actual repair. Do not unplug a production link without its change procedure.
Optics: given TX -2 dBm, RX -8 dBm, and minimum RX sensitivity -10 dBm, calculate 6 dB measured difference and 2 dB lower-limit margin. Then inspect the opposite direction and the receiver’s maximum rating before accepting the link. Distinguish a transceiver reading from a calibrated channel certification.
PoE: attach an approved test PD to a PoE-capable spare port. Record detection/classification, allocated and measured power, switch-wide budget, link state and device function. Compare a known-compatible power source if power is denied. Do not exceed device or injector ratings.
Service path: with physical link stable, introduce a VLAN mismatch only in the isolated lab. Observe that the link can remain up while traffic fails. Restore the VLAN and verify counters, neighbor discovery and end-to-end traffic.

On Linux, where the driver and tool are available, ip -s link show dev IFACE and ethtool IFACE provide complementary views; ethtool -S IFACE may expose driver-specific counters. Replace IFACE with the actual interface. Unsupported fields or counters are not proof of zero errors. The kernel’s twisted-pair diagnostic guide describes additional tests and cautions.

title: Physical Ethernet: Media, Optics, PoE and Fault Isolation
text:
Review
Why can a link be up but unusable? Which direction should you investigate when receive CRC errors rise? Why is a 6 dB loss figure alone insufficient to approve an optical path? Why can a powered endpoint still fail to pass data? What does a PoE budget describe that a port link-state indicator does not?
Further reading: IEEE 802.3 material on PoE detection and the Linux Ethernet diagnostic guide. Use the actual equipment and transceiver specifications for supported modes, power and optical limits.

On-link decision
A host first performs a routing lookup. Assigning an address normally installs a connected route, so a destination in that prefix will often use that interface directly; a more-specific route or a policy-selected table can change the result. For a selected unicast Ethernet route, ARP resolves the next hop: the destination for a direct route, or the gateway for a route with via. Local, broadcast, multicast, and other route types need different handling. ip route get asks the kernel for a lookup; it does not itself prove that a packet reaches the destination.

title: IPv4 Addressing and Subnetting
text:
Work the mask by hand
For 192.0.2.130/26, the last mask octet is 192 or 11000000 in binary. A bitwise AND keeps a bit only where both inputs have a 1:
address:  192.0.2.130   last octet 10000010
mask:     255.255.255.192          11000000
network:  192.0.2.128              10000000
The six host bits can vary from 000000 to 111111, giving .128 through .191. On a conventional broadcast subnet, .128 is the network address and .191 the directed broadcast, leaving .129–.190 for hosts. Equivalently, a /26 has blocks of 64 addresses; 130 falls in the block beginning at 128. This shortcut works because 64 divides the last octet. For a prefix that crosses an earlier octet, apply the same mask to all four octets.
A prefix describes a range of addresses; 192.0.2.130/26 is a host address with a prefix, while 192.0.2.128/26 names its network. A router may also hold a more-specific route inside an aggregate; that is deliberate route overlap. Address assignments to separate links should not accidentally overlap.

title: IPv4 Addressing and Subnetting
section: Lab: calculate and check without changing interfaces
text:
Lab: calculate and check without changing interfaces
Python’s standard ipaddress module checks arithmetic locally; it sends no packets and needs no administrator privilege. Save this as subnet_check.py and run python3 subnet_check.py:
from ipaddress import ip_interface, ip_network

host = ip_interface("192.0.2.130/26")
net = host.network
print("address:", host.ip)
print("network:", net)
print("mask:", net.netmask)
print("broadcast:", net.broadcast_address)
print("count:", net.num_addresses)
print("last host:", net.broadcast_address - 1)

for subnet in ip_network("198.51.100.0/24").subnets(new_prefix=26):
    print(subnet)
Expected output:
address: 192.0.2.130
network: 192.0.2.128/26
mask: 255.255.255.192
broadcast: 192.0.2.191
count: 64
last host: 192.0.2.190
198.51.100.0/26
198.51.100.64/26
198.51.100.128/26
198.51.100.192/26
broadcast_address - 1 here is a shortcut for this conventional /26, not a universal usable-host rule. For /31 and /32, use the special semantics above. To inspect a real Linux routing decision separately, run ip route get DESTINATION with a destination appropriate for your environment; the lookup is observational, but a later ping or application connection sends traffic.

title: IPv4 Addressing and Subnetting
text:
A worked longest-prefix example
Suppose a host has 192.0.2.130/26. A /26 mask is 255.255.255.192: the first 26 bits identify the prefix, leaving six host bits. Each block has 64 addresses. The blocks in the last octet start at 0, 64, 128, and 192, so the host belongs to 192.0.2.128/26, with network address .128 and directed broadcast .191. In a conventional subnet the usable host range is .129 through .190; point-to-point /31 and host /32 have special purposes, so do not apply the ordinary host-count rule mechanically.
Now compare routing entries 0.0.0.0/0 via A, 192.0.2.0/24 via B, and 192.0.2.128/26 via C. Destination 192.0.2.130 matches all three; /26 wins because it is the most specific matching prefix. Destination 192.0.2.70 uses /24. A default route matches anything not matched more specifically. Within the forwarding table selected for a lookup, route preferences or metrics choose among suitable alternatives for the same prefix; a less-specific forwarding entry does not override a more-specific one. Policy routing can select a different table first; see the policy lookup lab. See RFC 1812.
CIDR aggregation advertises a larger prefix covering several smaller ones. Aggregation saves state but can attract traffic for a destination that is not actually reachable inside the aggregate. Design the internal routes and failure behavior before advertising a summary.

Split 198.51.100.0/24 into four equal subnets. What prefix length and network addresses result?
A router has 198.51.100.0/24 via R1 and 198.51.100.128/25 via R2. Where does 198.51.100.200 go? What about 198.51.100.20?
Two hosts are in the same VLAN, but one has 192.0.2.10/24 and the other 192.0.2.130/25. Why can their on-link decisions differ?

Answers: (1) Four /26 networks: .0, .64, .128, .192. (2) .200 matches the more-specific /25 via R2; .20 uses the /24 via R1. (3) The first host considers the entire /24 on-link. The second considers only .128–.255 on-link and sends traffic to .10 through a gateway if it has a suitable route. Shared Ethernet membership does not make their subnet masks agree.

title: IPv6 Essentials
text:
IPv6 Essentials
IPv6 is not “IPv4 with longer addresses”. The address is longer, but the more useful changes for an operator are elsewhere: every interface has several addresses at once, each with a scope and a lifetime; the host checks that an address is unique before it uses it; neighbour resolution rides on multicast instead of broadcast; and the kernel, not the application, picks which of those addresses a packet leaves from. Most “IPv6 is broken” tickets in a lab are one of those four ideas misunderstood. This chapter builds them up on a Linux host, in an unprivileged namespace lab whose output is pasted below, and stops where SLAAC, the RA M/O flags and DHCPv6 begins.

title: IPv6 Essentials
text:
Learning goals

Write and read IPv6 addresses in the canonical form of RFC 5952, and classify an address by its prefix
Explain where a link-local address comes from (EUI-64 or RFC 7217 stable-privacy) and why it needs a zone index
Watch Duplicate Address Detection fail and read tentative / dadfailed / deprecated in ip -6 addr
Derive the solicited-node multicast group for an address and say why two addresses can share one
Predict which source address Linux will choose (RFC 6724), and move it with preferred_lft
Plan a dual-stack LAN with a ULA or documentation prefix and a /64 per link

Version note. The labs ran on 2026-11-13 on Linux 6.12.94+ with iproute2 6.15.0 and Python 3.13.5, as an unprivileged user inside unshare -rnm. That gives a throwaway user, network and mount namespace, inside which two further network namespaces (h1, h2) are joined by a veth pair. No sudo, no packages: ping, sysctl and tcpdump are not installed on the writing host, so sysctls are read and written through /proc/sys and the first datagram is sent from Python. MAC addresses and the random ULA in the listings are lab-local and will differ on your machine.
The lab host track has a hands-on dual-stack triangle on FRR, cEOS and SR Linux and a SLAAC switch lab. This chapter is the host-side foundation those labs assume; it does not repeat them.

title: IPv6 Essentials
section: Address format and the canonical text form
text:
Address format and the canonical text form
An IPv6 address is 128 bits written as eight 16-bit groups (“hextets”) in hex. Two rules make it short, and RFC 5952 makes the short form unique so that logs, ACLs and grep agree:







Rule (RFC 4291 2.2, RFC 5952 4)
Example




Drop leading zeros in each hextet
0db8 → db8


Replace the longest run of two or more zero hextets with ::, once
2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:10 → 2001:db8::1:0:0:10


If two runs tie, compress the first
2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1 → 2001:db8::1:0:0:1


Never compress a single zero hextet
2001:db8:0:1:1:1:1:1 stays as it is


Lower-case hex
2001:DB8:: → 2001:db8::



A prefix is written address/length, for example 2001:db8:10::/64. The documentation prefix 2001:db8::/32 (RFC 3849) is reserved for examples like the ones in this book, which is why it will never route on the internet.

Lab: notation, kinds and derived addresses
The standard library already implements RFC 5952 and the IANA special-purpose registries, so it is the quickest way to check yourself. The script below also derives an EUI-64 link-local, the solicited-node group and an RFC 4193 ULA prefix; the next sections use each result.
# v6tools.py: notation, EUI-64, solicited-node and an RFC 4193 ULA prefix. stdlib only.
import hashlib, ipaddress, time

print("-- RFC 5952 canonical text")
for s in ["2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0010", "2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:10",
          "2001:DB8::0:1:0:0:10", "fe80:0000::0ab0:00ff:fe00:0001"]:
    print(f"{s:42} -> {ipaddress.IPv6Address(s)}")
print(ipaddress.IPv6Address("2001:db8::1").exploded)

print("-- what kind of address is it?")
for s in ["::1", "::", "fe80::1", "fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::10", "2001:db8:10::10",
          "2606:4700:4700::1111", "ff02::1:ff00:10", "::ffff:192.0.2.7", "64:ff9b::c000:207"]:
    a = ipaddress.IPv6Address(s)
    kinds = [k for k in ("is_loopback", "is_unspecified", "is_link_local", "is_private",
                         "is_global", "is_multicast", "is_reserved") if getattr(a, k)]
    extra = f" ipv4_mapped={a.ipv4_mapped}" if a.ipv4_mapped else ""
    print(f"{s:24} {' '.join(k[3:] for k in kinds)}{extra}")

def eui64(mac):
    b = bytearray(int(x, 16) for x in mac.split(":"))
    b[0] ^= 0x02                                   # flip the universal/local bit
    iid = bytes(b[:3]) + b"\xff\xfe" + bytes(b[3:])
    return ipaddress.IPv6Address(b"\xfe\x80" + b"\x00" * 6 + iid)

print("-- EUI-64 link-local from the lab MAC")
print("f6:84:3f:52:2c:c0 ->", eui64("f6:84:3f:52:2c:c0"))

def solicited_node(addr):
    low24 = int(ipaddress.IPv6Address(addr)) & 0xFFFFFF
    return ipaddress.IPv6Address(int(ipaddress.IPv6Address("ff02::1:ff00:0")) | low24)

print("-- solicited-node groups")
for a in ["2001:db8:10::10", "fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::10", "fe80::f484:3fff:fe52:2cc0"]:
    print(f"{a:28} -> {solicited_node(a)}")

print("-- RFC 4193 section 3.2.2 ULA /48 (time + EUI-64, SHA-1, low 40 bits)")
ntp = int((time.time() + 2208988800) * (1 << 32)).to_bytes(8, "big")
eui = bytes.fromhex("f4843ffffe522cc0")
gid = hashlib.sha1(ntp + eui).digest()[-5:]
print(ipaddress.IPv6Network((b"\xfd" + gid + b"\x00" * 10, 48)))
print("-- a /48 holds", 2 ** (64 - 48), "/64 LANs; first three:",
      [str(n) for n in list(ipaddress.IPv6Network("fd3c:5a1e:77b0::/48").subnets(new_prefix=64))[:3]])
$ python3 v6tools.py
-- RFC 5952 canonical text
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0010    -> 2001:db8::1:0:0:10
2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:10                      -> 2001:db8::1:0:0:10
2001:DB8::0:1:0:0:10                       -> 2001:db8::1:0:0:10
fe80:0000::0ab0:00ff:fe00:0001             -> fe80::ab0:ff:fe00:1
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
-- what kind of address is it?
::1                      loopback private reserved
::                       unspecified private reserved
fe80::1                  link_local private
fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::10    private
2001:db8:10::10          private
2606:4700:4700::1111     global
ff02::1:ff00:10          global multicast
::ffff:192.0.2.7         private ipv4_mapped=192.0.2.7
64:ff9b::c000:207        global reserved
-- EUI-64 link-local from the lab MAC
f6:84:3f:52:2c:c0 -> fe80::f484:3fff:fe52:2cc0
-- solicited-node groups
2001:db8:10::10              -> ff02::1:ff00:10
fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::10        -> ff02::1:ff00:10
fe80::f484:3fff:fe52:2cc0    -> ff02::1:ff52:2cc0
-- RFC 4193 section 3.2.2 ULA /48 (time + EUI-64, SHA-1, low 40 bits)
fdfe:95bc:6ee7::/48
-- a /48 holds 65536 /64 LANs; first three: ['fd3c:5a1e:77b0::/64', 'fd3c:5a1e:77b0:1::/64', 'fd3c:5a1e:77b0:2::/64']
Things to take from that run:

Four spellings of one address produce one canonical string. Normalise before you compare addresses from different tools.
2001:db8:10::10 reports as private. Python follows the IANA special-purpose registry, where documentation space is “not globally reachable”. Do not read is_private as “RFC 1918 for IPv6”.
ff02::1:ff00:10 reports as global and multicast. is_global describes the registry entry, not the multicast scope. For multicast, the scope lives in the fourth hex digit (ff02 = link-local scope, ff05 = site, ff0e = global).
::ffff:192.0.2.7 is an IPv4-mapped address: how a dual-stack socket shows an IPv4 peer. 64:ff9b::/96 is the NAT64 well-known prefix (RFC 6052) that embeds 192.0.2.7 as c000:207.

title: IPv6 Essentials
text:
Address kinds you must know









Kind
Prefix
Scope / role
Seen where




Unspecified
::/128
“no address yet”
source of DAD probes, 0.0.0.0 equivalent in binds


Loopback
::1/128
this host
ip -6 addr show dev lo


Link-local unicast
fe80::/10 (used as fe80::/64)
one link only, never forwarded
on every IPv6 interface; router next hops


Unique local (ULA)
fc00::/7, in practice fd00::/8
inside a site; not routed on the internet
labs, internal services


Global unicast
2000::/3 today
routable
ISP / RIR space


Multicast
ff00::/8
scope in the 4th digit
ND, OSPFv3, mDNS


IPv4-mapped
::ffff:0:0/96
API representation
dual-stack sockets


NAT64 well-known
64:ff9b::/96
translation
DNS64/NAT64 networks



There is no broadcast in IPv6. What ARP used broadcast for, Neighbor Discovery does with multicast groups that only the right hosts join.

title: IPv6 Essentials
section: Many addresses per interface, each with a life
text:
Many addresses per interface, each with a life
On IPv4 a host interface usually has one address. On IPv6 a working host interface typically has at least:

one link-local address (always; the kernel generates it when the link comes up),
one or more global or ULA addresses (static, SLAAC, or DHCPv6),
under SLAAC, often a temporary (privacy) address that rotates (RFC 8981),
several multicast group memberships.

Each unicast address carries two lifetimes. Valid lifetime is how long it may be used at all. Preferred lifetime is how long it should be chosen for new connections. Between the two, the address is deprecated: existing connections keep it, new ones avoid it. That one distinction is how renumbering works without dropping sessions, and the lab below uses it to steer source selection.







ip -6 addr flag
Meaning




tentative
DAD has not finished; the address cannot be used as a source yet


dadfailed
Someone else on the link answered for it; the address will never become usable until removed and re-added


deprecated
Preferred lifetime is 0; kept for existing flows only


temporary
RFC 8981 privacy address


stable-privacy
Interface identifier generated per RFC 7217


mngtmpaddr
Template from which temporary addresses are made

title: IPv6 Essentials
section: Where the interface identifier comes from
text:
Where the interface identifier comes from
A /64 leaves 64 bits for the interface identifier (IID). A Linux interface builds its link-local address from one of several modes, selected by net.ipv6.conf.<if>.addr_gen_mode:








addr_gen_mode
IID
Trade-off




0 (default)
Modified EUI-64 from the MAC (RFC 4291 Appendix A)
Predictable; leaks the MAC; changes when the NIC changes


1
None (no link-local generated)
For interfaces you address by hand


2
RFC 7217 stable-privacy from stable_secret
Stable per prefix and interface, does not leak the MAC


3
RFC 7217 with a random secret
Stable until reboot



Modified EUI-64 splits the 48-bit MAC, inserts ff:fe in the middle and flips the universal/local bit (0x02 in the first byte). That flip is why the MAC f6:84:... became the IID f484:... in the lab: 0xf6 XOR 0x02 = 0xf4.
RFC 7217 replaces that with a hash of the prefix, the interface, a network identifier and a secret. Same inputs, same IID; different network, different IID. The address is stable for your monitoring and your ACLs, but does not let an observer track the hardware across networks. RFC 8064 recommends it as the default for SLAAC.

title: IPv6 Essentials
section: Lab: link-locals, DAD, multicast and source selection
text:
Lab: link-locals, DAD, multicast and source selection
The lab needs no root. unshare -rnm maps you to root inside a new user namespace, which is enough to create network namespaces and veths there; a tmpfs on /run gives ip netns somewhere to keep its bind mounts.
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -rnm ./lab.sh   (unprivileged user + net + mount namespace; no sudo)
set -e
mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
ip netns add h1; ip netns add h2
ip link add v1 netns h1 type veth peer v2 netns h2
for n in h1 h2; do ip netns exec $n ip link set lo up; done
ip netns exec h1 ip link set v1 up; ip netns exec h2 ip link set v2 up
sleep 2.5
echo "== 1. default link-local (addr_gen_mode 0 = EUI-64 from the MAC)"
ip netns exec h1 cat /proc/sys/net/ipv6/conf/v1/addr_gen_mode
ip netns exec h1 ip -br link show v1
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 -br addr show dev v1

echo "== 2. stable-privacy (RFC 7217): same secret, new MAC, same IID"
ip netns exec h2 ip link add sp0 type veth peer sp1
ip netns exec h2 sh -c 'echo 2001:db8:dead:beef:1:2:3:4 > /proc/sys/net/ipv6/conf/sp0/stable_secret'
ip netns exec h2 cat /proc/sys/net/ipv6/conf/sp0/addr_gen_mode
ip netns exec h2 ip link set sp1 up; ip netns exec h2 ip link set sp0 up; sleep 2.5
ip netns exec h2 ip -br link show sp0; ip netns exec h2 ip -6 -br addr show dev sp0
ip netns exec h2 ip link set sp0 down
ip netns exec h2 ip link set sp0 address 02:00:00:00:00:99
ip netns exec h2 ip link set sp0 up; sleep 2.5
ip netns exec h2 ip -br link show sp0; ip netns exec h2 ip -6 -br addr show dev sp0

echo "== 3. global + ULA on h1, then h2 claims h1's address (DAD)"
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:10::10/64 dev v1
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 addr add fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::10/64 dev v1
ip netns exec h2 ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:10::20/64 dev v2
sleep 2.5   # let h1 finish DAD first
ip netns exec h2 ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:10::10/64 dev v2
sleep 2.5
ip netns exec h2 ip -6 addr show dev v2 scope global

echo "== 4. multicast groups h1 joined on v1 (solicited-node = ff02::1:ff + low 24 bits)"
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 maddr show dev v1

echo "== 5. routes and source selection (RFC 6724)"
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 route show dev v1
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 route get 2001:db8:10::20
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 route get fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::99
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:10::8000/64 dev v1
sleep 2.5
echo "-- with ::10 and ::8000 both preferred"
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 route get 2001:db8:10::20
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 addr change 2001:db8:10::8000/64 dev v1 preferred_lft 0
echo "-- after ip -6 addr change 2001:db8:10::8000/64 preferred_lft 0"
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 addr show dev v1 scope global
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 route get 2001:db8:10::20

echo "== 6. link-local destinations and the zone index"
LL2=$(ip netns exec h2 ip -6 -br addr show dev v2 | grep -o 'fe80::[0-9a-f:]*' | head -1)
ip netns exec h1 python3 "$(dirname "$0")/ll.py" "$LL2" v1
ip netns exec h1 ip link add v3 type veth peer v4
ip netns exec h1 ip link set v3 up; ip netns exec h1 ip link set v4 up; sleep 2.5
echo "-- after adding a second link (v3/v4) to h1"
ip netns exec h1 ip -6 route show | grep fe80
ip netns exec h1 python3 "$(dirname "$0")/ll.py" "$LL2" v3
# ll.py LLADDR IFNAME: UDP-connect to a link-local address with and without a zone.
import socket, sys
ll, ifname = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
for target in (ll, f"{ll}%{ifname}"):
    sa = socket.getaddrinfo(target, 9, socket.AF_INET6, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)[0][4]
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET6, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    try:
        s.connect(sa)
        print(f"connect {target:34} scope_id={sa[3]} -> local {s.getsockname()[0]}%{s.getsockname()[3]}")
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"connect {target:34} scope_id={sa[3]} -> {e}")

1–2. Link-local addresses: EUI-64 and stable-privacy
$ unshare -rnm ./lab.sh
== 1. default link-local (addr_gen_mode 0 = EUI-64 from the MAC)
0
v1@if2           UP             f6:84:3f:52:2c:c0 <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> 
v1@if2           UP             fe80::f484:3fff:fe52:2cc0/64 
== 2. stable-privacy (RFC 7217): same secret, new MAC, same IID
2
sp0@sp1          UP             9a:00:d1:40:08:f5 <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> 
sp0@sp1          UP             fe80::f021:70b0:7b7c:a362/64 
sp0@sp1          UP             02:00:00:00:00:99 <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> 
sp0@sp1          UP             fe80::f021:70b0:7b7c:a362/64 
h1 uses the default mode 0, so its link-local is the EUI-64 of its MAC. On h2 a second veth sp0 was given a stable_secret; writing the secret switched the interface to mode 2 by itself. The MAC was then changed to 02:00:00:00:00:99 and the link bounced. The IID did not change. It also matched across separate runs of the lab, with different random MACs each time, because the secret, prefix (fe80::/64) and interface name were the same. That is RFC 7217 working as designed.


3. Duplicate Address Detection
Before a unicast address is used, the host sends a Neighbor Solicitation for it from :: to the address’s solicited-node group (RFC 4862 5.4). If anyone answers, or sends the same probe, the address fails DAD.
== 3. global + ULA on h1, then h2 claims h1's address (DAD)
2: v2@if2: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000 link-netns h1
    inet6 2001:db8:10::10/64 scope global dadfailed tentative 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
    inet6 2001:db8:10::20/64 scope global 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
h1 added 2001:db8:10::10 first and finished DAD. Then h2 tried to claim the same address. h1 defended it, so on h2 the address is stuck as dadfailed tentative: present in the list, never used as a source. Nothing was logged to the terminal. If an interface “has the address” but nothing works, look for these two words before you look at routing.
Gotcha seen while building this lab. In an earlier run both hosts added ::10 within the same second, while both were still tentative. Each saw the other’s probe and both addresses failed. DAD protects against duplicates; it does not elect a winner. Re-add the address on the host that should own it.


4. Solicited-node multicast
ND does not broadcast. To resolve 2001:db8:10::10, a neighbour sends a Neighbor Solicitation to the solicited-node group ff02::1:ff00:0/104 plus the low 24 bits of the target. Every address joins its group:
== 4. multicast groups h1 joined on v1 (solicited-node = ff02::1:ff + low 24 bits)
2:  v1
    inet6 ff02::1:ff00:10 users 2
    inet6 ff02::1:ff52:2cc0
    inet6 ff02::1
    inet6 ff01::1
h1 has three unicast addresses (one link-local, the GUA 2001:db8:10::10 and the ULA fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::10) but only two solicited-node groups. The GUA and the ULA share the low 24 bits 00:0010, so they share ff02::1:ff00:10, shown with users 2. The script in the first lab computed the same collision. On a switch with MLD snooping, that group is what decides which port a Neighbor Solicitation reaches; it is also why addresses like ::1 and ::10 on many hosts of a big L2 domain make ND multicast less selective than it looks.
ff02::1 (all nodes) and ff01::1 (interface-local all nodes) are joined by every IPv6 interface. A router also joins ff02::2.


5. Routes and source address selection
== 5. routes and source selection (RFC 6724)
2001:db8:10::/64 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium
fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::/64 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium
fe80::/64 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium
2001:db8:10::20 from :: dev v1 proto kernel src 2001:db8:10::10 metric 256 pref medium
fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::99 from :: dev v1 proto kernel src fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::10 metric 256 pref medium
-- with ::10 and ::8000 both preferred
2001:db8:10::20 from :: dev v1 proto kernel src 2001:db8:10::8000 metric 256 pref medium
-- after ip -6 addr change 2001:db8:10::8000/64 preferred_lft 0
2: v1@if2: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000 link-netns h2
    inet6 2001:db8:10::8000/64 scope global deprecated 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft 0sec
    inet6 fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::10/64 scope global 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
    inet6 2001:db8:10::10/64 scope global 
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
2001:db8:10::20 from :: dev v1 proto kernel src 2001:db8:10::10 metric 256 pref medium
Read it top to bottom:

Every address with a prefix length produces a connected route (proto kernel), and every interface gets its own fe80::/64.
For 2001:db8:10::20 the kernel picked 2001:db8:10::10; for a ULA destination it picked the ULA. That is RFC 6724 rule 8, longest matching prefix, doing the obvious thing when the candidates are in different prefixes.
When a second address in the same /64 was added (::8000), Linux switched to the new one. Rule 8 compares common prefix bits, but Linux caps the comparison at the source address’s prefix length (/64), as RFC 6724 allows. Both candidates tie at 64 bits, and the kernel takes the most recently added. Do not expect “the numerically closest address wins” inside one subnet.
Setting preferred_lft 0 on ::8000 marked it deprecated, and new traffic moved back to ::10 (rule 3, avoid deprecated addresses). The address still exists and still answers. That is the standard way to drain an address before removing it.

When the default choice is wrong for a service, set it explicitly: ip -6 route add ... src <addr>, or bind the socket. Do not rely on address order in a config file.


6. Link-local destinations need a zone
== 6. link-local destinations and the zone index
connect fe80::a8e5:aeff:fecb:e819          scope_id=0 -> [Errno 22] Invalid argument
connect fe80::a8e5:aeff:fecb:e819%v1       scope_id=2 -> local fe80::f484:3fff:fe52:2cc0%2
-- after adding a second link (v3/v4) to h1
fe80::/64 dev v1 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium
fe80::/64 dev v4 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium
fe80::/64 dev v3 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium
connect fe80::a8e5:aeff:fecb:e819          scope_id=0 -> [Errno 22] Invalid argument
connect fe80::a8e5:aeff:fecb:e819%v3       scope_id=4 -> local fe80::6862:11ff:fe83:5422%4
A link-local address is only unique per link, so a destination like fe80::a8e5:... is ambiguous until you name the link. Without a zone (scope_id=0) Linux refuses the connect() with EINVAL, even when only one link exists. With %v1 the socket gets scope_id=2 (the ifindex) and a link-local source on that link.
The second half of the output is the trap. After adding v3/v4, there are three fe80::/64 routes. %v3 connects without complaint, but h2 is not on v3; the datagram would leave on the wrong wire. A zone is a choice, not a check. The same applies to ping fe80::1%eth0, to BGP unnumbered sessions, and to OSPFv3 next hops, which are always link-local.

title: IPv6 Essentials
text:
Neighbor Discovery in one table
ND (RFC 4861) uses ICMPv6 types 133–137 and replaces ARP, ICMP router discovery and redirects:









ICMPv6 type
Message
Sent to
Purpose




133
Router Solicitation
ff02::2
“Routers, speak now”


134
Router Advertisement
ff02::1 or unicast
Prefixes, default router, flags (see 06b)


135
Neighbor Solicitation
solicited-node group (resolve), unicast (probe), or from :: (DAD)
Who has X?


136
Neighbor Advertisement
requester or ff02::1
X is at MAC M


137
Redirect
host
Better first hop



The states in ip -6 neigh are the same as for ARP (REACHABLE, STALE, DELAY, PROBE, FAILED); ARP, ND and local resolution shows them in a lab.
ICMPv6 is not optional. Blocking ICMPv6 breaks ND (no neighbours), SLAAC (no RAs) and Path MTU Discovery (type 2, Packet Too Big; IPv6 routers never fragment). RFC 4890 lists what a firewall must let through. A rule set that copies an IPv4 “drop ICMP” policy will appear to work for a few minutes, until the neighbour cache expires.

title: IPv6 Essentials
text:
Planning a dual-stack LAN







Decision
Boring default




Prefix per link
/64 on every LAN, even with two hosts. SLAAC, privacy addresses and many tools assume it (RFC 7421).


Point-to-point router links
/64, or /127 per RFC 6164 (check that the platform does not reserve the all-zeros address as Subnet-Router anycast, which is what made /127 unsafe on old gear)


Loopbacks
/128


Site size
A /48 = 65,536 /64s; a /56 = 256. Plan on nibble boundaries (/48, /52, /56, /60) so prefixes stay readable


Lab space
2001:db8::/32 in documentation; a random ULA /48 (RFC 4193) when you need something that might one day meet another lab


Gateway
::1 of the /64, matching .1 in IPv4, or a link-local learned from RAs



Generate the ULA with the RFC 4193 algorithm, as the script does, instead of picking fd00::/48. Two labs that both chose fd00:: will collide the day you join them with a VPN. Two random /48s will not.
A worked plan for one LAN:
  site ULA      fd3c:5a1e:77b0::/48
  LAN 10        fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::/64   gw fd3c:5a1e:77b0:10::1   IPv4 10.10.10.0/24 gw .1
  LAN 20        fd3c:5a1e:77b0:20::/64   gw fd3c:5a1e:77b0:20::1   IPv4 10.10.20.0/24 gw .1
  router links  fd3c:5a1e:77b0:ff00::/56 carved into /64 (or /127) per link
  loopbacks     fd3c:5a1e:77b0:ffff::<n>/128
Matching the IPv4 third octet to the IPv6 subnet ID (10.10.10.0/24 ↔︎ :10::/64) costs nothing and saves a lookup table during incidents.

Static configuration on Linux
ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:10::10/64 dev eth1
ip link set eth1 up
ip -6 route add default via fe80::1 dev eth1      # a link-local next hop needs "dev"
ip -6 addr show dev eth1                          # wait for "tentative" to clear
ip -6 route get 2001:db8:99::1                    # which source and next hop will be used
A link-local default gateway is normal (RAs announce one) and survives renumbering; dev is mandatory with it for the reason shown in lab step 6.

title: IPv6 Essentials
text:
Dual-stack failure isolation







Symptom
Check first




IPv4 works, IPv6 times out to everything
Default route present? ip -6 route show default. RA received? ICMPv6 filtered?


IPv6 to on-link host fails
ip -6 neigh shows FAILED? Address dadfailed?


Some sites slow, then load
AAAA answer but broken v6 path; client Happy Eyeballs hiding it


Large transfers stall, small ones fine
PMTUD: Packet Too Big filtered; check tunnel MTU


Logs show an unexpected source
RFC 6724 choice; ip -6 route get, then set src or bind



Test both families explicitly when dual-stack is in scope: curl -4 / curl -6, or ping -4 / ping -6 where ping is installed.

title: IPv6 Essentials
text:
Gotchas

dadfailed is silent and permanent. The address stays in the list and is never used. Remove it, fix the duplicate, add it again.
Simultaneous claims lose twice. Two hosts racing DAD can both fail.
Link-local needs %zone or dev. Without it, Linux returns EINVAL; with the wrong one it sends on the wrong link without warning.
Source selection inside one /64 is not “closest address”. Linux ties at the prefix length and takes the newest address. Use src or preferred_lft 0 to steer it.
is_private / is_global are registry facts. 2001:db8::/32 is “private”; multicast can be “global”.
Blocking ICMPv6 breaks IPv6. Follow RFC 4890, not an IPv4 ICMP policy.
Not every subnet is a /64, but every LAN should be. SLAAC needs a 64-bit IID; longer LAN prefixes break it and privacy addresses.
fd00::/48 is not a random ULA. Generate one.

title: IPv6 Essentials
text:
Boring rule
One /64 per link, /128 loopbacks, a generated ULA or the documentation prefix in labs, ICMPv6 allowed per RFC 4890. When something fails, read ip -6 addr flags and ip -6 route get before you touch the routing protocol.

title: IPv6 Essentials
section: Address scope and choosing a next hop
text:
Address scope and choosing a next hop
IPv6 is not simply IPv4 with longer addresses. A link-local address (fe80::/10) is valid only on its link and is often used as a router’s next hop. The same link-local address can exist on different interfaces, so a host may need an interface or zone identifier such as fe80::1%eth1. A global unicast address can be routed beyond the link subject to policy. Unique local addresses are intended for local communication, but their existence does not itself prevent a route or filter from leaking them.
A host learns on-link prefixes, default routers, and other parameters from router advertisements according to their flags and lifetimes. SLAAC and DHCPv6 are separate mechanisms: receiving an address is not the same as receiving a default route, and DHCPv6 does not normally provide the default router. Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6, including Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement, instead of ARP. IPv6 uses multicast rather than IPv4-style broadcast.
The IPv6 base header has a Hop Limit, reduced by forwarding routers. Routers do not fragment IPv6 packets; they report Packet Too Big when an outgoing link cannot carry a packet. Do not block ICMPv6 indiscriminately: Neighbor Discovery and path-MTU feedback depend on it. Inspect ip -6 addr, ip -6 route, and ip -6 neigh together to distinguish address, route, and neighbor failures. See RFC 8200.
