title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
text:
Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
Neighbour tables map network-layer IP addresses to link-layer MAC addresses. While ARP, ND, and Local Resolution established basic entry states and resolution flows, maintaining these tables across dense container environments, multi-homed hosts, and high-throughput routing platforms introduces significant operational challenges. Garbage collection thresholds, state transition timers, and multi-interface ARP behavior directly govern traffic reachability and host stability under load.
When neighbour tables exceed host-wide capacity limits or multi-homed hosts incorrectly advertise addresses across physical interfaces, networks experience packet drops, silent connection timeouts, or ARP flux. Understanding the exact kernel mechanisms driving neighbour table state transitions and memory bounds is critical for diagnosing low-level networking anomalies.

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
text:
Learning goals

Differentiate host-wide global garbage collection limits from per-namespace sysctl interfaces.
Calculate and trace state transition timelines for neighbour entries through REACHABLE, STALE, DELAY, PROBE, and FAILED.
Analyze the impact of host-wide neighbour table exhaustion and evaluate kernel overflow behaviors.
Diagnose ARP flux phenomena on multi-homed Linux systems using arp_ignore and arp_announce.
Configure production sysctls for high-density container hosts and Direct Server Return (DSR) load balancers.

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
text:
Version note
The behaviors, source code references, and sysctls documented in this chapter reflect Linux kernel v6.12 (net/core/neighbour.c, net/ipv4/arp.c), iproute2 v6.15.0, and Python 3.13 standard library executing on unprivileged Linux 6.12 network namespaces.

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
section: Host-Wide Limits and Garbage Collection Mechanics
text:
Host-Wide Limits and Garbage Collection Mechanics
The Linux kernel manages IPv4 ARP (arp_cache) and IPv6 Neighbour Discovery (ndisc_cache) tables via internal struct neigh_table instances. To limit kernel memory allocation, each table enforces a three-tier threshold model governed by global sysctls.








Sysctl Parameter
Default Value
Kernel Behavior / Action




gc_thresh1
128
Minimum entry threshold. Below this count, periodic garbage collection is completely inactive.


gc_thresh2
512
Soft entry threshold. Forced garbage collection runs during allocation if entries exceed this limit and last flush was > 5 seconds ago.


gc_thresh3
1024
Hard maximum threshold. Non-permanent entries cannot exceed this limit. Allocations failing at this limit trigger kernel overflow logs.


gc_stale_time
60 s
Per device. An unreferenced entry not used for this long is removed by periodic GC (only when the table holds at least gc_thresh1 entries).



Periodic garbage collection scans entries based on age and state. When entry counts exceed gc_thresh2, the kernel performs forced garbage collection during allocation cycles, removing unreferenced entries that are in FAILED or NOARP states, or entries that have not been updated within 5 seconds. Up to (gc_entries - gc_thresh2) entries are removed in a single pass. Note that gc_interval has been unused in the Linux kernel since version 2.6.8.






Important



PERMANENT entries (ip neigh add ... nud permanent) and NTF_EXT_LEARNED entries (extern_learn, installed by a control plane such as an EVPN daemon or by switchdev drivers) are exempt from gc_entries accounting and are never reclaimed by the garbage collector. The entries figure that ip -s ntable prints counts them; the thresholds do not.



Namespace Scope of Neighbour Limits
A critical architectural constraint in Linux container networking is the scope of table thresholds. While interface parameters (like base_reachable_time_ms) are namespaced, the table memory structures and gc_thresh* configuration parameters are strictly host-wide.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Initial Network Namespace (Host Netns)                                        |
| /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/default/gc_thresh1/2/3  <-- System-wide limits       |
|                                                                               |
| +-------------------------+ +-------------------------+ +-------------------+ |
| | Container Netns 'a'     | | Container Netns 'b'     | | Host Interfaces   | |
| | (No gc_thresh sysctls)  | | (No gc_thresh sysctls)  | | eth0, lo          | |
| +-------------------------+ +-------------------------+ +-------------------+ |
|              \                           |                         /          |
|               \                          |                        /           |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | Shared Host-Wide Kernel Table: arp_cache (All entries sum up here)       |  |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
The default sysctl directory containing gc_thresh1, gc_thresh2, and gc_thresh3 is registered exclusively in the initial network namespace (arp_init calls neigh_sysctl_register(NULL, &arp_tbl.parms, NULL)). Executing a sysctl write or netlink ntable change from inside a child network namespace returns ENOENT (No such file or directory).
Consequently, entries generated inside hundreds of independent network namespaces (such as Kubernetes pods) all aggregate into the same single host-wide arp_cache or ndisc_cache table.

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
section: State Machine Timers and Resolution Flow
text:
State Machine Timers and Resolution Flow
Neighbour entries transition through defined states as network traffic flows and timers expire. Per-device timers control the lifetime and probe behavior of each entry.
 new traffic                 ARP reply / NA
 ----------> INCOMPLETE ----------------------> REACHABLE <-----------------+
              |  mcast_probes requests,            |                       |
              |  retrans_time_ms apart             | reachable_time        |
              v  (no answer)                       | (0.5x..1.5x base)     |
            FAILED <----------+                    v                       |
                              |                  STALE                     |
                              |                    | next packet sent      |
                              |                    v                       |
                              |                  DELAY ---- upper-layer ---+
                              |                    |        confirmation   |
                              |                    | delay_first_probe_time|
                              |                    v                       |
                              +-- ucast_probes --- PROBE ---- reply -------+
                                  unanswered
A FAILED entry that sees new traffic starts again from INCOMPLETE.








Parameter
Default Value
Functional Description




base_reachable_time_ms
30000 ms (30 s)
Base for how long an entry stays REACHABLE. The kernel draws the real reachable_time uniformly from 0.5x to 1.5x of it, per device parameter set, and redraws it at most every 300 s.


delay_first_probe_time
5 s
Delay interval spent in DELAY state before sending the first unicast probe in PROBE state.


retrans_time_ms
1000 ms (1 s)
Retransmission interval between probe attempts.


ucast_probes
3
Maximum unicast probes sent while in PROBE state before marking entry FAILED.


mcast_probes
3
Maximum broadcast/multicast requests sent for an INCOMPLETE entry before failing.


unres_qlen_bytes
SK_WMEM_DEFAULT
Maximum memory queue limit for packets waiting for resolution (supersedes legacy unres_qlen).



When a host attempts to reach a non-existent or unconfigured IP target, the kernel enters INCOMPLETE state and broadcasts mcast_probes requests (default 3) spaced retrans_time_ms apart. If no response arrives, the entry transitions to FAILED. A TCP connect() to such a target fails after about 3 seconds with EHOSTUNREACH (No route to host), long before any SYN retransmission timer would give up.
Modern Linux kernels (v5.16+) also support NTF_MANAGED entries (ip neigh add ... managed). Managed entries are automatically maintained in a resolved state by periodic probes driven by the kernel at intervals governed by interval_probe_time_ms (default 5000 ms).

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
section: ARP Flux and Multi-Homed Host Mechanics
text:
ARP Flux and Multi-Homed Host Mechanics
Linux implements a weak host model (RFC 1122). Network interfaces are not isolated boundaries; IP addresses belong to the host system rather than to individual physical interfaces. By default, a Linux host receiving an ARP request on interface A for an IP address configured on interface B will issue an ARP response out of interface A using interface A’s MAC address.
This is the root of ARP flux. When two of a host’s interfaces sit in the same broadcast domain, both answer the same request with their own MAC, and the requester keeps whichever reply arrived last, so the address flips between MACs. The same rule makes a real server in a Direct Server Return pool answer for the load balancer’s VIP. The lab below cannot share one segment between two interfaces (the build box kernel cannot create bridges), so it shows the underlying rule with two separate links.
                         ARP Request: "Who has 10.9.2.1?"
                         -------------------------------->
  +--------------------+                                   +--------------------+
  | Remote Host (p1)   |                                   | Multi-Homed (h)    |
  | 10.9.1.2/24        |                                   |                    |
  | dev: p1            | <-------------------------------- | dev: e1 (10.9.1.1) |
  +--------------------+   ARP Reply (Default behavior):   | dev: e2 (10.9.2.1) |
                           "10.9.2.1 is-at e1's MAC"       +--------------------+
                           (weak host model: any local address)
To control ARP resolution logic on multi-homed hosts, two primary per-interface sysctl flags are provided:

arp_ignore Modes

0 (Default): Reply to ARP requests for any local IP configured on any interface.
1: Reply only if the target IP address is explicitly configured on the incoming interface receiving the request.
2: Reply only if the target IP is configured on the incoming interface AND the sender’s IP address resides in the same subnet.
3: Do not reply for scope host addresses; reply only for scope global and link addresses.
8: Never reply to ARP requests.

The active arp_ignore setting is calculated as max(conf/all/arp_ignore, conf/<if>/arp_ignore).


arp_announce Modes

0 (Default): Put the triggering packet’s source address in the ARP request, even if it belongs to a different interface.
1: Avoid source addresses that are not in the target’s subnet if possible.
2 (Recommended for multi-homed and DSR hosts): Ignore the packet’s source address and use the best local address for the target, preferring a primary address on the outgoing interface in the target’s subnet.

In Direct Server Return (DSR) load balancing (such as LVS-DR), real server nodes configure the Virtual IP (VIP) on the loopback interface (lo). Setting arp_ignore=1 and arp_announce=2 on all and physical interfaces prevents real servers from responding to ARP requests for the VIP, ensuring only the active load balancer answers ARP queries for the service address.

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
text:
The lab
The following environment executes inside unprivileged network namespaces using Linux 6.12, iproute2 6.15.0, and standard Python 3.13 scripts without host modification.


timeline.py

# timeline.py NS DEV ADDR SECONDS: print every change of one neighbour entry, with time.
import subprocess, sys, time
ns, dev, addr, dur = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3], float(sys.argv[4])
t0, last = time.monotonic(), None
while (t := time.monotonic() - t0) < dur:
    out = subprocess.run(["ip", "-n", ns, "neigh", "show", addr, "dev", dev],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.split()
    state = out[-1] if out else "(none)"
    if state != last:
        print(f"   t={t:5.2f}s  {state}", flush=True); last = state
    time.sleep(0.05)



send.py

# send.py DST [SRC]: one UDP datagram to DST:9, optionally from a chosen source address.
import socket, sys
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
if len(sys.argv) > 2: s.bind((sys.argv[2], 0))
s.sendto(b"x", (sys.argv[1], 9))



connect.py

# connect.py DST: time a TCP connect to a neighbour that never answers ARP.
import socket, sys, time
t = time.monotonic()
try:
    socket.create_connection((sys.argv[1], 80), timeout=30)
except OSError as e:
    print(f"   connect() -> {e.strerror} after {time.monotonic() - t:.2f} s")



arp.py

# arp.py ask IFACE SENDER_IP TARGET_IP   -> broadcast one ARP request, print replies for 1 s
# arp.py watch IFACE SECONDS              -> print every ARP request seen on IFACE
import socket, struct, sys, time, ipaddress
ETH_P_ARP = 0x0806
def mac(b): return ":".join(f"{x:02x}" for x in b)
def ip(b): return str(ipaddress.IPv4Address(b))
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_PACKET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.htons(ETH_P_ARP))
s.bind((sys.argv[2], 0)); s.settimeout(0.2)
me = s.getsockname()[4]
if sys.argv[1] == "ask":
    sip, tip = (ipaddress.IPv4Address(a).packed for a in sys.argv[3:5])
    arp = struct.pack("!HHBBH6s4s6s4s", 1, 0x0800, 6, 4, 1, me, sip, bytes(6), tip)
    s.send(b"\xff" * 6 + me + struct.pack("!H", ETH_P_ARP) + arp)
    end, n = time.time() + 1, 0
    while time.time() < end:
        try: f = s.recv(64)
        except socket.timeout: continue
        if struct.unpack("!H", f[20:22])[0] == 2 and f[38:42] == sip:
            print(f"reply: {ip(f[28:32])} is-at {mac(f[22:28])}"); n += 1
    if n == 0: print("no reply")
else:
    end = time.time() + float(sys.argv[3])
    while time.time() < end:
        try: f = s.recv(64)
        except socket.timeout: continue
        if struct.unpack("!H", f[20:22])[0] == 1:
            print(f"request: who-has {ip(f[38:42])} tell {ip(f[28:32])}", flush=True)



lab.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -urnm sh lab.sh   (unprivileged: user, net and mount namespaces; no sudo)
H=$(pwd); mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
for ns in a b h p1 p2; do ip netns add $ns; ip -n $ns link set lo up; done
ip link add a0 netns a type veth peer name b0 netns b
ip -n a addr add 10.9.0.1/24 dev a0; ip -n b addr add 10.9.0.2/24 dev b0
ip -n a link set a0 up; ip -n b link set b0 up
entries() { ip -s ntable show name arp_cache | awk '/entries/{print $NF; exit}'; }

echo "== 1. who owns the limits?"
echo "   /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/ inside netns a: $(ip netns exec a ls /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh | tr '\n' ' ')"
ip -s ntable show name arp_cache | awk '/thresh1/{print "   arp_cache:", $0; exit}'
ip netns exec a ip ntable change name arp_cache thresh3 4096 2>&1 | sed 's/^/   ntable change from a netns: /'
B=$(entries)
for i in $(seq 1 300); do echo "neigh add 10.9.$((100 + i / 250)).$((i % 250 + 1)) lladdr 02:00:00:00:00:01 nud stale dev a0"; done | ip -n a -batch -
echo "   host-wide arp_cache entries: before $B, after 300 adds inside netns a: $(entries)"
ip -n a neigh flush dev a0 nud stale; ip -n a neigh flush dev a0 >/dev/null 2>&1
echo "   after flush: $(entries)"

echo "== 2. one entry's life (a0: base_reachable_time_ms=4000, delay_first_probe_time=2)"
ip netns exec a sh -c 'echo 4000 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/a0/base_reachable_time_ms; echo 2 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/a0/delay_first_probe_time'
python3 $H/timeline.py a a0 10.9.0.2 24 & TL=$!
sleep 0.3; echo "   t~0   send"; ip netns exec a python3 $H/send.py 10.9.0.2
sleep 9;   echo "   t~9   send again"; ip netns exec a python3 $H/send.py 10.9.0.2
sleep 7;   echo "   t~16  peer loses its address, send again"
ip -n b addr del 10.9.0.2/24 dev b0; ip netns exec a python3 $H/send.py 10.9.0.2
wait $TL
ip -n a -s neigh show dev a0 | sed 's/^/   final: /'

echo "== 3. a neighbour that never answers"
ip netns exec b python3 $H/arp.py watch b0 6 > /tmp/arpseen & W=$!; sleep 0.3
ip netns exec a python3 $H/connect.py 10.9.0.77
wait $W; echo "   ARP requests seen on the wire: $(wc -l < /tmp/arpseen) ($(sort -u /tmp/arpseen | head -1))"
ip -n a neigh show 10.9.0.77 | sed 's/^/   entry: /'

echo "== 4. ARP flux: host h answers for addresses that live on other interfaces"
ip link add e1 netns h type veth peer name p1 netns p1
ip link add e2 netns h type veth peer name p2 netns p2
ip -n h addr add 10.9.1.1/24 dev e1; ip -n h addr add 10.9.2.1/24 dev e2
ip -n h addr add 10.9.1.100/32 dev lo                     # a load-balancer VIP (LVS-DR style)
ip -n p1 addr add 10.9.1.2/24 dev p1; ip -n p2 addr add 10.9.2.2/24 dev p2
for l in "h e1" "h e2" "p1 p1" "p2 p2"; do set -- $l; ip -n $1 link set $2 up; done
echo "   h: e1 MAC $(ip -n h -br link show e1 | awk '{print $3}'), e2 MAC $(ip -n h -br link show e2 | awk '{print $3}')"
for ign in 0 1; do
    ip netns exec h sh -c "echo $ign > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/arp_ignore"
    for t in 10.9.1.1 10.9.2.1 10.9.1.100; do
        printf '   arp_ignore=%s  p1 asks who-has %-10s -> %s\n' $ign $t "$(ip netns exec p1 python3 $H/arp.py ask p1 10.9.1.2 $t)"
    done
done
echo "== 5. arp_announce: which source IP goes into h's ARP request on e1"
for ann in 0 2; do
    ip netns exec h sh -c "echo $ann > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/arp_announce"; ip -n h neigh flush dev e1
    ip netns exec p1 python3 $H/arp.py watch p1 1.5 > /tmp/ann & W=$!; sleep 0.3
    ip netns exec h python3 $H/send.py 10.9.1.2 10.9.2.1; wait $W
    printf '   arp_announce=%s  (packet src 10.9.2.1)  p1 sees: %s\n' $ann "$(head -1 /tmp/ann)"
done

== 1. who owns the limits?
   /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/ inside netns a: a0 lo 
   arp_cache:     thresh1 128 thresh2 512 thresh3 1024 gc_int 30000 
   ntable change from a netns: RTNETLINK answers: No such file or directory
   host-wide arp_cache entries: before 3, after 300 adds inside netns a: 303
   after flush: 3
== 2. one entry's life (a0: base_reachable_time_ms=4000, delay_first_probe_time=2)
   t= 0.00s  (none)
   t~0   send
   t= 0.31s  REACHABLE
   t= 3.29s  STALE
   t~9   send again
   t= 9.35s  DELAY
   t=11.38s  REACHABLE
   t=14.28s  STALE
   t~16  peer loses its address, send again
   t=16.35s  DELAY
   t=18.37s  PROBE
   t=21.43s  FAILED
   final: 10.9.0.2  used 7/12/2probes 3 FAILED 
== 3. a neighbour that never answers
   connect() -> No route to host after 3.06 s
   ARP requests seen on the wire: 3 (request: who-has 10.9.0.77 tell 10.9.0.1)
   entry: 10.9.0.77 dev a0 FAILED 
== 4. ARP flux: host h answers for addresses that live on other interfaces
   h: e1 MAC 52:24:4a:f3:0a:97, e2 MAC 0a:91:42:da:96:c2
   arp_ignore=0  p1 asks who-has 10.9.1.1   -> reply: 10.9.1.1 is-at 52:24:4a:f3:0a:97
   arp_ignore=0  p1 asks who-has 10.9.2.1   -> reply: 10.9.2.1 is-at 52:24:4a:f3:0a:97
   arp_ignore=0  p1 asks who-has 10.9.1.100 -> reply: 10.9.1.100 is-at 52:24:4a:f3:0a:97
   arp_ignore=1  p1 asks who-has 10.9.1.1   -> reply: 10.9.1.1 is-at 52:24:4a:f3:0a:97
   arp_ignore=1  p1 asks who-has 10.9.2.1   -> no reply
   arp_ignore=1  p1 asks who-has 10.9.1.100 -> no reply
== 5. arp_announce: which source IP goes into h's ARP request on e1
   arp_announce=0  (packet src 10.9.2.1)  p1 sees: request: who-has 10.9.1.2 tell 10.9.2.1
   arp_announce=2  (packet src 10.9.2.1)  p1 sees: request: who-has 10.9.1.2 tell 10.9.1.1

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
text:
Reading the output

Section 1: Table Limits and Scope
The output confirms that inside child network namespace a, /proc/sys/net/ipv4/neigh/ contains only interface directories (a0, lo), with no global default directory present. Attempting to adjust thresh3 from inside namespace a fails with RTNETLINK answers: No such file or directory (kernel returns ENOENT). When 300 neighbour entries are added in namespace a, the global host-wide arp_cache counter increases from 3 to 303, demonstrating that namespace entries directly consume host-wide table budget.






Note



The lab deliberately does not fill the table to gc_thresh3. Because the table is host-wide, doing that from a namespace would force garbage collection and refuse new neighbours for the build box itself. It stays below gc_thresh2 (3 + 300 entries), and the overflow path is described from neigh_alloc() in the v6.12 source instead.




Section 2: Neighbour State Transitions
With base_reachable_time_ms=4000 (so reachable_time is drawn from 2 to 6 s; this run drew about 3 s) and delay_first_probe_time=2. The poller samples every 50 ms, so states shorter than that are not printed: 1. t=0.31s: Initial UDP datagram triggers resolution; receiving ARP reply sets state to REACHABLE. 2. t=3.29s: Timer expires (~3s), transitioning entry to STALE. 3. t=9.35s: The second datagram is sent while the entry is STALE. The packet goes out at once to the cached MAC and the entry moves to DELAY, waiting 2 s for an upper-layer confirmation (TCP progress would provide one; this UDP flow provides none). 4. t=11.38s: DELAY expired, the entry went to PROBE, sent one unicast ARP request and got a reply within milliseconds, so the poller only sees the result: REACHABLE. 5. t=14.28s: Reachable timer expires again, returning entry to STALE. 6. t=16.35s: Datagram sent after peer removes IP address. Entry enters DELAY. 7. t=18.37s: After 2s in DELAY, kernel transitions to PROBE and transmits 3 unicast probes (ucast_probes). 8. t=21.43s: Probes unacknowledged; entry transitions to FAILED.


Section 3: Non-Responding Target Resolution
Executing connect() against 10.9.0.77 starts broadcast ARP resolution (mcast_probes=3, one request per retrans_time_ms). Exactly 3 ARP requests are issued on the wire before the entry transitions to FAILED. The socket call terminates with connect() -> No route to host after 3.06 s (EHOSTUNREACH).


Section 4: ARP Flux Isolation
With arp_ignore=0, host h responds out of interface e1 for requests targeting 10.9.1.1 (on e1), 10.9.2.1 (on e2), and 10.9.1.100 (on lo), reporting e1’s MAC address (52:24:4a:f3:0a:97) for all three. Setting arp_ignore=1 forces host h to reply exclusively for 10.9.1.1 (configured directly on e1), suppressing responses for 10.9.2.1 and loopback VIP 10.9.1.100.


Section 5: ARP Request Source IP Selection
Host h sends a UDP datagram to 10.9.1.2 bound to source address 10.9.2.1. With arp_announce=0, the outgoing ARP request uses 10.9.2.1 as the ARP inner sender IP. With arp_announce=2, the kernel overrides the socket source IP and uses 10.9.1.1 (matching e1’s subnet), preventing remote hosts from updating their tables with invalid IP-to-interface bindings.

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
text:
Production Tuning and Configuration
For large-scale Kubernetes nodes, cloud routers, or flat L2 environments with thousands of endpoints, the defaults (gc_thresh3=1024 per table) are easy to hit: new neighbours stop being created and traffic to them is dropped, while existing entries keep working, which makes the symptom look random. Size the thresholds from the number of neighbours you expect across every namespace on the host; the values below are an example, not a recommendation for every box.

Tuning System-Wide Table Limits (Not run here)
Apply these settings in the root network namespace (/etc/sysctl.d/99-neighbour.conf):
# (not run here)
# Production scaling for Kubernetes worker nodes / Large L2 domains
net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh1 = 4096
net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh2 = 8192
net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh3 = 16384

net.ipv6.neigh.default.gc_thresh1 = 4096
net.ipv6.neigh.default.gc_thresh2 = 8192
net.ipv6.neigh.default.gc_thresh3 = 16384


Tuning DSR Load Balancer Real Servers (Not run here)
To suppress ARP flux on DSR nodes carrying VIPs on loopback adapters:
# (not run here)
# Prevent ARP flux across all interfaces
net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_ignore = 1
net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_announce = 2
net.ipv4.conf.default.arp_ignore = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.arp_announce = 2

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
text:
Checking a real host
On a running host (in the initial namespace for the kernel log):
# Display table entry limits and current entry count
ip -s ntable show name arp_cache

# Monitor kernel table statistics and overflow counters
cat /proc/net/stat/arp_cache

# Inspect kernel logs for table allocation failures
dmesg -T | grep "neighbor table overflow"

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
text:
Gotchas

Host-wide container impact: Neighbours created in any namespace count toward one host-wide gc_thresh3. A noisy pod that scans its subnet can stop other pods on the node from resolving new neighbours.
Asymmetric sysctl paths: Interface parameters like base_reachable_time_ms are per-namespace, whereas global gc_thresh* parameters only exist in the host init namespace.
Silent drops at thresh3: When gc_thresh3 is reached and forced GC frees no entries, the kernel logs ndisc_cache: neighbor table overflow! or arp_cache: neighbor table overflow!, increments table_fulls, and frees the packet with drop reason NEIGH_CREATEFAIL (ip_finish_output2() in net/ipv4/ip_output.c). The message is rate limited and only appears in the kernel log of the host, not of the container.
Reachable time randomisation: Setting base_reachable_time_ms to 30000 ms yields actual state durations anywhere from 15000 ms to 45000 ms due to mandatory kernel randomisation.
all versus the interface: Setting net.ipv4.conf.eth0.arp_ignore=1 while net.ipv4.conf.all.arp_ignore=0 results in effective value 0 because Linux uses the max() of all and <if>.
On-link failures are fast, not slow: with default probes a failed resolution surfaces as EHOSTUNREACH after about 3 s, not after the tcp_syn_retries timeout. If an application reports a 2-minute connect timeout to an on-link peer, ARP did resolve and something else is dropping the SYN.
PERMANENT entries bypass GC: entries added with ip neigh add ... nud permanent do not consume gc_thresh slots, but they silently break connectivity when the peer’s MAC changes (NIC swap, VM migration, VRRP failover).
Aggressive timers cost broadcasts: a low base_reachable_time_ms means more unicast probes, and a low gc_stale_time or low thresholds mean entries are deleted and re-resolved with broadcasts. On a big L2 segment that load lands on every host.
IPv6 is a separate table: ndisc_cache has its own net.ipv6.neigh.default.gc_thresh*. Raising only the IPv4 values leaves IPv6 at 1024, which is how hosts end up logging ndisc_cache: neighbor table overflow!.
arp_ignore=1 and /32 addresses on loopback: it is exactly what DSR needs, but it also stops the host from answering for any address it moved to lo on purpose (for example an anycast service address announced by BGP). Decide per address.

title: Linux Neighbour Tables in Production: Timers, Table Limits and ARP Flux
text:
Exercises

With default sysctls, how many dynamic IPv4 neighbour entries can a host hold in total across 50 network namespaces before forced garbage collection can start, and before new entries can be refused? Explain why the number of namespaces does not change the answer.
Modify lab.sh to adjust retrans_time_ms and ucast_probes on interface a0. Trace the altered timeline when communicating with a non-responsive destination.
Construct a multi-interface topology and demonstrate how enabling arp_filter=1 alters packet delivery compared to arp_ignore=1 when strict policy routing is enabled.
On a disposable VM (never a shared host), lower gc_thresh2/gc_thresh3 in the initial namespace to 64/128, generate traffic to 500 unused on-link addresses, and watch allocs, forced_gc_runs and table_fulls in ip -s ntable show name arp_cache. Find the overflow message in the kernel log.
Configure an IPv6 environment using ndisc_cache parameters and compare ndisc_cache garbage collection behavior against IPv4 arp_cache.

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
Duplicate IPv4 addresses are among the most frustrating operational anomalies in modern networking. When two hosts on the same Layer 2 segment share an IP address, neither host functions reliably. Traffic destined for the shared IP address is split across both hosts based on which machine last updated the surrounding switches and peer ARP caches. Because Layer 2 forwarding tables (MAC address tables) and Layer 3 neighbour tables (ARP caches) continuously flap between two distinct MAC addresses, network performance degrades into intermittent packet loss, asymmetric connection resets, and unexplained TCP timeouts.
From an operator’s perspective, duplicate IP address issues often manifest as “ghost” failures. A host may ping its default gateway successfully one second, only to drop all traffic the next when a peer sends an unsolicited ARP broadcast. Diagnostic tools like ping or traceroute become misleading because responses originate from different physical endpoints depending on exact packet timing. In automated provisioning environments, container networks, or statically addressed server subnets, human typo errors or misconfigured IPAM systems can easily introduce duplicate addresses that slip past standard OS checks.
Unlike IPv6, where duplicate address detection (DAD) is a mandatory, kernel-enforced phase of link initialization, IPv4 historically treated IP address assignment as a silent operation. The Linux kernel does not natively perform IPv4 conflict detection when an address is added to an interface. Unless an explicit user-space daemon or utility performs conflict detection prior to binding, the kernel immediately assigns the IP address, leaving the network vulnerable to instant address collisions. Understanding how IPv4 Address Conflict Detection (ACD) works—and how operating systems handle link-local address generation—is essential for building resilient network infrastructure.
As established in earlier chapters covering ARP fundamentals, neighbour tables, and neighbour state machines, IPv4 nodes rely on Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) to map 32-bit logical IPv4 addresses to 48-bit physical MAC addresses. Nodes maintain a local ARP cache mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses, transitioning entries through states such as REACHABLE, STALE, and FAILED. While gratuitous ARP (GARP) allows hosts to announce their presence or announce hardware updates, it also acts as a mechanism through which duplicate IP collisions propagate across a broadcast domain.

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
Learning goals

Explain the failure modes, frame sequences, and intermittent symptoms caused by duplicate IPv4 addresses on a shared Layer 2 segment.
Detail the Linux kernel net/ipv4/arp.c handling of incoming ARP replies, specifically net.ipv4.neigh.IFACE.locktime, arp_accept, and kernel responses to zero-source ARP probes.
Contrast IPv4 kernel behaviour during address assignment with mandatory IPv6 Duplicate Address Detection (RFC 4862).
Describe the packet structures, timer constants, state machines, and defence strategies of RFC 5227 Address Conflict Detection (ACD).
Analyze RFC 3927 IPv4 Link-Local autoconfiguration (169.254.0.0/16), including pseudo-random address selection, routing restrictions, and distinctions from fixed cloud metadata services.
Compare how production network management tools (NetworkManager, systemd-networkd, dhcpcd, arping, and DHCP server ping-checks) handle IPv4 ACD.
Diagnose and troubleshoot duplicate IP conditions using Linux kernel diagnostic tools, switch logs, and packet captures.

text:
Version note
The analysis and code examples in this chapter are based on Linux kernel version 6.12.94, iproute2 version 6.15.0, and Python version 3.13.5 running inside unprivileged user, network, and mount namespaces. Advanced networking utilities including NetworkManager, systemd-networkd, dhcpcd, and arping are referenced for production context, but are not installed in the isolated lab environment; their commands are provided for reference only.

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
section: IPv4 Address Collisions and Kernel ARP Internals
text:
IPv4 Address Collisions and Kernel ARP Internals
When two hosts on a single broadcast domain share an IPv4 address, Layer 2 switches and neighboring hosts experience constant cache corruption. Switches continuously update their MAC address tables as both hosts transmit frames, causing unicast traffic to switch ports back and forth. Simultaneously, neighboring hosts update their ARP caches whenever either host transmits an ARP request or reply.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        Layer 2 Switch                           |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
     | Port 1                                 | Port 2
     |                                        |
+----+--------------------+              +----+--------------------+
| Host A                  |              | Host B                  |
| IP: 10.0.0.5            |              | IP: 10.0.0.5            |
| MAC: 02:00:00:00:00:01  |              | MAC: 02:00:00:00:00:02  |
+-------------------------+              +-------------------------+
When a third host attempts to establish a TCP connection to 10.0.0.5, it emits an ARP request. Whichever host (A or B) processes the request and transmits an ARP reply last—or first, depending on host ARP locktime settings—wins the ARP cache entry on the prober. SYN packets flow to Host A, while subsequent ACK packets might end up at Host B if Host B transmitted a gratuitous ARP in the interim, causing immediate TCP resets (RST).

Silent IPv4 Binding vs IPv6 DAD
When a user executes ip addr add 10.0.0.5/24 dev eth0 on Linux, the kernel’s IPv4 stack adds the interface address immediately. The system calls return success (0), no frames are emitted by default to check for collisions, and the address scope becomes global.
In contrast, IPv6 implements mandatory DAD at the kernel layer per RFC 4862. When an IPv6 address is added (ip addr add fd00::5/64 dev eth0), the kernel sets the address state to tentative and emits a Neighbor Solicitation (NS) for its own address to the solicited-node multicast group. If another host replies with a Neighbor Advertisement (NA), the kernel marks the address as dadfailed, prevents any sockets from binding to it, and logs a kernel warning.


Linux Kernel ARP Processing (net/ipv4/arp.c)
The Linux IPv4 ARP implementation contains specific tuning knobs and hardcoded logical paths that determine how duplicate IP responses are handled.

ARP Cache Locktime (net.ipv4.neigh.IFACE.locktime)
The sysctl net.ipv4.neigh.default.locktime (and interface-specific variants under net.ipv4.neigh.IFACE.locktime) defaults to 100 USER_HZ ticks (1.0 second). The locktime parameter prevents ARP cache thrashing on segments with multiple responding bridges or redundant paths.
When the Linux kernel receives an ARP reply that would update an existing neighbour table entry, it checks the timestamp of the last update. If an update occurred less than locktime ago (e.g., within 1 second), the kernel discards the new mapping unless the incoming frame is a Gratuitous ARP. Thus, when two hosts respond simultaneously to an ARP request, the first reply to arrive at a listening node is committed to the neighbour table, and subsequent replies within the 1-second window are ignored.


Gratuitous ARP and Cache Updates
A Gratuitous ARP (GARP) is an ARP packet where the Sender IP Address (SPA) equals the Target IP Address (TPA). GARPs bypass the locktime restriction in net/ipv4/arp.c. If a neighbour entry already exists for that IP address, receiving a GARP forces the kernel to update the link-layer address immediately and transition the entry state to STALE.
The sysctl net.ipv4.conf.IFACE.arp_accept controls how the kernel handles GARPs for IP addresses that are not currently in its neighbour table: - 0 (default): no new neighbour entry is created from a gratuitous ARP for an address that is not already in the table. - 1: a new entry is created. - 2 (since Linux 6.0): a new entry is created only if the address is in one of the interface’s subnets.


Kernel Probe Replies for Local Addresses
When a host running RFC 5227 Address Conflict Detection probes an IP address, it sends an ARP Request with a Sender IP Address of 0.0.0.0. The Linux kernel (net/ipv4/arp.c function arp_process()) contains an explicit exception for these frames:
/* Special case: IPv4 duplicate address detection packet (RFC2131) */
If the kernel sees an ARP Request where SPA == 0.0.0.0 and TPA matches an IP address configured on the local interface, the kernel treats it as an ACD probe. It sends an ARP Reply unicast to the prober’s MAC address, with its own address as the sender IP and 0.0.0.0 as the target IP, and does not create a neighbour entry. Scenario 3 of the lab shows such a reply arriving. Note what this means: the kernel answers other hosts’ probes, but it never sends probes for its own addresses.

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
Address Conflict Detection (RFC 5227)
RFC 5227 standardizes a mechanism for IPv4 hosts to detect address conflicts before assigning an IP address (passive probing), and to detect and resolve conflicts after binding (active defence).

Frame Definitions: Probes vs Announcements
RFC 5227 defines two distinct ARP frame profiles:

ARP Probe: Used to check if an IP address is in use.

Hardware Type: 1 (Ethernet)
Protocol Type: 0x0800 (IPv4)
Opcode: 1 (ARP Request)
Sender Hardware Address (SHA): MAC address of probing interface
Sender Protocol Address (SPA): 0.0.0.0 (MUST be zero to avoid poisoning peer ARP caches)
Target Hardware Address (THA): 00:00:00:00:00:00 (Zeroes)
Target Protocol Address (TPA): Candidate IPv4 Address

ARP Announcement: Used to claim an IP address and update peer caches after probing succeeds.

Hardware Type: 1 (Ethernet)
Protocol Type: 0x0800 (IPv4)
Opcode: 1 (ARP Request)
Sender Hardware Address (SHA): MAC address of claiming interface
Sender Protocol Address (SPA): Candidate IPv4 Address
Target Hardware Address (THA): 00:00:00:00:00:00 (Zeroes)
Target Protocol Address (TPA): Candidate IPv4 Address













Packet Type
Opcode
Sender MAC (SHA)
Sender IP (SPA)
Target MAC (THA)
Target IP (TPA)




ACD Probe
1 (Request)
Own MAC
0.0.0.0
00:00:00:00:00:00
Candidate IP


ACD Announcement
1 (Request)

Candidate IP

RFC 5227 State Machine and Timers
RFC 5227 specifies exact parameters and intervals to ensure reliable detection while avoiding broadcast storms.








Timer Constant
Value
Description




PROBE_WAIT
1 second
Initial random delay before sending first probe (0 to 1 s)


PROBE_NUM
3
Number of probe packets sent during probe phase


PROBE_MIN
1 second
Minimum delay between successive probes


PROBE_MAX
2 seconds
Maximum delay between successive probes


ANNOUNCE_WAIT
2 seconds
Delay after last probe before configuration and first announcement


ANNOUNCE_NUM
2
Number of announcement packets sent


ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL
2 seconds

MAX_CONFLICTS
10
Max conflicts allowed before rate limiting


RATE_LIMIT_INTERVAL
60 seconds

DEFEND_INTERVAL
10 seconds
Minimum window during which a second conflict forces address relinquishment



Timeline of a successful RFC 5227 ACD sequence (lab scenario 4)

   t=0.0s          t=0.72s       t=1.92s       t=3.17s         t=5.18s                 t=7.18s
     |                |             |             |               |                       |
Start ACD       Probe 1       Probe 2       Probe 3       IP Configured &          Announce 2
(PROBE_WAIT)   (spa 0.0.0.0) (spa 0.0.0.0) (spa 0.0.0.0)  Announce 1 (spa=tpa)     (spa=tpa)
     |<---0.72s------>|<---1.20s--->|<---1.25s--->|<----2.00s---->|                       |
                      |<------- Probe Phase ----->| ANNOUNCE_WAIT |<--- ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL>|
The time from starting ACD to having a usable address is a random delay of 0–1 s, then two gaps of 1–2 s between the three probes, then ANNOUNCE_WAIT:
\[0 + 2 \times 1 + 2 = 4\text{ s (minimum)} \qquad 1 + 2 \times 2 + 2 = 7\text{ s (maximum)}\]
The lab run took 5.18 s. Every interface that comes up with RFC 5227 enabled therefore waits 4–7 seconds for its IPv4 address; this is why some tools shorten or disable it.


Conflict Detection Rules and Defence Options
During the Probing Phase, a conflict occurs if the host observes: 1. Any ARP packet (Request or Reply) with SPA == Candidate IP. 2. Any ARP Probe (SPA == 0.0.0.0 and TPA == Candidate IP) where SHA != Own MAC (simultaneous probing).
If a conflict occurs during probing, the host MUST NOT configure the candidate address.
During the Active/Defending Phase (after address is bound), if a host receives an ARP packet where SPA == Configured IP and SHA != Own MAC, a conflict has occurred. RFC 5227 defines three defence strategies:

Option (a) Passive / Give up immediately: The host unbinds the IP address at the first sign of a conflict.
Option (b) Defend once: if it has not seen another conflict in the last DEFEND_INTERVAL, the host broadcasts one ARP Announcement to defend the address, logs the event and keeps the address. If a second conflict occurs within DEFEND_INTERVAL (10 seconds), the host MUST immediately unbind the address and cease using it.
Option (c) Defend indefinitely: the host keeps the address whatever happens, still sending at most one defending announcement per DEFEND_INTERVAL. RFC 5227 intends this for devices that must keep a fixed address, such as a printer or router. Two such hosts on one segment never resolve the conflict.

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
IPv4 Link-Local Addressing (RFC 3927)
RFC 3927 defines the autoconfiguration of IPv4 Link-Local addresses in the 169.254.0.0/16 prefix. This allows ad-hoc networking between devices connected to the same switch without requiring a DHCP server or manual configuration.

Address Space and Selection
The IPv4 Link-Local prefix spans 169.254.0.0/16 (169.254.0.1 to 169.254.255.254). However, RFC 3927 reserves the first and last /24 subnets: - 169.254.0.0/24 (Reserved for future expansion) - 169.254.255.0/24 (Reserved for future expansion)
The usable host address range is 169.254.1.0 through 169.254.254.255.
Hosts pick an address within this range using a pseudo-random number generator. To ensure address stability across reboots, RFC 3927 recommends seeding the generator with the interface’s MAC address. Once an address is selected, the host MUST perform RFC 5227 ACD before binding it. If ACD reports a conflict, the host selects another pseudo-random address and repeats the process.


Operational Scope and Cloud Metadata
Link-Local addresses are explicitly non-routable. Routers MUST NOT forward packets with 169.254.0.0/16 source or destination addresses across network boundaries.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| WARNING: Cloud Metadata vs RFC 3927 Autoconfiguration                |
|                                                                       |
| Public cloud platforms (AWS, GCP, Azure, OpenStack) host an HTTP      |
| metadata server at fixed address 169.254.169.254.                     |
|                                                                       |
| This address falls within the 169.254.0.0/16 range, but it is NOT     |
| an RFC 3927 autoconfigured address. It is a statically routed, fixed  |
| service endpoint provided by hypervisors via host-local interception. |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
Production Implementation Landscape
Because the Linux kernel IPv4 stack does not implement RFC 5227 internally, user-space daemons and network management tools handle ACD in production environments.

NetworkManager
NetworkManager handles IPv4 ACD via the ipv4.dad-timeout setting (configured in milliseconds): - 0: Disables IPv4 ACD. - -1: Uses global default (or 200 ms if unset). - >0: Sets maximum time NetworkManager waits for DAD to complete.
The actual probing time is randomised between half and the full value of ipv4.dad-timeout. If a conflict is found, NetworkManager does not configure the address, and activation of the connection fails.
# (not run here)
# Set IPv4 DAD timeout to 3000 ms on connection eth0
nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv4.dad-timeout 3000
nmcli connection up eth0


systemd-networkd
systemd-networkd configures DAD via the [Address] section setting DuplicateAddressDetection=: - Values: ipv4, ipv6, both, none. - Default: ipv4 is enabled only for 169.254.0.0/16 link-local addresses. IPv6 DAD is enabled by default for all IPv6 addresses. none is the default for static global IPv4 addresses.
# (not run here)
# Example /etc/systemd/network/10-eth0.network
[Match]
Name=eth0

[Address]
Address=192.168.1.50/24
DuplicateAddressDetection=ipv4


dhcpcd
The dhcpcd daemon runs ARP probing by default on the addresses it configures (DHCP leases and IPv4LL) before adding them to the interface. To disable ACD in resource-constrained environments, use the noarp option in /etc/dhcpcd.conf.
# (not run here)
# Disable ARP probing in dhcpcd.conf
interface eth0
noarp


iputils arping
The arping utility from the iputils package can perform manual address conflict detection and broadcast announcements from shell scripts.
# (not run here)
# Perform RFC 5227 Duplicate Address Detection (-D)
# Exits with 0 if no conflict, 1 if address is in use
arping -D -I eth0 -c 3 10.0.0.5

# Send Unsolicited ARP Reply announcements (-A)
arping -A -I eth0 -c 2 10.0.0.5

# Send Unsolicited ARP Request announcements (-U)
arping -U -I eth0 -c 2 10.0.0.5


Kernel arp_notify
The kernel parameter net.ipv4.conf.IFACE.arp_notify triggers automatic gratuitous ARP announcements upon interface bring-up or link state changes: - 0 (default): do nothing. - 1: send gratuitous ARP requests when the device comes up or its hardware address changes. This announces addresses; it does not check for conflicts.
# (not run here)
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.eth0.arp_notify=1


DHCP Server Ping-Checks and Client Decline
Some DHCP servers check an address before offering it; ISC dhcpd’s ping-check is the best-known example. Before sending a DHCPOFFER, the server emits an ICMP Echo Request to the target IP address. If a reply is received, the server marks the IP address as abandoned and selects a different lease.
If a DHCP client receives an DHCPACK but subsequently fails RFC 5227 ACD probing, the client MUST transmit a DHCPDECLINE message to the DHCP server (RFC 2131 Sections 2.2 and 4.4.1), releasing the conflicting lease.

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
Operational Detection and Diagnostics
Operators encountering suspected IP address conflicts can use several diagnostic signals:

Switch Logs: Managed switches generate syslog alerts (on Cisco IOS, for example, %IP-4-DUPADDR: Duplicate address 10.0.0.5 on Vlan10, sourced by 0200.0000.0002 when someone else uses the switch’s own address).
MAC Flapping vs IP Conflict:

MAC Flapping: The same MAC address appears on multiple switch ports. Indicates a Layer 2 loop or VLAN misconfiguration.
IP Conflict: Two different MAC addresses appear associated with a single IP address on the network.

Kernel Monitoring (ip monitor neigh): Running ip monitor neigh captures live changes to the ARP cache, displaying rapid state transitions between MACs.
Daemon Monitoring (arpwatch): Tools like arpwatch log ethernet/IP address pairings to syslog and generate emails when an existing IP address changes its MAC association.

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
The lab
The lab environment uses rootless Linux namespaces (unshare -urnm) to simulate five hosts (h1 through h5) each connected by a veth pair (eth0 in the host, p-hN on the switch side) to a Linux bridge br0 inside a namespace named sw. Run it with unshare -urnm sh lab.sh; no root and no installs are needed.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    Bridge Namespace: "sw" (br0)                 |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
     | p-h1           | p-h2           | p-h3           | p-h4           | p-h5
     |                |                |                |                |
+----+----+      +----+----+      +----+----+      +----+----+      +----+----+
|   h1    |      |   h2    |      |   h3    |      |   h4    |      |   h5    |
| MAC:..01|      | MAC:..02|      | MAC:..03|      | MAC:..04|      | MAC:..05|
+---------+      +---------+      +---------+      +---------+      +---------+

Lab files
The script that creates the network topology, namespaces, and virtual interfaces. topo.sh:
#!/bin/sh
# One Ethernet segment: a Linux bridge in netns "sw" and five hosts h1..h5.
# Run inside: unshare -urnm sh ...   (no root, no installs)
set -e
mount -t tmpfs none /run 2>/dev/null || true
mkdir -p /run/netns
ip netns add sw; ip -n sw link set lo up
ip -n sw link add br0 type bridge; ip -n sw link set br0 up

A Python script implementing low-level ARP frame injection and sniffing using AF_PACKET raw sockets. arp.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Small ARP helpers over AF_PACKET (needs CAP_NET_RAW in the netns only).

arp.py garp IFACE IP          send one gratuitous ARP request (sender = target = IP)
arp.py sniff IFACE SECONDS [IP]  print ARP frames seen on IFACE (only those naming IP, if given)
"""
import socket, struct, sys, time

ETH_P_ARP = 0x0806
OPS = {1: "request", 2: "reply"}

def mac(b): return ":".join(f"{x:02x}" for x in b)

def frame(src_mac, dst_mac, op, sha, spa, tha, tpa):
    eth = dst_mac + src_mac + struct.pack("!H", ETH_P_ARP)
    arp = struct.pack("!HHBBH", 1, 0x0800, 6, 4, op) + sha + socket.inet_aton(spa) + tha + socket.inet_aton(tpa)
    return eth + arp

def parse(f):
    if len(f) < 42 or struct.unpack("!H", f[12:14])[0] != ETH_P_ARP:
        return None
    op = struct.unpack("!H", f[20:22])[0]
    return {"op": op, "sha": f[22:28], "spa": socket.inet_ntoa(f[28:32]),
            "tha": f[32:38], "tpa": socket.inet_ntoa(f[38:42])}

def open_sock(iface):
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_PACKET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.htons(ETH_P_ARP))
    s.bind((iface, 0))
    return s

def describe(p):
    kind = OPS.get(p["op"], p["op"])
    if p["op"] == 1 and p["spa"] == "0.0.0.0":
        kind = "PROBE (RFC 5227)"
    elif p["op"] == 1 and p["spa"] == p["tpa"]:
        kind = "ANNOUNCE/gratuitous"
    return f"{kind:20s} sha={mac(p['sha'])} spa={p['spa']:<10s} tpa={p['tpa']}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cmd, iface = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    s = open_sock(iface)
    me = s.getsockname()[4]
    if cmd == "garp":
        ip = sys.argv[3]
        s.send(frame(me, b"\xff" * 6, 1, me, ip, b"\x00" * 6, ip))
    elif cmd == "sniff":
        end = time.monotonic() + float(sys.argv[3]); t0 = time.monotonic()
        s.settimeout(0.2)
        while time.monotonic() < end:
            try:
                f = s.recv(2048)
            except socket.timeout:
                continue
            p = parse(f)
            if p and (len(sys.argv) < 5 or sys.argv[4] in (p["spa"], p["tpa"])):
                print(f"  {time.monotonic() - t0:6.2f}s {describe(p)}", flush=True)
acd.py IFACE IP|ll [--defend SECONDS] [--fast] probes, announces and (with --defend) defends one address as RFC 5227 describes; ll picks an RFC 3927 link-local candidate. --fast divides every timer by 10, for demonstrations only. acd.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""IPv4 Address Conflict Detection (RFC 5227) and link-local selection (RFC 3927).

acd.py IFACE IP|ll [--defend SECONDS] [--fast]

Probe: PROBE_WAIT random 0..1 s, then PROBE_NUM=3 probes (ARP request,
sender IP 0.0.0.0, target IP = candidate) PROBE_MIN..PROBE_MAX (1..2 s) apart,
then ANNOUNCE_WAIT=2 s. A conflict is any ARP packet whose sender IP is the
candidate (someone uses it), or a probe for the same address from another MAC
(someone else is probing it right now). With no conflict: configure the
address, send ANNOUNCE_NUM=2 announcements ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL=2 s apart.
Defend (2.4 option b): on a conflicting ARP for our address, defend once with
an announcement; a second conflict within DEFEND_INTERVAL=10 s -> give up
the address. "ll" picks 169.254.1.0-169.254.254.255 pseudo-randomly, seeded
from the MAC (RFC 3927 2.1), and moves on to another candidate after a conflict.
--fast divides every timer by 10 (for demonstrations only).
"""
import random, socket, subprocess, sys, time
from arp import frame, parse, open_sock, mac

PROBE_WAIT, PROBE_NUM, PROBE_MIN, PROBE_MAX = 1.0, 3, 1.0, 2.0
ANNOUNCE_WAIT, ANNOUNCE_NUM, ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL = 2.0, 2, 2.0
DEFEND_INTERVAL = 10.0

args = sys.argv[1:]
iface, want = args[0], args[1]
fast = "--fast" in args
defend_for = float(args[args.index("--defend") + 1]) if "--defend" in args else 0
k = 0.1 if fast else 1.0
s = open_sock(iface)
me = s.getsockname()[4]
t0 = time.monotonic()
rng = random.Random(int.from_bytes(me, "big"))      # RFC 3927: seed from the MAC

def log(msg):
    print(f"  [{mac(me)} {time.monotonic() - t0:5.2f}s] {msg}", flush=True)

def listen_until(deadline, ip, probing):
    s.settimeout(0.05)
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        try:
            p = parse(s.recv(2048))
        except socket.timeout:
            continue
        if not p or p["sha"] == me:
            continue
        if p["spa"] == ip:
            return f"{mac(p['sha'])} is using {ip} (ARP {'reply' if p['op'] == 2 else 'request'} with sender IP {ip})"
        if probing and p["op"] == 1 and p["spa"] == "0.0.0.0" and p["tpa"] == ip:
            return f"{mac(p['sha'])} is probing {ip} at the same time"
    return None

def probe(ip):
    time.sleep(rng.uniform(0, PROBE_WAIT) * k)
    for n in range(PROBE_NUM):
        s.send(frame(me, b"\xff" * 6, 1, me, "0.0.0.0", b"\x00" * 6, ip))
        log(f"probe {n + 1}/{PROBE_NUM} for {ip}")
        wait = ANNOUNCE_WAIT if n == PROBE_NUM - 1 else rng.uniform(PROBE_MIN, PROBE_MAX)
        c = listen_until(time.monotonic() + wait * k, ip, True)
        if c:
            log(f"CONFLICT: {c}")
            return False
    return True

def announce(ip):
    for n in range(ANNOUNCE_NUM):
        s.send(frame(me, b"\xff" * 6, 1, me, ip, b"\x00" * 6, ip))
        log(f"announce {n + 1}/{ANNOUNCE_NUM} {ip}")
        if n < ANNOUNCE_NUM - 1:
            time.sleep(ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL * k)

def ll_candidate():
    n = rng.randrange(0, 254 * 256)                  # 169.254.1.0 .. 169.254.254.255
    return f"169.254.{1 + n // 256}.{n % 256}"

ip = ll_candidate() if want == "ll" else want
for attempt in range(10):
    if probe(ip):
        break
    if want != "ll":
        log(f"not configuring {ip}"); sys.exit(1)
    ip = ll_candidate(); log(f"next link-local candidate {ip}")
plen = "16" if want == "ll" else "24"
subprocess.run(["ip", "addr", "add", f"{ip}/{plen}", "dev", iface], check=True)
log(f"configured {ip}/{plen} on {iface}")
announce(ip)
if defend_for:
    last = None
    end = time.monotonic() + defend_for * k
    while time.monotonic() < end:
        c = listen_until(end, ip, False)
        if not c:
            break
        now = time.monotonic()
        if last is None or now - last > DEFEND_INTERVAL * k:
            log(f"conflict while bound: {c}; defending once")
            s.send(frame(me, b"\xff" * 6, 1, me, ip, b"\x00" * 6, ip)); last = now
        else:
            log(f"second conflict within DEFEND_INTERVAL ({now - last:.2f}s): {c}; giving up {ip}")
            subprocess.run(["ip", "addr", "del", f"{ip}/{plen}", "dev", iface], check=True)
            break

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""who.py serve NAME: TCP 7777 answers with NAME.  who.py ask IP: print the answer."""
import socket, sys
if sys.argv[1] == "serve":
    l = socket.socket(); l.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    l.bind(("0.0.0.0", 7777)); l.listen(8)
    while True:
        c, _ = l.accept(); c.sendall(sys.argv[2].encode()); c.close()
else:
    try:
        c = socket.create_connection((sys.argv[2], 7777), timeout=2); print(c.recv(64).decode())
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"error: {e}")

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
Reading the output

Scenario 1: Silent IPv4 binding vs IPv6 DAD
In Scenario 1, host h1 holds IP address 10.0.0.5/24. Host h2 subsequently runs ip addr add 10.0.0.5/24 dev eth0.
The command executes with exit status 0. Standard output displays no warnings or error messages. Checking ip addr show dev eth0 on h2 confirms inet 10.0.0.5/24 scope global eth0 is actively bound. The Linux kernel performed no check against the network domain.
Next, h1 binds IPv6 address fd00::5/64. h2 then binds the same IPv6 address fd00::5/64. The kernel output for h2 shows:
inet6 fd00::5/64 scope global dadfailed tentative eth0
Because IPv6 DAD (RFC 4862) is built into the kernel stack, h2 detects h1’s reply to its Neighbor Solicitation. h2 immediately marks the IPv6 address as tentative and dadfailed, blocking applications from binding to the socket.


Scenario 2: Kernel locktime and GARP behaviour
Host h1 (02:00:00:00:00:01) and host h2 (02:00:00:00:00:02) both have 10.0.0.5/24 configured on their interfaces. Host h3 (02:00:00:00:00:03) attempts to open a TCP connection to 10.0.0.5:7777.

Host h3 emits an ARP request for 10.0.0.5. Both h1 and h2 transmit ARP replies at t=0.17s. Host h2’s reply arrives at h3 slightly before h1’s reply.
h3 stores 10.0.0.5 -> 02:00:00:00:00:02 as REACHABLE. h1’s reply arrived within the same 10 ms, but locktime (100 USER_HZ ticks = 1 s) stops a normal reply from overriding an entry updated less than a second ago, so it is ignored. With two answers, the first one to arrive wins; which host that is depends on timing. The TCP connection opens on h2.
h1 emits a Gratuitous ARP (arp.py garp 10.0.0.5). Because GARP bypasses locktime, h3 updates its neighbour table to 02:00:00:00:00:01 with state STALE. h3’s next TCP connection hits h1.
h2 emits a GARP (arp.py garp 10.0.0.5). h3 updates its neighbour entry back to 02:00:00:00:00:02 (STALE), and subsequent TCP connections hit h2.



Scenario 3: ACD probing against an occupied address
Host h4 runs acd.py eth0 10.0.0.5, with the RFC timers, while h1 holds 10.0.0.5.
At t=0.72s (after PROBE_WAIT), h4 broadcasts its first ARP Probe (SPA=0.0.0.0, TPA=10.0.0.5). Host h1 runs no ACD software, but its kernel answers the probe straight away with a unicast ARP reply (SPA=10.0.0.5, SHA=02:00:00:00:00:01).
acd.py intercepts h1’s reply, outputs CONFLICT: 02:00:00:00:00:01 is using 10.0.0.5 (ARP reply with sender IP 10.0.0.5), aborts configuration, and exits with status 1. Host h4 leaves eth0 unconfigured.


Scenario 4: ACD probing for a free address
Host h4 executes ACD for unassigned address 10.0.0.9. Host h3 runs arp.py sniff to monitor network frames.

Probe 1: t=0.72s (spa 0.0.0.0, tpa 10.0.0.9)
Probe 2: t=1.92s (spa 0.0.0.0, tpa 10.0.0.9) — 1.20s after Probe 1 (within PROBE_MIN..PROBE_MAX).
Probe 3: t=3.17s (spa 0.0.0.0, tpa 10.0.0.9) — 1.25s after Probe 2.
ANNOUNCE_WAIT: 2.00 seconds elapse without conflict frames.
Address Configuration: t=5.18s, 10.0.0.9/24 is bound to eth0.
Announcement 1: t=5.18s (spa 10.0.0.9, tpa 10.0.0.9).
Announcement 2: t=7.18s (spa 10.0.0.9, tpa 10.0.0.9) — 2.00s after Announcement 1.

h3’s sniffer captures exactly 3 probes (SPA=0.0.0.0) followed by 2 announcements (SPA=TPA=10.0.0.9).


Scenario 5: Simultaneous probing conflict
Hosts h4 and h5 simultaneously initiate ACD probing for 10.0.0.77 using --fast (which scales timer values down by 10).

At t=0.07s, h4 broadcasts an ARP Probe (SHA=02:00:00:00:00:04).
At t=0.10s, h5 broadcasts an ARP Probe (SHA=02:00:00:00:00:05).

h4 receives h5’s probe with SPA=0.0.0.0 and TPA=10.0.0.77. h5 receives h4’s probe. Both hosts detect simultaneous probing from a peer MAC address. Both acd.py instances decline configuration, log a conflict, and exit.


Scenario 6: Active defence and relinquishment
Host h5 claims 10.0.0.20 using --fast. Probing completes, and h5 configures the IP at t=0.60s, issuing announcements at t=0.60s and t=0.80s.
Host h2 is then given 10.0.0.20 by hand and sends a gratuitous ARP, which h5 sees at t=1.19s. - h5 detects the conflict while bound. Employing RFC 5227 Option (b), h5 broadcasts one ARP Announcement at t=1.19s to defend the IP (“conflict while bound … defending once”). - At t=1.56s (0.36 seconds later), h2 transmits a second GARP. - Because the second conflict occurred within DEFEND_INTERVAL (10s), h5 surrenders: “second conflict within DEFEND_INTERVAL … giving up”, removes 10.0.0.20 from eth0, and exits.
h2 now holds the address alone. That is the point of option (b): one of the two hosts gives up, so the segment stops flapping. Note that it was the host with the correct configuration that left. RFC 5227 cannot know which host is right, so a conflict still needs a human to look at it.


Scenario 7: IPv4 Link-Local autoconfiguration
Hosts h4 and h5 run acd.py eth0 ll --fast.
The pseudo-random number generator, seeded by interface MAC addresses, produces: - h4 (02:00:00:00:00:04) -> 169.254.184.163 - h5 (02:00:00:00:00:05) -> 169.254.249.72
Both hosts perform RFC 5227 ACD on their respective link-local candidates. Zero conflicts occur. Both hosts configure their addresses as /16. Because the generator is seeded from the MAC, running the scenario again picks the same addresses, which is what RFC 3927 recommends so that a host keeps its link-local address across restarts.

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
In production
# (not run here)
# View neighbour locktime setting for eth0

# Enable arp_notify to send gratuitous ARP when the device comes up or its MAC changes

    echo "ERROR: IP address 192.168.1.50 is already in use!"
    exit 1
fi

# Monitor ARP cache changes in real time
ip monitor neigh

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
Gotchas

Linux IPv4 silent bind: adding an IPv4 address never fails because of a duplicate on the wire. Linux does not send IPv4 probes itself; only user-space software (NetworkManager, systemd-networkd for link-local addresses, dhcpcd, arping -D) does.
Standard systemd-networkd default: systemd-networkd only enables IPv4 DAD for 169.254.0.0/16 link-local addresses by default. Static global IPv4 address definitions do not perform ACD unless explicitly configured.
Cloud Metadata is not RFC 3927 autoconfig: The address 169.254.169.254 used for instance metadata in AWS/GCP/Azure is a fixed service endpoint, not a dynamically selected autoconfigured address.
Locktime hides duplicate replies: The default net.ipv4.neigh.IFACE.locktime of 1 second prevents Linux from updating ARP entries if a second reply arrives within 100 USER_HZ ticks of the first.
Probe source IP must be zero: ARP Probes MUST use 0.0.0.0 as the Sender IP Address. Using the candidate IP during probing poisons peer ARP caches before address ownership is established.
Option (b) can evict the right host: Under standard RFC 5227 defence (Option b), a defending host surrenders its address if a second conflict occurs within 10 seconds, leaving the misconfigured intruder in control.
Option (c) never resolves a conflict: two hosts that both defend indefinitely keep the address on both machines, so the flapping continues. Use it only on devices whose address must not move.

title: Duplicate IPv4 Addresses: Address Conflict Detection and IPv4 Link-Local
text:
Exercises

Calculate ACD Timers: A host performs RFC 5227 ACD with PROBE_WAIT = 0.5s, PROBE_NUM = 3, PROBE_MIN = 1s, PROBE_MAX = 2s, and ANNOUNCE_WAIT = 2s. Assuming worst-case timer jitter (PROBE_MAX), calculate the maximum time elapsed before the address is configured.
Kernel Locktime Modification: Use sysctl to set net.ipv4.neigh.eth0.locktime = 0. Re-run Scenario 2 and observe how the ARP table responds when two hosts send simultaneous ARP replies.
Simulate DHCPDECLINE: Write a shell script using arping -D that tests candidate IP 10.0.0.5. If arping detects a conflict, print a log simulating a DHCPDECLINE frame sent back to the server.
Link-Local Exclusion Range: Write a Python function that generates random IP addresses in 169.254.0.0/16 but explicitly excludes 169.254.0.0/24 and 169.254.255.0/24.
Packet Capture Analysis: Capture an RFC 5227 exchange using tcpdump -e -n arp. Identify the fields that distinguish an ARP Probe from an ARP Announcement.
Systemd-networkd Audit: Inspect /etc/systemd/network/ configurations on a target system and verify whether DuplicateAddressDetection=ipv4 is enabled for static interface blocks.

title: ICMP and Path Diagnostics
text:
Interpret diagnostic replies carefully
An ICMP echo reply establishes that a particular endpoint or responding device returned an echo response for that flow and size. A timeout could be a route, neighbor, firewall, host, rate-limit, or return-path problem; it is not proof of a physical failure. A destination-unreachable message can identify a failure, but the source address tells you who generated the message, which may be a router rather than the target.
Traceroute sends probes with increasing IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit. A router that expires a probe may return Time Exceeded, revealing a responding address. Different traceroute tools use UDP, ICMP, or TCP probes, and multipath forwarding may send those flows on different paths. Rate limiting or filtering can hide a hop even while later hops respond. Asterisks do not automatically identify packet loss at that hop.
Path MTU is the smallest usable IP MTU along a particular path. Test progressively larger packets with the platform’s ping options, and distinguish an ICMP error from silent timeout. A smaller probe succeeding while a larger one stalls suggests an MTU or filtering issue; verify with capture and interface MTUs. The reverse direction can have a different path or MTU.

title: ICMP and Path Diagnostics
section: Lab: an MTU limit in isolated Linux namespaces
text:
Lab: an MTU limit in isolated Linux namespaces
This lab makes two Linux network namespaces connected by a virtual Ethernet pair with MTU 1200. It uses Linux unshare, mount, ip (iproute2), and iputils ping. It requires a system where unprivileged user and network namespaces and mounts are permitted. No external host is contacted. The first command starts a new user, network, and mount namespace; the script makes mounts private and mounts a temporary /run only inside that namespace, so the ip netns names and links disappear when the command exits. Do not run the script outside the shown unshare command.
Save as mtu-lab.sh:
#!/bin/sh
set -eu
mount --make-rprivate /
mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run
ip netns add a
ip netns add b
ip link add va type veth peer name vb
ip link set va netns a
ip link set vb netns b
ip -n a link set lo up
ip -n b link set lo up
ip -n a link set va mtu 1200 up
ip -n b link set vb mtu 1200 up
ip -n a addr add 192.0.2.1/30 dev va
ip -n b addr add 192.0.2.2/30 dev vb

ip netns exec a ping -n -c 1 -W 1 -M do -s 1172 192.0.2.2
if ip netns exec a ping -n -c 1 -W 1 -M do -s 1173 192.0.2.2; then
    echo "Unexpected: oversized probe succeeded" >&2
    exit 1
else
    echo "Oversized probe failed, as expected"
fi
Run unshare -Urnm sh ./mtu-lab.sh. A successful run shows one echo reply for the first probe, then a local Message too long error for the second. Exact ping statistics and timing vary. If namespace creation or mounts are denied, the lab has not reached the networking experiment; check your system’s namespace policy and available tools.
With a 20-byte IPv4 header (no options) and an 8-byte ICMP echo header, the first packet is \(1172 + 8 + 20 = 1200\) bytes. The next is 1201 bytes. -s specifies the echo data size, and -M do requests DF behavior. The local output interface already knows its MTU, so the kernel rejects the oversized probe locally; this does not demonstrate receiving a router’s ICMP fragmentation-needed message or discovering a remote path MTU. For a real path, tunnels, IP options, and routing changes can alter the calculation. Capture packets and inspect both directions before attributing a timeout to MTU.

title: ICMP and Path Diagnostics
text:
Practice and interpretation

An IPv4 echo request has 1400 data bytes and no IP options. What is the IP packet size? 1428 bytes: 1400 data + 8 ICMP + 20 IPv4.
A middle traceroute hop shows *, but later hops reply. Must that hop be dropping forwarded packets? No; its own diagnostic replies may be filtered or rate-limited while forwarding continues.
Does a ping reply prove that TCP port 443 works? No; it tests a different protocol and flow.
In the namespace lab, did the 1201-byte probe prove an intermediate router sent an ICMP error? No; the source kernel rejected it against its local interface MTU.

References: RFC 792 (ICMP), RFC 1191 (IPv4 PMTUD), RFC 8201 (IPv6 PMTUD), and Linux iputils ping.

title: Transport: TCP and UDP
section: TCP reliability is a byte-stream service
text:
TCP reliability is a byte-stream service
TCP numbers bytes, not application messages. If a segment starts at sequence 1001 and contains 500 bytes, the next in-order byte begins at 1501; an ACK of 1501 means the receiver has accepted all preceding bytes in sequence. SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number. Sequence values wrap modulo 2³². An ACK confirms transport receipt, not that the receiving application processed or stored the data. TCP preserves byte order but does not preserve write() boundaries: an application must frame its own messages. See RFC 9293.
The receiver advertises a receive window for available buffering. The sender also maintains a congestion window, reflecting its estimate of what the network can sustain. The effective amount of unacknowledged data is constrained by both, along with implementation and application behavior. Retransmission can follow a timer or loss inference; duplicate ACKs, selective acknowledgments, and modern loss-recovery algorithms help the sender identify missing data. Loss is not the only cause of a stalled application: a zero receive window, congestion, server processing, DNS, or policy can all matter.

Read a handshake and a failure
A SYN proposes an initial sequence number and may carry options such as MSS, window scaling, and SACK support. The SYN-ACK acknowledges that SYN and supplies the peer’s initial sequence number; the final ACK completes the normal handshake. A listener can exist while a firewall drops SYNs; a reset may indicate a closed port or a device actively rejecting traffic. A handshake proves that a TCP connection was established at that point, not that TLS, HTTP, or the application request succeeded.
FIN closes one direction of the byte stream; the peer may still send in the other direction. RST aborts a connection. TIME-WAIT supports safe connection closure and limits confusion with delayed packets; its presence alone is not a fault. UDP preserves datagram boundaries but provides no delivery, ordering, or duplicate suppression guarantee. Applications using UDP must handle their own requirements, including congestion behavior.
Try it: capture a TCP connection with tcpdump -ni eth1 -nn -S 'tcp port 8080'. Identify the SYN, SYN-ACK, final ACK, a data segment, and an ACK. With absolute sequence numbers shown by -S, calculate the next expected byte. Compare capture points if offload or retransmission makes the trace surprising.

title: Transport: TCP and UDP
section: How TCP estimates time, capacity, and loss
text:
How TCP estimates time, capacity, and loss
An RTT sample measures the interval between sending data and receiving an acknowledgment that covers it. That interval includes both directions, receiver behavior, and queueing; it is not a direct measurement of a single link’s propagation delay. TCP maintains smoothed RTT and variation estimates to set a retransmission timeout. A sudden queue can increase RTT variation even when the physical distance is unchanged. When an acknowledgment is missing, the sender cannot immediately distinguish a lost data segment, a lost ACK, reordering, and a slow path.
Consider bytes 1001–2000 sent in one segment and 2001–3000 in the next. If the first segment is missing and the second arrives, a cumulative ACK can continue to request byte 1001. With selective acknowledgment negotiated, the receiver can also report the later byte range it has received, helping the sender avoid retransmitting data unnecessarily. A timer expiration can trigger retransmission; implementations can also infer loss from subsequent acknowledgments. The retransmission timer is backed off after expiry. See RFC 6298 and RFC 9293.

Bandwidth-delay product and the windows
At 100 Mb/s with 40 ms RTT, the bandwidth-delay product is approximately 100,000,000 × 0.040 / 8 = 500,000 bytes. Roughly that much data must be in flight to fill an otherwise uncongested path at that rate. If the permitted flight size were only 64,000 bytes, a rough window/RTT upper bound would be about 12.8 Mb/s, before other limits. This is a teaching estimate, not a promise of throughput: congestion, packet loss, receiver processing, application pacing, and protocol overhead also matter.
The advertised receive window reflects receiver capacity; the sender’s congestion window limits traffic in response to network conditions. Window scaling, negotiated during the handshake, permits advertised windows larger than the unscaled 16-bit field. A zero receive window points toward receiver-side buffering or consumption, whereas a small congestion window concerns sender behavior and inferred path conditions. Use ss -tin on Linux to inspect available TCP statistics, but field names and support depend on the kernel; correlate them with captures and application timing.
Check yourself: if a receiver acknowledges through byte 2000 but has not yet received 2001–3000, the next cumulative ACK is 2001. An ACK is an endpoint’s claim about bytes accepted in sequence, not proof of application processing or disk persistence.

title: Transport: TCP and UDP

Practice: reason from the trace
A client sends 100 bytes starting at sequence 4001. The server receives all of them and returns ACK 4101. What has been acknowledged? If the application wrote those 100 bytes in two calls, can you infer that from the wire? If the ACK arrives but the application displays no response, which layer is proven to have made progress?
The ACK covers bytes 4001 through 4100. It says nothing about how the sending application divided its writes, and it does not prove that the receiving application processed the request. It does show that the remote TCP endpoint acknowledged those bytes. Continue by checking the application protocol and server behavior.

title: Common Application Protocols
text:
A name-to-response walkthrough
A name such as www.example.com is not an IP address. A resolver checks its configured sources and caches, then may ask a recursive DNS server. That server follows delegation from the root toward authoritative servers as necessary; cached answers can avoid repeated queries. A DNS record’s TTL limits how long it may be cached, but caches and clients can have their own behavior. A DNS answer can contain multiple IPv4 and IPv6 addresses; the client decides which connection attempts to make.
For an HTTPS request the client selects an address, establishes a transport connection, negotiates TLS, verifies the server certificate against its trust configuration and the requested name, and then exchanges HTTP messages. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP rather than a TCP connection. Name resolution success does not prove connectivity, a TCP handshake does not prove certificate validity, and a valid TLS connection does not prove an application returns the desired response.
A practical sequence is getent ahosts example.com, ip route get <address>, and curl -v https://example.com/. Record what each step proves. curl may use proxies or local configuration; its verbose output helps identify the endpoint actually contacted. DNS queries may use UDP or TCP; avoid treating port 53 or UDP as a universal description of every resolver path.

title: Common Application Protocols
text:
DNS answers, delegation, and caching
A recursive resolver takes responsibility for finding an answer on a client’s behalf; an authoritative server answers for data in a zone it serves. Delegation connects the hierarchy: a parent supplies information about a child zone’s authoritative servers, and the resolver can then query them. A zone is an administrative portion of the name hierarchy; it is not necessarily identical to a domain name and all descendants, because children can be delegated separately.
A and AAAA records carry IPv4 and IPv6 addresses; CNAME indicates an alias; NS identifies name servers; SOA describes zone authority and parameters; MX identifies mail exchangers. A resolver may answer from cache, so a repeated query is not proof that the authoritative server was contacted again. A record’s TTL is a caching lifetime, not a guarantee that every client observes an update at exactly the same instant.
A response of NXDOMAIN indicates that the queried name does not exist according to the answering authority, subject to aliases and resolver behavior. A NODATA answer means the name exists but the requested record type is absent. SERVFAIL signals a resolution failure, not that the name does not exist. Negative answers can also be cached: creating a record after a cached negative response may not make every resolver show it immediately. See RFC 2308.
Investigate: compare dig example.com A and dig example.com AAAA; inspect the response code, answer section, TTL, and server. For a lab zone, query the recursive resolver and authoritative server separately with dig @<server> <name> <type>. A direct authoritative answer and a cached recursive answer can legitimately differ during a change. Use only lab-controlled names when intentionally creating or removing records.
