title: Host Forwarding and Routing Intro
section: How a host chooses the outgoing path
text:
How a host chooses the outgoing path
For a typical locally generated packet, the operating system selects a route using the destination and any applicable policy. The selected route identifies an interface and may specify a gateway and preferred source address. It then resolves the next hop on that interface and transmits. Policy routing, multiple routing tables, multiple addresses, and application binding can make the result differ from an intuition based on the main table alone. On Linux, ip route get 198.51.100.20 shows the kernel’s decision for a representative lookup; supply a source address or other selectors when the real flow uses them.
A connected route says a prefix is reachable on a link; it does not prove that every address in the prefix exists. A default route says where to send otherwise unmatched destinations; it does not prove that the gateway can forward them. At each router the same distinction applies between a route being installed, a neighbor being reachable, and a packet actually being forwarded.

Exercise: predict before looking
A host has 10.0.0.10/24, a connected 10.0.0.0/24 route, and default gateway 10.0.0.1. For 10.0.0.20, it resolves .20. For 203.0.113.10, it resolves .1 but retains 203.0.113.10 as the IP destination. If the return path lacks a route to 10.0.0.0/24, the first packet can arrive while the exchange still fails. Check routes and captures in both directions.

title: Control, Data, and Management Planes
section: Trace one change across the planes
text:
Trace one change across the planes
Imagine an operator removes an OSPF adjacency. The configuration operation arrives through a management interface; OSPF’s neighbor and route calculations are control-plane behavior; traffic uses the installed forwarding entries in the data plane. These are conceptual roles, not necessarily separate processors or physical networks. An implementation may use a shared CPU, and operational traffic may share links with production traffic.
The state does not necessarily change everywhere at the same instant. A route may remain installed briefly while a protocol detects failure and recalculates; a device may retain a usable forwarding entry even when its management interface is unreachable. Conversely a healthy management session and an established routing neighbor do not prove that a particular data flow passes an ACL or that an egress link works. For a failure drill, record the time of the event, neighbor change, route change, and loss/recovery of probe traffic. That sequence explains convergence more reliably than a single final screenshot.

title: Encrypted DNS: DoT, DoH and Discovering Them
text:
Encrypted DNS: DoT, DoH and Discovering Them
Classic DNS goes over UDP port 53 in clear text. Anyone on the path can read every name a host looks up, and anyone on the path can answer first. That second point is not theoretical: the lab in this chapter sent a plain query to 1.1.1.1 from the writing host and got an answer, in about a millisecond, that Cloudflare never sent. DNS over TLS (DoT, RFC 7858) and DNS over HTTPS (DoH, RFC 8484) put the same DNS messages inside an authenticated, encrypted channel to a resolver you chose. This chapter sends one question over all of them by hand, shows the wire formats, pads the query, asks a resolver which encrypted endpoints it offers (DDR, RFC 9462), and ends with how to run encrypted DNS on Linux hosts without breaking split-horizon names.

title: Encrypted DNS: DoT, DoH and Discovering Them
text:
Learning goals

Say exactly what DoT and DoH protect, and what they do not (the resolver still sees everything; ECH and the IP still leak)
Build DoT and DoH requests from the RFCs with the Python standard library and read the replies
Explain EDNS(0) padding and why encrypted DNS without it still leaks names by size
Use Discovery of Designated Resolvers to upgrade from a plain resolver address to its encrypted endpoints
Choose between OS-level and application-level encrypted DNS for a fleet, and know what breaks with split-horizon DNS

Version note. The lab ran on 2026-11-13 from the writing host (Linux 6.12.94+, Python 3.13.5, OpenSSL 3.5.7, dnspython 2.9.1 used only to build and parse DNS messages). The transports themselves are standard library: socket, ssl and urllib. dnspython’s own DoH client was not used because its HTTP dependency is not installed and no installs are allowed. dig and kdig are not installed either. The resolver is Cloudflare’s public service. Timings are one run from one place and only useful as relative values.

DoT and DoH carry the same DNS message bytes. What changes is the wrapper and, with it, who can see or block the traffic. DoT on its own port is easy for a network to recognise, allow or block. DoH shares port 443 and often the same IPs with web traffic, which is exactly why browsers adopted it and why enterprises dislike it.
What none of them hide: the resolver still sees every query and the client IP; the destination IP of the connection you then open is visible; and the server name goes in clear in the TLS ClientHello unless Encrypted Client Hello is in use. Encrypted DNS moves trust from “every network on the path” to “the resolver operator”. That is a real improvement on hostile Wi-Fi and a policy question everywhere else.

title: Encrypted DNS: DoT, DoH and Discovering Them
text:
Lab: one question, four ways
The script sends a query for example.com A four ways, then repeats DoT with padding and asks for DDR records. Each request is built from the RFC text, not from a DNS library’s transport helpers, so you can see the framing.
# edns.py: one question, four transports (UDP/53, DoT/853, DoH POST, DoH GET), plus padding and DDR.
import base64, socket, ssl, struct, time, urllib.request
import dns.edns, dns.message, dns.rcode, dns.rdatatype

NAME = "example.com"

def q(name=NAME, rtype="A", pad=0):
    opts = [dns.edns.GenericOption(dns.edns.OptionType.PADDING, b"")] if pad else []
    m = dns.message.make_query(name, rtype, use_edns=0, options=opts, pad=pad)
    m.id = 0                                       # RFC 8484 4.1: id 0 for cache-friendly GET
    return m

def show(label, wire_q, wire_r, ms):
    r = dns.message.from_wire(wire_r)
    ans = [str(rd) for rr in r.answer for rd in rr][:2]
    print(f"{label:16} q={len(wire_q):3}B r={len(wire_r):4}B {ms:6.1f} ms "
          f"{dns.rcode.to_text(r.rcode())} {ans}")

def udp53(server="1.1.1.1"):
    w = q().to_wire(); s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.settimeout(3)
    t = time.perf_counter(); s.sendto(w, (server, 53)); r, _ = s.recvfrom(4096)
    show("UDP 53", w, r, (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)

def dot(server="1.1.1.1", sni="one.one.one.one", pad=0):
    w = q(pad=pad).to_wire()
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
    t = time.perf_counter()
    with socket.create_connection((server, 853), timeout=5) as raw, \
         ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname=sni) as s:
        hs = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000
        t = time.perf_counter()
        s.sendall(struct.pack("!H", len(w)) + w)      # RFC 7858: 2-byte length prefix, as DNS/TCP
        ln = struct.unpack("!H", s.recv(2))[0]; r = b""
        while len(r) < ln: r += s.recv(ln - len(r))
        show(f"DoT 853 pad={pad}", w, r, (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)
        print(f"{'':16} TLS {s.version()} {s.cipher()[0]}, handshake {hs:.1f} ms, "
              f"cert CN={dict(x[0] for x in s.getpeercert()['subject'])['commonName']}")

def doh_post(url="https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query"):
    w = q().to_wire()
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, data=w, headers={"Content-Type": "application/dns-message",
                                                        "Accept": "application/dns-message"})
    t = time.perf_counter()
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as resp:
        r = resp.read(); ct = resp.headers["Content-Type"]; cc = resp.headers.get("Cache-Control")
    show("DoH POST", w, r, (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)
    print(f"{'':16} Content-Type: {ct}  Cache-Control: {cc}")

def doh_get(url="https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query"):
    w = q().to_wire()
    b64 = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(w).rstrip(b"=").decode()   # RFC 8484 4.1: base64url, no padding
    print(f"{'':16} GET {url}?dns={b64}")
    req = urllib.request.Request(f"{url}?dns={b64}", headers={"Accept": "application/dns-message"})
    t = time.perf_counter()
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as resp:
        r = resp.read(); age = resp.headers.get("Age")
    show("DoH GET", w, r, (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)

def ddr(server="1.1.1.1", via="udp"):
    """RFC 9462: ask a resolver which encrypted endpoints it offers."""
    w = q("_dns.resolver.arpa", "SVCB").to_wire()
    if via == "udp":
        s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.settimeout(3)
        s.sendto(w, (server, 53)); r = dns.message.from_wire(s.recvfrom(4096)[0])
    else:
        req = urllib.request.Request("https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query", data=w, headers={
            "Content-Type": "application/dns-message", "Accept": "application/dns-message"})
        r = dns.message.from_wire(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5).read())
    print(f"  via {via}: {dns.rcode.to_text(r.rcode())}, {sum(len(x) for x in r.answer)} SVCB records")
    for rr in r.answer:
        for rd in rr:
            print(f"  SVCB {rd.priority} {rd.target} {' '.join(str(rd).split()[2:])}")

print("-- same query, four transports (resolver 1.1.1.1 / cloudflare-dns.com)")
udp53(); dot(); doh_post(); doh_get()
print("-- RFC 8467 padding: query padded to a multiple of 128 octets")
dot(pad=128)
print("-- RFC 9462 DDR: _dns.resolver.arpa SVCB, plain UDP to 1.1.1.1 vs DoH")
ddr(via="udp"); ddr(via="doh")
$ python3 edns.py
-- same query, four transports (resolver 1.1.1.1 / cloudflare-dns.com)
UDP 53           q= 40B r=  45B    1.1 ms NOERROR ['198.18.0.1']
DoT 853 pad=0    q= 40B r= 468B   45.6 ms NOERROR ['104.20.23.154', '172.66.147.243']
                 TLS TLSv1.3 TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, handshake 8.2 ms, cert CN=cloudflare-dns.com
DoH POST         q= 40B r=  72B   82.5 ms NOERROR ['172.66.147.243', '104.20.23.154']
                 Content-Type: application/dns-message  Cache-Control: None
                 GET https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?dns=AAABAAABAAAAAAABB2V4YW1wbGUDY29tAAABAAEAACkE0AAAAAAAAA
DoH GET          q= 40B r=  72B   72.2 ms NOERROR ['172.66.147.243', '104.20.23.154']
-- RFC 8467 padding: query padded to a multiple of 128 octets
DoT 853 pad=128  q=128B r= 468B   47.0 ms NOERROR ['104.20.23.154', '172.66.147.243']
                 TLS TLSv1.3 TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, handshake 7.4 ms, cert CN=cloudflare-dns.com
-- RFC 9462 DDR: _dns.resolver.arpa SVCB, plain UDP to 1.1.1.1 vs DoH
  via udp: NOERROR, 0 SVCB records
  via doh: NOERROR, 2 SVCB records
  SVCB 1 one.one.one.one. alpn="h2,h3" port="443" ipv4hint="1.1.1.1,1.0.0.1" ipv6hint="2606:4700:4700::1111,2606:4700:4700::1001" dohpath="/dns-query{?dns}"
  SVCB 2 one.one.one.one. alpn="dot" port="853" ipv4hint="1.1.1.1,1.0.0.1" ipv6hint="2606:4700:4700::1111,2606:4700:4700::1001"

Reading it
UDP 53 was not answered by Cloudflare. The reply came back in 1.1 ms with 198.18.0.1, an address from the benchmarking range 198.18.0.0/15 that Cloudflare does not hand out for example.com. The writing host’s network intercepts plain DNS to any address and answers it locally. The DoT and DoH replies, authenticated by a certificate for cloudflare-dns.com, give the real answer. This is the threat model in one line: plain DNS cannot tell you who answered. Corporate networks, hotel Wi-Fi, container sandboxes and some ISPs all do this, for reasons that range from captive portals to censorship.
DoT is DNS over TCP inside TLS: a 2-byte length, then the message (RFC 7858 3.3). The TLS handshake (about 8 ms here) is paid once per connection; real stubs keep the connection open and pipeline queries, so the steady-state cost is one round trip per query, like UDP. The 468-byte reply is padded by the server (below).
DoH POST sends the raw message as the HTTP body with Content-Type: application/dns-message. The reply is the same 72-byte wire message you would get over TCP.
DoH GET puts the message in the dns query parameter, base64url-encoded without padding (RFC 8484 4.1). The script sets the DNS ID to 0, as RFC 8484 recommends, so that identical questions produce identical URLs and HTTP caches can serve them. The base64 string above decodes to exactly the 40-byte query. GET is cache-friendly; POST is smaller for big queries and never cached by intermediaries.


Padding: encryption does not hide size
A TLS record hides content, not length. An observer who sees a 40-byte query and a 72-byte answer can often guess the name from sizes alone, especially for popular names. RFC 7830 defines an EDNS(0) Padding option, and RFC 8467 recommends a policy: pad queries to a multiple of 128 bytes and responses to a multiple of 468 bytes.
In the padded run the query grew from 40 to exactly 128 bytes. The responses were 468 bytes in both DoT runs: Cloudflare pads every DoT response to the 468-byte block, even when the query was not padded. Its DoH replies to the same unpadded query were 72 bytes: no padding. A client that wants size privacy must pad its own queries (which also signals that it wants padded replies, RFC 7830 section 4); it cannot assume every resolver or transport pads. Unbound pads queries and responses over TLS by default (pad-queries, pad-responses); check what your own stub does.


DDR: from “1.1.1.1” to its encrypted endpoints
A DHCP server or a router advertisement usually gives a host a resolver IP address. To use DoT or DoH the host needs a name to validate a certificate against, a port and, for DoH, a URI path. Discovery of Designated Resolvers (RFC 9462) lets the client ask the resolver itself: query _dns.resolver.arpa for SVCB records. The answers (RFC 9461 defines the DNS-specific keys) list the encrypted endpoints:

priority 1: one.one.one.one, alpn="h2,h3", dohpath="/dns-query{?dns}": DoH over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3,
priority 2: same name, alpn="dot", port 853: DoT,
with ipv4hint/ipv6hint addresses that include the IP the client already uses.

The client must then connect to the designated resolver and verify that its certificate covers both the name and the original IP address (1.1.1.1); that is what stops an on-path attacker from “designating” its own resolver. In the lab, the plain-UDP DDR query returned zero records: the intercepting network answered it, too, with an empty reply. A client that relied on DDR over unencrypted transport here would simply never upgrade, which is the designed, safe failure. The DoH query reached the real resolver and returned both records.
DDR is how Windows 11, Apple platforms and others auto-upgrade a configured resolver to encrypted transport. Its sibling, DNR (RFC 9463), carries the same information in DHCPv4, DHCPv6 and RA options, so the network can advertise an encrypted resolver directly.

title: Encrypted DNS: DoT, DoH and Discovering Them
section: Running encrypted DNS on Linux hosts
text:
Running encrypted DNS on Linux hosts
systemd-resolved (DoT only). In /etc/systemd/resolved.conf or a drop-in:
[Resolve]
DNS=1.1.1.1#cloudflare-dns.com 2606:4700:4700::1111#cloudflare-dns.com
DNSOverTLS=yes
DNSSEC=allow-downgrade
The #name suffix is the name to validate the certificate against. DNSOverTLS=opportunistic tries TLS and falls back to clear text, which protects against passive observers only; yes fails closed. resolvectl status shows +DNSOverTLS per link. resolved does not speak DoH.
Unbound as a local forwarder (DoT upstream).
server:
    tls-cert-bundle: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
forward-zone:
    name: "."
    forward-tls-upstream: yes
    forward-addr: 1.1.1.1@853#cloudflare-dns.com
    forward-addr: 2606:4700:4700::1111@853#cloudflare-dns.com
Both snippets are written from the systemd-resolved and Unbound documentation and were not run here (no root on the writing host, and its resolver is fixed by the sandbox).
Applications with their own DoH. Browsers resolve names themselves when DoH is on, bypassing the OS stub entirely. Firefox checks the canary domain use-application-dns.net: if the local resolver returns NXDOMAIN for it, Firefox leaves DoH off by default, which is how a network signals “use my resolver”. Enterprise browser policies can force or forbid DoH and pin the provider.

Troubleshooting
tcpdump port 53 shows nothing
Query the stub’s logs (resolvectl monitor), or use the client’s key log



The operator rule underneath all of them: encrypted DNS is a transport choice. Decide which resolver a host must use for which names, then encrypt the path to that resolver. Do not let each application decide.

title: Encrypted DNS: DoT, DoH and Discovering Them
text:
Gotchas

“DoH is on” can mean the OS stub is ignored. Check which resolver the application is using, not just resolv.conf.
Opportunistic means unauthenticated. It defeats passive snooping, not interception like the one in this lab.
No padding, little privacy. Sizes identify names. Pad queries to 128 and ask for padded replies.
Certificate names matter. 1.1.1.1@853 without a name to verify against accepts any certificate in many configs. Always give the #name.
DDR over clear text can be suppressed, not forged. A hostile network can stop the upgrade (as here); it cannot redirect you to its resolver if the client checks the certificate covers the original IP.
Port 853 is easy to block; 443 is not. Expect DoT to fail on restrictive networks where DoH works.
DNSSEC is still separate. Encrypted transport authenticates the resolver, not the data. Validate DNSSEC on the resolver, or locally if you do not trust it.

title: Encrypted DNS: DoT, DoH and Discovering Them
text:
Boring rule
Run your own validating resolver, offer it over DoT (and DoH if browsers matter), pad, and point managed hosts at it through the OS stub with strict TLS and a certificate name. Use DDR or DNR so unmanaged clients can find it. Treat any application that brings its own resolver as a policy exception, not a default.

title: Encrypted DNS: DoT, DoH and Discovering Them
text:
Try this

Change udp53() to query 9.9.9.9 and 8.8.8.8. Is your network intercepting plain DNS to every address, or only some? Compare with DoT to the same providers (dns.quad9.net, dns.google).
Add pad=468 to a DoH POST query. What sizes do the query and the response have now?
Decode the ?dns= string from the output with base64.urlsafe_b64decode (add the missing = padding) and parse it with dns.message.from_wire. Confirm the ID is 0.
Open one DoT connection and send ten queries on it, measuring each. How does the per-query time compare with the first one that included the handshake?
For your home or lab resolver, ask _dns.resolver.arpa SVCB over plain UDP. Does it advertise anything? What would a client have to validate before using it?

title: Ethernet & MAC Learning
section: The forwarding database as a hypothesis
text:
The forwarding database as a hypothesis
A bridge learns from source addresses, but forwards using the destination. Suppose h1 sends to h2 for the first time. The switch learns (VLAN 10, h1 MAC) → port 1. If h2 is unknown, it floods to the other forwarding ports in VLAN 10. When h2 replies, the switch learns h2’s source on port 2. Later traffic can be sent directly between those ports. The same MAC observed on two ports in the same VLAN moves the learned entry; repeated movement can indicate a loop, a redundant-path change, or a workload migration, so correlate it with topology and timing.
Unknown-unicast flooding is different from broadcast. It happens because the destination has not been learned, even if the destination MAC is unicast. A switch need not learn every active endpoint forever: entries age out, and traffic from a silent endpoint may be flooded again. Learning is scoped by VLAN; observing a MAC in VLAN 10 does not authorize forwarding it in VLAN 20. A port blocked by spanning tree does not serve as an ordinary forwarding port.
Evidence exercise: record the MAC table, send a frame in one direction, and record it again. Predict which entry appears from the source MAC, then send the reply and predict the second entry. Check the ingress VLAN as well as the port before explaining a result.

title: VLANs & Trunks
text:
VLANs & Trunks
VLANs split one physical switching fabric into multiple broadcast domains. Trunks carry many VLANs between switches with 802.1Q tags. Mis-matched tags and native VLANs are classic outage factories—this chapter makes them deliberate.

Without VLANs, one bridge = one flood domain. VLAN-aware bridging tags frames with a VLAN ID (VID) and keeps separate FDBs per VLAN (implementation details vary, model holds).

Behavior

One VLAN; frames untagged on the wire toward the host


Trunk
Multiple VLANs; tags on the wire (except optional native)

Untagged traffic on a trunk is mapped to this VLAN

Inserts TPID 0x8100 + PCP/DEI + VID. Capture shows tagged frames between switches:
tcpdump -ni eth1 -e vlan
# or
tcpdump -ni eth1 -e | head

Inter-VLAN traffic needs an L3 device (router-on-a-stick, SVI, separate routed ports). Same switch + different VLANs ⇒ no IP connectivity by design.

title: VLANs & Trunks
section: Follow one frame across an access port and a trunk
text:
Follow one frame across an access port and a trunk
A host sends an ordinary untagged Ethernet frame to an access port assigned to VLAN 10. The switch classifies it into VLAN 10 internally. When it sends the frame over a trunk that carries VLAN 10 as tagged traffic, the egress frame has an 802.1Q tag with VLAN ID 10. The receiving switch uses that tag to classify the frame into its VLAN 10, then normally removes the tag before sending it out an access port assigned to VLAN 10. The host does not need to understand VLAN tags for this access-port scenario.
The VLAN must exist and be permitted on every relevant trunk; an allowed VLAN does not prove that the far-side access port, spanning-tree state, or gateway is correct. Untagged or native-VLAN handling varies with platform configuration. A native mismatch can place untagged traffic into different VLANs at opposite ends, so inspect both sides rather than assuming a common default. VLANs provide L2 segmentation; they are not by themselves a substitute for filtering traffic routed between VLANs.
Predict: h1 and h2 are in VLAN 10 on different switches; the inter-switch trunk allows only VLAN 20. ARP broadcasts from h1 do not cross that trunk in VLAN 10, so h1 cannot resolve h2 through that path. After allowing VLAN 10 at both ends, verify VLAN membership, trunk state, MAC learning, and the ARP exchange rather than relying on the configuration alone.

title: VLANs & Trunks
text:
Practice: isolate the failed boundary
Two hosts on different switches use VLAN 10. Both access ports are up and assigned to VLAN 10. The trunk is up, but VLAN 10 is allowed at only one end. Predict what happens to an ARP request and which tables to inspect. Then allow VLAN 10 on both ends and verify the change.
The frame cannot traverse the end that excludes VLAN 10. Check each access port’s VLAN, the allowed and active trunk VLANs on both ends, spanning-tree forwarding state, and source MAC learning. A trunk’s physical link being up is necessary but does not prove that a particular VLAN is forwarded.

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
In high-density network environments—such as multi-tenant data centers, web hosting facilities, residential internet service provider (ISP) networks, hotel guest Wi-Fi networks, corporate DMZs, and out-of-band management networks—operators face a fundamental design dilemma. Multiple untrusted or semi-trusted workloads must reside within the same IPv4 subnet to conserve address space and simplify default gateway routing. However, allowing direct peer-to-peer Layer 2 communication between these hosts presents severe security and operational risks, including ARP spoofing, unauthorized lateral movement, malicious packet sniffing, and broadcast storm degradation.
The naive solution is to place each tenant host into its own dedicated IEEE 802.1Q Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) and assign each tenant a distinct IP subnet. While this achieves total Layer 2 and Layer 3 isolation, it consumes network administrative overhead rapidly and drains IPv4 address space due to subnetwork network IDs, broadcast addresses, and gateway allocations. In an IPv4 network allocating a /30 or /31 prefix per host, address space utilization is extremely inefficient. Furthermore, scaling an infrastructure to thousands of tenants exhausts the traditional 4,094 IEEE 802.1Q VLAN limit long before hardware capacity limits are reached.
Layer 2 isolation technologies solve this problem by decoupling Layer 2 forwarding topologies from Layer 3 IP subnetting. Techniques such as Private VLANs (described in RFC 5517), Linux bridge port isolation, sub-VLAN aggregation (RFC 3069), and IEEE 802.1ad Provider Bridging (Q-in-Q) let operators keep many hosts in one subnet without letting them talk to each other, and carry each customer’s own VLANs across a shared provider network.
As a systems or network engineer operating Linux-based infrastructure, software-defined networks (SDN), or bare-metal hypervisors, you will meet these features on switches and build their Linux equivalents yourself. This chapter covers private VLANs and port isolation, the proxy ARP that makes an isolated subnet usable, what changes for IPv6, and Q-in-Q tagging. The lab builds port isolation and RFC 3069-style routing on a Linux bridge without root.

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
Learning goals

Evaluate the architectural tradeoffs between standard 802.1Q VLAN subnets, Private VLANs (PVLANs), switch port isolation, and 802.1ad Q-in-Q tagging.
Map the functional roles of Private VLAN port types (promiscuous, isolated, community) and VLAN types (primary, secondary isolated, secondary community).
Configure and analyze Linux bridge port isolation using ip link and inspect kernel forwarding rules.
Explain the operational mechanics of kernel-level Proxy ARP for Private VLANs (net.ipv4.conf.IFACE.proxy_arp_pvlan), including routing table lookups, ICMP redirect generation, and dual-ARP race conditions.
Implement IPv6 host isolation within a shared Layer 2 domain using off-link Router Advertisement (RA) prefix flags (RFC 4861 / RFC 5942), RA Guard, and DHCPv6 Shield.
Analyze how Layer 2 security controls (DHCP Snooping, Option 82, Dynamic ARP Inspection) interact with isolated switch ports and broadcast/multicast containment.
Calculate frame size expansion and MTU overhead for 802.1ad Q-in-Q double-tagging across provider backbones.

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
Version note
The hands-on lab experiments in this chapter were executed on a Linux host running kernel Linux 6.12, iproute2 version 6.15.0, and Python 3.13. On the specific host environment used for generating outputs, the userland bridge utility (bridge(8)) was not present, the kernel had no 8021q module, and the bridge was built without VLAN filtering. Consequently, all Q-in-Q commands, bridge vlan syntaxes, and switch vendor configuration examples in this chapter are provided as production reference configurations and clearly marked as (not run here).

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
Private VLANs (RFC 5517) and Port Isolation
Private VLANs (PVLANs), formalized in RFC 5517, extend standard IEEE 802.1Q VLAN structure by partitioning a single broadcast domain (the primary VLAN) into multiple secondary sub-domains. This architecture enables Layer 2 segregation of end hosts while allowing all hosts to share a single IPv4 subnet and default gateway.

Primary and Secondary VLAN Concepts
A Private VLAN domain consists of one Primary VLAN and one or more Secondary VLANs. To the outside network and default gateway, the entire PVLAN structure appears as a single standard VLAN (the Primary VLAN).

Primary VLAN: The overarching VLAN that carries traffic from promiscuous ports downstream to isolated and community ports. It represents the shared Layer 3 IP subnet.
Secondary Isolated VLAN: A sub-VLAN whose ports can communicate only with promiscuous ports. Hosts connected to isolated ports within the same isolated VLAN cannot send traffic to or receive traffic from each other.
Secondary Community VLAN: A sub-VLAN whose ports can communicate with each other and with promiscuous ports, but cannot communicate with ports in any other community VLAN or isolated VLAN.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        PRIMARY VLAN (100)                         |
|                                                                   |
|  +--------------------+  +------------------+  +---------------+  |
|  | Promiscuous Port   |  | Secondary VLAN   |  | Secondary VLAN|  |
|  | (Router / Gateway) |  | Isolated (101)   |  | Community(102)|  |
|  +---------+----------+  +--------+---------+  +-------+-------+  |
+------------|----------------------|--------------------|----------+
             |                      |                    |
       [Default GW]           +-----+-----+        +-----+-----+
                              | Host1 Host2|        | Host3 Host4|
                              +-----------+        +-----------+
                              (Cannot talk)        (Can talk to
                                                   each other)


Port Roles and Communication Matrix
Ports assigned to a Private VLAN domain operate under three distinct functional roles:

Promiscuous Port (P-Port): Connects to Layer 3 routers, firewalls, or gateways. A promiscuous port can send and receive frames to and from all other ports in the PVLAN domain (isolated, community, or other promiscuous ports).
Isolated Port (I-Port): Connects to individual tenant hosts. An isolated port can send frames only to promiscuous ports. Frames received on an isolated port are blocked from reaching any other isolated or community port.
Community Port (C-Port): Connects to hosts belonging to a specific peer group (e.g., a server cluster). A community port can talk to promiscuous ports and other community ports in the same community VLAN, but is isolated from all other community VLANs and isolated ports.

Private VLAN Trunks
When a Private VLAN spans multiple physical Ethernet switches, the primary and secondary VLAN mappings must be preserved across inter-switch link trunks.
A PVLAN Trunk Port carries traffic for primary and secondary VLANs while retaining the double-tagging or secondary tag identification required for destination switch ASICs to enforce port isolation rules. In IEEE 802.1Q tagged frames traversing a standard switch trunk, frames originating from an isolated port travel across the trunk tagged with the Secondary Isolated VLAN ID. When the egress switch receives the frame, it maps the secondary VLAN ID back to the primary domain and permits egress only on promiscuous ports.


Switch Port Isolation (Protected Ports)
Full RFC 5517 Private VLAN configuration requires Enterprise-grade switch ASICs capable of secondary VLAN mapping tables. Simpler layer 2 managed switches offer a lightweight alternative known as Port Isolation or Protected Ports.
When ports on a managed switch are configured as “protected” or “isolated”: - Protected ports cannot forward Layer 2 frames (unicast, multicast, or broadcast) to other protected ports on the same switch. - Protected ports can forward frames to unprotected ports. - Unprotected ports can forward frames to any port (protected or unprotected).
Port isolation does not utilize secondary VLAN tags; it is an ASIC-level egress filtering mask enforced locally on the switch.


Enterprise Switch Configuration Reference
The following snippet illustrates a generic enterprise switch configuration establishing a Private VLAN domain with a gateway on a promiscuous port and tenant servers on isolated ports.
! (not run here)
! Step 1: Define Secondary and Primary VLANs
vlan 101
  private-vlan isolated
!
vlan 100
  private-vlan primary
  private-vlan association 101
!
! Step 2: Configure Promiscuous Gateway Port
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
  description Default Gateway Router
  switchport mode private-vlan promiscuous
  switchport private-vlan mapping 100 101
!
! Step 3: Configure Isolated Tenant Ports
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/2
  description Tenant A Server
  switchport mode private-vlan host
  switchport private-vlan host-association 100 101
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/3
  description Tenant B Server
  switchport mode private-vlan host
  switchport private-vlan host-association 100 101

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
VLAN Aggregation and Sub-VLANs (RFC 3069)
In service provider networks, assigning a full IP subnet per customer causes IP address fragmentation. RFC 3069 defines VLAN Aggregation for Efficient IP Address Allocation, introducing the concepts of Super-VLANs and Sub-VLANs.
In an RFC 3069 architecture: - Multiple Sub-VLANs (each containing a subset of customer hosts) share a single IPv4 subnet address space. - A Super-VLAN aggregates all Sub-VLANs into a logical Layer 3 interface on the router/switch. - Sub-VLANs have no default gateway IP assigned directly to their VLAN interfaces; instead, they share the single IP address assigned to the Super-VLAN interface. - Hosts within Sub-VLANs are prevented from communicating at Layer 2.
                 +--------------------------------+
                 |       Router / L3 Switch       |
                 | Super-VLAN 10 Interface        |
                 | IP: 10.20.0.1/24 (Proxy ARP)   |
                 +---------------+----------------+
                                 |
         +-----------------------+-----------------------+
         |                                               |
+--------+-------+                               +-------+--------+
| Sub-VLAN 11    |                               | Sub-VLAN 12    |
| Host A: 10.20.0.11                             | Host B: 10.20.0.12
+----------------+                               +----------------+
Because Hosts A and B share the same IP subnet (e.g., 10.20.0.0/24) but are segregated into isolated Sub-VLANs at Layer 2, Host A believes Host B is directly on-link. When Host A attempts to send traffic to Host B, it broadcasts an ARP request for 10.20.0.12.
Since Sub-VLAN 11 and Sub-VLAN 12 cannot bridge traffic directly, Host B never receives Host A’s ARP request. To enable communication, the Super-VLAN gateway router must act as a Proxy ARP agent. The router intercepts Host A’s ARP request for Host B, replies with its own MAC address, receives the Ethernet frames from Host A, and forwards them across Layer 3 into Sub-VLAN 12 toward Host B.

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
section: Port Isolation in the Linux Kernel
text:
Port Isolation in the Linux Kernel
The Linux kernel bridge implementation provides native port isolation functionality without requiring complex secondary VLAN definitions. This feature is controlled per-port using the isolated flag on bridge slave interfaces.

The isolated Slave Flag
When a Linux bridge slave interface has its isolated flag set to on: 1. Frames received on an isolated slave interface cannot be forwarded to any other slave interface that also has the isolated flag enabled. 2. Frames received on an isolated slave interface can be forwarded to non-isolated slave interfaces. 3. Frames received on non-isolated slave interfaces can be forwarded to both isolated and non-isolated slave interfaces.
This model directly implements the RFC 5517 promiscuous-versus-isolated port paradigm within a single Linux software bridge. Linux bridge port isolation does not support community groups; all isolated ports on a single bridge belong to a single isolation domain.


Linux Port Isolation Management Syntaxes
Port isolation can be managed using either ip link or the bridge link utility.
Setting isolation using ip link:
# (not run here)
# Set port eth1 as an isolated bridge port
ip link set dev eth1 type bridge_slave isolated on

# Disable isolation on port eth0 (e.g., router interface)
ip link set dev eth0 type bridge_slave isolated off
Setting isolation using bridge link:
# (not run here)
# Enable isolation on eth1
bridge link set dev eth1 isolated on

# Inspect bridge port flags
bridge link show
Checking isolation state via sysfs:
# (not run here)
cat /sys/class/net/eth1/brport/isolated
# Outputs: 1 (enabled) or 0 (disabled)

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
section: Linux Router Integration and Proxy ARP
text:
Linux Router Integration and Proxy ARP
When bridge port isolation prevents hosts on the same IPv4 subnet from reaching each other at Layer 2, inter-host communication requires Layer 3 hairpin forwarding through the default gateway router.
    +-------------------------------------------------------+
    |                    LINUX ROUTER (r)                   |
    |                                                       |
    |  ip_forward = 1                                       |
    |  proxy_arp_pvlan = 1                                  |
    |  send_redirects = 0                                   |
    |                                                       |
    |  IP:  10.20.0.1/24                                    |
    +---------------------------+---------------------------+
                                | (p-r)
    +---------------------------+---------------------------+
    |                     LINUX BRIDGE (sw)                 |
    |                                                       |
    |   p-r (isolated off)                                  |
    |   p-h1 (isolated on)        p-h2 (isolated on)        |
    +---------+----------------------------+----------------+
              |                            |
       (h1 eth0)                    (h2 eth0)
+-------------+-------------+  +-----------+----------------+
| Host 1 (h1)               |  | Host 2 (h2)                |
| IP:  10.20.0.11/24        |  | IP:  10.20.0.12/24        |
+---------------------------+  +----------------------------+

The proxy_arp_pvlan Kernel Parameter
Under standard Linux kernel behavior, Proxy ARP (net.ipv4.conf.IFACE.proxy_arp=1) responds to ARP requests for destinations reachable via other interfaces. However, if an ARP request arrives on eth0 for an IP address that the routing table states is reachable out of that same interface eth0, standard Proxy ARP ignores the request to prevent routing loops and unnecessary hairpinning.
In a Private VLAN or isolated port domain, Host 1 and Host 2 reside on the same interface from the router’s perspective. To force the router to answer ARP requests for addresses located on the same logical ingress interface, the kernel provides the proxy_arp_pvlan sysctl:
# (not run here)
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.eth0.proxy_arp_pvlan=1
When proxy_arp_pvlan=1 is enabled on an interface: 1. The kernel enables Proxy ARP behavior specifically for intra-interface traffic. 2. It does not require globally enabling proxy_arp=1 on the interface. 3. When Host 1 issues an ARP request for Host 2 (10.20.0.12), the router checks its routing table. Because 10.20.0.12 is reachable out of eth0, the router replies to Host 1 with its own MAC address. 4. Host 1 records 10.20.0.12 with the router’s MAC in its neighbour table. 5. Subsequent IP packets sent from Host 1 to Host 2 are framed at Layer 2 to the router’s MAC address. 6. The router receives the packets, decrements IP TTL, and forwards (hairpins) them back out eth0, this time addressed to Host 2’s real MAC address.


Requirements: ip_forward and send_redirects
For Private VLAN routing to function cleanly, two additional IP stack controls must be set on the gateway router:

IP Forwarding Enabled: net.ipv4.ip_forward must be set to 1. If packet forwarding is disabled, the router will answer ARP requests due to proxy_arp_pvlan, but will drop incoming data traffic.
ICMP Redirects Disabled: when a Linux router forwards a packet out the interface it arrived on, it assumes the sender could have reached the next hop directly and sends an ICMP Redirect (type 5, code 1, redirect for host), rate-limited per destination. Here the advice is wrong: the destination is already on-link for the sender, which is exactly the problem. In the lab the redirects were harmless (Linux hosts already treat the destination as on-link and keep using the MAC the router gave them), but they are noise, every hairpinned flow produces them, and you should not rely on how every host stack reacts. Turn them off on the gateway interface:

# (not run here)
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.eth0.send_redirects=0

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
section: IPv6 Considerations: Neighbor Discovery and Off-Link Prefixes
text:
IPv6 Considerations: Neighbor Discovery and Off-Link Prefixes
Unlike IPv4, IPv6 does not use ARP. Neighbor discovery in IPv6 relies on ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation (NS) and Neighbor Advertisement (NA) messages sent over multicast addresses (Solicited-Node Multicast ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX).

The IPv6 Proxy ND Challenge
Linux does not possess an IPv6 kernel equivalent to proxy_arp_pvlan. While Linux supports static Neighbor Discovery Proxying (ip -6 neigh add proxy ...), it does not offer a dynamic proxy_nd_pvlan sysctl that automatically replies to Neighbor Solicitations for all on-link hosts.


The RFC 4861 / RFC 5942 On-Link Model Solution
The standard IPv6 solution for Private VLAN and isolated host domains is to make hosts treat the IPv6 subnet prefix as off-link, as defined in RFC 4861 and refined in RFC 5942.
Under normal IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), a router sends Router Advertisements (RAs) containing Prefix Information Options (PIO). The PIO contains two critical control flags: - L-Flag (On-Link Indicator): When set (1), tells the host that addresses within this prefix are directly reachable on the local Layer 2 link without going through a router. - A-Flag (Autonomous Address-Configuration): When set (1), tells the host to use this prefix to autoconfigure a SLAAC IPv6 address.
To enforce IPv6 host isolation at Layer 3 without proxy ND: 1. The gateway router advertises RAs with the L-flag cleared (L=0) and the A-flag set (A=1). 2. Upon receiving the RA, the host autoconfigures an IPv6 address (e.g., 2001:db8:1::10/64) because A=1. 3. Because L=0, the host’s IPv6 protocol stack marks the /64 prefix as off-link. 4. When the host sends traffic to another IP in 2001:db8:1::/64 (e.g., 2001:db8:1::20), the host does not send a Neighbor Solicitation for the target host’s address. Instead, it immediately forwards the packet to the Default Gateway’s Link-Local IPv6 address (fe80::1). 5. The gateway router forwards the packet to the destination host.
# Generic radvd.conf prefix stanza enforcing off-link configuration
# (not run here)
prefix 2001:db8:1::/64 {
    AdvOnLink off;        # L-flag = 0 (Forces traffic to Default Gateway)
    AdvAutonomous on;     # A-flag = 1 (Enables SLAAC address generation)
};


IPv6 First-Hop Security
Because isolated ports block inter-host communication, rogue IPv6 hosts cannot directly launch Neighbor Advertisement spoofing against peers. However, to prevent tenant hosts on isolated ports from impersonating IPv6 routers, the switch infrastructure must deploy: - RA Guard (RFC 6105): Blocks incoming ICMPv6 Router Advertisement packets on isolated host-facing ports. - DHCPv6-Shield (RFC 7610): Blocks incoming DHCPv6 server response messages originating from host ports.

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
section: Operational Interactions: Broadcast, Multicast, DHCP, and DAI
text:
Operational Interactions: Broadcast, Multicast, DHCP, and DAI
Port isolation drastically alters standard Layer 2 broadcast and security protocol behaviors.

Broadcast and Multicast Containment
On a standard Linux bridge or Ethernet switch, broadcast frames (such as ARP requests or IPv4 subnet broadcasts) and unlearned multicast frames are flooded out every operational slave interface except the receiving ingress interface.
When port isolation (isolated on) is configured: - A broadcast or multicast frame received on an isolated port is flooded only to non-isolated ports. - Isolated ports never receive broadcast or multicast frames originated by another isolated port. - Non-isolated ports (e.g., gateway router ports) receive broadcast frames from isolated ports and can reply normally.
This limits who hears ARP, DHCP, mDNS and NetBIOS broadcasts, so tenants cannot discover each other by listening. It does not stop a tenant from flooding the gateway.


DHCP Snooping and Option 82
In Private VLAN environments, hosts depend on central DHCP servers attached to promiscuous/non-isolated ports. To prevent malicious hosts on isolated ports from running rogue DHCP servers, switches employ DHCP Snooping.
DHCP Snooping marks isolated ports as untrusted and promiscuous gateway ports as trusted: - DHCP client requests (DISCOVER, REQUEST) received on untrusted ports are forwarded only to trusted ports. - DHCP server responses (OFFER, ACK) received on untrusted ports are dropped immediately. - DHCP Option 82 (Relay Agent Information Info): Switch ASICs append Option 82 metadata (circuit-id, remote-id) specifying the physical switch port and PVLAN ID from which the request originated, allowing the central DHCP server to assign static or leased IP addresses tailored to exact port locations.


Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)
When Proxy ARP is utilized across isolated domains, tenant hosts receive ARP replies containing the router’s MAC address for peer IP destinations. If a malicious tenant attempts to broadcast falsified ARP replies to claim another host’s IP, Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) intercepts ARP packets on untrusted isolated ports. DAI validates the ARP sender IP-to-MAC binding against the hardware DHCP Snooping database before allowing the frame to traverse the switch.

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
IEEE 802.1ad Provider Bridging (Q-in-Q)
While Private VLANs and port isolation address tenant segregation within a single broadcast domain, service providers offering Metro Ethernet or Layer 2 VPN (L2VPN) services must transport hundreds of distinct customer VLAN topologies across a shared core network. IEEE 802.1ad (commonly known as Q-in-Q or Double-Tagging) solves this scaling challenge.

S-Tag and C-Tag Frame Architecture
Standard IEEE 802.1Q tagging appends a single 4-byte header to an Ethernet frame. IEEE 802.1ad prepends an outer Service Tag (S-Tag) to an inner customer frame that already contains a Customer Tag (C-Tag).
Standard Ethernet Frame (Un-tagged):
+-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+----------+
| Dest MAC (6B)     | Src MAC (6B)      | EtherType (2B)    | Payload  |
+-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+----------+

IEEE 802.1Q Single-Tagged Frame (C-Tag):
+---------------+---------------+-------------------+---------------+----------+
| Dest MAC (6B) | Src MAC (6B)  | TPID: 0x8100 (2B) | TCI/VID (2B)  | Payload  |
+---------------+---------------+-------------------+---------------+----------+

IEEE 802.1ad Double-Tagged Frame (Q-in-Q):
+---------------+---------------+-------------------+---------------+-------------------+---------------+----------+
| Dest MAC (6B) | Src MAC (6B)  | S-TPID: 0x88a8(2B)| S-VID (2B)    | C-TPID: 0x8100(2B)| C-VID (2B)    | Payload  |
+---------------+---------------+-------------------+---------------+-------------------+---------------+----------+
Key Protocol Differences: - C-Tag (Customer Tag): EtherType / TPID (Tag Protocol Identifier) = 0x8100. Carries customer-internal VLAN IDs (1–4094). - S-Tag (Service Tag): EtherType / TPID = 0x88a8 (IEEE 802.1ad standard). Carries service provider VLAN IDs (1–4094). Legacy provider implementations sometimes used 0x9100 or 0x8100 as outer TPIDs. - Tag Transparency: The provider core network routes traffic based exclusively on the outer S-VID (0x88a8). The inner C-Tag (0x8100) passes through the provider network completely unaltered, allowing customers to use arbitrary overlapping VLAN IDs inside their assigned S-VLAN.


Frame Overhead and MTU Calculations
Each 802.1Q/802.1ad VLAN tag adds 4 bytes of header overhead to the physical Ethernet frame.

Standard Un-tagged Ethernet Frame (Max Transmission Unit): 1500 bytes IP payload + 14 bytes Ethernet header + 4 bytes FCS = 1518 bytes.
Single-Tagged 802.1Q Frame: 1500 bytes IP + 14 bytes Eth + 4 bytes C-Tag + 4 bytes FCS = 1522 bytes.
Double-Tagged 802.1ad Q-in-Q Frame: 1500 bytes IP + 14 bytes Eth + 4 bytes S-Tag + 4 bytes C-Tag + 4 bytes FCS = 1526 bytes.

To prevent packet fragmentation or frame drops at provider edge interfaces, all intermediate switches, routers, and physical trunks in the provider core must be configured with an increased Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) headroom—typically setting physical interface MTUs to 1504 bytes (IP MTU equivalent) or jumbo frame sizes (e.g., 9000 bytes).


Linux Q-in-Q Configuration Reference
Linux supports 802.1ad double tagging via raw ip link sub-interface configurations or VLAN-aware bridges.
Stacked ip link syntax:
# (not run here)
# 1. Create outer Service VLAN interface (S-Tag VID 100, TPID 802.1ad)
ip link add link eth0 name eth0.100 type vlan proto 802.1ad id 100

# 2. Create inner Customer VLAN interface (C-Tag VID 10, TPID 802.1q)
ip link add link eth0.100 name eth0.100.10 type vlan id 10

# 3. Bring up interfaces
ip link set dev eth0.100 up
ip link set dev eth0.100.10 up
VLAN-Aware Bridge syntax for Q-in-Q Provider Edge:
# (not run here)
# Create a bridge using 802.1ad protocol for outer encapsulation
ip link add dev br-provider type bridge vlan_filtering 1 vlan_protocol 802.1ad
ip link set dev br-provider up

# Configure customer-facing port eth1 to push S-Tag 100 on untagged ingress
bridge vlan add dev eth1 vid 100 pvid untagged


Kernel Support Probe Script
The shell script below probes kernel module availability and tests whether 802.1ad VLAN device creation or bridge VLAN filtering are supported on the current execution host.
qinq-probe.sh:
#!/bin/sh
# Can this kernel do QinQ? Run as: unshare -urn sh qinq-probe.sh
ip link add eth0 type veth peer name eth1
echo '$ ip link add link eth0 name eth0.100 type vlan proto 802.1ad id 100'
ip link add link eth0 name eth0.100 type vlan proto 802.1ad id 100
echo '$ ip link add br0 type bridge vlan_filtering 1 vlan_protocol 802.1ad'
ip link add br0 type bridge vlan_filtering 1 vlan_protocol 802.1ad
echo '$ ip link add br0 type bridge   # plain bridge'
ip link add br0 type bridge && echo ok
echo "loaded bridge/vlan modules: $(ls /sys/module | grep -E '^(bridge|8021q)$' | tr '\n' ' ')"
Executing this script on the target environment generates diagnostic outputs indicating missing kernel modules or netlink attributes:
$ ip link add link eth0 name eth0.100 type vlan proto 802.1ad id 100
Error: Unknown device type.
$ ip link add br0 type bridge vlan_filtering 1 vlan_protocol 802.1ad
RTNETLINK answers: Operation not supported
$ ip link add br0 type bridge   # plain bridge
ok
loaded bridge/vlan modules: bridge

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
The lab
To demonstrate Linux bridge port isolation, Proxy ARP, ICMP redirect dynamics, and broadcast containment without requiring physical switches, we execute a rootless network namespace laboratory using unshare -urnmu.
The topology consists of a central Linux bridge (sw) holding four veth interfaces: 1. Port p-r connects router r (10.20.0.1/24). It stays a normal (promiscuous) port. 2. Port p-h1 connects tenant h1 (10.20.0.11/24); isolated from Section 2 on. 3. Port p-h2 connects tenant h2 (10.20.0.12/24); isolated from Section 2 on. 4. Port p-h3 connects h3 (10.20.0.13/24), which stays a normal port.
Every host’s interface is called eth0 inside its own namespace; MAC addresses are random on each run.
Every namespace, including r, runs udp.py as a UDP echo server that reports the TTL it received. This host’s ip_default_ttl is 127 rather than the usual 64, so 127 means the datagram was switched and 126 means it was routed once.
               +----------------------------------------+
               |           ROUTER NAMESPACE (r)         |
               |                                        |
               | IP:  10.20.0.1/24                      |
               +-------------------+--------------------+
                                   | eth0
                                   |
                                   | p-r (isolated off)
               +-------------------+--------------------+
               |           SWITCH NAMESPACE (sw)        |
               |           Bridge Device: br0           |
               |                                        |
               | p-h1 (isolated) p-h2 (isolated) p-h3   |
               +------+--------------+-------------+----+
                      |              |             |
                 eth0 |         eth0 |        eth0 |
                      |              |             |
           +----------+---+      +---+----------+  +-----+----------+
           | TENANT (h1)  |      | TENANT (h2)  |  | TENANT (h3)  |
           | 10.20.0.11   |      | 10.20.0.12   |  | 10.20.0.13   |
           | (Isolated)   |      | (Isolated)   |  | (Un-isolated)|
           +--------------+      +--------------+  +--------------+

Lab files
Two files: udp.py (echo server and client, with DF set) and pvlan.sh (the topology and the six tests). Run unshare -urnmu sh pvlan.sh.
udp.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Tiny UDP echo with DF set.  server: udp.py serve PORT
client: udp.py send IP PORT PAYLOAD_BYTES  -> prints reply TTL or timeout"""
import socket, sys
IP_MTU_DISCOVER, IP_PMTUDISC_DO, IP_RECVTTL, IP_TTL = 10, 2, 12, 2
if sys.argv[1] == "serve":
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_IP, IP_RECVTTL, 1)
    s.bind(("0.0.0.0", int(sys.argv[2])))
    while True:
        data, anc, _, peer = s.recvmsg(65535, 64)
        ttl = next((int.from_bytes(d[:4], "little") for l, t, d in anc if t == IP_TTL), -1)
        s.sendto(f"{socket.gethostname()} got {len(data)} B from {peer[0]} ttl={ttl}".encode(), peer)
else:
    ip, port, n = sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3]), int(sys.argv[4])
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_IP, IP_MTU_DISCOVER, IP_PMTUDISC_DO)
    s.settimeout(1.5)
    try:
        s.sendto(b"x" * n, (ip, port))
        print(f"  {n:4d} B -> {ip}: {s.recv(200).decode()}")
    except socket.timeout:
        print(f"  {n:4d} B -> {ip}: timeout")
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"  {n:4d} B -> {ip}: {e.strerror}")
pvlan.sh:
#!/bin/sh
# Private VLAN behaviour with Linux bridge port isolation.
# sw: bridge br0; r = router on a promiscuous (non-isolated) port;
# h1, h2 on isolated ports; h3 on a normal port.
# Run as: unshare -urnmu sh pvlan.sh   (no root, no installs)
set -e
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
mount -t tmpfs none /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
sc() { ip netns exec "$1" sh -c "echo $3 > /proc/sys/$(echo $2 | tr . /)"; }
rd() { ip netns exec "$1" cat /proc/sys/$(echo $2 | tr . /); }
for n in sw r h1 h2 h3; do ip netns add $n; ip -n $n link set lo up; done
ip -n sw link add br0 type bridge
ip -n sw link set br0 up
for h in r h1 h2 h3; do
  ip link add eth0 netns $h type veth peer name p-$h netns sw
  ip -n sw link set p-$h master br0
  ip -n sw link set p-$h up
  ip -n $h link set eth0 up
done
ip -n r  addr add 10.20.0.1/24  dev eth0
ip -n h1 addr add 10.20.0.11/24 dev eth0
ip -n h2 addr add 10.20.0.12/24 dev eth0
ip -n h3 addr add 10.20.0.13/24 dev eth0
for h in h1 h2 h3; do ip -n $h route add default via 10.20.0.1; done
PIDS=""

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
Reading the output

Section 1: a plain bridge
Every pair answers with ttl=127: one broadcast domain, frames switched directly, nothing routed.


Section 2: two isolated ports
ip -d link confirms isolated on for p-h1 and isolated off for p-r. The matrix is the private VLAN matrix: h1 -> 10.20.0.1 (router, normal port) works, h1 -> 10.20.0.13 (h3, normal port) works, h3 -> 10.20.0.12 works, and the two isolated hosts time out in both directions. The neighbour table explains why: 10.20.0.12 FAILED. h1’s ARP broadcast for h2 was flooded only to non-isolated ports, so h2 never saw it, and h1 never got as far as sending the datagram.


Section 3: the router answers ARP for the isolated hosts
On r: ip_forward=1, proxy_arp_pvlan=1, and proxy_arp left at 0, which shows the kernel documentation’s point that proxy_arp_pvlan works on its own. Now h1 -> h2 and h2 -> h1 both succeed with ttl=126, one routed hop. h1’s neighbour table maps 10.20.0.12 to the same MAC as 10.20.0.1, the router’s MAC, so h1 frames its packets to the router, which forwards them back out the same interface to h2. 10.20.0.13 still maps to h3’s own MAC and h1 -> h3 still arrives with ttl=127: h3 is not isolated, its own ARP reply reached h1, and that traffic stays switched.


Section 4: redirects
r’s Icmp OutRedirects is 3. Every packet r forwards out the interface it came in on qualifies for a redirect; the count is lower than the number of hairpinned packets because Linux rate-limits redirects per destination. ip route get 10.20.0.12 on h1 shows the destination as directly on-link (dev eth0, no via), so a redirect has nothing to change, and the traffic kept working.


Section 5: redirects off
After send_redirects=0 on all and eth0, the same matrix passes and the counter stays at 3: no new redirects.


Section 6: broadcast
h1 sends one UDP broadcast to 10.20.0.255. r and h3, on normal ports, hear it; h2, on an isolated port, hears nothing. Isolation applies to broadcast and multicast as well as unicast.

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
In production
When deploying Private VLANs, port isolation, and Proxy ARP in production Linux environments, configurations must be persisted using standard networking daemons, sysctl files, or enterprise switch templates.

Systemd-networkd Production Example
With systemd-networkd (version 251 or later), set Isolated= in the [Bridge] section of the port’s .network file (see systemd.network(5)):
# /etc/systemd/network/10-bridge-slave-eth1.network
# (not run here)
[Match]
Name=eth1

[Network]
Bridge=br0

[Bridge]
Isolated=yes


Production Gateway Sysctl Configuration
To ensure a Linux gateway router persistently handles Private VLAN Proxy ARP routing while suppressing ICMP redirects, create a dedicated /etc/sysctl.d/ drop-in configuration file:
# /etc/sysctl.d/90-pvlan-gateway.conf
# (not run here)
# Enable global IPv4 packet forwarding
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1

# Enable Proxy ARP for Intra-Interface Private VLAN Traffic on eth0
net.ipv4.conf.eth0.proxy_arp_pvlan = 1

# Disable ICMP Redirect Generation (Prevents path invalidation)
net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.eth0.send_redirects = 0
Apply immediately in production:
# (not run here)
sysctl --system

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
Gotchas

Two ARP replies for non-isolated hosts: with proxy_arp_pvlan, the router answers ARP for any address whose route points back out the same interface, including hosts on normal ports such as h3, while the real host answers too. Linux keeps the first answer for locktime (default one second) and ignores a different one inside that window, so usually the faster responder wins; in the lab, h3’s own answer won. If the router wins, the traffic just hairpins through it.
Redirects: without send_redirects=0, the gateway sends a redirect for hairpinned traffic. In the lab they changed nothing because the destination was already on-link, but they are wasted packets and log noise, and host stacks differ in what they do with them.
Lack of IPv6 proxy_arp_pvlan Kernel Dynamic Equivalent: Linux lacks a sysctl for dynamic intra-interface IPv6 Neighbor Discovery proxying. IPv6 tenant isolation must be designed using off-link prefix flags (L=0) in Router Advertisements or static ip -6 neigh add proxy configurations.
Q-in-Q MTU Blackholes: Adding 802.1ad outer S-Tags increases frame sizes by 4 bytes (or 8 bytes for double tagging). If provider core trunks are left at standard 1500-byte MTU, customer frames carrying 1500-byte IP payloads will be dropped silently due to MTU exhaustion.
DHCP Snooping Option 82 Rejection: Many enterprise switches automatically append Option 82 metadata to DHCP requests coming from isolated ports. If the upstream DHCP server or relay agent is not configured to accept Option 82 headers, it will drop client DHCP requests silently.
Asymmetric Traffic Paths with Promiscuous Trunks: When Private VLANs span multiple physical switches, primary and secondary VLAN mappings must be configured identically across all trunk interfaces. Mismatched secondary VLAN IDs cause frames to egress wrong port roles or drop silently at ASIC ingress.
The bridge device is not isolated: if the host that runs the bridge has an address on br0, every isolated port can reach that host. Isolation is between ports of one bridge only; a second path (another bridge, a routed interface, a VXLAN port left non-isolated) is a way around it.
Kernel Module Dependencies: Configuring 802.1ad VLAN sub-interfaces requires the 8021q kernel module. Without it, ip link add ... type vlan fails with Error: Unknown device type.; a bridge built without VLAN filtering rejects vlan_filtering 1 with RTNETLINK answers: Operation not supported, both seen in the probe above.

title: Private VLANs, Port Isolation and Q-in-Q: Separating Tenants at Layer 2
text:
Exercises

Calculate Q-in-Q Frame Sizes: A customer transmits a standard 1500-byte IP packet over an Ethernet connection. Calculate the precise frame byte length (including Ethernet header, C-Tag, S-Tag, and Frame Check Sequence) at the customer interface, single-tagged provider interface, and double-tagged Q-in-Q core trunk. Determine the minimum MTU required on the provider switches.
Diagnose Proxy ARP Redirect Failure: In a test lab, Host A (10.0.0.10) can ping Host B (10.0.0.20) for 5 seconds after clearing ARP caches, after which all ICMP traffic times out. Packet captures show Host A receiving ICMP Redirect messages from gateway 10.0.0.1. Explain the exact sequence of packet exchanges causing this failure and write the sysctl commands to fix it.
Simulate IPv6 Off-Link Prefix Isolation: Using unshare or network namespaces, set up an IPv6 gateway using radvd or dnsmasq. Configure the daemon to advertise prefix 2001:db8:100::/64 with the on-link flag disabled (L=0). Verify using ip -6 route show on a host namespace that the default route is targeted to the router link-local address and that no on-link route exists for the /64 prefix.
Isolation and the bridge’s own address: give br0 in sw the address 10.20.0.254/24, run the echo server there, and check from isolated h1 and h2. Explain the result and how you would stop it.
Who wins the ARP race: in Section 3, add a 50 ms delay on h3’s link with tc on a lab host (the lab host here has no tc), flush h1’s neighbour table, and send to h3 again. Which MAC does h1 store, what TTL arrives, and what changes if you set h1’s net.ipv4.neigh.eth0.locktime to 0?
Community ports: Linux has one isolation group per bridge. Design two “communities” using two bridges and a router, and list what you lose compared with a switch’s community VLANs.

title: Loop Prevention
text:
Loop Prevention
Redundant L2 links are good for resilience and catastrophic without loop control. Broadcasts and unknown unicasts circulate forever; MAC tables flap; the LAN melts. This chapter covers the spanning tree family as a model (not a vendor certification deep dive) and how to see loops in the lab.

title: Loop Prevention
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain why Ethernet needs loop prevention

Describe root bridge election and port roles at a conceptual level

Predict a blocked port in a simple triangle of switches

Build a loop, observe the blast, then enable prevention

Prefer design alternatives when L2 redundancy is the wrong tool

title: Loop Prevention
text:
Why loops kill L2
Ethernet has no TTL on frames. In a loop:

Broadcast / unknown unicast is flooded

Copies multiply around the cycle

CPUs and links saturate

Learning oscillates (MAC seen on alternating ports)

IP routers do not save you inside a pure L2 domain.

title: Loop Prevention
text:
Spanning tree behavior
Classic STP/RSTP/MSTP ideas:



Idea
Meaning




Root bridge
Reference switch (lowest priority/BID wins)


Root port
Each non-root switch’s best path toward root


Designated port
Best port on a segment toward downstream


Blocked / alternate
Redundant path held in reserve


BPDU
Control frames that build the tree



Modern networks often use RSTP or vendor rapid variants; data centers may avoid large L2 domains entirely (L3 fabric). Still, you must recognize STP language on campus gear and many NOS features.

Priority and ties
Lower bridge priority wins. Ties break by MAC. In labs, set priorities explicitly so root placement is intentional:
sw1 priority better (numerically lower) → root
sw2/sw3 farther


Port states (classic story)
Blocking → Listening → Learning → Forwarding (RSTP simplifies roles/states). During convergence, expect transient blackholes—measure them in drills.

title: Loop Prevention
text:
Design alternatives (model maturity)



Approach
Loop story




STP/RSTP on bridged triangle
Protocol blocks one link


L3 access / routed triangle
No L2 loop; ECMP at L3


MC-LAG / bundling
Multi-chassis tricks (complex)


Single homing
No redundancy, no loop



For many greenfield labs after this chapter, prefer L3 redundancy. Learn STP so you can operate brownfield and understand failure domains.

text:
Lab: three switches, intentional loop
    sw1

    - endpoints: ["sw1:eth2", "sw3:eth1"]

    - endpoints: ["h3:eth1", "sw3:eth3"]


Dangerous mode: dumb bridges without STP
#!/bin/sh
# config/sw-loop.sh — NO STP (for short controlled drill only!)
set -e
apk add --no-cache iproute2 bridge >/dev/null
ip link add br0 type bridge
ip link set br0 up
for i in 1 2 3; do
  ip link set eth$i up 2>/dev/null || true
  ip link set eth$i master br0 2>/dev/null || true
done
sleep infinity
Warning: Run the loop experiment briefly on an isolated lab host. Broadcast storms can stress CPU.


Observe storm (careful)
# terminal 1
docker exec clab-l2-loop-h2 ping -f 10.10.0.3 &
# or send broadcasts
docker exec clab-l2-loop-sw1 ip -s link
# counters explode
Destroy promptly:
sudo containerlab destroy -t l2-loop.clab.yml --cleanup


Safer mode: enable STP on the bridge
Linux bridge STP:
ip link add br0 type bridge
ip link set br0 type bridge stp_state 1
ip link set br0 up
# attach ports...
# inspect
docker exec clab-l2-loop-sw1 cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/stp_state
# port states under /sys/class/net/br0/brif/*/state
Predict: One of the triangle links is blocked; ping between h2 and h3 still works via remaining tree; storm does not persist.
Observe:
docker exec clab-l2-loop-h2 ping -c 5 10.10.0.3
# check which port is blocking on each sw
for s in sw1 sw2 sw3; do
  echo "== $s =="
  docker exec clab-l2-loop-$s sh -c 'for p in /sys/class/net/br0/brif/*/state; do echo $p $(cat $p); done'
done

Which link is most likely blocked?

title: Loop Prevention
section: Why a loop is a forwarding problem
text:
Why a loop is a forwarding problem
Ethernet frames do not carry an IP-style TTL. In a forwarding loop, a flooded broadcast or unknown-unicast frame can circulate and be replicated; source MACs may be learned repeatedly on different ports. High link utilization, MAC movement, and control-plane instability can reinforce each other. Spanning tree prevents a subset of redundant L2 paths from forwarding simultaneously while maintaining a loop-free active topology for its spanning-tree instance.
Bridges exchange BPDUs and elect a root based on bridge identifiers; other bridges choose a root port using path cost and tie-breakers. Port roles and states determine which paths forward. The exact state names and convergence behavior depend on STP variant and platform. A topology change can require MAC relearning, and a link failure is not necessarily invisible during convergence. Edge-port settings are for ports connected to end devices; applying them carelessly to a switch link can undermine loop protection.
In a lab, compare show spanning-tree on both switches with a link-down event and with a capture or counter from an actual data flow. A forwarding topology, a stable control-plane view, and end-to-end reachability are related but separate observations.

title: Spanning Tree: Elections, Roles and Failure Analysis
text:
Spanning Tree: Elections, Roles and Failure Analysis
Spanning tree does not simply disable the slowest link. For each tree or instance, bridges exchange information, select a root and calculate a loop-free set of forwarding ports. The result depends on bridge IDs, path costs, port IDs and the protocol instance. Work through the election before changing a production priority or cost.

title: Spanning Tree: Elections, Roles and Failure Analysis
text:
Compare information in order
A bridge ID combines priority-related bits with a MAC address; the exact priority field and any system-ID extension depend on the spanning-tree variant and instance. The lowest complete bridge ID wins the root election. Explicitly configure primary and secondary root intent rather than leaving root placement to MAC addresses. Confirm the actual root ID on every switch and instance; a configured priority is not evidence of the resulting election.
Each non-root bridge chooses its root port using the best received path to the root. Compare the root ID first, then the total root path cost including the receiving port’s cost. If those tie, compare the advertising bridge ID and advertising port ID; local port identification resolves a remaining tie where applicable. A segment’s designated port advertises the best information to that segment: root ID, root path cost, bridge ID, then port ID break ties. Read the actual implementation’s output and cost method, especially with per-VLAN trees, link aggregation, or MST regions.
A port role describes its place in the tree; a port state says how it handles ordinary data. In RSTP, root and designated ports normally forward after convergence, while an alternate port normally discards and provides an alternate route toward the root. A backup port represents a redundant connection to a segment for which the same bridge is designated; it is not simply another name for alternate. RSTP uses discarding, learning and forwarding states. Classic STP also names listening and blocking states. Control BPDUs can be processed while ordinary data is discarded.



RSTP triangle and port roles

title: Spanning Tree: Elections, Roles and Failure Analysis
text:
Worked triangle
Use the three-switch workbook topology as a physical pattern. For the calculation below assume one common RSTP instance, three point-to-point links, equal port costs of 4 on both ends of every link, and the following bridge IDs ordered A < B < C. These values are chosen for arithmetic; real defaults can use a different cost scale.



Bridge
Priority
MAC used in bridge ID
Ports




A
4096
02:00:00:00:00:01
a-b, a-c


B
8192
02:00:00:00:00:02
b-a, b-c


C
12288
02:00:00:00:00:03
c-a, c-b




Root: A has the lowest bridge ID, so A is root and has root cost 0. Its ports toward B and C are designated for those segments.
Root ports: B’s direct path through b-a costs 4; through C it costs 8. C’s direct path through c-a costs 4; through B it costs 8. Their direct ports are root ports.
B–C segment: both bridges advertise root cost 4. B has the lower bridge ID, so b-c is designated. C’s c-b is alternate and discarding. The root and designated ports forward in the converged tree.




Link
End 1
End 2




A–B
A designated / forwarding
B root / forwarding


A–C
A designated / forwarding
C root / forwarding


B–C
B designated / forwarding
C alternate / discarding



If A–C fails, C’s path through B costs 8. c-b becomes C’s root port and forwards after reconvergence; b-c remains designated. When A–C returns, the original calculation applies again. Actual interruption depends on link detection, BPDU exchange, transition behavior and endpoint traffic; it is not guaranteed to be zero.
Now restore all links and change only C’s receiving cost on c-a from 4 to 12. The path through B costs 8, so c-b becomes C’s root port; c-a is no longer its root port. A’s a-c remains designated, while C’s c-a is alternate/discarding in the stable tree. The values are directional: changing C’s local receiving cost does not change B’s port cost.

title: Spanning Tree: Elections, Roles and Failure Analysis
text:
Rapid transitions and topology changes
On suitable point-to-point links, RSTP uses proposal/agreement and synchronization to move toward forwarding without waiting for the full classic timer sequence. Edge ports are intended for end stations and can transition rapidly; connecting a bridge to an edge port changes the assumptions. Legacy peers, shared links, lost BPDUs and platform compatibility behavior can change convergence. Measure rather than promising a fixed failover time.
When the active topology changes, bridges need to update learned forwarding locations. Topology-change signaling accelerates handling of stale MAC information; the exact flushing or aging behavior depends on the protocol and implementation. Expect transient unknown-unicast flooding and inspect MAC movement as well as port state. A new tree can be correct while a VLAN mismatch, stale neighbor entry, or blocked upstream route still prevents the application from working.

title: Spanning Tree: Elections, Roles and Failure Analysis
text:
Protection controls and boundaries

BPDU guard on an intended host-facing edge port reacts to unexpected BPDUs, commonly by disabling the port. It protects root placement but can interrupt a legitimate downstream switch; recovery behavior varies.
Root guard prevents a downstream port from becoming a path to a superior root. It is useful at a defined boundary where a downstream device must not influence root placement.
Loop guard addresses certain cases where expected BPDUs stop arriving on a non-designated port, reducing the risk of it transitioning to forwarding incorrectly. It does not repair every physical fault or replace unidirectional-link detection.
BPDU filtering and disabling STP are not interchangeable with guard. Suppressing control traffic on a redundant bridge link can create a loop. Test features on the actual platform and understand which ports and instances they affect.

MST maps VLANs into spanning-tree instances. Region name, revision and VLAN-to-instance mapping must agree to form the intended region; inspect boundary behavior rather than assuming identical VLAN names imply matching configuration. Different per-VLAN or per-instance trees can have different root and blocked ports. Never infer the active path for VLAN 20 from the output for VLAN 10 without checking the relevant instance.

title: Spanning Tree: Elections, Roles and Failure Analysis
text:
Practice and verify
Using the workbook’s three-switch lab, record device software versions and configure the IDs and costs above using your platform’s syntax. The workbook may use a different STP mode and interface names, so align the instance, trunk VLANs and path-cost scale first. Predict each port’s role before reading output; then record root ID, root cost, port role/state and BPDU counters on all switches. Repeat the A–C failure and the C-side cost change, allowing convergence between steps. Send a modest continuous test stream between hosts, timestamp loss and recovery, and verify MAC learning and both traffic directions. Restore the baseline after each test.
For a guarded edge-port drill, use an isolated spare port and test switch. Record the expected guard action and recovery procedure first; introduce a BPDU, verify the event and affected port, then restore the original state. Do not connect the spare switch in a way that creates an uncontrolled loop. The exercise is a platform-neutral procedure and has not been validated on a particular switch implementation.
Questions: Why does B win designation on B–C even though its bridge priority is worse than A’s? How does an altered C-side cost affect C’s root port? Why can a port show physical link up while user traffic is blocked? What evidence distinguishes an STP issue from a trunk VLAN mismatch?
Further reading: IEEE 802.1w project, IEEE MST project, and Linux bridge documentation.

title: Link Aggregation
text:
Link Aggregation
Link aggregation (LAG / bonding / etherchannel-class ideas) combines multiple physical links into one logical link: more bandwidth, faster failover, and fewer STP blocked paths between the same pair of devices—when both ends agree.

Hashing
Flows distribute across members by a hash (MAC/IP/L4 ports depending on config). One TCP flow typically stays on one member—do not expect a single iperf stream to fill N× bandwidth.

apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils >/dev/null
# fallback if bonding unavailable: sequential routes demo only
if ip link add bond0 type bond mode 802.3ad 2>/dev/null; then

  ip link set eth2 down

  ip link set eth2 master bond0
