title: Link Aggregation
text:
Why a bundle has limits
A link aggregation group presents several physical links as one logical interface to the network. Member links must be compatible with the implementation’s aggregation rules and connected to the intended peer or supported multi-chassis system. LACP exchanges information that helps peers agree which links may participate; a configured member is not necessarily selected, synchronized, and forwarding. Static aggregation omits that negotiation and therefore depends even more on both ends matching.
A switch normally chooses a member using a hash over selected header fields so that packets of a given flow tend to remain ordered. The exact fields and hash are platform-dependent. Four 10 Gb/s members do not imply that one ordinary flow can use 40 Gb/s; a single flow may be limited to one 10 Gb/s member, and uneven flow distribution can leave one member busy while another is idle. More independent flows can improve distribution but do not guarantee perfect balance.
On member failure, surviving links may carry remapped flows, but total available capacity falls and transient loss or reordering is possible. A minimum-links setting can make the bundle unavailable when too few members remain, if the platform supports and configures it. Verify physical state, LACP partner and member state, port-channel state, member counters, and actual traffic. An up logical interface alone does not establish that every member forwards or that hashing is balanced.
Predict: with two equal members, one member fails while aggregate demand is greater than the survivor’s capacity. The logical bundle may remain up, but queues and drops can rise. Check per-member utilization and the configured minimum-links policy before concluding that aggregation failed to protect the link.

title: Link Aggregation
text:
Summary

LAG = one logical link from multiple physical members

Prefer LACP in real life; static only with tight control

Hashing limits single-flow throughput

Verify both ends; failover-test by shutting members

Unbundled parallel L2 links reintroduce STP/loop problems

title: L2 Failure Drills
text:
L2 Failure Drills
This chapter is a practice arena. You combine Ethernet, VLANs, loop prevention, and aggregation under intentional failure. Competence is measured by evidence and recovery, not by green first pings.

title: L2 Failure Drills
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Run a structured failure catalog against an L2 lab

Collect the minimum evidence set for each class of break

Recover cleanly and re-verify

Write short incident notes a peer can follow

Know when an “L2 issue” is actually L3 or host firewall

title: L2 Failure Drills
text:
Baseline lab
Use a multi-switch VLAN lab (from the VLANs chapter) with:

Two switches, trunk between them

VLAN 10 and VLAN 20

Hosts h1/h3 in VLAN 10, h2/h4 in VLAN 20

Optional inter-VLAN router for a subset of drills

Document addressing in addressing.md. Ensure ./verify.sh is green before any inject.

Evidence kit
# Host
ip -br a
ip neigh
ping -c 3 -W 1 <target>
tcpdump -ni eth1 -e -c 30 arp or icmp

# Switch / bridge
bridge vlan show
bridge fdb show
ip -s link
# STP port states if enabled
Save outputs under journal.md with timestamps.

title: L2 Failure Drills
text:
Drill catalog
For each drill: predict → inject → observe → restore → harden.

Drill 1 — Access port wrong VLAN
Inject: Move h1’s switch port from VLAN 10 to VLAN 20 (PVID change).
Predict: h1 cannot ARP h3; may see wrong subnet peers if any; verify.sh fails.
Observe: bridge vlan show, tcpdump for ARP who-has never answered by h3.
Restore: Correct PVID/untagged VLAN.
Harden: Label ports in diagrams; negative test in verify (optional).



Drill 2 — Trunk missing VLAN
Inject: Remove VLAN 10 from trunk allow list on one switch only.
Predict: Local VLAN 10 still works on that switch; cross-switch VLAN 10 dies; VLAN 20 may still work.
Observe: Asymmetric “works on same switch only.”
Restore: Re-add VID on both ends.
Harden: Checklist “both ends allow list.”



Drill 3 — Native VLAN mismatch
Inject: Native/PVID untagged mapping differs on trunk ends.
Predict: Untagged frames land in different broadcast domains; confusing intermittent leaks.
Observe: Captures show untagged where you expected tags; wrong FDB.
Restore: Align native VLAN; prefer tagged-only user VLANs.
Harden: Explicit lab policy: native VLAN unused for data.



Drill 4 — Cable / interface down
Inject:
docker exec clab-l2-vlan-sw1 ip link set eth3 down
Predict: Cross-switch traffic dies; FDB ages; local switching may live.
Observe: ping loss; interface counters; STP reconvergence if redundant path exists.
Restore: ip link set eth3 up; wait for learning/STP.
Harden: If no redundant path, document single point of failure.



Drill 5 — Broadcast storm (controlled)
Inject: Temporary bridging loop without STP on an isolated lab (very short).
Predict: CPU spikes, loss of management responsiveness, exploding counters.
Observe: ip -s link, host load.
Restore: containerlab destroy --cleanup immediately if unstable.
Harden: STP on; never lab this on a shared prod-like bridge.



Drill 6 — STP blocked port confusion
Inject: With STP triangle, shut the active root port path.
Predict: Alternate port activates; brief loss; new tree.
Observe: Port state sysfs or NOS show; ping -c 50 loss burst.
Restore: Bring link up; tree may revert depending on costs.
Harden: Note expected reconvergence budget.



Drill 7 — MAC move
Inject: Move host container link from sw1 to sw2 (redeploy link or migrate veth).
Predict: FDB updates; short blackhole until relearn; ARP may refresh.
Observe: bridge fdb show before/after; neigh on peers.
Restore: Stable attachment.
Harden: In virtualization, understand port channels / bond moves.



Drill 8 — Duplicate IP
Inject: Configure h4 temporarily with h3’s IP on VLAN 10 (careful).
Predict: Flapping ARP, intermittent delivery, wrong neigh.
Observe: ip neigh oscillating; tcpdump conflicting ARP replies.
Restore: Unique IPs.
Harden: Addressing plan ownership; IPAM habit.



Drill 9 — Duplicate MAC (advanced)
Inject: Spoof MAC on a second host (lab only).
ip link set eth1 down
ip link set eth1 address aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff
ip link set eth1 up
Predict: FDB flap; unstable delivery.
Restore: Original MAC; destroy/recreate if messy.
Harden: Understand L2 trust boundaries.



Drill 10 — LAG member down
Inject: On a bond/LAG lab, shut one member.
Predict: Traffic continues if min-links satisfied; single-flow rate unchanged.
Observe: /proc/net/bonding/bond0; ping continuity.
Restore: Member up.
Harden: Alert on member-down even if bond stays up.



Drill 11 — Inter-VLAN path mistaken for L2
Inject: Delete router inter-VLAN route or shut subinterface.
Predict: Same-VLAN ok; cross-VLAN fails—looks like “VLAN broken” if you misread.
Observe: traceroute never leaves gateway; ARP to gateway fails or gateway unreachable.
Restore: Router config.
Harden: Always check same-VLAN baseline before blaming trunk.



Drill 12 — Host firewall
Inject: On Linux host, drop ICMP.
# if nft/iptables available
iptables -A INPUT -p icmp -j DROP
Predict: Others cannot ping in; egress may still work.
Observe: Asymmetric ping stories.
Restore: Flush rule.
Harden: Include host endpoint in the failure picture.

title: Wireless LANs: Radio, Access, and Troubleshooting
text:
Wireless LANs: Radio, Access, and Troubleshooting
A wireless client shares radio airtime with other stations; an access point (AP) connects the wireless medium to the distribution network. An Ethernet link can be healthy while clients suffer retries, contention, roaming interruptions, or authentication failures over the air. Diagnose association, authorization, addressing and application reachability as separate stages.

title: Wireless LANs: Radio, Access, and Troubleshooting
text:
From radio to network
A service set identifier (SSID) is the network name presented to a user. A basic service set (BSS) is a radio cell; its BSSID identifies that BSS, normally with a MAC address. Multiple APs can advertise the same SSID as an extended service set, but matching names alone do not guarantee compatible security, mobility, VLANs, or seamless roaming. An AP can expose multiple BSSs per radio, with airtime overhead for each beacon. A controller-managed design may centralize policy and tunnel client traffic, or bridge it locally; determine the actual forwarding path before tracing a VLAN.
A client discovers BSSs through beacons and, when scanning actively, probe exchanges. It chooses a BSS based on its own policy and signal observations. It authenticates and associates at the 802.11 layer, negotiates security, and receives network authorization before ordinary traffic flows. The network then supplies addressing, a gateway and DNS. Association does not prove successful 802.1X authentication, DHCP or Internet access.

title: Wireless LANs: Radio, Access, and Troubleshooting
text:
Channels, airtime and capacity
Radios operate in bands and channels subject to local regulatory rules, device capabilities and configured channel width. Wider channels can increase peak physical rate but consume more spectrum and may reduce the number of independent channels available for neighboring cells. Channel plans must account for overlap, neighboring APs, non-Wi-Fi interference, and the client’s supported bands. Regulatory constraints, especially in 5 and 6 GHz, vary by jurisdiction and equipment; verify local requirements and device documentation before choosing channels or transmit power.
Wi-Fi is a shared medium. Stations generally use carrier sensing and contention before transmitting, and acknowledge unicast frames; collisions, interference and weak reception can trigger retries. A client that cannot hear another client can still collide at the AP: this is the hidden-node problem. RTS/CTS can help some hidden-node situations but adds overhead. High received signal alone does not guarantee good performance: noise, interference, channel utilization, retries and client rate selection matter. Signal-to-noise ratio compares received signal with the noise floor, both in dBm: -60 dBm - (-90 dBm) = 30 dB. Larger positive SNR is generally better, but thresholds depend on client, modulation and application.
A PHY rate is not application throughput. Airtime is spent on contention, interframe gaps, acknowledgments, management frames, retransmissions and protocol overhead. A slow or distant client can consume substantial airtime for a small amount of data. Measure both directions: an AP hearing a client poorly is different from a client hearing the AP poorly. A transmit-power increase at the AP cannot increase the client’s transmit power and can create an asymmetric cell.

title: Wireless LANs: Radio, Access, and Troubleshooting
text:
Security and access policy
Personal networks typically authenticate with a shared secret; enterprise access commonly uses 802.1X and EAP, with the client as supplicant, the AP or controller as authenticator, and a backend authentication server commonly reached over RADIUS. EAP is a framework for methods, not a single credential exchange. With EAP-TLS, validate the server certificate and expected identity on the client, and provision and revoke client credentials as required by policy. A client that accepts any server certificate can disclose credentials to an impostor when using susceptible methods. Protected management frames reduce certain management-frame attacks; support and enforcement depend on the configured security mode and clients.
Map authorization to the actual data path: an accepted identity may receive a VLAN, role, ACL or tunnel assignment. An authentication success with a wrong VLAN is an authorization or forwarding problem, not proof that DNS is broken. Do not assume every SSID maps to a separate VLAN or that isolation is automatic. Guest isolation, management access, certificate lifecycle and logging require explicit design.

title: Wireless LANs: Radio, Access, and Troubleshooting
text:
Roaming and design
The client makes the roaming decision. Neighbor information, transition suggestions and fast-transition mechanisms can assist compatible clients, but do not force every client to roam at the same signal threshold. Moving between APs while retaining the same subnet generally preserves IP addressing; crossing a Layer 3 boundary may change the address or require mobility mechanisms. Voice and real-time traffic expose brief interruptions that a web download may hide. Measure roaming time, packet loss and application impact rather than inferring success from a signal map.
A site survey starts with the floor plan, materials, user density and application requirements. Collect measurements at client height with representative clients, then validate coverage and capacity under expected load. Check AP uplink VLANs, PoE budget, switch capacity and controller reachability alongside radio performance. Coverage maps alone do not prove capacity, and maximum transmit power on every AP can increase contention.

title: Wireless LANs: Radio, Access, and Troubleshooting
text:
Troubleshooting exercise
Use an authorized test WLAN with two APs, a client, and an authentication server or personal-security profile. Record time, BSSID, channel, band, client signal and, where exposed, retries and channel utilization. Use the client and AP’s normal diagnostic tools; do not capture other users’ content. Walk through these tests, restoring the baseline after each intentional fault:

Discovery: confirm the intended SSID and BSSID are visible. Compare client-supported band and security capabilities with the AP configuration. If the SSID is absent, inspect radio state, channel and regulatory settings before DHCP.
Authentication: introduce an invalid test credential. Expect association or authentication progress to stop at the relevant stage; compare client and server logs. Restore the credential and verify authorization. For EAP-TLS, inspect time, certificate chain, identity and expiry without disabling validation.
Forwarding: on a disposable test SSID, change the assigned VLAN to one without the intended DHCP service. Authentication may succeed while addressing fails. Inspect assigned role, AP forwarding mode, trunk membership and DHCP exchange; restore the assignment and renew the lease.
Capacity: under controlled load compare idle and busy throughput, latency, retries, channel utilization and PHY rates at the same location. High utilization with low retries suggests contention; high retries with poor SNR suggests a radio-quality problem. These are hypotheses, not unique diagnoses.
Roaming: send a timestamped continuous probe to a local endpoint while moving between cells. Record old and new BSSIDs, loss interval and IP address; compare with AP and authentication logs. A stable BSSID suggests the client did not roam, whereas a BSSID change with a long outage requires investigation of security, VLAN and application behavior.

For each test record a baseline, observation at two points, hypothesis, repair and verification. Never generalize one client’s behavior to all clients.
Further reading: EAP architecture, RFC 3748, 802.1X RADIUS usage, RFC 3580, and EAP-TLS 1.3, RFC 9190.

Routing Fundamentals
Routing is longest-prefix match to a next hop or interface, plus the glue that resolves the next hop to L2. This chapter ties RIB/FIB, metrics, and host vs router behavior into one model you will reuse for statics and dynamic protocols.

title: Routing Fundamentals

title: Routing Fundamentals
text:
Concepts

Forwarding equation
For each packet:

Look up destination in FIB

Select winning route (longest prefix, then tie-breakers)

Find egress interface and L2 rewrite target

Decrement TTL / hop limit; drop if zero



RIB vs FIB



Store
Role




RIB
Routing information: all candidates, protocol owners


FIB
What data plane uses for forward



On Linux, ip route shows kernel FIB. FRR holds protocol RIB and installs selected routes into the kernel via zebra.
ip route
vtysh -c 'show ip route'   # FRR RIB view


Longest prefix match
Routes:

0.0.0.0/0 via gwA

10.0.0.0/8 via gwB

10.1.2.0/24 via gwC

Destination 10.1.2.5 → gwC. Destination 10.9.0.1 → gwB. Destination 1.2.3.4 → gwA.
ip route add 10.0.0.0/8 via 192.0.2.1
ip route add 10.1.2.0/24 via 192.0.2.2
ip route get 10.1.2.5


Metrics and distance (ideas)
Multiple protocols may offer the same prefix. Selection uses administrative preference (distance) then metric. Linux has metrics on routes; FRR has AD per protocol. Exact numbers differ—model is ranked sources.


Connected routes
Configuring 10.1.0.1/24 on eth1 installs connected route 10.1.0.0/24 dev eth1. Connected usually beats static/default for that space.

title: Routing Fundamentals
text:
Route selection versus packet forwarding
A routing protocol or a static configuration supplies candidate routes. The routing system selects eligible routes for a prefix using platform-specific route preference and metrics, then programs forwarding state. The data plane performs longest-prefix matching on that installed state. Thus a route shown in a protocol’s database is not necessarily installed in the forwarding table, and an installed route does not guarantee a reachable next hop or functioning return path. Equal-cost multipath may distribute flows across several next hops, typically using a hash; individual packets or test flows need not reveal every available path.
For 203.0.113.45, compare 0.0.0.0/0, 203.0.113.0/24, and 203.0.113.32/27. The /27 matches addresses .32 through .63 and wins. A lower metric on the /24 does not make it more specific. If the /27 is withdrawn, the /24 becomes the longest installed match. A discard route is also a route: it may deliberately prevent a summary from forwarding to a default route when a more-specific destination is missing.
Trace the evidence: inspect the control-plane route, the installed route and chosen next hop, the neighbor entry, egress counters or capture, and the reverse route. A packet arriving at the far router proves only the forward half of a bidirectional exchange.

title: Static Routing Labs
text:
Static Routing Labs
Static routes are the control plane you can see with your eyeballs. Master them in Containerlab with FRR or Linux before OSPF/BGP hide the decisions inside protocols.

FRR config sketches
Enable zebra in daemons. Example frr.conf for r1:

Floating statics
On r1, prefer r2 path, backup via r3:
ip route 192.168.2.0/24 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.2.0/24 10.0.13.2 200
In Linux:
ip route add 192.168.2.0/24 via 10.0.12.2 metric 10
ip route add 192.168.2.0/24 via 10.0.13.2 metric 200
Caveat: Floating statics failover when the route is withdrawn—often when the interface or next hop tracking says down. A silent next hop that stays “up” but blackholes may not fail over without tracking/BFD (advanced). In labs, shut the interface to force failover.

Failover drill

title: ICMP & Path MTU
text:
ICMP & Path MTU
Small pings succeed while large transfers hang: classic MTU / PMTUD failure. This chapter treats ICMP as a control helper and shows you how to find black holes with deliberate packet sizes.

title: ICMP & Path MTU
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain key ICMP types used in operations

Test reachability with controlled sizes and DF bit

Predict PMTUD behavior when ICMP “fragmentation needed” is filtered

title: ICMP & Path MTU
text:
ICMP essentials (IPv4)







Type
Role




Echo request/reply
ping


Destination unreachable
no route, port unreachable, frag needed


Time exceeded
TTL expired (traceroute)


Redirect
host guidance (often ignored/noisy)



ping -c 3 10.0.0.1
ping -c 3 -s 1400 10.0.0.1

-M do (Linux) sets Don’t Fragment. Adjust payload so total IP packet hits MTU boundary.

title: ICMP & Path MTU
section: The size budget is per path and encapsulation
text:
The size budget is per path and encapsulation
For an Ethernet IP MTU of 1500, a simple IPv4 TCP packet with 20-byte IP and TCP headers has 1460 bytes available for TCP data. Options reduce that amount. The TCP MSS advertises a receive-side maximum segment data size; actual transmitted payload can be lower because of path constraints and header options. UDP applications must also account for IP and UDP headers and should avoid assuming that a large datagram fits every path.
An IPv4 router that cannot forward an oversized packet may fragment it if permitted; when the Don’t Fragment bit prevents this, it drops the packet and normally sends ICMP Destination Unreachable, Fragmentation Needed. An IPv6 router never fragments forwarded packets and sends ICMPv6 Packet Too Big. The source can adjust its packet size based on this feedback. A tunnel must also fit its outer IP and tunnel headers in the underlay path MTU. If ICMP feedback is filtered, a handshake and small requests can succeed while larger transfers stall.
Test from the actual source to the actual destination, in both directions if relevant. Start below the suspected MTU, increase the size, and account for whether the test tool’s size flag counts application payload or the whole IP packet. Verify the observed interface MTUs and capture ICMP errors; an endpoint timeout alone is not proof of an MTU problem. RFC 8200 specifies IPv6 forwarding and fragmentation behavior.

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
text:
Learning goals

Understand how the Linux kernel caches Path MTU discovery results as route exceptions and inspect them using user-space networking tools.
Identify how network devices filtering ICMP messages create silent packet drops known as PMTU black holes.
Analyze the behavior of TCP connections during a PMTU black hole event when standard ICMP feedback is suppressed.
Explain the mechanics of Packetization-Layer Path MTU Discovery (PLPMTUD, RFC 4821) and configure Linux tcp_mtu_probing sysctls.
Contrast transport-layer kernel MTU probing with application-level Datagram Packetization-Layer PMTUD (DPLPMTUD, RFC 8899) used by protocols like QUIC.

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
text:
Version note
The execution logs and diagnostic outputs in this chapter were gathered on a cloud VM running Linux kernel 6.12.94, iproute2 6.15.0, and standard Python 3.13.5. All namespace operations were executed rootlessly using unshare -urnm across four network namespaces (c, r1, r2, s). All links are MTU 1500 except the r1-r2 link at MTU 1280. There is no ping, tcpdump, nft or iptables on this box: probes are small Python programs, and the TCP numbers come from TCP_INFO. The ICMP black hole was generated by adding an ip rule matching ipproto icmp directed to a routing table containing a blackhole default entry. The black-hole rule needs no firewall tool, so you can reproduce the whole lab as an ordinary user.
Earlier chapters established how classic Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) operates across IP networks. Under classic PMTUD (RFC 1191 for IPv4, RFC 8201 for IPv6), end hosts rely on intermediate routers to send back ICMP Destination Unreachable messages (Type 3 Code 4, Fragmentation Needed) or ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages (Type 2) whenever a packet exceeds a link’s MTU and cannot be fragmented. When firewalls, network ACLs, or misconfigured middleboxes silently drop these ICMP messages, a PMTU black hole is created. Small packets such as TCP SYN handshake frames flow unhindered, but bulk data packets carrying large payloads disappear into the network without notification.

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
section: The Linux PMTU Cache and Route Exceptions
text:
The Linux PMTU Cache and Route Exceptions
When a host receives an ICMP Fragmentation Needed message, the kernel must store this path constraint so subsequent outgoing packets are sized appropriately. Linux maintains these learned path constraints inside its routing subsystem as route exceptions (the PMTU cache).
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                              Linux Kernel                             |
|                                                                       |
|  +-------------------+        +------------------------------------+  |
|  | Socket Layer      |        | Routing Subsystem (PMTU Cache)     |  |
|  | IP_MTU_DISCOVER   |------->| IP Route Exception:                |  |
|  | IP_MTU            |        |   Dst: 10.0.2.2 -> MTU: 1280       |  |
|  +-------------------+        |   Expires: 600s                    |  |
|            |                  +------------------------------------+  |
|            |                                    ^                     |
|            v                                    |                     |
|    Packet Tx Logic <----------------------------+                     |
|  (Enforces EMSGSIZE if payload > Cached PMTU)                         |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
When a destination MTU is reduced by an incoming ICMP message, Linux creates an exception entry associated with the destination IP address. This entry can be observed using ip route get <DST>. The kernel limits the lifetime of these learned constraints using net.ipv4.route.mtu_expires (defaulting to 600 seconds). After the expiration timer elapses, the exception is invalidated, allowing the kernel to re-probe higher MTUs on the path.
To protect against malicious ICMP spoofing attacks that attempt to reduce host throughput by reporting artificially tiny MTUs, Linux enforces a lower boundary configured via net.ipv4.route.min_pmtu (defaulting to 552 bytes). Any ICMP message advertising a next-hop MTU below this floor is ignored or clamped to min_pmtu.
Applications inspect and control this path discovery machinery using IP-level socket options:

IP_MTU: A read-only option retrieved with getsockopt() that returns the current known path MTU for a connected socket.
IP_MTU_DISCOVER: Controls socket fragmentation behavior via several operating modes:

IP_PMTUDISC_DO: Sets the Don’t Fragment (DF) bit on outgoing IPv4 packets, enforces local MTU checks against the PMTU cache, and returns EMSGSIZE to send() if an application attempts to send a payload exceeding the cached MTU.
IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE: Sets the DF bit on outgoing packets but explicitly bypasses local PMTU cache checks. This allows applications to send out datagrams larger than the cached MTU to actively probe path capabilities.

IP_RECVERR: Enables delivery of extended asynchronous error information, including incoming ICMP messages, via the socket’s error queue (MSG_ERRQUEUE).

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
section: What Happens to TCP in a Black Hole
text:
What Happens to TCP in a Black Hole
TCP connections negotiate an initial Maximum Segment Size (MSS) during the three-way handshake based on the local outgoing interface MTU and the MSS option advertised by the remote peer. When TCP timestamps are enabled (RFC 7323), 12 bytes of TCP options are consumed in the header, resulting in standard MSS calculations:
MSS = MTU - 20 (IPv4 header) - 20 (TCP header) - 12 (timestamps option) = MTU - 52
On a standard 1500-byte MTU path, the MSS is 1500 - 52 = 1448 bytes. On a 1280-byte MTU path, it drops to 1280 - 52 = 1228 bytes.
When a network path contains a narrow link (such as 1280 bytes) and an upstream device drops ICMP packets, TCP handshake packets succeed because SYNs are small (about 60 bytes with options). However, when the sender transmits full-sized data segments (1448 bytes of payload), the bottleneck router silently drops the packet.
Because no ICMP message returns to update the sender’s PMTU cache, the TCP sender cannot distinguish between network congestion and an MTU mismatch. It enters exponential backoff, retransmitting the exact same oversized segment repeatedly. The Retransmission Timeout (RTO) doubles with each attempt (e.g., 400ms, 800ms, 1600ms, 3200ms). The connection stalls until the tcp_retries2 budget runs out (about 15 minutes with the default of 15), at which point the kernel aborts it with ETIMEDOUT.

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
text:
TCP MTU Probing (RFC 4821 PLPMTUD)
Packetization-Layer Path MTU Discovery (PLPMTUD) for TCP, specified in RFC 4821, removes the reliance on ICMP messages. Instead, the transport layer itself detects path MTU limits by validating which segment sizes successfully produce TCP acknowledgements.
Linux implements RFC 4821 through a suite of sysctls under net.ipv4:

net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing:

0: Disabled entirely. TCP relies exclusively on ICMP messages and local route settings.
1: Disabled by default, but automatically activated when a connection experiences repeated retransmission timeouts indicative of an ICMP black hole.
2: Always enabled for all TCP connections. Connections start using an initial MSS defined by tcp_base_mss and actively probe upward.

net.ipv4.tcp_base_mss: Default 1024. Specifies the starting MSS used when searching or when initiating connections under mode 2.
net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probe_floor: Default 48. Defines the minimum payload floor for probing operations.
net.ipv4.tcp_probe_interval: Default 600 seconds. Specifies the interval between upward MTU probing cycles.
net.ipv4.tcp_probe_threshold: Default 8. Stops probing when the search range is smaller than this threshold in bytes.

When tcp_mtu_probing is set to 1, Linux ties black-hole detection to repeated retransmission timeouts (the check uses tcp_retries1, default 3). After several consecutive timeouts without progress, the kernel suspects an MTU black hole, reduces the connection MSS to tcp_base_mss, and retransmits the lost data split into smaller segments. Once small segments are acknowledged, the kernel systematically probes upward by sending larger probe segments until it discovers the true path MTU.
When set to 2, every TCP connection avoids sending full-sized interface segments initially. It starts at tcp_base_mss and rapidly probes upward. While this adds minor probing overhead and initial throughput degradation on clean 1500-byte links, it guarantees that connections succeed immediately without stalling when operating behind tunnels or unknown network paths.

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
section: Application-Layer Probing: DPLPMTUD for UDP and QUIC (RFC 8899)
text:
Application-Layer Probing: DPLPMTUD for UDP and QUIC (RFC 8899)
UDP is stateless and lacks native retransmissions, sequence numbers, or segment tracking inside the kernel. Consequently, the Linux kernel cannot automatically repair UDP black holes. Applications operating over UDP must implement Datagram Packetization-Layer PMTUD (DPLPMTUD, RFC 8899).
DPLPMTUD places the responsibility of probing the path MTU on the application protocol itself. The application defines specific variables and state limits:

BASE_PLPMTU: The minimum guaranteed payload size that the application assumes the network supports without probing. For IPv4 over UDP, RFC 8899 Section 5.1.2 recommends a default of 1200 bytes (accounting for IP and UDP headers).
MIN_PLPMTU: The absolute lower limit of PLPMTU (1280 bytes for IPv6).
MAX_PLPMTU: The upper boundary (typically bounded by the local egress interface MTU).
PROBED_SIZE: The payload size currently being validated by an active probe.
MAX_PROBES: The maximum number of consecutive unacknowledged probe attempts allowed before declaring a probe size lost (typically 3 attempts).

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    Application Layer (QUIC / UDP)                     |
|                                                                       |
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | DPLPMTUD State Machine (RFC 8899)                               |  |
|  |   - BASE_PLPMTU = 1200 bytes                                    |  |
|  |   - Probes using IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE                              |  |
|  |   - Tracks ACK responses from remote peer                       |  |
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    v
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
|                            Linux Kernel                               |
|                                                                       |
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | UDP Socket (IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE)                                  |  |
|  |   - Forces DF bit = 1                                           |  |
|  |   - Ignores internal PMTU route cache                           |  |
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
QUIC (RFC 9000 Section 14) relies heavily on these principles:

Anti-Amplification and Initial Padding (Section 14.1): QUIC requires all Initial packets sent by a client to be padded to at least 1200 bytes. This ensures the network path supports the minimum required datagram size before establishing state.
PMTUD Integration (Section 14.2 & 14.3): QUIC implementations can utilize OS-level PMTUD notifications or execute application-driven DPLPMTUD by sending padded PING or PATH_CHALLENGE frames set to specific target sizes. If the peer acknowledges the frame, the path MTU is safely validated upward.

By opening sockets with IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE, UDP applications instruct the kernel to set the DF bit while bypassing local route cache restrictions, allowing precise binary search probing across unknown network paths.

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
text:
Hands-on Lab
The lab setup creates a four-namespace topology:
c (Client: 10.0.1.2) <—> r1 (Router 1) <—> r2 (Router 2) <—> s (Server: 10.0.2.2)
The link between r1 and r2 is set to MTU 1280. All other links remain at MTU 1500.

Lab Script (lab.sh)


lab.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -urnm sh lab.sh   (unprivileged: user, net and mount namespaces; no sudo)
H=$(pwd)
mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
for ns in c r1 r2 s; do ip netns add $ns; ip -n $ns link set lo up; done
ip link add c0 type veth peer name r1a;  ip link set c0 netns c;   ip link set r1a netns r1
ip link add r1b type veth peer name r2a; ip link set r1b netns r1; ip link set r2a netns r2
ip link add r2b type veth peer name s0;  ip link set r2b netns r2; ip link set s0 netns s
ip -n c  addr add 10.0.1.2/24 dev c0;  ip -n r1 addr add 10.0.1.1/24 dev r1a
ip -n r1 addr add 10.0.12.1/24 dev r1b; ip -n r2 addr add 10.0.12.2/24 dev r2a
ip -n r2 addr add 10.0.2.1/24 dev r2b; ip -n s  addr add 10.0.2.2/24 dev s0
ip -n r1 link set r1b mtu 1280; ip -n r2 link set r2a mtu 1280     # the narrow middle link
for d in c:c0 r1:r1a r1:r1b r2:r2a r2:r2b s:s0; do ip -n ${d%:*} link set ${d#*:} up; done
for r in r1 r2; do ip netns exec $r sh -c 'echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward'; done
ip -n c route add default via 10.0.1.1; ip -n s route add default via 10.0.2.1
ip -n r1 route add 10.0.2.0/24 via 10.0.12.2; ip -n r2 route add 10.0.1.0/24 via 10.0.12.1
C="ip netns exec c"; S="ip netns exec s"; sleep 0.5
rget() { echo "   \$ ip route get 10.0.2.2   (in c)"; ip -n c route get 10.0.2.2 | sed 's/^/   /'; }

echo "== 1. healthy path: the narrow link answers with Fragmentation Needed"
rget
$C python3 $H/dfprobe.py 10.0.2.2 1500 1400 1280
rget

echo "== 2. TCP upload of 4 MB over the healthy path (probing off)"
$S python3 $H/sink.py 10.0.2.2 5001 & K=$!; sleep 0.3
$C python3 $H/upload.py 10.0.2.2 5001 4000000 20
kill $K 2>/dev/null; wait $K 2>/dev/null

echo "== 3. break PMTUD: r1 may no longer send any ICMP (policy rule to a blackhole table)"
ip -n r1 route add blackhole default table 66
ip -n r1 rule add pref 100 ipproto icmp table 66
ip -n r1 rule show | sed 's/^/   /'
ip -n c route flush cache
rget
$C python3 $H/dfprobe.py 10.0.2.2 1500 1400 1280

for p in 0 1 2; do
  echo "== 4.$p TCP upload of 4 MB through the black hole, net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=$p"
  $C sh -c "echo $p > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_mtu_probing"
  ip -n c route flush cache
  $S python3 $H/sink.py 10.0.2.2 5001 & K=$!; sleep 0.3
  $C python3 $H/upload.py 10.0.2.2 5001 4000000 20
  kill $K 2>/dev/null; wait $K 2>/dev/null
done

echo "== 5. UDP has no kernel rescue: packetization-layer search with acknowledgements (RFC 8899 style)"
$S python3 $H/udpecho.py 10.0.2.2 5002 & K=$!; sleep 0.3
$C python3 $H/dplpmtud.py 10.0.2.2 5002
kill $K 2>/dev/null



Probing Tool (dfprobe.py)


dfprobe.py

# dfprobe.py DST SIZE...: send one UDP datagram per total IP size with DF set,
# then report what the kernel learned (IP_MTU) and any queued ICMP error.
import socket, sys, time, struct
IP_MTU_DISCOVER, IP_PMTUDISC_DO, IP_MTU, IP_RECVERR = 10, 2, 14, 11
dst = sys.argv[1]
for size in map(int, sys.argv[2:]):
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_IP, IP_MTU_DISCOVER, IP_PMTUDISC_DO)
    s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_IP, IP_RECVERR, 1)
    s.connect((dst, 9))
    try:
        s.send(b"x" * (size - 28))
        res = "sent"
    except OSError as e:
        res = "send refused: " + e.strerror
    time.sleep(0.3)
    err = "no ICMP came back"
    try:
        _, anc, _, _ = s.recvmsg(1, 512, socket.MSG_ERRQUEUE)
        for lvl, typ, data in anc:
            if lvl == socket.IPPROTO_IP and typ == IP_RECVERR:
                errno_, origin, itype, icode, _, info, _ = struct.unpack("=IBBBBII", data[:16])
                if origin == 1:
                    err = f"local error (kernel already knows mtu={info})"
                elif (itype, icode) == (3, 4):
                    err = f"ICMP frag-needed from the path, mtu={info}"
                elif (itype, icode) == (3, 3):
                    err = "ICMP port-unreachable from 10.0.2.2: it arrived"
                else:
                    err = f"ICMP type {itype} code {icode}"
    except BlockingIOError:
        pass
    except OSError as e:
        err = "errqueue: " + e.strerror
    print(f"   DF {size:4d} bytes: {res:30s} {err:45s} kernel path MTU now {s.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_IP, IP_MTU)}")
    s.close()



Upload Performance Tester (upload.py)


upload.py

# upload.py DST PORT BYTES DEADLINE: send BYTES, report progress, mss and retransmits
import socket, sys, time, struct
dst, port, total, deadline = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3]), float(sys.argv[4])
s = socket.create_connection((dst, port), timeout=deadline)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_SNDBUF, 262144)
def info():
    raw = s.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_INFO, 256)
    # struct tcp_info: retransmits at offset 2, total_retrans at 100, snd_mss at 16, rto at 8 (usec)
    rto = struct.unpack_from("I", raw, 8)[0]; snd_mss = struct.unpack_from("I", raw, 16)[0]
    total_retrans = struct.unpack_from("I", raw, 100)[0]
    return snd_mss, total_retrans, rto
t0 = time.monotonic(); sent = 0; buf = b"y" * 65536; s.setblocking(False); marks = []
print(f"   t=0.0s  snd_mss={info()[0]}")
next_mark = 0.5
while sent < total and time.monotonic() - t0 < deadline:
    try:
        sent += s.send(buf[: min(len(buf), total - sent)])
    except BlockingIOError:
        time.sleep(0.01)
    el = time.monotonic() - t0
    if el >= next_mark:
        m, r, rto = info()
        if not marks or marks[-1] != (m, r):
            print(f"   t={el:4.1f}s  queued={sent:8d}  snd_mss={m}  total_retrans={r}  rto={rto//1000}ms")
        marks.append((m, r)); next_mark += 0.5
# wait for the queue to drain (unacked bytes) before declaring done
while time.monotonic() - t0 < deadline:
    raw = s.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_INFO, 256)
    unacked = struct.unpack_from("I", raw, 24)[0]
    if sent == total and unacked == 0: break
    time.sleep(0.05)
el = time.monotonic() - t0; m, r, _ = info()
raw = s.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_INFO, 256); unacked = struct.unpack_from("I", raw, 24)[0]
state = "COMPLETE" if sent == total and unacked == 0 else "STALLED"
print(f"   {state}: queued {sent} of {total} bytes, unacked segments {unacked}, {el:.2f}s, final snd_mss={m}, total_retrans={r}")
s.close()



TCP Sink Server (sink.py)


sink.py

import socket, sys
l = socket.socket(); l.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)

Application UDP Server (udpecho.py)


udpecho.py

import socket, sys

while True:

DPLPMTUD Implementation (dplpmtud.py)


dplpmtud.py

# dplpmtud.py DST PORT: binary-search the largest UDP payload that is ACKED end to end.
# IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE sets DF but ignores the kernel's PMTU cache, so ICMP is not needed.
import socket, sys, time
IP_MTU_DISCOVER, IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE = 10, 3
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_IP, IP_MTU_DISCOVER, IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE)
s.connect((sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]))); s.settimeout(0.2)
def probe(ip_size, tries=3):
    for _ in range(tries):
        s.send(b"p" * (ip_size - 28))
        try:
            if int.from_bytes(s.recv(16), "big") == ip_size - 28: return True
        except socket.timeout:
            pass
    return False
lo, hi, n = 1200, 1500, 0          # BASE_PLPMTU 1200 (RFC 8899 section 5.1.2 recommends 1200 bytes for IPv4)
assert probe(lo); n += 1
t0 = time.monotonic()
while hi - lo > 1:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2; ok = probe(mid); n += 1
    print(f"   probe {mid:4d} bytes -> {'acked' if ok else 'lost (3 tries)'}")
    lo, hi = (mid, hi) if ok else (lo, mid)
print(f"   search done: PLPMTU = {lo} bytes (true path MTU 1280), {n} probe sizes, {time.monotonic()-t0:.1f}s")

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
text:
Reading the output

Section 1: PMTU Cache Initialization on a Healthy Path

ip route get 10.0.2.2: Initially shows no active route exception entry under the route lookup.
DF 1500 bytes: Sent from c. Router r1 attempts to forward it over r1b (MTU 1280). r1 generates an ICMP type 3 code 4 message containing mtu=1280. The kernel updates the active socket’s cached path MTU to 1280.
DF 1400 bytes: The application attempts to send a 1400-byte datagram. The kernel checks its internal route exception table prior to transmission, finds mtu=1280, rejects the system call locally with EMSGSIZE (“Message too long”), and generates an error queue origin 1 (SO_EE_ORIGIN_LOCAL).
DF 1280 bytes: Sent successfully. It traverses the path without fragmentation and arrives at s. Because port 9 is closed, s returns an ICMP port-unreachable (type 3 code 3), proving end-to-end path delivery.
cache expires 599sec mtu 1280: Re-running ip route get 10.0.2.2 reveals the newly populated route exception. The expiration timer starts at 599 seconds (counting down from net.ipv4.route.mtu_expires default of 600 seconds).



Section 2: TCP Transfer Over the Healthy Path

snd_mss=1228: TCP starts with snd_mss = 1228 (1280 - 52) because the kernel’s route cache exception learned in Section 1 remains active.
COMPLETE: ... 0.05s: The 4 MB transfer completes cleanly without retransmissions (total_retrans=0).



Section 3: ICMP Suppression and Black Hole Verification

Routing policy rule 100: from all ipproto icmp lookup 66 forces all ICMP traffic on r1 into table 66, which holds only a blackhole default route. Every ICMP message r1 would generate, including Fragmentation Needed, is discarded before it leaves.
After running ip route flush cache, dfprobe.py sends DF-flagged datagrams of 1500, 1400, and 1280 bytes. None receive ICMP replies. The path MTU stored in the kernel remains at the local link default of 1500 bytes.



Section 4.0: TCP Transfer with Probing Disabled (tcp_mtu_probing=0)

snd_mss=1448: Connection negotiates MSS assuming a 1500-byte path MTU (1500 - 52 = 1448).
queued=428608: Transmits initial window of data up to 428,608 bytes before the send buffer is full. Linux doubles the requested SO_SNDBUF of 262,144 to 524,288 bytes to account for bookkeeping overhead, and 428,608 bytes of payload fit in it.
rto=408ms to rto=13056ms: Exponential backoff occurs over 6 consecutive retransmission attempts (408ms, 816ms, 1632ms, 3264ms, 6528ms, 13056ms).
STALLED: After 20 seconds, the client application times out. 11 segments remain completely unacknowledged (unacked segments 11), and nothing moved after the first window. Left alone, this connection would sit there until the tcp_retries2 budget expired.



Section 4.1: TCP Black Hole Recovery (tcp_mtu_probing=1)

Connection initiates with snd_mss=1448 and stalls initially across retransmissions at 400ms, 800ms, 1600ms, and 3200ms.
After several consecutive timeouts (four retransmissions are visible before the MSS changes; the kernel’s check is tied to tcp_retries1, default 3), the kernel activates PLPMTUD recovery.
It drops snd_mss down to tcp_base_mss (1024 bytes) to flush the unacknowledged data across the bottleneck, then probes upward to discover the true MSS ceiling (1228). The intermediate 1024 is not visible in the half-second samples; only the result is.
COMPLETE: ... 6.40s, final snd_mss=1228, total_retrans=24: The 4 MB transfer recovers and finishes successfully. The 24 retransmissions reflect the accumulated backlog of large segments that had to be split and retransmitted as smaller frames.



Section 4.2: Proactive TCP Probing (tcp_mtu_probing=2)

snd_mss=1024: Connection immediately starts with MSS equal to tcp_base_mss (1024 bytes).
Probes larger segment sizes immediately during active data transmission without waiting for retransmission timeouts.
COMPLETE: ... 0.00s, final snd_mss=1228, total_retrans=2: Transfer completes instantly (under 10ms). The 2 retransmissions are most likely the upward probes that exceeded 1280 bytes and were dropped at r1; the data in them was resent at the confirmed size.



Section 5: UDP Application Binary Search (DPLPMTUD)

UDP application initiates binary search bounded between lo=1200 (BASE_PLPMTU) and hi=1500.
Socket option IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE forces DF on all probes while bypassing local route cache restrictions.
Probes at 1350, 1312, 1293, 1284, and 1281 bytes fail to receive application ACKs after 3 attempts (each timing out at 200ms).
Probes at 1275, 1279, and 1280 bytes receive application ACKs.
search done: PLPMTU = 1280 bytes: Discovers exact path MTU of 1280 bytes after 9 probe sizes and 3.0 seconds. Almost all of that time is waiting: 5 lost sizes x 3 tries x 200 ms = 3.0 s. A real implementation keeps sending data at the confirmed size while it probes, so the search costs no throughput.

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
text:
What to Do in Production

Do not filter the messages PMTUD needs. Permit ICMP type 3 code 4 and ICMPv6 type 2 (Packet Too Big) everywhere, including on host firewalls and cloud security groups. RFC 4890 lists Packet Too Big among the ICMPv6 messages that must not be dropped.
Turn on the safety net on servers. net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1 costs nothing on healthy paths and rescues connections that hit a black hole, at the price of a few seconds of stall (6.40 s in this lab, mostly RTO backoff). Despite the ipv4 in its name, the same sysctl drives the probing logic for TCP over IPv6 as well. Consider 2 on hosts that live behind tunnels or VPNs where the path MTU is routinely below 1500.
Clamp MSS where you add encapsulation. Tunnel endpoints and VPN gateways should clamp the MSS of TCP flows they carry; this is a local fix for TCP only and does not help UDP.
For UDP applications, pick software that does DPLPMTUD or stay at 1200 bytes. QUIC stacks implement it; home-grown UDP protocols usually do not.
When users report “small requests work, large ones hang”, compare ip route get DST (is there a cached MTU?), retransmission counters in ss -ti, and a DF probe at a few sizes from the affected host. A missing cache entry plus growing retransmissions is the black-hole signature reproduced in section 4.0.

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
text:
Gotchas

Belief: Setting net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1 fixes path MTU issues for UDP, ICMP, and QUIC.
Why it is wrong: tcp_mtu_probing is strictly a TCP stack feature within the kernel. UDP sockets and datagram protocols do not benefit from TCP sysctl settings; datagram protocols must implement application-layer mechanisms like RFC 8899 DPLPMTUD.
Belief: PMTU black holes always cause connection setup (SYN exchange) to fail.
Why it is wrong: SYN and SYN-ACK packets are small (typically 60 to 80 bytes) and easily pass through narrow link MTUs (such as 1280 bytes). The black hole only manifests after the handshake completes and the sender transmits full-sized data payload segments.
Belief: net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=2 should be enabled on all high-speed servers by default.
Why it is wrong: Mode 2 forces every TCP connection to start with a reduced MSS (tcp_base_mss, default 1024 bytes). On clean 1500-byte or 9000-byte jumbo-frame networks, this imposes unnecessary probing overhead and delays reaching maximum link bandwidth. Mode 1 is generally safer for heterogeneous environments.
Belief: Disabling ICMP completely across firewalls improves overall network security.
Why it is wrong: Blocking ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed) or ICMPv6 Type 2 (Packet Too Big) breaks RFC 1191 / RFC 8201 PMTUD, directly creating PMTU black holes that cause TCP stalls and broken UDP communications across tunneled or MTU-constrained paths.
Belief: MSS clamping on an edge router resolves all PMTU black holes across the Internet.
Why it is wrong: MSS clamping only modifies TCP SYN packets passing directly through the router executing the clamping rule. It cannot alter paths that do not traverse that specific router, nor can it inspect or resize UDP datagrams.
Belief: ip route flush cache alters permanent static routes configured on the host.
Why it is wrong: Flushing the route cache only purges temporary route exception entries (dynamically learned PMTUs and redirects) stored in memory. Main routing table entries remain intact.
Belief: Setting IP_MTU_DISCOVER to IP_PMTUDISC_DO prevents send failures when exceeding path limits.
Why it is wrong: IP_PMTUDISC_DO enforces path limits based on the kernel’s PMTU cache. If an application attempts to send a payload larger than the cached MTU, the kernel immediately rejects the call locally with an EMSGSIZE error.

title: When PMTUD Fails: the PMTU Cache, TCP MTU Probing and Packetization-Layer PMTUD
text:
Exercises

IPv6 Route Exception Verification: Modify lab.sh to configure IPv6 addresses (2001:db8:1::/64, 2001:db8:12::/64, 2001:db8:2::/64) across namespaces c, r1, r2, and s. Trigger a Path Too Big condition using dfprobe.py over IPv6 and verify the learned exception using ip -6 route get 2001:db8:2::2.
Impact of Lowering Base MSS: Change net.ipv4.tcp_base_mss to 512 in namespace c. Repeat Section 4.2 of the lab and observe how upload.py scales its probing sequence from 512 up to 1228 bytes.
Custom Intermediate MTU Limits: Modify the link MTU between r1 and r2 from 1280 to 1400. Execute upload.py under tcp_mtu_probing=1 and record the exact number of retransmissions and final snd_mss value achieved.
Enforcing min_pmtu Boundaries: Leave out the black-hole rule, set net.ipv4.route.min_pmtu to 1300 in namespace c (echo 1300 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/route/min_pmtu inside the namespace), and rerun section 1. What MTU does ip route get show in the cache now, and what happens to a 1300-byte DF datagram? Explain why a floor above the real path MTU recreates a black hole.
Monitoring Kernel MTU Probing Counters: Run nstat -az | grep MTUP inside namespace c before and after running Section 4.1. Identify the counters TcpExtTCPMTUPSuccess and TcpExtTCPMTUPFail and explain their increments.

title: Policy Routing and VRF
text:
Learning goals

See that “the” routing table is only one table, and that ip rule selects among tables.
Predict ip route get when two sources would otherwise share a destination.
Explain a VRF as a named L3 domain: a table, a set of enslaved interfaces, and a socket lookup, not just a label on a route.
Know why a kernel built without CONFIG_NET_VRF can still do policy routing, and what you lose.

Version note: the policy-routing lab ran on 2026-11-12 in an unprivileged user and network namespace (unshare -rn) on Linux 6.12.94+ with iproute2 6.15.0. Output is pasted verbatim. Creating a VRF device in the same namespace failed because this kernel is built with CONFIG_NET_VRF is not set (it does have CONFIG_NET_L3_MASTER_DEV=y). VRF semantics and the ip link add … type vrf / ip vrf exec commands are therefore taken from iproute2 and the kernel documentation, and are marked as not run.

title: Policy Routing and VRF
section: Two problems that look the same
text:
Two problems that look the same
A host with two uplinks often needs two answers to “how do I reach 10.99.1.1?”:

Packets from 10.10.10.1 should go via the first next hop.
Packets from 10.20.20.1 should go via the second.

The main table cannot hold two default or overlapping routes and pick by source. Policy routing adds a rule: “if the source is X, look up table N.” A VRF is the structured form of the same idea: a named device owns a table, and interfaces (and sockets) are bound to it so entire applications live in one routing domain.
On Linux the building blocks are:








Object
Command
Role




Routing table
ip route … table 10
A FIB, numbered or named in /etc/iproute2/rt_tables


Policy rule
ip rule add from … table 10
Selects a table; lower priority is earlier


VRF device
ip link add red type vrf table 10
A master device that is table 10


Enslaved interface
ip link set eth1 master red / ip link set eth1 vrf red
Traffic on that interface uses the VRF table


VRF-aware command
ip vrf exec red ping …
The process looks up routes and binds in that VRF



Reserved rules, always present, are priority 0 (from all lookup local), 32766 (from all lookup main) and 32767 (from all lookup default). Your rules sit between 0 and 32766.

title: Policy Routing and VRF
text:
Lab: two sources, two tables
The following ran inside unshare -rn. Two veth ends of one pair stand in for two uplinks. Each has an address. The destination 10.99.0.0/16 is not connected; it exists only as a route in table 10 or table 20. Rules send traffic from each address to the matching table.
unshare -rn bash
ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1
ip addr add 10.10.10.1/24 dev veth0
ip addr add 10.20.20.1/24 dev veth1
ip link set veth0 up
ip link set veth1 up
ip route add 10.99.0.0/16 via 10.10.10.2 table 10
ip route add 10.99.0.0/16 via 10.20.20.2 table 20
ip rule add from 10.10.10.1 table 10 priority 100
ip rule add from 10.20.20.1 table 20 priority 101
ip rule show after that:
0:  from all lookup local
100:    from 10.10.10.1 lookup 10
101:    from 10.20.20.1 lookup 20
32766:  from all lookup main
32767:  from all lookup default
The extra tables hold only the destination we care about:
# ip route show table 10
10.99.0.0/16 via 10.10.10.2 dev veth0
# ip route show table 20
10.99.0.0/16 via 10.20.20.2 dev veth1
The main table has the connected prefixes, and nothing for 10.99.0.0/16:
# ip route show
10.10.10.0/24 dev veth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.10.10.1
10.20.20.0/24 dev veth1 proto kernel scope link src 10.20.20.1
ip route get is the lookup the kernel will actually perform. With an explicit source, the rule fires and the next hop changes:
# ip route get 10.99.1.1 from 10.10.10.1
10.99.1.1 from 10.10.10.1 via 10.10.10.2 dev veth0 table 10 uid 0
    cache
# ip route get 10.99.1.1 from 10.20.20.1
10.99.1.1 from 10.20.20.1 via 10.20.20.2 dev veth1 table 20 uid 0
    cache
Without a source, no rule matches, the main table is used, and the destination is unreachable — which is what this lab intended:
# ip route get 10.99.1.1
RTNETLINK answers: Network is unreachable
The next hops 10.10.10.2 and 10.20.20.2 were not present on the other ends of the veths, so a ping would fail ARP. The point of the lab is the lookup, not an end-to-end echo.

title: Policy Routing and VRF
text:
What a VRF adds
A VRF wraps the table and the interfaces into one object:
# Not run on the writing host — CONFIG_NET_VRF is not set.
# The same unshare -rn namespace returned:
#   Error: Unknown device type.
ip link add vrf-red type vrf table 10
ip link set vrf-red up
ip link set veth0 master vrf-red
ip vrf show
ip route show vrf vrf-red
ip vrf exec vrf-red ping -c 1 10.99.1.1
Differences that matter once the device exists:

Enslaved interfaces use the l3mdev policy rule to consult the VRF table, and their connected routes appear there. On Linux, if that lookup finds no route, later policy rules can still consult main; an unreachable default in the VRF table can prevent that fallback. Higher-priority policy rules can override the VRF rule, so inspect the complete rule set.
ip vrf exec (or a cgroup / SO_BINDTODEVICE / VRF-aware ip vrf identify) makes a process’s sockets belong to that table, including the source address selection. Policy routing on from: alone does not move an application that bound 0.0.0.0 into the right domain.
One host can run overlapping prefixes — 10.0.0.0/24 in red and in blue — because they do not share a FIB.
Netplan persists this with a vrfs: block: compulsory table:, an interfaces: list, and routes / routing-policy that implicitly use that table.

On a containerlab or netlab topology, a VRF is usually a module or a Linux vrf device inside a namespace, not something you create on the shared lab host. The lookup rules are the same.

title: Policy Routing and VRF
text:
Gotchas

Rule order is numeric priority, not insertion order. A broad from all table 10 at priority 50 will steal traffic from a more specific rule at 100.
The local table (priority 0) wins for the host’s own addresses. Do not be surprised when a packet to 10.10.10.1 never reaches table 10.
ip route get without from uses a source the kernel picks, which may not be the source your application will use. Pass from when you are testing a from rule.
rp_filter will drop asymmetric paths. If traffic leaves via table 20 and the reply arrives on veth0, strict reverse-path filtering treats it as martian. This is a common “policy routing is broken” false alarm.
VRF is a kernel option. Userspace (ip link help lists vrf) can be present when the running kernel cannot create the device. Check /proc/config.gz or /boot/config-$(uname -r) for CONFIG_NET_VRF=y or a usable CONFIG_NET_VRF=m module before you debug syntax.
IPv6 has its own rules (ip -6 rule, ip -6 route). A working IPv4 policy is silent about IPv6.

title: Policy Routing and VRF
text:
Common mistakes

Adding routes to table 10 and never adding a rule that selects table 10.
Assuming that a default route in main can never be used by a VRF: when the VRF table has no match, later policy rules may select it. Install and test the intended VRF default or an unreachable default.
Forgetting ip link set vrf-red up — a down VRF is a down domain.
Copying ip rule into a lab journal but not into Netplan / routing-policy, then losing it at reboot.

title: Policy Routing and VRF
text:
Boring rule
If two sources (or two interfaces, or two applications) must not share a FIB, give them a table and a rule you can show with ip route get. If the whole interface and its sockets belong together, that table should be a VRF. If you cannot show the lookup, you do not have a design yet.

title: Policy Routing and VRF
text:
Try this

Repeat the lab and add a default route in main. Run ip route get 10.99.1.1 again. When does the default hide a missing from rule?
Add ip rule add iif veth0 table 10 priority 90 and compare from versus incoming-interface selection.
On a kernel with VRF support built in or available as a module, build two VRFs with the same prefix on each, and show that ip vrf exec pings the right next hop.
Persist the two-uplink example as Netplan routes + routing-policy (or as a vrfs: block) and confirm ip rule after netplan try.
Turn on rp_filter=1 for one interface and reproduce a silent drop on an asymmetric reply.
