title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) routing allows a host or router to balance traffic across multiple paths of equal cost to a given destination network. Instead of selecting a single gateway, the routing subsystem selects among several candidates based on a hash of packet fields. In modern networks, ECMP is essential for maximizing fabric throughput, providing redundancy, and supporting scale-out leaf-spine top-of-rack architectures.
Linux has supported ECMP routing in the kernel Forwarding Information Base (FIB) for decades. However, the legacy mechanism for configuring multipath routes scales poorly with large routing tables and exhibits disruption under topology changes. Recent Linux kernel releases introduced dedicated nexthop objects, custom hash policy field masks, and resilient nexthop groups.
This chapter details the internal mechanics of Linux IPv4 ECMP routing, contrasting legacy syntax with nexthop objects, explaining RFC 2992 hash-threshold behavior versus resilient hashing, evaluating kernel hash field policies, and troubleshooting real-world issues like hash polarization and packet reordering.

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Learning goals

Understand the difference between legacy inline multipath routes and standalone kernel nexthop objects.
Evaluate the mathematical and operational differences between hash-threshold algorithms (RFC 2992) and resilient hashing groups.
Configure sysctl parameters governing layer 3, layer 4, and custom field-based multipath hash calculations.
Measure flow migration and collateral disruption during link failure events.
Recognize potential edge cases, including IP fragment handling, hash polarization in multi-tier fabrics, and neighbor cache integration.

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Version note
The command outputs and empirical measurements in this chapter were gathered using Linux kernel version 6.12.94+, iproute2 6.15.0, and Python 3.13.5. The tests ran inside an unprivileged user and network namespace environment initialized via unshare -rn sh lab.sh without superuser privileges or external host package dependencies. The host namespace defaults on this test system were fib_multipath_hash_policy=0, fib_multipath_hash_fields=7 (0x0007), and fib_multipath_use_neigh=0. Kernel FIB queries were performed using ip route get ... iif in0 ipproto udp sport X dport Y against simulated forwarding interfaces without sending live packets.

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Evolution of Linux Multipath Routing

Legacy Multipath Syntax
Historically, Linux multipath routes were specified inline within the route definition itself. Each route entry carried a set of gateways and interface references.
# Legacy multipath route specification (not run here: written from the docs)
ip route add 198.51.100.0/24 nexthop via 10.0.1.2 dev r1 nexthop via 10.0.2.2 dev r2
While functional for basic multihoming, this inline model creates severe scaling bottlenecks when managing modern dynamic routing tables:

Memory Redundancy: If a BGP router receives 1,000,000 IPv4 prefixes pointing to the exact same pair of next hops, the kernel allocates and builds 1,000,000 separate route structures, each duplicating the gateway and interface pointers internally.
Slow Convergence: When an upstream link flaps, a control plane daemon such as FRR zebra must issue 1,000,000 individual Netlink route updates to remove or replace the affected path. This introduces noticeable convergence lag and heavy CPU utilization.
Non-atomic Updates: Modifying a path set requires deleting and re-adding or replacing whole routes, opening transient windows where packets may drop or misroute.



Modern Nexthop Objects
Linux kernel 5.3 introduced explicit nexthop objects managed via the ip nexthop command family. Next hops are decoupled from routing table prefixes. A nexthop object can represent a single gateway (via), a blackhole, or a multipath group referencing other nexthop IDs.
# The same commands the lab below runs (shortened to two next hops)
ip nexthop add id 1 via 10.0.1.2 dev r1
ip nexthop add id 2 via 10.0.2.2 dev r2
ip nexthop add id 100 group 1/2
ip route add 198.51.100.0/24 nhid 100
This architecture provides significant advantages:

Deduplication: Millions of routes can reference a single group ID (nhid 100).
Atomic Operations: When link r1 fails, deleting nexthop ID 1 or updating group 100 updates forwarding for every prefix that uses it with one netlink message, instead of one message per route.
Control plane decoupling: a routing daemon can track next-hop reachability (link state, BFD) separately from prefix churn, and change one group when a path fails while the prefixes stay untouched.

When querying routes using ip route show, the kernel expands the referenced nexthop group ID for display.

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Hash Algorithms and Group Types
When forwarding an IP packet toward a prefix backed by a nexthop group, the kernel computes a hash over key fields in the packet header. The calculated hash integer maps to one of the nexthop choices in the group.
Linux supports two distinct group types: multipath (mpath) and resilient (resilient).

Multipath Groups (Hash-Threshold / RFC 2992)
The default group type in Linux is mpath, which implements the hash-threshold algorithm defined in RFC 2992.
Under hash-threshold, the total hash key space \([0, 2^{32}-1]\) is partitioned into contiguous regions proportional to the weight assigned to each nexthop member.
For example, with three equal-weight next hops (\(A, B, C\)), the hash range is partitioned into three equal segments: - \([0, \frac{1}{3} \times 2^{32}-1] \rightarrow A\) - \([\frac{1}{3} \times 2^{32}, \frac{2}{3} \times 2^{32}-1] \rightarrow B\) - \([\frac{2}{3} \times 2^{32}, 2^{32}-1] \rightarrow C\)
Hash Space Partitioning (RFC 2992):
+-----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+
|     Nexthop A (33%)   |     Nexthop B (33%)   |     Nexthop C (33%)   |
+-----------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+
0                                                                    2^32-1
If Nexthop \(C\) is removed, the remaining hash space must be re-divided into two equal regions between \(A\) and \(B\): - \([0, \frac{1}{2} \times 2^{32}-1] \rightarrow A\) - \([\frac{1}{2} \times 2^{32}, 2^{32}-1] \rightarrow B\)
Hash Space Partitioning after removing C:
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
|          Nexthop A (50%)          |          Nexthop B (50%)          |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
0                                                                    2^32-1
Because the boundary dividing \(A\) and \(B\) shifted from \(33\%\) to \(50\%\), flows hashing into the region \([33\%, 50\%]\) that originally mapped to \(B\) now map to \(A\).
This shifting phenomenon is known as collateral disruption or flow churn. Mathematically, removing one member out of \(N\) equal-weight paths under hash-threshold causes more than just the \(1/N\) flows bound to the failed path to move; it shifts a substantial portion of healthy flows operating on surviving paths. In stateful network environments, this causes TCP resets or out-of-order packet delivery across unaffected uplinks.

Weights in Hash-Threshold Groups
Weights control relative region sizing. A nexthop group syntax like group 1/2/3,2 specifies that nexthop ID 3 receives weight 2, while IDs 1 and 2 receive weight 1. The total weight is 4 (\(1+1+2\)), allocating \(25\%\) of the hash space to ID 1, \(25\%\) to ID 2, and \(50\%\) to ID 3.



Resilient Nexthop Groups
Introduced in Linux kernel 5.13, resilient groups eliminate collateral disruption by replacing contiguous range partitioning with a fixed lookup table of discrete buckets.
When defining a resilient group (type resilient buckets N), the kernel creates \(N\) buckets and gives each next hop a share of them proportional to its weight. Buckets are not re-cut when membership changes: only the buckets that must change owner do.
# As run in section 3 of the lab
ip nexthop add id 200 group 1/2/3/4 type resilient buckets 64 idle_timer 0
When a packet arrives: 1. The kernel computes the flow hash value. 2. The hash value modulo the total number of buckets selects a specific bucket (\(B = \text{hash} \pmod N\)). 3. The packet is routed through the nexthop owning bucket \(B\).
Resilient Bucket Table (e.g., 64 buckets):
Bucket:  [ 0 ][ 1 ][ 2 ][ 3 ] ... [ 63 ]
Owner:   [NH1][NH2][NH3][NH4] ... [NH3]
When a nexthop member is deleted from a resilient group, only the buckets owned by the deleted nexthop are reassigned to the remaining healthy nexthops. The ownership of all other buckets remains unchanged.
Bucket Reassignment after deleting NH4:
Bucket:  [ 0 ][ 1 ][ 2 ][ 3 ] ... [ 63 ]
Owner:   [NH1][NH2][NH3][NH1] ... [NH3]  <-- Bucket 3 reassigned from NH4 to NH1
Consequently, zero flows on surviving nexthops suffer collateral remapping.

Resilient Timers and Buckets
Resilient groups accept specific tuning parameters:

buckets N: Total bucket count. The bucket count should be significantly larger than the number of next hops to ensure balanced distribution. For instance, allocating 64 buckets across 3 next hops results in an integer allocation of 21, 22, and 21 buckets per next hop, yielding a near-perfect \(33.3\%\) traffic split.
idle_timer S: Time in seconds a bucket must remain idle before it can be migrated to another next hop during rebalancing (such as when adding a new nexthop back into the group). Setting idle_timer 0 allows instant bucket migration.
unbalanced_timer S: how long the group may stay unbalanced before buckets are migrated even if they are not idle. 0 (the default) means never force it: only idle buckets move.

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
section: Multipath Hash Policies and Field Masks
text:
Multipath Hash Policies and Field Masks
The packet header fields included in the ECMP hash calculation are controlled by the sysctl parameter net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy. (IPv6 offers an equivalent configuration knob in net.ipv6.fib_multipath_hash_policy).








Value
Policy Mode
Description




0
Layer 3 (L3)
Hashes Source IP and Destination IP. For IPv6, includes Flow Label and Next Header.


1
Layer 4 (L4)
Hashes 5-tuple: Source IP, Destination IP, L4 Protocol, Source Port, Destination Port.


2
Inner Layer 3
Hashes Layer 3 headers, looking inside encapsulation headers (e.g., VXLAN/GRE inner IPs) if present.


3
Custom Bitmask
Uses explicit field bitmask defined in net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_fields.




Custom Hash Fields Bitmask (fib_multipath_hash_fields)
When fib_multipath_hash_policy is set to 3, the kernel evaluates fib_multipath_hash_fields as a bitmask to select exact packet header fields for hashing.
The bit flags are defined as follows:



Bit Flag (Hex)
Decimal Value
Selected Header Field




0x0001
1
Source IP Address


0x0002
2
Destination IP Address


0x0004
4
IP Protocol


0x0008
8
IPv6 Flow Label


0x0010
16
Layer 4 Source Port


0x0020
32
Layer 4 Destination Port


0x0040
64
Inner Source IP Address


0x0080
128
Inner Destination IP Address


0x0100
256
Inner IP Protocol


0x0200
512
Inner IPv6 Flow Label


0x0400
1024
Inner Layer 4 Source Port


0x0800
2048
Inner Layer 4 Destination Port



The default value of fib_multipath_hash_fields is 7 (0x0007), representing Source IP (0x01) + Destination IP (0x02) + IP Protocol (0x04).
Note: Reading /proc/sys/net/ipv4/fib_multipath_hash_fields in sysctl scripts returns values in decimal format. For example, a bitmask of 0x0021 (Source IP + Destination Port) prints as 33.

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Operational Mechanics and Edge Cases

Neighbor Cache Integration (fib_multipath_use_neigh)
By default, the Linux FIB selects next hops strictly based on hash values, regardless of whether the target gateway’s ARP or Neighbor Discovery (ND) state is valid.
Setting net.ipv4.fib_multipath_use_neigh=1 instructs the kernel FIB to consult the neighbor table before selecting a nexthop. If a candidate nexthop gateway enters a failed state (NUD_FAILED), the kernel skips that path during hash selection and routes traffic via remaining healthy gateways.


IP Fragment Handling
Layer 4 hashing policies reliance on transport-layer ports introduces challenges with IP fragmentation.
Only the initial fragment (fragment offset 0) contains transport protocol header fields like TCP/UDP source and destination ports. Subsequent fragments carry only IP headers and fragment offsets.
When L4 multipath hashing (policy 1) is enabled: - Fragment 0 hashes using the full 5-tuple. - Fragments 1..N lack port fields, forcing the kernel to fall back to L3 header fields (Source IP, Destination IP, Protocol).
Because the computed hash value for fragment 0 differs from subsequent fragments, initial and trailing fragments of the same IP datagram can be routed across different physical uplinks. If one path experiences higher latency or drops packets, receiver reassembly buffers fail, causing degraded application performance.


Hash Polarization
Hash polarization occurs in multi-tier leaf-spine network fabrics when every router in the path uses the identical hashing algorithm and identical header input fields.
            flows
              |
         [ leaf L1 ]   hash H(5-tuple) mod 2 -> keeps only flows with H even for S1
          /       \
     [ S1 ]       [ S2 ]
     /    \
 [L2a]   [L2b]    S1 hashes the same fields with the same function: every flow it
                  received has H even, so H mod 2 sends them all to L2a
If Leaf L1 splits incoming traffic across two spines using a 5-tuple hash, Spine S1 receives a pre-filtered subset of total flows. If Spine S1 uses the exact same hashing function and input fields to route traffic toward downstream Leaf L2, the hash calculation yields identical relative buckets. As a result, traffic concentrates heavily on a subset of links while adjacent uplinks sit completely idle.
To mitigate hash polarization: 1. Vary hash field bitmasks (fib_multipath_hash_fields) across different network tiers. 2. Give each router its own hash seed (net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_seed, added in Linux 6.11 and present on this box’s 6.12 kernel). By default the seed is random per boot, so polarization between Linux boxes mostly comes from a seed that has been pinned to the same value everywhere (done so that a group of routers hash consistently), or from hardware switches whose hash function and inputs really are identical.


Routing Daemon Integration
FRRouting’s zebra can install its next-hop groups as kernel nexthop objects on kernels that support them, so routes arrive as nhid N references rather than inline multipath routes; check ip nexthop show on an FRR box to see which objects it owns (not run here: no FRR on this box; see the FRR zebra documentation).

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Hands-on Lab
The following lab script creates a network namespace topology containing four uplink interfaces and tests hash-threshold groups, resilient groups, nexthop deletion, group weighting, and custom field hash policies.

Lab Script (lab.sh)


lab.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -rn sh lab.sh   (unprivileged user + network namespace, no sudo)
set -e
H=$(pwd); N=4000
ip link set lo up
ip link add in0 type veth peer name in1          # ingress: flows "arrive" here
ip addr add 203.0.113.254/24 dev in0; ip link set in0 up; ip link set in1 up
for i in 1 2 3 4; do                              # four uplinks, gateway .2 on each
  ip link add r$i type veth peer name p$i
  ip addr add 10.0.$i.1/24 dev r$i; ip link set r$i up; ip link set p$i up
  ip nexthop add id $i via 10.0.$i.2 dev r$i
done
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/fib_multipath_hash_policy    # L4: 5-tuple

echo "== 1. hash-threshold group of four, $N flows"
ip nexthop add id 100 group 1/2/3/4
ip route add 198.51.100.0/24 nhid 100
ip nexthop show id 100
python3 $H/flows.py $N ht-4.txt
echo "== 2. delete nexthop 4 (link down, BFD, withdrawn route...)"
ip nexthop del id 4
ip nexthop show id 100
python3 $H/flows.py $N ht-3.txt
python3 $H/compare.py ht-4.txt ht-3.txt 10.0.4.2

echo "== 3. same story with a resilient group (64 buckets)"
ip route del 198.51.100.0/24; ip nexthop del id 100
ip nexthop add id 4 via 10.0.4.2 dev r4
ip nexthop add id 200 group 1/2/3/4 type resilient buckets 64 idle_timer 0
ip route add 198.51.100.0/24 nhid 200
ip nexthop show id 200
python3 $H/flows.py $N rs-4.txt
ip nexthop del id 4
python3 $H/flows.py $N rs-3.txt
python3 $H/compare.py rs-4.txt rs-3.txt 10.0.4.2
echo "   bucket owners after the delete:"
ip nexthop bucket show id 200 | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sed 's/^/     /'

echo "== 4. weights: 1:1:2 (hash-threshold)"
ip route del 198.51.100.0/24; ip nexthop del id 200
ip nexthop add id 300 group 1/2/3,2
ip route add 198.51.100.0/24 nhid 300
ip nexthop show id 300
python3 $H/flows.py $N w.txt
python3 $H/compare.py w.txt

echo "== 5. policy 3: hash only on what you choose"
echo 3 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/fib_multipath_hash_policy
echo 0x0021 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/fib_multipath_hash_fields   # 0x0001 src IP | 0x0020 dst port
printf "   fields = %s\n" "$(cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/fib_multipath_hash_fields)"
for src in 10 11 12 13; do for sp in 1111 2222; do
  printf "   src 203.0.113.%s sport %s dport 53 -> " $src $sp
  ip route get 198.51.100.7 from 203.0.113.$src iif in0 ipproto udp sport $sp dport 53 | grep -o 'via [0-9.]*'
done; done



Flow Query Script (flows.py)


flows.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# flows.py N OUT: ask the kernel FIB which next hop each of N synthetic UDP flows gets.
# Uses one `ip -batch` run of `route get` and prints flow-key -> gateway lines to OUT.
import subprocess, sys, random
n, out = int(sys.argv[1]), sys.argv[2]
rnd = random.Random(7)          # fixed seed: the same N flows every time
lines, keys = [], []
for _ in range(n):
    src = f"203.0.113.{rnd.randrange(1, 254)}"   # .254 is our own in0
    dst = f"198.51.100.{rnd.randrange(1, 255)}"
    sp, dp = rnd.randrange(1024, 65535), rnd.choice([53, 443, 4789])
    keys.append(f"{src}:{sp}->{dst}:{dp}")
    lines.append(f"route get {dst} from {src} iif in0 ipproto udp sport {sp} dport {dp}")
r = subprocess.run(["ip", "-batch", "-"], input="\n".join(lines) + "\n",
                   capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
gws = [l.split(" via ")[1].split()[0] for l in r.stdout.splitlines() if " via " in l]
assert len(gws) == n, (len(gws), r.stderr[:200])
with open(out, "w") as f:
    for k, g in zip(keys, gws):
        f.write(f"{k} {g}\n")



Results Comparison Script (compare.py)


compare.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# compare.py BEFORE AFTER [REMOVED_GW]: spread per gateway, and how many flows moved.
import sys, collections
def load(p): return dict(l.split() for l in open(p))
a = load(sys.argv[1]); b = load(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
gone = sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else None
def spread(m):
    c = collections.Counter(m.values())
    return "  ".join(f"{g}={c[g]}" for g in sorted(c))
print("   before:", spread(a))
if b:
    print("   after: ", spread(b))
    moved = [k for k in a if a[k] != b[k]]
    innocent = [k for k in moved if a[k] != gone]
    print(f"   moved {len(moved)} of {len(a)} flows;"
          f" flows that were NOT on {gone} but moved anyway: {len(innocent)}")

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Reading the output

Step 1 & 2: Hash-Threshold Disruption
In Step 1, a hash-threshold group (ID 100) containing 4 equal next hops is evaluated across 4,000 synthetic UDP flows. The initial flow distribution across gateways is roughly equal: - 10.0.1.2: 964 flows - 10.0.2.2: 997 flows - 10.0.3.2: 999 flows - 10.0.4.2: 1040 flows
In Step 2, nexthop ID 4 (10.0.4.2) is removed from group 100. Comparing the flow mapping before and after deletion reveals massive collateral churn: - Total moved flows: 2,041 of 4,000 flows (\(51.0\%\)). - Innocent moved flows: 1,001 flows that were bound to healthy gateways (10.0.1.2, 10.0.2.2, 10.0.3.2) were forcibly remapped to different surviving gateways.
This occurs because removing nexthop 4 shifted the RFC 2992 hash range boundaries across all remaining gateways. Approximately \(25\%\) of all active network flows suffered collateral disruption despite operating on unaffected physical interfaces.


Step 3: Resilient Group Stabilization
In Step 3, group ID 200 is configured as a resilient group with 64 buckets. The initial distribution across 4,000 flows yields: - 10.0.1.2: 1024 flows - 10.0.2.2: 1001 flows - 10.0.3.2: 1042 flows - 10.0.4.2: 933 flows
Note: The initial flow counts differ slightly from Section 2 because consistent bucket hash indexing maps flow keys differently than hash-threshold range boundaries.
When nexthop ID 4 is deleted: - Total moved flows: 933 of 4,000 flows (\(23.3\%\)). - Innocent moved flows: 0.
Every single flow that was originally routed to surviving gateways (10.0.1.2, 10.0.2.2, 10.0.3.2) remained on its exact initial path. Only the 933 flows associated with the failed gateway (10.0.4.2) were reassigned to remaining healthy gateways.
The bucket inspection query displays the updated owner counts across the 64 buckets: - Gateway 10.0.1.2 (Nexthop 1): 21 buckets - Gateway 10.0.2.2 (Nexthop 2): 22 buckets - Gateway 10.0.3.2 (Nexthop 3): 21 buckets
The deleted nexthop’s buckets were evenly split across the surviving next hops, maintaining balance without disturbing unaffected flows.


Step 4: Weighted Hash-Threshold Distribution
In Step 4, group ID 300 is initialized with weights 1/2/3,2 (Nexthop 1 weight 1, Nexthop 2 weight 1, Nexthop 3 weight 2).
The 4,000 flows distribute as follows: - 10.0.1.2: 964 flows (\(24.1\%\)) - 10.0.2.2: 997 flows (\(24.9\%\)) - 10.0.3.2: 2039 flows (\(51.0\%\))
This matches the expected proportional weights of \(1:1:2\) (\(25\% / 25\% / 50\%\)).


Step 5: Custom Field Hash Policy Enforcement
In Step 5, the multipath policy is switched to mode 3 (custom), and fib_multipath_hash_fields is set to 0x0021 (decimal 33). This bitmask enables hashing on Source IP (0x0001) and Destination Port (0x0020), explicitly excluding Source Port (0x0010).
The output demonstrates that changing the source port (sport 1111 vs sport 2222) has zero effect on route selection: - 203.0.113.10 port 1111 and port 2222 both map to via 10.0.1.2. - 203.0.113.11 port 1111 and port 2222 both map to via 10.0.3.2. - 203.0.113.12 port 1111 and port 2222 both map to via 10.0.2.2. - 203.0.113.13 port 1111 and port 2222 both map to via 10.0.3.2.
Varying the source IP shifts the hash result to different next hops (10.0.1.2, 10.0.3.2, 10.0.2.2), but for any single source IP, all source ports land on the identical nexthop gateway.

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Gotchas

Belief: Deleting a single link from an ECMP group only affects flows on that specific link. Why it is wrong: Under default hash-threshold (mpath) groups, removing one gateway shifts the boundaries of all adjacent hash regions. As shown in the lab, deleting 1 of 4 gateways caused \(51\%\) of all flows to shift paths, including over 1,000 flows operating on healthy uplinks. Use resilient groups (type resilient) when minimal flow disruption is required.
Belief: Setting fib_multipath_hash_policy=1 guarantees equal distribution for fragmented IP traffic. Why it is wrong: Non-initial IP fragments lack UDP/TCP port headers. The kernel falls back to L3 headers when hashing non-initial fragments, causing trailing fragments to select different next hops than the initial fragment.
Belief: idle_timer 0 is the safe setting. Why it is wrong: it is the aggressive one. With idle_timer 0 a bucket can be handed to another next hop the moment the group is rebalanced (for example when a repaired next hop is added back), so live flows in that bucket change path. Through stateful firewalls, NAT or load balancers that is the same reset you were trying to avoid. A nonzero idle timer (the default is 120 seconds) waits for a bucket to go quiet first. The lab uses 0 only because it measures decisions, not live flows.
Belief: Modifying sysctl fib_multipath_hash_fields takes effect immediately while fib_multipath_hash_policy=1. Why it is wrong: The fib_multipath_hash_fields bitmask is strictly ignored by the kernel unless fib_multipath_hash_policy is explicitly set to 3.
Belief: a few buckets are enough, as long as there is one per next hop. Why it is wrong: bucket shares are integers. With 4 next hops and 4 buckets, losing one leaves 3 buckets for 3 next hops, fine, but weights cannot be expressed and a 5th next hop cannot get any share without stealing a whole bucket. Use many more buckets than next hops (64 gave 21/22/21 here; production setups use hundreds or thousands).
Belief: The kernel ARP/Neighbor table automatically withdraws failed ECMP gateways from routing decisions. Why it is wrong: By default (fib_multipath_use_neigh=0), the kernel forwards packets according to hash calculations even if the gateway’s ARP state is NUD_FAILED. To bypass dead neighbor entries, net.ipv4.fib_multipath_use_neigh must be explicitly set to 1.
Belief: Custom hash field values set via sysctl are entered in hexadecimal when using echo. Why it is wrong: While echo 0x0021 > /proc/sys/... accepts hex strings, reading back the sysctl parameter returns decimal values (e.g., 33). Automation scripts verifying configuration state must account for decimal conversion.

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Exercises

Resilient Idle Timers: Modify lab.sh to construct a resilient group with idle_timer 10. Delete nexthop 4, re-add nexthop 4 immediately, and measure flow migration before and after the 10-second idle window expires.
IPv6 Flow Label Hashing: Create an IPv6 variant of the lab using net.ipv6.fib_multipath_hash_policy=3 and configure fib_multipath_hash_fields to hash strictly on IPv6 Destination IP and Flow Label (0x000a). Verify that varying the IPv6 Flow Label spreads flows without altering port numbers.
Single Source ECMP Spread under L3 Policy: Set fib_multipath_hash_policy=0 (L3 mode). Write a script sending 4,000 flows originating from a single source IP address (203.0.113.10) toward random destination IPs in 198.51.100.0/24. Measure the resulting gateway distribution.
8-Way Hash-Threshold Disruption: Extend the hash-threshold lab to 8 equal-cost next hops. Remove 1 next hop and compute the percentage of innocent flows disrupted. Compare the result against theoretical predictions.
Resilient Group Weighting: Configure a resilient group with 64 buckets and weights 1/2/3,2. Query ip nexthop bucket show to verify the exact bucket count assigned to each nexthop ID.

title: Linux ECMP: Nexthop Objects, Hash Policies and Resilient Groups
text:
Verification
The tests and outputs in this chapter were executed and verified in the following environment:

Operating System / Kernel: Linux 6.12.94+

title: Multicast Membership and Distribution Trees
text:
Multicast Membership and Distribution Trees
A multicast sender sends one IP packet to a group address; the network replicates it where receiver paths diverge. This saves upstream bandwidth, but creates state in switches and routers. Multicast does not provide reliable delivery: loss and recovery remain the application’s responsibility.

title: Multicast Membership and Distribution Trees
text:
Addresses and LAN membership
IPv4 multicast uses 224.0.0.0/4; the 224.0.0.0/24 local network control block is not forwarded by multicast routers. Administratively scoped 239.0.0.0/8 addresses require boundary enforcement. IPv4 source-specific multicast (SSM) uses 232.0.0.0/8. IPv6 multicast begins with ff, with scope encoded in the address; IPv6 uses MLD rather than IGMP for membership.
Ethernet maps the low 23 bits of an IPv4 multicast group into 01:00:5e:00:00:00/25. Because a group has 28 variable bits, 32 groups map to each Ethernet address. For example, 239.1.1.1 and 239.129.1.1 both map to 01:00:5e:01:01:01. An Ethernet address alone does not identify a unique IP group.
IGMP connects IPv4 hosts to local multicast routers. An application joins a group through its operating system; routers query and hosts report reception state. IGMPv3 supports INCLUDE (accept listed sources) and EXCLUDE (accept sources except those listed). Router state aggregates interest on a LAN: one host leaving must not interrupt another. Query and last-member timers affect how quickly state disappears.
An IGMP-snooping switch observes control traffic and maintains VLAN-scoped entries toward receiver ports and multicast-router ports. It does not replace multicast routing. A querier refreshes membership; a switch’s snooping querier may provide queries without routing. Unknown multicast and fast-leave behavior vary by platform. Fast leave can interrupt other receivers when a port serves multiple hosts. IGMP reports do not authenticate receivers.

title: Multicast Membership and Distribution Trees
text:
Distribution trees and RPF
PIM uses routing information to build multicast distribution state. It is independent of the particular unicast routing protocol but needs a usable unicast or multicast-specific routing table. In PIM sparse mode, a receiver-side router sends a (*,G) join toward the rendezvous point (RP) for group G. The source-side router initially registers source traffic with the RP, allowing delivery down the shared tree. A receiver-side router may then join an (S,G) shortest-path tree toward source S and prune that source from the shared tree. Switchover policy varies. Any-source multicast (ASM) requires consistent group-to-RP mapping and RP reachability.
With SSM, the receiver specifies both source and group. Routers build an (S,G) tree toward the source, without an RP or shared tree. Source-aware host membership, such as IGMPv3, is required. SSM does not authenticate the source address.
A router checks whether a packet arrived on the expected upstream interface toward its source, or toward the RP while using the shared tree. This reverse-path forwarding (RPF) check prevents loops and duplicates. Traffic arriving on the wrong interface is normally discarded even when the receiver is reachable. Inspect the incoming interface (IIF), outgoing interface list (OIL), upstream neighbor, and counters. An empty OIL means no downstream forwarding. On shared LANs, PIM assert mechanisms select a forwarder. Equal-cost routing and multicast RIB overrides affect RPF selection, so inspect the actual selected state.







Observation
Investigate




No membership report
Application join, interface, IGMP version, filtering


Membership but no switch egress
VLAN, snooping entries, router port, querier and timers


PIM neighbors but no join
Membership, group policy, source or RP mapping


Wrong-IIF counter rises
RPF route, multicast RIB, asymmetry or stale state


Correct IIF and OIL but loss
TTL, MTU, ACL, congestion, hardware or receiver



TTL decreases across routers; a sender’s TTL of 1 typically prevents routed delivery. Capture at successive interfaces and compare timestamps. Hardware-forwarded traffic may not appear in a switch CPU capture; use a suitable mirror or port counters.
For packet captures and a routed PIM lab, continue with Multicast Essentials; use the multicast failure exercises to practice diagnosing the tree.

title: Multicast Membership and Distribution Trees
text:
Review and sources
Explain why IP groups can share an Ethernet address; distinguish a membership report from a PIM join; and explain why unicast reachability can coexist with RPF drops. What additional information does an SSM receiver supply?
Further reading: IGMPv3, RFC 9776, PIM sparse mode, RFC 7761, snooping considerations, RFC 4541, and SSM architecture, RFC 4607.

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
First-Hop Redundancy
Hosts rarely run a routing protocol. They send traffic to a default gateway. If that gateway dies, the LAN dies with it—unless you give the LAN a virtual first hop that can move between routers. This chapter builds the model and a free-stack lab: Linux + FRR + Containerlab (mid-2026 open path).

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain why a single gateway IP is a single point of failure

Contrast VRRP-class first-hop redundancy with floating statics and ECMP

Deploy a dual-router VRRP pair on FRR for a shared virtual IP (VIP)

Predict host behavior when the master fails and when it recovers

Verify with ip neigh, pings, and FRR VRRP state—not hope

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
Concepts

The problem
   h1 ---- [LAN] ---- gw 10.0.0.1  (one box)
              |
           Internet-ish
Host config: default via 10.0.0.1. When that box reboots, ARP still points at a MAC that is gone until the host relearns—or traffic blackholes forever if nothing answers.


First-hop redundancy idea
Two (or more) routers share:



Object
Role




Virtual IP (VIP)
Address hosts use as gateway


Virtual MAC (often)
Stable L2 identity for the VIP


Master / backup roles
Who owns the VIP right now


Hello / advertise
“I am alive and I claim priority”



Hosts keep one gateway IP. The active forwarder changes under them.


Protocol family (vendor-agnostic)



Name
Notes




VRRP
Open standard idea; FRR supports VRRP


HSRP / GLBP
Proprietary dialects of the same problem class


CARP
OpenBSD-family cousin



This book uses VRRP on FRR because it is free, documented, and works in Containerlab without licenses. Optional: Nokia SR Linux community images have their own FHRP configuration surface—same model, different CLI.


Priority, preempt, timers

Priority: higher wins master election (within rules).

Preempt: when a higher-priority router returns, does it take the VIP back?

Advertisement interval: how fast backups notice silence.

Skew / master-down interval: how long before backup promotes.



What FHRP is not







Not this
Because




Full routing protocol
Hosts do not learn remote prefixes via VRRP


Load balancing of arbitrary flows (unless designed)
Classic VRRP is active/standby for a VIP


Multihoming policy
That is BGP/statics + dual default; separate chapter lab



FHRP protects the LAN’s first hop. Dual-homing the site edge is complementary (see dual-home lab later in this part).


ARP and the VIP
When master changes, hosts may still have the old MAC in the neighbor cache briefly. Good implementations use a shared virtual MAC or gratuitous ARP so clients rebind quickly. In labs, clear neighbor cache deliberately when debugging:
# Linux host
ip neigh flush dev eth1
# or
ip neigh del 10.0.0.254 dev eth1

Topology YAML
name: vrrp-edge

topology:
  nodes:
    r1:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/r1:/etc/frr
    r2:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/r2:/etc/frr
    pe:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/pe:/etc/frr
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils
        - ip addr add 10.10.10.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 10.10.10.254

  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "r1:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth1", "r2:eth1"]   # same LAN: use bridge or multipoint
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth2", "pe:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r2:eth2", "pe:eth2"]
LAN wiring note: two point-to-point links do not make a shared segment. Prefer a Linux bridge node as “LAN switch,” or Containerlab multipoint / bridge patterns from your lab-craft notes:
    lan:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 bridge-utils
        - ip link add name br0 type bridge
        - ip link set br0 up
  # links: h1, r1, r2 all into lan with bridge enslavement in exec
Simpler teaching pattern: one host + two routers on a bridge so ARP and VRRP multicast behave like a campus LAN.

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
FRR VRRP sketch (r1)
frr version 10.2.1
frr defaults traditional
hostname r1
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.10.10.2/24
!
interface eth2
 ip address 172.16.1.1/30
!
interface eth1
 vrrp 1 ip 10.10.10.254
 vrrp 1 priority 200
 vrrp 1 advertisement-interval 1000
!
ip route 0.0.0.0/0 172.16.1.2
!
line vty
r2: real IP 10.10.10.3/24, priority 100, same VIP and VRID 1, default via its own uplink.
Syntax varies slightly by FRR minor version—always validate with:
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r1 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r1 vtysh -c 'show interface eth1'

Deploy and baseline
sudo containerlab deploy -t vrrp-edge.clab.yml

docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r1 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'

docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-h1 ping -c 3 10.10.10.254
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-h1 ping -c 3 172.16.1.2

Predict (baseline)

r1 is Master, r2 is Backup (priority 200 > 100)

h1 ARP for VIP resolves to master’s virtual/real MAC pattern for your stack

Ping VIP succeeds; traffic to upstream uses r1’s uplink



Observe
Record: VRRP state, VIP owner interface counters, ip neigh on h1, traceroute if upstream is reachable.

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
Drill 1 — Master failure
# Simulate master death (stop data plane or whole node)
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r1 ip link set eth1 down
# or: docker stop clab-vrrp-edge-r1

sleep 3
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r2 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-h1 ip neigh show 10.10.10.254
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-h1 ping -c 10 10.10.10.254
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-h1 ping -c 5 203.0.113.1   # if pe has this

Predict → observe → fix








Predict
Observe
Fix if wrong




r2 becomes Master after down-timer
show vrrp
timers, VRID mismatch, not same LAN


Short ping loss then recovery
count drops
ARP stuck—flush neigh; check VIP MAC


Upstream still works via r2
traceroute
r2 default / pe return routes



Restore:
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r1 ip link set eth1 up
# or docker start + wait FRR ready
sleep 5
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r1 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r2 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'
Preempt on: r1 reclaims Master. Preempt off: r2 may stay Master—document which you configured.

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
Drill 2 — Split brain / LAN partition (concept)
If both routers believe they are alone (broken LAN bridge), two masters can both answer the VIP → intermittent ARP thrash.

Predict
Duplicate VIP answers; flapping neighbor cache; odd packet loss.


Observe
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r1 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r2 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'
# tcpdump for VRRP (IP protocol 112) on the LAN
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-h1 sh -c 'apk add --no-cache tcpdump; tcpdump -ni eth1 proto 112 -c 10'


Fix / harden

Ensure single L2 domain for the VRID

BFD or link tracking to uplinks (advanced) so a “master” without upstream demotes

Monitoring on “two masters seen” is an ops smell

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
Drill 3 — Priority change live
docker exec -it clab-vrrp-edge-r2 vtysh
configure terminal
interface eth1
 vrrp 1 priority 250
end
write

Predict
If preempt allowed, r2 becomes Master; h1 may re-ARP; path to upstream shifts to r2’s uplink.


Observe
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r1 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r2 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-h1 traceroute -n 172.16.2.2
Revert priorities in git-mounted configs after the experiment.

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
Return path and asymmetric edges
VIP failover only moves the outbound first hop. If upstream routing always returns via r1 while r2 is master, you get asymmetric paths or blackholes. Pair FHRP with:

Shared upstream design, or

Dynamic routing so return traffic follows the active edge, or

State-aware NAT only on the active path (harder—prefer avoid state at edge in labs first)

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
Verification checklist



Check
Intent




show vrrp
One Master per VRID on the LAN


Host default route
Points at VIP only


ping VIP
L2/L3 ownership of first hop


Kill master
Backup promotes; host recovers


Capture proto 112
Hellos present on LAN


Upstream ping during fail
Data plane + return path

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
verify.sh sketch
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
fail() { echo "FAIL: $*" >&2; exit 1; }

docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-h1 ping -c 2 -W 1 10.10.10.254 || fail "VIP"
# Exactly one master is harder in shell—parse show vrrp or accept soft check:
docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r1 vtysh -c 'show vrrp' | grep -qi master \
  || docker exec clab-vrrp-edge-r2 vtysh -c 'show vrrp' | grep -qi master \
  || fail "no master"
echo OK

Symptom

Never form master/backup correctly

Two independent groups

title: First-Hop Redundancy
text:
Summary

Hosts need a stable first hop; VRRP-class protocols move a VIP between routers

FRR + Containerlab is enough to learn Master/Backup, preempt, and failure timers

Always verify host ARP, VRRP state, and end-to-end path after failover

FHRP is not multihoming policy—combine later with dual-home BGP/statics

Keep configs in binds; promote live priority experiments back to git

Next: DHCP relay and NAT—how edge services attach to this LAN model without becoming mysterious middleboxes.






Practice in the lab workbook



First Hop: VRRP and VARP

title: DHCP Relay and NAT
text:
DHCP Relay and NAT
Edges do more than forward packets. They hand out addresses (or relay DHCP) and often translate private space toward a provider. This chapter keeps both topics vendor-agnostic and lab-first: Linux services + FRR routing in Containerlab (mid-2026 free path).

title: DHCP Relay and NAT
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain DHCP discover/offer/request/ack across a relay

Configure a simple DHCP server and a relay path in a lab

Contrast source NAT (masquerade), static NAT, and “why not NAT everything forever”

Implement Linux nftables/iptables MASQUERADE on an edge

Predict breakage when relays, helpers, or return translations fail

title: DHCP Relay and NAT
text:
Concepts — DHCP

Why not static everything?
Labs love static host IPs. Real access LANs use DHCP for:



Benefit
Trade-off




Central policy (lease, DNS, gateway)
Dependency on server/relay


Fast readdressing
Lease timers and “sticky” clients


Audit of who got what
Need logging and hygiene





Four-way dance (v4)
Client          Relay (optional)         Server
  |-- Discover ------(unicast to server)-->|
  |<-- Offer -------------------------------|
  |-- Request ----------------------------->|
  |<-- Ack ---------------------------------|
On a flat LAN, broadcast Discover reaches the server. Across subnets, a relay agent (ip helper / DHCP relay) listens on the client VLAN and unicasts to the server, inserting giaddr (gateway IP of the client interface) so the server knows which pool to use.


Critical fields



Field / idea
Why it matters




Client MAC / Client-ID
Lease binding


giaddr
Selects pool / subnet


Options: router, DNS, domain
Host becomes usable


Lease time
How long address is “owned”





Relay failure modes

Wrong giaddr → wrong pool or no offer

ACL blocking UDP 67/68

Server unreachable from relay

Multiple relays or servers without coordinated scope and policy → unexpected offers or lease conflicts; multiple offers alone are normal

title: DHCP Relay and NAT
text:
Concepts — NAT family







Kind
Meaning




SNAT / MASQUERADE
Rewrite source as packets leave (common “PAT”)


DNAT
Rewrite destination (port forward / publish service)


1:1 static NAT
Stable mapping for a host


NAT64 / CLAT
v6/v4 transition tools (awareness only here)



NAT is state + rewrite. It is not a security model by itself. Stateful firewalls may sit with NAT; keep roles clear.

When NAT is appropriate in this book

Lab edge simulating consumer/ISP CPE

Hiding RFC1918 behind a single lab “public”

Temporary access during dual-stack migration

Prefer real global or ULA design for multi-site fabrics later—NAT at every hop becomes undebugable.

Addressing plan (combined edge lab)
  h-client (DHCP)          dhcp-srv
       |                      |
      lan ---- edge-rtr ---- pe (public-ish)
                 |

Net
Use

name: dhcp-nat-edge

Same subnet: client broadcast reaches server—no relay.

Off-subnet: relay required; server must understand the client subnet (shared-network / giaddr-aware config).


Minimal same-subnet lab (sanity first)
Place dnsmasq on edge’s LAN IP or a server on the bridge:

dhcp-option=option:router,10.20.30.1

Symptom
Checks

bridge, interface up, firewall, wrong interface in dnsmasq


Offer but wrong GW
dhcp-option router

UDP 67/68, giaddr, server route

title: DHCP Relay and NAT
text:
NAT — MASQUERADE on edge
Clients use private 10.20.30.0/24; PE only knows 198.51.100.0/30.
docker exec clab-dhcp-nat-edge-edge iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING \
  -o eth3 -j MASQUERADE
# nftables equivalent pattern:
# nft add table ip nat
# nft add chain ip nat postrouting { type nat hook postrouting priority 100 \; }
# nft add rule ip nat postrouting oifname "eth3" masquerade
PE needs a way to answer (connected route to 198.51.100.1 is enough for return of MASQUERADE traffic).

Predict

client → 203.0.113.1 works

On pe, sources appear as 198.51.100.1, not 10.20.30.x

Without MASQUERADE, pe has no return path to 10.20.30.0/24



Observe
docker exec clab-dhcp-nat-edge-client ping -c 3 203.0.113.1
docker exec clab-dhcp-nat-edge-pe sh -c 'apk add --no-cache tcpdump; tcpdump -ni eth1 -c 5 icmp'
docker exec clab-dhcp-nat-edge-edge iptables -t nat -L -n -v


Fix

ip_forward=1

Correct -o egress interface

title: DHCP Relay and NAT
section: DHCP lease state and relay reasoning
text:
DHCP lease state and relay reasoning
In the common initial IPv4 exchange, a client without an address broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER, one or more servers offer a configuration, the client requests one offer, and the selected server acknowledges it. A lease is time-limited: the client normally attempts renewal with the original server at T1 and, if necessary, rebinding with any available server at T2; T1 precedes T2 and lease expiry. A client that already has a lease may follow a different exchange, so do not expect every capture to show all four messages. See RFC 2131.
A router ordinarily does not forward a client’s local broadcast into a remote subnet. A DHCP relay receives the client message and forwards it to a configured server, identifying the client-side network using relay information including giaddr. The server uses its configuration and relay information to select an appropriate scope and send a response back through the relay. The precise policy can include additional relay options; giaddr is not the address being leased to the client.
When clients fail to acquire an address, capture on both the client-facing and server-facing interfaces. A DISCOVER on the client VLAN with no forwarded request suggests a relay, interface, or policy issue; a request reaching the server without an offer points toward server scope, policy, availability, or return routing. An ACK is evidence of a lease response, not proof that DNS, the default route, or external connectivity is correct. Compare the lease’s subnet mask, router, and DNS options with the intended VLAN.

title: DHCP Relay and NAT
section: NAT mapping is not a route or a firewall policy
text:
NAT mapping is not a route or a firewall policy
Suppose an inside client 172.16.10.10:40000 sends UDP to 203.0.113.10:53. A source-NAT device might translate it to 203.0.113.1:53001 and retain a mapping so the return packet can be translated back. The external port is an example, not a guaranteed choice. Concurrent clients need distinguishable mappings; an idle mapping can expire. The gateway must also have a route and permit the packet through its filtering policy.
A mapping answers how addresses and ports are translated; filtering decides which packets are allowed to use a mapping. These are related but separate behaviors. NAT does not authenticate a user or replace explicit firewall policy. Return traffic must pass through a device that has the appropriate translation state, so asymmetric paths and state expiry can break a flow even when routes exist in both directions. Compare captures inside and outside, and inspect the actual connection-tracking state where supported. RFC 4787 describes UDP mapping and filtering behaviors.

title: Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
text:
Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
Network booting allows a computer to load an operating system directly over a local or wide area network without using local storage devices like hard drives or NVMe SSDs. This capability forms the backbone of diskless workstations, automated OS installation pipelines, cloud hypervisor provisioning, and bare-metal server deployment.
The network boot lifecycle relies on a handoff between firmware execution, IP address acquisition, boot image retrieval, and kernel initialization. Historically, this lifecycle was governed by the Intel Preboot Execution Environment (PXE) specification over the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP). Modern infrastructure extends this foundation to support HTTP-based boot protocols, chainloading open-source bootloaders like iPXE, and leveraging UEFI firmware features for encrypted, authenticated image loading.
Understanding how network boot operates requires examining how network parameters and boot instructions are conveyed during address assignment. As introduced in DHCP Relay and NAT, Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) delivers IP addresses and network configuration to booting hosts. Beyond basic parameters like IP addresses and netmasks, network boot relies on specialized DHCP fields and options to direct firmware to boot binaries.

title: Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
text:
Learning goals

Understand the sequence of operations in PXE, iPXE, and UEFI HTTP boot processes.
Identify the DHCP options (60, 66, 67, 77, 93, 94, 97) used by client firmware to report capabilities and receive boot targets.
Explain the mechanism and configuration requirements of DHCP chainloading to prevent boot loops.
Analyze the internal protocol mechanics of TFTP (RFC 1350) and its option extensions (RFC 2347, 2348, 2349, 7440).
Evaluate performance bottlenecks of TFTP lock-step transmissions across high-RTT networks and quantify the impact of block size and window size optimizations.
Recognize security risks inherent in network boot protocols and identify strategies for hardening preboot environments.

title: Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
text:
Version note
The examples, lab outputs, and protocol demonstrations in this chapter were executed unprivileged on Linux kernel version 6.12 using iproute2 version 6.15.0 and Python 3.13 inside an isolated namespace (unshare -urnm). No root access or external daemon installations were required.

title: Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
text:
PXE Fundamentals and Protocol Sequence
The PXE 2.1 specification, introduced by Intel in 1999, defines a standard client-server environment for booting x86 systems over an Ethernet network. The client side consists of firmware embedded on the system board or Network Interface Card (NIC) Option ROM that implements a Universal Network Driver Interface (UNDI) and a minimal DHCP/TFTP stack.

PXE DHCP Discover and Options
When a machine initiates a PXE boot, the system firmware broadcasts a DHCP DISCOVER packet containing specific options to identify itself as a network boot client:

Option 60 (Vendor Class Identifier): Set to a string starting with PXEClient:Arch:xxxxx:UNDI:yyyzzz. The presence of PXEClient signals to the DHCP server or ProxyDHCP server that the client requires boot instructions.
Option 93 (Client System Architecture): A 16-bit integer specified in RFC 4578 identifying the system architecture.
Option 94 (Client Network Interface Identifier): Indicates the client UNDI version (e.g., \x01\x03\x10 for UNDI v3.16).
Option 97 (Client Machine Identifier / UUID): A 17-byte field containing a type prefix and a 128-bit GUID/UUID uniquely identifying the physical platform.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    DHCP DISCOVER (Option 60: PXEClient)                 |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | Option 93: Architecture (e.g. 0x0007 = x64 UEFI)                 |  |
|  | Option 97: Client UUID                                            |  |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     DHCP OFFER (Option 60: PXEClient)                   |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | siaddr: Next Server IP (TFTP Server)                              |  |
|  | file:   Bootloader filename (e.g., ipxe.efi)                      |  |
|  | Option 66: Server Name / IP                                     |  |
|  | Option 67: Bootfile Name                                          |  |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
When a DHCP server responds to a PXE client, it returns an OFFER containing standard lease parameters along with boot instructions: 1. siaddr (Server IP Address): Located in the fixed header of the BOOTP structure, specifying the IPv4 address of the TFTP boot server (referred to as next-server). 2. file (Boot File Name): A 128-byte field in the fixed header containing the null-terminated file path of the boot image. 3. Option 66 (TFTP Server Name): A string representation of the TFTP server hostname or IP address. 4. Option 67 (Bootfile Name): An option string specifying the boot file path, overriding or supplementing the BOOTP file field. 5. Option 60 (Vendor Class Identifier): the PXE specification expects a boot server or ProxyDHCP server to put PXEClient in option 60 of its reply. Many firmware implementations ignore boot instructions from a reply without it, so echo it whenever you hand out a boot file.


Architecture Identification (Option 93)
Because BIOS and UEFI targets execute binary code differently, serving the wrong boot file (such as sending a BIOS boot sector to a 64-bit UEFI system) causes boot failure. DHCP option 93 conveys the exact system architecture:








Option 93 Value
Architecture Description
Boot File Target Example




0
x86 BIOS
pxelinux.0, undionly.kpxe


6
x86 UEFI (IA32)
bootia32.efi


7
x64 UEFI
bootx64.efi, ipxe.efi


9
x64 UEFI (EFI Byte Code)
bootx64.efi, ipxe.efi


10
ARM 32-bit UEFI
bootarm.efi


11
ARM 64-bit UEFI
bootaa64.efi, ipxe-arm64.efi


16
x64 UEFI HTTP Boot
http://10.66.0.1/ipxe.efi


19
ARM64 UEFI HTTP Boot
http://10.66.0.1/bootaa64.efi





ProxyDHCP Operation
In enterprise environments where the existing DHCP server cannot be modified to output PXE options, a ProxyDHCP server can be deployed alongside it.
The primary DHCP server provides IP leases on UDP port 67, while the ProxyDHCP server listens on UDP port 67 for DISCOVER packets containing PXEClient in option 60. The ProxyDHCP server sends a separate DHCP OFFER on UDP port 68 containing siaddr and Option 67 without offering an IP address. Alternatively, the ProxyDHCP service listens on UDP port 4011, where the client communicates directly via unicast after completing its initial address assignment to retrieve boot filenames.

title: Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
text:
UEFI HTTP Boot
UEFI specification version 2.5 introduced UEFI HTTP Boot as a modern replacement for TFTP-based PXE booting. Rather than pulling small binaries over UDP using TFTP, UEFI firmware retrieves boot payloads over TCP using standard HTTP or encrypted HTTPS GET requests.

Protocol Differences








Characteristic
Traditional PXE
UEFI HTTP Boot




Transport Protocol
UDP (TFTP)
TCP (HTTP/HTTPS)


Vendor Class (Option 60)
PXEClient:Arch:xxxxx...
HTTPClient:Arch:xxxxx...


Boot File Payload Location
Relative path on TFTP server
Fully qualified HTTP/HTTPS URL


Reliability Mechanism
Application-layer lock-step ACK
TCP windowing and congestion control


Security
None (Plaintext UDP)
TLS Certificate Verification (HTTPS Boot)


Architecture Identifiers
0, 7, 9, 11
16 (x64 HTTP), 19 (ARM64 HTTP)



During UEFI HTTP Boot, the client broadcasts a DHCP DISCOVER with Option 60 set to HTTPClient:Arch:00016:UNDI:... and Option 93 set to 16. The DHCP server returns an OFFER where Option 67 (or the BOOTP file field) contains a URI starting with http:// or https://, and echoes HTTPClient in Option 60.
Once the client accepts the DHCP lease, it initializes its TCP/IP stack, performs a TCP handshake with the destination HTTP server, issues a standard GET request for the specified boot file, and executes the payload.

title: Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
text:
iPXE and Chainloading
iPXE is an open-source boot firmware designed to replace aging or limited PXE ROMs. While standard NIC PXE firmware is restricted to TFTP transfers, iPXE supports HTTP, HTTPS, iSCSI, SAN booting, and scripting.

Chainloading Logic and Loop Prevention
Because replacing physical NIC Option ROMs across a fleet is impractical, administrators use chainloading. The machine performs a standard PXE boot to retrieve a tiny iPXE binary (ipxe.efi or undionly.kpxe) via TFTP. Upon execution, iPXE takes control of the NIC, initializes its own network stack, and issues a second DHCP DISCOVER to locate its actual instructions.
This creates a potential infinite loop: if the DHCP server responds to iPXE with the same boot filename (ipxe.efi), iPXE will re-download itself over TFTP indefinitely.
[System Firmware] ---> DHCP DISCOVER #1 (Option 60: PXEClient)
                  <--- DHCP OFFER #1 (File: ipxe.efi)
[System Firmware] ---> TFTP GET ipxe.efi
[System Firmware] ---> Executes ipxe.efi

[iPXE Executing]  ---> DHCP DISCOVER #2 (Option 60: PXEClient, Option 77: iPXE)
                  <--- DHCP OFFER #2 (File: http://10.66.0.1/boot.ipxe)
[iPXE Executing]  ---> HTTP GET http://10.66.0.1/boot.ipxe
[iPXE Executing]  ---> Executes boot.ipxe Script
To break the loop, the DHCP server must differentiate between the original system firmware and the executing iPXE binary. When iPXE issues a DHCP DISCOVER, it includes Option 77 (User Class) set to the ASCII string iPXE (and encapsulates internal features in Option 175).
The DHCP server uses Option 77 to branch its logic: 1. If Option 77 is absent: The client is the raw system firmware. Return ipxe.efi via TFTP. 2. If Option 77 is “iPXE”: The client is already running iPXE. Return an HTTP URL pointing to an iPXE script (e.g., http://10.66.0.1/boot.ipxe).


Minimal iPXE Script Structure
An iPXE boot script is a text file beginning with #!ipxe. It drives network configuration, fetches operating system artifacts (vmlinuz, initrd), passes command-line options to the kernel, and boots:
#!ipxe
dhcp
kernel http://10.66.0.1/vmlinuz initrd=initrd.img ip=dhcp console=ttyS0,115200
initrd http://10.66.0.1/initrd.img
boot

title: Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
section: Across Subnets: Relaying and TFTP Mechanics
text:
Across Subnets: Relaying and TFTP Mechanics
When the network boot client and the provisioning servers reside on different VLANs or subnets, network boot traffic must cross routers and firewalls.

DHCP Relay Integration
As covered in DHCP Relay and NAT, a DHCP relay agent (such as Cisco ip helper-address) receives client broadcast DISCOVER packets on UDP port 67, populates the giaddr field with its own interface IP, and unicasts the request to the central DHCP server.
The DHCP server processes the request, inspects giaddr to choose the appropriate IP pool, and includes the siaddr (next-server) field pointing to the TFTP or HTTP server. The relay forwards the unicast OFFER back to the client subnet.


TFTP Protocol Mechanics (RFC 1350)
TFTP is a minimalist transfer protocol operating over UDP. Unlike FTP or HTTP, TFTP implements no user authentication, directory listing, or complex command structure.
RFC 1350 defines five basic packet types: 1. Read Request (RRQ): Opcode 1. Sent by the client to request a file read. 2. Write Request (WRQ): Opcode 2. Sent by the client to request a file write. 3. Data Packet (DATA): Opcode 3. Contains a 2-byte block number and up to 512 bytes of payload. 4. Acknowledgment (ACK): Opcode 4. Contains a 2-byte block number acknowledging receipt of a DATA packet. 5. Error (ERROR): Opcode 5. Sent when a request cannot be fulfilled or an invalid state occurs.

Lock-Step Operation
TFTP operates using a simple lock-step transmission model. The client sends an RRQ to the server on well-known UDP port 69. The server allocates a new ephemeral UDP port (known as a Transfer Identifier or TID) and transmits DATA block 1. The client responds with ACK block 1 sent to the server’s new TID port. The server waits to receive ACK block 1 before transmitting DATA block 2.
Client (Port 50123)                    Server (Port 69)
       |                                      |
       |--- RRQ "ipxe.efi", octet ----------->| (Allocates TID Port 41002)
       |                                      |
       |                                      Server (Port 41002)
       |<-- DATA Block 1 (512 bytes) ---------|
       |                                      |
       |--- ACK Block 1 --------------------->|
       |                                      |
       |<-- DATA Block 2 (512 bytes) ---------|
       |                                      |
       |--- ACK Block 2 --------------------->|
       |                                      |
       |<-- DATA Block 3 (120 bytes) ---------| (Final block < 512 bytes)
       |                                      |
       |--- ACK Block 3 --------------------->|
Transfer completion is governed by block size: every full data block contains exactly blksize payload bytes (512 bytes by default). Receipt of a DATA packet containing fewer than blksize bytes (including a 0-byte payload) signals the end of the transfer.
Because block numbers are stored as unsigned 16-bit integers (0 to 65535), standard RFC 1350 TFTP transfers without block counter rollover are limited to \(65535 \times 512 = 33{,}553{,}920\) bytes, just under 32 MiB. Many servers and clients roll the counter over (to 0 or to 1, which is not standardised), and a larger blksize raises the limit proportionally.



TFTP Protocol Extensions
To address performance limitations and file size bounds, several RFC extensions expand TFTP capabilities:

RFC 2347 (Option Extension): Allows clients to append option key-value pairs to RRQ packets. If accepted, the server responds with an Option Acknowledgment (OACK) packet (Opcode 6) before data transfer begins.
RFC 2348 (Blocksize Option): Negotiates a custom blksize between 8 and 65464 bytes. Increasing blksize from 512 to 1468 bytes allows payload data to fit entirely inside standard Ethernet MTU frames (1500 bytes) without IP fragmentation, significantly raising throughput.
RFC 2349 (Timeout and Transfer Size Options): Adds timeout (retransmission window) and tsize (total size of the requested file in bytes, allowing clients to pre-allocate memory buffers).
RFC 7440 (Windowsize Option): Introduces sliding windows to TFTP. The windowsize parameter allows the server to send \(N\) consecutive DATA blocks before waiting for an ACK matching the last block in the window.



Firewalls, NAT, and State Tracking
Because TFTP transfers switch from UDP port 69 to an dynamically allocated server TID port, stateful firewalls and NAT gateways will drop returning DATA packets unless specialized state tracking is enabled.
In Linux Netfilter environments, the nf_conntrack_tftp kernel module acts as an Application Layer Gateway (ALG). It inspects RRQ/WRQ packets to UDP port 69 and creates a conntrack expectation that admits the server’s reply from its new TID port back to the client’s port. Since Linux 4.7 the kernel no longer attaches helpers to connections automatically by default, and Linux 6.0 removed the old nf_conntrack_helper switch entirely, so the firewall must assign the helper explicitly, for example with an nftables ct helper object bound to udp dport 69.

title: Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
text:
Security Considerations
Traditional network boot stack components (PXE, TFTP, standard DHCP) operate entirely unauthenticated and unencrypted. Deploying network boot safely requires compensating controls:

Rogue DHCP Attacks: Any unauthorized device on the local Layer 2 broadcast domain can send rapid DHCP OFFER responses containing malicious siaddr and bootfile directives. Network switches must enforce DHCP Snooping, restricting DHCP OFFER/ACK packets exclusively to trusted switch ports connected to authorized infrastructure.
TFTP Tampering and Eavesdropping: TFTP carries no authentication or checksum validation beyond basic UDP integrity. An attacker can inject modified bootloader images or capture unencrypted boot parameters.
UEFI Secure Boot and Shim: UEFI Secure Boot ensures that only cryptographically signed binaries execute during preboot. On most PCs the firmware trusts the Microsoft UEFI CA, so Linux distributions boot a Microsoft-signed shim, which then verifies the next stage (GRUB, or an iPXE build signed with a key shim trusts) against the distribution’s certificate or an enrolled Machine Owner Key. A self-built, unsigned ipxe.efi will not run with Secure Boot on until you sign it with a key the platform or shim accepts.
HTTPS Boot: Utilizing UEFI HTTP Boot over TLS (HTTPS Boot) requires enrolling trusted root CA certificates into the firmware PKI storage. Firmware validates the HTTPS server’s TLS certificate before downloading boot payloads.
Network Isolation: Provisioning interfaces should be bound to dedicated management VLANs, isolated from standard user traffic.
The firmware network stack is itself attack surface: the code that runs PXE executes before Secure Boot has verified anything. In January 2024 the “PixieFail” set (CVE-2023-45229 to CVE-2023-45237) showed buffer overflows in the EDK II NetworkPkg DHCPv6 and IPv6 code. In October 2026 EDK II published GHSA-99cj-7hg9-mp4m (CVE-2026-97631): the PXE Base Code driver copies received ICMP error messages into a fixed 504-byte field with wrong bounds handling, so an unauthenticated attacker who can send an oversized ICMP error to a machine while it PXE-boots can corrupt memory and run code before the OS loads. Treat firmware updates as part of the boot infrastructure. Keep PXE disabled in firmware on machines that do not need it, and on the provisioning VLAN filter what can reach booting clients, ICMP errors from arbitrary sources included.

title: Network Boot: PXE, iPXE, UEFI HTTP Boot and TFTP
text:
The lab
The following script environment demonstrates PXE architecture matching, HTTP chainload options, iPXE loop prevention via Option 77, and TFTP performance across various block sizes and window options.


pxedhcp.py

# pxedhcp.py server IFACE ADDR   : a DHCP server that only answers PXE/iPXE/HTTP-boot clients
# pxedhcp.py client IFACE PROFILE: send one DISCOVER as a given firmware and print the OFFER
#   PROFILE bios | uefi | httpboot | ipxe | ipxe-noefi
import socket, struct, sys, random
MAGIC = b"\x63\x82\x53\x63"
def opts(b):
    o, i = {}, 0
    while i < len(b) and b[i] != 255:
        if b[i] == 0: i += 1; continue
        o[b[i]] = b[i + 2:i + 2 + b[i + 1]]; i += 2 + b[i + 1]
    return o
def enc(o): return b"".join(bytes([k, len(v)]) + v for k, v in o.items()) + b"\xff"
def sock(iface, port):
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BROADCAST, 1)
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BINDTODEVICE, iface.encode())
    s.bind(("", port)); return s

ARCH = {0: "x86 BIOS", 7: "x64 UEFI", 9: "x64 UEFI", 11: "ARM64 UEFI", 16: "x64 UEFI HTTP", 19: "ARM64 UEFI HTTP"}

def choose(o, server):
    """The chainload decision: what boot file does this client get?"""
    vci = o.get(60, b"").decode()
    arch = struct.unpack("!H", o[93])[0] if 93 in o else None
    if not (vci.startswith("PXEClient") or vci.startswith("HTTPClient")):
        return None, "not a network-boot client, no boot file"
    if o.get(77) == b"iPXE":                                     # already running iPXE: stop the loop
        return f"http://{server}/boot.ipxe", "iPXE (option 77) -> boot script over HTTP"
    if vci.startswith("HTTPClient"):
        return f"http://{server}/ipxe.efi", f"{ARCH.get(arch)} -> HTTP URL, option 60 echoed"
    if arch == 0:
        return "undionly.kpxe", f"{ARCH[0]} -> undionly.kpxe over TFTP"
    if arch in (7, 9, 11):
        return ("ipxe.efi" if arch != 11 else "ipxe-arm64.efi"), f"{ARCH[arch]} -> iPXE EFI binary over TFTP"
    return None, f"unknown arch {arch}, no boot file"

if sys.argv[1] == "server":
    iface, me = sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
    s = sock(iface, 67); pool = iter(range(100, 200))
    while True:
        pkt, _ = s.recvfrom(1500)
        xid, chaddr = pkt[4:8], pkt[28:44]
        o = opts(pkt[240:])
        if o.get(53) != b"\x01": continue                       # DISCOVER only, for brevity
        boot, why = choose(o, me)
        print(f"   server: xid {xid.hex()} class {o.get(60, b'-').decode()!r} "
              f"user-class {o.get(77, b'-').decode()!r}: {why}", flush=True)
        yiaddr = socket.inet_aton(f"10.66.0.{next(pool)}")
        ro = {53: b"\x02", 54: socket.inet_aton(me), 51: struct.pack("!I", 600), 1: socket.inet_aton("255.255.255.0")}
        file = b""
        if boot:
            ro[60] = o[60][:10] if o[60].startswith(b"HTTPClient") else b"PXEClient"   # required echo
            if boot.startswith("http"): file = boot.encode()
            else: ro[66] = me.encode(); ro[67] = boot.encode(); file = boot.encode()
        hdr = struct.pack("!BBBB4sHH4s4s4s4s16s64s128s", 2, 1, 6, 0, xid, 0, 0x8000, bytes(4), yiaddr,
                          socket.inet_aton(me), bytes(4), chaddr, b"", file)   # siaddr = next-server
        s.sendto(hdr + MAGIC + enc(ro), ("255.255.255.255", 68))
else:
    iface, prof = sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
    P = {"bios": (b"PXEClient:Arch:00000:UNDI:002001", 0, None),
         "uefi": (b"PXEClient:Arch:00007:UNDI:003016", 7, None),
         "httpboot": (b"HTTPClient:Arch:00016:UNDI:003001", 16, None),
         "ipxe": (b"PXEClient:Arch:00007:UNDI:003016", 7, b"iPXE"),
         "ipxe-noefi": (b"PXEClient:Arch:00007:UNDI:003016", 7, None)}[prof]
    s = sock(iface, 68); s.settimeout(2)
    xid = random.randbytes(4); mac = bytes.fromhex("020000000066")
    o = {53: b"\x01", 60: P[0], 93: struct.pack("!H", P[1]), 94: b"\x01\x03\x10"}
    if P[2]: o[77] = P[2]
    hdr = struct.pack("!BBBB4sHH4s4s4s4s16s64s128s", 1, 1, 6, 0, xid, 0, 0x8000, bytes(4), bytes(4),
                      bytes(4), bytes(4), mac.ljust(16, b"\0"), b"", b"")
    s.sendto(hdr + MAGIC + enc(o), ("255.255.255.255", 67))
    while True:
        pkt = s.recv(1500)
        if pkt[4:8] == xid: break
    ro = opts(pkt[240:])
    file = pkt[108:236].rstrip(b"\0").decode()
    print(f"   client {prof}: offer {socket.inet_ntoa(pkt[16:20])}, next-server {socket.inet_ntoa(pkt[20:24])}, "
          f"file {file!r}, opt66 {ro.get(66, b'-').decode()!r}, opt67 {ro.get(67, b'-').decode()!r}, "
          f"opt60 {ro.get(60, b'-').decode()!r}")



tftp.py

# tftp.py server ADDR DIR        : RFC 1350 TFTP server (read only) with RFC 2347/2348/2349/7440 options
# tftp.py get SERVER FILE [blksize=N] [windowsize=N] [tsize=0]
import os, socket, struct, sys, time
RRQ, DATA, ACK, ERROR, OACK = 1, 3, 4, 5, 6
def serve(addr, root):
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.bind((addr, 69))
    while True:
        pkt, peer = s.recvfrom(1500)
        if struct.unpack("!H", pkt[:2])[0] != RRQ: continue
        parts = pkt[2:].split(b"\0")[:-1]
        name, mode, rest = parts[0].decode(), parts[1], parts[2:]
        req = {rest[i].decode().lower(): rest[i + 1].decode() for i in range(0, len(rest) - 1, 2)}
        t = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); t.bind((addr, 0)); t.settimeout(1)  # new TID
        path = os.path.join(root, os.path.basename(name))
        if not os.path.isfile(path):
            t.sendto(struct.pack("!HH", ERROR, 1) + b"File not found\0", peer); continue
        data = open(path, "rb").read()
        blk, win, ack = 512, 1, {}
        if "blksize" in req: blk = max(8, min(int(req["blksize"]), 65464)); ack["blksize"] = blk
        if "windowsize" in req: win = max(1, min(int(req["windowsize"]), 64)); ack["windowsize"] = win
        if "tsize" in req: ack["tsize"] = len(data)
        if ack:
            t.sendto(struct.pack("!H", OACK) + b"".join(f"{k}\0{v}\0".encode() for k, v in ack.items()), peer)
            t.recvfrom(1500)                             # ACK 0
        nblocks = len(data) // blk + 1                   # a short (possibly empty) final block ends it
        n = 1
        while n <= nblocks:
            for b in range(n, min(n + win, nblocks + 1)):
                t.sendto(struct.pack("!HH", DATA, b % 65536) + data[(b - 1) * blk:b * blk], peer)
            a = struct.unpack("!HH", t.recvfrom(1500)[0][:4])[1]
            n += ((a - n) % 65536) + 1                   # resume after the last acknowledged block
        t.close()

def get(server, name, opts):
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.settimeout(2)
    o = dict(x.split("=") for x in opts)
    s.sendto(struct.pack("!H", RRQ) + name.encode() + b"\0octet\0" +
             b"".join(f"{k}\0{v}\0".encode() for k, v in o.items()), (server, 69))
    t0, got, sent, recvd, blk, win, expect, last = time.monotonic(), bytearray(), 1, 0, 512, 1, 1, 0
    while True:
        pkt, peer = s.recvfrom(70000); recvd += 1
        op = struct.unpack("!H", pkt[:2])[0]
        if op == ERROR: return print(f"   get {name}: ERROR {pkt[4:-1].decode()}")
        if op == OACK:
            f = pkt[2:].split(b"\0")[:-1]; neg = {f[i].decode(): f[i + 1].decode() for i in range(0, len(f), 2)}
            blk, win = int(neg.get("blksize", 512)), int(neg.get("windowsize", 1))
            s.sendto(struct.pack("!HH", ACK, 0), peer); sent += 1; continue
        b = struct.unpack("!H", pkt[2:4])[0]
        if b == expect % 65536:
            got += pkt[4:]; expect += 1
            final = len(pkt) - 4 < blk
            if final or (expect - 1) % win == 0:
                s.sendto(struct.pack("!HH", ACK, b), peer); sent += 1
            if final: break
    dt = time.monotonic() - t0
    print(f"   get {name} {' '.join(opts) or '(no options)'}: {len(got)} bytes, blksize {blk}, window {win}, "
          f"{recvd} packets in, {sent} out (lock-step round trips), {dt * 1000:.0f} ms")

if sys.argv[1] == "server": serve(sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3])
else: get(sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3], sys.argv[4:])
