title: SVCB and HTTPS Records: Service Binding in the DNS (RFC 9460 and 9461)
text:
Gotchas

The trap: publishing stale or wrong ipv4hint/ipv6hint values. Because Happy Eyeballs v3 clients may race hinted addresses immediately before A/AAAA answers arrive, a stale hint sends initial SYN or QUIC Initial packets to the wrong host. If you automate CDN or load-balancer IP changes, update ipv4hint/ipv6hint in lockstep with A/AAAA—or omit hints entirely (as www.google.com does) and let A/AAAA carry the addresses.
The trap: assuming presentation order equals wire order. Zone files and CLI tools often display SvcParams in arbitrary order, or let you write ipv4hint before alpn. On the wire, SvcParamKeys must be strictly increasing. Any custom packet builder or signer that serializes keys in input order produces an invalid RR that strict resolvers and clients drop.
The trap: attaching SvcParams to AliasMode. An AliasMode record (priority = 0) is purely a pointer. Adding alpn, port, or hints to a priority-0 record violates RFC 9460 and causes compliant parsers to discard the entire record.
The trap: treating hints as a replacement for A/AAAA. Hints are unauthenticated shortcuts when A/AAAA are delayed; they do not replace A/AAAA resolution or DNSSEC validation of address records. Never configure a client or resolver to skip A/AAAA lookups permanently just because hints were present.
The trap: middlebox stripping of HTTPS/SVCB. In some enterprise or ISP networks, DNS forwarders or interception proxies strip or block HTTPS queries and responses—often to prevent clients from learning ech keys and hiding the TLS SNI. When troubleshooting missing ECH or unexpected http/1.1 fallbacks, compare what the authoritative nameserver returns against what the local stub resolver receives.
The trap: using CNAME at the zone apex instead of HTTPS AliasMode. Placing a CNAME at example.com breaks SOA/NS coexistence and violates DNS standards. Use HTTPS 0 target.example.net. for https origins at the apex, rather than relying on non-standard zone-flattening workarounds where HTTPS AliasMode is supported.

title: SVCB and HTTPS Records: Service Binding in the DNS (RFC 9460 and 9461)
text:
Exercises

Wire-format decoding: Decode the following RFC 9460-encoded HTTPS RDATA hex dump into SvcPriority, TargetName, and each (SvcParamKey, Length, Value) tuple. Verify that every invariant holds:
00 01 00 00 01 00 06 02 68 32 02 68 33 00 03 00 02 20 fb 00 04 00 04 c0 00 02 01
Presentation order vs. wire order: In RFC 9460 Appendix D Figure 9, the presentation format lists mandatory, alpn, and ipv4hint, and the wire encoder must emit keys in strictly increasing order (0, 1, 4). Explain why RFC 9460 mandates strictly increasing key order on the wire rather than allowing arbitrary order like presentation format. What breaks for single-pass parsers and DNSSEC canonicalization if keys arrive out of order or duplicated?
Zone apex design: You operate example.com, whose web traffic is served by a CDN at edge.cdn.example.net. Design the HTTPS record(s) at example.com. and at edge.cdn.example.net. so that https://example.com avoids a CNAME at the apex, prefers HTTP/3 (h3) with HTTP/2 (h2) fallback, and advertises IPv4/IPv6 hints at the CDN target. Explain why SvcParams belong on the ServiceMode record at edge.cdn.example.net. rather than on example.com..
Mandatory vs. optional ech: Suppose a server publishes an HTTPS ServiceMode record containing alpn=h2 and ech=<71 bytes>. Compare what a legacy client (one that does not implement ech, key 5) does in two cases:

Case A: mandatory is omitted.
Case B: mandatory=ech. Also explain why mandatory=mandatory is explicitly forbidden by RFC 9460.

Interpreting live DoH answers: Based on the four live HTTPS queries from the lab:

cloudflare.com: priority=1, target=., alpn=['h3','h2'], ipv4hint, ipv6hint
www.google.com: priority=1, target=., alpn=['h2','h3'] (no hints)
github.com: 0 HTTPS RRs (rcode=0)
crypto.cloudflare.com: priority=1, target=., alpn=['h2'], ipv4hint, ipv6hint, ech=71 bytes For each domain, trace what an RFC 9460-compliant browser does immediately after receiving the HTTPS response: which protocols it offers, whether it can start racing TCP/QUIC before A/AAAA arrive, and how it handles TLS ClientHello construction.

Failure-case triage: Each of the following wire encodings corresponds to an Appendix D.3 failure case. Identify the specific RFC 9460 rule violated by each and explain why a strict parser must reject the entire RR:

SvcPriority = 0, TargetName = cdn.example.net., SvcParams = [alpn="h2"]
SvcPriority = 1, TargetName = ., SvcParams = [port=empty (0 bytes)]
SvcPriority = 1, TargetName = ., SvcParams = [no-default-alpn=0x01]
SvcPriority = 1, TargetName = ., SvcParams = [mandatory=port, alpn="h2"]

text:
The boring rule
Always sort SvcParamKeys in strictly increasing numeric order on the wire, keep AliasMode completely free of SvcParams, and treat ipv4hint/ipv6hint as racing hints rather than authoritative replacements for A and AAAA.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Learning goals

Understand the historical 512-byte UDP payload limit for standard DNS messages.
Learn how EDNS(0) advertises client UDP buffer capacity using the OPT pseudo-RR.
Recognize how responders use the TrunCation (TC) bit to trigger TCP fallback.
Evaluate why blocking TCP/53 causes silent resolution failure for large DNS responses.
Analyze the impact of IP fragmentation, DNSSEC keys, and post-quantum algorithms on DNS message budgets.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Thesis
DNS is a UDP protocol only until the answer gets big. Every query carries, implicitly or explicitly, a size budget: 512 bytes without EDNS, or whatever the client advertises in its OPT record. A server that cannot fit the answer in that budget sends an empty answer with the TC bit set, and the client must ask again over TCP. That design works only if three things hold: the client advertises a sensible budget, the server honours it, and TCP/53 is open end to end. Break any of them and resolution fails for exactly the names with the largest answers, which are often the most important ones: DNSSEC keys during a rollover, big round-robin sets, and in future post-quantum signatures. This chapter watches glibc’s real stub resolver go through each case against a server you control, and then does the byte arithmetic for signed answers.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Core transport constraints: RFC 1035 limits
Classic DNS framing, defined in RFC 1035, specifies that DNS messages transmitted over User Datagram Protocol (UDP) cannot exceed 512 bytes, excluding IP and UDP headers. If an authoritative or recursive server generates a response that exceeds this 512-byte limit, it must truncate the response payload and set the TrunCation (TC) bit in the DNS message header.
Upon receiving a response with the TC bit set, a compliant DNS client drops the incomplete answer section and re-issues the identical query over Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) to port 53. Over TCP, DNS messages are prefixed with a 2-byte length field, removing the size limit inherent to UDP datagrams and permitting transfers up to 65,535 bytes per message frame.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
section: Extension Mechanisms for DNS: RFC 6891 EDNS(0)
text:
Extension Mechanisms for DNS: RFC 6891 EDNS(0)
To avoid forcing every response larger than 512 bytes onto TCP, RFC 6891 specifies Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0)). EDNS(0) introduces an OPT pseudo-Resource Record (type 41) positioned inside the Additional section of a DNS message.
The OPT record does not represent actual domain data. Instead, its fields are repurposed for protocol negotiation: - CLASS field: Carries the sender’s maximum acceptable UDP payload size (in bytes). - TTL field: Split into sub-fields carrying extended RCODE bits, EDNS version, and flags such as the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit.
When a client advertises an EDNS buffer size to a responder, the responder may send UDP answers up to that advertised size. If a client sends an advertised size smaller than 512 bytes, the responder treats the limit as 512 bytes.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
section: Fragmented UDP and the DNS Flag Day 2020 recommendation
text:
Fragmented UDP and the DNS Flag Day 2020 recommendation
EDNS(0) lets a client advertise up to 65,535 bytes. A UDP response larger than the path MTU (1500 bytes on plain Ethernet, less through tunnels) has to be fragmented at the IP layer: by the sender for IPv6, by the sender or a router for IPv4.
IP fragments present severe operational risks: - Middleboxes, stateful firewalls, and NAT devices often drop secondary IP fragments. - Fragments after the first carry no UDP header, so they carry no DNS ID or port. An off-path attacker who can guess the IP fragment ID can forge a later fragment that is reassembled with a genuine first fragment, and replace records without ever guessing the DNS query ID. That is a cache-poisoning path that the usual DNS ID and source-port randomisation does not protect.
To remediate these failure modes, major DNS vendors established DNS Flag Day 2020, recommending a maximum default EDNS buffer size of 1232 bytes. This number derives from the minimum IPv6 MTU (1280 bytes) minus the 40-byte IPv6 header and the 8-byte UDP header (\(1280 - 40 - 8 = 1232\)). Capping the UDP payload at 1232 bytes avoids fragmentation on nearly every path, at the cost of sending more answers over TCP.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
section: Modern TCP requirements: RFC 7766 and RFC 9210
text:
Modern TCP requirements: RFC 7766 and RFC 9210
Historically, DNS over TCP was viewed purely as a fallback mechanism for truncated UDP answers. RFC 7766 and RFC 9210 (BCP 235) updated this requirement: TCP support is mandatory for all standard Internet DNS implementations.
RFC 9210 is blunt: “network operators MUST allow DNS service over both UDP and TCP transports.” Firewalls or security policies that filter TCP/53 break DNS resolution whenever answers exceed the path’s UDP buffer budget, leading to resolution failures even when UDP functionality is healthy.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Causes of large DNS payloads
Multiple production requirements drive DNS message sizes past default UDP boundaries: - Large RRsets: Domains operating numerous A or AAAA records for load balancing or round-robin routing. - TXT records: Security policies relying on large TXT records, such as long DKIM keys, complex SPF policies, and openpgpkey data. - DNSSEC cryptographic material: Inclusion of RRSIG signatures and DNSKEY records alongside data records significantly inflates wire size. - Key Rollovers: During DNSSEC KSK or ZSK rollovers, multiple active and published keys exist simultaneously inside the DNSKEY RRset. - Post-Quantum Cryptography: Emerging post-quantum signing schemes require vastly larger public keys and signatures. For instance, ML-DSA-44 (FIPS 204) features a 1312-byte public key and a 2420-byte signature. ML-DSA has no standardized DNSSEC algorithm number yet; it appears here only as an experiment in sizing.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Operator checks and daemon configuration
Network engineers use command-line diagnostics and configuration directives to inspect and manage DNS buffer limits.
# Querying with an explicit EDNS buffer size and DNSSEC validation (not run here; written from the docs)
dig +bufsize=1232 +dnssec example.com DNSKEY

# Forcing TCP transport directly (not run here; written from the docs)
dig +tcp example.com A

# Disabling automatic TCP fallback to observe truncated UDP responses (not run here; written from the docs)
dig +ignore example.com A
For DNS server daemons, buffer limits are explicitly configured:
# Unbound resolver configuration (not run here; written from the docs)
server:
    edns-buffer-size: 1232

# BIND 9 configuration (not run here; written from the docs)
options {
    edns-udp-size 1232;
    max-udp-size 1232;
};

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
section: Lab: DNS payload dynamics, truncation, and TCP fallback
text:
Lab: DNS payload dynamics, truncation, and TCP fallback
The lab environment executes Python scripts inside isolated user, mount, and network namespaces via unshare -rmn.

Lab setup
The first program, dns-size.py, runs a tiny DNS server on 127.0.0.1:53 and points glibc at it. It needs a private user, mount and network namespace (unshare -rmn): inside it you are root, so you can bind port 53 and bind-mount a private /etc/resolv.conf. Nothing outside the namespace changes. The server answers big.example.test/A with N records and truncates over UDP exactly as RFC 1035 and RFC 6891 describe. socket.getaddrinfo() is the real glibc stub resolver, the same code path as curl or ssh use. In the “TCP broken” case the server accepts the TCP connection and closes it without answering.
dns-size.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""EDNS(0), the TC bit and TCP fallback, seen through glibc's stub resolver.

Run inside a private user+mount+net namespace (no root needed):
    unshare -rmn python3 dns-size.py
A tiny authoritative-style server on 127.0.0.1:53 answers
big.example.test/A with N A records. It truncates over UDP exactly the way
RFC 1035 / RFC 6891 say: if the answer does not fit the requester's UDP
limit (512 without EDNS, else the OPT payload size, capped at 1232 here), it
sends the header + question with TC=1 and no answers. Over TCP it sends
everything. The script logs every query the server sees.
"""
import os, socket, struct, subprocess, threading, time

A, OPT = 1, 41
SERVER_MAX_UDP = 1232
log = []
cfg = {"records": 10, "tcp": True}

def name(n):
    out = b""
    for label in n.rstrip(".").split("."):
        out += bytes([len(label)]) + label.encode()
    return out + b"\x00"

def parse(q):
    i, labels = 12, []
    while q[i]:
        labels.append(q[i + 1:i + 1 + q[i]].decode()); i += q[i] + 1
    qtype, = struct.unpack("!H", q[i + 1:i + 3])
    qsec = q[12:i + 5]
    arcount, = struct.unpack("!H", q[10:12])
    edns = None
    if arcount:  # glibc puts only the OPT record in the additional section
        j = i + 5
        if q[j] == 0 and struct.unpack("!H", q[j + 1:j + 3])[0] == OPT:
            edns = struct.unpack("!H", q[j + 3:j + 5])[0]
    return ".".join(labels), qtype, qsec, edns

def build(q, transport):
    qid, = struct.unpack("!H", q[:2])
    qname, qtype, qsec, edns = parse(q)
    rrs, n = b"", 0
    if qname == "big.example.test" and qtype == A:
        for k in range(cfg["records"]):
            rrs += (b"\xc0\x0c" + struct.pack("!HHIH", A, 1, 300, 4)
                    + socket.inet_aton(f"198.51.100.{k + 1}"))
            n += 1
    opt = b""
    if edns is not None:
        opt = b"\x00" + struct.pack("!HHIH", OPT, SERVER_MAX_UDP, 0, 0)
    full = struct.pack("!HHHHHH", qid, 0x8580, 1, n, 0, 1 if opt else 0) + qsec + rrs + opt
    limit = 512 if edns is None else min(max(edns, 512), SERVER_MAX_UDP)
    tc = transport == "udp" and len(full) > limit
    log.append(f"{transport} qtype={qtype:<3} edns={edns} full={len(full)}B "
               f"limit={limit if transport == 'udp' else '-'} -> "
               + ("TC=1, answers dropped" if tc else f"sent {len(full)}B"))
    if tc:
        return struct.pack("!HHHHHH", qid, 0x8780, 1, 0, 0, 1 if opt else 0) + qsec + opt
    return full

def udp_loop(s):
    while True:
        q, peer = s.recvfrom(4096)
        s.sendto(build(q, "udp"), peer)

def tcp_loop(s):
    while True:
        c, _ = s.accept()
        with c:
            while True:
                hdr = c.recv(2)
                if len(hdr) < 2:
                    break
                ln, = struct.unpack("!H", hdr)
                q = b""
                while len(q) < ln:
                    q += c.recv(ln - len(q))
                if not cfg["tcp"]:
                    break
                r = build(q, "tcp")
                c.sendall(struct.pack("!H", len(r)) + r)

def resolve(options):
    with open("/tmp/dns-size-resolv.conf", "w") as f:
        f.write("nameserver 127.0.0.1\noptions attempts:1 timeout:1 " + options + "\n")
    log.clear()
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    try:
        res = socket.getaddrinfo("big.example.test", 80, socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        out = f"OK, {len(res)} addresses"
    except socket.gaierror as e:
        out = f"FAIL ({e.strerror})"
    ms = (time.monotonic() - t0) * 1000
    return out, ms, list(log)

def main():
    subprocess.run(["ip", "link", "set", "lo", "up"], check=True)
    open("/tmp/dns-size-resolv.conf", "w").close()
    subprocess.run(["mount", "--bind", "/tmp/dns-size-resolv.conf", "/etc/resolv.conf"], check=True)
    u = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); u.bind(("127.0.0.1", 53))
    t = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    t.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1); t.bind(("127.0.0.1", 53)); t.listen()
    threading.Thread(target=udp_loop, args=(u,), daemon=True).start()
    threading.Thread(target=tcp_loop, args=(t,), daemon=True).start()
    cases = [
        ("10 A records, no EDNS", 10, True, ""),
        ("40 A records, no EDNS", 40, True, ""),
        ("40 A records, options edns0", 40, True, "edns0"),
        ("100 A records, options edns0", 100, True, "edns0"),
        ("100 A records, edns0, TCP broken", 100, False, "edns0"),
        ("10 A records, options use-vc", 10, True, "use-vc"),
    ]
    for title, n, tcp_ok, opts in cases:
        cfg["records"], cfg["tcp"] = n, tcp_ok
        out, ms, lines = resolve(opts)
        print(f"== {title}: {out} in {ms:.0f} ms")
        for line in lines:
            print("   " + line)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Run it:
unshare -rmn python3 dns-size.py
Output:
== 10 A records, no EDNS: OK, 10 addresses in 1 ms
   udp qtype=1   edns=None full=194B limit=512 -> sent 194B
== 40 A records, no EDNS: OK, 40 addresses in 1 ms
   udp qtype=1   edns=None full=674B limit=512 -> TC=1, answers dropped
   tcp qtype=1   edns=None full=674B limit=- -> sent 674B
== 40 A records, options edns0: OK, 40 addresses in 0 ms
   udp qtype=1   edns=1200 full=685B limit=1200 -> sent 685B
== 100 A records, options edns0: OK, 100 addresses in 1 ms
   udp qtype=1   edns=1200 full=1645B limit=1200 -> TC=1, answers dropped
   tcp qtype=1   edns=1200 full=1645B limit=- -> sent 1645B
   udp qtype=1   edns=1200 full=1645B limit=1200 -> TC=1, answers dropped
   tcp qtype=1   edns=1200 full=1645B limit=- -> sent 1645B
== 100 A records, edns0, TCP broken: FAIL (Name or service not known) in 0 ms
   udp qtype=1   edns=1200 full=1645B limit=1200 -> TC=1, answers dropped
== 10 A records, options use-vc: OK, 10 addresses in 0 ms
   tcp qtype=1   edns=None full=194B limit=- -> sent 194B


Reading Lab 1 output
The output from Lab 1 demonstrates how glibc’s stub resolver handles truncated answers and TCP fallback under different configuration settings:

10 A records, no EDNS: The wire payload size is 194 B, which fits under the default 512 B UDP limit. Resolution succeeds directly over UDP in 1 ms.
40 A records, no EDNS: The full answer requires 674 B, exceeding the 512 B limit. The server truncates the payload, sets TC=1, and drops the answer records. glibc automatically opens a TCP connection, re-sends the query, receives the full 674 B payload, and resolves 40 addresses in 1 ms.
40 A records, options edns0: glibc 2.41 advertises an EDNS buffer size of 1200 B. The answer payload is 685 B (including the 11-byte OPT record). Because \(685\text{ B} \le 1200\text{ B}\), the response fits in a single UDP packet without setting TC=1.
100 A records, options edns0: The answer payload is 1645 B, exceeding the advertised 1200 B EDNS limit. The server returns TC=1 over UDP. glibc retries over TCP, receiving 1645 B.
100 A records, edns0, TCP broken: When TCP/53 is blocked, the server sets TC=1 over UDP, but glibc cannot establish a TCP stream. Resolution fails with FAIL (Name or service not known). That is the same text an application prints for a name that does not exist (EAI_NONAME), so the transport problem is invisible to the user. In the lab the TCP side closes at once. A firewall that silently drops the SYN instead adds the resolver timeout on top, so the failure is also slow.
10 A records, options use-vc: The use-vc option forces glibc to bypass UDP entirely and query over TCP, returning the 194 B payload directly over a stream socket.

Notice that the 100-record case shows the whole UDP-then-TCP exchange twice. A separate sweep with the same program and other record counts showed the following record threshold dynamics: - With edns0, 60 records (1005 B) fit in UDP. - At 80 records (1325 B), resolution required one UDP query followed by one TCP exchange. - From 90 to 130 records (1485–2125 B), glibc repeated the full UDP+TCP retry sequence twice. - At 170 records (2765 B), glibc repeated the full UDP+TCP exchange three times.
This pattern was observed during execution and is consistent with getaddrinfo retrying resolution with a larger internal allocation buffer when the parsed DNS answer does not fit its initial buffer allocation (an ERANGE-style retry). Huge RRsets incur significant performance costs in redundant network round trips even when resolution eventually succeeds.


Size budget comparison
The second program, size-budget.py, is plain arithmetic over the wire formats in RFC 1035 and RFC 4034. It builds no packets.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Byte budget for a signed DNS answer, per DNSSEC algorithm.

Counts wire bytes the way RFC 1035 / 4034 lay them out: header, question,
answer RRs (name compressed to a 2-byte pointer), one RRSIG per RRset, and an
OPT record. Key and signature sizes are the algorithm's fixed sizes.
"""
HEADER, OPT = 12, 11
QNAME = len(b"\x03www\x07example\x03com\x00")    # 17 bytes
QUESTION = QNAME + 4
SIGNER = len(b"\x07example\x03com\x00")           # signer name in RRSIG, 13 bytes
RR_FIXED = 2 + 10                                 # compressed owner + type/class/ttl/rdlen

ALGS = {  # name: (DNSKEY public key bytes, signature bytes)
    "RSASHA256 (2048-bit)": (260, 256),
    "ECDSAP256SHA256 (13)": (64, 64),
    "ED25519 (15)": (32, 64),
    "ML-DSA-44 (experimental)": (1312, 2420),
}

def rrsig(sig):
    return RR_FIXED + 18 + SIGNER + sig           # 18 = fixed RRSIG rdata fields

def a_answer(sig, n_a=2):
    return HEADER + QUESTION + n_a * (RR_FIXED + 4) + rrsig(sig) + OPT

def dnskey_answer(pub, sig):
    keys = 2 * (RR_FIXED + 4 + pub)               # KSK + ZSK, 4 = flags/proto/alg
    return HEADER + QUESTION + keys + 2 * rrsig(sig) + OPT   # signed by KSK and ZSK

print(f"{'algorithm':26} {'A (2 RRs)+RRSIG':>16} {'DNSKEY RRset':>13}   fits 1232?")
for alg, (pub, sig) in ALGS.items():
    a, k = a_answer(sig), dnskey_answer(pub, sig)
    fits = lambda x: "yes" if x <= 1232 else "TC -> TCP"
    print(f"{alg:26} {a:>14} B {k:>11} B   A:{fits(a):9} DNSKEY:{fits(k)}")
Run it:
python3 size-budget.py
Output:
algorithm                   A (2 RRs)+RRSIG  DNSKEY RRset   fits 1232?
RSASHA256 (2048-bit)                  375 B        1194 B   A:yes       DNSKEY:yes
ECDSAP256SHA256 (13)                  183 B         418 B   A:yes       DNSKEY:yes
ED25519 (15)                          183 B         354 B   A:yes       DNSKEY:yes
ML-DSA-44 (experimental)             2539 B        7626 B   A:TC -> TCP DNSKEY:TC -> TCP


Reading Lab 2 output
Lab 2 models the wire byte size of DNSSEC-signed answers against the standard 1232-byte EDNS safety budget:

RSASHA256 (2048-bit): An answer with 2 A records and signatures occupies 375 B, fitting comfortably in 1232 B. However, a DNSKEY RRset with two keys occupies 1194 B. Adding a third key during a key rollover pushes the RRset past the 1232 B UDP budget, triggering TC=1 and TCP fallback.
ECDSA P-256 (Algorithm 13) and Ed25519 (Algorithm 15): Produce small public keys and signatures. An answer with RRSIG occupies 183 B, while the DNSKEY RRset occupies 418 B (ECDSA) or 354 B (Ed25519), fitting well within 1232 B.
ML-DSA-44 (experimental): Post-quantum signatures dramatically inflate payload sizes. A simple 2-A-record answer requires 2539 B, and the DNSKEY RRset requires 7626 B. Neither fits within 1232 B, so every signed answer would be truncated and retried over TCP. Post-quantum DNSSEC therefore assumes TCP (or DoT/DoH/DoQ) as the normal transport, not the exception. The model counts one answer RRset and its RRSIGs only; real responses can add NS, glue and NSEC records on top.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Case
This is an illustrative scenario, not a real named incident.
An enterprise enabled DNSSEC on its primary zone using 2048-bit RSA keys. Several months later, the network engineering team initiated a planned Zone Signing Key (ZSK) rollover.
During the rollover window, the DNS server published three DNSKEY records along with their corresponding RRSIG records in the apex DNSKEY RRset. Using the lab’s model, the third 2048-bit key adds 276 bytes to the 1194-byte RRset, so DNSKEY answers grew to about 1,470 bytes.
Branch office locations were connected via security appliances enforcing strict firewall policies that allowed UDP port 53 outbound but blocked TCP port 53. Before the rollover, standard A and AAAA record queries returned payloads under 512 bytes, allowing branch office hosts to resolve internal and external names without issue.
Each branch ran its own validating recursive resolver. When those resolvers fetched the apex DNSKEY RRset to validate the zone, the authoritative servers truncated the answer over UDP (TC=1), because about 1,470 bytes exceeded the 1232-byte limit. The resolvers retried over TCP port 53, and the branch firewalls dropped the SYNs.
Without the keys the resolvers could not validate anything in the zone, so they returned SERVFAIL for every internal name. Users saw “Temporary failure in name resolution”. Engineers spent hours inspecting local recursive resolver logs and authoritative server health before diagnosing that TCP/53 blocking was preventing fallback for truncated DNSSEC key responses.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Trap

Assuming UDP health equals DNS health: a monitoring probe that asks for one small A record over UDP stays green while every large answer fails. Probe over TCP too (dig +tcp), and probe a large answer such as your own DNSKEY RRset.
Misinterpreting client error codes: Stub resolvers like glibc return generic errors (Name or service not known) when TCP fallback fails, masking network transport blocks as non-existent domains.
Raising EDNS buffer sizes “to avoid TCP”: anything above 1232 bytes risks fragmentation on some paths, which means silent drops and the fragment-poisoning risk above. Fix TCP instead.
Ignoring key rollover payload growth: Planning DNSSEC key rollovers without factoring in the temporary payload size spike when multiple keys co-exist in the DNSKEY RRset.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Boring rule
Allow TCP/53 wherever UDP/53 is allowed. Cap EDNS UDP sizes at 1232 bytes on servers and resolvers. Monitor DNS over both transports, with at least one probe whose answer is larger than 1232 bytes.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Try this

Change SERVER_MAX_UDP in dns-size.py from 1232 to 1480 and rerun the 100-record case. Does anything change? Work out from the log lines whose limit actually applied, the client’s or the server’s.
Make the “TCP broken” case behave like a firewall: instead of closing, accept the connection and never answer (or don’t listen on TCP at all and add a DROP-like delay with time.sleep). Measure how long getaddrinfo() takes with timeout:1 and with timeout:5 in the generated resolv.conf.
Edit size-budget.py to add a third RSA-2048 key to the DNSKEY RRset model and calculate the resulting wire payload size.
Use struct to make the server answer AAAA queries too, and resolve with socket.AF_UNSPEC. How many queries does glibc send now, and are they sent in parallel?
Extend size-budget.py to include NSEC3 record overhead (hashed owner name, salt, type bitmap) alongside an RRSIG record to evaluate negative response size budgets.

title: DNS Message Size: EDNS(0), the TC Bit and TCP Fallback
text:
Verification
This chapter’s lab materials were verified on Linux 6.12.94+, Python 3.13.5, glibc 2.41 (Debian), running unprivileged with unshare -rmn and no external package dependencies on 2026-11-13. The /etc/resolv.conf bind mount existed strictly inside the isolated network namespace. The listings are the exact files that ran, and both outputs are pasted unedited. Millisecond timings are on loopback and vary per run. The extra-round sweep (60 to 170 records) used the same program with a different cases list; only its summary is reported. The repeated-exchange behaviour was observed, not traced in the glibc source.
Diagnostic tools such as dig, unbound, and BIND were not installed on the system; all command snippets for these daemons are marked as (not run here; written from the docs). Public external resolvers were not queried because outbound DNS on the host appeared to be intercepted (a DNSKEY query directed to two public resolvers returned an empty 29-byte answer).

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
Learning goals

State the CNAME rules that are precise in the RFCs: one CNAME per owner name, no other data at that name, and chains followed by the resolver
Explain the difference between the order of records inside an RRset, which never matters, and the order of RRsets in the answer section, which the RFCs leave unclear
Reproduce, without root, the glibc getaddrinfo() failure that hit users of a large public resolver on 2026-01-08, and show the same bytes parsed correctly by an order-independent algorithm
Write CNAME-heavy zones and DNS-serving code that do not depend on this ambiguity
Know which “illegal” CNAME data glibc silently tolerates, so you are not fooled when a broken zone still works on Linux

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
Thesis
A CNAME says “this name is an alias; ask about that other name instead”. When a recursive resolver answers for an alias, it puts the whole chain in the answer section: each CNAME, then the final records. Every DNS client has to follow that chain. There are two ways to do it. You can index the whole section and then walk from the question name. Or you can read records top to bottom, updating the name you are looking for each time you pass a CNAME. The second way is shorter and works as long as the server sends the chain in order. RFC 1034 describes answers as “possibly preface[d] by one or more CNAME RRs”, which nearly every server follows, but no RFC makes it a requirement. In January 2026, a resolver change put the CNAMEs after the address records for some cached answers. Every sequential parser, including glibc’s, started returning “no such name”. This chapter rebuilds that failure on a laptop in a few milliseconds and draws two rules from it: servers should send chains in order, and clients should not need them to.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
Mental model
  question:  www.example.test  A

  answer section as sent (in order):         answer section as sent (reordered):
    www.example.test   CNAME cdn.example.test    edge.cdn.test      A     192.0.2.80
    cdn.example.test   CNAME edge.cdn.test       www.example.test   CNAME cdn.example.test
    edge.cdn.test      A     192.0.2.80          cdn.example.test   CNAME edge.cdn.test

  sequential parser, "expected name" = www.example.test
    in order : match CNAME -> expect cdn...      reordered: A for edge.cdn.test != www -> skip
               match CNAME -> expect edge...                CNAME www -> expect cdn...
               match A     -> 192.0.2.80                     CNAME cdn -> expect edge...
                                                             end of section -> NO ADDRESS
  indexed parser: build {owner -> CNAME} and {owner -> A} first, then walk from the
                  question name. Same result for both orders.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
section: What the RFCs are clear about
text:
What the RFCs are clear about
Three CNAME rules are precise, and you should treat them as hard constraints in any zone you run.
One CNAME per name, and nothing else there. RFC 1034 section 3.6.2 says that if a CNAME RR is present at a node, no other data should be present. RFC 2181 section 10.1 tightens this: an alias name can have only one CNAME record. (DNSSEC’s RRSIG and NSEC records at the alias are the standard exceptions.) This is why you cannot put a CNAME at a zone apex, which must have SOA and NS records. “CNAME flattening” and ALIAS/ANAME records exist to work around that, by having the server resolve the target and answer with A/AAAA records instead.
RRset order never matters. RFC 1034 section 3.6 defines an RRset as all records with the same owner, type and class, and says “the order of RRs in a set is not significant, and need not be preserved by name servers, resolvers, or other parts of the DNS”. That is why round-robin works and why no client may rely on getting a particular address first.
Resolvers restart at the target. RFC 1034 section 5.2.2: “In most cases a resolver simply restarts the query at the new name when it encounters a CNAME.” A full recursive resolver does exactly that and then assembles the chain in its answer.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
What the RFCs leave open
The ambiguity sits between those rules. Each CNAME in a chain is its own RRset, because each has a different owner name. The final A records are another RRset. The “order is not significant” rule is about records within one RRset. It says nothing about the order of different RRsets in a section. RFC 1034 section 4.3.1 says a recursive response will be “the answer to the query, possibly preface by one or more CNAME RRs that specify aliases encountered on the way to an answer”. It is a description, written ten years before RFC 2119 gave the IETF its MUST and SHOULD keywords, so it is not a requirement either.
So a server that sends the A record first, or sends the chain links out of order, has not clearly broken any rule. A client that only works when the chain comes first and in order has not clearly broken one either. Both readings were deployed for decades. They only collided when one large server changed its behaviour.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
The 2026-01-08 incident, briefly
Cloudflare’s post-incident write-up describes the cause. A memory optimisation in the 1.1.1.1 cache changed how a partially cached CNAME chain was merged with the final records. The old code built a new list with the CNAMEs first, then the answer. The new code appended the CNAMEs to the existing answer list, so for some responses the CNAMEs came after the A or AAAA records. The global release started late on 2026-01-07 (UTC) and reached 90% of servers on 2026-01-08. glibc’s getaddrinfo() started failing for affected names, and some Cisco switches that used 1.1.1.1 went into reboot loops. The incident was declared at 18:19 UTC, the revert started at 18:27 and impact ended at 19:55 UTC the same day. Cloudflare says it will keep CNAMEs first and in order, and it has proposed an Internet-Draft (draft-jabley-dnsop-ordered-answer-section) to make that ordering explicit.
The interesting part for an operator is not the bug. It is that the “obviously fine” response broke clients on millions of Linux machines, and that you can reproduce it in a few milliseconds.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
section: Lab: serve one chain in six orders, ask glibc each time
text:
Lab: serve one chain in six orders, ask glibc each time
The lab runs a tiny DNS server on 127.0.0.1:53 and calls socket.getaddrinfo(), which is the real glibc stub resolver, the same code path curl, ssh and most Linux programs use. To avoid touching the host, it runs inside a private user, mount and network namespace (unshare -rmn). Inside, you are root, so the script can bind port 53 and bind-mount a private /etc/resolv.conf that says nameserver 127.0.0.1. That mount exists only inside the namespace. When the script exits, the namespace and the mount are gone.
For each case the server returns the same records in a different order. The script prints what glibc returned and, for comparison, what an order-independent follow() function makes of the same records.
cname-order.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Serve one CNAME chain in two orders and ask glibc to resolve it.

Run inside a private user+mount+net namespace (no root needed):
    unshare -rmn python3 cname-order.py
The script points /etc/resolv.conf at 127.0.0.1 with a bind mount that only
exists inside the namespace, starts a tiny DNS server on 127.0.0.1:53, and
calls socket.getaddrinfo(), which is glibc's stub resolver.
"""
import os, socket, struct, subprocess, threading, sys

def name(n):
    out = b""
    for label in n.rstrip(".").split("."):
        out += bytes([len(label)]) + label.encode()
    return out + b"\x00"

def rr(owner, rtype, ttl, rdata):
    return name(owner) + struct.pack("!HHIH", rtype, 1, ttl, len(rdata)) + rdata

A, CNAME = 1, 5
CHAIN = [
    ("www.example.test", CNAME, 3600, name("cdn.example.test")),
    ("cdn.example.test", CNAME, 300, name("edge.cdn.test")),
    ("edge.cdn.test", A, 60, socket.inet_aton("192.0.2.80")),
    ("unrelated.test", A, 60, socket.inet_aton("192.0.2.99")),         # 3
    ("www.example.test", A, 60, socket.inet_aton("192.0.2.66")),       # 4: illegal sibling
    ("www.example.test", CNAME, 3600, name("other.cdn.test")),         # 5: second CNAME
    ("other.cdn.test", A, 60, socket.inet_aton("192.0.2.77")),         # 6
]
ORDERS = {
    "cname-first": [0, 1, 2],
    "cname-last": [2, 0, 1],
    "chain-reversed": [1, 0, 2],
    "unrelated-first": [3, 0, 1, 2],
    "cname-plus-a": [0, 4, 1, 2],
    "two-cnames": [0, 5, 1, 2, 6],
}
mode = {"order": "cname-first"}

def parse_question(msg):
    i = 12
    labels = []
    while msg[i]:
        labels.append(msg[i + 1:i + 1 + msg[i]].decode())
        i += msg[i] + 1
    qtype, qclass = struct.unpack("!HH", msg[i + 1:i + 5])
    return ".".join(labels), qtype, msg[12:i + 5]

def answer(query):
    qid, = struct.unpack("!H", query[:2])
    qname, qtype, qsec = parse_question(query)
    rrs = b""
    count = 0
    if qname == "www.example.test" and qtype == A:
        for idx in ORDERS[mode["order"]]:
            rrs += rr(*CHAIN[idx])
            count += 1
    flags = 0x8180  # QR, RD, RA, NOERROR
    return struct.pack("!HHHHHH", qid, flags, 1, count, 0, 0) + qsec + rrs

def follow(records, qname, max_hops=8):
    """Order-independent: index the whole answer section, then walk the chain."""
    cname = {}
    addrs = {}
    for owner, rtype, _, rdata in records:
        if rtype == CNAME:
            cname.setdefault(owner, rdata)        # first CNAME per owner, like glibc
        elif rtype == A:
            addrs.setdefault(owner, []).append(socket.inet_ntoa(rdata))
    name_, hops = qname, 0
    while name_ in cname and hops < max_hops:
        raw, labels, i = cname[name_], [], 0
        while raw[i]:
            labels.append(raw[i + 1:i + 1 + raw[i]].decode()); i += raw[i] + 1
        name_, hops = ".".join(labels), hops + 1
    return name_, addrs.get(name_, [])

def serve(sock):
    while True:
        q, peer = sock.recvfrom(4096)
        sock.sendto(answer(q), peer)

def main():
    subprocess.run(["ip", "link", "set", "lo", "up"], check=True)
    with open("/tmp/cname-order-resolv.conf", "w") as f:
        f.write("nameserver 127.0.0.1\noptions attempts:1 timeout:1\n")
    subprocess.run(["mount", "--bind", "/tmp/cname-order-resolv.conf",
                    "/etc/resolv.conf"], check=True)
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 53))
    threading.Thread(target=serve, args=(s,), daemon=True).start()
    for order in ORDERS:
        mode["order"] = order
        seq = " | ".join(f"{CHAIN[i][0]} {'CNAME' if CHAIN[i][1]==CNAME else 'A'}"
                         for i in ORDERS[order])
        try:
            res = socket.getaddrinfo("www.example.test", 80, socket.AF_INET,
                                     socket.SOCK_STREAM, 0, socket.AI_CANONNAME)
            addrs = ",".join(sorted({r[4][0] for r in res}))
            out = f"OK  {addrs}  canonname={res[0][3]}"
        except socket.gaierror as e:
            out = f"FAIL  gaierror {e.errno}: {e.strerror}"
        target, robust = follow([CHAIN[i] for i in ORDERS[order]], "www.example.test")
        print(f"{order:15} [{seq}]\n{'':15} glibc  -> {out}"
              f"\n{'':15} follow -> {','.join(robust) or 'NODATA'}  canonname={target}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Run it:
unshare -rmn python3 cname-order.py
Output:
cname-first     [www.example.test CNAME | cdn.example.test CNAME | edge.cdn.test A]
                glibc  -> OK  192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test
                follow -> 192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test
cname-last      [edge.cdn.test A | www.example.test CNAME | cdn.example.test CNAME]
                glibc  -> FAIL  gaierror -2: Name or service not known
                follow -> 192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test
chain-reversed  [cdn.example.test CNAME | www.example.test CNAME | edge.cdn.test A]
                glibc  -> FAIL  gaierror -2: Name or service not known
                follow -> 192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test
unrelated-first [unrelated.test A | www.example.test CNAME | cdn.example.test CNAME | edge.cdn.test A]
                glibc  -> OK  192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test
                follow -> 192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test
cname-plus-a    [www.example.test CNAME | www.example.test A | cdn.example.test CNAME | edge.cdn.test A]
                glibc  -> OK  192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test
                follow -> 192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test
two-cnames      [www.example.test CNAME | www.example.test CNAME | cdn.example.test CNAME | edge.cdn.test A | other.cdn.test A]
                glibc  -> OK  192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test
                follow -> 192.0.2.80  canonname=edge.cdn.test

Reading the first three cases: order is the whole difference
cname-first is the conventional order and works. cname-last is the shape of the January incident: the A record first, then the chain. glibc returns EAI_NONAME, “Name or service not known”, the same error as a name that does not exist. chain-reversed keeps the A record last but swaps the two CNAMEs. It fails as well. That case matters because “CNAMEs before other records” is not enough: a sequential parser also needs the links of the chain in order, starting from the question name.
follow() gets 192.0.2.80 and the canonical name edge.cdn.test in all three cases, from identical bytes. The data was never wrong. Only the parsing strategy differs.


Reading unrelated-first: glibc skips, it does not stop
An unrelated A record at the top does not break glibc. Its parser skips records whose owner is not the name it is currently expecting, then carries on. That explains exactly why cname-last fails: the A record for edge.cdn.test is skipped as “unrelated” because, when glibc reaches it, it is still looking for www.example.test. By the time the CNAMEs have moved the expected name to edge.cdn.test, the A record is behind it.


Reading cname-plus-a and two-cnames: broken zones that still “work”
These two answers break the hard rules: www.example.test has a CNAME and an A record, and in the last case two different CNAMEs. A correct zone loader would refuse both. glibc returns an address anyway. With a CNAME and an A record at the alias, it followed the CNAME and ignored 192.0.2.66. With two CNAMEs, it followed the first one and ignored other.cdn.test. So did follow(), because it was written to keep the first CNAME too.
That is the trap. If you test a broken zone only from a Linux host, it looks fine. A different resolver may pick the other CNAME, or return the sibling A record, or SERVFAIL. RFC 2181 section 10.1 allows none of these zones, and the only safe behaviour is not to publish them. Validate zones with your server’s checker (for example named-checkzone or kzonecheck; not run here, neither is installed), not by resolving names from one client.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
section: How to be robust on both sides
text:
How to be robust on both sides
If you serve DNS (an authoritative server, a resolver, a load balancer that answers DNS, a test fake like the one in the lab):

Send the chain first, in order from the question name, then the final RRset. That is what the RFC 1034 text describes and what deployed clients expect.
Keep that order on every code path, including cache merges and partially cached chains. Write a test that asserts it. The incident came from an optimisation in code that had no such test.
Keep chains short. Each CNAME hop costs the resolver at least one more lookup when it is not cached, and some resolvers cap the chain length.

If you parse DNS (a stub resolver, a monitoring probe, an embedded client):

Index the whole answer section, then walk from the question name, as follow() does. It is a dozen lines and handles every order.
Put a hop limit on the walk (the lab uses 8) so a CNAME loop in a broken answer cannot spin forever.
Treat a CNAME and other data at the same owner, or two CNAMEs, as a broken answer. Do not quietly pick one.

If you run Linux hosts, you cannot fix glibc’s parser from configuration. You can choose what sits in front of it. A local caching resolver (for example systemd-resolved, unbound or dnsmasq on 127.0.0.x) parses upstream answers with its own code and re-serialises them for glibc. Cloudflare’s write-up notes that systemd-resolved was not affected because it parses answers into a set before following the chain.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
Case
This is an illustrative scenario, not a real named incident.
A team ran an internal DNS-based service discovery layer: a small Go service answering for *.svc.internal, with aliases such as api.svc.internal CNAME api-blue.svc.internal. During a refactor, someone changed the answer builder to append the alias records after looking up the final A records, because that made the code simpler. Unit tests compared answers as sets and passed. Staging used a resolver library that parsed answers as a set, and it passed too. In production, every service that called getaddrinfo() through glibc began failing to resolve aliased names with “Name or service not known”. Services that resolved non-aliased names were fine, which made the problem look like a data issue. A packet capture showed the answer section in the new order. The fix was one line. The lasting fix was a test that compared the answer section as a list: CNAMEs first, in chain order.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
Trap
Testing DNS answers as sets. Sets are the right model for RRset contents and the wrong model for what clients actually parse. If you write or proxy DNS, assert the order of the answer section in tests. And do not take “it resolves on my Linux box” as proof a zone is valid: glibc forgives some illegal zones, as the last two cases showed.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
Boring rule
Serve CNAME chains first and in order. Parse them without depending on order. Never publish a CNAME with sibling data or a second CNAME, and check zones with a zone checker, not a client.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
Try this

Add a case where the chain is complete but the final A record is missing (a “dangling” CNAME). What does glibc return? What does follow() return, and how would you make it say NODATA explicitly?
Add a CNAME loop: www -> cdn -> www. Does glibc return, and how fast? Does follow() stop at its hop limit?
Change getaddrinfo() to use socket.AF_UNSPEC and teach the server to answer AAAA with the same chain plus 2001:db8::80. Reorder only the AAAA answer. What do you get back now?
Make follow() reject answers with two CNAMEs for one owner or a CNAME plus other data, instead of picking the first. Which of the six cases does it reject?
Write the server-side test the Case describes: given an answer section, assert that the CNAMEs come first and that each CNAME’s owner is the previous one’s target, starting from the question name.

title: CNAME Chains and Answer Order: What the RFCs Say and What glibc Does
text:
Verification

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Learning goals

Explain what anycast is at the routing layer: the same service prefix announced from several places, with ordinary best-path selection choosing which one each client reaches
Name the parts RFC 4786 uses (service address, anycast node, local vs global node) and the rule that matters most: the route announcement must follow the health of the service
Reproduce, without root, the three behaviours that decide whether an anycast deployment is safe: best-path stickiness, a black hole when a dead node keeps announcing, and failover when it withdraws
Show how ECMP hashing (fib_multipath_hash_policy) decides whether one client is pinned to one instance or spread across several
Reproduce a TCP connection being reset when the routing system moves it to a different instance, and say why DNS and other short transactions tolerate this
Identify which instance answered a query (id.server / hostname.bind, NSID) when debugging

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Thesis
Anycast is not a protocol. No packet carries an “anycast” bit, and no router knows it is doing it. You put the same address on several servers in different places, announce the prefix that contains it from each place, and let routing do what it always does: pick one best path per destination. Each client reaches whichever instance is “closest” in routing terms, which is not always closest on a map. Root and TLD DNS servers, public resolvers and CDNs all work this way because it gives you load spreading, DDoS dilution and failover without a single extra protocol.
The price is that routing now decides which server holds a client’s state. That has two consequences, and both are easy to get wrong. First, the announcement must be tied to the health of the service. A node whose daemon died but whose router still announces the prefix is a black hole for every client routed to it. Second, a routing change in the middle of a connection silently moves the client to another instance, one that has never heard of the connection. For a one-packet DNS query that is harmless. For a long TCP download it is a reset. This chapter builds both failures in four network namespaces and draws the operating rules from them.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Mental model
                         192.0.2.53/32 is configured on BOTH servers' loopbacks

   client 10.0.1.2 ----- r (router) ---- 10.0.2.2  s1 "mumbai"   lo: 192.0.2.53
                          |  \
                          |   `--------- 10.0.3.2  s2 "chennai"  lo: 192.0.2.53
                          |
   r's routing table decides who "is" 192.0.2.53 for this client:

     best path    192.0.2.53 via s1 metric 10      -> every packet to s1
                  192.0.2.53 via s2 metric 20      -> backup, used only if s1's route goes
     ECMP         192.0.2.53 nexthop s1 nexthop s2 -> per-flow hash picks one
     withdrawal   delete "via s1"                  -> everything moves to s2

   On the Internet, "r" is the whole BGP system and "metric" is AS-path length,
   local preference and the rest of best-path selection. The behaviour is the same.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Words RFC 4786 uses
RFC 4786 (BCP 126, Operation of Anycast Services) is the operator’s document. Its vocabulary is worth adopting because it keeps the routing part separate from the service part:







Term
Meaning




Service address
The address clients use, e.g. 192.0.2.53. It is configured on every node.


Service supernet
The prefix announced in routing that covers the service address. On the global Internet it has to be at least a /24 (IPv4) or /48 (IPv6) to survive common prefix filters.


Anycast node
One location that offers the service and originates the supernet.


Global node
A node whose announcement propagates everywhere.


Local node
A node whose announcement is meant to stay near it. RFC 4786 suggests tagging it with the NO_EXPORT community, so that only the networks peering at that exchange point use it.



Two pieces of RFC 4786 advice matter more than the rest:

Tie the route to the service. It recommends that a node withdraw its announcement when the service fails, and treats that as part of the node, not an afterthought. The usual way to do it is a local health check that drives the BGP speaker: a script that probes the daemon on the node and enables or disables the BGP announcement (a BIRD protocol, an FRR network statement behind a route-map, or ExaBGP’s health-check helper).
Give every node a unique unicast management address, so you can reach a specific instance for debugging and monitoring. The service address can never do that, by definition.

RFC 3258 describes the same idea specifically for authoritative DNS (“shared unicast addresses”). RFC 7094 explains why anycast works for stateful protocols in practice even though nothing guarantees it. RFC 9199, written by large authoritative DNS operators, recommends anycast and covers how routing choices shape latency and attack absorption.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
section: Why DNS is the canonical anycast service
text:
Why DNS is the canonical anycast service
A classic DNS query is one UDP datagram in and one out. There is no connection to break: if routing moves between two queries, the second one simply lands on another instance with the same zone data. That is why the root servers and almost every large authoritative and recursive DNS service are anycast. The same reasoning covers NTP, and any protocol whose transactions are short compared with how often routes change.
TCP, TLS and QUIC carry state in the server. Anycast still works for them, and CDNs serve HTTP over anycast every day, because Internet routes are stable for most clients for minutes or hours at a time (RFC 7094 section 4.2, “Transport Implications”, discusses this assumption). Stable is not guaranteed, though, and the lab below shows what the rare unlucky connection sees.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
section: Lab: four namespaces, one service address
text:
Lab: four namespaces, one service address
The lab runs as an unprivileged user with unshare -urnm (a user, network and mount namespace), then creates four named network namespaces inside it: client, router r, and two servers s1 and s2. Both servers put 192.0.2.53/32 on their loopback and run the same small responder. It needs only iproute2 and Python 3; nothing is installed and sudo is never used.

The responder
Each instance answers CHAOS-class TXT queries with its own name. This is the convention RFC 4892 describes for id.server and hostname.bind, and real servers (BIND, NSD, Knot, Unbound) support it. It also offers a tiny TCP echo on port 5300 so we can watch a long-lived connection.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Tiny DNS responder for the anycast lab.
Answers CHAOS TXT queries for id.server / hostname.bind (RFC 4892) with this
instance's name, so a client can tell which anycast instance answered.
Also serves a TCP echo-ish service on port 5300 to show what a path change
does to an established TCP connection.
usage: dnsid.py ADDR NAME
"""
import socket, struct, sys, threading

addr, name = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]

def answer(q: bytes) -> bytes:
    qid, flags, qd = struct.unpack("!HHH", q[:6])
    i = 12
    while q[i]:
        i += q[i] + 1
    qend = i + 5                       # zero label + QTYPE + QCLASS
    qtype, qclass = struct.unpack("!HH", q[i + 1:qend])
    txt = name.encode()
    rdata = bytes([len(txt)]) + txt
    rr = b"\xc0\x0c" + struct.pack("!HHIH", 16, qclass, 0, len(rdata)) + rdata
    ok = qtype == 16 and qclass == 3   # TXT CH
    hdr = struct.pack("!HHHHHH", qid, 0x8400 | (0 if ok else 4), 1, 1 if ok else 0, 0, 0)
    return hdr + q[12:qend] + (rr if ok else b"")

def udp():
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    s.bind((addr, 53))
    while True:
        q, peer = s.recvfrom(512)
        s.sendto(answer(q), peer)

def tcp():
    s = socket.socket()
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind((addr, 5300)); s.listen()
    while True:
        c, _ = s.accept()
        threading.Thread(target=serve, args=(c,), daemon=True).start()

def serve(c):
    with c:
        while (d := c.recv(100)):
            c.sendall(name.encode() + b":" + d)

threading.Thread(target=tcp, daemon=True).start()
udp()


The client
ask.py sends N id.server CH TXT queries. Each query uses a new socket, and therefore a new ephemeral source port. It then counts which instance answered. tcpprobe.py holds one TCP connection and sends a line every 0.3 s.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Send N CHAOS TXT id.server queries (RFC 4892), each from a fresh source
port, and count which anycast instance answered.  usage: ask.py ADDR N"""
import collections, socket, struct, sys

addr, n = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
QNAME = b"\x02id\x06server\x00"
seen = collections.Counter()
for qid in range(n):
    q = struct.pack("!HHHHHH", qid, 0x0100, 1, 0, 0, 0) + QNAME + struct.pack("!HH", 16, 3)
    with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) as s:
        s.settimeout(0.3)
        s.bind(("0.0.0.0", 0))                 # new ephemeral port every time
        s.sendto(q, (addr, 53))
        try:
            r, _ = s.recvfrom(512)
        except socket.timeout:
            seen["timeout"] += 1
            continue
    rdata = r[12 + len(QNAME) + 4 + 2 + 10:]   # header, question, RR name ptr + fixed part
    seen[rdata[1:1 + rdata[0]].decode()] += 1
print("  ".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in sorted(seen.items())))
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Hold one TCP connection to the anycast address and send a line every
0.3 s; print who answered.  A path change mid-connection shows up here.
usage: tcpprobe.py ADDR ROUNDS"""
import socket, sys, time
addr, rounds = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
c = socket.create_connection((addr, 5300), timeout=2)
print("   local port", c.getsockname()[1])
for i in range(rounds):
    try:
        c.sendall(b"ping%d" % i)
        d = c.recv(100)
        print("   round", i, "->", d.decode() if d else "EOF (peer closed)")
        if not d:
            break
    except OSError as e:
        print("   round", i, "->", type(e).__name__, e.errno, e.strerror)
        break
    time.sleep(0.3)


The topology and the six experiments
The box has no sysctl binary, so the script writes /proc/sys directly inside the router’s namespace.
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -urnm sh lab.sh
# client --- router ===( two paths )=== s1, s2   both s1 and s2 own 192.0.2.53/32
set -e
mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
for ns in client r s1 s2; do ip netns add $ns; ip -n $ns link set lo up; done
link() { ip link add $1 type veth peer name $3; ip link set $1 netns $2; ip link set $3 netns $4
         ip -n $2 link set $1 up; ip -n $4 link set $3 up; }
link c0 client r0 r; link r1 r s1e s1; link r2 r s2e s2
ip -n client addr add 10.0.1.2/24 dev c0; ip -n r addr add 10.0.1.1/24 dev r0
ip -n r addr add 10.0.2.1/24 dev r1;      ip -n s1 addr add 10.0.2.2/24 dev s1e
ip -n r addr add 10.0.3.1/24 dev r2;      ip -n s2 addr add 10.0.3.2/24 dev s2e
ip -n client route add default via 10.0.1.1
ip -n s1 route add default via 10.0.2.1;  ip -n s2 route add default via 10.0.3.1
ip -n s1 addr add 192.0.2.53/32 dev lo;   ip -n s2 addr add 192.0.2.53/32 dev lo
sysw() { ip netns exec r sh -c "echo $2 > /proc/sys/${1}" && echo "   $(echo $1 | tr / .) = $(ip netns exec r cat /proc/sys/$1)"; }
sysw net/ipv4/ip_forward 1 >/dev/null
H=$(pwd)
ip netns exec s1 python3 $H/dnsid.py 192.0.2.53 s1-mumbai & P1=$!
ip netns exec s2 python3 $H/dnsid.py 192.0.2.53 s2-chennai & P2=$!
sleep 0.5
C="ip netns exec client python3"

echo "== 1. one best path (s1 metric 10, s2 metric 20): who answers 50 queries?"
ip -n r route add 192.0.2.53/32 via 10.0.2.2 metric 10
ip -n r route add 192.0.2.53/32 via 10.0.3.2 metric 20
ip -n r route show 192.0.2.53/32 | sed 's/^/   /'
$C $H/ask.py 192.0.2.53 50 | sed 's/^/   /'

echo "== 2. s1 process dies but its route stays (no health-tied withdrawal)"
kill $P1; wait $P1 2>/dev/null || true
$C $H/ask.py 192.0.2.53 20 | sed 's/^/   /'
ip netns exec s1 python3 $H/dnsid.py 192.0.2.53 s1-mumbai & P1=$!; sleep 0.3

echo "== 3. health check withdraws s1 (route deleted): who answers now?"
ip -n r route del 192.0.2.53/32 via 10.0.2.2 metric 10
$C $H/ask.py 192.0.2.53 20 | sed 's/^/   /'
ip -n r route add 192.0.2.53/32 via 10.0.2.2 metric 10

echo "== 4. ECMP at the router, hash policy 0 (L3: src+dst IP only)"
ip -n r route del 192.0.2.53/32 metric 10; ip -n r route del 192.0.2.53/32 metric 20
ip -n r route add 192.0.2.53/32 nexthop via 10.0.2.2 nexthop via 10.0.3.2
ip -n r route show 192.0.2.53/32 | sed 's/^/   /'
sysw net/ipv4/fib_multipath_hash_policy 0
$C $H/ask.py 192.0.2.53 200 | sed 's/^/   /'

echo "== 5. same ECMP, hash policy 1 (L4: 5-tuple), fresh source port per query"
sysw net/ipv4/fib_multipath_hash_policy 1
$C $H/ask.py 192.0.2.53 200 | sed 's/^/   /'

echo "== 6. TCP across a path change: connection pinned to one instance, then the route moves"
ip -n r route replace 192.0.2.53/32 via 10.0.2.2
$C $H/tcpprobe.py 192.0.2.53 6 > /tmp/tcp.out 2>&1 & T=$!
sleep 0.8
ip -n r route replace 192.0.2.53/32 via 10.0.3.2
echo "   (route moved to s2 at ~0.8 s)"
wait $T || true; cat /tmp/tcp.out

kill $P1 $P2 2>/dev/null || true
Run it:
unshare -urnm sh lab.sh
Output, unedited (kernel 6.12.94+, iproute2 6.15.0, Python 3.13.5):
== 1. one best path (s1 metric 10, s2 metric 20): who answers 50 queries?
   192.0.2.53 via 10.0.2.2 dev r1 metric 10 
   192.0.2.53 via 10.0.3.2 dev r2 metric 20 
   s1-mumbai=50
== 2. s1 process dies but its route stays (no health-tied withdrawal)
   timeout=20
== 3. health check withdraws s1 (route deleted): who answers now?
   s2-chennai=20
== 4. ECMP at the router, hash policy 0 (L3: src+dst IP only)
   192.0.2.53 
    nexthop via 10.0.2.2 dev r1 weight 1 
    nexthop via 10.0.3.2 dev r2 weight 1 
   net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy = 0
   s1-mumbai=200
== 5. same ECMP, hash policy 1 (L4: 5-tuple), fresh source port per query
   net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy = 1
   s1-mumbai=109  s2-chennai=91
== 6. TCP across a path change: connection pinned to one instance, then the route moves
   (route moved to s2 at ~0.8 s)
   local port 46118
   round 0 -> s1-mumbai:ping0
   round 1 -> s1-mumbai:ping1
   round 2 -> s1-mumbai:ping2
   round 3 -> ConnectionResetError 104 Connection reset by peer


Reading the output
1. Best path is sticky. With s1 at metric 10 and s2 at metric 20, all 50 queries went to s1. s2 was healthy the whole time and received nothing. This is what most of the Internet sees for most anycast services: one site per client, chosen by routing, with no regard for load. If your Mumbai node takes 80 percent of your traffic, the fix is in routing (prepend, communities, more nodes, local nodes), not in the server.
2. A dead daemon behind a live route is a black hole. We killed the responder on s1 but left the router’s route in place. Every one of the 20 queries timed out. s2 was up, and it did not matter. Note how it failed: the client saw silence, not an error. s1’s kernel may answer with an ICMP port unreachable, but an unconnected UDP socket does not report it to the application, so a stub resolver just waits for its retry timer. In production this looks like “DNS is slow for users in one region”, which is one of the hardest outages to see from a central monitoring point. It is the reason RFC 4786 wants the announcement tied to the service.
3. Withdrawal is the failover. Once the route via s1 was deleted (the equivalent of the health check telling BGP to withdraw), the next query went to s2 and all 20 succeeded. No client changed anything. How fast this happens on the real Internet depends on how quickly the withdrawal propagates. That ranges from sub-second inside one network to tens of seconds across the Internet, because of MRAI timers and path exploration.
4 and 5. ECMP hash policy decides spreading. Same two equal next hops, two hash policies:

fib_multipath_hash_policy = 0 hashes on source and destination IP only. One client, one destination, one hash result: all 200 queries went to s1, even though each used a new source port.
fib_multipath_hash_policy = 1 adds the protocol and ports (the 5-tuple). The same 200 queries split 109 / 91.

Neither is “right”. Policy 0 keeps a client’s flows together, which suits stateful services and a resolver that sends many queries from the same address. Policy 1 spreads load better when there are few clients and many flows. The kernel documentation (ip-sysctl, fib_multipath_hash_policy) also lists policy 2 (inner headers for encapsulated traffic) and 3 (a custom field set chosen with fib_multipath_hash_fields). The common in-site pattern is several servers behind a router, each announcing the service /32 over BGP with ECMP enabled, and it relies on exactly this hash.
6. TCP does not survive a move. The TCP connection was established to s1 and three round trips worked. Then the route moved to s2. The next segment arrived at s2, which has a listener on port 5300 but no connection matching that 4-tuple, so s2’s kernel answered with a RST. The client got ECONNRESET. Nothing was misconfigured. This is what anycast means for stateful protocols: correctness depends on routing not changing for the life of the connection.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Debugging which instance you reached
From the outside, every instance has the same address, so ping and traceroute do not tell you which one answered. Use the service itself:
dig @192.0.2.53 id.server CH TXT +short       # RFC 4892 convention; also hostname.bind
dig @192.0.2.53 example.test +nsid            # RFC 5001 NSID option in the EDNS OPT record
Both depend on the server being configured to reveal an identity. Most operators publish a site code rather than a hostname. These commands are not run here because dig is not installed on this box; the lab’s ask.py does the same id.server query by hand. From many vantage points at once, the RIPE Atlas built-in measurements query hostname.bind against the root servers continuously, which is how people map anycast catchments.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
section: Operating rules that fall out of the lab
text:
Operating rules that fall out of the lab

Health-checked announcements, always. The check should exercise the real service, for example by asking the local daemon for a known record. A process check alone is not enough. Withdraw on failure, and add hold-down or dampening so a flapping daemon does not flap your routes across the Internet.
Announce the same supernet everywhere, and cover it with ROAs. If several sites originate from the same ASN, one ROA for that ASN covers them all. If some sites use a different origin ASN (a partner network, a local node hosted by an IXP member), each origin ASN needs its own ROA, or RPKI-validating networks drop those announcements as Invalid. Keep the ROA’s maxLength equal to the announced length unless you really announce more-specifics.
Never anycast without per-node unicast addresses for management, health monitoring and log collection.
Keep catchments observable. Log which node served each query, and alert on sudden shifts of traffic share between nodes. A shift with no event on your side is often someone else’s routing change.
Think about state per protocol. DNS over UDP is fine. DNS over TCP and DoT, HTTP and TLS work because routes are usually stable, so keep connection lifetimes modest. QUIC can survive some path changes with connection IDs plus a load balancer that routes on them, but only within a site. Two different anycast sites do not share QUIC state either.
Local nodes stay local. If a node is meant only for one exchange, use NO_EXPORT (or your upstreams’ scoping communities) and check from a looking glass that it does not leak.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Case
A small authoritative DNS operator runs three nodes (Mumbai, Chennai, Singapore), each announcing 198.51.100.0/24 from the same ASN over two transit providers. After a kernel upgrade, the DNS daemon on the Chennai node fails to start because of a bad configuration line. The BGP daemon starts fine. For forty minutes, resolvers in South India get timeouts for every zone the operator hosts. External monitoring probes from Europe and the US all pass, because they reach Singapore. The fix was two lines: a health check that queries the local daemon for the zone’s SOA every two seconds and disables the BGP announcement after three failures, plus a monitoring probe that queries id.server from each region and alerts when one region stops answering.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Trap
“Anycast gives me load balancing.” It gives you routing-defined distribution, which can be very uneven (experiment 1 sent 100 percent to one site). If you need even load, you need more nodes, routing adjustments, or a load balancer behind each site.
“ECMP across instances is free redundancy.” In experiment 6 the route moved on purpose, but an ECMP group losing a next hop has the same effect on some surviving flows. With plain hash-threshold ECMP, removing one next hop can remap flows that were going to the healthy ones. Linux resilient next-hop groups (ip nexthop add ... type resilient, see ip-nexthop(8)) exist to limit that churn.
“The daemon is up, so the node is healthy.” A daemon serving an empty or stale zone is worse than a dead one: it answers quickly and wrongly. Health checks should verify content, such as the SOA serial or a canary record, not just liveness.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Boring rule
Announce only what you can serve: the BGP announcement and the service’s health are one switch, not two. Give every node a unicast name, every query an instance ID in the logs, and every origin ASN a ROA.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Try this

Add a third server s3 with weight 2 in the ECMP group (nexthop via ... weight 2) and check that the policy-1 split moves towards 50/25/25.
Run experiment 6 again with the ECMP group and policy 1, and delete one next hop instead of replacing the route. Run tcpprobe.py several times: some connections survive, some are reset, depending on where their hash lands.
Change ask.py to use one socket for all queries (fixed source port) and rerun experiment 5. Explain the result.
Write a ten-line health checker that runs in s1, queries 127.0.0.1 for id.server, and calls ip -n r route del ... after three failures (it can reach the router namespace because everything is inside the same user namespace). Kill the responder and time the failover.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Verification

unshare -urnm sh lab.sh was run on this box as an unprivileged user (no sudo, nothing installed). The output above is pasted verbatim. Kernel 6.12.94+, iproute2 6.15.0, Python 3.13.5.
The ECMP split (109 / 91) depends on the random source ports, so expect different numbers each run. With policy 0, expect all queries on one instance.
Not run: real BGP (BIRD, FRR, ExaBGP), RPKI, dig (not installed) and RIPE Atlas. These parts are written from the cited documentation.

title: Anycast Services: One Address, Many Servers, and Withdrawing When Sick
text:
Sources

RFC 4786 / BCP 126, Operation of Anycast Services: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4786
RFC 3258, Distributing Authoritative Name Servers via Shared Unicast Addresses: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3258
RFC 7094, Architectural Considerations of IP Anycast: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7094
RFC 9199, Considerations for Large Authoritative DNS Server Operators: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9199
RFC 4892, Requirements for a Mechanism Identifying a Name Server Instance: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4892
RFC 5001, DNS Name Server Identifier (NSID) Option: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5001
