title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Learning goals

Differentiate distance-vector and link-state control planes by how they compute and propagate routing information across a topology.
Trace the Bellman-Ford algorithm, infinity thresholds, split horizon, and poison reverse to explain why count-to-infinity occurs and where classic mitigations break down.
Contrast flooding and Dijkstra’s Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm in link-state protocols against neighborhood metric exchanges in distance-vector protocols.
Evaluate trade-offs between distance-vector, link-state, path-vector, and hybrid protocols regarding CPU usage, memory footprint, convergence speed, and troubleshooting visibility.
Run a Python simulation of distance-vector updates and SPF to observe convergence, metric laddering, and loop mechanics on simple topologies.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Thesis
Dynamic routing protocols automate how routers discover paths, calculate best routes, update kernel routing tables, and react to topology failures. Distance-vector protocols pass summarized routing tables between immediate neighbors, calculating paths using distributed Bellman-Ford operations that conserve memory but suffer from transient loops and slow convergence when links fail. Link-state protocols flood raw adjacency state to every node in an area, giving each router an identical topology database from which it runs Dijkstra’s algorithm to compute shortest paths locally. Understanding the trade-offs between local rumor-based routing and global map-based routing allows network operators to select, optimize, and troubleshoot interior gateway protocols effectively.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Mental model
Distance-vector protocols pass path costs to immediate neighbors, whereas link-state protocols flood link conditions to all routers so every node builds an identical topology map.
Distance-Vector (Distributed Rumor)
  [ Router A ] <--- Distance Vector (Cost=3) ---> [ Router B ] <--- Distance Vector (Cost=2) ---> [ Router C ]
  (A only knows B offered cost 3; A has no map of what lies beyond B)

Link-State (Global Map & Local SPF)
  [ Router A ] <--- Flooded LSA (Adjacency State) ---> [ Router B ] <--- Flooded LSA (Adjacency State) ---> [ Router C ]
  (A receives link states from B and C, builds identical topology database, then runs Dijkstra locally)

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Core functions of dynamic routing
Static routing works well for predictable topologies with few nodes, but manual configuration scales poorly and cannot re-route around unexpected link failures automatically. A dynamic routing protocol automates four continuous operations:

Neighbor discovery: Identifying adjacent routers over directly connected links and verifying bidirectionality.
Information propagation: Exchanging route reachability or link status metrics across the network domain.
Path computation and installation: Evaluating available paths according to metric algorithms and inserting the optimal routes into the kernel Routing Information Base (RIB) and Forwarding Information Base (FIB).
Topology change detection and reaction: Detecting link failures or metric shifts, invalidating bad paths, recomputing alternatives, and updating neighbors.

Different routing protocol families accomplish these four duties through fundamentally distinct mathematical models and data structures.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Distance-vector architecture
Distance-vector (DV) protocols implement a distributed variant of the Bellman-Ford algorithm. In a distance-vector system, each router maintains a vector of distances (metrics) to all known destination networks alongside the next-hop router IP address used to reach each destination.
Nodes do not share network topology. Instead, each router periodically transmits its local routing table—its vector of reachability estimates—to its directly connected neighbors. Upon receiving an update from neighbor N advertising metric m to destination D, a receiving node computes its candidate cost to D via N as m + c, where c is the cost of its own link to N. If this total cost is lower than the node’s current recorded distance to D, the node updates its table to record the new distance and sets N as its next hop.

RIP characteristics and RFC 2453
Routing Information Protocol (RIP) version 2 (RFC 2453) is the classic distance-vector protocol. Its design choices illustrate the operational mechanics of distance-vector routing:

Metric: Hop count only. Every active IP link carries a metric of 1, regardless of bandwidth, latency, or reliability.
Infinity threshold: Set strictly to 16 hops. A metric of 16 indicates an unreachable destination.
Periodic updates: Routers broadcast or multicast (224.0.0.9) their full routing table every 30 seconds.
Expiration timeout: If no update is received for a route within 180 seconds, the route is marked invalid (metric set to 16) and enters a hold-down state.
Garbage collection timer: Invalid routes remain in the table for an additional 120 seconds to allow the metric 16 advertisement to propagate before the entry is pruned completely.
Triggered updates: When a router detects a local metric change or link failure, it immediately transmits an unsolicited update without waiting for the 30-second timer.

Because distance-vector routing relies on indirect information (“B told me it can reach D in 2 hops”), it is often characterized as “routing by rumor.” A node trusts its neighbor’s advertised distance without knowing the physical path or node sequence behind that distance.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Link-state architecture
Link-state (LS) protocols replace rumor propagation with deterministic database synchronization. Instead of distributing calculated routing tables, link-state nodes flood uncalculated reports about local physical links—known as Link-State Advertisements (LSAs) in OSPF or Link-State Packets (LSPs) in IS-IS.
Every router in a link-state area collects these advertisements and populates a Link-State Database (LSDB). Because every router in the area receives the same set of LSAs via reliable flooding, every router constructs an identical graph representation of the network topology.

Flooding, sequence numbers, and ageing
Link-state updates rely on three mechanisms to keep topology databases synchronized across the network:

Reliable flooding: When a node receives a new LSA, it acknowledges the LSA to the sender, writes it to its local LSDB, and retransmits it out all other active interfaces.
Sequence numbers: LSAs carry explicitly incrementing sequence numbers (for example, starting at 0x80000001 in OSPF). If a router receives an LSA with a sequence number higher than the entry in its current database, it replaces its database entry and floods the new LSA. Older or duplicate sequence numbers are discarded.
MaxAge and refresh timers: LSAs include an age field (in seconds) that counts upward while stored in memory. If an LSA reaches MaxAge (typically 3600 seconds in OSPF), it is flushed from the database. To prevent expiry during normal operation, the originating router re-floods each LSA periodically (every 1800 seconds by default in OSPF).



Local Dijkstra SPF computation
Once the LSDB is synchronized, each router independently executes Dijkstra’s Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm, using itself as the root node of the graph. Dijkstra calculates the shortest path tree to every reachable destination based on configured link costs (such as interface bandwidth metrics).
Because Dijkstra operates on a complete graph rather than a neighbor’s computed table, link-state protocols prevent routing loops during steady-state operation. The primary implementations are Open Shortest Path First (OSPFv2 RFC 2328, OSPFv3 RFC 5340) and Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS ISO/IEC 10589, RFC 1195).

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Count-to-infinity and loop mitigations
The vulnerability of classic distance-vector protocols is count-to-infinity. When a network link fails, routers using distributed Bellman-Ford can accept stale advertisements from neighbors that still route traffic through the failed link.
Consider a linear path: A --- B --- C --- D. If the link between C and D breaks, C detects the failure and sets its distance to D to 16 (unreachable). However, before C can propagate this update, B might send its periodic update to C, stating: “I can reach D at cost 2” (because B previously routed via C at cost 1 + 1 = 2).
C receives B’s update, sees that B offers a path to D at cost 2, and updates its own table entry for D to cost 3 via B. In the next round, B receives C’s update and increases its metric to 4 via C. The nodes continually increment their distance to D (3, 4, 5, 6…) until the metric hits the defined infinity value of 16. During this count-to-infinity process, packets addressed to D bounce between B and C, causing a transient routing loop and consuming link capacity. (In this line example the loop is between B and C; A simply forwards into it.)
Setting a small infinity value (such as 16 in RIP) bounds the time required for count-to-infinity to settle, stopping the increment loop after 16 iterations instead of running indefinitely up to standard integer limits.

Split horizon and poison reverse
To mitigate simple two-node count-to-infinity loops, distance-vector protocols use two techniques:

Split horizon: A router never advertises a route out the interface through which it learned that route. In A --- B --- C, B learns about D from C. Under split horizon rules, B suppresses its advertisement of destination D when sending updates out its interface back to C.
Poison reverse: Instead of suppressing the route, B explicitly advertises destination D back to C with an infinite metric (cost 16). This explicitly informs C that B relies on C for that destination, preventing C from considering B as a fallback path to D.



Multi-node loop failure modes
Split horizon and poison reverse prevent two-node mutual feedback loops. However, they fail on topologies containing loops of three or more nodes (such as triangles or rings).
Take a triangle X, Y, Z (every pair linked), where Z also connects to destination T. In steady state X and Y both reach T through Z at cost 2. If link Z --- T drops, Z invalidates its route. Split horizon stops X and Y from advertising T back to Z, but it does not stop them from advertising it to each other: each still holds cost 2 via Z, so in the next round X learns cost 3 via Y and Y learns cost 3 via X. The stale route is now circulating.
However, split horizon does not prevent X from advertising its path to Z (since X learned the route from Y, not Z). Z receives X’s advertisement (cost 3), updates its table to route to T via X at cost 4, and advertises this new path. Y then updates its path through Z, creating a circular metric ladder that counts to 16 despite split horizon rules.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Path-vector architecture
Path-vector routing is an explicit extension of distance-vector principles designed to eliminate count-to-infinity in arbitrary topologies. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP, RFC 4271) is the primary path-vector protocol.
Instead of passing only a destination and a scalar metric, a path-vector update carries an ordered list of traversal path identifiers—such as the AS_PATH attribute listing Autonomous System numbers. When a router receives a path-vector update containing its own identifier in the path list, it rejects the advertisement immediately. This path record detects and blocks loops of any length on the first update round, preventing count-to-infinity without placing artificial limits on maximum network hop metrics.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Protocol comparison









Dimension
Distance-Vector (e.g., RIP)
Link-State (e.g., OSPF, IS-IS)
Path-Vector (e.g., BGP)




State maintained
Routing table (distances and next hops to destinations)
Complete graph topology (LSDB containing all nodes and links)
Prefix routes with full attribute lists (e.g., AS_PATH)


CPU usage
Low (simple scalar comparisons)
High (runs Dijkstra SPF across full graph)
Moderate to high (complex policy matching)


Memory usage
Low (proportional to destination count)
High (proportional to total nodes and links)
High (proportional to global Internet prefixes and paths)


Convergence speed
Slow (limited by periodic timers and metric step-up iterations)
Fast (floods raw state changes immediately and recomputes SPF)
Variable (constrained by path selection policies and MRAI timers)


Failure modes
Transient routing loops, count-to-infinity
Database desynchronization, SPF CPU spikes, LSA thrashing
Path oscillation, route flapping, misconfigurations


Scaling scope
Small networks (bounded by small max hop counts)
Hierarchical areas/domains (thousands of routers per domain)
Global scale (hundreds of thousands of prefixes inter-domain)


Visibility
Low (only sees next-hop metrics; no topology visibility)
High (complete map of area topology visible on every router)
Moderate (sees sequence of autonomous systems, not internal nodes)

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Operator view: Control plane visibility
Network operators troubleshoot distance-vector and link-state networks using different diagnostic workflows.
In a distance-vector environment, inspection is limited to examining the local routing table. If a route is missing or incorrect, an operator inspects neighbor updates to determine which adjacent router sent an unexpected metric. The operator cannot determine the path beyond the neighbor without querying each intermediate hop individually.
In a link-state environment, operators separate control plane state into the neighbor table, the topology database, and the routing table:
1. Neighbor Table  ---> Verifies bidirectionality and adjacency state
2. LSDB Database   ---> Inspects flooded node/link records (identical across all routers in area)
3. Routing Table   ---> Verifies local SPF output installed into RIB/FIB
If an OSPF router lacks a route, an operator inspects the LSDB (show ip ospf database). If the LSA exists in the LSDB but the route is not in the RIB, the issue is not network propagation; it is a local SPF calculation failure, an administrative distance override, or a local interface metric configuration.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Modern hybrids: Babel and EIGRP
Modern interior routing protocols address the limitations of classic distance-vector protocols without requiring the memory footprint of full link-state databases.

Babel (RFC 8966) and the feasibility condition
Babel is a distance-vector protocol optimized for wireless mesh and wired networks. It uses explicit sequence numbers to prevent routing loops and count-to-infinity without imposing a low hop limit.
Babel enforces a feasibility condition in the same family as EIGRP’s: a router accepts a route update from a neighbor only if it carries a newer sequence number for that source, or the same sequence number with a metric strictly less than the receiving router’s feasibility distance (the best metric it has advertised for that source and sequence number). If a neighbor advertises a metric equal to or higher than the feasibility distance, the receiver rejects it, preventing metric updates from feeding back into a loop.


EIGRP and DUAL
Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) is a proprietary protocol developed by Cisco that incorporates distance-vector and link-state characteristics. EIGRP uses the Diffusing Update Algorithm (DUAL) to guarantee loop-free operations at every instant. EIGRP routers store backup routes (feasible successors) reported by neighbors if those neighbors satisfy the feasibility condition. If a primary route fails and a feasible successor exists, EIGRP installs the backup route immediately without waiting for global recomputation or timer expirations.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
section: Lab: Simulating DV convergence, SPF, and loop mechanics
text:
Lab: Simulating DV convergence, SPF, and loop mechanics
The simulation script dvls.py demonstrates the mathematical mechanics of distance-vector updates, SPF calculation, and count-to-infinity behavior on a shared network topology.

Simulation setup
The test graph consists of five routers (A, B, C, D, E) with weighted links:
       (1)       (1)       (1)
  [A] ------ [B] ------ [C] ------ [D]
   |                                |
   +-------------- [E] -------------+
         (4)               (1)
The script runs four test cases: 1. Distance-vector convergence from a cold start targeting destination D. 2. Link-state (Dijkstra) shortest path calculation from each node targeting D. 3. Link failure and count-to-infinity when destination D becomes disconnected, comparing plain DV, split horizon, and poison reverse. 4. Triangle topology failure where split horizon and poison reverse fail to prevent count-to-infinity.
The Python implementation in dvls.py uses synchronous rounds: every router reads updates from the previous round simultaneously and publishes new metrics for the next round. Real-world RIP operates asynchronously with independent timers, which introduces variable delays between updates.
The executable script dvls.py contains the following code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Distance-vector vs link-state on the same five-router graph.

Run: python3 dvls.py
Prints DV rounds to convergence, a count-to-infinity run, the effect of
split horizon / poison reverse, and the link-state (Dijkstra) answer.
"""
import heapq

INF = 16  # RIP's "infinity"

LINKS = {("A", "B"): 1, ("B", "C"): 1, ("C", "D"): 1,
         ("A", "E"): 4, ("E", "D"): 1}


def neighbours(links):
    nbr = {}
    for (u, v), c in links.items():
        nbr.setdefault(u, {})[v] = c
        nbr.setdefault(v, {})[u] = c
    return nbr


def dv_converge(links, dest, tables=None, mode="plain", max_rounds=40,
                trace=False):
    """Synchronous Bellman-Ford rounds toward a single destination.

    tables: {router: (metric, next_hop)}; mode: plain | split | poison.
    Returns (rounds, tables, history)."""
    nbr = neighbours(links)
    routers = sorted(nbr)
    if tables is None:
        tables = {r: (0, r) if r == dest else (INF, None) for r in routers}
    history = []
    for rnd in range(1, max_rounds + 1):
        # each router advertises its metric to each neighbour
        adverts = {}
        for r in routers:
            m, nh = tables[r]
            for n in nbr[r]:
                if nh == n and r != dest:
                    if mode == "split":
                        continue            # say nothing back toward next hop
                    if mode == "poison":
                        adverts.setdefault(n, {})[r] = INF
                        continue
                adverts.setdefault(n, {})[r] = m
        new = {}
        for r in routers:
            if r == dest:
                new[r] = (0, r)
                continue
            best = (INF, None)
            for n, m in adverts.get(r, {}).items():
                cand = min(INF, m + nbr[r][n])
                if cand < best[0]:
                    best = (cand, n)
            new[r] = best
        history.append(new)
        if trace:
            row = "  ".join(f"{r}={new[r][0]:>2}/{new[r][1] or '-'}"
                            for r in routers)
            print(f"  round {rnd:>2}: {row}")
        if new == tables:
            return rnd, new, history
        tables = new
    return max_rounds, tables, history


def dijkstra(links, src):
    nbr = neighbours(links)
    dist, first = {src: 0}, {src: src}
    pq = [(0, src, src)]
    while pq:
        d, u, fh = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if d > dist.get(u, INF * 99):
            continue
        for v, c in nbr[u].items():
            nd = d + c
            if nd < dist.get(v, INF * 99):
                dist[v] = nd
                first[v] = v if u == src else fh
                heapq.heappush(pq, (nd, v, first[v]))
    return dist, first


def main():
    print("== 1. DV from cold start toward D ==")
    rounds, tables, _ = dv_converge(LINKS, "D", trace=True)
    print(f"  converged after {rounds} rounds (last round = no change)")

    print("\n== 2. Link-state: every router runs SPF on the same map ==")
    for r in "ABCE":
        dist, first = dijkstra(LINKS, r)
        print(f"  SPF at {r}: D cost {dist['D']} via {first['D']}")

    # Count to infinity: C-D and E-D both fail, so D is unreachable.
    print("\n== 3. Count to infinity: D disappears (C-D and E-D fail) ==")
    broken = {k: v for k, v in LINKS.items() if "D" not in k}
    # D is gone; keep its old table entries as a stale starting point
    start = {r: tables[r] for r in "ABCE"}
    for mode in ("plain", "split", "poison"):
        rounds, final, hist = dv_converge(
            broken, "D", tables=dict(start), mode=mode)
        peak = [h["A"][0] for h in hist]
        print(f"  mode={mode:<6} rounds={rounds:>2}  "
              f"A's metric per round: {peak}")

    # Split horizon fails with a triangle loop (three routers).
    print("\n== 4. Where split horizon is not enough: a triangle ==")
    tri = {("X", "Y"): 1, ("Y", "Z"): 1, ("X", "Z"): 1, ("Z", "T"): 1}
    _, t0, _ = dv_converge(tri, "T")
    tri_broken = {k: v for k, v in tri.items() if k != ("Z", "T")}
    t0 = {r: t0[r] for r in "XYZ"}
    # Z notices first: only Z's own route is invalidated before the next round
    t0["Z"] = (INF, None)
    for mode in ("split", "poison"):
        rounds, final, hist = dv_converge(
            tri_broken, "T", tables=dict(t0), mode=mode)
        print(f"  mode={mode:<6} rounds={rounds:>2}  "
              f"Z's metric per round: {[h['Z'][0] for h in hist]}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Executing python3 dvls.py generates the following output:
== 1. DV from cold start toward D ==
  round  1: A=16/-  B=16/-  C= 1/D  D= 0/D  E= 1/D
  round  2: A= 5/E  B= 2/C  C= 1/D  D= 0/D  E= 1/D
  round  3: A= 3/B  B= 2/C  C= 1/D  D= 0/D  E= 1/D
  round  4: A= 3/B  B= 2/C  C= 1/D  D= 0/D  E= 1/D
  converged after 4 rounds (last round = no change)

== 2. Link-state: every router runs SPF on the same map ==
  SPF at A: D cost 3 via B
  SPF at B: D cost 2 via C
  SPF at C: D cost 1 via D
  SPF at E: D cost 1 via D

== 3. Count to infinity: D disappears (C-D and E-D fail) ==
  mode=plain  rounds=16  A's metric per round: [3, 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 13, 13, 15, 15, 16, 16]
  mode=split  rounds= 5  A's metric per round: [3, 3, 16, 16, 16]
  mode=poison rounds= 5  A's metric per round: [3, 3, 16, 16, 16]

== 4. Where split horizon is not enough: a triangle ==
  mode=split  rounds=15  Z's metric per round: [16, 4, 16, 16, 7, 16, 16, 10, 16, 16, 13, 16, 16, 16, 16]
  mode=poison rounds=15  Z's metric per round: [16, 4, 16, 16, 7, 16, 16, 10, 16, 16, 13, 16, 16, 16, 16]


Analysis of simulation output

Section 1: Good news travels fast
In Round 1, only direct neighbors of D (C and E) have non-infinite metrics (cost 1). Node A has no direct connection to D.
In Round 2, A receives advertisements from B (metric 16) and E (metric 1 via D). Node A calculates its cost via E as 1 + 4 = 5 and updates its entry to 5/E.
In Round 3, B publishes its updated metric of 2 (learned from C in Round 2). Node A evaluates B’s offering: 2 + 1 = 3. Because 3 is less than 5, A switches its next hop from E to B.
Round 4 produces identical routing state across all nodes, confirming convergence after 4 rounds.


Section 2: Link-state single-pass calculation
Section 2 demonstrates how Dijkstra’s algorithm reaches the same optimal next-hop decisions in a single computation locally per router. Each router processes the global map, identifying that A reaches D via B at cost 3, B via C at cost 2, and C/E via D directly at cost 1.


Section 3: Bad news travels slowly
When links C-D and E-D fail simultaneously, destination D becomes unreachable.
In plain mode, A’s metric step-up output displays classic count-to-infinity:
[3, 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 9, 9, 11, 11, 13, 13, 15, 15, 16, 16]
Node A increments its metric by 2 every two rounds (3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 16) because neighbors keep re-advertising the stale route to each other, each time one link’s cost higher. With nothing but RIP’s 30-second periodic updates, 16 rounds is about 8 minutes. Triggered updates shorten that a lot in practice, but the loop still exists while the metrics climb.
In split and poison modes on this linear/tree topology, split horizon and poison reverse prevent B from advertising its route back to C. The stale route is cleared after round 3, reaching metric 16 by round 5.


Section 4: Breakdown on three-node triangle loops
Section 4 models a triangle topology X-Y-Z attached to destination T via Z. When link Z-T breaks, Z invalidates its direct route (Z metric = 16).
Both split and poison modes fail to prevent count-to-infinity:
Z's metric per round: [16, 4, 16, 16, 7, 16, 16, 10, 16, 16, 13, 16, 16, 16, 16]
Node Z sets its metric to 16 in round 1. In round 2, Z receives an update from X, which is advertising a route to T at cost 3 (learned from Y). Split horizon allows X to advertise this route to Z because X learned it from Y, not Z. Z adopts X as its next hop at cost 3 + 1 = 4.
In later rounds the stale route keeps coming back around the triangle: Z sees 4, then 7, then 10, then 13, each time three hops’ worth higher, until every router reaches 16 after 15 rounds. Split horizon fails because reachability information recirculated through a third node, disguising the original source of the path.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Case
This is an illustrative scenario, not a real named incident.
A utility company operated a regional telemetry network linking sub-stations over leased serial circuits. The operator deployed RIPv2 across 45 small routers because the hardware lacked the memory required for OSPF databases.
During a maintenance window, a fiber cut isolated a remote branch router hosting a master control server. Immediately following the outage, network operators noticed that CPU usage spiked across three intermediate routers. Furthermore, traceroute commands directed to the isolated master server IP address showed packets bouncing in an infinite loop between two core aggregation nodes (core-01 and core-02).
The operators assumed split horizon was misconfigured. However, checking show ip rip status confirmed that split-horizon was active on all serial interfaces.
Analyzing the topology revealed that core-01, core-02, and a backup distribution node formed a triangular ring. When the master server link failed, core-01 suppressed updates back to core-02, but core-02 accepted a path advertised by the distribution node. The metric incremented step-by-step from 3 to 16 over a four-minute period. During those four minutes, telemetry control traffic intended for other reachable sub-stations experienced packet drops due to interface queue saturation caused by the circulating loop packets.
The engineering team replaced RIPv2 with OSPF. Following the migration, repeating the fiber cut test produced LSA flooding, a local SPF run on every router, and the route withdrawn everywhere within seconds, with no counting phase at all. The lesson they wrote down was not “RIP is bad” but “our topology has rings, and split horizon only protects lines”.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Trap
Believing that split horizon and poison reverse eliminate distance-vector loops. They only stop a router from feeding a route straight back to the neighbor it came from, which fixes two-router loops and tree-shaped topologies. Any ring of three or more routers can still count to infinity, exactly as section 4 of the lab shows. Hold-down timers and triggered updates make the window shorter. They do not close it. Only extra information closes it: a full path (path-vector), sequence numbers with a feasibility condition (Babel, EIGRP), or a full map (link-state).
The second trap is the opposite: assuming link-state can never loop. While the LSDBs are being re-synchronized after a change, two routers can briefly run SPF on different databases and point at each other. These microloops last milliseconds to a few hundred milliseconds, and they are the reason fast-reroute features exist.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Boring rule
Run a link-state IGP (OSPF or IS-IS) inside anything with a ring in it. Use distance-vector only where the topology is a tree or the devices cannot do better, and then turn on split horizon with poison reverse and triggered updates. Use BGP between administrative domains. Whatever you run, know how many rounds or seconds “bad news” takes on your topology before an outage teaches you.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Try this

Change INF = 16 to INF = 64 and rerun section 3 in plain mode. Predict the number of rounds first. This is why RIP chose a small infinity.
Add a link ("B", "E"): 1 to LINKS and rerun sections 1 and 2. Does DV still agree with SPF? How many rounds does DV need now?
Add a fourth router W to the triangle in section 4, linked to X and Y. Does Z’s metric climb in steps of 3 or 4? Why?
Implement hold-down: once a router’s metric goes to INF, ignore every advertisement for that destination for three rounds. Rerun section 4 and compare the round count and the highest stale metric.
Implement a Babel-style feasibility condition: keep a per-router feasibility distance and reject any advertisement whose metric is not strictly lower. Show that section 4 no longer counts up.

title: Dynamic Routing Ideas: Distance-Vector vs Link-State
text:
Verification

The lab ran on Linux 6.12.94+ (a KVM guest) with Python 3.13.5, as an unprivileged user with no sudo and no extra packages, on 2026-11-13. It is pure Python and needs no network.
The listing is the exact file that was run, and the output is pasted unedited.
The model is deliberately simplified: synchronous rounds, one destination, link cost as the metric, no timers. Real RIP is asynchronous and timer-driven, so absolute timings differ. The shape of each result (fast good news, slow bad news, split horizon failing on a triangle) is what carries over.
Not run here: RIP, OSPF, IS-IS or Babel daemons (no FRR on the box, no installs). The protocol details above come from the RFCs listed below.

title: OSPF Basics
text:
OSPF Basics
OSPF is a link-state IGP: routers flood topology information within an area, run SPF, and install routes. This chapter builds a single-area triangle on FRR in Containerlab—the highest-ROI dynamic routing lab in the book.

title: OSPF Basics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Contrast link-state vs distance-vector at a model level

Bring up OSPF adjacencies on FRR and read neighbor states

Advertise loopbacks and LANs into OSPF

Predict reconvergence when a link costs out or dies

Verify RIB/FIB and traceroute paths

title: OSPF Basics
text:
Concepts

Distance-vector vs link-state




Distance-vector (idea)
Link-state (OSPF)




What is shared
Vectors to prefixes
Topology (LSAs)


Loop risk
Needs careful rules
SPF on common map


Visibility
Partial
Area-wide topology view


Example
Classic RIP
OSPF, IS-IS





OSPF adjacency state machine (short)
Down → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full
On point-to-point transit links, expect Full with the other router. On a broadcast LAN, two routers that are neither DR nor BDR normally remain at 2-Way with each other. Unexpected states can indicate MTU, authentication, layer-2, or network type problems; see OSPF Adjacencies and Database Troubleshooting.


Areas
Single-area (0) is enough here. Multi-area adds ABR summarization later in your journey; do not rush.


Cost
OSPF picks lowest cost path. Cost often derives from reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth. In FRR you can set ip ospf cost on interfaces for drills.


Network types (awareness)
Point-to-point vs broadcast affects adjacency count and DR/BDR. P2P links in labs are simple; Ethernet multipoint may elect DR.

section: Method A: The Fast Netlab Workflow (Recommended)
text:
Method A: The Fast Netlab Workflow (Recommended)
Using Netlab (with provider: clab), you declare only the protocol intent and node interconnections. Netlab automatically plans IP subnets, allocates loopbacks, writes the FRR configurations, and stands up the Containerlab environment:
# topology.yml
---
provider: clab
defaults.device: frr
module: [ ospf ]

nodes:
  r1:
  r2:
  r3:
  h1:
    device: linux
  h2:
    device: linux

links:
  - r1:
    r2:
  - r2:
    r3:
  - r3:
    r1:
  - h1:
    r1:
  - h2:
    r2:

validate:
  ospf_neighbors:
    description: "Verify all routers reach Full OSPF adjacency with 2 neighbors"
    nodes: [ r1, r2, r3 ]
    plugin: ospf_neighbor(count=2, state='Full')
  end_to_end_ping:
    description: "Verify end-to-end connectivity between endpoints h1 and h2"
    nodes: [ h1 ]
    exec:
      ping_h2: ping -c 3 10.0.0.5

Deploy and Validate with Netlab
# Compile configurations and bring up the Containerlab environment
netlab up

# Run automated OSPF adjacency and ping assertions
netlab validate

# Connect to any router CLI directly without memorizing container IDs
netlab connect r1

section: Method B: Raw Containerlab & Manual FRR Configurations
text:
Method B: Raw Containerlab & Manual FRR Configurations
If you are inspecting low-level container plumbing or deploying on a system without Python/Netlab, you can author the Containerlab topology and FRR configurations by hand.

Topology YAML (ospf-tri.clab.yml)
name: ospf-tri

topology:
  nodes:
    r1:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/r1:/etc/frr
    r2:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/r2:/etc/frr
    r3:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/r3:/etc/frr
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils
        - ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth1 && ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils
        - ip addr add 192.168.2.10/24 dev eth1 && ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 192.168.2.1

  links:
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth1", "r2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r2:eth2", "r3:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r3:eth2", "r1:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "r1:eth3"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "r2:eth3"]


FRR Daemons File (config/r1/daemons)
daemons file must enable:
zebra=yes
ospfd=yes


FRR OSPF Config (config/r1/frr.conf)
frr version 10.2.1
frr defaults traditional
hostname r1
!
interface lo
 ip address 1.1.1.1/32
 ip ospf area 0
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.0.12.1/24
 ip ospf area 0
!
interface eth2
 ip address 10.0.13.1/24
 ip ospf area 0
!
interface eth3
 ip address 192.168.1.1/24
 ip ospf area 0
!
router ospf
 ospf router-id 1.1.1.1
!
line vty
Advertise by putting interfaces in area 0 (common FRR style). Equivalent network statements exist; be consistent across nodes.
r2/r3: unique router-ids 2.2.2.2, 3.3.3.3; matching interface IPs; LANs in OSPF so remote LANs appear in RIB.


Deploy and Verify Manually
sudo containerlab deploy -t ospf-tri.clab.yml

docker exec clab-ospf-tri-r1 vtysh -c 'show ip ospf neighbor'

docker exec clab-ospf-tri-r1 vtysh -c 'show ip route'
docker exec clab-ospf-tri-r1 vtysh -c 'show ip ospf database'

docker exec clab-ospf-tri-h1 ping -c 3 192.168.2.10
docker exec clab-ospf-tri-h1 traceroute -n 192.168.2.10

Each router: 2 neighbors Full (triangle)

RIB contains remote LAN and loopbacks via OSPF

Path prefers lower cost sides



Neighbor not Full?

title: OSPF Adjacencies and Database Troubleshooting
text:
OSPF Adjacencies and Database Troubleshooting
An OSPF neighbor table is a sequence of clues, not a connectivity test. Diagnose the relationship in stages: can the routers exchange valid Hellos, should they form an adjacency, can they synchronize databases, and does the resulting route reach the forwarding table? This chapter uses OSPFv2 for concrete packet fields. OSPFv3 has different addressing and LSA details; verify its instance and interface configuration independently.

title: OSPF Adjacencies and Database Troubleshooting
text:
Packet and state vocabulary
OSPF runs directly over IP protocol 89, not TCP or UDP port 89. The five main OSPF packet types are Hello, Database Description (DD), Link State Request (LSR), Link State Update (LSU) and Link State Acknowledgment (LSAck). DD packets summarize database entries; requests ask for missing or newer LSAs; updates carry LSAs; acknowledgments confirm flooding. An LSA describes routing information inside an LSU, whereas an LSU is the packet carrying one or more LSAs.








State
What it tells you
What to investigate if unexpected




Down
No currently valid Hello from that neighbor
Link, addressing, OSPF enabled on interface, filtering, area and authentication


Attempt
On configured non-broadcast networks, attempting contact
Neighbor configuration and unicast reachability


Init
A valid Hello arrived, but the local router ID is absent from the neighbor’s Hello list
One-way delivery, filtering, multicast or peer processing


2-Way
Each router has seen itself in the other’s Hello
On broadcast networks, check DR/BDR roles before declaring a fault


ExStart
Neighbors negotiate DD exchange roles and sequence
MTU, duplicate router IDs, DD delivery or implementation logs


Exchange
DD summaries are being exchanged
DD retransmissions, MTU, sequence errors and packet loss


Loading
Requested LSAs are being obtained
LSR/LSU/LSAck loss, retransmission and database errors


Full
The adjacency’s initial database synchronization is complete
Still verify the specific LSA, route, forwarding entry and reverse path



The states may be too brief to observe on a healthy link; transitions can also move backward after an event. Full does not mean all traffic can pass, and it does not mean databases across different areas are identical. A router synchronizes the appropriate scoped database with its adjacent neighbor.

title: OSPF Adjacencies and Database Troubleshooting
text:
Point-to-point and broadcast behavior
On a point-to-point link, the two routers normally form a full adjacency. On a broadcast LAN, the designated router (DR) and backup designated router (BDR) reduce the number of full adjacencies. Two ordinary routers that are neither DR nor BDR normally stay at 2-Way with one another while each forms Full with the DR and BDR. Check the interface’s actual network type and roles before resetting a healthy 2-Way neighbor.
For DR/BDR election, a router with interface priority zero is ineligible; otherwise priority and then router ID influence selection. Election is not ordinarily preemptive: a newly arrived router with a higher priority does not automatically replace the current DR. A mismatch in intended network types can produce unexpected election, neighbor and flooding behavior; inspect both ends rather than assuming every Ethernet interface must be broadcast.

title: OSPF Adjacencies and Database Troubleshooting
text:
Evidence before changes
Collect the following from both sides with timestamps:

Interface state, IP address and prefix, VLAN or link membership, physical MTU, OSPF network type, area, timers, authentication and router ID.
Neighbor state, dead timer, DR/BDR role where applicable, transition counts, retransmissions and relevant logs. Look for duplicate router IDs within the OSPF routing domain.
Packet captures or counters in both directions. Verify Hello arrival and contents before assuming the configuration is active. A capture on one interface proves observation at that point, not acceptance by the protocol process.
For an established adjacency, inspect the LSA by type, link-state ID and advertising router; compare age and sequence where useful. Then inspect OSPF’s calculated route, the device’s selected RIB route and the actual FIB entry.

Area ID, Hello/dead intervals, authentication and relevant area options must be compatible for OSPFv2 Hellos to be accepted. Other checks depend on network type and implementation. If the neighbor does not appear, a mismatch can cause the receiver to discard a Hello before a neighbor entry is created. A passive interface may advertise its connected network while intentionally suppressing neighbor formation; confirm intent before changing it.
OSPFv2 DD packets advertise interface MTU. A receiver rejects a DD packet that advertises a datagram size larger than it can accept without fragmentation. This can leave an adjacency repeatedly negotiating or exchanging. Compare the actual link and tunnel MTUs, not just an OSPF display; repairing inconsistent MTUs is preferable to hiding the check because a synchronized control plane does not guarantee large data packets will work. MTU is one hypothesis, not the only explanation for ExStart or Exchange.

title: OSPF Adjacencies and Database Troubleshooting
section: A route can fail after Full
text:
A route can fail after Full
If an expected prefix is missing, identify its origin and area, then follow evidence:

No originating LSA: check the source interface, OSPF enablement, passive setting, redistribution policy and originator’s database. Passive suppresses Hellos; it does not inherently suppress advertisement of that connected network.
LSA present, no OSPF route: check LSA scope, area connectivity, reachability of the advertising router or forwarding address, route type and the calculation’s eligibility rules.
OSPF route exists but not selected: compare competing routes to the same prefix, protocol preferences and policy. Next-hop resolution matters.
Selected RIB route but forwarding fails: inspect FIB programming, outgoing link, neighbor resolution, ACLs, MTU and return path. A ping to a loopback and an application flow may take different policy or ECMP paths.

In OSPFv2, router and network LSAs describe topology within an area; ABRs advertise inter-area reachability; external LSAs describe imported routes subject to area type and flooding scope. Distinguish an LSA’s existence from its eligibility to produce a route. For external route metrics, forwarding addresses and redistribution feedback, use Redistribution Design.

title: OSPF Adjacencies and Database Troubleshooting
text:
Failure drills
Start from OSPF in One Area. Record neighbor states and loopback routes on each router. Perform one fault at a time in the isolated lab; platform syntax and exact logs vary. These exercises are test procedures, not a claim that every platform displays the same state.

Hello acceptance: change the OSPF area on one end of one link. Observe the affected neighbor and Hellos on both sides. Restore the area and verify the adjacency and routes return; other triangle paths may keep the destination reachable throughout.
One-way observation: selectively filter OSPF packets in one direction on one transit link. Compare both captures and neighbor timers. Depending on timing and implementation, one side can briefly show Init or other transitions before a timeout. Remove the filter and verify recovery. Do not filter unrelated production control traffic.
DD MTU: use a dedicated point-to-point link and create a documented MTU mismatch between its ends. Compare the DD MTU fields and logs; the smaller side can reject a DD advertising an excessive MTU. Confirm whether a session reset is needed on your platform, restore matching MTUs and verify both adjacency and a suitably sized data packet.
Healthy 2-Way: connect at least three routers to one broadcast segment, ensure distinct IDs and eligible DR/BDR priorities, and identify the DR/BDR. To observe two ordinary routers in 2-Way with each other and still have both a DR and a BDR, use at least four routers with eligible priorities. Verify Full toward the DR and BDR, then restore the topology.
Full but missing route: keep the transit adjacency intact and remove OSPF advertisement of a test loopback. Verify the adjacency stays Full while the originating LSA and route change. Restore the advertisement and validate the route and forwarding path.

For every drill document the hypothesis, expected state, observations on both ends, the repair and the restored baseline. Do not use neighbor state alone to claim forwarding success.
References: OSPFv2, RFC 2328, OSPF terminology update, RFC 9454, and OSPFv3, RFC 5340.

title: BGP Basics
text:
BGP Basics
BGP is the inter-domain workhorse and also appears inside modern DC fabrics. This chapter stays vendor-agnostic and free-image-only: eBGP and iBGP ideas, sessions, advertisements, and path selection at a practitioner level—implemented with FRR.

title: BGP Basics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain ASNs, eBGP vs iBGP roles

Bring up a BGP session on FRR to Established

Advertise a prefix and see it on the peer

Apply the path selection process at a high level

Break a session and observe withdrawal

text:
Concepts

Autonomous systems
An AS is a policy domain with an ASN. Labs use private ASNs:



Range
Notes




64512–65534
16-bit private


4200000000+
32-bit private space (use docs for exact ranges)



Example: AS65001 and AS65002 as “two sites” or “customer and ISP.”


eBGP vs iBGP









eBGP
iBGP




Between
Different ASNs
Same ASN


Typical TTL
1 (direct)
multi-hop ok with care


Default next-hop
Peer address
Needs next-hop-self often for reachability


Scale
Edge policy
Route reflection / confed for large iBGP





Session state
Idle → Connect → Active → OpenSent → OpenConfirm → Established
Only Established exchanges routes.


Path selection overview
BGP is policy-heavy. Simplified order of preference ideas:

Prefer higher local preference (inbound influence)

Prefer shorter AS path

Origin, MED, eBGP over iBGP, IGP metric to next hop, router-id, etc.

You will not memorize every tie-breaker today—know that policy beats pure shortest path.


NLRI and attributes
Routes carry attributes (AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, MED, communities…). Filters rewrite attributes; that is policy.

text:
Lab A: two AS eBGP
h1--r1 (AS65001) -------- r2 (AS65002)--h2

Topology

title: Policy & Filters
text:
Policy & Filters
Routing without policy is a demo; routing with policy is operations. This chapter covers prefix filters, distribute ideas, route-maps as a pattern, and loop-prevention instincts using FRR—still free and vendor-agnostic.

title: Policy & Filters
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Write prefix-lists that match intended space only

Apply import/export filters on BGP neighbors

Use route-map style logic (match → set → permit/deny)

Predict leaks and loops from redistribution mistakes

Build a lab that rejects unauthorized prefixes

title: Policy & Filters
text:
Why policy exists







Goal
Mechanism ideas




Do not accept bogons / your own space from customers
Inbound prefix filter


Do not advertise internal-only nets to Internet
Outbound filter


Prefer one uplink
local-pref on import


De-prefer backup path
AS-path prepend on export


Redistribute without feedback loops
Tags, filters, distance

title: Policy & Filters
text:
Prefix lists (FRR)
ip prefix-list OWN-NETS seq 10 permit 192.168.1.0/24
ip prefix-list OWN-NETS seq 20 permit 1.1.1.1/32
ip prefix-list OWN-NETS seq 30 deny any
ip prefix-list CUST-ALLOW seq 10 permit 198.51.100.0/24
ip prefix-list CUST-ALLOW seq 20 deny any
Order matters: first match wins. Always know your implicit/default at the end.

title: Policy & Filters
text:
Route-maps as idea
Regardless of vendor syntax, the pattern is:
if match prefix-list X:
  set local-preference 200
  permit
else deny
FRR example:
route-map FROM-CUST permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list CUST-ALLOW
 set local-preference 200
route-map FROM-CUST deny 99
!
route-map TO-CUST permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list OWN-NETS
Attach:
router bgp 65002
 neighbor 10.0.0.1 route-map FROM-CUST in
 neighbor 10.0.0.1 route-map TO-CUST out

title: Policy & Filters
text:
Lab: filter unauthorized prefixes
Extend eBGP lab: r2 (ISP) should only accept 192.168.1.0/24 from r1 (customer), not a hijack prefix.

Customer r1 advertises extra junk
address-family ipv4 unicast
 network 192.168.1.0/24
 network 203.0.113.0/24


ISP r2 policy

ip prefix-list CUST-R1 seq 10 deny any
!
route-map FROM-R1 permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list CUST-R1
route-map FROM-R1 deny 20
!
router bgp 65002
 neighbor 10.0.0.1 route-map FROM-R1 in


Predict

ISP installs 192.168.1.0/24

203.0.113.0/24 is rejected

show bgp on r2 lacks the junk



Observe
docker exec clab-bgp-ebgp-r2 vtysh -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast'

docker exec clab-bgp-ebgp-r1 vtysh -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast neighbors 10.0.0.2 advertised-routes'


Harden
Return to explicit export on customer too—only advertise owned space.
route-map EXPORT-OWN permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list OWN-NETS
!
neighbor 10.0.0.2 route-map EXPORT-OWN out
Remove no bgp ebgp-requires-policy when policies are in place if you want FRR to enforce the discipline.

Local-pref steer drill
Two ISPs: isp1 and isp2; customer prefers isp1 for inbound to customer… actually:

Local pref (on customer) influences outbound exit from customer AS

AS prepend / MED / communities influence how others send inbound


Outbound preference (customer)

 set local-preference 300
route-map PREFER-ISP2 permit 10

!
neighbor <isp1> route-map PREFER-ISP1 in
neighbor <isp2> route-map PREFER-ISP2 in
Predict: traffic leaves via isp1 when both paths exist.

vtysh -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast'

title: Policy & Filters
text:
Redistribution loop awareness
Redistributing OSPF ↔︎ BGP (or static ↔︎ OSPF) without filters can:

Re-inject prefixes with changed metrics

Create loops or suboptimal paths

Explode tables

Rules of thumb:

Redistribute on purpose, on as few points as possible

Tag routes; filter on tags

Never blindly mutual redistribute two IGPs

Prefer BGP for policy domains, IGP for underlay topology


Example static→OSPF with filter (sketch)
ip prefix-list STATICS seq 5 permit 192.168.9.0/24
route-map REDIST-STATIC permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list STATICS
!
router ospf
 redistribute static route-map REDIST-STATIC

title: Policy & Filters
section: ACL-style packet filters vs routing policy
text:
ACL-style packet filters vs routing policy
Do not confuse:



Routing policy
Packet filter




Which routes enter RIB
Which packets pass


BGP/OSPF route-maps
nftables/iptables/ACLs


Control plane
Data plane



Both appear in hardening. A permit route does not mean packets are allowed through a firewall mid-path.

title: Policy & Filters
text:
Distribute-list / filter-list ideas
Older or alternate forms filter by ACL or AS-path lists:
bgp as-path access-list 1 permit _65001$
neighbor x filter-list 1 in
Same intent: accept only what policy allows.

title: Policy & Filters
text:
Failure drills

Drill 1 — over-broad permit any
Export permit any to a lab “ISP.”
Observe: internal lab nets leave the AS.
Fix: prefix-list OWN only.
Harden: default-deny export mindset.


Drill 2 — accidental deny all
Route-map deny first line matches everything.
Symptom: Established but zero prefixes.
Debug: show bgp neighbors ... routes / policy counters if available; simplify map.


Drill 3 — next-hop-self missing (iBGP)
Learned eBGP route reflected iBGP with remote next hop unreachable.
Symptom: BGP has path; FIB lacks usable route.
Fix: next-hop-self or IGP reachability to next hop.

title: Redistribution Design and Route Provenance
text:
Redistribution Design and Route Provenance
Redistribution creates a new routing advertisement from a route learned through another source. It is useful during migrations and at boundaries between routing domains, but a second boundary can feed the advertisement back into the domain where it began. The result may be a misleading path, persistent black hole, or forwarding loop even while all routing adjacencies are healthy.
Start with the redistribution and route-tag workbook lab, which shows a single OSPF–BGP boundary. This chapter examines what changes when boundaries are redundant. Commands, redistribution eligibility and default administrative distances differ across implementations; inspect the actual platform rather than assuming a universal behavior.

title: Redistribution Design and Route Provenance
text:
Follow a route across boundaries
Imagine domain A and domain B connected by two boundary routers, X and Y. A originates prefix P. X imports P from A into B. Y learns that B advertisement and could import it back into A. A path can return with a new protocol identity and attributes even though its destination prefix is unchanged. Protocol-local loop prevention, such as BGP AS-path checks, cannot by itself prevent every loop involving a different routing protocol. Multiple redistribution points also create transient risks while a failure is converging.
Before configuring anything, draw each permitted crossing and write its direction, eligible sources, exact prefixes, metric, provenance marker and return filter. Prefer one-way exchange or a controlled default route where the requirements permit. If both directions are required, use explicit prefix allowlists and provenance controls at every boundary. Define what happens if the preferred boundary fails; do not assume that changing a route preference fixes route feedback.

title: Redistribution Design and Route Provenance
text:
Route selection has separate stages

A routing protocol computes or selects its own candidate. OSPF, for example, compares OSPF path types and costs; BGP selects among its eligible paths using its own decision process.
The device’s route manager chooses among candidates for the same prefix and prefix length, commonly using a local protocol preference or administrative distance. Defaults and tie-breaking are implementation-specific.
The forwarding table performs longest-prefix matching on the packet destination. A /25 wins over a /24 for addresses it covers, even when the /24 has a more preferred protocol source.
Redistribution exports only routes eligible under the implementation’s rules and policy. A route in a protocol database is not necessarily selected in the main RIB, installed in the forwarding table, or eligible for export. Verify all three and the advertisement at the next router.

For example, A has native 198.51.100.0/24 and also receives a copy from B. If a boundary chooses the B-derived candidate and forwards back toward a neighbor whose next hop points to that boundary, traffic can loop. The exact outcome depends on the topology, next-hop resolution and platform selection rules; redistribution does not inevitably cause a loop.

title: Redistribution Design and Route Provenance
text:
Metrics and OSPF external routes
Metrics from different protocols do not have a universal exchange rate. A hop count of 3, an OSPF cost of 3 and a BGP MED of 3 are not equivalent measurements. Set an intentional seed metric and route type at the target boundary; test the result from multiple locations. Changing the metric can influence which exit a domain uses but does not prove a route is safe to re-export.
For OSPFv2 external routes to the same destination, intra-area and inter-area paths are preferred over external paths; type 1 external paths are preferred over type 2. Within type 1, compare the sum of internal cost to the ASBR or forwarding address and external cost. For type 2, the external metric is the primary cost; internal cost is considered when the relevant higher-priority criteria tie. Other selection details, including ASBR path preference and compatibility settings, can matter. These comparisons are within OSPF, before a platform compares a selected OSPF route with candidates from other protocols.
Consider two otherwise comparable external advertisements for the same prefix:










Exit
Internal cost X
External metric Y
E1 total X+Y
E2 primary Y




X
10
20
30
20


Y
30
10
40
10



If both are E1, X wins on total cost. If both are E2, Y wins on the lower external metric. If X advertises E1 and Y E2, X wins by path type despite Y’s lower displayed number. This example assumes all other applicable selection conditions are equal and the forwarding addresses are reachable.
An OSPF external LSA may specify a forwarding address. When it is nonzero, the router resolves that address through an eligible intra-area or inter-area path; it does not simply forward toward the advertising ASBR. An unreachable forwarding address can leave an LSA visible in the database without an installed usable external route. A zero forwarding address instead directs traffic toward the ASBR. Inspect the LSA, reachability, selected route and forwarding entry separately.

title: Redistribution Design and Route Provenance
section: Mark provenance and deny the return trip
text:
Mark provenance and deny the return trip
A route tag can record where an external route came from. It is policy metadata, not an automatic loop-prevention mechanism: every relevant boundary must match it and deny the inappropriate return crossing. OSPF external tags are carried in external LSAs, but a tag is not automatically an equivalent BGP community or a universally preserved end-to-end label. Check whether each platform can match, set, copy or translate the metadata at each protocol boundary. A device may discard it on export or summarization; a native route may not have the same tag field as an external route.
Example policy contract, expressed as intent rather than vendor syntax:









Crossing
Permit
Mark in destination
Deny before permit




A → B
Approved A-origin prefixes
provenance A, if B supports it
anything marked B


B → A
Approved B-origin prefixes
provenance B, if A supports it
anything marked A



Apply the contract at X and Y, in both directions. Match exact prefix and length ranges, and include explicit default-deny behavior according to the platform’s policy semantics. Test a permitted prefix, a more-specific not intended for export, a route with a return marker, an unmarked route, and the default route. If markers cannot survive a boundary, use other enforceable controls such as disjoint prefix ownership and explicit filtering; do not claim tagging alone protects the design. Allocate tags centrally and document reserved values.
Summarization complicates provenance: an aggregate may cover prefixes from different origins or remain advertised when a component disappears. Test partial and total component failure, discard routes, and whether the aggregate accurately reflects reachability. Never assume a summary’s tag represents all of its components without checking the platform’s behavior.

title: Redistribution Design and Route Provenance
text:
Failure exercises
Use the workbook topology as a baseline, then add a second independently configured boundary with separate transit links and equivalent policy. Keep both source domains isolated from production. Use your lab platform’s route database, RIB, FIB, policy counters and packet capture tools to gather evidence:

Originate an approved test prefix in A and confirm that both boundaries may advertise it into B with the intended metric and provenance. Verify the selected and alternate paths in B; multiple LSAs do not necessarily imply multiple installed next hops.
Verify that both B → A policies reject the returning A-origin route. Inspect the actual tag or translated attribute and the matching policy counter at each boundary; an absent returning route alone does not prove which control stopped it.
Withdraw A’s original prefix. Observe withdrawals in each protocol and verify that no stale or unmarked return copy sustains reachability. Record convergence times and loss, and restore the prefix.
Fail X’s transit link. Verify that traffic reaches the destination through Y and that the reverse path works. Restore X, observe reconvergence, and compare forwarding with the pre-failure baseline.
In the isolated lab only, remove Y’s return filter. Introduce a controlled route that would be eligible for return, inspect the resulting advertisements and next hops, then restore the filter. Whether a loop actually forms depends on route preference and platform export behavior; do not infer a loop solely from duplicate advertisements.
Test an unapproved more-specific and a default route. Neither should cross unless the written policy permits it. Check policy counters and advertisements on the receiving side, then remove the test routes.

For each test capture the prefix, source protocol, best path, next hop, route type, metric, tag, export decision, forwarding entry and return path. State the observed outcome rather than assuming a feature is working because the configuration is present.

title: Redistribution Design and Route Provenance
text:
Review and references
Why can a route exist in an OSPF database but not in the RIB? Why does a route tag need a corresponding deny rule? What changes if an aggregate remains present after the last reachable component fails? Explain why E1 versus E2 cannot be compared by looking only at their external metric numbers.
References: OSPFv2, RFC 2328, particularly external route calculation and external LSAs; FRR OSPF redistribution; and FRR BGP redistribution. Consult the exact version and platform used in your lab for commands and defaults.

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
BFD — Fast Failure Detection
Routing protocols are good at choosing paths and bad at noticing that a path died. When the failure is not a local link-down — a switch in the middle, a provider handoff, a hung line card, a VM whose host froze — BGP waits for its hold timer and OSPF for its dead interval. That is minutes of blackholed traffic with every session looking healthy. Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is the boring fix: a tiny, protocol-independent hello that proves the forwarding path works and tells its clients (BGP, OSPF, static routes) within a second when it does not. This chapter runs the failure first without BFD, then with it, on two FRR routers behind a Linux bridge — and measures both.

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain why carrier loss on one side does not reach the other side through a switch

Predict BGP failure detection time from keepalive/hold timers (and why it is a range)

Describe BFD control packets, the session states, and the detection-time formula

Enable BFD for an FRR BGP neighbor with a profile and verify the negotiated timers

Show that the slower side wins timer negotiation

Attach BFD to a static route so it is withdrawn when the next hop dies

Choose timers that do not turn CPU hiccups into routing flaps

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Why carrier is not enough
           r1-eth1                        r2-eth1
 r1 (AS65001) ──────── sw (bridge) ──────── r2 (AS65002) ── h2
 10.0.12.1/24        sw-r1      sw-r2       10.0.12.2/24     203.0.113.10/24
                                  ✖
                     failure here: r2 sees NO-CARRIER,
                     r1's port to the switch stays UP
Direct cable: either end losing light usually drops the link at both ends, and routing reacts to the interface event in milliseconds. Through a switch, a media converter, a provider’s L2 service, or a virtual switch, each side only sees its own port. r2 notices instantly and tears its session down; r1 still has carrier, still has an Established BGP session, and still forwards toward a next hop that will never answer.








Mechanism
Default (FRR “traditional”)
Detects




Local carrier
Immediate
Only your link


BGP hold timer
keepalive 60 s, hold 180 s
Peer silent for hold time


OSPF dead interval
hello 10 s, dead 40 s
Neighbor silent for dead interval


BFD (async)
300 ms × 3 = 900 ms
Forwarding path silent for detect time



Tuning BGP to keepalive 3 / hold 9 helps, but it puts liveness inside a TCP session handled by a busy control-plane process, it is per-protocol, and you still get several seconds. BFD exists so that every protocol can share one cheap, sub-second liveness check.

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Concepts — BFD in one page
What it is. RFC 5880 defines BFD; RFC 5881 maps it onto single-hop IPv4/IPv6 (UDP destination port 3784, sent with TTL/hop-limit 255 and checked on receipt so only a directly connected peer can inject packets); RFC 5883 covers multihop sessions (UDP 4784, e.g., between loopbacks); RFC 5882 describes how clients such as BGP and OSPF should react.
Asynchronous mode. Both sides send control packets periodically. Each packet carries the sender’s My Discriminator and the receiver’s Your Discriminator (session IDs), the state, a diagnostic code, and three timer values: Desired Min TX, Required Min RX, and Detect Mult.
States. AdminDown → Down → Init → Up. A three-way handshake brings a session up; while not Up, packets are sent at most once per second (slow start), so a flapping peer cannot generate a burst.
Timer negotiation — the slower side wins.
r1 transmit interval = max(r1 Desired Min TX, r2 Required Min RX)
r1 detection time    = r2 Detect Mult × max(r1 Required Min RX, r2 Desired Min TX)
Each side declares what it wants to send and what it can receive; nobody is forced to receive faster than it said. Transmit times are jittered (75–100% of the interval) so sessions do not synchronize.
Diagnostics. When a session goes down the reason is in the packet and in show bfd peer: control detection time expired (no packets in time — the classic failure), neighbor signaled session down, administratively down (the peer disabled it on purpose — RFC 5882 says clients should not treat this as a path failure), and others.
Echo mode (optional) sends packets that the peer loops back in its forwarding plane, testing the data path rather than the peer’s BFD process. Single-hop only. In FRR it works only when the peer is also FRR, unless you have hardware-offloaded BFD.
Clients. BFD itself changes nothing in the RIB. A client registers interest in a peer; when BFD declares it Down, the client acts — BGP closes the session and withdraws routes, OSPF drops the adjacency, a static route is removed. Several clients share one session to the same peer.
