title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Lab build (Linux namespaces + FRR)
This lab needs no container images: four network namespaces, veth pairs, a Linux bridge as the switch, and one FRR instance per router namespace using FRR’s pathspace option (-N), which gives each instance its own sockets and PID files under /var/run/frr/<name>/ and its own vtysh -N <name>. It was run on Debian 13 with the distro frr package (FRR 10.3), as root. Outputs below are copied from those runs; ages, IDs, and PIDs will differ on yours.
The same frr.conf snippets drop unchanged into the FRR containers used in other labs in this book — add bfdd=yes to their daemons file.
Install FRR and helpers (Debian/Ubuntu), and make sure the system-wide FRR service is not running (it would use the default pathspace, not these):
sudo apt-get install -y frr iputils-ping bc
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab.sh — r1 and r2 (FRR) behind a Linux-bridge "switch", h2 on r2's LAN
# usage: sudo ./lab.sh up | down
set -euo pipefail
FRR=/usr/lib/frr
DAEMONS="mgmtd zebra bgpd bfdd staticd"

up() {
  for ns in r1 r2 sw h2; do ip netns add "$ns"; ip -n "$ns" link set lo up; done

  # the switch: one bridge, two access ports
  ip -n sw link add br0 type bridge
  ip -n sw link set br0 up
  for r in r1 r2; do
    ip link add "$r-eth1" netns "$r" type veth peer name "sw-$r" netns sw
    ip -n sw link set "sw-$r" master br0 up
    ip -n "$r" link set "$r-eth1" up
  done
  ip -n r1 addr add 10.0.12.1/24 dev r1-eth1
  ip -n r2 addr add 10.0.12.2/24 dev r2-eth1

  # r2's customer LAN with one host
  ip link add r2-eth2 netns r2 type veth peer name h2-eth0 netns h2
  ip -n r2 addr add 203.0.113.1/24 dev r2-eth2
  ip -n h2 addr add 203.0.113.10/24 dev h2-eth0
  ip -n r2 link set r2-eth2 up
  ip -n h2 link set h2-eth0 up
  ip -n h2 route add default via 203.0.113.1
  ip netns exec r2 sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
  ip netns exec r1 sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

  for ns in r1 r2; do
    install -d -o frr -g frr "/var/run/frr/$ns" "/etc/frr/$ns"
    : > "/etc/frr/$ns/vtysh.conf"
    for d in $DAEMONS; do
      ip netns exec "$ns" "$FRR/$d" -d -N "$ns" -F traditional \
        -u frr -g frr --limit-fds 1024 >/dev/null 2>&1
    done
    vtysh -N "$ns" -f "$ns.conf" >/dev/null
  done
}

down() {
  for ns in r1 r2; do
    for d in $DAEMONS; do
      pidf="/var/run/frr/$ns/$d.pid"
      [ -f "$pidf" ] && kill "$(cat "$pidf")" 2>/dev/null || true
    done
  done
  for ns in r1 r2 sw h2; do ip netns del "$ns" 2>/dev/null || true; done
}

"$@"
Router configs — plain eBGP first, no BFD:
! r1.conf — AS 65001, plain eBGP (no BFD yet)
hostname r1
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.0.12.1
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor 10.0.12.2 remote-as 65002
! r2.conf — AS 65002, originates the customer LAN
hostname r2
router bgp 65002
 bgp router-id 10.0.12.2
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor 10.0.12.1 remote-as 65001
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 203.0.113.0/24
 exit-address-family
The failure drill — it fails r2’s switch port, confirms r1’s port is still up, and times how long r1 keeps the dead route in its kernel FIB:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# drill.sh — fail r2's switch port, time how long r1 keeps a dead route
# usage: sudo ./drill.sh [prefix]   (default 203.0.113.0/24)
set -euo pipefail
PFX=${1:-203.0.113.0/24}

ip -n r1 route show "$PFX" | grep -q . || { echo "no route to $PFX on r1"; exit 1; }
echo "before: $(ip -n r1 route show "$PFX")"

start=$(date +%s.%N)
ip -n sw link set sw-r2 down            # r2 loses carrier; r1's port stays up
echo "r1-eth1 state after failure: $(ip -n r1 -br link show r1-eth1 | awk '{print $2}')"

while ip -n r1 route show "$PFX" | grep -q .; do sleep 0.05; done
end=$(date +%s.%N)
printf 'route withdrawn on r1 after %.2f s\n' "$(echo "$end - $start" | bc)"

ip -n sw link set sw-r2 up               # heal for the next run
Bring it up and check the baseline:
chmod +x lab.sh drill.sh
sudo ./lab.sh up
sleep 10
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show ip route bgp'
sudo ip netns exec r1 ping -c2 -W1 203.0.113.10
Output (tails):
IPv4 unicast VRF default:
B>* 203.0.113.0/24 [20/0] via 10.0.12.2, r1-eth1, weight 1, 00:00:08
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1023ms
Each daemon prints a [pid|daemon] done line as vtysh -f applies configuration; that is normal.

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Drill 1 — the silent failure (no BFD)

Predict
r1’s hold time is 180 s and keepalives arrive every 60 s. The failure happens at a random point in the keepalive cycle. How long will r1 keep the route?
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show ip bgp neighbors 10.0.12.2' | grep -i 'hold time'
  Hold time is 180 seconds, keepalive interval is 60 seconds
  Configured hold time is 180 seconds, keepalive interval is 60 seconds


Observe
sudo ./drill.sh
While it waits, in a second terminal:
sudo ip netns exec r1 ping -c3 -W1 203.0.113.10 | tail -2
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show ip bgp summary' | grep -A1 Neighbor
sudo vtysh -N r2 -c 'show ip bgp summary' | grep -A1 Neighbor
3 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 2039ms

Neighbor        V         AS   MsgRcvd   MsgSent   TblVer  InQ OutQ  Up/Down State/PfxRcd   PfxSnt Desc
10.0.12.2       4      65002         4         5        1    0    0 00:00:35            1        1 N/A
Neighbor        V         AS   MsgRcvd   MsgSent   TblVer  InQ OutQ  Up/Down State/PfxRcd   PfxSnt Desc
10.0.12.1       4      65001         4         4        0    0    0 00:00:13       Active        0 N/A
r2 already knows (its port lost carrier). r1 shows Established with 1 prefix and drops every packet. The drill finishes:
before: 203.0.113.0/24 nhid 6 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 proto bgp metric 20 
r1-eth1 state after failure: UP
route withdrawn on r1 after 158.87 s


Explain
Not 180 s: the hold timer restarts on every keepalive, so detection is anywhere from hold − keepalive (120 s) to hold (180 s), depending on when the last keepalive landed. Two and a half minutes of blackhole with a green dashboard.

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Drill 2 — add BFD and repeat
Define a profile on each router and attach it to the BGP neighbor. The profile asks for 100 ms intervals with multiplier 3 (300 ms detection). FRR’s defaults are 300 ms × 3.
! r1-bfd.conf — add a BFD profile and attach it to the BGP neighbor
bfd
 profile fast
  detect-multiplier 3
  receive-interval 100
  transmit-interval 100
 exit
exit
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 10.0.12.2 bfd profile fast
! r2-bfd.conf — add a BFD profile and attach it to the BGP neighbor
bfd
 profile fast
  detect-multiplier 3
  receive-interval 100
  transmit-interval 100
 exit
exit
router bgp 65002
 neighbor 10.0.12.1 bfd profile fast
sudo vtysh -N r1 -f r1-bfd.conf
sudo vtysh -N r2 -f r2-bfd.conf
sleep 3
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bfd peers brief'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bfd peer 10.0.12.2'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show ip bgp neighbors 10.0.12.2' | grep -A3 'BFD'
Output (session IDs will differ):
Session count: 1
SessionId  LocalAddress                             PeerAddress                             Status         
=========  ============                             ===========                             ======         
3526470594 10.0.12.1                                10.0.12.2                               up             
BFD Peer:
    peer 10.0.12.2 local-address 10.0.12.1 vrf default interface r1-eth1
        ID: 3526470594
        Remote ID: 1869221485
        Active mode
        Status: up
        Uptime: 2 second(s)
        Diagnostics: ok
        Remote diagnostics: ok
        Peer Type: dynamic
        RTT min/avg/max: 0/0/0 usec
        Local timers:
            Detect-multiplier: 3
            Receive interval: 100ms
            Transmission interval: 100ms
            Echo receive interval: 50ms
            Echo transmission interval: disabled
        Remote timers:
            Detect-multiplier: 3
            Receive interval: 100ms
            Transmission interval: 100ms
            Echo receive interval: 50ms
  BFD: Type: single hop
  Detect Multiplier: 3, Min Rx interval: 300, Min Tx interval: 300
  Status: Up, Last update: 0:00:00:02
(That last block was captured right after the first apply, before the 100 ms profile values were in place — BGP’s neighbor view shows what the session had at registration. Trust show bfd peer for live timers.) Peer Type: dynamic means a client (BGP) created the session; you did not declare a peer under bfd.
Run the drill again, a few times:
sudo ./drill.sh
before: 203.0.113.0/24 nhid 6 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 proto bgp metric 20 
r1-eth1 state after failure: UP
route withdrawn on r1 after 0.38 s
Repeated runs: 0.33 s, 0.33 s, 0.33 s — the 300 ms detection time plus BGP and zebra doing their work. After a failure the session records why:
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bfd peer 10.0.12.2' | grep -E 'Status|Diagnostics|Downtime'
        Status: down
        Downtime: 0 second(s)
        Diagnostics: control detection time expired
From 158.87 s to 0.33 s, with the same BGP timers.

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Drill 3 — the slower side wins
Put r2 back to 300 ms while r1 stays at 100 ms:
sed 's/interval 100/interval 300/g' r2-bfd.conf > r2-slow.conf
sudo vtysh -N r2 -f r2-slow.conf
sleep 3
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bfd peer 10.0.12.2 json' | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E 'interval|multiplier'
    "receive-interval": 100,
    "transmit-interval": 100,
    "echo-receive-interval": 50,
    "echo-transmit-interval": 0,
    "detect-multiplier": 3,
    "remote-receive-interval": 300,
    "remote-transmit-interval": 300,
    "remote-echo-receive-interval": 50,
    "remote-detect-multiplier": 3,

Predict
r1 detection time = r2 Detect Mult × max(r1 Required Min RX, r2 Desired Min TX) = 3 × max(100, 300) = 900 ms.


Observe
sudo ./drill.sh | tail -1
route withdrawn on r1 after 0.86 s
Configuring one end aggressively buys nothing; detection follows the slower declaration. Restore r2 with sudo vtysh -N r2 -f r2-bfd.conf.

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
section: Drill 4 — BFD for a static route
text:
Drill 4 — BFD for a static route
Static routes are the other place silent failures hurt: a static next hop “stays up” as long as the interface does. FRR’s staticd can make a static route a BFD client — installed only while the session is Up.
sudo ip -n r2 addr add 198.51.100.1/24 dev lo
! r1-static.conf — a static route that is only installed while BFD says the next hop is alive
ip route 198.51.100.0/24 10.0.12.2 bfd profile fast
! r2-static.conf — answer BFD for r1 even without a routing protocol
bfd
 peer 10.0.12.1 interface r2-eth1
  profile fast
 exit
exit
r2 has no routing protocol for this prefix, so it gets an explicit peer under bfd to answer the session (in this lab BGP’s session to the same address already exists and is shared — one session, two clients).
sudo vtysh -N r1 -f r1-static.conf
sudo vtysh -N r2 -f r2-static.conf
sleep 3
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show ip route 198.51.100.0/24'
sudo ./drill.sh 198.51.100.0/24
Routing entry for 198.51.100.0/24
  Known via "static", distance 1, metric 0, best
  Last update 00:00:03 ago
  * 10.0.12.2, via r1-eth1, weight 1
before: 198.51.100.0/24 nhid 6 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 proto static metric 20 
r1-eth1 state after failure: UP
route withdrawn on r1 after 0.27 s
A few seconds after the drill heals the port, both the static and the BGP route are back. While a monitored static is uninstalled it disappears from show ip route; use show bfd static route to see it. This is what makes a floating static (a backup with a higher distance) actually float when the primary next hop dies behind a switch.

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Drill 5 — one-sided BFD (predict, then try)
Tear the lab down and up again, and apply r1-bfd.conf only on r1.
sudo ./lab.sh down && sudo ./lab.sh up
sudo vtysh -N r1 -f r1-bfd.conf
sleep 10
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bfd peers brief'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show ip bgp summary'
Predict before you look: does BGP come up? Is the BFD session Up? Does the drill now take 0.3 s or ~150 s? (FRR’s default BGP–BFD integration reacts to a session going down; a session that never came up does not hold BGP back. Newer FRR releases add neighbor … bfd strict, which refuses to bring BGP up until BFD is Up — check neighbor 10.0.12.2 bfd ? on your build.) The lesson either way: BFD must be configured on both ends, and your verification must check BFD state, not just BGP state.
Clean up when done:
sudo ./lab.sh down

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Choosing timers








Environment
Starting point
Why




Physical routers, hardware/offloaded BFD
50–100 ms × 3
Packets handled off the main CPU


Software routers (FRR on servers)
300 ms × 3 (default)
Survives scheduler hiccups and GC pauses


VMs / containers / cloud
300–1000 ms × 3–5
Noisy neighbors, live migration, steal time


Over a provider L2/L3 service
Agree with the provider
Their policers may drop small UDP



Rules of thumb:

Detection time is the number you choose; interval and multiplier are how you get there. 900 ms that never false-positives beats 150 ms that flaps every afternoon.
A false BFD-down is not free: it tears down BGP, withdraws routes, and triggers reconvergence across the network. Combine with BGP graceful restart awareness (bfd check-control-plane-failure in FRR) when routers restart their control planes.
Protect BFD from your own filters and QoS: allow UDP 3784/4784 (and the echo port 3785 if used) in control-plane policy, and do not let it queue behind bulk traffic.
Use multihop BFD (RFC 5883) for loopback-to-loopback iBGP; single-hop rules (TTL 255) do not apply, so set minimum-ttl sensibly.

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Verification checklist








Check
Command
Intent




Session up on both ends
show bfd peers brief (r1 and r2)
No one-sided config


Live timers
show bfd peer <ip>
Negotiated values, not just configured


Client attached
show ip bgp neighbors <ip> → BFD: block
BGP actually registered


Monitored statics
show bfd static route
Uninstalled statics are visible here


Last failure reason
show bfd peer <ip> → Diagnostics
Detection expired vs admin down


Filters
Control-plane ACL permits UDP 3784/4784
BFD not dropped by your own policy


Drill
drill.sh or equivalent
Measured, not assumed, detection time

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Common mistakes







Mistake
Symptom




BFD on one side only
BFD never Up; failures still take hold-timer time


Aggressive timers on VMs
Random BGP flaps under load; control detection time expired with no link event


Tuning only one end
Detection follows the slower side (Drill 3)


Filtering UDP 3784 in control-plane policy
BFD Down, BGP Up — or worse, BGP reset by strict modes


Treating AdminDown as a failure
Maintenance on the peer causes an outage


Single-hop BFD between loopbacks
Session never forms; needs multihop


Trusting show ip bgp summary alone
“Established” while forwarding is dead (Drill 1)

title: BFD — Fast Failure Detection
text:
Summary

Through a switch or L2 service, carrier loss is local: the far router keeps its port, its session, and its route

BGP detection is hold − keepalive … hold (120–180 s by default) — measured here at 158.87 s

BFD is a shared sub-second liveness check; clients (BGP, OSPF, statics) act on its Down event — measured here at 0.33 s

Detection time = remote multiplier × max(local Required Min RX, remote Desired Min TX): the slower side wins

Configure both ends, verify negotiated timers, size timers for your platform, and drill the failure

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
text:
RPKI — Route Origin Validation
BGP believes whatever its neighbors say. If a peer announces your prefix with someone else’s AS at the end of the path, your router installs it, prefers it if it is more specific, and forwards your customers’ traffic into the wrong network. Prefix lists help for the handful of customers you know; they do nothing for the 1,000,000 routes arriving from a transit provider. RPKI route origin validation (ROV) is the boring, widely deployed answer: address holders publish signed statements of which AS may originate which prefix, up to which length, a validator turns those into a flat table, and your router labels every route Valid, Invalid, or NotFound. Policy then drops the Invalids. This chapter builds the whole chain on one Linux box — a cache, a validating FRR router, and a misbehaving peer — and then breaks it the three ways it breaks in production.

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain the chain ROA → validator → VRP → RTR → router, and what each piece is trusted for

Apply the RFC 6811 algorithm by hand: covering VRPs, origin AS, maxLength

Enable RPKI in FRR, connect it to an RTR cache, and read validation state per route

Show that validation without policy changes nothing about forwarding

Write an inbound route-map that drops Invalid and de-prefers NotFound

Explain why a loose maxLength turns a sub-prefix hijack into a Valid route

Predict what happens to routing when the cache is unreachable, and when VRPs change underneath accepted routes

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
text:
Concepts — RPKI in one page



RPKI ROV lab


Who signs what. The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RFC 6480) mirrors the address allocation hierarchy: the five RIRs hold trust anchors, they certify the address blocks they hand out, and a holder can publish a Route Origin Authorization (ROA) for its space. A ROA says: prefix P, origin AS A, maximum length M. It says nothing about the rest of the AS path.
Who validates. A relying-party validator (Routinator, rpki-client, FORT, OctoRPKI…) fetches every repository, checks every signature and expiry, and emits a flat list of Validated ROA Payloads (VRPs): (prefix, maxLength, ASN) tuples. Your routers never touch certificates.
How the router learns them. The validator (or a small cache in front of it, such as StayRTR) serves VRPs to routers over the RPKI-to-Router protocol (RTR, RFC 8210 for version 1), normally TCP port 8282 or 323. It is a serial-numbered, incremental feed: routers get a full table once, then diffs.
The algorithm (RFC 6811). For a route with prefix R and origin AS O (the last AS in the path):

Collect the covering VRPs: those whose prefix contains R.

None → NotFound. Nobody made a claim about this space.

Any covering VRP with ASN = O and length(R) ≤ maxLength → Valid.

Covering VRPs exist but none match → Invalid. Either the wrong AS, or a longer prefix than the holder authorised.

What the router does with the label. Nothing, until you write policy. RFC 7115 describes operational practice; the common baseline today is drop Invalid, accept NotFound (much of the table still has no ROAs), accept Valid.



Term
Meaning




ROA
Signed object: prefix, maxLength, origin ASN


VRP
One validated (prefix, maxLength, ASN) tuple


RP / validator
Software that turns the RPKI into VRPs


RTR
Protocol that carries VRPs from cache to router


Covering VRP
A VRP whose prefix contains the route’s prefix


ROV
Labelling routes by RFC 6811; policy acts on the label



The algorithm fits in a page of Python. Feeding it the lab’s VRPs first makes the router output later look familiar:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# rov.py — RFC 6811 route origin validation, nothing else
import ipaddress, json, sys

def load_vrps(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        roas = json.load(f)["roas"]
    return [(ipaddress.ip_network(r["prefix"]), r["maxLength"],
             int(str(r["asn"]).removeprefix("AS"))) for r in roas]

def validate(route, origin, vrps):
    route = ipaddress.ip_network(route)
    covering = [v for v in vrps
                if v[0].version == route.version and route.subnet_of(v[0])]
    if not covering:
        return "NotFound", []
    for pfx, maxlen, asn in covering:
        if asn == origin and route.prefixlen <= maxlen:
            return "Valid", [(str(pfx), maxlen, asn)]
    return "Invalid", [(str(p), m, a) for p, m, a in covering]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    vrps = load_vrps(sys.argv[1])
    for line in sys.stdin:
        route, origin = line.split()
        state, why = validate(route, int(origin), vrps)
        print(f"{route:<18} AS{origin:<6} {state:<9} {why}")
{
  "metadata": { "buildtime": "2026-10-08T00:00:00Z" },
  "roas": [
    { "prefix": "203.0.113.0/24", "maxLength": 24, "asn": "AS65002" },
    { "prefix": "198.51.100.0/24", "maxLength": 24, "asn": "AS65099" },
    { "prefix": "100.64.0.0/22",  "maxLength": 22, "asn": "AS65002" }
  ]
}
Save the JSON as vrps.json (StayRTR reads the same file later) and run:
printf '%s\n' "203.0.113.0/24 65002" "198.51.100.0/24 65002" "192.0.2.0/24 65002" \
  "100.64.0.0/22 65002" "100.64.1.0/24 65002" "100.64.1.0/24 65099" \
  | python3 rov.py vrps.json
203.0.113.0/24     AS65002  Valid     [('203.0.113.0/24', 24, 65002)]
198.51.100.0/24    AS65002  Invalid   [('198.51.100.0/24', 24, 65099)]
192.0.2.0/24       AS65002  NotFound  []
100.64.0.0/22      AS65002  Valid     [('100.64.0.0/22', 22, 65002)]
100.64.1.0/24      AS65002  Invalid   [('100.64.0.0/22', 22, 65002)]
100.64.1.0/24      AS65099  Invalid   [('100.64.0.0/22', 22, 65002)]
Read the last two lines carefully: the /24 inside the /22 is Invalid whoever originates it, because the holder only authorised the /22. That is the property that makes sub-prefix hijacks fail — and the property a loose maxLength gives away (Drill 3).

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
text:
Lab build (Linux namespaces + FRR + StayRTR)
No container images and no Internet RPKI: three network namespaces, two veth pairs, one FRR instance per router namespace (FRR’s pathspace option -N, exactly like the BFD chapter’s lab), and StayRTR serving the vrps.json file above as an RTR cache. A real deployment points the same router configuration at a validator such as Routinator or rpki-client; only the cache address changes.
It was run on Debian 13 with the distro packages FRR 10.3 (frr, frr-rpki-rtrlib) and StayRTR 0.6.2, as root. Outputs below are copied from those runs; timestamps and PIDs will differ on yours.
sudo apt-get install -y frr frr-rpki-rtrlib stayrtr
sudo systemctl disable --now frr      # the lab starts its own instances
frr-rpki-rtrlib ships the bgpd module bgpd_rpki.so; bgpd only loads it when started with -M rpki. Without the package bgpd refuses to start with that flag.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab.sh — r1 (validating FRR) peers with r2 (announcing FRR); "cache" runs StayRTR
# usage: sudo ./lab.sh up | down
set -euo pipefail
FRR=/usr/lib/frr
DAEMONS="mgmtd zebra bgpd staticd"
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)

up() {
  for ns in r1 r2 cache; do ip netns add "$ns"; ip -n "$ns" link set lo up; done

  # eBGP link r1 <-> r2
  ip link add r1-eth1 netns r1 type veth peer name r2-eth1 netns r2
  ip -n r1 addr add 10.0.12.1/24 dev r1-eth1
  ip -n r2 addr add 10.0.12.2/24 dev r2-eth1
  ip -n r1 link set r1-eth1 up; ip -n r2 link set r2-eth1 up

  # management link r1 <-> RPKI cache (RTR runs over plain TCP here)
  ip link add r1-eth2 netns r1 type veth peer name cache-eth0 netns cache
  ip -n r1 addr add 10.0.13.1/24 dev r1-eth2
  ip -n cache addr add 10.0.13.2/24 dev cache-eth0
  ip -n r1 link set r1-eth2 up; ip -n cache link set cache-eth0 up

  # the relying-party cache: StayRTR serving VRPs from a local JSON file
  ip netns exec cache stayrtr -bind 10.0.13.2:8282 -cache "$HERE/vrps.json" \
    -checktime=false -refresh 5 -metrics.addr "" >"$HERE/stayrtr.log" 2>&1 &
  echo $! > "$HERE/stayrtr.pid"

  for ns in r1 r2; do
    install -d -o frr -g frr "/var/run/frr/$ns" "/etc/frr/$ns"
    : > "/etc/frr/$ns/vtysh.conf"
    for d in $DAEMONS; do
      extra=""; [ "$d" = bgpd ] && [ "$ns" = r1 ] && extra="-M rpki"
      ip netns exec "$ns" "$FRR/$d" -d -N "$ns" -F traditional $extra \
        -u frr -g frr --limit-fds 1024 >/dev/null 2>&1
    done
    vtysh -N "$ns" -f "$HERE/$ns.conf" >/dev/null
  done
}

down() {
  for ns in r1 r2; do
    for d in $DAEMONS; do
      pidf="/var/run/frr/$ns/$d.pid"
      [ -f "$pidf" ] && kill "$(cat "$pidf")" 2>/dev/null || true
    done
  done
  [ -f "$HERE/stayrtr.pid" ] && kill "$(cat "$HERE/stayrtr.pid")" 2>/dev/null || true
  for ns in r1 r2 cache; do ip netns del "$ns" 2>/dev/null || true; done
}

"$@"
StayRTR flags used: -cache accepts a URL or a local file; -checktime=false stops it rejecting our hand-written file for having no fresh validator timestamp; -refresh 5 re-reads the file every five seconds so the drills move quickly (the default is 600 s).
r2 announces all five prefixes; the blackhole statics only exist so that network statements have something in the RIB to match:
! r2.conf — AS 65002, announces four prefixes with four different RPKI outcomes
hostname r2
ip route 203.0.113.0/24 blackhole
ip route 198.51.100.0/24 blackhole
ip route 192.0.2.0/24 blackhole
ip route 100.64.0.0/22 blackhole
ip route 100.64.1.0/24 blackhole
router bgp 65002
 bgp router-id 10.0.12.2
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor 10.0.12.1 remote-as 65001
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 203.0.113.0/24
  network 198.51.100.0/24
  network 192.0.2.0/24
  network 100.64.0.0/22
  network 100.64.1.0/24
 exit-address-family
r1 connects to the cache and validates — but has no RPKI policy yet:
! r1.conf — AS 65001, validates origins against the RPKI cache (no policy yet)
hostname r1
rpki
 rpki cache tcp 10.0.13.2 8282 preference 1
exit
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.0.12.1
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor 10.0.12.2 remote-as 65002
preference orders several caches: the router uses the lowest-numbered group it can reach. Production routers should have at least two caches on different hosts.
Bring it up and check the RTR session:
chmod +x lab.sh
sudo ./lab.sh up
sleep 12
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show rpki cache-connection'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show rpki prefix-table'
Connected to group 1
rpki tcp cache 10.0.13.2 8282 pref 1 (connected)
RPKI/RTR prefix table
Prefix                                   Prefix Length  Origin-AS
100.64.0.0                                  22 -  22   65002
203.0.113.0                                 24 -  24   65002
198.51.100.0                                24 -  24   65099
Number of IPv4 Prefixes: 3
Number of IPv6 Prefixes: 0
22 - 22 is “prefix length 22, maxLength 22”. You can ask the cache directly what it serves, from r1’s namespace, with StayRTR’s companion tool:
sudo ip netns exec r1 rtrdump -connect 10.0.13.2:8282 -file /dev/stdout
{"metadata":{"vrps":3,"bgpsec_pubkeys":0,"sessionid":16344,"serial":0},"roas":[{"prefix":"198.51.100.0/24","maxLength":24,"asn":65099},{"prefix":"203.0.113.0/24","maxLength":24,"asn":65002},{"prefix":"100.64.0.0/22","maxLength":22,"asn":65002}]}

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
section: Drill 1 — validation is a label, not a filter
text:
Drill 1 — validation is a label, not a filter

Predict
r1 knows that 198.51.100.0/24 belongs to AS65099 and that nothing more specific than /22 should exist inside 100.64.0.0/22. Which of r2’s five routes will r1 install?


Observe
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast'
sudo ip netns exec r1 ip route show proto bgp
RPKI validation codes: V valid, I invalid, N Not found

     Network          Next Hop            Metric LocPrf Weight Path
V*>  100.64.0.0/22    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
I*>  100.64.1.0/24    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
N*>  192.0.2.0/24     10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
I*>  198.51.100.0/24  10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
V*>  203.0.113.0/24   10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i

Displayed 5 routes and 5 total paths
100.64.0.0/22 nhid 10 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 metric 20 
100.64.1.0/24 nhid 10 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 metric 20 
192.0.2.0/24 nhid 10 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 metric 20 
198.51.100.0/24 nhid 10 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 metric 20 
203.0.113.0/24 nhid 10 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 metric 20 
The per-route view names the state explicitly:
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast 100.64.1.0/24'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast rpki invalid'
BGP routing table entry for 100.64.1.0/24, version 2
Paths: (1 available, best #1, table default)
  Advertised to non peer-group peers:
  10.0.12.2
  65002
    10.0.12.2 from 10.0.12.2 (10.0.12.2)
      Origin IGP, metric 0, valid, external, best (First path received), rpki validation-state: invalid
...
     Network          Next Hop            Metric LocPrf Weight Path
I*>  100.64.1.0/24    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
I*>  198.51.100.0/24  10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i

Displayed 2 routes and 5 total paths


Explain
All five are best (*>) and all five are in the kernel FIB, Invalids included. FRR’s documentation says so plainly: enabling RPKI does not change best-path selection. Note the two meanings of “valid” in one line — valid, external, best is BGP’s next-hop/attribute validity, rpki validation-state: invalid is origin validation. Do not grep for the wrong one.

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
text:
Drill 2 — drop Invalid, de-prefer NotFound
! r1-policy.conf — drop Invalid, de-prefer NotFound, keep Valid
route-map RPKI-IN deny 10
 match rpki invalid
exit
route-map RPKI-IN permit 20
 match rpki notfound
 set local-preference 50
exit
route-map RPKI-IN permit 30
exit
router bgp 65001
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  neighbor 10.0.12.2 soft-reconfiguration inbound
  neighbor 10.0.12.2 route-map RPKI-IN in
 exit-address-family
soft-reconfiguration inbound keeps an unmodified Adj-RIB-In copy of what the peer sent, including routes your policy rejected. FRR’s RPKI documentation requires it for cache updates to be applied to routes; Drill 4 shows why you want it anyway.
sudo vtysh -N r1 -f r1-policy.conf
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'clear bgp ipv4 unicast 10.0.12.2 soft in'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast neighbors 10.0.12.2 received-routes'
sudo ip netns exec r1 ip route show proto bgp
     Network          Next Hop            Metric LocPrf Weight Path
V*>  100.64.0.0/22    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
N*>  192.0.2.0/24     10.0.12.2                0     50      0 65002 i
V*>  203.0.113.0/24   10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i

Displayed 3 routes and 3 total paths
     Network          Next Hop            Metric LocPrf Weight Path
 *> 100.64.0.0/22    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
 *> 100.64.1.0/24    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
 *> 192.0.2.0/24     10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
 *> 198.51.100.0/24  10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
 *> 203.0.113.0/24   10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i

Total number of prefixes 5 (2 filtered)
100.64.0.0/22 nhid 10 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 metric 20 
192.0.2.0/24 nhid 10 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 metric 20 
203.0.113.0/24 nhid 10 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 metric 20 
The hijacked 198.51.100.0/24 is gone. The too-specific 100.64.1.0/24 is gone, but traffic to 100.64.1.x still flows via the legitimate /22 — dropping an Invalid more-specific does not blackhole the space, it just stops the more-specific from winning longest-match. received-routes proves the peer still sends all five and the filter is doing the work.
Why set local-preference 50 on NotFound rather than dropping it: a large share of the Internet table still has no ROAs. Dropping NotFound would cut you off from it. De-preferring means a Valid path wins whenever one exists.

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
text:
Drill 3 — the maxLength trap

Predict
The holder of 100.64.0.0/22 decides to “save time” and publishes its ROA with maxLength 24, so it can announce /24s later without touching RPKI. It still announces only the /22. What happens to r2’s 100.64.1.0/24?
Edit vrps.json, changing only the /22 line to "maxLength": 24. StayRTR notices within five seconds and bumps its serial:
time="2026-10-08T09:03:09+05:30" level=info msg="New update (3 uniques, 3 total prefixes, 0 router keys)."
time="2026-10-08T09:03:09+05:30" level=info msg="Update added, new serial 1"
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show rpki prefix-table'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'clear bgp ipv4 unicast 10.0.12.2 soft in'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast'
Prefix                                   Prefix Length  Origin-AS
100.64.0.0                                  22 -  24   65002
...
     Network          Next Hop            Metric LocPrf Weight Path
V*>  100.64.0.0/22    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
V*>  100.64.1.0/24    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
N*>  192.0.2.0/24     10.0.12.2                0     50      0 65002 i
V*>  203.0.113.0/24   10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i


Explain
The /24 is now Valid. In the lab r2 really is AS65002, but on the Internet the attacker does not need to be: a forged-origin hijack announces 100.64.1.0/24 with an AS path ending in 65002. ROV checks only the last AS, so the forged route validates, and because it is more specific than the real /22 it attracts all the traffic for that quarter of the block. With maxLength 22, the same forgery is Invalid and dropped by every ROV network.
RFC 9319 (BCP 185) turns this into the rule: do not use maxLength unless every prefix it authorises is actually announced; publish one ROA per announced prefix instead (“minimal ROAs”). Put the setting back to 22 before the next drill.

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
section: Drill 4 — state changes under accepted routes
text:
Drill 4 — state changes under accepted routes

Predict
You tighten the ROA back to maxLength 22. The cache updates; r1’s prefix-table updates. Is 100.64.1.0/24 withdrawn from r1’s FIB?


Observe
About ten seconds after the edit, and again twenty seconds later:
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast'
sudo ip netns exec r1 ip route show 100.64.1.0/24
     Network          Next Hop            Metric LocPrf Weight Path
V*>  100.64.0.0/22    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
I*>  100.64.1.0/24    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
N*>  192.0.2.0/24     10.0.12.2                0     50      0 65002 i
V*>  203.0.113.0/24   10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i

Displayed 4 routes and 4 total paths
100.64.1.0/24 nhid 10 via 10.0.12.2 dev r1-eth1 proto bgp metric 20 
The label flipped to I — and the route stayed best and installed. On this FRR 10.3 build, the new validation state was recorded but the inbound route-map was not re-run for an already-accepted route. Re-running inbound policy fixes it:
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'clear bgp ipv4 unicast 10.0.12.2 soft in'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast'
sudo ip netns exec r1 ip route show 100.64.1.0/24
     Network          Next Hop            Metric LocPrf Weight Path
V*>  100.64.0.0/22    10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i
N*>  192.0.2.0/24     10.0.12.2                0     50      0 65002 i
V*>  203.0.113.0/24   10.0.12.2                0             0 65002 i

Displayed 3 routes and 3 total paths
(no FIB line — the /24 is gone). The same happened in the other direction in Drill 3: the /24 rejected under maxLength 22 did not reappear when the ROA was loosened until the soft clear.


Explain
FRR’s RPKI guide says cache updates are applied and path selection updated, provided soft reconfiguration is enabled. Whether a particular release re-applies policy (not just the label) on every VRP change is exactly the kind of thing to measure on your version rather than assume. Operational answers that work everywhere: keep soft-reconfiguration inbound on RPKI-filtered sessions, alert on show bgp ipv4 unicast rpki invalid being non-empty, and schedule a periodic clear bgp * soft in (cheap with an Adj-RIB-In) until you have proved your release does it for you.

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
section: Drill 5 — the cache goes away (predict, then try)
text:
Drill 5 — the cache goes away (predict, then try)
Stop the cache and look at r1:
sudo kill "$(cat stayrtr.pid)"
sleep 8
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show rpki cache-connection'
sudo vtysh -N r1 -c 'show rpki prefix-table' | tail -2
Connected to group 1
rpki tcp cache 10.0.13.2 8282 pref 1
Number of IPv4 Prefixes: 3
Number of IPv6 Prefixes: 0
The (connected) marker is gone but the VRPs remain: RTR data lives until the expire interval (StayRTR advertises 7200 s by default; FRR has rpki expire_interval). Routing continues unchanged. After expiry, every route becomes NotFound — Invalids included — and your “drop Invalid” policy silently stops dropping anything. ROV fails open by design: a dead validator must not take the network down, but it does take your protection away. Hence two caches, on different hosts, monitored. Newer FRR releases add neighbor PEER rpki strict to hold a session down until a cache is connected; FRR 10.3 rejects that command (% Unknown command), so check your version.

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
text:
Checking real-world origins
The same three states exist on the live Internet, and RIPEstat exposes a validator over HTTPS. A real ROA, then a deliberately wrong origin:
curl -s 'https://stat.ripe.net/data/rpki-validation/data.json?resource=AS13335&prefix=1.1.1.0/24' \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys;d=json.load(sys.stdin)['data'];print(json.dumps({k:d[k] for k in ('resource','prefix','status','validating_roas')},indent=1))"
curl -s 'https://stat.ripe.net/data/rpki-validation/data.json?resource=AS64500&prefix=1.1.1.0/24' \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys;d=json.load(sys.stdin)['data'];print(d['resource'],d['prefix'],d['status'])"
{
 "resource": "13335",
 "prefix": "1.1.1.0/24",
 "status": "valid",
 "validating_roas": [
  {
   "origin": "13335",
   "prefix": "1.1.1.0/24",
   "validity": "valid",
   "max_length": 24
  }
 ]
}
64500 1.1.1.0/24 invalid_asn
Use it to check your own prefixes before you publish a ROA, and after: the holder can make its own routes Invalid with a mistake, and every ROV network will then drop them.

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
text:
Deploying it for real








Step
What
Why




1
Publish ROAs for your own space (RIR portal, hosted RPKI) — one per announced prefix, maxLength = prefix length
Others can protect you; avoids Drill 3


2
Run two validators/caches (e.g., Routinator and rpki-client) on separate hosts
Fail-open is fine only if it is rare (Drill 5)


3
Point every border router at both (rpki cache … preference 1/2)
Cache failover


4
Start with monitor-only: label, do not filter; review rpki invalid
Find your customers’ broken ROAs first


5
Enable deny invalid on transit and peer sessions, then on customers
The RFC 7115 path


6
Re-run inbound policy on VRP changes, or prove your release does (Drill 4)
No stale accepts


7
Alert on cache disconnect, VRP count drops, and serial not advancing
Validator outages are silent



ROV protects against wrong origins. It does not stop route leaks (valid origin, wrong path) or forged-origin hijacks of space with loose ROAs; path validation (ASPA, BGPsec) is the next layer and is outside this chapter.

title: RPKI — Route Origin Validation
text:
Verification checklist








Check
Command
Intent




Cache connected
show rpki cache-connection
(connected) on at least one group


VRPs loaded
show rpki prefix-table
Non-zero, plausible count


State per route
show bgp ipv4 unicast <prefix>
rpki validation-state: line


Invalids accepted
show bgp ipv4 unicast rpki invalid
Should be empty with policy on


Policy attached
show running-config → route-map RPKI-IN in
Labels mean nothing without it


Filter doing work
… neighbors <ip> received-routes

title: Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA
text:
Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA
IGP shortest paths are easy to explain and slow to heal. Classic Loop-Free Alternates (LFA) and Remote LFA cover many failures but not all topologies. Segment Routing (SR) (RFC 8402) lets the ingress (or a repair point) encode an explicit path as a list of segments. On IPv6, that list lives in the SR Header and is programmed with SRv6 network programming (RFC 8986). TI-LFA (RFC 9855) uses those segments so a Point of Local Repair (PLR) can pre-install a loop-free backup that follows the expected post-convergence path — topology-independent coverage in two-connected IGP areas, without Targeted LDP tunnels. This chapter stays vendor-neutral and RFC-first.

title: Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

State the SR architecture: Prefix-SID / Adjacency-SID, SR-MPLS vs SRv6
Explain SRv6 SID lists, active segment, and head-end behaviors at a PLR
Define TI-LFA, P-space / Q-space, and Repair List (RL)
Predict what the PLR pushes when the active segment is a node SID vs an adjacency SID
Relate TI-LFA to BFD-scale detection: FRR is local and precomputed; IGP still converges

title: Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA
text:
Thesis
TI-LFA is not a new IGP. It is a local repair algorithm that expresses post-failure shortest paths as SR segment lists the PLR can push the moment a link (or protected node/SRLG) dies — then withdraws that repair when the IGP SPF at the PLR catches up.

title: Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA
text:
Mental model
Before failure (IGP SPF):     S ──→ F ──→ … ──→ D
                                \                 ↑
After local repair (TI-LFA):    └─ RL → P ⋯ Q ────┘



TI-LFA repair at the PLR









Term (RFC 9855 / 8402)
Meaning




PLR
Router that detects local failure and activates a precomputed backup


RL (Repair List)
Segment list encoding a loop-free path avoiding the protected resource


P-space
Nodes reachable from the PLR without traversing the failed resource


Q-space
Nodes that can reach the destination without traversing the failed resource


Post-convergence path
SPF path the PLR would use after the IGP absorbs the failure




SR data planes








Plane
How a segment is carried
Primary RFCs




SR-MPLS
MPLS label stack
RFC 8402, RFC 8660


SRv6
IPv6 destination + optional SRH (RFC 8754); behaviors in RFC 8986
RFC 8402, 8754, 8986



SRv6 Adjacency SIDs are often globally routed, so RLs can be shorter than SR-MPLS (less need to precede an Adj-SID with a Prefix-SID) — RFC 9855 §7.2.

title: Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Architecture in one page (RFC 8402)
A segment is an instruction. Common kinds:

Prefix-SID (node segment) — “go to this node via the IGP algorithm (usually SPF)”
Adjacency-SID — “take this specific link / adjacency”

An SR Policy is an ordered list of segments. On SRv6, the active segment is the IPv6 Destination Address; Segments Left in the SRH walks the list (RFC 8402 §3.1.3 summary).
Operators instantiate SRv6 SIDs explicitly — ordinary interface addresses are not SIDs by default.


Case 2: TI-LFA repair flavours (RFC 9855 §5)







Situation along post-convergence path
RL shape




Direct neighbor in P ∩ Q
Empty RL; just change next hop (post-convergence LFA)


Remote PQ node
Single node segment to that PQ


Adjacent P then Q
Node-SID(P) then Adj-SID(P→Q)


Distant P and Q
Node-SID(P) + explicit path EP(P,Q) (Adj-SID list or optimized mix)



Protection modes: link, node, or SRLG failure assumptions when computing the backup.


Case 3: What the PLR does to the packet (RFC 9855 §6–7)
Active segment is a node SID. Keep it; add the RL so the node SID becomes the first segment after the repair list.
Active segment is an adjacency SID S–F (protected). Apply NEXT on that Adj-SID, then PUSH an RL that restores traffic toward F (or toward a Q whose path to the following node SID avoids the failure) — details in §6.2.1–6.2.2.
SRv6 transit PLR. Add the SID list using RFC 8986 head-end behaviors (e.g. H.Encaps / SRH push as implemented). Endpoint PLR: run endpoint processing first, then protect as transit.
USD flavor (RFC 8986) is often cited so the last repair endpoint can decapsulate the outer header the PLR added and forward the inner packet — useful for TI-LFA encapsulation on P routers.


Case 4: Numbers from RFC 9855 Appendix B (SR-MPLS measurements)
On real SP/enterprise topologies measured in the RFC:

Link / local SRLG protection: ≤1 SID repair path covers >99% of prefixes in the data set
Node protection: ≤2 SIDs yields about 99% coverage

Exact hardware MSD limits still matter; implementations may optimize RL length.

title: Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA
text:
The trap

Expecting TI-LFA to protect inter-domain exits or non-IGP destinations — RFC 9855 limits scope to link-state IGP areas.
Forgetting micro-loops during distributed convergence: TI-LFA is complementary to loop-free convergence methods (RFC 5715, RFC 8333, etc.), not a full substitute.
Building RLs from protected Adj-SIDs and then suffering double FRR if a repair hop fails (RFC 9855 §9); some implementations prefer unprotected Adj-SIDs in RLs.
Assuming SR Policies with custom constraints stay on-policy during local repair — TI-LFA does not know head-end TE constraints; use policy-level protection or Flexible Algorithm-aware TI-LFA (RFC 9855 §8) when constraints matter.
Confusing detection (BFD, carrier) with repair encoding (TI-LFA): you need both for fast restoration.

title: Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA
text:
The boring rule
Run a link-state IGP with SR enabled; precompute TI-LFA RLs toward post-convergence paths; detect failures quickly; keep RL depth inside MSD; let SPF release the repair after convergence.

title: TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks
text:
TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks
The previous chapter introduced Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA), P-space, Q-space and repair lists. This chapter does the computation. You will build the shortest-path trees a Point of Local Repair (PLR) builds, find the P and Q nodes on the post-convergence path, turn the result into an SR-MPLS label stack, and check it against the platform’s Maximum SID Depth (MSD). The lab is a small standard-library Python program. It reproduces both worked examples in RFC 9855 and then measures how much classic LFA, remote LFA and TI-LFA cover on rings and on a meshed core.
Doing this by hand once pays off in operations. When a router reports a backup path with three labels you can check it is the one you expect. When a platform warns that some prefixes are unprotected because the repair exceeds MSD you will know which topologies cause it. And when a vendor’s “show” output disagrees with your mental model you will have a reference to compare against.

title: TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks
text:
Learning goals

Compute P-space, extended P-space and Q-space for a link or node failure, including the strict treatment of equal-cost paths.
Find the expected post-convergence path and pick the P and Q nodes on it.
Express a repair as a repair list (RL) in each of the four RFC 9855 forms, from empty to Node-SID plus Adj-SIDs.
Turn an RL into SR-MPLS labels with an SRGB and Adj-SIDs, and apply the RFC 9855 section 7.1 rules for the active segment and penultimate-hop popping (PHP).
Compare LFA, remote LFA and TI-LFA coverage on a topology, and spot repairs that exceed MSD.
Read FRR’s TI-LFA configuration and backup-route output with that model in mind.

title: TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks
text:
Version note
Everything in the lab ran on the book’s build box with Python 3.13.5 (standard library only), as an unprivileged user. No routers or MPLS data plane are involved; the program models the control-plane computation a PLR does. The FRR configuration near the end is written from the FRR isisd and ospfd documentation and is not run here. Check the documentation for your FRR version before using it, because SR and TI-LFA options have changed between releases.

title: TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks
text:
The computation in one page
A PLR S protects a resource X: a link S-F, a neighbour node F, or a shared-risk link group. For every destination D whose primary path uses X, S precomputes what to do in the moment X fails, before the IGP has reconverged. TI-LFA’s answer is to send the packet along the path the network will use after convergence, and to add just enough segments that no router on the way loops the packet back toward X while the rest of the network still has the old topology.
The steps, following RFC 9855 sections 4 and 5:

Post-convergence path. Run SPF from S on the topology with X removed. Pick the path to D. This is where traffic will go anyway once the IGP converges, so repairing onto it avoids a second path change.
P-space. P(S, X) is the set of nodes S reaches on its pre-failure shortest paths without any of those paths, including equal-cost splits, crossing X. Sending a packet to a P node with that node’s Node-SID is safe: every router on the way still uses old shortest paths, and none of them cross X.
Extended P-space. P’(S, X) is the union of the P-spaces of S’s neighbours that are not reached through X. S can hand the packet to such a neighbour directly, so the neighbour’s view counts. RFC 9855 section 4.1 restricts this to neighbours on the post-convergence path.
Q-space. Q(D, X) is the set of nodes whose shortest paths to D do not cross X. Once a packet reaches a Q node, plain shortest-path forwarding toward D is safe.
Pick P and Q. Intersect both sets with the post-convergence path. Take P as the deepest P node along the path and Q as the first Q node at or after P.
Build the RL. If P is Q, one Node-SID (or nothing at all if P is the next hop). If P and Q are adjacent, Node-SID(P) plus Adj-SID(P-Q). If they are further apart, Node-SID(P) plus Adj-SIDs along the path to Q. RFC 9855 leaves shorter encodings of the P-to-Q stretch to implementations (section 5.4).

The four repair forms match the four subsections of RFC 9855 section 5:









Form
When
RL
Older technique it resembles




Direct neighbour
next hop on the post-convergence path is in P’ and Q
empty
post-convergence LFA


PQ node
a remote node is in both P’ and Q
Node-SID(PQ)
remote LFA tunnel


P and Q adjacent
P and Q are neighbours on the path
Node-SID(P), Adj-SID(P-Q)
directed LFA (DLFA)


Distant P and Q
gap between P and Q
Node-SID(P), Adj-SIDs to Q
none: this is what only SR can express



 PLR S                 post-convergence path                       D
   o-----o-----o-------o=========o=========o-------o-----o
         ^             ^                   ^
         |             P (deepest node     Q (first node whose
         |               S can reach on      own path to D avoids X)
     next hop            old paths)
                 <-- Node-SID(P) -->< Adj-SIDs P..Q ><-- shortest path -->
Two properties make this “topology independent”. First, the RL can always be built if the post-convergence path exists, because Adj-SIDs can pin every hop if needed. Second, the repair follows the post-convergence path, so when the IGP converges the traffic does not move again.

title: TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks
section: From a repair list to labels
text:
From a repair list to labels
On SR-MPLS (RFC 8660), segments become labels:

A Node-SID is advertised as an index. Each router turns it into a label by adding the index to its own Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB) base. With the same SRGB everywhere (the common and recommended deployment), Node-SID index 5 is label 16005 on every router when the SRGB starts at 16000.
An Adj-SID is a local label that means “pop and send out of this specific adjacency”. It is only meaningful on the router that allocated it. The lab gives each node its own block (24100s for the first node, 24200s for the second and so on) so you can see whose label is whose.

The packet arriving at S already carries an active segment, typically Node-SID(D). RFC 9855 section 7.1 says what to do with it:

If the active segment is a Node-SID signalled with PHP, and the RL ends with an Adj-SID that terminates on D’s penultimate node, pop the active segment. The last Adj-SID delivers the packet to the router that would have popped it anyway.
Otherwise pop and re-push the active segment using the label value in Q’s SRGB, then push the RL on top. With a uniform SRGB the value does not change.

So the label depth on the repaired packet is the RL length plus zero or one. That depth is what has to fit the MSD the PLR can push, which routers advertise in the IGP (RFC 8491 for IS-IS, RFC 8476 for OSPF). Most routers push only a handful of labels at line rate, so the RL length is an operational constraint, not just an elegance metric. RFC 9855 section 3 makes the point directly: an RL made only of Adj-SIDs always works but can be too long for hardware.

title: TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks
text:
The lab
Three files. tilfa.py is the model: a topology class with ECMP-aware Dijkstra, the P/Q-space computations, the RL builder and the label rules. rfc-figures.py reproduces RFC 9855 Figures 1 and 2. coverage.py runs every PLR against every destination on four topologies, with link protection of the primary next hop.
The model makes these simplifications, all stated in the code: metrics are symmetric (so the reverse SPF for Q-space equals a forward SPF from D), one path is picked deterministically when the post-convergence path has equal-cost options, the SRGB is uniform, and SRLGs are not modelled.


tilfa.py

"""TI-LFA (RFC 9855) repair lists over SR-MPLS (RFC 8660), computed from a link-state graph.
Standard library only. Metrics are symmetric unless a topology says otherwise."""
import heapq, itertools

class Topo:
    def __init__(self, links, srgb_base=16000):
        self.adj = {}
        for a, b, m in links:
            self.adj.setdefault(a, {})[b] = m
            self.adj.setdefault(b, {})[a] = m
        self.nodes = sorted(self.adj)
        self.index = {n: i + 1 for i, n in enumerate(self.nodes)}      # prefix-SID index per node
        self.srgb = srgb_base
        # Adj-SIDs are local labels; give each node its own block for readability
        self.adj_sid = {}
        for i, n in enumerate(self.nodes):
            for j, nb in enumerate(sorted(self.adj[n])):
                self.adj_sid[(n, nb)] = 24000 + 100 * (i + 1) + j

    def node_label(self, n):
        return self.srgb + self.index[n]

    def spf(self, root, x=None):
        """Dijkstra with ECMP predecessors. x = ('link', a, b) or ('node', n) is removed."""
        dist, preds, heap = {root: 0}, {root: set()}, [(0, root)]
        while heap:
            d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
            if d > dist[u]:
                continue
            for v, m in self.adj[u].items():
                if x and (x[0] == "node" and v == x[1] or x[0] == "link" and {u, v} == {x[1], x[2]}):
                    continue
                nd = d + m
                if nd < dist.get(v, float("inf")):
                    dist[v], preds[v] = nd, {u}
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, v))
                elif nd == dist[v]:
                    preds[v].add(u)
        return dist, preds

    def clean_set(self, root, x):
        """Nodes reachable from root on pre-failure shortest paths, with no ECMP branch through x."""
        dist, preds = self.spf(root)
        tainted = {}
        for v in sorted(dist, key=dist.get):
            if v == root:
                tainted[v] = False
                continue
            t = False
            for p in preds[v]:
                if tainted[p] or (x[0] == "link" and {p, v} == {x[1], x[2]}) or (x[0] == "node" and p == x[1]):
                    t = True
            if x[0] == "node" and v == x[1]:
                t = True
            tainted[v] = t
        return {v for v, t in tainted.items() if not t}

    def p_space(self, s, x):
        return self.clean_set(s, x)

    def ext_p_space(self, s, x, on_path=None):
        """P'(S,X): union of P(N,X) for neighbors N not reached through X (RFC 9855 s2.1, s4.1)."""
        out = set(self.p_space(s, x))
        for n in self.adj[s]:
            if x[0] == "node" and n == x[1] or x[0] == "link" and {s, n} == {x[1], x[2]}:
                continue
            if on_path is not None and n not in on_path:
                continue
            out |= self.clean_set(n, x)
        return out

    def q_space(self, d, x):
        # symmetric metrics: reverse SPF from D equals forward SPF from D
        return self.clean_set(d, x)

    def path(self, s, d, x=None):
        dist, preds = self.spf(s, x)
        if d not in dist:
            return None, None
        hops, v = [d], d
        while v != s:
            v = min(preds[v])            # deterministic tie-break: lowest name
            hops.append(v)
        return hops[::-1], dist[d]

    def repair(self, s, d, x):
        """Return dict describing the TI-LFA repair at PLR s for destination d when x fails."""
        pc, cost = self.path(s, d, x)
        if pc is None:
            return None
        P = self.ext_p_space(s, x, on_path=set(pc))
        Q = self.q_space(d, x)
        p_idx = max(i for i, n in enumerate(pc) if n in P)
        q_idx = next(i for i in range(p_idx, len(pc)) if pc[i] in Q)
        p, q = pc[p_idx], pc[q_idx]
        segs = []
        if p == d:
            pass                                       # D itself is reachable loop-free: the active segment suffices
        elif p_idx > 1:                                  # P is not the first hop: steer to it with its Node-SID
            segs.append(("node", p))
        for a, b in zip(pc[p_idx:q_idx], pc[p_idx + 1:q_idx + 1]) if p != d else ():
            segs.append(("adj", a, b))
        kind = ("empty RL (post-convergence next hop already loop-free)" if not segs else
                "PQ node (one Node-SID)" if p == q else
                "P and Q adjacent (Node-SID + Adj-SID)" if q_idx - p_idx == 1 and p_idx > 1 else
                "Adj-SIDs from P to Q")
        return dict(pc=pc, cost=cost, P=sorted(P & set(pc)), Q=sorted(Q & set(pc)), p=p, q=q,
                    segs=segs, nexthop=pc[1], kind=kind)

    def labels(self, r, d, php=True):
        """SR-MPLS labels on the repaired packet, top first, for active segment Node-SID(d) (RFC 9855 s7.1)."""
        stack = [self.node_label(s[1]) if s[0] == "node" else self.adj_sid[(s[1], s[2])] for s in r["segs"]]
        q, segs = r["q"], r["segs"]
        if segs and q == d:
            return stack                      # the repair itself delivers to D
        if not segs:
            # only the active segment, swapped toward the repair next hop; popped if that hop is D (PHP)
            return [] if php and r["nexthop"] == d else [self.node_label(d)]
        q_path = self.path(q, d)[0]
        if php and segs[-1][0] == "adj" and len(q_path) == 2:
            return stack                      # rule 1: Q is D's penultimate hop, active segment popped
        return stack + [self.node_label(d)]   # rule 2: re-push Node-SID(D) per Q's SRGB (homogeneous here)

def fmt_seg(t, s):
    return f"Node-SID({s[1]})={t.node_label(s[1])}" if s[0] == "node" else f"Adj-SID({s[1]}-{s[2]})={t.adj_sid[(s[1], s[2])]}"

def lfa_ok(t, s, d, f):
    """RFC 5286 link-protecting LFA: some neighbor N != F with dist(N,D) < dist(N,S) + dist(S,D)."""
    ds = t.spf(s)[0]
    for n in t.adj[s]:
        if n == f:
            continue
        dn = t.spf(n)[0]
        if dn[d] < dn[s] + ds[d]:
            # and N's own shortest path must not use S-F (guaranteed by the inequality for link protection)
            return True
    return False

def rlfa_ok(t, s, d, x):
    """RFC 7490 remote LFA: a PQ node exists (extended P-space of S intersect Q-space of D)."""
    return bool(t.ext_p_space(s, x) & t.q_space(d, x))

The P-space test is the part to read closely. clean_set walks the shortest-path DAG from the root in distance order and marks a node tainted if any predecessor on any equal-cost path is tainted, is the failed node, or reaches it over the failed link. That is the strict definition: a node with one clean path and one equal-cost path through X is not in P-space, because the routers on the way may hash the packet onto the bad branch.


rfc-figures.py

"""Reproduce the two worked examples in RFC 9855 (Figures 1 and 2)."""
from tilfa import Topo, fmt_seg

K = 1000
fig1 = Topo([("S", "N1", 1), ("N1", "D", 1), ("S", "N2", 1), ("S", "N3", K), ("N1", "R1", 1),
             ("N1", "R2", 1), ("D", "R3", 1), ("N2", "R1", 1), ("R1", "R2", K), ("R2", "R3", K), ("N3", "R1", K)])
x = ("node", "N1")
print("== RFC 9855 Figure 1: PLR S, destination D, protect node N1")
print("  P(S,N1)            =", sorted(fig1.p_space("S", x) - {"S"}), " strict: S->R1 has an ECMP branch via N1")
print("  P'(S,N1) extended  =", sorted(fig1.ext_p_space("S", x) - {"S", "N1"}), " R1 enters via neighbor N2")
print("  Q(D,N1)            =", sorted(fig1.q_space("D", x) - {"D"}))
r = fig1.repair("S", "D", x)
print("  post-convergence   =", " -> ".join(r["pc"]), f"(cost {r['cost']})")
print("  P on path / Q on path =", r["P"], "/", r["Q"], f"-> P={r['p']} Q={r['q']}")
print("  repair list        =", ", ".join(fmt_seg(fig1, s) for s in r["segs"]), f"| out via {r['nexthop']}")
print("  label stack (PHP)  =", fig1.labels(r, "D", php=True), " top first")
print("  label stack (no PHP)=", fig1.labels(r, "D", php=False))

fig2 = Topo([("S", "R2", 1), ("R2", "R3", 1), ("R3", "R4", 1), ("R4", "R5", 1), ("R5", "D", 1),
             ("R2", "R7", K), ("R3", "R7", 1), ("R3", "R8", 1), ("R7", "R8", K), ("R8", "R4", K),
             ("R7", "R9", K), ("R9", "R10", 1), ("R8", "R10", 1)])
x = ("node", "R3")
print("\n== RFC 9855 Figure 2: PLR R2, destination D, protect node R3")
r = fig2.repair("R2", "D", x)
print("  post-convergence   =", " -> ".join(r["pc"]), f"(cost {r['cost']})")

Figure 1: node protection with distant P and Q
RFC 9855 Figure 1 (metric 1 except the starred links at 1000):
     S --------- N1 --------- D
     *\          | \          |
     * \         |  \         |
     *  \        |   \        |
     *   N2----- R1***R2 *** R3
     *           *
     N3 **********
S protects traffic to D against the failure of node N1. The post-convergence path is S, N2, R1, R2, R3, D at cost 2003: the only way around N1 uses the two expensive links R1-R2 and R2-R3.
The first output line is worth stopping on. The RFC text says P(S, N1) is [N3, N2, R1]. The program says [N2, N3] and puts R1 only in the extended P-space. Both paths S-N1-R1 and S-N2-R1 cost 2, so S’s shortest paths to R1 include an equal-cost split through N1, and the RFC’s own definition (“without any of those paths (including equal-cost path splits) transiting through X”) excludes R1. R1 is still usable as the P node, because S can hand the packet to its neighbour N2 and N2’s only shortest path to R1 is the direct link. That is exactly why the extended P-space exists. The repair list comes out the same as the RFC’s: Node-SID(R1), Adj-SID(R1-R2), Adj-SID(R2-R3), sent out via N2.
Why the Adj-SIDs? R2 is not in Q-space: its shortest path to D goes R2-N1-D at cost 2. If the packet arrived at R2 with only Node-SID(D) on it, R2 would send it straight back toward the failed N1. Only R3 is in Q(D, N1). So the RL has to pin both expensive links.
The two label lines show RFC 9855 section 7.1 in action. R3 is D’s penultimate hop, and the RL ends with an Adj-SID into R3. With PHP, rule 1 applies: the active segment (16001, D’s label) is popped and not re-pushed, so the repaired packet carries three labels. If D’s Node-SID was advertised with the no-PHP flag, rule 2 applies and D’s label goes back on the bottom: four labels.


Figure 2: the P node is the next hop
RFC 9855 Figure 2 (metric 1 except R2-R7, R7-R8, R8-R4 and R7-R9 at 1000):
     S --- R2 --- R3 ---- R4 --- R5 --- D
              *   |  \   *
                * |   \ *
                 R7 ** R8
                  *    |
                  *    |
                 R9 -- R10
R2 protects traffic for D against the failure of R3. The post-convergence path is R2, R7, R8, R4, R5, D. R7 is the deepest P node, and it is R2’s own next hop, so no Node-SID is needed to reach it. Q is R4. The RL is two Adj-SIDs, Adj-SID(R7-R8) and Adj-SID(R8-R4), out via R7, which is exactly the RFC’s answer. R4 is not D’s penultimate hop (R5 is), so rule 2 applies and D’s label 16001 is re-pushed under the RL: three labels.
RFC 9855 uses this figure for a different warning (section 9). If the Adj-SID for R7-R8 is itself protected, and R7-R8 fails during the repair, R7 applies its own repair and the packet gets a second RL. Implementations may prefer unprotected Adj-SIDs in RLs to avoid such double FRR. Fast reroute is for one planned failure. When more fails at once, IGP convergence speed is what saves you.


Coverage: LFA, remote LFA and TI-LFA


coverage.py

"""Coverage of LFA vs remote LFA vs TI-LFA for every PLR, every protected link, every destination."""
import collections
from tilfa import Topo, fmt_seg, lfa_ok, rlfa_ok

def survey(name, t, msd):
    cases = lfa = rlfa = ti = 0
    sizes, over, adj_only = collections.Counter(), [], 0
    for s in t.nodes:
        for d in t.nodes:
            if d == s:
                continue
            pc, _ = t.path(s, d)
            f = pc[1]                                   # primary next hop
            x = ("link", s, f)
            r = t.repair(s, d, x)
            if r is None:
                continue
            cases += 1
            lfa += lfa_ok(t, s, d, f)
            rlfa += lfa_ok(t, s, d, f) or rlfa_ok(t, s, d, x)
            ti += 1
            st = t.labels(r, d)
            sizes[len(st)] += 1
            adj_only = max(adj_only, len(r["pc"]) - 1)     # an Adj-SID for every post-convergence hop
            if len(st) > msd:
                over.append((s, d, f, r, st))
    pct = lambda n: f"{n}/{cases} ({100 * n / cases:.0f}%)"
    print(f"== {name}: {len(t.nodes)} nodes, link protection, {cases} (PLR, destination) pairs")
    print(f"  LFA (RFC 5286)        {pct(lfa)}")
    print(f"  LFA + remote LFA      {pct(rlfa)}")
    print(f"  TI-LFA (RFC 9855)     {pct(ti)}")
    print("  SR labels on the repaired packet:",
          ", ".join(f"{k} labels: {v}" for k, v in sorted(sizes.items())))
    for s, d, f, r, st in over[:3]:
        print(f"  over MSD {msd}: PLR {s} -> {d}, link {s}-{f}: {len(st)} labels {st} via",
              " -> ".join(r["pc"]))
    print(f"  pairs over MSD {msd}: {len(over)}  (deepest TI-LFA stack {max(sizes)}; Adj-SID-only would need up to {adj_only})")

# 1. A plain ring: the classic LFA failure case
ring = Topo([(a, b, 10) for a, b in zip("ABCDEF", "BCDEFA")])
survey("6-node ring, all metrics 10", ring, msd=3)

# 2. The same ring with one expensive link, as you get with a long-haul or a costed-out span
ring2 = Topo([(a, b, 10) for a, b in zip("ABCDEF", "BCDEF")] + [("F", "A", 100)])
survey("6-node ring, F-A metric 100", ring2, msd=3)

# 3. Ring of 8 with one costly span: repairs get deeper
ring8 = Topo([(a, b, 10) for a, b in zip("ABCDEFGH", "BCDEFGH")] + [("H", "A", 100)])
survey("8-node ring, H-A metric 100", ring8, msd=2)

# 4. A small two-plane core with a costed cross-link (well meshed)
core = Topo([("P1", "P2", 10), ("P2", "P3", 10), ("P3", "P4", 10), ("P4", "P1", 10), ("P1", "P3", 15),
             ("PE1", "P1", 10), ("PE1", "P2", 10), ("PE2", "P3", 10), ("PE2", "P4", 10)])
survey("core: 4 P routers + 2 dual-homed PEs", core, msd=3)

r = ring8.repair("C", "E", ("link", "C", "D"))
print("\nWorked case: 8-node ring, PLR C, destination E, protect link C-D")
print("  primary path   ", " -> ".join(ring8.path("C", "E")[0]))
print("  post-converge  ", " -> ".join(r["pc"]), f"(cost {r['cost']})")
print("  P on path      ", r["P"], " Q on path", r["Q"], " kind:", r["kind"])
print("  repair list    ", ", ".join(fmt_seg(ring8, s) for s in r["segs"]), "| out via", r["nexthop"])
print("  label stack    ", ring8.labels(r, "E"), "top first")
print("  LFA? ", lfa_ok(ring8, "C", "E", "D"), "  remote LFA?", lfa_ok(ring8, "C", "E", "D") or rlfa_ok(ring8, "C", "E", ("link", "C", "D")))

lfa_ok is the RFC 5286 link-protection test: a neighbour N other than the primary next hop is a loop-free alternate for D if dist(N, D) < dist(N, S) + dist(S, D), meaning N’s own shortest path to D does not come back through S. rlfa_ok is the remote LFA condition from RFC 7490: there is some node in both S’s extended P-space and D’s Q-space, to which S could tunnel the packet. Remote LFA as deployed uses a targeted LDP session to that PQ node; with SR the same node is reached with one Node-SID.

title: TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks
text:
Reading the results
Rings are where plain LFA fails. On the six-node ring with equal metrics, only 6 of 30 (PLR, destination) pairs have an LFA. In an even ring, a neighbour’s shortest path to most destinations runs back through the PLR. Remote LFA fixes all of them: there is always a node half-way round that is in both spaces.
One expensive span breaks remote LFA too. Give one link of the same ring metric 100 (a long-haul span, or a link someone costed out) and remote LFA adds nothing over LFA: 10 of 30 either way. The expensive span pushes the P-space and Q-space apart so that no single node is in both. TI-LFA still covers all 30, and two of the repairs need three labels.
Bigger rings make deeper stacks. On the eight-node ring with one costly span, TI-LFA again covers 56 of 56, but 12 pairs need three labels. The printed examples are all PLR C losing link C-D: the post-convergence path goes the whole way round, C, B, A, H and on. A is the deepest node C can reach on old paths without crossing C-D, and H is the first node whose own path to the destination avoids C-D. Pinning the costly A-H link takes Node-SID(A) and Adj-SID(A-H), and the destination’s label sits underneath. If this PLR could only push two labels, those 12 pairs would be unprotected. Pinning every hop with Adj-SIDs instead would need up to seven.
Well-meshed cores barely need SR. The four-router core with two dual-homed PEs has 100% LFA coverage and every repair is a plain swap toward a different next hop (one label: the destination’s). That matches field experience: TI-LFA’s value shows on rings, long chains and sparse regional networks, not on dense fabrics. Run the coverage numbers on your own topology before arguing about it.
The worked case. The last block is C protecting link C-D toward E on the eight-node ring. Neither LFA nor remote LFA works. TI-LFA sends the packet to B with labels [16001, 24101, 16005]: B forwards on A’s Node-SID (and pops it, being A’s penultimate hop under PHP), A pops its own Adj-SID 24101 and sends the packet over A-H, and H forwards on E’s label along H, G, F, E. When C’s own SPF finishes, C installs the post-convergence route and the repair is withdrawn; because the repair already followed that path, traffic does not move.

show isis route ... backup lists the backup next hop and the label stack per prefix. Feed the same topology and metrics into tilfa.py and compare. Differences usually come from one of: a different tie-break among equal-cost post-convergence paths, the implementation shortening the P-to-Q stretch with an extra Node-SID, node protection versus link protection, or a non-uniform SRGB.

title: TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks
text:
Gotchas

Equal-cost paths shrink P-space. A node reachable over two equal paths, one through X, is not in P-space. The RFC 9855 Figure 1 text is loose on this; the lab shows the strict result and why the extended P-space still finds R1. If your mental calculation disagrees with the router, check for ECMP first.
Node protection needs more labels than link protection. Protecting against F’s failure removes all of F’s links, so the post-convergence path is longer and Q is further away. Some platforms fall back to link protection if no node-protecting repair fits (FRR’s link-fallback keyword).
MSD is per platform, and per line card. A repair the IGP happily computes is useless if the hardware cannot push it. Watch for “unprotected” counters in the FRR summary and vendor equivalents after enabling node protection.
Non-uniform SRGBs change labels mid-path. Rule 2 re-pushes the active segment with the label from Q’s SRGB. With different SRGBs per router, a label that is correct at S is wrong at Q. Keep one SRGB network-wide unless you have a migration reason.
PHP decides whether the destination label is on the packet. The same repair can be three or four labels depending on the no-PHP and explicit-null flags of the destination’s Node-SID. Count both when sizing MSD.
The repair is only as fast as detection. TI-LFA is precomputed, but it starts when S notices the failure. Loss of light is fast; a silent failure behind a media converter needs BFD.
Microloops are a separate problem. TI-LFA protects traffic until S converges. Other routers converge in a different order and can loop briefly. Microloop avoidance (RFC 8333 for local convergence) and ordered updates are complementary.
Policies and Flex-Algo. TI-LFA follows IGP shortest paths. Traffic on an SR Policy or a Flexible Algorithm may be repaired off its constraint unless the implementation computes repairs per algorithm (RFC 9855 section 8).
SRLGs are invisible to plain SPF. Two links in the same conduit fail together. Without SRLG-aware TI-LFA, the computed repair can use the other link in the same duct.

title: IGP Flexible Algorithm (RFC 9350): Constraint Planes Without RSVP-TE
text:
IGP Flexible Algorithm (RFC 9350): Constraint Planes Without RSVP-TE
You want traffic for one service to avoid high-delay satellite hops, traffic for another to stay exclusively on the blue physical plane, and traffic for a third to steer around a shared fibre duct. Historically, you had two choices: build separate physical or virtual topologies with Multi-Topology Routing, or deploy RSVP-TE with Constrained Shortest Path First (CSPF) and maintain thousands of signalled LSP states across your core. Neither scales cleanly when all you really want is a handful of distinct forwarding planes with different rules for what “shortest” and “usable” mean.
IGP Flexible Algorithm (Flex-Algo), specified in RFC 9350, solves this inside the link-state IGP itself. Instead of signalling point-to-point tunnels from every ingress to every egress, every router runs Shortest Path First (SPF) over a pruned view of the topology using a chosen metric and a shared set of link constraints. Each algorithm produces its own routing table and its own Segment Routing forwarding state—a dedicated Prefix-SID label in SR-MPLS or a dedicated locator in SRv6—so a packet’s outer label or IPv6 destination address selects the entire constraint plane hop by hop.
Because every router computes the same pruned SPF independently, loop freedom depends on strict consensus. Every router participating in an algorithm must agree on the exact Flexible Algorithm Definition (FAD), apply the exact same pruning rules in the exact same order, and drop out completely if it cannot honour any part of the definition.

title: IGP Flexible Algorithm (RFC 9350): Constraint Planes Without RSVP-TE
text:
Learning goals

Explain how Flex-Algo creates isolated forwarding planes using IGP-computed SPF trees and Segment Routing identifiers without RSVP-TE signalling state.
Decode and construct an IS-IS Flexible Algorithm Definition (FAD) sub-TLV (type 26) inside Router CAPABILITY TLV 242, including metric types, calculation types, priorities, and constraint sub-TLVs.
Trace the RFC 9350 Section 5.3 FAD election rules and predict how priority changes, tie-breaks, or withdrawn advertisements alter the active plane.
Apply the RFC 9350 Section 13 link-pruning order and node-participation checks to determine reachability, path selection, and failure modes.
Map SR-MPLS Prefix-SID indices and SRGB bases to per-algorithm forwarding labels, and describe how TI-LFA repairs stay within an algorithm’s constraints.
Configure and audit basic Flex-Algo parameters in FRR isisd (from documentation) while accounting for implementation limits around metric types and flags.

title: IGP Flexible Algorithm (RFC 9350): Constraint Planes Without RSVP-TE
text:
Why constraint planes without RSVP-TE
When you run plain IS-IS or OSPF, every router computes a single shortest-path tree per destination based on the standard IGP metric. That single tree is algorithm 0. As the SRv6 and SR-MPLS TI-LFA chapters earlier in this part showed, Segment Routing replaces LDP and RSVP-TE label distribution with IGP-advertised Prefix-SIDs and Adjacency-SIDs, and TI-LFA computes loop-free backup paths using the same link-state database. Yet by default, all of that still runs on a single topology and a single metric.
RSVP-TE solved traffic engineering by moving path computation to the headend. Each ingress router ran CSPF against a Traffic Engineering Database (TED), found a path that satisfied bandwidth, affinity, and SRLG constraints, and signalled an explicit-route LSP with PATH and RESV messages. Every transit router had to store soft state for every LSP passing through it, refresh that state periodically, and tear down and re-signal tunnels whenever a link flapped. In a full mesh of \(N\) edge routers, that meant \(O(N^2)\) tunnels—and \(O(N^2)\) state on core P routers that had no business knowing about edge-to-edge service SLAs.
Flex-Algo takes the opposite trade-off. You do not get per-flow bandwidth reservation or arbitrary explicit hop lists; for those, you still need an SR Policy with a Segment Routing Traffic Engineering (SR-TE) stack or a central PCE. What you do get is up to 128 topology-wide constraint planes computed natively by the IGP with zero transit signalling state:
RSVP-TE (Headend CSPF + Signalling)
  PE1 --[PATH/RESV state]--> P1 --[PATH/RESV state]--> P3 --[PATH/RESV state]--> PE2
  State on P1, P3: O(N^2) LSPs

Flex-Algo (Distributed IGP SPF + SR Forwarding)
  Algo 0   (IGP metric):      PE1 ---> P1 ---> SAT ---> PE2   (Label 16002)
  Algo 128 (Min Delay):       PE1 ---> P1 ---> P3  ---> PE2   (Label 16102)
  Algo 133 (No SAT/SRLG 103): PE1 ---> P2 ---> P4  ---> PE2   (its own Prefix-SID)
  State on P1..P4: O(Algorithms * Prefixes), zero per-tunnel state
Every router in the area already holds the full link-state database (LSDB). If every router agrees on the rules for Algorithm 128—say, “prune links without a delay metric, then run SPF using minimum unidirectional link delay”—then every router computes a loop-free shortest-path tree toward every destination advertising Algorithm 128. Packets entering at PE1 simply receive the label or locator bound to PE2 in Algorithm 128. Transit routers never inspect service intent or run CSPF on demand; they do a standard MPLS label swap or IPv6 longest-prefix match in that algorithm’s forwarding table.
