title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
A BGP route says two things: where (the prefix) and through whom (the next hop). For years the address family of the prefix fixed the family of the next hop: IPv4 prefixes got IPv4 next hops. RFC 8950 (which replaced RFC 5549 in 2020) breaks that link. An IPv4 prefix can carry an IPv6 next hop, so a link, or a whole core, can run with IPv6 addresses only and still forward IPv4. This is what makes “BGP unnumbered” fabrics work. Two routers peer over IPv6 link-local addresses and swap IPv4 routes, and nobody hands out a /31 per link. This chapter encodes the two wire pieces by hand: the Extended Next Hop Encoding capability and an MP_REACH_NLRI with a 32-octet next hop. It then builds the forwarding result in a Linux network namespace, an IPv4 route via inet6, and shows that the kernel finds the next hop’s MAC address with IPv6 neighbour discovery, not ARP. Last comes the FRR configuration for a two-router containerlab lab.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
Learning goals

Say why a next hop’s address family doesn’t have to match the prefix’s
Encode and decode capability code 5 and its <NLRI AFI, NLRI SAFI, Nexthop AFI> triples
Read an MP_REACH_NLRI and use the next-hop length to decide whether the next hop is IPv4, IPv6 or VPN-IPv6
Know what changed from RFC 5549: VPN next hops are 24 or 48 octets with a zero RD, and IPv4 multicast VPN (1/129) is allowed
Install and inspect an IPv4 route with an IPv6 gateway on Linux, and see neighbour discovery resolve it
Configure FRR for extended next hop, on both interface (link-local) peers and global-address peers

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
Thesis
A next hop is not a destination. It is a neighbour to hand the frame to. A router forwarding an IPv4 packet needs only a layer-2 address for that neighbour, and IPv6 neighbour discovery gives one as well as ARP does. RFC 8950 is the BGP half of that idea: a way to say “IPv6 next hop” for IPv4 routes, and a capability that makes sure the peer understands it before you say it.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
Mental model



RFC 8950 on one link: the capability in OPEN, the MP_REACH_NLRI layout, how the receiver decides the next-hop family, and the IPv4 route the kernel installs


Keep three layers apart:

Negotiation. In OPEN, each speaker lists the NLRI families for which it accepts an IPv6 next hop. No capability, no IPv6 next hop: RFC 8950 §4 says a speaker MUST NOT send one until the peer has advertised support for that AFI/SAFI.
Encoding. The IPv4 route moves out of the classic IPv4-only UPDATE fields into the multiprotocol attribute MP_REACH_NLRI (RFC 4760). That attribute has its own next-hop field with an explicit length.
Forwarding. The RIB entry 198.51.100.0/24 via fe80::2 needs a data plane that can resolve an IPv6 gateway for an IPv4 route. On Linux, that is the RTA_VIA route attribute.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
Concepts

Why the classic NEXT_HOP can’t do it
The original BGP-4 UPDATE (RFC 4271) carries IPv4 prefixes in its NLRI field and the next hop in the NEXT_HOP path attribute, type 3. That attribute is exactly four octets: an IPv4 address. There is no room for 16 octets. Multiprotocol BGP (RFC 4760) added MP_REACH_NLRI, type 14. It carries AFI, SAFI, length of next hop, next hop, reserved octet, NLRI, so any family can say any next hop as long as the receiver knows how to read the length. RFC 8950 uses MP_REACH_NLRI with AFI 1 (IPv4) and says which lengths are legal.


The length rule (RFC 8950 §3)
The receiver decides the next hop’s family from the Length of Next Hop Address field:



NLRI AFI/SAFI
Length
Next hop is




1/1 unicast, 1/2 multicast, 1/4 labeled
4
IPv4 (the old case)


1/1, 1/2, 1/4
16
IPv6 global


1/1, 1/2, 1/4
32
IPv6 global, then IPv6 link-local


1/128 VPN, 1/129 VPN multicast
12
VPN-IPv4 (8-octet RD + IPv4)


1/128, 1/129
24
VPN-IPv6, RD set to zero


1/128, 1/129
48
VPN-IPv6 global + VPN-IPv6 link-local, RDs zero



The 32-octet form follows RFC 2545 §3, the same rule IPv6 BGP uses: global address first, link-local second. A router that shares the link uses the link-local address to forward.


What changed from RFC 5549
RFC 8950 §2 lists two changes. First, for VPN-IPv4 (1/128), RFC 5549 had said the next hop was a plain 16- or 32-octet IPv6 address. Deployed code actually sent a VPN-IPv6 address, 24 or 48 octets with a zero route distinguisher, matching how VPNv4 over IPv4 and VPNv6 over IPv6 already worked (erratum 5253). RFC 8950 writes down what the implementations did. Second, IPv4 multicast VPN (1/129) gets the same treatment. Plain IPv4 unicast didn’t change, so a 5549-era unicast speaker and an 8950 speaker interoperate.


The capability (RFC 8950 §4)
Capability code 5, Extended Next Hop Encoding, rides in the OPEN message’s Capabilities optional parameter (RFC 5492). Its value is a list of 6-octet triples:
+--------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+
| NLRI AFI (2 octets)| NLRI SAFI (2 octets)| Nexthop AFI (2 octets)|  ...repeated
+--------------------+---------------------+-----------------------+
RFC 8950 allows only NLRI AFI 1, NLRI SAFI 1, 2, 4, 128 or 129, and Nexthop AFI 2. The capability doesn’t enable an address family. That is still the job of the Multiprotocol Extensions capability (code 1). It only says how a family that is already enabled may encode its next hop. It isn’t meant for families that already allow both next-hop types. IPv6 prefixes with IPv4 next hops, for instance, have their own older mechanism (RFC 4798, RFC 4659).


Route reflectors and mixed peers (RFC 8950 §5)
A route reflector passes the next hop on unchanged, and RFC 8950 says its encoding MUST NOT change. If one client can’t take IPv6 next hops (it didn’t send capability 5 for that family), the reflector can’t send it that route at all. It doesn’t translate. In practice, every client of a reflector that carries RFC 8950 routes needs the capability.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
section: Lab 1: the bytes, by hand (run here)
text:
Lab 1: the bytes, by hand (run here)
enh.py builds the capability and an MP_REACH_NLRI for two IPv4 prefixes with a global + link-local IPv6 next hop. It then decodes them the way a receiver would, using only the length to pick the next-hop family. It is plain Python 3, standard library only.
"""Encode and decode the RFC 8950 pieces of a BGP session by hand."""
import ipaddress, struct

AFI = {1: "IPv4", 2: "IPv6"}
SAFI = {1: "unicast", 2: "multicast", 4: "labeled", 128: "VPN", 129: "VPN multicast"}

def ext_nh_capability(triples):
    """Capability code 5: a list of <NLRI AFI, NLRI SAFI, Nexthop AFI>, 2 octets each."""
    value = b"".join(struct.pack("!HHH", a, s, n) for a, s, n in triples)
    return struct.pack("!BB", 5, len(value)) + value

def decode_capability(blob):
    code, length = blob[0], blob[1]
    assert code == 5, code
    out = []
    for i in range(2, 2 + length, 6):
        a, s, n = struct.unpack("!HHH", blob[i:i + 6])
        out.append(f"NLRI {AFI[a]}/{SAFI[s]} may use an {AFI[n]} next hop")
    return out

def mp_reach_ipv4_unicast(next_hops, prefixes):
    """MP_REACH_NLRI (type 14) for AFI 1 / SAFI 1 with one or two IPv6 next hops."""
    nh = b"".join(ipaddress.IPv6Address(h).packed for h in next_hops)
    nlri = b""
    for p in prefixes:
        net = ipaddress.IPv4Network(p)
        nbytes = (net.prefixlen + 7) // 8
        nlri += bytes([net.prefixlen]) + net.network_address.packed[:nbytes]
    value = struct.pack("!HBB", 1, 1, len(nh)) + nh + b"\x00" + nlri
    # flags 0x80 = optional, non-transitive; type code 14
    return struct.pack("!BBB", 0x80, 14, len(value)) + value

def decode_mp_reach(attr):
    flags, typ, length = attr[0], attr[1], attr[2]
    v = attr[3:3 + length]
    afi, safi, nhlen = struct.unpack("!HBB", v[:4])
    nh = v[4:4 + nhlen]
    pos = 4 + nhlen + 1          # skip the reserved octet
    prefixes = []
    while pos < len(v):
        plen = v[pos]; nbytes = (plen + 7) // 8
        raw = v[pos + 1:pos + 1 + nbytes] + b"\x00" * (4 - nbytes)
        prefixes.append(f"{ipaddress.IPv4Address(raw)}/{plen}")
        pos += 1 + nbytes
    # RFC 8950 section 3: the length alone says which protocol the next hop is
    kinds = {4: "IPv4", 16: "IPv6 global", 32: "IPv6 global + link-local",
             12: "VPN-IPv4", 24: "VPN-IPv6 (RD 0)", 48: "VPN-IPv6 global + link-local"}
    hops = []
    if nhlen in (16, 32):
        hops = [str(ipaddress.IPv6Address(nh[i:i + 16])) for i in range(0, nhlen, 16)]
    return {"afi/safi": f"{afi}/{safi}", "nh length": nhlen,
            "nh kind": kinds.get(nhlen, "invalid for this AFI/SAFI"),
            "next hops": hops, "nlri": prefixes}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cap = ext_nh_capability([(1, 1, 2), (1, 128, 2)])
    print("capability bytes:", cap.hex(" "))
    for line in decode_capability(cap):
        print("  ", line)

    attr = mp_reach_ipv4_unicast(["2001:db8:12::2", "fe80::2"],
                                 ["198.51.100.0/24", "203.0.113.128/25"])
    print("MP_REACH_NLRI bytes:", attr.hex(" "))
    for k, val in decode_mp_reach(attr).items():
        print(f"   {k:10} {val}")

    single = mp_reach_ipv4_unicast(["2001:db8:12::2"], ["10.0.0.0/8"])
    d = decode_mp_reach(single)
    print("global-only next hop:", d["nh length"], "octets ->", d["nh kind"], d["next hops"])
$ python3 enh.py
capability bytes: 05 0c 00 01 00 01 00 02 00 01 00 80 00 02
   NLRI IPv4/unicast may use an IPv6 next hop
   NLRI IPv4/VPN may use an IPv6 next hop
MP_REACH_NLRI bytes: 80 0e 2e 00 01 01 20 20 01 0d b8 00 12 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 02 fe 80 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 02 00 18 c6 33 64 19 cb 00 71 80
   afi/safi   1/1
   nh length  32
   nh kind    IPv6 global + link-local
   next hops  ['2001:db8:12::2', 'fe80::2']
   nlri       ['198.51.100.0/24', '203.0.113.128/25']
global-only next hop: 16 octets -> IPv6 global ['2001:db8:12::2']
Read the capability bytes left to right: 05 is the code, 0c the length (12 octets, two triples), then 00 01 00 01 00 02 (IPv4 unicast may use an IPv6 next hop) and 00 01 00 80 00 02 (VPN-IPv4, SAFI 128 = 0x80). In the attribute, 80 0e 2e is flags (optional, non-transitive), type 14, and a value length of 46. Then come AFI 00 01 and SAFI 01, and 20, the next-hop length: 32. After it sit the two 16-octet addresses, the reserved 00, and the NLRI: 18 c6 33 64 is /24 198.51.100 and 19 cb 00 71 80 is /25 203.0.113.128. Nothing in the attribute says “IPv6” outright. The length of 32 is the whole signal.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
section: Lab 2: an IPv4 route with an IPv6 gateway (run here, no sudo)
text:
Lab 2: an IPv4 route with an IPv6 gateway (run here, no sudo)
This is what bgpd hands the kernel once it accepts such a route. unshare -rn gives an unprivileged user a private network namespace in which they’re root, so the lab touches nothing on the host. A veth pair stands in for the link, and v0 gets no IPv4 address at all. (A dummy interface would be simpler, but loading its kernel module needs real root, so a veth pair it is.) nh.py sends one UDP datagram to 198.51.100.7 and listens on the far end, v1, for whatever v0 sends to find the next hop.
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -rn sh lab.sh   (a private network namespace, no sudo)
ip link add v0 type veth peer name v1
ip link set lo up; ip link set v0 up; ip link set v1 up
ip addr add 192.0.2.1/32 dev lo            # a source address for our own packets
ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:12::1/64 dev v0 nodad
ip route add 198.51.100.0/24 via inet6 2001:db8:12::2 dev v0
echo "--- ipv4 routes";  ip -4 route show
echo "--- route lookup"; ip -4 route get 198.51.100.7
echo "--- ipv4 addresses on v0"; ip -4 addr show dev v0
sleep 1
python3 nh.py                              # send one UDP datagram, watch v1
echo "--- ipv6 neighbours on v0"; ip -6 neigh show dev v0
echo "--- ipv4 neighbours on v0"; ip -4 neigh show dev v0
"""Send one IPv4 datagram to 198.51.100.7 and report how v0 resolves the next hop."""
import socket, struct

cap = socket.socket(socket.AF_PACKET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.htons(0x0003))  # all frames
cap.bind(("v1", 0))          # the far end of the veth pair sees what v0 transmits
cap.settimeout(3)

socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM).sendto(b"hello", ("198.51.100.7", 9))

while True:
    try:
        f = cap.recv(2048)
    except socket.timeout:
        print("nothing seen"); break
    src, ethertype = f[6:12], struct.unpack("!H", f[12:14])[0]
    if ethertype == 0x0806:
        print(f"{src.hex(':')} sent an ARP request"); break
    # IPv6 (0x86dd), next header 58 = ICMPv6, ICMPv6 type 135 = neighbour solicitation
    if ethertype == 0x86dd and len(f) >= 78 and f[20] == 58 and f[54] == 135:
        target = socket.inet_ntop(socket.AF_INET6, f[62:78])
        if not target.startswith("fe80"):          # skip the link-local DAD noise
            print(f"{src.hex(':')} -> {f[:6].hex(':')} ICMPv6 neighbour solicitation"
                  f" for {target}")
            break
$ unshare -rn sh lab.sh
--- ipv4 routes
198.51.100.0/24 via inet6 2001:db8:12::2 dev v0 
--- route lookup
198.51.100.7 via inet6 2001:db8:12::2 dev v0 src 192.0.2.1 uid 0 
    cache 
--- ipv4 addresses on v0
ce:c8:07:ce:15:7e -> 33:33:ff:00:00:02 ICMPv6 neighbour solicitation for 2001:db8:12::2
--- ipv6 neighbours on v0
2001:db8:12::2 INCOMPLETE 
--- ipv4 neighbours on v0
Three things to notice:

ip route takes via inet6 <addr> on an IPv4 route. iproute2 sends this as the RTA_VIA attribute, and Linux has accepted IPv6 gateways for IPv4 routes since kernel 5.2. This run used kernel 6.12 with iproute2 6.15.
v0 has no IPv4 address, and the lookup still works. The source address, 192.0.2.1, comes from the loopback, the way a router uses its loopback /32 in an unnumbered fabric.
To send the IPv4 datagram, the kernel sent an ICMPv6 neighbour solicitation to the solicited-node multicast group of 2001:db8:12::2 (33:33:ff:00:00:02). The IPv4 neighbour table stays empty, because no ARP is involved. (INCOMPLETE is expected: nobody owns ::2 on this veth.)

In a real fabric, bgpd installs the link-local form, via inet6 fe80::2 dev eth1. A link-local gateway is only meaningful together with the interface, which is why the route always names the device.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
section: Lab 3: two FRR routers in containerlab (from the docs, not run here)
text:
Lab 3: two FRR routers in containerlab (from the docs, not run here)
Running containers needs a container runtime and root, which this book’s build box doesn’t have. The topology below follows the containerlab topology-file format, and the FRR commands come from the FRR BGP documentation. Run it yourself and compare against the checks below.
rfc8950.clab.yml:
name: rfc8950
topology:
  nodes:
    r1:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - r1/daemons:/etc/frr/daemons
        - r1/frr.conf:/etc/frr/frr.conf
    r2:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - r2/daemons:/etc/frr/daemons
        - r2/frr.conf:/etc/frr/frr.conf
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth1", "r2:eth1"]
r1/daemons sets bgpd=yes (zebra always runs). r1/frr.conf, an interface peer with no addresses on eth1 at all:
frr defaults datacenter
!
interface lo
 ip address 192.0.2.1/32
!
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 192.0.2.1
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor eth1 interface remote-as external
 !
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 192.0.2.1/32
 exit-address-family
!
r2 is the same with AS 65002, router ID and loopback 198.51.100.1, and network 198.51.100.0/24 backed by a static ip route 198.51.100.0/24 blackhole.
What FRR does for you here, per its documentation:

neighbor eth1 interface peers over the IPv6 link-local address it learns from the other side’s router advertisements. bgpd asks zebra to send RAs on that interface (the bgp ipv6-auto-ra behaviour, on by default).
On a link-local peering, FRR turns capability extended-nexthop on automatically. For a peer reached by a global IPv6 address you set it yourself: neighbor 2001:db8:12::2 capability extended-nexthop. That’s what lets bgpd install IPv4 routes with IPv6 next hops when the interfaces have no IPv4.

Checks to run after containerlab deploy -t rfc8950.clab.yml:
docker exec clab-rfc8950-r1 vtysh -c "show bgp neighbors eth1"   # look for the Extended nexthop line: advertised and received, IPv4 Unicast
docker exec clab-rfc8950-r1 vtysh -c "show ip route bgp"         # 198.51.100.0/24 via fe80::..., eth1
docker exec clab-rfc8950-r1 ip -4 route show proto bgp           # ... via inet6 fe80::... dev eth1
docker exec clab-rfc8950-r1 ip -4 neigh show dev eth1            # empty: no ARP on this link
If the neighbour output shows the capability advertised but not received, the peer won’t accept IPv6 next hops for IPv4, and per RFC 8950 §4 your router must not send them. On a global-address peer, the usual cause is a missing capability extended-nexthop on the far side.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
Case: an unnumbered leaf-spine
A leaf-spine fabric with 64 leaves and 4 spines has 256 links. Numbered with IPv4 /31s, that’s 256 /31s to allocate, document and keep consistent in two configs per link. With RFC 8950 and interface peering, each switch needs one IPv4 /32 on its loopback (for sourcing and management) and nothing on its links: IPv6 link-local addresses come up on their own. The price is a hard dependency on IPv6 being enabled on every fabric port. You also have to watch three things:

Traceroute replies come from the loopback (or whatever the vendor picks), because the link has no IPv4 address to answer from.
Out-of-band tools that assume an IPv4 next hop in BGP (old collectors, some BMP pipelines) may print the IPv6 next hop oddly, or drop the route.
Every reflector client needs the capability (RFC 8950 §5), so one old box can quietly miss routes.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
The trap
“The session is up, so the routes will be fine.” Capability 5 is negotiated per family, and only if both sides advertise it. A global-address IPv6 session with IPv4 unicast activated, but no capability extended-nexthop on one end, comes up fine and exchanges IPv6 routes. The IPv4 routes then fail to install, or are never sent. Check the capability line in the neighbour output, not just Established.
Second trap: the 32-octet next hop is global then link-local. A hand-built decoder, or a filter that reads only the first 16 octets, gets the global address. That’s fine for a multihop peer, but on a shared link the router actually forwards to the link-local one.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
The boring rule
Peer over interfaces where you can, so the capability is on automatically. Turn it on explicitly for global-address IPv6 peers that carry IPv4. Then verify three things: capability received, the IPv4 route installed via inet6, and the IPv4 neighbour table empty on the link.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
Try this

Change mp_reach_ipv4_unicast in enh.py to send a 24-octet next hop for AFI/SAFI 1/1. What does decode_mp_reach call it? What should a real receiver do with it? (RFC 8950 §3 and RFC 7606 on malformed attributes.)
Add a third triple, (2, 1, 1): IPv6 unicast with an IPv4 next hop. Why does RFC 8950 §4 rule it out?
In Lab 2, add 2001:db8:12::2/64 on v1 and re-run. What changes in ip -6 neigh, and why does nh.py now see a different frame?
Re-run Lab 2 with fe80::2 as the gateway. Why does ip route add 198.51.100.0/24 via inet6 fe80::2 fail without dev v0?

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
Next
Use this with route reflectors (RFC 8950 §5): a reflector won’t translate next-hop encodings for a client that lacks the capability.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
Verification

enh.py was run with Python 3 (standard library only). The capability and MP_REACH_NLRI bytes and decodes shown are its real output.
Lab 2 (lab.sh + nh.py) was run unprivileged with unshare -rn on Linux 6.12 with iproute2 6.15. The routes, the lookup, the neighbour-solicitation capture and the neighbour tables are genuine output. MAC addresses are random per run.
Lab 3 (containerlab + FRR) was not run: it needs a container runtime and root. It is written from the containerlab and FRR documentation, and the expected output is described, not pasted.

title: IPv4 Routes over IPv6 Next Hops: BGP Extended Next Hop (RFC 8950)
text:
Sources

RFC 8950, Advertising IPv4 Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) with an IPv6 Next Hop: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8950. §2 changes from RFC 5549, §3 next-hop lengths, §4 capability, §5 operations.
RFC 4760, Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4 (MP_REACH_NLRI): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4760
RFC 5492, Capabilities Advertisement with BGP-4: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5492
RFC 2545, Use of BGP-4 Multiprotocol Extensions for IPv6 Inter-Domain Routing (global + link-local next hop): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2545
RFC 4271, A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (NEXT_HOP attribute): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4271
IANA, BGP Capability Codes (code 5): https://www.iana.org/assignments/capability-codes/
FRR documentation, BGP (capability extended-nexthop, interface peers, bgp ipv6-auto-ra): https://docs.frrouting.org/en/latest/bgp.html
containerlab documentation, topology definition: https://containerlab.dev/manual/topo-def-file/
iproute2 ip-route(8) (via [ FAMILY ] ADDRESS): https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-route.8.html

title: IS-IS Basics
text: IS-IS Basics

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
Learning goals

Place IS-IS next to OSPF as a second link-state IGP: LSPs, flooding, SPF, but a different addressing and level model.
Read a NET (area + system ID + NSEL) and choose level-1, level-2 or level-1-2 on purpose.
Write a minimal FRR isisd configuration for a point-to-point triangle, including wide metrics and IPv4/IPv6.
Know the operational traps: mismatched levels, narrow versus wide metrics, the overload bit, and hello authentication that drops adjacencies.

Version note: FRR and Containerlab/netlab were not installed on the writing host, and no IS-IS adjacency was formed (no root, no installs). Commands, defaults and configuration syntax are taken from FRR’s current isisd documentation, ISO 10589, RFC 1195 and RFC 5308, and from netlab’s IS-IS module listing. Run the lab on your Containerlab or netlab host and treat the “expected” show output as a checklist, not as a capture from this machine.
OSPF Basics already covers link-state versus distance-vector, areas, cost and a triangle lab. This chapter does not repeat that pedagogy; it maps the same ideas onto IS-IS.

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
Why another link-state IGP?
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is specified in ISO 10589. RFC 1195 added IPv4 (“integrated IS-IS”); RFC 5308 describes IPv6. Like OSPF, each router floods a link-state database and runs SPF. Unlike OSPF:

Packets are not encapsulated in IP. IS-IS PDUs are exchanged directly over the link (on Ethernet, as an 802.3 / 802.2 LLC frame to the AllIS and AllL1/AllL2 multicast addresses). A broken IP stack can still form an IS-IS adjacency. A capture filter is isis or clns, not ip proto 89.
Addressing of the protocol itself is ISO: each router has a NET, not an OSPF router-id plus area.
The two-level hierarchy is level-1 (inside an area) and level-2 (the backbone). A router is L1, L2, or L1/L2. There is no named “area 0” that every ABR must touch in the OSPF sense; the backbone is the set of L2 adjacencies.
Information is carried in TLVs, which is why IPv6, TE, SR and SRv6 were added without changing the core FSM.

ISPs and large fabrics often prefer IS-IS for that extensibility and for the fact that IPv4 and IPv6 can share one SPF (or use multi-topology, RFC 5120, when you do not want them to). The protocol is not Cisco-only and is first-class in FRR.

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
The NET
A Network Entity Title is an NSAP that identifies this IS. The usual lab form is 8–20 bytes, written in dotted hex, and ends with NSEL 00:
49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00
│  │    │              └─ n-selector (00 = the router itself)
│  │    └──────────────── system ID (6 bytes) — must be unique in the domain
│  └───────────────────── area (here 0001; can be longer)
└──────────────────────── AFI 49 = private (ISO)

Pick a convention and keep it. Two common lab habits:

Encode an IPv4 loopback in the system ID: 10.0.0.1 → 0100.0000.0001.
Use simple integers: r1 → 0000.0000.0001.

FRR takes the whole NET under router isis:
router isis lab
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
FRR does not support multiple IS-IS processes yet, but you still have to name the instance (lab above). That name must match ip router isis lab / ipv6 router isis lab on the interfaces. A VRF-aware instance is router isis lab vrf RED.

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
Levels, DIS and circuit type








Role
Adjacencies
Typical use




level-1
L1 only, same area
Stub or access area


level-2-only
L2 only
Backbone / inter-area


level-1-2 (default-ish behaviour on many platforms)
Both
Area border, leaks L1 prefixes into L2 when configured



On broadcast media IS-IS elects a DIS (Designated Intermediate System) per level, by priority then system ID. The DIS does not become a permanent transit stub the way an OSPF DR can; it mainly originates the pseudonode LSP and paces CSNPs. On point-to-point links, skip the DIS: in FRR, isis network point-to-point. That is the right type for almost every veth or Containerlab link.
Hello, CSNP and PSNP timers, and the hello multiplier, are per interface and per level. FRR defaults to the three-way handshake on P2P (RFC 5303) and to periodic CSNPs even on P2P; you can turn the latter off to save bandwidth once you know why they exist (a periodic CSNP is how a neighbor notices a hole in its LSP database).

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
Metrics: use wide
ISO 10589 metrics were 6-bit (narrow, max 63). RFC 5305 wide metrics are 24-bit. FRR’s default metric-style is wide. Do not mix narrow and wide in a lab unless you are practising a migration (metric-style transition sends and accepts both).
With wide metrics, the value 16777215 (2^24 - 1) is still advertised but ignored in SPF, as RFC 5305 requires. That is how you take a link out of the topology without tearing the adjacency. FRR’s advertise-high-metrics (RFC 3277) sets 63, 62 or 16777215 depending on style, to shift traffic off a node you are draining.
The overload bit (set-overload-bit) tells others not to use this IS as transit. set-overload-bit on-startup (0-86400) holds the bit after boot so BGP or LDP can settle first. Use it; do not just slash all interface metrics and hope.

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
A triangle in FRR (not run)
Three point-to-point links, one area, level-2 only, IPv4 and IPv6 on each router. This is the documentation form of the lab; deploy it with Containerlab + FRR or with netlab’s module: [ isis ].
! r1 — /etc/frr/frr.conf  (integrated config; zebra must be up first)
interface eth1
 ip router isis lab
 ipv6 router isis lab
 isis network point-to-point
 isis circuit-type level-2-only
 isis metric 10
!
interface eth2
 ip router isis lab
 ipv6 router isis lab
 isis network point-to-point
 isis circuit-type level-2-only
 isis metric 10
!
interface lo
 ip router isis lab
 ipv6 router isis lab
 isis passive
!
router isis lab
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 is-type level-2-only
 metric-style wide
 hostname dynamic
 log-adjacency-changes
r2 and r3 differ only in the NET system ID (…0002.00, …0003.00) and in which interfaces face whom. Enable isisd in /etc/frr/daemons alongside zebra.
On a running router you would check, in order:
vtysh -c 'show isis neighbor'
vtysh -c 'show isis interface detail'
vtysh -c 'show isis database'
vtysh -c 'show isis topology'
vtysh -c 'show isis route'
Expect: two neighbors in Up (or Full-equivalent adjacency state in the neighbor listing), a database with an LSP per IS, a topology that lists both peers, and routes to the other loopbacks. If a neighbor is missing, check NET uniqueness, matching levels, point-to-point vs broadcast, and whether both ip router isis and addresses are present.

The same graph in netlab (not run)
defaults.device: frr
provider: clab
module: [ isis ]
isis:
  net: 49.0001.0000.0000.0000.00
  type: level-2

nodes:
  r1:
  r2:
  r3:

links:
  - r1-r2
  - r2-r3
  - r3-r1
Confirm attribute names with netlab show modules -m isis on your version before you rely on isis.type / isis.net. netlab will allocate system IDs and render the FRR snippets. Add a validate: plugin or an exec: ping once the module lab comes up.

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
IPv4, IPv6 and one SPF
ip router isis lab carries IPv4; ipv6 router isis lab carries IPv6. On an interface with both, a single adjacency can advertise both families. Multi-topology (topology ipv6-unicast in FRR) splits the SPF so an IPv6-only link does not black-hole IPv4.
FRR also has isis ipv4-over-ipv6-nexthop: IPv4 routes via the neighbor’s IPv6 link-local when the link has no IPv4 address (Linux 5.2+). Enable it on every router on that link, or one side will forward IPv4 into a neighbor that will not. This is the IS-IS analogue of BGP RFC 8950, and it has the same operational rule: both ends, or neither.

title: IS-IS Basics
section: Fast reroute, SR and the rest (awareness)
text:
Fast reroute, SR and the rest (awareness)
FRR IS-IS implements local LFA, remote LFA (LDP), TI-LFA, a TE database, SR-MPLS (experimental, RFC 8667) and SRv6 (RFC 9352). Those are later studies; the Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA chapter already covers the ideas. Get a clean L2 triangle and show isis route before you turn segment-routing on.
Authentication (clear text, HMAC-MD5, or RFC 5310 key chains) and RFC 7602 extended sequence numbers are how you stop a lab from accepting replayed hellos. Enable send on everyone before verify on anyone — the same “both ends” rule.

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
Common mistakes

Two routers with the same system ID. The database looks haunted; neighbors flap or LSPs overwrite each other.
is-type level-1 on one side and level-2-only on the other. No adjacency, no error you will notice unless you read show isis neighbor and the hello log.
Leaving the default broadcast type on a veth, then debugging DIS election that the lab did not need.
Narrow metrics in a topology that also has wide-metric routers.
Forgetting isis passive on the loopback, so IS-IS hellos go out a stub interface — or the opposite, forgetting it and never advertising the loopback.
Starting isisd before zebra, or restarting zebra and not isisd.
Setting the overload bit for a maintenance window and never clearing it.

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
Boring rule
One unique NET per IS, matching levels on the link, point-to-point on lab veths, wide metrics, and a show isis neighbor / show isis database / show isis route pass before you talk about policy or SR. If the LSP database does not agree, SPF will not save you.

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
Try this

Deploy the triangle with netlab or Containerlab. Capture show isis neighbor and show isis database. Shut one link and watch SPF and the remaining path.
Change r3 to is-type level-1 only, leave r1 and r2 at level-2, and predict which adjacencies die.
Set isis metric 100 on one side of a link and not the other. IS-IS is not required to have symmetric costs; look at each router’s show isis route.
Set set-overload-bit on r2 and confirm r1–r3 no longer transit r2, while r2 can still reach others.
Enable IPv6 on all three, then an IPv6-only link, with and without multi-topology, and see whether IPv4 is dragged into a black hole.

title: IS-IS Basics
text:
Sources

ISO/IEC 10589 (IS-IS intra-domain routing)
RFC 1195 — Use of OSI IS-IS for routing in TCP/IP and dual environments
RFC 5308 — Routing IPv6 with IS-IS
RFC 5305 — IS-IS extensions for traffic engineering (wide metrics)
RFC 5120 — M-ISIS: multi-topology IS-IS
RFC 5303 — Three-way handshake for IS-IS point-to-point
FRR isisd
netlab configuration modules

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
text:
A First BGP Lab with netlab
The fastest way to feel eBGP and iBGP is not to start from a blank frr.conf. netlab takes a short YAML topology, assigns addresses and AS numbers, builds the sessions the module’s design rules describe, and renders device configs. This chapter is that first BGP lab: three routers, one iBGP pair, one eBGP peer, one originated prefix, and the reports you use to check that netlab built what you think it built.
It is not a catalog of every BGP module knob — that belongs in the modules / provisioning / validation chapter — and it is not a vendor-CLI walkthrough of eBGP or a route reflector. Those exist later as hands-on labs on cEOS and FRR. Here the skill is reading a YAML file and predicting the sessions.

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
text:
Learning goals

Predict which sessions netlab will create from AS numbers and links (eBGP on the link, iBGP between loopbacks)
Write a first topology that combines bgp and ospf so iBGP next hops are reachable
Originate a prefix with bgp.originate and explain why it is a discard route, not a pingable subnet
Use netlab up, netlab report, netlab connect, and a small validate block as the lab loop
Avoid the first-lab traps: editing generated configs, forgetting an IGP under iBGP, and expecting originated prefixes to answer ICMP

Version note. netlab, containerlab, FRR, Docker, and Ansible were not installed and were not run on the writing host (2026-11-13, Linux 6.12.94+). Every topology, command, and “expected shape” below is written from the netlab.tools BGP module documentation and is illustrative. Run the lab on a machine that already has netlab and a device image (this book’s usual choice is FRR).
Installation of netlab itself is in Netlab Fundamentals. This chapter assumes netlab up is a command you already have.

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
section: What netlab will build if you only give it AS numbers
text:
What netlab will build if you only give it AS numbers
The BGP module follows a small set of design rules (netlab.tools, BGP Configuration Module). They are the whole mental model for a first lab.
eBGP. On every link where the attached routers have different AS numbers, netlab builds eBGP sessions between the directly connected addresses on that link. If the link has more than one address family, you get a session per family.
iBGP. When two routers share an AS, netlab builds iBGP sessions between their loopbacks (or the first external interface if a node has no loopback). With no route reflector, you get a full mesh. With bgp.rr / bgp.rr_list, clients peer with the reflectors. iBGP should sit on an IGP so those loopbacks are reachable; netlab warns if you create iBGP without one.
External links leave the IGP. By default, a link that carries eBGP is given role external (defaults.bgp.ebgp_role). OSPF or IS-IS is not run on that link. That is deliberate: the IGP stays inside the AS.
        AS 65001                         AS 65002
     +-------------+                  +-------------+
     | r1   r3     |                  |     r2      |
     |  \  /  iBGP |                  |             |
     |   \/  (lo)  |---- eBGP, p2p ---|             |
     |  OSPF here  |                  |             |
     +-------------+                  +-------------+
Sessions (IBGP or EBGP) are also created when local-as or confederation AS values differ; that is later territory. For this lab, “different bgp.as → eBGP on the link; same bgp.as → iBGP on loopbacks” is enough.

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
section: A first topology: two ASNs, three FRR routers
text:
A first topology: two ASNs, three FRR routers
Three nodes, two links, both modules. r1 and r3 are AS 65001 and need OSPF so the iBGP session between loopbacks can come up. r2 is AS 65002 and talks eBGP to r1 only. r2 originates 172.16.0.0/19 as a discard prefix so there is something to look at in the BGP table besides loopbacks.
# topology.yml — first BGP lab (illustrative; not executed here)
defaults.device: frr

module: [ bgp, ospf ]

nodes:
  r1:
    bgp.as: 65001
  r2:
    bgp.as: 65002
    bgp.originate:
      - 172.16.0.0/19
  r3:
    bgp.as: 65001

links:
  - r1-r2
  - r1-r3
Read it once, slowly:

Global module: [ bgp, ospf ] is inherited by all three routers. Do not later set module: [ bgp ] on a node thinking you are adding BGP; a node module: list replaces the global one and would drop OSPF. The modules chapter covers that trap in more detail.
bgp.as is required for every node that uses the module. Here it is set per node because the lab has two ASNs. A single-AS lab can set a global bgp.as and override only the external routers.
r1–r3 share 65001 → one iBGP session, loopback to loopback, plus OSPF on r1–r3 (and not on r1–r2).
r1–r2 differ in AS → one eBGP session on the link addresses.
r2 does not need iBGP and does not need OSPF for this graph, but inheriting OSPF on r2 is harmless: the r1–r2 link is external, so OSPF is not run there. r2 simply has no internal OSPF neighbor.

Default prefix advertisement (same docs page) also matters before you type show ip bgp:

Loopbacks are advertised unless you set bgp.advertise_loopback: false.
Stub links (a single router attached) are advertised by default.
bgp.originate installs a discard static (usually Null0) and advertises the prefix. It is not a connected subnet with reachable hosts.
bgp.advertise on a link or as a list advertises a prefix that is expected to be in the routing table already.

bgp.next_hop_self defaults to true on iBGP. Communities default to standard and extended toward iBGP neighbors, and standard toward eBGP. You do not need to set either for this lab; you do need to know they are on.

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
text:
The lab loop (illustrative)
From the directory that holds topology.yml:
# illustrative — netlab was not run on the writing host
netlab up
netlab report
netlab connect r1
netlab up is the pipeline the modules chapter unpacks (create → addressing → provider deploy → initial config). For this lab you only need the result: three FRR nodes, wiring, OSPF on the internal link, BGP sessions as above.
netlab report (and netlab create -o report, or netlab show reports bgp) is how you check the design before you argue with vtysh. The BGP ASN report should list 65001 with r1 and r3, 65002 with r2, and the advertised prefixes — at least each router’s loopback, plus 172.16.0.0/19 on r2. The neighbor report should show:



Node
Neighbor
Type
Transport




r1
r2
eBGP
address on the r1–r2 link


r1
r3
iBGP
loopbacks


r3
r1
iBGP
loopbacks


r2
r1
eBGP
address on the r1–r2 link



There is no r2–r3 session: they are not on a common link (so no eBGP) and they are not in the same AS (so no iBGP). If your report shows that session, the topology is not the one above.
On r1, the FRR shape you are looking for — illustrative, not pasted from a run — is:
# netlab connect r1
# vtysh
# show bgp summary
#  - an eBGP neighbor (r2's link address) in state Established
#  - an iBGP neighbor (r3's loopback) in state Established
# show ip bgp
#  - r2's loopback and 172.16.0.0/19, learned from the eBGP peer
#  - r3's loopback, learned from iBGP (next-hop likely r1 itself, next-hop-self)
On r3, 172.16.0.0/19 should be present because r1 re-advertises it over iBGP with next-hop-self (the default). On r2, you should see 65001 loopbacks. None of those listings were produced here; treat them as a prediction to confirm on your lab host.
A small validation block, in the same YAML, will fail the lab for you:
validate:
  r1_peers:
    nodes: [ r1 ]
    plugin: bgp_neighbor(count=2, state='Established')
  r2_origin:
    nodes: [ r1, r3 ]
    plugin: bgp_prefix(prefix='172.16.0.0/19')
Plugin names and parameters are those documented by netlab’s validation plugins; if your installed version uses a slightly different signature, believe netlab show / the module docs over this sketch. netlab validate is the command. netlab down tears the lab down.

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
section: IPv4, IPv6, and what you can ignore in a first lab
text:
IPv4, IPv6, and what you can ignore in a first lab
The module configures IPv4 and IPv6 address families in the same way: a family is enabled when the device has at least one interface address in that family, and netlab prefers separate sessions for IPv4 and IPv6 rather than carrying one family over the other. Unnumbered IPv6 LLA eBGP and RFC 8950 (IPv4 NLRI with an IPv6 next hop) are supported on a subset of platforms; they are not part of this first lab. If you add IPv6 addresses to the links and loopbacks, predict a second session per pair and confirm it with netlab report before you debug vtysh.
Addressing itself is netlab’s usual pool logic (documented in the addressing and fundamentals pages): P2P links and loopbacks are allocated for you unless you pin them. You should not need to write IP addresses in the first topology. If a report shows a session you cannot trace to a link or a loopback, the address family or the bgp.sessions / bgp.activate knobs (advanced, documented, easy to misuse) have been changed — leave them alone until this lab is boring.

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
section: bgp.originate is not a subnet you can ping
text:
bgp.originate is not a subnet you can ping
This is the first-lab surprise. The module docs are direct: when a node has bgp.originate, netlab adds discard static routes for those prefixes and advertises the BGP prefix. The prefix does not have reachable IP addresses. ping 172.16.0.1 from r1 should fail even when the BGP path is perfect. You are proving advertisement, not a host route.
If you want a pingable target, give r2 a stub link (or a loopback you already advertise) and ping that, or use a later plugin that creates a real interface for originated prefixes. The first lab should keep the discard route and a show ip bgp check.

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
text:
Traps

Editing generated device configs and re-running netlab up. The rendered files are outputs. They will be overwritten. Change topology.yml, or a documented extra-config hook, not frr.conf in the work directory.
iBGP without an IGP. A topology that is module: [ bgp ] only, with two nodes in the same AS, will still configure iBGP between loopbacks. Those sessions will sit idle unless the loopbacks are reachable some other way. Add OSPF or IS-IS, or do not use iBGP in that lab.
Expecting 172.16.0.0/19 to answer ICMP. See above.
Replacing the module list by accident. Node module: [ bgp ] is not a merge.
Looking for r2–r3. There is no link and no shared AS.
A 4-octet ASN in as.dot notation is supported by the module; it is not needed for this lab and is easy to typo. Stay in 65000–65534 until the graph is boringly correct.

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
text:
Boring rule
Write the sessions on paper from the AS numbers and the links, then ask netlab report if it agrees, then look at show bgp summary. If you start in vtysh, you will debug a design error as if it were a daemon error.

title: A First BGP Lab with netlab
text:
Try this

Add bgp.originate: [ 172.16.32.0/19 ] on r1 and predict which tables show it, and whether it is pingable.
Move r3 into AS 65003 and add a link r2–r3. Predict the new sessions before netlab up.
Add a second node in 65001 as a route reflector (bgp.rr: true, or bgp.rr_list) and draw the iBGP graph again. A later lab-host track chapter runs iBGP and a reflector on vendor CLIs; keep this exercise in YAML.
Tag an originated prefix with no_export (community policy is a later skill) and confirm a downstream eBGP peer does not see it.

Sources

Simple BGP example
netlab.tools and github.com/ipspace/netlab
RFC 4271, A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4) (session types and advertisement; this lab does not implement the protocol by hand)

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
text:
IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
Giving a router an IPv6 address does not make its IPv4 IGP carry those prefixes. OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) is an IPv4 protocol. To run a link-state IGP for IPv6 you either start a different protocol, OSPFv3, or you teach IS-IS — which can already carry more than one address family in one process — to advertise IPv6 reachability. This chapter is the IPv6 IGP note: what is actually different, how FRR names the knobs, and when a single IS-IS process with multi-topology is a better fit than “OSPFv2 plus OSPFv3.”
It is not a second OSPF basics chapter, and it is not a second IS-IS basics chapter. Those already cover areas, costs, NETs, levels, and DIS. A later lab-host track runs IPv6 and IS-IS on cEOS and FRR; this chapter is the conceptual and config-shape layer those labs assume. Address assignment (SLAAC, RA flags, DHCPv6) is a different chapter and is not retold here.

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
text:
Learning goals

Explain why OSPFv3 is not “OSPFv2 with IPv6 addresses,” including the 32-bit router ID, link-local hellos, and where prefixes actually travel
Configure a minimal FRR router ospf6 and a minimal dual-stack IS-IS (RFC 5308 TLVs, ipv6 router isis)
Say when single-topology IS-IS black-holes IPv6, and why multi-topology IS-IS (RFC 5120) plus metric-style wide exists
Place RFC 5838 (OSPFv3 address families, including IPv4) and RFC 7166 (authentication trailer) in that picture
Pick a dual-stack IGP approach for a lab without declaring a universal winner

Version note. FRR, netlab, and containerlab were not installed and were not run on the writing host (2026-11-13, Linux 6.12.94+). Every FRR snippet, show command, and netlab topology below is written from the FRR ospf6d / isisd documentation, the cited RFCs, and netlab.tools, and is illustrative.

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
section: Two protocols, or one process with two topologies
text:
Two protocols, or one process with two topologies
  IPv4-only IGP                  Dual-stack choices
  -------------                  ------------------
  OSPFv2  ─────────────┬───────► OSPFv2  +  OSPFv3     (two LSDB, two adjacencies)
                       │
                       └───────► IS-IS, IPv4 + IPv6
                                   ├─ single topology (one SPF for both)
                                   └─ multi-topology  (RFC 5120: e.g. ipv6-unicast SPF)
OSPFv3 began as the IPv6-only counterpart of OSPFv2 (RFC 2740, updated by RFC 5340). You run it as a separate process, with its own LSDB and its own adjacencies, even on a link that already has OSPFv2. RFC 5838 later added address-family support so an OSPFv3 process can also carry IPv4; that is the modern option, not the historical default, and not every lab image will be configured for it.
IS-IS started as an ISO IGP and grew IPv4 reachability (RFC 1195) and then IPv6 reachability (RFC 5308) as TLVs in the same LSP. One adjacency, one flooding machine, optionally one SPF — or, with multi-topology, a second SPF for IPv6 so an IPv4-only neighbor does not drag IPv6 down.

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
text:
OSPFv3: what actually changed
A few properties surprise people who treat OSPFv3 as a paint job.
Router ID is still 32 bits. It is written as a dotted quad (192.0.2.1) and is not an IPv6 address. On an IPv6-only box there may be no IPv4 address to derive it from, so you configure it. FRR: ospf6 router-id A.B.C.D. If you change it, FRR documents clear ipv6 ospf6 process rather than “just restart later and hope.”
Hellos go to IPv6 multicast, from a link-local source. All-SPF-Routers is FF02::5, All-DRouters FF02::6. The adjacency is built with link-local addresses. Global or ULA addresses on the interface are not required for OSPFv3 signalling, and FRR’s own documentation is blunt that there is no OSPFv3 reason to put them on the interface if you do not otherwise need them.
Interface IPv6 prefixes are not in the hello the way OSPFv2 carried IPv4 addresses. Prefixes travel in Intra-Area-Prefix LSAs (and Link LSAs for on-link information). That split is why you can have a working adjacency and still be missing a prefix: the neighbor is up, the LSA type is different.
Instance ID exists. Multiple OSPFv3 instances can share a link. FRR’s interface sample uses ipv6 ospf6 instance-id 0. Mismatched instance IDs do not form an adjacency.
Areas, costs, DR/BDR, stubs and NSSAs are still there. The IPv4 OSPF chapter’s mental model of areas and types still applies. FRR’s ipv6 ospf6 area, ipv6 ospf6 cost, hello/dead/retransmit, and area … range / NSSA commands are the IPv6-named counterparts. PtP vs broadcast is still a configuration choice; FRR does not support NBMA for IPv6 and says it likely never will.
Authentication is not “use IPsec or go home.” The original OSPFv3 text assumed IPsec. RFC 7166 defines an authentication trailer. FRR supports it as ipv6 ospf6 authentication with a manual key (MD5 or HMAC-SHA-256 in the internal crypto build; more algorithms with OpenSSL) or a keychain. Do not write “OSPFv3 has no authentication.”

FRR shape (illustrative)
From the FRR ospf6d documentation, a one-interface, one-area process looks like this:
interface eth0
 ipv6 ospf6 area 0.0.0.0
 ipv6 ospf6 instance-id 0
!
router ospf6
 ospf6 router-id 192.0.2.1
 area 0.0.0.0 range 2001:db8:105:2::/64
!
Enable it on every interface that should participate, including a loopback if you want that prefix in the area (loopbacks are often point-to-point / passive, as in OSPFv2). Useful show commands, also illustrative:
show ipv6 ospf6
show ipv6 ospf6 neighbor
show ipv6 ospf6 route
show ipv6 ospf6 interface
A later lab-host-track IPv6 lab is where you would paste real output from cEOS or FRR. Nothing here was executed.

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
section: IS-IS for IPv6: TLVs, then multi-topology
text:
IS-IS for IPv6: TLVs, then multi-topology
RFC 5308 adds two TLVs: IPv6 Reachability (prefixes, metric, up/down and external bits) and IPv6 Interface Address. IPv6 IS-IS uses the same levels, the same LSP flooding, and the same NET as IPv4 IS-IS. On FRR you attach IPv6 to an already-defined process with an interface command, not a second NET:
interface eth0
 ip router isis CORE
 ipv6 router isis CORE
!
router isis CORE
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 metric-style wide
!
ip router isis is IPv4 on that interface; ipv6 router isis is IPv6. The process name (CORE) must match router isis. Other platforms (for example some EOS-style CLIs) enable the IPv6 address-family under the IS-IS process instead of on the interface. Believe the image you are running.

Single topology is the trap
If IPv4 and IPv6 share one topology, they share one SPF. A neighbor that is IPv4-only, or a link that has IPv4 but no IPv6, still sits in that graph. IPv6 prefixes can be advertised with a next hop or a path that cannot forward IPv6, or an IPv6-only island can look closer than it is. The failure is quiet: the IPv4 adjacency is up, IPv6 routes appear, packets do not.
Multi-topology IS-IS (RFC 5120) gives IPv6 its own topology identifier and its own SPF. A router without IPv6 on a link simply does not participate in the IPv6 topology on that link. FRR enables this under the process:
router isis CORE
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 metric-style wide
 topology ipv6-unicast
FRR requires wide metrics when any multi-topology is configured. metric-style narrow with topology ipv6-unicast is a configuration error (the daemon will refuse it). Enable MT on every router that should agree on the IPv6 graph; a mixed MT / single-topology area is not a lab you will enjoy debugging.
With MT, a three-router line where the third router has no IPv6 toward the others will still have IPv4 reachability to all three loopbacks, and IPv6 reachability only where the IPv6 topology is actually connected. That is the behaviour you want, and the reason to turn MT on in a dual-stack lab before the topology gets interesting.

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
section: Which one should a dual-stack lab use?
text:
Which one should a dual-stack lab use?
There is no single right answer. The useful trade-offs are:








Approach
You gain
You pay




OSPFv2 + OSPFv3
Familiar IPv4 OSPF stays untouched; IPv6 is a second, well-understood protocol
Two processes, two LSDBs, two authentications, two places a link can be in the wrong area


OSPFv3 with RFC 5838 AFs
One OSPFv3 process can carry IPv6 and IPv4
Support and default config vary; do not assume the image is in AF mode


IS-IS, single topology
One adjacency, one set of LSPs
IPv4-only or IPv6-only links can black-hole the other family


IS-IS, multi-topology
One adjacency and flooding, separate SPFs
Wide metrics, MT on every speaker, a slightly larger mental model



A network that already runs OSPFv2 often adds OSPFv3 rather than introducing IS-IS only to get IPv6. A network that already runs IS-IS, or a green-field dual-stack core, often prefers one IS-IS process with topology ipv6-unicast. In this book’s labs, pick one approach and keep it consistent across the topology.

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
text:
A netlab sketch (illustrative, not run)
netlab will configure OSPF or IS-IS from the corresponding module once the nodes have IPv6 addresses. A three-router dual-stack triangle, still just YAML, might look like this (check your netlab version’s OSPF/IS-IS module pages for exact IPv6 / MT attributes before you rely on a flag name):
# illustrative — not executed; confirm module knobs with netlab.tools
defaults.device: frr
addressing.p2p.ipv6: 2001:db8:0:1::/64

module: [ ospf ]
# or: module: [ isis ]  and an isis area/NET, plus IPv6 / MT if the module supports it

nodes:
  r1:
  r2:
  r3:

links:
  - r1-r2
  - r2-r3
  - r1-r3
For OSPF, expect OSPFv2 for IPv4 and OSPFv3 for IPv6 unless you have deliberately chosen an AF mode the image supports. For IS-IS, expect a single process; enable IPv6 and multi-topology explicitly rather than hoping the default matches RFC 5120. netlab report and netlab validate are the same loop as in the BGP and modules chapters; no report was generated here.

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
text:
Gotchas

Forgetting the OSPFv3 router ID on an IPv6-only box. The process may not come up the way you expect, or it may pick an ID you did not plan for. Set it.
Filtering ICMPv6 and “allowing OSPF.” OSPFv3 is ICMPv6-adjacent in the operator’s mind but it is its own protocol (89) on IPv6. Also do not filter the link-local traffic it uses to hello.
Single-topology IS-IS on a mixed IPv4/IPv6 graph. The adjacency is not a guarantee that IPv6 follows IPv4.
Narrow metrics plus MT in FRR. The daemon should reject it; if you pasted a snippet from an IPv4-only lab, this is why.
Assuming OSPFv3 has no authentication. RFC 7166 and FRR’s ipv6 ospf6 authentication exist. Use them in any lab that is not a closed netns.
Pinging a prefix that the IGP advertised from a loopback /128 or a discard. Reachability of a prefix and presence in the LSDB are different checks.

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
text:
Boring rule
Treat IPv6 as a first-class topology, not a second address on an IPv4 IGP. Either run OSPFv3 properly (router ID, link-local, prefixes in the right LSAs) or run IS-IS with an IPv6 topology you can draw, preferably multi-topology.

title: IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocols: OSPFv3 and IS-IS
text:
Try this

title: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly
text: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly

title: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly
text:
Learning goals

Explain why path-vector routing protocols experience path exploration during route withdrawals.
Contrast BGP path exploration with distance-vector count-to-infinity behavior.
Describe how the Minimum Route Advertisement Interval (MRAI) timer limits BGP control-plane message rate.
Distinguish between standard MRAI behavior and withdrawal rate-limiting (WRATE).
Analyze how network topology, MRAI timers, and WRATE affect convergence time during prefix withdrawals versus additions (\(T_{down}\) vs \(T_{up}\)).
Identify network architectural patterns and features that mitigate BGP path exploration in production networks.

title: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly
text:
Thesis
When a primary destination prefix is withdrawn, BGP routers attempt to converge on valid backup paths. However, because routers evaluate local policy asynchronously and possess incomplete topological context, they often explore multiple increasingly longer invalid backup paths before ultimately recognizing that the destination is unreachable. This phenomenon—path exploration—causes a severe asymmetry between rapid route originations (\(T_{up}\)) and delayed route withdrawals (\(T_{down}\)). Applying the Minimum Route Advertisement Interval (MRAI) drastically reduces control-plane message churn during path exploration, but it forces withdrawal convergence times to scale linearly with the network diameter and timer duration.

title: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly
text:
Mental model
+------+             +------+             +------+
| AS 1 |-------------| AS 2 |-------------| AS 3 |
+------+             +------+             +------+
   \                    |                    /
    \                   |                   /
     \                  |                  /
      +-----------------+-----------------+
                        |
                    [ Prefix P ]
                      (AS 0)

1. AS 0 withdraws Prefix P.
2. AS 1 receives withdrawal, but AS 2 and AS 3 still advertise paths to P (e.g., 2-0, 3-0).
3. AS 1 switches to path 1-2-0.
4. AS 2 processes withdrawal from AS 0, switches to path 2-3-0, sends UPDATE to AS 1.
5. AS 1 switches to path 1-2-3-0 (Path Exploration / Path Hunting).
6. Cycle repeats across stale intermediate states until all nodes process all withdrawals.

title: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly
text:
Path Vectoring and Path Exploration
Distance-vector routing protocols suffer from count-to-infinity when a link fails, as adjacent nodes repeatedly increment metrics while passing stale routing state in loops. Path-vector protocols like BGP eliminate traditional routing loops by appending every Autonomous System (AS) traversed to an explicit path attribute (AS_PATH). When a router receives an UPDATE containing its own AS number in the AS_PATH, it rejects the route immediately.
While AS_PATH prevents routing loops, it does not prevent path exploration (often called “path hunting”). When a destination prefix loses its primary egress path or is withdrawn at the origin, a router must select its next-best path. If adjacent peers have not yet processed or propagated the withdrawal, their advertised paths still appear valid. The local router selects one of these stale paths, advertises the newly selected path to its neighbors, and subsequently receives further updates as those neighbors process downstream failures.
Consequently, the protocol “hunts” through combinations of stale paths of increasing path length. BGP does not count to infinity, but it does count to the maximum path length permitted by local policy or topology before settling on an unreachability state (a withdrawal).

title: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly
text:
The Minimum Route Advertisement Interval (MRAI)
To protect router CPUs and link bandwidth from the exponential message volume generated by path exploration, BGP defines a rate-limiting mechanism called the Minimum Route Advertisement Interval (MRAI).

Standard RFC 4271 Dynamics
RFC 4271 specifies that MinRouteAdvertisementIntervalTimer is the minimum period that must elapse between consecutive advertisements or withdrawals of routes to a given destination sent to a specific peer. The MRAI operates on a per-destination, per-peer basis.
Key properties specified in RFC 4271 include: - The MRAI controls the rate of route advertisement, not local route selection. A router may recalculate its best path hundreds of times per second locally, but it buffers outbound updates. - If multiple route changes occur while the MRAI timer is running for a peer, the router transmits only the last selected best route upon timer expiration. - To prevent synchronization of BGP updates across large networks, implementation timers MUST be jittered. The timer value is multiplied by a random factor uniformly distributed between 0.75 and 1.0. - RFC 4271 suggests default values of 30 seconds for external BGP (eBGP) sessions and 5 seconds for internal BGP (iBGP) sessions. It permits shorter or zero-valued MRAI timers on internal sessions.


Rate-Limiting Withdrawals (WRATE)
An important historical distinction exists between update types. The older specification (RFC 1771) explicitly exempted explicit withdrawals from MRAI rate limiting, allowing explicit unreachability notifications to bypass queueing delays. RFC 4271 changed this rule to include withdrawals under the MRAI umbrella.
In academic literature and vendor terminology, applying MRAI rate-limiting to withdrawals is termed “WRATE” (Withdrawal Rate-Limiting). When WRATE is off, withdrawals are transmitted instantly, while path announcements remain subject to MRAI pacing. When WRATE is on, both explicit withdrawals and path announcements share the MRAI timer.


Industry Implementation Reality: FRR Defaults
In production hardware and software routing suites, default MRAI behaviors vary. FRR (Free Range Routing) provides the neighbor command to set MRAI explicitly:
! (not run here; written from the docs)
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.0.2.2 advertisement-interval 0
FRR’s documented default advertisement-interval is 0 seconds for both iBGP and eBGP peers. Setting this interval to 0 disables MRAI update buffering completely, preferring immediate control-plane propagation at the expense of potential update processing churn.

title: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly
text:
Delayed Convergence: Tup vs Tdown
BGP convergence dynamics exhibit a severe structural asymmetry between route announcements (\(T_{up}\)) and route withdrawals (\(T_{down}\)). This phenomenon was rigorously documented by Labovitz et al. in “Delayed Internet Routing Convergence” (SIGCOMM 2000).
When a new prefix is announced (\(T_{up}\)), the implicit path priority favors short, direct paths. The moment a node receives a short path from an upstream neighbor, it typically accepts it immediately as its best path. \(T_{up}\) convergence is bounded primarily by physical link propagation delay and local serialization times.
When an established prefix is withdrawn (\(T_{down}\)), nodes must invalidate existing routes. Because nodes learn of the failure asynchronously, they traverse intermediate stale topologies. In a fully connected clique or dense topology of \(n\) Autonomous Systems, the number of distinct paths that can be explored during a withdrawal grows explosively with \(n\): in the worst case it is factorial, because any ordering of the other ASes is a loop-free path.
Labovitz et al. demonstrated that when MRAI timers are non-zero, \(T_{down}\) convergence time does not scale with physical propagation latency; instead, it scales linearly with the product of the network diameter (or clique size) and the MRAI timer duration:
\[\text{Convergence Time} \approx O(n \times \text{MRAI})\]

title: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly
text:
Mitigations and Architectural Controls
Network operators use several design patterns and protocol extensions to limit the operational impact of path exploration and slow withdrawal convergence.

MRAI Tuning: Lowering MRAI intervals on low-latency eBGP handoffs or setting MRAI to 0 on internal iBGP networks accelerates path processing. Modern high-performance router control planes can process updates fast enough that update dampening via MRAI is often unnecessary within enterprise or data center environments.
BGP PIC (Prefix Independent Convergence): Control-plane path exploration delays FIB programming if the router waits for BGP to resolve to a final state. BGP PIC precomputes backup next-hops directly in the data plane. When an interface or session fails, the FIB switches traffic to the precomputed backup path in milliseconds, decoupling data-plane disruption from control-plane \(T_{down}\) path hunting.
BGP Add-Path (RFC 7911): Standard BGP allows a router to advertise only its single best path to a peer. BGP Add-Path allows nodes to advertise multiple path options for the same prefix. By providing visibility into alternative paths prior to failure, nodes do not need to query or wait for sequential update passes during a failover.
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD): BFD (RFC 5880) is a lightweight hello protocol that detects a dead forwarding path in milliseconds and tears down the BGP session, so the withdrawal starts sooner. It does not shorten the hunt that follows; it removes the hold-timer wait in front of it.

title: BGP Path Exploration and MRAI: Why Withdrawals Converge Slowly
text:
Lab: Discrete-Event Path Exploration Simulator
The following lab experiment uses a discrete-event Python simulation (pathhunt.py) modeling a full-mesh clique of \(n\) Autonomous Systems to analyze path exploration dynamics, MRAI timing impact, and WRATE behavior.
pathhunt.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Path exploration ("path hunting") in a BGP clique, with and without MRAI.

A discrete-event model of path-vector routing. Every AS runs the BGP
decision process in its simplest form (shortest AS_PATH, then lowest
neighbour id), drops paths that contain its own ASN (loop prevention),
and tells every neighbour about its best path. Messages take a random
1-10 ms each. With MRAI on, an AS waits at least MRAI (jittered to
0.75-1.0x, RFC 4271 9.2.1.1) between two announcements to the same
neighbour; withdrawals are not delayed unless --wrate is set.

Events: AS 0 originates 203.0.113.0/24, the network converges, then AS 0
withdraws it (Tdown) or re-announces it (Tup).
"""
import argparse, heapq, itertools, random

class Net:
    def __init__(self, n, mrai, wrate, seed):
        self.n, self.mrai, self.wrate = n, mrai, wrate
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)
        self.nbrs = {a: [b for b in range(n) if b != a] for a in range(n)}  # clique
        self.rib_in = {a: {} for a in range(n)}      # a -> {neighbour: path}
        self.best = {a: None for a in range(n)}
        self.sent = {a: {} for a in range(n)}        # what a last told each neighbour
        self.next_ok = {a: {} for a in range(n)}     # MRAI: earliest next send
        self.pending = {a: set() for a in range(n)}  # neighbours waiting on MRAI
        self.q, self.seq, self.now = [], itertools.count(), 0.0
        self.updates = self.withdrawals = 0
        self.last_change = 0.0
        self.trace = []

    def at(self, t, fn, *args):
        heapq.heappush(self.q, (t, next(self.seq), fn, args))

    def run(self):
        while self.q:
            self.now, _, fn, args = heapq.heappop(self.q)
            fn(*args)

    def decide(self, a):
        cands = [(len(p), nb, p) for nb, p in self.rib_in[a].items() if p is not None]
        new = None
        if a == 0 and self.originating:
            new = (0,)
        elif cands:
            new = (a,) + min(cands)[2]
        if new != self.best[a]:
            self.best[a] = new
            self.last_change = self.now
            if a == 1:
                self.trace.append((self.now, new))
            for b in self.nbrs[a]:
                self.schedule_send(a, b)

    def schedule_send(self, a, b):
        adv = self.best[a]
        is_withdraw = adv is None
        if self.mrai and (not is_withdraw or self.wrate):
            t = self.next_ok[a].get(b, 0.0)
            if self.now < t:
                if b not in self.pending[a]:
                    self.pending[a].add(b)
                    self.at(t, self.flush, a, b)
                return
        self.send(a, b)

    def flush(self, a, b):
        self.pending[a].discard(b)
        self.send(a, b)

    def send(self, a, b):
        adv = self.best[a]
        if self.sent[a].get(b, "never") == adv:
            return
        self.sent[a][b] = adv
        if adv is None:
            self.withdrawals += 1
        else:
            self.updates += 1
        if self.mrai and (adv is not None or self.wrate):
            self.next_ok[a][b] = self.now + self.mrai * self.rng.uniform(0.75, 1.0)
        self.at(self.now + self.rng.uniform(0.001, 0.010), self.recv, b, a, adv)

    def recv(self, b, a, path):
        if path is not None and b in path:
            path = None                               # loop: treat as withdrawn
        self.rib_in[b][a] = path
        self.decide(b)

    def event(self, originate):
        self.updates = self.withdrawals = 0
        self.trace = []
        start = self.now
        self.originating = originate
        self.at(self.now, self.decide, 0)
        self.run()
        return self.last_change - start

def experiment(n, mrai, wrate, seed, show_trace=False):
    net = Net(n, mrai, wrate, seed)
    net.event(True)                                    # initial announce
    net.now += 100; net.last_change = net.now
    tdown = net.event(False)
    down_u, down_w, trace = net.updates, net.withdrawals, net.trace
    net.now += 100; net.last_change = net.now
    tup = net.event(True)
    up_u = net.updates
    if show_trace:
        print(f"  AS1's best path during Tdown (clique of {n}, MRAI={mrai}s):")
        for t, p in trace:
            print(f"    +{t - trace[0][0] + 0.0:8.3f}s  {' '.join(map(str, p)) if p else 'WITHDRAWN'}")
    return tdown, down_u, down_w, tup, up_u

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=7)
    ap.add_argument("--big", action="store_true",
                    help="also run n=16 with MRAI=0 (millions of messages, slow)")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    print("1) One AS watching the hunt")
    experiment(6, 0, False, args.seed, show_trace=True)
    print()
    print("2) Clique size vs MRAI (announcements / withdrawals sent, convergence time)")
    print(f"  {'n':>3} {'MRAI':>5} {'WRATE':>5} | {'Tdown':>8} {'ann':>6} {'wdr':>5} | {'Tup':>7} {'ann':>5}")
    for n in (4, 8, 12, 16):
        for mrai, wrate in ((0, False), (5, False), (30, False), (30, True)):
            if n == 16 and mrai == 0 and not args.big:
                print(f"  {n:>3} {mrai:>4}s   off | (skipped: run with --big)")
                continue
            tdown, du, dw, tup, uu = experiment(n, mrai, wrate, args.seed)
            print(f"  {n:>3} {mrai:>4}s {('on' if wrate else 'off'):>5} | "
                  f"{tdown:7.2f}s {du:>6} {dw:>5} | {tup:6.3f}s {uu:>5}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Run it (no root, no packages, about half a second):
python3 pathhunt.py
Output:
