title: QoS: Queues, Token Buckets and Congestion Evidence
text:
QoS: Queues, Token Buckets and Congestion Evidence
QoS decides how a finite link and its buffers are shared during contention. A DSCP label alone does not reserve bandwidth or guarantee latency: each hop must classify and apply an appropriate policy, and the path must have enough capacity. Start with QoS Vocabulary, then quantify the behavior here.

title: QoS: Queues, Token Buckets and Congestion Evidence
text:
The bottleneck and the queue
For a constant-rate link, a rough serialization time is packet bits / link bits per second. A 1,500-byte packet at 10 Mbit/s takes about 1.2 ms to serialize, before link-layer overhead. A queue of 100,000 bytes drained at 10 Mbit/s adds approximately 100,000 × 8 / 10,000,000 = 0.08 s, or 80 ms, to a packet at the tail. Actual delay varies with packet sizes, scheduling, competing queues and hardware. Increasing a queue can absorb bursts but can also increase latency; a full queue must drop or mark traffic according to its policy.
Traffic need not average above the link rate to create a queue: short bursts can exceed service rate. Measure utilization at a sufficiently fine interval and inspect queue occupancy, drops and delay under the workload. A one-minute average can hide a millisecond burst. Input drops, output queue drops, policer drops, interface errors and remote congestion are different counters with different remedies.

title: QoS: Queues, Token Buckets and Congestion Evidence
text:
Token-bucket reasoning
A token bucket is a useful model for a meter or shaper. Tokens accumulate at a configured rate up to a burst capacity; transmitting or admitting a packet consumes tokens. An initially full bucket permits a burst above the sustained rate. With a single ideal bucket of 100,000 bytes and a refill rate of 1,000,000 bytes/s, the bucket represents 100 ms of tokens. This does not mean all traffic experiences 100 ms of delay: packet timing, queue size and implementation matter. When accounting includes different headers at different devices, a nominally matching rate may still exceed a provider’s measured rate.
A policer evaluates traffic against a profile and typically drops or remarks nonconforming packets; it does not normally smooth excess by holding a large queue. A shaper queues traffic until its transmission conforms, subject to finite buffer capacity; excess can still be dropped. Either can allow bursts, and neither automatically guarantees application performance. Bucket size and rate use explicit units: 1 Mbit/s is 125,000 bytes/s before accounting differences; a 16,000-byte bucket is not 16,000 bits.

title: QoS: Queues, Token Buckets and Congestion Evidence
text:
Class, mark, queue and schedule
Classify traffic using available fields and policy, apply a trust boundary, and map accepted markings to local queues. DSCP is the upper six bits of the IP DS field; the lower two bits carry ECN. For example, EF is DSCP 46 (101110); with ECN bits 00, the full field is binary 10111000, or hex 0xb8. If ECN changes to 11, the DSCP remains 46 while the full byte becomes 0xbb. Do not compare an entire byte to a DSCP value without masking or accounting for ECN.
A scheduler chooses which eligible queue to serve. Strict priority can reduce delay for a bounded critical class, but an unbounded priority stream can starve other queues. Weighted schedulers distribute service among eligible queues; the exact weights, minimums, maximums and borrowing rules are platform-specific and depend on offered load. A configured minimum is not necessarily unused capacity permanently reserved from others. An active queue management algorithm may drop or ECN-mark before a queue is full to signal congestion; ECN needs compatible endpoints and a suitable path, and is not a substitute for capacity.

title: QoS: Queues, Token Buckets and Congestion Evidence
section: Lab: observe a shaper under burst load
text:
Lab: observe a shaper under burst load
The following Linux example needs unshare, nsenter, ip, tc, Python 3, permission for user/network namespaces, and kernel support for veth and TBF. It sends traffic only between disposable namespaces. Run it as shown; do not add a qdisc to a host or production interface. The peer need not run a UDP server: the experiment observes the sender’s egress queue, not application delivery. The namespace holders last at most 60 seconds and the trap cleans them up on normal exit.
Save as shape-lab.sh, then run unshare -rn bash shape-lab.sh:
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 60 & peer=$!
trap 'kill "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link add tx0 type veth peer name rx0
ip link set rx0 netns "$peer"
ip addr add 10.77.0.1/24 dev tx0
ip link set tx0 up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip addr add 10.77.0.2/24 dev rx0
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set rx0 up

tc qdisc add dev tx0 root tbf rate 1mbit burst 16kb latency 100ms
python3 - <<'PY'
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
for _ in range(2000):
    s.sendto(b'x' * 1000, ('10.77.0.2', 9999))
s.close()
PY
sleep 1
tc -s qdisc show dev tx0
tc qdisc del dev tx0 root
On the test host, the displayed TBF reported 47 packets sent and 1,957 dropped, with 2,039 overlimits; extra control packets can also pass through the qdisc, so these are not a packet-conservation equation for the 2,000 UDP sends. Values vary with scheduling, kernel, ARP, queueing and machine speed. overlimits is a qdisc-specific indication of rate enforcement, not a synonym for loss. A nonzero drop count shows the queue discarded packets; it does not show which application packets arrived at the peer. A local UDP sendto success only indicates local acceptance, not delivery.
Repeat with a slower sender or a lower packet count and predict how drops change. Record elapsed time, rate, burst, qdisc statistics and peer observations. To measure end-to-end delivery, run an application receiver with sequence numbers and compare sent and received packets. For latency under load use a separate probe and compare idle and loaded distributions; a single ping is not a latency percentile. For bidirectional service, test both directions because qdiscs here operate on egress only.

title: QoS: Queues, Token Buckets and Congestion Evidence
text:
Design checks

At 20 Mbit/s, approximately how long does a 50,000-byte FIFO backlog take to drain, ignoring overhead and new arrivals? 20 ms.
If only a few packets are dropped but latency is high, inspect queue depth and the bottleneck rather than assuming a policer.
If a marked voice stream enters the best-effort queue, inspect classification, trust and mapping at each hop; packet marking alone is not a queue counter.
If a priority queue consumes a whole congested link, verify its admission or rate controls and measure the impact on other classes.
Record platform, link speed, traffic direction, offered load, frame sizes, rate accounting, queue configuration and counter deltas when reporting a QoS result.

References: Differentiated Services field, RFC 2474, single-rate three-color marker, RFC 2697, and Linux TBF manual.

Hardening is not a one-time “secure the router” checkbox. It is a repeatable set of gates you run after every design change. This chapter consolidates edge, control-plane, ACL, and ops hygiene into checklists you can attach to Containerlab labs (mid-2026 open stack: FRR, Linux, optional SR Linux notes).

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
text:
SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
A TCP server commits memory before it knows the client is real. The first SYN makes the kernel allocate a request socket, send a SYN-ACK, and wait. A SYN flood sends SYNs from spoofed addresses that will never send the final ACK, so those half-open entries pile up until the listener refuses real clients. Linux has two queues per listener, two different limits, and a stateless escape hatch, SYN cookies, that is on by default. Most “we tuned it and nothing changed” incidents come from mixing up which queue overflowed. This chapter separates them, measures each one with real counters, and runs an actual spoofed flood, without root, inside a throwaway network namespace.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
text:
Learning goals

Draw the SYN queue (request sockets, SYN_RECV) and the accept queue (ESTABLISHED, waiting for accept()) and say which limit applies to each
Explain why net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog does not size the SYN queue on a modern kernel, and what it actually does
Read ss -lnt Recv-Q/Send-Q on a listener and the TcpExt counters (ListenOverflows, ListenDrops, TCPReqQFullDrop, TCPReqQFullDoCookies, Syncookies*)
Say what a SYN cookie encodes, and what a cookie-built connection loses (MSS precision, and every option when timestamps are off)
Tell a flood from an application that accepts too slowly, and fix the right one
Reproduce a spoofed SYN flood safely with an unprivileged user + network namespace

Lab platform: Linux 6.12, iproute2 6.15 (ss, ip, nstat), Python 3.13.5, run as an unprivileged user. Each lab runs in its own unshare -rn namespace: root there, with its own sysctls, raw sockets, and veth, and no effect on the host. Every listing output below is pasted from those runs. Kernel behaviour is quoted from net/ipv4/tcp_input.c, tcp_minisocks.c, and syncookies.c in Linux 6.12.
This chapter covers the host’s own defences. Upstream scrubbing, SYN proxies in front of the server (nftables synproxy, load balancers), and XDP drop paths are out of scope here.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
text:
Mental model



One listener, two queues


             SYN                         final ACK                 accept()
 client ───────────► [ SYN queue ] ─────────────────► [ accept queue ] ───────► application
                     request socks, SYN_RECV           full sockets, ESTABLISHED
                     limit: len > min(backlog,          limit: count > min(backlog,
                            somaxconn)                         somaxconn)
                     overflow: cookie or drop          overflow: drop SYN; ignore ACK
                                                                 (RST if abort_on_overflow)
Both queues hang off the same listen() call. In Linux 6.12, tcp_conn_request() checks them in this order for every incoming SYN:

tcp_syncookies == 2, or the SYN queue is full (inet_csk_reqsk_queue_len(sk) > sk_max_ack_backlog)? Then tcp_syn_flood_action(): with cookies enabled, answer with a cookie (TCPReqQFullDoCookies); otherwise drop (TCPReqQFullDrop).
The accept queue is full (sk_ack_backlog > sk_max_ack_backlog)? Drop the SYN (ListenOverflows). Cookies do not help here.
Cookies off and the SYN queue more than three quarters of tcp_max_syn_backlog? Drop SYNs from peers the kernel has not seen before (tcp_peer_is_proven() is false). ListenDrops only.
Otherwise allocate a request socket (≈300 bytes), send the SYN-ACK, and retransmit it up to tcp_synack_retries times (5 → about 63 s before giving up).

sk_max_ack_backlog is the backlog you passed to listen(), silently capped at net.core.somaxconn (default 4096 since Linux 5.4). The > comparisons mean listen(N) holds N + 1 entries.








Knob
Default here
What it really does on 6.12




listen(fd, backlog)
app-chosen
Sets both queue limits (sk_max_ack_backlog)


net.core.somaxconn
4096
Caps backlog without telling the application


net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
1
0 = never, 1 = when the SYN queue is full, 2 = always


net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog
1024 (≥128, scales with RAM)
Only with cookies off: keep the last quarter for proven peers


net.ipv4.tcp_synack_retries
5
How long a half-open entry occupies a slot


net.ipv4.tcp_abort_on_overflow
0
Final ACK into a full accept queue: 0 = ignore it, 1 = send RST



All of these are per network namespace, which is what makes the labs below safe.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
section: Concepts — what a SYN cookie is
text:
Concepts — what a SYN cookie is
With a cookie, the server keeps no state. It encodes the essentials in the 32-bit initial sequence number of its SYN-ACK: a keyed hash of the 4-tuple and a coarse timestamp, plus a 2-bit index into a table of four MSS values (msstab = {536, 1300, 1440, 1460} in net/ipv4/syncookies.c). When an ACK arrives with no request socket behind it, the kernel checks ack − 1 against the hash (valid for two 60-second periods), rebuilds the connection, and counts SyncookiesRecv (or SyncookiesFailed).
The price is the TCP options. The ISN has no room for window scale, SACK, or ECN. Linux hides them in the low 6 bits of the TCP timestamp value if the client sent timestamps (TS_OPT_WSCALE_MASK, TS_OPT_SACK, TS_OPT_ECN). If timestamps are off, a cookie connection has no window scaling (64 KiB window), no SACK, and an MSS rounded down to the table. The kernel’s own sysctl documentation is blunt: cookies are a fallback and “seriously violate TCP protocol”; if you see SYN-flood warnings from legitimate load, fix the backlog, not the cookies.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
section: Lab — setup: a private network namespace with a void
text:
Lab — setup: a private network namespace with a void
unshare -rn gives an unprivileged user a new user namespace (mapped to root) and a new network namespace. The helper below adds a veth so the server has a real address (10.9.0.1) and routes TEST-NET-2 (198.51.100.0/24, RFC 5737) to a fake next hop. SYN-ACKs to “spoofed” clients leave v0 and are never answered, exactly like a real spoofed flood.
#!/bin/sh
# netns_lab.sh — run CMD inside a throwaway network namespace:
#   lo up, veth v0 = 10.9.0.1/24, and 198.51.100.0/24 (TEST-NET-2) routed into a void
# usage: unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh CMD [ARGS...]
set -e
ip link set lo up
ip link add v0 type veth peer name v1
ip link set v0 up && ip link set v1 up
ip addr add 10.9.0.1/24 dev v0
ip route add 198.51.100.0/24 via 10.9.0.2 dev v0
# a fake next hop: SYN-ACKs to the "spoofed" clients leave v0 and are never answered
ip neigh replace 10.9.0.2 lladdr 02:00:00:00:00:02 dev v0 nud permanent
exec "$@"
#!/bin/sh
# listen_defaults.sh — the knobs that size and protect a TCP listener (this netns)
for k in net/ipv4/tcp_syncookies net/ipv4/tcp_max_syn_backlog \
         net/ipv4/tcp_synack_retries net/ipv4/tcp_abort_on_overflow net/core/somaxconn; do
  printf '%-32s %s\n' "$k" "$(cat /proc/sys/$k)"
done
nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops TcpExtTCPReqQFullDrop \
          TcpExtTCPReqQFullDoCookies TcpExtSyncookiesSent TcpExtSyncookiesRecv
chmod +x netns_lab.sh listen_defaults.sh
./listen_defaults.sh                                # host namespace, read-only
unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh ip route                 # the lab namespace
net/ipv4/tcp_syncookies          1
net/ipv4/tcp_max_syn_backlog     1024
net/ipv4/tcp_synack_retries      5
net/ipv4/tcp_abort_on_overflow   0
net/core/somaxconn               4096
#kernel
TcpExtSyncookiesSent            0                  0.0
TcpExtSyncookiesRecv            0                  0.0
TcpExtListenOverflows           0                  0.0
TcpExtListenDrops               0                  0.0
TcpExtTCPReqQFullDoCookies      0                  0.0
TcpExtTCPReqQFullDrop           0                  0.0
10.9.0.0/24 dev v0 proto kernel scope link src 10.9.0.1 
198.51.100.0/24 via 10.9.0.2 dev v0 
The host counters are all zero, and they stay zero after every lab below: each unshare -rn namespace has its own /proc/net/netstat and its own sysctls.
tcpext.py is the shared counter reader (the same numbers nstat prints):
# tcpext.py — read TcpExt counters from /proc/net/netstat (what `nstat` reports)
KEYS = ("ListenOverflows", "ListenDrops", "TCPReqQFullDrop",
        "TCPReqQFullDoCookies", "SyncookiesSent", "SyncookiesRecv", "SyncookiesFailed")

def tcpext():
    lines = open("/proc/net/netstat").read().splitlines()
    for names, values in zip(lines[::2], lines[1::2]):
        if names.startswith("TcpExt:"):
            return dict(zip(names.split()[1:], map(int, values.split()[1:])))

def delta(before, after):
    return {k: after[k] - before[k] for k in KEYS if after[k] != before[k]}

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
section: Lab — accept queue: a server that never calls accept()
text:
Lab — accept queue: a server that never calls accept()
# accept_queue_lab.py — a listener that never calls accept(): what happens to client #5?
# usage: unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 accept_queue_lab.py BACKLOG CLIENTS ABORT_ON_OVERFLOW
import socket, subprocess, sys, time
from tcpext import tcpext, delta

backlog, clients, abort = map(int, sys.argv[1:4])
with open("/proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_abort_on_overflow", "w") as f:
    f.write(str(abort))

lsock = socket.socket()
lsock.bind(("10.9.0.1", 8080))
lsock.listen(backlog)                       # never accept()

before = tcpext()
socks = []
for i in range(clients):
    c = socket.socket()
    c.setblocking(False)
    c.connect_ex(("10.9.0.1", 8080))        # non-blocking: SYN goes out now
    socks.append(c)
    time.sleep(0.05)
time.sleep(1.5)                             # let one SYN retransmit (RTO 1 s) happen

print(f"listen({backlog}), {clients} clients, tcp_abort_on_overflow={abort}")
print(subprocess.run(["ss", "-ltn", "sport = :8080"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout, end="")
states = subprocess.run(["ss", "-Htn", "dport = :8080"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
count = {}
for line in states.splitlines():
    count[line.split()[0]] = count.get(line.split()[0], 0) + 1
print("client-side states:", count)
srv = subprocess.run(["ss", "-Htn", "state", "syn-recv", "sport = :8080"],
                     capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
print("server SYN-RECV:", len(srv.splitlines()))
print("TcpExt deltas:", delta(before, tcpext()))
unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 accept_queue_lab.py 3 8 0
unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 accept_queue_lab.py 3 8 1
listen(3), 8 clients, tcp_abort_on_overflow=0
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port
LISTEN 4      3           10.9.0.1:8080      0.0.0.0:*   
client-side states: {'SYN-SENT': 4, 'ESTAB': 4}
server SYN-RECV: 0
TcpExt deltas: {'ListenOverflows': 8, 'ListenDrops': 8}

listen(3), 8 clients, tcp_abort_on_overflow=1
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port
LISTEN 4      3           10.9.0.1:8080      0.0.0.0:*   
client-side states: {'ESTAB': 4, 'SYN-SENT': 4}
server SYN-RECV: 0
TcpExt deltas: {'ListenOverflows': 8, 'ListenDrops': 8}
How to read it:

On a listening socket, ss reuses the columns: Recv-Q is the current accept-queue length (4), Send-Q is its limit (3). Recv-Q = Send-Q + 1 is the “full” signature, because the check is >.
Four clients completed the handshake and sit ESTAB in the queue. The application has not seen them, but the clients think they are connected and may already be sending.
The other four never got a SYN-ACK. Their SYNs hit step 2 (accept queue full) and were dropped. Each client retransmitted once after the 1 s initial RTO, so 4 × 2 = 8 ListenOverflows. They stay in SYN-SENT and keep retrying with backoff; if the application wakes up and calls accept(), they get in.
tcp_abort_on_overflow=1 changed nothing. It acts only in tcp_check_req() when a final ACK arrives for a request whose accept queue filled in the meantime (listen_overflow: → embryonic_reset). Here the SYNs were refused before any handshake. In production it turns a short burst into connection resets for clients that would have recovered, which is why the kernel docs say to enable it only if the daemon really cannot keep up.
No SYN_RECV entries and no cookie counters: this is not a flood. It is an application that does not accept fast enough, and the fix is in the application or its listen() backlog.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
section: Lab — somaxconn silently caps the backlog
text:
Lab — somaxconn silently caps the backlog
# somaxconn_lab.py — listen() backlog is silently capped by net.core.somaxconn
# usage: unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 somaxconn_lab.py
import socket, subprocess

def show(somaxconn, backlog):
    open("/proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn", "w").write(str(somaxconn))
    s = socket.socket()
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind(("10.9.0.1", 8080))
    s.listen(backlog)
    line = subprocess.run(["ss", "-Hltn", "sport = :8080"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.split()
    print(f"somaxconn={somaxconn:<5} listen({backlog:<6}) -> ss Send-Q={line[2]}")
    s.close()

show(4096, 128)
show(4096, 65535)
show(128, 1024)
unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 somaxconn_lab.py
somaxconn=4096  listen(128   ) -> ss Send-Q=128
somaxconn=4096  listen(65535 ) -> ss Send-Q=4096
somaxconn=128   listen(1024  ) -> ss Send-Q=128
listen() never fails because the backlog is too large. __sys_listen_socket() in net/socket.c clamps it to somaxconn, and only ss -lnt Send-Q shows what the kernel actually used. Many servers have their own setting (nginx listen … backlog=, default 511 on Linux; HAProxy backlog; Go’s net package passes somaxconn itself; Java’s ServerSocket defaults to 50). Raising somaxconn without raising the application value does nothing, and the reverse is capped.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
section: Lab — a spoofed SYN flood, three ways
text:
Lab — a spoofed SYN flood, three ways
The flood builds IPv4 + TCP SYN headers by hand on a raw socket (allowed in the namespace, where the user is root). Sources cycle through 198.51.100.1–254. After the flood, one real client in the same namespace tries to connect with a 3 s timeout.
# synflood_lab.py — spoofed SYN flood against a listener, inside a private netns.
# usage: unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 synflood_lab.py COOKIES MAX_SYN_BACKLOG BACKLOG SYNS
import os, random, socket, struct, sys, time
from tcpext import tcpext, delta

cookies, max_syn_backlog, backlog, syns = map(int, sys.argv[1:5])
SERVER, PORT = "10.9.0.1", 8080

def sysctl(name, value):
    with open("/proc/sys/" + name.replace(".", "/"), "w") as f:
        f.write(str(value))

sysctl("net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies", cookies)
sysctl("net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog", max_syn_backlog)

lsock = socket.socket()
lsock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
lsock.bind((SERVER, PORT))
lsock.listen(backlog)

def csum(data):
    if len(data) % 2:
        data += b"\0"
    s = sum(struct.unpack(f"!{len(data)//2}H", data))
    s = (s >> 16) + (s & 0xFFFF)
    return ~(s + (s >> 16)) & 0xFFFF

def syn(src, sport):
    dst = socket.inet_aton(SERVER)
    seq = random.getrandbits(32)
    tcp = struct.pack("!HHIIBBHHH", sport, PORT, seq, 0, 5 << 4, 0x02, 64240, 0, 0)
    pseudo = socket.inet_aton(src) + dst + struct.pack("!BBH", 0, 6, len(tcp))
    tcp = tcp[:16] + struct.pack("!H", csum(pseudo + tcp)) + tcp[18:]
    ip = struct.pack("!BBHHHBBH4s4s", 0x45, 0, 20 + len(tcp), 0, 0, 64, 6, 0,
                     socket.inet_aton(src), dst)
    return ip + tcp

def syn_recv_count():
    n = 0
    with open("/proc/net/tcp") as f:
        next(f)
        for line in f:
            local, state = line.split()[1], line.split()[3]
            if state == "03" and local.endswith(f":{PORT:04X}"):   # 03 = SYN_RECV
                n += 1
    return n

before = tcpext()
raw = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.IPPROTO_RAW)
for i in range(syns):
    src = f"198.51.100.{1 + i % 254}"
    raw.sendto(syn(src, 1024 + i), (SERVER, 0))
time.sleep(0.5)
print(f"tcp_syncookies={cookies} tcp_max_syn_backlog={max_syn_backlog} "
      f"listen({backlog}) spoofed SYNs={syns}")
print(f"  SYN_RECV entries on :{PORT}: {syn_recv_count()}")

c = socket.socket()
c.settimeout(3)
t0 = time.monotonic()
try:
    c.connect((SERVER, PORT))
    conn, _ = lsock.accept()
    print(f"  real client: connected in {1000*(time.monotonic()-t0):.1f} ms, accepted")
except OSError as e:
    print(f"  real client: FAILED after {time.monotonic()-t0:.1f} s ({e})")
print(f"  TcpExt deltas: {delta(before, tcpext())}")
unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 synflood_lab.py 0  128 4096 1000   # cookies off, small max_syn_backlog
unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 synflood_lab.py 0 4096   64 1000   # cookies off, small listen backlog
unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 synflood_lab.py 1  128   64 1000   # default: cookies when full
unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 synflood_lab.py 2  128   64   10   # cookies always
tcp_syncookies=0 tcp_max_syn_backlog=128 listen(4096) spoofed SYNs=1000
  SYN_RECV entries on :8080: 97
  real client: FAILED after 3.0 s (timed out)
  TcpExt deltas: {'ListenDrops': 906}
tcp_syncookies=0 tcp_max_syn_backlog=4096 listen(64) spoofed SYNs=1000
  SYN_RECV entries on :8080: 65
  real client: FAILED after 3.0 s (timed out)
  TcpExt deltas: {'ListenDrops': 938, 'TCPReqQFullDrop': 938}
tcp_syncookies=1 tcp_max_syn_backlog=128 listen(64) spoofed SYNs=1000
  SYN_RECV entries on :8080: 65
  real client: connected in 0.2 ms, accepted
  TcpExt deltas: {'TCPReqQFullDoCookies': 936, 'SyncookiesSent': 936, 'SyncookiesRecv': 1}
tcp_syncookies=2 tcp_max_syn_backlog=128 listen(64) spoofed SYNs=10
  SYN_RECV entries on :8080: 0
  real client: connected in 0.1 ms, accepted
  TcpExt deltas: {'TCPReqQFullDoCookies': 11, 'SyncookiesSent': 11, 'SyncookiesRecv': 1}
Every number is accounted for:

Cookies off, listen(4096), tcp_max_syn_backlog=128. The SYN queue is nowhere near the listen limit, but it stops at 97 entries: step 3 drops unproven peers once fewer than 128 >> 2 = 32 slots of tcp_max_syn_backlog remain (128 − 97 < 32). 1000 − 97 = 903 spoofed SYNs dropped, plus the real client’s SYN and its two retransmits (at 1 s and 3 s) = 906 ListenDrops. This path does not count TCPReqQFullDrop because the queue is not “full”, it is being rationed. The real client is a new, unproven peer, so it loses too.
Cookies off, listen(64), tcp_max_syn_backlog=4096. Now the listen backlog is the limit: 65 entries (> 64), then step 1 drops: 935 + 3 client attempts = 938, counted as both TCPReqQFullDrop and ListenDrops. A large tcp_max_syn_backlog did not buy a single extra slot.
Default cookies (1). The same 65 entries fill, then every further SYN gets a cookie: 935 spoofed + 1 real = 936 SyncookiesSent. The real client’s ACK validates (SyncookiesRecv 1) and it connects in 0.2 ms, with a queue full of junk.
Cookies always (2). No request sockets at all (SYN_RECV 0). Every SYN, including the real one, is answered statelessly. This is a test mode, and it costs every client its options (next lab).

The kernel also logged the event once per listener (ratelimited, tcp_syn_flood_action()), on the host’s dmesg, which is shared by all namespaces:
TCP: request_sock_TCP: Possible SYN flooding on port 10.9.0.1:8080. Dropping request.
TCP: request_sock_TCP: Possible SYN flooding on port 10.9.0.1:8080. Sending cookies.
Case 1 logs nothing: step 3 drops are reported only through pr_drop_req() at debug level. A host can be shedding real clients with no warning in the log, which is one more reason to read the counters.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
section: Lab — what a cookie connection keeps
text:
Lab — what a cookie connection keeps
# cookie_options_lab.py — what a SYN-cookie connection keeps of the client's TCP options
# usage: unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 cookie_options_lab.py
import socket, struct

TS, SACK, WSCALE = 1, 2, 4                  # TCPI_OPT_* bits in tcp_info.tcpi_options

def sysctl(name, value):
    with open("/proc/sys/" + name.replace(".", "/"), "w") as f:
        f.write(str(value))

def options(sock):
    raw = sock.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_INFO, 104)
    opts, wscale = raw[5], raw[6]
    snd_mss = struct.unpack_from("I", raw, 16)[0]
    names = [n for bit, n in ((TS, "timestamps"), (SACK, "sack"), (WSCALE, "wscale")) if opts & bit]
    if opts & WSCALE:
        names[-1] += f"={wscale & 0xF}/{wscale >> 4}"
    return f"{' '.join(names) or '(no options)'}  snd_mss={snd_mss}"

def handshake(cookies, timestamps):
    sysctl("net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies", cookies)
    sysctl("net.ipv4.tcp_timestamps", timestamps)
    lsock = socket.socket()
    lsock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    lsock.bind(("10.9.0.1", 8080))
    lsock.listen(16)
    c = socket.socket()
    c.connect(("10.9.0.1", 8080))
    conn, _ = lsock.accept()
    print(f"syncookies={cookies} timestamps={timestamps}: server sees {options(conn)}")
    for s in (c, conn, lsock):
        s.close()

handshake(0, 1)   # normal handshake
handshake(2, 1)   # always cookies, timestamps on: options ride in the TS value
handshake(2, 0)   # always cookies, no timestamps: only an MSS bucket survives
unshare -rn ./netns_lab.sh python3 cookie_options_lab.py
syncookies=0 timestamps=1: server sees timestamps sack wscale=7/7  snd_mss=32768
syncookies=2 timestamps=1: server sees timestamps sack wscale=7/7  snd_mss=1448
syncookies=2 timestamps=0: server sees (no options)  snd_mss=1460

A normal handshake negotiates timestamps, SACK, and window scale 7 in both directions. The MSS is large because the path is local (veth address over loopback, MTU 65536).
With a cookie and timestamps, window scale and SACK survive (they rode in the timestamp’s low bits). The MSS drops to 1448: 1460 from msstab minus 12 bytes of timestamp option. A loopback-class path now uses Ethernet-sized segments.
With a cookie and no timestamps, nothing survives: no window scaling (receive window capped at 64 KiB, which caps throughput at 64 KiB per RTT), no SACK (loss recovery without selective acknowledgements, one hole per RTT), MSS 1460. Some middleboxes and hosts disable TCP timestamps for privacy or legacy reasons; their users pay this price on every cookie connection.

That is why cookies are the default fallback (1), not the default mode (2).

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
text:
Case — reading a production listener
The same counters tell three different stories. Take two samples a few seconds apart (nstat with no -a prints the delta since its last run):








You see
It is
Do




ListenOverflows rising, Recv-Q = Send-Q + 1 on ss -lnt, cookie counters flat
Accept queue full: the application is slow (GC pause, blocked event loop, too few workers) or the backlog is tiny
Fix the accept loop, raise the app’s listen backlog and somaxconn


TCPReqQFullDoCookies / SyncookiesSent rising, many SYN_RECV from scattered sources, SyncookiesRecv small
SYN flood (or a burst far above the backlog), cookies are absorbing it
Nothing urgent on the host; raise the backlog if real clients also trigger it; push filtering upstream


SyncookiesRecv ≈ SyncookiesSent, few distinct sources
Legitimate load above the SYN-queue limit, served by cookies
Raise the listen backlog; this is the case the sysctl docs warn about


TCPReqQFullDrop or ListenDrops rising with cookies off
Real clients are being refused
Turn cookies back on (tcp_syncookies=1)



ss -lnt '( sport = :443 )'                       # Recv-Q / Send-Q per listener
ss -Htn state syn-recv '( sport = :443 )' | wc -l  # half-open count
nstat TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops TcpExtTCPReqQFullDoCookies TcpExtSyncookiesSent TcpExtSyncookiesRecv
(Commands for a production host; their output here would be the zero counters shown in the setup.)

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
text:
The trap
Trap: “raise tcp_max_syn_backlog to survive a SYN flood.” On current kernels the SYN queue limit is the listen backlog (capped by somaxconn). tcp_max_syn_backlog matters only when cookies are off, and then it is a rationing threshold, not a size. Lab case 2 set it to 4096 and still got 65 slots. The ip-sysctl text still calls it a “maximal number of remembered connection requests”; the code in tcp_conn_request() is the authority.
Trap: “SYN cookies protect against a full accept queue.” They do not. Step 2 drops SYNs when the accept queue is full, cookies or not. A slow accept() loop looks like a SYN flood to clients (timeouts in SYN-SENT) but shows ListenOverflows, not cookie counters.
Trap: “listen(65535) gives me a 64 K backlog.” somaxconn clamps it without an error. Check Send-Q on the listener.
Trap: “turn on tcp_abort_on_overflow so clients fail fast.” It only resets handshakes whose final ACK arrives into a full accept queue, and it turns a recoverable burst into hard ECONNRESETs. Fix the accept rate instead.
Trap: “tcp_syncookies=2 is safer.” It disables request sockets entirely, so every client gets cookie-quality options (MSS table, no options without timestamps). Leave it at 1.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
text:
The boring rule
Size the listen backlog in the application and in somaxconn together, leave tcp_syncookies=1, and when clients time out, read ss -lnt and the TcpExt counters before touching a sysctl: ListenOverflows means accept faster, SyncookiesSent means you are being flooded and the host is coping.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
text:
Try this

Re-run the accept-queue lab, then add an accept() loop after 2 s. How long do the SYN-SENT clients take to get in, and why (SYN retransmit backoff 1, 2, 4 s …)?
In the flood lab, set tcp_synack_retries=1 with cookies off. Re-run the real client after 5 s instead of immediately. What changed, and what does that tell you about how long a flood must be sustained?
Add IPv6 to netns_lab.sh (2001:db8::/32 routed into the void) and repeat case 3. Which counters are shared between IPv4 and IPv6?
With tcp_timestamps=0 on the client side only, make a cookie connection and send 10 MB over the veth. Compare throughput with a normal connection.
Put an nft synproxy rule in front of the lab listener (the namespace lets you load rules there) and compare which counters move during the flood.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
text:
Verification

Linux 6.12.94+ (Debian 13), iproute2 6.15.0, Python 3.13.5, unprivileged user uid=1000; each lab ran in its own unshare -rn user + network namespace. All outputs above are pasted from those runs.
The flood was real (1000 hand-built SYN packets on a raw socket per case) but never left the namespace: spoofed sources are TEST-NET-2, SYN-ACKs went to a static fake neighbour on a veth with no peer stack. Host TcpExt counters stayed 0.
Counter arithmetic was checked against tcp_conn_request(), tcp_syn_flood_action(), inet_csk_reqsk_queue_is_full(), sk_acceptq_is_full() (Linux 6.12) and the SYN retransmit timing of the real client (initial RTO 1 s).
Not shown: the tcp_abort_on_overflow RST path (it needs a final ACK to race a filling accept queue, which local handshakes do not do); it is described from tcp_check_req() in tcp_minisocks.c. Production ss/nstat commands in the Case section were not run against a production host.
No packages installed, no sudo, no host sysctl changed.

title: SYN Floods and Listen Queues: SYN_RECV, SYN Cookies, and Accept Overflow
text:

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
text:
FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
A link that is full does not have to be slow. When a bulk upload makes a video call stutter, the culprit is almost never bandwidth. It is a queue in front of the bottleneck that fills with the upload’s packets until each call packet waits hundreds of milliseconds behind them. That is bufferbloat. Linux has two well-known answers. FQ-CoDel (RFC 8290) gives each flow its own small queue and keeps each queue short with the CoDel AQM (RFC 8289). CAKE adds a shaper so that you own the bottleneck queue rather than the modem. This chapter builds the algorithms from the RFC pseudocode in a small simulator, measures FIFO against CoDel and FQ-CoDel, and ends with the configuration and checks that matter on a real router.

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
text:
Learning goals

Explain why a full FIFO causes delay without causing loss, and why loss-based TCP keeps filling it
Describe CoDel’s control law: sojourn time, target, interval, and drop spacing interval/sqrt(count)
Describe FQ-CoDel’s DRR scheduler with new and old flow lists, and why sparse flows skip the queue
Know when FQ-CoDel is enough and when you need CAKE’s shaper (or HTB + FQ-CoDel)
Verify which qdisc is really running, and whether the queue you are managing is the one that fills

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
text:
Mental model



FIFO, CoDel and FQ-CoDel in front of a 10 Mbit/s bottleneck, with the sparse-flow latency each one produced in the lab.


              one queue                         per-flow queues + DRR
FIFO       [b b b b b b b b b b v b b b] ─►    FQ-CoDel   new: [v] ──┐
           v waits behind everything            old: [b b] [b b] [b b] [b b] ─┴─► link
CoDel      [b b b v b] ─► drop at head when     each queue has its own CoDel,
           sojourn > 5 ms for 100 ms            a sparse flow is served from "new"
Three rules:

Delay is queue length divided by link rate. A thousand 1514-byte packets at 10 Mbit/s is 1.2 seconds. Memory is cheap, so buffers are deep.
Loss-based TCP grows until something drops. A deep tail-drop buffer gives no signal, so every bulk flow fills it. AQM sends the signal (drop or ECN mark) early, based on time spent queued rather than bytes.
You can only manage a queue you own. The qdisc must sit on the bottleneck. On a home router the bottleneck is usually the modem’s buffer, so you shape slightly below line rate (CAKE bandwidth, or HTB) to move the queue into Linux.

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
text:
Concepts

CoDel in four lines (RFC 8289)

Stamp every packet at enqueue. At dequeue compute its sojourn time.
If sojourn has been above target (5 ms) continuously for at least interval (100 ms), enter the dropping state and drop the head packet.
While dropping, drop the next packet after interval / sqrt(count), so the drop rate rises until TCP backs off.
Leave the dropping state as soon as sojourn falls below target. If you re-enter soon, resume near the previous count rather than starting over.

Dropping at the head matters: the sender learns about congestion one queue-length sooner than it would with tail drop.


FQ-CoDel (RFC 8290)

Packets are hashed on the 5-tuple into one of 1024 queues (flows). Each queue has its own CoDel state.
A deficit round robin scheduler with a 1514-byte quantum serves two lists. A queue that becomes active joins new_flows and is served first. When it uses up its quantum, it moves to the tail of old_flows.
A flow that never builds a queue (DNS, game traffic, voice, TCP ACKs) is served from new_flows almost every time it has a packet, which is why its latency collapses.
The defaults in tc-fq_codel(8) are limit 10240 packets, memory_limit 32 MB, target 5ms, interval 100ms, and ecn on, which unlike plain codel marks ECN-capable packets instead of dropping them.



CAKE (tc-cake(8))
CAKE is “a shaping-capable queue discipline which uses both AQM and FQ”. Its parts:

COBALT, which is CoDel combined with BLUE for unresponsive flows
a deficit-mode shaper
DRR++ flow isolation with 8-way set-associative hashing
diffserv tins (diffserv3 by default)
triple-isolate per-host fairness by default, with nat to see through masquerading
overhead keywords (docsis, ethernet, pppoe-*, atm) that make the shaper count bytes the way the link does



Who is on by default

The kernel’s built-in net.core.default_qdisc is pfifo_fast. Virtual devices such as lo and veth ignore it and default to noqueue.
systemd’s sysctl.d/50-default.conf sets net.core.default_qdisc = fq_codel, so most systemd distributions get FQ-CoDel on new interfaces.
Multi-queue NICs get mq with a per-queue child of that default.
Interfaces created before the sysctl applied, and kernels without the module, keep whatever they had.

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
section: Lab 1: what this host actually runs
text:
Lab 1: what this host actually runs
$ cat /proc/sys/net/core/default_qdisc
pfifo_fast
$ ip link show enp0s4 | head -1
2: enp0s4: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc pfifo_fast state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000
The box has pfifo_fast, not fq_codel. tc is not installed, so kernel.py asks the kernel directly over netlink (pyroute2 0.9.7 in a user venv) inside an unprivileged network namespace (unshare -rn). It creates a veth pair and tries to attach each qdisc:
from pyroute2 import IPRoute
ip = IPRoute()
ip.link('add', ifname='a', kind='veth', peer='b')
i = ip.link_lookup(ifname='a')[0]
for kind in ('pfifo', 'fq_codel', 'cake'):
    try:
        ip.tc('add', kind, i, '1:'); print(f"{kind:9} available"); ip.tc('del', kind, i, '1:')
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{kind:9} {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
$ unshare -rn python kernel.py
pfifo     available
fq_codel  NetlinkError: (2, 'No such file or directory')
cake      NetlinkError: (2, 'No such file or directory')
ENOENT from RTM_NEWQDISC means the kernel does not know that qdisc, either because sch_fq_codel / sch_cake is not built or because the module cannot be loaded. This kernel (6.12) is a minimal build with neither. On a real router the same check is tc qdisc add dev X root fq_codel failing with “No such file or directory”. Check this before you tune parameters that are not running.

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
text:
Lab 2: the algorithms, simulated
Because the kernel here has no FQ-CoDel, aqm.py implements both from the RFCs. CoDel follows the RFC 8289 §5 pseudocode. FQ-CoDel follows RFC 8290 §4: DRR over new/old lists with a CoDel per queue. The bottleneck is 10 Mbit/s with a 1000-packet buffer. Four Reno-like bulk flows run with a 20 ms base RTT, alongside one sparse flow sending a 200-byte packet every 20 ms. Delay is measured from enqueue to the end of transmission:
"""Bottleneck simulator: FIFO vs CoDel (RFC 8289) vs FQ-CoDel (RFC 8290).
10 Mbit/s link, 1514-byte bulk packets, 4 Reno-like bulk flows (base RTT 20 ms),
plus one sparse flow: a 200-byte packet every 20 ms (a VoIP-ish probe)."""
import heapq, math, statistics, sys
from collections import deque

RATE = 10e6 / 8            # bytes per second
BASE_RTT = 0.020
TARGET, INTERVAL = 0.005, 0.100   # RFC 8289 defaults
LIMIT = 1000               # packets, a "bufferbloated" tail-drop buffer
SIM = float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 30.0

class CoDel:                       # RFC 8289 section 5 pseudocode, one instance per queue
    def __init__(s): s.first_above = 0.0; s.drop_next = 0.0; s.count = 0; s.lastcount = 0; s.dropping = False
    def _ok_to_drop(s, sojourn, now, qlen_bytes):
        if sojourn < TARGET or qlen_bytes <= 1514:
            s.first_above = 0.0; return False
        if s.first_above == 0.0:
            s.first_above = now + INTERVAL; return False
        return now >= s.first_above
    def dequeue(s, q, now, drop):
        """q: deque of (enq_time, size, flow, seq); returns a packet or None; drop(p) records a drop."""
        if not q: s.dropping = False; return None
        p = q.popleft(); ok = s._ok_to_drop(now - p[0], now, sum(x[1] for x in q) + p[1])
        if s.dropping:
            if not ok: s.dropping = False
            while s.dropping and now >= s.drop_next:
                drop(p); s.count += 1
                if not q: s.dropping = False; return None
                p = q.popleft()
                if not s._ok_to_drop(now - p[0], now, sum(x[1] for x in q) + p[1]): s.dropping = False
                else: s.drop_next += INTERVAL / math.sqrt(s.count)
        elif ok:
            drop(p)
            if not q: return None
            p = q.popleft(); s.dropping = True
            delta = s.count - s.lastcount
            s.count = delta if (delta > 1 and now - s.drop_next < 16 * INTERVAL) else 1
            s.drop_next = now + INTERVAL / math.sqrt(s.count); s.lastcount = s.count
        return p

class Fifo:
    def __init__(s, aqm): s.q = deque(); s.codel = CoDel() if aqm else None
    def enqueue(s, p, drop):
        if len(s.q) >= LIMIT: drop(p)
        else: s.q.append(p)
    def dequeue(s, now, drop):
        if s.codel: return s.codel.dequeue(s.q, now, drop)
        return s.q.popleft() if s.q else None
    def __len__(s): return len(s.q)

class FqCodel:                     # RFC 8290 section 4: DRR over new/old flow lists, CoDel per queue
    QUANTUM = 1514
    def __init__(s): s.qs = {}; s.new = deque(); s.old = deque(); s.n = 0
    def enqueue(s, p, drop):
        f = p[2]
        if f not in s.qs: s.qs[f] = [deque(), CoDel(), 0, None]   # queue, codel, deficit, list
        st = s.qs[f]; st[0].append(p); s.n += 1
        if st[3] is None: st[2] = s.QUANTUM; st[3] = 'new'; s.new.append(f)
        if s.n > LIMIT * 10:       # drop from the fattest queue (section 4.1)
            fat = max(s.qs, key=lambda k: sum(x[1] for x in s.qs[k][0])); drop(s.qs[fat][0].popleft()); s.n -= 1
    def dequeue(s, now, drop):
        while s.new or s.old:
            lst = s.new if s.new else s.old
            f = lst[0]; st = s.qs[f]
            if st[2] <= 0:
                st[2] += s.QUANTUM; lst.popleft(); s.old.append(f); st[3] = 'old'; continue
            before = len(st[0])
            p = st[1].dequeue(st[0], now, drop); s.n -= before - len(st[0])
            if p is None:
                lst.popleft()
                if lst is s.new: s.old.append(f); st[3] = 'old'
                else: st[3] = None
                continue
            st[2] -= p[1]; return p
        return None
    def __len__(s): return s.n

def run(name, qdisc):
    ev, now, seq = [], 0.0, 0
    cwnd = {f: 2.0 for f in range(4)}; inflight = {f: 0 for f in range(4)}; last_cut = {f: -1.0 for f in range(4)}
    delays = {f: [] for f in range(5)}; delivered = {f: 0 for f in range(5)}; drops = [0]
    busy = [False]
    def push(t, kind, data=None):
        nonlocal seq; seq += 1; heapq.heappush(ev, (t, seq, kind, data))
    def drop(p):
        drops[0] += 1
        if p[2] < 4: push(now + BASE_RTT, 'loss', p)     # sender notices about one RTT later
    def send(f, size):
        qdisc.enqueue((now, size, f, seq), drop)
        if f < 4: inflight[f] += 1
        if not busy[0]: push(now, 'tx')
        busy[0] = True
    def pump(f):
        while inflight[f] < int(cwnd[f]): send(f, 1514)
    for f in range(4): push(0.01 * f, 'start', f)
    push(0.5, 'sparse')
    while ev:
        now, _, kind, d = heapq.heappop(ev)
        if now > SIM: break
        if kind == 'start': pump(d)
        elif kind == 'sparse': send(4, 200); push(now + 0.020, 'sparse')
        elif kind == 'tx':
            p = qdisc.dequeue(now, drop)
            if p is None: busy[0] = False; continue
            done = now + p[1] / RATE
            if now > 5.0: delays[p[2]].append(done - p[0]); delivered[p[2]] += p[1]
            if p[2] < 4: push(done + BASE_RTT, 'ack', p)
            push(done, 'tx')
        elif kind == 'ack':
            f = d[2]; inflight[f] -= 1; cwnd[f] += 1 / cwnd[f]; pump(f)
        elif kind == 'loss':
            f = d[2]; inflight[f] -= 1
            if now - last_cut[f] > BASE_RTT: cwnd[f] = max(2.0, cwnd[f] / 2); last_cut[f] = now
            pump(f)
    ms = lambda xs, q: 1000 * statistics.quantiles(xs, n=100)[q - 1]
    bulk = [x for f in range(4) for x in delays[f]]
    tput = sum(delivered[f] for f in range(4)) * 8 / (SIM - 5.0) / 1e6
    share = [round(delivered[f] / sum(delivered[g] for g in range(4)), 2) for f in range(4)]
    print(f"{name:9} sparse p50 {ms(delays[4],50):6.1f} ms  p99 {ms(delays[4],99):6.1f} ms | "
          f"bulk p50 {ms(bulk,50):6.1f} ms | bulk {tput:4.2f} Mbit/s shares {share} | drops {drops[0]}")

print(f"10 Mbit/s bottleneck, 4 bulk flows + 1 sparse flow, {SIM:.0f} s simulated, stats after 5 s")
run('fifo', Fifo(False)); run('codel', Fifo(True)); run('fq_codel', FqCodel())
$ python3 aqm.py
10 Mbit/s bottleneck, 4 bulk flows + 1 sparse flow, 30 s simulated, stats after 5 s
fifo      sparse p50  385.3 ms  p99  511.7 ms | bulk p50  385.3 ms | bulk 9.92 Mbit/s shares [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] | drops 0
codel     sparse p50   12.4 ms  p99   21.3 ms | bulk p50   13.0 ms | bulk 9.92 Mbit/s shares [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] | drops 850
fq_codel  sparse p50    0.8 ms  p99    1.4 ms | bulk p50   14.2 ms | bulk 9.92 Mbit/s shares [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] | drops 740
$ python3 aqm.py 120
10 Mbit/s bottleneck, 4 bulk flows + 1 sparse flow, 120 s simulated, stats after 5 s
fifo      sparse p50  755.6 ms  p99 1048.2 ms | bulk p50  755.2 ms | bulk 9.92 Mbit/s shares [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] | drops 0
codel     sparse p50   12.7 ms  p99   21.8 ms | bulk p50   13.0 ms | bulk 9.92 Mbit/s shares [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] | drops 3405
fq_codel  sparse p50    0.8 ms  p99    1.4 ms | bulk p50   14.2 ms | bulk 9.92 Mbit/s shares [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] | drops 2975
What the numbers say:

FIFO never drops, and gets worse with time. With 0 drops TCP gets no signal, so the queue keeps growing. The sparse flow’s median delay rises from 385 ms after 30 s to 756 ms after 120 s, for the same 9.92 Mbit/s of throughput.
CoDel holds the queue near target. About 13 ms (5 ms target, plus the time it takes the four flows to react, plus serialisation) at the same throughput, by dropping roughly one bulk packet in 30.
FQ-CoDel isolates. The bulk flows see the same ~14 ms as under CoDel, but the sparse flow sees 0.8 ms, because it is almost always on the new-flows list. That is the effect you notice on a call.

This is a model, not a kernel. There is no ECN, no pacing, no GSO, no hash collisions, and a simplified Reno. Treat the ratios as the lesson, not the milliseconds.

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
section: Lab 3: configuring it (from the man pages; not run here)
text:
Lab 3: configuring it (from the man pages; not run here)
The box has no tc and no FQ-CoDel/CAKE in its kernel, so these come from tc-fq_codel(8), tc-cake(8) and systemd.network(5) and were not run:
# What is running, with drop/mark/backlog counters
tc -s qdisc show dev eth0

# Hosts and servers where the NIC is the bottleneck: FQ-CoDel at root
tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root fq_codel

# Router WAN on a 100/20 Mbit/s cable line: shape upload just below the line rate
tc qdisc replace dev wan0 root cake bandwidth 19mbit docsis nat
# systemd-networkd equivalent (/etc/systemd/network/10-wan.network)
[Match]
Name=wan0

[CAKE]
Parent=root
Bandwidth=19M
NAT=yes
OverheadBytes=18
MPUBytes=64
For download, the queue forms at the ISP side, so shaping ingress requires redirecting it to an ifb device and attaching CAKE there with the ingress keyword.

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
text:
The trap

Managing a queue that never fills. FQ-CoDel on the WAN NIC of a router with a 1 Gbit/s port in front of a 20 Mbit/s modem does nothing: the queue builds in the modem. Shape below line rate, or the AQM has nothing to manage.
Shaping exactly at line rate. Shape slightly below the measured rate, so the queue moves into Linux and not into the modem. The man pages leave the margin to you, and setting CAKE’s overhead keyword correctly matters as much as the number.
Believing the sysctl. default_qdisc applies only to qdiscs created after it is set, and only where the kernel has the module. Lab 1 shows a 6.12 kernel without it. Always read tc -s qdisc.
Tuning target for a LAN-only path. interval should be on the order of the worst-case RTT through the bottleneck (tc-fq_codel(8)). Lowering it for a datacentre path makes Internet flows back off too hard.
Benchmarking with one flow. Fairness and isolation show up only with several bulk flows plus a latency probe, as in Lab 2. A single iperf3 stream mostly measures the shaper.

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
text:
The boring rule
Make sure FQ-CoDel (or fq with paced TCP on servers) is actually attached wherever Linux is the bottleneck. On routers in front of slower links, run CAKE (or HTB + FQ-CoDel) with bandwidth just under the real rate and the right overhead keyword, in both directions. Then measure latency under load, with several flows, before and after.

title: FQ-CoDel and CAKE: How Linux Fights Bufferbloat, and How to Check It Is Actually On
text:
Try this

In aqm.py, raise LIMIT to 5000 and run FIFO for 300 s. When do the first drops appear, and what is the sparse delay then?
Add an unresponsive bulk flow, a constant 6 Mbit/s that ignores loss. What happens to the Reno flows’ shares under CoDel versus FQ-CoDel? This is the case BLUE in CAKE’s COBALT is for.
Send the sparse flow at 2 Mbit/s instead of 80 kbit/s, so it is no longer sparse. Does it stay on the new-flows list?
Change INTERVAL to 10 ms with the 20 ms RTT. Watch throughput and drops, and explain them with rule 2.
On a Linux machine you control, run tc -s qdisc while a large upload is running, and read dropped, ecn_mark and new_flows_len.

Sources

RFC 8289 — Controlled Delay Active Queue Management: §3 building blocks, §4 overview, §5 annotated pseudocode
