title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
text:
Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
Netfilter connection tracking (nf_conntrack) is a table of flows, not of sockets. NAT, stateful firewall rules, and many “related” helpers consult it on every packet. When the table cannot hold a new entry, the kernel logs nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet and the new flow dies. Existing entries keep working, which is why the symptom is so confusing: SSH sessions that are already up stay up, pings to the host may still answer, and a fresh TCP handshake or a burst of short UDP (DNS is the classic) starts failing.
A system-level nftables chapter (in review, or already in this part) is where tables, chains, and ct matchers live. This chapter is the table underneath: how big it is, how long an entry lives, why it fills, and what to change without guessing.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
text:
Learning goals

Read nf_conntrack_max, nf_conntrack_count, and nf_conntrack_buckets, and interpret the “table full” log line
Explain that each flow occupies the hash table in both directions, so a full table has an average chain length of about two with the default max == buckets
Use timeouts (tcp_timeout_established, udp_timeout, udp_timeout_stream, tcp_timeout_time_wait) as the other half of capacity planning
Know which sysctls are only writable in the initial network namespace, and that a namespace without nft/iptables rules may not track local sockets at all
Distinguish “raise max” from “shorten timeouts,” “do not track this traffic,” and “stop making so many flows”

Version note. Host sysctls were read on 2026-11-13 on Linux 6.12.94+. This writing user cannot read /proc/net/nf_conntrack (permission denied) and must not paste other tenants’ tuples in any case. A throwaway netns (unshare -urnm, root in a user namespace) showed a separate nf_conntrack_count of 0, read-only nf_conntrack_max and nf_conntrack_buckets, and still count = 0 after eight localhost TCP connections — there is no nftables/iptables on this host, so no conntrack hook was attached and no table-full event could be produced. A genuine exhaustion run was not performed (and must not be performed on a shared host). Timeouts, the log message, and the “entries are inserted twice” hash-table note are from the kernel’s Netfilter Conntrack Sysfs variables documentation. nft and the conntrack userspace tool are not installed.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
section: The table, the hash, and the counter
text:
The table, the hash, and the counter
Three numbers matter first:








Sysctl
This host
Meaning




net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count
393 (it moves)
Entries currently allocated (read-only)


net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
262144
Hard cap; a new flow is dropped when it would exceed this


net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_buckets
262144
Hash-table size



On this host, at 00:45 IST:
# uname -r
6.12.94+
# cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max
262144
# cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count
393
# cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_buckets
262144
# cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_expect_max
4096
The kernel documentation is explicit about two things operators regularly get backwards.
First, nf_conntrack_max defaults to nf_conntrack_buckets. Raising max without raising buckets makes each hash chain longer and lookups slower. nf_conntrack_buckets is only writable in the initial network namespace. It may also be set as a module parameter at load time. The default bucket count is derived from memory (total RAM / 16384), then clamped to [1024, 262144]. This host is already at the documented clamp for buckets.
Second, each flow is entered twice — once for the original direction and once for the reply (addresses reversed). With max == buckets, a full table has an average hash chain length of two, not one. That is expected, not a misconfiguration.
nf_conntrack_count approaching nf_conntrack_max is the warning. The log line when a new insertion fails is:
nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet
(older kernels said ip_conntrack: table full, dropping packet). Established flows already in the table are not evicted to make room. That is why a “the server is down” ticket can coexist with a working ping and an existing SSH session.
This host’s count was a few hundred against a 262144 cap — not in danger. A busy NAT gateway, a DNS recursive resolver, or a node doing per-flow NAT for many short connections will be.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
text:
Timeouts are capacity
An entry lives until its protocol timer expires without traffic. The documented defaults, and the values on this host, agree:
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established = 432000
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait = 120
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_close_wait = 60
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_fin_wait = 120
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_syn_sent = 120
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_syn_recv = 60
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_udp_timeout = 30
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_udp_timeout_stream = 120
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_icmp_timeout = 30
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_generic_timeout = 600
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_loose = 1
tcp_timeout_established = 432000 is five days. A long-lived TCP flow is cheap in count (one entry) and expensive only if you have a huge number of them. The usual exhaustion pattern is the opposite: many short flows that still occupy a slot.

TCP that open and close quickly still sit in TIME_WAIT in conntrack for tcp_timeout_time_wait (120 s here), which is a different timer from the socket’s TCP_TIMEWAIT and can outlast what the application expects.
UDP is worse for churn. A single DNS query is a flow. The default udp_timeout is 30 s; once the kernel decides the 4-tuple looks like a stream, udp_timeout_stream (120 s) applies. A resolver or a log shipper that talks to many destinations can fill the table with entries that are already application-done.
tcp_loose defaults to 1: conntrack will pick up an already-established TCP session that it did not see the handshake for (common after a failover or a ruleset reload). Set it to 0 only if you understand that mid-flow packets may then be invalid.

Capacity is roughly “how many new flows per second × how long each entry lives.” Raising max is one lever. Shortening udp_timeout or tcp_timeout_time_wait is another, and it has a correctness cost (late packets may no longer match). Not tracking traffic that does not need NAT or stateful policy is a third.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
section: What fills the table in real networks
text:
What fills the table in real networks
Typical causes, in the order they are usually worth checking:

NAT of high-churn UDP, especially DNS from many sources through one gateway, or a node that SNATs a fleet of short connections.
A ruleset that attached conntrack as a side effect. Loading a NAT table, or even listing one on some systems, can start tracking all seen flows, not just the ones you intended to translate. A router that did not need conntrack yesterday can start filling a table after one diagnostic command. (This host already had 393 entries, so something in the environment already attached hooks in the initial netns. We did not inspect those tuples.)
Expect table growth (nf_conntrack_expect_max, 4096 here) from helpers (FTP, SIP, …). Exhaustion of expects is a different cap, but it shows up as “related” traffic failing first.
Scanning or a flood of new 4-tuples aimed at a stateful filter. Each SYN can become an entry until tcp_timeout_syn_sent / syn_recv expires.

“Just raise max” without looking at which entries dominate (TCP established, UDP, SYN-sent) postpones the same outage. The conntrack userspace tool (conntrack -C, conntrack -L -o extended, counts by state) is the usual way to see that mix. It is not installed here and was not run. nft list ruleset plus ct matchers belong to the nftables chapter; notrack in the raw table (or nft equivalent) is how you exempt a class of traffic, for example a host-local DNS resolver talking to a known forwarder, if you do not also need to NAT it.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
section: Lab — what this host can and cannot show
text:
Lab — what this host can and cannot show
In a fresh netns the count starts at zero, which already tells you conntrack accounting is per-netns on this 6.12 kernel:
# unshare -urnm, then:
# ls -l /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_buckets
-r--r--r-- 1 root root 0 Nov 13 00:46 /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max
-r--r--r-- 1 root root 0 Nov 13 00:46 /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_buckets
# cat ...
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 262144
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count = 0
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_buckets = 262144
Writing a lower max (to exhaust the table safely) is not permitted in that namespace:
# echo 64 > /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max
bash: .../nf_conntrack_max: Permission denied
# echo 128 > /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_buckets
bash: .../nf_conntrack_buckets: Permission denied
That matches the kernel documentation for nf_conntrack_buckets (initial netns only). On this kernel nf_conntrack_max was similarly read-only for the unprivileged user namespace. Do not lower max in the initial netns of a shared machine to force a table-full event.
Eight localhost TCP connections, with lo up, left the counter at zero:
# 8 localhost TCP connections on 127.0.0.1:34279
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count = 0
No nft/iptables hook, no tracking. /proc/net/nf_conntrack was also unreadable in that namespace (PermissionError). An exhaustion lab therefore needs three things this writing host does not offer: a writable cap (or a dedicated machine), a ruleset that attaches conntrack, and enough new flows to hit the cap. On a machine where you can do that, the shape is:

Isolated netns or a dedicated lab VM, never a shared production table.
Attach a minimal stateful rule (a simple nft ct state filter or a masquerade).
Set a small nf_conntrack_max in a namespace where it is writable, or use a fresh VM.
Open more flows than max (many short TCP or UDP 4-tuples).
Confirm count sticks at max, new connects fail, dmesg shows table full, dropping packet, and a flow that was already established still works.
Restore max, tear the namespace down.

That procedure was not run here.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
text:
What to change, in order

Look at count / max and at recent table full lines in the kernel log. If you are not actually full, you are debugging a different failure.
See which states dominate, with conntrack -L or a distribution’s conntrack exporter, before you move a cap.
Fix the creator of churn if you can: a DNS ndots pattern that generates bursts of useless queries, a client that opens a new 4-tuple per request, a NAT that should not be in the path.
Exempt traffic that does not need a state table (notrack / nft equivalent), especially high-rate UDP that you are not NATing.
Tune timeouts only with a reason: shortening udp_timeout on a busy resolver is common; shortening tcp_timeout_established from five days is rarely the first fix for a churn problem.
Raise nf_conntrack_max and nf_conntrack_buckets together, in the initial netns, as a planned change. Memory: each entry is on the order of a few hundred bytes, and both directions are hashed. Persist the values in /etc/sysctl.d/ so a reboot does not surprise you. On this host buckets is already at the documented 262144 clamp; a larger max here would mean longer chains unless the kernel you run allows a bigger hash.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
text:
Gotchas

Raising only max. Longer hash chains, slower packet path, same timeout-driven accumulation.
Tuning timeouts on a shared gateway without measuring. Late DNS replies or a hung TCP close can break in ways that look like an application bug.
Assuming a new netns is a safe place to lower max. On this kernel those sysctls were not writable there, and local sockets were not tracked without a hook.
Reading count as “number of client connections.” It is flows × directions in the hash, including NAT, forwarded traffic, and mid-stream pickups (tcp_loose).
Clearing the table as a fix (conntrack -F) drops stateful NAT and firewall memory; existing NAT sessions break. Use it only as a lab or last-resort tool.
Forgetting that listing or loading a NAT ruleset can start tracking on a box that was previously stateless.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
text:
Boring rule
Treat nf_conntrack_count / nf_conntrack_max as a first-class capacity signal. When it is high, ask what is creating flows and how long they live before you add zeros to max.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
text:
Try this

On a disposable VM with nft, attach a simple ct state filter, watch nf_conntrack_count as you make a few TCP and UDP flows, and identify them with conntrack -L (or by reading /proc/net/nf_conntrack as root).
Without touching production, compute “new UDP flows per second × udp_timeout” for a resolver you run and compare it to max.
Confirm whether nf_conntrack_buckets is writable on your kernel, and whether it is already at 262144.
After you have a test ruleset, use notrack for one UDP port and confirm those 4-tuples stop appearing in the table.

title: Conntrack Exhaustion: Limits, Timeouts and the Table-Full Drop
text:
Sources

Linux kernel documentation, Netfilter Conntrack Sysfs variables: https://docs.kernel.org/networking/nf_conntrack-sysctl.html
The nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet diagnostic, as documented by distributions and the kernel log
nft(8) / nftables wiki for ct matching and notrack (see also the nftables fundamentals chapter in this part)

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
text:
MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
Media Access Control Security (MACsec), defined in IEEE 802.1AE, provides point-to-point security at the Data Link Layer (Layer 2) of the OSI model. Unlike Layer 3 encryption solutions like IPsec or application-layer mechanisms like TLS, MACsec operates directly on Ethernet frames, protecting everything the host or switch sends through the secured (controlled) port: IPv4, IPv6, ARP, ND and every routing protocol that rides on them. Key agreement (EAPOL-MKA) and, on most platforms, link-local control frames such as LLDP and LACP use the unsecured (uncontrolled) port and stay in the clear. Because MACsec operates between adjacent MAC entities, frames are decrypted at each receiving interface and re-encrypted on outbound interfaces, making it a hop-by-hop security mechanism rather than an end-to-end transport encryption protocol. Dynamic key management, peer discovery, and Secure Association Key (SAK) distribution are governed by the MACsec Key Agreement (MKA) protocol, defined in IEEE 802.1X-2010 and 802.1X-2020. This chapter covers the architectural components of 802.1AE, frame formats, cryptographic operations, packet number (PN) limits, key agreement via MKA, Linux kernel operational considerations, and cryptographic test vectors.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
text:
Learning goals

Explain the scope, positioning, and hop-by-hop boundaries of IEEE 802.1AE relative to network-layer security protocols.
Identify the core architectural elements of MACsec: SecY, KaY, CA, SC, SA, SCI, AN, SAK, CAK, and CKN.
Decode the 802.1AE SecTAG header structure, flag bits, EtherType values, and payload layout.
Calculate the framing overhead, MTU impact, and Packet Number (PN) exhaustion times across high-speed link rates.
Distinguish standard 32-bit PN MACsec from Extended Packet Numbering (XPN, 802.1AEbw) and explain the role of the SSCI and salt.
Evaluate Linux ip macsec commands, wpa_supplicant MKA configuration structures, and hardware offload architectures.
Analyze Python implementation output verifying IEEE published GCM-AES test vectors, replay protection rules, and receiver drop conditions.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
text:
Version note
The specifications and command structures detailed in this chapter reflect IEEE Std 802.1AE-2018 (incorporating 802.1AEbw-2013 XPN), IEEE Std 802.1X-2020, and the Linux iproute2 ip-macsec(8) interface present in modern kernel releases. Command syntax for user-space control relies on standard iproute2 and wpa_supplicant v2.10 or newer.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
text:
MACsec architecture and positioning
MACsec operates at the Media Access Control sublayer. It secures single physical or logical Ethernet links between two hosts, host-to-switch interfaces, or switch-to-switch links.

Layer 2 positioning and security boundaries
Because MACsec operates directly above the physical layer MAC entity, it secures everything inside the Ethernet frame after the Source MAC address for traffic on the controlled port. EAPOL frames used to bootstrap the keys never pass through the SecY.









Feature
MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE)
IPsec (ESP / ip xfrm)
WireGuard




OSI Layer
Data Link Layer (Layer 2)
Network Layer (Layer 3)
Layer 3 over UDP


Scope
Hop-by-Hop (adjacent nodes)
End-to-End or Site-to-Site
End-to-End or Site-to-Site


Secured Protocols
Everything on the controlled port (IP, ARP, ND)
IPv4, IPv6 (IP payloads only)
IPv4, IPv6 (IP payloads only)


Encapsulation Overhead
24 or 32 bytes
roughly 50 to 70+ bytes, depending on mode and cipher
60 bytes (IPv4 outer) / 80 bytes (IPv6 outer)


Intermediate Inspection
Decrypted at every L2 hop
Transparent to L2/L3 switches
Transparent to L2/L3 routers


Hardware Offload
Line-rate PHY/MAC ASIC support
Crypto co-processors / smartNIC
Software / Crypto offload



An Ethernet frame secured by MACsec contains a plain text Destination MAC address, Source MAC address, and a SecTAG header, followed by encrypted or authenticated payload data and an Integrity Check Value (ICV). Because intermediate switches process frames at Layer 2, a non-MACsec switch cannot bridge MACsec frames without explicit L2 pass-through, and any L2 device terminating MACsec will decrypt the frame into plain text inside its switching fabric before forwarding it to another port.


Core terminology and object model
MACsec defines a specific entity hierarchy for link protection:

SecY (MAC Security Entity): The functional protocol entity in a device’s stack that performs frame encryption, decryption, replay checking, and ICV validation.
KaY (MACsec Key Agreement Entity): The control-plane entity (typically implemented in user-space daemons like wpa_supplicant) that runs MKA to discover peers, authenticate them, elect a Key Server, and install keys into the SecY.
CA (Connectivity Association): A logical security relationship between two or more stations on a shared medium that share a Connectivity Association Key (CAK).
SC (Secure Channel): A unidirectional point-to-point vector transmitting secure traffic from a single transmitter to one or more receivers in a CA. Each SC is identified by a 64-bit SCI (Secure Channel Identifier), which consists of a 48-bit MAC address combined with a 16-bit Port Identifier (MAC + Port).
SA (Secure Association): A specific cryptographic instance within an SC containing active keys and counters. Up to 4 SAs can exist simultaneously per SC to facilitate zero-hit key rollover. An SA is selected using a 2-bit AN (Association Number) values 0 through 3.
SAK (Secure Association Key): The symmetric key used by the SecY to encrypt and/or authenticate data frames within a specific SA.
CAK / CKN: The long-term symmetric root key (CAK) and its corresponding hex-encoded name (CKN) used by MKA to authenticate peers and securely derive or wrap SAKs.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
section: MACsec frame format and cryptographic operations
text:
MACsec frame format and cryptographic operations
IEEE 802.1AE modifies the standard Ethernet frame format by prepending a 8-byte or 16-byte SecTAG after the Source MAC address and appending a 16-byte ICV at the end of the frame.
Standard Ethernet Frame:
+---------+---------+-----------+----------------+----------+
| DA (6B) | SA (6B) | Type (2B) |  Payload (N B) | FCS (4B) |
+---------+---------+-----------+----------------+----------+

MACsec Frame (SC=1, SCI included):
+---------+---------+----------------+-----------------+---------------+----------+
| DA (6B) | SA (6B) | SecTAG (16B)   | Secure Payload  |  ICV (16B)    | FCS (4B) |
|         |         | EtherType=88E5 | (Encrypted/Auth)| (GCM-AES tag) |          |
+---------+---------+----------------+-----------------+---------------+----------+

SecTAG header bit field detail
The SecTAG is identified by the registered EtherType value 0x88E5. Its internal binary layout is structured as follows:

EtherType (16 bits): Always 0x88E5.
TCI/AN Byte (8 bits): Tag Control Information and Association Number.

Bit 7 (V): Version. Must be 0.
Bit 6 (ES): End Station. Set to 1 when the transmitter’s SCI is its source MAC address plus port 1, so a receiver can rebuild the SCI from the frame’s MAC SA.
Bit 5 (SC): SCI present. If 1, the 8-byte SCI follows the PN and the SecTAG is 16 bytes. If 0, the SCI is left out (8-byte SecTAG) and the receiver derives it: from the MAC SA when ES=1, or from the only peer it knows on a point-to-point link.
Bit 4 (SCB): Single Copy Broadcast. Used in multi-access LAN topologies.
Bit 3 (E): Encryption bit. Set to 1 if payload is encrypted (Confidentiality). Set to 0 if payload is plain text (Integrity-only).
Bit 2 (C): Changed Text bit. Set to 1 if encryption is applied or if a non-zero confidentiality offset is used.
Bits 1–0 (AN): Association Number (0–3), identifying which of the 4 active SAs within the SC contains the decryption key.

SL (Short Length, 8 bits): Contains the length of the payload if it is less than 48 bytes. If the payload is 48 bytes or greater, SL is set to 0.
PN (Packet Number, 32 bits): A monotonically increasing sequence number per SA. Used to construct the Initialization Vector (IV) and prevent replay attacks.
SCI (Optional, 64 bits / 8 bytes): Present only when SC=1. Contains the 48-bit MAC address and 16-bit Port ID of the transmitting SecY.



Cryptographic modes: Integrity-only vs Confidentiality
MACsec uses Galois/Counter Mode with Advanced Encryption Standard (GCM-AES). It supports two primary modes of operation controlled by the E and C flags in the TCI byte:

Integrity-Only Mode (E=0, C=0): The payload remains in plain text, but the entire frame (excluding FCS) is authenticated. The ICV is calculated across the Destination MAC, Source MAC, SecTAG, and payload. Any alteration of the plain text in transit causes an ICV mismatch drop. Decoding TCI/AN = 0x22 yields binary 00100010, mapping to V=0, ES=0, SC=1, SCB=0, E=0, C=0, AN=2.
Confidentiality and Integrity Mode (E=1, C=1): The payload is encrypted using GCM-AES, and the ICV authenticates both the unencrypted headers (Additional Authenticated Data, or AAD) and the encrypted payload ciphertext. Decoding TCI/AN = 0x2E yields binary 00101110, mapping to V=0, ES=0, SC=1, SCB=0, E=1, C=1, AN=2.



Confidentiality Offsets
In specialized deployments, MACsec supports a Confidentiality Offset of 0, 30, or 50 bytes. A non-zero offset leaves the first 30 or 50 bytes of the payload following the SecTAG unencrypted (in plain text) while still calculating authentication over them. For example, a 30-byte offset leaves the IPv4 and TCP/UDP headers readable by intermediate L3/L4 hardware classification engines while encrypting the user data payload.


Cryptographic Construction: IV and AAD
For standard GCM-AES-128 and GCM-AES-256, MACsec builds a 96-bit (12-byte) Initialization Vector (IV) by concatenating the 64-bit SCI with the 32-bit PN:
IV (96 bits) = SCI (64 bits) || PN (32 bits)
The Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) fed into the GCM engine consists of: 1. Destination MAC address (6 bytes) 2. Source MAC address (6 bytes) 3. SecTAG (8 bytes or 16 bytes depending on the SC flag bit)
In integrity-only mode there is nothing to encrypt: the user data is appended to the AAD and GCM runs with an empty plaintext (this is GMAC, and it is exactly what macsec.py does for vector 2.1.1).
Because the Destination and Source MAC addresses are included in the AAD, any MAC address translation or tampering in transit invalidates the ICV at the receiver.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
section: Packet Number (PN) exhaustion and Extended Packet Numbering (XPN)
text:
Packet Number (PN) exhaustion and Extended Packet Numbering (XPN)
A fundamental constraint of Galois/Counter Mode (GCM-AES) is that an Initialization Vector (IV) must never be repeated under the same key (SAK). Repeating an IV under the same GCM key leaks the XOR of the two plaintexts and lets an attacker recover the GHASH key and forge tags, which is why a SecY stops transmitting on an SA before its PN wraps.

32-Bit PN Exhaustion at High Link Rates
Standard IEEE 802.1AE uses a 32-bit Packet Number (PN). A single SA can transmit a maximum of 2^32 - 1 = 4,294,967,295 frames before the PN space is completely exhausted and the SAK must be replaced.
At modern line rates transmitting minimum-size 64-byte Ethernet frames (84 bytes on the wire including preamble and inter-frame gap), high frame rates exhaust 32-bit PNs in seconds:

1 Gb/s: 1.49 million frames/s, so 2^32 PNs exhaust in 2886.2 seconds (~48 minutes).
10 Gb/s: 14.88 million frames/s, so 2^32 PNs exhaust in 288.6 seconds (~4.8 minutes).
100 Gb/s: 148.81 million frames/s, so 2^32 PNs exhaust in 28.9 seconds.
400 Gb/s: 595.24 million frames/s, so 2^32 PNs exhaust in 7.2 seconds.

At 100 Gb/s or 400 Gb/s, dynamic MKA re-keying would have to take place continuously every few seconds, introducing control plane instability and processing overhead.


Extended Packet Numbering (IEEE 802.1AEbw XPN)
To address high-speed PN exhaustion, IEEE 802.1AEbw introduced Extended Packet Numbering (XPN), which expands the sequence number space from 32 bits to 64 bits.
Under XPN: - The SecTAG header still transmits a 32-bit PN field on the wire to maintain physical frame structure. - The SecY maintains an internal 64-bit PN counter, where the lower 32 bits match the wire PN and the upper 32 bits represent an internal extension counter. - The 96-bit IV construction is updated to incorporate a 32-bit Short Secure Channel Identifier (SSCI) and a 96-bit Salt derived during MKA negotiation:
IV (96 bits) = Salt (96 bits) XOR ( SSCI (32 bits) || PN (64 bits) )
A 64-bit PN space (2^64 frames) running continuously at 400 Gb/s line rate lasts about 980 years (2^64 divided by 595.24 million frames per second) without requiring a SAK rotation due to PN limit bounds.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
section: MACsec Key Agreement (MKA) and Key Management
text:
MACsec Key Agreement (MKA) and Key Management
While MACsec (802.1AE) provides data plane encapsulation and cryptographic processing, the MACsec Key Agreement (MKA) protocol (defined in IEEE 802.1X) operates in the control plane to manage keys dynamically.

MKA Protocol Operation
MKA frames are transmitted as EAPOL-MKA frames using EtherType 0x888E. MKA uses a pre-shared or EAP-derived root key called the Connectivity Association Key (CAK) and its identifier, the CKN.
    Host A (Priority 16)                        Host B (Priority 128)
             |                                           |
             |--- EAPOL-MKA (MKPDU: CKN, Priority 16) -->|
             |<-- EAPOL-MKA (MKPDU: CKN, Priority 128) --|
             |                                           |
             |       [Key Server Election: Host A]       |
             |                                           |
             |--- SAK Distributed (Wrapped with KEK) --->|
             |                                           |
             |-- Transmit SA active (AN=0, Key=SAK1) --->|
             |<-- Transmit SA active (AN=0, Key=SAK1) ---|

Peer Discovery: Nodes connected to a link send EAPOL-MKA packets containing their CKN, SCI, and an assigned Key Server Priority (0–255, where lower numerical values indicate higher priority).
Key Server Election: The participant with the lowest numerical Key Server Priority value is elected as the Key Server for the Connectivity Association. If priorities are equal, the lowest SCI byte value wins.
SAK Generation and Distribution: The Key Server generates a random symmetric SAK (GCM-AES-128 or GCM-AES-256). It derives a Key Encryption Key (KEK) from the CAK and encrypts the SAK inside an MKA PDU (MKPDU) sent to all authenticated peers.
Seamless SA Rollover: Before an active SA reaches its PN exhaustion limit or when a peer leaves/joins, the Key Server generates a new SAK, assigns it to a new Association Number (e.g., changing AN from 0 to 1), and distributes it. Both SecYs install the new key into their secondary SA slot and switch active AN flags without dropping a single frame on the wire.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
text:
Linux Implementation: ip-macsec and wpa_supplicant
The Linux kernel supports MACsec via the macsec netdriver module (introduced in Linux 4.6). Administration is performed via iproute2 (ip macsec) for static key deployment, or via wpa_supplicant / macsec_daemon for dynamic MKA.

Static MACsec Configuration via ip-macsec (Not Run Here)
Static configuration installs SAKs directly into the kernel SecY driver without running MKA control plane daemons.
# Static MACsec setup between two hosts (Not run here)
# Host A configuration
# eth1 is the physical (or veth) link to Host B; Host B's eth1 MAC is 52:54:00:12:34:56
ip link add link eth1 macsec0 type macsec port 1 encrypt on replay on window 64 cipher gcm-aes-128
# our transmit SA: AN 0, key ID 01, 128-bit SAK
ip macsec add macsec0 tx sa 0 pn 1 on key 01 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f
# Host B's receive channel and its SA (Host B uses its own SAK for its direction)
ip macsec add macsec0 rx port 1 address 52:54:00:12:34:56
ip macsec add macsec0 rx port 1 address 52:54:00:12:34:56 sa 0 pn 1 on key 02 0f0e0d0c0b0a09080706050403020100
ip address add 192.168.100.1/24 dev macsec0
ip link set dev macsec0 up
# Host B mirrors this: its tx key is 0f0e..00 (ID 02), its rx SA for Host A uses 0001..0f (ID 01)
The command’s own usage text on this box (iproute2 6.15.0, ip macsec help) lists the full grammar, including the XPN options xpn, salt and ssci:
Usage: ip macsec add DEV tx sa { 0..3 } [ OPTS ] key ID KEY
       ip macsec set DEV tx sa { 0..3 } [ OPTS ]
       ip macsec del DEV tx sa { 0..3 }
       ip macsec add DEV rx SCI [ on | off ]
       ip macsec set DEV rx SCI [ on | off ]
       ip macsec del DEV rx SCI
       ip macsec add DEV rx SCI sa { 0..3 } [ OPTS ] key ID KEY
       ip macsec set DEV rx SCI sa { 0..3 } [ OPTS ]
       ip macsec del DEV rx SCI sa { 0..3 }
       ip macsec show
       ip macsec show DEV
       ip macsec offload DEV [ off | phy | mac ]
where  OPTS := [ pn <u32> | xpn <u64> ] [ salt SALT ] [ ssci <u32> ] [ on | off ]
       ID   := 128-bit hex string
       KEY  := 128-bit or 256-bit hex string
       SCI  := { sci <u64> | port { 1..2^16-1 } address <lladdr> }
       SALT := 96-bit hex string


Dynamic MKA via wpa_supplicant (Not Run Here)
In production deployments, dynamic MKA manages keys to eliminate manual key coordination. The following wpa_supplicant.conf snippet demonstrates an MKA setup using pre-shared CAK/CKN keys:
# /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant-eth1.conf (Not run here)
eapol_version=3
ap_scan=0
fast_reauth=1

network={
    key_mgmt=NONE
    macsec_policy=1
    macsec_integ_only=0
    mka_cak=000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f
    mka_ckn=0102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f101112131415161718191a1b1c1d1e1f20
    mka_priority=16
}
When started via wpa_supplicant -i eth1 -D macsec_linux -c /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant-eth1.conf, wpa_supplicant communicates with the kernel Netlink interface to instantiate the macsec0 interface, run MKA peer discovery over eth1, elect the Key Server, and dynamically inject SAKs into the SecY kernel driver.


Hardware Offloading
Software-based MACsec encryption in the Linux kernel introduces CPU overhead at multi-gigabit speeds. Modern network interface cards (NICs) and PHY transceivers support hardware offload via iproute2:
# Enable hardware offload on PHY or MAC layer (Not run here)
ip macsec offload macsec0 mac

offload mac: Offloads MACsec encryption and processing to the integrated MAC ASIC within the network interface controller.
offload phy: Offloads MACsec processing to an external Ethernet PHY transceiving chip on the board.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
text:
Operational checklist and troubleshooting counters
When deploying MACsec in enterprise campus, data center interconnect (DCI), or metro Ethernet environments, follow this operational checklist:

MTU Adjustment: MACsec adds 24 bytes (without explicit SCI) or 32 bytes (with explicit SCI) of framing overhead. Ensure the underlying physical link MTU is incremented (e.g., from 1500 to 1532) to prevent IP packet fragmentation.
Key Server Priority Alignment: Explicitly configure mka_priority on participating nodes to control which switch or host becomes the MKA Key Server.
Cipher Suite Matching: Both endpoints must agree on the cipher suite (e.g., GCM-AES-128, GCM-AES-256, GCM-AES-XPN-128, or GCM-AES-XPN-256).
Replay Window Size: On link-aggregated or multi-path links where out-of-order frame delivery occurs, adjust the replay window size (replay on window N) to prevent legitimate frames from being dropped.


Kernel Diagnostic Counters (ip -s macsec show)
The receive counters below are the 802.1AE names that ip -s macsec show prints (described from the standard and the man page; not run here):

InPktsUntagged: Received frames without a SecTAG on an interface configured to require MACsec validation. Indicates a misconfigured peer sending plain text frames.
InPktsNoTag: Received frames missing a valid MACsec tag structure.
InPktsBadTag: Frames containing invalid or corrupted SecTAG header fields.
InPktsUnknownSCI: Frames received with an SCI that does not match any configured inbound Secure Channel (RX SC).
InPktsNotValid: Frames failing ICV integrity verification. Indicates bit errors on the physical medium, incorrect SAK mismatch, or frame data tampering.
InPktsLate: Frames received with a PN below the lowest acceptable replay window threshold. Indicates severe out-of-order delivery or replay attacks.
InPktsNotUsingSA: Frames received for an SA that is present but not currently marked active for reception.
InPktsUnusedSA: Frames received matching an unassigned or unallocated SA slot.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
section: Lab: Verifying IEEE 802.1AE GCM-AES Test Vectors
text:
Lab: Verifying IEEE 802.1AE GCM-AES Test Vectors
This lab uses a specialized Python script (macsec.py) to execute cryptographic verification against IEEE-published GCM-AES MACsec test vectors. It parses SecTAG headers, verifies ICVs, evaluates receiver decisions across various packet tampering scenarios, and demonstrates packet number exhaustion across link speeds.
macsec.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""macsec.py: build and check MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) frames with GCM-AES-128.
Checks two published test vectors (Randall, IEEE 802.1 2011), then shows
what a receiver rejects: a flipped bit, a replayed PN, and a wrong key."""
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag
import struct

H = bytes.fromhex
KEY = H("AD7A2BD03EAC835A6F620FDCB506B345")
DA, SA = H("D609B1F05663"), H("7A0D46DF998D")
SCI = H("12153524C0895E81")
PN = 0xB2C28465

def tci_an(es=0, sc=1, scb=0, e=0, c=0, an=2):
    # TCI bits, most significant first: V(0) ES SC SCB E C, then 2-bit AN
    return (es << 6) | (sc << 5) | (scb << 4) | (e << 3) | (c << 2) | an

def sectag(tcian, sl, pn, sci):
    return H("88E5") + bytes([tcian, sl]) + struct.pack("!I", pn) + (sci or b"")

def decode_tci(b):
    names = ["V", "ES", "SC", "SCB", "E", "C"]
    bits = {n: (b >> (7 - i)) & 1 for i, n in enumerate(names)}
    return " ".join(f"{n}={v}" for n, v in bits.items()) + f" AN={b & 3}"

def protect(key, da, sa, tag, sci, pn, user, encrypt):
    iv = sci + struct.pack("!I", pn)          # 96-bit IV = SCI || PN
    g = AESGCM(key)
    if encrypt:
        out = g.encrypt(iv, user, da + sa + tag)  # returns C || ICV
        return da + sa + tag + out
    icv = g.encrypt(iv, b"", da + sa + tag + user)  # GMAC: P empty, all in A
    return da + sa + tag + user + icv

def verify(key, frame, encrypt, sci, lowest_pn):
    da, sa, tag = frame[:6], frame[6:12], frame[12:28]
    pn = struct.unpack("!I", tag[4:8])[0]
    if pn < lowest_pn:
        return f"DROP replay: PN {pn:#x} < lowest acceptable {lowest_pn:#x}"
    iv = sci + struct.pack("!I", pn)
    body, icv = frame[28:-16], frame[-16:]
    try:
        if encrypt:
            AESGCM(key).decrypt(iv, body + icv, da + sa + tag)
        else:
            AESGCM(key).decrypt(iv, icv, da + sa + tag + body)
    except InvalidTag:
        return "DROP ICV mismatch"
    return "ACCEPT"

user54 = H("08000F101112131415161718191A1B1C1D1E1F202122232425262728292A2B2C2D2E2F3031323334" "0001")
user60 = H("08000F101112131415161718191A1B1C1D1E1F202122232425262728292A2B2C2D2E2F303132333435363738393A0002")

print("== SecTAG fields")
for name, b in [("2.1 auth-only", tci_an(an=2)), ("2.2 encrypted", tci_an(e=1, c=1, an=2))]:
    print(f"{name:14} TCI/AN=0x{b:02X}  {decode_tci(b)}")

print("\n== Test vector 2.1.1 (54-byte packet, integrity only)")
tag = sectag(tci_an(an=2), 0x2A, PN, SCI)
f1 = protect(KEY, DA, SA, tag, SCI, PN, user54, encrypt=False)
icv = f1[-16:].hex().upper()
print("SecTAG  ", tag.hex().upper())
print("ICV     ", icv)
print("expected F09478A9B09007D06F46E9B6A1DA25DD ->", icv == "F09478A9B09007D06F46E9B6A1DA25DD")
print(f"frame {len(DA+SA+user54)} -> {len(f1)} bytes (+{len(f1)-len(DA+SA+user54)})")

print("\n== Test vector 2.2.1 (60-byte packet, encrypted)")
tag = sectag(tci_an(e=1, c=1, an=2), 0x00, PN, SCI)
f2 = protect(KEY, DA, SA, tag, SCI, PN, user60, encrypt=True)
ct, icv = f2[28:-16].hex().upper(), f2[-16:].hex().upper()
print("C[1..3] ", ct[:32], ct[32:64], ct[64:], sep="\n         ")
print("ICV     ", icv)
print("expected 4F8D55E7D3F06FD5A13C0C29B9D5B880 ->", icv == "4F8D55E7D3F06FD5A13C0C29B9D5B880")
print("first C block matches 701AFA1CC039C0D765128A665DAB6924 ->", ct[:32] == "701AFA1CC039C0D765128A665DAB6924")

print("\n== Receiver decisions (replay window 0, lowest acceptable PN = last PN + 1)")
print("original frame, fresh SA       :", verify(KEY, f2, True, SCI, PN))
bad = bytearray(f2); bad[40] ^= 0x01
print("one ciphertext bit flipped     :", verify(KEY, bytes(bad), True, SCI, PN))
bad = bytearray(f2); bad[0] ^= 0x01
print("destination MAC changed        :", verify(KEY, bytes(bad), True, SCI, PN))
print("same frame replayed            :", verify(KEY, f2, True, SCI, PN + 1))
print("wrong SAK                      :", verify(H("00" * 16), f2, True, SCI, PN))
print("SCI not the sender's           :", verify(KEY, f2, True, H("0000000000000001"), PN))

print("\n== Overhead per frame")
for label, sci_len in [("SecTAG with SCI (SC=1)", 8), ("SecTAG without SCI (SC=0)", 0)]:
    print(f"{label:28}: SecTAG {8+sci_len:2} + ICV 16 = {24+sci_len} bytes")
print("\n== PN exhaustion at line rate (32-bit PN, minimum-size 64-byte frames)")
for gbps in (1, 10, 100, 400):
    pps = gbps * 1e9 / ((64 + 20) * 8)   # 64B frame + 20B preamble/IFG
    print(f"{gbps:3} Gb/s: {pps/1e6:7.2f} Mpps -> 2^32 PNs last {2**32/pps:8.1f} s")
To execute the test vector verification script and verify host system kernel driver capabilities, the following commands are issued:
python3 macsec.py
== SecTAG fields
2.1 auth-only  TCI/AN=0x22  V=0 ES=0 SC=1 SCB=0 E=0 C=0 AN=2
2.2 encrypted  TCI/AN=0x2E  V=0 ES=0 SC=1 SCB=0 E=1 C=1 AN=2

== Test vector 2.1.1 (54-byte packet, integrity only)
SecTAG   88E5222AB2C2846512153524C0895E81
ICV      F09478A9B09007D06F46E9B6A1DA25DD
expected F09478A9B09007D06F46E9B6A1DA25DD -> True
frame 54 -> 86 bytes (+32)

== Test vector 2.2.1 (60-byte packet, encrypted)
C[1..3] 
         701AFA1CC039C0D765128A665DAB6924
         3899BF7318CCDC81C9931DA17FBE8EDD
         7D17CB8B4C26FC81E3284F2B7FBA713D
ICV      4F8D55E7D3F06FD5A13C0C29B9D5B880
expected 4F8D55E7D3F06FD5A13C0C29B9D5B880 -> True
first C block matches 701AFA1CC039C0D765128A665DAB6924 -> True

== Receiver decisions (replay window 0, lowest acceptable PN = last PN + 1)
original frame, fresh SA       : ACCEPT
one ciphertext bit flipped     : DROP ICV mismatch
destination MAC changed        : DROP ICV mismatch
same frame replayed            : DROP replay: PN 0xb2c28465 < lowest acceptable 0xb2c28466
wrong SAK                      : DROP ICV mismatch
SCI not the sender's           : DROP ICV mismatch

== Overhead per frame
SecTAG with SCI (SC=1)      : SecTAG 16 + ICV 16 = 32 bytes
SecTAG without SCI (SC=0)   : SecTAG  8 + ICV 16 = 24 bytes

== PN exhaustion at line rate (32-bit PN, minimum-size 64-byte frames)
  1 Gb/s:    1.49 Mpps -> 2^32 PNs last   2886.2 s
 10 Gb/s:   14.88 Mpps -> 2^32 PNs last    288.6 s
100 Gb/s:  148.81 Mpps -> 2^32 PNs last     28.9 s
400 Gb/s:  595.24 Mpps -> 2^32 PNs last      7.2 s

# Run as: unshare -urn sh probe.sh   (no sudo)
ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1 && echo "veth: ok"
ip link add link veth0 macsec0 type macsec port 1 encrypt on 2>&1 || echo "macsec: exit $?"
ip macsec show 2>&1 || echo "ip macsec show: exit $?"

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
text:
Reading the output
The output from the test execution provides direct cryptographic verification of the IEEE 802.1AE standard and illustrates local kernel module support status.

SecTAG Control Field Decoding
In Section 2 of the script output, two distinct SecTAG TCI byte values are decoded: - Test Vector 2.1.1 (Integrity-Only): The TCI/AN byte value 0x22 decodes to binary 00100010. Mapping these bits to TCI flags yields V=0, ES=0, SC=1, SCB=0, E=0, C=0, and AN=2. Because E=0 and C=0, the frame payload remains in plain text, but the entire frame structure is authenticated by the trailing ICV. - Test Vector 2.2.1 (Confidentiality and Integrity): The TCI/AN byte value 0x2E decodes to binary 00101110. Mapping these bits yields V=0, ES=0, SC=1, SCB=0, E=1, C=1, and AN=2. Because E=1 and C=1, the payload data is encrypted using GCM-AES.


Cryptographic Vector Validation
The output validates the script implementation against the IEEE published test vectors authored by Karen Randall: - Vector 2.1.1: The input 54-byte plain text Ethernet frame expands to 86 bytes after appending a 16-byte SecTAG (with explicit SC=1) and a 16-byte ICV (54 + 32 = 86 bytes). The computed ICV F09478A9B09007D06F46E9B6A1DA25DD matches the expected test vector ICV exactly (expected ... -> True). - Vector 2.2.1: The input 60-byte payload is encrypted into 3 ciphertext blocks (C[1..3]). The first computed ciphertext block matches 701AFA1CC039C0D765128A665DAB6924 (first C block matches ... -> True), and the computed ICV matches 4F8D55E7D3F06FD5A13C0C29B9D5B880 (expected ... -> True). This confirms that the 96-bit Initialization Vector (SCI || PN) and Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) are correctly formatted.


Receiver Security Decisions
The receiver simulation evaluates tamper detection rules: - Fresh Frame: Evaluates as ACCEPT. - Ciphertext Bit Flip: Changing a single bit in the ciphertext causes immediate frame DROP ICV mismatch. - Destination MAC Change: Modifying the unencrypted Destination MAC address in the Ethernet header causes frame DROP ICV mismatch. This occurs because the Destination MAC is explicitly included in the GCM Additional Authenticated Data (AAD). - Frame Replay: Submitting the same frame a second time results in DROP replay: PN 0xb2c28465 < lowest acceptable 0xb2c28466. Replay drop occurs at the PN checking stage before executing cryptographic decryption. - Wrong SAK or SCI Mismatch: Alters the decryption key or IV construction, resulting in DROP ICV mismatch.


PN Exhaustion Timing
The lab output quantifies the operational lifespan of a 32-bit PN space when transmitting minimum-size 64-byte Ethernet frames: - At 1 Gb/s (1.49 Mpps), 2^32 PNs last 2886.2 seconds. - At 10 Gb/s (14.88 Mpps), 2^32 PNs last 288.6 seconds. - At 100 Gb/s (148.81 Mpps), 2^32 PNs last 28.9 seconds. - At 400 Gb/s (595.24 Mpps), 2^32 PNs last 7.2 seconds.
This rapid exhaustion demonstrates why high-speed links must utilize Extended Packet Numbering (XPN, IEEE 802.1AEbw).


Host Kernel Module Probe Analysis
The kernel probe script output demonstrates system-level driver dependencies: - veth: ok: Confirms that the host kernel supports virtual Ethernet pair interfaces. - Error: Unknown device type. / macsec: exit 2: Indicates that the macsec kernel module is not loaded or not supported by the execution environment’s kernel build. - RTNETLINK answers: No such file or directory: Confirms the kernel Netlink subsystem cannot find the requested MACsec device driver module. - Because the local execution environment lacks the macsec kernel module, static Linux MACsec commands and wpa_supplicant dynamic MKA configurations are explicitly labeled as not run here.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
text:
Gotchas

MTU mismatch black holes: Linux sets the macsec0 MTU to the parent MTU minus the overhead (1500 - 32 = 1468 with an SCI), so a host is safe on its own. The trap is a switch port or peer that still assumes 1500 bytes of IP: full-size frames grow by 32 bytes and are dropped on any 1500-byte hop. Raise the physical MTU (1532 or more) or lower the IP MTU everywhere on the segment.
EAPOL Frame Unencrypted Path: MACsec encrypts all upper-layer L2/L3 protocols, but EAPOL frames (EtherType 0x888E) used by MKA are explicitly transmitted in plain text so peers can perform key agreement.
Loss of L2 Control Protocol Visibility: Intermediate Layer 2 provider networks that do not support MACsec frame pass-through will drop frames containing EtherType 0x88E5, breaking connectivity.
Out-of-Order Packet Drops on Link Aggregation: Port Channel / LACP bundles that distribute packets across physical paths can deliver frames out of sequence. If the packet sequence skew exceeds the configured MACsec replay window size, valid packets are dropped as InPktsLate.
Replay Window Size vs. Security: Setting the replay window size to a very large value tolerates significant packet reordering, but widens the vulnerability window for replay attacks on the link.
32-Bit PN Exhaustion at High Speed: Running standard 32-bit PN MACsec on 100 Gbps links causes SAK exhaustion in 28.9 seconds. Failure to deploy 802.1AEbw XPN or configure frequent MKA re-keying will cause link failure when the counter hits 2^32 - 1.
MAC Address Tampering Drops: Changing the Source or Destination MAC address via upstream NAT or L2 MAC rewriting breaks the MACsec ICV check, because header MAC addresses are bound into the GCM Additional Authenticated Data (AAD).
Offload ASIC Support Constraints: Enabling hardware offload via ip macsec offload phy|mac will fail if the underlying Network Interface Card driver does not support hardware MACsec crypto co-processing.

title: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) and MKA: Hop-by-Hop Ethernet Encryption
text:
Exercises

SecTAG Binary Parsing: Given a received MACsec frame containing a SecTAG with TCI/AN byte value 0x2B, convert this byte to binary, determine the status of the V, ES, SC, SCB, E, and C flags, and identify the selected Association Number (AN).
MTU Overhead Calculation: A network engineer needs to transport jumbo frames with an IP payload of 9000 bytes across a MACsec link using explicit SCI inclusion (SC=1). Calculate the minimum physical interface MTU required on the underlying Ethernet switch ports to prevent packet fragmentation.
XPN Salt and IV Construction: Explain step-by-step how a 96-bit Initialization Vector (IV) is constructed under IEEE 802.1AEbw XPN using the SSCI, 64-bit PN, and Salt, and contrast this with standard 802.1AE 32-bit PN IV derivation.
Replay Protection Counter Evaluation: A MACsec receiver has a recorded last-received PN of 1000 and a configured replay window size of 32. Evaluate whether the receiver will ACCEPT or DROP incoming frames with the following sequence numbers: (a) PN 1005, (b) PN 980, (c) PN 965, (d) PN 1000.
Troubleshooting Counter Diagnostics: A network administrator notices that ip -s macsec show displays rapidly incrementing InPktsNotValid counters while InPktsLate remains zero. Identify the two most likely root causes for this behavior and outline the steps to resolve it.

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
text:
Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
When a volumetric attack fills your upstream links, filters on your own routers are too late: the damage is done on the link before your ACL sees a packet. The only place to drop that traffic is further upstream, on routers you do not configure. Operators solved this years ago by reusing the one control channel they already share with their neighbours and inside their own network: BGP. Announce a route with the right attributes, and every router that honours it drops the matching traffic at line rate.
There are three generations of this idea, and each fixes a problem of the previous one:
This chapter shows all three working: RTBH and source RTBH on Linux namespaces, where you can watch which packets survive, and FlowSpec through a stdlib encoder, decoder and matcher that reproduces the RFC’s own encoding examples byte for byte.

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
text:
Learning goals

Explain destination-based RTBH, the BLACKHOLE community (RFC 7999) and the discard next-hop trick (RFC 5635), including what “completing the attack” means.
Explain source-based RTBH, why it needs uRPF, why loose mode is used at the edge, and why spoofed sources make it risky.
Reproduce both on Linux with blackhole routes and rp_filter, and read the counters that prove which packets were dropped.
Read and write RFC 8955 FlowSpec NLRI: component types, numeric and bitmask operators, AND/OR precedence, and the length encoding.
Know the FlowSpec traffic-filtering actions (extended communities) and the validation rule that stops a neighbour from filtering traffic it does not own.
Avoid the classic FlowSpec mistake: port-based rules do not match non-first fragments.

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
text:
Version note
Ran on this box as an unprivileged user: Linux 6.12.94, iproute2 6.15.0, Python 3.13.5 (standard library only). The RTBH lab uses unshare -urnm and three named network namespaces joined by veth pairs; Linux plays the edge router, with ip route add blackhole standing in for the route a BGP policy would install, and rp_filter standing in for uRPF. The FlowSpec part is a pure Python program that encodes, decodes and evaluates RFC 8955 NLRI. All outputs are pasted unedited.
Not run here: any BGP daemon. FRR, BIRD and ExaBGP configuration later in the chapter is written from their documentation and marked “not run here”; the box has no routing daemons and nothing may be installed. The counting helper netdelta.py is a small snapshot-and-diff tool: it reads nstat, ip -s link and the kernel-wide routing and neighbour statistics before and after a command and prints the drop-related counters that moved. It is listed in the lab so the chapter stands alone.

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
text:
Destination-based RTBH
The mechanism in RFC 5635 has two halves, prepared in advance and triggered in seconds.
Preparation on every edge router. Configure a static route for an unused address (the RFC uses 192.0.2.1 from documentation space; many networks use something in 192.0.2.0/24 or a dedicated prefix) pointing at the discard interface (Null0, discard, or on Linux a blackhole route). Then configure an inbound BGP policy: routes from the trigger router carrying the RTBH community get their next hop rewritten to that discard address.
Trigger. When an address is under attack, a single trigger router (often a small box or a route server dedicated to the job) announces the victim’s /32 via iBGP with the community. Every edge router installs “victim /32 via 192.0.2.1”, resolves 192.0.2.1 to the discard interface, and drops every packet to the victim at the ingress edge, at forwarding-plane speed.
          trigger router --iBGP: 192.0.2.10/32, community RTBH, next hop 192.0.2.1-->
                                                  |
   upstream A --> [edge 1]  192.0.2.10/32 -> 192.0.2.1 -> discard     (drop at ingress)
   upstream B --> [edge 2]  192.0.2.10/32 -> 192.0.2.1 -> discard     (drop at ingress)
                          \--> core --> 192.0.2.0/24 servers (everything else still flows)
Dropping inside your own edge saves your core, but the attack still fills the links from your upstreams. To push the drop into their networks you announce the /32 to them with a community they honour. RFC 7999 standardised one well-known value for this: BLACKHOLE, 65535:666 (0xFFFF029A). Its rules are short and worth knowing exactly:

Honouring it is a bilateral decision, agreed before use; networks that do not use it should ignore it.
A receiver should add NO_EXPORT or NO_ADVERTISE so the blackhole does not travel further than intended.
Accept a blackhole announcement only for a prefix covered by an equal or shorter prefix the neighbour is authorised to announce. Without that check, anyone could blackhole anyone.
Blackhole prefixes should be as specific as possible, /32 for IPv4 and /128 for IPv6, even though prefixes longer than /24 and /48 are normally filtered. Your import policy needs an explicit exception for them.
Origin validation (ROV) must not accidentally reject legitimate blackhole announcements; a ROA with a maxLength of /24 makes a /32 “Invalid”, so blackhole sessions need their own ROV handling.
Implementations should not drop traffic for BLACKHOLE-tagged routes without explicit configuration, and the RFC suggests the keyword blackhole for the community.
Store every BLACKHOLE update for audit.

The price is in the name. Destination RTBH drops all traffic to the victim, legitimate users included. It “completes the attack” for that address in exchange for saving everything else that shares the links. That is often the right trade (a single customer IP versus a whole data centre), and it is why destination RTBH is usually the first lever pulled.

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
text:
Source-based RTBH
RFC 5635’s second technique turns the same machinery around. Instead of blackholing the destination, you blackhole the sources: the trigger announces the attackers’ addresses with the community, and every edge installs “attacker /32 via discard”. By itself that only stops return traffic to the attacker, which is useless. The trick is uRPF on the ingress interfaces. uRPF checks the source address of each arriving packet against the forwarding table:

Strict mode: the best route back to the source must point out of the interface the packet arrived on.
Loose mode: there must be some route back to the source, and that route must not be a discard route.

With a discard route for the attacker installed, both modes now fail for packets from the attacker, and the edge drops them before they enter. Loose mode is the one used at Internet edges, because traffic from a given source routinely arrives on a different upstream than the one you would use to reach it (asymmetric routing); strict mode would drop legitimate traffic there. RFC 3704 describes both modes.
The weakness is just as clear. If the sources are spoofed (as in reflection and many SYN floods), blackholing them blocks innocent addresses that happen to be forged, and the attacker can pick which addresses you block. Source RTBH is the right tool against a botnet of real hosts, not against spoofed floods.

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
text:
The RTBH lab
The topology has an upstream namespace inet holding two source addresses on its loopback, an edge router r, and a victim namespace v with two servers on one /24:
   inet                         r (edge)                         v
   198.51.100.66 (attacker) ]   up0 10.255.0.1/30                192.0.2.10 (under attack)
   203.0.113.10  (client)   ]-- i0 10.255.0.2/30 -- up0 | dn0 -- v0 192.0.2.20 (neighbour)
                                default route via inet           192.0.2.1/24 on dn0
blast.py sends 50 datagrams from each source to each victim address; count.py on the victim counts what arrives per (source, destination) pair, using IP_PKTINFO to learn which local address each datagram was sent to. netdelta.py measures the router.


count.py

# count.py PORT SECONDS: count UDP datagrams per (source, destination) for SECONDS
import collections, socket, sys
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_IP, socket.IP_PKTINFO, 1)
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", int(sys.argv[1]))); s.settimeout(float(sys.argv[2]))
seen = collections.Counter()
try:
    while True:
        data, anc, _, src = s.recvmsg(2048, 256)
        dst = socket.inet_ntoa(anc[0][2][8:12])      # in_pktinfo.ipi_addr
        seen[(src[0], dst)] += 1
except socket.timeout:
    pass
for (src, dst), n in sorted(seen.items()):
    print(f"   {src:>15} -> {dst:<12} {n:>3} received")
if not seen:
    print("   nothing received")



blast.py

# blast.py N: from each source, send N datagrams to each victim address (UDP 5300)
import socket, sys
n = int(sys.argv[1])
for src in ("198.51.100.66", "203.0.113.10"):          # attacker, legitimate client
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.bind((src, 0))
    for dst in ("192.0.2.10", "192.0.2.20"):           # attacked host, its neighbour
        for _ in range(n):
            s.sendto(b"q" * 40, (dst, 5300))



netdelta.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""netdelta.py: snapshot the kernel's drop-related counters, run a command, print what moved.

Usage: netdelta.py [--all] [--ns NAME]... -- command args...
Only counters whose names look like drops or errors are printed, unless --all.
Sources: nstat -saz (SNMP + netstat MIBs, per namespace), ip -s -j link (per device),
and three kernel-wide tables: /proc/net/softnet_stat, /proc/net/stat/rt_cache, /proc/net/stat/arp_cache.
"""
import json, re, subprocess, sys

DROPPY = re.compile(r"Drop|Discard|Err|NoRoute|NoPort|Overflow|Fail|Filter|TimeExcd|DestUnreach|Prune|Collapse|dropped|errors|squeeze|InAddr|Csum|RateLimit")

def sh(ns, *argv):
    pre = ["ip", "netns", "exec", ns] if ns else []
    return subprocess.run(pre + list(argv), capture_output=True, text=True).stdout

def snapshot(ns):
    snap = {}
    data = json.loads(sh(ns, "nstat", "-saz", "--json") or "{}")
    for table in data.values():
        for k, v in table.items():
            snap[k] = v
    for dev in json.loads(sh(ns, "ip", "-s", "-j", "link") or "[]"):
        st = dev.get("stats64", {})
        for d in ("rx", "tx"):
            for k in ("dropped", "errors"):
                snap[f"{dev['ifname']}.{d}_{k}"] = st.get(d, {}).get(k, 0)
    return snap

def global_snapshot():
    """Kernel-wide counters: NOT per network namespace, so other traffic on the host shows up too."""
    snap = {}
    for cpu, row in enumerate(open("/proc/net/softnet_stat")):
        f = [int(x, 16) for x in row.split()]
        snap[f"softnet.cpu{cpu}.dropped"] = f[1]
        snap[f"softnet.cpu{cpu}.time_squeeze"] = f[2]
    rows = open("/proc/net/stat/rt_cache").read().split("\n")
    names = rows[0].split()
    for name in ("in_no_route", "in_martian_dst", "in_martian_src"):
        i = names.index(name)
        snap[f"rt_cache.{name}"] = sum(int(r.split()[i], 16) for r in rows[1:] if r.strip())
    # /proc/net/stat/arp_cache only exists in the initial namespace; ip ntable works everywhere
    out = subprocess.run(["ip", "-s", "ntable", "show", "name", "arp_cache"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    for name in ("res_failed", "unresolved_discards", "table_fulls"):
        m = re.search(rf"\b{name} (\d+)", out)
        if m:
            snap[f"arp_cache.{name}"] = int(m.group(1))
    return snap

def main():
    args = sys.argv[1:]
    nss, show_all = [], False
    if args and args[0] == "--all":
        show_all, args = True, args[1:]
    while args and args[0] == "--ns":
        nss.append(args[1]); args = args[2:]
    if args and args[0] == "--":
        args = args[1:]
    nss = nss or [None]
    before = {ns: snapshot(ns) for ns in nss}
    gbefore = global_snapshot()
    rc = subprocess.run(args).returncode
    gafter = global_snapshot()
    for ns in nss:
        after = snapshot(ns)
        moved = {k: after[k] - before[ns].get(k, 0) for k in after
                 if after[k] != before[ns].get(k, 0) and (show_all or DROPPY.search(k))}
        for k in sorted(moved):
            print(f"   [{ns or 'host'}] {k:<34} +{moved[k]}")
    for k in sorted(gafter):
        if gafter[k] != gbefore[k] and (show_all or DROPPY.search(k) or k.startswith(("rt_cache", "arp_cache"))):
            print(f"   [kernel-wide] {k:<28} +{gafter[k] - gbefore[k]}")
    return rc

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

The script runs five rounds, each measured on the edge router with netdelta.py:


lab.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -urnm sh lab.sh   (user + net + mount namespaces, no sudo)
H=$(pwd); D="python3 $H/netdelta.py"
mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
for ns in inet r v; do ip netns add $ns; ip -n $ns link set lo up; done
ip link add up0 type veth peer name i0; ip link set up0 netns r; ip link set i0 netns inet
ip link add dn0 type veth peer name v0; ip link set dn0 netns r; ip link set v0 netns v
ip -n inet addr add 10.255.0.2/30 dev i0; ip -n r addr add 10.255.0.1/30 dev up0
ip -n inet addr add 198.51.100.66/32 dev lo; ip -n inet addr add 203.0.113.10/32 dev lo
ip -n r addr add 192.0.2.1/24 dev dn0
ip -n v addr add 192.0.2.10/24 dev v0; ip -n v addr add 192.0.2.20/24 dev v0
for d in inet:i0 r:up0 r:dn0 v:v0; do ip -n ${d%:*} link set ${d#*:} up; done
ip netns exec r sh -c 'echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward'
ip -n inet route add 192.0.2.0/24 via 10.255.0.1
ip -n r route add default via 10.255.0.2          # "the Internet" is behind up0
ip -n v route add default via 192.0.2.1
sleep 1
round() {   # round LABEL: 50 datagrams per (source, destination) pair, count at the victim
  echo "   $1"
  ip netns exec v python3 $H/count.py 5300 1.5 & C=$!; sleep 0.3
  $D --ns r -- ip netns exec inet python3 $H/blast.py 50
  wait $C
}

echo "== 1. baseline: attacker and client both reach both servers"
round "no mitigation"

echo "== 2. destination-based RTBH: the /32 under attack goes to discard"
ip -n r route add blackhole 192.0.2.10/32
ip -n r route show 192.0.2.10/32
round "blackhole 192.0.2.10/32"
ip -n r route del blackhole 192.0.2.10/32

echo "== 3. source-based RTBH without uRPF: blackhole the attacker's /32"
ip -n r route add blackhole 198.51.100.66/32
round "blackhole 198.51.100.66/32, rp_filter=$(ip netns exec r cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/up0/rp_filter)"

echo "== 4. source-based RTBH with loose uRPF on the upstream interface"
ip netns exec r sh -c 'echo 2 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/up0/rp_filter'
round "blackhole 198.51.100.66/32, rp_filter=2 on up0"

echo "== 5. S-RTBH aimed at a whole /24 that also holds a legitimate client"
ip -n r route del blackhole 198.51.100.66/32
ip -n r route add blackhole 203.0.113.0/24
round "blackhole 203.0.113.0/24, rp_filter=2 on up0"

unshare -urnm sh lab.sh

Baseline
== 1. baseline: attacker and client both reach both servers
   no mitigation
     198.51.100.66 -> 192.0.2.10    50 received
     198.51.100.66 -> 192.0.2.20    50 received
      203.0.113.10 -> 192.0.2.10    50 received
      203.0.113.10 -> 192.0.2.20    50 received
Four flows, fifty datagrams each, all delivered.


Destination RTBH
== 2. destination-based RTBH: the /32 under attack goes to discard
blackhole 192.0.2.10 
   blackhole 192.0.2.10/32
   [kernel-wide] rt_cache.in_no_route         +100
     198.51.100.66 -> 192.0.2.20    50 received
      203.0.113.10 -> 192.0.2.20    50 received
The route blackhole 192.0.2.10/32 is what a BGP policy installs when it rewrites the next hop of a BLACKHOLE-tagged /32 to the discard address. The neighbour 192.0.2.20 is untouched and both sources still reach it. Everything to 192.0.2.10 is gone, including the legitimate client. This is “completing the attack”: the victim is offline, but by your hand and only that one address.
Note how quiet the drop is. No per-namespace counter moved in r; the only evidence is the kernel-wide routing statistic rt_cache.in_no_route +100 (two sources, 50 datagrams each). Linux treats a blackhole route as a lookup error (EINVAL in ip_error()) and frees the packet without SNMP accounting or ICMP. If you rely on blackholing, count the drops somewhere else, for example with flow export or a firewall counter, or you will not be able to tell your customer how much traffic you discarded.


Source RTBH without uRPF
== 3. source-based RTBH without uRPF: blackhole the attacker's /32
   blackhole 198.51.100.66/32, rp_filter=0
     198.51.100.66 -> 192.0.2.10    50 received
     198.51.100.66 -> 192.0.2.20    50 received
      203.0.113.10 -> 192.0.2.10    50 received
      203.0.113.10 -> 192.0.2.20    50 received
Blackholing the attacker’s /32 on its own changes nothing for the attack. The route only affects packets to 198.51.100.66, and the attack consists of packets from it. rp_filter=0 means the router never asks where the source lives. This is the most common way source RTBH is deployed wrongly: the trigger works, the route is installed everywhere, and the graphs do not move.


Source RTBH with loose uRPF
== 4. source-based RTBH with loose uRPF on the upstream interface
   blackhole 198.51.100.66/32, rp_filter=2 on up0
   [r] TcpExtIPReversePathFilter          +100
   [kernel-wide] rt_cache.in_martian_src      +100
      203.0.113.10 -> 192.0.2.10    50 received
      203.0.113.10 -> 192.0.2.20    50 received
Now the upstream interface has rp_filter=2, Linux’s loose mode. Every packet from 198.51.100.66 fails the check because the only route back to it is the blackhole, and the router counts them: TcpExtIPReversePathFilter +100 (the reverse-path filter counter, which lives in the TcpExt table despite its name) and the kernel-wide in_martian_src +100. The legitimate client reaches both servers. This is the outcome RFC 5635 promises: drop the attacker, keep the victim online.
Two details about Linux matter if you build this on Linux edges. The effective rp_filter on an interface is the maximum of net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and the interface’s own value. And in loose mode a blackhole (or unreachable, or prohibit) route to the source fails the check, which is exactly the behaviour RTBH needs; a default route covering the source passes.


Source RTBH aimed too wide
== 5. S-RTBH aimed at a whole /24 that also holds a legitimate client
   blackhole 203.0.113.0/24, rp_filter=2 on up0
   [r] TcpExtIPReversePathFilter          +100
   [kernel-wide] rt_cache.in_martian_src      +100
     198.51.100.66 -> 192.0.2.10    50 received
     198.51.100.66 -> 192.0.2.20    50 received
The last round blackholes 203.0.113.0/24 as a source prefix. Every packet from the legitimate client fails uRPF and is dropped, while the attacker, outside that prefix, sails through. It is a contrived mistake here, but the same thing happens in production when an attack is attributed by prefix rather than by address, or when the “attacker” addresses were spoofed and belong to someone you wanted to talk to. Source blackholes deserve the same review as destination ones: as specific as possible, time-limited, and logged.

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
section: FlowSpec: a filter rule in a BGP route
text:
FlowSpec: a filter rule in a BGP route
RTBH can only say “this address”. FlowSpec, defined for IPv4 in RFC 8955 (which obsoleted RFC 5575) and for IPv6 in RFC 8956, lets a BGP route carry a full match expression. The route is in its own address family: AFI 1, SAFI 133 for IPv4, and SAFI 134 for flow rules inside BGP/MPLS VPNs. The “prefix” of the route is the rule itself, and the action rides along as extended communities.

Components
The NLRI is a list of components, each starting with a one-octet type, and the types must appear in strictly increasing order with each type at most once. A packet matches the rule only if it matches every component present.









Type
Component
Operand
Notes




1
Destination prefix
prefix length + prefix
as in BGP UPDATE


2
Source prefix
prefix length + prefix



3
IP protocol
numeric



4
Port
numeric
matches source or destination port


5
Destination port
numeric



6
Source port
numeric



7
ICMP type
numeric



8
ICMP code
numeric



9
TCP flags
bitmask
1 octet = flags octet; 2 octets = data offset (as 0) + flags


10
Packet length
numeric
total IP length, header included, no L2


11
DSCP
numeric
6 low bits


12
Fragment
bitmask
DF 0x01, IsF 0x02 (not first), FF 0x04 (first), LF 0x08 (last)





Operators
Every non-prefix component is a list of {operator, value} pairs. The numeric operator octet is e a len 0 lt gt eq: e (0x80) marks the last pair, a (0x40) means “AND with the previous pair” (otherwise OR), len gives the value size as 1, 2, 4 or 8 octets, and the three comparison bits combine into ==, >, >=, <, <=, !=, always-true and always-false. AND binds tighter than OR, so >=137 AND <=139 OR ==8080 means “137 to 139, or 8080”. The bitmask operator octet is e a len 0 0 not m: with m set the test is “all these bits set”, without it “any of these bits set”, and not negates the result.
The NLRI starts with its length: one octet if the length is under 240, otherwise two octets with the top nibble 0xF (so the maximum is 4095).


Ordering and validation
Several FlowSpec rules may match one packet, so RFC 8955 section 5.1 defines a deterministic order that every router computes the same way regardless of arrival order: compare component by component, a rule that has a lower component type wins over one that lacks it, more-specific prefixes win, and other components are compared as byte strings. Appendix A of the RFC gives Python for the comparison.
Validation is the part that keeps FlowSpec from being an attack tool. By default (section 6) a received rule is feasible only if:

it contains a destination prefix;
the originator of the rule is also the originator of the best unicast route for that destination prefix; and
no more-specific unicast routes for parts of that prefix were learned from a different neighbouring AS.

In plain words: only the network you would send the traffic to may ask you to filter it. RFC 9117 revises this procedure, mainly so it works when rules and unicast routes arrive through route reflectors or from a centralised controller inside one AS. Rule 1 may be relaxed by configuration, which is common for rules distributed internally from a mitigation controller.


Actions
Actions are transitive extended communities (RFC 8955 section 7):








Community type
Action
Encoding




0x8006
traffic-rate-bytes
2-octet id + IEEE 754 float, bytes per second; 0 means discard


0x800c
traffic-rate-packets
same encoding, packets per second


0x8007
traffic-action
two bits: S (sample and log) and T (“terminal action”; read the gotcha below)


0x8008 (and 0x8108, 0x8208)
rt-redirect
redirect into the VRF whose import route target matches


0x8009
traffic-marking
set DSCP



Rate 0 is “drop”. Redirect is how scrubbing works with FlowSpec: matching traffic is pushed into a VRF whose route leads to a scrubbing centre, cleaned traffic comes back, and everything else takes the normal path.

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
section: Configuration you would use (not run here)

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
text:
Gotchas

Destination RTBH completes the attack. It saves shared capacity by taking the victim offline. Agree with the customer in advance when it may be used, and remove it as soon as the attack stops.
Source RTBH without uRPF does nothing. A blackhole route for a source affects only traffic to it. The lab’s third round is the failure mode: routes everywhere, attack unchanged.
Spoofed sources turn source RTBH against you. Against reflection or spoofed floods, blocking “sources” blocks forged addresses that belong to others. Use it only for verified, non-spoofed sources.
Blackholes are silent on Linux. No per-namespace counter, no ICMP: only the kernel-wide in_no_route moves. Measure discarded volume with flow export or firewall counters.
Your /32 will be filtered unless the session expects it. Upstreams accept long prefixes only on sessions where BLACKHOLE handling is agreed, often a separate session or a specific community. ROV can mark the /32 Invalid if your ROAs have a short maxLength.
Port rules miss fragments. FlowSpec port, ICMP and TCP-flag components never match non-first fragments. Always add a fragment rule for the same destination.
Validation surprises. A FlowSpec rule without a destination prefix, or one for a destination whose best unicast route came from another neighbour, is not feasible by default and will be ignored. When a rule “does not install”, check validation before suspecting the encoding.
FlowSpec is control-plane code that parses attacker-influenced input. Implementations have had serious bugs in FlowSpec handling, including ones that crash or compromise the routing engine. Accept FlowSpec only from sessions that need it, cap the number of rules per session, keep router software patched, and test rule sets on a lab router first.
The T bit reads backwards. RFC 8955 section 7.3 says that when the traffic-action T (“terminal action”) bit is set, evaluation continues with later FlowSpec rules, and when it is clear, evaluation stops at this rule. The name suggests the opposite, and it is easy to get wrong in a controller. Check what your platform documents before relying on rule chaining.
Hardware limits. Each FlowSpec rule consumes filter (TCAM) entries; rate actions consume policers. A detector that pushes hundreds of fine-grained rules during an attack can exhaust them. Aggregate rules and set a hard maximum.

title: Dropping Attack Traffic with Routing: RTBH, Source-Based RTBH and BGP FlowSpec
text:
Exercises

Strict mode at the edge. Rerun the RTBH lab with rp_filter=1 instead of 2 on up0. Does the result change for this topology? Then add a second upstream namespace and route the client’s prefix back through it, and explain why strict mode now drops the legitimate client.
Measure what you discarded. Extend count.py and blast.py so the sender numbers its datagrams, and report how many were lost per flow during the destination RTBH round. Compare with the kernel-wide counter while unrelated traffic runs.
Encode your own rule. Use flowspec.py to encode “to 192.0.2.0/24, TCP, destination port 80 or 443, TCP SYN set and ACK clear”. You will need the bitmask operator with the match bit for SYN and the not bit for ACK. Decode the result and check the operator octets by hand.
Order two rules. Encode rule A and rule B and sort them with the RFC 8955 Appendix A comparison (copy the function from the RFC). Which one is evaluated first, and does it matter here?
Extended length. Build a rule with enough port pairs to make the NLRI 240 octets or longer, and extend encode() to emit the two-octet 0xFnnn length. Check that 240 encodes as f0 f0, as the RFC says.
Plan a BLACKHOLE policy. Write the import policy for an upstream session that honours 65535:666: which prefix lengths you accept, which ownership check you apply, which community you add, and how ROV is handled for these routes.
