ScopedPDU failed to decrypt or parse as ASN.1
Wrong privacy passphrase/cipher, or corrupted packet

title: SNMPv3 Done Properly: USM Keys, Engine IDs, Time Windows and VACM Views
text:
VACM: least-privilege views
USM answers who sent the message and whether it was tampered with. VACM (RFC 3415) answers what that user is allowed to read, write, or receive. Configuring a USM user without a VACM entry leaves the user unable to access any OID.
VACM evaluates access in three steps:
(securityModel, securityName)
       |
       v
vacmSecurityToGroupTable  --->  groupName
                                    |
(groupName, contextName,            |
 securityModel, securityLevel)      v
                           vacmAccessTable  --->  readViewName
                                                  writeViewName
                                                  notifyViewName
                                                       |
                                                       v
                                          vacmViewTreeFamilyTable
                                          (OID subtrees + bitmask,
                                           included / excluded)

Group mapping: (securityModel=3, securityName) maps to a groupName (for example, netops -> rw_group, monitor -> ro_group).
Access rule: (groupName, contextName, securityModel, securityLevel) selects the readView, writeView, and notifyView, enforcing a minimum securityLevel (always authPriv in production).
View tree: Each view is a list of OID subtrees marked included or excluded, optionally with a bitmask for row-level or column-level filtering.

Two VACM behaviours matter operationally:

Silent denial per varbind. If a user queries an OID outside their readView, the agent does not return an authorization error for the whole packet; it returns noSuchObject for that specific varbind. This prevents an unprivileged user from probing which MIBs or interfaces exist on a box.
Protect the security MIBs. If you grant a read-only monitoring user a view of the entire ISO tree (.1) or mib-2 plus snmpV2 (.1.3.6.1), you may expose the usmUser subtree, including usmUserTable (1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.2.2), and vacmAccessTable (1.3.6.1.6.3.16.1.4). Even though usmUserTable does not return raw Kul values over the wire, it exposes every configured username, authentication protocol, and privacy protocol. Restrict read-only views to the specific subtrees your NMS actually polls (such as system and interfaces / ifMIB), or explicitly exclude the snmpUsmMIB and snmpVacmMIB subtrees.

title: SNMPv3 Done Properly: USM Keys, Engine IDs, Time Windows and VACM Views
section: Operations: Net-SNMP, traps vs informs, and when to leave SNMP behind
text:
Operations: Net-SNMP, traps vs informs, and when to leave SNMP behind

Configuring Net-SNMP (from the docs, not run)
On Linux hosts running Net-SNMP’s snmpd, USM users are created with createUser (typically placed in /var/lib/snmp/snmpd.conf so snmpd replaces the plaintext passphrases with localized usmUser entries on startup) and bound to VACM with view and rouser in /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf. The following syntax is from the Net-SNMP snmpd.conf(5) manual page (not run here):
# From the Net-SNMP snmpd.conf(5) docs, not run
createUser netops SHA-256 "StrongAuthPassphrase!" AES "StrongPrivPassphrase!"

view system_if included 1.3.6.1.2.1.1
view system_if included 1.3.6.1.2.1.2
view system_if included 1.3.6.1.2.1.31

rouser netops priv -V system_if
Notice the priv keyword on rouser: it enforces authPriv as the minimum security level, rejecting noAuthNoPriv or authNoPriv attempts even if the user exists. Never use rwuser unless you have a specific, audited requirement for SNMP SET—configuration changes belong in NETCONF, RESTCONF, or gNMI, not SNMP.
To query that agent from a collector (not run):
# Not run
snmpget -v3 -l authPriv -u netops -a SHA-256 -A 'StrongAuthPassphrase!' \
  -x AES -X 'StrongPrivPassphrase!' 192.0.2.10 sysDescr.0


Traps vs Informs
SNMPv3 notifications come in two forms:

SNMPv2-Trap: unacknowledged, reportableFlag = 0. The sender (the router) is authoritative. The collector needs a USM user entry localized to each router’s snmpEngineID.
InformRequest: acknowledged with a Response PDU, reportableFlag = 1. The receiver (the collector) is authoritative. Every router sending informs needs the collector’s snmpEngineID (discovered automatically or configured statically) to localize its keys.

Prefer InformRequest when delivery matters (link down, BGP peer state change) and your collector handles discovery cleanly, or avoid SNMP traps altogether in favour of syslog over TLS and streaming telemetry.


Network hygiene and scaling

Management VRF and ACLs: Bind the SNMP agent to your out-of-band or management VRF only, and filter UDP 161 (and UDP 162 on collectors) to explicit NMS source prefixes.
Monitor usmStats: Poll or alert on usmStatsWrongDigests.0 (brute-force attempts or misconfigured collector credentials), usmStatsNotInTimeWindows.0 (reboot loops or replay attempts), and unexpected spikes in usmStatsUnknownUserNames.0.
64-bit counters: RFC 2863 requires 64-bit octet counters on interfaces faster than 20 Mbps, and for good reason: at 10 Gbps a 32-bit octet counter wraps in roughly 3.4 seconds. Poll the 64-bit High Capacity (HC) counters in IF-MIB::ifXTable (ifHCInOctets, ifHCOutOctets, RFC 2863).
GETBULK sizing: GetBulkRequest amplifies a small request into a large Response. Setting max-repetitions too high pushes the response past msgMaxSize or your path MTU, causing tooBig errors or IP fragmentation across management tunnels. Test max-repetitions (commonly 10–25 for wide tables) against your actual msgMaxSize.



When to stop using SNMP
SNMPv3 solves wire confidentiality and integrity, but it cannot fix SNMP’s underlying operational limits:

Polling overhead: Walking large BGP or ARP tables with GetNext/GetBulk burns router control-plane CPU.
Flat, untyped OIDs: Mapping vendor MIBs and table indexes is brittle compared to strongly typed YANG schemas.
No native streaming: Sub-second interface telemetry requires push-based gRPC/gNMI rather than 60-second UDP polling.

As covered in the YANG/NETCONF/gNMI chapter, move high-frequency counters, routing state, and configuration to gNMI and streaming telemetry wherever your hardware supports it. Keep SNMPv3 strictly for legacy gear, out-of-band power/environmental devices, and low-frequency inventory checks.

title: SNMPv3 Done Properly: USM Keys, Engine IDs, Time Windows and VACM Views
text:
The lab
To see every RFC 3414, 3415, 3826, and 7860 rule in action on real wire bytes, the lab runs a self-contained Python agent and manager (snmpv3.py, Python standard library plus the cryptography package for AES-128-CFB, talking over loopback UDP). The agent uses snmpEngineID 80001f8804 + "edge-r1" (80001f8804656467652d7231) with snmpEngineBoots = 7 and snmpEngineTime = 1000, and defines two users:

netops: HMAC-SHA-256-192 + AES-128-CFB (authPriv), read view 1.3.6.1 (deliberately broad, for contrast with monitor).
monitor: HMAC-SHA-96 (authNoPriv), VACM read view restricted to 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 (system) only.

Across seven automated checks, the lab verifies:

Exact reproduction of both RFC 3414 Appendix A.3 "maplesyrup" test vectors (MD5 and SHA-1 Ku and Kul).
Key localization isolation: the same passphrase produces different SHA-256 Kul keys on edge-r1 (1bf9d82e...) versus edge-r2 (71d2f038...).
Discovery: an empty-engineID probe triggers a Report with usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs=1, returning 80001f8804656467652d7231, boots 7, time 1000.
authPriv vs SNMPv2c on the wire: netops polls sysDescr.0 and ifDescr.1 (154 B request, 185 B response) returning 'lab-agent Linux 6.12 router' and 'eth0' with payloads hidden—though netops remains in clear text—compared to a 67 B SNMPv2c response exposing "public" and sysDescr in clear text.
All major usmStats Reports: wrong password (usmStatsWrongDigests=1), unknown user admin (usmStatsUnknownUserNames=1), monitor requesting authPriv (usmStatsUnsupportedSecLevels=1), stale engineTime by 200 s (usmStatsNotInTimeWindows=1, sent authNoPriv with flags 0x01), and pre-reboot boots (usmStatsNotInTimeWindows=2).
VACM scoping: monitor reads sysName.0 ('edge-r1') but receives noSuchObject for ifDescr.1.
Replay behaviour: a byte-identical replay of the netops authPriv request 2 seconds later (at time = 1002) is accepted and answered again.



snmpv3.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""SNMPv3 USM + VACM on loopback UDP, stdlib + cryptography (AES-CFB only).
Agent and manager are both in this file; every message crosses a real socket."""
import hashlib, hmac, os, socket, struct, threading, time
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes

# ---------------- BER ----------------
def tlv(tag, val):
    n = len(val)
    if n < 0x80: ln = bytes([n])
    else:
        b = n.to_bytes((n.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big"); ln = bytes([0x80 | len(b)]) + b
    return bytes([tag]) + ln + val
def ber_int(v):
    b = v.to_bytes(max(1, (v.bit_length() + 8) // 8), "big", signed=True); return tlv(0x02, b)
def ber_oct(b): return tlv(0x04, b)
def ber_null(): return b"\x05\x00"
def ber_oid(s):
    p = [int(x) for x in s.split(".")]; out = bytes([40 * p[0] + p[1]])
    for n in p[2:]:
        enc = [n & 0x7F]; n >>= 7
        while n: enc.append(0x80 | (n & 0x7F)); n >>= 7
        out += bytes(reversed(enc))
    return tlv(0x06, out)
def seq(*items, tag=0x30): return tlv(tag, b"".join(items))

def parse(buf, i=0):
    tag = buf[i]; ln = buf[i + 1]; i += 2
    if ln & 0x80:
        k = ln & 0x7F; ln = int.from_bytes(buf[i:i + k], "big"); i += k
    return tag, buf[i:i + ln], i + ln
def children(buf):
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(buf):
        t, v, i = parse(buf, i); out.append((t, v))
    return out
def dec_int(v): return int.from_bytes(v, "big", signed=True)
def dec_oid(v):
    p = [v[0] // 40, v[0] % 40]; n = 0
    for b in v[1:]:
        n = (n << 7) | (b & 0x7F)
        if not b & 0x80: p.append(n); n = 0
    return ".".join(map(str, p))

# ---------------- USM crypto ----------------
def password_to_key(pw: bytes, engine_id: bytes, h):
    """RFC 3414 A.2 (MD5/SHA-1) and RFC 7860 (SHA-2): 1 MiB of repeated password, then localize."""
    count, buf = 0, b""
    d = h()
    rep = (pw * (64 // len(pw) + 2))
    while count < 1048576:
        chunk = rep[count % len(pw):count % len(pw) + 64]; d.update(chunk); count += 64
    ku = d.digest()
    return ku, h(ku + engine_id + ku).digest()

AUTH = {"sha1-96": (hashlib.sha1, 12), "sha256-192": (hashlib.sha256, 24)}

def aes_cfb(key16, boots, etime, salt, data, enc=True):
    iv = struct.pack("!II", boots, etime) + salt
    c = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key16), modes.CFB(iv))
    x = c.encryptor() if enc else c.decryptor()
    return x.update(data) + x.finalize()

# ---------------- message build/parse ----------------
GET, RESPONSE, REPORT = 0xA0, 0xA2, 0xA8
STATS = {"1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.1.0": "usmStatsUnsupportedSecLevels", "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.2.0": "usmStatsNotInTimeWindows",
         "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.3.0": "usmStatsUnknownUserNames", "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.4.0": "usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs",
         "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.5.0": "usmStatsWrongDigests", "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.6.0": "usmStatsDecryptionErrors"}

def pdu(tag, reqid, varbinds, err=0, idx=0):
    vbs = seq(*[seq(ber_oid(o), v) for o, v in varbinds])
    return seq(ber_int(reqid), ber_int(err), ber_int(idx), vbs, tag=tag)

def build_v3(msgid, flags, eng, boots, etime, user, scoped, auth=None, priv_key=None, salt=b""):
    auth_len = AUTH[auth[0]][1] if auth else 0
    privp = b""
    body = scoped
    if priv_key:
        privp = salt
        pad = scoped  # CFB needs no padding
        body = ber_oct(aes_cfb(priv_key[:16], boots, etime, salt, pad))
    def assemble(authp):
        usm = seq(ber_oct(eng), ber_int(boots), ber_int(etime), ber_oct(user), ber_oct(authp), ber_oct(privp))
        hdr = seq(ber_int(msgid), ber_int(65507), ber_oct(bytes([flags])), ber_int(3))
        return seq(ber_int(3), hdr, ber_oct(usm), body)
    if not auth: return assemble(b"")
    blank = assemble(b"\x00" * auth_len)
    h, n = AUTH[auth[0]]
    mac = hmac.new(auth[1], blank, h).digest()[:n]
    return assemble(mac)

def parse_v3(dgram):
    _, top, _ = parse(dgram); parts = children(top)
    hdr = children(parts[1][1]); usm = children(parse(parts[2][1])[1])
    m = dict(msgid=dec_int(hdr[0][1]), flags=hdr[2][1][0], eng=usm[0][1], boots=dec_int(usm[1][1]),
             etime=dec_int(usm[2][1]), user=usm[3][1], authp=usm[4][1], privp=usm[5][1],
             data_tag=parts[3][0], data=parts[3][1])
    return m

def parse_scoped(raw):
    _, sp, _ = parse(raw); ch = children(sp)
    tag, body = ch[2]; f = children(body)
    vbs = [children(v) for _, v in children(f[3][1])]
    return tag, dec_int(f[0][1]), dec_int(f[1][1]), [(dec_oid(vb[0][1]), vb[1][0], vb[1][1]) for vb in vbs]

# ---------------- agent ----------------
class Agent:
    def __init__(self, engine_id):
        self.eng, self.boots, self.t0 = engine_id, 7, time.monotonic() - 1000
        self.mib = {"1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0": ber_oct(b"lab-agent Linux 6.12 router"),
                    "1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0": ber_oct(b"edge-r1"),
                    "1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.1": ber_oct(b"eth0")}
        self.users = {}
        self.stats = {k: 0 for k in STATS}
        self.sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); self.sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
        self.addr = self.sock.getsockname()
    def etime(self): return int(time.monotonic() - self.t0)
    def add_user(self, name, pw, auth, priv_pw=None, view="1.3.6.1"):
        h = AUTH[auth][0]
        self.users[name] = dict(auth=auth, ak=password_to_key(pw, self.eng, h)[1],
                                pk=password_to_key(priv_pw, self.eng, h)[1] if priv_pw else None, view=view)
    def report(self, m, oid, flags=0):
        self.stats[oid] += 1
        sp = seq(ber_oct(self.eng), ber_oct(b""), pdu(REPORT, 0, [(oid, tlv(0x41, self.stats[oid].to_bytes(4, "big")))]))
        u = self.users.get(m["user"].decode(errors="replace"))
        auth = (u["auth"], u["ak"]) if (flags & 1 and u) else None
        return build_v3(m["msgid"], flags, self.eng, self.boots, self.etime(), m["user"], sp, auth=auth)
    def handle(self, d):
        m = parse_v3(d)
        if m["eng"] != self.eng:
            return self.report(m, "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.4.0")
        u = self.users.get(m["user"].decode(errors="replace"))
        if not u: return self.report(m, "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.3.0")
        if m["flags"] & 2 and not u["pk"]: return self.report(m, "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.1.0")
        if m["flags"] & 1:
            h, n = AUTH[u["auth"]]
            blank = d.replace(m["authp"], b"\x00" * n, 1)
            if not hmac.compare_digest(hmac.new(u["ak"], blank, h).digest()[:n], m["authp"]):
                return self.report(m, "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.5.0")
            if m["boots"] != self.boots or abs(m["etime"] - self.etime()) > 150:
                return self.report(m, "1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.2.0", flags=1)
        raw = m["data"]
        if m["flags"] & 2:
            raw = aes_cfb(u["pk"][:16], m["boots"], m["etime"], m["privp"], raw, enc=False)
        else:
            raw = seq(raw)  # plaintext ScopedPDU was a SEQUENCE; rewrap value
        tag, reqid, _, vbs = parse_scoped(raw)
        out = []
        for oid, _, _ in vbs:
            if not (oid + ".").startswith(u["view"] + "."): out.append((oid, b"\x80\x00"))     # noSuchObject (notInView)
            else: out.append((oid, self.mib.get(oid, b"\x80\x00")))
        sp = seq(ber_oct(self.eng), ber_oct(b""), pdu(RESPONSE, reqid, out))
        salt = os.urandom(8) if m["flags"] & 2 else b""
        return build_v3(m["msgid"], m["flags"] & 3, self.eng, self.boots, self.etime(), m["user"], sp,
                        auth=(u["auth"], u["ak"]) if m["flags"] & 1 else None,
                        priv_key=u["pk"] if m["flags"] & 2 else None, salt=salt)
    def serve(self):
        while True:
            d, a = self.sock.recvfrom(65535)
            if d == b"stop": break
            self.sock.sendto(self.handle(d), a)

# ---------------- manager helpers ----------------
def xchg(agent, d):
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.settimeout(2)
    s.sendto(d, agent.addr); r, _ = s.recvfrom(65535); s.close(); return r

def show(label, r, key=None, h=None):
    m = parse_v3(r)
    raw = m["data"]
    if m["flags"] & 2: raw = aes_cfb(key[:16], m["boots"], m["etime"], m["privp"], raw, enc=False)
    else: raw = seq(raw)
    tag, reqid, err, vbs = parse_scoped(raw)
    kind = {RESPONSE: "Response", REPORT: "Report"}[tag]
    items = []
    for oid, t, v in vbs:
        if oid in STATS: items.append(f"{STATS[oid]}={int.from_bytes(v, 'big')}")
        elif t == 0x80: items.append(f"{oid}=noSuchObject")
        else: items.append(f"{oid}={v.decode()!r}")
    print(f"  {label:44s} -> {kind} flags=0x{m['flags']:02x} boots={m['boots']} time={m['etime']} {'; '.join(items)}")
    return m

def section(t): print(f"\n=== {t} ===")

def main():
    section("1. RFC 3414 A.3 password-to-key vectors")
    e2 = bytes.fromhex("000000000000000000000002")
    for name, h, want in [("MD5", hashlib.md5, "526f5eed9fcce26f8964c2930787d82b"),
                          ("SHA-1", hashlib.sha1, "6695febc9288e36282235fc7151f128497b38f3f")]:
        ku, kul = password_to_key(b"maplesyrup", e2, h)
        print(f"  {name:5s} Ku={ku.hex()} Kul={kul.hex()} match={kul.hex() == want}")

    section("2. Same password, two engines (key localization)")
    eA = bytes.fromhex("80001f8804") + b"edge-r1"; eB = bytes.fromhex("80001f8804") + b"edge-r2"
    for e in (eA, eB):
        print(f"  engineID {e.hex()} -> SHA-256 Kul {password_to_key(b'correct horse 1', e, hashlib.sha256)[1].hex()[:32]}...")

    ag = Agent(eA)
    ag.add_user("netops", b"correct horse 1", "sha256-192", priv_pw=b"battery staple 2")
    ag.add_user("monitor", b"monitor-pass-9", "sha1-96", view="1.3.6.1.2.1.1")
    th = threading.Thread(target=ag.serve, daemon=True); th.start()
    _, ak = password_to_key(b"correct horse 1", eA, hashlib.sha256)
    _, pk = password_to_key(b"battery staple 2", eA, hashlib.sha256)
    _, mk = password_to_key(b"monitor-pass-9", eA, hashlib.sha1)
    get = lambda oids, rid=1: seq(ber_oct(eA), ber_oct(b""), pdu(GET, rid, [(o, ber_null()) for o in oids]))

    section("3. Engine discovery (RFC 3414 s4)")
    probe = build_v3(100, 0x04, b"", 0, 0, b"", seq(ber_oct(b""), ber_oct(b""), pdu(GET, 9, [])))
    m = show("noAuthNoPriv probe, empty engineID", xchg(ag, probe))
    print(f"  learned engineID={m['eng'].hex()} boots={m['boots']} time={m['etime']}")

    section("4. authPriv GET as netops (HMAC-SHA-256-192 + AES-128-CFB)")
    salt = os.urandom(8)
    req = build_v3(101, 0x07, eA, m["boots"], m["etime"], b"netops", get(["1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0", "1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.1"]),
                   auth=("sha256-192", ak), priv_key=pk, salt=salt)
    r = xchg(ag, req)
    show("GET sysDescr.0, ifDescr.1", r, key=pk)
    print(f"  request {len(req)} B, response {len(r)} B; b'lab-agent' visible on the wire: {b'lab-agent' in r}; "
          f"b'netops' visible: {b'netops' in req}")
    v2c = seq(ber_int(1), ber_oct(b"public"), pdu(RESPONSE, 1, [("1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0", ber_oct(b"lab-agent Linux 6.12 router"))]))
    print(f"  same answer as SNMPv2c: {len(v2c)} B; b'public' and b'lab-agent' visible: {b'public' in v2c and b'lab-agent' in v2c}")

    section("5. Failures the agent reports")
    _, bad = password_to_key(b"wrong password", eA, hashlib.sha256)
    show("netops, wrong auth password", xchg(ag, build_v3(102, 0x05, eA, m["boots"], m["etime"], b"netops", get(["1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0"]), auth=("sha256-192", bad))))
    show("unknown user 'admin'", xchg(ag, build_v3(103, 0x04, eA, m["boots"], m["etime"], b"admin", get(["1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0"]))))
    show("monitor asks for authPriv (no priv key)", xchg(ag, build_v3(104, 0x07, eA, m["boots"], m["etime"], b"monitor", get(["1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0"]), auth=("sha1-96", mk), priv_key=mk, salt=os.urandom(8))))
    show("netops, engineTime 200 s stale", xchg(ag, build_v3(105, 0x05, eA, m["boots"], m["etime"] - 200, b"netops", get(["1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0"]), auth=("sha256-192", ak))))
    show("netops, engineBoots from before a reboot", xchg(ag, build_v3(106, 0x05, eA, m["boots"] - 1, m["etime"], b"netops", get(["1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0"]), auth=("sha256-192", ak))))

    section("6. VACM: monitor's view is 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 (system)")
    show("monitor authNoPriv GET sysName.0, ifDescr.1", xchg(ag, build_v3(107, 0x05, eA, m["boots"], m["etime"], b"monitor", get(["1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0", "1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.1"]), auth=("sha1-96", mk))))

    section("7. Replay inside the 150 s window")
    time.sleep(2)
    show("byte-identical replay of step 4 request", xchg(ag, req), key=pk)
    print(f"  usm counters: " + ", ".join(f"{STATS[k]}={v}" for k, v in ag.stats.items() if v))
    socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM).sendto(b"stop", ag.addr)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it with python3 snmpv3.py. It needs the cryptography package for AES (already present on many Linux systems; if not, install it in a virtual environment). No root is needed: agent and manager use an unprivileged loopback port. Output, pasted unedited from a run on 2026-11-16:
=== 1. RFC 3414 A.3 password-to-key vectors ===
  MD5   Ku=9faf3283884e92834ebc9847d8edd963 Kul=526f5eed9fcce26f8964c2930787d82b match=True
  SHA-1 Ku=9fb5cc0381497b3793528939ff788d5d79145211 Kul=6695febc9288e36282235fc7151f128497b38f3f match=True

=== 2. Same password, two engines (key localization) ===
  engineID 80001f8804656467652d7231 -> SHA-256 Kul 1bf9d82e1f187a553f6babc310d97c8c...
  engineID 80001f8804656467652d7232 -> SHA-256 Kul 71d2f038b110a140cc3b3458104f22f5...

=== 3. Engine discovery (RFC 3414 s4) ===
  noAuthNoPriv probe, empty engineID           -> Report flags=0x00 boots=7 time=1000 usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs=1
  learned engineID=80001f8804656467652d7231 boots=7 time=1000

=== 4. authPriv GET as netops (HMAC-SHA-256-192 + AES-128-CFB) ===
  GET sysDescr.0, ifDescr.1                    -> Response flags=0x03 boots=7 time=1000 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0='lab-agent Linux 6.12 router'; 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.1='eth0'
  request 154 B, response 185 B; b'lab-agent' visible on the wire: False; b'netops' visible: True
  same answer as SNMPv2c: 67 B; b'public' and b'lab-agent' visible: True

=== 5. Failures the agent reports ===
  netops, wrong auth password                  -> Report flags=0x00 boots=7 time=1000 usmStatsWrongDigests=1
  unknown user 'admin'                         -> Report flags=0x00 boots=7 time=1000 usmStatsUnknownUserNames=1
  monitor asks for authPriv (no priv key)      -> Report flags=0x00 boots=7 time=1000 usmStatsUnsupportedSecLevels=1
  netops, engineTime 200 s stale               -> Report flags=0x01 boots=7 time=1000 usmStatsNotInTimeWindows=1
  netops, engineBoots from before a reboot     -> Report flags=0x01 boots=7 time=1000 usmStatsNotInTimeWindows=2

=== 6. VACM: monitor's view is 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 (system) ===
  monitor authNoPriv GET sysName.0, ifDescr.1  -> Response flags=0x01 boots=7 time=1000 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0='edge-r1'; 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.1=noSuchObject

=== 7. Replay inside the 150 s window ===
  byte-identical replay of step 4 request      -> Response flags=0x03 boots=7 time=1002 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0='lab-agent Linux 6.12 router'; 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.1='eth0'
  usm counters: usmStatsUnsupportedSecLevels=1, usmStatsNotInTimeWindows=2, usmStatsUnknownUserNames=1, usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs=1, usmStatsWrongDigests=1
Two lines deserve a second look. In section 4, the request is 154 bytes and the string netops is visible in it while lab-agent is not: the username rides in clear text and the payload does not. In section 7, the replayed request is answered again at engine time 1002, which is USM working exactly as specified.

title: SNMPv3 Done Properly: USM Keys, Engine IDs, Time Windows and VACM Views
text:
Gotchas
The trap: authNoPriv feels like “SNMPv3 is enabled.” Because authNoPriv sets msgFlags = 0x01, operators sometimes assume traffic is protected. It is authenticated, not encrypted: every OID, interface description, IP address, and counter value travels in clear text. Always require authPriv for operational polling.
The trap: assuming authPriv hides usernames. msgUserName lives in msgSecurityParameters, outside the encrypted ScopedPDU. Anyone sniffing management traffic can harvest valid usernames. Combine authPriv with management-VRF isolation and strict UDP 161 ACLs.
The trap: assuming USM stops replay attacks. USM checks only that boots matches and engineTime is within +/-150 seconds. It has no replay cache. A captured authPriv GetRequest or SetRequest can be replayed for up to 300 seconds—another reason to disable SNMP SET entirely.
The trap: cloning snmpEngineID in golden images. Copying /var/lib/snmp/snmpd.conf (or a vendor persistent config) into a VM or router template gives every device the same snmpEngineID. That breaks key localization isolation and confuses collector time-window caches. Strip persisted engine IDs before sealing images.
The trap: passphrases shorter than 8 characters. RFC 3414 recommends passphrases of at least 8 octets, and agents such as Net-SNMP commonly refuse shorter passphrases outright. Use long, randomly generated passphrases (16+ characters) stored in your secrets manager.
The trap: polling 32-bit IF-MIB counters on high-speed links. ifInOctets and ifOutOctets wrap every few seconds on 10G/100G interfaces, producing flat or sawtooth graphs. Always poll the 64-bit HC counters in ifXTable (RFC 2863).
The trap: oversized GETBULK max-repetitions. Requesting 100 repetitions of a wide table can exceed msgMaxSize or force IP fragmentation across management GRE/IPsec tunnels, causing silent drops or tooBig errors. Tune max-repetitions conservatively.
The trap: VACM views that expose usmUserTable. Granting a read-only user access to .1 or .1.3.6.1 lets them read usmUserTable and vacmAccessTable. Scope read-only views to the specific MIB subtrees your NMS needs, and explicitly exclude security tables.
The trap: leaving CBC-DES in legacy device templates. Some older templates still specify DES as a fallback privacy protocol. Audit your fleet and migrate every capable device to AES-128-CFB (AES) with SHA-256 (usmHMAC192SHA256).

title: SNMPv3 Done Properly: USM Keys, Engine IDs, Time Windows and VACM Views
text:
Exercises

Key localization by hand or script. Using the RFC 3414 Appendix A.2 algorithm, compute Ku and Kul for the passphrase "maplesyrup" with SHA-1 and engine ID 80001f8804656467652d7231 (edge-r1), then repeat for edge-r2. Explain why a compromise of edge-r1’s localized key does not grant access to edge-r2.
Packet dissection. Capture (or inspect from the lab) an SNMPv3 discovery probe, its Report response, and the subsequent authPriv GetRequest. Identify the exact byte offsets or fields for msgFlags, msgUserName, msgPrivacyParameters, and the encrypted ScopedPDU. Confirm which fields are visible in clear text.
Timeliness and replay analysis. An attacker captures a valid authPriv SetRequest that bounces an interface (ifAdminStatus.1 = down) at snmpEngineTime = 1000. At what snmpEngineTime values will the router accept a byte-identical replay? What happens if the router reboots (snmpEngineBoots increments) 30 seconds after the capture?
Least-privilege VACM design. Design a Net-SNMP view and rouser configuration for a capacity-planning collector that needs system (1.3.6.1.2.1.1) and ifXTable (1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1) only, must use authPriv, and must receive noSuchObject for usmUserTable and ipRouteTable.
Triage with usmStats. Your NMS alerts that polling to core-r4 stopped after a maintenance window. You query usmStats from a working collector and see usmStatsNotInTimeWindows.0 climbing rapidly while usmStatsWrongDigests.0 is 0. What happened, and what are the two most likely root causes?
Migration decision. A campus switch stack supports SNMPv3 (SHA-256 + AES-128) and gNMI over TLS. You need 5-second interface drop counters and BGP session state, plus daily hardware serial inventory. Decide which protocol handles which workload and justify your split.

title: SNMPv3 Done Properly: USM Keys, Engine IDs, Time Windows and VACM Views
text:
The boring rule
Use authPriv with SHA-256 and AES-128, keep a unique snmpEngineID on every device, scope VACM views to read-only operational subtrees, and move high-frequency telemetry to gNMI wherever the platform allows it.

title: SNMPv3 Done Properly: USM Keys, Engine IDs, Time Windows and VACM Views
text:
Sources

RFC 3411: An Architecture for Describing Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Management Frameworks
RFC 3412: Message Processing and Dispatching for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)
RFC 3414: User-based Security Model (USM) for version 3 of the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv3)
RFC 3415: View-based Access Control Model (VACM) for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)

title: Automation & Lab-as-Code
text:
Automation & Lab-as-Code
A lab you cannot rebuild is a rumor. This chapter automates the Containerlab lifecycle, config push patterns, and smoke verification so your networking skill compounds in git.

title: Automation & Lab-as-Code
text:
Templating addressing: DIY vs. Netlab

The DIY Approach (Jinja2 + custom scripts)
# addressing.yml
links:
  r1_r2: { r1: 10.0.12.1/24, r2: 10.0.12.2/24 }
lans:
  h1: { gw: 192.168.1.1/24, host: 192.168.1.10/24 }
You can render frr.conf.j2 → config/r1/frr.conf with a custom Python/Jinja script or Ansible template module. Generated files can be committed for diff visibility or generated in CI.


The Netlab Declarative Approach
Writing custom Python Jinja compilers and manual IPAM spreadsheets becomes difficult to maintain when topologies exceed 3–4 nodes. Netlab provides a turnkey, declarative engine designed specifically for network labs:
# topology.yml
---
provider: clab
defaults.device: frr
module: [ ospf, bfd ]

nodes:
  r1:
  r2:
  r3:

links:
  - r1:
    r2:
  - r2:
    r3:
  - r3:
    r1:

validate:
  ospf_full:
    description: "Verify all OSPF adjacencies reach Full"
    nodes: [ r1, r2, r3 ]
    plugin: ospf_neighbor(count=2, state='Full')
Running netlab up calculates IPAM, renders Jinja2 templates for each device, stands up the Containerlab environment, and configures the routers. Running netlab validate executes the validation suite automatically.

title: Automation & Lab-as-Code
text:
Verification: verify.sh vs. netlab validate

Custom Shell Script (verify.sh)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
fail() { echo "FAIL: $*" >&2; exit 1; }

need_full() {
  local node=$1
  docker exec "$node" vtysh -c 'show ip ospf neighbor' | grep -q Full \
    || fail "$node missing Full neighbor"
}

need_full clab-ospf-tri-r1
need_full clab-ospf-tri-r2
need_full clab-ospf-tri-r3

docker exec clab-ospf-tri-h1 ping -c 2 -W 1 192.168.2.10 || fail "h1->h2"
docker exec clab-ospf-tri-h2 ping -c 2 -W 1 192.168.1.10 || fail "h2->h1"

echo "OK $(date -Is)"


Netlab Automated Validation
With Netlab, assertions are declared directly in YAML and executed with exit codes suitable for CI:
# Returns exit code 0 on pass, non-zero on failure
netlab validate

title: Automation & Lab-as-Code
text:
CI smoke (GitHub Actions sketch)
Conceptual job (runner must support Docker + Containerlab—often self-hosted):
# conceptual — adapt to your runners
jobs:
  lab-smoke:
    runs-on: self-hosted-linux
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: deploy+verify
        working-directory: books/Networking/labs/ospf-tri
        run: |
          sudo containerlab deploy -t topology.clab.yml
          ./verify.sh
      - name: cleanup
        if: always()
        working-directory: books/Networking/labs/ospf-tri
        run: sudo containerlab destroy -t topology.clab.yml --cleanup
This book’s monorepo CI renders Quarto; lab smoke is optional local/self-hosted. Do not assume GitHub-hosted runners allow nested Containerlab without setup.

title: network-xray: see why BGP picked that path in containerlab
text:
network-xray: see why BGP picked that path in containerlab
After reading this chapter, you can run network-xray alongside Containerlab or Netlab to inspect BGP path selection decisions and routing state directly in your web browser.
Understanding why a router selected one BGP path over competing candidates usually requires manually logging into individual nodes, executing multiple diagnostic show commands, and evaluating path attributes step-by-step against standard decision rules. network-xray automates this process by polling live router state from FRRouting (FRR), Nokia SR Linux, and Cisco IOL nodes running inside Containerlab or Netlab, visualizing topology links and path selection logic in real time.

title: network-xray: see why BGP picked that path in containerlab
text:
Architectural Overview
network-xray functions as a read-only live-state visualizer. It operates as a local HTTP server that reads container metadata and topology structures from Containerlab or Netlab, issues standard diagnostic show commands to participating router instances, and renders the compiled state in an interactive web interface.
  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
  |                           Browser UI                              |
  |             http://127.0.0.1:8600/ (or recorded demo)             |
  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    ^
                                    | HTTP / Web Sockets
                                    v
  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
  |                       network-xray container                      |
  |      Reads clab topology & polls routers via show commands        |
  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
             |                                           |
             | /var/run/docker.sock                      | CLI Execution
             v                                           v
  +-----------------------+                 +-------------------------+
  |  Docker Engine Host   |                 | Containerlab Router     |
  |  (Reads container ID) |                 | Nodes (FRR, SRL, IOL)   |
  +-----------------------+                 +-------------------------+
Rather than modifying routing engine logic or inserting proprietary telemetry agents, network-xray uses non-disruptive inspection. It queries nodes for control-plane data—such as show bgp detail or show ip ospf neighbor—and parses the raw text or JSON outputs into structured graph visualizers.

title: network-xray: see why BGP picked that path in containerlab
text:
Supported Routing Platforms and Protocols
network-xray supports live state visual extraction for three main network operating systems running within Containerlab environments:








Operating System
Supported Protocols
Inspection Mechanism




FRRouting (FRR)
BGP (IPv4/IPv6), OSPF
vtysh -c 'show ...' queries


Nokia SR Linux
BGP, OSPF
sr_cli JSON state queries


Cisco IOL
BGP, OSPF
Standard CLI show outputs



The tool captures key control-plane characteristics, including: - BGP Best-Path Decision logic: Highlighting why a specific prefix candidate won (e.g., Local Preference, AS-Path length, Origin, MED, eBGP vs. iBGP, IGP metric, or Router ID). - OSPF Adjacency states: Real-time inspection of neighbor states (e.g., Full, 2-Way, Init) across active topology interfaces.

title: network-xray: see why BGP picked that path in containerlab
text:
Running network-xray with Containerlab






Note



Not run here. Running network-xray requires access to a local Docker daemon and a running Containerlab environment. Because this environment does not run containerlab or host a Docker socket, execution steps below illustrate local workstation commands.


To launch network-xray alongside a running Containerlab topology, execute the official Docker container inside your lab directory.
docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$(pwd)":/lab:ro -p 127.0.0.1:8600:8600 ghcr.io/rclab-dev/network-xray:1 --topo /lab/topology.clab.yml






Note



Security note from upstream: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock gives the container root-equivalent privileges on the host system. network-xray requires read access to execute docker exec commands into running lab nodes. Run network-xray only on isolated development workstations or dedicated lab machines.



Image Pinning and Security Digest
In production automation or stable testing environments, pin the container image using its exact SHA256 digest rather than a floating tag like :1. Refer to the upstream release page to obtain the exact digest string:
docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$(pwd)":/lab:ro -p 127.0.0.1:8600:8600 ghcr.io/rclab-dev/network-xray@sha256:e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855 --topo /lab/topology.clab.yml
Once launched, navigate to http://127.0.0.1:8600/ in a browser to interact with the topology graph and route decision panels.

title: network-xray: see why BGP picked that path in containerlab
text:
Integration with Netlab
Netlab allows declarative lab deployment across multiple virtualization drivers. network-xray can be integrated directly into Netlab configurations using standard tool definitions.
To enable network-xray within Netlab, declare the tool inside your topology file (topology.yml) and reference the extra defaults loader provided by the tool package:

---
provider: clab
defaults.device: frr
defaults.sources.extra:
  - docker/netlab-defaults.yml

module: [ bgp, ospf ]

nodes:
  r1:
    bgp.as: 65001
  r2:
    bgp.as: 65002
  r3:
    bgp.as: 65003

links:
  - r1:
    r2:
  - r1:
    r3:

tools:
  network_xray:
When you start the lab environment via netlab up, Netlab parses the network_xray tool declaration, loads the configuration from docker/netlab-defaults.yml, and automatically starts the visualizer container attached to the lab topology.

title: network-xray: see why BGP picked that path in containerlab
section: Example Scenario: Live BGP Best-Path Decision Tracking
text:
Example Scenario: Live BGP Best-Path Decision Tracking
Consider a standard dual-homed topology where router r1 receives updates for prefix 8.8.8.0/24 from two separate upstream peers: r2 (via Local Preference 100) and r3 (via Local Preference 100 default).

Diagnostic Script for State Verification
To verify that FRR state changes dynamically when attributes are altered, the following script modifies Local Preference on r1 for updates arriving from r3, causing the best path selection to change without tearing down the underlying session.

import subprocess
import time


def exec_vtysh(node: str, command: str) -> str:
    """Execute a vtysh command inside a container host."""
    cmd = ["docker", "exec", node, "vtysh", "-c", command]
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    return result.stdout


def main():
    node = "clab-bgp-demo-r1"

    print("Checking initial BGP route table for 8.8.8.0/24...")
    output_before = exec_vtysh(node, "show ip bgp 8.8.8.0/24")
    print(output_before)

    print("Updating Local Preference for peer r3 (10.0.13.3) to 150...")
    config_cmds = (
        "configure terminal\n"
        "route-map SET_LP_150 permit 10\n"
        " set local-preference 150\n"
        "exit\n"
        "router bgp 65001\n"
        " neighbor 10.0.13.3 route-map SET_LP_150 in\n"
        "end\n"
        "clear ip bgp 10.0.13.3 soft in\n"
    )
    exec_vtysh(node, config_cmds)

    time.sleep(2)

    print("Checking updated BGP route table for 8.8.8.0/24...")
    output_after = exec_vtysh(node, "show ip bgp 8.8.8.0/24")
    print(output_after)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Run the script to execute the Local Preference change inside the lab node:
The following command runs the path modification test script:
<<OUTPUT:run1>>


Visualizing the Decision in network-xray
After changing the configuration: 1. Open the network-xray interface at http://localhost:8600/. 2. Click on router node r1 to view its routing state. 3. In the BGP inspection table, observe candidate entries for 8.8.8.0/24. 4. Check the Best-Path Decision panel. The UI highlights that the winner candidate changed from via r2 (LocPref 100) to via r3 (LocPref 150) due to Local Preference evaluation, reflecting FRR’s re-calculated state without requiring a full container restart.

title: network-xray: see why BGP picked that path in containerlab
text:
Pitfalls








Mistake
Consequence
Remedy




Forgetting to mount /var/run/docker.sock
network-xray cannot query container details or execute show commands
Always include -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock in the docker run command


Specifying incorrect relative path to --topo file
Container fails to load topology map
Mount the current directory using -v "$(pwd)":/lab:ro and provide --topo /lab/<filename>.clab.yml


Running on public or un-sanitised host interfaces
Exposing Docker host control socket to host networks
Bind published port strictly to localhost using -p 127.0.0.1:8600:8600


Using floating latest image tags in persistent automation
Unintended upstream container version drift
Pin specific digest hashes using ghcr.io/rclab-dev/network-xray@sha256:<digest>

network-xray offers live, read-only visualization of BGP path selection and OSPF neighbor states in Containerlab and Netlab environments.
It parses diagnostic output from FRR, Nokia SR Linux, and Cisco IOL without requiring agent installation inside router nodes.

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
text: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
text:
Learning goals

Ask ss a precise question (state, port, process, timer) instead of dumping every socket on the host.
Read a TCP ss -ti line far enough to see the congestion control, RTT and window, and know what it cannot tell you.
Know when to move from sockets to packets (tcpdump) and from one hop to a path (mtr), and what each tool needs on the wire.

Version note: the ss lab ran on 2026-11-12 on Linux 6.12.94+ with iproute2 6.15.0 and Python 3. A process bound a TCP listener on 127.0.0.1:47931, accepted one connection from itself, and bound a UDP socket on 127.0.0.1:47932. The ss listings below are pasted verbatim from that process. tcpdump and mtr were not installed and were not run. Their flags and output shape are taken from the tcpdump(1) and mtr(8) manuals and should be verified on a lab host that has them.

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
text:
Three questions, three tools








Question
Tool
Looks at




What is listening, what is established, which process, which TCP counters?
ss
Kernel socket tables


What actually went on the wire, with headers and timing?
tcpdump / tshark
Packets on an interface or a namespace


Where on the path does loss or delay show up?
mtr
A series of probes, hop by hop



ss is the one you can run first, usually without root, and the one this chapter can demonstrate here. It replaced netstat on modern Linux (ss is from iproute2; this host reports ss utility, iproute2-6.15.0). The ICMP chapter covers ping and the idea of path diagnostics; this chapter is the socket and capture counterpart.

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
text:
Ask ss a narrow question
ss filter syntax is a small language: sport, dport, src, dst, state, and boolean and / or. Add -t / -u / -x for TCP, UDP, Unix; -l for listening; -n to skip service-name lookups; -p for the process (often needs enough permission to read /proc); -i for TCP internal info; -s for a summary.
The lab process (Python, pid 2740604) listened on 47931, had one established connection, and a UDP socket on 47932. First, the listener:
# ss -tlnp sport = 47931
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:PortProcess
LISTEN 0      1          127.0.0.1:47931      0.0.0.0:*    users:(("python3",pid=2740604,fd=5))
Recv-Q on a listener is the accept queue (completed connections not yet accepted), not unread application data. Send-Q on a listener is the backlog the process passed to listen() — here 1, because the lab called s.listen(1). A production SYNflood chapter will use these two columns hard; here they just mean “this is a listener, and its backlog is tiny.”
Both ends of the accepted connection, same pid, ephemeral port 47202 picked by the kernel:
# ss -tnp dport = 47931 or sport = 47931
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:47931    127.0.0.1:47202 users:(("python3",pid=2740604,fd=7))
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:47202    127.0.0.1:47931 users:(("python3",pid=2740604,fd=6))
ESTAB is the short name for ESTABLISHED. Recv-Q / Send-Q on an established socket are unread and unsent bytes. Both zero: nothing was written after the handshake.
UDP does not have LISTEN. An unbound-to-peer UDP socket is UNCONN:
# ss -ulnp sport = 47932
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:PortProcess
UNCONN 0      0          127.0.0.1:47932      0.0.0.0:*    users:(("python3",pid=2740604,fd=8))

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
text:
Reading ss -ti
Internal TCP info is the reason to keep ss open during a performance drill:
# ss -ti sport = 47931 or dport = 47931
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:47931    127.0.0.1:47202
     cubic wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:0.018/0.009 mss:32768 pmtu:65535 rcvmss:536 advmss:65483 cwnd:10 segs_in:2 send 146Gbps lastsnd:20 lastrcv:20 lastack:20 pacing_rate 291Gbps delivered:1 app_limited rcv_space:65483 rcv_ssthresh:65483 minrtt:0.018 snd_wnd:65536 rcv_wnd:65483
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:47202    127.0.0.1:47931
     cubic wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:0.026/0.013 mss:32741 pmtu:65535 rcvmss:536 advmss:65483 cwnd:10 bytes_acked:1 segs_out:2 segs_in:1 send 101Gbps lastsnd:20 lastrcv:20 lastack:20 pacing_rate 201Gbps delivered:1 app_limited rcv_space:65495 rcv_ssthresh:65495 minrtt:0.026 snd_wnd:65483 rcv_wnd:65536
What to trust on this listing, and what not to:

cubic is the congestion-control module. This host’s default is CUBIC. A BBR flow would say bbr (or bbr1 / bbr3 depending on the kernel).
rtt:0.018/0.009 is smoothed RTT and RTT variance, in milliseconds. A localhost handshake really is this fast. On a WAN path you should see tens or hundreds of milliseconds, not “146Gbps” of implied send rate.
cwnd:10 is the congestion window in segments. app_limited means the application has not offered enough data to fill the window — so the huge send / pacing_rate figures are arithmetic on a nearly idle loopback flow, not a benchmark. Do not quote them.
wscale:7,7 is window scaling in each direction. pmtu:65535 is loopback. A real path will show 1500 or whatever the tunnel allows.
rto:204 is the retransmission timeout in milliseconds. On a lossy path this is the number you watch rise.

Useful one-liners for later labs (not captured here):
ss -tan state syn-recv
ss -tan state time-wait
ss -ti dst 192.0.2.1
ss -tnp dport = :443
ss -s
ss -s prints host-wide counters (TCP established, time-wait, and so on). It is a snapshot of the whole machine, so this chapter does not paste one: the writing host has many unrelated sockets. Use it to watch TIME-WAIT accumulate during a load test, not as evidence about a single listener.

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
section: tcpdump: when the socket table is not enough (not run)
text:
tcpdump: when the socket table is not enough (not run)
ss will not show a packet that was dropped before a socket existed, a wrong VLAN tag, or the difference between a SYN and a SYN-ACK. That is tcpdump.
# documented usage — tcpdump was not installed here, not run
tcpdump -ni eth1 -s 0 'tcp port 47931'
tcpdump -ni eth1 -s 0 -w capture.pcap 'host 10.0.0.2 and icmp'
tcpdump -n -r capture.pcap 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'
Flags worth making boring and habitual:

-n — no DNS. Captures should not wait on a resolver, and should not leak names into a file you might share.
-i — pick the interface (or any). In a netns or a Containerlab node, that is the veth or eth1, not the host’s uplink.
-s 0 (or a snaplen large enough for the headers you care about) — do not truncate before the TCP options.
-w — write a pcap, read later with tcpdump -r or Wireshark. Do not try to debug a one-shot flood from a scrolling terminal only.
A BPF filter (tcp port 80, host, net, icmp, vlan 100) keeps the file small. Filter as tightly as you can without hiding the failure.

Root or CAP_NET_RAW is required for most live captures. In Containerlab, run tcpdump inside the node or on the host veth that represents the link; capturing on the wrong namespace is the usual empty-file bug. Rotate or delete pcaps that may contain payload from even a lab — payloads are still data.
For IS-IS, remember the packets are not IP: a filter like isis or ether proto 0x8870 (depending on encapsulation) is the starting point, not ip. For VXLAN, capture the outer UDP 4789 and, if you need the inner headers, a tool that can decap, or a capture point inside the overlay.

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
section: mtr: a path, not a hop (not run)
text:
mtr: a path, not a hop (not run)
ping asks one destination. traceroute asks each hop once (or a few times). mtr keeps probing and refreshes a table of loss and RTT per hop.
# documented usage — mtr was not installed here, not run
mtr -n 192.0.2.1
mtr -n -r -c 50 192.0.2.1
mtr -n -u -P 443 192.0.2.1
-n again skips DNS. -r -c 50 is report mode: 50 cycles, then a static table you can paste into a journal. Default probes are ICMP; -u / -T and -P change the probe to UDP or TCP, which is what you want when ICMP is policed but port 443 is not.
How to read a hop that shows loss: the hop may be rate-limiting ICMP, or it may be genuinely dropping traffic. If hop 5 shows 40 % loss and hop 6 through the destination show 0 %, the path is probably fine and hop 5 is just rude to probes. If loss appears at hop 5 and stays through the destination, the problem is at or after hop 5. Always read the last hop and the destination together.
mtr needs permission to open raw sockets for ICMP; TCP/UDP modes have their own constraints. It is a path tool, not a socket tool: it will not tell you that ss is in SYN-RECV. Use both.

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
text:
A working order

Can I see a socket? ss -tlnp / ss -tnp for the port.
Is the state the one I predicted (LISTEN, ESTAB, SYN-RECV, TIME-WAIT)?
If it is established but slow, ss -ti for RTT, cwnd, app_limited, retransmissions.
If there is no socket, or the handshake never completes, tcpdump on the right interface and namespace.
If this host is fine and the far end is not, mtr -n to the destination, and do not over-interpret a single ICMP-lossy hop.

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
text:
Common mistakes

Running ss -tulpna on a busy host and trying to read it like a story. Filter.
Treating loopback send 146Gbps as a capacity measurement.
Capturing on the host when the packet only exists in a netns, or vice versa.
Forgetting -n and stalling on DNS, or writing names into a pcap you later share.
Declaring “the network is lossy” from an mtr hop that does not propagate loss to the destination.
Using tcpdump without a filter on a high-rate link and dropping packets in the capture itself (the tool will tell you how many it dropped — believe it).

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
text:
Boring rule
Start with ss and a filter. Move to packets only when the socket table cannot explain the failure. Move to mtr only when the failure is on the path, not on this host. Paste output that you actually captured, with the command that produced it.

title: Seeing Packets and Sockets: ss, tcpdump and mtr
text:
Try this

Repeat the Python listener lab, then ss -tlnp sport = <port> before and after accept(). Watch Recv-Q on the listener if you connect twice with listen(1) and do not accept the second client.
Send a few megabytes on the connection and re-run ss -ti. Confirm app_limited disappears and bytes_acked moves.
On a host with tcpdump, capture the handshake of that lab (tcp port <port>) and match SYNs to the ss state transitions.
Run mtr -n -r -c 50 to a well-known name and to a lab default gateway. Practise reading a hop that shows isolated loss.
In a Containerlab triangle, shut a data-plane link, then use ss on an FRR node (vtysh neighbors, plus ss -tlnp for BGP TCP 179) and tcpdump on the veth to see which tool answered first.

title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
text:
Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
A packet that leaves a client and never reaches the application on the other side died somewhere. tcpdump can show you where it was last seen, but it cannot tell you why the kernel threw it away, and it shows nothing at all for packets that never made it to the capture point. The kernel, on the other hand, keeps score: almost every drop path in Linux increments a counter, and since Linux 5.17 most of them also attach a drop reason to the freed packet. The trouble is that the counters are spread across half a dozen files, some are per network namespace and some are kernel-wide, and a few drop paths count nothing at all.
This chapter builds a map. You will reproduce nine distinct ways to lose a packet on a three-namespace Linux path, watch exactly which counter moves for each, and end up with a small tool, netdelta.py, that snapshots every relevant counter around a command and prints only what changed. The last part shows where the counters stop and drop reasons take over.

title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
text:
Learning goals

Know which file or command holds each class of Linux drop counter: SNMP and netstat MIBs (nstat), per-device statistics (ip -s link), per-CPU backlog statistics (/proc/net/softnet_stat), routing-cache statistics and neighbour-table statistics.
Tell per-namespace counters from kernel-wide ones, and know which ones silently include other traffic on the host.
Reproduce and recognise the counter signature of the common drops: closed UDP port, full socket buffer, full accept queue, TTL expiry, missing route, disabled forwarding, reverse-path filtering, failed neighbour resolution, blackhole and prohibit routes.
Explain why some ICMP errors never get sent even though the drop was counted, and which two rate limiters are responsible.
Map each drop to its kernel drop reason (enum skb_drop_reason) and know how to read drop reasons with perf, bpftrace or dropwatch on a host where you have root.
Use a before/after counter diff as the first step of any “packets are disappearing” investigation.

title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
text:
Version note
Every listing in the lab ran on this box as an unprivileged user: Linux 6.12.94, iproute2 6.15.0 (ip, nstat), Python 3.13.5 standard library only. The topology lives inside unshare -urnm (new user, network and mount namespaces) with three named network namespaces joined by veth pairs, so no sudo and no installs were needed and the host’s own networking was never touched. All outputs are pasted unedited from those runs.
Kernel behaviour quoted in this chapter was checked against the Linux v6.12 source: net/ipv4/route.c (ip_error()), net/ipv4/ip_forward.c, net/ipv4/ip_input.c, net/ipv4/udp.c, net/core/neighbour.c, net/core/net-procfs.c and include/net/dropreason-core.h.
Not run here: anything that reads drop reasons (perf, bpftrace, dropwatch, pwru), because attaching to the skb:kfree_skb tracepoint needs root or CAP_SYS_ADMIN/CAP_BPF, and ethtool -S, because veth devices expose few driver statistics and ethtool is not installed. Those commands are shown from their documentation and marked.

title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
section: The five places Linux keeps score
text:
The five places Linux keeps score
Before reproducing anything, it helps to know where to look. Linux exposes drop accounting in five layers, and each answers a different question.









Source
Scope
Answers
Read with




SNMP MIBs: /proc/net/snmp, /proc/net/snmp6
per network namespace
IP/ICMP/UDP/TCP drops defined by the IETF MIBs (IpInHdrErrors, UdpNoPorts, …)
nstat, netstat -s


Linux MIBs: /proc/net/netstat (TcpExt, IpExt)
per network namespace
Linux-specific events: listen overflows, reverse-path filter, no-route on input
nstat


Device statistics
per device
drops and errors at the interface: queue full, peer down, driver errors
ip -s -s link, ethtool -S


/proc/net/softnet_stat
per CPU, kernel-wide
the per-CPU input backlog: overflow drops, NAPI budget exhaustion
cat, a small decoder


/proc/net/stat/rt_cache, neighbour-table stats
kernel-wide
input packets with no route, martian sources and destinations, ARP failures
cat, ip -s ntable



nstat deserves a word because it is the one you will use most. It reads the three MIB files and keeps a history file so that, by default, each invocation prints the change since the last one. For scripting you usually want the opposite: -a (absolute values), -z (include zero counters), and -s (do not update the history file, so you do not disturb anyone else’s deltas). nstat -saz --json gives you every counter in the current network namespace as JSON. Counter names are the MIB table name glued to the field name, which is why the reverse-path filter counter is called TcpExtIPReversePathFilter even though it has nothing to do with TCP: it lives in the TcpExt table of /proc/net/netstat.
The scope column is the trap. MIB counters are per network namespace, so in a container or a lab namespace they describe only that namespace’s traffic. Softnet, routing-cache and neighbour-table statistics are kernel-wide: read from inside any namespace, they include every packet on the machine. On a busy host a kernel-wide counter moving by three tells you nothing unless you control the traffic.

title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
text:
The lab
The topology is a client c, a router r and a server s on two point-to-point veth links:
   c (10.0.1.2) ---- c0 | ra (10.0.1.1)  r  (10.0.2.1) rb | s0 ---- (10.0.2.2) s
                         ip_forward=1, default routes on c and s point at r
Four tiny helpers generate traffic. udpsend.py fires datagrams and never reads; slowsink.py binds a UDP socket with a 2 KiB receive buffer and never reads it; fulllisten.py listens with a backlog of 1 and never accepts; connectmany.py opens several non-blocking connects at once.


udpsend.py

# udpsend.py HOST PORT COUNT [TTL]: fire COUNT small UDP datagrams, never read anything back
import socket, sys
host, port, n = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3])
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
if len(sys.argv) > 4:
    s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_IP, socket.IP_TTL, int(sys.argv[4]))
for i in range(n):
    try:
        s.sendto(b"x" * 64, (host, port))
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"   sendto #{i}: {e.strerror}")
        break



slowsink.py

# slowsink.py HOST PORT: bind a UDP socket with a tiny receive buffer and never read it
import socket, sys, time
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_RCVBUF, 2048)
s.bind((sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])))
time.sleep(30)



fulllisten.py

# fulllisten.py HOST PORT: listen with backlog 1 and never call accept()
import socket, sys, time
s = socket.socket()
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind((sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])))
s.listen(1)
time.sleep(30)



connectmany.py

# connectmany.py HOST PORT N: open N non-blocking connects and wait 3 s
import socket, sys, time
socks = []
for _ in range(int(sys.argv[3])):
    c = socket.socket(); c.setblocking(False)
    c.connect_ex((sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]))); socks.append(c)
time.sleep(3)

The driver script builds the namespaces and runs nine scenarios, each wrapped in netdelta.py with the namespaces that matter for it:


lab.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -urnm sh lab.sh   (user + net + mount namespaces, no sudo)
H=$(pwd); D="python3 $H/netdelta.py"
mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
for ns in c r s; do ip netns add $ns; ip -n $ns link set lo up; done
ip link add c0 type veth peer name ra; ip link set c0 netns c; ip link set ra netns r
ip link add rb type veth peer name s0; ip link set rb netns r; ip link set s0 netns s
ip -n c addr add 10.0.1.2/24 dev c0; ip -n r addr add 10.0.1.1/24 dev ra
ip -n r addr add 10.0.2.1/24 dev rb; ip -n s addr add 10.0.2.2/24 dev s0
for d in c:c0 r:ra r:rb s:s0; do ip -n ${d%:*} link set ${d#*:} up; done
ip netns exec r sh -c 'echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward'
ip -n c route add default via 10.0.1.1; ip -n s route add default via 10.0.2.1
ping() { ip netns exec c python3 $H/udpsend.py "$@"; }
sleep 1

echo "== 1. UDP to a port nobody listens on (c -> s:9999)"
$D --ns c --ns s -- ip netns exec c python3 $H/udpsend.py 10.0.2.2 9999 5

echo "== 2. UDP to a socket that never reads (SO_RCVBUF 2048)"
ip netns exec s python3 $H/slowsink.py 10.0.2.2 9000 & P=$!; sleep 0.5
$D --ns s -- ip netns exec c python3 $H/udpsend.py 10.0.2.2 9000 200
kill $P

echo "== 3. TCP listener with backlog 1 that never accepts"
ip netns exec s python3 $H/fulllisten.py 10.0.2.2 8000 & P=$!; sleep 0.5
$D --ns s -- ip netns exec c python3 $H/connectmany.py 10.0.2.2 8000 8
kill $P

echo "== 4. TTL runs out on the router (IP TTL 1)"
$D --ns r --ns c -- ip netns exec c python3 $H/udpsend.py 10.0.2.2 9999 3 1

echo "== 5. router has no route for the destination"
$D --ns r -- ip netns exec c python3 $H/udpsend.py 172.16.9.9 9999 3

echo "   same three packets after a 6 s pause (route error tokens refilled):"
sleep 6
$D --ns r -- ip netns exec c python3 $H/udpsend.py 172.16.9.9 9999 3

echo "== 6. forwarding switched off on the router"
ip netns exec r sh -c 'echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/forwarding'
$D --ns r -- ip netns exec c python3 $H/udpsend.py 10.0.2.2 9999 3
ip netns exec r sh -c 'echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/forwarding'

echo "== 7. strict rp_filter on r: a source r would not route back out of ra"
ip netns exec r sh -c 'echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/rp_filter; echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/ra/rp_filter'
ip -n c addr add 10.0.2.77/32 dev c0
$D --ns r -- ip netns exec c sh -c "python3 -c \"
import socket; s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.bind(('10.0.2.77',0))
[s.sendto(b'x'*64,('10.0.2.2',9999)) for _ in range(4)]\""
echo "   same packets with rp_filter=2 (loose) on ra:"
ip netns exec r sh -c 'echo 2 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/rp_filter; echo 2 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/ra/rp_filter'
$D --ns r --ns s -- ip netns exec c sh -c "python3 -c \"
import socket; s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.bind(('10.0.2.77',0))
[s.sendto(b'x'*64,('10.0.2.2',9999)) for _ in range(4)]\""
ip -n c addr del 10.0.2.77/32 dev c0

echo "== 8. the far end of a veth is down"
ip -n s link set s0 down
$D --ns r -- ip netns exec c sh -c "python3 $H/udpsend.py 10.0.2.2 9999 3; sleep 4"
ip -n s link set s0 up

echo "== 9. blackhole and prohibit routes on r"
sleep 6
ip -n r route add blackhole 10.0.2.0/25
$D --ns r --ns c -- ip netns exec c python3 $H/udpsend.py 10.0.2.2 9999 3
ip -n r route del blackhole 10.0.2.0/25
ip -n r route add prohibit 10.0.2.0/25; sleep 6
$D --ns r --ns c -- ip netns exec c python3 $H/udpsend.py 10.0.2.2 9999 3
ip -n r route del prohibit 10.0.2.0/25

Run it from the directory holding the files:
unshare -urnm sh lab.sh
The output follows, scenario by scenario.

1. Nobody is listening
== 1. UDP to a port nobody listens on (c -> s:9999)
   [c] IcmpInDestUnreachs                 +5
   [s] IcmpOutDestUnreachs                +5
   [s] UdpNoPorts                         +5
The simplest drop has a complete paper trail on both ends. The server counted UdpNoPorts (the IETF name for “datagram arrived for a port with no socket”) and sent an ICMP port unreachable for each, IcmpOutDestUnreachs +5; the client counted the five ICMP errors arriving. In the kernel this is __udp4_lib_rcv() setting drop reason SKB_DROP_REASON_NO_SOCKET. If you see UdpNoPorts climbing on a DNS server, something is querying a port your daemon is not bound to, often after a restart or an address change.


2. A socket that does not keep up
== 2. UDP to a socket that never reads (SO_RCVBUF 2048)
   [s] UdpInErrors                        +195
   [s] UdpRcvbufErrors                    +195
This time the port is open but the application never reads, and its receive buffer was set to 2048 bytes (the kernel doubles SO_RCVBUF for bookkeeping and accounts the full skb truesize, so only a handful of small datagrams fit). Of 200 datagrams, 195 were dropped and counted twice: UdpRcvbufErrors (the specific reason) and UdpInErrors (the MIB total that includes it). No ICMP is sent, because from the network’s point of view the datagram was delivered. Drop reason: SKB_DROP_REASON_SOCKET_RCVBUFF. On a real server this is the signature of a slow consumer or a receive buffer left at the default for a bursty protocol (syslog, DNS, telemetry).


3. A full accept queue
== 3. TCP listener with backlog 1 that never accepts
   [s] TcpExtListenDrops                  +18
   [s] TcpExtListenOverflows              +18
The listener has a backlog of 1 and never calls accept(), so after the first completed connection or two the accept queue is full and further handshakes are dropped. TcpExtListenOverflows counts “the accept queue was full”; TcpExtListenDrops counts all drops at the listen stage and is always at least as large. Eight connects produced 18 drops because TCP clients retransmit their SYN (and the server may retransmit SYN-ACKs) while the queue stays full. Every retransmission is another drop. In production, both counters rising together is the classic sign of an application that cannot accept fast enough, or a backlog capped by net.core.somaxconn.


4. TTL runs out on the router
== 4. TTL runs out on the router (IP TTL 1)
   [r] IcmpOutTimeExcds                   +3
   [r] IpInHdrErrors                      +3
   [c] IcmpInTimeExcds                    +3
With IP TTL 1 the router must discard the packet instead of forwarding it. ip_forward() increments IpInHdrErrors (TTL expiry is classed as a header error by the MIB), sends ICMP time exceeded (IcmpOutTimeExcds), and frees the packet with reason SKB_DROP_REASON_IP_INHDR. This is exactly the mechanism traceroute uses. Seeing it unexpectedly in production usually means a routing loop: packets bounce until their TTL is gone, and every router in the loop counts IpInHdrErrors.


5. No route on the router, and the two ICMP rate limiters
== 5. router has no route for the destination
   [r] IcmpOutDestUnreachs                +1
   [r] IcmpOutRateLimitHost               +1
   [r] IpExtInNoRoutes                    +3
   [kernel-wide] rt_cache.in_no_route         +3
   same three packets after a 6 s pause (route error tokens refilled):
   [r] IcmpOutDestUnreachs                +2
   [r] IcmpOutRateLimitHost               +1
   [r] IpExtInNoRoutes                    +3
   [kernel-wide] rt_cache.in_no_route         +3
The client’s default route takes packets for 172.16.9.9 to r, which has no route for them. Three counters agree that three packets died: IpExtInNoRoutes +3 in the router’s namespace and the kernel-wide rt_cache.in_no_route +3. But only one ICMP net unreachable left the router, with one more counted as suppressed in IcmpOutRateLimitHost. The third packet produced no ICMP and no counter at all.
Two independent limiters are at work:

ip_error() in net/ipv4/route.c, which handles every packet that hit an unreachable route, keeps a token bucket per source host. Its parameters are net.ipv4.route.error_cost (one second’s worth of tokens per ICMP) and net.ipv4.route.error_burst (five seconds’ worth). These two sysctls exist only in the initial network namespace, and a suppression here increments nothing.
The general ICMP limiter, net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit (1000 ms by default, per namespace) applied to the message types in net.ipv4.icmp_ratemask (6168, which includes destination unreachable and time exceeded). Suppressions here are counted in IcmpOutRateLimitHost (and IcmpOutRateLimitGlobal for the global icmp_msgs_per_sec limit).

The second burst, sent after a six-second pause that refilled the route-error bucket, sent two ICMP errors and rate-limited one, and all three packets are now accounted for. The lesson: a missing ICMP error is not evidence that a router did not drop your packet, and “ping works but my burst of probes gets only one unreachable back” is normal behaviour.


6. Forwarding switched off
== 6. forwarding switched off on the router
   [r] IpInAddrErrors                     +3
   [kernel-wide] rt_cache.in_no_route         +3
Turn off forwarding on r and packets for a non-local destination are dropped with IpInAddrErrors (“address errors”: the packet was not for us and we do not forward). No ICMP is sent at all. In ip_error() the forwarding check comes first: with forwarding off, an EHOSTUNREACH result is counted as IPSTATS_MIB_INADDRERRORS with reason SKB_DROP_REASON_IP_INADDRERRORS, and the function returns without touching ICMP. The kernel-wide in_no_route moves too, because the input route lookup failed. On a Linux router that “suddenly stopped routing” after a configuration management run or a container runtime upgrade, IpInAddrErrors climbing is the quickest confirmation that ip_forward was reset.


7. Reverse-path filtering, strict versus loose
== 7. strict rp_filter on r: a source r would not route back out of ra
   [r] TcpExtIPReversePathFilter          +4
   [kernel-wide] rt_cache.in_martian_src      +4
   same packets with rp_filter=2 (loose) on ra:
   [s] IcmpOutDestUnreachs                +4
   [s] UdpNoPorts                         +4
The client sends from 10.0.2.77, an address that r would route out of rb, not back out of ra where the packet arrived. With strict reverse-path filtering (rp_filter=1) the router asks “would I send a reply to this source out of the interface it came in on?”, gets “no”, and drops the packet. The counter is TcpExtIPReversePathFilter (LINUX_MIB_IPRPFILTER, set in ip_input.c when route validation returns -EXDEV), the drop reason is SKB_DROP_REASON_IP_RPFILTER, and the kernel-wide in_martian_src moves as well. No ICMP is sent.
With loose mode (rp_filter=2) the question becomes “is this source reachable via any interface?”, the answer is yes, and the packets are forwarded: the server’s UdpNoPorts +4 shows they arrived. Two operational notes. First, the effective value on an interface is the maximum of net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and the interface’s own value, which is why the lab sets both. Second, strict mode breaks legitimate asymmetric routing (multihomed hosts, ECMP with different return paths, policy routing), and the only symptom is this counter. If an asymmetric flow dies silently on a Linux box, read TcpExtIPReversePathFilter first.


8. The next hop is gone
== 8. the far end of a veth is down
   [r] IcmpOutDestUnreachs                +3
   [r] rb.tx_dropped                      +4
   [kernel-wide] arp_cache.res_failed         +1
Here the far end of rb is administratively down and the router has no neighbour entry for 10.0.2.2. The forwarded packets wait in the neighbour entry’s queue while ARP solicitations are attempted; the solicitations go nowhere (rb.tx_dropped +4 on the device with a dead peer), resolution fails (arp_cache.res_failed +1, reason SKB_DROP_REASON_NEIGH_FAILED for the queued packets), and the router sends ICMP host unreachable back to the client, IcmpOutDestUnreachs +3.
Notice what is not in the filtered output. A separate --all run of the same scenario showed IpForwDatagrams +3: the MIB counted all three packets as forwarded, because the counter is incremented when a packet is handed to the output path, before neighbour resolution. “Forwarded” in IpForwDatagrams means “routed”, not “transmitted”. The scenario also needed sleep 4 inside the measured command, because ARP gives up only after mcast_solicit probes spaced retrans_time (one second by default) apart; a snapshot taken immediately after sending would miss the failure entirely.


9. Blackhole and prohibit routes
== 9. blackhole and prohibit routes on r
   [kernel-wide] rt_cache.in_no_route         +3
   [r] IcmpOutDestUnreachs                +2
   [r] IcmpOutRateLimitHost               +1
   [c] IcmpInDestUnreachs                 +2
   [kernel-wide] rt_cache.in_no_route         +3
This is the scenario that justifies the kernel-wide columns in the tool. A blackhole route drops matching packets without an ICMP error, which is the point of it, but it also drops them without any per-namespace counter. The only trace is rt_cache.in_no_route +3, and that is a kernel-wide counter which on a real router moves for every unroutable packet from every source. In ip_error() the blackhole case is the EINVAL branch: goto out, free the packet with reason NOT_SPECIFIED, count nothing.
A prohibit route is the polite version. It sends ICMP destination unreachable with code 13 (communication administratively prohibited), so the client saw IcmpInDestUnreachs +2, but again there is no SNMP drop counter for the packets themselves, only the ICMP that announced them, with one ICMP suppressed by the host rate limiter. An unreachable route behaves the same way with code 1 (host unreachable). If you use blackhole routes for DDoS mitigation or null-routing, count the drops somewhere else: an nftables counter on a matching rule, the drop-reason tracepoint, or flow export.

title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
text:
Reading the per-CPU backlog: softnet_stat
The last kernel-wide source sits below IP. When a NIC driver receives packets it either processes them in NAPI context or, for RPS, loopback and veth traffic, queues them on a per-CPU input backlog. /proc/net/softnet_stat has one line per online CPU, all hexadecimal. In Linux 6.12 (softnet_seq_show() in net/core/net-procfs.c) the columns are: packets processed, packets dropped, time squeeze, five zero columns (formerly fastroute), a zero column (formerly cpu_collision), packets received via RPS, flow-limit count, current backlog length, the CPU index, and the input and process queue lengths separately. The column count changed over the years, so decode it from the source of the kernel you run rather than from a blog post.


softnet.py

# softnet.py: decode /proc/net/softnet_stat (column layout from net/core/net-procfs.c, Linux 6.12)
cols = {0: "processed", 1: "dropped", 2: "time_squeeze", 9: "received_rps",
        10: "flow_limit", 11: "backlog", 12: "cpu"}
print(f"{'cpu':>4} {'processed':>10} {'dropped':>8} {'squeeze':>8} {'rps':>5} {'flow_lim':>8} {'backlog':>8}")
for row in open("/proc/net/softnet_stat"):
    f = [int(x, 16) for x in row.split()]
    print(f"{f[12]:>4} {f[0]:>10} {f[1]:>8} {f[2]:>8} {f[9]:>5} {f[10]:>8} {f[11]:>8}")
print("netdev_max_backlog =", open("/proc/sys/net/core/netdev_max_backlog").read().strip(),
      "| netdev_budget =", open("/proc/sys/net/core/netdev_budget").read().strip(),
      "| netdev_budget_usecs =", open("/proc/sys/net/core/netdev_budget_usecs").read().strip())

 cpu  processed  dropped  squeeze   rps flow_lim  backlog
   0    3967934        0       22     0        0        0
   1    4202784        0       21     0        0        0
   2    4085750        0       22     0        0        0
   3    4096244        0       22     0        0        0
   4   21389927        0     1429     0        0        0
   5    4088564        0      157     0        0        0
   6    4196121        0       34     0        0        0
   7    4177096        0       22     0        0        0
netdev_max_backlog = 1000 | netdev_budget = 300 | netdev_budget_usecs = 8000
How to read it:

dropped counts packets thrown away because the per-CPU backlog already held net.core.netdev_max_backlog packets (1000 here). Non-zero and growing means one CPU is receiving faster than it can process, typically because all flows hash to one receive queue. Fixes are RSS or RPS spreading, or a larger backlog as a stop-gap. This idle box shows zero everywhere.
time_squeeze counts how often the receive softirq ran out of budget (net.core.netdev_budget packets or netdev_budget_usecs microseconds, 300 and 8000 here) with work still pending. A few, as here, are normal. CPU 4 processed about five times more packets than any other and has by far the most squeezes (1429), which tells you the box’s receive load lands mostly on one CPU. A squeeze is not a drop, but a steadily rising rate means packets wait longer in ring buffers, and if the NIC ring fills, the drops happen in hardware and show up only in ethtool -S as something like rx_missed_errors or rx_fifo_errors.
received_rps and flow_limit stay at zero unless RPS or the flow limiter (net.core.flow_limit_cpu_bitmap) are configured.
