title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
section: When counters are not enough: drop reasons
text:
When counters are not enough: drop reasons
The table shows the limit of counters: some drops count nothing, some count only kernel-wide, and none tell you which packet died. Since Linux 5.17 most kfree_skb() calls in the stack have become kfree_skb_reason(), and the skb:kfree_skb tracepoint carries the reason, the protocol and the code location. On a host where you have root, these are the usual ways to read it (not run here: tracepoints need root or CAP_SYS_ADMIN/CAP_BPF):
# not run here: count drops by reason for 10 seconds (bpftrace)
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:skb:kfree_skb { @[args->reason] = count(); }
                  interval:s:10 { exit(); }'

# not run here: record drops with call stacks, then summarise (perf)
sudo perf record -e skb:kfree_skb -a -g -- sleep 10
sudo perf script | head

# not run here: dropwatch prints drop locations live
sudo dropwatch -l kas
bpftrace prints numeric reasons; map them through the enum in dropreason-core.h for your kernel. perf script prints symbolic names, because the tracepoint’s own format string (include/trace/events/skb.h) decodes the reason with __print_symbolic. pwru (packet, where are you?) goes further and traces one packet through every kernel function with a filter expression, at the cost of an eBPF-capable host. Treat these as the second step: run netdelta.py (or plain nstat) first to learn which class of drop you have, then trace with a filter for that class rather than tracing every freed skb on a busy host. A note on volume: kfree_skb also fires for packets freed for normal reasons on some paths in older kernels, and consume_skb is the “not a drop” counterpart; filter on a non-NOT_SPECIFIED reason to keep the signal.

title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
text:
Production checklist
None of this needs a lab. On a real host, the same investigation looks like this (not run here; these are standard iproute2 and procfs reads):
# not run here: baseline, reproduce, compare (per namespace)
nstat -n                     # reset history so the next call shows deltas
# ... reproduce the problem ...
nstat | grep -Ei 'drop|err|overflow|noroute|noport|filter|ratelimit'

ip -s -s link show dev eth0  # device rx/tx dropped, errors, missed, fifo
ethtool -S eth0 | grep -Ei 'drop|miss|fifo|err'   # driver/NIC counters
cat /proc/net/softnet_stat   # per-CPU backlog drops and squeezes
ip -s ntable show name arp_cache   # res_failed, unresolved_discards, table_fulls
sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter net.ipv4.ip_forward
In a container, run the same commands inside the container’s network namespace (nsenter -t <pid> -n), and remember which counters are kernel-wide. For monitoring, the Prometheus node exporter’s netstat and softnet collectors export exactly these counters; alert on rates of UdpRcvbufErrors, TcpExtListenOverflows, TcpExtIPReversePathFilter and softnet dropped, not on absolute values.

title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
text:
Gotchas

Kernel-wide counters lie in shared environments. softnet_stat, rt_cache and the neighbour-table statistics include every namespace on the host. In a container, a moving in_no_route may be your neighbour’s traffic.
Blackhole drops are invisible to SNMP. The only per-packet evidence of a blackhole route doing its job is the kernel-wide in_no_route counter or the drop-reason tracepoint. Add a counting firewall rule if you need numbers.
Missing ICMP does not mean no drop. ip_error() has its own uncounted per-source token bucket (route.error_cost/error_burst, initial namespace only), and icmp_ratelimit adds a second, counted one. Bursts of probes get one or two errors back.
IpForwDatagrams counts routed, not transmitted. Packets that later die in neighbour resolution or a full qdisc are already counted as forwarded.
The counter name lies about the protocol. TcpExtIPReversePathFilter is an IP counter stored in the TcpExt table. Search by meaning, not by prefix.
rp_filter is the maximum of all and the interface. Setting conf/eth0/rp_filter=0 does nothing while conf/all/rp_filter=1.
Snapshots need to wait for slow drops. Neighbour resolution fails seconds after the packet was sent; TCP retransmits SYNs for over a minute. Measure across the whole failure, not just the send.
/proc/net/stat/arp_cache is missing outside the initial namespace. Scripts that read it break inside containers; use ip -s ntable.
The softnet_stat layout changes between kernels. Columns were added (backlog length, CPU index, queue lengths) and retired columns are kept as zeros. Decode with the source of your running kernel.

title: Where Did the Packet Die? Linux Drop Counters from nstat to Drop Reasons
text:
Exercises

Strict rp_filter on the server side. Leave rp_filter=1 on r and instead give the server a second address in a subnet routed via a different interface. Predict which counter moves on which namespace before you run netdelta.py --ns r --ns s.
Find the receive-buffer knee. Rerun scenario 2 with SO_RCVBUF values of 2048, 8192, 65536 and 212992. Record how many of 200 datagrams survive each time and explain why the numbers are not proportional to the buffer size (hint: skb->truesize).
Make the router talk. In scenario 5, send 10 packets one per 1.1 seconds instead of a burst. How many ICMP errors come back? Then set net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit=0 inside r and repeat the burst. Which limiter is left, and how can you tell?
Count a blackhole properly. Pick a method that counts blackholed packets per prefix without root on the router (for example, a UDP receiver on the far side and a sender that numbers its datagrams), and compare its count with rt_cache.in_no_route while another process generates unrelated unroutable traffic.
Watch the accept queue. During scenario 3, run ip netns exec s ss -ltn in another shell. Compare Recv-Q and Send-Q on the listening socket with the backlog of 1, and relate them to TcpExtListenOverflows.
Read drop reasons for real. On a machine where you have root, run the bpftrace one-liner while repeating scenarios 1, 2, 7 and 9. Confirm the reasons in the map table, and note what blackhole reports.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
When network operators troubleshoot path latency, packet loss, or routing policy across modern IP networks, traceroute is often the first tool they run. However, on networks that employ Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing or Link Aggregation Groups (LAGs), traditional traceroute tools frequently produce misleading or impossible results. Instead of reporting real network paths, standard traceroute often reports non-existent links, missing intermediate routers, false loops, and phantom parallel paths.
These anomalies occur because classic traceroute varies header fields that multi-path load balancers use to assign packets to flow paths. As traceroute increments the IP Time-To-Live (TTL) field to discover successive hops, it simultaneously alters header parameters like source ports, destination ports, or sequence numbers. To a flow-aware load balancer performing 5-tuple hashing, each probe appears as an entirely separate flow and may be dispatched across a different physical path. Consequently, each Hop Count response comes from a different path, rendering the stitched-together sequence of reported hops a synthetic composite that no single packet ever traversed.
Understanding how ECMP load balancing interacts with probe packet structure is essential for modern network operations. By controlling which packet header fields vary and which remain fixed, operators can eliminate multi-path measurement artifacts. This chapter walks through why classic traceroute fails, the Paris traceroute method for flow-consistent path discovery, how Linux routers hash flows, and how to enumerate every path through a load-balanced network. The lab reproduces the anomalies on seven network namespaces without root.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
Learning goals

Explain how classic UDP traceroute increments packet parameters across probe attempts and why this triggers ECMP load-balancing anomalies.
Identify the four classical path measurement anomalies defined by Augustin et al.: false links, missing nodes, false loops, and false diamonds.
Describe how Paris traceroute keeps the hashed header fields constant across TTLs and still tells its probes apart.
Contrast per-packet, per-flow, and per-destination load balancing mechanisms and evaluate their impact on path measurement.
Configure and analyze Linux kernel IPv4 and IPv6 multipath hash policies (fib_multipath_hash_policy, fib_multipath_hash_fields, and fib_multipath_hash_seed).
Evaluate how router ICMP source address selection (icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr) introduces router interface aliasing during path discovery.
Run flow-pinned traces with traceroute, mtr, Paris traceroute, Dublin Traceroute and scamper, and know which flags pin the flow.

text:
Version note
The lab ran on Linux 6.12 with iproute2 6.15.0 and Python 3.13, unprivileged, inside user, network and mount namespaces (unshare -urnm). The tracer uses ordinary UDP sockets and the Linux IP_RECVERR socket option, so it needs no raw sockets. fib_multipath_hash_seed needs Linux 6.11 or later. traceroute, mtr, paris-traceroute, dublin-traceroute and scamper are not installed on the lab host, so their commands below are not run.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
section: Classic UDP traceroute and flow hashing
text:
Classic UDP traceroute and flow hashing
Classic UNIX traceroute—including the default implementation of traceroute(8) on Linux—operates by transmitting a sequence of UDP datagrams toward an unallocated UDP port at the target destination (typically starting at destination port 33434). Discovery proceeds in rounds based on the IP Time-To-Live (TTL) header field:

The probing host sends datagrams with TTL set to 1. The first-hop router decrements the TTL to 0, drops the packet, and returns an ICMP Time Exceeded message (Type 11, Code 0) back to the source.
The host processes the ICMP message, extracts the source IP address of the ICMP payload to identify the first-hop router interface, and records the round-trip time.
The host increments the IP TTL to 2 and repeats the procedure. Intermediate routers return ICMP Time Exceeded messages until a probe reaches the final destination.
Upon reaching the destination host, the packet is received by the network stack. Because no application is listening on UDP port 33434, the destination returns an ICMP Destination Unreachable message (Type 3, Code 3: Port Unreachable), signaling the end of the trace.

Host (Prober)                  Hop 1 Router                   Hop 2 Router                   Destination
  |                                 |                              |                              |
  |-- UDP TTL=1, DPort=33434 ------>|                              |                              |
  |<- ICMP Time Exceeded -----------|                              |                              |
  |                                 |                              |                              |
  |-- UDP TTL=2, DPort=33435 ------------------------------------->|                              |
  |<- ICMP Time Exceeded ------------------------------------------|                              |
  |                                 |                              |                              |
  |-- UDP TTL=3, DPort=33436 ---------------------------------------------------------------------->|
  |<- ICMP Port Unreachable ----------------------------------------------------------------------|
To correlate incoming ICMP responses with outgoing probes, classic traceroute alters packet parameters for every single probe. Standard Linux traceroute(8) increments the UDP destination port number by 1 for each transmitted probe (Port 33434 for TTL 1 Probe 1, 33435 for TTL 1 Probe 2, 33436 for TTL 2 Probe 1, and so forth). ICMP-echo traceroute changes the ICMP sequence number per probe, which also changes the ICMP checksum.

The conflict with ECMP hashing
Modern high-performance routers and switches do not forward packets purely on a per-packet round-robin basis due to out-of-order packet delivery issues, which severely degrade TCP performance. Instead, layer-3 switches and routers implement Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing and Layer-2 Link Aggregation (LAG) using per-flow deterministic hashing.
To route a packet across one of \(N\) parallel equal-cost paths, the router extracts a set of fields from the packet headers—the flow 5-tuple—and computes a hash. The hash is reduced to one of the next hops (modulo, hash-threshold ranges or a resilient bucket table, depending on the implementation):
next hop = select( hash(src addr, dst addr, protocol, src port, dst port, seed), N next hops )
Because classic UDP traceroute increments the destination UDP port (or source port) with every probe, every single probe packet generated by classic traceroute constitutes a unique flow 5-tuple.
(illustrative hash values)
Probe 1 (TTL=1): [10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.6.2, UDP, sport 40000, dport 33434] => hash 0x8A31 => path A
Probe 2 (TTL=2): [10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.6.2, UDP, sport 40000, dport 33435] => hash 0x3F12 => path B
Probe 3 (TTL=3): [10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.6.2, UDP, sport 40000, dport 33436] => hash 0xC194 => path A
When probes pass through an ECMP load balancer, probe 1 (TTL=1) may hash to Path A, probe 2 (TTL=2) may hash to Path B, and probe 3 (TTL=3) may hash back to Path A. The probing host collects responses from router interfaces along disparate physical paths and combines them into a single linear chain.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
Path measurement anomalies
In their landmark IMC 2006 paper “Avoiding traceroute anomalies with Paris traceroute”, Brice Augustin and co-authors named the structural measurement errors that occur when flow-varying traceroute runs over load-balanced topologies.
Actual Topology (Diamond):
         +---> Router B (10.0.1.2) ---> Router D (10.0.3.2) ---+
        /                                                       \
Router A (10.0.0.2)                                            Router E (10.0.4.2)
        \                                                       /
         +---> Router C (10.0.2.2) ----------------------------+
When classic traceroute probes this diamond topology where Router A load-balances traffic across upper and lower paths, four distinct anomalies can manifest depending on how probes hash at Router A.








Anomaly Type
Mechanism
Resulting Output Representation




False Link
TTL k hits one path; TTL k+1 hits a different path.
Reports a direct physical link between two nodes on different parallel paths (e.g., C -> D).


Missing Node
A router on one branch is never hit by the probe whose TTL expires at its distance.
A router that carries traffic never appears in the trace.


False Loop
The TTL k probe reaches router X over a short branch and the TTL k+1 probe reaches X over a longer branch.
X appears twice in a row (or under two aliases), which looks like a forwarding loop.


False Diamond
Several probes per TTL (Linux traceroute sends three by default) land on different branches at TTL k and k+1.
Links drawn between every TTL k router and every TTL k+1 router, a mesh that hides the real adjacencies.




Mechanics of a false link
Consider the diamond topology shown above. The top path through B and D requires 3 hops from A to E (A -> B -> D -> E). The bottom path through C requires 2 hops from A to E (A -> C -> E).
Suppose an operator runs classic traceroute where the probes hash as follows: - The TTL=1 probe expires at A. Response from A. - Probe for TTL=2 (different destination port) hashes to the lower path (A -> C). Response from C. - Probe for TTL=3 (different destination port) hashes to the upper path (A -> B -> D). Response from D. - Probe for TTL=4 hashes to destination T via E. Response from T.
The traceroute output displays: 1. 10.0.0.2 (Router A) 2. 10.0.2.2 (Router C) 3. 10.0.3.2 (Router D) 4. 10.0.6.2 (Target T)
The operator concludes that Router C connects directly to Router D (C -> D). In reality, no physical link or IP adjacency exists between C and D. The link reported by classic traceroute is completely fictional.


Uneven-length diamonds and node repetition
When parallel paths through an ECMP network contain an unequal number of layer-3 hops (an uneven-length diamond), classic traceroute creates additional artifacts.
If a probe with TTL=3 takes the shorter lower path (A -> C -> E), the packet reaches Router E at TTL=3. Router E returns an ICMP Time Exceeded message from its interface 10.0.5.2.
If the subsequent probe with TTL=4 takes the longer upper path (A -> B -> D -> E), the packet reaches Router E at TTL=4. Router E returns an ICMP Time Exceeded message from its interface 10.0.4.2.
The output displays Router E at TTL 3 and Router E again at TTL 4 (under different IP addresses). This makes it appear as if the packet passed through Router E twice or encountered an extra intermediate router, when in fact two different probe flows simply encountered the same router at different hop counts.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
The Paris Traceroute solution
To eliminate flow-hashing anomalies, Paris Traceroute maintains invariant values across all 5-tuple header fields that routers evaluate during ECMP hashing:

Source IP Address (Constant for a host)
Destination IP Address (Constant for the target)
IP Protocol Field (Fixed to UDP, TCP, or ICMP)
Source Port (Fixed per probe flow)
Destination Port (Fixed per probe flow)

By fixing all five fields, every probe packet generated for a given trace yields an identical hash value at every ECMP router along the path. Consequently, all probes within that trace follow an identical physical path, ensuring that responses at TTL 1, TTL 2 and onwards represent a true, contiguous linear route.
Classic Traceroute Probe Stream:
[TTL=1, SPort=40000, DPort=33434] -> Hash 0x1A (Path 1)
[TTL=2, SPort=40000, DPort=33435] -> Hash 0x8B (Path 2)
[TTL=3, SPort=40000, DPort=33436] -> Hash 0x3F (Path 1)

Paris Traceroute Probe Stream (Flow ID 1):
[TTL=1, SPort=40000, DPort=33434, FlowIdentifier=1] -> Hash 0x1A (Path 1)
[TTL=2, SPort=40000, DPort=33434, FlowIdentifier=2] -> Hash 0x1A (Path 1)
[TTL=3, SPort=40000, DPort=33434, FlowIdentifier=3] -> Hash 0x1A (Path 1)

Telling probes apart without changing the flow
If source and destination ports cannot be changed between probes, how does the probing host match returning ICMP Time Exceeded messages to specific probe attempts and TTLs?
When a router drops a packet because its TTL expired, RFC 792 requires the ICMP error to quote the original IP header plus at least the first 8 bytes of its payload (RFC 1812 asks routers to quote as much as fits in 576 bytes). For UDP those 8 bytes are the whole UDP header: ports, length and checksum. Paris traceroute hides its probe identifier in a quoted field that load balancers do not hash.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| IPv4 Header (20 Bytes)                                            |
| Src: 192.168.1.10 | Dst: 10.0.6.2 | Protocol: UDP (17)             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| UDP Header (8 Bytes)                                              |
| Src Port: 40000    | Dst Port: 33434    | Length: 12  | Checksum    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| UDP Payload (4 Bytes)                                             |
| Probe Sequence Number / Magic Identifier                          |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+

UDP Probes (Checksum Manipulation): Paris traceroute fixes both ports and makes the UDP checksum itself the probe identifier: it chooses payload bytes so that the checksum takes the value it wants for each probe. The checksum is quoted in every ICMP error, so the reply can be matched, and load balancers hash on ports, not on the checksum.
IP Identification: The IPv4 Identification field is quoted too and is not part of any common flow hash, so it can also carry a probe number. Some routers rewrite or zero it, so tools treat it as a secondary signal.
ICMP Probes: A load balancer that has no ports to hash for ICMP may hash the first four bytes after the IP header instead: type, code and checksum. Classic ICMP traceroute changes the sequence number, and with it the checksum. Paris traceroute changes the Identifier and Sequence Number together so that the checksum stays the same while the pair still identifies the probe.
TCP Probes: For TCP probes, Paris traceroute keeps the ports constant and puts the probe identifier in the sequence number, which is inside the first 8 quoted bytes and is not hashed.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
Multipath path enumeration (MDA)
While pinning the 5-tuple guarantees that a single trace discovers a valid, non-anomalous path, a single trace only uncovers one of many potential paths through an ECMP network. To map the complete topology, an operator must enumerate all available paths.
Systematically varying the flow identifier (for example, incrementing the source port for each distinct trace) allows a measurement tool to explore different branches of an ECMP diamond.
Flow 1 (SPort 40000): S -> A -> B -> D -> E -> T  (Path 1)
Flow 2 (SPort 40001): S -> A -> C -> E -> T       (Path 2)
Flow 3 (SPort 40002): S -> A -> B -> D -> E -> T  (Path 1)

The Multipath Detection Algorithm (MDA)
Simply sending a random number of flows does not guarantee that all equal-cost paths have been discovered. If a router load-balances traffic across \(k\) outbound links, how many probe flows must be transmitted to guarantee with high statistical confidence that every link has been sampled at least once?
This problem is modeled by the Multipath Detection Algorithm (MDA), formulated by Veitch, Augustin, Friedman, and Teixeira (INFOCOM 2009). MDA applies probability theory (specifically coupon collector problem formulations) to multi-path route tracing.
The stopping rule is the useful part. Suppose a hop has shown k distinct next hops so far. Before concluding that there are only k, MDA asks how many flows it would take to see a (k+1)th next hop with high probability if there really were k+1 equally loaded ones. With k+1 next hops, the chance that n random flows all miss a particular one is (k/(k+1))^n, and the chance that some next hop is missed is at most (k+1)(k/(k+1))^n. MDA keeps sending flows until that bound drops below the failure probability it accepts, alpha:
\[ (k+1)\left(\frac{k}{k+1}\right)^{n_k} \le \alpha \]
The short program mda-table.py in the lab prints n_k for a few values (genuine output):
seen k test k+1  n_k a=0.10  n_k a=0.05  n_k a=0.01
     1        2           5           6           8
     2        3           9          11          15
     3        4          13          16          21
     4        5          18          21          28
     7        8          33          39          51
    15       16          79          90         115
Read the first row as: after one next hop has answered six different flows, you may stop with 95% confidence that there is no second one. The lab sends 16 flows, more than the 11 needed at 95% to rule out a third next hop after seeing two. The published MDA spreads the failure probability across all hops of a trace and so uses somewhat larger numbers; this table shows the shape of the rule, not the exact constants of any tool. Uneven load balancing (weighted ECMP) needs more flows still.
MDA dynamically measures the number of distinct interfaces discovered at hop \(m\), updates its estimate of \(k\), and transmits additional flow-pinned probes until the probability of an undiscovered interface drops below \(\alpha\).


Tooling landscape for flow-consistent tracing
Modern networking toolsets incorporate flow-pinned measurement techniques:

paris-traceroute: the original implementation from the 2006 paper; it also has an exhaustive multipath mode.
scamper: CAIDA’s measurement tool; its tracelb command implements MDA.
Dublin Traceroute: a Paris-style tracer that sends many flows (by default it varies the destination port) and writes the result as JSON that can be drawn as a graph; it also tracks NAT along the path using the IP ID.
Linux traceroute(8): the default method increments the destination port, so it is not flow-stable. -U uses a constant UDP destination port (default 53), -T a constant TCP port (default 80), and --sport=PORT pins the source port (and implies -N 1 -w 5). Combine -U or -T with --sport to pin the whole 5-tuple.
mtr: -u (UDP) or -T (TCP) with -P PORT for the destination port and -L LOCALPORT for the source port pins the flow; with default ICMP mode, check what your version varies before trusting per-hop numbers.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
section: Load balancing modes and Linux kernel hashing
text:
Load balancing modes and Linux kernel hashing
The effectiveness of traceroute flow-pinning depends directly on the load-balancing strategy implemented by intermediate routers.
+---------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Load Balancing Mode | Description & Impact on Tracing                                   |
+---------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Per-Packet          | Packets are distributed round-robin regardless of headers.         |
|                     | Flow pinning CANNOT prevent anomalies; MDA must be used.          |
+---------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Per-Flow (5-Tuple)  | Hash calculated over Src/Dst IP, Protocol, Src/Dst Port.           |
|                     | Standard ECMP mode. Flow pinning fully prevents anomalies.        |
+---------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Per-Destination     | Hash calculated over Destination IP address only.                |
|                     | All probes to a target take the exact same path regardless of L4. |
+---------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------+

Linux fib_multipath_hash_policy
Linux selects the fields its IPv4 ECMP hash uses with net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy (and net.ipv6.fib_multipath_hash_policy for IPv6). The kernel’s ip-sysctl documentation lists the values:

Policy 0 (Layer 3 Hashing): Source and destination addresses only (the default). For IPv6, policy 0 also includes the flow label.

Impact: Source and destination ports are ignored. Classic traceroute (which varies ports) produces consistent results without false links because L4 port changes do not alter the calculated hash.

Policy 1 (Layer 4 Hashing): The 5-tuple: addresses, protocol and ports.

Impact: Standard 5-tuple ECMP. Classic traceroute produces path anomalies. Paris Traceroute flow-pinning is required.

Policy 2 (Layer 3 Inner / Outer Hashing): Layer 3, or the inner Layer 3 header of encapsulated packets when present (useful for GRE and similar tunnels).
Policy 3 (Custom Fields): Custom: the fields come from the fib_multipath_hash_fields bitmask.



Multipath hash seeds and IPv6 flow labels
Linux mixes a per-namespace random key into the hash, so two routers with the same configuration do not make the same choice for the same flow (which would polarise traffic onto the same branches hop after hop). Since Linux 6.11, net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_seed sets that key explicitly. The lab sets it to 42 on A, which is why its output repeats exactly from run to run; without it, which flow takes which branch changes every time the namespace is recreated. A fixed seed is also what you want across a fleet if you need two routers to agree, and what you do not want on two consecutive tiers.

IPv6 Flow Labels and RFC 6438
IPv6 adds the 20-bit flow label. RFC 6437 lets a source put a per-flow value there and RFC 6438 describes using it for ECMP and LAG, so routers can balance without parsing extension headers to reach the ports. Linux’s IPv6 policy 0 hashes addresses plus flow label. A tracer therefore has to keep the flow label constant as well as the ports, and any host that changes its flow label mid-connection (Linux does so on some TCP retransmission timeouts to steer around a failed path) changes path through such networks. traceroute -l sets the flow label explicitly.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
section: Router ICMP response behavior and interfaces
text:
Router ICMP response behavior and interfaces
Understanding traceroute output requires analyzing how intermediate routers construct ICMP error responses.
When a router interface receives a packet whose TTL expires, it generates an ICMP Time Exceeded packet. The source IP address chosen for this ICMP response depends on router kernel configuration and interface architecture.
   from D --- e-d 10.0.4.2 ---+
                              [ E ] --- e-t 10.0.6.1 --- T
   from C --- e-c 10.0.5.2 ---+

icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr
On Linux routers, the sysctl parameter net.ipv4.icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr governs ICMP source IP selection:

icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr = 0 (Default): The source is chosen like any locally generated packet: normally an address of the interface the ICMP error leaves through towards the prober. With asymmetric routing that can be an interface the probe never touched.
icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr = 1: The router answers from an address of the interface the expired packet arrived on, which makes the trace describe the forward path.

In multi-path topologies where a router (such as Router E in our lab) connects to two upstream nodes via different interfaces (10.0.4.2 on interface eth0 toward D, and 10.0.5.2 on interface eth1 toward C), icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr=1 causes Router E to respond as 10.0.5.2 for traffic arriving via C, and as 10.0.4.2 for traffic arriving via D.
This behavior causes a single physical router to appear under different IP addresses (aliases) depending on which ingress link a probe flow traverses.


ICMP rate limiting
Routers rate-limit ICMP generation to protect the control plane. On Linux, net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit (default 1000 ms between bursts per destination, applied to the types in icmp_ratemask, which include Time Exceeded and Destination Unreachable) and the host-wide token bucket icmp_msgs_per_sec (default 1000) both apply. Hardware routers usually generate ICMP in software on a slow path and police it hard. The lab sets icmp_ratelimit=0 and raises icmp_msgs_per_sec so that no probe is lost to rate limiting.
When traceroute sends high-frequency probes, intermediate routers may silently drop TTL-expired probes due to rate-limiting thresholds. This results in asterisks (* * *) at specific intermediate hops.
Rule of thumb: if packet loss appears at an intermediate hop (e.g., Hop 4 shows 20% loss) but does not persist at subsequent hops (Hops 5, 6, and 7 show 0% loss), the observed loss is an artifact of ICMP control-plane rate limiting on Hop 4, NOT real data-plane forwarding loss.


Asymmetric routing and return paths
Traceroute discovers the forward path, but every round-trip time includes the return path of the ICMP error, which each router routes towards the prober independently. If return paths are asymmetric, latency spikes or packet drops reported at a specific hop may reflect congestion on the return path from the router to the probing host, rather than on the forward path to the destination.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
The lab
To explore ECMP load-balancing behavior hands-on, we construct an unprivileged network topology featuring an uneven diamond graph.
                    10.0.1.0/30        10.0.3.0/30        10.0.4.0/30
                  +------------- B ------------- D -------------+
                  |          10.0.1.2        10.0.3.2      10.0.4.2
   10.0.0.0/30    |                                             |       10.0.6.0/30
 S ------------- A  (ECMP for 10.0.6.0/24, L4 hash, seed 42)    E ------------- T
 10.0.0.1  10.0.0.2                                             |  10.0.6.1  10.0.6.2
                  |          10.0.2.2                      10.0.5.2
                  +------------- C -----------------------------+
                    10.0.2.0/30             10.0.5.0/30

 Path via B: S A B D E T  (T answers at TTL 5)
 Path via C: S A C E T    (T answers at TTL 4)

Topology specification
The lab topology consists of 7 interconnected Linux network namespaces (S, A, B, C, D, E, T):

Path via B (5 Hops): S -> A -> B (10.0.1.2) -> D (10.0.3.2) -> E (10.0.4.2) -> T (10.0.6.2)
Path via C (4 Hops): S -> A -> C (10.0.2.2) -> E (10.0.5.2) -> T (10.0.6.2)

Node A load-balances traffic destined for 10.0.6.0/24 across Node B (10.0.1.2) and Node C (10.0.2.2) using kernel multipath routing with L4 hashing (net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy=1) and a fixed seed (net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_seed=42). Every router has net.ipv4.icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr=1, ICMP rate limiting off, and plain static routes back to S.


Lab files
The lab setup script creates the namespaces, configures veth pairs, sets up routing tables, and applies sysctl hash policies.
topo.sh:
#!/bin/sh

  ip -n $1 addr add $3/30 dev $2; ip -n $1 link set $2 up
  ip -n $4 addr add $6/30 dev $5; ip -n $4 link set $5 up
}

  sc $n net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit 0

trace.py implements both methods with one UDP socket per probe and IP_RECVERR, which queues the ICMP error on the socket together with the address of the router that sent it. Classic mode increments the destination port per probe; Paris mode keeps both ports and changes only the first two payload bytes. It sends one probe at a time and waits for the answer, so the order of replies identifies the probe and no checksum trick is needed. Changing the payload does change the UDP checksum; that is harmless here because Linux does not hash the checksum.
trace.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Classic vs Paris UDP traceroute using IP_RECVERR (no raw sockets needed).

classic : destination port increments per probe (33434, 33435, ...), like
          the original Van Jacobson traceroute, so every probe is a new flow.
paris   : source and destination ports stay fixed for the whole trace; only
          the payload changes, so every probe hashes onto the same ECMP path.
"""
import socket, struct, sys, select

IP_RECVERR = 11
SO_EE_ORIGIN_ICMP = 2

def probe(dst, ttl, sport, dport, payload, timeout=1.0):
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_IP, IP_RECVERR, 1)
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_IP, socket.IP_TTL, ttl)
    s.bind(("0.0.0.0", sport))
    s.sendto(payload, (dst, dport))
    r, _, _ = select.select([s], [], [], timeout)
    if not r:
        s.close(); return None, None
    _, anc, _, _ = s.recvmsg(512, 512, socket.MSG_ERRQUEUE)
    s.close()
    for level, typ, data in anc:
        if level == socket.SOL_IP and typ == IP_RECVERR:
            errno_, origin, itype, icode, _, info, _ = struct.unpack("=IBBBBII", data[:16])
            offender = socket.inet_ntoa(data[16 + 4:16 + 8])  # sockaddr_in: family, port, addr
            return offender, (itype, icode)
    return None, None

def trace(dst, mode, sport=40000, max_ttl=6, base_port=33434):
    hops = []
    seq = 0
    for ttl in range(1, max_ttl + 1):
        dport = base_port + seq if mode == "classic" else base_port
        who, kind = probe(dst, ttl, sport, dport, struct.pack("!H", seq) + b"x" * 30)
        seq += 1
        hops.append(who)
        print(f"{ttl:2d}  {who or '*':<10}  sport={sport} dport={dport}"
              + ("  (port unreachable: destination)" if kind == (3, 3) else ""))
        if kind == (3, 3):
            break
    return hops

if __name__ == "__main__":
    dst, mode = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    sport = int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 40000
    trace(dst, mode, sport)
mda.py runs a Paris trace for 16 different source ports and merges the results.
mda.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Enumerate every interface at every TTL by varying the flow (source port),
then print the links that each individual flow actually used.
A tiny version of the Multipath Detection Algorithm idea used by Paris
traceroute / Dublin traceroute / scamper (no stopping rule, fixed flow count)."""
import sys
from trace import probe

dst = sys.argv[1]
flows = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 16
paths = {}
for f in range(flows):
    sport = 41000 + f
    path = []
    for ttl in range(1, 7):
        who, kind = probe(dst, ttl, sport, 33434, b"mda")
        path.append(who or "*")
        if kind == (3, 3):
            break
    paths.setdefault(tuple(path), []).append(sport)

print(f"{flows} flows, {len(paths)} distinct paths")
for p, sports in sorted(paths.items()):
    print(f"  {' -> '.join(p):<52} flows={len(sports)} e.g. sport {sports[0]}")
hop_sets = {}
for p in paths:
    for i, h in enumerate(p, 1):
        hop_sets.setdefault(i, set()).add(h)
for i in sorted(hop_sets):
    print(f"  ttl {i}: {sorted(hop_sets[i])}")
links = set()
for p in paths:
    links.update(zip(p, p[1:]))
print("  real links:", sorted(links))
mda-table.py prints the MDA stopping numbers used earlier in the chapter:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""How many flows must reach a hop before you may stop looking for one more
next hop?  MDA's rule (Veitch et al., 2009): having seen k next hops, keep
sending until the hypothesis "there are k+1 equally loaded next hops" would
have shown the (k+1)th with probability >= 1 - alpha:
    (k+1) * (k/(k+1))**n <= alpha     ->  smallest such n is n_k"""
import math
print(f"{'seen k':>6} {'test k+1':>8} {'n_k a=0.10':>11} {'n_k a=0.05':>11} {'n_k a=0.01':>11}")
for k in (1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 15):
    row = [math.ceil(math.log(a / (k + 1)) / math.log(k / (k + 1))) for a in (0.10, 0.05, 0.01)]
    print(f"{k:>6} {k+1:>8} {row[0]:>11} {row[1]:>11} {row[2]:>11}")

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
Reading the output

Section 0 and 1: the map and the ECMP route
Section 0 is the key for the rest: E owns both 10.0.4.2 (towards D) and 10.0.5.2 (towards C). Section 1 shows the multipath route on A with two equal-weight next hops and the two sysctls that decide which flow takes which: policy 1 (hash the 5-tuple) and seed 42.


Section 2: classic traceroute
Each run uses one source port and increments the destination port from 33434, one probe per TTL, so every TTL is a new flow at A.

sport 40000 reports A, 10.0.2.2 (C), 10.0.3.2 (D), then T at TTL 4. The TTL 2 probe went via C, the TTL 3 probe via B and expired at D. The trace implies a link C -> D that does not exist, and a four-hop path that no packet took: the C path really is four hops but does not contain D, and the path containing D is five hops.
sport 40001 reports A, C, 10.0.5.2 (E), T at TTL 4. This one happens to be a real path, because the TTL 2, 3 and 4 probes all hashed to C. Nothing in the output tells you it is real.
sport 40002 reports A, 10.0.1.2 (B), 10.0.5.2, 10.0.4.2, T at TTL 5. The TTL 3 probe went via C and expired at E’s C-facing interface; the TTL 4 probe went via B and D and expired at E’s D-facing interface. The output shows a false link B -> E(10.0.5.2) and then E twice in a row under two different addresses. Without alias resolution, that looks like an extra router; with it, it looks like a loop.



Section 3: Paris traceroute
With both ports fixed, a trace is one flow. Source ports 40000 and 40002 both hash to B and report the true five-hop path A B D E(10.0.4.2) T. Source port 40001 hashes to C and reports the true four-hop path A C E(10.0.5.2) T. Every trace is a real path. A single Paris trace still shows only one of the paths, and which one depends on the flow you picked.


Section 4: enumerating the paths
Sixteen source ports found exactly two paths: seven flows via B and nine via C. That split is what a hash over 16 flows looks like, not a configured weight. The per-TTL sets show two interfaces at TTL 2, 3 and 4, and the TTL 4 set mixes a router (10.0.4.2) with the destination (10.0.6.2), the signature of an uneven diamond. The link list is built only from adjacent hops of the same flow, so it holds the seven real links and none of the false ones from Section 2.


Section 5: hash policy 0
With policy 0 on A, the hash only covers addresses, so changing ports moves nothing. Classic traceroute with source ports 40000 and 40001 both report the five-hop path via B. Classic traceroute is only wrong where something hashes on ports; Paris traceroute is right either way. Note that with policy 0 every flow between S and T takes the same branch, so no source-port trick will reveal the C path; a tool would have to vary the source or destination address.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
In production
When operating in production data centers or service provider networks, operators should utilize flow-pinned tracing commands and audit kernel multipath configurations.

Production tool invocations

Paris Traceroute (Production CLI)
To execute Paris Traceroute using fixed-flow UDP probes:
# (not run here)
paris-traceroute -p udp -s 40000 -d 33434 10.0.6.2
# multipath (MDA) mode
paris-traceroute -n -a exh 10.0.6.2
To execute Paris Traceroute using ICMP probes with checksum alignment:
# (not run here)
paris-traceroute -p icmp 10.0.6.2


Scamper / Tracelb (CAIDA)
To perform complete MDA multipath enumeration using CAIDA’s scamper:
# (not run here)
scamper -O json -I "tracelb -P udp-sport 10.0.6.2"


Linux traceroute(8)
To enforce flow-pinned UDP tracing with standard Linux traceroute:
# (not run here)
traceroute -U --sport=40000 -p 33434 10.0.6.2
To perform flow-pinned TCP SYN tracing:
# (not run here)
traceroute -T --sport=40000 -p 80 10.0.6.2


MTR (My Traceroute)
To run mtr in flow-pinned mode using TCP or UDP:
# (not run here)
mtr --udp -P 33434 -L 40000 10.0.6.2
mtr --tcp -P 80 -L 40000 10.0.6.2


Dublin Traceroute
To run Dublin Traceroute with 16 flows and save the JSON result:
# (not run here)
# option names vary between releases; check dublin-traceroute --help
dublin-traceroute --npaths=16 --output-file=trace.json 10.0.6.2



Kernel sysctl configuration for routers
To view and set Linux router ECMP hash policies in production environments:
# (not run here)
# Inspect current IPv4 multipath policy and seed
sysctl net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy
sysctl net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_seed

# Configure 5-tuple L4 hashing for balanced ECMP
sysctl -w net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy=1

# Fixed seed (Linux 6.11+); 0 returns to a random seed
sysctl -w net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_seed=1337

# Enable inbound interface IP addressing for ICMP errors
sysctl -w net.ipv4.icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr=1

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
Gotchas

Assuming intermediate packet loss indicates network outages: Asterisks or loss at intermediate hops (e.g., Hop 3 showing 50% loss while Hop 4 shows 0% loss) are almost always caused by control-plane ICMP rate limiting (net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit), not data-plane forwarding drops.
Misassembling asymmetric return paths: Latency spikes reported at an intermediate hop may reflect path congestion on the return route from that router to the prober, rather than on the forward route to the target destination.
Ignoring IPv6 Flow Labels: IPv6 routers often incorporate the 20-bit IPv6 Flow Label into ECMP hashes. Failing to pin the Flow Label during IPv6 tracing causes ECMP path jumping even when L4 ports are fixed.
Mistaking router interface aliases for distinct physical routers: When a router responds with icmp_errors_use_inbound_ifaddr=1, probes arriving via different interfaces yield different source IPs for the same physical router.
Overlooking Stateful Firewall Session Limits: Transmitting hundreds of MDA probe flows with distinct source ports can fill stateful firewall connection tables (e.g., conntrack), triggering drop actions or state table exhaustion.
Evaluating uneven ECMP path lengths as routing loops: In uneven diamonds, probes taking longer paths hit a router at TTL k+1, while probes taking shorter paths hit the same router at TTL k, making the router appear twice in sequence.
A fixed seed hides nothing, a random one hides everything: with the default random hash key, the same flow can take a different branch after a router reboot. Compare traces taken before and after a change only if you know the seed did not change.
LAG members are invisible: a LAG hashes the same way, but its members are one IP hop, so traceroute never shows them. Pinning the flow keeps you on one member; it does not tell you which.

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
Exercises

MDA sample size: extend mda-table.py to k = 31 and explain why a 32-way ECMP hop needs hundreds of flows before MDA may stop. Then make mda.py stop at each hop using the table instead of a fixed 16 flows.
Identify False Links: Given the classic traceroute output: Hop 1: 10.0.0.1, Hop 2: 10.1.1.1, Hop 3: 10.2.2.1, Hop 4: 10.9.9.9. If 10.1.1.1 is on a 3-hop path and 10.2.2.1 is on a 4-hop parallel path, reconstruct the true graph topology and prove why link 10.1.1.1 -> 10.2.2.1 is false.
Custom hash fields: on A, set fib_multipath_hash_policy=3 and fib_multipath_hash_fields to hash only the destination port (bit 0x0020 per the kernel’s ip-sysctl documentation; check your kernel’s documentation for the bit values). Predict, then check, what classic and Paris traces now show, and why changing only the source port no longer enumerates paths.
Implement UDP Checksum Alignment: Write a Python function that takes a fixed source port, fixed destination port, and desired probe sequence number, and calculates a 2-byte compensating payload suffix that keeps the overall UDP checksum constant across all sequence numbers.
IPv6: add IPv6 addresses and an IPv6 ECMP route on A, keep net.ipv6.fib_multipath_hash_policy=0, and trace with fixed ports from a host where you can set the flow label (for example traceroute -l on a lab host). Show that changing only the flow label moves the probe between branches.
Rate limiting: restore net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit=1000 on C only and run mda.py with 64 flows. Which hops now show *, and why does the destination still answer?

title: ECMP-Aware Tracing: Why traceroute Lies Through Load Balancers, and Paris Traceroute
text:
Verification

Ran: lab.sh (all five sections) and mda-table.py, on Linux 6.12.94, iproute2 6.15.0, Python 3.13.5, unprivileged in unshare -urnm. The full output above is pasted unedited. lab.sh was run twice and the outputs diffed identical, which the fixed fib_multipath_hash_seed makes possible.
Not run: traceroute, mtr, paris-traceroute, scamper and dublin-traceroute (not installed, and no installs were allowed). Their command lines are from the man pages and project documentation; option names, especially Dublin Traceroute’s, can differ between versions.
Not run: IPv6 tracing. Setting a fixed flow label on a socket needs privileges this environment does not have, so the IPv6 notes are from RFC 6437/6438 and the kernel documentation.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
text:
Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
Screen-scraping show output works until the vendor changes a column. Model-driven management replaces text with a schema: the device publishes YANG models of its configuration and state, and clients read and write that tree over NETCONF or gNMI. The lab host track has a short hands-on chapter, Reading SR Linux with gNMI, that does one get and one subscribe. This chapter is the model behind it: how to read a YANG module, what a NETCONF transaction actually guarantees, how gNMI paths and Set operations work, and which tool to pick for configuration versus telemetry.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Read a YANG tree and tell configuration from state, lists from containers, and native models from OpenConfig
Explain NETCONF datastores, edit-config operations, locks and confirmed commit, and why a candidate datastore makes changes safer
Write gNMI paths with list keys correctly, including keys that contain a slash
Choose between gNMI Set update, replace and delete, and between Subscribe modes ONCE, POLL and STREAM
Turn a gNMI JSON_IETF notification into path/value pairs, the way a telemetry collector does
Enable the management APIs on the lab NOS images and know what each listens on

Version note. The three small Python programs in this chapter ran on 2026-11-13 on the writing host (Python 3.13.5, standard library only), and their output is pasted verbatim. Their inputs are hand-written samples, not data from a device: the JSON file follows the shape SR Linux uses for JSON_IETF, and the NETCONF RPC uses the OpenConfig interfaces namespace. No device, gnmic, pyang or ncclient was available on the writing host, so every device command and every device output in this chapter is from vendor and project documentation and was not run there. Device outputs are labelled illustrative.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
text:
Why a model








Approach
What you parse
What breaks it




CLI scraping (Expect, regex, TextFSM)
Human-formatted text
New column, new release, different vendor


SNMP
MIB objects, polled
Thin write support, poll intervals average away spikes


Model-driven (NETCONF, RESTCONF, gNMI)
A typed tree defined by YANG
Model version changes, which are versioned and visible



The model gives three things scraping never does: types (an MTU is an integer with a range, not a string), transactions (several changes succeed or fail together), and a way to ask the device what it supports before you send anything.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
text:
YANG in one page
YANG (RFC 7950) is the schema language. A module defines a tree of nodes:








Statement
What it is
Path example




container
A grouping node with no value
/interfaces


list with key
Repeated entries identified by key leaves
/interfaces/interface[name=Ethernet1]


leaf
One typed value
.../config/description


leaf-list
A list of values
.../dns/server


config false
State, read-only: counters, oper-status
.../state/counters/in-octets


augment
Another module adds nodes into this tree
Vendor additions to OpenConfig


deviation
A vendor declares where it does not implement the model
“not-supported” leaves


grouping / uses
Reusable blocks, flattened into the tree




Nobody reads YANG source to find a path. They read a tree. pyang -f tree (and gnmic’s path generator) print one. Illustrative, abridged from the OpenConfig interfaces model in pyang tree format:
module: openconfig-interfaces
  +--rw interfaces
     +--rw interface* [name]
        +--rw name      -> ../config/name
        +--rw config
        |  +--rw name?          string
        |  +--rw description?   string
        |  +--rw enabled?       boolean
        +--ro state
           +--ro oper-status    enumeration
           +--ro counters
              +--ro in-octets?    oc-yang:counter64
How to read it: rw is configuration, ro is state. interface* [name] is a list keyed by name. ? means optional. -> is a leafref, a pointer to another leaf.

Native models and OpenConfig
Every vendor publishes native models that mirror its own configuration (SR Linux srl_nokia-interfaces, Arista EOS native paths, and so on). OpenConfig is a vendor-neutral set of models written by operators. The trade:









Native
OpenConfig




Coverage
Everything the box can do
The common subset, plus vendor augments


Portability
One vendor
The same path on several vendors


Structure
Vendor’s choice
Always config (intended) and state (applied) side by side



OpenConfig’s config/state split matters in practice: you write .../config/description and read .../state/description to see what the device actually applied. A tool that writes and then reads back config only proves the device stored your intent.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
section: gNMI: gRPC paths, Set and Subscribe
text:
gNMI: gRPC paths, Set and Subscribe
gNMI (gRPC Network Management Interface, from OpenConfig) runs over gRPC on HTTP/2 with TLS. Four RPCs:







RPC
Purpose




Capabilities
Models, versions and encodings the target supports


Get
Read a snapshot of one or more paths


Set
Apply delete, replace and update operations in one transaction


Subscribe
Telemetry: receive values once, on poll, or as a stream



The port is not fixed by the specification. IANA assigned 9339 for gNMI; SR Linux listens on 57400 by default and Arista EOS on 6030. Check the device.

Paths and keys
A gNMI path is a list of PathElem: a name plus an optional map of keys. The string form puts keys in brackets. The parsing trap is that key values may contain /, as SR Linux interface names do. A client that splits on every / sends nonsense. This program does what gNMI clients do: split on / only outside brackets:


gnmi-path.py

"""Split a gNMI path string into PathElem name + keys, the way gNMI clients do."""
import sys

def split_path(p):
    elems, buf, depth = [], "", 0
    for ch in p.strip("/"):
        if ch == "[":
            depth += 1
        elif ch == "]":
            depth -= 1
        if ch == "/" and depth == 0:
            elems.append(buf); buf = ""
        else:
            buf += ch
    if buf:
        elems.append(buf)
    out = []
    for e in elems:
        name, _, rest = e.partition("[")
        keys = {}
        for kv in ("[" + rest).split("[")[1:] if rest else []:
            k, _, v = kv.rstrip("]").partition("=")
            keys[k] = v
        out.append((name, keys))
    return out

for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    print(path)
    for name, keys in split_path(path):
        print(f"  elem name={name!r} keys={keys}")

Captured output:
$ python3 gnmi-path.py "/interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/subinterface[index=0]/ipv4/address[ip-prefix=10.12.0.1/30]" "/interfaces/interface[name=Ethernet1]/state/counters/in-octets"
/interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/subinterface[index=0]/ipv4/address[ip-prefix=10.12.0.1/30]
  elem name='interface' keys={'name': 'ethernet-1/1'}
  elem name='subinterface' keys={'index': '0'}
  elem name='ipv4' keys={}
  elem name='address' keys={'ip-prefix': '10.12.0.1/30'}
/interfaces/interface[name=Ethernet1]/state/counters/in-octets
  elem name='interfaces' keys={}
  elem name='interface' keys={'name': 'Ethernet1'}
  elem name='state' keys={}
  elem name='counters' keys={}
  elem name='in-octets' keys={}
ethernet-1/1 and 10.12.0.1/30 stay intact as key values. On a shell command line, quote the whole path: the brackets are glob characters to the shell.
Path rules worth knowing:

An origin selects the schema: openconfig or a vendor’s native origin. Some targets need it set explicitly when they support both.
A prefix in a request is prepended to every path in it, which keeps large requests small.
Wildcards: * for any element or key value (/interface[name=*]/oper-state), ... for any depth. Support for wildcards in Set is limited; use them in Get and Subscribe.



Set: update, replace, delete
A single SetRequest can carry many operations. The target applies deletes first, then replaces, then updates, and the whole request succeeds or fails as one transaction.








Operation
Meaning
Use it for




update
Merge the given value into the tree
Changing a few leaves


replace
Make the subtree at this path exactly the given value; anything not sent is removed or reset to defaults
Declaring a whole object, such as one interface’s complete config


delete
Remove the subtree
Removing a list entry



replace at a high path is how people delete half a device’s configuration by accident. Replace the narrowest path that holds the whole object you mean.


Encodings







Encoding
What it is




JSON_IETF
JSON per RFC 7951: module-qualified names on the top node (srl_nokia-interfaces:interface), 64-bit integers as strings


JSON
Plain JSON, no module prefixes. Implementation-defined details


PROTO
Typed scalar values in protobuf; efficient for telemetry


ASCII
Vendor CLI text


BYTES
Opaque



Ask Capabilities which encodings a target supports. Most model-driven work uses JSON_IETF for config and PROTO or JSON_IETF for telemetry.


Subscribe modes







Mode
Behaviour




ONCE
Send current values, then a sync marker, then close


POLL
Keep the stream open; send values each time the client polls


STREAM with SAMPLE
Send values every sample_interval


STREAM with ON_CHANGE
Send only when a value changes (oper-status, BGP state)


STREAM with TARGET_DEFINED
Let the device choose per leaf: usually on-change for state, sample for counters



Every stream starts with the full current state followed by a sync_response. A collector that does not wait for sync_response cannot tell the initial snapshot from real changes. Counters belong in SAMPLE; anything with a meaningful transition belongs in ON_CHANGE. A five-minute SNMP poll averages a thirty-second microburst into nothing, which is the operational reason streaming telemetry exists.


From a notification to time series
A gNMI notification carries a path prefix and a set of updates. With JSON_IETF, an update for a container holds a JSON object. A collector flattens it into path/value pairs before writing a time series database. This program does that for a JSON_IETF value:


flatten.py

"""Flatten a JSON_IETF notification value into path/value pairs, as a collector would."""
import json, sys

def walk(node, path, out):
    if isinstance(node, dict):
        for k, v in node.items():
            walk(v, path + [k], out)
    elif isinstance(node, list):
        for item in node:
            # YANG list entries: use the first scalar member as the key
            key = next((k for k, v in item.items() if not isinstance(v, (dict, list))), None)
            rest = {k: v for k, v in item.items() if k != key}
            elem = f"{path[-1]}[{key}={item[key]}]"
            if rest:
                walk(rest, path[:-1] + [elem], out)
            else:  # list entry that is only its key: emit the key leaf
                out.append(("/" + "/".join(path[:-1] + [elem, key]), item[key]))
    else:
        out.append(("/" + "/".join(path), node))

doc = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
prefix = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else ""
pairs = []
walk(doc, [prefix] if prefix else [], pairs)
for p, v in pairs:
    print(f"{p} = {v!r}")

The input is a hand-written sample in the shape SR Linux returns for an interface (not captured from a device):


sample-srl-interface.json

{
  "srl_nokia-interfaces:interface": [
    {
      "name": "ethernet-1/1",
      "description": "to-leaf2",
      "admin-state": "enable",
      "mtu": 9232,
      "subinterface": [
        {
          "index": 0,
          "admin-state": "enable",
          "ipv4": {
            "admin-state": "enable",
            "address": [ { "ip-prefix": "10.12.0.1/30" } ]
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Captured output:
$ python3 flatten.py sample-srl-interface.json
/srl_nokia-interfaces:interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/description = 'to-leaf2'
/srl_nokia-interfaces:interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/admin-state = 'enable'
/srl_nokia-interfaces:interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/mtu = 9232
/srl_nokia-interfaces:interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/subinterface[index=0]/admin-state = 'enable'
/srl_nokia-interfaces:interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/subinterface[index=0]/ipv4/admin-state = 'enable'
/srl_nokia-interfaces:interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/subinterface[index=0]/ipv4/address[ip-prefix=10.12.0.1/30]/ip-prefix = '10.12.0.1/30'
Two things to see. The module prefix appears once, on the top node, as RFC 7951 requires; children inherit the module. And the list keys (name, index, ip-prefix) move out of the values and into the path. The last line shows a list entry that consists only of its key. The first version of this program dropped such entries silently, which is the kind of bug that makes a dashboard miss every IPv4 address. Real collectors (gnmic’s outputs, Telegraf’s gNMI input) use the schema to identify keys. This program guesses the first scalar member, which is only good enough for a demonstration.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
section: Turning it on in the lab images
text:
Turning it on in the lab images
The lab host track uses Arista cEOS, Nokia SR Linux and FRR. Not run on the writing host; check each against the vendor documentation for your image version.









NOS
gNMI
NETCONF
Notes




SR Linux
Enabled in the default config Containerlab gives the SR Linux kind, port 57400
Supported in recent releases; enable it as the SR Linux NETCONF documentation for your release describes
Native models srl_nokia-*; OpenConfig models must be enabled explicitly (see the SR Linux OpenConfig docs)


Arista cEOS
management api gnmi / transport grpc default (port 6030)
management api netconf / transport ssh default (port 830)
OpenConfig paths by default


FRR
Northbound gRPC is experimental and not gNMI
No
Use vtysh JSON output (show ... json) for automation



On cEOS, illustrative EOS configuration:
management api gnmi
   transport grpc default
management api netconf
   transport ssh default
The same gnmic container image the gNMI lab uses can then read either NOS. Illustrative gnmic invocations, not run on the writing host:
# What does this target support?
gnmic -a 172.20.20.2:57400 -u admin -p 'NokiaSrl1!' --skip-verify capabilities

# Get with JSON_IETF, native SR Linux path
gnmic -a 172.20.20.2:57400 -u admin -p 'NokiaSrl1!' --skip-verify \
  get --path '/interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/description' --encoding json_ietf

# Update one leaf, then replace a whole subtree
gnmic -a 172.20.20.2:57400 -u admin -p 'NokiaSrl1!' --skip-verify \
  set --update-path '/interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/description' --update-value 'to-leaf2'

# Sample counters every 10 s
gnmic -a 172.20.20.2:57400 -u admin -p 'NokiaSrl1!' --skip-verify \
  subscribe --path '/interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/statistics' \
  --mode stream --stream-mode sample --sample-interval 10s
--skip-verify accepts the lab’s self-signed certificate. Never carry it into production; use real certificates and --tls-ca.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
section: Lab: read, change, confirm (not run on the writing host)
text:
Lab: read, change, confirm (not run on the writing host)
On your lab host, with a single SR Linux node as in Reading SR Linux with gNMI:

Run capabilities and find the srl_nokia-interfaces module and the encodings list. Predict: JSON_IETF is listed.
get the description of ethernet-1/1 with --encoding json_ietf. Compare the response with the sample JSON in this chapter, and run flatten.py on the values object of the response.
Start a subscribe --mode stream --stream-mode on-change on /interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/oper-state in one terminal. In another, set --update-path .../admin-state --update-value disable. Predict: one notification with down. Set it back and watch the second.
Use set --replace-path '/interface[name=ethernet-1/1]' --replace-value '{"admin-state":"enable"}' on a throwaway node. Predict: the description you set earlier is gone, because replace removed every leaf you did not send.
On cEOS, enable management api netconf, connect with ssh -s admin@<mgmt-ip> -p 830 netconf, and read the server’s <hello>. Find urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:candidate:1.0 and confirmed-commit in the list, or note that they are absent.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
text:
Gotchas

Writing config, reading config. With OpenConfig, read state to confirm what was applied.
replace too high in the tree deletes everything you did not send under that path.
Unprefixed operation attributes in NETCONF XML are in no namespace and may be ignored.
Unquoted paths on the shell: brackets glob, and [name=*] may expand to a filename.
Keys containing / break naive path splitting.
Telemetry without sync_response handling treats the initial snapshot as a storm of changes.
64-bit counters in JSON_IETF are strings. A collector that expects numbers drops them or graphs zero.
Self-signed certificates and --skip-verify belong in the lab only.
Model versions. Paths change between OpenConfig releases and NOS versions. Record capabilities output with each automation release.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
text:
Boring rule
Ask the device what it supports, write the narrowest path that holds the whole object, read back the applied state, and use a confirmed commit or equivalent rollback for anything that could cut your session.

title: Model-Driven Management: YANG, NETCONF and gNMI
text:
Try this

Run gnmi-path.py on /network-instance[name=default]/protocols/bgp/neighbor[peer-address=2001:db8::1]/session-state. Expected: the IPv6 address survives as one key value, colons and all.
Change netconf-edit.py to send operation="replace" on <interfaces> instead of <config>. Explain in one sentence what that would do to every other interface on a real device.
Add a second list entry to sample-srl-interface.json (ethernet-1/2, admin-state disable) and run flatten.py. Expected: each leaf appears once per interface, with the key in the path.
Change the registration in netconf-edit.py to ET.register_namespace("", NC) and run it. Expected: the elements lose their nc: prefix and the attribute prints as operation="merge", now in no namespace. Find the sentence in RFC 6241 section 7.2 that shows the attribute with a namespace prefix.
On your lab host, subscribe to the same counter with sample at 1 s and at 30 s while running a ping flood across the link. Expected: the 30 s series hides the burst shape that the 1 s series shows.
