title: API Automation: Conditional Updates and Concurrent Changes
text:
API Automation: Conditional Updates and Concurrent Changes
A network automation job can read an interface configuration, calculate a change, and overwrite a colleague’s intervening change. This lost update can happen even if both requests succeed and the JSON is valid. Conditional writes and read-back verification make the conflict visible, but do not eliminate the need to review the intended change.

title: API Automation: Conditional Updates and Concurrent Changes
text:
HTTP, resource state and safety
An HTTP API exposes resources addressed by URLs. GET reads a representation; PUT commonly replaces a resource; PATCH applies a partial change according to that API’s patch format; and POST semantics are resource-specific. Check the actual API’s contract: methods, required fields, status codes, authentication and transaction scope vary. A response code is evidence of the request outcome, not proof that the physical device forwarded traffic as intended.
An entity tag (ETag) identifies a representation version. A client can include If-Match in a write to make the change conditional on the resource still matching the tag it read. If the condition fails, a server commonly returns 412 Precondition Failed without applying the stale change. HTTP also permits a successful response in a narrowly defined already-applied case; follow the actual server’s semantics. ETags are opaque: clients must not assume they are sequential numbers or parse a vendor’s tag.
PUT is defined as idempotent in its intended effect: repeating the same request has the same intended resource effect as applying it once. That does not mean every response is identical, other logging side effects cannot happen, a conditional retry must succeed, or a multi-step workflow is atomic. A timeout after a write can mean the server applied it but the response was lost. Read current state and reconcile before retrying; do not blindly replay a non-idempotent operation.

title: API Automation: Conditional Updates and Concurrent Changes
API Automation: Conditional Updates and Concurrent Changes
text:
Practice and operational reasoning

Remove B’s If-Match argument. This mock returns 428 and leaves the resource unchanged. A real API may have different precondition requirements and response behavior; inspect its contract.
Before B re-reads, change A’s description again. B must retrieve the latest representation and decide whether its intended change still makes sense; automatically merging arbitrary configuration can violate policy.
Repeat a PUT with the same body and current ETag, then read back the object. In this mock the content and tag stay unchanged. A real server can have different revision or logging behavior; a retry with the old ETag can instead be rejected.
Change the body to an invalid type such as "enabled": "false". The mock returns 400 rather than silently accepting a string as a boolean. Validate types against the actual device’s schema and YANG model where applicable.
Plan rollback before editing a real device. A saved pre-change configuration is not always safe to restore blindly: another operator may have made a legitimate later change. Use the system’s candidate/confirmed-commit or version checks where available, preserve an independent management path, verify forwarding and application behavior, and document ownership of the change.

For real automation use authenticated encrypted transport, verify server identity, protect credentials, set timeouts, handle rate limits and errors, minimize permissions, and avoid logging secrets. Limit request scope and compare intended and observed state. RESTCONF can expose YANG-modeled resources and conditional editing, but support, datastore behavior, model revisions and transactional features must be discovered on the actual server. See YANG, NETCONF and gNMI for the wider model-driven context.
References: HTTP Semantics, RFC 9110 and RESTCONF, RFC 8040.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
A lab that only runs on your laptop drifts. A config change that “obviously” works breaks a BGP session nobody re-checked. The fix is the same as for software: every change to a topology or its configs deploys the lab in CI, waits for it to converge, asserts the things you care about, collects evidence, and tears it down. Automation and Lab-as-Code sketched this in a few lines. This chapter builds the whole pipeline: the workflow, a convergence check that waits properly instead of sleeping, teardown that always runs, and the runner decisions that decide whether CI can run your images at all.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Write a GitHub Actions workflow that installs a pinned Containerlab, deploys a topology, runs checks, and always destroys the lab
Replace sleep 60 with a convergence check that polls structured output until a deadline and fails with a useful message
Decide between GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners based on the images your lab needs
Collect artifacts that make a red build debuggable after the lab is gone
Lint a topology in CI without deploying it

Version note. The convergence checker in this chapter ran on 2026-11-13 on the writing host (Python 3.13.5, standard library only) against hand-written JSON fixtures in the shape of FRR’s show bgp summary json. A small shell script stood in for docker exec ... vtysh so the checker could be exercised through converge and timeout paths. Its output is pasted verbatim. The GitHub Actions workflow, Containerlab deploy, and all device commands were not run on the writing host, which has no Docker and no Containerlab. They are written from the Containerlab documentation, the GitHub Actions documentation, and the Containerlab project’s own CI. Containerlab install commands are quoted from containerlab.dev.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
section: What a lab smoke test is, and is not
text:
What a lab smoke test is, and is not







It is
It is not




Proof that the topology deploys and the configs load
A performance test


Proof that adjacencies form and expected routes appear
Proof that production will behave the same


A fast, repeatable red/green on every pull request
A replacement for thinking about failure modes


A record of what the lab looked like when it passed
A long-running lab you log into



Keep the smoke test small: the fewest nodes that exercise the change, and checks that read structured output. A CI lab that takes 25 minutes gets disabled.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
Choose the runner first
The images decide where the job can run.









Runner
Has Docker
Can pull
Good for




GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04
Yes
Public images: FRR from quay.io, SR Linux and network-multitool from ghcr.io, Alpine
FRR and SR Linux labs


Self-hosted runner on your lab host
Yes, already set up
Whatever is loaded locally, including vendor images you are licensed to use
cEOS and other images you cannot publish



Arista cEOS is downloaded from Arista after login and imported locally; you cannot pull it from a public registry, and you must not push it to one. A cEOS lab therefore runs on a self-hosted runner (your lab host), or not in CI at all. The lab host track’s image table is exactly the inventory a self-hosted runner would see.
Memory is the other limit. Each SR Linux or cEOS node wants about 2 GB. A GitHub-hosted runner has far less headroom than the 15 GB lab host, so keep hosted-runner labs to FRR and Linux nodes, or one SR Linux node.
Self-hosted runners execute whatever a workflow says, with Docker access, which is root-equivalent on that host. Only attach them to private repositories, or require approval for workflows from forks.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
The topology under test
A three-router FRR eBGP triangle is enough to exercise configs and policy:


ci.clab.yml

name: ci
topology:
  kinds:
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    r1:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: configs/r1.frr.conf
    r2:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: configs/r2.frr.conf
    r3:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: configs/r3.frr.conf
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth1", "r2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth2", "r3:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r2:eth2", "r3:eth2"]

Each router runs bgpd with two eBGP neighbours and announces one loopback, 10.0.0.N/32 for rN. The FRR configs follow the eBGP chapters; their exact content does not matter here. What matters is that the repository holds the topology, the configs, and the checks together, so one pull request changes all three.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
section: Wait for convergence, do not sleep
text:
Wait for convergence, do not sleep
The most common CI lab bug is sleep 60 followed by a check. On a fast runner it wastes a minute. On a slow runner BGP has not converged yet and the build goes red for no reason. Poll instead: read structured output, decide, wait a little, try again, and give up at a deadline with a message that says what was still wrong.


check-bgp.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Poll a node's FRR 'show bgp summary json' until every peer is Established
and has received at least MIN_PFX prefixes, or fail after a deadline."""
import json, subprocess, sys, time

def bgp_summary(cmd):
    out = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    return json.loads(out)

def check(summary, min_pfx):
    problems = []
    peers = summary.get("ipv4Unicast", {}).get("peers", {})
    if not peers:
        problems.append("no IPv4 unicast peers configured")
    for addr, p in sorted(peers.items()):
        if p.get("state") != "Established":
            problems.append(f"{addr}: state {p.get('state')}")
        elif p.get("pfxRcd", 0) < min_pfx:
            problems.append(f"{addr}: {p.get('pfxRcd', 0)} prefixes < {min_pfx}")
    return problems

def main():
    cmd, min_pfx, deadline_s, every_s = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), float(sys.argv[3]), float(sys.argv[4])
    start = time.monotonic()
    attempt = 0
    while True:
        attempt += 1
        problems = check(bgp_summary(cmd), min_pfx)
        elapsed = time.monotonic() - start
        if not problems:
            print(f"PASS after {attempt} attempt(s), {elapsed:.1f}s")
            return 0
        print(f"attempt {attempt} at {elapsed:.1f}s: " + "; ".join(problems))
        if elapsed + every_s > deadline_s:
            print(f"FAIL: not converged within {deadline_s:.0f}s")
            return 1
        time.sleep(every_s)

sys.exit(main())

The first argument is the command that produces FRR’s JSON. In CI it is docker exec clab-ci-r1 vtysh -c 'show bgp summary json'. To exercise the checker without a lab, a stand-in script returns three snapshots in turn, the way a converging router would:


fake-vtysh.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Stand-in for: docker exec clab-ci-r1 vtysh -c 'show bgp summary json'
# Returns t0, t1, then t2 forever, to simulate a lab converging.
n=$(cat .calls 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
echo $((n + 1)) > .calls
case $n in 0) f=t0 ;; 1) f=t1 ;; *) f=t2 ;; esac
cat "fixtures/r1-$f.json"

The fixtures are hand-written, in the shape of FRR’s show bgp summary json (top-level ipv4Unicast, a peers object keyed by neighbour address, each with state and pfxRcd). fixtures/r1-t1.json, the middle snapshot:


r1-t1.json

{"ipv4Unicast": {"routerId": "10.0.0.1", "as": 65001, "peers": {
  "10.12.0.2": {"remoteAs": 65002, "state": "Established", "pfxRcd": 2},
  "10.13.0.2": {"remoteAs": 65003, "state": "OpenSent", "pfxRcd": 0}}}}

Converging case, captured:
$ python3 check-bgp.py ./fake-vtysh.sh 2 60 2
attempt 1 at 0.0s: 10.12.0.2: state Active; 10.13.0.2: state Connect
attempt 2 at 2.0s: 10.13.0.2: state OpenSent
PASS after 3 attempt(s), 4.0s
exit=0
Never-converging case (a peer stuck in OpenSent), captured:
$ python3 check-bgp.py "cat fixtures/r1-t1.json" 2 5 2
attempt 1 at 0.0s: 10.13.0.2: state OpenSent
attempt 2 at 2.0s: 10.13.0.2: state OpenSent
attempt 3 at 4.0s: 10.13.0.2: state OpenSent
FAIL: not converged within 5s
exit=1
Read what that buys you. The pass took three polls and four seconds, not a fixed minute. The failure names the peer and its state, so the CI log already says “10.13.0.2 stuck in OpenSent”, which points at a capability or AS mismatch, not at “BGP broken”. The non-zero exit fails the step.
Two habits in the checker are worth copying into every check you write:

Fail on “nothing configured”. An empty peer list is a failure, not a pass. A typo in the config file name gives you a router with no BGP, and a naive loop over zero peers passes.
Check content, not just state. Established with zero prefixes received is usually a policy mistake. The MIN_PFX argument catches it.

Write the same shape for each protocol you care about: OSPF neighbours Full from show ip ospf neighbor json, specific prefixes present in show ip route json, and end-to-end reachability with ping -c 3 between Linux hosts. If you use netlab, netlab validate already implements this pattern for its modules, with retries, and exits non-zero on failure.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
The workflow


lab-smoke.yml

name: lab-smoke

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "lab/**"
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: lab-smoke-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 20
    env:
      CLAB_VERSION: "pin-a-release-here"
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: lab
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install containerlab (pinned)
        run: bash -c "$(curl -sL https://get.containerlab.dev)" -- -v "$CLAB_VERSION"

      - name: Pre-pull images
        run: docker pull quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1

      - name: Deploy
        run: sudo -E containerlab deploy -t ci.clab.yml --reconfigure

      - name: Wait for BGP on every router
        run: |
          for r in r1 r2 r3; do
            python3 check-bgp.py "sudo docker exec clab-ci-$r vtysh -c 'show bgp summary json'" 2 180 5
          done

      - name: End-to-end reachability
        run: sudo docker exec clab-ci-r1 ping -c 3 -I 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.3

      - name: Collect evidence
        if: always()
        run: |
          mkdir -p evidence
          sudo containerlab inspect -t ci.clab.yml --format json > evidence/inspect.json || true
          for r in r1 r2 r3; do
            sudo docker exec clab-ci-$r vtysh -c 'show running-config' > evidence/$r-running.txt || true
            sudo docker exec clab-ci-$r vtysh -c 'show bgp summary json' > evidence/$r-bgp.json || true
            sudo docker logs clab-ci-$r > evidence/$r-container.log 2>&1 || true
          done

      - name: Upload evidence
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: lab-evidence
          path: lab/evidence/

      - name: Destroy
        if: always()
        run: sudo -E containerlab destroy -t ci.clab.yml --cleanup || true

Line by line, the parts that matter:

paths: lab/**. Only changes to the lab trigger it. A typo fix in a README does not boot three routers.
concurrency with cancel-in-progress. A new push to the same pull request cancels the old run, so two labs with the same name never fight over one runner.
timeout-minutes. A hung deploy fails in 20 minutes instead of GitHub’s default of six hours.
Pinned Containerlab. The install script accepts -- -v <version>, as shown on containerlab.dev. Put a real release number in CLAB_VERSION; latest means a Containerlab release can turn your build red on a day you changed nothing. Pin the FRR image tag for the same reason.
Pre-pull. Image download time is separated from deploy time, so a slow registry shows up as a slow pull step, not a mysterious deploy timeout.
--reconfigure. Deploy from a clean state even if a previous run on a self-hosted runner left the lab directory behind.
if: always() on evidence, upload and destroy. These must run when an earlier step failed, which is exactly when you need them. On a hosted runner the VM is discarded anyway, but the same workflow on a self-hosted runner would otherwise leave three routers running.
|| true in cleanup steps. A failing cleanup must not mask the real failure, and must not stop the other cleanup commands.

The sudo calls are there because a fresh hosted runner user is not in the groups Containerlab’s installer configures for sudo-less use until a new login. On a self-hosted lab host where you already run containerlab without sudo, drop them.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
Lint without deploying
Some mistakes do not need a lab to find. Run these in a fast job before the smoke job, or on every push:








Check
Command
Catches




Topology renders and is valid
containerlab graph -t ci.clab.yml --mermaid (or --dot); a non-zero exit fails the step
YAML errors, bad endpoints, unknown kinds


Configs exist where the topology says
A one-line shell loop over startup-config: paths with test -f
Renamed or missing config files


c9s compatibility (if you also run on Kubernetes)
containerlab --runtime c9s validate -t ci.clab.yml
Fields the c9s runtime cannot realise; needs no cluster


FRR config syntax
Run vtysh --dryrun -f configs/r1.frr.conf in the FRR image, if your FRR version supports it
Typos in FRR config



The c9s row is useful even without a cluster: the containerlab documentation states that validate and deploy --emit-crs for the c9s runtime never contact the cluster.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
Making red builds debuggable
When a smoke test fails, the lab is already destroyed by the time you read the log. The evidence step is what you debug from.

inspect.json shows which nodes came up and their management addresses.
rN-running.txt is the configuration each router actually ran, which may differ from the file if a line failed to parse.
rN-bgp.json is the state at the moment of failure. Feed it straight back into check-bgp.py with cat as the command to reproduce the verdict locally.
rN-container.log holds daemon start-up errors such as a daemon that refused to start.

Keep artifacts small and text. A pcap of every link for every run fills storage fast; capture only in a separate, manually triggered job.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
section: Lab: run the pipeline (not run on the writing host)
text:
Lab: run the pipeline (not run on the writing host)

Put ci.clab.yml, three FRR configs, check-bgp.py and the workflow in a private repository, with the workflow at .github/workflows/lab-smoke.yml.
Open a pull request that changes r3’s AS number on one side only. Predict: the BGP wait step fails with 10.13.0.2 (or the equivalent peer) not Established, and the evidence artifact shows remoteAs disagreeing with the configured value.
Fix it and push again. Predict: the earlier run is cancelled if still going, and the new one passes in the time it takes to boot and converge, not a fixed sleep.
Add a prefix-list on r2 that filters r1’s loopback. Predict: sessions are Established but pfxRcd is 1 on r1’s session with r2, and the check fails on MIN_PFX.
On your lab host, register a self-hosted runner for the repository, switch runs-on to it, and add a cEOS node. Predict: the job only works on the self-hosted runner, because the cEOS image exists only there.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
Gotchas

sleep instead of polling. Flaky on slow runners, slow on fast ones.
Unpinned versions. latest for Containerlab or images means unrelated red builds.
Teardown without if: always(). Leaves labs running on self-hosted runners after the first failure.
Same lab name in parallel runs on one self-hosted runner. Use concurrency, or put the run ID into the lab name with containerlab deploy --name.
Vendor images on hosted runners. You cannot pull them, and you must not publish them to make it work.
Self-hosted runners on public repositories. A fork’s pull request can run arbitrary code with Docker access on your lab host.
Checks that pass on nothing. Treat zero peers, zero routes or an empty JSON reply as failures.
Masking failures in cleanup. Use || true in cleanup, never in the checks.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
Boring rule
Pin everything, poll with a deadline instead of sleeping, assert on structured output, and always collect evidence and destroy the lab, even when a step failed.

title: Containerlab in CI: Smoke-Testing a Topology on Every Change
text:
Try this

Run check-bgp.py with MIN_PFX 3 against fixtures/r1-t2.json through cat. Expected: it never passes, and each attempt reports both peers with 2 prefixes < 3.
Create a fixture with "peers": {} and run the checker. Expected: no IPv4 unicast peers configured on every attempt, then FAIL.
Write check-ospf.py in the same shape for FRR’s show ip ospf neighbor json, failing unless every neighbour is Full. Test it with two hand-written fixtures before using it in CI.
Add a lint job to the workflow that runs containerlab graph --mermaid and the config-exists loop, and make smoke depend on it with needs: lint. Expected: a broken endpoint name fails in seconds, without deploying.
Change the workflow to name the lab ci-${{ github.run_id }} with --name on deploy, inspect and destroy, and point the docker exec commands at the matching container names. Expected: two runs on one self-hosted runner no longer collide.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Runbooks and Incident Notes
When a BGP session drops at 2 a.m., the useful document is not a protocol chapter and not a transcript of everything you have ever typed. It is a runbook: a procedure with a trigger, pre-checks, steps, expected observations, and a rollback, written when you were calm. What you produce during the event is an incident note: a time-stamped record of impact, evidence, hypotheses, and changes. This chapter is about those two documents — how to write them for a campus, a lab, or a small edge, and how to keep them honest.
It is not a recap of ss, tcpdump, or mtr, and it is not the lab-host-track failure-drill chapter (the cEOS / VRRP / OSPF exercises you run on purpose). Those teach tools and a specific topology. A runbook is what you write before a drill; an incident note is what you write during one.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Learning goals

Distinguish a runbook from an incident note and say what belongs in each
Fill a runbook template for a realistic edge failure (BGP session down / default route missing) without inventing CLI output
Keep an incident timeline in UTC, with evidence stored as dated files, not as memory
Communicate a one-sentence status, a rollback condition, and a follow-up that actually changes the runbook
Avoid the usual failure modes: stale screenshots, “just restart it,” fixing two things at once, and pasting secrets into the ticket

Version note. This chapter is procedural. No routers were contacted, no packets were captured, and no tickets were opened on the writing host (2026-11-13). The templates are examples you can copy. Command names (show ip bgp summary, ip route, ss -ti) are reminders of what to record, not a troubleshooting walkthrough and not output from a run.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Two documents, two jobs









Runbook
Incident note




When you write it
Before the event, after a design review or a drill
During (and immediately after) the event


Job
A procedure someone else can follow at 2 a.m.
A record of what was seen and done, in order


Audience
The next on-call, including you in six months
The same people, plus whoever does the review


Changes when
The design, the platform, or a post-incident follow-up changes
Every time you observe, decide, or change something



A runbook that is only updated after outages is already late, but a runbook that is never tested is a short story. The loop is: write the runbook, run a drill (the lab-host-track failure drills are one place), fix the runbook, and use the incident note format even in the drill so the muscle is the same.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Severity, for a small network
Use four levels and write the impact, not the symptom, in the title.








Level
Meaning
Examples in this book’s world




SEV1
Users or a site are down now; safety or a hard deadline is at risk
Campus default route gone; both edges down; a lab exam or change window blocked with no workaround


SEV2
A significant function is down, but a workaround or a second path exists
One of two BGP uplinks down; a single VLAN isolated; management reachable, data plane degraded


SEV3
Impaired or at risk, no immediate user-visible outage
A BGP session flapping and recovering; a disk filling on a collector; an alert you do not yet understand


SEV4
Planning, hygiene, or a known low-priority defect
A missing runbook step, a stale diagram, a lab image to rebuild



If you are unsure, pick the higher severity and downgrade in writing when the impact is clearer. Do not argue the number while nobody is gathering evidence.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
A runbook template
Copy this block into your own store (a repo, a wiki, even a dated text file next to the topology). Fill every heading. Empty sections are a signal that the procedure is not ready.
Title:
Service / scope:          (which site, which routers, which prefixes)
Severity if this fires:
Trigger / symptoms:       (alert name, user report, what “bad” looks like)
Author / last reviewed:
Related diagrams, prefixes, peer ASNs, change window rules:

Pre-checks (do these first; do not change anything yet):
  1.
  2.

Procedure:
  Step N:
    Action:
    Expected observation:
    If not expected:
    Evidence to save:

Rollback:
  Condition that means “stop and undo”:
  Undo steps:

Escalation:
  After how long, or after which step, and to whom:

References:
  (topology file, prefix list, peer contract — not a pile of screenshots)

Example: site default missing, edge BGP down
This is a complete runbook you could actually keep. Placeholders are in angle brackets. Do not paste it into production until the names match your network.
Title: Site default route missing / edge BGP session down
Service / scope: <site-edge>, routers <edge-rtr> and <core-rtr>,
                 default of last resort for <site-prefixes>, eBGP to <peer-asn>
Severity if this fires: SEV1 if the site has no other default; SEV2 if the
                 second edge is still advertising a default
Trigger / symptoms:
  - users at <site> cannot reach off-site prefixes
  - monitoring: eBGP session <edge-rtr> to <peer-ip> is not Established
  - <edge-rtr> has no default, or the default’s next hop is recursive-fail
Author / last reviewed: <name>, <YYYY-MM-DD>

Pre-checks:
  1. Confirm impact. Can a host on <site-prefix> reach a known off-site
     address? Can it reach <edge-rtr>? Write the test and the result.
  2. Confirm the second edge (if any) is still up, so you know the severity.
  3. Look at the last change: last commit / last human session / last
     netlab or config push to <edge-rtr> or the peer. Do not roll it back yet.
  4. Save a snapshot (see Evidence, below) before you clear a counter or
     bounce a session.

Procedure:
  Step 1 — session state
    Action: on <edge-rtr>, show the BGP session to <peer-ip>
            (FRR: show bgp summary / show bgp neighbors <peer-ip>).
    Expected: state Established, prefixes received > 0 if this peer
              should send a default or a full table.
    If not: record last error / last reset reason / how long it has been down.
    Evidence: dated text file, command + output.

  Step 2 — reachability of the peer
    Action: from <edge-rtr>, check the connected route and ARP/ND entry
            for <peer-ip>, and a one-shot ping or a TCP check to the
            session port if policy allows.
    Expected: on-link next hop resolved, no FAILED neighbor, the
              interface is up.
    If not: this is a link or L2 problem, not a policy problem. Do not
            start editing route-maps.

  Step 3 — policy and last change
    Action: if the session is up but the default is missing, compare the
            inbound policy and the received default (or lack of it) with
            the last known-good config.
    Expected: a default (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0) accepted, next hop resolvable.
    If not: prefer rolling back the last policy change on *this* box
            over inventing a new one during the incident.

  Step 4 — rollback or escalate
    Action: if Step 3 pointed at our last change, apply the rollback
            in Rollback, below. If the peer appears to have withdrawn
            the default, escalate with the evidence pack; do not “fix”
            it by redistributing something you did not run a drill for.

Rollback:
  Condition: a config change on <edge-rtr> in the last change window
             is the likely cause, AND the second path (if any) is still
             safe, AND you have the snapshot from pre-check 4.
  Undo: revert that change only; do not combine it with an unrelated edit.
        Re-run Step 1 and the impact test.

Escalation:
  If the session stays down after the link is verified, or if rollback
  did not restore the default within <N minutes>, call <role> and send
  the evidence pack. If this is a peer-side withdrawal, call <peer-contact>
  with times in UTC and the last-error text, not a theory.

References:
  Topology / addressing: <path>
  Peer ASN and expected prefixes: <path>
The commands are deliberately not spelled out as a vendor cookbook. Your runbook should name the exact CLI for the NOS you run, after you have tried it in a lab.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
An incident-note template
Write this as the event unfolds, not the next morning. Use UTC in the timeline (and add local time once, in the header, if your team lives in one zone). Asia/Calcutta is UTC+5:30; a note that says “1:30” with no zone is how reviews go wrong.
Incident: <short impact statement>
Severity: SEV<n> (and why)
Start (UTC):
Detected by:          (alert, user, drill)
Status:               (investigating / mitigating / monitoring / closed)
Local time note:      (e.g. Asia/Calcutta = UTC+5:30; used only as a hint)
Recorder:

Impact:
  Who / what is broken, what still works, workaround if any.

Timeline (UTC):
  HH:MM  observation or action. Evidence: <filename or link>.
  HH:MM  hypothesis considered: …  rejected because: …
  HH:MM  change made: …  rollback plan: …

Evidence index:
  - 2026-11-13T191200Z-edge-rtr-bgp-summary.txt
  - 2026-11-13T191400Z-edge-rtr-ip-route.txt

Hypotheses:
  - …
Current status:
Follow-ups:           (owner, due, “update runbook X”)

Example timeline (fictional, no fake command output)
Incident: Site office cannot reach off-site prefixes; eBGP on edge-rtr appears down
Severity: SEV2 (backup edge still advertises a default; office is on the backup)
Start (UTC): 2026-11-13 19:06
Detected by: user report, then the session-down alert
Status: monitoring
Local time note: Asia/Calcutta, UTC+5:30
Recorder: <name>

Impact:
  About 40 users at <site> are on the backup edge. Primary edge is not
  passing a default. Internal site traffic is normal.

Timeline (UTC):
  19:06  user report: off-site sites slow or failing. Ticket opened.
  19:08  alert: eBGP <edge-rtr> to <peer-ip> not Established.
  19:10  pre-checks: backup edge is up; last config push to <edge-rtr>
         was 18:40 UTC (policy change). Snapshot saved
         (2026-11-13T191000Z-edge-rtr-*.txt).
  19:12  session is Idle/Active, last error recorded in the snapshot.
         Peer ARP entry is REACHABLE; link is up. Not an L2 miss.
  19:18  hypothesis “fibre cut” rejected (link up, ARP ok).
         hypothesis “last policy change” still open.
  19:22  rollback of the 18:40 UTC change on <edge-rtr> only.
  19:24  session Established; default present; users recovering.
  19:40  monitoring; no further changes.

Follow-ups:
  - Review the 18:40 policy in a lab before it is re-applied (owner: …).
  - Add a runbook pre-check: “diff against last-known-good before commit.”
  - Alert fired two minutes late; check the poll interval (SEV4).
There is no pasted show output on purpose. The output lives in the evidence files.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Evidence discipline

Save first. A command’s output goes into a dated file (<UTC-timestamp>-<device>-<check>.txt) before you bounce a session, clear a counter, or reboot. If safety requires an immediate action (the box is on fire), take the action and write that you could not snapshot.
Write the command in the file, not only the output, and the device and the time.
Note the clock. If NTP is wrong, every timestamp in the note is a guess; say so.
Do not clear counters to “get a clean look” until the first snapshot exists. You cannot un-clear them.
Point, do not paste walls. The incident note lists files. The ticket can attach them. This also reduces the chance of pasting a key or a community string into a channel that is wider than you think.
Tools you already have chapters for — ss, tcpdump, mtr, ip neigh, BGP show — are sources of evidence, not a substitute for the note.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Communication
While the incident is open, other people need one sentence they can repeat:

SEV2: office traffic is on the backup edge; we are rolling back the 18:40 UTC policy on the primary; next update at 19:35 UTC.

That sentence has severity, impact, current action, and a next-update time. It does not contain a theory about the vendor. Customer-facing or class-facing lines should be even plainer (“off-site access is on a backup path; we are restoring the primary”). The rollback condition belongs in the runbook and in the note (“if the session is not Established by 19:30 UTC, undo step 4”).

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
After the incident
Three kinds of leftover, and they are not the same:

Runbook edit. A missing pre-check, a wrong command, a stale peer IP. Do this before the memory fades.
A drill. If you only discovered the failure in production, add a lab or lab-host-track style drill that reproduces it safely.
A tracked follow-up. Capacity, a missing alert, unclear ownership, a policy that should not have shipped. An owner and a date, or it did not happen.

A write-up that only says “root cause: human error” teaches nothing. Name the change, the missing check, and the document that will carry the check next time.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Gotchas

Runbooks made of screenshots. They rot on the first CLI redesign and they are unsearchable. Prefer commands and expected conditions (“state is Established,” “a default is present”).
“Restart it” as step 1. A restart can clear the only evidence you had, and it is not a diagnosis. If a restart is the actual fix, it is a late step, after a snapshot, with a rollback if the box does not come back.
Notes written the next day from memory. Times will be wrong and two actions will collapse into one. Keep the timeline in the moment, even if it is ugly.
Fixing two things at once. You will not know which one restored service, and you will not know what to put in the runbook.
No rollback plan. Every change during an incident needs an undo, written before the change.
Secrets in the ticket. Community strings, private keys, pastes from startup-config. Evidence files can be restricted; a group chat usually cannot.
A runbook that has never been walked. If nobody has followed it in a drill, assume a step is wrong.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Boring rule
Write the procedure when you are calm, take notes when you are not, and put evidence in dated files before you change the network.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Try this

Pick one failure you already know how to cause in a lab (a BGP session shut, a missing VLAN on a trunk, a static route typo). Write a runbook for it using the template, then run the failure and follow the runbook as written. Edit whatever was wrong.
During that drill, keep an incident note in UTC with an evidence index. Have a second person try to reconstruct the story from the note alone.
Take an old runbook (or a lab README) and remove every screenshot, replacing it with a command and an expected condition.
Add a “last reviewed” date and a six-month reminder. A runbook without a review date is already suspect.

title: Runbooks and Incident Notes
text:
Sources

The templates in this chapter (operator practice for a small network; adapt them)
RFC 2350, Expectations for Computer Security Incident Response, for the idea of a published, reviewed CSIRT document — not as a process you must adopt wholesale
Your own lab-host-track failure drills and the troubleshooting chapters in this book, as the place the evidence comes from

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Why Encapsulate
Encapsulation is not a fashion—it is how networks reuse an underlay while giving tenants or sites a different topology, address space, or policy domain. This chapter builds durable models before GRE/IPsec/VXLAN/EVPN syntax (Containerlab + FRR + Linux, mid-2026 free path).

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Separate underlay from overlay responsibilities

List reasons to tunnel or encapsulate (and reasons not to)

Trace a packet through outer/inner headers

Predict MTU, ECMP entropy, and troubleshooting failure modes

Map encapsulation choices to common design problems

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
The core picture
        overlay topology (what apps believe)
     ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────┐
     │  site A  │ ······· │  site B  │
     └────┬─────┘         └────┬─────┘
          │  encapsulated path │
     ┌────▼─────────────────────▼────┐
     │     underlay IP fabric/WAN     │
     └───────────────────────────────┘







Plane
Job




Underlay
Deliver outer packets between tunnel endpoints (IP reachability, IGP/BGP, ECMP)


Overlay
Present virtual links, L2 segments, or VRFs to tenants/sites


Control (overlay)
Who is where (EVPN-class, controller, static maps)


Data (overlay)
Encapsulation format (VXLAN, GRE, Geneve, IPsec…)






Underlay vs overlay

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Why people encapsulate



Driver
What encapsulation buys




Overlap addresses
Two tenants both use 10.0.0.0/8


L2 adjacency over L3
VM mobility, some clusters, legacy apps


Policy domains
Separate routing tables / VRFs


Traffic engineering
Steer logical topology ≠ physical


Multi-site stretch
Same segment in two DCs (careful!)


Security boundary
IPsec provides crypto + integrity


Abstraction
Apps ignore underlay renumbering

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Why not to encapsulate



Temptation
Cost




Tunnel everything by default
MTU tax, state, debug opacity


Stretch L2 globally
Failure domains explode


Overlay without underlay skill
“EVPN down” actually IGP down


Double NAT + tunnel + hairpin
Undebuggable piles



Rule: prefer plain IP routing until a requirement forces an overlay.

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Encapsulation as Russian dolls



Encapsulation


Example mental stack (VXLAN-ish):
[ Eth ][ IP underlay ][ UDP ][ VXLAN ][ Eth inner ][ IP inner ][ TCP ][ payload ]



Header
Owned by




Outer IP
Underlay endpoints (VTEPs / tunnel routers)


Outer L4
Often UDP for ECMP entropy (VXLAN)


Overlay header
VNI / keys / flags


Inner frame
Tenant



GRE classic:
[ Eth ][ IP ][ GRE ][ IP inner ][ ...]
IPsec tunnel mode adds crypto headers and often transports inner IP.

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Identifiers you must name



Identifier
Role




Tunnel endpoint IP
Underlay address of VTEP/router


VNI / VPN id / GRE key
Separates segments


VRF
Routing table isolation


Route target / RD (EVPN/MPLS-ish)
Control-plane membership


Mapping
End-host IP/MAC → endpoint



Without a clear mapping system (static, flood-and-learn, EVPN), overlays become amateur radio.

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Failure domains
Underlay down → all overlays using it down
One VTEP down → locals on that leaf isolated from fabric overlay
VNI mis-map → blackhole or cross-tenant leak (severe)
MTU blackhole → big packets die, small pings live
Always ask: is this underlay, overlay data, or overlay control?

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
MTU tax
Every header steals bytes. If underlay MTU is 1500 and you add ~50–100 bytes, inner needs lower MTU or underlay needs jumbo.



Symptom
Likely




Ping works, TCP hangs
PMTUD broken + encapsulation


Only large transfers fail
MTU


DF set drops
Need clamp or larger underlay



Lab habit: set explicit MTU on overlay interfaces and test large pings.
ping -M do -s 1472 10.0.0.1   # classic Ethernet payload probe
# inside overlay, lower size until success; compute header tax

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
ECMP and entropy
Underlays load-balance on outer five-tuple. If outer UDP/TCP ports are fixed, many inner flows hash to one path → polarization.



Design
Entropy




VXLAN UDP source port from inner flow hash
Good


GRE without entropy helpers
Often poor


IPsec without cleverness
Can polarize



When debugging “uneven spines,” check outer headers, not only inner apps.

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Control plane vs data plane (again)




Data plane only
With control plane




Static GRE
Manual who-to-whom
—


Flood-and-learn VXLAN
Dynamic MAC via flood
Limited scale


EVPN-class
Advertises reachability
Mapping distributed



This book’s later chapters: site tunnels (mostly static/service), VXLAN data plane, EVPN intro where free images allow.

title: Why Encapsulate
section: Mini lab — see encapsulation with tcpdump
text:
Mini lab — see encapsulation with tcpdump
name: encap-why

topology:
  nodes:
    a:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils tcpdump
    b:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils tcpdump
    under:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils tcpdump
        - sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

  links:
    - endpoints: ["a:eth1", "under:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["b:eth1", "under:eth2"]

GRE between a and b across under
# addresses: a 10.0.0.1/24, under eth1 10.0.0.254; b 10.0.1.1/24, under eth2 10.0.1.254
# underlay route a↔b via under

docker exec clab-encap-why-a sh -c '
  ip tunnel add gre1 mode gre remote 10.0.1.1 local 10.0.0.1 ttl 64
  ip link set gre1 up
  ip addr add 172.16.0.1/30 dev gre1
'
docker exec clab-encap-why-b sh -c '
  ip tunnel add gre1 mode gre remote 10.0.0.1 local 10.0.1.1 ttl 64
  ip link set gre1 up
  ip addr add 172.16.0.2/30 dev gre1
'


Predict → observe → fix
docker exec clab-encap-why-a ping -c 2 172.16.0.2
docker exec clab-encap-why-under tcpdump -ni eth1 -c 5 proto gre
# or: tcpdump -ni eth1 proto 47
Predict: underlay capture shows outer IP a→b with GRE; inner ICMP not as plain on underlay without decap.
Observe: header stack.
Fix: if no gre, check tunnel remote/local and underlay ping 10.0.1.1 from a.

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Design questions checklist
Before choosing an overlay:

What problem is pure IP routing failing to solve?

L2 stretch or L3 VPN?

Who allocates VNIs / VRFs?

What is the underlay routing design?

MTU strategy?

How do we debug (mirror, drop counters, inner/outer captures)?

Failure domain acceptable?

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Mapping to the journey map
Models (planes, encap) 
  → underlay skill (L2/L3/IGP/BGP)
  → edge services
  → overlays (this part)
  → fabrics (scale the underlay + overlay)
Skipping underlay competence makes overlay chapters mystical.

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Common mistakes



Mistake
Symptom




Troubleshooting only inner
Miss underlay loss


Ignoring MTU
Mystery TCP issues


One giant L2 VNI
Broadcast storms / failure blast


No inventory of VNIs
Collisions and leaks


Encrypt + fragment chaos
Performance cliff

title: Why Encapsulate
text:
Summary

Encapsulation reuses underlays to build different logical networks

Always name underlay, overlay data, overlay control, and identifiers

MTU and ECMP entropy are not footnotes

Prefer routing until requirements force tunnels

A tiny GRE lab + tcpdump makes the model real

Next: site tunnels—practical GRE/IPsec-style site-to-site patterns on free Linux/FRR labs.

title: Site Tunnels
text:
Site Tunnels
Site-to-site tunnels connect islands of private addressing across a routed underlay (lab “Internet” or WAN). This chapter implements GRE and policy-based / route-based IPsec-style patterns with Linux in Containerlab, optionally fronted by FRR for routing (mid-2026 free tools).

title: Site Tunnels
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Build a GRE tunnel and route site prefixes across it

Explain route-based vs policy-based VPN approaches

Run a simple WireGuard or LibreSwan/strongSwan-style lab path (tool availability permitting)

Fail underlay links and predict overlay behavior

Clamp MTU and verify with large pings and tcpdump

title: Site Tunnels
section: When site tunnels are the right tool
text:
When site tunnels are the right tool







Use
Not the first tool for




Two branches over untrusted WAN
DC fabric east-west (use fabric overlay)


Quick lab multi-site
Massive multi-tenant scale (EVPN fabrics)


Crypto requirement
Cleartext GRE alone on hostile nets

title: Site Tunnels
text:
Topology — two sites + “Internet”
h1--siteA--\                /--siteB--h2
            +---- inet ----+
name: site-tun

topology:
  nodes:
    sitea:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils tcpdump iptables wireguard-tools || true
    siteb:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils tcpdump iptables wireguard-tools || true
    inet:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils tcpdump
        - sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils

  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sitea:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "siteb:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["sitea:eth2", "inet:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["siteb:eth2", "inet:eth2"]

title: Site Tunnels
text:
Addressing plan



Object
Address




Site A LAN
192.168.10.0/24 (sitea .1, h1 .10)


Site B LAN
192.168.20.0/24 (siteb .1, h2 .10)


sitea WAN
198.51.100.1/30


inet eth1
198.51.100.2/30


siteb WAN
203.0.113.1/30


inet eth2
203.0.113.2/30


GRE outer
WAN IPs


GRE inner
10.255.255.0/30 (.1 a, .2 b)



# site A
docker exec clab-site-tun-sitea sh -c '
  sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
  ip addr add 192.168.10.1/24 dev eth1; ip link set eth1 up
  ip addr add 198.51.100.1/30 dev eth2; ip link set eth2 up
  ip route add 203.0.113.0/30 via 198.51.100.2
'
docker exec clab-site-tun-h1 sh -c '
  ip addr add 192.168.10.10/24 dev eth1; ip link set eth1 up
  ip route add default via 192.168.10.1
'
# site B + h2 analogous with 192.168.20.0/24 and 203.0.113.1
docker exec clab-site-tun-inet sh -c '
  ip addr add 198.51.100.2/30 dev eth1; ip link set eth1 up
  ip addr add 203.0.113.2/30 dev eth2; ip link set eth2 up
'

title: Site Tunnels
text:
Lab 1 — GRE + static routes
docker exec clab-site-tun-sitea sh -c '
  ip tunnel add gre1 mode gre remote 203.0.113.1 local 198.51.100.1 ttl 64
  ip link set gre1 up mtu 1400
  ip addr add 10.255.255.1/30 dev gre1
  ip route add 192.168.20.0/24 dev gre1
'
docker exec clab-site-tun-siteb sh -c '
  ip tunnel add gre1 mode gre remote 198.51.100.1 local 203.0.113.1 ttl 64
  ip link set gre1 up mtu 1400
  ip addr add 10.255.255.2/30 dev gre1
  ip route add 192.168.10.0/24 dev gre1
'

Predict

Underlay: sitea pings 203.0.113.1

Overlay: h1 pings h2

tcpdump on inet shows GRE (proto 47), not plain inner ICMP as clear tenant IP without decap context



Observe
docker exec clab-site-tun-sitea ping -c 2 203.0.113.1
docker exec clab-site-tun-h1 ping -c 3 192.168.20.10
docker exec clab-site-tun-inet tcpdump -ni eth1 -c 8 proto 47
docker exec clab-site-tun-sitea ip route get 192.168.20.10


Fix







Symptom
Check




No underlay
inet addrs, routes


Underlay OK overlay fail
gre remote/local swap, routes to LAN via gre


One-way
missing return route

title: Site Tunnels
text:
Lab 2 — MTU blackhole drill
docker exec clab-site-tun-h1 ping -c 2 -M do -s 1472 192.168.20.10
docker exec clab-site-tun-h1 ping -c 2 -M do -s 1372 192.168.20.10

Predict
Large DF pings fail; smaller succeed if gre mtu 1400.
Fix: lower inner interface MTU, TCP MSS clamp, or raise underlay MTU.
docker exec clab-site-tun-sitea iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu

title: Site Tunnels
text:
Lab 3 — Underlay failure
docker exec clab-site-tun-inet ip link set eth2 down
docker exec clab-site-tun-h1 ping -c 5 192.168.20.10
docker exec clab-site-tun-inet ip link set eth2 up

Predict
Overlay dies with underlay; no magic. Multi-homed underlay would need dual tunnels + routing.

title: Site Tunnels
text:
Route-based vs policy-based VPN








Model
Idea
Lab analogue




Route-based
Tunnel is an interface; RIB steers prefixes into it
GRE, WireGuard wg0, VTI


Policy-based
SPD selects traffic by ACL selectors for crypto
classic “interesting traffic” IPsec



Route-based composes better with dynamic routing (run OSPF/BGP over tunnel—carefully).

title: Site Tunnels
text:
Lab 4 — WireGuard route-based (if packages available)
# Generate keys on both sides (persist in lab folder for real work)
docker exec clab-site-tun-sitea sh -c '
  apk add --no-cache wireguard-tools
  wg genkey | tee /tmp/a.key | wg pubkey > /tmp/a.pub
'
# exchange pubs out of band in lab notes
docker exec clab-site-tun-sitea sh -c '
  ip link add wg0 type wireguard
  ip addr add 10.255.255.1/30 dev wg0
  wg set wg0 private-key /tmp/a.key listen-port 51820 \
    peer B_PUBLIC_KEY endpoint 203.0.113.1:51820 allowed-ips 192.168.20.0/24,10.255.255.2/32
  ip link set wg0 up
  ip route add 192.168.20.0/24 dev wg0
'
Mirror on siteb with allowed-ips 192.168.10.0/24. Open UDP 51820 on path (inet forwards by default).

Predict → observe
docker exec clab-site-tun-h1 ping -c 3 192.168.20.10
docker exec clab-site-tun-inet tcpdump -ni eth1 -c 5 udp port 51820
docker exec clab-site-tun-sitea wg show
If wireguard-tools or kernel module missing in container, treat as optional—GRE still teaches site tunnels. Host-level WireGuard between namespaces is an alternate craft path from lab-craft chapters.

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
text:
WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
The site-tunnel chapter used WireGuard as one route-based VPN option among several. This chapter opens it up. WireGuard has two ideas you must understand before you run it in production. Cryptokey routing means that a peer’s AllowedIPs list is both its routing table and its source-address filter. The optional pre-shared key (PSK) is a 32-byte symmetric secret mixed into every handshake. In 2026 the PSK is getting attention as a cheap post-quantum hedge: VPN providers now generate it by default for router and native-client configs. Both ideas are easy to misconfigure, and both fail silently. This chapter makes them fail on purpose in a two-namespace lab and reads the evidence.

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Build a WireGuard tunnel between two Linux network namespaces with wg and ip, without config files
Explain why AllowedIPs drops a correctly encrypted packet and where that drop is counted
Recognise WireGuard’s “no peer for this destination” behaviour
Add a PSK, explain exactly what it does and does not protect against, and rotate it live
Diagnose a PSK mismatch from a packet capture (both handshake messages are on the wire, yet the tunnel never comes up)

Lab platform: Debian 13, Linux 6.12, wireguard-tools v1.0.20210914 (the current Debian package), iproute2, tcpdump 4.99.5. All commands need root. Every output below is pasted from a run.

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
text:
Concepts in one page
           siteA (198.51.100.1)                         siteB (198.51.100.2)
 ┌────────────────────────────────────┐ veth "internet" ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ wg0 10.0.0.1/24                    │◄──── UDP ──────►│ wg0 10.0.0.2/24     lo 192.0.2.1/24│
 │ peer B: allowed 10.0.0.2/32,       │   51820         │ peer A: allowed 10.0.0.1/32        │
 │         192.0.2.0/24               │                 │                                    │
 └────────────────────────────────────┘                 └────────────────────────────────────┘







Direction
What AllowedIPs does




Outbound (a packet leaves via wg0)
Longest-prefix match of the destination against every peer’s AllowedIPs picks the peer, and so the key and endpoint. No match means the packet is not sent, and the sender gets an error.


Inbound (a packet arrives and decrypts)
The decrypted inner source must fall inside the AllowedIPs of the peer whose key decrypted it. Otherwise it is dropped.



The kernel route only gets a packet to wg0. AllowedIPs decides which peer, if any.
The handshake is Noise IKpsk2 (Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2s). There are two messages. The initiation (type 1, 148 bytes of UDP payload) carries the initiator’s encrypted static key and a timestamp. The response (type 2, 92 bytes) carries the responder’s ephemeral key and an empty AEAD box. The PSK is hashed into the chaining key while the response is being built. Without a PSK the protocol uses 32 zero bytes in its place.
What the PSK buys: if Curve25519 is broken later (the “harvest now, decrypt later” scenario with a large quantum computer), traffic recorded today stays confidential, provided the PSK itself was never exposed. What it does not buy: it is not a post-quantum key exchange, it does not replace the public keys, and a PSK that was sent over a classical channel (for example a TLS session protected by ECDHE) is only as strong as that channel. Protocols such as Rosenpass run a post-quantum key exchange alongside WireGuard and feed the result into the PSK slot, rotating it. That is the direction to take when this matters.

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
text:
Lab build
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-up.sh - two namespaces, a veth "internet", and a WireGuard tunnel between them
set -euo pipefail
ip netns add siteA; ip netns add siteB
ip link add vA netns siteA type veth peer name vB netns siteB
ip -n siteA addr add 198.51.100.1/24 dev vA; ip -n siteA link set vA up; ip -n siteA link set lo up
ip -n siteB addr add 198.51.100.2/24 dev vB; ip -n siteB link set vB up; ip -n siteB link set lo up

umask 077
for s in A B; do wg genkey | tee $s.key | wg pubkey > $s.pub; done
wg genpsk > ab.psk

# create wg0 inside each namespace: a WireGuard interface sends its UDP from the namespace it was born in
ip -n siteA link add wg0 type wireguard
ip -n siteB link add wg0 type wireguard
ip netns exec siteA wg set wg0 private-key A.key listen-port 51820 \
   peer "$(cat B.pub)" preshared-key ab.psk endpoint 198.51.100.2:51820 allowed-ips 10.0.0.2/32,192.0.2.0/24
ip netns exec siteB wg set wg0 private-key B.key listen-port 51820 \
   peer "$(cat A.pub)" preshared-key ab.psk endpoint 198.51.100.1:51820 allowed-ips 10.0.0.1/32
ip -n siteA addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev wg0; ip -n siteA link set wg0 up
ip -n siteB addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev wg0; ip -n siteB link set wg0 up
# siteB also owns a LAN prefix that siteA routes into the tunnel
ip -n siteB addr add 192.0.2.1/24 dev lo
ip -n siteA route add 192.0.2.0/24 dev wg0
echo "lab up"
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-down.sh - remove everything lab-up.sh created
ip netns del siteA 2>/dev/null; ip netns del siteB 2>/dev/null
rm -f A.key A.pub B.key B.pub ab.psk wrong.psk
echo "lab down"
wg genpsk produces 32 random bytes in base64, the same format as a private key. The PSK is configured per peer and must be identical on both ends. umask 077 keeps the key files private. In production these values live in /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf (mode 600) or in your configuration management tool’s secret store, never in a world-readable file.
$ sudo ./lab-up.sh
lab up
$ sudo ip netns exec siteA ping -c 2 10.0.0.2 | tail -2
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1015ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.547/0.590/0.633/0.043 ms
$ sudo ip netns exec siteA wg show
interface: wg0
  public key: SfKQSp7pB2JRf6CnHF048gHOIul0sUi0k9lCH/V9P2I=
  private key: (hidden)
  listening port: 51820

peer: SVXjcMNZVP6LGPEc+CYMNGGQ0/4KHY05bo34Oc5MuVg=
  preshared key: (hidden)
  endpoint: 198.51.100.2:51820
  allowed ips: 10.0.0.2/32, 192.0.2.0/24
  latest handshake: 1 second ago
  transfer: 348 B received, 404 B sent
$ sudo ip -n siteA link show wg0
3: wg0: <POINTOPOINT,NOARP,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1420 qdisc noqueue state UNKNOWN mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000
The handshake completed on the first ping (latest handshake: 1 second ago), and wg show reports the PSK as (hidden). Its presence is visible and its value is not. The interface MTU is 1420 by default. That leaves room for the outer IPv6 header (40), UDP (8), and WireGuard’s 32 bytes of data-message overhead (a 16-byte header plus a 16-byte Poly1305 tag) inside a 1500-byte path. Over IPv4 there are 20 bytes to spare.

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
section: Drill 1: cryptokey routing drops a perfectly encrypted packet
text:
Drill 1: cryptokey routing drops a perfectly encrypted packet
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# drill-cryptokey.sh - AllowedIPs is a routing table outbound and a source filter inbound
set -euo pipefail
ip -n siteA addr add 203.0.113.5/32 dev lo           # an address siteB never allowed for this peer
echo "== inside the allowed source (10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.0.2)"
ip netns exec siteA ping -c 2 -W 1 10.0.0.2 | tail -2
echo "== outside it (203.0.113.5 -> 10.0.0.2)"
ip netns exec siteA ping -c 3 -W 1 -I 203.0.113.5 10.0.0.2 | tail -2 || true
echo "== siteB wg0 counters (decrypted fine, then dropped: src not in peer's allowed-ips)"
ip -n siteB -s link show wg0 | sed -n '3,4p'
echo "== a route into wg0 that no peer's allowed-ips covers"
ip -n siteA route add 198.18.0.0/15 dev wg0
ip netns exec siteA ping -c 1 -W 1 198.18.0.1 2>&1 | head -2 || true
$ sudo ./drill-cryptokey.sh
== inside the allowed source (10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.0.2)
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1028ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.138/0.334/0.531/0.196 ms
== outside it (203.0.113.5 -> 10.0.0.2)
3 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 2040ms

== siteB wg0 counters (decrypted fine, then dropped: src not in peer's allowed-ips)
    RX:  bytes packets errors dropped  missed   mcast           
           660       5      3       0       0       0 
== a route into wg0 that no peer's allowed-ips covers
PING 198.18.0.1 (198.18.0.1) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.0.0.1 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable
Read it in order:

From the allowed source, the ping works.
From 203.0.113.5, siteA’s kernel still routes the packet into wg0, because the destination 10.0.0.2 matches peer B’s AllowedIPs. WireGuard encrypts it and siteB decrypts it successfully. Then siteB checks the inner source against peer A’s AllowedIPs (10.0.0.1/32), finds no match, and drops it. The only trace is the RX errors counter on siteB’s wg0 (3 packets, one per ping). Nothing is logged, and no ICMP message goes back.
A destination that the kernel routes into wg0 but that no peer allows (198.18.0.0/15) is never sent. WireGuard rejects it at transmit, and the sender sees Destination Host Unreachable.

That makes AllowedIPs a security boundary as well as a convenience. A peer that holds a valid key still cannot inject traffic from addresses it was not given. The flip side is that every new subnet behind a peer means editing AllowedIPs on both sides: the outbound list on one end, the inbound filter on the other.

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
section: Drill 2: a PSK mismatch, seen from the wire
text:
Drill 2: a PSK mismatch, seen from the wire
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# drill-psk-mismatch.sh - same keypairs, different PSK on each side: the handshake never completes
set -euo pipefail
umask 077; wg genpsk > wrong.psk
# re-adding the peer throws away its current session, forcing a new handshake
for ns in siteA siteB; do
  peer=$(ip netns exec $ns wg show wg0 peers)
  ep=$(ip netns exec $ns wg show wg0 endpoints | cut -f2)
  aips=$(ip netns exec $ns wg show wg0 allowed-ips | cut -f2 | tr ' ' ',')
  psk=ab.psk; [ $ns = siteB ] && psk=wrong.psk
  ip netns exec $ns wg set wg0 peer "$peer" remove
  ip netns exec $ns wg set wg0 peer "$peer" preshared-key $psk endpoint "$ep" allowed-ips "$aips"
done
ip netns exec siteB timeout 8 tcpdump -lnni vB -c 4 udp port 51820 2>/dev/null &
sleep 1
ip netns exec siteA ping -c 3 -W 1 10.0.0.2 | tail -2 || true
wait
echo "siteA latest-handshake (0 = never):"; ip netns exec siteA wg show wg0 latest-handshakes
echo "siteB latest-handshake (0 = never):"; ip netns exec siteB wg show wg0 latest-handshakes
$ sudo ./drill-psk-mismatch.sh
03:40:05.224460 IP 198.51.100.1.51820 > 198.51.100.2.51820: UDP, length 148
03:40:05.224668 IP 198.51.100.2.51820 > 198.51.100.1.51820: UDP, length 92
3 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 2049ms

03:40:10.317113 IP 198.51.100.1.51820 > 198.51.100.2.51820: UDP, length 148
03:40:10.317315 IP 198.51.100.2.51820 > 198.51.100.1.51820: UDP, length 92
siteA latest-handshake (0 = never):
SVXjcMNZVP6LGPEc+CYMNGGQ0/4KHY05bo34Oc5MuVg=    0
siteB latest-handshake (0 = never):
SfKQSp7pB2JRf6CnHF048gHOIul0sUi0k9lCH/V9P2I=    0
This is the most confusing failure in WireGuard, and the capture explains it:

The 148-byte initiation goes out, and siteB accepts it. The initiation is authenticated with the static keys and does not depend on the PSK, so siteB has no reason to be silent.
siteB answers with a 92-byte response. It mixes its PSK into the chaining key while building that response, so the empty AEAD box inside is sealed under a key that siteA cannot derive.
siteA fails to open the response and discards it without logging. About five seconds later (REKEY_TIMEOUT plus jitter) it tries again. Note the timestamps.
Neither side records a handshake (0 means never).

So “packets in both directions on UDP 51820, tunnel down” points to a PSK mismatch (or a corrupted PSK). A wrong public key looks different: the responder cannot authenticate the initiation, so it sends nothing back, and you see only the 148-byte packets.

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
section: Drill 3: fix and rotate the PSK live
text:
Drill 3: fix and rotate the PSK live
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# drill-psk-fix.sh - put the right PSK back on siteB (live, no restart) and watch the tunnel recover
set -euo pipefail
peer=$(ip netns exec siteB wg show wg0 peers)
ip netns exec siteB wg set wg0 peer "$peer" preshared-key ab.psk
ip netns exec siteA ping -c 8 -W 1 10.0.0.2 | tail -2
now=$(date +%s)
for ns in siteA siteB; do
  echo "$ns latest handshake: $(( now - $(ip netns exec $ns wg show wg0 latest-handshakes | cut -f2) )) s ago"
done
$ sudo ./drill-psk-fix.sh
8 packets transmitted, 8 received, 0% packet loss, time 7114ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.268/1859.476/5006.915/1836.351 ms, pipe 5
siteA latest handshake: 2 s ago
siteB latest handshake: 2 s ago
$ sudo ./lab-down.sh
lab down
wg set ... preshared-key changes the PSK on a running interface. Existing sessions keep their keys until the next handshake, and new handshakes use the new PSK. Here the first ping waited for siteA’s next retry (the 5-second maximum RTT), and after that the tunnel ran normally. To rotate a PSK in production, change both ends inside one rekey window (sessions rekey about every two minutes) so that at most one handshake attempt fails. Or let a key-exchange daemon do it for you.

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
text:
Deploying it for real

Generate a separate PSK per peer pair with wg genpsk. One PSK shared across a whole fleet becomes a single secret whose leak removes the hedge for everyone.
Distribute it like a private key, over a channel you would trust in 2040: out of band, through a secret store, or from a post-quantum key exchange. A PSK pasted into a TLS-protected web form is protected only by that TLS session.
Store it with the private key: PresharedKey = ... under [Peer] in wg0.conf (mode 600), or PresharedKeyFile= in a systemd-networkd .netdev.
Monitor the handshake age. wg show wg0 latest-handshakes returns epoch seconds. Alert when the value is 0 or older than about three minutes for a peer that should be up.
Watch RX errors on wg0. A rising count usually means AllowedIPs is filtering traffic someone expects to pass.

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
text:
Verification checklist

wg show lists preshared key: (hidden) on both ends for every peer that should have one
latest-handshakes is recent (non-zero and under about 3 minutes) on both ends
Capture shows both 148-byte initiations and 92-byte responses, and data packets follow
Each remote prefix appears in the sender’s AllowedIPs and in the receiver’s AllowedIPs for the return path
ip -s link show wg0 RX errors are flat during normal traffic
Large pings at your path MTU (ping -M do -s 1392 over IPv4 with MTU 1420) succeed

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix

Initiations and responses on the wire, no handshake
Same wg genpsk value on both peers


Subnet added to the route but not to AllowedIPs
Destination Host Unreachable from the local wg0
Add the prefix to the peer’s AllowedIPs

Silent loss, RX errors on the far wg0

Traffic goes to the “wrong” peer (longest prefix wins, and a later wg set moves the prefix)

Calling the PSK “post-quantum encryption”

It is a symmetric hedge for recorded traffic. Distribute it safely or use a PQ key exchange


One fleet-wide PSK
One leak removes the hedge everywhere
One PSK per peer pair

title: WireGuard: Cryptokey Routing and the Pre-Shared Key
text:
Summary
WireGuard’s configuration is small because AllowedIPs does two jobs: it chooses the peer on the way out and filters the source on the way in, and both outcomes are silent unless you read wg show and the interface counters. The PSK adds a symmetric secret to the Noise IKpsk2 handshake. That protects recorded traffic against a future break of Curve25519, as long as the PSK itself stays secret. A PSK mismatch has a distinctive signature on the wire: both handshake messages appear and no session forms, because the responder cannot detect the mismatch and the initiator cannot open its reply. Rotate PSKs per peer pair, distribute them like private keys, and monitor handshake age.

title: OpenVPN Data Channel Offload (DCO)
text: OpenVPN Data Channel Offload (DCO)

title: OpenVPN Data Channel Offload (DCO)
text:
Thesis
Classic OpenVPN runs the control plane and the data plane in userspace. Every encrypted packet crosses the kernel↔︎userspace boundary twice. That copy-and-context-switch tax is why OpenVPN used to lose throughput races against kernel-native VPNs. Data Channel Offload (DCO) moves encryption, decryption, and encapsulation into a Linux kernel module (ovpn since Linux 6.16; earlier out-of-tree ovpn-dco / ovpn-dco-v2). Userspace OpenVPN keeps TLS, authentication, and option negotiation; the kernel keeps the hot path. The security model does not change — only where the ciphertext is processed. On modern hardware, published UDP benchmarks regularly show roughly 2× legacy OpenVPN throughput, and independent tests put DCO in the same ballpark as other high-performance VPN designs.

title: OpenVPN Data Channel Offload (DCO)
text:
Mental model
  Before DCO (userspace data path)          With DCO (kernel data path)

  NIC ──► kernel ──► openvpn(userspace)     NIC ──► kernel ovpn module
              │  encrypt / decrypt                     │  encrypt / decrypt
              │  encapsulate                           │  encapsulate
              ▼                                        ▼
         kernel ──► NIC                            NIC (no userspace hop)

  Control plane (TLS, auth, PUSH) stays in userspace either way.







Piece
Role




Control plane
TLS handshake, certificates, --push / NCP, peer lifecycle — always userspace


Data plane
AEAD encrypt/decrypt, tunnel encapsulation, peer forwarding — kernel with DCO


ovpn module
In-tree since Linux 6.16; needs OpenVPN 2.7+


ovpn-dco / backports
Out-of-tree path for kernels < 6.16 or OpenVPN 2.6.x


--disable-dco
Force the legacy userspace data path (benchmarks, unsupported options)



Cipher and topology constraints (by design). DCO is L3 / dev tun only. Supported data-channel ciphers are AES-GCM-128/192/256 and ChaCha20-Poly1305. Compression framing is out; servers use --topology subnet. Older CBC-only peers force a non-DCO fallback. Routing to clients uses the host routing table (a client VPN IP as nexthop) rather than OpenVPN’s internal iroute machinery — see the official README.dco.md.
Version pairing that matters in 2026:








Kernel / userspace
Module name
Notes




Linux ≥ 6.16 + OpenVPN ≥ 2.7
ovpn (in-tree)
Preferred; no DKMS on stock distro kernels


Older kernel or OpenVPN 2.6
ovpn-dco via ovpn-backports / distro DKMS
Still fine; package names differ by distro


Windows
ovpn-dco-win
Ships with official Windows builds since 2.6; multi-core workers improved further in 2026

title: OpenVPN Data Channel Offload (DCO)
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Confirm the kernel side before you touch configs
On a host that already runs Linux 6.16+ with OpenVPN 2.7+, you do not install a third-party module. Check what you have:
# dco-probe.sh — inventory for OpenVPN DCO (read-only; no packages installed here)
uname -r
modinfo ovpn 2>/dev/null | head -5 || echo "ovpn module metadata not present"
lsmod | grep -E '^ovpn' || echo "ovpn not loaded yet (normal until openvpn starts)"
openvpn --version 2>/dev/null | head -3 || echo "openvpn binary not on PATH"
Expected shape on a DCO-ready box (versions will differ):
$ uname -r
6.16.3-1-amd64
$ modinfo ovpn | head -3
filename:       /lib/modules/6.16.3-1-amd64/kernel/drivers/net/ovpn/ovpn.ko
description:    OpenVPN data channel offload
license:        GPL
If modinfo ovpn is missing on an older kernel, use the ovpn-backports project or your distro’s ovpn-dkms / kmod-ovpn package — not covered as an install lab in this chapter (no package installs in the book environment).


Case 2: Let OpenVPN auto-enable DCO (and force it off for A/B)
OpenVPN auto-detects DCO when the module is present and the config is compatible. You only need an explicit flag to disable it.
# Minimal server sketch — AEAD + subnet topology so DCO can engage
# openvpn-server-dco.conf
port 1194
proto udp
dev tun
topology subnet
server 10.8.0.0 255.255.255.0
dh none
tls-groups X25519:secp256r1
data-ciphers AES-256-GCM:AES-128-GCM:CHACHA20-POLY1305
persist-key
keepalive 10 60
verb 3
# certificates omitted — use your existing PKI
# Run with DCO (default when available):
#   openvpn --config openvpn-server-dco.conf
# Force userspace data path for a throughput comparison:
#   openvpn --config openvpn-server-dco.conf --disable-dco
Log lines to look for:







Message
Meaning




DCO / ovpn enabled (wording varies by version)
Kernel data path is live


Note: Kernel support for ovpn-dco missing, disabling data channel offload.
Module absent or userspace too old for in-tree ovpn


Warning that an option disabled DCO
Config used a feature DCO cannot implement (compression, unsupported cipher, …)



Antonio Quartulli’s workstation numbers (Ryzen 9 9950X, 25 Gbps NIC, iperf3 UDP, published via the OpenVPN DCO guide, Feb 2026): legacy userspace ≈ 3.61 Gbps; DCO ≈ 7.15 Gbps — about 2× on the same box. Third-party reports (IPFire, consumer VPN vendors, router vendors) show similar order-of-magnitude gains; treat any single percentage as hardware-specific.


Case 3: One-sided DCO still helps
You do not need DCO on both ends for a win. A DCO server alone cuts server CPU and raises aggregate capacity; both ends DCO maximizes the path. Clients that speak OpenVPN 2.6+/Connect 3.4+ with AEAD are enough for the control plane to negotiate a DCO-capable data channel when the server supports it.
  laptop (no DCO) ──TLS──► gateway (DCO / ovpn)
       ▲                         │
       │   ciphertext still      │  encrypt/decrypt + forward
       └──── encrypted tunnel ───┘  stays in kernel on the gateway


Case 4: Routing mental shift under DCO
With DCO, “iroutes” become ordinary host routes whose nexthop is the client’s VPN address. Client-to-client is no longer a special userspace hairpin: packets hit the tunnel interface and the system routing table decides the next peer.
# Example: send 192.0.2.0/24 to the client that owns 10.8.0.5
# ip route add 192.0.2.0/24 via 10.8.0.5
If you still need a blackhole when that client is offline, add an explicit companion route that only exists while the peer is connected — DCO will not invent OpenVPN’s old internal routing table for you.

title: OpenVPN Data Channel Offload (DCO)
text:
The trap

CBC or compression “just for compatibility”. A single --data-ciphers entry that forces CBC, or leftover --compress, silently (or with a warning) drops you back to userspace. You keep the old config working and wonder why the benchmark looks unchanged.
OpenVPN 2.6 + in-tree ovpn. The Linux 6.16 ovpn module speaks the 2.7 netlink API. On 2.6 you still want the older ovpn-dco out-of-tree module (or upgrade userspace). Mixing them yields “kernel support missing” even though a DCO module is loaded.
Assuming DCO changes cryptography. It does not. TLS, certificates, and cipher selection stay in userspace; DCO only relocates AEAD packet processing. Threat modeling stays the same; capacity planning does not.
Comparing protocols by blog headlines alone. Marketing posts crown a winner every quarter. Measure your NIC, CPU crypto offload, and MTU. DCO removes OpenVPN’s historical userspace tax; it does not erase the need for sound AEAD choice, MSS clamping, and CPU affinity on multi-gigabit paths.

title: OpenVPN Data Channel Offload (DCO)
text:
The boring rule
Ship OpenVPN ≥ 2.7 on Linux ≥ 6.16 with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, --topology subnet, and no compression. Let DCO auto-enable. Keep --disable-dco in your lab toolkit for A/B tests. On older kernels, use the matching out-of-tree module — do not assume the in-tree ovpn name. Verify with modinfo / logs before you trust a speed claim.

title: OpenVPN Data Channel Offload (DCO)
text:
Try this

On a 6.16+ lab host, run modinfo ovpn and openvpn --version. Confirm the 2.7 + ovpn pairing.
Bring up a two-namespace UDP tunnel (reuse your existing PKI). Capture a short iperf3 run with DCO on, then the same run with --disable-dco. Record throughput and top CPU for openvpn.
Intentionally add a DCO-incompatible option (e.g. force a CBC cipher). Confirm the log shows DCO disabled, then remove it.
Add a host route via a client VPN IP and traceroute from the server VRF/namespace to prove DCO is using the system FIB.
