BLACKHOLE (RFC 7999, 0xFFFF029A or ASN:666): Signals transit providers and peers to discard all traffic destined for the prefix in hardware (Remote Triggered Blackholing).



Extended (RFC 4360) and Large Communities (RFC 8092)

Extended Communities (8 octets): Provide typed metadata such as Route Targets (RT) and Route Distinguishers (RD) in EVPN and MPLS-VPN deployments.
Large Communities (12 octets): Formatted as Global-Admin:Action:Function (e.g., 65000:1:100). Designed to support full 32-bit AS numbers alongside flexible operator tagging.

title: BGP Path Attributes and Policy Expression
section: ADD-PATH, GTSM and Modern Security Attributes
text:
ADD-PATH, GTSM and Modern Security Attributes

ADD-PATH (RFC 7911): By default, BGP only advertises its single best path to peers. ADD-PATH allows a router to advertise multiple alternative paths for the same prefix, each identified by a unique Path ID. This eliminates route-reflector hiding and accelerates convergence.
Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM, RFC 5082): Mitigates CPU denial-of-service by verifying that eBGP packets have traversed exactly one hop (TTL = 255).
BGP Only to Customer (OTC, RFC 9234): An attribute designed to enforce provider-customer hierarchy and automatically block route leaks.

title: The BGP Decision Process and Route Selection
text:
The BGP Decision Process and Route Selection
BGP receives advertisements for prefixes, applies policy, checks feasibility and selects paths. A best BGP path is not automatically the route used to forward a packet: it must be eligible for the main routing table, installed in the forwarding table, and match the destination more specifically than other installed prefixes. Route selection is a major security boundary because policy and validation determine which information can influence forwarding.

title: The BGP Decision Process and Route Selection
section: Follow a route through the router
text:
Follow a route through the router

Session and address family: an Established session only proves the BGP session is up. Check that the desired address family is negotiated and enabled, and that the peer actually advertises the prefix.
Import and eligibility: evaluate inbound policy, origin validation where configured, AS-loop rules, attribute handling, and next-hop resolution. An unresolved or rejected path may appear in some diagnostic views but cannot be assumed eligible. Implementations differ in whether they retain pre-policy paths and how they label them.
BGP selection: compare eligible paths for the same prefix using local policy and the implementation’s decision process. Document software version, options, defaults and any route-reflector behavior; there is no single vendor-independent list of every tie-breaker.
RIB and FIB: the selected BGP path competes with candidates from other sources according to the platform’s route preference and installation rules. The forwarding table must contain a usable next hop. A route can be BGP-best yet absent from the FIB because a static or IGP route wins or hardware installation fails.
Packet lookup and export: forwarding selects the longest matching installed prefix within the relevant forwarding table. Export policy independently decides what can be advertised to each peer. A path used locally is not necessarily exported, and an advertised path does not prove remote acceptance.

The RFC’s Adj-RIB-In, Loc-RIB and Adj-RIB-Out describe logical stages; they need not be implemented as three literal copies of every route. Commands named “received,” “accepted,” “best,” or “advertised” can expose different stages. Check the documentation for the exact command and policy visibility.

title: The BGP Decision Process and Route Selection
text:
Common decision inputs








Input
Typical treatment
Scope and caveats




Local proprietary preference, often called weight
Higher may win before standard attributes
Local to one router; not a BGP path attribute; range and order vary


LOCAL_PREF
Higher preferred
Internal AS policy; propagated to internal peers; normally not sent to external peers


Locally originated status
May be preferred
Placement and interpretation vary


AS_PATH length
Shorter commonly preferred when earlier criteria tie
AS sequence, AS sets and confederation segments have specific counting rules; configuration can change comparison


ORIGIN
IGP preferred to EGP, then incomplete
Attribute ordering, not proof the route is authentic or physically shorter


MED
Lower commonly preferred
Usually compared for routes from the same neighboring AS; missing values, grouping and always-compare options vary


eBGP versus iBGP
eBGP commonly preferred if earlier criteria tie
Confed and platform rules may differ


IGP cost to next hop
Lower often preferred
Hot-potato behavior depends on a reachable next hop and earlier tie-breaks


Later tie-breaks
Router ID, cluster information, peer address or path age may matter
Ordering, eligibility and oldest-path behavior are implementation-specific



Multipath is an implementation capability with its own eligibility rules. Multiple paths in the BGP table do not prove multiple next hops are installed or that traffic is distributed evenly. Inspect FIB next hops and test several flows; a single flow often follows one hash bucket.

title: The BGP Decision Process and Route Selection
text:
Worked comparisons
Assume the following explicit lab policy: both candidates are eligible for 203.0.113.0/24; higher LOCAL_PREF is considered before shorter AS_PATH; remaining attributes are equal. A has LOCAL_PREF 200 and path 64510 64496; B has LOCAL_PREF 100 and path 64520. A wins despite its longer AS_PATH. If A’s next hop becomes unresolvable, A is ineligible and B can win. Restoring reachability can restore A’s eligibility; observe both BGP and FIB changes rather than assuming an immediate switch.
For two paths received from the same neighboring AS, with all earlier criteria equal, MED 50 is typically preferred to MED 200. If the lower-MED path has a longer AS_PATH and that implementation compares AS_PATH before MED, the shorter path can win instead. MED comparison across different neighboring ASes depends on policy and implementation; compare-med and deterministic-MED settings affect outcomes and stability. Do not infer the winner from MED alone.
Now add an installed 203.0.113.128/25 via another path. A packet to 203.0.113.150 uses the /25, even if the /24 has higher BGP LOCAL_PREF, provided both are installed in the same forwarding table. LOCAL_PREF compares candidate paths for the same NLRI; it does not make an aggregate override a more-specific forwarding entry. Policy routing and VRFs can select a different table first.

title: The BGP Decision Process and Route Selection
text:
Security implications
An unauthorized shorter path or more-specific announcement can attract traffic where it is accepted and selected. It is not guaranteed to win globally: different networks apply different import policies, validation, prefix-length filters and preferences, and some may not receive the advertisement. Origin validation checks an origin against validated authorizations; it does not authenticate the complete AS path or prove that a route is leak-free. Prefer explicit import/export filters, maximum-prefix safeguards, validation policy, and monitoring of both accepted and rejected routes.
AS-path prepending is an external signal, not a command to remote networks. A remote AS can prefer a longer path because of its own policy, ignore some prepends, or see a different set of routes. Similarly, changing LOCAL_PREF generally controls your AS’s exit, not how another AS sends traffic toward you.

title: The BGP Decision Process and Route Selection
section: Troubleshoot a missing or unexpected route
text:
Troubleshoot a missing or unexpected route
For a specific prefix and neighbor, collect evidence in order:

Confirm the session, negotiated address family and counters; ask what the neighbor actually advertises. An Established session can carry zero accepted prefixes.
Inspect inbound policy, prefix length, AS-loop detection and validation state. Distinguish no advertisement from an advertisement rejected at import. A platform may not retain rejected pre-policy routes unless configured to do so.
Inspect all candidate paths, their next-hop resolution, eligibility flags and best-path reason. Confirm the routing table used for recursion and check that resolution does not depend recursively on the route itself.
Compare the BGP best path to the main RIB and FIB. Check VRF, address family, competing routes, hardware installation and longest matching prefixes.
Inspect export policy and the actual advertised route at the sending peer, then confirm reception at the remote peer. A route-refresh capability can request re-advertisement after an inbound policy change if supported; it does not force the peer to export a route its own policy denies. Resetting a session can disrupt unrelated prefixes.
Verify data traffic and the reverse path separately. Record timestamps so that transient convergence is not mistaken for a stable policy result.

title: The BGP Decision Process and Route Selection
text:
Practice
Use BGP MED, Prepend, and ECMP for the two-link topology, and BGP Policy for import/export controls. Before each change, record the peer’s advertised path, local pre- and post-policy view if available, best-path explanation, next-hop reachability and FIB. Change one attribute at a time, predict the winner, apply the policy using the platform’s documented refresh mechanism, and compare evidence. Withdraw next-hop reachability without dropping the BGP session, observe eligibility and forwarding, then restore it. Exact commands and observed behavior depend on the chosen NOS; these are exercises to validate in that environment.
Review: Why can an Established session have no usable routes? How can a /25 win over a /24 with higher LOCAL_PREF? What does a route refresh ask the peer to do, and what can export policy still prevent? Why is a shorter AS_PATH not a guarantee of global hijack success?
References: BGP-4, RFC 4271, Route Refresh, RFC 2918, and FRRouting BGP documentation. Consult the exact version of your implementation for its decision order and multipath rules.

title: Convergence, Stability and Propagation Dynamics
text:
Convergence, Stability and Propagation Dynamics
The global routing system is never in a perfectly static state. Across tens of thousands of networks, physical fiber cuts, hardware reboots, BFD timeouts, and maintenance windows trigger a continuous stream of BGP updates and withdrawals. Understanding how these updates ripple through the planetary topology—and how that dynamics can be weaponized—is essential for securing the routing control plane.

title: Convergence, Stability and Propagation Dynamics
section: Convergence Time and Global Propagation Delays
text:
Convergence Time and Global Propagation Delays
Convergence is the process by which all routers across the Internet transition from an old state to an agreed new consistent forwarding state following a topology change.
Unlike IGP link-state databases that synchronize in tens of milliseconds, interdomain BGP convergence operates on the order of seconds to minutes. The total delay is governed by four factors:
\[T_{\text{convergence}} = \sum (T_{\text{processing}} + T_{\text{MRAI}} + T_{\text{queuing}} + T_{\text{propagation}})\]

Minimum Route Advertisement Interval (MRAI, RFC 4271): To prevent routers from bombarding neighbors with continuous updates during a flap, BGP enforces a rate-limiting timer on eBGP sessions (historically default: 30 seconds; modern implementations allow 5 seconds or 0 seconds). A router cannot send successive updates for the same prefix until the MRAI timer expires.
Path Exploration (BGP Hunting): When a preferred path is withdrawn, a router does not immediately know that backup paths traversing the same failing link are also broken. It will iteratively explore each candidate path in order of length, advertising and withdrawing multiple intermediate paths before settling on the true surviving route.
Propagation Delay: Speed-of-light delays across transoceanic fiber links (e.g., London to Singapore: ~160 ms round-trip).

title: Convergence, Stability and Propagation Dynamics
text:
Route Flapping and Dampening (RFC 2439)
A route flap occurs when a prefix is repeatedly advertised and withdrawn in rapid succession. Left unchecked, a single flapping prefix on a flapping DSL line or unstable BGP session would force hundreds of thousands of routers worldwide to continuously recompute their FIBs.
To combat this, BGP Route Flap Dampening (RFD, RFC 2439) was introduced: - Every time a route flaps, the router adds a numerical penalty (typically \(1000\)). - If the penalty exceeds a configured Suppress Threshold (e.g., \(2000\)), the route is suppressed: the router stops using it and stops advertising it to peers, even if it is currently advertised as reachable. - While suppressed, the penalty decays exponentially according to a Half-Life timer (e.g., 15 minutes). - Once the penalty falls below a Reuse Threshold (e.g., \(750\)), the route is unsuppressed and restored to service.
Penalty
   ^
   |        +-- Flap 2 (Penalty = 2000) -> SUPPRESSED
   |       / \
   |      /   \ 
   |     /     \ Exponential Decay (Half-Life = 15m)
   |    +-- Flap 1 (Penalty = 1000)
   |   /         \
   +----------------------------------------------------> Time
              Reuse Threshold (750) -> RE-ENABLED

[!CAUTION] The RFD Trap: In the early 2000s, measurement research (Mao et al.) revealed that normal BGP path exploration during a single failover event caused benign prefixes to flap 3–5 times within seconds. Aggressive RFD suppressed legitimate networks for hours. Consequently, RIPE-378 and RFC 7454 advise operators to either disable RFD entirely or set conservative thresholds that only trigger on persistent, sustained oscillations.

title: Convergence, Stability and Propagation Dynamics
section: Hot Potato Routing and Path Instability
text:
Hot Potato Routing and Path Instability
In Hot-Potato Routing, an Autonomous System sheds outbound traffic at the closest exit router according to its internal IGP metric.
While computationally efficient, hot-potato routing ties interdomain forwarding decisions directly to intradomain topology. A link flap inside an ISP’s internal backbone can shift the lowest IGP metric from Exit Router \(A\) in Chicago to Exit Router \(B\) in Dallas. Because BGP recomputes the best path, the ISP sends an UPDATE with a changed NEXT_HOP to external peers, triggering global route churn despite the external destination remaining entirely stable.

title: Convergence, Stability and Propagation Dynamics
section: Slow Convergence as an Attack Surface
text:
Slow Convergence as an Attack Surface
The latency of interdomain convergence creates significant operational and security vulnerabilities:

Transient Forwarding Loops and Blackholes: During the minutes when Router \(A\) has converged to a new path but downstream Router \(B\) is still evaluating an old path, packets can bounce between routers in a transient loop or be dropped into a blackhole until TTL expires.
Volumetric Churn Attacks: An adversary with control of a flapping BGP speaker can intentionally cycle announcements and withdrawals at intervals timed to defeat MRAI filters, forcing upstream route processors to continuously consume CPU cycles in state recalculation.
Attack Opportunity Window: In an intentional origin hijacking attack, the minutes taken for global looking glasses and monitoring systems to converge and alert operators give attackers an uncontested window to intercept credentials or siphon cryptocurrency.

title: Convergence, Stability and Propagation Dynamics
text:
Measurement Data on Convergence Behavior
Data gathered from global route collection projects (RIPE RIS, RouteViews, CAIDA) indicates: - Up-Convergence (a newly announced prefix becoming globally reachable): typically achieves 95% global visibility within 10 to 45 seconds. - Down-Convergence (withdrawing an active prefix): can take 90 to 240 seconds due to path exploration across Tier-1 networks. - Over 60% of observed global routing updates are duplicate announcements or attribute modifications that do not change the underlying forwarding next-hop.

title: Historical Design Decisions and Their Security Consequences
text:
Historical Design Decisions and Their Security Consequences
The architectural weaknesses of interdomain routing are neither oversights nor accidental engineering flaws. They are the deliberate, logical consequences of design trade-offs made in the late 1980s and early 1990s under intense operational pressure to save a rapidly collapsing Internet.

title: Historical Design Decisions and Their Security Consequences
section: EGP, CGE and the Origins of Interdomain Routing Protocols
text:
EGP, CGE and the Origins of Interdomain Routing Protocols
In the early ARPANET and early NSFNET eras, the network was organized around a strict tree topology with a single centralized core backbone. The protocol used to connect external networks to this core was the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP, RFC 904).
EGP had severe limitations: - It was strictly a reachability protocol, incapable of detecting loops in arbitrary mesh topologies. - It required a single hierarchical root; it could not support horizontal peering between commercial networks. - As regional networks proliferated, the centralized architecture became an unsustainable bottleneck.
In 1989, during the “Three Dirt Clods” meeting (Kirk Lougheed of Cisco and Yakov Rekhter of IBM), BGP-1 was famously sketched on two ketchup-stained napkins (RFC 1105). BGP introduced the path-vector concept: by including the complete sequence of Autonomous Systems in the route announcement (AS_PATH), routers could detect and discard loops in arbitrary, uncoordinated mesh topologies without requiring a centralized backbone.

title: Historical Design Decisions and Their Security Consequences
section: The Scalability Imperative: Why End-to-End Verification Was Abandoned
text:
The Scalability Imperative: Why End-to-End Verification Was Abandoned
By 1993, the Internet faced an existential scaling crisis: the 32-bit IPv4 address space was depleting rapidly under classful allocation (\(A\), \(B\), \(C\)), and global routing tables were expanding exponentially. BGP-4 (RFC 1654, later RFC 4271) was developed specifically to introduce Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR, RFC 1519), allowing route aggregation and supernetting.
At the time, typical backbone routers operated with CPU clock speeds measured in tens of megahertz and RAM measured in megabytes. Adding cryptographic signatures to routing updates: - Would have required asymmetric public-key cryptography (RSA or DSA) on every router. - Would have caused packet-processing engines and control processors to grind to a halt. - Would have required a global, authoritative Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) when even the commercial DNS infrastructure was barely nascent.
The engineering consensus was unequivocal: scalability and survival took absolute precedence over cryptographic verification.

title: Historical Design Decisions and Their Security Consequences
section: The Trust Assumptions Embedded in BGP-4’s Design
text:
The Trust Assumptions Embedded in BGP-4’s Design
BGP-4 was architected on fundamental trust assumptions reflecting the collegial academic environment of the early Internet:

Physical Session Trust: It was assumed that if two organizations established a physical cable or leased line and configured a BGP peering session, they knew each other and could be trusted.
Implicit Origin Authority: If a peer announced an IP prefix \(P\), the receiver assumed the peer had legitimate authority to originate \(P\).
Implicit Path Honesty: It was assumed that intermediate transit networks would accurately append their own ASN to the AS_PATH and would not delete, reorder, or fabricate AS hops.
Benevolent Operation: Routing anomalies were viewed as rare equipment failures, not malicious asymmetric attacks by state actors or cybercriminals.

title: Historical Design Decisions and Their Security Consequences
section: Operational Flexibility Over Consistency: A Deliberate Choice
text:
Operational Flexibility Over Consistency: A Deliberate Choice
BGP was explicitly designed to allow operators to implement arbitrary, confidential business policies. An AS can modify attributes (LOCAL_PREF, MED, communities) arbitrarily on import and export without explaining its reasoning to its neighbors.
This design priority produced the Gao-Rexford model of Internet stability: routing converges stably if and only if commercial relationships follow strict hierarchical patterns (prefer customer over peer over provider). However, because policy expression is purely local and unauthenticated: - An operator cannot independently verify whether a path received from a neighbor represents the actual physical or topological path packets will take. - An operator cannot detect if an upstream peer is silently rewriting or stripping policy communities.

title: Historical Design Decisions and Their Security Consequences
section: Why Security Was Added as an Afterthought
text:
Why Security Was Added as an Afterthought
For nearly two decades, the Internet functioned on informal operator cooperation and out-of-band communication (the NANOG mailing list, IRC channels, telephone calls between network operations centers). When an operator misconfigured a router and hijacked traffic, people called each other to fix it.
This social trust model collapsed as the Internet transformed into critical economic infrastructure: - The rise of financial technology, cryptocurrency, and e-commerce created massive monetary incentives to steal traffic. - State-sponsored espionage groups recognized that interdomain routing could be used for covert surveillance without breaking end-to-end cryptography. - The sheer scale of the global network (over 75,000 ASes) rendered informal human relationships obsolete.
Because cryptographic security could not be retrofitted into the core BGP-4 state machine without breaking backwards compatibility across thousands of hardware vendors, security had to be built out-of-band: through Internet Routing Registries (IRR), the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), and Route Origin Validation (ROV).

title: The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
text:
The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
Securing an interdomain network requires an adversarial threat model. Disruption in global routing falls along a continuum: from benign clerical typos committed by tired engineers during maintenance windows, to sophisticated, state-sponsored cyber operations designed to covertly intercept encrypted communications.

title: The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
section: Accidental Misconfiguration: The Most Common Disruption
text:
Accidental Misconfiguration: The Most Common Disruption
Historically, over 90% of global routing anomalies are caused not by malicious attackers, but by accidental human misconfigurations. The most common root causes include: - Fat-finger errors: Entering 10.0.0.0/8 or a public IP block instead of a private internal block in an IGP redistribution statement. - Leaked IGP into BGP: Redistributing an entire interior routing table (containing hundreds of subnets) into external BGP without an attached route-map or prefix filter. - Omission of export filters: Bringing up a new eBGP transit session with an upstream provider while forgetting to apply an outbound route filter, inadvertently advertising full-table routes learned from other upstreams.
Because BGP treats every received UPDATE with equal validity, a single typo in a remote edge router in Melbourne can disrupt connectivity for millions of users in North America within 60 seconds.

title: The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
text:
Origin Prefix Hijacking and Impersonation
In an Origin Prefix Hijack, an unauthorized Autonomous System (\(AS_{\text{bad}}\)) announces an IP prefix \(P\) that belongs to another network (\(AS_{\text{victim}}\)), falsely claiming that it is the legitimate origin:
\[\text{Legitimate Announcement:} \quad P \longleftarrow [AS_{\text{transit}}, AS_{\text{victim}}]\] \[\text{Hijack Announcement:} \quad P \longleftarrow [AS_{\text{bad}}]\]
+------------------------------------+
|  Remote Internet Observer (AS400)  |
+-----------------+------------------+
                  |
     +------------+------------+
     |                         |
     v                         v
AS_PATH: [AS200, AS100]    AS_PATH: [AS300, AS666]
(Length: 2 AS hops)        (Length: 2 AS hops)
     |                         |
     v                         v
+---------+               +---------+
|  AS200  |               |  AS300  |
+----+----+               +----+----+
     |                         |
     v                         v
+----+----+               +----+----+
|  AS100  |               |  AS666  |
| Legitimate Origin       | Adversary Origin
| Prefix: 198.51.100.0/24 | Prefix: 198.51.100.0/24 (Exact-Match Hijack)
+---------+               +---------+
When an exact-match hijack occurs, the Internet splits: routers topologically closer to \(AS_{\text{bad}}\) route traffic to the attacker, while routers closer to \(AS_{\text{victim}}\) continue routing to the legitimate owner.

title: The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
text:
Subprefix Hijacking and Splitting
A Subprefix Hijack exploits the fundamental rule of IP packet forwarding: Longest Prefix Match (LPM). Forwarding hardware in every router always prefers a more specific route over a covering aggregate.
If the legitimate owner announces an aggregate block: \[\text{Legitimate:} \quad 198.51.100.0/22 \quad (\text{Addresses: } 198.51.100.0 - 198.51.103.255)\]
The attacker announces two constituent subprefixes: \[\text{Attacker:} \quad 198.51.100.0/24 \quad\text{and}\quad 198.51.101.0/24\]
Because /24 is a longer mask than /22, every router on Earth will prefer the attacker’s route, regardless of LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH length, or topological distance. The hijack is 100% effective globally.

title: The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
text:
Route Leaks: Transit Rules Violated
Formally defined in RFC 7908, a Route Leak occurs when a multihomed Autonomous System receives a route from one transit provider or peer, and re-advertises it to another transit provider or peer in violation of standard commercial transit agreements.
       +--------------------+          +--------------------+
       | Transit Provider A |          | Transit Provider B |
       +---------+----------+          +---------+----------+
                 |                               ^
                 | (Sends Google /24)            | (Illegitimate Leak)
                 v                               |
            +----+-------------------------------+----+
            |      Small Customer / Enterprise        |
            |              (Leaking AS)               |
            +-----------------------------------------+
When Customer AS advertises routes learned from Provider A to Provider B, Provider B sees Customer as the lowest-cost path. Provider B diverts massive traffic streams destined for major content networks (Google, AWS, Cloudflare) through Customer’s modest 1 Gbps uplink. The customer router’s interfaces instantly saturate, inducing massive global packet loss.

title: The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
text:
Blackholing and Traffic Interception
Depending on how the attacker configures its data plane, a hijack manifests in one of two ways: - Blackholing (Denial of Service): The attacker advertises the prefix but discards all incoming packets (null0 / drop). Legitimate services become completely unreachable. - Traffic Interception (Man-in-the-Middle): The attacker captures, inspects, or modifies incoming traffic, and then forwards the packets onward to the true destination via a clean, secondary tunnel (e.g., GRE or WireGuard) to avoid detection.

title: The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
text:
AS_PATH Manipulation and Policy Exploitation
Because BGP lacks cryptographic path integrity, an attacker can modify the AS_PATH attribute before transmitting an UPDATE: - AS_PATH Prepending Abuse: An attacker injects victim ASNs into the path to trigger loop-detection defenses in targeted networks, effectively cutting off their visibility. - Fake 1-Hop Paths: An attacker announces a stolen route while forging a direct connection to a Tier-1 provider (AS_PATH: [Tier1_ASN]), tricking downstream networks into preferring the forged path over legitimate multi-hop routes.

title: The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
text:
Control-Plane Exhaustion and Volumetric Attacks
Routers maintain routing tables in expensive Ternary Content-Addressable Memory (TCAM) and process updates using onboard CPUs. Attackers can exploit this through: - Table Bloat: Inundating an edge router with hundreds of thousands of disaggregated /24 prefixes, exhausting router RAM or exceeding hardware TCAM limits, causing line cards to crash. - Update Churn: Generating rapid bursts of advertisements and withdrawals designed to drive control-plane CPU utilization to 100%, causing BGP keepalive timeouts and triggering cascading session resets across the network.

title: The Threat Landscape: Accidents and Intentional Attacks
text:
Compromised Routers and Network Operators
The threat model must account for insider threats: - Rogue / Hostile ISPs: Commercial or state-owned telcos that intentionally weaponize their transit sessions to hijack financial services or suppress dissidents. - Compromised Edge Devices: Internet-exposed router management interfaces (SSH, RESTCONF, SNMP) compromised via credential stuffing or zero-day vulnerabilities, allowing adversaries to directly alter BGP configurations.

title: Origin Hijacking Attacks: Mechanics, Impact and Detection
text:
Origin Hijacking Attacks: Mechanics, Impact and Detection
Origin prefix hijacking is the archetypal interdomain routing attack. In an origin hijack, an attacker illegitimately announces an IP block from its own Autonomous System, corrupting the global mapping between prefixes and authoritative origin networks.

title: Origin Hijacking Attacks: Mechanics, Impact and Detection
text:
Attack Prerequisites and Execution Steps
Executing an origin prefix hijack requires minimal technical resources:
[Attacker with BGP Peering]
             |
             | 1. Configure prefix under local BGP daemon (e.g., FRR/BIRD)
             v
   "network 203.0.113.0/24"
             |
             | 2. Upstream transit provider lacks strict prefix filtering
             v
  [Upstream ISP Border Router]
             |
             | 3. ISP accepts and propagates UPDATE to peers and Tier-1s
             v
 [Global Internet DFZ (Default-Free Zone)]

Step 1: Upstream Peering Access
The attacker must operate or control an Autonomous System with an active eBGP peering session to at least one upstream transit provider or IXP.


Step 2: Identification of Unfiltered Upstream
The attacker identifies an upstream provider that fails to enforce strict prefix-list filtering (e.g., relying on loose customer filters or failing to validate against IRR databases).


Step 3: Prefix Injection
The attacker adds the victim’s prefix to its BGP configuration (e.g., in FRR: network 203.0.113.0/24) and applies an export policy.


Step 4: Upstream Propagation
The upstream provider accepts the announcement, prepends its own ASN, and propagates the UPDATE across its transit mesh. Within 30 to 60 seconds, routers globally evaluate the new path.

title: Origin Hijacking Attacks: Mechanics, Impact and Detection
text:
Complete vs. Partial Hijacking
The blast radius of an origin hijack depends entirely on prefix specificity:

1. Complete Hijacking (Subprefix / More-Specific)
If the victim announces /22 and the attacker announces /24, every BGP speaker in the world that receives the announcement will direct traffic to the attacker due to Longest Prefix Match (LPM). The victim experiences a complete global blackout for that /24 address space.


2. Partial Hijacking (Exact-Match)
If both the victim and the attacker announce the identical /24 prefix, the Internet bifurcates based on the BGP decision process (principally LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH length): - Networks that have a direct peering or shorter AS path to the attacker route to the attacker. - Networks closer to the victim continue routing to the victim. - Upstream Tier-1 providers with high-degree mesh connectivity become battlegrounds where small differences in propagation time or path length decide the winner.

title: Origin Hijacking Attacks: Mechanics, Impact and Detection
text:
Confidentiality and Integrity Implications
Once an attacker intercepts traffic, severe security breaches become possible: - Traffic Sniffing and Decryption: Unencrypted traffic (DNS, HTTP, unauthenticated database replication) is captured in plaintext. If TLS is used, the attacker can log metadata (IP flows, SNI headers, packet timing) or attempt SSL stripping. - Data Modification: The attacker acts as an active proxy, altering DNS responses or inserting malicious payloads into unencrypted data streams.

title: Origin Hijacking Attacks: Mechanics, Impact and Detection
section: How Hijacking Enables Phishing and MITM
text:
How Hijacking Enables Phishing and MITM
Origin hijacking is frequently combined with automated Certificate Authority (CA) exploitation:
+----------+      1. BGP Hijack of /24      +----------+
| Attacker | -----------------------------> |  Victim  |
+----+-----+                                +----------+
     |
     | 2. Attacker now controls HTTP on victim's IP
     v
+----+------------------------------------------------+
| ACME Automated Certificate Authority (Let's Encrypt)|
+----+------------------------------------------------+
     |
     | 3. Attacker requests TLS cert for victim.com
     | 4. CA issues HTTP-01 challenge to http://victim.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/
     | 5. Challenge arrives at ATTACKER's server!
     v
+----+-----+
| Attacker | ---> Challenge Validated! CA issues signed, valid TLS Certificate!
+----------+

The attacker hijacks the IP prefix hosting the victim’s web infrastructure.
The attacker requests a new TLS certificate from an ACME-based Certificate Authority (such as Let’s Encrypt) for target-bank.com.
The CA performs an HTTP-01 domain validation challenge, sending an HTTP GET request to target-bank.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/<TOKEN>.
Because the attacker controls the IP in BGP, the CA’s probe routes directly to the attacker’s server, which responds with the token.
The CA issues a cryptographically valid, trusted TLS certificate.
The attacker can now terminate TLS connections from legitimate users with green browser padlocks, capturing credentials and session tokens without triggering browser certificate warnings.

title: Origin Hijacking Attacks: Mechanics, Impact and Detection
section: Detection via Route Monitors, Looking Glasses and Real-Time Alerts
text:
Detection via Route Monitors, Looking Glasses and Real-Time Alerts
Detecting an origin hijack requires external vantage points:

Public Route Collectors: Projects like RouteViews (University of Oregon) and RIPE RIS (Routing Information Service) peer with hundreds of border routers globally, logging all BGP updates and periodic table dumps into public archives.
Looking Glasses: Public web interfaces provided by Tier-1 providers allowing operators to execute show ip bgp <prefix> from their internal core routers.
Real-Time Streaming Telemetry:

RIS-Live: Real-time WebSocket firehose of global BGP updates.
BGPStream: Open-source framework for processing real-time BGP telemetry.
Commercial Alerting: Tools like Cloudflare Radar, Cisco ThousandEyes, and Kentik monitor customer prefixes and trigger SMS/webhook alerts when an unexpected origin ASN appears in an AS_PATH.

title: Origin Hijacking Attacks: Mechanics, Impact and Detection
section: The Role of RPKI and ROV in Origin Hijacking Prevention
text:
The Role of RPKI and ROV in Origin Hijacking Prevention
The definitive cryptographic defense against origin hijacking is Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) combined with Route Origin Validation (ROV).
Under RPKI: 1. The prefix owner signs a cryptographic Route Origin Authorization (ROA) stating: Only AS100 is authorized to originate 198.51.100.0/24 up to maxLength /24. 2. Remote routers fetch these validated ROAs. 3. When the attacker (\(AS666\)) announces 198.51.100.0/24, routers evaluating ROV flag the announcement as Invalid. 4. The router automatically drops the Invalid announcement, completely neutralizing the hijack at the border.

title: Route Leaks and Policy Abuse
text:
Route Leaks and Policy Abuse
While prefix hijacking involves the illegitimate origination of IP address space, route leaks represent a distinct, highly disruptive class of interdomain routing anomalies. Route leaks violate commercial routing policy agreements, causing traffic to flow through unauthorized networks without changing the authoritative origin ASN.

title: Route Leaks and Policy Abuse
section: What Is a Route Leak and How It Differs From Hijacking
text:
What Is a Route Leak and How It Differs From Hijacking
Formally defined in RFC 7908, a route leak is: > “The propagation of routing announcement(s) beyond their intended scope. That is, an announcement from an Autonomous System (AS) of a learned BGP route to another AS in violation of the intended rules of the receiver, the sender, and/or one of the preceding ASes in the path.”
The critical distinction between a hijack and a leak:








Characteristic
Origin Hijack
Route Leak




Origin ASN
Illegitimate; changed to attacker’s ASN
Legitimate; original authoritative ASN preserved


AS_PATH
Forged or newly originated (\([AS_{\text{bad}}]\))
Contains valid origin, but path contains an illegal valley


Root Cause
Malicious injection or misorigination
Policy violation / export filter omission


RPKI ROV Defense
Effective (evaluates prefix vs. origin ASN)
Ineffective (origin ASN is valid!)



Because RPKI Route Origin Validation only checks the rightmost (origin) ASN in the AS_PATH, ROV cannot prevent or detect a standard route leak.

title: Route Leaks and Policy Abuse
text:
The Customer-Concentrator-Provider Leak Pattern
The most damaging and widespread route leak pattern is the Customer-Provider Leak (RFC 7908 Type 1):
       +-----------------------+              +-----------------------+
       | Upstream Transit ISP1 |              | Upstream Transit ISP2 |
       |     (e.g., Level3)    |              |     (e.g., Telia)     |
       +-----------+-----------+              +-----------+-----------+
                   |                                      ^
                   | 1. Sends full routing table          | 3. Illegitimate Leak!
                   |    to Customer AS                    |    Customer exports ISP1
                   v                                      |    routes to ISP2!
       +-----------+--------------------------------------+-----------+
       |                  Multihomed Customer AS                      |
       |                     (Small Enterprise)                       |
       +--------------------------------------------------------------+

Multihomed Customer AS purchases transit from ISP1 and ISP2.
ISP1 announces a full global routing table (over 900,000 routes) to Customer.
Customer accidentally misconfigures its outbound export route-map on its session to ISP2, failing to restrict exports to its own locally originated prefixes.
Customer advertises ISP1’s routes to ISP2.
In ISP2’s BGP decision process:

Routes learned from Customer have a higher LOCAL_PREF (e.g., \(200\), customer route) than routes learned from peers (\(150\)) or other transit providers (\(100\)).

ISP2 accepts the leaked routes and directs all traffic destined for those prefixes into Customer’s network!

title: Route Leaks and Policy Abuse
text:
Accidental vs. Intentional Policy Violations

Accidental Leaks: Caused by missing outbound prefix-lists, regex typos in BGP community filters, or software crashes during route-map recompilation.
Intentional / Adversarial Leaks: An adversary intentionally leaks routes to:

Force competitor traffic onto saturated links (economic sabotage).
Act as a transparent Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) snooping node between two major transit backbones.
Exploit asymmetric peering billing structures.

title: Route Leaks and Policy Abuse
section: Propagation Patterns and Impact on Reachability
text:
Propagation Patterns and Impact on Reachability
When a route leak occurs: 1. Traffic Funneling: Upstream providers divert petabits of planetary transit traffic through the leaking AS. 2. Buffer Exhaustion and Packet Loss: The leaking network’s edge routers, typically provisioned with 1 Gbps or 10 Gbps uplinks, are instantly overwhelmed by 500+ Gbps of incoming traffic. Queues drop 99.9% of packets. 3. Global Service Collapse: Remote users attempting to reach major cloud providers, CDNs, or financial hubs experience total timeouts.

title: Route Leaks and Policy Abuse
section: Prevention Through Policy, Filtering and Community Tags
text:
Prevention Through Policy, Filtering and Community Tags
Mitigating route leaks requires defense in depth:

1. Strict Outbound Prefix Filtering
Every non-transit customer must configure strict outbound export filters that only allow the exact prefixes originated by the organization:
ip prefix-list OWN-PREFIXES permit 198.51.100.0/24
!
route-map EXPORT-TO-TRANSIT permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list OWN-PREFIXES
route-map EXPORT-TO-TRANSIT deny 20


2. BGP Communities for Leak Prevention
Operators use communities to classify routes upon ingress and reject them upon egress: - Tag all routes learned from Transit/Peers with COMMUNITY 65000:TRANSIT. - Drop any route carrying 65000:TRANSIT before advertising to any other Transit/Peer.


3. RFC 9234: Autonomous System Provider Authorization (ASPA) and Only to Customer (OTC)
RFC 9234 defines the Only to Customer (OTC) BGP attribute: - When a provider or peer advertises a route to a customer or lateral peer, it attaches the OTC attribute set to its own ASN. - If a downstream network receives a route with an OTC attribute from a customer or lateral peer, it recognizes an illegal “valley” path and automatically rejects the route.

title: Route Leaks and Policy Abuse
text:
Detection via Monitoring and Analysis
Route leaks are detected by analyzing AS_PATH patterns across public collectors: - Valley Detection: Identifying sequences in the AS_PATH where a route moves from Customer \(\to\) Provider \(\to\) Customer \(\to\) Provider. - Volume Anomalies: Sudden spikes in prefix count advertised by small stub ASes (e.g., an AS normally originating 3 prefixes suddenly originates 400,000 prefixes).

title: Advanced and Emerging Routing Threats
text:
Advanced and Emerging Routing Threats
As basic origin prefix filtering and RPKI Route Origin Validation gain adoption across Tier-1 and Tier-2 networks, sophisticated adversaries and nation-state intelligence agencies have shifted to advanced evasion techniques, targeting routing infrastructure, telemetry systems, and policy manipulation.

title: Advanced and Emerging Routing Threats
text:
Compromised Routers and Rogue Operators
Traditional threat models assume that router operating systems adhere strictly to the BGP state machine and RFC specifications. This assumption collapses when the router itself is compromised: - Router Implant Malware: State-sponsored actors have successfully compromised edge and core router platforms (e.g., Cisco IOS XE implants, Juniper Junos backdoors), injecting modified routing binaries directly into system memory. - Rogue Bulletproof Hosting Operators: Specialized transit entities operate with the explicit commercial model of providing routing transit to bulletproof hosting networks, phishing cartels, and botnet command-and-control operators. These rogue ASes frequently forge peering agreements, cycle through discarded or stolen AS numbers, and announce unallocated address space (bogon squatting).

title: Advanced and Emerging Routing Threats
section: Competitive Manipulation: Steering Traffic for Advantage
text:
Competitive Manipulation: Steering Traffic for Advantage
Routing manipulation is not limited to espionage; it is increasingly weaponized for economic and commercial advantage: - Asymmetric De-peering and Traffic Dumping: A large network intentionally manipulates MED or AS_PATH prepending to force a rival peer to carry heavy transit payloads across its internal backbone while taking minimal return traffic. - Latency Degraded Peering: Manipulating routing policies to detour traffic destined for a competitor’s cloud or gaming platform through high-latency transoceanic paths, degrading user experience and inducing customer churn.

title: Advanced and Emerging Routing Threats
section: Attacks on Route Collectors and Validation Infrastructure
text:
Attacks on Route Collectors and Validation Infrastructure
The global routing monitoring ecosystem relies heavily on public collectors (RouteViews, RIPE RIS, BGPStream): - Telemetry Poisoning: An attacker peering with public collectors can intentionally inject false or deceptive routes directly into collector sessions while filtering those same routes from commercial transit links. This blinds detection systems or floods analysts with false positive alerts. - Denial-of-Service against RPKI Validators: By flooding RPKI repositories with millions of deeply nested manifests, invalid certificates, or malicious rsync directories, attackers attempt to trigger algorithmic complexity attacks (denial-of-service) against relying party validators like Routinator or rpki-client.

title: Advanced and Emerging Routing Threats
text:
Long-Term Reconnaissance and Persistent Manipulation
Sophisticated adversaries rarely announce noisy /24 subprefixes that trigger immediate alarms on Twitter/X or Slack channels: - Micro-burst Hijacking: Announcing a target prefix for only 60 to 120 seconds—long enough to complete an automated TLS certificate challenge or siphon authentication tokens—and withdrawing the route before global NOCs can initiate diagnostic traceroutes. - Low-and-Slow Interception: Manipulating the AS_PATH by appending legitimate ASNs so the route appears to be a normal multi-hop path. The adversary diverts a small percentage of global traffic through an offshore intercept facility, decrypts or logs the data, and forwards it to the true destination without dropping packets.

title: Advanced and Emerging Routing Threats
section: Threats Specific to Large Networks and Cloud Providers
text:
Threats Specific to Large Networks and Cloud Providers
Hyperscale cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP, Cloudflare) operate massive, globally distributed Anycast networks. This architecture exposes distinct threat vectors: - Anycast Localization Attacks: Announcing an Anycast prefix from a single rogue geographic location (e.g., Eastern Europe) to capture local user traffic destined for a global DNS resolver (like 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8). - Internal Cross-Tenant Leaks: In multi-tenant cloud environments where thousands of enterprise customers run virtual BGP sessions over Direct Connect or ExpressRoute, configuration bugs in cloud software-defined network (SDN) controllers can allow one customer’s private routes to leak into another tenant’s virtual private cloud (VPC).

title: The Routing Registries: IRRs and Their Limitations
text:
The Routing Registries: IRRs and Their Limitations
Long before cryptographic validation through RPKI was deployed, the network operations community created the Internet Routing Registry (IRR) system to record routing policies, prefix ownership, and transit relationships. While IRRs remain widely used to generate automated prefix-lists, their fundamental design weaknesses highlight why cryptographic authentication became necessary.

title: The Routing Registries: IRRs and Their Limitations
section: What Routing Registries Are and How They Store Route Objects
text:
What Routing Registries Are and How They Store Route Objects
An Internet Routing Registry is a distributed database storing text-based policy statements formatted in Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL, RFC 2622).
The IRR system is not a single database; it is a confederation of more than 30 independent registries worldwide: - Authoritative RIR Registries: Run by Regional Internet Registries (RIPE, APNIC, AFRINIC, LACNIC, and ARIN-RR), containing records tied to actual resource allocations. - Third-Party / Commercial Registries: Including RADB (Merit), NTT, Level3/Lumen, and ALTDB, established historically to allow multi-region operators to register policy objects without cross-RIR coordination.
Registries mirror each other’s databases via daily or hourly bulk dumps, but synchronization is loose, partial, and frequently inconsistent.

title: The Routing Registries: IRRs and Their Limitations
section: Creating Route Objects: Route, Route6, AS-SET and Related Classes
text:
Creating Route Objects: Route, Route6, AS-SET and Related Classes
RPSL defines several core object classes:

1. route (IPv4) and route6 (IPv6) Objects
A route object binds an IP prefix to an authoritative origin Autonomous System:
route:         198.51.100.0/24
descr:         Example Production Web Backbone
origin:        AS65001
mnt-by:        EXAMPLE-MNT
source:        RADB


2. aut-num Objects
An aut-num object specifies the routing policy of an Autonomous System, detailing its import, export, and peering rules:
aut-num:       AS65001
as-name:       EXAMPLE-NET
import:        from AS65002 action pref=100; accept ANY;
export:        to AS65002 announce AS-EXAMPLE;
mnt-by:        EXAMPLE-MNT
source:        RADB


3. as-set Objects
An as-set is a hierarchical grouping of Autonomous Systems representing an entire customer cone. Upstream transit providers use as-set objects to recursively build prefix-lists for an entire downstream customer hierarchy:
as-set:        AS-EXAMPLE-CUSTOMERS
descr:         Downstream customers of AS65001
members:       AS65010, AS65020, AS-SUB-CLIENTS
mnt-by:        EXAMPLE-MNT
source:        RADB

title: The Routing Registries: IRRs and Their Limitations
section: Policy-Based Filtering: Using IRR Data to Build Filters
text:
Policy-Based Filtering: Using IRR Data to Build Filters
Modern Tier-1 and Tier-2 transit providers use open-source tools such as bgpq4 or irrpt to query IRR databases and automatically generate vendor-specific prefix filters:
# Query RADB and generate a Cisco IOS XR prefix-list for AS-EXAMPLE-CUSTOMERS
bgpq4 -X -l CUSTOMER-IN AS-EXAMPLE-CUSTOMERS
Output:
prefix-set CUSTOMER-IN
  198.51.100.0/24,
  203.0.113.0/24 le 24
end-set
These generated prefix-lists are applied to customer-facing eBGP sessions, preventing customers from advertising arbitrary unauthorized prefixes.

title: The Routing Registries: IRRs and Their Limitations
section: Weaknesses: No Authorization Checking, No Cryptographic Binding
text:
Weaknesses: No Authorization Checking, No Cryptographic Binding
Despite its widespread operational use, the legacy IRR system suffers from critical security flaws:

No Authorization Checking in Third-Party IRRs: In non-authoritative registries (such as RADB or legacy ALTDB), anyone with a paid account could register a route object for any IP address on Earth. An attacker could create a fake route object claiming that 1.1.1.1/32 originates from AS666. If an upstream transit provider built its filters using an unvetted query (-S radb), the attacker’s route would be automatically permitted through the provider’s border filters!
Stale and Ghost Objects: When organizations renumber, merge, or return IP blocks to an RIR, they rarely delete their old IRR objects. Millions of obsolete route objects remain active in mirrored registries decades after the addresses were reassigned.
No Cryptographic Signatures: IRR objects are plaintext text files. They contain no digital signatures, no public-key certificates, and no cryptographic binding to the resource holder’s cryptographic keys.

title: The Routing Registries: IRRs and Their Limitations
section: The Transition from IRR Filtering to RPKI-Based Validation
text:
The Transition from IRR Filtering to RPKI-Based Validation
Because the legacy IRR system could not guarantee origin authenticity or prevent rogue registrations, the IETF developed the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI).
While RPKI provides cryptographic truth for origin validation, IRRs remain operationally necessary for expanding as-set customer cones and generating strict inbound prefix-lists at transit borders. In modern network operations, IRR and RPKI are deployed as complementary controls: IRR validates the path and customer cone, while RPKI cryptographically verifies the origin.

title: The RPKI Architecture: Resource Certificates and Trust Anchors
text:
The RPKI Architecture: Resource Certificates and Trust Anchors
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), standardized in RFC 6480, is a specialized Public Key Infrastructure designed to cryptographically bind Internet number resources (IPv4 blocks, IPv6 blocks, and Autonomous System Numbers) to public-key certificates held by the organizations to which those resources were formally allocated.

title: The RPKI Architecture: Resource Certificates and Trust Anchors
section: The RPKI Trust Model: Hierarchical Certification from RIRs
text:
The RPKI Trust Model: Hierarchical Certification from RIRs
Unlike the commercial Web PKI (where hundreds of commercial Certificate Authorities can issue TLS certificates for any domain on Earth), RPKI strictly follows the hierarchical allocation chain of the Internet:
                       +-----------------------+
                       |         IANA          |
                       +-----------+-----------+
                                   |
         +------------+------------+------------+------------+
         |            |            |            |            |
         v            v            v            v            v
     AFRINIC TA   APNIC TA     ARIN TA      LACNIC TA   RIPE NCC TA
         |            |            |            |            |
         +------------+------------+------------+------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                       +-----------------------+
                       |  LIR / ISP Sub-CA     |
                       |  (e.g., Enterprise)   |
                       +-----------+-----------+
                                   |
                       +-----------+-----------+
                       |                       |
                       v                       v
               +---------------+       +---------------+
               |   ROA (AS100, |       |   Manifest    |
               |  198.51.100/24|       |  (.mft file)  |
               +---------------+       +---------------+
The tree begins at IANA and cascades down through the five Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) to Local Internet Registries (ISPs, telcos, cloud providers) and enterprise end-users. A certificate in RPKI cannot authorize resources that were not explicitly delegated down the parent chain.

title: The RPKI Architecture: Resource Certificates and Trust Anchors
section: Trust Anchors and Root Certificates at Each RIR
text:
Trust Anchors and Root Certificates at Each RIR
Every relying party (validator) bootstraps its validation process using Trust Anchor Locators (TALs) (RFC 8630). A TAL is a small text file containing: - The URI of the RIR’s root certificate (hosted over HTTPS or rsync). - The subject public key identifier (SPKI) and public key of the RIR’s self-signed Trust Anchor root certificate.
There are five primary Trust Anchors corresponding to the five RIRs: 1. arin.tal 2. ripe.tal 3. apnic.tal 4. lacnic.tal 5. afrinic.tal
A validator reads these TALs on startup, downloads the root certificates from the specified publication points, verifies their cryptographic fingerprints, and constructs the root of the validation tree.

title: The RPKI Architecture: Resource Certificates and Trust Anchors
section: Resource Certificates: Structure, Extensions and Resource Holders
text:
Resource Certificates: Structure, Extensions and Resource Holders
RPKI certificates are standard X.509 v3 public key certificates with a critical addition: the IP Address and AS Number Extensions (RFC 3779).
In standard TLS certificates, the certificate subject is a Common Name or Domain (e.g., CN=example.com). In an RPKI certificate: - The Subject field contains a non-identifying pseudonym. - The RFC 3779 extensions explicitly list the exact IP address ranges and Autonomous System Numbers the certificate holder is authorized to manage:
X509v3 extensions:
  IP Address Delegation:
    IPv4: 198.51.100.0/24
    IPv6: 2001:db8:abcd::/48
  Autonomous System Numbers:
    AS65001
A parent CA can only issue a child certificate for a subset of the resources listed in the parent’s own certificate. If a rogue administrator at an ISP attempts to issue a certificate for someone else’s /16 block, chain validation fails immediately because the parent certificate does not contain those resources.

title: The RPKI Architecture: Resource Certificates and Trust Anchors
text:
CA Certificates and Chain Validation
RPKI distinguishes between two certificate types: - CA Certificates (Certificate Authority): Used to sign child certificates, Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), and signed object lists. - End-Entity (EE) Certificates: Ephemeral, single-use certificates created solely to sign a specific payload object—such as a Route Origin Authorization (ROA) or an ASPA object. Once the object is signed, the private key is discarded.
During chain validation, a relying party walks down the cryptographic path from the RIR Trust Anchor to the EE certificate, verifying: 1. That all signatures across the path are mathematically valid (RSA or ECDSA). 2. That each certificate is within its valid start and expiration dates (notBefore / notAfter). 3. That the resources in the child certificate are strictly a sub-allocation of the parent’s RFC 3779 extensions. 4. That no certificate in the chain has been revoked on an active CRL.

title: The RPKI Architecture: Resource Certificates and Trust Anchors
section: Manifests and Signed Object Lists: What They Protect
text:
Manifests and Signed Object Lists: What They Protect
Every RPKI repository publication point publishes a Manifest (RFC 6486). A manifest is a signed CMS object (.mft) that lists the filenames and SHA-256 cryptographic hashes of every valid object currently published in that repository directory.
Manifests protect relying parties against replay and deletion attacks: - If an adversary compromises a local repository mirror and deletes a valid ROA, the validator checks the manifest, detects that a listed file is missing, and raises an alarm. - If an attacker attempts to inject a revoked, stale ROA from six months ago, the manifest’s hash check fails, preventing the stale authorization from entering the router’s decision engine.

title: Route Origin Authorizations: The Core Authorization Object
text:
Route Origin Authorizations: The Core Authorization Object
In the RPKI ecosystem, the digital object that directly governs BGP route validation is the Route Origin Authorization (ROA), defined in RFC 6482. A ROA is a cryptographically signed statement that specifies which Autonomous System is authorized to originate a given IP prefix into the global BGP routing system.

title: Route Origin Authorizations: The Core Authorization Object
section: What a ROA Is and What It Proves
text:
What a ROA Is and What It Proves
A ROA is an encapsulated Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) signed object. It contains a signed payload that binds: 1. An Autonomous System Number (ASN). 2. One or more IP prefixes (IPv4 or IPv6). 3. An optional Maximum Length (maxLength) for each prefix.
A valid ROA proves that the legitimate holder of the IP address space has authorized the specified AS to originate BGP announcements for that address block up to the specified prefix length.
Crucially, a ROA proves origin authorization only. It does not prove: - That the originating AS has active physical connectivity to the Internet. - That the AS path between the origin and the receiving router is honest or loop-free. - That the originating AS will actually forward data plane traffic.

title: Route Origin Authorizations: The Core Authorization Object
section: Creating a ROA: Prefix, AS Number and Maximum Length

title: Route Origin Authorizations: The Core Authorization Object
section: Max-Length: How It Controls Subprefix Authorization
text:
Max-Length: How It Controls Subprefix Authorization
The maxLength attribute is an operational convenience, but it represents the most dangerous trap in RPKI:








ROA Configuration
Authorized Announcements
Unauthorized Announcements (Flagged INVALID)




198.51.100.0/22 without maxLength
Exactly 198.51.100.0/22 only from AS65001
Any /23, /24, or subprefix from any AS (including AS65001)


198.51.100.0/22 with maxLength: 24
198.51.100.0/22, and any /23 or /24 from AS65001
Any /25 or longer from AS65001; ANY prefix from any other AS




The maxLength Security Vulnerability (RFC 9319)
If an operator announces only 198.51.100.0/22 in BGP, but creates a ROA with maxLength: 24 “just in case we want to split it later”, an attacker can execute a forged-origin subprefix hijack: 1. The attacker announces 198.51.100.0/24 with AS_PATH: [Attacker_AS, 65001]. 2. The router evaluating ROV checks the origin: the origin is AS65001. 3. The router checks prefix length: /24 is \(\le 24\) (maxLength). 4. The router flags the attacker’s announcement as VALID! 5. Longest Prefix Match directs all traffic for that /24 to the attacker.

[!IMPORTANT] RFC 9319 Best Current Practice: Do not use maxLength unless actively necessary. Instead, create explicit minimal ROAs matching the exact prefix lengths currently advertised in BGP. If you announce a /22 and two /24s, publish three distinct ROAs with exact lengths.

title: Route Origin Authorizations: The Core Authorization Object
text:
ROA Lifespan, Expiration and Revocation
ROAs are cryptographic objects with a defined validity period (notBefore and notAfter dates, typically 12 to 36 months).

Automated Re-signing: Hosted RIR CAs automatically re-sign ROAs prior to expiration. If an operator runs a delegated CA (e.g., Krill) and lets the daemon crash or neglect automated re-signing, the ROA expires. Once expired, the prefix transitions from Valid to NotFound.
Revocation: If a network changes upstream providers or reassigns an IP block, the old ROA is revoked. The CA signs a Certificate Revocation List (CRL) and publishes a new manifest.

title: Route Origin Authorizations: The Core Authorization Object
section: Common Mistakes: Over-Permissive, Under-Covered and Conflicting ROAs
text:
Common Mistakes: Over-Permissive, Under-Covered and Conflicting ROAs

Under-Covered ROAs (Self-Inflicted Outage): An operator announces 198.51.100.0/24 in BGP, but registers a ROA for 198.51.100.0/22 without maxLength. The router running ROV flags the operator’s own /24 announcement as INVALID because the announced prefix length (\(24\)) exceeds the authorized length (\(22\)). Upstream transit networks drop the route, severing connectivity.
Conflicting Multi-Origin ROAs: When transitioning between transit providers, an operator must ensure that ROAs for both ASNs exist concurrently before shifting BGP traffic, preventing temporary Invalid states during convergence.
Ghost ROAs: Retaining active ROAs for IP space that was transferred or sold to another organization.

title: RPKI Validation: Validators, VRPs and Relying Parties
text:
RPKI Validation: Validators, VRPs and Relying Parties
Routers cannot directly walk the planetary RPKI certificate tree. Public-key signature verification, recursive repository crawling, and cryptographic certificate chain parsing require substantial computational power, memory, and disk I/O that router control-plane processors do not possess.
This structural reality necessitates an architectural split: an external server software package—the RPKI Relying Party (RP) or Validator—performs the heavy cryptographic heavy lifting and delivers a simple, flattened table to routers.

title: RPKI Validation: Validators, VRPs and Relying Parties
section: What an RPKI Validator Does: Download, Verify, Extract
text:
What an RPKI Validator Does: Download, Verify, Extract
An RPKI Validator performs four primary tasks in a continuous operational loop (typically every 10 to 20 minutes):
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|                  RPKI Repository Tree                     |
|  (ARIN, RIPE, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC Publication Points)  |
+-----------------------------+-----------------------------+
                              |
                              | 1. Sync via RRDP (HTTPS) / rsync
                              v
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|                  RPKI Relying Party (Validator)          |
|                  (Routinator, rpki-client, FORT)          |
|                                                           |
|  2. Cryptographic Verification:                           |
|     - Walk TAL root anchors -> EE certificates            |
|     - Check cryptographic signatures (RSA/ECDSA)          |
|     - Verify RFC 3779 resource inclusions                 |
|     - Check CRLs and Manifest hashes                      |
|                                                           |
|  3. Extraction: Flatten valid ROAs into VRP table         |
+-----------------------------+-----------------------------+
                              |
                              | 4. RTR Protocol (Port 3323)
                              v
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|                     Edge & Core Routers                   |
|                   (Cisco, Juniper, Nokia, FRR)            |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+

Repository Synchronization: Synchronizes local cache with all global RPKI publication repositories.
Cryptographic Validation: Validates the entire certificate chain from the 5 Trust Anchor Locators (TALs) down through intermediate CAs to End-Entity certificates and ROAs.
Revocation and Integrity Checking: Confirms that certificates have not been revoked on Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) and that all files match the hashes recorded on signed manifests.
VRP Extraction: Extracts valid authorizations into a flattened list of Validated ROA Payloads (VRPs) and serves them to routers over the RPKI-to-Router (RTR) protocol.

title: RPKI Validation: Validators, VRPs and Relying Parties
section: Validator Architecture and Repository Sync: RRDP vs. rsync
text:
Validator Architecture and Repository Sync: RRDP vs. rsync
Historically, RPKI repositories synchronized using rsync. In production, rsync proved disastrously fragile: - Scaling bottlenecks: Thousands of validators executing concurrent rsync crawls overwhelmed RIR server CPU and memory. - Partial updates: Network dropouts during rsync transfers left directories with missing or inconsistent certificate sets.
The IETF resolved this by introducing RPKI Repository Delta Protocol (RRDP, RFC 8182): - Operates over standard HTTPS. - Uses an XML-based Notification File (notification.xml), Snapshot Files, and Delta Files. - Enables caching through commercial Content Delivery Networks (CDNs), allowing millions of queries per second without placing load on RIR origin servers. - Validators only fall back to rsync if an RRDP publication endpoint fails.

title: RPKI Validation: Validators, VRPs and Relying Parties
section: Validated ROA Payloads (VRPs): The Validator’s Output
text:
Validated ROA Payloads (VRPs): The Validator’s Output
The final output of an RPKI validation cycle is a flat table of Validated ROA Payloads (VRPs). A VRP is a simplified 4-tuple:
VRP = (Prefix, PrefixLength, MaxLength, OriginASN)
Example VRP table dump:









IP Prefix
Prefix Length
Maximum Length (maxLength)
Authorized Origin ASN




198.51.100.0
24
24
AS65001


203.0.113.0
24
24
AS65002


2001:db8::
32
48
AS65001


192.0.2.0
24
24
AS65100



This compact table is all a router needs to make real-time forwarding decisions.

title: RPKI Validation: Validators, VRPs and Relying Parties
section: CRL and SKI/IAI: Revocation and Validation Accuracy
text:
CRL and SKI/IAI: Revocation and Validation Accuracy

Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs): Each CA periodically signs a CRL listing the serial numbers of revoked certificates. Validators must download the CRL before evaluating any certificate issued by that CA.
Subject Key Identifier (SKI) & Authority Key Identifier (AKI): Ensure exact cryptographic matching between the public key in a parent CA certificate and the issuer signature on a child certificate, preventing key substitution attacks.

title: RPKI Validation: Validators, VRPs and Relying Parties
section: Validator Outages, Stale Data and Recovery Behavior
text:
Validator Outages, Stale Data and Recovery Behavior
What happens when an RPKI validator server crashes, loses Internet connectivity, or is partitioned from the RIR repositories?

Local Cache Persistence: Validators do not purge their databases when an upstream sync fails. They continue serving the last known valid VRP set to routers until certificates and manifests reach their cryptographic expiration dates.
Router Cache Timer: Routers maintain an RTR expiry timer (default typically 60 to 120 minutes). If all RTR sessions to all local validators drop, the router preserves its VRP table in memory until the timer expires.
Redundant Validator Architecture: Best operational practice dictates deploying at least two independent validator instances running different software implementations (e.g., Routinator by NLnet Labs and rpki-client by the OpenBSD project) in separate physical data centers to prevent single-vendor software bugs from taking down the routing policy.

title: RPKI-to-Router (RTR) and Route Origin Validation (ROV)
text:
RPKI-to-Router (RTR) and Route Origin Validation (ROV)
Once an RPKI validator has downloaded, cryptographically verified, and extracted the global set of Validated ROA Payloads (VRPs), this data must be delivered into router memory. The protocol that bridges external validators and router control planes is the RPKI-to-Router (RTR) protocol, defined in RFC 6810 (RTRv0) and RFC 8210 (RTRv1).

title: RPKI-to-Router (RTR) and Route Origin Validation (ROV)
section: The RPKI-to-Router Protocol: Messages and Mechanics
text:
The RPKI-to-Router Protocol: Messages and Mechanics
RTR is a lightweight, binary client-server protocol running over TCP (default port 323 for plaintext; port 3323 when wrapped in TLS or SSH).
The protocol operates using explicit Protocol Data Units (PDUs):
+-------------------------------------------------------+
|                    RTR Session Lifecycle              |
|                                                       |
|  Router (Client)                    Validator (Server)|
|         |                                  |          |
|         | -------- Reset Query (PDU 2) --> |          |
|         | <------- Cache Response (PDU 3)- |          |
|         | <------- IPv4/IPv6 Prefix PDUs - |          |
|         | <------- End of Data (PDU 7) --- |          |
|         |                                  |          |
|         | --- [Wait Refresh Timer] ------- |          |
|         |                                  |          |
|         | <------- Serial Notify (PDU 0) - | (Changes)|
|         | -------- Serial Query (PDU 1) -> |          |
|         | <------- Incremental Deltas ---- |          |
|         | <------- End of Data ----------- |          |
+-------------------------------------------------------+








PDU Type
Name
Purpose




0
Serial Notify
Sent asynchronously by the validator to inform routers that the VRP cache has been updated to a new Serial Number.


1
Serial Query
Sent by the router requesting incremental changes (adds/deletes) since its last known Serial Number.


2
Reset Query
Sent by the router upon initial startup or cache corruption, requesting a complete, full dump of all VRPs.


3
Cache Response
Acknowledges a query and precedes payload transmission.


4
IPv4 Prefix
Transmits an IPv4 VRP: [Flags (Add/Del), Prefix, Length, MaxLength, OriginASN].


6
IPv6 Prefix
Transmits an IPv6 VRP with identical fields formatted for 128-bit addresses.


7
End of Data
Marks the conclusion of a data transfer and specifies refresh, retry, and expire timers.


8
Cache Reset
Sent by the validator if the router’s requested serial is too old to compute an incremental delta, forcing a Reset Query.


10
Error Report
Signals an encapsulation, syntax, or cryptographic error.

title: RPKI-to-Router (RTR) and Route Origin Validation (ROV)
section: Session Establishment, Keepalive and Data Transfer
text:
Session Establishment, Keepalive and Data Transfer
When a router boots: 1. It establishes a TCP session to the configured RTR validator IP on port 323. 2. It sends a Reset Query (PDU 2). 3. The validator responds with Cache Response (PDU 3), followed by a stream of IPv4 Prefix and IPv6 Prefix PDUs (over 500,000 records). 4. The validator terminates the transfer with End of Data (PDU 7), containing: - Refresh Interval: How often the router should query for updates (default: 3600 seconds). - Retry Interval: How long to wait before retrying after a failed query (default: 600 seconds). - Expire Interval: How long the router may continue using its cached VRPs if all RTR sessions fail before purging them (default: 7200 seconds).

title: RPKI-to-Router (RTR) and Route Origin Validation (ROV)
section: How VRPs Become Route Decision Criteria: Route Origin Validation (ROV)
text:
How VRPs Become Route Decision Criteria: Route Origin Validation (ROV)
With the VRP table resident in router memory, the router executes Route Origin Validation (ROV) (RFC 6811) on every incoming BGP route received from peers.
For an incoming route advertisement \(R = (\text{Prefix } P, \text{Length } L, \text{Origin AS } O)\): The router queries its local VRP database for any entry \(V = (P_V, L_V, M_V, O_V)\) that covers \(P\) (where \(P\) is a subprefix of or equal to \(P_V\)):
                        +--------------------------------+
                        |  Incoming Route Update:        |
                        |  Prefix P, Length L, Origin O  |
                        +---------------+----------------+
                                        |
                                        v
                 Does any VRP in memory cover Prefix P?
                                        |
                     +------------------+------------------+
                     | No                                  | Yes
                     v                                     v
               +-----------+           Does at least ONE covering VRP match:
               | NotFound  |           - Origin AS == O  AND
               | (Unknown) |           - Length L <= MaxLength?
               +-----------+                               |
                                           +---------------+---------------+
                                           | Yes                           | No
                                           v                               v
                                     +-----------+                   +-----------+
                                     |   Valid   |                   |  Invalid  |
                                     +-----------+                   +-----------+

Valid: At least one covering VRP exists where the VRP ASN matches the origin ASN (\(O_V == O\)) AND the route prefix length is less than or equal to the VRP maximum length (\(L \le M_V\)).
Invalid: At least one covering VRP exists, but neither the origin ASN matches nor the prefix length satisfies the maximum length requirement (\(L > M_V\)).
NotFound (Unknown): No covering VRP exists in the database for prefix \(P\).

title: RPKI-to-Router (RTR) and Route Origin Validation (ROV)
section: ROV Integration with the BGP Decision Process
text:
ROV Integration with the BGP Decision Process
ROV states are integrated into the BGP decision engine via router policy (route-maps):
! Standard Production ROV Policy (FRR / Cisco Syntax)
route-map BGP-PEER-IN permit 10
 match rpki invalid
 set local-preference 10      <-- Or direct drop: drop / reject
!
route-map BGP-PEER-IN permit 20
 match rpki valid
 set local-preference 200     <-- Prefer cryptographically validated routes
!
route-map BGP-PEER-IN permit 30
 match rpki notfound
 set local-preference 100     <-- Neutral default preference for unvalidated space
In strict production hardening (RFC 7454), all Invalid routes are immediately dropped upon receipt:
route-map BGP-TRANSIT-IN deny 10
 match rpki invalid
!
route-map BGP-TRANSIT-IN permit 20

title: RPKI-to-Router (RTR) and Route Origin Validation (ROV)
section: Handling State Transitions: Valid, Invalid, NotFound and Pending
text:
Handling State Transitions: Valid, Invalid, NotFound and Pending
When a new ROA is published or revoked: - The validator pushes an update over RTR. - The router dynamically re-evaluates all affected routes in its Adj-RIB-In. - If a currently installed route transitions from NotFound \(\to\) Invalid, the router drops it and re-runs the BGP best-path selection algorithm to pick an alternative path. - During initial session bring-up, routes reside in a temporary Pending state for a few seconds until the initial RTR sync concludes, preventing premature route drops.

title: Operational Consequences of ROV: Invalid, Valid, NotFound and Real-World Effects
text:
Operational Consequences of ROV: Invalid, Valid, NotFound and Real-World Effects
Enabling Route Origin Validation (ROV) changes packet forwarding in the global data plane. While ROV provides definitive protection against origin prefix hijacking, its operational enforcement requires navigating nuanced failure modes, operator errors, and unintended collateral reachability loss.

title: Operational Consequences of ROV: Invalid, Valid, NotFound and Real-World Effects
section: Rejecting Invalid Routes vs. De-Prioritizing Them
text:
Rejecting Invalid Routes vs. De-Prioritizing Them
When deploying ROV, an operator must choose between two policy philosophies:

Option A: Hard Dropping (Drop Invalids)
route-map INBOUND-POLICY deny 10
 match rpki invalid

Security Guarantee: 100% immune to origin hijacks and unauthorized subprefix injections.
Operational Risk: If a legitimate content provider misconfigures its ROA, your network will drop all routes to that service, rendering it completely unreachable for your users.



Option B: Soft De-prioritizing (Deprecate Invalids)
route-map INBOUND-POLICY permit 10
 match rpki invalid
 set local-preference 10

Security Guarantee: Fails against subprefix hijacks! If an attacker announces a /24 subprefix, Longest Prefix Match overrides LOCAL_PREF = 10. The router still sends traffic to the attacker.
