Operational Consensus: The global networking community (MANRS, RFC 7454) firmly rejects Option B. To achieve routing security, operators must drop Invalid routes entirely.

title: Operational Consequences of ROV: Invalid, Valid, NotFound and Real-World Effects
section: The Risk of Rejecting Legitimate Traffic
text:
The Risk of Rejecting Legitimate Traffic
The primary barrier preventing hesitant network operators from enabling ROV enforcement is the fear of self-inflicted collateral outages.
If a large university, government agency, or SaaS vendor creates a typo in its ROA (or fails to update its ROA when shifting traffic to a new CDN partner), the route is classified as Invalid. A Tier-1 ISP that drops Invalids will cut off access to that vendor for all its subscribers, prompting support escalation and angry executive inquiries.

title: Operational Consequences of ROV: Invalid, Valid, NotFound and Real-World Effects
text:
NotFound: The Ambiguous Middle State
Currently, approximately 50% to 55% of global IPv4 prefixes have valid ROAs. The remaining 45% reside in the NotFound (Unknown) state.

NotFound does not mean a route is legitimate; it merely means the prefix owner has not signed an RPKI ROA.
Routers cannot drop NotFound routes; doing so would break connectivity to nearly half the Internet.
Consequently, attackers targeting NotFound address space can still execute classic origin prefix hijacks uncontested by ROV.

title: Operational Consequences of ROV: Invalid, Valid, NotFound and Real-World Effects
section: Max-Length Policy Errors and Collateral Damage
text:
Max-Length Policy Errors and Collateral Damage
As discussed in Chapter 14, maxLength mismatches account for over 80% of all benign Invalid route states observed globally:
[Legitimate Enterprise Allocation: 203.0.113.0/22]
                       |
        ROA published: 203.0.113.0/22 (No maxLength)
                       |
   Enterprise Network Operations adds DDoS Mitigation:
      Announces: 203.0.113.0/24 to Akamai/Cloudflare
                       |
               ROV Evaluation:
       Prefix Length (24) > Authorized Length (22)
                       |
                       v
         ROUTE FLAGGED INVALID AND DROPPED!
The enterprise inadvertently blackholes its own DDoS protection service because its network engineers did not coordinate with the team managing its RPKI portal.

title: Operational Consequences of ROV: Invalid, Valid, NotFound and Real-World Effects
section: Documented Incidents: When ROV Went Wrong
text:
Documented Incidents: When ROV Went Wrong

1. The Cloudflare / AWS Route 53 Incident (2018)
When attackers hijacked Amazon Route 53 DNS IP space (205.251.192.0/24) to drain MyEtherWallet cryptocurrency wallets, authoritative DNS queries were redirected to Russian servers. Networks that had enabled ROV dropped the hijack because Amazon had published valid ROAs, but networks lacking ROV fell victim.


2. The Orange España RPKI Account Takeover (January 2024)
A rogue actor accessed Orange España’s RIPE NCC administrator portal via compromised credentials that lacked Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). The intruder created fraudulent ROAs for Orange’s primary infrastructure prefixes with bogus origin ASNs. Within minutes, global validators downloaded the new ROAs, flagged Orange España’s legitimate BGP announcements as Invalid, and Tier-1 ISPs dropped the routes, knocking the entire national telco offline for several hours until RIPE administrators manually intervened.

title: The Scope and Limits of RPKI and ROV
text:
The Scope and Limits of RPKI and ROV
RPKI Route Origin Validation is the cornerstone of modern routing defense, but it is not a silver bullet. Understanding what RPKI can and cannot prove is essential for architects designing resilient network perimeters.

title: The Scope and Limits of RPKI and ROV
section: What Origin Validation Proves and What It Does Not
text:
What Origin Validation Proves and What It Does Not
The scope of RPKI ROV is strictly limited to the rightmost element of the BGP announcement:








Security Claim
Can RPKI ROV Prove It?
Explanation




Origin ASN Authorization
YES
Proves the rightmost ASN in AS_PATH is authorized by the resource holder to originate the prefix.


Prefix Length Authorization
YES
Enforces that announced prefix mask does not exceed maxLength.


Path Authenticity / Integrity
NO
Cannot verify whether intermediate ASNs in AS_PATH actually forwarded or received the route.


Data Plane Forwarding
NO
A router with a Valid route may still drop, blackhole, or snoop packets in the data plane.


Prevention of Route Leaks
NO
In a route leak, the origin ASN is legitimate; therefore, the route evaluates as Valid under ROV.

title: The Scope and Limits of RPKI and ROV
section: Why RPKI Cannot Prevent All Route Leaks
text:
Why RPKI Cannot Prevent All Route Leaks
Consider the classic route leak scenario: - Google originates 8.8.8.0/24 with origin AS15169. - Google creates a valid ROA: (8.8.8.0/24, maxLength=24, Origin=15169). - Transit Provider \(A\) sends the route to Customer \(B\). - Customer \(B\) leaks the route to Transit Provider \(C\) with AS_PATH: [Customer_B, Provider_A, 15169].
When Transit Provider \(C\) receives the route: 1. It inspects the origin ASN: 15169. 2. It compares 8.8.8.0/24 against the VRP cache. 3. The origin matches 15169. The prefix length matches /24. 4. Result: Valid.
Provider \(C\) installs the leaked route, directing its traffic into Customer \(B\)’s saturated connection. RPKI ROV validated the route as legitimate because the origin was never altered.

title: The Scope and Limits of RPKI and ROV
section: The Dependency on Accurate, Complete ROA Data
text:
The Dependency on Accurate, Complete ROA Data
RPKI is entirely dependent on human operators keeping their registry data synchronized with physical network changes: - If a network migrates its data center from one transit provider to another but forgets to update its ROA, legitimate traffic will be dropped as Invalid. - If an enterprise delegates address management to a regional branch that fails to pay its RIR maintenance fees, the parent RIR can revoke the resource certificate, instantly invalidating the enterprise’s global routing.

title: The Scope and Limits of RPKI and ROV
text:
Cryptographic Soundness vs. Operational Fragility
RPKI introduces an explicit coupling between interdomain routing (traditionally a distributed, loosely coupled control plane) and centralized cryptographic infrastructure: - Centralized Dependencies: If an RIR’s publication server or TAL repository goes offline for extended periods or suffers DNS failures, validator caches decay. - Clock Drift: Because X.509 certificates and manifests rely on UTC timestamps, routers or validator servers with unsynchronized clocks (NTP drift) will reject valid certificates as either expired or not yet valid.

title: The Scope and Limits of RPKI and ROV
text:
Misconceptions About What RPKI “Solves”

“RPKI encrypts Internet traffic.” — False. RPKI validates BGP control-plane assertions; it does not touch or encrypt data-plane payload packets.
“If I enable ROV, nobody can hijack my traffic.” — False. An attacker can execute a forged-origin path hijack by prepending your ASN to their announcement (AS_PATH: [Attacker_AS, Victim_AS]), tricking ROV into evaluating your ASN as the origin.
“RPKI eliminates the need for prefix filtering.” — False. Strict customer prefix-lists, IRR filters, and maximum-prefix limits remain essential complementary controls.

title: Complementary Mechanisms: IRR Filtering, Prefix Filters and AS_PATH Filters
text:
Complementary Mechanisms: IRR Filtering, Prefix Filters and AS_PATH Filters
Because RPKI ROV only authenticates the origin of a route, robust edge security requires defense in depth. Network operators must combine ROV with deterministic inbound and outbound prefix filtering, regular-expression AS_PATH filtering, and hardware resource limits.

title: Complementary Mechanisms: IRR Filtering, Prefix Filters and AS_PATH Filters
section: Prefix Filters: What Prefixes Should Be Announced
text:
Prefix Filters: What Prefixes Should Be Announced
Every eBGP session must enforce strict boundaries on what prefixes may be received and transmitted:

1. Bogon and Special-Purpose Filtering
Routers must unconditionally discard advertisements for IP space that should never appear on the public Internet (RFC 6890): - IPv4 Bogons: 0.0.0.0/8, 10.0.0.0/8, 100.64.0.0/10, 127.0.0.0/8, 169.254.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12, 192.0.2.0/24, 192.168.0.0/16, 198.18.0.0/15, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 224.0.0.0/4 (Multicast), 240.0.0.0/4. - IPv6 Bogons: ::/8, 0100::/64, 2001:db8::/32, fe80::/10, fc00::/7 (ULA), ff00::/8 (Multicast).


2. Prefix Length Boundaries

In IPv4: drop any prefix smaller than /8 or longer than /24.
In IPv6: drop any prefix smaller than /19 or longer than /48.

title: Complementary Mechanisms: IRR Filtering, Prefix Filters and AS_PATH Filters
section: AS_PATH Filters: Detecting and Rejecting Suspicious Paths
text:
AS_PATH Filters: Detecting and Rejecting Suspicious Paths
Operators use regular expressions (regex) to inspect AS_PATH segments:
! Reject private ASNs, reserved ASNs, or path anomalies (Cisco IOS XR / Junos)
as-path-set BOGON-ASNS
  64512-65534,          # 16-bit Private ASNs
  65535,                # Reserved
  4200000000-4294967294 # 32-bit Private ASNs
end-set

! Reject routes containing bogon ASNs in transit
if as-path enters-with BOGON-ASNS then
  drop
endif

! Customer session enforcement: enforce that the first hop in AS_PATH matches customer's configured ASN
if not as-path starts-with ^65001 then
  drop
endif
By enforcing that the first ASN in the AS_PATH matches the neighbor’s ASN, an ISP prevents a customer from spoofing direct peering sessions with other networks.

title: Complementary Mechanisms: IRR Filtering, Prefix Filters and AS_PATH Filters
section: IRR-Based Filtering: Still Relevant After RPKI
text:
IRR-Based Filtering: Still Relevant After RPKI
While RPKI validates origins, IRR filters validate topology and customer cones: - An ISP queries the customer’s as-set (e.g., AS-HURRICANE) using bgpq4. - The tool recursively expands all downstream customer ASNs and their registered route objects into an explicit prefix-list. - Even if an attacker uses a valid origin ASN to execute a route leak, the route is rejected at the ISP’s border because it is not registered inside the customer’s legitimate IRR cone.

title: Complementary Mechanisms: IRR Filtering, Prefix Filters and AS_PATH Filters
section: Maximum-Prefix Limits: Protection Against Table Poisoning
text:
Maximum-Prefix Limits: Protection Against Table Poisoning
Every BGP session must be configured with a hardware safety valve: the Maximum-Prefix Limit:
! FRR / Cisco IOS Syntax
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.0.2.2 maximum-prefix 100 80 restart 15

If a customer who normally announces 5 prefixes accidentally leaks 100,000 routes, the moment the count crosses \(80\) (80%), the router issues a high-severity syslog alarm.
When the count exceeds \(100\), the router immediately sends a BGP NOTIFICATION (Cease / Maximum Number of Prefixes Reached) and tears down the TCP session.
This protects the router’s control-plane CPU and TCAM from buffer exhaustion.

title: Complementary Mechanisms: IRR Filtering, Prefix Filters and AS_PATH Filters
section: BGP Communities for Policy Signaling and Leak Prevention
text:
BGP Communities for Policy Signaling and Leak Prevention
Operators classify every imported route using internal BGP communities:








Community
Operational Meaning
Policy Action




65000:100
Learned from Customer
Propagate to Transit, Peers, and Customers


65000:200
Learned from Settlement-Free Peer
Propagate to Customers only; NEVER to Transit


65000:300
Learned from Paid Transit Provider
Propagate to Customers only; NEVER to Peers or Transit



Before exporting routes to any external transit provider or lateral peer, an export route-map checks the community. Any route carrying 65000:200 or 65000:300 is unconditionally suppressed, programmatically guaranteeing that the network cannot become an accidental transit pipe.

title: Route Leak Detection and Prevention Mechanisms
text:
Route Leak Detection and Prevention Mechanisms
Route leaks remain one of the most volatile disruptions on the global Internet. Because traditional RPKI ROV does not detect route leaks, the industry has developed architectural standards, automated telemetry systems, and industry self-regulation frameworks to systematically detect and prevent them.

title: Route Leak Detection and Prevention Mechanisms
text:
Community-Based Leak Prevention and RFC 9234
Operators have long relied on proprietary BGP communities to tag routes. However, proprietary communities do not cross organizational boundaries: upstream ISP \(A\) strips or ignores customer \(B\)’s internal communities.
To standardize leak prevention across administrative domains, the IETF published RFC 9234: Route Leak Prevention and Detection Using BGP Roles:
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|               BGP Role Negotiation (RFC 9234)             |
|                                                           |
|  Provider AS                                  Customer AS |
|     Role: Provider <=========================> Role: Customer
|                                                           |
|  - When Provider advertises route to Customer:            |
|    Attaches "Only to Customer" (OTC) Attribute: OTC=Provider_ASN
|                                                           |
|  - When Customer advertises route to another Provider:    |
|    Second Provider inspects OTC attribute:                |
|    "Wait! This route has an OTC set, but I received it    |
|     from a Customer/Peer! This is an illegal leak!"       |
|    --> ROUTE REJECTED AT BORDER!                          |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+

Role Negotiation: When establishing a BGP session, peers negotiate their commercial relationship in the OPEN message: Provider, Customer, Peer, or RS-Client.
OTC Attribute: When a route moves down a hierarchy (Provider \(\to\) Customer) or laterally across peers (Peer \(\leftrightarrow\) Peer), the router attaches the Only to Customer (OTC) path attribute (Type 35), recording its own ASN.
Automatic Leak Rejection: If an upstream router receives a route from a customer or lateral peer that already contains an OTC attribute, it detects an illegal “valley” path and automatically rejects the route, neutralizing the leak in software without requiring complex manual prefix-lists.

title: Route Leak Detection and Prevention Mechanisms
section: Automated Leak Detection via Route Collectors and Monitors
text:
Automated Leak Detection via Route Collectors and Monitors
When route leaks occur, real-time monitoring algorithms detect them through anomalous propagation signatures: - Valley-Path Algorithms: Automated telemetry engines inspect the AS_PATH streams received by RIPE RIS and RouteViews. By maintaining a global inferred topology map (customer-provider pairs), algorithms flag any path containing a Customer \(\to\) Provider \(\to\) Customer sequence as a probable route leak. - Traffic Shift Probes: Automated synthetic measurement networks (e.g., RIPE Atlas, ThousandEyes) detect sudden 200ms latency spikes and buffer-bloat jitter on paths that previously converged in 15ms.

title: Route Leak Detection and Prevention Mechanisms
text:
BGPsec Route Leak Prevention Potential
While BGPsec (RFC 8205) was designed to protect path integrity by having each AS cryptographically sign its announcement to the next hop, base BGPsec does not inherently prevent route leaks: - In a route leak, the customer legally received the route from Provider \(A\) with a valid cryptographic signature. - The customer appends its own valid signature and passes it to Provider \(B\). - The signature chain is mathematically flawless! - To prevent leaks, cryptographic protocols must incorporate role metadata (such as ASPA or signed OTC attributes) into the signature envelope.

title: Route Leak Detection and Prevention Mechanisms
section: MANRS Principles and Their Implementation Status
text:
MANRS Principles and Their Implementation Status
The Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security (MANRS) is a global, industry-led initiative operated under the Internet Society (ISOC) that establishes a baseline of routing hygiene:








MANRS Action
Technical Requirement
Operational Focus




Action 1: Filtering
Prevent propagation of incorrect routing information
Strict prefix-lists on customer sessions; RPKI ROV enforcement


Action 2: Anti-Spoofing
Prevent traffic with spoofed source IP addresses
Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF, RFC 3704) on edge access links


Action 3: Coordination
Facilitate global operational communication
Accurate, maintained contact info in PeeringDB and RIR WHOIS


Action 4: Global Validation
Publicly document routing policy
Publish valid ROAs in RPKI and maintained route/as-set objects in IRR



MANRS participation has become a mandatory procurement requirement for Tier-1 telcos, major cloud operators, and financial enterprises.

title: Route Leak Detection and Prevention Mechanisms
section: Coordination and Incident Response When Leaks Occur
text:
Coordination and Incident Response When Leaks Occur
When a severe leak bypasses filters and floods a network: 1. Out-of-Band NOC Communication: Operators contact the leaking network’s 24/7 Network Operations Center (NOC) via phone numbers published in PeeringDB. 2. Session Teardown: If the leaking customer does not answer, the upstream provider immediately executes shutdown on the BGP neighbor session. 3. Emergency Disaggregation: The victim network temporarily announces more-specific /24 subprefixes to reclaim its traffic until the leak converges out of the global DFZ.

title: BGPsec: Architecture, Security Guarantees and Deployment Reality
text:
BGPsec: Architecture, Security Guarantees and Deployment Reality
For over a decade, the Holy Grail of interdomain routing security was BGPsec, standardized by the IETF in RFC 8205 (Protocol Specification) and RFC 8206–8211. BGPsec was conceived to solve the fundamental flaw of path-vector routing: the inability to cryptographically verify the integrity of the AS_PATH.

title: BGPsec: Architecture, Security Guarantees and Deployment Reality
section: BGPsec’s Threat Model: Protecting AS_PATH Integrity
text:
BGPsec’s Threat Model: Protecting AS_PATH Integrity
While RPKI ROV authenticates the origin of a prefix, it leaves the intermediate hops completely unverified. An adversary can execute a forged-origin path hijack: - The attacker operates \(AS_{666}\). - The attacker announces a victim’s prefix (\(AS_{100}\)) with AS_PATH: [AS_{666}, AS_{100}]. - A remote router running ROV inspects the rightmost ASN: it sees \(AS_{100}\). Because \(AS_{100}\) is the legitimate owner with a valid ROA, the router marks the announcement as Valid, and the attacker succeeds in diverting traffic.
BGPsec was designed to make path forgery mathematically impossible: every single Autonomous System along the path must cryptographically sign its routing update to the next hop.

title: BGPsec: Architecture, Security Guarantees and Deployment Reality
section: The BGPsec Path Attribute and Signature Chain
text:
The BGPsec Path Attribute and Signature Chain
BGPsec replaces the traditional AS_PATH with a new optional non-transitive path attribute: BGPsec_Path:
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       BGPsec Path Segment                     |
|                                                               |
|  [Origin AS 100]                                              |
|  - Signs: (Prefix P, Target AS 200, Algorithm ID, Key ID)     |
|    Signature = Sig_100                                        |
|         |                                                     |
|         v                                                     |
|  [Transit AS 200]                                             |
|  - Validates Sig_100 using AS 100's RPKI Router Certificate   |
|  - Appends its own Secure Path Segment:                       |
|    Signs: (Sig_100, Target AS 300, Algorithm ID, Key ID)      |
|    Signature = Sig_200                                        |
|         |                                                     |
|         v                                                     |
|  [Destination AS 300]                                         |
|  - Validates complete cryptographic chain: Sig_200 -> Sig_100 |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
Each signature binds: 1. The preceding signature block. 2. The local ASN. 3. The ASN of the intended downstream peer (Target AS). 4. A cryptographic timestamp.
An adversary cannot delete an AS hop, rearrange hops, or insert an arbitrary AS into the middle of the path without breaking the cryptographic digital signature chain.

title: BGPsec: Architecture, Security Guarantees and Deployment Reality
text:
Key Management and Certificate Infrastructure
To support BGPsec: - Every router in an AS must possess a private key paired with an RPKI Router Certificate (RFC 8209). - Router certificates are issued under the AS holder’s RPKI CA and published in the global RPKI repository tree. - The cryptographic algorithm mandated is ECDSA with the P-256 curve and SHA-256 (RFC 8208).

title: BGPsec: Architecture, Security Guarantees and Deployment Reality
section: Operational Barriers: Complexity, Interoperability and Performance
text:
Operational Barriers: Complexity, Interoperability and Performance
Despite being a complete IETF standard since 2017, BGPsec has seen near-zero production deployment across the global Internet DFZ. The reasons are structural:

1. The Asymmetric Cryptographic Compute Penalty
Verifying an ECDSA signature requires significant CPU cycles. A backbone router receiving a full routing table during a global convergence storm would need to verify hundreds of thousands of cryptographic signatures per second. Router control processors would immediately suffer complete CPU exhaustion, causing sessions to flap and collapse.


2. Message Size and MTU Fragmentation
Standard BGP messages are capped at 4096 bytes. A 5-hop BGPsec signature chain consumes several kilobytes of overhead, requiring universal support for Extended BGP Messages (RFC 8654, 65,535 bytes) and risking IP-layer packet fragmentation across transit links.


3. The All-or-Nothing Deployment Trap
BGPsec requires an unbroken chain of cryptographic signatures. If even a single intermediate transit provider along a path does not support BGPsec, the signature chain is broken, and the route drops back to legacy unauthenticated BGP. There is zero economic incentive for an early adopter to invest in expensive hardware upgrades if their upstreams do not.

title: BGPsec: Architecture, Security Guarantees and Deployment Reality
section: Current Deployment Status and Future Prospects
text:
Current Deployment Status and Future Prospects
As of 2026, BGPsec remains an academic reference architecture rather than an operational defense. The global networking community has largely pivoted toward lighter, out-of-band path verification mechanisms—most notably Autonomous System Provider Authorizations (ASPA)—which provide robust path protection without requiring in-band cryptographic signing on wire-speed routers.

title: ASPA: Autonomous System Provider Authorizations
text:
ASPA: Autonomous System Provider Authorizations
Recognizing that BGPsec’s in-band cryptographic overhead rendered it operationally unviable, the IETF SIDROPS working group designed Autonomous System Provider Authorization (ASPA) (draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-profile and draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification). ASPA provides practical, scalable protection against both route leaks and forged-origin path hijacks using the existing out-of-band RPKI infrastructure.

title: ASPA: Autonomous System Provider Authorizations
section: What ASPA Is and the Problem It Solves
text:
What ASPA Is and the Problem It Solves
ASPA shifts the security verification model from signing every dynamic route announcement to publishing verified out-of-band statements of upstream provider relationships:

In BGP, a route leak occurs when a customer forwards a route learned from one provider to another provider.
A forged-origin hijack occurs when an attacker fakes an adjacency to a legitimate origin.
Both attacks violate the fundamental commercial topology of the Internet: a customer only sends routes to its upstream providers; a provider never routes through a customer to reach the global transit web.

ASPA allows an Autonomous System to formally publish a signed object stating: “These are the only ASNs that are authorized to act as my upstream transit providers.”

title: ASPA: Autonomous System Provider Authorizations
section: ASPA Structure: Customer, Provider and Peer Relationships
text:
ASPA Structure: Customer, Provider and Peer Relationships
An ASPA is an RPKI signed object cryptographically bound to a Customer ASN:
ASPA Object Payload:
  CustomerASID: AS65001
  ProviderASSet: [
    AS174 (Cogent),
    AS2914 (NTT),
    AS3356 (Lumen)
  ]
This simple list asserts that AS65001 only purchases transit from AS174, AS2914, and AS3356. If a route appears on the Internet with AS_PATH: [AS7018, AS65001, ...], but AS7018 is not listed in AS65001’s ASPA object, downstream routers know that AS7018 has no legitimate commercial authority to act as AS65001’s provider!

title: ASPA: Autonomous System Provider Authorizations
section: Integration with the RPKI Trust Infrastructure
text:
Integration with the RPKI Trust Infrastructure
Like ROAs, ASPA objects: - Are issued under the resource holder’s RPKI CA. - Are verified against the RIR Trust Anchor root certificates. - Are downloaded and validated by relying party validators (such as Routinator or rpki-client). - Are delivered to routers over the RPKI-to-Router (RTR) protocol version 2 (RFC 8210-bis).
Because ASPA objects represent static business contracts rather than dynamic route states, a single ASPA object covers all prefixes originated by that AS. The total global ASPA dataset requires only tens of thousands of records, fitting comfortably inside router RAM.

title: ASPA: Autonomous System Provider Authorizations
section: How ASPA Validation Affects Route Selection
text:
How ASPA Validation Affects Route Selection
When a router evaluates an incoming AS_PATH, it runs the ASPA Verification Algorithm:
[Inbound BGP Route]
         |
         v
Deconstruct AS_PATH into directional hop pairs: (AS_i -> AS_{i+1})
         |
         v
Compare hop pairs against local ASPA database:
- Is AS_{i+1} listed in ASPA(AS_i)? (Valid Upstream)
- Is AS_i listed in ASPA(AS_{i+1})? (Valid Downstream)
         |
         +---------------------------------------+
         |                                       |
         v                                       v
No valley violations found?             Illegal valley sequence detected:
State: VALID                            - Customer -> Provider -> Customer -> Provider
                                        - Forged direct adjacency
                                                 |
                                                 v
                                        State: INVALID -> REJECT ROUTE!
ASPA assigns one of three verification states to the path: 1. Valid: The sequence of AS hops complies strictly with the Gao-Rexford model of provider-customer hierarchy. 2. Invalid: At least one hop pair is demonstrably contradicted by an authoritative ASPA record (e.g., an unlisted AS acting as a provider, or an illegal valley route leak). 3. Unknown: Insufficient ASPA records exist to determine path validity.
Routers configure inbound policies to unconditionally drop ASPA Invalid routes, neutralizing route leaks and forged-origin hijacks before they can enter the Loc-RIB.

title: ASPA: Autonomous System Provider Authorizations
section: Current Deployment Status and Standardization Progress
text:
Current Deployment Status and Standardization Progress
As of 2026, ASPA represents the most actively developed and promising routing security protocol in the IETF: - Supported in open-source validators (Routinator, rpki-client, FORT). - Production implementations running on open routing platforms (BIRD 2.15+, FRR). - Active commercial trials and interoperability testing across Tier-1 backbones (NTT, Cloudflare, Lumen). - Widespread deployment of ASPA alongside RPKI ROV promises to close the path-manipulation loophole that has plagued BGP for thirty years.

title: Designing and Implementing Routing Security in Your Network
text:
Designing and Implementing Routing Security in Your Network
Deploying routing security across an active production network requires a structured, multi-phase engineering process. Implementing controls haphazardly—such as enforcing hard ROV drops before auditing address allocations—is a guaranteed recipe for self-inflicted outages.
This chapter outlines an end-to-end, seven-step blueprint for hardening an Autonomous System.

title: Designing and Implementing Routing Security in Your Network
section: Step 1: Inventory and Audit Your Address Space and Announcements
text:
Step 1: Inventory and Audit Your Address Space and Announcements
Before touching a single firewall or router configuration, create an authoritative inventory: - Query public route collectors (e.g., whois -h whois.radb.net -- "-i origin AS<YOUR_ASN>") to list all prefixes currently seen on the global Internet. - Check internal IP Address Management (IPAM) systems to identify all assigned, unassigned, and delegated subnets. - Reconcile differences: identify any ghost prefixes being announced without business justification, or internal subnets missing from external tables.

title: Designing and Implementing Routing Security in Your Network
section: Step 2: Verify Ownership and Create or Update ROAs
text:
Step 2: Verify Ownership and Create or Update ROAs
Log into your organization’s RIR portal (ARIN, RIPE, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC): - Verify that your organization is listed as the authoritative Org-ID on all resource certificates. - Generate cryptographically valid ROAs matching your active BGP announcements. - Enforce the Minimal ROA rule (RFC 9319): Set maxLength equal to the announced prefix length. If you announce a /22 and two /24 subprefixes, create three explicit ROAs rather than a single /22 max-length 24.

title: Designing and Implementing Routing Security in Your Network
section: Step 3: Design and Deploy Import Filters
text:
Step 3: Design and Deploy Import Filters
Apply deterministic inbound hygiene filters on all transit and peering sessions: - Unconditionally deny IPv4/IPv6 bogon ranges (RFC 6890). - Unconditionally deny default routes (0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0) from lateral peers and IXPs. - Enforce prefix length sanity: drop IPv4 \(< /8\) or \(> /24\); drop IPv6 \(< /19\) or \(> /48\). - Configure hardware maximum-prefix limits on every neighbor session with an 80% warning threshold and auto-restart cooldown.

title: Designing and Implementing Routing Security in Your Network
section: Step 4: Design and Deploy Export Filters
text:
Step 4: Design and Deploy Export Filters
Prevent accidental route leaks at your outbound border: - Define an explicit prefix-list containing only your locally owned and operated address space. - Apply this prefix-list to all outbound route-maps facing transit providers and settlement-free peers. - Tag all inbound routes from providers and peers with internal NO-TRANSIT communities, and ensure export policies discard any route bearing those tags.

title: Designing and Implementing Routing Security in Your Network
section: Step 5: Enable ROV with Staged Enforcement
text:
Step 5: Enable ROV with Staged Enforcement
Never transition directly from zero validation to hard drops in production. Execute a staged migration:

Stage A: Validation Without Enforcement (Telemetry Mode)
Deploy validators (Routinator / rpki-client) and establish RTR sessions with border routers. Configure the router to evaluate ROV states, but do not alter forwarding:
route-map PEER-IN permit 10
 match rpki invalid
 set community 65000:666 additive   <-- Tag only; do not drop
Monitor logs and NetFlow data for 30 days to identify legitimate partners whose routes evaluate as Invalid due to clerical errors.


Stage B: Hard Drop Enforcement
Once telemetry confirms that no critical business services are flagged as Invalid, activate hard drops across all transit and peer borders:
route-map PEER-IN deny 10
 match rpki invalid
!
route-map PEER-IN permit 20

title: Designing and Implementing Routing Security in Your Network
section: Step 6: Implement Monitoring, Logging and Alerting
text:
Step 6: Implement Monitoring, Logging and Alerting
Set up automated alerting infrastructure: - Stream BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP, RFC 7854) data from border routers to an internal collector. - Subscribe to real-time public telemetry (RIS-Live or BGPStream). - Configure automated alerts that trigger immediately if an unauthorized ASN originates your prefixes or if a validator RTR session drops.

title: Designing and Implementing Routing Security in Your Network
section: Step 7: Document Policies, Plan Rollback and Test Recovery
text:
Step 7: Document Policies, Plan Rollback and Test Recovery
Every security configuration must have an emergency recovery procedure: - Document the exact CLI command required to bypass ROV globally if an RIR infrastructure outage corrupts the VRP cache. - Schedule bi-annual fire drills in staging or containerized lab environments (Containerlab) where engineers practice mitigating simulated hijacks, invalid states, and validator synchronization failures.

title: Configuration Examples and Vendor-Specific Considerations
text:
Configuration Examples and Vendor-Specific Considerations
Routing security concepts are universal, but syntax, execution semantics, and memory structures vary significantly across routing operating systems. This chapter provides production-ready configuration stanzas across major commercial and open-source platforms.

title: Configuration Examples and Vendor-Specific Considerations
section: Cisco IOS XR: ROV, Filtering and RTR Configuration
text:
Cisco IOS XR: ROV, Filtering and RTR Configuration
Cisco IOS XR manages RPKI caches using the RPKI-to-Router protocol under the global routing configuration, and applies policy using Routing Policy Language (RPL):
! Configure RTR connection to two redundant RPKI validators
router bgp 65001
 rpki server 192.0.2.10
  transport tcp port 3323
  refresh-time 1800
  response-time 60
 !
 rpki server 192.0.2.20
  transport tcp port 3323
  refresh-time 1800
  response-time 60
 !
! Define RPL policy to drop Invalids and prefer Valids
route-policy EBGP-INBOUND
  # Bogon filtering
  if destination in BOGON-PREFIXES then
    drop
  endif
  # Enforce RPKI Route Origin Validation
  if rpki origin state is invalid then
    drop
  elseif rpki origin state is valid then
    set local-preference 200
    pass
  else
    # NotFound / Unknown
    set local-preference 100
    pass
  endif
end-policy

title: Configuration Examples and Vendor-Specific Considerations
section: Juniper Junos: ROV, Filtering and RPKI Integration

title: Configuration Examples and Vendor-Specific Considerations
section: Nokia SR OS: Routing Security Configuration
text:
Nokia SR OS: Routing Security Configuration
In Nokia SR OS (Service Router Operating System), RPKI sessions are established under the global router context, and validation is integrated into routing policy:
/configure router
    origin-validation
        rpki-session 192.0.2.10
            port 3323
            admin-state enable
        exit
        rpki-session 192.0.2.20
            port 3323
            admin-state enable
        exit
    exit
    policy-options
        begin
        policy-statement "ROV-POLICY"
            entry 10
                from
                    protocol bgp
                    origin-validation-state invalid
                exit
                action drop
            exit
            entry 20
                from
                    protocol bgp
                    origin-validation-state valid
                exit
                action accept
                    local-preference 200
                exit
            exit
            default-action accept
                local-preference 100
            exit
        exit
        commit

title: Configuration Examples and Vendor-Specific Considerations
section: Open Source and Research Platforms: FRR and BIRD

title: Configuration Examples and Vendor-Specific Considerations
text:
Common Pitfalls Across Platforms

Failure to Commit: On modular systems (IOS XR and Junos), policy edits require explicit commit. Uncommitted RPKI changes remain inactive while misleading administrators.
Implicit Fall-Through Behavior: In some platforms (Cisco IOS XE), failing to specify an explicit permit term after an RPKI deny causes an implicit deny-all, blackholing all valid traffic!
Session Flap CPU Spikes: Configuring RTR refresh timers too aggressively (e.g., 10 seconds) forces continuous re-evaluation of full tables, spiking router CPU. Maintain default timers (1800 to 3600 seconds).

title: Troubleshooting Routing Security Controls
text:
Troubleshooting Routing Security Controls
When routing security mechanisms malfunction, legitimate traffic is dropped, peering sessions flap, and reachability breaks. Diagnosing these failures requires a disciplined, hypothesis-driven methodology that isolates whether the fault resides in the router’s local policy, the RTR transport layer, the validator cache, or the upstream RIR cryptographic hierarchy.

title: Troubleshooting Routing Security Controls
text:
Unexpected Invalid Routes: Systematic Diagnosis
When a route unexpectedly evaluates as Invalid: 1. Identify the exact announced parameters: Run show bgp <prefix> to extract: - Announced Prefix (e.g., 198.51.100.0/24) - Origin ASN (the rightmost ASN in the AS_PATH) 2. Compare against local VRP entries: On Cisco: show bgp rpki prefix 198.51.100.0/24. On Junos: show validation database 198.51.100.0/24. 3. Determine the exact invalid condition: - AS Mismatch: A covering VRP exists for the prefix, but specifies a different authorized ASN (e.g., authorized AS65001, but received AS65002). - Length Mismatch: The ASN matches, but the announced prefix length exceeds maxLength (e.g., announced /24, but ROA maxLength is /22).

title: Troubleshooting Routing Security Controls
section: RTR Session Failures and Stale Validation Data
text:
RTR Session Failures and Stale Validation Data
If border routers report that all routes have reverted to NotFound or that RPKI tables are empty: - Check TCP Layer Connectivity: Ensure firewalls permit TCP port 323 / 3323 between the router loopback and the validator IP. - Inspect Serial Number Desynchronization: If a validator server reboots and resets its internal database without properly incrementing its serial number, the router may reject updates. Force an explicit reset query: - Cisco: clear bgp rpki server <IP> reset - Junos: clear validation session <IP> - Examine Expire Timers: If the validator fails to respond to keepalives, verify whether the router’s expire-time has lapsed, purging the cache from memory.

title: Troubleshooting Routing Security Controls
section: ROA Lookup: Verifying What Validators See

title: Troubleshooting Routing Security Controls
text:
Legitimate Routes Rejected by Filters
If a route is dropped despite having a Valid RPKI state, the drop is typically caused by a static filter placed before the RPKI evaluation term in the route policy: - Bogon filter misconfiguration: The prefix falls within an overly broad bogon regex. - Prefix-list length restriction: The inbound prefix-list permits only /8 to /22, rejecting a legitimate /24. - Maximum-prefix trip: The neighbor’s total prefix count exceeded the configured ceiling, causing the router to drop all routes from that session.

title: Troubleshooting Routing Security Controls
text:
Cross-Validator Consistency Checks
Running a single validator instance creates a single point of failure and vulnerability to implementation bugs: - Operate at least two distinct validator engines: e.g., Validator A running Routinator (Rust) and Validator B running rpki-client (C/OpenBSD). - Run automated cron scripts comparing the total VRP count output by each validator. If the VRP counts diverge by more than 2%, trigger an administrative alert to investigate repository sync failures or parsing discrepancies.

title: Troubleshooting Routing Security Controls
text:
Post-Incident Forensics: Reconstructing What Happened
When a routing security incident concludes: 1. Pull BGP Table Dumps and BMP Archives: Capture historical updates from the incident window to reconstruct the exact timestamps when the illegitimate announcement appeared, propagated, and was withdrawn. 2. Review RIR Audit Logs: Determine whether the incident was caused by an account takeover, a revoked resource certificate, or an operator typo in the RIR portal. 3. Conduct Root-Cause Analysis (RCA): Document why local and upstream filters did or did not mitigate the issue, and update automated test suites to prevent recurrence.

title: Monitoring, Measurement and Testing
text:
Monitoring, Measurement and Testing
You cannot defend what you cannot see, and you cannot observe global interdomain routing anomalies from the perspective of a single border router. Comprehensive routing defense requires continuous global measurement, real-time streaming telemetry, and isolated testing environments where security controls can be validated safely before live deployment.

title: Monitoring, Measurement and Testing
section: Real-Time Route Monitoring: BGPStream, RIS-Live and RouteViews
text:
Real-Time Route Monitoring: BGPStream, RIS-Live and RouteViews
Modern security operations centers (SOCs) and network operations centers (NOCs) rely on distributed telemetry frameworks to monitor their prefixes from hundreds of external vantage points:
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|                   Global Telemetry Collectors             |
|                                                           |
|  +-------------------+             +-------------------+  |
|  | RouteViews (UO)   |             | RIPE RIS (Europe) |  |
|  | Hundreds of peers |             | Distributed RRCs  |  |
|  +---------+---------+             +---------+---------+  |
|            |                                 |            |
+------------|---------------------------------|------------+
             |                                 |
             v                                 v
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|               Real-Time Streaming Pipelines               |
|                                                           |
|  - RIS-Live (WebSocket JSON stream of raw updates)        |
|  - BGPStream (C++ / Python framework for MRT and streams) |
|  - BGPalerter (Automated standalone monitoring daemon)    |
+-----------------------------+-----------------------------+
                              |
                              v
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|                 Operator Alerting & Defense               |
|                                                           |
|  - Instant Slack / PagerDuty / Webhook alarms             |
|  - Automated mitigation: disaggregate / activate ROA      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+

1. RIPE RIS and RIS-Live
The RIPE Routing Information Service (RIS) operates remote route collectors (RRCs) at major Internet Exchange Points globally (London, Amsterdam, Tokyo, New York). RIS-Live exposes a real-time WebSocket firehose delivering BGP UPDATE messages within milliseconds of their occurrence on global backbones.


2. RouteViews
Operated by the University of Oregon, RouteViews provides multi-decade historical MRT archives and live multihop BGP peering with Tier-1 and Tier-2 service providers, serving as the gold standard for routing research and forensic investigation.


3. BGPStream and BGPalerter

BGPStream: An open-source software framework for parsing, filtering, and analyzing historical MRT dumps and real-time live BGP data streams.
BGPalerter: A self-hosted open-source monitoring application that tracks an organization’s prefixes, ASNs, and ROAs, firing instant webhook alerts if a prefix is hijacked, a route leaks, or a ROA nears expiration.

title: Monitoring, Measurement and Testing
section: Looking Glasses and Prefix Monitoring Services
text:
Looking Glasses and Prefix Monitoring Services
When an alert fires, engineers need interactive visibility into remote routing tables: - Looking Glasses (LG): Publicly accessible web portals hosted by Tier-1 operators (e.g., Level3/Lumen, NTT, Hurricane Electric) allowing operators to execute ping, traceroute, and show ip bgp <prefix> from specific points of presence across the planet. - Commercial SaaS Monitors: Services such as Cloudflare Radar, Cisco ThousandEyes, and Kentik provide graphical dashboards mapping global propagation paths, prefix visibility percentages, and AS path changes.

title: Monitoring, Measurement and Testing
section: Safe Testing: Lab Environments and Controlled Announcements
text:
Safe Testing: Lab Environments and Controlled Announcements
Deploying new route policies or RPKI validators directly into production is unacceptably risky. Safe verification requires staging in containerized and software-defined testbeds:

1. Containerlab Network Topologies
Using Containerlab, engineers spin up multi-vendor containerized topologies (FRR, Nokia SR Linux, Arista cEOS, BIRD) running on a single developer workstation or CI/CD runner. Topologies simulate upstream transit providers, lateral peers, relying party validators (Routinator), and malicious rogue ASes.
# Example Containerlab test snippet simulating an upstream validator
name: bgp-security-lab
topology:
  nodes:
    validator:
      kind: linux
      image: routinator/routinator:latest
    border-router:
      kind: linux
      image: frrouting/frr:latest
    attacker-as:
      kind: linux
      image: frrouting/frr:latest


2. The PEERING Testbed
For academic and controlled research, the PEERING testbed (operated by USC and partner universities) allows vetted researchers to announce experimental prefixes into the real global Internet from multiple worldwide locations to measure live propagation dynamics without disrupting commercial traffic.

title: Monitoring, Measurement and Testing
section: Public Incident Detection Systems and Alerts
text:
Public Incident Detection Systems and Alerts
Automated detection engines scan global feeds to identify attacks: - CAIDA BGP Mon: Automatically reconstructs prefix hijack events and tracks global prefix churn. - MANRS Observatory: Aggregates routing incidents per Autonomous System, scoring network operators on their compliance with anti-spoofing, filtering, and RPKI deployment standards.

title: Monitoring, Measurement and Testing
section: Metrics That Matter: Convergence, Stability and Coverage
text:
Metrics That Matter: Convergence, Stability and Coverage
To evaluate the operational health of an organization’s routing posture, operators track five primary Key Performance Indicators (KPIs): 1. ROA Coverage: Percentage of announced IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes covered by valid ROAs (Target: 100%). 2. ROV Filtering Rate: Percentage of peering sessions actively enforcing hard drops on Invalid routes (Target: 100% of transit and peer sessions). 3. Prefix Stability / Flap Rate: Number of route withdrawal events per hour across peering sessions. 4. Convergence Latency: Time required for a planned BGP withdrawal or announcement to achieve 95% global propagation across RouteViews collectors (Target: \(< 60\) seconds). 5. ASPA Compliance: Progress in documenting and publishing upstream transit relationships in ASPA objects.

title: Case Studies: Documented Routing Incidents
text:
Case Studies: Documented Routing Incidents
Analyzing historical routing incidents reveals how protocol vulnerabilities, operator errors, and intentional exploits manifest in real-world networks. These landmark case studies shaped the modern routing security landscape and demonstrate why specific defense layers were developed.

title: Case Studies: Documented Routing Incidents
text:
Pakistan Telecom YouTube Hijack (February 24, 2008)
The 2008 YouTube hijack remains the classic textbook demonstration of a subprefix origin hijack:
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
|                    The 2008 YouTube Hijack                    |
|                                                               |
|  [YouTube (AS36561)]                                          |
|  - Announces legitimate covering aggregate: 208.65.152.0/22   |
|                                                               |
|  [Pakistan Telecom (AS17557)]                                 |
|  - Government censorship order: block YouTube domestically    |
|  - Configured internal blackhole null route: 208.65.153.0/24  |
|  - Omitted export filter! Leaked /24 to PCCW Global (AS3491)  |
|                                                               |
|  [PCCW Global (AS3491)]                                       |
|  - Accepted announcement without customer prefix filtering    |
|  - Propagated /24 to global Tier-1 transit backbones          |
|                                                               |
|  [Global Outcome]                                             |
|  - 208.65.153.0/24 (LPM) won against YouTube's /22 globally   |
|  - YouTube went completely dark worldwide for nearly 2 hours  |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+

Context: Following a domestic censorship order by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority to block YouTube video clips, engineers at Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) configured an internal null route on an edge router for YouTube’s IP block: 208.65.153.0/24.
The Mechanism: YouTube legitimately originated the covering /22 aggregate: 208.65.152.0/22. Pakistan Telecom originated the /24 subprefix. Crucially, Pakistan Telecom accidentally leaked this /24 advertisement to its international transit provider, PCCW Global (AS3491).
The Failure: PCCW Global accepted the announcement without enforcing an inbound customer prefix-list, and propagated the /24 to its global transit peers.
The Impact: Because /24 is a longer prefix than /22, Longest Prefix Match directed global Internet traffic for YouTube into Pakistan Telecom’s network, instantly saturating its international links and knocking YouTube completely offline globally for nearly two hours.
Mitigation: YouTube engineers resolved the outage by disaggregating their space, announcing two matching /24 prefixes to compete, and broadcasting emergency out-of-band requests to PCCW Global to filter Pakistan Telecom’s session.

title: Case Studies: Documented Routing Incidents
section: Safe Host / China Telecom Route Leak (June 6, 2019)
text:
Safe Host / China Telecom Route Leak (June 6, 2019)
On June 6, 2019, a Swiss data center provider caused a massive European and international traffic disruption through a Customer-Provider Route Leak:

The Mechanism: Safe Host (AS21217), a Swiss hosting company, received full Internet routing tables from its upstream providers. Due to a configuration error during maintenance, Safe Host re-announced approximately 70,000 global prefixes to China Telecom (AS4134).
The Failure: China Telecom accepted the leaked routes and, because they were learned from a customer session, assigned them high preference and propagated them to other international transit networks.
The Impact: Over 70,000 prefixes—including critical IP blocks belonging to European mobile operators (Swisscom, Bouygues Telecom) and major European cloud services—were detoured through China Telecom’s internal network in China. Massive packet loss, severe latency spikes, and complete connection drops lasted for over two hours.
Root Cause: Complete absence of basic export filtering at Safe Host, combined with the lack of RFC 9234 Only to Customer (OTC) enforcement at China Telecom.

title: Case Studies: Documented Routing Incidents
text:
Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 Incident (June 27, 2024)
Even modern, highly protected Anycast DNS resolvers remain vulnerable to misrouting anomalies when upstream transit providers misbehave:

The Incident: On June 27, 2024, a regional ISP in Asia accidentally originated 1.1.1.0/24—the primary IP address of Cloudflare’s public DNS service.
The Defense in Action: Cloudflare had published a valid, exact-match ROA: (1.1.1.0/24, maxLength=24, Origin=AS13335).
The Divergence:

Tier-1 and Tier-2 networks that had deployed RPKI Route Origin Validation immediately flagged the regional ISP’s announcement as Invalid and dropped it, keeping DNS reachability clean for their users.
However, networks and ISPs that had not deployed ROV accepted the illegitimate announcement, directing user DNS queries into a blackhole.

Key Takeaway: ROV successfully protected adopters, but highlighted that incomplete global deployment leaves non-adopting networks exposed to disruptions.

title: Case Studies: Documented Routing Incidents
text:
3ve BGP Hijacking Campaign (2018)
In 2018, the US Department of Justice unsealed indictments against the operators of 3ve, a massive international cybercrime syndicate that stole tens of millions of dollars through fraudulent digital advertising:

The Mechanism: The 3ve syndicate used compromised routing infrastructure and rogue BGP speakers to hijack hundreds of dormant, unannounced IP blocks (bogon and legacy address space) from legitimate corporate holders who were not actively using them.
The Exploitation: The attackers registered fraudulent route objects in permissive third-party IRR databases (such as RADB) to convince transit providers to accept the routes. They then announced the hijacked blocks and used them to host thousands of fake websites and botnet servers, generating billions of fraudulent ad impressions.
The Catalyst for RPKI: The 3ve campaign served as the wake-up call for the global advertising and financial industries, proving that dormant IP blocks could be weaponized indefinitely unless cryptographically protected by RPKI ROAs.

title: Economics, Governance and the Human Dimension
text:
Economics, Governance and the Human Dimension
Securing global routing is fundamentally an economic, political, and human governance challenge. Technology alone does not secure the Internet; rather, protocols are adopted when economic incentives align, institutional frameworks mandate compliance, and operational liability outweighs the friction of change.

title: Economics, Governance and the Human Dimension
section: Who Is Responsible for What: A Stakeholder Map
text:
Who Is Responsible for What: A Stakeholder Map
The global routing ecosystem comprises multiple distinct stakeholder groups, each operating under conflicting incentives:
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       Global Routing Stakeholder Map                     |
|                                                                          |
|  +--------------------+                                                  |
|  | Standards & Policy | ---> IETF / IRTF / Regional Internet Registries  |
|  +---------+----------+      (Defines RFCs, operates Trust Anchors)      |
|            |                                                             |
|            v                                                             |
|  +--------------------+                                                  |
|  | Infrastructure Core| ---> Tier-1 Transit Providers & Hyperscale Cloud |
|  +---------+----------+      (Cogent, NTT, Lumen, AWS, Google, Cloudflare|
|            |                 High deployment of ROV and strict filters)  |
|            v                                                             |
|  +--------------------+                                                  |
|  | Access & Regional  | ---> Regional Telcos, ISPs, Mobile Operators     |
|  +---------+----------+      (Mixed adoption; sensitive to support costs)|
|            |                                                             |
|            v                                                             |
|  +--------------------+                                                  |
|  | Enterprise & Stubs | ---> Banks, Universities, Municipalities, SMBs   |
|  +--------------------+      (Lowest awareness; slowest to create ROAs)  |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Standards Bodies (IETF, IRTF): Engineer protocols (BGPsec, ASPA, RTR). They operate by consensus and have zero authority to force commercial networks to deploy standards.
Regional Internet Registries (RIRs): Allocate IP addresses and AS numbers; operate RPKI Trust Anchors and repository infrastructure.
Tier-1 Transit Providers: Maintain the global backbone. They bear the heaviest computational load and traffic volume during incidents.
Content Providers and Cloud Hyperscalers: Heavily motivated to adopt security to protect customer trust and latency SLAs.
Stub Networks and Enterprises: Tens of thousands of small organizations that view routing as a utility, lacking dedicated BGP engineering expertise.

title: Economics, Governance and the Human Dimension
section: Economic Incentives and Disincentives for Adoption
text:
Economic Incentives and Disincentives for Adoption
The persistent delay in achieving universal routing security is rooted in a classic positive externality problem: - When Network \(A\) signs its ROAs, it protects itself from being hijacked, but it expends engineering labor to do so. - When Network \(B\) deploys ROV filtering (dropping Invalids), it expends CPU power, risks support tickets from broken third-party ROAs, and protects everyone else on the Internet, while receiving no direct commercial revenue for doing so. - Customers rarely choose an Internet Service Provider based on whether the provider validates RPKI routes; they choose based on price, bandwidth, and geographic availability.

title: Economics, Governance and the Human Dimension
section: The Role of RIRs, Regional Communities and IETF
text:
The Role of RIRs, Regional Communities and IETF
The five RIRs (ARIN, RIPE NCC, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC) have transitioned from passive allocation registries to critical operational certificate authorities: - Hosted vs. Delegated RPKI: RIRs provide hosted web portals allowing non-technical operators to create ROAs with a few clicks, driving the majority of global RPKI adoption. - RIR Coordination: RIRs coordinate via the Number Resource Organization (NRO) to standardize TAL formats, certificate expiration policies, and repository architectures. - Regional Operator Groups (NANOG, RIPE, APRICOT): Serve as the primary forums where network engineers share post-mortem analyses, establish informal social pressure, and develop shared operational norms.

title: Economics, Governance and the Human Dimension
text:
MANRS, IRTF and Industry Self-Regulation
In the absence of a global regulatory body with binding jurisdiction over Internet routing, the industry has turned to self-regulation through Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security (MANRS): - The MANRS Observatory: Provides public transparency by grading operators on their routing hygiene, making poor security visible to enterprise procurement officers. - Peer Pressure and Commercial Mandates: Major financial institutions and cloud providers now require transit providers to be MANRS-compliant as a mandatory condition in Request for Proposal (RFP) vendor contracts.

title: Economics, Governance and the Human Dimension
section: Why Technically Sound Mechanisms Fail to Deploy
text:
Why Technically Sound Mechanisms Fail to Deploy
History demonstrates that technical elegance does not guarantee adoption: 1. The Curse of BGPsec: A mathematically brilliant protocol (RFC 8205) that failed because it demanded massive hardware upgrades, high CPU latency, and universal deployment before delivering value. 2. The Success of RPKI and ASPA: Pragmatic, out-of-band protocols that deliver immediate security benefits to early adopters without requiring router ASIC replacements. 3. The Lesson: On the global Internet, incremental deployability and backwards compatibility always defeat cryptographic purity.

title: The Current State and Future of Internet Routing Security
text:
The Current State and Future of Internet Routing Security
The journey from a completely unauthenticated, trust-based experimental network to a hardened, cryptographically verified planetary communication system is one of the most remarkable transitions in engineering history. As we evaluate the contemporary landscape, we must balance clear-eyed realism about persistent vulnerabilities against the undeniable progress achieved over the past decade.

title: The Current State and Future of Internet Routing Security
section: The Baseline: How Secure Is Global Routing Today?
text:
The Baseline: How Secure Is Global Routing Today?
As of 2026, the baseline of interdomain routing security is fundamentally stronger than at any point in the history of the Internet: - RPKI ROA Deployment: Over 55% of global IPv4 prefixes and more than 60% of IPv6 prefixes announced in the Default-Free Zone are covered by valid Route Origin Authorizations. - Route Origin Validation Enforcement: Major Tier-1 transit backbones (including Cogent, NTT, Lumen, Telia/Arelion, Hurricane Electric) and hyperscale cloud networks (Cloudflare, Google, AWS) actively enforce hard drops on RPKI Invalid routes. - Disappearance of Naive Hijacks: The era of simple, accidental origin prefix hijacks surviving for hours across the global Internet is over. When a misconfigured router announces an exact-match or more-specific subprefix for a protected block today, the announcement is discarded at the first transit border within seconds.

title: The Current State and Future of Internet Routing Security
section: Deployment Gaps: Who Has Not Adopted and Why?
text:
Deployment Gaps: Who Has Not Adopted and Why?
Despite significant progress, substantial gaps remain across the global network topology:
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|               Global Routing Adoption Spectrum              |
|                                                             |
|  [Hyperscalers & Tier-1s]   [Regional ISPs]    [Enterprise] |
|   High ROA & ROV Coverage   Mixed Adoption      Slowest     |
|   Strict Inbound Filters    Lagging Software    Unaware     |
|            |                      |                |        |
|            v                      v                v        |
|     +-------------+        +-------------+   +-----------+  |
|     |  Hardened   |        | Partial Hole|   | Uncovered |  |
|     +-------------+        +-------------+   +-----------+  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Enterprise and Stub Network Inertia: Tens of thousands of small and medium enterprises, regional municipalities, and educational institutions have never signed into their RIR portal to generate ROAs. Their address space remains in the vulnerable NotFound state.
Access-Network Economics: Many consumer broadband and mobile operators in developing markets run legacy router hardware that lacks sufficient memory or software support to run RTR sessions and maintain local VRP tables.
The Unprotected Path: Because path validation (ASPA or BGPsec) is still in its early operational rollout, adversaries can still forge AS_PATH attributes or trigger devastating route leaks that bypass origin validation.

title: The Current State and Future of Internet Routing Security
section: Open Research Problems and Protocol-Level Unknowns
text:
Open Research Problems and Protocol-Level Unknowns
Several critical questions remain active frontiers in academic research and IETF working groups: - RPKI Repository Centralization: As reliance on RPKI increases, the five RIR trust anchors represent potential single points of administrative and geopolitical failure. How can the Internet ensure survivability if a major RIR repository is seized, sanctioned, or subjected to sustained volumetric DDoS attacks? - ASPA Convergence Dynamics: In a hybrid Internet where only 20% of networks have published ASPA objects, how do ASPA-enabled routers safely interpret ambiguous multi-hop path sequences without causing transient forwarding loops? - AI/ML in Real-Time Anomaly Mitigation: Can machine learning models trained on BGPStream telemetry reliably distinguish between legitimate emergency traffic engineering and malicious micro-burst hijacks without generating false-positive disconnects?

title: The Current State and Future of Internet Routing Security
section: Plausible Developments: ASPA, BGPsec Revival, or New Directions?
text:
Plausible Developments: ASPA, BGPsec Revival, or New Directions?
Over the next decade, the interdomain routing security trajectory will likely unfold across three phases:

Near-Term (ASPA Ubiquity): Autonomous System Provider Authorization will follow the adoption path of RPKI. Once major Tier-1 transit providers deploy ASPA verification at their peering borders, the vast majority of accidental route leaks will be permanently eliminated.
Medium-Term (Decentralized Trust Anchors): Research into multi-party threshold signatures and transparency logs (analogous to Certificate Transparency in Web PKI) will be integrated into RPKI to prevent unilateral RIR certificate revocation without public audit trails.
Long-Term (SCION and Next-Generation Path-Aware Architectures): Clean-slate architectures such as SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-Generation Networks) are already running in production across Swiss banking and academic backbones. SCION replaces single-path hop-by-hop forwarding with cryptographically signed, multipath packet routing where senders select verified end-to-end paths through cryptographically isolated failure domains.

title: The Current State and Future of Internet Routing Security
section: A Grounded Assessment: Progress Made, Work Remaining
text:
A Grounded Assessment: Progress Made, Work Remaining
Building global routing security is not an engineering project with a static finish line; it is an ongoing immune response. The decentralized, sovereign nature of the Internet means that security will always be negotiated at the boundaries between independent networks.
By deploying RPKI Route Origin Validation, enforcing strict IRR-generated customer prefix-lists, rejecting bogons, deploying RFC 9234 roles, and preparing for ASPA path verification, network engineers transform BGP from a fragile, trust-based relic into a hardened, resilient foundation capable of supporting the next century of planetary civilization.

title: BGP no_export and Well-Known Communities
text: BGP no_export and Well-Known Communities

title: BGP no_export and Well-Known Communities
text:
Thesis
Well-known BGP communities are a portable policy language. no_export (65535:65281) means “do not announce this route to eBGP peers”; no_advertise keeps it off all peers; no_export_subconfed stops it at confederation boundaries. Mis-applying them is a classic route-leak footgun.

title: BGP no_export and Well-Known Communities
text:
Mental model
  route with community no_export
       │
       ├─ iBGP: still propagated inside the AS (usual)
       └─ eBGP: stripped from announcements to external peers
Vendor knobs differ: some require send-community on the neighbor before communities travel at all.

title: BGP no_export and Well-Known Communities
text:
Worked example
Conceptual FRR / policy sketch (lab with netlab/containerlab — not executed on this box; no sudo/lab installs):
! tag a prefix so upstreams do not re-advertise it onward
ip prefix-list LOCAL-ONLY permit 192.0.2.0/24
route-map TAG-NO-EXPORT permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list LOCAL-ONLY
 set community no-export
!
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 remote-as 65002
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  neighbor 203.0.113.1 route-map TAG-NO-EXPORT out
  neighbor 203.0.113.1 send-community
Verification on a lab router after the session is up:
show bgp ipv4 uni 192.0.2.0/24
# expect Community: no-export
# on the eBGP peer: prefix absent (or present only if they ignore well-known — treat as bug)

title: BGP no_export and Well-Known Communities
text:
Trap
Assuming communities are sent by default. Many implementations require an explicit send-community [both]. Also: no_export does not replace NO_PEER / RFC 7999 peer communities — pick the community that matches the business intent.

title: BGP no_export and Well-Known Communities
text:
Boring rule
Document each tagged prefix: who may see it, which community encodes that, and whether send-community is on. Test with an eBGP session in the lab before production.

title: BGP no_export and Well-Known Communities
text:
Try this

In netlab/containerlab, announce a prefix with and without no_export and watch the second-hop AS.
Compare no_export vs no_advertise on an iBGP mesh.
Read IANA well-known community registry values.

title: BGP no_export and Well-Known Communities
text:
Sources

RFC 1997 (BGP Communities Attribute)
RFC 3765 (NOPEER) / RFC 7999 (BLACKHOLE) as related well-knowns
FRR docs: BGP communities / route maps

title: RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap
text: RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap

title: RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap
text:
Thesis
A ROA (Route Origin Authorization) signs that an ASN may originate a prefix. The optional maxLength widens which more-specifics are also valid. Broad maxLength (for example /8 ROA with maxLength=24) makes hijacks of punched-out space look RPKI-valid — RFC 9319 warns against that.

title: RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap
text:
Mental model
  ROA: ASN 64500 may originate 192.0.2.0/24, maxLength=24
       → /24 only (tight)

  ROA: ASN 64500 may originate 192.0.2.0/24, maxLength=32
       → any more-specific through /32 also "valid" under that ASN
Validators classify announcements as Valid / Invalid / NotFound. Invalid should be dropped (Route Origin Validation).

title: RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap
text:
Worked example
Operational checklist (docs-based; no RPKI validator installed here):
1. Inventory prefixes you originate.
2. For each, publish a ROA with ASN = your origin AS.
3. Set maxLength to the longest prefix you actually announce —
   not "32 just in case".
4. After every IPv4 transfer, re-check ROAs (stale ROAs → NotFound/Invalid pain).
Example of a tight vs loose posture:



Prefix
ASN
maxLength
Comment




192.0.2.0/24
64500
24
Only the /24


198.51.100.0/22
64500
24
Allows /23–/24 you plan to announce


203.0.113.0/8
64500
24
Avoid — huge attack surface

title: RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap
text:
Trap
Copy-pasting maxLength=24 on large aggregates “for flexibility”. Attackers who can somehow announce more-specifics under your ASN (or who compromise your CA workflow) get free cover. Prefer multiple tight ROAs over one loose one.

title: RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap
text:
Boring rule
ROA maxLength = maximum length you intentionally announce today. Re-issue when that policy changes. Monitor Valid/Invalid/NotFound with a relying party (routinator, rpki-client, vendor RPKI RTR).

title: RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap
text:
Try this

Look up your ASN’s ROAs on a public RPKI viewer.
Read RFC 9319 §3 on maxLength.
In a lab, announce a /25 covered by a /24 ROA with maxLength=24 and watch it become Invalid.

title: RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap
text:
Sources

RFC 6482 (ROA format)
RFC 6811 (BGP Prefix Origin Validation)
RFC 9319 (RPKI best practices — maxLength guidance)
