title: Specialized Forensics by Domain
text:
Specialized Forensics by Domain
Enterprise IT networks are only one facet of modern connected infrastructure. A comprehensive network forensics methodology must extend to specialized operational and mission-critical domains: Industrial Control Systems (ICS/SCADA), the Internet of Things (IoT), Cloud and Containerized Platforms, Healthcare and Medical Devices (IoMT), and Interdependent Smart City Infrastructures.
Each domain features specialized network architectures, proprietary protocols, legacy constraints, and distinct failure modes. An anomaly that represents benign developer traffic in a cloud development cluster (e.g., thousands of rapid ephemeral socket connections) indicates an existential physical safety threat inside an industrial control system.

title: Specialized Forensics by Domain
text:
Operational Technology (OT) and ICS/SCADA Forensics
Industrial control systems operate physical plants: electrical grids, oil refineries, water treatment facilities, and nuclear generation sites. OT networks are architected according to the Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture (ISA-95):
[ Enterprise IT / Corporate Network (Level 4/5) ]
                       │ (Firewall / DMZ Level 3.5)
                       ▼
[ Site Operations & Plant Monitoring (Level 3: Historians, Engineering Workstations) ]
                       │ (Internal Industrial Firewall)
                       ▼
[ Control Systems (Level 2: SCADA HMIs, Supervisory Servers) ]
                       │
                       ▼
[ Basic Control (Level 1: Programmable Logic Controllers [PLCs], RTUs) ]
                       │ (Hard Real-Time Industrial Fieldbus)
                       ▼
[ Physical Process (Level 0: Actuators, Valves, Turbines, Pumps) ]

Behavioral Invariants in Industrial Telemetry

Extreme Protocol Determinism: In an industrial network, protocol communications are virtually clockwork. A PLC polls an RTU every \(250.0\text{ ms} \pm 2\text{ ms}\) over Modbus TCP. Any packet arrival with high jitter, non-standard transaction IDs, or irregular payload sizes is an immediate forensic anomaly.
Read vs. Write Function Codes: Normal supervisory SCADA traffic consists almost entirely of read operations (e.g., Modbus Function Code 0x03 - Read Holding Registers). An unauthorized write command (e.g., Modbus Function Code 0x06 - Write Single Register or 0x10 - Write Multiple Registers) attempting to modify centrifuge speeds or valve limits represents a critical physical attack (e.g., Stuxnet or Industroyer2 tradecraft).
Engineering Workstation Firmware Uploads: Unauthorized invocation of proprietary diagnostic functions (such as Siemens S7comm Download Block or Stop CPU) from an IP address other than the designated, audited engineering console.

title: Specialized Forensics by Domain
text:
Cloud, Multi-Cloud, and Containerized Forensics
In cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP) and container orchestrators (Kubernetes), traditional network visibility (physical taps and switch SPAN ports) does not exist. Network forensics must adapt to virtualized, software-defined fabrics:

1. Ephemeral IP Addresses and Identity Disconnects
In Kubernetes, pods terminate and spawn within seconds, recycling IP addresses. If an incident occurred at 10:14:22, an alert referencing IP 10.244.2.84 is useless without correlating the IP to the exact Pod UID, Namespace, and Container Image running at that precise microsecond: - Kubernetes Audit Logs: Correlating network flows against API server audit trails (requestURI: /api/v1/namespaces/prod/pods). - Cilium eBPF Tetragon: Capturing kernel-level network socket events enriched with Kubernetes container metadata directly at socket creation.


2. Cloud Control Plane Forensics
Adversaries in cloud networks rarely pivot through physical cables; they pivot through the control plane: - Inspecting AWS CloudTrail or Azure Activity logs for AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress, CreateVpcPeeringConnection, or ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute. - VPC Flow Logs capturing communication with unusual internal metadata services (169.254.169.254 IMDSv1 queries attempting SSRF token theft).

title: Specialized Forensics by Domain
section: Internet of Things (IoT) and Smart Cities
text:
Internet of Things (IoT) and Smart Cities
Smart cities deploy millions of constrained sensors across traffic control, automated metering, public surveillance, and environmental monitoring:

Lightweight Protocols: IoT devices communicate via MQTT, CoAP, or lightweight REST over UDP/DTLS.
Botnet Enlistment (Mirai / Mozi Archetype): IoT devices are targeted for recruitment into massive DDoS botnets. Forensic behavioral indicators include:

Spikes in outbound TCP port 23 (Telnet), 22 (SSH), or 2323 sweeps with hardcoded default credentials.
Abrupt shifts in DNS querying behavior from local NTP/manufacturer gateways to public resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1).
High-volume outbound UDP/GRE floods originating from low-power microcontroller MAC addresses.

title: Specialized Forensics by Domain
text:
Healthcare and Medical Devices (IoMT)
Hospital networks host Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) hardware: infusion pumps, patient monitors, MRI/CT scanners, and surgical robotics.

Vulnerable Legacy Stacks: Many IoMT devices run embedded, unpatchable legacy operating systems (Windows XP Embedded, legacy VxWorks).
Protocol Specifics: Traffic revolves around DICOM (medical imaging) and HL7 (patient health records).
Forensic Behavioral Constraints: Active vulnerability scanning (e.g., aggressive Nmap scans) can crash sensitive infusion pumps or disrupt heart-rate monitors. Forensic evidence must be gathered purely out-of-band via passive network taps and statistical flow inspection.

title: Specialized Forensics by Domain
text:
Chapter Summary

Operational technology (OT/ICS) networks demand extreme timing determinism; unauthorized write function codes signal direct threats to physical safety.
Cloud and container forensics requires synchronizing ephemeral IP lifecycles with container identities and control plane audit logs (CloudTrail, K8s API).
IoT networks reveal botnet staging through sudden shifts from lightweight telemetry to outbound port sweeps and high-volume UDP floods.
Medical device forensics must operate strictly out-of-band to prevent active scanning tools from destabilizing critical patient-care systems.

title: Case Studies in Advanced Behavior-Based Network Forensics
text:
Case Studies in Advanced Behavior-Based Network Forensics
Theoretical forensic frameworks prove their value only when tested against sophisticated, determined threat actors in operational networks. This chapter examines three comprehensive, end-to-end case studies based on real-world incidents.
Each case study demonstrates the operational deployment of Cyber Forensics Behavioral Analysis (CFBA), Anomaly-Based Scoring (ABS), and Cyber-Behavioral Forensics Modeling (CBFM). We trace how behavior-driven analytics identified micro-deviations that bypassed static signature defenses, reduced adversary dwell time from months to minutes, and prevented catastrophic breaches.

title: Case Studies in Advanced Behavior-Based Network Forensics
section: Case Study 1: APT Nation-State Supply-Chain Intrusion
text:
Case Study 1: APT Nation-State Supply-Chain Intrusion

Background and Intrusion Mechanics
A nation-state threat group compromised the build pipeline of a widely deployed network monitoring appliance. The attackers inserted a trojanized update signed with a legitimate cryptographic certificate. Once installed inside an enterprise network, the backdoor lay dormant for 14 days to defeat sandbox analysis before establishing outbound command-and-control over HTTPS (TCP 443).

Static Defense Failure: Because the malicious DLL was legitimately signed, antivirus and endpoint detection engines generated zero alerts. The outbound C2 traffic resolved to dynamic Amazon AWS IP addresses, bypassing IP reputation blocklists.



CFBA and Anomaly-Based Scoring (ABS) in Action
While the content of the TLS sessions was fully encrypted, the network behavioral cadence violated historical baselines:
Normal Appliance Telemetry Cadence:
[ Beacon ] ──────── (Exact 3600.0s Interval) ────────> [ Legitimate Update Server ]
* Payload Size: 450 bytes ± 10 bytes | SNI: updates.vendor.com

Compromised Appliance C2 Beaconing:
[ Beacon ] ── (3241s) ──> [ Beacon ] ── (3892s) ──> [ Beacon ] ── (3110s) ──>
* Payload Size: 1,840 bytes | Artificial Jitter: ~15% | Rare SNI: aws-telemetry-east.net

Jitter Regularity Analysis: The appliance’s legitimate traffic was rigidly scheduled (exactly once per hour via cron). The trojan introduced pseudorandom jitter (\(15\%\)) to evade simple periodic counters. However, CBFM time-series modeling identified that the underlying distribution was an artificial uniform random variable over \([3000\text{ s}, 4000\text{ s}]\)—a pattern characteristic of automated C2 implants, completely absent from legitimate Linux system services.
JA4 Cryptographic Fingerprinting: The TLS Client Hello emitted by the trojan utilized the Go standard library TLS stack, whereas the legitimate vendor appliance was written in Python/OpenSSL. The resulting JA4 fingerprint mismatch triggered an immediate anomaly flag.
CBS Calculation: \[\text{CBS} = 100 \times (0.35 \times 0.85_I + 0.20 \times 0.90_C + 0.20 \times 0.95_P + 0.25 \times 0.80_E) \times 1.2_{\Phi} = 100.0\] An automated SOAR playbook initiated packet mirroring on the switch port, capturing the initial stage-2 payload download and terminating the session before the adversary could harvest Active Directory credentials.

title: Case Studies in Advanced Behavior-Based Network Forensics
section: Case Study 2: Privileged Insider Data Exfiltration
text:
Case Study 2: Privileged Insider Data Exfiltration

Background and Intrusion Mechanics
A senior systems administrator with valid administrative credentials accepted a financial bribe to exfiltrate proprietary source code and intellectual property. The administrator accessed the internal Git repository server from their corporate-issued laptop using their normal SSH keys, packaged repositories into encrypted archives, and staged the files on an internal development server before attempting exfiltration.

Static Defense Failure: No malware was used. All commands (tar, ssh, rsync) were standard native administrative utilities. No alerts fired on endpoint security software.



Behavioral Profiling and Peer-Group Analytics
The intrusion was uncovered through peer-group working window and flow volume deviations:
Engineering Peer Group Behavioral Matrix:
- Working Hours: 08:30 - 18:00 Local Time
- Mean Daily Egress Volume: 1.8 GB (Standard Deviation: 0.4 GB)
- Primary Destination Protocols: HTTPS (TCP 443), SSH (TCP 22)

Suspect Administrator Observed Metrics:
- Timestamp: 02:45:12 Local Time (Severe Temporal Anomaly, Z = +4.8)
- Connection: High-Throughput Egress Stream to Unregistered Cloud Storage
- Transferred Volume: 68.4 GB within 45 Minutes (Volume Anomaly, Z = +16.2)
- Flow Symmetry: Highly Asymmetric Outbound Flow (Bytes_Out / Bytes_In = 142.0)

Temporal and Volume Anomaly Flagging: The UEBA baseline identified that the administrator’s account had never initiated a session between 00:00 and 06:00 in over three years of historical telemetry.
DNS Entropy and Covert Staging: While staging the archive, the administrator executed DNS queries containing high-entropy subdomains, attempting to verify egress tunnel reachability.
Forensic Response: The SIEM correlation engine grouped the temporal anomaly, the peer-group volume breach, and the egress byte asymmetry into an emergency Priority-1 incident. An automated playbook revoked the administrator’s Active Directory ticket, terminated active SSH sessions via TCP RST injection, and initiated a forensic snapshot of the target development server.

title: Case Studies in Advanced Behavior-Based Network Forensics
section: Case Study 3: Enterprise Ransomware Precursor Neutralization
text:
Case Study 3: Enterprise Ransomware Precursor Neutralization

Background and Intrusion Mechanics
A ransomware affiliate (operating BlackCat/ALPHV tradecraft) obtained external credentials to an edge SSL-VPN gateway through a darknet credential dump. Upon establishing a VPN tunnel into the corporate network, the attacker immediately attempted internal network discovery using AdFind.exe and Nmap to locate Domain Controllers and unpatched SMB file shares.

Objective: Complete domain reconnaissance, stage Cobalt Strike beacons, disable volume shadow copies, and execute enterprise-wide encryption within 6 hours.



Deception Networks and SPADE Traps in Action
The organization had deployed a deception layer utilizing SPADE Canary Honey-Accounts and synthetic honey-ports:
[ Compromised VPN Gateway: 10.200.5.88 ]
                   │
                   ▼ (Executes Internal Subnet Scan)
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Touches Decoy Honey-Port (IP: 10.10.40.250:445)        │
└──────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘
                   │ Immediate Forensic Alarm (Zero-Tolerance)
                   ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SOAR Dynamic Trap Execution:                           │
│ 1. Feeds synthetic decoy Domain Controller responses   │
│ 2. Seeds fake admin credentials (canary Kerberos user) │
│ 3. Attacker attempts Kerberoast against canary account │
└──────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘
                   │ Confirmed Hostile Intent
                   ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Micro-Quarantine Isolation via 802.1X SDN in 42 seconds│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Zero-Tolerance Canary Touch: The attacker’s initial discovery sweep probed 10.10.40.250—an IP address reserved for an OpenCanary decoy. Because no legitimate host communicates with this IP, the touch event generated a high-severity alert instantly.
Adversary Prolongation: Rather than immediately severing the connection, the deception system responded with an emulated, highly vulnerable Windows Server 2016 instance. The attacker paused their automated scan to interact manually with the decoy, wasting 25 minutes of operational time while the SOC verified the source VPN session.
Automated Quarantine: When the attacker used the decoy credentials to query Active Directory, the identity provider flagged the canary ticket request. The SOAR platform dispatched an API call to the VPN concentrator, terminating the session and blacklisting the external source IP across all perimeter routers. Total dwell time: 38 minutes. Zero production systems were encrypted.

title: Case Studies in Advanced Behavior-Based Network Forensics
text:
Chapter Summary

Real-world case studies prove that behavioral models detect advanced threats that completely bypass static signatures and cryptographic certificate validation.
APT command-and-control exhibits detectable mathematical micro-deviations in protocol timing, inter-arrival jitter, and cryptographic fingerprints (JA4).
Insider threats are exposed through multi-dimensional peer-group clustering, temporal anomalies, and asymmetric egress flow ratios.
Deception canaries and honey-ports provide zero-false-positive forensic tripwires, collapsing ransomware dwell times from days to minutes.

title: The Future of Network Forensics and Cyberpsychology
text:
The Future of Network Forensics and Cyberpsychology
The convergence of artificial intelligence, high-speed photonic networks, quantum computation, and advanced behavioral science is reshaping the landscape of digital network defense. Network forensics is transitioning from a human-driven, retrospective investigative discipline into an autonomous, proactive, and predictive cognitive science.
This concluding chapter examines the emerging frontiers that will define network forensics and cyberpsychology over the coming decade: AI-scaled automated evidence processing, Sense-making and Proactive Adaptive Deception (SPADE), cognitive forensics, the disruptive impact of quantum computation and post-quantum cryptography (PQC), and the evolving legal, ethical, and privacy frameworks governing behavioral monitoring.

title: The Future of Network Forensics and Cyberpsychology
text:
AI-Scaled Automated Evidence Processing
As telemetry volumes grow exponentially with the expansion of 5G/6G fabrics, edge computing, and satellite constellations (Starlink/Kuiper), human forensic analysis of raw data will become physically impossible. The future belongs to autonomous multi-agent forensic systems:

1. Multi-Agent Autonomous Investigators
Future forensic architectures will deploy specialized swarms of LLM-powered autonomous agents: - Triage Agents: Ingest millions of raw alerts, querying local databases to discard false positives with zero human intervention. - Hypothesis Generation Agents: Automatically formulate competing forensic theories (e.g., “Is this traffic an external supply-chain intrusion or an internal insider credential misuse?”) and generate specific search queries to prove or refute each theory. - Dossier Synthesis Agents: Automatically assemble comprehensive, court-admissible forensic narratives complete with cited packet timestamps, extracted payloads, and timeline graphs within seconds of containment.


2. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for Global Campaign Reconstruction
By treating global Internet routing events, DNS resolutions, and TLS certificate transparency logs as an interconnected knowledge graph, GNNs will identify distributed threat campaigns across disparate corporate boundaries, attributing attacks to common threat actors before individual organizations realize they have been targeted.

title: The Future of Network Forensics and Cyberpsychology
section: SPADE: Sense-Making and Proactive Adaptive Deception
text:
SPADE: Sense-Making and Proactive Adaptive Deception
Current deception technologies are largely static: an administrator deploys a honeypot, and it remains static until discovered. SPADE (Sense-making and Proactive Adaptive Deception) represents the next evolutionary step: living, morphing deception fabrics:
[ Attacker Scans Network Segment ]
                │
                ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SPADE Dynamic Deception Controller:                    │
│ 1. Evaluates incoming probe velocity and tool fingerprint│
│ 2. Dynamically manifests synthetic virtual subnets ahead│
│    of the attacker's scan path                         │
│ 3. Injects subtle, simulated vulnerabilities tailored  │
│    to the attacker's observed psychological profile    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                │
                ▼
[ Attacker Enters Infinite Synthetic Maze of Decoys ]
(Adversary computational and human resources exhausted)
SPADE continuously measures the attacker’s behavioral state and dynamically mutates the perceived network topology in real time. If an attacker favors web application exploits, SPADE dynamically generates an emulated web portal with realistic synthetic databases, keeping the attacker occupied in a harmless simulation while defenders study their tradecraft.

title: The Future of Network Forensics and Cyberpsychology
text:
Cognitive Forensics and Psychological Friction
Cognitive forensics examines the psychological feedback loop between the defender’s network maneuvers and the attacker’s mental state:

Injecting Cognitive Friction: By introducing micro-delays (artificial TCP window throttling, simulated packet drops, intermittent connection resets) exclusively into suspected malicious connections, defenders increase the attacker’s frustration and cognitive fatigue.
Inducing Operational Mistakes: Stressed, fatigued human attackers make mistakes: they accidentally disable proxy configurations, execute commands with unescaped characters, or reuse identifying credentials across sessions.
Psycholinguistic Profiling in Artifacts: Natural language processing over chat logs, ransom negotiation portals, and command-line comments extracts psycholinguistic markers (native language syntax interference, emotional valence, dominance/submission dynamics), providing deep psychological profiling of the human extortionists.

title: The Future of Network Forensics and Cyberpsychology
text:
Quantum-Era Network Forensics
The advent of fault-tolerant quantum computers will disrupt digital network forensics:

Collapse of Classical Asymmetric Cryptography: Shor’s algorithm will render current RSA and ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) obsolete. Encrypted network captures collected today by adversaries (“Harvest Now, Decrypt Later”) will eventually be decrypted.
Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Evidence Integrity: Forensic evidence chains must transition immediately to NIST-standardized quantum-resistant algorithms (such as ML-KEM / Kyber for key encapsulation and ML-DSA / Dilithium for digital signatures) to guarantee that forensic logs cannot be forged or tampered with in a post-quantum world.
Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) Forensics: In networks secured by quantum entanglement (QKD), any attempt by an adversary to tap optical fibers physically alters the quantum state of the photons, creating an immediate, mathematically proven physical forensic trace of eavesdropping.

title: The Future of Network Forensics and Cyberpsychology
text:
Legal, Ethical, and Privacy Frameworks
As behavioral monitoring becomes increasingly granular—tracking keystroke cadences, working hours, and cognitive state—it collides directly with global privacy laws, labor regulations, and civil liberties:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           The Tension: Security Telemetry vs. Personal Privacy         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
             ▲                                          ▲
             │                                          │
    [ Security Objective ]                     [ Legal / Ethical Boundary]
  - Identify insider threats                 - GDPR Article 88 (Employee Data)
  - Profile attacker behavior                - EU AI Act (High-Risk AI Systems)
  - Prevent data exfiltration                - Admissibility under Fed. R. Evid. 702

The EU Artificial Intelligence Act: AI systems used for biometric categorization, emotion recognition, or workplace behavioral surveillance face stringent regulatory oversight and potential prohibitions. Behavioral forensic engines must be engineered with strict purpose-limitation controls.
Privacy-Preserving Telemetry: Modern forensics is adopting Differential Privacy and Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs). Organizations can verify that an employee’s network access conforms to legitimate behavioral baselines without exposing the private, personal contents of their communications to investigators.
Evidentiary Admissibility (Daubert and Frye Standards): For machine-learning-derived behavioral attribution to be admissible in a court of law, the underlying models must satisfy rigorous evidentiary tests: known error rates, peer-reviewed methodology, standardized controls, and full explainability (XAI).

title: The Future of Network Forensics and Cyberpsychology
text:
The Path Forward
Network engineering and forensic science have entered an era where transport mechanics and human behavioral intelligence are inseparable. The defenders who succeed in the coming decade will not be those with the longest lists of static IP blocklists or the most rigid perimeter firewalls. They will be the architects who design resilient, self-aware network fabrics capable of measuring behavior, modeling adversary psychology, orchestrating automated deception, and preserving transparent, legally defensible evidence at wire speed.

title: The Future of Network Forensics and Cyberpsychology
text:
Chapter Summary

Autonomous multi-agent systems and Graph Neural Networks will automate forensic hypothesis generation and global campaign correlation.
Sense-making and Proactive Adaptive Deception (SPADE) replaces static honeypots with living, mutating synthetic networks that exhaust adversary resources.
Cognitive forensics exploits attacker psychological vulnerabilities, using deliberate latency and friction to induce operational mistakes.
Post-quantum cryptography (ML-DSA / Dilithium) is urgently required to ensure long-term evidence integrity against quantum decryption.
Next-generation behavioral monitoring must balance deep security visibility with legal compliance (GDPR, EU AI Act) using privacy-preserving mathematics.

title: QUIC Version 2 and Compatible Version Negotiation
text:
QUIC Version 2 and Compatible Version Negotiation
QUIC version 1 (RFC 9000) won the Internet. That success is also a risk: middleboxes that only ever see 0x00000001 in the long-header Version field, or that hard-code the version-1 Initial salt, will quietly break the next version. QUIC version 2 (RFC 9369) is deliberately almost identical to version 1 — same streams, same TLS, same congestion control — with a handful of wire-image changes whose only job is to break that ossification and to exercise the negotiation machinery. Compatible version negotiation (RFC 9368) is how endpoints switch between v1 and v2 (or any pair of compatible versions) without paying an extra round trip. This chapter teaches the Version field, Compatible VN versus Incompatible VN, when v2 actually matters on the wire, and how to observe it in a modern browser stack.

title: QUIC Version 2 and Compatible Version Negotiation
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

State what QUICv2 changes (and what it deliberately does not change)

Decode a long-header Version field: 0x00000001 vs 0x6b3343cf

Explain Compatible VN vs Incompatible VN, and why v1 ↔︎ v2 is Compatible

Predict which packets keep the Original Version and which must use the Negotiated Version

Name the version_information transport parameter (0x11) and why v2 endpoints MUST use it

Observe negotiated version in Firefox (Nightly 154+, all channels from 155) and reason about server support

title: QUIC Version 2 and Compatible Version Negotiation
section: Concepts — why a “version 2” that does nothing new?
text:
Concepts — why a “version 2” that does nothing new?
RFC 9369 is explicit: QUICv2 exists to mitigate ossification and to exercise version negotiation. Application capabilities are unchanged. ALPN tokens defined for QUICv1 (h3, doq, …) also work over v2. Extensions that work with v1 work with v2 unless they say otherwise.
What does change:








Knob
QUICv1 (RFC 9000 / 9001)
QUICv2 (RFC 9369)




Long-header Version field
0x00000001
0x6b3343cf


Long-header Type bits
Initial 0b00, 0-RTT 0b01, Handshake 0b10, Retry 0b11
Initial 0b01, 0-RTT 0b10, Handshake 0b11, Retry 0b00


Initial salt
v1 salt
0x0dede3def700a6db819381be6e269dcbf9bd2ed9


HKDF labels
quic key / quic iv / quic hp / quic ku
quicv2 key / quicv2 iv / quicv2 hp / quicv2 ku


Retry Integrity Tag keying
v1 secret
v2 secret / key / nonce (RFC 9369 §3.3.3)



The version number is not the integer 2. It is the first four bytes of sha256("QUICv2 version number"), chosen randomly on purpose so middleboxes cannot guess “the next number”. A provisional draft codepoint 0x709a50c4 also sits in the IANA registry for historical draft traffic.
Long header (RFC 8999 invariants):
  Header Form (1) = 1
  Fixed Bit    (1) = 1
  Long Packet Type (2)   ← different encoding in v2
  Type-Specific (4)
  Version (32)           ← 0x00000001 or 0x6b3343cf
  DCID Len / DCID / SCID Len / SCID / …

title: QUIC Version 2 and Compatible Version Negotiation
section: Concepts — Compatible VN vs Incompatible VN
text:
Concepts — Compatible VN vs Incompatible VN
RFC 9000 gave servers a Version Negotiation packet that says “I do not speak the version you chose”, but it never defined a safe client reaction. RFC 9368 fills that hole with two mechanisms:
Incompatible VN. Server cannot parse the client’s first flight. It sends a Version Negotiation packet listing Offered Versions. Client starts a new connection attempt with a mutually supported version. Cost: one extra RTT. Works between any versions.
Compatible VN. Server can parse the first flight, extracts the client’s Version Information, and may switch to another version that (1) it supports and (2) it knows is compatible with the client’s Chosen Version. It converts the first flight and replies as if that converted flight had arrived. Cost: zero extra RTT, but only when the versions share a convertible first-flight format.
RFC 9369 states that v2 is compatible with v1 and v1 is compatible with v2. Endpoints that speak both SHOULD use Compatible VN.
Compatible VN (happy path, client offers v1+v2, prefers v1 as Chosen):

  Client                                         Server
  Chosen=v1, Available=(v1,v2)  --------------->
                                (server prefers v2, converts first flight)
                                <--------------- CRYPTO in v2 long headers
  (client sees Version 0x6b3343cf ≠ Chosen) → Negotiated = v2
  subsequent Initial / Handshake / 1-RTT use v2

Version Information (transport parameter 0x11)
Version Information {
  Chosen Version (32),
  Available Versions (32) ...,
}

Client Available Versions: every version this first flight is compatible with, preference order descending. Chosen Version MUST appear in the list.

Server Available Versions: the deployment’s Fully Deployed Versions (may be empty during rollouts; ordering carries no meaning).

QUICv2 endpoints MUST send, process, and validate this parameter (downgrade defence). QUICv1 endpoints that only ever speak v1 may omit it; RFC 9368 §8 special-cases that.



Packet-version rules after a Compatible switch (v1 ↔︎ v2)







Packet class
Rule




Retry
Always Original Version; client must not switch version in the next Initial that carries the Retry token


Server Initial before client TP processed
May use Original Version


All CRYPTO frames from the server
Negotiated Version


Handshake and 1-RTT
MUST be Negotiated Version; other versions dropped


Client 0-RTT
MUST stay on Original Version even after seeing Negotiated Version


Session tickets / NEW_TOKEN
Version-scoped; do not resume v1 tickets on a v2 connection (and vice versa). After Compatible VN, issued tokens belong to the Negotiated version



The client learns the Negotiated Version by watching the first long-header Version field that differs from the Original Version. If the server answers with CRYPTO still in the Original Version, negotiation landed on Original == Negotiated.

title: QUIC Version 2 and Compatible Version Negotiation
section: When v2 matters vs when it does not
text:
When v2 matters vs when it does not







Situation
Prefer




Fighting middleboxes that ossify on v1 Initial crypto / Version bytes
Offer v2; some clients start with v2 when they know the server supports it (accepts Incompatible VN cost on miss)


Maximising reach to old clients / Alt-Svc h3 without version signalling
Keep speaking v1; RFC 9369 says HTTP servers SHOULD support multiple versions


Measuring deployment health
Log negotiated version per handshake (Firefox Glean: networking.http_3_version)


Application features (streams, datagrams, HTTP/3)
Irrelevant — v2 adds none



v2 does not deprecate v1. Treating “we enabled v2” as “we can drop v1” breaks clients that only offer v1, and Alt-Svc still does not distinguish versions.

title: QUIC Version 2 and Compatible Version Negotiation
section: Worked observation — Firefox and Compatible VN
text:
Worked observation — Firefox and Compatible VN
As of mid-2026, Mozilla’s neqo stack can offer QUICv2. Bug 2040450 enabled Compatible VN on Firefox Nightly 154 via the pref network.http.http3.version_negotiation.enabled (Nightly-only at first). Bug 2059947 later set that pref to true on all channels (Firefox 155). When the pref is true, the client offers Version::all() (v2 preferred, then v1); when false, v1 only. The server still chooses:
Client offers: [v2, v1]     Server speaks only v1  → connection uses v1
Client offers: [v2, v1]     Server prefers v2        → Compatible VN → v2
Client offers: [v1]         Server prefers v2        → stays v1 (client never offered v2)

Try this (browser)

Firefox 155+ (or Nightly 154+ with the pref true).

Visit an HTTP/3 origin you control that advertises QUICv2 (or a public origin known to prefer v2).

about:networking#httpconn (or your TLS/QUIC debugger) — confirm HTTP/3 and note the negotiated QUIC version if exposed.

On Nightly builds that still gate the pref, toggle network.http.http3.version_negotiation.enabled and compare.

Server-side (conceptual checklist, library-specific):

Advertise both version codepoints in Compatible VN.

Emit version_information on every v2 (and dual-stack) handshake.

Log Original vs Negotiated Version.

Keep issuing version-scoped session tickets.

Roll versions through Acceptable → Offered → Fully Deployed with ≥1 MSL between steps (RFC 9368 §5) so downgrade detection does not false-positive during fleet upgrades.

Libraries commonly cited for dual-version support include quiche, quic-go, and browser stacks built on neqo / NSS-adjacent HTTP/3 plumbing. Always check the current release notes for your pin — Compatible VN and v2 landed at different times in different stacks.

title: QUIC Version 2 and Compatible Version Negotiation
text:
The trap

Assuming the Version field integer “2”. The wire value is 0x6b3343cf. Fingerprinting scripts that look for version == 2 will miss every real v2 packet.

Enabling v2 only on the client. Without servers that select v2 from Available Versions, you negotiate v1 forever and learn nothing.

Reusing tickets across versions. A v1 session ticket on a v2 attempt must be rejected (full handshake, no 0-RTT).

Skipping version_information on a v2 endpoint. Mandatory; without it you lose downgrade protection and violate RFC 9369.

Expecting application-visible differences. If your HTTP/3 metrics are identical on v1 and v2, that is success — the change is at the transport wire image.

title: QUIC Version 2 and Compatible Version Negotiation
text:
The boring rule
Offer QUICv1 and QUICv2 together. Use Compatible VN so the upgrade is free when both sides agree. Keep v1 around for reachability. Authenticate negotiation with version_information. Measure which version you actually land on.

title: QUIC Loss Recovery: Packet Threshold, Time Threshold and PTO (RFC 9002)
text:
QUIC Loss Recovery: Packet Threshold, Time Threshold and PTO (RFC 9002)
QUIC replaces TCP’s sequence-number ACKs, SACK blocks, and retransmission timeouts with a single monotonically increasing packet number per encryption level and an explicit, receiver-driven acknowledgement model. Because packet numbers never repeat—even on retransmission—a sender never faces TCP’s retransmission ambiguity. Every ACK tells you unambiguously which transmission arrived and when.
RFC 9002 builds loss detection and recovery directly on that property. Instead of inferring loss from duplicate ACKs or a single monolithic RTO, QUIC separates loss detection into two mechanisms—a packet threshold and a time threshold—and reserves the Probe Timeout (PTO) strictly for eliciting an ACK when the loss timer is not armed or no feedback arrives. Loss state, RTT estimates, and timers are tracked independently across three packet number spaces: Initial, Handshake, and Application Data.
If you already know TCP loss recovery (RTO, fast retransmit, SACK, RACK, and TLP), you will recognize the ideas here. QUIC’s time threshold is close in spirit to RACK, and PTO plays a role similar to TLP, but the state machine is cleaner because QUIC encrypts transport headers and never reuses packet numbers.

title: QUIC Loss Recovery: Packet Threshold, Time Threshold and PTO (RFC 9002)
text:
Learning goals
After working through this chapter, you will be able to:

Explain why QUIC tracks packet numbers, in-flight state, and loss timers separately for Initial, Handshake, and Application Data spaces.
Compute whether an unacknowledged packet is declared lost under the packet threshold (kPacketThreshold = 3) or the time threshold (kTimeThreshold = 9/8).
Calculate smoothed_rtt, rttvar, and loss_delay from raw RTT samples and peer-reported ack_delay values.
Determine when to arm the loss timer versus the Probe Timeout (PTO), including exponential backoff before the first RTT sample (kInitialRtt = 333 ms) and max_ack_delay rules after handshake confirmation.
Identify why PTO must prioritize Initial and Handshake spaces over Application Data until the handshake is confirmed.
Evaluate a loss timeline against the persistent congestion threshold (3 * smoothed_rtt) to determine when congestion control must collapse cwnd to the minimum.

title: QUIC Loss Recovery: Packet Threshold, Time Threshold and PTO (RFC 9002)
text:
Three packet number spaces
A QUIC connection does not have one shared sequence space. It has three separate packet number spaces, each tied to an encryption level and each starting at packet number 0:









Space
Encryption level
Purpose
When discarded




Initial
Initial keys
Client/Server Hello, initial cryptographic frames
When Handshake keys are installed/used


Handshake
Handshake keys
TLS handshake completion, certificates, Finished
When handshake is confirmed


Application Data
0-RTT and 1-RTT keys
Stream data, connection control, post-handshake ACKs
Connection close



Loss detection runs per space. An ACK frame in Application Data acknowledging packet number 40 tells you nothing about whether Handshake packet number 2 arrived. You cannot declare Handshake packet 2 lost just because Application Data packet 40 was acknowledged, and you cannot mix packet numbers across spaces when checking thresholds.
Initial Space          : [PN 0] [PN 1]                     (ack-eliciting)
Handshake Space        : [PN 0] [PN 1] [PN 2]              (ack-eliciting)
Application Data Space : [PN 0] [PN 1] [PN 2] ... [PN 40]  (separate PN counter)

ACK for App Data PN 40 does NOT advance largest_acked in Initial or Handshake.
The only shared state across spaces is the RTT estimator (smoothed_rtt, rttvar, min_rtt, latest_rtt) and the congestion controller. Once a space is discarded, its in-flight packets are dropped from bytes_in_flight and its loss timers no longer fire.

title: QUIC Loss Recovery: Packet Threshold, Time Threshold and PTO (RFC 9002)
text:
Packet threshold and time threshold
When an ACK arrives in a given space, it updates largest_acked for that space. Any unacknowledged, ack-eliciting packet in that same space with pn < largest_acked becomes a candidate for loss. RFC 9002 declares a packet lost if it satisfies either of two conditions:

Packet threshold (kPacketThreshold = 3): A later packet at least 3 packet numbers ahead has been acknowledged:
largest_acked - pn >= kPacketThreshold
Reordering of 1 or 2 packets is tolerated as normal network jitter and is not treated as loss. If packet 0 is still in flight and packets 1 and 2 are acknowledged, packet 0 is not declared lost by the packet threshold (2 - 0 = 2 < 3). If packet 4 is acknowledged while packet 1 is still unacknowledged, packet 1 is declared lost (4 - 1 = 3 >= 3), whereas packets 2 and 3 remain in flight.
Time threshold (kTimeThreshold = 9/8): The unacknowledged packet was sent at least loss_delay ago, where:
loss_delay = max(kTimeThreshold * max(smoothed_rtt, latest_rtt), kGranularity)
With kGranularity = 1 ms and an RTT of 20 ms, loss_delay = max(9/8 * 20 ms, 1 ms) = 22.5 ms.
Why max(smoothed_rtt, latest_rtt)? If the path RTT suddenly spikes (latest_rtt > smoothed_rtt), using smoothed_rtt alone would declare packets lost too aggressively before their ACKs return. Conversely, if a single sample is unusually fast (latest_rtt < smoothed_rtt), using latest_rtt alone would ignore the smoothed baseline. Taking the maximum protects against both.

t = 0 ms       Send PN 0, PN 1
t = 20 ms      ACK arrives for PN 1  (largest_acked = 1)
               -> Packet threshold: 1 - 0 = 1 < 3 (not lost)
               -> Time threshold:   elapsed = 20 ms < 22.5 ms (not lost)
               -> Arm loss timer for t = 0 + 22.5 ms = 22.5 ms

t = 22.5 ms    Loss timer fires -> PN 0 is declared lost
If an unacknowledged packet with pn < largest_acked has not yet hit loss_delay, the sender does not declare it lost immediately. Instead, it arms a loss detection timer for time_sent + loss_delay. When that timer fires, the packet is declared lost without waiting for another ACK.
Notice the distinction from TCP’s classic fast retransmit. TCP’s 3-DUPACK rule counts three duplicate acknowledgements for the same cumulative sequence number, which usually implies three later segments arrived. QUIC’s kPacketThreshold = 3 is a direct arithmetic difference between packet numbers (largest_acked - pn >= 3), regardless of whether intermediate packets were acknowledged or lost.

title: QUIC Loss Recovery: Packet Threshold, Time Threshold and PTO (RFC 9002)
text:
RTT estimation and ack_delay
Every time an ACK newly acknowledges at least one ack-eliciting packet—and the largest newly acknowledged packet in that frame is ack-eliciting—the sender takes a raw RTT sample:
latest_rtt = ack_receive_time - largest_acked_packet.time_sent
Before feeding latest_rtt into smoothed_rtt and rttvar, RFC 9002 §5 adjusts for the peer’s reported ack_delay (the time the peer intentionally waited before sending the ACK, encoded in the ACK frame):

First RTT sample: min_rtt = latest_rtt, smoothed_rtt = latest_rtt, rttvar = latest_rtt / 2. On the very first sample, ack_delay is not subtracted.
Subsequent RTT samples:

Update min_rtt = min(min_rtt, latest_rtt).
Cap ack_delay at max_ack_delay if the handshake is confirmed (for Initial and Handshake spaces, max_ack_delay does not apply because peers must acknowledge handshake packets immediately).
Subtract ack_delay from latest_rtt only if latest_rtt - ack_delay >= min_rtt. If subtracting ack_delay would push the sample below min_rtt, the ack_delay value is unreliable (for example, min_rtt was measured on a slightly different path or clock), so you keep the unadjusted latest_rtt.
Update the EWMA:

rttvar = 3/4 * rttvar + 1/4 * |smoothed_rtt - adjusted_rtt|
smoothed_rtt = 7/8 * smoothed_rtt + 1/8 * adjusted_rtt



Because ack_delay is subtracted only when it produces a valid sample (>= min_rtt) and is capped by max_ack_delay in Application Data, a peer claiming an inflated ack_delay cannot artificially drive your smoothed_rtt down to zero.

title: QUIC Loss Recovery: Packet Threshold, Time Threshold and PTO (RFC 9002)
text:
Probe Timeout (PTO)
What happens when you have ack-eliciting packets in flight, no later packet has been acknowledged (largest_acked has not moved past them), and therefore the time-threshold loss timer is not armed? You cannot wait forever. You arm the Probe Timeout (PTO).
Crucially, a PTO firing does not declare packets lost. It tells the sender to transmit one or two probe packets (either new data or copies of unacknowledged frames) to elicit an ACK from the peer. Only when the resulting ACK arrives—or when the loss timer later fires—are earlier packets actually declared lost.

PTO before and after an RTT sample
The PTO duration depends on whether an RTT sample exists:








State
PTO formula
Notes




No RTT sample yet
2 * kInitialRtt * (2 ^ pto_count)
kInitialRtt = 333 ms. First PTO at 666 ms, second 1332 ms later (4 * kInitialRtt), and so on.


RTT sample exists (Initial / Handshake)
(smoothed_rtt + 4 * rttvar + kGranularity) * (2 ^ pto_count)
max_ack_delay is not added.


RTT sample exists (Application Data)
(smoothed_rtt + 4 * rttvar + kGranularity + max_ack_delay) * (2 ^ pto_count)
max_ack_delay is included once the handshake is confirmed.



In RFC 9002 §6.2.1, the 4 * rttvar term is floored at kGranularity (max(4 * rttvar, kGranularity)), and max_ack_delay is included for Application Data because the peer is allowed to delay 1-RTT ACKs by up to max_ack_delay (typically 25 ms). Before the handshake is confirmed, peers must not delay Initial or Handshake ACKs, so adding max_ack_delay there would inflate handshake recovery times unnecessarily.


Exponential backoff on consecutive PTOs
Each time a PTO fires without an ACK arriving for an ack-eliciting packet, pto_count increments by 1 and the next PTO doubles (2 ^ pto_count). Before any RTT sample is collected:
t = 0 ms       Send Initial PN 0 (no RTT sample yet, kInitialRtt = 333 ms)
               Arm PTO_0 = 2 * 333 ms = 666 ms
t = 666 ms     PTO_0 fires -> send probe PN 1, pto_count becomes 1
               Arm PTO_1 = 4 * 333 ms = 1332 ms from now (fires at t = 1998 ms)
t = 1998 ms    PTO_1 fires -> send probe PN 2, pto_count becomes 2
               Arm PTO_2 = 8 * 333 ms = 2664 ms from now (fires at t = 4662 ms)
Once an ACK arrives for an ack-eliciting packet, pto_count resets to 0.


Space priority before handshake confirmation
A connection can have ack-eliciting packets in flight in multiple spaces at the same time—for instance, Handshake packets waiting for the server’s Finished ACK alongside early 1-RTT Application Data. RFC 9002 §6.2.2.1 enforces a strict rule: until the handshake is confirmed, PTO must prioritize Initial and Handshake spaces over Application Data.
Specifically, if there are any in-flight ack-eliciting packets in Initial or Handshake, you arm the PTO timer for the earliest space among Initial and Handshake that has in-flight ack-eliciting packets (without max_ack_delay). You must not arm an Application Data PTO alone while Initial or Handshake still has unacknowledged ack-eliciting packets, because a peer that has not yet completed the handshake cannot process or acknowledge 1-RTT Application Data.

title: QUIC Loss Recovery: Packet Threshold, Time Threshold and PTO (RFC 9002)
text:
Persistent congestion
Individual packet losses trigger fast recovery, halving the congestion window (cwnd). A sustained outage—where every packet sent over multiple RTTs is lost—signals something worse: persistent congestion.
RFC 9002 §7.6 defines persistent congestion using a time span across newly lost packets rather than a fixed packet count:

Compute the persistent congestion duration:
pc_duration = (smoothed_rtt + max(4 * rttvar, kGranularity) + max_ack_delay) * kPersistentCongestionThreshold
where kPersistentCongestionThreshold = 3. (In simplified terms, the threshold scales with 3 * smoothed_rtt plus variance and max_ack_delay, depending on whether an RTT sample exists.)
Inspect the set of newly lost ack-eliciting packets (packets that were sent after the first RTT sample was obtained).
Find the earliest and latest send timestamps among contiguous ranges of lost packets. If the time span latest_lost.time_sent - earliest_lost.time_sent is at least the persistent congestion threshold (>= 3 * smoothed_rtt in the simplified check, or >= pc_duration in the full RFC calculation), persistent congestion is declared.

When persistent congestion is detected, the loss detector signals the congestion controller, which collapses cwnd to the minimum window (typically 2 * max_datagram_size) and resets congestion_recovery_start_time so the connection probes capacity from scratch. A brief burst of losses—even 5 or 10 packets—that all left the sender within a few milliseconds does not trigger persistent congestion; the loss period must span multiple RTTs.

title: QUIC Loss Recovery: Packet Threshold, Time Threshold and PTO (RFC 9002)
text:
The lab
There is no live aioquic or quic-go traffic on this box (aioquic is not installed). Instead, the lab runs a faithful RFC 9002 state machine in Python, exercising the exact packet-number, time-threshold, RTT, PTO, and persistent-congestion rules rather than capturing Chrome or nginx off the wire.
It walks through seven deterministic scenarios: 1. Reordering of 1–2 packets is not loss (ACKing PNs 1 and 2 leaves PN 0 in flight at t = 20 ms, arming the loss timer at 22.500 ms). 2. Packet threshold (kPacketThreshold = 3): ACKing PNs 0 and 4 declares PN 1 lost, leaving PNs 2 and 3 in flight. 3. Time threshold (kTimeThreshold = 9/8): ACKing PN 1 at 20 ms causes PN 0 to be declared lost when the loss timer fires at 22.500 ms. 4. PTO before an RTT sample starts at 2 * kInitialRtt (666 ms) and doubles (1332 ms later). 5. PTO prefers Initial and Handshake spaces until the handshake is confirmed. 6. ack_delay adjustment in RTT estimation (not subtracted on the first sample, subtracted and capped on the second sample of 40 ms yielding smoothed_rtt = 48.75 ms) and max_ack_delay (25 ms) in the Application Data PTO (158.75 ms with max_ack_delay, 133.75 ms without it). 7. Persistent congestion: losing PNs 1–7 across a 90.0 ms send span exceeds 3 * smoothed_rtt = 58.1 ms, setting persistent_congestion = True.
The lab program is quic-loss-lab.py, a Python RFC 9002 state machine. It is not a capture of a live QUIC stack.
quic-loss-lab.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""QUIC loss detection and PTO (RFC 9002 Appendix A), event-driven simulation."""
from __future__ import annotations
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import IntEnum
import math, sys

class Space(IntEnum):
    Initial = 0
    Handshake = 1
    ApplicationData = 2
    def short(self):
        return {0: "Init", 1: "Hs", 2: "App"}[int(self)]

K_PACKET_THRESHOLD = 3
K_TIME_THRESHOLD = 9 / 8
K_GRANULARITY = 0.001   # 1 ms
K_INITIAL_RTT = 0.333   # 333 ms
K_WINDOW_INITIAL = 12000  # not used beyond persistent-congestion period

@dataclass
class Sent:
    pn: int
    time_sent: float
    size: int
    ack_eliciting: bool
    in_flight: bool = True
    pkt_space: Space = Space.ApplicationData

@dataclass
class Conn:
    now: float = 0.0
    latest_rtt: float = 0.0
    smoothed_rtt: float = K_INITIAL_RTT
    rttvar: float = K_INITIAL_RTT / 2
    min_rtt: float = 0.0
    first_rtt_sample: float = 0.0
    max_ack_delay: float = 0.025  # 25 ms typical
    pto_count: int = 0
    handshake_confirmed: bool = False
    sent: dict[Space, dict[int, Sent]] = field(default_factory=lambda: {s: {} for s in Space})
    largest_acked: dict[Space, int] = field(default_factory=lambda: {s: -1 for s in Space})
    loss_time: dict[Space, float] = field(default_factory=lambda: {s: 0.0 for s in Space})
    time_of_last_ack_eliciting: dict[Space, float] = field(default_factory=lambda: {s: 0.0 for s in Space})
    lost: list[tuple[float, Space, int]] = field(default_factory=list)
    pto_events: list[tuple[float, Space]] = field(default_factory=list)
    next_pn: dict[Space, int] = field(default_factory=lambda: {s: 0 for s in Space})
    log: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def note(self, msg):
        self.log.append(f"t={self.now*1000:8.2f} ms  {msg}")

    def send(self, space: Space, size=1200, ack_eliciting=True) -> int:
        pn = self.next_pn[space]
        self.next_pn[space] += 1
        self.sent[space][pn] = Sent(pn, self.now, size, ack_eliciting, True, space)
        if ack_eliciting:
            self.time_of_last_ack_eliciting[space] = self.now
        self.note(f"send {space.short()} pn={pn} size={size} ack_elicit={ack_eliciting}")
        return pn

    def on_ack(self, space: Space, acked: list[int], ack_delay: float = 0.0):
        newly = []
        for pn in acked:
            pkt = self.sent[space].get(pn)
            if pkt is None:
                continue
            newly.append(pkt)
            if pn > self.largest_acked[space]:
                self.largest_acked[space] = pn
        if not newly:
            return
        # RTT: first newly acked largest + ack-eliciting (RFC 9002 §5, A.7)
        largest = max(newly, key=lambda p: p.pn)
        if largest.ack_eliciting and largest.pn == self.largest_acked[space]:
            self._update_rtt(self.now - largest.time_sent, ack_delay, space)
        for p in newly:
            self.sent[space].pop(p.pn, None)
        self.note(f"ack  {space.short()} pns={sorted(p.pn for p in newly)}  "
                  f"latest_rtt={self.latest_rtt*1000:.2f}ms srtt={self.smoothed_rtt*1000:.2f}ms "
                  f"rttvar={self.rttvar*1000:.2f}ms")
        self.pto_count = 0
        self.detect_lost(space)

    def _update_rtt(self, latest, ack_delay, space):
        self.latest_rtt = latest
        if self.first_rtt_sample == 0.0:
            self.min_rtt = latest
            self.smoothed_rtt = latest
            self.rttvar = latest / 2
            self.first_rtt_sample = self.now
            self.note(f"rtt first sample {latest*1000:.2f}ms")
            return
        self.min_rtt = min(self.min_rtt, latest)
        if space == Space.ApplicationData:
            ack_delay = min(ack_delay, self.max_ack_delay)
        adjusted = latest
        if adjusted >= self.min_rtt + ack_delay:
            adjusted -= ack_delay
        self.rttvar = 0.75 * self.rttvar + 0.25 * abs(self.smoothed_rtt - adjusted)
        self.smoothed_rtt = 0.875 * self.smoothed_rtt + 0.125 * adjusted

    def loss_delay(self) -> float:
        return max(K_TIME_THRESHOLD * max(self.latest_rtt, self.smoothed_rtt), K_GRANULARITY)

    def detect_lost(self, space: Space):
        if self.largest_acked[space] < 0:
            return
        lost_pns = []
        self.loss_time[space] = 0.0
        delay = self.loss_delay()
        for pn, pkt in list(self.sent[space].items()):
            if pn > self.largest_acked[space]:
                continue
            time_thresh = self.now >= pkt.time_sent + delay
            pkt_thresh = (self.largest_acked[space] - pn) >= K_PACKET_THRESHOLD
            if time_thresh or pkt_thresh:
                lost_pns.append((pn, "time" if time_thresh else "packet"))
            else:
                # next loss time
                when = pkt.time_sent + delay
                if self.loss_time[space] == 0.0 or when < self.loss_time[space]:
                    self.loss_time[space] = when
        for pn, why in lost_pns:
            self.note(f"LOST {space.short()} pn={pn} by {why}-threshold")
            self.lost.append((self.now, space, pn))
            self.sent[space].pop(pn, None)

    def get_pto(self, space: Space) -> float:
        # RFC 9002 §6.2.1 / A.8
        if self.first_rtt_sample == 0.0:
            duration = 2 * K_INITIAL_RTT
        else:
            duration = self.smoothed_rtt + max(4 * self.rttvar, K_GRANULARITY)
            if space == Space.ApplicationData:
                duration += self.max_ack_delay
        duration *= 2 ** self.pto_count
        return duration

    def next_timeout(self) -> tuple[float, str, Space] | None:
        # loss timer first (A.8)
        candidates = []
        for s in Space:
            if self.loss_time[s] > 0:
                candidates.append((self.loss_time[s], "loss", s))
        if candidates:
            return min(candidates, key=lambda x: x[0])
        # PTO
        ptos = []
        for s in Space:
            if not any(p.ack_eliciting for p in self.sent[s].values()):
                continue
            # Before handshake confirmed, do not arm PTO for App Data if Init/Hs in flight? 
            # RFC 6.2.1: the PTO is armed for the space that has in-flight ack-eliciting packets,
            # preferring Initial / Handshake until the handshake is confirmed.
            t = self.time_of_last_ack_eliciting[s] + self.get_pto(s)
            ptos.append((t, "pto", s))
        if not self.handshake_confirmed:
            ptos = [p for p in ptos if p[2] != Space.ApplicationData] or ptos
        if not ptos:
            return None
        return min(ptos, key=lambda x: x[0])

    def fire_timeout(self):
        ev = self.next_timeout()
        if ev is None:
            return
        when, kind, space = ev
        self.now = when
        if kind == "loss":
            self.note(f"loss timer fired for {space.short()}")
            self.detect_lost(space)
        else:
            self.pto_count += 1
            self.pto_events.append((self.now, space))
            self.note(f"PTO  {space.short()} (pto_count={self.pto_count}, duration={self.get_pto(space)*1000:.2f}ms)")
            # send two probe packets in that space (RFC 6.2.4)
            self.send(space, size=1200, ack_eliciting=True)

def run_scenario(title, fn):
    print(f"\n== {title} ==")
    c = Conn()
    fn(c)
    for line in c.log:
        print("  " + line)
    return c

def main():
    # Scenario 1: reordering within packet threshold is not loss
    def s1(c: Conn):
        # Send a burst, then ACK the later PNs after one RTT. Packet threshold
        # is 3, so pn 0 is only 2 behind 2 and must stay in flight until the
        # time threshold (9/8 RTT) expires.
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)  # 0
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)  # 1
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)  # 2
        c.now = 0.020
        c.on_ack(Space.ApplicationData, [1, 2], ack_delay=0)
        in_flight = list(c.sent[Space.ApplicationData])
        delay = c.loss_delay()
        c.note(f"in flight after ack 1,2: {in_flight}; loss_delay={delay*1000:.3f}ms; now={c.now*1000:.1f}ms")
        assert in_flight == [0], in_flight
        assert not any(pn == 0 for _,_,pn in c.lost)
        ev = c.next_timeout()
        assert ev and ev[1] == "loss"
        c.note(f"loss timer armed at {ev[0]*1000:.3f} ms (9/8 * {c.smoothed_rtt*1000:.2f} ms)")
    c1 = run_scenario("1. Reordering of 1-2 packets is not loss (threshold is 3)", s1)

    # Scenario 2: packet threshold
    def s2(c: Conn):
        for _ in range(5):
            c.send(Space.ApplicationData)
        # Burst at t=0, ACK after 20 ms — inside the 9/8 RTT time window
        # so only the packet threshold can declare loss. 4-1=3 so pn 1 is
        # lost; 4-2=2 so 2 and 3 stay in flight.
        c.now = 0.020
        c.on_ack(Space.ApplicationData, [0, 4])
        lost = [pn for _,_,pn in c.lost]
        inflight = list(c.sent[Space.ApplicationData])
        c.note(f"lost={lost} in_flight={inflight}")
        assert lost == [1], lost
        assert inflight == [2, 3], inflight
    run_scenario("2. Packet threshold: ack 0 and 4 declares pn 1 lost, not 2 or 3", s2)

    # Scenario 3: time threshold (9/8 * RTT)
    def s3(c: Conn):
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)  # 0 at t=0
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)  # 1 at t=0
        c.now = 0.020
        c.on_ack(Space.ApplicationData, [1], ack_delay=0)  # rtt = 20 ms
        delay = c.loss_delay()
        c.note(f"loss_delay={delay*1000:.3f} ms (9/8 * max(latest,srtt), min 1ms)")
        assert list(c.sent[Space.ApplicationData]) == [0]
        ev = c.next_timeout()
        assert ev and ev[1] == "loss"
        c.fire_timeout()
        assert any(pn == 0 for _,_,pn in c.lost)
        expected = K_TIME_THRESHOLD * 0.020
        c.note(f"expected fire {expected*1000:.3f} ms, actual {c.now*1000:.3f} ms")
        assert abs(c.now - expected) < 1e-12
    run_scenario("3. Time threshold: pn 0 lost 9/8 RTT after a later packet is acked", s3)

    # Scenario 4: PTO before any RTT sample is 2 * kInitialRtt
    def s4(c: Conn):
        c.send(Space.Initial)
        ev = c.next_timeout()
        assert ev and ev[1] == "pto" and ev[2] == Space.Initial
        c.note(f"first PTO armed at {ev[0]*1000:.1f} ms (2 * kInitialRtt={2*K_INITIAL_RTT*1000:.1f})")
        assert abs(ev[0] - 2 * K_INITIAL_RTT) < 1e-12
        c.fire_timeout()
        # backoff: next PTO is 2x
        ev2 = c.next_timeout()
        c.note(f"second PTO armed at {ev2[0]*1000:.1f} ms (4 * kInitialRtt={4*K_INITIAL_RTT*1000:.1f} from last probe)")
    run_scenario("4. PTO before an RTT sample is 2 * kInitialRtt, then doubles", s4)

    # Scenario 5: three packet number spaces — Handshake PTO, not App, until confirmed
    def s5(c: Conn):
        c.send(Space.Initial)
        c.now = 0.010
        c.send(Space.Handshake)
        c.now = 0.020
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)
        ev = c.next_timeout()
        c.note(f"next timeout kind={ev[1]} space={ev[2].short()} at {ev[0]*1000:.1f} ms")
        # both Init and Hs have in-flight ack-eliciting; earliest last_ack_elicit + PTO
        # Init sent at 0, Hs at 0.010, same PTO duration 2*333ms, Init is earlier
        assert ev[2] == Space.Initial
        c.handshake_confirmed = True
        ev2 = c.next_timeout()
        c.note(f"after handshake confirmed: kind={ev2[1]} space={ev2[2].short()} at {ev2[0]*1000:.1f} ms")
        # App sent at 0.020 also eligible; Init still earliest
        assert ev2[2] == Space.Initial
    run_scenario("5. PTO prefers Initial/Handshake until the handshake is confirmed", s5)

    # Scenario 6: ack delay is subtracted, but not below min_rtt; App Data adds max_ack_delay to PTO
    def s6(c: Conn):
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)  # 0 at 0
        c.now = 0.050
        c.on_ack(Space.ApplicationData, [0], ack_delay=0.025)
        # first sample does not subtract ack delay (RFC 5.3 / A.7 first sample uses latest as-is)
        c.note(f"after first sample (no ack_delay subtracted): srtt={c.smoothed_rtt*1000:.2f}")
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)  # 1
        c.now = 0.090
        c.on_ack(Space.ApplicationData, [1], ack_delay=0.025)
        c.note(f"after second sample (ack_delay capped at max_ack_delay={c.max_ack_delay*1000:.0f}ms): "
               f"latest={c.latest_rtt*1000:.2f} srtt={c.smoothed_rtt*1000:.2f}")
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)  # 2 still in flight
        pto = c.get_pto(Space.ApplicationData)
        pto_no_app = c.smoothed_rtt + max(4 * c.rttvar, K_GRANULARITY)
        c.note(f"App PTO={pto*1000:.2f} ms includes max_ack_delay; without it {pto_no_app*1000:.2f} ms")
        assert abs(pto - (pto_no_app + c.max_ack_delay)) < 1e-12
    run_scenario("6. ACK Delay in RTT and max_ack_delay in the Application Data PTO", s6)

    # Scenario 7: persistent congestion — two lost packets spanning a long enough window
    def s7(c: Conn):
        # Establish RTT = 20 ms
        c.send(Space.ApplicationData)  # 0
        c.now = 0.020
        c.on_ack(Space.ApplicationData, [0])
        # Send a burst, lose a span longer than persistent congestion duration
        # PC duration = smoothed_rtt * 3  (kPersistentCongestionThreshold, RFC 9002 7.6.1 = 3)
        start = c.now
        pns = []
        for i in range(8):
            pns.append(c.send(Space.ApplicationData))
            c.now += 0.015
        # ack only the last, so earlier ones will be packet-threshold lost once enough later pns are acked
        c.on_ack(Space.ApplicationData, [pns[-1]])
        lost = [pn for _,_,pn in c.lost]
        # first of the burst is pns[0]; last lost is those >= 3 behind largest
        # persistent congestion if the interval between first and last lost ack-eliciting
        # packets is >= smoothed_rtt * 3
        if len(lost) >= 2:
            # times of first/last lost among the burst
            # We popped lost packets; recover times from the log? Keep a side map — use c.lost times
            # lost entries are (time_detected, space, pn). Need send times: reconstruct from start
            send_time = {pns[i]: start + i * 0.015 for i in range(8)}
            lost_times = [send_time[pn] for pn in lost if pn in send_time]
            span = max(lost_times) - min(lost_times)
            pc_period = c.smoothed_rtt * 3
            in_pc = span >= pc_period
            c.note(f"lost pns={lost} send-span={span*1000:.1f} ms  "
                   f"PC period 3*srtt={pc_period*1000:.1f} ms  persistent_congestion={in_pc}")
            assert in_pc
        else:
            raise AssertionError("expected several packet-threshold losses")
    run_scenario("7. Persistent congestion: lost span >= 3*smoothed_rtt", s7)

    print("\n== constants used (RFC 9002 A.2 / §6.1 / §6.2.2 / §7.6.1) ==")
    print(f"  kPacketThreshold={K_PACKET_THRESHOLD}  kTimeThreshold={K_TIME_THRESHOLD}  "
          f"kGranularity={K_GRANULARITY*1000}ms  kInitialRtt={K_INITIAL_RTT*1000}ms  "
          f"kPersistentCongestionThreshold=3")
    print("\n== summary ==")
    print("failures: 0")
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
