title: Zero-Copy Sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY: Completions, Deferred Copies, and When It Loses
text: Zero-Copy Sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY: Completions, Deferred Copies, and When It Loses

title: Zero-Copy Sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY: Completions, Deferred Copies, and When It Loses
text:
Learning goals

Explain what MSG_ZEROCOPY changes about send(). The kernel pins your pages instead of copying them, which means you may not reuse the buffer until the kernel says so.
Turn the feature on correctly. SO_ZEROCOPY has to be set first, because without it the flag is silently ignored.
Read completion notifications from the socket error queue (MSG_ERRQUEUE), including the coalesced ranges and the SO_EE_CODE_ZEROCOPY_COPIED flag.
Predict when zero-copy is slower than copying (small writes, loopback and veth, NICs without scatter-gather), and measure it rather than assume.

Version note: the lab ran on Linux 6.12 with plain Python 3 sockets, with no root and no extra packages. The constants come from the kernel UAPI headers because Python’s socket module does not export them. Every number below comes from the pasted run. Throughput on a shared box varies by tens of percent between runs, so read the shape of the results, not the digits.



MSG_ZEROCOPY send path, completion notifications, and the loopback deferred copy.

title: Zero-Copy Sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY: Completions, Deferred Copies, and When It Loses
text:
The contract
Per the kernel’s MSG_ZEROCOPY documentation:

Socket setup. send() ignores flags it does not know, so the kernel will not enable copy avoidance just because a legacy program happens to pass the bit. You must first set setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_ZEROCOPY, 1).
Transmission. send(fd, buf, len, MSG_ZEROCOPY). The call can fail with ENOBUFS if the socket exceeds its optmem limit or the user exceeds the locked-pages ulimit. Calls with and without the flag can be mixed on the same socket.
Completion. Each successful zero-copy send call increments an unsigned 32-bit counter, starting at 0. It counts system calls, not bytes. When the kernel is done with the pages, it queues a sock_extended_err with ee_origin = SO_EE_ORIGIN_ZEROCOPY. ee_info holds the first number of the completed range and ee_data the last. Consecutive completions are coalesced, and for TCP there is usually at most one outstanding. The notification has a zero error code, so it does not block normal send/recv.
Deferred copies. The flag is “a hint … not a guarantee”. If the kernel had to copy after all, it sets SO_EE_CODE_ZEROCOPY_COPIED in ee_code, and a program can then stop passing the flag.
Loopback. All MSG_ZEROCOPY packets “looped to a local socket will incur a deferred copy”, because a local receiver might never read and the pages would stay pinned indefinitely.
Size. Page pinning and notification costs mean it is “generally only effective at writes over around 10 KB”.

title: Zero-Copy Sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY: Completions, Deferred Copies, and When It Loses
text:
Lab: measure it on loopback
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""MSG_ZEROCOPY over TCP: send, then read completions from the error queue."""
import socket, struct, sys, threading, time

SO_ZEROCOPY = 60          # asm-generic/socket.h
MSG_ZEROCOPY = 0x4000000  # linux/socket.h
SO_EE_ORIGIN_ZEROCOPY = 5
SO_EE_CODE_ZEROCOPY_COPIED = 1

def sink(srv):
    c, _ = srv.accept()
    while c.recv(1 << 20):
        pass

def run(addr, size, count, zc, flag_only=False):
    fam = socket.AF_INET6 if ':' in addr else socket.AF_INET
    srv = socket.socket(fam, socket.SOCK_STREAM); srv.bind((addr, 0)); srv.listen()
    threading.Thread(target=sink, args=(srv,), daemon=True).start()
    s = socket.socket(fam, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    if zc and not flag_only:
        s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, SO_ZEROCOPY, 1)
    s.connect(srv.getsockname()[:2])
    buf = bytearray(size)
    t = time.perf_counter(); c0 = time.thread_time()
    for _ in range(count):
        s.sendall(buf, MSG_ZEROCOPY if zc else 0)
    # drain notifications
    lo = hi = None; copied = 0; notes = 0; first = None
    if zc:
        deadline = time.time() + (0.5 if flag_only else 2)
        while time.time() < deadline and (hi is None or hi < count - 1):
            try:
                _, anc, _, _ = s.recvmsg(0, 512, socket.MSG_ERRQUEUE | socket.MSG_DONTWAIT)
            except BlockingIOError:
                time.sleep(0.001); continue
            for lvl, typ, data in anc:
                first = first or (lvl, typ)
                errno_, origin, _t, code, _p, info, data_ = struct.unpack('IBBBBII', data[:16])
                if origin == SO_EE_ORIGIN_ZEROCOPY:
                    notes += 1
                    lo = info if lo is None else min(lo, info)
                    hi = data_ if hi is None else max(hi, data_)
                    copied += code & SO_EE_CODE_ZEROCOPY_COPIED
    el = time.perf_counter() - t; cpu = time.thread_time() - c0
    s.close()
    print(f"  {addr:9} size={size:>7} zc={int(zc)} sends={count} "
          f"{size*count/el/1e9:6.2f} GB/s sender_cpu={cpu:5.2f}s"
          + (f" notifications={notes} range=[{lo},{hi}] copied_flag={copied} cmsg={first}" if zc else "")
          + (" (MSG_ZEROCOPY without SO_ZEROCOPY)" if flag_only else ""))

print("== loopback TCP, 256 MiB per run (per-run sizes below)")
for addr in ('127.0.0.1',):
    for size in (4096, 65536, 1048576):
        cnt = max(200, (256 << 20) // size)
        run(addr, size, cnt, False); run(addr, size, cnt, True)
print("== flag passed but socket option not set")
run('127.0.0.1', 65536, 64, True, flag_only=True)
$ python3 zc.py
== loopback TCP, 256 MiB per run (per-run sizes below)
  127.0.0.1 size=   4096 zc=0 sends=65536   2.46 GB/s sender_cpu= 0.10s
  127.0.0.1 size=   4096 zc=1 sends=65536   2.47 GB/s sender_cpu= 0.11s notifications=8 range=[0,65535] copied_flag=8 cmsg=(0, 11)
  127.0.0.1 size=  65536 zc=0 sends=4096   6.41 GB/s sender_cpu= 0.04s
  127.0.0.1 size=  65536 zc=1 sends=4096   2.86 GB/s sender_cpu= 0.08s notifications=1 range=[0,4095] copied_flag=1 cmsg=(0, 11)
  127.0.0.1 size=1048576 zc=0 sends=256   8.80 GB/s sender_cpu= 0.03s
  127.0.0.1 size=1048576 zc=1 sends=256   5.45 GB/s sender_cpu= 0.05s notifications=1 range=[0,255] copied_flag=1 cmsg=(0, 11)
== flag passed but socket option not set
  127.0.0.1 size=  65536 zc=1 sends=64   0.01 GB/s sender_cpu= 0.01s notifications=0 range=[None,None] copied_flag=0 cmsg=None (MSG_ZEROCOPY without SO_ZEROCOPY)

title: Zero-Copy Sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY: Completions, Deferred Copies, and When It Loses
text:
Reading the numbers

The flag without the socket option does nothing. There were no notifications and no error, so the last run behaved exactly like a normal copy. Its GB/s figure is meaningless because it includes the script’s 0.5-second wait for notifications that never come. This is the documented legacy-safety behaviour, and it is also the most common bug: “we enabled zero-copy” when nothing changed.
Completions really are coalesced. 65,536 sends of 4 KiB produced only 8 notifications covering [0, 65535]. The 64 KiB and 1 MiB runs produced a single notification for the whole run. Your reclaim loop must handle ranges, not one completion per send. The ranges end exactly at sends − 1, which confirms the counter counts calls: every Python sendall() here was satisfied by a single send syscall.
The control message is (0, 11), which is SOL_IP/IP_RECVERR. That matches the documentation (IPv6 sockets report IPV6_RECVERR).
Every notification carried copied_flag. On loopback the kernel copied anyway, later. The result is no gain at 4 KiB, and a loss at 64 KiB (6.41 → 2.86 GB/s) and 1 MiB (8.80 → 5.45 GB/s), with more sender CPU. You pay for pinning, notifications and a copy that is now cold in cache.

title: Zero-Copy Sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY: Completions, Deferred Copies, and When It Loses
section: What changes on a real NIC (not run here)
text:
What changes on a real NIC (not run here)
The box has no physical NIC to test against. Between two hosts, the selftest tools/testing/selftests/net/msg_zerocopy.c (driven by msg_zerocopy.sh) is the reference measurement. The documentation warns that running it between namespaces over veth “will not show any improvement”, for the same loopback reason seen above. Expect gains only when all of these hold:

writes are large (well above about 10 KB) and the sender is CPU-bound on copies
the NIC does scatter-gather, so the kernel can send headers and user pages together
the application can afford to hold buffers until completion, which is easiest with a ring of buffers reclaimed on each notification range

ss -tmi and perf top (look for copy_user_* / _copy_from_iter) on the sender are the quickest ways to see whether copying was the bottleneck in the first place.

title: Zero-Copy Sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY: Completions, Deferred Copies, and When It Loses
text:
The boring rule

Default to copying. Try MSG_ZEROCOPY only for big writes on a sender proven to be copy-bound.
Always set SO_ZEROCOPY, always drain MSG_ERRQUEUE (non-blocking, every few sends), and never touch a buffer before its range completes.
Watch SO_EE_CODE_ZEROCOPY_COPIED. If it shows up on a path, turn the flag off for that socket.
Benchmark between real hosts, never over loopback or veth.

title: Zero-Copy Sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY: Completions, Deferred Copies, and When It Loses
text:
Try this

Change the address to ::1. What cmsg level and type do you see now?
Drain the error queue after every 16 sends instead of at the end. Does the notification count go up?
Lower the locked-memory limit (ulimit -l 64) and try 1 MiB sends. Do you get ENOBUFS, or does the deferred-copy path on loopback avoid pinning altogether?

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
After reading this chapter, you will be able to design and operate multi-process network services using SO_REUSEPORT, explain how the Linux kernel hashes incoming TCP handshakes and UDP datagrams across distinct listening sockets, diagnose queue draining and connection reset risks during server reloads, and contrast kernel-level load balancing with traditional single-listener architectures.
Version note: All code listings and socket behaviors in this chapter were verified on an unprivileged Linux 6.12 system over the loopback interface using the Python 3.14 standard library.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
section: The Scaling Limits of a Single Listener
text:
The Scaling Limits of a Single Listener
High-concurrency network servers running on multi-core systems must distribute incoming connection handling across multiple CPU cores. In traditional Unix socket programming, services achieved this through one of two models:

Single-process event loop with worker threads: A single listening socket is managed by one thread or event loop, which accepts connections and passes accepted client file descriptors to worker threads. The single accept queue and its associated socket lock quickly become a bottleneck at high connection rates.
Shared listening socket across processes: A parent process opens and binds a socket, calls listen(), and then calls fork() to spawn worker processes that inherit the listening file descriptor. Each worker independently adds the shared descriptor to its own event loop (such as epoll) and calls accept().

While the inherited-socket approach distributes worker execution, it creates severe kernel-level contention. When a new TCP connection completes the three-way handshake, the kernel wakes up waiting processes. Historically, this caused a thundering herd, where every worker process woke up to call accept(), but only one succeeded while the others received EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK.
Linux introduced the EPOLLEXCLUSIVE flag (Linux 4.5) for epoll_ctl to wake only one worker per event. However, all workers still contend on a single underlying kernel listening socket lock (struct sock::sk_lock) and compete for entries in the same listen queue (icsk_accept_queue). Under heavy connection churn, lock contention in inet_csk_accept() limits scalability across NUMA nodes and multiple CPU cores.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
The SO_REUSEPORT Architecture
Introduced in Linux 3.9, the SO_REUSEPORT socket option fundamentally alters listener architecture. Rather than forcing worker processes to share a single listening socket data structure in the kernel, SO_REUSEPORT allows completely independent sockets—each with its own file descriptor, its own listen backlog queue, and its own lock—to bind to the exact same IP address and port combination.
Traditional Shared Listener (Inherited FD):
                           ┌─ Worker 1 (accepts from queue)
Incoming SYN ──> [ Shared Listen Socket ] ─┼─ Worker 2 (accepts from queue)
                 [ Single Accept Queue  ] ─┼─ Worker 3 (accepts from queue)
                 [ Single Spinlock      ] └─ Worker 4 (accepts from queue)

SO_REUSEPORT Listener Group:
                 ┌─> [ Socket 1 / Backlog Queue ] ──> Worker 1 (isolated)
Incoming SYN ──> ┼─> [ Socket 2 / Backlog Queue ] ──> Worker 2 (isolated)
  (4-tuple hash) ┼─> [ Socket 3 / Backlog Queue ] ──> Worker 3 (isolated)
                 └─> [ Socket 4 / Backlog Queue ] ──> Worker 4 (isolated)
When an incoming connection arrives, the kernel selects which socket in the reuseport group will receive it:

TCP distribution: During the initial SYN packet handling, the kernel computes a hash of the connection’s 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). The kernel scales that hash onto the group (reciprocal_scale(hash, N), which behaves like a modulo) to pick the receiving socket. The connection’s three-way handshake and subsequent accept() occur entirely on that specific socket.
UDP distribution: For SOCK_DGRAM sockets, the kernel computes the 4-tuple hash for every incoming datagram, distributing packets among the bound sockets in the group.
Lock isolation: Because each worker process operates on its own socket, there is zero cross-worker spinlock contention on accept queues.


Group Security Requirements
Allowing arbitrary processes to bind to an already open port would present an obvious security vulnerability: an unprivileged local attacker could bind to port 80 or 443 and hijack a portion of incoming traffic.
To prevent port hijacking, the kernel enforces strict security constraints:

Explicit opt-in: Every socket participating in the group must set the SO_REUSEPORT socket option before calling bind(). If a socket attempts to bind without the option set, the call fails with EADDRINUSE.
Effective UID matching: All sockets binding to the same address and port with SO_REUSEPORT must share the same effective user ID (euid). A process running under a different user ID cannot join an existing reuseport group.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
SO_REUSEPORT vs SO_REUSEADDR
Network engineers frequently conflate SO_REUSEADDR and SO_REUSEPORT. Although their names sound similar, they solve distinct problems.








Feature
SO_REUSEADDR
SO_REUSEPORT




Primary purpose
Rebind to a port currently in TIME_WAIT state
Distribute load across multiple active listeners


Simultaneous active listeners
No (only one active listening socket on a specific IP:port)
Yes (multiple listening sockets on the exact same IP:port)


Kernel distribution
None
Hash-based 4-tuple load balancing


Security barrier
Any process with bind privileges to that port
Enforces matching effective UID across all group sockets


Linux introduction
Historic BSD / Linux 1.0+
Linux 3.9



SO_REUSEADDR permits a server to restart immediately after a crash while previous connections linger in the kernel’s TIME_WAIT state. It does not allow multiple processes to listen concurrently on 127.0.0.1:8080. Attempting to bind a second active listener using only SO_REUSEADDR will fail immediately with EADDRINUSE.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
Lab: Default Binding Behavior
To observe the baseline kernel restriction, attempt to bind two independent sockets to the same address and port without enabling SO_REUSEPORT.
The following script requests an ephemeral port from the kernel on loopback (127.0.0.1:0), reads the assigned port, and then attempts to bind a second socket to the identical address and port.

import errno
import socket

def main():
    s1 = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    s1.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
    s1.listen(128)
    addr, port = s1.getsockname()
    print(f"Socket 1 bound to {addr}:{port}")

    s2 = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    try:
        s2.bind((addr, port))
        s2.listen(128)
        print("Socket 2 bound successfully")
    except OSError as err:
        print(f"Socket 2 failed to bind: {err.strerror} (errno {err.errno} == EADDRINUSE: {err.errno == errno.EADDRINUSE})")
    finally:
        s1.close()
        s2.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
The following command executes the script:
python3 without.py
Running without.py attempts to bind a second socket to the same address and port, raising an address-in-use error:
Socket 1 bound to 127.0.0.1:33855
Socket 2 failed to bind: Address already in use (errno 98 == EADDRINUSE: True)
Notice that the second bind() call fails immediately with OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use. Without explicit socket options, the network stack strictly forbids duplicate bindings to prevent port collision.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
Inspecting Listener Groups with ss
When SO_REUSEPORT is active, multiple listening sockets coexist on the same address. You can observe all sockets in the reuseport group using the Linux iproute2 utility ss.
ss -ltnp 'sport = :PORT'
(Not captured in the labs below, which use ephemeral ports.) When run against a service configured with four reuseport workers, ss reports four distinct socket inodes and separate receive queues (Recv-Q) and send queues (Send-Q), each mapped to a distinct worker process ID.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
section: Lab: Distributing TCP Connections Across Workers
text:
Lab: Distributing TCP Connections Across Workers
To demonstrate how SO_REUSEPORT distributes traffic, we construct a multi-process server.
The master process locates an available port, forks four worker processes, and directs each worker to create its own socket, apply SO_REUSEPORT, and bind to that exact port. The master process then initiates 400 separate TCP client connections, reads the responding worker’s identifier from each, and tallies the result into a histogram.

import collections
import multiprocessing
import os
import socket
import sys
import time

def worker_process(worker_id: int, port: int, ready_event: multiprocessing.Event, stop_event: multiprocessing.Event):
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEPORT, 1)
    sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", port))
    sock.listen(128)
    sock.settimeout(0.2)

    ready_event.set()

    while not stop_event.is_set():
        try:
            conn, _ = sock.accept()
        except socket.timeout:
            continue
        except OSError:
            break
        with conn:
            conn.sendall(f"worker-{worker_id}\n".encode("ascii"))

    sock.close()

def find_free_port() -> int:
    temp_sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    temp_sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
    port = temp_sock.getsockname()[1]
    temp_sock.close()
    return port

def main():
    multiprocessing.set_start_method("fork", force=True)
    port = find_free_port()
    num_workers = 4
    num_connections = 400

    stop_event = multiprocessing.Event()
    workers = []

    for wid in range(num_workers):
        ready = multiprocessing.Event()
        p = multiprocessing.Process(
            target=worker_process,
            args=(wid, port, ready, stop_event),
        )
        p.start()
        ready.wait()
        workers.append(p)

    counts = collections.Counter()

    for _ in range(num_connections):
        with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as client:
            client.connect(("127.0.0.1", port))
            response = client.recv(64).decode("ascii").strip()
            counts[response] += 1

    stop_event.set()
    for p in workers:
        p.join()

    print(f"Total connections handled: {sum(counts.values())}")
    for worker, count in sorted(counts.items()):
        print(f"  {worker}: {count} connections ({count / num_connections * 100:.1f}%)")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
The following command runs the listener group:
python3 group.py
Running group.py distributes 400 TCP handshakes across all four workers:
Total connections handled: 400
  worker-0: 111 connections (27.8%)
  worker-1: 85 connections (21.2%)
  worker-2: 106 connections (26.5%)
  worker-3: 98 connections (24.5%)
When reviewing the output, observe that all four workers receive and service a share of the 400 connections. Because the kernel assigns sockets using a hash of the 4-tuple, connections arriving from changing ephemeral source ports distribute across the workers. Variations between worker totals reflect natural statistical variance in 4-tuple hashing rather than an equal round-robin counter.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
Lab: 4-Tuple Hashing and Connection Stickiness
The default socket selection mechanism in Linux is deterministic: it computes a seeded Jenkins hash (jhash, via inet_ehashfn) over the connection 4-tuple and maps it onto the \(N\) sockets. Conceptually:
\[\text{index} = \text{hash}(\text{src\_ip}, \text{src\_port}, \text{dst\_ip}, \text{dst\_port}) \pmod N\]
where \(N\) is the number of sockets in the group. If the 4-tuple does not change, the hash does not change, and the incoming connection routes to the exact same listening socket every time.
We can verify this property directly. In standard TCP implementations, closing a connection leaves the local endpoint in the TIME_WAIT state for two Maximum Segment Lifetimes (typically 60 seconds), which prevents reusing the same source port. However, by enabling SO_REUSEADDR and setting SO_LINGER to an abortive zero-second timeout (l_onoff = 1, l_linger = 0), the client forces an immediate RST teardown, bypassing TIME_WAIT. This permits the client to rebind immediately to the exact same source port.

import collections
import multiprocessing
import os
import socket
import struct
import time

def worker_process(worker_id: int, port: int, ready_event: multiprocessing.Event, stop_event: multiprocessing.Event):
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEPORT, 1)
    sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", port))
    sock.listen(128)
    sock.settimeout(0.2)

    ready_event.set()

    while not stop_event.is_set():
        try:
            conn, _ = sock.accept()
        except socket.timeout:
            continue
        except OSError:
            break
        with conn:
            conn.sendall(f"worker-{worker_id}\n".encode("ascii"))

    sock.close()

def find_free_port() -> int:
    temp = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    temp.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
    port = temp.getsockname()[1]
    temp.close()
    return port

def main():
    multiprocessing.set_start_method("fork", force=True)
    server_port = find_free_port()
    client_port = find_free_port()
    num_workers = 4
    num_trials = 20

    stop_event = multiprocessing.Event()
    workers = []

    for wid in range(num_workers):
        ready = multiprocessing.Event()
        p = multiprocessing.Process(
            target=worker_process,
            args=(wid, server_port, ready, stop_event),
        )
        p.start()
        ready.wait()
        workers.append(p)

    counts = collections.Counter()
    linger_struct = struct.pack("ii", 1, 0)  # l_onoff=1, l_linger=0 (send RST)

    for _ in range(num_trials):
        client = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        client.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        client.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_LINGER, linger_struct)
        client.bind(("127.0.0.1", client_port))
        client.connect(("127.0.0.1", server_port))
        
        reply = client.recv(64).decode("ascii").strip()
        counts[reply] += 1
        client.close()
        time.sleep(0.01)

    stop_event.set()
    for p in workers:
        p.join()

    print(f"Fixed client 4-tuple trials: {num_trials}")
    for worker, hits in sorted(counts.items()):
        print(f"  {worker}: {hits} hits")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
The following command runs the stickiness test:
python3 sticky.py
Running sticky.py connects 20 times from the exact same source port, showing that all attempts route to the same worker:
Fixed client 4-tuple trials: 20
  worker-1: 20 hits
Notice that across all 20 connection cycles, exactly one worker receives 100% of the connections, while the other three workers receive none. Because the 4-tuple (127.0.0.1, client_port, 127.0.0.1, server_port) remains constant, the kernel’s hash function computes the identical group index every time.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
Lab: UDP Datagram Load Balancing
For UDP sockets, SO_REUSEPORT works on individual datagrams rather than TCP handshakes. This enables multi-threaded or multi-process DNS, syslog, or media servers to read from independent UDP queues on the same port.
In the following script, three worker processes form an SO_REUSEPORT UDP group. A test client sends 300 datagrams, creating a fresh ephemeral client socket for each datagram.

import collections
import multiprocessing
import os
import socket
import time

def udp_worker(worker_id: int, port: int, ready_event: multiprocessing.Event, stop_event: multiprocessing.Event, results_queue: multiprocessing.Queue):
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEPORT, 1)
    sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", port))
    sock.settimeout(0.2)

    ready_event.set()
    handled = 0

    while not stop_event.is_set():
        try:
            data, addr = sock.recvfrom(1024)
            handled += 1
        except socket.timeout:
            continue
        except OSError:
            break

    sock.close()
    results_queue.put((worker_id, handled))

def find_free_udp_port() -> int:
    temp = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    temp.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
    port = temp.getsockname()[1]
    temp.close()
    return port

def main():
    multiprocessing.set_start_method("fork", force=True)
    port = find_free_udp_port()
    num_workers = 3
    num_packets = 300

    stop_event = multiprocessing.Event()
    results_queue = multiprocessing.Queue()
    workers = []

    for wid in range(num_workers):
        ready = multiprocessing.Event()
        p = multiprocessing.Process(
            target=udp_worker,
            args=(wid, port, ready, stop_event, results_queue),
        )
        p.start()
        ready.wait()
        workers.append(p)

    for i in range(num_packets):
        with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) as client:
            client.sendto(f"msg-{i}".encode("ascii"), ("127.0.0.1", port))

    time.sleep(0.1)
    stop_event.set()

    worker_counts = {}
    for _ in range(num_workers):
        wid, count = results_queue.get()
        worker_counts[f"worker-{wid}"] = count

    for p in workers:
        p.join()

    print(f"Total UDP datagrams received: {sum(worker_counts.values())}")
    for worker, count in sorted(worker_counts.items()):
        print(f"  {worker}: {count} datagrams ({count / num_packets * 100:.1f}%)")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
The following command executes the UDP load test:
python3 udp_group.py
Running udp_group.py transmits 300 datagrams from distinct ephemeral ports, distributing them across the three UDP sockets:
Total UDP datagrams received: 300
  worker-0: 86 datagrams (28.7%)
  worker-1: 105 datagrams (35.0%)
  worker-2: 109 datagrams (36.3%)
Notice that all three workers process datagrams, with each worker handling roughly one-third of the total volume. Unlike TCP, where hashing occurs once per connection during SYN reception, UDP evaluates the 4-tuple hash on every individual packet.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
Operational Caveats and Edge Cases
While SO_REUSEPORT provides lock-free concurrency, it introduces specific operational hazards during dynamic resizing, process restarts, and rolling reloads.

The Accept Queue Drain Problem
When a worker process closes its listening socket—either during a graceful shutdown or after a process crash—any established TCP connections sitting in that socket’s accept backlog queue that have not yet been accepted via accept() are immediately discarded by the kernel, sending TCP RST packets to the connected clients.
Furthermore, any half-open connections in the SYN backlog associated with that specific socket fail completion during the handshake.
To solve this, Linux 5.14 introduced the net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req sysctl. When enabled:
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1   # needs root; not run here
If a listening socket in an SO_REUSEPORT group closes while requests remain in its child queues, the kernel automatically migrates those pending requests to another active listening socket within the same reuseport group instead of resetting them.


Hash Reshuffling on Group Resizing
Since the selection is effectively \(\text{hash} \bmod N\), adding or removing a socket changes which listener most 4-tuples map to.
For TCP this matters less than it looks:

Established connections no longer touch the listener at all.
Since Linux 4.4, handshakes in flight are stored as request sockets in the established hash table. The client’s final ACK finds its request socket by direct lookup. It isn’t hashed across the group again.

The real TCP hazard is removing a listener, as described in the previous section. Its queued requests and unaccepted connections go with it, unless tcp_migrate_req is enabled.
For UDP, resizing matters a great deal. Every datagram is hashed again, so a “flow” that stayed on worker 2 (a QUIC connection, or a DNS client retrying from the same port) can land on a different worker as soon as \(N\) changes. Protocols that keep per-flow state in the worker need BPF steering, or another way to find the owner, to survive scaling.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
section: Advanced Steering: BPF and CPU Affinity
text:
Advanced Steering: BPF and CPU Affinity
The standard 4-tuple modulo hash treats all worker processes identically and ignores CPU cache locality. The Linux kernel provides two mechanisms to override or tune this behavior.

CPU Locality with SO_INCOMING_CPU
When workers run bound to specific CPU cores, setting the SO_INCOMING_CPU socket option informs the kernel which CPU core handles the socket:
int cpu = worker_cpu_id;
setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_INCOMING_CPU, &cpu, sizeof(cpu));
When packets arrive on a network interface card (NIC) configured with Receive Side Scaling (RSS) or Receive Packet Steering (RPS), the kernel directs the connection to the SO_REUSEPORT socket whose configured CPU matches the CPU servicing the packet’s network interrupt, maximizing L1/L2 CPU cache hits.


Programmable Steering with eBPF






Note



Not run here. Loading custom BPF programs onto socket reuseport groups requires the CAP_BPF or CAP_NET_ADMIN capability and specialized BPF toolchains, which are not configured in this unprivileged lab environment.


According to the kernel documentation and primary sources, applications requiring precise connection dispatch can attach a BPF program to the reuseport group using the socket options:

SO_ATTACH_REUSEPORT_CBPF (classic BPF)
SO_ATTACH_REUSEPORT_EBPF (extended BPF)

In modern kernels, you write a program of type BPF_PROG_TYPE_SK_REUSEPORT. Instead of the kernel evaluating a 4-tuple hash, the kernel invokes your BPF program on each incoming packet. The program can inspect packet headers, check NUMA topology, look up worker load metrics in a BPF map, and explicitly return the array index of the target worker socket. If a worker is overloaded, the BPF program steers new connections to less busy workers, avoiding queue buildup.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
section: Production Implementations: Nginx, HAProxy, and Envoy

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
Common Pitfalls
Understanding these common mistakes prevents subtle production outages:

Setting the option after bind(): SO_REUSEPORT must be applied using setsockopt() before invoking bind(). Setting the option on an already bound socket has no effect on group registration, and subsequent bind() calls by other processes will raise EADDRINUSE.
Assuming round-robin distribution: SO_REUSEPORT does not use round-robin scheduling. It uses a 4-tuple hash. When testing with synthetic benchmark tools (such as load generators running from a single client machine with a narrow port range), traffic may land disproportionately on a subset of workers due to hash collisions.
Uneven load from long-lived connections: Because distribution occurs strictly at connection establishment time, a worker that accepts a handful of heavy, long-running connections (such as WebSocket or gRPC streams) will experience high CPU usage, while adjacent workers handling short-lived HTTP/1.1 requests sit idle. Application-level balancing or BPF steering is needed to balance persistent streams.
Neglecting the accept queue on shutdown: If a worker receives SIGTERM and immediately terminates its listening socket, clients with handshakes completed in the kernel accept queue receive connection resets. Production code must first stop accepting new connections while continuing to drain existing backlog descriptors, or rely on net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req.
Mixing differing UIDs: Attempting to bind a worker process running as a non-privileged user (e.g., www-data) to an existing reuseport group created by a process running under another user ID fails with EADDRINUSE, even if the socket option is set on both.

title: SO_REUSEPORT: Many Listeners on One Port
text:
Key Takeaways

SO_REUSEPORT allows multiple independent listening sockets on the exact same IP and port, provided every socket sets the option before binding and all processes share the same effective UID.
Unlike single-socket architectures where workers compete for a shared accept queue lock or suffer from thundering herd wakeups, SO_REUSEPORT gives each worker an independent socket, an independent accept queue, and independent lock state.
For TCP, incoming connections are assigned during SYN processing using a deterministic 4-tuple hash. Fixed client-server 4-tuples always map to the same worker socket.
For UDP, every datagram is independently hashed by its 4-tuple across the group sockets.
Closing a listener drops its queued handshakes and unaccepted connections. Graceful restarts need careful draining, socket hand-off, or the Linux 5.14+ net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req sysctl. Resizing the group also remaps UDP flows.
Advanced routing can be accomplished using SO_INCOMING_CPU for CPU cache locality and BPF_PROG_TYPE_SK_REUSEPORT for custom load-aware connection steering.

title: Multipath TCP: Subflows, Path Managers and a Rootless Lab
text:
Multipath TCP: Subflows, Path Managers and a Rootless Lab
After reading this chapter, you will be able to configure Linux Multipath TCP (MPTCP) path managers, inspect active MPTCP connections and underlying TCP subflows, observe kernel path-manager event streams, and audit hosts for MPTCP listener exposure without requiring root privileges.

title: Multipath TCP: Subflows, Path Managers and a Rootless Lab
section: Concepts: Connections, Subflows, and the Path Manager
text:
Concepts: Connections, Subflows, and the Path Manager
Multipath TCP (MPTCP), specified in RFC 8684, extends TCP so that one connection can use several paths at once and survive losing one of them. To an application, an MPTCP socket behaves like a standard byte stream socket. Underneath the hood, the Linux kernel manages one or more individual TCP subflows that traverse distinct network paths or IP addresses.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        Application Layer                          |
|             socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_MPTCP)           |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       MPTCP Token / Connection                    |
|       (one data sequence space; schedules data onto subflows)      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
                 /                                 \
                v                                   v
+-------------------------------+   +-------------------------------+
|   TCP Subflow 1 (Primary)     |   |   TCP Subflow 2 (Secondary)   |
|   127.0.0.1:48394 -> :7000    |   |   127.0.0.2:58777 -> :7000    |
+-------------------------------+   +-------------------------------+

The Protocol Handshake and Subflow Join
An MPTCP connection begins when a client opens a socket using the MPTCP protocol family (IPPROTO_MPTCP, numeric value 262 on Linux).

Initial Handshake (MP_CAPABLE): The client initiates a TCP handshake containing the TCP option MP_CAPABLE (Option Kind 30, Subtype 0). This option exchanges keying material and capability flags. If the peer supports MPTCP and no middlebox strips the option, both sides establish an MPTCP connection context identified by 32-bit tokens.
Additional Subflows (MP_JOIN): Once the initial subflow is established, either host can declare additional IP addresses or initiate new TCP subflows targeting the peer. Secondary subflows perform a standard TCP handshake containing the MP_JOIN option (Option Kind 30, Subtype 1), referencing the initial connection’s token and presenting an authentication HMAC to prove ownership.
Fallback to Plain TCP: If middleboxes (such as firewalls or deep-packet inspection appliances) remove the MPTCP TCP options during the initial SYN exchange, or if the destination server does not support MPTCP, the Linux kernel falls back to plain single-path TCP. The application gets no error.



The In-Kernel Path Manager
Linux delegates subflow lifecycle decisions to an in-kernel path manager. The path manager decides when to announce local IP addresses to peers, when to accept address announcements from peers, and when to proactively initiate new subflows.
Path management relies on two kernel configuration primitives configured per network namespace:

Limits: Control how many additional subflows can be established or accepted (subflow limit) and how many IP addresses advertised by the peer can be accepted (add_addr_accepted limit). By default, Linux sets add_addr_accepted to 0, preventing automatic subflow creation when a peer advertises new addresses.
Endpoints: Specific local IP addresses registered with the path manager. An endpoint can act as a subflow endpoint (causing the local host to initiate a new subflow from this address toward the peer) or a signal endpoint (causing the local host to advertise the address to the remote peer via ADD_ADDR TCP options). Endpoints can also carry flags such as backup to indicate standby links.

In Python 3.10 and later, MPTCP sockets are created by passing socket.IPPROTO_MPTCP (or constant integer 262) as the protocol argument to socket.socket(). Linux allows or refuses MPTCP socket creation per network namespace through the sysctl net.mptcp.enabled (1 in the lab below).

title: Multipath TCP: Subflows, Path Managers and a Rootless Lab
text:
The Rootless Lab Setup
You do not need dedicated hardware, multiple physical network interfaces, or root privileges to build a complete MPTCP laboratory. Using unprivileged network namespaces via unshare -rn, an ordinary user account creates an isolated network stack. Because the entire 127.0.0.0/8 block is automatically routed to the loopback interface (lo), assigning subflow endpoints to addresses like 127.0.0.2 allows multiple TCP subflows to be established locally over loopback.
The lab consists of two files: a Python echo client/server script (mptcp_echo.py) and a Bash orchestration script (lab.sh).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Tiny MPTCP echo pair: server on 127.0.0.1:7000, client sends for a few seconds."""
import socket
import sys
import time

IPPROTO_MPTCP = getattr(socket, "IPPROTO_MPTCP", 262)


def serve():
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_MPTCP)
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 7000))
    s.listen()
    print("server: listening with proto", IPPROTO_MPTCP, flush=True)
    conn, peer = s.accept()
    total = 0
    while data := conn.recv(65536):
        total += len(data)
        conn.sendall(data)
    print("server: echoed", total, "bytes from", peer, flush=True)


def client(seconds):
    c = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_MPTCP)
    c.connect(("127.0.0.1", 7000))
    end = time.time() + seconds
    sent = 0
    while time.time() < end:
        c.sendall(b"x" * 4096)
        c.recv(65536)
        sent += 4096
        time.sleep(0.01)
    c.shutdown(socket.SHUT_WR)
    while c.recv(65536):
        pass
    print("client: done", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if sys.argv[1] == "serve":
        serve()
    else:
        client(float(sys.argv[2]))
The accompanying orchestration script configures the namespace path manager, starts background event monitoring via ip mptcp monitor, launches the echo server, executes the client, and inspects the sockets using ss.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run inside: unshare -rn bash lab.sh   (unprivileged user + network namespace)
set -euo pipefail
ip link set lo up
echo "net.mptcp.enabled = $(cat /proc/sys/net/mptcp/enabled)"
echo "--- limits before"
ip mptcp limits show
ip mptcp limits set subflow 2 add_addr_accepted 2
ip mptcp endpoint add 127.0.0.2 dev lo subflow
echo "--- limits and endpoints after"
ip mptcp limits show
ip mptcp endpoint show
ip mptcp monitor > monitor.log 2>&1 &
MON=$!
python3 mptcp_echo.py serve > server.log 2>&1 &
SRV=$!
sleep 0.5
python3 mptcp_echo.py client 3 &
CLI=$!
sleep 1.5
echo "--- ss -M (MPTCP sockets)"
ss -Mn
echo "--- ss -tn (the TCP subflows underneath)"
ss -tn
wait $CLI
wait $SRV
kill $MON
echo "--- server log"
cat server.log
echo "--- monitor events"
cat monitor.log

title: Multipath TCP: Subflows, Path Managers and a Rootless Lab
section: Executing the Lab and Reading Output
text:
Executing the Lab and Reading Output
To run the experiment, execute lab.sh within an unprivileged network namespace user wrapper:
unshare -rn bash lab.sh

Path Manager Initialization
The initial portion of lab.sh verifies net.mptcp.enabled, displays default path manager limits, increases subflow and address acceptance limits to 2, and registers 127.0.0.2 as a local subflow endpoint on interface lo.
The following command printed the initial path manager state and the updated limits and endpoint definitions.
net.mptcp.enabled = 1
--- limits before
add_addr_accepted 0 subflows 2 
--- limits and endpoints after
add_addr_accepted 2 subflows 2 
127.0.0.2 id 1 subflow dev lo 
Key things to observe in this output: - net.mptcp.enabled returns 1, confirming MPTCP socket creation is active. - A fresh namespace starts with add_addr_accepted 0 subflows 2. Raising add_addr_accepted to 2 lets this namespace act on addresses a peer announces with ADD_ADDR. The extra subflow in this lab comes from the local subflow endpoint, which the existing subflows 2 limit already allows. - The ip mptcp endpoint add command registers 127.0.0.2 with id 1 and flag subflow.


Inspecting MPTCP Sockets (ss -M)
While traffic flows between the echo client and server, ss -Mn queries the Linux kernel for active MPTCP-level connections (-M filters for MPTCP sockets, -n prevents port/IP resolution).
The following command displayed the high-level MPTCP socket entries.
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port 
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:48394    127.0.0.1:7000 
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:7000     127.0.0.1:48394
ss -M shows the MPTCP layer: one connection, listed twice because both ends live in this namespace (client port 48394 and server port 7000). It shows one row per MPTCP socket, however many subflows that socket has.


Inspecting Underlying Subflows (ss -tn)
To view the concrete TCP connections carrying the data stream, ss -tn queries standard IPv4 TCP sockets.
The following command displayed the active TCP subflows operating beneath the MPTCP connection.
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port 
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:7000     127.0.0.2:58777
ESTAB 0      0          127.0.0.1:48394    127.0.0.1:7000 
ESTAB 0      0       127.0.0.2%lo:58777    127.0.0.1:7000 
ESTAB 0      4096       127.0.0.1:7000     127.0.0.1:48394
Observe the difference between ss -M and ss -tn: - ss -tn shows four rows: two TCP subflows, each seen from both ends. - 127.0.0.1:48394 -> 127.0.0.1:7000 is the initial subflow, set up with MP_CAPABLE. - 127.0.0.2:58777 -> 127.0.0.1:7000 is the second subflow, the MP_JOIN that the path manager opened from the 127.0.0.2 endpoint (%lo shows it is bound to dev lo).


Application Completion and Event Logs
Once the client completes its timed transmission, it performs a socket shutdown, causing the server to log the total byte count and exit.
The following command printed the completed server execution log.
client: done
server: listening with proto 262
server: echoed 1191936 bytes from ('127.0.0.1', 48394)
Simultaneously, ip mptcp monitor captures netlink kernel events emitted by the MPTCP path manager throughout the socket lifecycle.
The following command printed the path-manager event trace captured during execution.
[LISTENER_CREATED] saddr4=127.0.0.1 sport=7000
[         CREATED] token=02c31fc4 remid=0 locid=0 saddr4=127.0.0.1 daddr4=127.0.0.1 sport=48394 dport=7000
[         CREATED] token=096d3203 remid=0 locid=0 saddr4=127.0.0.1 daddr4=127.0.0.1 sport=7000 dport=48394
[     ESTABLISHED] token=096d3203 remid=0 locid=0 saddr4=127.0.0.1 daddr4=127.0.0.1 sport=7000 dport=48394
[     ESTABLISHED] token=02c31fc4 remid=0 locid=0 saddr4=127.0.0.1 daddr4=127.0.0.1 sport=48394 dport=7000
[  SF_ESTABLISHED] token=02c31fc4 remid=0 locid=1 saddr4=127.0.0.2 daddr4=127.0.0.1 sport=58777 dport=7000 backup=0 ifindex=1
[  SF_ESTABLISHED] token=096d3203 remid=1 locid=0 saddr4=127.0.0.1 daddr4=127.0.0.2 sport=7000 dport=58777 backup=0
[ LISTENER_CLOSED] saddr4=127.0.0.1 sport=7000
[          CLOSED] token=096d3203
[          CLOSED] token=02c31fc4
In the monitor output, look for the chronological sequence of events: 1. LISTENER_CREATED: The server opens an MPTCP listening socket on port 7000. 2. CREATED / ESTABLISHED: The initial subflow forms via MP_CAPABLE. 3. SF_ESTABLISHED: The path manager detects endpoint 127.0.0.2 and triggers an additional subflow via MP_JOIN. 4. CLOSED / LISTENER_CLOSED: Sockets tear down cleanly upon transfer completion.

title: Multipath TCP: Subflows, Path Managers and a Rootless Lab
text:
Production Configuration: Multi-Homed Hosts
In production, hosts typically possess multiple physical network interfaces (for example, eth0 on 192.168.1.50 and eth1 on 10.0.0.50). The role of each endpoint depends on whether the host acts primarily as a server or a client.









Goal
Endpoint Type
Local Command Example
Protocol Action




Server announcing an extra IP to clients
signal
ip mptcp endpoint add 10.0.0.50 dev eth1 signal
Sends an ADD_ADDR option to the client over existing subflows.


Client actively opening extra subflows
subflow
ip mptcp endpoint add 10.0.0.50 dev eth1 subflow
Initiates an outgoing MP_JOIN TCP handshake from 10.0.0.50 to the server.


Reserve an interface for failover only
backup flag
ip mptcp endpoint add 10.0.0.50 dev eth1 subflow backup
Sets the MP_JOIN backup bit; traffic stays on primary paths unless they fail.


Permit inbound peer address join requests
Limit adjustment
ip mptcp limits set subflow 4 add_addr_accepted 4
Allows the kernel to accept up to 4 peer-advertised addresses and subflows.

title: Multipath TCP: Subflows, Path Managers and a Rootless Lab
section: Operations: Security Auditing and Emergency Mitigation
text:
Operations: Security Auditing and Emergency Mitigation
Understanding where MPTCP listening sockets exist is critical for infrastructure security operations. MPTCP introduces distinct code paths inside the kernel network stack, expanding the attack surface of listening ports.

CVE-2026-98432 Vulnerability Context
CVE-2026-98432, published in October 2026, is a critical (CVSS 9.8) vulnerability in the Linux kernel network subsystem. The defect stems from IPv4 option structures (inet_opt/ireq_opt) being freed without honoring an RCU (Read-Copy Update) grace period during socket state transitions.
The vulnerability affects Linux kernel versions starting from 4.4. The public exploit released on 27 October 2026 needs a reachable MPTCP listener socket (IPPROTO_MPTCP). Certain application runtimes and framework defaults create MPTCP listeners automatically when binding stream sockets on supporting kernels.
The vulnerability is resolved in fixed kernel releases: - 5.10.272 - 5.15.223 - 6.1.190 - 6.6.159 - 6.12.113 - 6.18.56 - 7.2.10 - 7.3


Inventorying MPTCP Listeners
Standard socket tools like netstat or default ss -tnl output do not explicitly differentiate MPTCP listeners from standard TCP listeners. To inventory active MPTCP listeners across host network namespaces, query the socket statistics utility using the -M flag:
ss -Mlnp
This command flags listening (-l), numeric (-n), process-associated (-p) MPTCP (-M) sockets. Any listening socket reported by ss -Mlnp accepts MPTCP option handshakes and exposes the kernel’s MPTCP state machine.


Immediate Emergency Mitigation (Kill Switch)
Until you can reboot into a fixed kernel, the interim mitigation is to stop new MPTCP sockets being created in the host namespace:
sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0






Note



Not run here (it needs root on the host). Setting net.mptcp.enabled=0 prevents the creation of new MPTCP sockets and forces new connection attempts to fall back to standard TCP. It does not retroactively close or alter existing, already-established MPTCP sockets. Restart services whose MPTCP listeners already exist, then check that ss -Mlnp is empty. The sysctl is per network namespace, so containers with their own namespace need the same treatment. Add the setting to a sysctl configuration file if it should survive a reboot.

title: Multipath TCP: Subflows, Path Managers and a Rootless Lab
text:
Pitfalls

Default add_addr_accepted is zero: Fresh network namespaces default to add_addr_accepted 0. Even if a remote server advertises additional IP addresses via ADD_ADDR, the client kernel silently ignores them until ip mptcp limits set add_addr_accepted N is configured.
Middlebox option stripping: Enterprise firewalls, NAT boxes, or WAN accelerators may strip unknown TCP options (Option Kind 30). When this occurs, MPTCP falls back to single-path TCP during the initial handshake without raising an error to the application.
Per-namespace limits and endpoints: MPTCP endpoint tables and limits are isolated within network namespaces. Running ip mptcp endpoint add in the root namespace does not propagate rules into container namespaces or unshare environments.
ss -M appears empty after fallback: If an MPTCP socket falls back to plain TCP due to peer incompatibility or option stripping, ss -M no longer tracks the socket. The connection continues operating as a standard TCP socket and appears exclusively under ss -t.

title: Multipath TCP: Subflows, Path Managers and a Rootless Lab
text:
Summary

MPTCP (IPPROTO_MPTCP / 262) wraps multiple TCP subflows into a single logical socket, so it can use several paths and survive losing one.
The in-kernel path manager controls subflow creation using per-namespace limits (ip mptcp limits) and configured IP endpoints (ip mptcp endpoint).
Client hosts use subflow endpoints to initiate secondary TCP connections (MP_JOIN), while servers use signal endpoints to advertise IP addresses (ADD_ADDR).
ss -M inspects MPTCP connection tokens and top-level session state; ss -tn displays the underlying constituent TCP subflows.
For a kernel MPTCP bug such as CVE-2026-98432: inventory listeners with ss -Mlnp, use net.mptcp.enabled=0 plus service restarts as the stopgap, and upgrade the kernel as the fix.
