title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
TCP will send as much as the path will hold, not as much as the application can write. The congestion-control algorithm is the part of the stack that decides how large that in-flight window is allowed to be, and how it reacts when the path seems busy. On Linux the default has been CUBIC for many years. Reno (and its NewReno repair) is the historical loss-based baseline. BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time) is a model-based alternative that estimates the bottleneck rate and the minimum RTT instead of treating every lost packet as a signal to cut the window in half. This chapter shows how to see which algorithm a socket is using, how to select one per socket, and what CUBIC and BBR actually optimise — including the cases where a popular “just enable BBR” tip is wrong.

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
Learning goals

Read net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control, tcp_available_congestion_control and tcp_allowed_congestion_control, and pick an algorithm with TCP_CONGESTION
Read the algorithm name, cwnd, rtt, pmtu, and app_limited from ss -ti, and know which numbers you must not quote as a benchmark
Explain CUBIC’s loss-based cubic growth (RFC 8312 / RFC 9438) versus Reno’s linear growth after a multiplicative decrease
Explain what BBRv1 estimated, why BBRv2/v3 exist, and when BBR can be harder on a loss-based neighbor
Say what this kernel can and cannot load (no BBR module here)

Version note. Sysctls and labs ran on 2026-11-13 on Linux 6.12.94+ with iproute2 6.15.0 and Python 3.13.5. The host reports tcp_available_congestion_control = reno cubic and the default tcp_congestion_control = cubic. There is no loadable tcp_bbr module in /lib/modules on this writing host. setsockopt(TCP_CONGESTION, "bbr") and a sysctl write of bbr both failed with No such file or directory. CUBIC and Reno transfers ran in two unshare network namespaces connected by a veth (192.0.2.1 → 192.0.2.2, MTU 1500). ss -ti listings below are pasted from those runs. There is no tc / netem on this host, so the path has essentially no delay and no induced loss: the transfer finishes in a few milliseconds and the implied send rates are arithmetic, not capacity measurements. BBR behaviour is written from the kernel’s TCP BBR documentation and the IETF work, and is not run here.
The transport chapter covers TCP and UDP generally. A sibling chapter already uses ss -ti as a troubleshooting tool; this one is about the congestion-control name on that line.

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
The knobs Linux actually exposes
Three sysctls, all under /proc/sys/net/ipv4/:








Sysctl
This host
Role




tcp_available_congestion_control
reno cubic
Algorithms compiled in or already loaded


tcp_allowed_congestion_control
reno cubic
Algorithms a non-privileged socket may choose


tcp_congestion_control
cubic
Default for new sockets



On this host they were:
# uname -r
6.12.94+
# cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_available_congestion_control
reno cubic
# cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_allowed_congestion_control
reno cubic
# cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_congestion_control
cubic
reno is built into the core TCP code. CUBIC is a module that this kernel has already loaded (or compiled in). BBR is a different module (tcp_bbr). If it is not in available, you cannot select it:
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='cubic' -> getsockopt='cubic' OK
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='reno' -> getsockopt='reno' OK
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='bbr' -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='bbr2' -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='bbr3' -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='yeah' -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
write tcp_congestion_control=bbr -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
value still: cubic
That ENOENT is the kernel telling you the algorithm is not present, not that you lacked capability. Loading tcp_bbr would take a privileged modprobe (and a module that exists). This host has neither; nothing was loaded. Do not assume “modern Linux means BBR is there.” Check available first.
A process chooses an algorithm for one socket with setsockopt level IPPROTO_TCP, option TCP_CONGESTION (value 13), passing the name as a string. Unprivileged processes may only pick names in tcp_allowed_congestion_control. Changing the default sysctl is a system-wide (or netns-wide) act and is usually the wrong first move; prefer a per-service setsockopt or a systemd / ip-tcp_metrics policy you can roll back.

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
section: Reading ss -ti without lying to yourself
text:
Reading ss -ti without lying to yourself
The algorithm name is the first token on the indented ss -ti line. Next to it sit cwnd (congestion window, in segments), rtt (smoothed RTT / variance, in milliseconds), pmtu, mss, and often app_limited or a huge send figure.
An 8 MiB write from 192.0.2.1 to 192.0.2.2 across a veth, mid-transfer, CUBIC on the sending socket:
# ss -ti mid-transfer cubic client 192.0.2.1 -> 192.0.2.2:45111
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
ESTAB 0      0          192.0.2.1:53180    192.0.2.2:45111
     cubic wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:0.049/0.058 mss:1448 pmtu:1500 rcvmss:536 advmss:1448 cwnd:897 bytes_sent:2162688 bytes_acked:2162689 segs_out:1506 segs_in:30 data_segs_out:1504 send 212Gbps lastsnd:4 lastrcv:4 lastack:4 pacing_rate 424Gbps delivery_rate 5.79Gbps delivered:1505 rcv_space:14480 rcv_ssthresh:64088 minrtt:0.002 snd_wnd:4138624 rcv_wnd:64256
The same transfer with the sending socket set to Reno:
# ss -ti mid-transfer reno client 192.0.2.1 -> 192.0.2.2:45112
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
ESTAB 0      0          192.0.2.1:34960    192.0.2.2:45112
     reno wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:0.044/0.035 mss:1448 pmtu:1500 rcvmss:536 advmss:1448 cwnd:994 bytes_sent:2162688 bytes_acked:2162689 segs_out:1501 segs_in:20 data_segs_out:1499 send 262Gbps pacing_rate 516Gbps delivery_rate 644Mbps delivered:1500 rcv_space:14480 rcv_ssthresh:64088 minrtt:0.003 snd_wnd:1575808 rcv_wnd:64256
Both sides received the full 8 MiB (recvd=8388608) in about 5–6 ms. What to trust:

The name (cubic / reno) is the algorithm on that socket. The listening side, if you snapshot it, may still say cubic because the server never called setsockopt. Congestion control is a sender decision.
pmtu:1500 and mss:1448 show this is a real Ethernet-sized path (1500 minus headers), not the loopback pmtu:65535 / 32 KiB MSS you will see on 127.0.0.1.
cwnd:897 and cwnd:994 are huge because the path has no delay and no loss. The window opened as fast as ACKs returned. On a 30 ms, slightly lossy WAN path you would see a much smaller cwnd and a meaningful difference between the algorithms.
send 212Gbps is cwnd * mss / rtt with an RTT of 49 microseconds. It is not a measurement of the NIC, the veth, or CUBIC. Do not publish it. delivery_rate is a little closer to observed throughput, and even that is a nearly idle or already-finished burst on this path.
The transfer time (0.0060s / 0.0045s) is also not a CUBIC-versus-Reno result. Without queueing delay or loss, both algorithms just get out of the way.

If you need a fair comparison, you want a path with a known bandwidth-delay product and a controlled loss or queue (for example netem on a lab host that has tc). That lab was not run here.

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
Loss-based control: Reno and CUBIC
Classic TCP, as popularised by Reno / NewReno, treats a lost segment (or a sufficient ECN mark, when ECN is in use) as congestion. The window is cut — multiplicatively, typically to about half for a fast retransmit — and then grows linearly, one more segment per RTT in congestion avoidance. On a high-bandwidth, high-RTT path that linear climb is slow: after a single loss it can take many RTTs to fill the pipe again.
CUBIC (RFC 8312, later RFC 9438) stays loss-based, but the window is a cubic function of time since the last congestion event, not of ACK count. After a cut, CUBIC grows slowly around the previous operating point (to probe whether the path is still full), then more quickly if that point is left behind, and it flattens again as it approaches the old window. Time-based growth is why CUBIC is less punished by a long RTT than Reno is, and why it became the Linux default.
CUBIC still believes loss is congestion. On a path with random wireless loss, or a shallow switch queue that drops while the path is not actually full, both Reno and CUBIC back off. That is the design. It is also the complaint that motivated BBR.

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
Model-based control: BBR
BBR, originally from Cardwell et al. at Google and documented in the Linux kernel’s tcp_bbr notes and subsequent IETF drafts, estimates two numbers: the bottleneck bandwidth (from delivered rate over time) and the round-trip propagation delay (from the minimum RTT seen). The product is the bandwidth-delay product, the amount of data that should be in flight to fill the pipe but not the queue. BBR paces at the estimated rate and caps in-flight data around that product, with periodic probes for more bandwidth and for a new minimum RTT.
The intended contrast with CUBIC is simple:









CUBIC / Reno
BBR




Primary signal
Loss (and ECN, if enabled)
Estimated rate and min RTT


Reaction to random loss
Shrink cwnd
Should keep the rate if the model still says the pipe is not full


Risk
Underfills a long-fat path after loss
Can fill a shared queue more aggressively than a loss-based neighbor, and early BBRv1 was known to do so



BBRv1’s queueing behaviour on paths it shared with CUBIC was the reason for BBRv2 and later BBRv3: more conservative reaction to loss and ECN, better coexistence. Linux module and ss names vary by tree (bbr, sometimes a versioned name). This host has none of them, so there is no ss -ti line to paste.
Two operational consequences matter more than the brand name:

You cannot enable BBR if it is not in available. The ENOENT above is the whole story until the module exists and is allowed.
Switching a whole server to BBR because a blog said “three sysctls make it faster” is not a measurement. BBR can help a long, slightly lossy path where CUBIC keeps backing off; it can also change how your flows share a bottleneck with CUBIC-only peers. Measure with ss -ti and an application-level goodput on a representative path, and keep a way to revert the default.

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
Choosing one, in practice

Leave the system default at CUBIC unless you have a reason and a rollback.
If a single service needs a different algorithm, set TCP_CONGESTION in that process (or its unit / container) after checking tcp_allowed_congestion_control.
Compare algorithms on a path that looks like production (delay, modest loss, a real MTU), not on a veth with a 50 µs RTT.
Watch app_limited. If the application is not offering enough data, the algorithm is not the bottleneck and cwnd / send will mislead you.

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
Gotchas

Quoting send …Gbps from a lab with a tiny RTT. The formula will invent a fantasy rate. Look at elapsed time, delivery_rate, and application counters instead.
Assuming both ends of ss -ti show the algorithm you set. Only the sending socket’s choice matters for that direction; the listener may still say cubic.
Loopback or same-namespace local delivery. pmtu:65535 means you are not on a 1500-byte path. The veth lab above was set up in two netns precisely so pmtu:1500 would show up.
“The kernel is 6.12, so BBR is there.” Availability is a module/config question, not a version number. Read tcp_available_congestion_control.
No netem, no comparison. Without delay or loss, CUBIC and Reno mid-transfer windows in this lab were both enormous (cwnd 897 vs 994) and the elapsed times were within a couple of milliseconds. That is not a result.

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
Boring rule
Read the algorithm name and cwnd from ss -ti, but only trust a comparison when the path has a real RTT and a reason to lose or queue packets. Check available before you try to “turn on BBR.”

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
Try this

On a lab host that has tc, add 20–50 ms and a fraction of a percent of loss on a veth, repeat the 8 MiB transfer with CUBIC and Reno, and compare elapsed time and mid-transfer cwnd. Then, if bbr is in available, add it as a third run.
Set TCP_CONGESTION to reno on only the client and confirm the server’s ss -ti line still says cubic.
Start a transfer, pause the sender so the socket goes app_limited, and watch send and cwnd stop meaning “path capacity.”

title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR
text:
Sources

RFC 8312, CUBIC for Fast Long-Distance Networks; RFC 9438, CUBIC for Fast and Long-Distance Networks (standards-track update)
RFC 5681, TCP Congestion Control (Reno-style loss-based control)
Linux kernel documentation for tcp_congestion_control / BBR (Documentation/networking/bbr-quick-start and the tcp_bbr module notes in the tree you run)
ss(8), iproute2 6.15; tcp(7) (TCP_CONGESTION)
Cardwell, Cheng, Gunn, Yeganeh, Jacobson, BBR: Congestion-Based Congestion Control (the original description); later IETF CCWG work on BBRv2/v3 for coexistence

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Learning goals

Break one-way UDP latency into stages you can name: the send syscall and stack, the driver hand-off, the wire and switches, the receive stack, the socket queue, and the wake-up of the application
Use the kernel’s software timestamps (SO_TIMESTAMPING with SOF_TIMESTAMPING_TX_SOFTWARE and SOF_TIMESTAMPING_RX_SOFTWARE) to measure those stages yourself, without root
Show with real numbers that, on an idle path, waking a blocked receiver costs more than the whole network stack, and that under load, queueing in the socket buffer costs more than everything else combined
Read the drop counter that tells you a socket buffer overflowed (Udp: RcvbufErrors), and size receive buffers from evidence
Place the parts this lab cannot measure (serialization, propagation, interrupt coalescing, kernel bypass) in the same budget with simple arithmetic

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Thesis
“The network is slow” usually means “somewhere between sendto() and recvfrom() time went missing”. On a single host, or two hosts in the same rack, very little of that time is on the wire. A 64-byte frame takes about 67 ns to serialize at 10 Gb/s, including preamble and inter-frame gap, and light covers a 2 m cable in about 10 ns. The rest is software: the syscall, building and routing the skb, the qdisc, the driver, the receive path, the socket buffer, and most of all the scheduler deciding when the receiving thread runs again.
The kernel can stamp a packet at the two points where it crosses the device boundary. Add two user-space clock reads and you get four timestamps per datagram, and the differences between them are the latency budget. This chapter builds that tool in about 130 lines of C, runs it across a veth pair between two network namespaces, and reads three experiments: an idle blocked receiver, a spinning receiver, and a slow receiver under a burst.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Mental model
  sender (netns a)                                   receiver (netns b)
  ----------------                                   ------------------
  t0 = clock_gettime()      user
     send()                 syscall, UDP/IP, route, neighbour, qdisc
  t1 = TX software stamp    driver hands skb to the device   (SOF_TIMESTAMPING_TX_SOFTWARE)
        |                   NIC queue, serialization, wire, switches, remote NIC,
        |                   interrupt (or coalescing), NAPI poll
  t2 = RX software stamp    skb handed to the receive stack  (SOF_TIMESTAMPING_RX_SOFTWARE)
                            IP/UDP receive, socket lookup, enqueue on socket,
                            wake the blocked thread, scheduler runs it, syscall returns
  t3 = clock_gettime()      user

  send path = t1 - t0      "network" = t2 - t1      sock->app = t3 - t2
All four timestamps are CLOCK_REALTIME on one host, so they can be subtracted directly. Across two hosts you would need PTP-synchronized clocks to compare t1 and t2. On one host with veth they are the same clock.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
What the kernel timestamps mean
The kernel’s timestamping documentation (Documentation/networking/timestamping.rst) defines the flags used here:







Flag
What it asks for




SOF_TIMESTAMPING_TX_SOFTWARE
A timestamp when the packet leaves the kernel: “generated in the device driver as close as possible, but always prior to, passing the packet to the network interface”. Delivered later on the socket’s error queue.


SOF_TIMESTAMPING_RX_SOFTWARE
A timestamp “just after a device driver hands a packet to the kernel receive stack”. Delivered with the data as a control message.


SOF_TIMESTAMPING_SOFTWARE
Report software timestamps (the reporting flag that goes with the two above).


SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_ID
Tag each TX timestamp with a per-socket counter, so you can match it to the datagram it belongs to.


SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_TSONLY
Return only the timestamp on the error queue, not a copy of the packet.



Hardware timestamps (SOF_TIMESTAMPING_TX_HARDWARE / RX_HARDWARE) are taken by the NIC itself and remove the driver’s own jitter from the measurement. They need a NIC that supports them and SIOCSHWTSTAMP, which requires CAP_NET_ADMIN on the real device. They are out of reach here, and veth has no hardware clock anyway.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Reading the numbers

Run 1: the idle path is dominated by wake-up, not by networking
With one datagram per millisecond and the receiver blocked in recvmsg():

Send path, p50 1.7 µs. Syscall entry, UDP header, route lookup, neighbour lookup, qdisc (the default noqueue on veth) and the driver call. This is the part people usually blame, and it is small.
veth + rx, p50 0.2 µs. This is not a wire. veth passes the skb straight into the peer’s receive path in the same call chain, so t1 and t2 are taken a few hundred nanoseconds apart on the same CPU. On real hardware this interval holds the NIC queue, serialization, the cable, any switches, the remote NIC and its interrupt moderation. See the budget table below.
sock->app, p50 13.8 µs, p90 169 µs. This interval holds the IP/UDP receive work, the socket lookup and enqueue, and then the wait while the scheduler wakes the receiving thread and the syscall returns. The long tail comes from the receiving CPU having gone idle (deeper idle states take longer to leave) and from this being a virtual machine whose vCPUs are themselves scheduled.

So on an idle path, about 80 percent of the median and nearly all of the tail is the cost of the receiver not running when the packet arrived.


Run 2: spinning removes the wake-up
Same traffic, but the receiver loops on recvmsg(MSG_DONTWAIT) and never sleeps:

sock->app falls from 13.8 µs to 1.4 µs at p50, and from 264 µs to 9.5 µs at p99.
The total one-way median falls from 17 µs to 2.7 µs.

The difference, roughly 12 µs at the median, is the wake-up cost on this machine. Spinning buys it back at the cost of one CPU at 100 percent all the time. That is the trade every low-latency system makes in some form. Kernel busy polling (SO_BUSY_POLL, net.core.busy_read, net.core.busy_poll) is the in-kernel version: the receiving syscall polls the device’s NAPI queue directly instead of sleeping. It only applies to devices with NAPI, so it is not exercised over plain veth here. The SO_BUSY_POLL description is in socket(7).


Run 3: under load, the queue is the latency
A back-to-back burst of 2000 datagrams into a receiver with SO_RCVBUF set to 4096 bytes, doing 20 µs of “work” per datagram:

Only 121 of 2000 arrived. The kernel counted the rest: RcvbufErrors went from 0 to 1879, exactly the number lost. This counter, in /proc/net/snmp (or nstat -az UdpRcvbufErrors, or the drops column of /proc/net/udp), is the first thing to check when a UDP application “loses packets” that tcpdump saw arrive.
The ones that did arrive waited 260 µs at p50 and 396 µs at worst between the receive stamp and the application. The send path and the “wire” did not change at all. All of the extra latency is datagrams sitting in the socket queue behind other datagrams.

Two details explain the small number. First, socket(7) says the kernel doubles the requested SO_RCVBUF to allow for bookkeeping overhead, so 4096 becomes 8192 bytes. Second, the buffer is charged with each skb’s truesize (the payload plus the skb and its memory slab), not with the 64-byte payload. That is why only a handful of tiny datagrams fit. A buffer sized as “messages × payload size” is always too small.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
The full one-way budget
The lab measured the host parts. The parts on the wire are arithmetic:








Stage
Typical size
Measured here?




Send syscall + UDP/IP + qdisc + driver
1–10 µs
yes (t1−t0: 1.7 µs p50)


NIC TX queue and DMA
sub-µs to µs when the queue is empty; unbounded when it is full
no


Serialization: 64 B frame (84 B on the wire with preamble and IFG)
672 ns at 1 Gb/s, 67 ns at 10 Gb/s, 6.7 ns at 100 Gb/s
no (arithmetic)


Serialization: 1500 B frame (1538 B on the wire)
12.3 µs at 1 Gb/s, 1.23 µs at 10 Gb/s
no (arithmetic)


Propagation in fibre or copper
about 5 µs per km (2 m: about 10 ns)
no (arithmetic)


Switch, cut-through
hundreds of ns per hop
no


Switch, store-and-forward
one extra serialization per hop + lookup
no


RX interrupt moderation (ethtool -c, rx-usecs)
up to the configured value, often tens of µs; driver-dependent
no


IP/UDP receive + socket enqueue + wake-up + syscall return
2–15 µs idle, ms when queued
yes (t3−t2: 13.8 µs blocking, 1.4 µs spinning)



Read it as a ladder of fixes, cheapest first:

Don’t queue. Size socket buffers from measured bursts. Read the drop counters. Keep the consumer faster than the producer. Run 3 shows a queue can cost a hundred times more than everything else.
Don’t sleep. Spin (run 2), busy-poll, or pin the receiving thread to a CPU that is kept out of deep idle states.
Don’t moderate. Lower rx-usecs on the NIC when latency matters more than CPU use.
Don’t enter the kernel. AF_XDP (in-kernel, zero-copy to a user-space ring, still using the kernel driver) and full kernel bypass such as DPDK remove the syscall, the skb and the socket from the path. They also remove the tools you just used: no socket, no RcvbufErrors, no ss. You take on the job of measuring.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Case
A trading-adjacent team saw “network jitter” of up to 400 µs between two hosts in the same rack and asked for a faster switch. They added SO_TIMESTAMPING to their UDP receiver (RX software and hardware stamps) and logged t2 and t3 for a day. The hardware-to-application time was 3 µs at the median. The tail came entirely from the consumer thread being descheduled behind a logging thread on the same core, plus a 256 KiB receive buffer that filled during bursts and produced RcvbufErrors every market open. The fix was CPU pinning, a busy-polling receive loop, and a buffer sized from the measured burst. The switch stayed.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Trap
“tcpdump saw it, so the application got it.” tcpdump taps the packet on the receive path, before UDP checks the socket buffer. A datagram can show up in a capture and still be dropped at the socket. Check RcvbufErrors.
“Bigger buffers fix latency.” Bigger buffers fix drops. Run 3 with a larger buffer would deliver more datagrams, each waiting longer. If the consumer is slower than the producer, a bigger buffer turns loss into delay.
“veth timings are network timings.” veth has no wire, no interrupt and no coalescing. The 0.2 µs between t1 and t2 here is not a benchmark of anything. The host stages and the wake-up effect carry over to real NICs; the middle column does not.
“Software timestamps are exact.” They are taken by the CPU at points near the driver, so they include some driver and scheduling jitter. For sub-microsecond work use hardware timestamps and a PTP-disciplined clock.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Boring rule
Measure the four timestamps before tuning anything. If t3−t2 dominates, the problem is your process (sleeping or queueing), not the network. Watch RcvbufErrors in every UDP service’s dashboard.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Try this

Pin sender and receiver to different CPUs (taskset -c 2 ... inside each ip netns exec) and rerun run 1. Then pin both to the same CPU. Which stage moves?
Rerun run 3 with SO_RCVBUF at 262144 and then 4194304 (the kernel caps it at net.core.rmem_max unless you use SO_RCVBUFFORCE, which needs CAP_NET_ADMIN). Plot lost vs median sock->app.
Add SOF_TIMESTAMPING_TX_SCHED to the sender flags. The kernel then also reports when the packet entered the qdisc. Split t1−t0 into “before the qdisc” and “after”.
Replace the 20 µs busy-wait in the receiver with usleep(20) and explain why the latency gets much worse than 20 µs per datagram.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Verification

udplat.c was compiled with gcc 14.2.0 and run with unshare -urnm sh lab.sh as an unprivileged user on an 8-vCPU VM (kernel 6.12.94+). No root, no sudo, nothing installed. The output is pasted verbatim.
Absolute numbers are specific to this VM and will vary between runs and machines, especially the tails. The relationships (wake-up much larger than the stack when idle; queueing larger than everything else under load; lost = RcvbufErrors delta) are what to check.
Not run: hardware timestamps, kernel busy polling, ethtool -C, AF_XDP and DPDK. The table rows marked “no” are arithmetic or come from the cited documentation.

title: Where the Microseconds Go: Timestamping One UDP Datagram Through the Linux Stack
text:
Sources

Linux kernel documentation, Timestamping: https://docs.kernel.org/networking/timestamping.html
socket(7) (SO_RCVBUF doubling, SO_BUSY_POLL, SO_TIMESTAMPING): https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/socket.7.html
udp(7) and the Udp: counters in /proc/net/snmp: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/udp.7.html
Linux kernel documentation, NAPI (busy polling): https://docs.kernel.org/networking/napi.html
Linux kernel documentation, AF_XDP: https://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
Learning goals

Explain why an idle TCP socket cannot detect a broken network path or a crashed peer by default.
Calculate detection times and configure socket options for TCP keepalives (SO_KEEPALIVE, TCP_KEEPIDLE, TCP_KEEPINTVL, TCP_KEEPCNT).
Contrast TCP keepalives with application-layer heartbeats and understand why stateful middleboxes cause silent connection deadlocks.
Differentiate between unacknowledged data retransmissions (tcp_retries2) and user-level timeout bounds (TCP_USER_TIMEOUT).
Identify how Linux processes soft ICMP errors (such as host or network unreachable) versus user timeouts.

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
Version note
The experiments in this chapter were run on a Linux kernel 6.12.94 host inside an unprivileged multi-namespace container (unshare -urnm). Network tools include iproute2 version 6.15.0 (ss) and Python 3.13.5 standard library script execution. Three network namespaces (c, r, s) were chained sequentially to model a client-router-server topology. Path failures were injected via ip route replace blackhole and ip route replace unreachable commands on router r.

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
section: Detection of Dead Peers in TCP
text:
Detection of Dead Peers in TCP
TCP is a stateful, connection-oriented protocol designed to operate over an unreliable datagram IP layer. However, TCP endpoints maintain connection state locally. If a remote host crashes, reboots, or suffers a silent network path outage while no data is actively flowing across the wire, neither endpoint receives explicit notification of the failure.
The protocol relies on packets in flight to trigger state transitions or error timers. When a connection is idle, neither side sends traffic. If a physical line is severed or a router drops state silently, both endpoints remain in the ESTABLISHED state indefinitely.
+----------+            +----------+            +----------+
|  Client  |            |  Router  |            |  Server  |
|   (c)    |------------|   (r)    |------------|   (s)    |
+----------+            +----------+            +----------+

Stateful Middleboxes and Silent Expiry
Modern IP networks frequently employ stateful middleboxes such as Network Address Translation (NAT) gateways, stateful firewalls (Linux conntrack), and Network Load Balancers (NLBs). These middleboxes maintain translation or connection tables mapping internal flows to external endpoints.
Because memory resources on middleboxes are finite, inactive entries must be purged. For example, Linux Netfilter defaults to a 5-day timeout (nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established = 432000) for established TCP connections, but cloud infrastructure implements far shorter thresholds. An AWS Network Load Balancer, for example, defaults to a 350-second TCP idle timeout (configurable from 60 to 6000 seconds per listener); after it forgets a flow, the next packet on that flow is answered with a TCP RST. TCP keepalive packets do reset that idle timer.
When a middlebox purges a flow entry due to inactivity: 1. No TCP packets are sent to either endpoint to announce the table purge. 2. Subsequent packets sent by either client or server hit the middlebox without an active table mapping. 3. The middlebox typically responds with a RST packet or drops the frame silently.
If an application does not generate periodic traffic, it will not discover that its session has been dropped by a middlebox until it attempts to send data after long periods of silence.

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
TCP Keepalive Mechanisms
TCP keepalive is an optional mechanism defined in RFC 9293 Section 3.8.4. When enabled on a socket, the protocol stack generates empty probe segments (or segments containing a single garbage payload byte with a previously acknowledged sequence number) after a period of channel silence.

Kernel Sysctls vs Socket Options
Linux maintains three global sysctl defaults within each network namespace:








Sysctl Path
Meaning
Default Value




/proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_keepalive_time
Inactivity delay before sending the first probe
7200 s (2 hours)


/proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_keepalive_intvl
Interval between subsequent unacknowledged probes
75 s


/proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_keepalive_probes
Number of unacknowledged probes before dropping socket
9 probes



By default, socket keepalive functionality is disabled. An application must explicitly issue setsockopt() with the SO_KEEPALIVE flag to enable probe generation.
Applications can override the global sysctl configurations on a per-socket basis using raw IPPROTO_TCP options: - TCP_KEEPIDLE: Overrides tcp_keepalive_time. - TCP_KEEPINTVL: Overrides tcp_keepalive_intvl. - TCP_KEEPCNT: Overrides tcp_keepalive_probes.


Keepalive Probe Timing Calculation
For an idle socket, the time from the last segment received from the peer to the abort is:
detection time = TCP_KEEPIDLE + TCP_KEEPCNT x TCP_KEEPINTVL
With the Linux defaults that is 7200 s + 9 x 75 s = 7875 s, or 2 hours, 11 minutes and 15 seconds.
Because default idle thresholds on intermediate infrastructure (e.g., 350 seconds) are drastically lower than 7,200 seconds, stock OS keepalive parameters are insufficient to prevent idle session drops across stateful middleboxes.


Socket Diagnostics (ss Output)
The ss utility inspects active socket timers. When keepalive probes are enabled and active, socket output includes timer metrics:
timer:(keepalive,800ms,2)
Here, keepalive identifies the active timer type, 800ms indicates the remaining duration before the next probe attempt, and 2 indicates the count of unacknowledged probes sent so far.

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
Transmitting Data: tcp_retries2 and TCP_USER_TIMEOUT
Keepalive mechanisms monitor idle connections. When an application has active data in flight, connection reliability is governed by retransmission parameters.

Retransmission Limits: tcp_retries2
When data is transmitted but unacknowledged, Linux starts a retransmission timer using exponential backoff starting from TCP_RTO_MIN (typically 200 ms). The sysctl /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_retries2 determines how many times TCP retransmits unacknowledged segments before aborting the connection.
Despite the name, tcp_retries2 is not used as a plain retry counter. The kernel documentation explains that it is converted into a time budget, computed as if the RTO started at TCP_RTO_MIN (200 ms) and doubled on every retransmission up to the 120 s maximum. The default of 15 yields a hypothetical timeout of 924.6 seconds (about 15.4 minutes), and the documentation calls this a lower bound for the effective timeout, because a connection with a larger RTO takes longer. RFC 1122 recommends at least 100 seconds, which corresponds to a value of at least 8.


Transmit Timeout Bounding: TCP_USER_TIMEOUT
Introduced in Linux 2.6.37 (RFC 5482), TCP_USER_TIMEOUT is a socket option specifying the maximum time in milliseconds that sent data may remain unacknowledged before the kernel forcibly closes the connection and returns ETIMEDOUT.
TCP_USER_TIMEOUT operates independently of retransmission counts: 1. When data remains unacknowledged, the retransmission timer fires periodically. 2. If the total elapsed time of unacknowledged transmission exceeds TCP_USER_TIMEOUT, the socket aborts immediately regardless of remaining tcp_retries2 attempts. 3. When combined with SO_KEEPALIVE, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT overrides probe counting logic: if a keepalive probe remains unacknowledged past the TCP_USER_TIMEOUT duration, the kernel terminates the connection instantly.

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
section: ICMP Soft Errors vs Hard Errors
text:
ICMP Soft Errors vs Hard Errors
When a intermediate router cannot forward a packet, it emits ICMP Destination Unreachable messages.
RFC 1122 classifies ICMP Destination Unreachable codes 0 (net unreachable), 1 (host unreachable), and 5 (source route failed) as soft errors. Soft errors signal transient network conditions. Consequently, Linux does not terminate an ESTABLISHED TCP socket immediately upon receiving an ICMP soft error.
Instead: 1. Linux stores the error as a soft error (sk_err_soft), separate from the hard error (sk_err) that ends a connection. 2. Retransmissions continue. Linux implements RFC 6069 (TCP-LCD), which reverts the RTO backoff when ICMP unreachable messages arrive for retransmitted segments, so the sender keeps re-probing the path at short intervals instead of backing off for minutes. 3. If the user timeout or tcp_retries2 budget expires while the path remains down, the socket closes. The error code exposed to the application via SO_ERROR or system calls reflects the pending soft error (e.g., EHOSTUNREACH) rather than generic ETIMEDOUT.

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
Lab Architecture & Execution
The lab setup creates three network namespaces (c, r, s) connected via virtual ethernet pairs (veth). Router r forwards traffic between subnet 10.0.1.0/24 (client c) and 10.0.2.0/24 (server s).
 +------------------+      +------------------+      +------------------+
 | Namespace: c     |      | Namespace: r     |      | Namespace: s     |
 | c0 10.0.1.2/24   |------| ra 10.0.1.1/24   |------| s0 10.0.2.2/24   |
 | (client)         |      | rb 10.0.2.1/24   |      | (server)         |
 +------------------+      +------------------+      +------------------+

Lab Scripts
Below are the complete, verbatim scripts used to run the experiments.


lab.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -urnm sh lab.sh   (unprivileged: user, net and mount namespaces; no sudo)
H=$(pwd)
mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /run; mkdir -p /run/netns
for ns in c r s; do ip netns add $ns; ip -n $ns link set lo up; done
ip link add c0 type veth peer name ra; ip link set c0 netns c; ip link set ra netns r
ip link add rb type veth peer name s0; ip link set rb netns r; ip link set s0 netns s
ip -n c addr add 10.0.1.2/24 dev c0; ip -n r addr add 10.0.1.1/24 dev ra
ip -n r addr add 10.0.2.1/24 dev rb; ip -n s addr add 10.0.2.2/24 dev s0
for d in c:c0 r:ra r:rb s:s0; do ip -n ${d%:*} link set ${d#*:} up; done
ip netns exec r sh -c 'echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward'
ip -n c route add default via 10.0.1.1; ip -n s route add default via 10.0.2.1
ip netns exec s python3 $H/server.py 10.0.2.2 7000 & SV=$!; sleep 0.5
echo "   c: tcp_retries2=$(ip netns exec c cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_retries2) keepalive_time=$(ip netns exec c cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_keepalive_time)s intvl=$(ip netns exec c cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_keepalive_intvl)s probes=$(ip netns exec c cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_keepalive_probes)"
# run CASE-ROUTE MODE ARGS: start client, wait for its signal, break the path on r, let it run
run() {
  how=$1; shift; rm -f /tmp/ka-break
  ip netns exec c python3 $H/client.py 10.0.2.2 7000 "$@" & C=$!
  while [ ! -f /tmp/ka-break ]; do sleep 0.05; done
  ip -n r route replace $how 10.0.2.0/24; rm -f /tmp/ka-break
  if [ -n "$SS" ]; then sleep $SS; echo "   ss -tno in c, ${SS}s after the break:"; ip netns exec c ss -tno state established | sed 's/^/      /'; fi
  wait $C
  ip -n r route replace 10.0.2.0/24 dev rb
}
echo "== 1. path dies silently (blackhole on r), application is idle"
SS=3 run blackhole idle limit=12
echo "== 2. same, with keepalive idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=3"
SS=3 run blackhole idle idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=3 limit=12
SS=
echo "== 3. path dies while the application is sending"
ip netns exec c sh -c 'echo 6 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_retries2'; echo "   (c: tcp_retries2=6 for the next run only)"
run blackhole send limit=40
ip netns exec c sh -c 'echo 15 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_retries2'; echo "   (c: tcp_retries2 back to 15)"
run blackhole send uto=3000 limit=40
echo "== 4. TCP_USER_TIMEOUT together with keepalive (cnt=100 would mean 100 probes)"
run blackhole idle idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=100 uto=5000 limit=40
echo "== 5. the router says so: unreachable route (ICMP net-unreachable) instead of a blackhole"
run unreachable send uto=3000 limit=40
run unreachable idle idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=3 limit=12
kill $SV



server.py

# server.py ADDR PORT: accept connections and hold them open; read and discard data.
import socket, sys, threading
l = socket.socket(); l.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
l.bind((sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]))); l.listen(16)
def hold(c):
    try:
        while c.recv(65536): pass
    except OSError: pass
while True:
    c, _ = l.accept(); threading.Thread(target=hold, args=(c,), daemon=True).start()



client.py

# client.py DST PORT MODE [key=value...]: connect, signal the lab to break the path,
# then either sit idle or keep sending, and report when (and how) the kernel gives up.
# keys: idle, intvl, cnt (keepalive), uto (TCP_USER_TIMEOUT ms), limit (seconds to wait)
import socket, sys, time, os, errno, select
dst, port, mode = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), sys.argv[3]
kv = dict(a.split("=") for a in sys.argv[4:]); limit = float(kv.get("limit", 30))
s = socket.create_connection((dst, port))
if "idle" in kv:
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_KEEPALIVE, 1)
    s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_KEEPIDLE, int(kv["idle"]))
    s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_KEEPINTVL, int(kv["intvl"]))
    s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_KEEPCNT, int(kv["cnt"]))
if "uto" in kv:
    s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_USER_TIMEOUT, int(kv["uto"]))
s.send(b"hello"); time.sleep(0.2)
open("/tmp/ka-break", "w").close()                 # lab breaks the path now
while os.path.exists("/tmp/ka-break"): time.sleep(0.05)
t0 = time.monotonic(); s.setblocking(False); result = None; soft = None
while time.monotonic() - t0 < limit:
    try:
        if mode == "send":
            s.send(b"z" * 1000)
        r, _, x = select.select([s], [], [s], 0.1)
        if r and s.recv(1) == b"": result = "peer closed"; break
    except BlockingIOError:
        time.sleep(0.1)
    except OSError as e:
        result = f"{errno.errorcode[e.errno]} ({e.strerror})"; break
    if soft is None:      # SO_ERROR returns (and clears) sk_err, or else the ICMP soft error
        err = s.getsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_ERROR)
        if err: soft = f"{errno.errorcode[err]} at {time.monotonic() - t0:.1f}s"
el = time.monotonic() - t0
print(f"   {mode:4s} {' '.join(sys.argv[4:]):38s} -> " + (f"{result} after {el:.1f}s" if result else f"still ESTABLISHED after {el:.1f}s, no error")
      + (f"   [first non-zero SO_ERROR: {soft}]" if soft else ""))



Lab Execution Output
The verbatim execution output from running unshare -urnm sh lab.sh:
   c: tcp_retries2=15 keepalive_time=7200s intvl=75s probes=9
== 1. path dies silently (blackhole on r), application is idle
   ss -tno in c, 3s after the break:
      Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
      0      0           10.0.1.2:60454     10.0.2.2:7000
   idle limit=12                               -> still ESTABLISHED after 12.0s, no error
== 2. same, with keepalive idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=3
   ss -tno in c, 3s after the break:
      Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
      0      0           10.0.1.2:55260     10.0.2.2:7000 timer:(keepalive,800ms,2)
   idle idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=3 limit=12          -> ETIMEDOUT (Connection timed out) after 4.8s
== 3. path dies while the application is sending
   (c: tcp_retries2=6 for the next run only)
   send limit=40                               -> EPIPE (Broken pipe) after 26.6s   [first non-zero SO_ERROR: ETIMEDOUT at 26.6s]
   (c: tcp_retries2 back to 15)
   send uto=3000 limit=40                      -> ETIMEDOUT (Connection timed out) after 3.4s
== 4. TCP_USER_TIMEOUT together with keepalive (cnt=100 would mean 100 probes)
   idle idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=100 uto=5000 limit=40 -> ETIMEDOUT (Connection timed out) after 4.9s
== 5. the router says so: unreachable route (ICMP net-unreachable) instead of a blackhole
   send uto=3000 limit=40                      -> EHOSTUNREACH (No route to host) after 5.0s   [first non-zero SO_ERROR: EHOSTUNREACH at 0.1s]
   idle idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=3 limit=12          -> ETIMEDOUT (Connection timed out) after 4.8s

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
Reading the Output
Each test phase demonstrates a specific timeout interaction:

Phase 1: Silent Path Blackhole on Idle Connection
idle limit=12 -> still ESTABLISHED after 12.0s, no error
Without SO_KEEPALIVE configured, an idle TCP connection generates zero segments. Inspecting ss -tno confirms no timer is scheduled on the socket. Even though ip route replace blackhole drops all transit frames, the client socket remains in state ESTABLISHED indefinitely.


Phase 2: Keepalive Probe Execution
idle idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=3 limit=12 -> ETIMEDOUT (Connection timed out) after 4.8s
Here SO_KEEPALIVE is configured with idle=2, intvl=1, and cnt=3. 1. The client sends b"hello" (acknowledged at once), sleeps 0.2 s, signals the lab, and starts its clock (t = 0) once the path is broken, roughly 0.25 s after the last segment. 2. The first keepalive probe goes out 2 s after the last activity, at about t = 1.75 s. 3. Probes 2 and 3 follow at 1 s intervals, at about t = 2.75 s and t = 3.75 s. 4. ss at t = 3 s shows timer:(keepalive,800ms,2): two probes are unanswered and the next timer event is 800 ms away (at about 3.75 s). 5. One interval after the third unanswered probe (t of about 4.75 s) the kernel gives up and the socket reports ETIMEDOUT: printed as 4.8 s.


Phase 3: Active Transmit Deadlocks (tcp_retries2 vs TCP_USER_TIMEOUT)
(c: tcp_retries2=6 for the next run only)
send limit=40 -> EPIPE (Broken pipe) after 26.6s   [first non-zero SO_ERROR: ETIMEDOUT at 26.6s]
When transmitting continuously while the route is blackholed, Linux relies on exponential retransmission backoffs. Lowering /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_retries2 to 6 shrinks the time budget. The model gives 0.2 s x (2^7 - 1) = 25.4 s; the kernel dropped the session after 26.6 seconds, a little later because the real RTO started slightly above 200 ms and the check runs only when the retransmission timer fires.
Notice that the program’s send() got EPIPE, not ETIMEDOUT. The lab client polls getsockopt(SO_ERROR) on every loop iteration, and that call returns and clears the pending error: the poll took ETIMEDOUT, and the next send() on the now-closed socket could only report EPIPE. Real applications that poll SO_ERROR (some event loops do, after a writable event) see exactly this.
When uto=3000 (TCP_USER_TIMEOUT set to 3000 ms) is applied with default tcp_retries2=15:
send uto=3000 limit=40 -> ETIMEDOUT (Connection timed out) after 3.4s
Unacknowledged data in flight causes the connection to close after 3.4 seconds. The nominal overshoot (3.4 s versus 3.0 s) occurs because the user timeout threshold is evaluated whenever the active retransmission timer fires.


Phase 4: Overriding Keepalives with TCP_USER_TIMEOUT
idle idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=100 uto=5000 limit=40 -> ETIMEDOUT (Connection timed out) after 4.9s
TCP_KEEPCNT is set to 100, which would normally require 102 seconds to fail (2 s + 100 x 1 s). However, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT is set to 5000 ms (5.0 s). The connection aborts at 4.9 s. This verifies that TCP_USER_TIMEOUT overrides keepalive probe counting to enforce a firm upper bound on unacknowledged probe duration.


Phase 5: ICMP Soft Error Handling
send uto=3000 limit=40 -> EHOSTUNREACH (No route to host) after 5.0s   [first non-zero SO_ERROR: EHOSTUNREACH at 0.1s]
With an unreachable route rule configured, router r immediately returns an ICMP Net Unreachable packet to client c. 1. At t = 0.1 s, getsockopt(SO_ERROR) detects the pending soft error (EHOSTUNREACH). 2. The socket remains ESTABLISHED and retransmissions continue according to RFC 6069. 3. Once TCP_USER_TIMEOUT terminates the connection at t = 5.0 s, the recorded soft error (EHOSTUNREACH) is surfaced as the primary socket abort error instead of generic ETIMEDOUT.
For an idle socket with keepalives enabled (idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=3), the result is ETIMEDOUT at 4.8 s, identical to the blackhole case, and no soft error was recorded at all. The router did answer every probe with ICMP unreachable, but a Linux keepalive probe carries sequence number snd_una - 1, deliberately just outside the window, and when an ICMP error quotes a sequence number outside snd_una..snd_nxt the kernel discards it as an out-of-window ICMP. A second run of just this case, with the same namespace setup as lab.sh, ip netns exec c nstat -n before it and ip netns exec c nstat after it, shows the counters:
   idle idle=2 intvl=1 cnt=3 limit=12          -> ETIMEDOUT (Connection timed out) after 4.9s
IcmpInMsgs                      4                  0.0
IcmpInErrors                    1                  0.0
IcmpInDestUnreachs              4                  0.0
IcmpMsgInType3                  4                  0.0
TcpExtOutOfWindowIcmps          3                  0.0
TcpExtTCPAbortOnTimeout         1                  0.0
TcpExtTCPKeepAlive              3                  0.0
Three keepalive probes (TcpExtTCPKeepAlive 3), three ICMP errors ignored as out of window (TcpExtOutOfWindowIcmps 3), and one abort on timeout. (The Icmp6Out* lines from the same nstat output are IPv6 neighbour discovery noise and are left out.) Keepalive detection on Linux therefore never gets faster because a router reports the path as unreachable.

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
Choosing Values
Work backwards from the shortest idle timeout on the path and from how fast you need to notice a failure:








Knob
Starting point for long-lived connections
Why




SO_KEEPALIVE
on
Nothing else detects a dead peer on an idle socket


TCP_KEEPIDLE
below the smallest middlebox idle timeout, for example 60 s
Keeps NAT, conntrack and load-balancer state alive (350 s on an AWS NLB)


TCP_KEEPINTVL
10 to 15 s
Spacing between probes once the peer stops answering


TCP_KEEPCNT
3 to 5
Tolerates a lost probe or two without false aborts


TCP_USER_TIMEOUT
about KEEPIDLE + KEEPINTVL x KEEPCNT
Bounds failures that happen while data is in flight, which keepalive does not cover



Set these per socket in the application (database drivers, message-broker clients and HTTP connection pools usually expose them) rather than lowering the sysctls for the whole host. Be careful with tcp_retries2: lowering it globally also kills connections that are merely slow or crossing a brief outage, and RFC 1122 asks for at least 100 seconds. Where a proxy terminates TCP, add application-level liveness (HTTP/2 PING frames, WebSocket ping/pong, SSH ServerAliveInterval, gRPC keepalive), because TCP keepalives only ever test the hop to the proxy.

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
Gotchas

Belief: TCP sockets naturally detect dead peers or broken cables. Why it is wrong: TCP sends packets only when an application writes data or when protocol timers (such as keepalives) fire. An idle connection without keepalive enabled will remain in state ESTABLISHED indefinitely despite host crashes or severed lines.
Belief: Linux kernel keepalives protect applications against cloud middlebox flow entry timeouts. Why it is wrong: The default Linux tcp_keepalive_time is 7200 seconds (2 hours). AWS NLB defaults to a 350-second idle timeout, and many NAT devices and firewalls use idle timeouts well below two hours. Standard OS keepalives fire far too late to prevent middlebox drops.
Belief: Application-level heartbeats and TCP keepalives perform identical functions. Why it is wrong: TCP keepalives monitor transport-layer reachability between OS kernels. If an intermediate proxy (e.g., an HTTP reverse proxy or layer-7 load balancer) terminates the TCP connection, TCP keepalives only test the leg between the client and the proxy. Application-layer heartbeats (such as gRPC keepalives or WebSocket ping/pong) test end-to-end application responsiveness.
Belief: tcp_retries2 = 15 means TCP will retransmit a packet 15 times at 1-second intervals. Why it is wrong: Linux converts tcp_retries2 into a time duration using exponential backoff starting from TCP_RTO_MIN (200 ms). A setting of 15 corresponds to a timeout of roughly 924.6 seconds (~15.4 minutes), not 15 seconds or 15 probes.
Belief: Inspecting SO_ERROR with getsockopt has no side effects on subsequent socket operations. Why it is wrong: Reading SO_ERROR retrieves and clears the pending socket error (sk_err). In Phase 3, polling SO_ERROR consumed ETIMEDOUT, causing the subsequent send() invocation to return EPIPE (Broken pipe) due to writing to a closed socket without a pending error state.
Belief: ICMP Destination Unreachable messages cause TCP sockets to abort immediately. Why it is wrong: ICMP Destination Unreachable codes 0, 1, and 5 are treated as soft errors under RFC 1122. Linux logs the error code internally and continues retransmitting until user timeouts or retransmission limits expire.
Belief: TCP_USER_TIMEOUT only controls active data retransmissions. Why it is wrong: TCP_USER_TIMEOUT also controls unacknowledged keepalive probes. When configured alongside SO_KEEPALIVE, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT terminates the socket as soon as the total unacknowledged probe duration exceeds the configured threshold.

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
Exercises

Calculate Custom Keepalive Durations: An application configures TCP_KEEPIDLE = 30, TCP_KEEPINTVL = 5, and TCP_KEEPCNT = 4. Calculate the exact elapsed duration from the last received ACK until the kernel closes the connection.
Observe Socket Timers with ss: Modify lab.sh to execute ss -tno continuously every 0.5 seconds during Phase 2. Track the decay of the remaining timer interval and the incremental count of unacknowledged probes.
Analyze SO_ERROR Consumption: Write a Python script that causes a socket to time out. Compare the return value of send() when getsockopt(SOL_SOCKET, SO_ERROR) is called prior to send() versus when it is omitted.
Tune BGP-Style Session Failover: Given a network with a stateful firewall enforcing a 120-second TCP idle timeout, select appropriate values for TCP_KEEPIDLE, TCP_KEEPINTVL, TCP_KEEPCNT, and TCP_USER_TIMEOUT to detect path loss within 15 seconds while preventing middlebox flow drops.
Differentiate Hard vs Soft ICMP Errors: In phase 5, replace ip route replace unreachable with ip route replace prohibit, which makes r answer with ICMP code 13 (communication administratively prohibited) instead of net unreachable. Run the send uto=3000 case again. Does the socket still survive until the user timeout, and which error does it report? Compare with the soft-error list in RFC 1122 section 4.2.3.9.

Networking Tools: iproute2 ss utility version 6.15.0

title: Dead Peers and Silent Paths: TCP Keepalive, TCP_USER_TIMEOUT and tcp_retries2
text:
Sources

RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) - Section 3.8.4 details TCP keep-alive requirements.
RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts – Communication Layers - Section 4.2.3.9 defines ICMP soft error handling.
RFC 5482: TCP User Timeout Option - Specifies user timeout options for TCP.
RFC 6069: Making TCP More Robust to Long Connectivity Disruptions (TCP-LCD) - Reverting RTO backoff on ICMP unreachable messages.
