The Python link emulator handles packet forwarding, rate-limiting, delay simulation, and queueing. link.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Userspace impaired link between two network namespaces.

Opens one TUN device inside netns "c" and one inside netns "s" and moves
IPv4 packets between them with a fixed one-way delay, an optional rate
limit with a byte-limited queue, and scripted drops/delays of TCP data
segments selected by their offset in the stream. Logs every scripted
event and every retransmission it sees (same seq seen twice).
"""
import argparse, fcntl, heapq, json, os, select, struct, sys, time

TUNSETIFF, IFF_TUN, IFF_NO_PI = 0x400454CA, 0x0001, 0x1000

def open_tun(nspath, name):
    here = os.open("/proc/self/ns/net", os.O_RDONLY)
    fd_ns = os.open(nspath, os.O_RDONLY)
    os.setns(fd_ns, os.CLONE_NEWNET)
    fd = os.open("/dev/net/tun", os.O_RDWR)
    fcntl.ioctl(fd, TUNSETIFF, struct.pack("16sH", name.encode(), IFF_TUN | IFF_NO_PI))
    os.setns(here, os.CLONE_NEWNET)
    os.close(here); os.close(fd_ns)
    os.set_blocking(fd, False)
    return fd

def tcp_info(pkt):
    if len(pkt) < 20 or pkt[0] >> 4 != 4 or pkt[9] != 6:
        return None
    ihl = (pkt[0] & 15) * 4
    tot = struct.unpack("!H", pkt[2:4])[0]
    sp, dp, seq, ack = struct.unpack("!HHII", pkt[ihl:ihl + 12])
    doff = (pkt[ihl + 12] >> 4) * 4
    flags = pkt[ihl + 13]
    plen = tot - ihl - doff
    return sp, dp, seq, ack, flags, plen

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--delay-ms", type=float, default=10.0, help="one-way delay, each direction")
    ap.add_argument("--rate-mbit", type=float, default=0.0, help="c->s bottleneck, 0 = unlimited")
    ap.add_argument("--queue-bytes", type=int, default=0, help="bottleneck queue limit")
    ap.add_argument("--drop", default="", help="comma list of data segment indexes to drop (first transmission, c->s)")
    ap.add_argument("--drop-again", default="", help="indexes whose first retransmission is dropped too")
    ap.add_argument("--drop-tail", type=int, default=0, help="drop the first transmission of every segment that carries any of the last N stream bytes")
    ap.add_argument("--total", type=int, default=300000, help="stream length in bytes (for --drop-tail)")
    ap.add_argument("--hold-ms", default="", help="idx:ms reorder, e.g. 30:15 delays segment 30 by 15 ms extra")
    ap.add_argument("--port", type=int, default=5001)
    ap.add_argument("--log", default="")
    a = ap.parse_args()

    tc = open_tun("/run/netns/c", "tun0")
    ts = open_tun("/run/netns/s", "tun0")
    drop = {int(x) for x in a.drop.split(",") if x}
    drop2 = {int(x) for x in a.drop_again.split(",") if x}
    hold = dict((int(k), float(v)) for k, v in (x.split(":") for x in a.hold_ms.split(",") if x))
    d = a.delay_ms / 1000
    heap, n = [], 0                 # (due, n, fd, pkt)
    seen = {}                       # seq -> times seen
    isn = None
    order = {}
    log = []
    t0 = None
    link_free = 0.0                 # bottleneck: when the link finishes sending current packet
    qdrops = 0
    pending = []                    # bottleneck FIFO of (pkt) waiting to be serialized

    def now():
        return time.monotonic()

    while True:
        timeout = None
        if heap:
            timeout = max(0, heap[0][0] - now())
        r, _, _ = select.select([tc, ts], [], [], timeout)
        t = now()
        for fd in r:
            while True:
                try:
                    pkt = os.read(fd, 65535)
                except BlockingIOError:
                    break
                out = ts if fd == tc else tc
                extra = 0.0
                info = tcp_info(pkt)
                if fd == tc and info and info[1] == a.port:
                    sp, dp, seq, ack, flags, plen = info
                    if flags & 0x02:            # SYN
                        isn = (seq + 1) & 0xffffffff
                        t0 = t
                    if plen and isn is not None:
                        off = (seq - isn) & 0xffffffff
                        if seq not in order:          # index = order of first transmission
                            order[seq] = len(order)
                        idx = order[seq]
                        cnt = seen.get(seq, 0)
                        seen[seq] = cnt + 1
                        ms = round((t - t0) * 1000, 1)
                        if cnt >= 1:
                            log.append(f"{ms:9.1f} ms  retransmit seg {idx:4d} (seq+{off}, {plen} B, copy {cnt + 1})")
                        if cnt == 0 and (idx in drop or (a.drop_tail and off + plen > a.total - a.drop_tail)):
                            log.append(f"{ms:9.1f} ms  DROP       seg {idx:4d} (seq+{off}, {plen} B)")
                            continue
                        if cnt == 1 and idx in drop2:
                            log.append(f"{ms:9.1f} ms  DROP again seg {idx:4d} (first retransmission)")
                            continue
                        if cnt == 0 and idx in hold:
                            extra = hold[idx] / 1000
                            log.append(f"{ms:9.1f} ms  HOLD       seg {idx:4d} +{hold[idx]:.0f} ms (reorder)")
                    if flags & 0x01 and t0 is not None and seen.get(seq, 0) <= 1:
                        log.append(f"{round((t - t0) * 1000, 1):9.1f} ms  FIN from client")
                due = t + d + extra
                if fd == tc and a.rate_mbit > 0:
                    qbytes = max(0.0, link_free - t) * a.rate_mbit * 1e6 / 8
                    if a.queue_bytes and qbytes + len(pkt) > a.queue_bytes:
                        log.append(f"{round((t - (t0 or t)) * 1000, 1):9.1f} ms  QUEUE FULL drop ({int(qbytes)} B queued)")
                        qdrops += 1
                        continue
                    start = max(t, link_free)
                    link_free = start + len(pkt) * 8 / (a.rate_mbit * 1e6)
                    due = link_free + d + extra
                n += 1
                heapq.heappush(heap, (due, n, out, pkt))
        t = now()
        while heap and heap[0][0] <= t:
            _, _, out, pkt = heapq.heappop(heap)
            try:
                os.write(out, pkt)
            except OSError:
                pass
        if a.log and log:
            with open(a.log, "a") as f:
                f.write("\n".join(log) + "\n")
            log.clear()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
The BDP test harness executes bulk data transfers (8,000,000 bytes) under varying socket and sysctl options, reporting socket memory and tcp_info metrics. bdp.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Bulk transfer across the emulated long fat link, with the kernel's view.

serve [--rcvbuf N]        sink on 10.9.0.2:5001; prints the receive-side numbers
send BYTES [--sndbuf N]   source in netns c; prints goodput and what limited it
SO_RCVBUF/SO_SNDBUF are set before listen()/connect(), which turns off the
kernel's autotuning for that direction (see tcp(7), socket(7)).
"""
import socket, struct, sys, time

def info(s):
    b = s.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_INFO, 232)
    g = lambda fmt, off: struct.unpack_from(fmt, b, off)[0]
    return {   # offsets from struct tcp_info, include/uapi/linux/tcp.h
        "snd_wscale": b[6] & 15, "rcv_wscale": b[6] >> 4,
        "rtt_ms": g("I", 68) / 1000, "snd_cwnd": g("I", 80),
        "rcv_space": g("I", 96), "rcv_ssthresh": g("I", 64),
        "busy_us": g("Q", 168), "rwnd_limited_us": g("Q", 176), "sndbuf_limited_us": g("Q", 184),
        "total_retrans": g("I", 100),
        "snd_wnd": g("I", 228) if len(b) >= 232 else None,
    }

def opt(name, default=0):
    return int(sys.argv[sys.argv.index(name) + 1]) if name in sys.argv else default

def serve():
    l = socket.socket()
    l.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    if opt("--rcvbuf"):
        l.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_RCVBUF, opt("--rcvbuf"))
    l.bind(("10.9.0.2", 5001)); l.listen(1)
    c, _ = l.accept()
    rb0 = c.getsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_RCVBUF)
    n = 0
    while True:
        d = c.recv(1 << 20)
        if not d:
            break
        n += len(d)
    i = info(c)
    rb1 = c.getsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_RCVBUF)
    print(f"  receiver: SO_RCVBUF at accept={rb0} at end={rb1} rcv_wscale={i['rcv_wscale']} "
          f"rcv_space={i['rcv_space']} rcv_ssthresh={i['rcv_ssthresh']}", flush=True)
    c.sendall(b"%d\n" % n); c.close()

def send(nbytes):
    s = socket.socket()
    if opt("--sndbuf"):
        s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_SNDBUF, opt("--sndbuf"))
    s.connect(("10.9.0.2", 5001))
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    chunk = b"x" * 65536
    left = nbytes
    while left:
        left -= s.send(chunk[:min(left, len(chunk))])
    i = info(s)
    sb = s.getsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_SNDBUF)
    s.shutdown(socket.SHUT_WR); s.recv(64)
    el = time.monotonic() - t0
    busy = i["busy_us"] or 1
    print(f"  sender:   goodput={nbytes * 8 / el / 1e6:5.2f} Mbit/s in {el:.2f} s  rtt={i['rtt_ms']:.1f} ms "
          f"retrans={i['total_retrans']} cwnd={i['snd_cwnd']} snd_wnd={i['snd_wnd']} SO_SNDBUF={sb} snd_wscale={i['snd_wscale']}\n"
          f"  sender:   time limited by receive window {100 * i['rwnd_limited_us'] / busy:4.1f}%, "
          f"by send buffer {100 * i['sndbuf_limited_us'] / busy:4.1f}%  (busy {busy / 1e6:.2f} s)", flush=True)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    serve() if sys.argv[1] == "serve" else send(int(sys.argv[2]))
The LOWAT latency test harness measures arrival delays for urgent single-line messages transmitted behind bulk stream traffic. lowat.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""How long does an urgent message wait behind bulk data already in the kernel?

serve        : reads everything; for each urgent message prints how long it
               took from "the application decided to send it" to arrival
send [LOWAT] : keeps the socket full of 16 KiB bulk chunks for 5 s; every
               0.5 s from t=1 s it decides an urgent message must go next and
               writes it at the next writable event. The message carries the
               decision time (CLOCK_MONOTONIC is shared by both namespaces).
               With LOWAT set, TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT (tcp(7)) keeps unsent bytes
               in the kernel below LOWAT and the rest waits in the application.
"""
import re, select, socket, struct, sys, time

TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT = getattr(socket, "TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT", 25)

def notsent(s):
    b = s.getsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_INFO, 232)
    return struct.unpack_from("I", b, 144)[0]     # tcpi_notsent_bytes

def serve():
    l = socket.socket(); l.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    l.bind(("10.9.0.2", 5001)); l.listen(1)
    c, _ = l.accept()
    buf = b""; lat = []
    while True:
        d = c.recv(1 << 16)
        if not d:
            break
        now = time.monotonic()
        buf = buf[-64:] + d
        for m in re.finditer(rb"<U(\d+)\|(\d+\.\d+)\|(\d+)>", buf):
            i, t, ns = int(m.group(1)), float(m.group(2)), int(m.group(3))
            if i >= len(lat):
                lat.append((i, (now - t) * 1000, ns))
    for i, ms, ns in lat:
        print(f"  urgent #{i}: {ns:7d} unsent bytes ahead of it in the sender's kernel -> arrived {ms:6.1f} ms after the decision")
    print(f"  mean {sum(x[1] for x in lat) / len(lat):.1f} ms over {len(lat)} urgent messages", flush=True)

def send(lowat):
    s = socket.socket()
    if lowat:
        s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT, lowat)
    s.connect(("10.9.0.2", 5001)); s.setblocking(False)
    bulk = b"b" * 16384
    t0 = time.monotonic(); k = 0; pending = None; peak = 0
    while time.monotonic() - t0 < 5.0:
        select.select([], [s], [], 0.01)
        now = time.monotonic()
        if pending is None and k < 8 and now - t0 >= 1.0 + 0.5 * k:
            pending = b"<U%d|%.6f|%d>" % (k, now, notsent(s)); k += 1
        try:
            if pending is not None:
                s.send(pending); pending = None      # tiny; fits whenever writable
            else:
                s.send(bulk)
        except BlockingIOError:
            pass
        peak = max(peak, notsent(s))
    print(f"  sender: peak unsent bytes in the kernel {peak}, TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT={lowat or 'unset'}", flush=True)
    s.setblocking(True); s.shutdown(socket.SHUT_WR); s.recv(1); s.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    serve() if sys.argv[1] == "serve" else send(int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 0)

title: TCP Windows, Buffers and the Bandwidth-Delay Product: Autotuning, Buffer Caps and Unsent-Data Latency
text:
Reading the output

The defaults and the BDP
The header lines give the numbers everything else is measured against. The BDP is 250000 bytes. The kernel defaults are tcp_rmem = 4096 131072 6291456 and tcp_wmem = 4096 16384 4194304. net.core.rmem_max and wmem_max are 212992, which is host-wide and read-only inside the namespaces. tcp_adv_win_scale still reads 1 even though it is obsolete on this kernel.


Scenario 1: autotuning on both ends
The receiver accepted the connection with a 131072-byte buffer and finished with 6291456, which is tcp_rmem[2]. It offered wscale 7 from the first SYN-ACK because the shift is sized for the maximum. The sender saw a window of up to 3930752 bytes, 16 times the BDP, and the receive window never limited it (0.0 %). Goodput was 17.14 Mbit/s rather than 20 for two reasons, and both show in the snapshot taken at 2.5 s:

Slow-start overshoot. The sender shows retrans:0/18 and bytes_retrans:26064 (18 segments of 1448 bytes). CUBIC’s exponential start overran the 250000-byte bottleneck queue and lost a burst, which cost time to repair.
A full queue. The sender’s rtt:148.354 at 2.5 s, and its smoothed RTT of 167.1 ms at the end, are well above the 100 ms path. Once the window is bigger than the BDP, the extra data waits in the bottleneck queue. The window does not limit the flow, but the RTT grows.

The sender snapshot also shows the send side autotuning: tb1617408 (the send buffer grew from 16384 towards tcp_wmem[2]), notsent:702280 (700 KB written by the application but not yet sent), and w1188216 of memory queued for sending. That unsent backlog is the problem scenarios 7 and 8 measure. On the receiver, rcv_space:838392 is the autotuner’s estimate of one RTT of reading, and rcv_wnd:2804352 is the window it was advertising at that moment.


Scenario 2: SO_RCVBUF=65536 before listen()
The kernel stored 131072 (double the request) and never changed it, because setting the option turns autotuning off. The shift was sized for that small buffer: the receiver snapshot shows wscale:7,1, meaning the peer sends with scale 7 and this socket receives with scale 1. The usable window was 80480 bytes, 61 % of the buffer. The ceiling is 80480 × 8 / 0.1015 s = 6.34 Mbit/s, and the flow measured 6.18 Mbit/s. The sender snapshot names the cause: rwnd_limited:2080ms(87.0%) at 2.5 s, rising to 96.8 % by the end. The application had plenty of data waiting (notsent:253136). The RTT stayed at 101.5 ms and nothing was retransmitted, because a window this small never reaches the bottleneck queue.


Scenarios 3 and 4: the rmem_max cap
A request for 262144 was first capped at net.core.rmem_max (212992) and then doubled to 425984. A request for 524288 went through the same two steps and produced the same 425984, so scenario 4 is scenario 3 again (17.13 and 17.04 Mbit/s). Asking for more than rmem_max silently gets you rmem_max.
The window here is 262140 bytes, which is exactly 65535 × 2². The buffer could have backed a larger window, but with a shift of 2 the largest value the 16-bit field can express is 262140. It happens to sit just above the 250000-byte BDP. Window and BDP being nearly equal explains the other numbers: goodput matched scenario 1, the RTT was only 108.6 ms (the queue barely filled), there were no retransmissions, and the flow still counts as receive-window-limited for 84.7 % of the time, because it kept bumping against a window that only just fitted the pipe. A window close to the BDP gives you full throughput without the queue.


Scenario 5: autotuning capped by tcp_rmem[2]
Autotuning stayed on but could only grow the buffer from 131072 to 262144. The shift was sized for that maximum (3). The advertised window reached 162400, which is 62 % of 262144, below the BDP. The ceiling is 162400 × 8 / 0.1014 = 12.81 Mbit/s; the flow got 11.98 Mbit/s and was receive-window-limited 91.5 % of the time. A distribution or container image with a low tcp_rmem maximum produces exactly this ceiling on every long path.


Scenario 6: no window scaling
With tcp_window_scaling=0 the receiver sent no window-scale option, so neither direction scales (rcv_wscale=0, snd_wscale=0). Autotuning still grew the buffer to 667238 bytes, and rcv_ssthresh reached 416223, but the 16-bit field cannot express more than 65535. rcv_space stayed near that limit (66983). The ceiling is 65535 × 8 / 0.1015 = 5.17 Mbit/s and the flow got 5.08 Mbit/s, receive-window-limited 97.4 % of the time. A middlebox that strips the option from SYNs has the same effect.


Scenarios 7 and 8: what the urgent message waits behind
Without a low-water mark, the sender kernel held up to 611283 unsent bytes. The eight urgent messages found between 331984 and 579219 bytes ahead of them and arrived 257.7 to 476.3 ms after the application decided to send them, with a mean of 337.1 ms. Draining 400–580 kB at 20 Mbit/s takes 160–230 ms. Add the 50 ms one-way delay and the time spent in the bottleneck queue, and you get the measured values. The 476.3 ms outlier (#1) was most likely caught behind a loss-recovery period, since this run fills the queue as scenario 1 did.
With TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT=16384, the socket only reported writable when fewer than 16384 unsent bytes were queued. The peak of 65160 shows that a single 16 KiB write can still overshoot the mark. The urgent messages found 5955 to 12870 bytes ahead of them and arrived 107.4 to 146.7 ms after the decision, a mean of 127.6 ms against 337.1 ms. What remains, about 125 ms, is the 50 ms propagation delay plus the bottleneck queue inside the network. No sender-side socket option can remove that; only queue management on the bottleneck can.

title: TCP Windows, Buffers and the Bandwidth-Delay Product: Autotuning, Buffer Caps and Unsent-Data Latency
text:
In production

Diagnosing Active Sockets with ss
To inspect socket buffer metrics, window scaling factors, and throttling constraints on live production servers, use ss:
# (not run here)
# Display detailed TCP socket memory and tcp_info telemetry for established HTTP/HTTPS flows
ss -tmi state established '( dport = :http or dport = :https )'
Inspect the output for critical diagnostic indicators: - rwnd_limited: Indicates performance is constrained by remote receive buffer size or WSCALE negotiation issues. - sndbuf_limited: Indicates local sender buffer exhaustion (SO_SNDBUF too small or autotuning capped by tcp_wmem[2]). - notsent: High values (e.g., > 100 KiB) indicate large amounts of un-transmitted data queued in kernel memory, causing high head-of-line blocking latency.


Benchmarking Path BDP with iperf3
When performing path capacity tests, compare autotuned TCP throughput against explicitly restricted window sizes:
# (not run here)
# Run standard autotuned parallel TCP test to measure true path capacity
iperf3 -c 192.168.10.50 -P 4 -t 30

# (not run here)
# Force legacy socket buffer size (64 KB) to verify WSCALE impact
iperf3 -c 192.168.10.50 -w 64K -t 30


Tuning System-Wide TCP Buffers in /etc/sysctl.conf
For core routers, storage nodes, or edge proxies attached to high-speed WAN links (10G/40G/100G with > 50 ms RTT), append the following parameters to /etc/sysctl.conf:
# (not run here)
# Increase max TCP receive buffer to 128 MB (min, default, max)
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096 131072 134217728

# Increase max TCP send buffer to 128 MB (min, default, max)
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem = 4096 65536 134217728

# Optional: host-wide unsent-data limit. Only helps applications that write
# when poll/epoll says the socket is writable; blocking writers just wake more often.
net.ipv4.tcp_notsent_lowat = 131072

# Ensure Window Scaling and Receive Autotuning remain enabled
net.ipv4.tcp_window_scaling = 1
net.ipv4.tcp_moderate_rcvbuf = 1
Apply configured sysctl changes immediately without rebooting:
# (not run here)
sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.conf


Configuring TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT in Application Code
In C/C++ services, set TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT per socket:
// (not run here)
int lowat_val = 16384; // 16 KiB threshold
if (setsockopt(sockfd, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT, &lowat_val, sizeof(lowat_val)) < 0) {
    perror("failed to set TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT");
}
In Python:
# (not run here)
import socket

sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
# socket.TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT where the module defines it; 25 is the Linux value
sock.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, getattr(socket, "TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT", 25), 16384)

title: TCP Windows, Buffers and the Bandwidth-Delay Product: Autotuning, Buffer Caps and Unsent-Data Latency
text:
Gotchas

Disabling Autotuning via setsockopt: Calling setsockopt() with SO_RCVBUF or SO_SNDBUF permanently disables kernel autotuning for that direction on that socket.
The Kernel Memory Doubling Rule: Linux doubles whatever value you pass to SO_RCVBUF or SO_SNDBUF to reserve memory for sk_buff control headers. Asking for 128 KiB allocates 256 KiB of kernel memory.
net.core.rmem_max Capping: Manual SO_RCVBUF calls are hard-capped by net.core.rmem_max. Requesting a 1 MB buffer on a system with rmem_max = 212992 silently caps your request to 212,992 bytes (doubled to 425,984 bytes). Autotuning ignores rmem_max.
The Pre-Listen WSCALE Trap: Setting SO_RCVBUF to a small value before calling listen() or connect() locks in a small WSCALE shift factor during the SYN handshake. That shift factor cannot be changed later, even if SO_RCVBUF is expanded.
Unilateral WSCALE Disabling: If a middlebox, firewall, or remote host omits WSCALE in its SYN or SYN-ACK, window scaling is disabled for both directions, restricting maximum window size to 65,535 bytes.
Misinterpreting sndbuf_limited = 0.0%: the kernel only runs that clock when the write queue is empty, the flow is not cwnd-limited and the application is blocked on the buffer. A value of 0.0% does not prove the send buffer was big enough.
tcp_adv_win_scale advice is out of date: it is obsolete since Linux 6.6. Tuning guides that change it are describing older kernels.
Over-estimating TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT Granularity: TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT prevents application socket writability when unsent data exceeds the threshold, but a single large write() call can still overshoot the threshold by the size of that write block.
Conflating net.ipv4.tcp_rmem with net.core.rmem_max: tcp_rmem[2] dictates the max memory ceiling for dynamic receive autotuning. net.core.rmem_max dictates the max memory ceiling for manual setsockopt(SO_RCVBUF) calls.

title: TCP Windows, Buffers and the Bandwidth-Delay Product: Autotuning, Buffer Caps and Unsent-Data Latency
text:
Exercises

Calculate the Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) in bytes for a 10 Gbit/s cross-country link with a 60 ms RTT. If WSCALE is disabled (\(S=0\)), what is the maximum achievable throughput across this path?
An application developer sets SO_RCVBUF to 1048576 (1 MiB) on a host where net.core.rmem_max = 212992. Calculate the exact value stored in sk_rcvbuf by the kernel and explain the clamping/doubling sequence.
Using ss -tmi, capture diagnostic telemetry from an active bulk download. Identify rcv_space, snd_wnd, wscale, rtt, and rwnd_limited. Calculate whether the flow is constrained by receive window or congestion window.
Write a minimal Python script that creates a TCP listening socket, sets SO_RCVBUF to 32,768 bytes, and invokes listen(). Run tcpdump or wireshark to capture the SYN-ACK packet generated during an incoming connection. Extract the WSCALE option value and explain how it was derived.
In an environment with an 80 ms RTT and a 50 Mbit/s bottleneck link, an application encounters severe head-of-line blocking when sending urgent RPC commands over a shared TCP connection. Explain how configuring TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT reduces latency, and calculate the maximum unsent queue size recommended to maintain low latency without starving path throughput.
Scenario 1 in the lab achieved 17.14 Mbit/s on a 20 Mbit/s link despite rwnd_limited reporting 0.0%. Explain the root causes of this throughput shortfall, referencing packet retransmissions, RTT inflation, and slow-start overshoot.

text:
Verification
The experiments and telemetry data presented in this chapter were gathered using the following execution environment and tool versions:

Operating System / Kernel: Linux 6.12.94 (x86_64).
Networking Tooling: iproute2 version 6.15.0 (ss, ip netns, ip link).
Runtime Environment: Python 3.13.5 (standard library socket, struct, select, fcntl modules).
TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC (default kernel module).
Containerization / Isolation: Unprivileged Linux namespaces (unshare -urnm). No root privileges were required.


Executed vs. Non-Executed Environment Elements

Executed in Lab: All topology generation (topo.sh), Python software rate-limiting and delay simulation (link.py), bulk socket transfers (bdp.py), and unsent queue latency probes (lowat.py) were executed directly inside unprivileged user/network namespaces.
Not Run in Lab: the commands in “In production” (iperf3, sysctl -p changes, the C snippet) and anything needing tcpdump. None of those tools are installed, and host-wide sysctls such as net.core.rmem_max are read-only inside the namespaces. A seventh scenario, a 64 KiB sender SO_SNDBUF, was dropped from the lab: it lost 141 segments in slow start, so its goodput could not be attributed to the send buffer alone.
Repeatability: earlier runs of the same script gave the same buffer, scale and window values. Goodput, retransmissions and latency vary a little from run to run, so the text quotes only the run shown above.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
text:
Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
In high-throughput networking applications—such as QUIC protocol stacks, authoritative DNS resolvers, WireGuard VPN concentrators, and real-time media relays—the traditional POSIX socket interface presents a severe performance bottleneck. Processing UDP traffic one packet at a time using sendto() and recvfrom() imposes a high CPU cost per datagram. When packet rates reach hundreds of thousands or millions of packets per second (pps), kernel context switches, socket lock contention, memory allocation, and layer-by-layer protocol traversal consume the majority of host CPU cycles.
Without batching techniques, a single CPU core quickly reaches a performance ceiling long before saturating high-bandwidth network interfaces. If the kernel network stack or user-space application cannot drain incoming socket buffers quickly enough, the receiver’s socket queue fills up. This leads to silent packet drops inside the kernel, visible in metrics as socket buffer overflows (RcvbufErrors). For latency-sensitive media protocols or packet-loss-sensitive QUIC transport connections, these drops introduce heavy jitter, head-of-line blocking, and throughput collapse.
Linux offers several generations of socket API extensions to solve UDP throughput and CPU efficiency challenges: 1. Syscall-level batching via sendmmsg() and recvmmsg(), which amortize the overhead of entering and exiting the kernel across multiple messages. 2. Kernel and hardware segmentation offloads via UDP Generic Segmentation Offload (UDP GSO / UDP_SEGMENT) and UDP Generic Receive Offload (UDP GRO / UDP_GRO), which allow applications to pass multi-kilobyte buffers representing dozens of datagrams in a single operation.
Understanding how these mechanisms function, how they interact across virtual interface boundaries (such as veth and loopback), and how they behave under buffer pressure is essential for operating high-performance UDP infrastructure.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
text:
Learning goals

Quantify the CPU overhead and packet rate limits of single-datagram UDP syscalls versus batched syscalls.
Differentiate between syscall-level batching (sendmmsg/recvmmsg) and packet-level offloading (UDP_SEGMENT/UDP_GRO).
Implement UDP GSO (Generic Segmentation Offload) on socket buffers using control messages (cmsg).
Implement UDP GRO (Generic Receive Offload) on receiver sockets and parse incoming segment sizing metadata.
Analyze kernel UDP drop mechanics, specifically why fast GSO senders cause elevated RcvbufErrors on non-GRO receivers.
Observe packet counter semantics across virtual interfaces when hardware and software offloads are active.
Identify the structural constraints, MTU limits, and socket state requirements for UDP GSO offloading.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
text:
Version note
The concepts, kernel socket options, and lab measurements described in this chapter were compiled on Linux kernel version 6.12.94 using gcc 14.2.0 and iproute2 6.15.0 in unprivileged user, network, and mount namespaces. UDP GSO (UDP_SEGMENT) was introduced in Linux 4.18, and UDP GRO (UDP_GRO) was added in Linux 5.0.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
section: Per-datagram overhead in standard UDP sockets
text:
Per-datagram overhead in standard UDP sockets
A standard sendto() or recvfrom() call requires a complete transition across the user-kernel boundary for every single datagram. The kernel must copy memory, perform socket lock management, check access permissions, build or parse headers, and manage socket buffer state (sk_buff or skb).
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       User Space App                            |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
   | sendto()        | sendto()        | sendto()        | sendto()
   v                 v                 v                 v
====================== Kernel Boundary ============================
   |                 |                 |                 |
   v                 v                 v                 v
+---------+       +---------+       +---------+       +---------+
| sk_buff |       | sk_buff |       | sk_buff |       | sk_buff |
+---------+       +---------+       +---------+       +---------+
   |                 |                 |                 |
   v                 v                 v                 v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     Network Driver / Wire                       |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
When operating at 1,000,000 packets per second, executing a sendto() or recvfrom() call 1,000,000 times per second incurs substantial overhead: - Syscall Entry/Exit: Execution of instruction-pointer isolation barriers, context saving/restoration, and security mitigations (e.g., KPTI, spec-store bypass controls). - Buffer allocation: Allocating and initialising an sk_buff for every payload, however small. - Locking and Traversal: Acquiring socket lock structures, updating socket queue pointers, computing IP/UDP header fields, and updating kernel statistics.
For high-packet-rate workloads, the cost of packet processing is dominated by per-packet fixed overhead rather than payload byte copying.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
text:
Syscall batching: sendmmsg and recvmmsg
Linux added recvmmsg() in 2.6.33 and sendmmsg() in 3.0 to allow applications to pass arrays of datagram buffers to or from the kernel in a single system call.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       User Space App                            |
|             mmsghdr array: [ msg1, msg2, msg3, msg4 ]           |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
                                  |
                                  | sendmmsg(batch=4)
                                  v
====================== Kernel Boundary ============================
                                  |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                        |                        |
         v                        v                        v
    +---------+              +---------+              +---------+
    | sk_buff |              | sk_buff |              | sk_buff |
    +---------+              +---------+              +---------+
         |                        |                        |
         +------------------------+------------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     Network Driver / Wire                       |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+

sendmmsg semantics
The sendmmsg() system call accepts an array of struct mmsghdr structures:
struct mmsghdr {
    struct msghdr msg_hdr;  /* Message header */
    unsigned int  msg_len;  /* Number of transmitted bytes */
};
The application populates the msg_hdr array with distinct payload buffer pointers, destination addresses, and ancillary data controls. sendmmsg() iterates over the array inside the kernel, allocating an sk_buff for each element and queuing it to the network stack.


recvmmsg semantics and MSG_WAITFORONE
recvmmsg() receives multiple messages from a socket into an array of struct mmsghdr elements. By default, recvmmsg() blocks until the entire array is filled or a socket timeout occurs.
The MSG_WAITFORONE flag alters this behavior: it causes recvmmsg() to block until at least one packet is available, fill as many remaining array elements as are immediately present in the receive buffer without blocking further, and then return instantly. This prevents latency penalties for low-rate or sporadic traffic while maintaining high batching efficiency during traffic spikes.


Performance characteristics of syscall batching
Syscall batching reduces CPU instruction count by crossing the kernel boundary once per batch instead of once per packet. However, inside the kernel, sendmmsg() still constructs individual sk_buff instances for every datagram. The stack continues to process each packet individually through routing, netfilter/iptables rules, and queueing disciplines (qdisc). Consequently, while sendmmsg() improves efficiency over sendto(), it does not eliminate per-packet kernel stack overhead.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
section: Packet-level batching: UDP GSO and UDP GRO
text:
Packet-level batching: UDP GSO and UDP GRO
Generic Segmentation Offload (GSO) and Generic Receive Offload (GRO) move batching from the system call API down into packet buffer processing in the network layer.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       User Space App                            |
|        Single Buffer (e.g. 38,400 Bytes) + GSO Size (1200)      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
                                  |
                                  | sendmsg() with UDP_SEGMENT
                                  v
====================== Kernel Boundary ============================
                                  |
                                  v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|           Single Super-skb (38,400 Bytes, gso_size=1200)        |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
                                  |
                 (Traverses Stack, Netfilter, qdisc)
                                  |
            +---------------------+---------------------+
            | Virtual / Software  |  Hardware NIC       |
            | Segmentation        |  (USO / Offload)    |
            v                     v                     v
       +---------+           +---------+           +---------+
       | Packet  |           | Packet  |           | Packet  |  (Separated at driver or wire)
       +---------+           +---------+           +---------+

UDP Generic Segmentation Offload (UDP GSO / UDP_SEGMENT)
With UDP GSO (UDP_SEGMENT), an application passes a single large memory buffer (up to ~64 KiB) containing multiple concatenated UDP payload segments to the kernel via sendmsg(). The application attaches ancillary data (cmsg) specifying the target segment length (gso_size).
The kernel constructs a single large sk_buff (“super-skb”). This super-skb traverses the routing engine, socket queues, and netfilter chains as a single entity. The payload is segmented into standard MTU-sized wire packets at the last possible moment: - In software, inside the IP layer or driver queue before transmission. - In hardware, offloaded to the Network Interface Card via UDP Segmentation Offload (USO / NETIF_F_GSO_UDP_L4).


UDP Generic Receive Offload (UDP GRO / UDP_GRO)
UDP GRO reverses this process on the receive path. When consecutive UDP datagrams arrive from a single source address and port destined for a matching target socket, the kernel or network interface coalesces them into a single super-skb.
When an application enables the UDP_GRO socket option, calling recvmsg() returns a single large payload buffer along with a UDP_GRO control message indicating the original segment size (gso_size). The application then iterates over the buffer in memory, slicing segments of length gso_size.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
section: Interface boundaries and packet counter semantics
text:
Interface boundaries and packet counter semantics
The behavior of GSO super-skbs varies depending on the underlying network interface type:
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         Sender Namespace                           |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                  |
                                  | GSO Super-skb (32 segs)
                                  v
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     veth Pair (Virtual Device)                     |
|    GSO skb stays INTACT across virtual interface boundary          |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
         +------------------------+------------------------+
         |                                                 |
         | GRO Enabled Receiver                            | GRO Disabled Receiver
         v                                                 v
+----------------------------------+             +-------------------+
| Received as 1 Super-skb (32 segs)|             | Kernel splits into|
| App reads 32 segs in 1 syscall   |             | 32 individual skbs|
+----------------------------------+             +-------------------+
                                                           |
                                                           v
                                                 +-------------------+
                                                 | Recv queue bursts |
                                                 | Drops occur if    |
                                                 | rmem is full      |
                                                 +-------------------+

Physical NICs: a NIC that advertises USO (tx-udp-segmentation) splits the super-skb into wire frames in hardware; otherwise the kernel segments it in software just before the driver. On the receive side, NAPI GRO only coalesces plain UDP datagrams of one flow when the destination socket has UDP_GRO enabled, or when the device has the forwarding features (rx-udp-gro-forwarding, rx-gro-list) turned on.
Virtual interfaces (veth, lo): both advertise the GSO features, so the kernel never needs to segment a super-skb on its way through them. It arrives in the peer namespace as the same single skb.
Interface counters: on veth and lo the packet counters (ip -s link, /sys/class/net/*/statistics) count skbs. Sending 32 datagrams as one GSO buffer adds 1 to tx_packets, not 32. Physical drivers differ: many report wire frames for offloaded packets, so compare counters only on the same kind of device.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
section: Buffer pressure, fast senders, and drop mechanics
text:
Buffer pressure, fast senders, and drop mechanics
When a GSO sender transmits packets to a non-GRO receiver, a significant speed imbalance occurs.
The GSO sender converts tens of thousands of datagrams into super-skbs with minimal CPU overhead. When these super-skbs arrive at a receiver socket that does not have UDP_GRO enabled, the kernel’s receive path must segment the super-skb into individual standard sk_buff instances before enqueuing them into the socket receive buffer (sk_rcvbuf).
GSO sender: 1 sendmsg = 32 datagrams, ~290 ns CPU each
       |
       |  one super-skb across the veth
       v
receiver without UDP_GRO: kernel segments it back into 32 skbs
       |
       v  each skb is charged to sk_rcvbuf separately
+-----------------------------------------------------+
| socket receive queue (SO_RCVBUF, capped by rmem_max)|
+-----------------------------------------------------+
       |  drained by recvfrom(), one datagram per syscall
       v
queue full -> the datagram that does not fit is dropped, RcvbufErrors += 1

receiver with UDP_GRO: the super-skb is queued as ONE skb
       -> if it does not fit, all 32 datagrams are dropped together
If the receiver application processes datagrams using single-datagram calls (recvfrom()), its consumption rate will be far slower than the sender’s transmission rate. Once the receiver’s sk_rcvbuf limit is reached, the kernel rejects new incoming datagrams.
The unit of loss depends on the receiver. A socket without UDP_GRO gets the super-skb segmented before queueing, so each datagram is accounted and dropped on its own: the 86,052 losses in scenario D are not a multiple of 32. A socket with UDP_GRO queues the whole super-skb as one buffer, so a drop takes all of its segments at once. RcvbufErrors counts dropped skbs, not datagrams: in one GRO run of this lab the counter rose by 77 while the receiver came up 2,464 datagrams short, which is 77 x 32.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
text:
Constraints, limits, and pacing
To use UDP GSO and GRO safely in production, several architectural constraints must be observed:

Maximum Segment Count: The kernel enforces a maximum of 128 segments per GSO super-skb.
Maximum Payload Size: The total aggregated length of a GSO super-skb cannot exceed the maximum IPv4 UDP datagram payload limit of 65,507 bytes (65,535 byte IP limit minus 20-byte IP header and 8-byte UDP header).
MTU Alignment: The gso_size parameter must be chosen such that individual segmented frames do not exceed the path MTU when IP and UDP headers are added (e.g., maximum gso_size of 1472 bytes for a 1500-byte MTU under standard IPv4).
Checksums and paths that refuse GSO: the kernel leaves the UDP checksum to be completed per segment, so GSO is refused on a socket with checksums disabled (SO_NO_CHECK: EINVAL), for UDP-Lite, and when the route goes through an IPsec (xfrm) transform (EIO), per udp_send_skb() in v6.12. QUIC stacks treat EIO at send time as “turn GSO off for this socket”.
Burstiness and Pacing: Transmitting large GSO super-skbs causes bursts of back-to-back packets at line rate when segmented. In networks with shallow-buffered switches, these bursts can induce packet drops. Production deployments running QUIC often combine GSO with Fair Queueing (fq) and rate pacing (SO_TXTIME).
Connected vs Unconnected Sockets: UDP_SEGMENT functions on both connected sockets (where connect() sets the default destination) and unconnected sockets (where sendmsg() specifies destination addresses via sockaddr_in).

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
text:
Reading the output

1. 200000 x 1200 B datagrams, one call each vs batched

Scenario A: sender sendto (batch 1) -> receiver recvfrom

Sender performance: 200,000 datagrams sent in 200,000 system calls (sendto). Wall time: 0.340s, CPU time: 0.340s, throughput: 588 kpps, CPU cost: 1701 ns-cpu/datagram.
Receiver performance: Received 199,798 datagrams (239,757,600 bytes) across 199,798 system calls (recvfrom). CPU time: 0.231s.
Counters: Interface tx v0 counted 200,002 packets (including IPv6 background neighbor discovery). UDP SNMP statistics recorded InDatagrams=199798 and RcvbufErrors=202. A minor loss of 202 packets occurred due to socket queue transient saturation during unpinned execution.



Scenario B: sender mmsg (batch 32) -> receiver recvfrom

Sender performance: 200,000 datagrams sent using sendmmsg() in 6,250 system calls (200000 / 32 = 6250). Wall time: 0.296s, throughput: 676 kpps, CPU cost: 1478 ns-cpu/datagram.
Syscall Overhead Analysis: Converting from sendto to sendmmsg reduced system calls from 200,000 to 6,250. CPU cost dropped slightly from 1,701 ns to 1,478 ns per datagram. On this kernel, per-datagram network stack allocation overhead (sk_buff creation, IP routing) dominates total CPU consumption, meaning syscall elimination provides a modest boost (~15%) rather than an order-of-magnitude shift.
Receiver performance: 200,000 datagrams received via 200,000 recvfrom calls (datagrams/syscall=1.0). No additional drops occurred (RcvbufErrors=202).



Scenario C: sender mmsg (batch 32) -> receiver mmsg

Sender performance: 200,000 datagrams sent in 6,250 sendmmsg calls (579 kpps, 1727 ns-cpu/datagram).
Receiver performance: 200,000 datagrams received across 97,637 recvmmsg system calls. Average yield: datagrams/syscall=2.0.
Batching Analysis: Even though the receiver requested batches of up to 32 datagrams, recvmmsg returned an average of 2.0 datagrams per call. This occurs because the receiver drained incoming socket buffers as quickly as single packet sk_buff items were enqueued by the kernel thread, demonstrating that recvmmsg batching yield is limited by receiver scheduling and incoming queue depth.



Scenario D: sender gso (batch 32) -> receiver recvfrom

Sender performance: Wall time: 0.058s, CPU time: 0.058s, throughput: 3449 kpps, CPU cost: 290 ns-cpu/datagram.
Throughput Jump: GSO reduced sender CPU overhead from ~1,478 ns to 290 ns per datagram, driving a 5x increase in transmission speed (3.45 Mpps). Passing 38,400-byte buffers (32 segments * 1,200 bytes) allows the kernel stack to process 1 super-skb instead of 32 individual skbs.
Receiver Buffer Overflow: The receiver obtained only 113,948 datagrams. Receiver RcvbufErrors jumped from 202 to 86,254 (a loss of 86,052 datagrams).
Root cause: the sender got cheaper, the receiver did not. The receiver still pays one recvfrom() per datagram, so the queue (8 MiB requested, capped by rmem_max) filled and the kernel dropped datagrams individually after segmenting each super-skb. 86,052 is not a multiple of 32, which confirms the per-datagram accounting. The sender is unaware: GSO makes it possible to send faster than the peer can read.
Interface Counters: tx v0 counted exactly 6,250 packets. This confirms that virtual interfaces (veth) treat GSO super-skbs as single packet entities in network driver statistics.



Scenario E: sender gso (batch 32) -> receiver gro

Sender performance: Wall time: 0.023s, throughput: 8632 kpps, CPU cost: 116 ns-cpu/datagram.
Receiver performance: Received all 200,000 datagrams (240,000,000 bytes) across exactly 6,250 system calls (datagrams/syscall=32.0). Receiver active CPU time: 0.020s.
Coalescing efficiency: coalesced-reads=6250, max-segs-per-read=32. RcvbufErrors stayed at 86,254, so nothing was lost in this run. In the two other runs the same scenario lost 2,464 and 2,048 datagrams: 77 and 64 whole 32-segment buffers.
Optimization Alignment: Combining UDP GSO on the sender with UDP GRO on the receiver eliminated the processing bottleneck on both sides of the socket. The receiver read 38,400 bytes per recvmsg() call, allowing kernel and user space to operate entirely on 32-segment super-units.



Scenario F: sender sendto (batch 1) -> receiver gro

Sender performance: 764 kpps, 1309 ns-cpu/datagram.
Receiver performance: 199,689 datagrams received in 199,689 system calls (coalesced-reads=0).
GRO Ineffectiveness: Enabling UDP_GRO on a receiver provides no performance benefit when the sender transmits individual sendto frames over a veth interface without NAPI hardware GRO support. The receiver processed 1 datagram per call (datagrams/syscall=1.0), proving that software GRO requires either GSO super-skbs from the sender or GRO support in the network driver.




2. UDP_SEGMENT limits on a 1500-byte MTU veth
The second lab section tests kernel enforcement of payload and segment boundary constraints:

64 x 1000 B (64000 B total) -> ok: Valid (64 segments <= 128 max limit; total payload <= 65507 bytes).
65 x 1000 B (65000 B total) -> ok: Valid (65 segments <= 128 max limit; total payload <= 65507 bytes).
128 x 500 B -> ok: Valid (128 segments matches the maximum segment count limit).
129 x 500 B -> Invalid argument (EINVAL): Transmitting 129 segments violates the kernel constraint of 128 segments per GSO payload.
segment 1472 B on a 1500 MTU -> ok: Valid (1472 bytes payload + 8 bytes UDP header + 20 bytes IP header = 1500 bytes, fitting MTU).
segment 1473 B on a 1500 MTU -> Message too long (EMSGSIZE): A segment size of 1473 bytes produces an IP packet of 1501 bytes, exceeding the link MTU of 1500 bytes.
66 x 1000 B (66000 B > 65507) -> Message too long (EMSGSIZE): Total payload exceeds the maximum IPv4 UDP datagram limit of 65,507 bytes.
last segment short: 10 x 1000 + 1 -> ok: Valid. The kernel allows the final segment in a GSO buffer to be smaller than gso_size (e.g., 10 full 1000-byte segments followed by 1 trailing byte).



3. The same GSO send on loopback (MTU 65536)
The final lab section runs GSO benchmarks over the loopback interface (lo, MTU 65536):

GSO -> GRO: 9143 kpps and 109 ns-cpu/datagram. The receiver read 197,376 datagrams in 6,168 reads of 32, so 82 buffers (2,624 datagrams) were dropped whole this time. Loopback behaves like the veth: the super-skb stays intact, and the large loopback MTU changes nothing because the segment size, not the MTU, decides what the receiver sees.
GSO -> recvfrom: Throughput fell to 3397 kpps (294 ns-cpu/datagram), with significant packet drops resulting from receiver queue saturation.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
text:
Gotchas

GSO Creates Micro-Bursts: Transmitting 64 KiB GSO super-skbs emits back-to-back packets at line rate. This can saturate queue buffers on intermediate switches, causing packet drops. Use SO_TXTIME or fq (Fair Queueing) pacing where necessary.
GRO receivers lose whole buffers: a socket with UDP_GRO queues a coalesced buffer as one skb, so when its queue is full all 32 datagrams go at once and RcvbufErrors rises by 1. Divide nothing by the counter without knowing which kind of receiver you are looking at.
A fast sender is not a healthy sender: scenario D shows GSO making the sender five times cheaper while the receiver lost 43 % of the datagrams. Pair GSO on the sender with UDP_GRO on the receiver, and rely on the protocol’s own flow and congestion control (QUIC has both) rather than on the socket buffer.
Software segmentation is silent: on a NIC without USO the kernel segments in software. It still beats one sendto() per datagram, but the savings are smaller than with hardware USO.
Receiver App Must Split GRO Buffers: UDP_GRO returns concatenated payloads in a single buffer. If the application does not inspect the UDP_GRO cmsg and parse the payload into gso_size chunks, it will treat multiple distinct datagrams as one corrupted payload.
Truncated Final Segment: In both GSO transmission and GRO reception, the final payload segment can be shorter than gso_size. Receiver parsing loops must handle trailing partial segments correctly.
128 Segment Limit: Attempting to pass more than 128 segments in a single UDP_SEGMENT sendmsg() call fails immediately with EINVAL (Invalid argument).
MTU Enforcement: The gso_size value passed to UDP_SEGMENT must account for outer headers. Setting a segment size that causes IP frames to exceed the path MTU results in EMSGSIZE errors.
Virtual Interface Counter Artifacts: Tools monitoring veth or loopback interfaces report super-skb counts rather than wire packet counts. A single reported packet on a veth link may represent up to 128 UDP datagrams.

title: Batching UDP on Linux: sendmmsg, recvmmsg, UDP GSO and GRO
text:
Exercises

Verify Syscall Reduction: Modify udpbench.c to send 500,000 datagrams using sendmmsg() with batch sizes of 1, 8, 32, and 128. Use strace -c to count total system call invocations and compare overall runtime.
Observe Drop Thresholds: Reduce rmem_max and the socket receive buffer (SO_RCVBUF) to 64 KiB. Run a GSO sender (batch 32) against a non-GRO recvfrom() receiver. Calculate the exact ratio of lost datagrams using nstat -az UdpRcvbufErrors.
Implement GRO Parsing: Write a standalone receiver loop in C that accepts incoming datagrams, inspects SOL_UDP / UDP_GRO cmsg headers, and prints the timestamp, total bytes read, segment count, and payload length of every parsed segment.
Test Trailing Partial Segments: Construct a GSO payload containing 5 full segments of 1,000 bytes plus one partial segment of 350 bytes (total 5,350 bytes). Transmit the payload using UDP_SEGMENT set to 1000 and verify that the receiver correctly parses 6 distinct segments.
Measure Loopback MTU Interaction: Change the loopback interface MTU from 65536 to 1500 (ip link set dev lo mtu 1500). Rerun the GSO benchmark suite and compare performance metrics against the high-MTU baseline.
Simulate Offload Disabling: Use ethtool -K to disable GRO on a physical network interface. Compare CPU utilization and packet loss for a high-rate QUIC traffic stream before and after toggling the setting.

Toolchain: gcc 14.2.0, iproute2 6.15.0

The per-datagram scenarios lost 0 to 202 datagrams; GSO towards a recvfrom() receiver lost 83,729 to 87,875 every time; GSO towards a UDP_GRO receiver lost 0 to 2,464 over the veth and 0 to 8,896 over loopback, always a multiple of 32. title: Choosing a Source Port: connect(), bind() and the Ephemeral Range
text:
Choosing a Source Port: connect(), bind() and the Ephemeral Range
When building high-throughput systems, reverse proxies, API gateways, and load-test engines, network operators often encounter socket allocation failures long before CPU or memory capacity limits are reached. A common operational crisis occurs when an outbound proxy or HTTP load generator suddenly begins throwing EADDRNOTAVAIL (Cannot assign requested address) or EADDRINUSE (Address already in use) errors while attempting to establish TCP connections.
While these errors are frequently blamed on TCP TIME-WAIT socket accumulation (covered in the TIME-WAIT chapter of this part), system engineers frequently encounter port exhaustion in scenarios where TIME-WAIT plays no role at all. Active long-lived connections, rapid microservice fan-out, explicit IP binding in multi-homed systems, and misconfigured socket options can completely deplete the host’s available local source port budget even when zero sockets reside in TIME-WAIT.
Understanding how the Linux kernel selects local source ports during connect() and bind() system calls is critical for capacity planning and troubleshooting high-concurrency network services. The kernel relies on specific data structures, hashing strategies, and sysctl boundaries to enforce socket uniqueness across the system. Misinterpreting how bind() interacts with connect() can reduce an application’s outbound connection budget from tens of thousands of concurrent streams down to a single socket pool per target service.
This chapter details the low-level mechanics of source port selection in Linux, examines how socket state structures govern 4-tuple sharing, evaluates the performance impacts of socket options like IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT, and demonstrates capacity planning calculations for edge gateways and service meshes.

title: Choosing a Source Port: connect(), bind() and the Ephemeral Range
text:
Learning goals

Understand how the TCP 4-tuple enables source port reuse across distinct remote endpoints.
Differentiate between implicit port allocation via connect() and explicit port reservation via bind().
Identify the root cause of EADDRINUSE vs. EADDRNOTAVAIL during outbound connection establishment.
Explain the Linux kernel’s parity-based port allocation algorithm (__inet_hash_connect vs. inet_csk_get_port).
Evaluate the operational impact of socket options IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT, IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE, and sysctl net.ipv4.ip_autobind_reuse.
Apply accurate capacity planning formulas for outgoing connections based on connection rate, duration, source IPs, and ephemeral range bounds.

title: Choosing a Source Port: connect(), bind() and the Ephemeral Range
text:
Version note
The kernel implementation details, parity split algorithms, and code paths discussed in this chapter are accurate as of Linux kernel version 6.12.94. IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT arrived in Linux 4.2 and the per-socket IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE in Linux 6.3 (both per their man pages). The lab ran on 6.12.94 with Python 3.13.5 and iproute2 6.15.0.

title: Choosing a Source Port: connect(), bind() and the Ephemeral Range
section: Ephemeral Port Range and the TCP 4-Tuple
text:
Ephemeral Port Range and the TCP 4-Tuple
Every active TCP connection on a Linux host is uniquely identified within the network stack by a 4-tuple structure:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                              TCP 4-Tuple                              |
|                                                                       |
|  [ Source IP ]  :  [ Source Port ]  <--->  [ Dst IP ]  :  [ Dst Port ] |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
Because uniqueness is enforced across all four fields, a single local source IP address and source port combination can be reused simultaneously across multiple connections, provided each connection targets a distinct remote IP address or remote port.

The Ephemeral Range
When an application creates a stream socket and initiates an outbound connection using connect() without explicitly specifying a local port, the Linux kernel automatically assigns an unused local port from the ephemeral port range. This range is defined by the sysctl parameter net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range.
The default range is 32768 to 60999 inclusive: 28,232 ports. RFC 6335 assigns 49152–65535 (16,384 ports) as the IANA dynamic range, and RFC 6056 recommends that port selection use the whole 1024–65535 space. Linux defaults to a larger range than IANA’s and leaves room above 61000 for services that listen there. The range must start at or above net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start (1024 by default).









Parameter / Standard
Range Start
Range End
Total Available Ports




Linux Sysctl Default
32768

28,232


IANA Recommendation (RFC 6335)

Widest allowed by default

Per-Destination Budgeting
Because uniqueness depends on the full 4-tuple, an application issuing plain connect() calls can establish up to ~28,232 concurrent connections from a single local IP to target destination 192.168.1.100:443. If the same application simultaneously connects to target destination 192.168.1.101:443, the kernel can reuse the exact same set of 28,232 source ports. Thus, the outbound connection budget for plain connect() operations is per destination endpoint (Destination IP + Destination Port).
Source: 10.0.0.1                         Destinations:
+----------------+                       +--------------------+
|                |--- src port 40000 --->| 192.168.1.100:443  | (Tuple A)
|  Local Client  |                       +--------------------+
|                |                       +--------------------+
|                |--- src port 40000 --->| 192.168.1.101:443  | (Tuple B)
+----------------+                       +--------------------+

title: Choosing a Source Port: connect(), bind() and the Ephemeral Range
text:
The bind() Trap and IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT
A common architecture in multi-homed hosts, egress gateways, and reverse proxies (such as NGINX, HAProxy, or Envoy) involves binding outbound sockets to a specific source IP address before establishing outbound connections. This is done to force outbound traffic onto specific egress interfaces or policy routes.

The bind(src, 0) Problem
To select a source IP while allowing the kernel to auto-select a free port, applications call bind() with port 0 (e.g., bind("10.0.0.1", 0)) prior to calling connect().
Calling bind(src, 0) forces the kernel to immediately select and reserve a local port within the host’s binding table at the time bind() is executed. However, at the moment bind() is invoked, the kernel does not know the remote destination IP or port, because connect() has not yet been called.
Sequence for bind(src, 0) followed by connect():

Step 1: bind(10.0.0.1, 0)
        Kernel reserves port X globally for source IP 10.0.0.1.
        Dest IP/Port are unknown. Port X cannot be bound again.

Step 2: connect(192.168.1.100, 443)
        Connection completes using local 10.0.0.1:X.
Because the kernel must guarantee that the bound address is usable for whatever connect() comes next, a port chosen by bind(src, 0) is taken out of the pool for every destination: later bind(src, 0) calls will not hand it out again (unless SO_REUSEADDR and ip_autobind_reuse are involved, see below). Consequently, the source port budget is transformed from a per-destination limit of 28,232 connections to a global limit of 28,232 connections across all combined destinations for that bound source IP.
When all 28,232 ports are bound, subsequent calls to bind(src, 0) immediately fail with the error EADDRINUSE (Address already in use)—even if the application intends to connect to a completely new destination IP address.


Resolving the Trap: IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT
To solve this architectural issue, Linux 4.2 introduced the socket option IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT. When this option is set on a socket before calling bind(src, 0), it informs the kernel to bind the socket to the requested source IP address, but to defer source port selection until connect() is executed.
Sequence with IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT:

Step 1: setsockopt(..., IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT, 1)
Step 2: bind(10.0.0.1, 0)
        Kernel records source IP 10.0.0.1. No port is reserved yet.

Step 3: connect(192.168.1.100, 443)
        Kernel evaluates full 4-tuple and selects port X.
        Port X is bound only in the context of destination 192.168.1.100:443.
Because port assignment occurs during connect(), the kernel evaluates the complete 4-tuple. This restores the outbound connection capacity back to ~28,232 connections per unique destination endpoint. If port allocation fails at connect() time because all 4-tuples for that specific destination are occupied, the kernel returns EADDRNOTAVAIL rather than EADDRINUSE.

title: Choosing a Source Port: connect(), bind() and the Ephemeral Range
text:
Kernel Port Allocation Mechanics
The Linux kernel implements specific strategies in its networking subsystem to allocate ephemeral ports efficiently and avoid resource contention between active outgoing connections and listening services.

Parity Splitting (__inet_hash_connect vs inet_csk_get_port)
Since 2016 (Eric Dumazet’s “tcp/dccp: try to not exhaust ip_local_port_range in connect()”), the kernel uses a parity-based split to ensure that applications making automatic client connections (connect()) and applications explicitly binding local ports (bind(0)) do not exhaust each other’s available port supplies.
Internal kernel routines govern port selection based on the call path: - __inet_hash_connect(): Invoked during implicit port selection for outbound connect() calls. - inet_csk_get_port() / inet_csk_find_open_port(): Invoked when an application calls bind(0).
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = [ 40000 , 40009 ]  (Low end = 40000: EVEN)
                                  |
            +---------------------+---------------------+
            |                                           |
            v                                           v
   __inet_hash_connect()                     inet_csk_get_port()
     (Plain connect)                              (Explicit bind)
            |                                           |
            v                                           v
Prefers EVEN Ports (40000, 40002...)       Prefers ODD Ports (40001, 40003...)
The algorithm evaluates the starting bound (the low end) of net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range: 1. If the lower range bound is even (e.g., 32768 or 40000), __inet_hash_connect() attempts to allocate even ports first. Conversely, inet_csk_get_port() attempts to allocate odd ports first. 2. If the lower range bound is odd (e.g., 32769), __inet_hash_connect() attempts to allocate odd ports first, while inet_csk_get_port() attempts to allocate even ports first.
Because of this separation, Linux kernel sysctl documentation recommends that operators configure net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range such that the low and high bounds have different parities (e.g., an even low bound and an odd high bound like 32768 60999).


Exclude Ports with ip_local_reserved_ports
Systems often run control-plane applications or administrative daemons on known static ports inside the ephemeral port range (e.g., port 41000). If an outbound connect() call automatically claims port 41000 as its local ephemeral source port, a subsequent attempt by a daemon to execute bind() on port 41000 will fail with EADDRINUSE.
The sysctl parameter net.ipv4.ip_local_reserved_ports specifies a comma-separated list or range of ports to exclude from automatic selection:
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_reserved_ports = 40000-40004
Ports listed in ip_local_reserved_ports are skipped by every automatic selection (connect() and bind() with port 0). Explicit calls such as bind(src, 40002) still succeed; the kernel documentation says “Explicit port allocation behavior is unchanged”. The list must be cleared by writing a newline; writing an empty string does not clear it (we hit this in the lab).


UDP Autobind Behavior
Unlike TCP, UDP is a connectionless transport protocol. While UDP sockets can invoke connect() to lock in a default remote destination address, the kernel’s port allocation table does not support 4-tuple sharing for UDP sockets undergoing automatic port allocation (autobind).
When a UDP socket calls connect() or sendto() without a prior bind(), the kernel autobinds it through udp_lib_get_port(), which looks only at the local port (and address), never at the destination. Each autobound UDP socket therefore consumes one port of the range. When the range is exhausted, autobind fails with EAGAIN no matter how many different destinations the sockets talk to.


ip_autobind_reuse
The sysctl net.ipv4.ip_autobind_reuse (default 0) controls whether bind(0) may hand out a port that is already bound, when the new socket and every socket on that port have SO_REUSEADDR. The kernel documentation says it “may break some applications”, names IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT as the preferred solution, and says it “should only be set by experts”.
Setting net.ipv4.ip_autobind_reuse = 1 modifies inet_csk_get_port() to allow port sharing for sockets configured with SO_REUSEADDR. However, because bind() takes place without knowledge of the eventual destination IP and port, the kernel may assign a port whose resulting 4-tuple conflicts with an existing connection once connect() is subsequently invoked. Lab section 8 shows exactly that: the shared port is handed out again and connect() fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL once the 4-tuple is taken.


Per-Socket Ephemeral Range (IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE)
Linux 6.3 introduced the IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE socket option, allowing individual user-space applications to override the global net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range sysctl on a per-socket basis.
The value is one 32-bit integer: the upper bound in the high 16 bits, the lower bound in the low 16 bits (hi << 16 | lo); 0 for either half means “use the sysctl’s bound”. The effective range is the intersection with the sysctl range. In __inet_hash_connect() (v6.12) a per-socket range turns the parity split off:
/* net/ipv4/inet_hashtables.c, Linux v6.12 (excerpt) */
local_ports = inet_sk_get_local_port_range(sk, &low, &high);
step = local_ports ? 1 : 2;
...
/* In first pass we try ports of @low parity.
 * inet_csk_get_port() does the opposite choice.
 */
if (!local_ports)
    offset &= ~1U;
With a per-socket range the scan starts at a hashed offset and walks every port (step 1) instead of every other one, which matters for small ranges: all of them are usable by connect() in one pass.

title: Choosing a Source Port: connect(), bind() and the Ephemeral Range
text:
The lab
The lab script lab-ports.sh executes Python script ports.py inside a private, unprivileged network namespace (unshare -urn). Network namespaces isolate sysctl settings, ensuring host configuration parameters remain completely untouched.
Run it as unshare -urn sh lab-ports.sh (no root, nothing installed). Inside the namespace, all of 127.0.0.0/8 is local once lo is up, and the script adds 127.0.0.10 explicitly for section 4. TCP listeners are started on 127.0.0.2:80 and 127.0.0.3:80. To trigger immediate port exhaustion without creating thousands of sockets, net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range is restricted inside the test namespace to 40000 40009 (a total budget of 10 ports). All client sockets configured in ports.py set SO_LINGER to 0 upon closure, forcing a TCP RST packet to bypass the TIME-WAIT state completely so residual sockets do not influence subsequent test steps.

Lab files
The wrapper that enters the namespace:
lab-ports.sh:
#!/bin/sh
# Run as: unshare -urn sh lab-ports.sh   (private network namespace: the sysctls below are per-netns)
ip link set lo up
ip addr add 127.0.0.10/8 dev lo 2>/dev/null || true
uname -r
python3 "$(dirname "$0")/ports.py"
The experiments, one function call per section:
ports.py:
"""Source-port selection on Linux: connect() vs bind(0), IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT, reserved ports, UDP."""
import errno, socket, sys, time
IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT = getattr(socket, "IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT", 24)
P = "/proc/sys/net/ipv4/"
def sysctl(name, value=None):
    if value is not None:
        open(P + name, "w").write(value)
    return open(P + name).read().split()
DST = [("127.0.0.2", 80), ("127.0.0.3", 80)]
listeners = []
for d in DST:
    l = socket.create_server(d, backlog=200); listeners.append(l)
held = []
LINGER0 = (1).to_bytes(4, "little") + (0).to_bytes(4, "little")
def close_all():
    for s in held:                       # SO_LINGER 0: close with RST, so no TIME-WAIT keeps the port
        s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_LINGER, LINGER0); s.close()
    held.clear()
def opener(dst, src=None, no_port=False, reuse=False):
    s = socket.socket()
    held.append(s)
    if reuse: s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    if no_port: s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_IP, IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT, 1)
    if src is not None: s.bind((src, 0))
    s.connect(dst)
    return s.getsockname()[1]
def fill(label, dst, **kw):
    ports, err = [], None
    while True:
        try:
            ports.append(opener(dst, **kw))
        except OSError as e:
            err = errno.errorcode[e.errno]; break
        if len(ports) > 100: break
    print(f"  {label:52} {len(ports):3} connections, then {err}; ports {ports[:6]}{'...' if len(ports) > 6 else ''}")
    return ports
def part(t): print(f"\n== {t}")

sysctl("ip_local_port_range", "40000 40009")
print("ip_local_port_range =", " ".join(sysctl("ip_local_port_range")), "(10 ports)")

part("1. plain connect(): the limit is per destination")
a = fill("to 127.0.0.2:80", DST[0]); b = fill("to 127.0.0.3:80", DST[1])
print(f"  same source ports reused toward both destinations: {sorted(a) == sorted(b)}"); close_all()

part("2. bind(src, 0) before connect(): the port is reserved for every destination")
fill("to 127.0.0.2:80, bind 127.0.0.1:0 first", DST[0], src="127.0.0.1")
fill("to 127.0.0.3:80, bind 127.0.0.1:0 first", DST[1], src="127.0.0.1"); close_all()

part("3. bind(src, 0) with IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT: port chosen at connect() time")
fill("to 127.0.0.2:80, bind + NO_PORT", DST[0], src="127.0.0.1", no_port=True)
fill("to 127.0.0.3:80, bind + NO_PORT", DST[1], src="127.0.0.1", no_port=True); close_all()

part("4. a second source address doubles the per-destination budget")
fill("to 127.0.0.2:80 from 127.0.0.1 (NO_PORT)", DST[0], src="127.0.0.1", no_port=True)
fill("to 127.0.0.2:80 from 127.0.0.10 (NO_PORT)", DST[0], src="127.0.0.10", no_port=True); close_all()

part("5. parity: connect() starts on even ports, bind(0) on odd ones (20-port range)")
sysctl("ip_local_port_range", "40000 40019")
c = [opener(DST[0]) for _ in range(6)]
bnd = []
for _ in range(6):
    s = socket.socket(); held.append(s); s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); bnd.append(s.getsockname()[1])
print(f"  connect() picked {sorted(c)}\n  bind(0)   picked {sorted(bnd)}")
close_all()

part("6. ip_local_reserved_ports: autoselection skips them, explicit bind still works")
sysctl("ip_local_port_range", "40000 40009"); sysctl("ip_local_reserved_ports", "40000-40004")
fill("to 127.0.0.2:80 with 40000-40004 reserved", DST[0])
s = socket.socket(); held.append(s); s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 40002)); print(f"  explicit bind to reserved port 40002: ok, got {s.getsockname()[1]}")
close_all(); sysctl("ip_local_reserved_ports", "\n")
print("  ip_local_reserved_ports cleared:", sysctl("ip_local_reserved_ports") == [])

part("7. UDP autobind has no 4-tuple sharing")
socks, err = [], None
while True:
    u = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    try:
        u.connect(DST[len(socks) % 2]); socks.append(u)
    except OSError as e:
        err = errno.errorcode[e.errno]; break
print(f"  connected UDP sockets alternating between 2 destinations: {len(socks)}, then {err}")
for u in socks: u.close()

part("8. bind(0) with SO_REUSEADDR and net.ipv4.ip_autobind_reuse")
for v in ("0", "1"):
    try:
        sysctl("ip_autobind_reuse", v)
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"  cannot set ip_autobind_reuse={v}: {e}"); continue
    fill(f"ip_autobind_reuse={v}: SO_REUSEADDR + bind(0), to .2 then .3", DST[0], src="127.0.0.1", reuse=True)
    fill(f"ip_autobind_reuse={v}:   (second destination)", DST[1], src="127.0.0.1", reuse=True)
    close_all()
sysctl("ip_autobind_reuse", "0")

part("9. per-socket range with IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE (Linux 6.3+): 40100-40103 for this client only")
IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE = getattr(socket, "IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE", 51)
sysctl("ip_local_port_range", "40000 40999")
got, err = [], None
while True:
    s = socket.socket(); held.append(s)
    s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_IP, IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE, ((40103 << 16) | 40100).to_bytes(4, "little"))  # hi<<16 | lo
    try:
        s.connect(DST[0]); got.append(s.getsockname()[1])
    except OSError as e:
        err = errno.errorcode[e.errno]; break
print(f"  {len(got)} connections, then {err}; ports {sorted(got)} (system range is 40000-40999)")
close_all()


Execution output
6.12.94+

== 1. plain connect(): the limit is per destination
  to 127.0.0.2:80                                       10 connections, then EADDRNOTAVAIL; ports [40000, 40002, 40004, 40006, 40008, 40007]...
  to 127.0.0.3:80                                       10 connections, then EADDRNOTAVAIL; ports [40006, 40002, 40004, 40008, 40000, 40001]...
  same source ports reused toward both destinations: True

== 2. bind(src, 0) before connect(): the port is reserved for every destination
  to 127.0.0.2:80, bind 127.0.0.1:0 first               10 connections, then EADDRINUSE; ports [40005, 40007, 40001, 40009, 40003, 40004]...
  to 127.0.0.3:80, bind 127.0.0.1:0 first                0 connections, then EADDRINUSE; ports []

== 3. bind(src, 0) with IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT: port chosen at connect() time
  to 127.0.0.2:80, bind + NO_PORT                       10 connections, then EADDRNOTAVAIL; ports [40004, 40008, 40006, 40000, 40002, 40005]...
  to 127.0.0.3:80, bind + NO_PORT                       10 connections, then EADDRNOTAVAIL; ports [40000, 40002, 40004, 40006, 40008, 40001]...

== 4. a second source address doubles the per-destination budget
  to 127.0.0.2:80 from 127.0.0.1 (NO_PORT)              10 connections, then EADDRNOTAVAIL; ports [40004, 40002, 40006, 40008, 40000, 40005]...
  to 127.0.0.2:80 from 127.0.0.10 (NO_PORT)             10 connections, then EADDRNOTAVAIL; ports [40008, 40002, 40000, 40004, 40006, 40005]...

== 5. parity: connect() starts on even ports, bind(0) on odd ones (20-port range)
  connect() picked [40000, 40002, 40006, 40008, 40014, 40018]
  bind(0)   picked [40001, 40003, 40011, 40013, 40015, 40017]

== 6. ip_local_reserved_ports: autoselection skips them, explicit bind still works
  to 127.0.0.2:80 with 40000-40004 reserved              5 connections, then EADDRNOTAVAIL; ports [40006, 40008, 40005, 40007, 40009]

  ip_local_reserved_ports cleared: True

== 7. UDP autobind has no 4-tuple sharing
  connected UDP sockets alternating between 2 destinations: 10, then EAGAIN

== 8. bind(0) with SO_REUSEADDR and net.ipv4.ip_autobind_reuse
  ip_autobind_reuse=0: SO_REUSEADDR + bind(0), to .2 then .3  10 connections, then EADDRINUSE; ports [40001, 40003, 40002, 40000, 40007, 40009]...
  ip_autobind_reuse=0:   (second destination)            0 connections, then EADDRINUSE; ports []
  ip_autobind_reuse=1: SO_REUSEADDR + bind(0), to .2 then .3  10 connections, then EADDRNOTAVAIL; ports [40001, 40003, 40002, 40000, 40009, 40005]...
  ip_autobind_reuse=1:   (second destination)            1 connections, then EADDRNOTAVAIL; ports [40001]

== 9. per-socket range with IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE (Linux 6.3+): 40100-40103 for this client only
