title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
text:
TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
TLS session resumption allows a client and server to re-establish a secure channel using cryptographic state established in a prior handshake. A full TLS handshake costs the server a certificate signature (RSA or ECDSA) and a key exchange, and costs the client a certificate chain to verify. Resumption lets a returning client prove it holds a secret from an earlier session, so the server can skip the certificate and the signature. In TLS 1.2 it also skipped the key exchange. In TLS 1.3, as deployed by OpenSSL and every browser, a fresh (EC)DHE exchange still happens on resumption, which changes how much CPU resumption actually saves, as the lab measures.
For systems operators managing load balancers, reverse proxies, and API gateways, understanding how session resumption works under the hood is critical. Misconfigurations in ticket issuance, key management, or multi-tenant SNI routing can degrade connection latency, cause mysterious CPU spikes, or introduce subtle security vulnerabilities. When front-end servers operate as a multi-node fleet behind round-robin load balancers, an improper session resumption design can reduce cache hit rates to zero, invalidating performance optimization efforts entirely.
Furthermore, session resumption introduces distinct security trade-offs. The mechanism used to encrypt session state across cluster nodes relies on Session Ticket Encryption Keys (STEKs). If an operator fails to rotate STEKs properly or persists them insecurely, an attacker who later obtains a key and holds packet captures can decrypt TLS 1.2 sessions after the fact, and can impersonate the server to TLS 1.3 clients holding tickets under that key. Sharing ticket keys across virtual hosts also lets a session established for one name be resumed under another.
This chapter examines the practical architecture of TLS session resumption across TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3, ticket management mechanics, fleet-wide key rotation schemes, and the concrete performance impact across different signature schemes and post-quantum hybrid key exchange groups.

title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
text:
Learning goals

Differentiate between server-side session ID caching and stateless session tickets (RFC 5077 / RFC 8446).
Explain how TLS 1.3 resumption operates via NewSessionTicket messages, Pre-Shared Key (PSK) identities, and mode selection (psk_ke vs psk_dhe_ke).
Quantify the security risks of Session Ticket Encryption Keys (STEKs) regarding forward secrecy and server impersonation.
Design ticket key distribution and rotation for an nginx or HAProxy fleet.
Analyze how anti-replay protection mechanisms for early data alter session ticket reuse single-use semantics.
Evaluate the CPU performance delta between full handshakes and resumed sessions across RSA-2048, ECDSA P-256, and post-quantum hybrid groups (X25519MLKEM768).
Scope ticket keys so that sessions cannot be resumed across tenants on a shared terminator.

title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
text:
Version note
The lab exercises and benchmark outputs in this chapter were generated on a test host running Linux kernel 6.12.94, Python 3.13.5, and OpenSSL 3.5.7 (built June 9, 2026). All network execution took place over the local loopback interface (127.0.0.1). No external edge proxies such as NGINX or HAProxy were running during the execution of the lab scripts; production configurations for those proxies are provided in designated reference sections.

title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
section: Session Resumption Mechanics: TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3
text:
Session Resumption Mechanics: TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3
The primary objective of session resumption is to establish cryptographic material for a new connection using state derived from a previous connection. How that state is identified, stored, and exchanged differs fundamentally between TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246 / RFC 5077) and TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446).

TLS 1.2: State Caches and RFC 5077 Tickets
In TLS 1.2, session resumption historically relied on two mechanisms: Session IDs and Session Tickets.

Session ID (Stateful)
The server generates a unique 32-byte identifier during a full handshake and stores the master secret alongside connection metadata in an in-memory session cache. The server sends this identifier in the ServerHello. When the client re-connects, it sends the 32-byte identifier in its ClientHello. If the server finds a matching entry in its memory cache, it resumes the session.
Client                                   Server
  |                                         |
  |--- ClientHello (Session ID: 0x4f2a...) ->|  [Lookup 0x4f2a in RAM Cache]
  |                                         |  --> Found!
  |<-- ServerHello (Session ID: 0x4f2a...) -|
  |<-- [ChangeCipherSpec] ------------------|
  |<-- Finished ----------------------------|
  |--- [ChangeCipherSpec] ----------------->|
  |--- Finished --------------------------->|
This model requires the server (or fleet) to maintain synchronized state across all instances. If the client connects to a different backend node that lacks the Session ID in its RAM cache, the resumption fails, triggering a full handshake.


Session Tickets (Stateless - RFC 5077)
To avoid maintaining large distributed RAM caches, RFC 5077 introduced stateless session tickets. During a full handshake, after negotiating keys, the server serializes the session state (master secret, cipher suite, client identity) into a data structure, encrypts and authenticates it using a symmetric key known only to the server (the Session Ticket Encryption Key, or STEK), and transmits it to the client inside a NewSessionTicket handshake message.
Client                                   Server
  |                                         |
  |--- ClientHello (Session Ticket) ------->|  [Decrypt Ticket with STEK]
  |                                         |  --> Unpack Master Secret
  |<-- ServerHello -------------------------|
  |<-- [ChangeCipherSpec] ------------------|
  |<-- Finished ----------------------------|
  |--- [ChangeCipherSpec] ----------------->|
  |--- Finished --------------------------->|
When returning, the client passes this opaque blob back in the SessionTicket extension of its ClientHello. The server decrypts the ticket using its STEK, restores the session state, and completes a abbreviated handshake without consulting an in-memory cache.



TLS 1.3: Post-Handshake Tickets and PSK Modes
TLS 1.3 unifies session resumption under the Pre-Shared Key (PSK) architecture. Rather than emitting session tickets during the main handshake phase, the server transmits zero, one, or more NewSessionTicket messages after the main handshake completes and application data is flowing.
Client                                   Server
  |                                         |
  |=========================================|  <-- Handshake Completed
  |                                         |
  |<-- NewSessionTicket (Ticket 1, PSK 1) --|
  |<-- NewSessionTicket (Ticket 2, PSK 2) --|
  |                                         |
  |-- Application Data -------------------->|
Each ticket includes a ticket value (which acts as a PSK identity), an obfuscated ticket age, a lifetime hint (up to a maximum of 604,800 seconds / 7 days per RFC 8446), and a flag set for early data limits.
When the client wishes to resume a session, it sends a psk_key_exchange_modes extension in its ClientHello alongside a pre_shared_key extension listing the saved ticket identities.
TLS 1.3 defines two key exchange modes for PSKs:

psk_ke: Pure Pre-Shared Key exchange. The key derived for the new connection is based entirely on the secret stored within the ticket. No Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE/DHE) key exchange occurs.
psk_dhe_ke: Pre-Shared Key with Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange. The client and server present ephemeral key shares (e.g., X25519, P-256, or post-quantum hybrid groups such as X25519MLKEM768) alongside the PSK binder.

OpenSSL offers and accepts only psk_dhe_ke unless SSL_OP_ALLOW_NO_DHE_KEX is set, and browsers behave the same way. A resumed handshake therefore still runs the full key exchange, including the ML-KEM half of a hybrid group, and skips only the Certificate, CertificateVerify (the server’s signature) and the client’s chain validation.









Feature / Mechanism
TLS 1.2 Session ID
TLS 1.2 Session Ticket (RFC 5077)
TLS 1.3 PSK (psk_dhe_ke)




State Storage
Server In-Memory Cache
Client-side Encrypted Blob
Client-side Encrypted Blob (or Stateful Index)


Server Key Required
None (Cache lookup)
Symmetric STEK
Symmetric STEK


Key Exchange on Resumption
None
None
Ephemeral DH / Post-Quantum Hybrid


What a key or cache leak exposes
Master secrets in the cache
Master secret of every recorded session whose ticket was seen
Ability to impersonate the server to ticket holders; no passive decryption


Asymmetric Signatures
Skipped
Skipped
Skipped





Stateless vs Stateful Tickets in OpenSSL
While TLS 1.3 session tickets are conceptually client-side state blobs, OpenSSL supports two operational modes:

Stateless (default): the ticket is the session itself (resumption PSK, cipher suite, timestamps, SNI) encrypted under the server’s ticket key. The server keeps nothing per ticket.
Stateful (SSL_OP_NO_TICKET): Setting the SSL_OP_NO_TICKET flag in OpenSSL for TLS 1.3 does not disable session resumption. Instead, it changes the structure of the ticket. The server issues a NewSessionTicket containing an opaque database key, while storing the session parameters in its own local in-memory cache.

Understanding this operational difference is important: when an application sets SSL_OP_NO_TICKET in TLS 1.3, it forces stateful server-side caching, causing ticket validation to fail if the client presents the ticket to a sibling node in a multi-server fleet without shared memory or cache synchronization.


Anti-Replay Protection and Single-Use Rules
TLS 1.3 introduces 0-RTT (Early Data), allowing clients to send application data inside the first flight of packets along with the ClientHello. Because 0-RTT data relies on the ticket’s pre-shared key before server authentication finishes, it is vulnerable to replay attacks by network eavesdroppers unless protected by anti-replay mechanisms.
OpenSSL turns replay protection on automatically when the server’s maximum early data is non-zero (SSL_CTX_set_max_early_data, s_server -max_early_data). Its documentation describes the mechanism: the server then behaves as if SSL_OP_NO_TICKET were set, adds every issued session to its internal cache, and removes it on first resumption. A second use of the same ticket gets a full handshake, “even if a client does not send any early data”. SSL_OP_NO_ANTI_REPLAY switches this off for applications that protect against replay themselves.
Two consequences matter for operators. Tickets become single use, which RFC 8446 Appendix C.4 recommends for privacy anyway, so clients must keep the fresh tickets each connection delivers. And because the state is back in one server’s memory, enabling early data on an OpenSSL-based fleet makes resumption node-local: a shared ticket key no longer helps a client that lands on another node.

title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
section: STEK Architecture, Security Risks, and Fleet Design
text:
STEK Architecture, Security Risks, and Fleet Design
Session Ticket Encryption Keys (STEKs) enable stateless session resumption across web server fleets. However, their security implications must be carefully managed.

STEK Cryptographic Structure
nginx and HAProxy accept 48-byte (AES-128) or 80-byte (AES-256) ticket keys. In nginx’s 80-byte format the bytes split into three fields:
+------------------------+------------------------+------------------------+
|   Key Name (16 bytes)  |  HMAC Key (32 bytes)   |  AES Key (32 bytes)    |
| (Identifier in wire)   | (SHA-256 Authentication)| (AES-256 Encryption)   |
+------------------------+------------------------+------------------------+
Tickets built from such a key follow the structure RFC 5077 section 4 recommends: 1. The encrypting key is chosen and a random IV generated. 2. The serialized session is encrypted (AES-CBC with the key’s AES part). 3. An HMAC-SHA256 with the key’s HMAC part covers key name, IV and ciphertext. 4. The ticket is key name, IV, ciphertext and MAC; the key name tells the server which key to try.
Upon resumption, the server reads the first 16 bytes of the incoming ticket, identifies the corresponding key in its configured STEK list, verifies the HMAC, and decrypts the payload.


Cryptographic Compromise Dynamics
The security risk of a compromised STEK depends on the protocol version and negotiated key exchange mode.

TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 (psk_ke)
In TLS 1.2 (or TLS 1.3 running pure psk_ke), the ticket payload contains the raw session master secret. If an attacker captures encrypted wire traffic from a target connection and later steals the STEK, the attacker can decrypt the ticket, extract the master secret, and retroactively decrypt the target connection and any other session resumed using that ticket. (See Springall et al., “Measuring the Security Harm of TLS Crypto Shortcuts”, IMC 2016).


TLS 1.3 (psk_dhe_ke)
When psk_dhe_ke is used, the final connection key is derived from both the ticket PSK and an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange. If an attacker steals a TLS 1.3 STEK, passive decryption of past recorded traffic remains impossible because the attacker lacks the private ephemeral key shares exchanged over the wire. However, possessing the active STEK allows the attacker to execute active Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks: they can forge valid tickets, authenticate as the server to any client presenting a ticket encrypted under that STEK, and intercept future connections.
Treat ticket keys like private keys, with one difference: they should be short-lived. HAProxy’s manual suggests rotating at least every 12 hours and keeping the files on tmpfs, off any permanent storage.



Fleet STEK Synchronization
In a load-balanced infrastructure with multiple edge nodes terminating TLS, a client’s consecutive requests may hit different backend nodes.
                     +-----------------------+
                     |  Layer 4 Load Balancer|
                     |     (Round Robin)     |
                     +-----------+-----------+
                                 |
                 +---------------+---------------+
                 |                               |
                 v                               v
       +-------------------+           +-------------------+
       |    Node A (STEK 1)|           |    Node B (STEK 2)|
       +-------------------+           +-------------------+
If Node A and Node B generate independent STEKs locally at startup: 1. Client connects to Node A, receives a ticket encrypted with Node A’s STEK 1. 2. Client sends a subsequent request; Load Balancer routes it to Node B. 3. Node B reads the 16-byte Key Identifier, finds no matching key in its local memory, rejects the ticket, and forces a full handshake.
Under this configuration, the fleet’s session resumption rate drops significantly, proportional to the number of nodes.
To achieve consistent session resumption across a fleet, all nodes behind the load balancer must share identical STEK key chains.
                               Centralized STEK Generator
                               (Rotates keys every 1 hr)
                                           |
                    +----------------------+----------------------+
                    | Push active + decryption key list           |
                    v                                             v
        +-----------------------+                     +-----------------------+
        |   Node A (Primary: K2) |                     |   Node B (Primary: K2) |
        |   Keys: [K2, K1]      |                     |   Keys: [K2, K1]      |
        +-----------------------+                     +-----------------------+


Key Rotation Lifecycle
A rotation scheme keeps a short window of keys:

Encryption key: encrypts every new ticket.
Previous keys: decrypt tickets issued before the last rotation, for one ticket lifetime.
Next key (HAProxy’s model): distributed one period early and accepted for decryption, so a node that rotates a few seconds before its neighbours does not break resumption on them.

Time Window T0:   Active: [ Key A (Encrypt/Decrypt) ]
Time Window T1:   Active: [ Key B (Encrypt/Decrypt) ], Secondary: [ Key A (Decrypt) ]
Time Window T2:   Active: [ Key C (Encrypt/Decrypt) ], Secondary: [ Key B (Decrypt) ] (Key A retired)
With OpenSSL’s default lifetime of 7,200 seconds, keep a retired encryption key for decryption for at least two more hours. Keeping it longer buys nothing: the server rejects older tickets on age anyway.


Multi-Tenant SNI Boundaries
RFC 8446 section 4.6.1 puts the rule on the client: it MUST only resume if the new SNI is valid for the certificate of the original session, and SHOULD only resume if the SNI is the same. Nothing in the protocol stops a server from accepting a ticket under a different name, and section 7 of the lab shows OpenSSL client and server resuming an a.lab session with SNI b.lab, because the certificate covers both.
That matters wherever one terminator serves many tenants: a session authenticated for one virtual host (including any client-certificate authentication) can be carried into another that shares the ticket key. Scope ticket keys to a trust boundary: one key set per tenant or per group of names that may share sessions. Where the software allows, also check the hostname recorded in the resumed session against the new SNI.

title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
text:
The lab
The following hands-on lab demonstrates session resumption behaviors in OpenSSL and Python. It consists of three primary scripts:

tlslab.py: A Python test suite using the ssl module to evaluate stateless vs stateful tickets, server restarts, multi-node fleets, and SNI isolation.
cli.sh: A shell script using openssl s_server and openssl s_client to inspect session structures, ticket reuse, and anti-replay fallback mechanisms.
srvcpu.py: A benchmark tool measuring server CPU consumption across full and resumed handshakes using ECDSA, RSA, and post-quantum hybrid groups.


Lab files
Before running the scripts, execute the certificate generation script to establish the local PKI test assets.
mkcerts.sh:
#!/bin/sh
# Self-signed lab certificates: one ECDSA P-256, one RSA-2048, both for a.lab and b.lab
set -e
for k in ec rsa; do
  if [ $k = ec ]; then alg="-newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256"; else alg="-newkey rsa:2048"; fi
  openssl req -x509 $alg -nodes -days 2 -subj /CN=a.lab \
    -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:a.lab,DNS:b.lab" -keyout $k-key.pem -out $k-cert.pem 2>/dev/null
done
ls ec-*.pem rsa-*.pem
tlslab.py:
"""TLS session resumption lab: tickets, ticket keys, fleets and cost (stdlib only)."""
import socket, ssl, sys, threading, time

def server_ctx(cert="ec", tls12=False, no_ticket=False, tickets=None):
    c = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
    c.load_cert_chain(f"{cert}-cert.pem", f"{cert}-key.pem")
    if tls12:
        c.maximum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2
    if no_ticket:
        c.options |= ssl.OP_NO_TICKET
    if tickets is not None:
        c.num_tickets = tickets
    return c

class Node:
    """One TLS listener on 127.0.0.1 that answers each connection with b'hi'."""
    def __init__(self, ctx):
        self.ctx, self.sock = ctx, socket.create_server(("127.0.0.1", 0))
        self.port = self.sock.getsockname()[1]
        threading.Thread(target=self.loop, daemon=True).start()
    def loop(self):
        while True:
            raw, _ = self.sock.accept()
            try:
                with self.ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_side=True) as s:
                    s.recv(16); s.sendall(b"hi")
            except (ssl.SSLError, OSError):
                pass

CLIENT = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)
CLIENT.check_hostname = False
CLIENT.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE

def connect(node, session=None, sni="a.lab"):
    """Return (reused, new_session, tls_version, seconds)."""
    t = time.perf_counter()
    with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", node.port)) as raw:
        with CLIENT.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname=sni, session=session) as s:
            s.sendall(b"x"); s.recv(16)   # read, so TLS 1.3 tickets sent after the handshake arrive
            return s.session_reused, s.session, s.version(), time.perf_counter() - t

def show(label, r):
    print(f"  {label:44} reused={str(r[0]):5} {r[2]}")

def part(title):
    print(f"\n== {title}")

part("1. full handshake, then resume with the saved session (TLS 1.3, defaults)")
n = Node(server_ctx())
r1 = connect(n); show("first connection", r1)
s = r1[1]
print(f"  saved session: has_ticket={s.has_ticket} ticket_lifetime_hint={s.ticket_lifetime_hint}s timeout={s.timeout}s")
print(f"  server num_tickets={n.ctx.num_tickets}")
r2 = connect(n, s); show("second connection, session from first", r2)
r3 = connect(n, s); show("third connection, SAME session again", r3)

part("2. stateless vs stateful TLS 1.3 tickets: where the state lives")
for label, kw in [("stateless (default)", {}), ("stateful (OP_NO_TICKET)", {"no_ticket": True})]:
    n = Node(server_ctx(**kw))
    for _ in range(50):
        connect(n)
    s = connect(n)[1]
    show(f"{label}: resume", connect(n, s))
    show(f"{label}: resume same ticket again", connect(n, s))
    st = n.ctx.session_stats()
    print(f"    server session cache: number={st['number']} hits={st['hits']} misses={st['misses']}")

part("3. num_tickets=0: server issues no tickets")
n = Node(server_ctx(tickets=0))
r = connect(n); print(f"  session after connection: has_ticket={r[1].has_ticket}")
show("try to resume", connect(n, r[1]))

part("4. server restart = new ticket key")
ctx = server_ctx(); n = Node(ctx)
s = connect(n)[1]
show("same process, same key", connect(n, s))
n2 = Node(server_ctx())      # a fresh SSLContext gets a fresh random ticket key
show("restarted server (new SSLContext)", connect(n2, s))

part("5. two-node fleet behind round-robin, 200 connections, client keeps latest session")
def fleet(nodes, n_conn=200):
    sess, reused = None, 0
    for i in range(n_conn):
        r = connect(nodes[i % len(nodes)], sess)
        reused += r[0]; sess = r[1]
    return reused
print(f"  per-node keys (two SSLContexts): resumed {fleet([Node(server_ctx()), Node(server_ctx())])}/200")
shared = server_ctx()
print(f"  shared key   (one SSLContext)  : resumed {fleet([Node(shared), Node(shared)])}/200")

part("6. TLS 1.2: session tickets vs session-ID cache")
for label, kw in [("tickets (default)", {}), ("session IDs only (OP_NO_TICKET)", {"no_ticket": True})]:
    shared = server_ctx(tls12=True, **kw)
    a, b = Node(shared), Node(server_ctx(tls12=True, **kw))
    s = connect(a)[1]
    print(f"  {label}: has_ticket={s.has_ticket}")
    show("    same context", connect(a, s))
    show("    other node, own context", connect(b, s))

part("7. SNI changes between connections")
n = Node(server_ctx())
s = connect(n, sni="a.lab")[1]
try:
    show("resume a.lab session while sending SNI b.lab", connect(n, s, sni="b.lab"))
except Exception as e:
    print(f"  resume a.lab session while sending SNI b.lab -> {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

print(f"\n{ssl.OPENSSL_VERSION}, Python {sys.version.split()[0]}")
cli.sh:
#!/bin/sh
# openssl s_server / s_client / s_time view of the same mechanics (loopback only)
P=44330
srv() { tail -f /dev/null | openssl s_server -quiet -accept $P -cert ${CERT:-ec}-cert.pem -key ${CERT:-ec}-key.pem "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1 & S=$!; sleep 0.5; }
stop() { pkill -f "s_server -quiet -accept $P"; wait 2>/dev/null; }
cli() { sleep 0.3 | openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:$P -servername a.lab "$@" 2>/dev/null; }
reuse() { cli "$@" | grep -E "^(New|Reused),|^Negotiated TLS1.3 group|^Peer signature type" | sed 's/^/    /'; }

echo "== A. stateless tickets (default): save, inspect, resume twice"
srv
cli -sess_out t.pem >/dev/null
openssl sess_id -in t.pem -noout -text | grep -E "Protocol|Cipher|Session-ID:|Resumption PSK|lifetime hint|Timeout|Max Early" | sed 's/Resumption PSK: .*/Resumption PSK: (48 bytes, elided)/; s/Session-ID: .*/Session-ID: (32 bytes, elided)/' | sed 's/^/    /'
echo "  resume 1:"; reuse -sess_in t.pem
echo "  resume 2 (same ticket):"; reuse -sess_in t.pem
stop

echo "== B. stateful tickets + early data enabled (anti-replay on): single use"
srv -no_ticket -max_early_data 1024
cli -sess_out t2.pem >/dev/null
echo "  resume 1:"; reuse -sess_in t2.pem
echo "  resume 2 (same ticket):"; reuse -sess_in t2.pem
stop

echo "== C. stateless tickets + early data enabled (anti-replay on)"
srv -max_early_data 1024
cli -sess_out t3.pem >/dev/null
echo "  resume 1:"; reuse -sess_in t3.pem
echo "  resume 2 (same ticket):"; reuse -sess_in t3.pem
stop
srvcpu.py:
"""Server-side CPU per handshake: drive a real openssl s_server, read its CPU time from /proc."""
import os, socket, ssl, subprocess, sys, time
HZ = os.sysconf("SC_CLK_TCK")
def cpu(pid):
    f = open(f"/proc/{pid}/stat").read().rsplit(")", 1)[1].split()
    return (int(f[11]) + int(f[12])) / HZ          # utime + stime, seconds
ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT); ctx.check_hostname = False; ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
def conn(port, sess=None):
    with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port)) as raw, ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname="a.lab", session=sess) as s:
        s.sendall(b"GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n"); s.recv(64)
        return s.session_reused, s.session
N = 2000
for i, (cert, group) in enumerate([(c, g) for g in ("X25519MLKEM768", "X25519") for c in ("ec", "rsa")]):
    port = 44400 + i
    p = subprocess.Popen(["openssl", "s_server", "-quiet", "-www", "-accept", str(port), "-cert", f"{cert}-cert.pem",
                          "-key", f"{cert}-key.pem", "-groups", group], stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    time.sleep(0.5)
    _, sess = conn(port)
    c0 = cpu(p.pid)
    for _ in range(N): conn(port)
    c1 = cpu(p.pid)
    hits = 0
    for _ in range(N):
        r, s2 = conn(port, sess); hits += r
    c2 = cpu(p.pid)
    p.kill(); p.wait()
    full, res = (c1 - c0) / N * 1e6, (c2 - c1) / N * 1e6
    print(f"  {group:14} {cert:3} cert: server CPU per full handshake {full:6.0f} us, per resumed {res:6.0f} us ({hits}/{N} resumed)  ratio {full/res:.1f}x")

title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
text:
Reading the output
Analyzing the laboratory outputs reveals the practical mechanics of session resumption.

Reading tlslab.py Output

Part 1: Default TLS 1.3 Resumption
== 1. full handshake, then resume with the saved session (TLS 1.3, defaults)
  first connection                             reused=False TLSv1.3
  saved session: has_ticket=True ticket_lifetime_hint=7200s timeout=7200s
  server num_tickets=2
  second connection, session from first        reused=True  TLSv1.3
  third connection, SAME session again         reused=True  TLSv1.3

Connection 1 is a full handshake (reused=False).
OpenSSL’s default configuration issues 2 tickets post-handshake (num_tickets=2), each configured with a 7200-second (2-hour) lifetime hint.
Subsequent connections using the saved session object return reused=True. With no early data configured there is no replay protection, so the same stateless ticket works any number of times.



Part 2: Stateless vs Stateful State Locations
== 2. stateless vs stateful TLS 1.3 tickets: where the state lives
  stateless (default): resume                  reused=True  TLSv1.3
  stateless (default): resume same ticket again reused=True  TLSv1.3
    server session cache: number=0 hits=2 misses=0
  stateful (OP_NO_TICKET): resume              reused=True  TLSv1.3
  stateful (OP_NO_TICKET): resume same ticket again reused=True  TLSv1.3
    server session cache: number=104 hits=2 misses=0

In stateless mode, the server session cache counter remains number=0. The session state is embedded within the client’s ticket payload, so the server maintains zero local cache allocations.
In stateful mode (SSL_OP_NO_TICKET), the server session cache contains number=104 entries. This is calculated as 52 initial connections multiplied by 2 tickets issued per connection. Here, SSL_OP_NO_TICKET does not disable resumption; instead, it forces ticket state to reside in the server’s local RAM cache.



Part 3: Disabling Tickets Entirely
== 3. num_tickets=0: server issues no tickets
  session after connection: has_ticket=False
  try to resume                                reused=False TLSv1.3

When SSL_CTX_set_num_tickets(0) is configured, the server emits no NewSessionTicket messages.
The client receives no ticket data (has_ticket=False), preventing subsequent session resumption attempts.



Part 4: Server Restart Effects
== 4. server restart = new ticket key
  same process, same key                       reused=True  TLSv1.3
  restarted server (new SSLContext)            reused=False TLSv1.3

A new SSLContext gets a fresh random ticket key when it is created.
Restarting the server process invalidates all previously issued tickets because the new instance cannot decrypt tickets encrypted by the previous instance’s STEK.



Part 5: Multi-Node Fleet Simulation
== 5. two-node fleet behind round-robin, 200 connections, client keeps latest session
  per-node keys (two SSLContexts): resumed 0/200
  shared key   (one SSLContext)  : resumed 199/200

In a two-node round-robin setup where each node maintains its own independent STEK, the client stores only the most recently received ticket. Because each subsequent request alternates to the sibling node, ticket validation fails every time (resumed 0/200).
When both nodes share the same STEK, 199 out of 200 connections resume successfully (with only the initial connection requiring a full handshake).



Part 6: TLS 1.2 Stateless vs Stateful
== 6. TLS 1.2: session tickets vs session-ID cache
  tickets (default): has_ticket=True
      same context                             reused=True  TLSv1.2
      other node, own context                  reused=False TLSv1.2
  session IDs only (OP_NO_TICKET): has_ticket=False
      same context                             reused=True  TLSv1.2
      other node, own context                  reused=False TLSv1.2

In TLS 1.2, session tickets and Session IDs operate as separate paths.
With OP_NO_TICKET enabled in TLS 1.2, has_ticket is False. Resumption falls back to the 32-byte Session ID cache, which succeeds within the same context but fails across isolated nodes.



Part 7: Cross-SNI Ticket Reuse
== 7. SNI changes between connections
  resume a.lab session while sending SNI b.lab reused=True  TLSv1.3

The test demonstrates that an OpenSSL client presenting a ticket acquired from a.lab while requesting SNI b.lab will resume successfully if the server processes both names within the same SSLContext and the underlying certificate is valid for both hostnames. This highlights the importance of scoping ticket contexts per tenant in multi-tenant environments.




Reading cli.sh Output
== A. stateless tickets (default): save, inspect, resume twice
        Protocol  : TLSv1.3
        Cipher    : TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
        Session-ID: (32 bytes, elided)
        Resumption PSK: (48 bytes, elided)
        TLS session ticket lifetime hint: 7200 (seconds)
        Timeout   : 7200 (sec)
        Max Early Data: 0
  resume 1:
    Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768
    Reused, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  resume 2 (same ticket):
    Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768
    Reused, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
In section A, without anti-replay protection configured, the client reuses the exact same saved session file twice. Both attempts negotiate the X25519MLKEM768 key exchange group, confirming that TLS 1.3 psk_dhe_ke performs a Diffie-Hellman key exchange on resumption.
== B. stateful tickets + early data enabled (anti-replay on): single use
  resume 1:
    Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768
    Reused, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  resume 2 (same ticket):
    Peer signature type: ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256
    Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768
    New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
In section B, setting -max_early_data 1024 enables OpenSSL’s internal anti-replay mechanism.

On resume 1, the ticket is accepted (Reused, TLSv1.3) and OpenSSL removes the session from its internal cache.
On resume 2, the same ticket finds no cache entry, so the server performs a full TLS 1.3 handshake. The client sent no early data at all.
The appearance of the line Peer signature type: ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 in resume 2 confirms that an asymmetric signature was calculated by the server, proving that a full handshake occurred instead of resumption.

Section C shows the same result without -no_ticket: with early data enabled OpenSSL switches to stateful tickets on its own, so there is no “stateless and single use” mode.


Reading srvcpu.py Output
  X25519MLKEM768 ec  cert: server CPU per full handshake    385 us, per resumed    300 us (2000/2000 resumed)  ratio 1.3x
  X25519MLKEM768 rsa cert: server CPU per full handshake    600 us, per resumed    305 us (2000/2000 resumed)  ratio 2.0x
  X25519         ec  cert: server CPU per full handshake    315 us, per resumed    255 us (2000/2000 resumed)  ratio 1.2x
  X25519         rsa cert: server CPU per full handshake    530 us, per resumed    245 us (2000/2000 resumed)  ratio 2.2x
The microbenchmark results quantify the server CPU time required for full versus resumed handshakes across different crypto configurations:

Baseline Protocol Overhead: The execution CPU baseline for a resumed connection ranges between 245 µs and 305 µs. This baseline represents TCP connection handling, socket I/O, event processing, and memory allocation within openssl s_server.
RSA-2048 Optimization Impact:

Full handshake with RSA-2048 certificates requires 530 µs to 600 µs per connection due to private key signature calculations.
Resuming an RSA session drops CPU execution time to 245 µs – 305 µs, achieving a 2.0x to 2.2x performance improvement.
Session resumption saves approximately 280 µs to 300 µs of server CPU processing per connection by eliminating the RSA signature operation.

ECDSA P-256 Optimization Impact:

Full handshakes using ECDSA P-256 require 315 µs to 385 µs per connection.
Resuming an ECDSA session reduces execution time to 255 µs – 300 µs, yielding a smaller 1.2x to 1.3x speedup.
Because ECDSA P-256 signatures are computationally lighter than RSA-2048 operations, session resumption saves 60 µs to 85 µs of CPU time per connection.

Post-Quantum Hybrid Group Overhead (X25519MLKEM768):

Evaluating X25519MLKEM768 relative to standard X25519 shows a modest CPU overhead increment of 55 µs to 70 µs across both full and resumed connection modes.
Because TLS 1.3 psk_dhe_ke executes key agreement on resumed connections, post-quantum key exchange calculations affect both initial and resumed handshakes.

title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
text:
In production
Implementing session resumption across web server fleets requires configuring primary edge software to manage STEK lifecycles and ticket distribution.

NGINX Configuration
In NGINX, stateless session ticket decryption is configured using the ssl_session_ticket_key directive within the http or server context.
# (not run here) nginx.conf
http {
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

    # Enable server-side session cache as fallback for TLS 1.2 / stateful modes
    ssl_session_cache   shared:SSL:50m;
    ssl_session_timeout 1d;

    # Configure STEK key file list
    # The first file listed is used to ENCRYPT new tickets.
    # Subsequent files are used strictly to DECRYPT existing client tickets.
    ssl_session_ticket_key /etc/nginx/stek/active.key;
    ssl_session_ticket_key /etc/nginx/stek/prev_1h.key;
    ssl_session_ticket_key /etc/nginx/stek/prev_2h.key;

    # Define custom log format to monitor session resumption rates
    log_format ssl_monitor '$remote_addr - [$time_local] "$request" '
                           'ssl_proto=$ssl_protocol ssl_cipher=$ssl_cipher '
                           'ssl_reused=$ssl_session_reused';

    access_log /var/log/nginx/access.log ssl_monitor;
}


HAProxy Configuration
HAProxy defines ticket key chains within its global settings and allows dynamic, zero-downtime key rotation via its Unix Control Socket.
# (not run here) haproxy.cfg
global
    # tls_keys: base64 keys, one per line (openssl rand 80 | openssl base64 -A).
    # The last 3 keys are used (TLS_TICKETS_NO build default): the penultimate
    # encrypts, all three decrypt. Rotate by appending a key and reloading.
    stats socket /var/run/haproxy.sock mode 660 level admin

frontend tls_in
    bind :443 ssl crt /etc/haproxy/certs/site.pem tls-ticket-keys /etc/haproxy/stek/tls_keys.bin
    mode http
    default_backend web_servers


Generating and Rotating STEKs
To generate an 80-byte OpenSSL-compatible STEK file:
# (not run here)
# Generate an 80-byte random binary STEK key
openssl rand 80 > /etc/nginx/stek/active.key
chmod 0400 /etc/nginx/stek/active.key
A production STEK rotation pipeline typically executes the following workflow:
# (not run here)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Production STEK Rotation Script (hourly execution)
STEK_DIR="/etc/nginx/stek"

# Rotate file hierarchy
mv "${STEK_DIR}/prev_1h.key" "${STEK_DIR}/prev_2h.key" 2>/dev/null || true
mv "${STEK_DIR}/active.key"  "${STEK_DIR}/prev_1h.key" 2>/dev/null || true

# Generate new primary key
openssl rand 80 > "${STEK_DIR}/active.key"
chmod 0400 "${STEK_DIR}"/*.key

# Reload NGINX gracefully to load updated key paths
systemctl reload nginx
For HAProxy, key chains can be updated dynamically at runtime without reloading the process:
# (not run here)
echo "show tls-keys" | socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock
# add the next key; it becomes the last one, the previous last one starts encrypting
echo "set ssl tls-key /etc/haproxy/stek/tls_keys $(openssl rand 80 | openssl base64 -A)" | socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock
The runtime command changes one process only. Push the same key to every node, or the fleet is back to per-node keys.


Monitoring Resumption Metrics and Client Behavior

Verification via NGINX Access Logs
Monitor the $ssl_session_reused log variable in NGINX. A healthy fleet architecture should demonstrate a session reuse ratio exceeding 80% for recurring client traffic patterns:
# (not run here)
awk '{print $NF}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c
$ssl_session_reused is r for a resumed session and . otherwise. Count per connection, not per request: keep-alive requests on one connection all repeat the same value.


Verification via OpenSSL CLI
To verify that an external endpoint supports session resumption over the network:
# (not run here)
# five reconnects with the first session: look for "Reused" vs "New"
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -reconnect < /dev/null | grep -E '^(New|Reused),'
# the same test restricted to TLS 1.2 session IDs
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -tls1_2 -no_ticket -reconnect < /dev/null | grep -E '^(New|Reused),'


Client Diagnostics (curl and Session Caching)
curl keeps TLS sessions in memory for the life of one process, so resumption only happens between URLs fetched in the same invocation. --no-sessionid turns that off, which is useful when you want every connection of a test to pay for a full handshake:
# (not run here)
curl -sv -o /dev/null -o /dev/null https://example.com/ https://example.com/ 2>&1 | grep -i 'resum\|reus'
curl --no-sessionid -sv -o /dev/null -o /dev/null https://example.com/ https://example.com/

title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
text:
Gotchas

SSL_OP_NO_TICKET in TLS 1.3 does not disable resumption: Setting SSL_OP_NO_TICKET switches OpenSSL from stateless client tickets to stateful server-cached tickets. To completely disable session ticket issuance in TLS 1.3, call SSL_CTX_set_num_tickets(0).
Anti-replay protection forces single-use tickets: Enabling early data (max_early_data > 0) causes OpenSSL to record ticket identities in an anti-replay cache. Presenting the same ticket twice triggers fallback to a full handshake.
psk_dhe_ke does not bypass key exchange latency: While TLS 1.3 session resumption skips asymmetric signature generation, it still performs an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange. It saves CPU cycles, but does not eliminate key agreement computation.
A node with different key bytes fails silently: nothing logs an error when a ticket fails to decrypt; the client just gets a full handshake. Watch the resumption rate per node after every key push.
Early data makes OpenSSL tickets node-local: with max_early_data above zero, replay protection turns tickets stateful and single use, so a shared ticket key no longer helps clients that move between nodes (sections B and C).
Patch the terminator: CVE-2026-97629 is an nginx bug, not an HAProxy one. When automatic TLS session-ticket key rotation was in use — shared ssl_session_cache without an explicit ssl_session_ticket_key file — one of the three in-memory keys was left uninitialised, which “might allow to forge a session” and, on servers that verify client certificates, skip that check. nginx 1.31.7 (mainline) and 1.30.6 (stable), both released 14 October 2026, fix it. The vulnerable range is 1.23.2 through 1.31.6. Workarounds on an unpatched build are ssl_session_tickets off; or loading managed keys with ssl_session_ticket_key, which leaves the automatic-rotation path. See the nginx security advisories and the 1.31.7 / 1.30.6 CHANGES entries. HAProxy is not listed as affected.
Unsynchronized STEKs break multi-node fleets: Deploying edge termination nodes behind a round-robin load balancer without shared STEKs causes session resumption rates to drop toward zero.
Long-lived ticket keys undo forward secrecy: a key kept for months lets whoever steals it decrypt every recorded TLS 1.2 session from those months and impersonate the server to TLS 1.3 ticket holders. Rotate on a schedule and keep keys off disk.
Multi-tenant cross-SNI resumption vulnerabilities: Sharing a single SSLContext or STEK across separate tenant domains can allow clients to resume sessions across distinct virtual hosts if SNI validation callbacks are omitted.
Restarts invalidate generated keys: without configured key files, nginx, HAProxy and OpenSSL generate random keys at startup, so every restart or deploy turns all outstanding tickets into full handshakes (section 4). nginx 1.23.2 and later rotate generated keys automatically when ssl_session_cache uses shared memory.

title: TLS Session Resumption in Practice: Tickets, Ticket Keys and Fleets
text:
Exercises

Calculate Fleet Cache Hit Rate Probability: Given a fleet of \(N\) web nodes operating behind a layer-4 round-robin load balancer without shared STEKs, write a mathematical expression representing the probability \(P\) that a returning client successfully resumes its session on its second request. Evaluate \(P\) for \(N = 2, 5, 10\).
Rotation without a cliff: extend the fleet test in tlslab.py to three nodes that share one SSLContext while a fourth uses its own. Predict the resumption rate for round-robin and for random node choice, then measure both.
Configure NGINX TLS Session Cache Isolation: Construct an NGINX configuration snippet featuring two separate server blocks matching tenant-a.lab and tenant-b.lab. Configure distinct ssl_session_ticket_key paths for each server block and demonstrate that a session ticket generated by tenant-a is rejected when presented to tenant-b.
Benchmarking Post-Quantum Hybrid Group Impact: Modify srvcpu.py to benchmark performance across X25519, SecP256r1, and post-quantum hybrid modes (X25519MLKEM768). Compute the percentage CPU overhead increase introduced by post-quantum key exchange during full versus resumed handshakes.
Clean shutdown matters for stateful tickets: run cli.sh section B again, but kill s_client before it sends close_notify on the first connection. Per the s_server manual the server then drops the session from its cache; confirm that resume 1 becomes a full handshake.
Diagnose Single-Use Ticket Behavior under 0-RTT: Execute cli.sh using openssl s_client and openssl s_server with early data enabled (-early_data). Capture wire outputs showing ticket rejection and full handshake fallback when presenting the same ticket twice.

Unexecuted Production Examples

STEK rotation shell scripts and dynamic socket commands (socat) are provided as production reference designs and were not executed during the automated lab run.

title: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt
text: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt

title: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt
text:
Learning goals

Explain why hashing or truncating client IPs is a weak way to share network logs, and what keyed, invertible IP encryption gives you.
Choose between IPCrypt’s three families: deterministic, prefix-preserving (ipcrypt-pfx) and non-deterministic (ipcrypt-nd / ipcrypt-ndx). Each one keeps different analytics possible and leaks different things.
Implement three of the modes in about 70 lines of Python and check them against the specification’s test vectors.
Spot the operational traps: equal pfx key halves, IPv4 turning into IPv6, and blobs that are no longer IP addresses.

Version note: this follows draft-denis-ipcrypt-14 (Informational, IETF Internet-Draft, Barber & Denis, expires February 2027). The labs ran on 31 Oct 2026 with Python 3.13 and the cryptography 43 package already on the box. No installs were needed. All addresses come from the documentation ranges (RFC 5737, RFC 3849), and the keys are demo values only. The output blocks are pasted from the runs.



The four IPCrypt modes, what each output looks like and which log questions still work.

title: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt
section: Why not just hash or truncate?
text:
Why not just hash or truncate?
The common shortcuts each fail in a different way:

Unkeyed hashes of IPv4 addresses are not private. There are only 2^32 inputs, so anyone can hash them all and reverse the mapping.
Truncation (zeroing the last octet) destroys the data you need for abuse handling, and still identifies small networks.
Ad hoc encryption with a library’s default mode gives outputs that are not addresses, so they break every downstream tool.

The draft’s motivation (§1.1) is to provide a common, specified set of constructions with test vectors, so that two implementations of the same mode, with the same key, produce the same output.

title: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt
text:
The modes in one table










Mode
Construction (draft §)
Output
Same IP, same output?
Keeps subnet structure?




ipcrypt-deterministic
one AES-128 block, 16-byte key (§5.1)
16 bytes, an IPv6 address
yes
no


ipcrypt-pfx
per-bit PRF = AES(K1)⊕AES(K2), 32-byte key (§6.2)
native size: IPv4 stays IPv4
yes
yes


ipcrypt-nd
KIASU-BC, 8-byte random tweak (§7.4.1)
24 bytes
no
no


ipcrypt-ndx
single-block AES-XTS, 16-byte random tweak (§7.4.2)
32 bytes
no
no



All four modes are invertible with the key. The draft states plainly that they provide confidentiality, not integrity (§8): someone who can edit the log can still swap or forge ciphertexts.
Every mode except pfx first maps an address to 16 bytes, turning IPv4 into ::ffff:a.b.c.d (§3.1.2). That is why 192.0.2.1 and ::ffff:192.0.2.1 encrypt identically.

title: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt
section: Lab 1: implement it and check the test vectors
text:
Lab 1: implement it and check the test vectors
ipcrypt.py covers deterministic, pfx and ndx. ipcrypt-nd is left out because KIASU-BC (AES with a tweak mixed into every round key) is not in standard crypto libraries. The pfx loop follows the draft’s §9.6 pseudocode. The PRF input at each step is zeros || 1 || prefix-so-far, where the prefix is always the plaintext prefix. That is what makes equal prefixes encrypt to equal prefixes.
"""ipcrypt-deterministic, ipcrypt-pfx and ipcrypt-ndx, following
draft-denis-ipcrypt-14 sections 3, 5.1, 6.2, 7.4.2 and 9.  AES from `cryptography`."""
import ipaddress, os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes

def aes(key, block, dec=False):
    c = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.ECB())
    op = c.decryptor() if dec else c.encryptor()
    return op.update(block) + op.finalize()

def to16(ip):                      # section 3.1: IPv4 -> ::ffff:a.b.c.d
    a = ipaddress.ip_address(ip)
    if a.version == 4:
        return bytes(10) + b"\xff\xff" + a.packed
    return a.packed

def from16(b):                     # section 3.2
    if b[:12] == bytes(10) + b"\xff\xff":
        return str(ipaddress.IPv4Address(b[12:]))
    return str(ipaddress.IPv6Address(b))

def xor(a, b): return bytes(x ^ y for x, y in zip(a, b))

# --- 5.1 ipcrypt-deterministic: one AES-128 block --------------------------
def det_encrypt(ip, key): return from16(aes(key, to16(ip)))
def det_decrypt(ip, key): return from16(aes(key, to16(ip), dec=True))

# --- 6.2 / 9.6 ipcrypt-pfx: one PRF bit per address bit ----------------------
def _get(d, pos): return (d[15 - pos // 8] >> (pos % 8)) & 1
def _set(d, pos, v): d[15 - pos // 8] |= (v & 1) << (pos % 8)
def _shl(d):
    r, carry = bytearray(16), 0
    for i in range(15, -1, -1):
        r[i] = ((d[i] << 1) | carry) & 0xFF
        carry = (d[i] >> 7) & 1
    return r

def _pfx(ip, key, decrypt):
    assert len(key) == 32
    k1, k2 = key[:16], key[16:]
    src = to16(ip)
    out = bytearray(16)
    pad = bytearray(16)
    if src[:12] == bytes(10) + b"\xff\xff":
        start = 96; out[10] = out[11] = 0xFF
        pad[3] = 0x01; pad[14] = pad[15] = 0xFF
    else:
        start = 0; pad[15] = 0x01
    for n in range(start, 128):
        e = xor(aes(k1, bytes(pad)), aes(k2, bytes(pad)))
        pos = 127 - n
        bit = _get(src, pos) ^ (e[15] & 1)
        _set(out, pos, bit)
        plain_bit = bit if decrypt else _get(src, pos)
        pad = _shl(pad); _set(pad, 0, plain_bit)   # prefix is always the PLAINTEXT prefix
    return from16(bytes(out))

def pfx_encrypt(ip, key): return _pfx(ip, key, False)
def pfx_decrypt(ip, key): return _pfx(ip, key, True)

# --- 7.4.2 / 9.8 ipcrypt-ndx: single-block AES-XTS (XEX), random 16-byte tweak
def ndx_encrypt(ip, key, tweak=None):
    tweak = tweak or os.urandom(16)
    et = aes(key[16:], tweak)
    return tweak + xor(aes(key[:16], xor(to16(ip), et)), et)

def ndx_decrypt(blob, key):
    tweak, c = blob[:16], blob[16:]
    et = aes(key[16:], tweak)
    return from16(xor(aes(key[:16], xor(c, et), dec=True), et))
vectors.py checks every encryption against the draft’s Appendix A and decrypts it back:
# Check ipcrypt.py against draft-denis-ipcrypt-14 Appendix A (A.1, A.2, A.4).
from ipcrypt import *
H = bytes.fromhex
det = [("0123456789abcdeffedcba9876543210", "0.0.0.0", "bde9:6789:d353:824c:d7c6:f58a:6bd2:26eb"),
       ("1032547698badcfeefcdab8967452301", "255.255.255.255", "aed2:92f6:ea23:58c3:48fd:8b8:74e8:45d8"),
       ("2b7e151628aed2a6abf7158809cf4f3c", "192.0.2.1", "1dbd:c1b9:fff1:7586:7d0b:67b4:e76e:4777")]
K1 = "0123456789abcdeffedcba98765432101032547698badcfeefcdab8967452301"
K2 = "2b7e151628aed2a6abf7158809cf4f3ca9f5ba40db214c3798f2e1c23456789a"
pfx = [(K1, "0.0.0.0", "151.82.155.134"), (K1, "255.255.255.255", "94.185.169.89"),
       (K1, "192.0.2.1", "100.115.72.131"), (K1, "2001:db8::1", "c180:5dd4:2587:3524:30ab:fa65:6ab6:f88"),
       (K2, "10.0.0.47", "19.214.210.244"), (K2, "10.0.0.129", "19.214.210.80"),
       (K2, "172.16.5.193", "210.78.229.136"), (K2, "172.16.97.42", "210.78.179.241"),
       (K2, "2001:db8::a5c9:4e2f:bb91:5a7d", "7cec:702c:1243:f70:1956:125:b9bd:1aba"),
       (K2, "2001:db8:3a5c:0:e7d1:4b9f:2c8a:f673", "7cec:702c:3503:bef:e616:96bd:be33:a9b9")]
ndx = [("0123456789abcdeffedcba98765432101032547698badcfeefcdab8967452301", "0.0.0.0",
        "21bd1834bc088cd2b4ecbe30b70898d7", "21bd1834bc088cd2b4ecbe30b70898d782db0d4125fdace61db35b8339f20ee5"),
       ("2b7e151628aed2a6abf7158809cf4f3c3c4fcf098815f7aba6d2ae2816157e2b", "2001:db8::1",
        "21bd1834bc088cd2b4ecbe30b70898d7", "21bd1834bc088cd2b4ecbe30b70898d76089c7e05ae30c2d10ca149870a263e4")]
ok = 0; total = 0
for k, ip, want in det:
    got = det_encrypt(ip, H(k)); back = det_decrypt(got, H(k)); total += 1
    ok += got == want and back == ip
    print(f"det  {ip:<36} -> {got:<40} {'OK' if got == want and back == ip else 'FAIL'}")
for k, ip, want in pfx:
    got = pfx_encrypt(ip, H(k)); back = pfx_decrypt(got, H(k)); total += 1
    ok += got == want and back == ip
    print(f"pfx  {ip:<36} -> {got:<40} {'OK' if got == want and back == ip else 'FAIL'}")
for k, ip, tw, want in ndx:
    got = ndx_encrypt(ip, H(k), H(tw)).hex(); back = ndx_decrypt(H(got), H(k)); total += 1
    ok += got == want and back == ip
    print(f"ndx  {ip:<36} -> {got[32:]:<40} {'OK' if got == want and back == ip else 'FAIL'}")
print(f"{ok}/{total} Appendix A vectors match (encrypt and decrypt round-trip)")
$ python3 vectors.py

det  255.255.255.255                      -> aed2:92f6:ea23:58c3:48fd:8b8:74e8:45d8   OK

pfx  10.0.0.129                           -> 19.214.210.80                            OK

title: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt
section: Lab 2: anonymise a log, then ask analyst questions
text:
Lab 2: anonymise a log, then ask analyst questions
A tiny access log:
198.51.100.7 GET /login 200
198.51.100.7 POST /login 401
198.51.100.7 POST /login 401
198.51.100.42 POST /login 401
203.0.113.9 GET / 200
2001:db8:1::5 GET /api 200
2001:db8:1::5 GET /api 200
2001:db8:2::77 GET /api 503
logs.py encrypts it in each mode, then asks the questions an analyst would ask: how many distinct clients, who failed login most, and how traffic splits per subnet.
# Anonymise access.log three ways, then ask the questions an analyst asks.
import ipaddress, os, collections
from ipcrypt import *
k16 = bytes.fromhex("000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f")              # demo keys only
k32 = bytes.fromhex("000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f" "f0e1d2c3b4a5968778695a4b3c2d1e0f")
rows = [l.split(" ", 1) for l in open("access.log").read().splitlines()]
modes_ = {"deterministic": lambda ip: det_encrypt(ip, k16),
          "pfx":           lambda ip: pfx_encrypt(ip, k32),
          "ndx":           lambda ip: ndx_encrypt(ip, k32).hex()}
for name, f in modes_.items():
    out = [(f(ip), rest) for ip, rest in rows]
    print(f"== {name}")
    for ip, rest in out: print(f"   {ip:<66} {rest}")
    ips = [ip for ip, _ in out]
    print(f"   distinct clients seen: {len(set(ips))} (true: {len(set(i for i, _ in rows))})")
    fails = collections.Counter(ip for ip, r in out if r.endswith("401"))
    print(f"   top failed-login source: {fails.most_common(1)[0]}")
    if name == "pfx":
        nets = collections.Counter(str(ipaddress.ip_network(ip + ("/24" if "." in ip else "/48"), strict=False))
                                   for ip in ips)
        print(f"   requests per encrypted /24 or /48: {dict(nets)}")
print("== pitfalls")
same = k16 + k16
print(f"   pfx with K1 == K2:            198.51.100.7 -> {pfx_encrypt('198.51.100.7', same)}")
print(f"   deterministic IPv4 output is an IPv6 address: 198.51.100.7 -> {det_encrypt('198.51.100.7', k16)}")
print(f"   ::ffff:198.51.100.7 and 198.51.100.7 encrypt alike: "
      f"{det_encrypt('::ffff:198.51.100.7', k16) == det_encrypt('198.51.100.7', k16)}")
blob = ndx_encrypt("198.51.100.7", k32)

== pitfalls
   pfx with K1 == K2:            198.51.100.7 -> 198.51.100.7
   deterministic IPv4 output is an IPv6 address: 198.51.100.7 -> 6cf6:bc3b:adc5:c807:7270:735:8db6:e26e
   ::ffff:198.51.100.7 and 198.51.100.7 encrypt alike: True
   ndx decrypts with the key: 198.51.100.7  (32-byte blob, not an IP)
The ndx rows will differ on every run, because the tweak comes from os.urandom. Everything else is deterministic for these keys.
Reading it:

Deterministic: counting and joins still work: 5 distinct clients, and the brute-force source is visible with 2 failures. But 198.51.100.7 and 198.51.100.42 are now unrelated values, so you cannot tell they sit in the same /24. Every IPv4 client also becomes an IPv6-looking address, which surprises tools that bucket by family.
pfx: everything deterministic gives, plus structure. The two 198.51.100.x clients share 138.109.141.0/24. 2001:db8:1::/48 and 2001:db8:2::/48 become …:1d26::/48 and …:1d24::/48, which share 46 bits exactly as the originals do. That is useful for “which subnet is attacking us”. It is also a leak: anyone with outside knowledge of one host can learn about its neighbours. §6.2.3 says it outright: prefix-preserving encryption “intentionally reveals network structure”, and organisations needing complete obfuscation should use a non-prefix-preserving mode. §7.4.3 lists network analytics, subnet monitoring and DDoS mitigation as its use cases.
ndx: 8 rows give 8 distinct values. Without the key you cannot even tell that one client failed login twice. Use it when the log reader should not be able to link anything. The output is a 32-byte blob, not an IP, so the schema has to change.

title: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt
text:
Pitfalls the lab shows

pfx with equal key halves is the identity function. The PRF is AES(K1)⊕AES(K2), so K1 = K2 cancels out. The draft says the halves MUST NOT be identical (§6.2.2), and the lab shows 198.51.100.7 -> 198.51.100.7. Generate the 32-byte key randomly, and never by repeating a 16-byte key.
Format change in deterministic mode. IPv4 goes in and IPv6 comes out. Size and parse columns accordingly.
Keys are the whole security. Anyone holding the key decrypts everything; that is by design (§8). Store the key like any other secret, and rotate it on a schedule. Rotation also breaks correlation across periods, which may be exactly what a retention policy wants.
Tweak collisions in the nd modes are bounded by about 2^32 encryptions per key for nd and 2^64 for ndx (§7.4.1, §7.4.2). A collision reveals only a repetition, not the address.

title: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt
text:
The boring rule

Logs shared outside the team that only need “same client?” get ipcrypt-deterministic.
Abuse and DDoS work that needs subnets gets ipcrypt-pfx, accepting the neighbour leak, with a random 32-byte key.
Anything that must not be linkable gets ipcrypt-ndx, with a schema that stores 32 bytes.
Keep the key in your secret store, rotate it, and never treat ciphertext as tamper-proof.

title: Encrypting IP Addresses in Logs with IPCrypt
text:
Try this

Encrypt every address in 10.0.0.0/24 with pfx_encrypt and confirm that all 256 outputs fall into one /24. Then try 10.0.0.0/23.
Change one bit of a det_encrypt output and decrypt it. What comes back? (There is no integrity, so you get a different, valid-looking address.)
Add ipcrypt-nd by implementing KIASU-BC from the draft’s §9.9 and check it against Appendix A.3.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
text: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
text:
Learning goals

Explain what TLS 1.3 still leaks in the clear (the server name, ALPN and extensions in the ClientHello) and which part Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) hides.
Walk through the ECH handshake: the HTTPS DNS record that carries the key, the outer and inner ClientHello, accept confirmation, GREASE and the retry_configs recovery path.
Fetch and decode a live ECHConfigList with about 60 lines of Python, and read every field.
Know what ECH does not hide, why it depends on encrypted DNS, and what it changes for firewalls, SNI routing and incident response.
Decide what you need to deploy it: a CDN that does it for you, or your own server plus automated key rotation in DNS.

Version note: ECH is RFC 9849 (TLS Encrypted Client Hello, Standards Track, March 2026). Publishing its keys in DNS is RFC 9848 (Bootstrapping TLS Encrypted ClientHello with DNS Service Bindings). The labs ran on 13 Nov 2026 from an unprivileged Linux host with Python 3.13 and dnspython 2.9.1, curl 8.14.1 and OpenSSL 3.5.7. Neither curl nor OpenSSL 3.5 on that host can send ECH, and that limitation is part of the lab. All DNS queries went over DoH (RFC 8484), because the host’s plain UDP/53 is intercepted. The output blocks are pasted from the runs. The server configuration near the end is written from the Caddy documentation and was not run.



Where each piece of an ECH connection travels and who can see it.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
text:
What TLS 1.3 still shows
TLS 1.3 encrypts the certificate and everything after the ServerHello. But the ClientHello goes out before any keys exist, so it is plaintext. It carries:

server_name (SNI): the exact host the client wants, for example private.example. The server needs it to choose a certificate, and a reverse proxy or CDN needs it to route.
application_layer_protocol_negotiation (ALPN): h2, http/1.1 and similar, which hints at the application.
Every other extension and its order. That is enough to fingerprint the client software (JA3/JA4-style fingerprints).

Encrypted DNS (DoT/DoH) hides the lookup, but the next packet then announces the same name in SNI. Any on-path device can log it, block on it or rewrite policy around it. SNI is the main remaining plaintext name in a modern HTTPS connection, which is why so many firewalls and parental-control products filter on it.
An earlier attempt, ESNI, encrypted only the SNI extension. It shipped experimentally around 2018–2020 and was abandoned because encrypting one extension left the rest of the hello, and the fact that ESNI was in use, visible. ECH encrypts the whole ClientHello instead.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
text:
How ECH works

The keys come from DNS
A server operator publishes an ECHConfigList in the ech parameter (SvcParamKey 5) of the domain’s HTTPS record (RFC 9460, RFC 9848). Each ECHConfig holds:







Field
Meaning




version
0xfe0d for the RFC 9849 format. Clients skip configs with versions they do not know.


config_id
One byte that tells the server which private key to try.


kem_id, public_key
The HPKE (RFC 9180) key-encapsulation algorithm and public key.


cipher_suites
The HPKE KDF/AEAD pairs the server accepts.


maximum_name_length
Helps the client pad the inner name so its length does not leak. 0 means “no hint”.


public_name
The name the client puts in the outer SNI and the name the server must hold a valid certificate for.


extensions
Optional ECHConfig extensions (none are in common use).





Two ClientHellos in one
The client builds its real hello, the ClientHelloInner, with the true SNI, ALPN and extensions. It then builds a ClientHelloOuter with the config’s public_name as SNI and puts the inner hello, HPKE-encrypted to the server’s public key, into an encrypted_client_hello extension. Only the outer hello crosses the network in the clear. The inner hello is padded so its length says little about the real name.
The server that holds the private key is the client-facing server. It tries to decrypt the inner hello:

Shared mode: the client-facing server is also the origin and serves the inner hello itself.
Split mode: the client-facing server only decrypts and forwards the connection to a separate backend server that finishes the handshake. This is how a CDN can hide many customer names behind one public name.

If decryption works, the server continues the handshake with the inner hello. It signals acceptance by setting the last 8 bytes of ServerHello.random to a value derived from the inner transcript. The client checks those bytes: matching means “ECH accepted, you are talking to the real host”; anything else means the server used the outer hello.


Rejection and retry_configs
Keys rotate. A client may hold a cached or slightly old ECHConfig, and decryption fails. RFC 9849 handles this without a silent downgrade:

The server completes the handshake as the public_name, presenting a certificate valid for that name, and puts its current configs in retry_configs in EncryptedExtensions.
The client authenticates that certificate against the public_name. Only then does it trust the retry configs.
The client aborts that connection with an ech_required alert and opens a new one using the fresh config.

A client should not accept a second retry_configs on the retried connection. If it gets one, the RFC treats that as server misconfiguration: two nodes behind the same name hold different keys, so the client keeps landing on the wrong one.
If the rejecting server sends no retry_configs, it is authenticated as public_name saying “I no longer do ECH”, and the client should reconnect with ECH disabled. Because the certificate must be valid for the public name, an attacker cannot forge this opt-out without that certificate.


GREASE
A client that has no ECHConfig for a site still sends an encrypted_client_hello extension filled with random bytes of a plausible size (“GREASE ECH”). The observer then cannot tell “real ECH to a CDN site” from “a browser that just always sends the extension”. It also keeps middleboxes from ossifying around the extension’s absence.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
section: Lab 1: fetch and decode a live ECHConfigList
text:
Lab 1: fetch and decode a live ECHConfigList
This script asks for HTTPS records over DoH using only the Python standard library’s HTTP client plus dnspython for the DNS message format. It then decodes the ech parameter byte by byte, following the ECHConfig structure in RFC 9849 section 4.


ech.py

# ech.py NAME...: fetch HTTPS RRs over DoH and decode the ECHConfigList (RFC 9849 section 4).
import base64, struct, sys, urllib.request
import dns.message, dns.rcode, dns.rdatatype, dns.rdtypes.svcbbase

def doh(q, url="https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query"):
    """RFC 8484 POST with application/dns-message, stdlib HTTP client."""
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, data=q.to_wire(), headers={
        "Content-Type": "application/dns-message", "Accept": "application/dns-message"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as resp:
        return dns.message.from_wire(resp.read())

KEM = {0x0010: "DHKEM(P-256)", 0x0020: "DHKEM(X25519)", 0x0021: "DHKEM(X448)"}
KDF = {1: "HKDF-SHA256", 2: "HKDF-SHA384", 3: "HKDF-SHA512"}
AEAD = {1: "AES-128-GCM", 2: "AES-256-GCM", 3: "ChaCha20Poly1305"}

def vec(b, off, n):                      # TLS vector with an n-byte length prefix
    ln = int.from_bytes(b[off:off + n], "big")
    return b[off + n:off + n + ln], off + n + ln

def decode_ech_config_list(raw):
    body, _ = vec(raw, 0, 2)
    off = 0
    while off < len(body):
        version, length = struct.unpack("!HH", body[off:off + 4])
        c = body[off + 4:off + 4 + length]; off += 4 + length
        if version != 0xFE0D:
            print(f"    skip ECHConfig version 0x{version:04x}"); continue
        cid = c[0]; kem = struct.unpack("!H", c[1:3])[0]
        pk, p = vec(c, 3, 2)
        suites, p = vec(c, p, 2)
        max_name = c[p]; p += 1
        pub_name, p = vec(c, p, 1)
        ext, p = vec(c, p, 2)
        ss = [f"{KDF.get(k, k)}/{AEAD.get(a, a)}" for k, a in
              (struct.unpack("!HH", suites[i:i + 4]) for i in range(0, len(suites), 4))]
        print(f"    ECHConfig v0x{version:04x} config_id={cid} kem={KEM.get(kem, hex(kem))} "
              f"pk={len(pk)}B\n      suites={ss}\n      public_name={pub_name.decode()} "
              f"maximum_name_length={max_name} extensions={len(ext)}B")

for name in sys.argv[1:]:
    q = dns.message.make_query(name, "HTTPS")
    r = doh(q)
    print(f"{name}: rcode={dns.rcode.to_text(r.rcode())}")
    for rrset in r.answer:
        for rd in rrset:
            if rd.rdtype != dns.rdatatype.HTTPS:
                print(f"  {rrset.name} {dns.rdatatype.to_text(rrset.rdtype)} {rd}"); continue
            keys = [dns.rdtypes.svcbbase.key_to_text(k) for k in rd.params]
            print(f"  HTTPS {rd.priority} {rd.target} keys={keys}")
            if 5 in rd.params:
                raw = rd.params[5].ech
                print(f"    ech= {len(raw)} bytes, base64 {base64.b64encode(raw)[:32].decode()}...")
                decode_ech_config_list(raw)

Run against Cloudflare’s ECH test host and three comparison names:
python3 ech.py crypto.cloudflare.com cloudflare.com example.com www.google.com
crypto.cloudflare.com: rcode=NOERROR
  HTTPS 1 . keys=['alpn', 'ipv4hint', 'ech', 'ipv6hint']
    ech= 71 bytes, base64 AEX+DQBBqgAgACCVJ6nEVFI2GoHbi5RX...
    ECHConfig v0xfe0d config_id=170 kem=DHKEM(X25519) pk=32B
      suites=['HKDF-SHA256/AES-128-GCM']
      public_name=cloudflare-ech.com maximum_name_length=0 extensions=0B
cloudflare.com: rcode=NOERROR
  HTTPS 1 . keys=['alpn', 'ipv4hint', 'ipv6hint']
example.com: rcode=NOERROR
  HTTPS 1 . keys=['alpn', 'ipv4hint', 'ipv6hint']
www.google.com: rcode=NOERROR
  HTTPS 1 . keys=['alpn']
Reading it:

Only crypto.cloudflare.com publishes an ech key. cloudflare.com itself and example.com publish HTTPS records with alpn and address hints but no ECH, and www.google.com only advertises alpn. ECH is per name, and publishing an HTTPS record does not imply ECH.
The config is version 0xfe0d, the RFC 9849 format, with one HPKE suite: X25519 for the KEM, HKDF-SHA256 and AES-128-GCM. The public key is 32 bytes, an X25519 point.
public_name=cloudflare-ech.com is what the outer SNI will say for every ECH-enabled Cloudflare site. That shared name, plus the shared anycast addresses, is the anonymity set.
maximum_name_length=0 means the server gives no name-length hint, so no extra name padding is added. The client still rounds the whole encoded inner hello up to a multiple of 32 bytes (RFC 9849 section 6.1.3), which hides small differences in name length.
The config_id is the key Cloudflare is using right now. A run of the same script about 25 minutes earlier, at 03:25 IST, returned config_id=112, and this one returned 170: the key had rotated in between. Cloudflare rotates often and publishes the new key in DNS with a short TTL. Old clients recover through retry_configs.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
section: Lab 2: what this host’s client actually sends
text:
Lab 2: what this host’s client actually sends
Cloudflare’s trace endpoint reports, from the server’s side, how the TLS connection arrived. Asked from curl:
curl -s https://crypto.cloudflare.com/cdn-cgi/trace | grep -E '^(http|tls|sni|kex)='
http=http/2
tls=TLSv1.3
sni=plaintext
kex=X25519MLKEM768
sni=plaintext is the important line: the server received an ordinary ClientHello with the real name in the clear. The key exchange is the X25519 + ML-KEM-768 hybrid, so this connection is post-quantum for confidentiality, yet it still leaks the hostname. Encryption strength and metadata privacy are separate properties.
Why plaintext? The client cannot do ECH:
curl --version | head -1
curl --ech true https://crypto.cloudflare.com/
openssl version
curl 8.14.1 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.14.1 OpenSSL/3.5.7 zlib/1.3.1 brotli/1.1.0 zstd/1.5.7 libidn2/2.3.8 libpsl/0.21.2 libssh2/1.11.1 nghttp2/1.64.0 nghttp3/1.8.0 librtmp/2.3 OpenLDAP/2.6.10
curl: option --ech: the installed libcurl version does not support this
curl: try 'curl --help' or 'curl --manual' for more information
OpenSSL 3.5.7 9 Jun 2026 (Library: OpenSSL 3.5.7 9 Jun 2026)
curl has an --ech option, but it only works when libcurl is built against a TLS library with an ECH API and with ECH enabled at build time. OpenSSL gained that API in 4.0. Older releases, such as the 3.5 LTS on this host, have no ECH at all, so openssl s_client also has no ECH options here. BoringSSL, wolfSSL and rustls have ECH client support, and Chrome and Firefox ship it on by default. With a browser you can check the same trace URL: it shows sni=encrypted when ECH was used.
The lesson for operators: ECH is a property of the client build. Server-side support plus a published key changes nothing for a command-line tool, monitoring probe or older library that cannot use it.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
text:
What ECH does not hide

The IP address. If a site has its own address, ECH hides nothing useful. The privacy comes from many names sharing one client-facing server, which in practice means large CDNs or big shared hosting.
The public name. An observer learns “this is a Cloudflare ECH connection” (or whoever’s public name it is).
Sizes and timing. Traffic analysis still works, and padding only covers the hello.
DNS, unless DNS is private too. The ECHConfig arrives in a DNS answer. Over plain UDP an on-path attacker can read the query name directly, or just strip the ech parameter, and the client then connects without ECH. Real deployments pair ECH with DoH or DoT; Firefox, for example, only uses ECH when its own DoH is enabled.
The server’s own logs. The client-facing server decrypts the hello and sees everything.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
text:
Operational consequences
SNI-based controls go blind. A firewall, proxy or parental-control product that allows or blocks by SNI now sees only cloudflare-ech.com. Its options are coarse: block the public name (and every site behind it), block ECH as a whole, or control the endpoint. In managed fleets the practical levers are browser policy (Chrome’s EncryptedClientHelloEnabled enterprise policy, Firefox’s network.dns.echconfig.enabled preference) and a managed resolver. Clients only learn ECH keys from DNS, so a resolver you control decides which configs they see, as long as clients cannot bypass it with their own DoH.
SNI routing still works, but on the outer name. A TCP-level SNI router in front of an ECH-terminating server must route on the public_name. Only the box with the private key (the client-facing server) can see the real name and route on it.
Keys must stay in sync with DNS. If the private key rotates but the HTTPS record does not, or the record changes but some servers lack the key, clients take the retry_configs path. It costs an extra round trip and a second handshake. That is not an outage, but it is a latency regression you will only see if you measure ECH accept/retry rates.
The public name needs a real certificate. Retry and opt-out are authenticated against public_name, so every client-facing server needs a valid certificate for it. An expired public-name certificate breaks the recovery path for every hidden site at once.
Incident response loses a field. Packet captures and NetFlow-style logs no longer contain the hostname. Plan for logging at the point that decrypts, the CDN or your client-facing server.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
text:
Pitfalls

Testing with a tool that cannot do ECH. curl or OpenSSL builds without ECH silently send plaintext SNI (or reject --ech, as in Lab 2). Check the client build before concluding the server is broken.
Publishing ech with no secure DNS on the client side. Clients that will not trust plaintext DNS for ECH configs simply ignore them. Clients that would trust them are trivially downgraded.
Rotating keys without DNS automation. A hand-edited HTTPS record falls behind the first key rotation, and every connection then takes the retry path.
A single-tenant “hidden” site. If only one site sits behind the public name and IP, the observer knows which site it is anyway.
Forgetting the public name’s certificate. It is used only on rejection paths, so it fails silently until keys rotate.
Inconsistent keys across a server pool. If node A and node B behind one name hold different ECH keys, a client can be told to retry by A and then land on B. RFC 9849 tells clients not to follow a second retry_configs, so those connections fail. Roll keys to every node before publishing them.
Assuming ECH defeats SNI-based allowlists in your own network. It does, if clients use their own DoH. Write the policy for that case before rolling out managed browsers with ECH enabled.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
text:
The boring rule
Let the CDN do ECH if you are behind one. If you run your own, use a server that rotates keys and publishes the HTTPS record itself, make sure the public name has a valid certificate everywhere, and measure accepted versus retried ECH handshakes. On managed networks, decide your SNI-filtering policy explicitly: control ECH with browser policy and a managed resolver, not by blocking random TLS extensions.

title: Encrypted Client Hello: Hiding the Server Name
text:
Try this

Run ech.py against crypto.cloudflare.com every 15 minutes for two hours and record the config_id. How often does it change, and how does that compare with the record’s TTL?
Extend ech.py to print the HTTPS record’s TTL and the ipv4hint addresses, then explain why the hints point at the same anycast addresses as many other Cloudflare sites.
Point ech.py at five sites you use. Which publish ech? Which share a public_name?
In a browser with DoH enabled, open https://crypto.cloudflare.com/cdn-cgi/trace and compare sni= with Lab 2. Then disable the browser’s secure DNS and check again.
On paper: a client holds an ECHConfig that is one rotation old. Write down every message of the resulting connection attempt, including the alert and the second ClientHello.
