title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
text:
DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
When DNSSEC validation fails, a validating resolver does the safe thing: it refuses to answer and returns SERVFAIL. From a user’s point of view the name has vanished. From an operator’s point of view SERVFAIL is the least informative answer DNS has, because a dead authoritative server, a firewall dropping TCP/53, an expired signature and a botched key rollover all look identical. This chapter takes public test zones that are broken on purpose, asks two large validating resolvers about them, and reads the Extended DNS Errors (EDE, RFC 8914) that say why. It then covers what validator operators can do in the minutes after a zone they depend on breaks (serve-stale, negative trust anchors) and what zone operators should monitor so they are not that zone.
DNS authoritative and recursive introduces the chain of trust and the AD bit; the 2026 root KSK rollover covers trust anchors. This chapter assumes both and stays on failure.

title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
text:
Learning goals

Map the common DNSSEC breakages to the EDE codes a resolver returns, and tell DNSSEC failures from reachability failures
Use the CD bit to separate “the data is there” from “the data does not validate”
Explain why two validators can disagree about the same zone (unsupported algorithms)
Configure serve-stale and a negative trust anchor, and know the risk each one takes
Monitor signature expiry in a way that works for both offline and online signers

Version note. The probes ran on 2026-11-13 around 03:45 IST from the writing host with Python 3.13.5 and dnspython 2.9.1 (message building and parsing only), sending DNS-over-HTTPS POSTs with the standard library to cloudflare-dns.com and dns.google. The broken names are maintained test zones (dnssec-failed.org by Comcast, and the extended-dns-errors.com suite); their exact breakage and the resolvers’ wording can change. The resolver configuration snippets near the end are from the Unbound and BIND documentation and were not run (no resolver daemons, no root on the writing host).

Failure
Typical cause
Validator result
EDE




DS at parent matches no DNSKEY in the child
KSK rolled without updating DS; DS published for the wrong key; registrar typo
Bogus → SERVFAIL
9 DNSKEY Missing (sometimes 6)


RRSIG expired
Signer stopped (cron died, HSM offline), zone transferred unsigned copies stopped updating
Bogus → SERVFAIL

RRSIG not yet valid

Bogus → SERVFAIL

Signature does not verify

Bogus → SERVFAIL

Partial signing, broken secondaries
Bogus → SERVFAIL

New or retired algorithm

Authoritative servers refuse or unreachable
ACLs, outage, firewall
SERVFAIL (not a DNSSEC problem at all)
18 Prohibited, 22 No Reachable Authority, 23 Network Error



The last row is there on purpose. Half of the SERVFAILs blamed on DNSSEC are not DNSSEC.

title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
section: Lab: ask two validators about broken zones
text:
Lab: ask two validators about broken zones
For each name the probe asks Cloudflare and Google with the DO bit set, then asks Cloudflare again with CD (Checking Disabled, RFC 4035 3.2.2), which tells the resolver “give me the data even if it does not validate”. It prints the RCODE, whether the AD (validated) bit is set, the first A record, and every EDE option with the first part of its free-text explanation.
# probe.py NAME...: ask DoH resolvers about broken-DNSSEC test names; show RCODE, AD, EDE (RFC 8914).
import sys, time, urllib.request
import dns.edns, dns.flags, dns.message, dns.rcode, dns.rdatatype

RESOLVERS = {"cloudflare": "https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query",
             "google": "https://dns.google/dns-query"}

def doh(url, q):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, data=q.to_wire(), headers={
        "Content-Type": "application/dns-message", "Accept": "application/dns-message"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=8) as r:
        return dns.message.from_wire(r.read())

def ask(url, name, rtype="A", cd=False):
    q = dns.message.make_query(name, rtype, want_dnssec=True, use_edns=0)
    if cd:
        q.flags |= dns.flags.CD
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = doh(url, q)
    ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    ad = "AD" if r.flags & dns.flags.AD else "--"
    ede = [f"EDE {o.code} {dns.edns.EDECode.to_text(o.code)}" + (f' "{o.text[:44]}"' if o.text else "")
           for o in r.options if o.otype == dns.edns.OptionType.EDE]
    ans = [str(rd) for rrset in r.answer for rd in rrset if rrset.rdtype == dns.rdatatype.from_text(rtype)]
    out = f"{dns.rcode.to_text(r.rcode()):8} {ad} {ms:5.0f} ms {','.join(ans[:1]) or '-':15}"
    return out + ("".join(f"\n{'':24}{e}" for e in ede))

names = sys.argv[1:]
for name in names:
    print(name)
    for rn, url in RESOLVERS.items():
        print(f"  {rn:10}    {ask(url, name)}")
    print(f"  {'cloudflare':10} CD {ask(RESOLVERS['cloudflare'], name, cd=True)}")
$ python3 probe.py example.com unsigned.extended-dns-errors.com dnssec-failed.org rrsig-exp-all.extended-dns-errors.com rrsig-not-yet-all.extended-dns-errors.com ds-unassigned-key-algo.extended-dns-errors.com ds-unassigned-digest-algo.extended-dns-errors.com allow-query-none.extended-dns-errors.com

  google        SERVFAIL --   404 ms -              
                        EDE 18 PROHIBITED
                        EDE 23 NETWORK_ERROR "[65.21.51.117] rcode=REFUSED for allow-query"
                        EDE 22 NO_REACHABLE_AUTHORITY "At delegation allow-query-none.extended-dns-"
  cloudflare CD SERVFAIL --   442 ms -              
                        EDE 18 PROHIBITED
                        EDE 22 NO_REACHABLE_AUTHORITY "at delegation allow-query-none.extended-dns-"

Reading it, name by name

example.com: validated (AD) at both. With CD the answer comes back without AD, because the resolver was told not to validate. This is the baseline to compare everything else to.
unsigned.extended-dns-errors.com: no AD, NOERROR. Unsigned is not broken. A zone without a DS at its parent is insecure, and validators answer normally.
dnssec-failed.org: the parent publishes a DS that matches no DNSKEY in the zone, the classic botched-rollover state. Both validators return SERVFAIL with EDE 9; their texts differ, the code does not. With CD the A record 96.99.227.255 is right there. That is the diagnostic: if CD gets an answer and normal resolution does not, the data exists and validation is the problem.
rrsig-exp-all: signatures expired. EDE 7 at both, and Cloudflare’s text includes the expiry as a Unix timestamp (1782814088 = 2026-06-30 10:08 UTC). The sigcheck.py lab below reads those timestamps directly.
rrsig-not-yet-all: signatures whose inception is in the future (2027-06-30). EDE 8. On a real network the same code appears when a validator’s clock is a year behind, for example a lab VM restored from an old snapshot without NTP. Every signed zone on the internet then fails at once. Check the validator’s clock before you blame the zone.
ds-unassigned-key-algo: the validators disagree. The DS names an algorithm number that is not assigned. RFC 4035 section 5.2 and RFC 6840 section 5.2 say a validator that supports none of the algorithms in the DS set must treat the zone as insecure. Google did that (NOERROR, no AD). Cloudflare failed closed with EDE 9. Neither is “down”, and a user on one resolver sees the site while a user on the other does not. When a ticket says “works for some users”, ask which resolver.
ds-unassigned-digest-algo: an unknown DS digest type. Both treat the zone as insecure and answer; Cloudflare adds EDE 2 as an informational note to a successful answer. EDE is not only for failures.
allow-query-none: the authoritative servers refuse queries. SERVFAIL at both, with and without CD, and the EDE codes (18 Prohibited, 22 No Reachable Authority, 23 Network Error with the server IP and REFUSED) say plainly that this is reachability, not DNSSEC. CD does not help here because there is no data to return.

Two rules fall out. CD separates data problems from validation problems. And EDE separates DNSSEC from everything else, when the resolver sends it. Clients see EDE only if they look: recent BIND dig versions print an EDE: line in the OPT pseudosection, kdig decodes it too, and browsers and stub resolvers mostly throw it away.

title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
text:
Extended DNS Errors worth knowing








Code
Name
What to do




1 / 2
Unsupported DNSKEY Algorithm / DS Digest Type
Usually informational: zone treated as insecure. Check whether the zone moved to an algorithm your validator lacks.


3
Stale Answer
The resolver served expired cache (serve-stale). Upstream is broken; you are on borrowed time.


6
DNSSEC Bogus
Generic validation failure. Read the text.


7 / 8
Signature Expired / Not Yet Valid
Zone signer stopped, or a clock is wrong (signer or validator).


9
DNSKEY Missing
DS ↔︎ DNSKEY mismatch. Rollover or registrar problem at the zone owner.


10 / 12
RRSIGs Missing / NSEC Missing
Partially signed zone or a broken secondary.


13
Cached Error
The resolver is returning a cached SERVFAIL; fixing the zone may not show for a while.


15–17
Blocked / Censored / Filtered
Policy on the resolver (RPZ, filtering service), not the zone.


18
Prohibited
The resolver or an upstream refused you or it.


22 / 23
No Reachable Authority / Network Error
Authoritative servers down or unreachable. Not DNSSEC.

title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
text:
Lab: watch signature expiry
Expired signatures are the most common self-inflicted DNSSEC outage, and the easiest to see coming. This check asks for the RRSIGs over the SOA and DNSKEY sets, with CD so that already-broken zones still answer, and prints how long each signature has left.
# sigcheck.py ZONE...: days left on the RRSIGs over SOA and DNSKEY (asked with CD so bogus data still comes back).
import datetime as dt, sys, urllib.request
import dns.flags, dns.message, dns.rdatatype

def doh(q, url="https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query"):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, data=q.to_wire(), headers={
        "Content-Type": "application/dns-message", "Accept": "application/dns-message"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=8) as r:
        return dns.message.from_wire(r.read())

now = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc)
for zone in sys.argv[1:]:
    for rtype in ("SOA", "DNSKEY"):
        q = dns.message.make_query(zone, rtype, want_dnssec=True)
        q.flags |= dns.flags.CD
        for rrset in doh(q).answer:
            if rrset.rdtype != dns.rdatatype.RRSIG:
                continue
            for sig in rrset:
                inc = dt.datetime.fromtimestamp(sig.inception, dt.timezone.utc)
                exp = dt.datetime.fromtimestamp(sig.expiration, dt.timezone.utc)
                left = (exp - now).total_seconds() / 86400
                state = "EXPIRED" if left < 0 else ("NOT YET VALID" if inc > now else
                        ("WARN <7d" if left < 7 else "ok"))
                print(f"{zone:40} {rtype:6} key {sig.key_tag:5} alg {sig.algorithm:2} "
                      f"inc {inc:%Y-%m-%d} exp {exp:%Y-%m-%d} {left:7.1f} d  {state}")
$ python3 sigcheck.py example.com rrsig-exp-all.extended-dns-errors.com rrsig-not-yet-all.extended-dns-errors.com
example.com                              SOA    key 34505 alg 13 inc 2026-11-11 exp 2026-11-13     1.0 d  WARN <7d
example.com                              DNSKEY key  2371 alg 13 inc 2026-10-19 exp 2026-12-19    36.8 d  ok
rrsig-exp-all.extended-dns-errors.com    SOA    key 50880 alg  8 inc 2026-06-30 exp 2026-06-30  -135.5 d  EXPIRED
rrsig-exp-all.extended-dns-errors.com    DNSKEY key 16126 alg  8 inc 2026-06-30 exp 2026-06-30  -135.5 d  EXPIRED
rrsig-exp-all.extended-dns-errors.com    DNSKEY key 50880 alg  8 inc 2026-06-30 exp 2026-06-30  -135.5 d  EXPIRED
rrsig-not-yet-all.extended-dns-errors.com SOA    key 53458 alg  8 inc 2027-06-30 exp 2028-06-30   595.5 d  NOT YET VALID
rrsig-not-yet-all.extended-dns-errors.com DNSKEY key 53458 alg  8 inc 2027-06-30 exp 2028-06-30   595.5 d  NOT YET VALID
rrsig-not-yet-all.extended-dns-errors.com DNSKEY key 54334 alg  8 inc 2027-06-30 exp 2028-06-30   595.5 d  NOT YET VALID
The broken test zones are flagged correctly. The surprise is example.com: its SOA signature was made two days ago and expires in one, so a fixed “warn at 7 days” threshold calls a healthy zone unhealthy. Zones signed by an online signer (most large DNS providers sign on the fly) use short validity periods and re-sign continuously; zones signed offline (a nightly dnssec-signzone run, an HSM ceremony) typically carry weeks. The DNSKEY signature on the same zone has 36 days. Alert on the fraction of the validity period remaining (for example, warn below 25%, page below 10%), and alert on any signature already expired or not yet valid. Run the check from outside your own network, against every authoritative server separately, because one stale secondary is enough to fail validation for the resolvers that pick it.

title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
section: When a zone you depend on breaks: options for validator operators
text:
When a zone you depend on breaks: options for validator operators
You run the resolver. A partner’s zone just went bogus and your users cannot reach it. In order of preference:

Tell the zone owner, with the EDE code and text. EDE 9 means “your DS and DNSKEY do not match”: that is a five-minute fix at their registrar once they know.
Serve-stale (RFC 8767) keeps answering from cache with expired records when upstream resolution fails, and marks them with EDE 3. It helps when the authoritative servers are unreachable, and for records already in cache. It does not rescue names that were never cached. RFC 8767 recommends a stale TTL of 30 seconds and a cap of one to three days on how stale data may get.
A negative trust anchor (RFC 7646) tells your validator to treat one zone as insecure for a limited time. Users get answers again; they also lose DNSSEC protection for that zone, which is exactly what an attacker would want if the “breakage” is an attack. Scope it to the one zone, give it a lifetime, log it, and remove it when the owner fixes the zone.

Not run here; from the Unbound and BIND documentation:
# unbound.conf: serve-stale per RFC 8767
server:
    serve-expired: yes
    serve-expired-ttl: 86400             # do not serve data more than a day past expiry
    serve-expired-client-timeout: 1800   # try upstream for 1.8 s first, then serve stale

# Unbound: negative trust anchor at runtime (and remove it later)
unbound-control insecure_add partner.example
unbound-control insecure_remove partner.example
# BIND 9 named.conf options
    stale-answer-enable yes;
    stale-cache-enable yes;
    max-stale-ttl 1d;

# BIND 9: NTA with an explicit lifetime
rndc nta -lifetime 2h partner.example
rndc nta -dump
What you should not do: turn validation off globally, or point users at a non-validating resolver “until it is fixed”. That trades one partner’s outage for every user’s exposure.

title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
section: For zone operators: not being the outage
text:
For zone operators: not being the outage







Practice
Why




Automate signing and re-signing; monitor it as in sigcheck.py
Expired signatures are the top cause


Use algorithm 13 (ECDSA P-256) or 8 (RSA/SHA-256) for new zones; plan any algorithm change as a double-signature rollover
RFC 8624 algorithm guidance; validators that do not know a new algorithm treat you as insecure, which is safe but silent


Change the DS at the parent only after the new KSK is published and cached; remove the old DS before the old KSK
DS mismatch (EDE 9) is the classic rollover failure


Use CDS/CDNSKEY (RFC 7344, RFC 8078) if your parent supports it
Removes the human from DS updates


Check every authoritative server, not the one behind your nearest anycast node
Secondaries can serve stale signatures


Keep signer and validator clocks on NTP
EDE 7/8 for everyone

title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
text:
Gotchas

SERVFAIL is not proof of a DNSSEC problem. Check EDE, then retry with CD. If CD also fails, look at reachability.
CD is for diagnosis, not a workaround. Applications that set CD to “fix” DNS turn validation off for themselves.
Validators can legitimately disagree. Unsupported-algorithm handling and resolver policy differ. Ask users which resolver they use.
A wrong validator clock breaks every signed zone at once. EDE 8 (or 7) for names that are fine elsewhere points at your own clock.
Fixed expiry thresholds fail for online signers. Use the fraction of validity left.
Negative cache of errors. Resolvers cache SERVFAIL briefly (EDE 13). After a fix, expect a delay, or flush the resolver cache for that name.
NTAs are security exceptions. Time-limit them, log them, and remove them.
EDE text is free-form. Match on the code in automation, not on the string.

title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
text:
Boring rule
Validate, and let it fail closed. When it fails, read the EDE code, retry with CD, and fix the zone or ask its owner to; use a time-limited NTA only for a zone you have confirmed is broken rather than attacked. If you sign zones, automate re-signing and monitor the fraction of signature validity left on every authoritative server.

title: DNSSEC Failure Modes: SERVFAIL, Extended DNS Errors, Serve-Stale and NTAs
text:
Try this

Run probe.py against your own resolver (change the URL list, or add a plain-UDP path). Does it return EDE at all? Which codes?
Change sigcheck.py to warn when less than 25% of each signature’s validity period remains. Re-run it against example.com and a zone you know is signed offline.
Query dnssec-failed.org with CD set and DO set, and print the RRSIG and DNSKEY records you get back. Compute the key tag of each DNSKEY with dns.dnssec.key_id() and compare it with the DS at .org.
Write a short runbook entry for “partner zone bogus”: the commands to confirm (EDE, CD), who to contact, the exact NTA command with its lifetime, and the removal step.
Set a lab VM’s clock one year back and query a signed name through a validating resolver on that VM. Which EDE do you get? Restore the clock.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
Server-to-server mail has a weak spot that HTTPS does not. A sending mail server (an MTA) looks up the recipient domain’s MX records, connects to port 25, and upgrades to TLS only if the server announces STARTTLS in its cleartext greeting. An attacker on the path can delete that one line, and the sender falls back to cleartext. An attacker who can forge DNS can do worse: hand out an MX record pointing at their own host. Even when the sender insists on TLS, it has no good way to know which certificate is right. Most MTAs accept any certificate on port 25, because insisting on a public CA certificate whose name matches the MX host would bounce a lot of legitimate mail.
DANE (DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities, RFC 6698) fixes this with DNSSEC. The receiving domain publishes a TLSA record that says “the TLS server at _25._tcp.mx.example.net uses this key”. The record is signed, so a validating sender can trust it. If a signed TLSA record exists, the sender must use TLS and the server must present a matching key. Strip STARTTLS and delivery waits instead of going out in cleartext. Present the wrong key and the sender moves to another MX or keeps the message queued.
DANE is deployed for SMTP: Postfix, Exim and several large mail providers implement it. For HTTPS it barely matters, because no mainstream browser validates TLSA records. This chapter therefore spends most of its time on SMTP (RFC 7672), with HTTPS servers used only as easy live examples.
You will compute TLSA records by hand and with OpenSSL, run OpenSSL’s own DANE verifier against toy STARTTLS servers, check real TLSA records on the Internet, walk through what a sending MTA decides for several real domains, and practise a key rollover that does not drop mail.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
Learning goals

Read a TLSA record: owner name, certificate usage, selector, matching type and data.
Explain why 3 1 1 (DANE-EE, SPKI, SHA2-256) is the usual choice, and what 3 0 1 and 2 1 1 cost you.
Compute a TLSA record from a certificate and check it against a live TLS server.
Follow the RFC 7672 decision a sending MTA makes for each MX host: authenticated TLS, encrypted-only, opportunistic, or “do not deliver here”.
Roll a server key without an outage, and lint a TLSA RRset against the chain the server serves now.
Configure DANE in Postfix and know which parts depend on a local validating resolver.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
Version note
Everything in the lab ran on the book’s build box as an unprivileged user: Linux 6.12, OpenSSL 3.5.7 (9 Jun 2026) and Python 3.13 with the standard library only. Nothing was installed. The toy SMTP servers listen on 127.0.0.1. Live DNS answers come from Google Public DNS over its DoH JSON API (https://dns.google/resolve) on 2026-11-14 (IST); live TLS chains were fetched from port 443 with openssl s_client. Outbound port 25 is blocked from the build box, so no real MX host was contacted over SMTP. The Postfix, zone file and resolver snippets in the production section come from the Postfix documentation and the RFCs and are not run here.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
The TLSA record
A TLSA record (RR type 52) lives at a name built from the port, the transport and the server’s host name:
_25._tcp.mx1.example.net.   IN TLSA  3 1 1  cb66729efbc13da1...0f215767655
 |    |    |                         | | |  |
 port proto  TLS server host name    | | |  certificate association data (hex)
                                     | | matching type: 0 Full, 1 SHA2-256, 2 SHA2-512
                                     | selector:      0 Cert (whole certificate), 1 SPKI (public key only)
                                     certificate usage: 0 PKIX-TA, 1 PKIX-EE, 2 DANE-TA, 3 DANE-EE
The acronyms come from RFC 7218 and are what logs and tools print. The four usages mean:









Usage
Name
What must match
Public CA validation?




0
PKIX-TA
a CA certificate in the chain
yes, and the chain must also reach a CA the client trusts


1
PKIX-EE
the server’s own certificate
yes


2
DANE-TA
a CA certificate the server sends; the chain is then validated up to it
no; the TLSA record is the trust anchor


3
DANE-EE
the server’s own certificate or key
no; names and validity dates are not checked (RFC 7671 section 5.1)



The selector chooses what gets hashed. Selector 0 hashes the whole DER certificate, so every renewal changes it, even when the key stays the same. Selector 1 hashes only the SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI): the algorithm and the public key. Reissue the certificate on the same key and the SPKI hash does not move.
RFC 7671 section 5.1 recommends 3 1 1 for most servers: pin the key, ignore the CA, survive renewals that keep the key. Two further rules matter for SMTP:

With DANE-TA (usage 2) the server must send the trust anchor certificate in its handshake. Clients do not fetch it from anywhere else.
RFC 7672 section 3.1.3 says SMTP server operators SHOULD NOT publish usages 0 and 1, and SMTP clients MAY treat them as unusable. There is no agreed set of public CAs for port 25, so a PKIX check has nothing to anchor to.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
What a sending MTA decides
RFC 7672 turns DNSSEC results into delivery actions. Every lookup ends in one of four states defined in RFC 4035: secure (validated), insecure (provably unsigned), bogus (signatures fail) or indeterminate. RFC 7672 section 2.1.1 treats bogus, indeterminate, SERVFAIL and timeouts all as one thing: a lookup failure. A secure or insecure “no such record” is not a failure; it is an answer.
recipient domain example.net
  |
  |  MX lookup
  |-- failure (bogus / SERVFAIL / timeout) ------------> defer delivery (section 2.1.2)
  |-- insecure -----------------------------------------> pre-DANE opportunistic TLS for this domain
  |                                                        (a client MAY still use TLSA records of the
  |                                                         MX hosts it found, section 2.2.1)
  |-- secure: for each MX host, in preference order
        |
        |  TLSA lookup at _25._tcp.<mx host>
        |-- failure -----------------------------> skip this host; MUST NOT deliver through it
        |-- insecure, or secure "no TLSA" -------> opportunistic TLS; cleartext allowed
        |-- secure, all records unusable --------> TLS required, no authentication
        |-- secure, at least one usable record --> TLS required AND the chain must match;
                                                    on failure try the next MX or defer
Three consequences are easy to miss:

A failed TLSA lookup is not “no DANE”. If it were, an attacker would just drop TLSA queries. The host is treated as unreachable instead.
MX preference beats security. Section 2.2.1 says an MX host with TLSA records must not jump ahead of a better-preference host without them. Protection is per host, so a domain is only as protected as its weakest MX.
A TLSA record is a promise to offer STARTTLS. Section 2.2 says clients may read its presence as a commitment by the operator. Publish one for a server without TLS and DANE senders will stop delivering to it.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
The lab
Six files. mkcerts.sh makes a private CA and a set of certificates designed to hit each rule. dane.py computes and matches TLSA records with no crypto library. lab.py runs the matching cases, a rollover lint and a live check. toysmtp.py and openssl-dane.sh repeat the matching cases with OpenSSL’s built-in DANE verifier over a real STARTTLS handshake. smtp.py walks the MTA decision for real domains.

A private CA and certificates that break the rules


mkcerts.sh

#!/bin/sh
# A private CA, a leaf key and certificate, a renewed certificate on the SAME key, a next key,
# an expired certificate and one with the wrong name. EC P-256 keeps the output short.
set -e
mkdir -p pki && cd pki
o="openssl"
$o req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -keyout ca.key -out ca.pem \
   -days 3650 -subj "/CN=Lab Issuing CA" -addext basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE 2>/dev/null
sign() { # sign <key> <cn> <out> <days-ago-start> <days>
  $o req -new -key "$1" -subj "/CN=$2" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:$2" -out "$3.csr" 2>/dev/null
  $o x509 -req -in "$3.csr" -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out "$3.pem" \
     -copy_extensions copy -not_before "$4" -not_after "$5" 2>/dev/null
}
$o genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out cur.key 2>/dev/null
$o genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out next.key 2>/dev/null
sign cur.key  mail.lab.example leaf      20261101000000Z 20270201000000Z
sign cur.key  mail.lab.example renewed   20261114000000Z 20270214000000Z
sign next.key mail.lab.example rotated   20261114000000Z 20270214000000Z
sign cur.key  mail.lab.example expired   20260101000000Z 20260401000000Z
sign cur.key  www.other.example wrongname 20261101000000Z 20270201000000Z
echo "certificates: $(ls *.pem | tr '\n' ' ')"

certificates: ca.pem expired.pem leaf.pem renewed.pem rotated.pem wrongname.pem 
renewed reuses cur.key, rotated uses next.key, expired ended in April 2026 and wrongname is issued for a different host. EC P-256 keys keep the hashes and certificates short.


Computing and matching TLSA records


dane.py

"""DANE TLSA (RFC 6698, RFC 7671): compute, look up and check TLSA records. Stdlib + openssl CLI."""
import base64, hashlib, json, re, ssl, subprocess, tempfile, urllib.request

USAGE = {0: "PKIX-TA", 1: "PKIX-EE", 2: "DANE-TA", 3: "DANE-EE"}
SELECTOR = {0: "Cert", 1: "SPKI"}
MTYPE = {0: "Full", 1: "SHA2-256", 2: "SHA2-512"}

def _tlv(b, i):
    """Return (tag, header_len, value_len) of the DER element at offset i."""
    tag, l = b[i], b[i + 1]
    if l < 0x80:
        return tag, 2, l
    n = l & 0x7F
    return tag, 2 + n, int.from_bytes(b[i + 2:i + 2 + n], "big")

def spki(cert_der):
    """subjectPublicKeyInfo of an X.509 certificate, as DER bytes (no crypto library needed)."""
    _, h, _ = _tlv(cert_der, 0)                  # Certificate ::= SEQUENCE
    i = h
    _, h, _ = _tlv(cert_der, i)                  # tbsCertificate ::= SEQUENCE
    i += h
    if cert_der[i] == 0xA0:                      # [0] version (optional)
        _, h, l = _tlv(cert_der, i); i += h + l
    for _ in range(5):                           # serial, signature, issuer, validity, subject
        _, h, l = _tlv(cert_der, i); i += h + l
    _, h, l = _tlv(cert_der, i)                  # subjectPublicKeyInfo
    return cert_der[i:i + h + l]

def association(cert_der, selector, mtype):
    data = cert_der if selector == 0 else spki(cert_der)
    return {0: lambda d: d, 1: lambda d: hashlib.sha256(d).digest(),
            2: lambda d: hashlib.sha512(d).digest()}[mtype](data).hex()

def tlsa(cert_der, usage=3, selector=1, mtype=1):
    return (usage, selector, mtype, association(cert_der, selector, mtype))

def pem_to_der(pem):
    return [ssl.PEM_cert_to_DER_cert(m) for m in
            re.findall(r"-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----.+?-----END CERTIFICATE-----", pem, re.S)]

def doh_tlsa(name):
    """TLSA lookup over DoH (JSON API). Returns (AD flag, [records])."""
    url = f"https://dns.google/resolve?name={name}&type=TLSA"
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) as r:
        d = json.load(r)
    recs = []
    for a in d.get("Answer", []):
        if a["type"] == 52:
            u, s, m, h = a["data"].split(" ", 3)
            recs.append((int(u), int(s), int(m), h.replace(" ", "").lower()))
    return d.get("AD", False), d["Status"], recs

def server_chain(host, port, starttls=None):
    cmd = ["openssl", "s_client", "-showcerts", "-connect", f"{host}:{port}", "-servername", host]
    if starttls:
        cmd += ["-starttls", starttls]
    out = subprocess.run(cmd, input=b"", capture_output=True, timeout=15).stdout.decode(errors="replace")
    return pem_to_der(out)

def _pem(der):
    return ssl.DER_cert_to_PEM_cert(der)

def pkix_to(ta_der, chain, name):
    """Does chain[0] verify up to ta_der (trusted as a partial chain) with the right name?"""
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".pem") as ta, \
         tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".pem") as inter, \
         tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".pem") as leaf:
        ta.write(_pem(ta_der)); ta.flush()
        inter.write("".join(_pem(c) for c in chain[1:]) or _pem(ta_der)); inter.flush()
        leaf.write(_pem(chain[0])); leaf.flush()
        r = subprocess.run(["openssl", "verify", "-partial_chain", "-trusted", ta.name,
                            "-untrusted", inter.name, "-verify_hostname", name, leaf.name],
                           capture_output=True, text=True)
        lines = (r.stdout + r.stderr).strip().splitlines()
        errs = [l.split("lookup: ")[-1] for l in lines if " depth lookup" in l]
        return r.returncode == 0, "OK" if r.returncode == 0 else errs[0] if errs else lines[-1]

def check(records, chain, name, ad=True):
    """RFC 6698/7671 matching for DANE-EE(3) and DANE-TA(2). Returns (ok, reason)."""
    if not ad:
        return False, "TLSA answer not DNSSEC-validated (AD=0): DANE must not be used"
    usable = [r for r in records if r[0] in (2, 3) and r[1] in SELECTOR and r[2] in MTYPE]
    if not usable:
        return False, "no usable TLSA records"
    for u, s, m, h in usable:
        if u == 3 and association(chain[0], s, m) == h:
            return True, f"leaf matches {u} {s} {m} (DANE-EE: names and dates ignored)"
    for u, s, m, h in usable:
        if u == 2:
            for c in chain[1:]:
                if association(c, s, m) == h:
                    ok, why = pkix_to(c, chain, name)
                    return ok, f"TA matches {u} {s} {m}; chain to TA with name check: {why}"
    return False, "no TLSA record matches the presented chain"

def publisher_lint(records, chain):
    """RFC 7671 section 8: every (usage, selector, mtype) combination must match the CURRENT chain."""
    combos, out = {}, []
    for u, s, m, h in records:
        combos.setdefault((u, s, m), []).append(h)
    for (u, s, m), hashes in sorted(combos.items()):
        certs = chain[:1] if u in (1, 3) else chain[1:] or chain
        live = {association(c, s, m) for c in certs}
        matched = [x for x in hashes if x in live]
        state = "OK" if matched else "BROKEN: only past/future keys"
        out.append(f"{u} {s} {m}: {len(hashes)} record(s), {len(matched)} match current chain -> {state}")
    return out

spki() walks the certificate’s DER structure just far enough to cut out the subjectPublicKeyInfo element: certificate, then tbsCertificate, then skip the optional version, serial, signature algorithm, issuer, validity and subject. That is all a TLSA selector 1 needs. check() implements the client side for usages 2 and 3; pkix_to() hands DANE-TA chains to openssl verify -partial_chain, which accepts a non-root certificate as the trust anchor. publisher_lint() is the server-side check from RFC 7671 section 8, discussed below.


lab.py

"""DANE lab: compute TLSA records, match chains, lint rollovers, then check live servers."""
import subprocess, dane

def der(name):
    return dane.pem_to_der(open(f"pki/{name}.pem").read())[0]

def show(title, records, chain, name="mail.lab.example"):
    ok, why = dane.check(records, chain, name)
    print(f"  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {title:46} {why}")

ca, leaf = der("ca"), der("leaf")
print("1. TLSA 3 1 1 for the leaf, two ways")
cli = subprocess.run("openssl x509 -in pki/leaf.pem -noout -pubkey | openssl pkey -pubin -outform DER"
                     " | openssl dgst -sha256 -r", shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.split()[0]
print(f"  openssl pipeline : {cli}")
print(f"  dane.spki()      : {dane.association(leaf, 1, 1)}")
for rec in [dane.tlsa(leaf, 3, 1, 1), dane.tlsa(leaf, 3, 0, 1), dane.tlsa(ca, 2, 1, 1)]:
    u, s, m, h = rec
    print(f"  _25._tcp.mail.lab.example. IN TLSA {u} {s} {m} {h[:16]}...   "
          f"({dane.USAGE[u]} {dane.SELECTOR[s]} {dane.MTYPE[m]})")

ee_spki = [dane.tlsa(leaf, 3, 1, 1)]
ee_cert = [dane.tlsa(leaf, 3, 0, 1)]
ta = [dane.tlsa(ca, 2, 1, 1)]
print("\n2. Matching (chain = leaf + issuing CA, as the server sends it)")
show("3 1 1, original cert", ee_spki, [leaf, ca])
show("3 1 1, renewed cert on the same key", ee_spki, [der("renewed"), ca])
show("3 0 1, renewed cert on the same key", ee_cert, [der("renewed"), ca])
show("3 1 1, new key, TLSA not updated", ee_spki, [der("rotated"), ca])
show("3 1 1, expired cert", ee_spki, [der("expired"), ca])
show("3 1 1, cert for another name", ee_spki, [der("wrongname"), ca])
show("2 1 1, new key from the same CA", ta, [der("rotated"), ca])
show("2 1 1, expired cert", ta, [der("expired"), ca])
show("2 1 1, cert for another name", ta, [der("wrongname"), ca])
show("2 1 1, server forgot to send the CA", ta, [der("rotated")])
ok, why = dane.check(ee_spki, [leaf, ca], "mail.lab.example", ad=False)
print(f"  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {'3 1 1, but the answer had AD=0':46} {why}")

print("\n3. Key rollover, RFC 7671 section 8 lint against what the server serves NOW")
nxt = dane.tlsa(der("rotated"), 3, 1, 1)
plans = {
    "step 0: current only": (ee_spki, [leaf, ca]),
    "step 1: current + next, old key still served": (ee_spki + [nxt], [leaf, ca]),
    "step 2: new key deployed (>= 2 TTLs later)": (ee_spki + [nxt], [der("rotated"), ca]),
    "step 3: old record removed": ([nxt], [der("rotated"), ca]),
    "mistake: next only, old key still served": ([nxt], [leaf, ca]),
    "mistake: added 3 0 1 for the next cert only": (ee_spki + [dane.tlsa(der("rotated"), 3, 0, 1)], [leaf, ca]),
}
for title, (recs, chain) in plans.items():
    print(f"  {title}")
    for line in dane.publisher_lint(recs, chain):
        print(f"      {line}")

print("\n4. Live: TLSA over DoH (AD = validated by the resolver), then the real chain")
for host in ("www.huque.com", "www.nlnetlabs.nl", "www.freebsd.org", "www.ietf.org"):
    ad, status, recs = dane.doh_tlsa(f"_443._tcp.{host}")
    if not recs:
        print(f"  {host:18} AD={ad} rcode={status} no TLSA -> DANE does not apply, plain WebPKI")
        continue
    chain = dane.server_chain(host, 443)
    ok, why = dane.check(recs, chain, host, ad)
    print(f"  {host:18} AD={ad} {len(recs)} TLSA, chain of {len(chain)}: {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'} {why}")

1. TLSA 3 1 1 for the leaf, two ways
  openssl pipeline : cb66729efbc13da169811daaad01ec870538e2c3ccac2579dcc630f215767655
  dane.spki()      : cb66729efbc13da169811daaad01ec870538e2c3ccac2579dcc630f215767655
  _25._tcp.mail.lab.example. IN TLSA 3 1 1 cb66729efbc13da1...   (DANE-EE SPKI SHA2-256)
  _25._tcp.mail.lab.example. IN TLSA 3 0 1 7ef1469ea953e2bf...   (DANE-EE Cert SHA2-256)
  _25._tcp.mail.lab.example. IN TLSA 2 1 1 7bbeada201d92c56...   (DANE-TA SPKI SHA2-256)

2. Matching (chain = leaf + issuing CA, as the server sends it)
  PASS  3 1 1, original cert                           leaf matches 3 1 1 (DANE-EE: names and dates ignored)
  PASS  3 1 1, renewed cert on the same key            leaf matches 3 1 1 (DANE-EE: names and dates ignored)
  FAIL  3 0 1, renewed cert on the same key            no TLSA record matches the presented chain
  FAIL  3 1 1, new key, TLSA not updated               no TLSA record matches the presented chain
  PASS  3 1 1, expired cert                            leaf matches 3 1 1 (DANE-EE: names and dates ignored)
  PASS  3 1 1, cert for another name                   leaf matches 3 1 1 (DANE-EE: names and dates ignored)
  PASS  2 1 1, new key from the same CA                TA matches 2 1 1; chain to TA with name check: OK
  FAIL  2 1 1, expired cert                            TA matches 2 1 1; chain to TA with name check: certificate has expired
  FAIL  2 1 1, cert for another name                   TA matches 2 1 1; chain to TA with name check: hostname mismatch
  FAIL  2 1 1, server forgot to send the CA            no TLSA record matches the presented chain
  FAIL  3 1 1, but the answer had AD=0                 TLSA answer not DNSSEC-validated (AD=0): DANE must not be used

3. Key rollover, RFC 7671 section 8 lint against what the server serves NOW
  step 0: current only
      3 1 1: 1 record(s), 1 match current chain -> OK
  step 1: current + next, old key still served
      3 1 1: 2 record(s), 1 match current chain -> OK
  step 2: new key deployed (>= 2 TTLs later)
      3 1 1: 2 record(s), 1 match current chain -> OK
  step 3: old record removed
      3 1 1: 1 record(s), 1 match current chain -> OK
  mistake: next only, old key still served
      3 1 1: 1 record(s), 0 match current chain -> BROKEN: only past/future keys
  mistake: added 3 0 1 for the next cert only
      3 0 1: 1 record(s), 0 match current chain -> BROKEN: only past/future keys
      3 1 1: 1 record(s), 1 match current chain -> OK

4. Live: TLSA over DoH (AD = validated by the resolver), then the real chain
  www.huque.com      AD=True 5 TLSA, chain of 3: PASS leaf matches 3 1 1 (DANE-EE: names and dates ignored)
  www.nlnetlabs.nl   AD=True 1 TLSA, chain of 4: PASS leaf matches 3 1 1 (DANE-EE: names and dates ignored)
  www.freebsd.org    AD=True 2 TLSA, chain of 4: PASS leaf matches 3 1 1 (DANE-EE: names and dates ignored)
  www.ietf.org       AD=True rcode=0 no TLSA -> DANE does not apply, plain WebPKI


The same cases through OpenSSL’s DANE verifier
Section 2 above is my own matcher. To check it against an independent implementation, openssl s_client has DANE support built in (-dane_tlsa_domain, -dane_tlsa_rrdata). The toy server below speaks just enough SMTP to offer STARTTLS and then completes a real TLS handshake with whatever certificate chain it is given.


toysmtp.py

"""A toy SMTP server that offers STARTTLS with a chosen certificate (loopback only)."""
import socket, ssl, sys, threading

def serve(port, cert, key):
    ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
    ctx.load_cert_chain(cert, key)        # cert file = leaf + issuing CA
    s = socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", port)); s.listen()
    def handle(c):
        f = c.makefile("rwb")
        def say(x): f.write(x.encode() + b"\r\n"); f.flush()
        say("220 mail.lab.example ESMTP toy")
        while (line := f.readline()):
            cmd = line.strip().upper()
            if cmd.startswith(b"EHLO"):
                say("250-mail.lab.example"); say("250 STARTTLS")
            elif cmd == b"STARTTLS":
                say("220 2.0.0 go ahead")
                try:
                    t = ctx.wrap_socket(c, server_side=True)
                    tf = t.makefile("rwb")
                    while (l2 := tf.readline()):
                        if l2.strip().upper() == b"QUIT":
                            tf.write(b"221 bye\r\n"); tf.flush(); break
                        tf.write(b"250 ok\r\n"); tf.flush()
                except (ssl.SSLError, OSError):
                    pass
                return
            elif cmd == b"QUIT":
                say("221 bye"); return
            else:
                say("250 ok")
    while True:
        c, _ = s.accept()
        threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(c,), daemon=True).start()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    serve(int(sys.argv[1]), sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3])



openssl-dane.sh

#!/bin/sh
# OpenSSL's built-in DANE verifier against two toy STARTTLS servers on loopback.
# 2525 serves the current key, 2526 the rotated key, 2527 an expired cert on the current key.
python3 toysmtp.py 2525 pki/leaf-chain.pem    pki/cur.key & p1=$!
python3 toysmtp.py 2526 pki/rotated-chain.pem pki/next.key & p2=$!
python3 toysmtp.py 2527 pki/expired-chain.pem pki/cur.key & p3=$!
sleep 1
ee=$(openssl x509 -in pki/leaf.pem -noout -pubkey | openssl pkey -pubin -outform DER | openssl dgst -sha256 -r | cut -d' ' -f1)
ta=$(openssl x509 -in pki/ca.pem   -noout -pubkey | openssl pkey -pubin -outform DER | openssl dgst -sha256 -r | cut -d' ' -f1)
try() { # try <port> <tlsa rrdata> <domain> <label> [extra s_client flag]
  r=$(echo QUIT | timeout 5 openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:$1 -starttls smtp \
        -dane_tlsa_domain "$3" -dane_tlsa_rrdata "$2" $5 2>&1)
  code=$(echo "$r" | grep -m1 'Verify return code' | sed 's/.*code: //')
  match=$(echo "$r" | grep -m1 '^DANE TLSA' | sed 's/.*matched/matched/')
  printf '%-44s %s %s\n' "$4" "$code" "$match"
}
try 2525 "3 1 1 $ee" mail.lab.example "3 1 1, current key"
try 2525 "3 1 1 $ee" mx.wrong.example "3 1 1, current key, other name"
try 2525 "3 1 1 $ee" mx.wrong.example "same, -dane_ee_no_namechecks" -dane_ee_no_namechecks
try 2527 "3 1 1 $ee" mail.lab.example "3 1 1, expired cert on current key"
try 2526 "3 1 1 $ee" mail.lab.example "3 1 1, rotated key, TLSA not updated"
try 2526 "2 1 1 $ta" mail.lab.example "2 1 1, rotated key"
try 2526 "2 1 1 $ta" mx.wrong.example "2 1 1, rotated key, other name"
try 2527 "2 1 1 $ta" mail.lab.example "2 1 1, expired cert"
kill $p1 $p2 $p3

3 1 1, current key, other name               62 (hostname mismatch) 
same, -dane_ee_no_namechecks                 0 (ok) matched the EE certificate at depth 0
3 1 1, expired cert on current key           0 (ok) matched the EE certificate at depth 0
3 1 1, rotated key, TLSA not updated         65 (no matching DANE TLSA records) 
2 1 1, rotated key                           0 (ok) matched the TA certificate at depth 1
2 1 1, rotated key, other name               62 (hostname mismatch) 
2 1 1, expired cert                          10 (certificate has expired) 


What a sender decides for real domains


smtp.py

"""RFC 7672 sender view: what a DANE-aware MTA decides for each recipient domain (DNS only)."""
import json, urllib.request

def q(name, rtype):
    url = f"https://dns.google/resolve?name={name}&type={rtype}"
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) as r:
        return json.load(r)

def decide(domain):
    mx = q(domain, "MX")
    hosts = sorted((int(a["data"].split()[0]), a["data"].split()[1].rstrip("."))
                   for a in mx.get("Answer", []) if a["type"] == 15)
    if not mx.get("AD"):
        sts = q(f"_mta-sts.{domain}", "TXT")
        has_sts = any("v=STSv1" in a["data"] for a in sts.get("Answer", []))
        return [f"{domain}: MX RRset insecure (AD=0) -> no DANE; "
                f"MTA-STS TXT {'present' if has_sts else 'absent'}"]
    out = [f"{domain}: MX RRset validated (AD=1), {len(hosts)} MX host(s)"]
    for pref, h in hosts:
        t = q(f"_25._tcp.{h}", "TLSA")
        recs = [a["data"] for a in t.get("Answer", []) if a["type"] == 52]
        if recs:
            kinds = sorted({" ".join(r.split()[:3]) for r in recs})
            verdict = "DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext"
            out.append(f"  {pref:>3} {h:28} AD={t.get('AD')} TLSA {', '.join(kinds)} -> {verdict}")
        else:
            out.append(f"  {pref:>3} {h:28} AD={t.get('AD')} rcode={t['Status']} no TLSA -> opportunistic TLS")
    return out

for d in ("nlnetlabs.nl", "posteo.de", "freebsd.org", "ietf.org", "gmail.com"):
    print("\n".join(decide(d)))

nlnetlabs.nl: MX RRset validated (AD=1), 4 MX host(s)
   10 mxext1.mailbox.org           AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
   10 mxext2.mailbox.org           AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
   10 mxext3.mailbox.org           AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
   10 mxext4.mailbox.org           AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
posteo.de: MX RRset validated (AD=1), 4 MX host(s)
   10 mx01.posteo.de               AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
   10 mx02.posteo.de               AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
   10 mx03.posteo.de               AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
   10 mx04.posteo.de               AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
freebsd.org: MX RRset validated (AD=1), 2 MX host(s)
   10 mx1.freebsd.org              AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
   30 mx66.freebsd.org             AD=True rcode=3 no TLSA -> opportunistic TLS
ietf.org: MX RRset validated (AD=1), 1 MX host(s)
    0 mx.ietf.org                  AD=True TLSA 3 1 1 -> DANE: authenticated TLS REQUIRED, no fallback to cleartext
gmail.com: MX RRset insecure (AD=0) -> no DANE; MTA-STS TXT present
smtp.py takes the strict reading for an insecure MX RRset (no DANE). A real MTA may still use the TLSA records of the MX hosts, as section 2.2.1 allows. It also trusts the AD bit from Google’s resolver, which is acceptable for a lab over HTTPS but not for a production MTA (see the production section).

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
Reading the results
The SPKI hash is easy to compute twice. The OpenSSL pipeline and the 30-line DER walker agree on cb66729e.... That pipeline is what you will run in production, and the Python version shows there is nothing magic in it: SHA-256 over the DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo.
Selector 1 survives renewals; selector 0 does not. 3 1 1 passes for the renewed certificate on the same key; 3 0 1 fails. Any change to serial, dates or extensions changes a selector-0 hash. A new key breaks 3 1 1 too (the “new key, TLSA not updated” row), which is why key changes need the rollover below.
DANE-EE ignores dates and, by the RFC, names. In lab.py, 3 1 1 passes for an expired certificate and for one issued to www.other.example. The DNS zone owner pinned that key; nothing else about the certificate matters. DANE-TA is different: the chain is validated normally up to the pinned CA, so expiry (certificate has expired) and name (hostname mismatch) are enforced.
OpenSSL checks names for DANE-EE unless told not to. The OpenSSL rows mostly agree with my matcher, with one exception: 3 1 1, current key, other name fails with code 62. OpenSSL’s SSL_CTX_dane_enable(3) page explains why: name checks stay on for DANE-EE by default because, for web browsers, skipping them opens “unknown key share” attacks. Applications such as MTAs that follow RFC 7671 set DANE_FLAG_NO_DANE_EE_NAMECHECKS, which is what -dane_ee_no_namechecks does, and the row passes. Expiry is ignored for DANE-EE even by default (the expired row is 0 (ok)).
DANE-TA needs the CA in the handshake. 2 1 1 keeps working across a key change from the same CA (row “rotated key”), which is its main attraction. In lab.py, the “server forgot to send the CA” case fails: with only the leaf on the wire there is nothing for the TLSA record to match.
Unvalidated answers are ignored. The AD=0 row fails even though the hash matches. An unsigned TLSA record is just a hint an attacker can forge.
On the Internet. www.huque.com, www.nlnetlabs.nl and www.freebsd.org publish signed TLSA records whose 3 1 1 hash matches the key they serve today; www.ietf.org publishes none, so plain WebPKI applies. For mail, nlnetlabs.nl (hosted at mailbox.org), posteo.de and ietf.org have signed MX RRsets and TLSA records on every MX host, so a DANE sender will not deliver to them in cleartext. freebsd.org is the instructive case: mx1 has a TLSA record, but the backup mx66 returns a secure NXDOMAIN for _25._tcp.mx66.freebsd.org. That is a valid “no DANE here” answer, so mail to that host goes out with opportunistic TLS. gmail.com has an unsigned MX RRset, so DANE does not apply; it publishes an MTA-STS record (RFC 8461) instead.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
Rolling keys without an outage
TLSA records are cached for their TTL. If you change the server’s key before every resolver has seen a record for the new key, DANE senders with the old RRset cached will refuse to deliver. RFC 7671 section 8 gives the rule that prevents this:

each and every parameter combination that appears in the TLSA RRset is, on its own, sufficient to match the server’s current certificate chain

and section 8.1 gives the procedure for a fixed 3 1 1 setup:
step 0   RRset: 3 1 1 <cur>               server: cur key
step 1   RRset: 3 1 1 <cur>, 3 1 1 <next> server: cur key     wait at least 2 x TTL
step 2   RRset: 3 1 1 <cur>, 3 1 1 <next> server: next key    check delivery works
step 3   RRset: 3 1 1 <next>              server: next key
Section 3 of lab.py lints each step against the chain the server serves at that moment, and shows two mistakes. Publishing only the next key while the old key is still served leaves no matching record. The subtler one is adding a record with a different parameter combination (3 0 1) that matches only the future certificate. A client that only implements 3 0 1, or that prefers it, sees a combination with no current match. Every combination you publish has to match what is on the wire now.
A practical routine is to keep a pre-generated next key at all times, publish 3 1 1 for both current and next, and renew certificates on the current key. When you want to rotate, swap to the next key (it is already in DNS), generate a new next key, publish its hash, and remove the old one after two TTLs.
RFC 7671 section 13 adds the TTL trade-off: long TTLs mean long waits before a planned change and long outages after an unplanned one (lost or compromised key). Pick a TTL short enough that an emergency key change with a few hours of failed deliveries is acceptable. Mail queues retry, so a delay of hours costs much less for SMTP than for HTTPS.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
Production configuration (not run here)

Publishing the record
Compute the hash from the certificate the server actually uses, then publish it in a DNSSEC-signed zone:


tlsa-hash.sh

# not run here
openssl x509 -in /etc/ssl/mx1.example.net.pem -noout -pubkey \
  | openssl pkey -pubin -outform DER \
  | openssl dgst -sha256 -r | cut -d' ' -f1

; zone example.net, signed (not run here)
example.net.                 3600 IN MX    10 mx1.example.net.
mx1.example.net.             3600 IN A     192.0.2.25
mx1.example.net.             3600 IN AAAA  2001:db8::25
_25._tcp.mx1.example.net.    3600 IN TLSA  3 1 1 <64 hex digits>
Both the zone holding the MX records and the zone holding the MX host’s TLSA record must be signed and correctly delegated with DS records. If your mail is hosted by a provider, the TLSA records belong to the provider’s zone (_25._tcp.mxext1.mailbox.org in the nlnetlabs.nl example), and your part is signing your own zone so the MX RRset validates.
If certificates come from an ACME client, make it reuse the key on renewal (for certbot, --reuse-key), or hook the DNS update into the renewal so the new key is published two TTLs before it is used. Otherwise each renewal is an unannounced key change.


Sending side: Postfix
From postconf(5) and TLS_README:


main.cf

# /etc/postfix/main.cf (not run here)
# Postfix only treats "#" at the start of a line as a comment.
# Ask the resolver for DNSSEC and honour its AD bit:
smtp_dns_support_level = dnssec
# Opportunistic DANE: authenticate where usable signed TLSA records exist:
smtp_tls_security_level = dane
smtp_tls_loglevel = 1

dane is opportunistic DANE: authenticated TLS where signed TLSA records exist, ordinary opportunistic TLS elsewhere. dane-only makes DANE mandatory, so mail to destinations without usable TLSA records is deferred; use it in a per-destination policy table, not as a global default. (Since Postfix 3.11 the default smtp_tls_security_level is may instead of empty.)
Postfix does not validate DNSSEC itself. It trusts the AD bit from the resolver in /etc/resolv.conf, so that resolver must be a validating one on the same host, for example Unbound on 127.0.0.1. An AD bit received over an untrusted network can be forged as easily as the answer.


Receiving side
Publishing the record is the whole receiving-side change, plus making sure every MX host offers STARTTLS with the pinned key on every address it answers on, IPv4 and IPv6 alike.


MTA-STS
MTA-STS (RFC 8461) solves the same downgrade problem without DNSSEC: a TXT record at _mta-sts.<domain> and a policy file over HTTPS, with certificates checked against public CAs. A domain can publish both. A sender may implement either or both; check your MTA’s documentation for what it does when both are present.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
Gotchas

OpenSSL name checks on DANE-EE. Applications that use OpenSSL’s DANE API get name checks on DANE-EE by default. For SMTP, RFC 7671 says to skip them, and Postfix does. If you write your own client, decide deliberately and set DANE_FLAG_NO_DANE_EE_NAMECHECKS only where unknown-key-share attacks do not matter.
3 0 1 breaks on every renewal. Pin the SPKI (3 1 1) unless you have a specific reason not to.
DANE-TA without the CA on the wire fails. Configure the server to send the full chain, including the certificate the 2 x x record matches.
The AD bit is only as trustworthy as the path to the resolver. Use a validating resolver on loopback for the MTA.
ACME renewals rotate keys by default. Reuse keys or automate the TLSA update with the two-TTL wait.
One unprotected MX host weakens the domain. An attacker who blocks the DANE-protected hosts can push senders to a host without TLSA records. Publish TLSA for every MX host or none.
TLSA without working STARTTLS stops your inbound mail. DANE senders will defer instead of delivering in cleartext.
SERVFAIL on TLSA queries is an outage. Broken signatures, a missing DS, or nameservers that mishandle the TLSA query type (RFC 7672 section 2.2.2 mentions load-balancing nameservers that do) all make the MX host unreachable for DANE senders.
Secure NXDOMAIN is not an error. mx66.freebsd.org shows that a signed “no TLSA here” is a valid answer and leads to opportunistic TLS.
Emergency key changes run into cached RRsets. Senders keep the old TLSA RRset until its TTL expires. Keep the TTL modest and a pre-published next key ready.

title: DANE and TLSA: Pinning TLS Keys in DNSSEC
text:
Exercises

Run openssl s_client -connect www.freebsd.org:443 -servername www.freebsd.org and compute the 3 1 1 hash of the leaf with the pipeline from lab.py. Compare it with the TLSA records lab.py fetched. Which of the two published records matches, and what might the other one be for?
Add matching type 2 (SHA2-512) records to section 2 of lab.py, then add a case where the RRset holds a 3 1 2 record for the next key only. What does publisher_lint report, and which client would break?
Change openssl-dane.sh so the server on 2526 sends only the leaf (use pki/rotated.pem instead of pki/rotated-chain.pem). Which 2 1 1 rows change and why?
Extend smtp.py to sort MX hosts by preference and print, for each domain, whether an attacker who blocks the DANE-protected hosts could get mail delivered in cleartext.
Pick a domain you run. Is the MX RRset secure? Do all MX hosts have TLSA records? Write down the steps and TTL waits needed to roll the key on one MX host without deferring mail.

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
The DANE chapter showed DANE/TLSA (RFC 7672) as a mechanism to secure SMTP connections against active man-in-the-middle attacks, cleartext downgrades, and DNS MX spoofing. DANE provides cryptographic guarantees for transport layer security directly via DNS. However, its operation strictly depends on DNSSEC. Many mail domains are not signed, and the largest mail providers’ MX zones are among them (the DANE chapter’s survey found gmail.com with an insecure MX RRset).
SMTP Mail Transfer Agent Strict Transport Security (MTA-STS, RFC 8461) and SMTP TLS Reporting (TLSRPT, RFC 8460) were created to provide MTA-to-MTA TLS enforcement and visibility without requiring DNSSEC. By anchoring trust in standard Web PKI certificates and serving enforcement policies over HTTPS, MTA-STS allows domain owners to declare that incoming mail MUST be delivered over encrypted TLS connections to verified hostnames.

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
Learning goals

Understand the architecture of RFC 8461 (MTA-STS) and how HTTPS-based policy distribution bypasses the need for DNSSEC.
Analyze the Trust-On-First-Use (TOFU) security model and its trade-offs compared to DANE.
Parse and validate _mta-sts TXT records and HTTPS policy files using exact RFC 8461 syntax rules.
Evaluate RFC 8460 TLSRPT structure, URI schemas, media types, and aggregate reporting JSON payloads.
Observe real-world MTA-STS deployment patterns across major email providers.
Implement server-side policy hosting (Nginx) and client-side policy resolution architecture (postfix-mta-sts-resolver).
Identify critical deployment edge cases, caching pitfalls, and operational failures.

text:
Version note
The lab ran on the book’s build box as an unprivileged user: Linux 6.12, OpenSSL 3.5.7 and Python 3.13 with the standard library only. Nothing was installed. The toy policy hosts are real HTTPS servers on 127.0.0.1 with a private CA. Live DNS answers come from Google Public DNS over its DoH JSON API, and live policies were fetched over HTTPS from the real mta-sts.<domain> hosts on 2026-11-14 (IST). Outbound port 25 is blocked from the build box, so no SMTP session was made; the MX TLS outcomes in section 4 of the lab are given as data. The nginx, DNS, Postfix and postfix-mta-sts-resolver snippets are not run here.

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
How MTA-STS works
MTA-STS (RFC 8461) relies on two distinct protocols to establish TLS enforcement: DNS for signaling policy presence and updates, and HTTPS for serving the actual policy definition.
+-------------------+             1. TXT Query _mta-sts.example.com
|                   | --------------------------------------------------------> +------------+
|                   | <-------------------------------------------------------- | DNS Server |
|                   |             "v=STSv1; id=20261114T0900Z;"                 +------------+
|  Sending Mail     |
|  Transfer Agent   |             2. HTTPS GET /.well-known/mta-sts.txt
|     (MTA)         | --------------------------------------------------------> +------------------------+
|                   | <-------------------------------------------------------- | https://mta-sts.example|
|                   |             version: STSv1                                +------------------------+
|                   |             mode: enforce ...
|                   |
|                   |             3. Authenticated TLS SMTP Session
|                   | --------------------------------------------------------> +------------+
|                   |                                                           | Mail Exch. |
+-------------------+                                                           +------------+

DNS Discovery Record
A domain supporting MTA-STS publishes a DNS TXT record at _mta-sts.<domain>. According to RFC 8461 Section 3.1, this record must adhere to specific formatting rules:

The value must begin with v=STSv1;.
Exactly one v=STSv1 record must be present at _mta-sts.<domain>. If multiple STSv1 records are found, the sending MTA MUST treat the domain as having no valid MTA-STS policy.
The record must contain an id field formatted as 1 to 32 alphanumeric characters ([A-Za-z0-9]{1,32}). This ID serves as a policy version tracker.
Multiple character strings in a single TXT record must be concatenated without spaces during parsing.
CNAME records are explicitly permitted for delegating the _mta-sts record to third-party providers.



HTTPS Policy File Fetch
When a sending MTA detects a new or updated id in the DNS TXT record, it issues an HTTPS GET request to:
https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt
The HTTPS request and response must obey these strict operational bounds (RFC 8461 Section 3.3): - TLS Validation: The server certificate presented at mta-sts.<domain> MUST be valid according to standard Web PKI rules (X.509 chain of trust to a public CA, matching SAN/CN). - HTTP Status Code: Only an HTTP 200 OK response indicates success. - No Redirects: HTTP redirects (301, 302, 307, 308) MUST NOT be followed. Any redirect response must be treated as a policy fetch error. - No HTTP caching: Sending MTAs MUST NOT use HTTP caching (RFC 7234) for the fetch. How long a policy lives is set only by its max_age field. - Media Type: Senders SHOULD check that the media type is text/plain, so that a web server which lets users upload HTML or images under arbitrary paths cannot be used to plant a policy. The lab treats any other media type as invalid. - Resource Limits: Implementations SHOULD enforce a timeout (suggested 1 minute) and limit the maximum response body read (suggested 64 KiB) to prevent denial-of-service vectors.


Policy File Syntax and Fields
The policy file uses key-value formatting separated by colons (:), with lines delimited by LF or CRLF (RFC 8461 Section 3.2). Key parsing follows a “first copy wins” rule for non-mx fields:

version: Must be STSv1.
mode: Must be one of enforce, testing, or none.
max_age: Lifetime of the policy in seconds (max allowed value is 31557600, approximately 1 year).
mx: One or more domain patterns specifying valid receiving MX hosts. Required for enforce and testing modes; optional/ignored for none.

mx pattern matching rules (Section 4.1) permit wildcarding: - A leading *. wildcard matches exactly one left-most domain label (e.g., *.example.com matches mail.example.com, but does NOT match example.com or a.b.example.com). - Explicit hostnames match exact string representations (case-insensitive).


Policy Modes and Cache Semantics
The three operational modes defined in RFC 8461 Section 5 govern MTA delivery behavior:

enforce: Sending MTAs MUST verify that the destination MX host matches an mx field in the policy AND that the MX presents a valid Web PKI TLS certificate matching its hostname. If TLS cannot be negotiated or validation fails, delivery MUST NOT proceed over cleartext; messages must be deferred/queued.
testing: Sending MTAs attempt TLS negotiation and validation. If verification fails, the failure is recorded for TLSRPT reporting, but the mail is still delivered over unauthenticated TLS or cleartext.
none: Senders treat the domain as having no active policy. This mode exists so a domain can switch MTA-STS off cleanly (section 8.3) and senders can tell an opt-out from an attack.

Section 3.3 outlines sender caching semantics: 1. Valid Cache Available: Senders apply the cached policy without re-fetching over HTTPS for every mail transaction, provided max_age has not elapsed. 2. Fetch Failure with Valid Cache: If DNS or HTTPS policy fetches fail, but a valid, non-expired cache exists, the cached policy MUST continue to be applied. 3. Fetch Failure with No Cache: If no cache exists and the policy fetch fails (or no valid TXT record exists), the message is delivered normally as if MTA-STS were not supported by the domain. 4. Proactive Refresh: Senders SHOULD refresh cached policies before they expire, about once a day, and alert an administrator when refreshes keep failing (sections 3.3 and 10.2). 5. No bounce without a recheck: Per section 5.1, a message that cannot be delivered because of an enforce policy must not be failed permanently until the sender has checked the TXT record for a new policy id. 6. Subdomain Isolation: MTA-STS policies do not automatically apply to subdomains. A policy for example.com does not protect sub.example.com unless sub.example.com explicitly publishes its own _mta-sts.sub.example.com DNS record (Section 3.4).

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
Trust on first use
The core structural weakness of MTA-STS is its reliance on Trust-On-First-Use (TOFU), detailed in RFC 8461 Section 10.2.
Because initial policy discovery depends on unauthenticated DNS queries (_mta-sts.<domain>) and cleartext network paths prior to TLS establishment, an active network adversary can intercept a sender’s initial contact with a domain. The attacker can strip the _mta-sts TXT record or block the HTTPS fetch to mta-sts.<domain>. Under standard behavior, a sender experiencing initial fetch failure simply falls back to standard SMTP delivery without enforcement.
Initial Uncached Contact:
Sender ------------------ TXT Query? ------------------> Unsigned DNS (Vulnerable to MITM stripping)
Sender ------------------ HTTPS Fetch? ----------------> mta-sts.domain (can be blocked)

Subsequent Contacts (Active Cache Valid):
Sender ------------------ Enforces Policy ---------------> TLS to an MX that matches the policy, cert checked
To mitigate TOFU vulnerabilities, domain operators specify large max_age values (e.g., several weeks or months). Once a sending MTA successfully fetches a policy, that policy is pinned locally. While an enforce policy is cached, an attacker who controls DNS can no longer downgrade the connection or redirect it to a forged MX; the most they can do is delay mail. They can still try again at refresh time, which is why section 10.2 asks senders to refresh daily and long before expiry, so an attacker has to block every refresh for the whole max_age.
By contrast, DANE/TLSA (RFC 7672) does not rely on TOFU. Every connection attempt using DANE dynamically validates TLSA records authenticated via DNSSEC signatures. DANE protects the very first connection attempt without requiring warmup caches or secondary HTTPS servers, provided the sender performs DNSSEC validation. However, MTA-STS trades this instant first-use guarantee for ease of deployment on standard Web PKI infrastructure.

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
TLSRPT
SMTP TLS Reporting (TLSRPT, RFC 8460) works alongside MTA-STS and DANE by giving domain owners visibility into transport security failures occurring during mail delivery.

Reporting Discovery Record
Domains declare where senders should submit automated aggregate reports by publishing a DNS TXT record at _smtp._tls.<domain>:
_smtp._tls.example.com. IN TXT "v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:tlsrpt@example.com,https://tlsrpt.example.com/submit"
The rua parameter accepts a comma-separated list of reporting endpoints using either mailto: or https: URI schemas.


Delivery and Formats
Sending MTAs aggregate diagnostic events over a 24-hour period and generate a JSON document. Reports are transmitted via HTTPS POST or email (mailto:).

Media Types:

Standard JSON: application/tlsrpt+json
Compressed JSON: application/tlsrpt+gzip


By mail, the report is an attachment with a recommended file name of the form sender!policy-domain!begin-timestamp!end-timestamp!unique-id.json.gz, and the message carries TLS-Report-Domain and TLS-Report-Submitter header fields so receivers can sort reports automatically (RFC 8460 section 5.3).


Standard Result Types
RFC 8460 defines explicit result type strings covering both MTA-STS and DANE failure modes:

starttls-not-supported: Target MX did not announce STARTTLS capability.
certificate-host-mismatch: MX certificate identity does not match the expected hostname or policy patterns.
certificate-expired: MX certificate timestamp is outside its validity window.
certificate-not-trusted: a catch-all for chain problems (unknown CA, name constraints, chain errors); senders SHOULD add a failure-reason-code.
validation-failure: a failure that fits none of the other types; again with a failure-reason-code.
tlsa-invalid: none of the records in the TLSA RRset were found to be valid.
dnssec-invalid: no valid records were returned from the recursive resolver.
dane-required: the sender is configured to require DANE for this destination, but the MX host had no DNSSEC-validated TLSA records.
sts-policy-fetch-error: Could not retrieve the MTA-STS policy over HTTPS (connect timeout, DNS failure, 404/500 HTTP code).
sts-policy-invalid: Policy file contents failed RFC 8461 syntax parsing.
sts-webpki-invalid: HTTPS certificate presented by mta-sts.<domain> failed Web PKI trust checks.

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
The lab
Six files. mkpki.sh makes a private CA and two policy-host certificates. mtasts.py holds the parsers, the MX pattern matcher and a policy fetcher that follows section 3.3. policyhost.py serves nine kinds of policy host over real HTTPS on 127.0.0.1. sender.py is a small sending MTA with a policy cache and TLSRPT counters. lab.py drives sections 1 to 5, and survey.py asks the real Internet.

A private CA for the policy hosts


mkpki.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Private CA, one policy-host certificate covering the lab domains, one with the wrong name.
set -e
mkdir -p pki && cd pki
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -keyout ca.key -out ca.pem \
  -days 30 -subj "/CN=STS Lab CA" -addext basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE \
  -addext keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign 2>/dev/null
cert() { # cert <name> <subjectAltName>
  openssl req -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -keyout "$1.key" -subj "/CN=$1" \
    -addext "subjectAltName=$2" -out "$1.csr" 2>/dev/null

Parsing, matching and fetching

"""MTA-STS (RFC 8461) and TLSRPT (RFC 8460) building blocks. Standard library only."""
import http.client, json, re, socket, ssl, urllib.request

MAX_AGE_LIMIT = 31557600            # RFC 8461 section 3.2: about one year

def doh(name, rtype):
    with urllib.request.urlopen(f"https://dns.google/resolve?name={name}&type={rtype}", timeout=10) as r:
        return json.load(r)

def txt_records(name):
    ans = doh(name, "TXT").get("Answer", [])
    # A TXT record may hold several strings; RFC 8461 says join them without spaces.
    return ["".join(re.findall(r'"((?:[^"\\]|\\.)*)"', a["data"])) or a["data"]
            for a in ans if a["type"] == 16]

def parse_sts_txt(records):
    """Section 3.1: keep records starting with v=STSv1; exactly one must remain and carry an id."""
    cand = [r for r in records if re.match(r"v=STSv1\s*;", r)]
    if len(cand) != 1:
        return None, f"{len(cand)} v=STSv1 record(s) -> no policy"
    fields = dict(f.strip().split("=", 1) for f in cand[0].split(";") if "=" in f)
    sid = fields.get("id", "")
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9]{1,32}", sid):
        return None, f"bad id {sid!r} -> no policy"
    return sid, "ok"

def parse_policy(body, content_type="text/plain"):
    """Section 3.2: key: value lines, LF or CRLF; first copy of a non-mx key wins."""
    if content_type.split(";")[0].strip().lower() != "text/plain":
        return None, f"media type {content_type!r} is not text/plain"
    pol = {"mx": []}
    for line in body.replace("\r\n", "\n").split("\n"):
        if ":" not in line:
            continue
        k, v = (x.strip() for x in line.split(":", 1))
        if k == "mx":
            pol["mx"].append(v.lower())
        elif k not in pol:
            pol[k] = v
    if pol.get("version") != "STSv1":
        return None, "version is not STSv1"
    if pol.get("mode") not in ("enforce", "testing", "none"):
        return None, f"bad mode {pol.get('mode')!r}"
    if not re.fullmatch(r"\d{1,10}", pol.get("max_age", "")) or int(pol["max_age"]) > MAX_AGE_LIMIT:
        return None, f"bad max_age {pol.get('max_age')!r}"
    if pol["mode"] != "none" and not pol["mx"]:
        return None, "no mx lines"
    pol["max_age"] = int(pol["max_age"])
    return pol, "ok"

def mx_match(pattern, host):
    """Section 4.1: '*.' matches exactly one left-most label."""
    host, pattern = host.lower().rstrip("."), pattern.lower().rstrip(".")
    if pattern.startswith("*."):
        head, _, rest = host.partition(".")
        return bool(head) and rest == pattern[2:]
    return host == pattern

def fetch_policy(domain, connect_to=None, port=443, cafile=None, timeout=10):
    """Section 3.3: HTTPS GET, certificate valid for mta-sts.<domain>, only 200 counts,
    redirects are NOT followed. connect_to lets the lab dial 127.0.0.1 while still
    verifying the real policy host name. Returns (policy or None, reason)."""
    host = f"mta-sts.{domain}"
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context(cafile=cafile)
    conn = http.client.HTTPConnection(host, port, timeout=timeout)
    try:
        raw = socket.create_connection((connect_to or host, port), timeout=timeout)
        conn.sock = ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname=host)
        conn.putrequest("GET", "/.well-known/mta-sts.txt", skip_host=True)
        conn.putheader("Host", host)
        conn.endheaders()
        r = conn.getresponse()
        body = r.read(65536).decode("utf-8", "replace")      # 64 KiB cap, section 3.3
    except ssl.SSLCertVerificationError as e:
        return None, f"sts-webpki-invalid: {e.verify_message}"
    except (OSError, http.client.HTTPException) as e:
        return None, f"sts-policy-fetch-error: {type(e).__name__}"
    finally:
        conn.close()
    if r.status != 200:
        loc = r.getheader("Location")
        return None, f"sts-policy-fetch-error: HTTP {r.status}" + (f", redirect to {loc} not followed" if loc else "")
    pol, why = parse_policy(body, r.getheader("Content-Type", ""))
    return (pol, "ok") if pol else (None, f"sts-policy-invalid: {why}")

def tlsrpt_record(domain):
    cand = [r for r in txt_records(f"_smtp._tls.{domain}") if re.match(r"v=TLSRPTv1\s*;", r)]
    if len(cand) != 1:
        return None
    m = re.search(r"rua=([^;]+)", cand[0])
    return m.group(1).strip() if m else None

fetch_policy() connects with a normal ssl.create_default_context(), so the policy host’s certificate is checked exactly like a web browser would check it, against the name mta-sts.<domain>. The connect_to argument lets the lab dial 127.0.0.1 while still verifying the real name. Redirects are reported, never followed, and the body is capped at 64 KiB.
