"""Toy MTA-STS policy hosts on 127.0.0.1, one behaviour per Host header."""
import http.server, ssl, sys, threading

POLICIES = {
    "good":     ("200", "text/plain", "version: STSv1\r\nmode: enforce\r\nmx: mx1.good.example\r\n"
                                      "mx: *.backup.good.example\r\nmax_age: 1209600\r\n"),
    "testing":  ("200", "text/plain; charset=utf-8", "version: STSv1\nmode: testing\nmx: mx.testing.example\nmax_age: 86400\n"),
    "none":     ("200", "text/plain", "version: STSv1\nmode: none\nmax_age: 86400\n"),
    "redirect": ("301", "text/plain", ""),
    "html":     ("200", "text/html", "<html>version: STSv1<br>mode: enforce</html>"),
    "missing":  ("404", "text/plain", "not found\n"),
    "dupmode":  ("200", "text/plain", "version: STSv1\nmode: testing\nmode: enforce\nmx: mx.dupmode.example\nmax_age: 86400\n"),
    "bigage":   ("200", "text/plain", "version: STSv1\nmode: enforce\nmx: mx.bigage.example\nmax_age: 63115200\n"),
    "nomx":     ("200", "text/plain", "version: STSv1\nmode: enforce\nmax_age: 86400\n"),
}

class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        dom = self.headers["Host"].removeprefix("mta-sts.").removesuffix(".example")
        code, ctype, body = POLICIES.get(dom, ("404", "text/plain", ""))
        self.send_response(int(code))
        self.send_header("Content-Type", ctype)
        if code == "301":
            self.send_header("Location", "https://evil.example/.well-known/mta-sts.txt")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body.encode())
    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

def serve(port, cert, key):
    ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
    ctx.load_cert_chain(cert, key)
    srv = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), H)
    srv.socket = ctx.wrap_socket(srv.socket, server_side=True)
    threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    return srv



A sender with a policy cache


sender.py

"""A sending MTA's MTA-STS logic (RFC 8461 sections 3.3, 5, 5.1) with a policy cache and
TLSRPT counters (RFC 8460). DNS, HTTPS and the MX TLS handshakes are passed in as data,
so every case is reproducible; the parsing and matching are the real functions."""
import collections, mtasts

class Sender:
    def __init__(self):
        self.cache = {}                                   # domain -> (policy, id, fetched_at)
        self.ok = collections.Counter()
        self.fail = collections.Counter()   # (domain, result-type, mx, reason) -> sessions

    def refresh(self, domain, now, txt, fetch):
        sid, _ = mtasts.parse_sts_txt(txt)
        cached = self.cache.get(domain)
        fresh = cached and now - cached[2] < cached[0]["max_age"]
        if sid and not (fresh and cached[1] == sid):
            pol, why = fetch()
            if pol:
                self.cache[domain] = (pol, sid, now)
                return f"fetched policy id={sid} mode={pol['mode']}"
            if not (fresh and cached[0]["mode"] == "none"):
                self.fail[(domain, why.split(":")[0], None, why.split(": ", 1)[1])] += 1
            return f"fetch failed ({why})" + ("; keeping cached policy" if fresh else "")
        if not sid:
            return "no usable TXT" + ("; cached policy still valid" if fresh else "")
        return f"TXT id={sid} unchanged; cached policy valid"

    def deliver(self, domain, now, mxs, tls):
        """mxs: MX hosts in preference order; tls: host -> 'ok' or an RFC 8460 result type."""
        cached = self.cache.get(domain)
        pol = cached[0] if cached and now - cached[2] < cached[0]["max_age"] else None
        mode = pol["mode"] if pol else "none"
        for mx in mxs:
            if mode == "none":
                how = "TLS" if tls[mx] == "ok" else "CLEARTEXT/unauthenticated"
                return f"delivered to {mx} via {how} (no active policy)"
            problem, code = None, None
            if not any(mtasts.mx_match(p, mx) for p in pol["mx"]):
                problem = "validation-failure"   # RFC 8460 has no MX-specific type
                code = "mx host not in policy"
            elif tls[mx] != "ok":
                problem = tls[mx]
            if problem is None:
                self.ok[domain] += 1
                return f"delivered to {mx} via authenticated TLS ({mode})"
            self.fail[(domain, problem, mx, code)] += 1
            if mode == "testing":
                return f"delivered to {mx} despite {problem} (testing: reported only)"
        return "deferred: no MX passed the enforce policy; recheck TXT before bouncing"

    def report(self, domain, org="sender.example", day="2026-11-14"):
        pol = self.cache[domain][0]
        details = []
        for (d, rt, mx, code), n in sorted(self.fail.items(), key=str):
            if d != domain:
                continue
            item = {"result-type": rt}
            if mx:
                item["receiving-mx-hostname"] = mx
            item["failed-session-count"] = n
            if code:
                item["failure-reason-code"] = code
            details.append(item)
        return {
            "organization-name": org,
            "date-range": {"start-datetime": f"{day}T00:00:00Z", "end-datetime": f"{day}T23:59:59Z"},
            "contact-info": f"tlsrpt@{org}",
            "report-id": f"{day}-{domain}",
            "policies": [{
                "policy": {"policy-type": "sts",
                           "policy-string": [f"version: STSv1", f"mode: {pol['mode']}"]
                                            + [f"mx: {m}" for m in pol["mx"]] + [f"max_age: {pol['max_age']}"],
                           "policy-domain": domain, "mx-host": pol["mx"]},
                "summary": {"total-successful-session-count": self.ok[domain],
                            "total-failure-session-count": sum(n for k, n in self.fail.items() if k[0] == domain)},
                "failure-details": details}]}

The sender takes DNS answers, HTTPS fetch results and the outcome of each MX TLS handshake as arguments. Outbound port 25 is blocked on the build box, so the MX handshakes in section 4 are given as data (“ok” or an RFC 8460 result type). The parsing, MX matching, cache expiry and mode logic are the real functions above.

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
Reading the results
The execution outputs highlight key aspects of MTA-STS parsing, state management, real-world deployment practices, and Python strict validation quirks.

Section 1: TXT Parsing Mechanics
Section 1 demonstrates the string parsing rules from RFC 8461 Section 3.1: - split into two strings, joined: Demonstrates DNS TXT chunk concatenation. DNS responses splitting strings across 255-byte boundaries are joined seamlessly. - two STSv1 records: two v=STSv1 TXT records mean no policy at all. RFC 8461 requires exactly one. A leftover record from a migration silently switches MTA-STS off for new senders. - id with a dash: Fails validation (bad id '2026-11-14'). RFC 8461 strictly limits the id field to alphanumeric characters ([A-Za-z0-9]). Dashes, underscores, or special characters render the TXT record invalid. - version not first: id=abc; v=STSv1 fails because RFC 8461 dictates that v=STSv1 must be the absolute first tag in the record.


Section 2: MX Wildcard Matching
Matching tests verify Section 4.1 rule compliance: - *.example.com matches mail.example.com but fails against example.com (wildcard requires a left-most label) and a.b.example.com (wildcard matches exactly one label level).


Section 3: Toy Policy Host Verification
Testing against HTTPS endpoints on 127.0.0.1 illustrates mandatory HTTP client checks: - redirect.example: Returns HTTP 301. MTA-STS fetch engines MUST NOT follow redirects. The fetch fails instantly (HTTP 301... not followed). - html.example: rejected because the Content-Type is text/html. Section 3.2 says senders SHOULD check for text/plain; the lab does. - dupmode.example: Demonstrates first-wins parsing logic. mode: testing followed by mode: enforce evaluates to mode=testing. - bigage.example: Fails parsing because 63115200 exceeds the maximum max_age cap of 31,557,600 seconds. - missing.example: a 404 is a fetch error. With no cached policy, the sender continues as if the domain had no MTA-STS at all. - nomx.example: an enforce policy without mx lines is invalid; only mode: none may omit them (none.example parses fine with mx=[]). - good.example (wrong cert): the policy host presents a certificate for www.unrelated.example, and the fetch fails with sts-webpki-invalid. This is what happens when mta-sts.<domain> is a CNAME to a shared web host that has no certificate for that name.


Section 4: 17-Day Sender Timeline Dynamics
The time-series simulation highlights caching state transitions over a 17-day period: - Day 0.0 (First Contact): Senders fetch policy A1 and cache it (mode=enforce, max_age=1209600 / 14 days). Mail is successfully delivered via authenticated TLS. - Day 1.0 (Active Attack): An attacker strips DNS TXT records and blocks HTTPS policy fetches while spoofing MX records to point to evil.attacker.example. Because the sender has a valid unexpired cache for good.example, it ignores the DNS/HTTPS failure, applies the cached policy, checks the forged MX against the policy mx: list, rejects evil.attacker.example, and defers message delivery. - Day 2.0 (Operator Configuration Error): The domain operator provisions a new MX host (mx2.newhost.example) but forgets to update the HTTPS policy file. Delivery to mx2.newhost.example fails because the host is not matched by the cached policy mx: patterns. - Day 2.1 (Corrected Update): Policy body is updated to include mx2.newhost.example and the TXT record id is incremented to B2. Senders fetch the updated policy and resume successful delivery. - Day 3.0 (Primary MX Outage): Primary host mx1 presents an expired certificate. The sender seamlessly falls back to mx9.backup.good.example which matches the wildcard policy *.backup.good.example. - Day 17.0 (Policy Expiration): The policy fetched on day 2.1 has passed its 14-day max_age, and the HTTPS fetch fails. With no valid cached policy, protection lapses and mail goes out without authentication, here in cleartext. The toy sender only refetches when the TXT id changes or the cache has expired. A real sender should refresh daily in the background (section 10.2), so a refresh would have succeeded on some day between 3 and 16 and the policy would still be valid. - Testing Mode Behavior: For testing.example, STARTTLS stripping is logged as a failure for TLSRPT reporting, but the sender proceeds with delivery regardless. - Uncached Attacker Interaction: For fresh.example (never before seen), an attacker stripping TXT/HTTPS prevents policy pinning. Delivery falls back to cleartext without protection, highlighting TOFU exposure.


Section 5: TLSRPT Serialization
The resulting JSON document summarizes delivery statistics. Note that RFC 8460 lacks a distinct result type for “MX host not explicitly listed in MTA-STS policy.” The lab models this event using validation-failure supplemented by failure-reason-code: "mx host not in policy".


Real-World Domain Survey Observations
The live survey reveals distinct operational strategies: - Gmail & Yahoo: Set max_age to 86,400 seconds (1 day). This is significantly shorter than the “weeks or greater” expectation suggested in RFC 8461 Section 10.2. A short max_age reduces TOFU resistance but minimizes operational lock-out risks during infrastructure changes. - Testing Status: Yahoo (yahoo.com) and Fastmail (fastmail.com) publish mode=testing. They capture diagnostic TLSRPT telemetry without blocking unauthenticated sessions. - Both mechanisms: posteo.de and mailbox.org publish TLSA records (see the DANE chapter’s survey) and an enforce MTA-STS policy, so senders get protection whichever mechanism they implement. Gmail’s policy also lists *.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com, so the alt1 to alt4 MX hosts match with one wildcard. - No policy published: github.com and ietf.org publish no _mta-sts record. ietf.org relies on DANE instead (TLSA 3 1 1 on mx.ietf.org).


Python 3.13 Standard Library Strictness
During initial lab setup, Section 3 policy fetches failed for every local endpoint with the following error:
sts-webpki-invalid: CA cert does not include key usage extension
Since Python 3.13, ssl.create_default_context() sets VERIFY_X509_STRICT, which asks OpenSSL to enforce RFC 5280 rules it otherwise tolerates, including that a CA certificate carries a keyUsage extension. The first version of mkpki.sh made the CA with only basicConstraints, and every fetch failed. Adding -addext keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign fixed it. Public CAs already comply; the trap is home-made lab and internal CAs.

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
Sending side
Postfix does not natively contain built-in MTA-STS caching or parsing logic. In a Postfix production deployment, MTA-STS policy resolution is handled by an external daemon such as postfix-mta-sts-resolver.
+-------------------+                   +----------------------------+
|  Postfix (smtp)   | -- SocketMap ---->| postfix-mta-sts-resolver   |
|                   | <-- (secure/ta) --| (mta-sts-daemon)           |
+-------------------+                   +----------------------------+
                                                    |
                                          DNS TXT + HTTPS fetch
                                                    v
                                        +----------------------------+
                                        |  Remote _mta-sts Domain    |
                                        +----------------------------+

Postfix Integration (postfix-mta-sts-resolver)
The daemon runs as a local service listening on a TCP or Unix socket, implementing the Postfix socketmap protocol.
Its configuration file (/etc/mta-sts-daemon.yml) is described in the project’s man page; the defaults listen on 127.0.0.1 port 8461.
Postfix configuration, from the project README (not run here):


main.cf

# /etc/postfix/main.cf (not run here)
smtp_tls_policy_maps = socketmap:inet:127.0.0.1:8461:postfix
smtp_tls_CAfile = /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
smtp_tls_loglevel = 1

When Postfix routes mail for destination.example, it queries the socketmap service. The resolver checks its policy cache (fetching _mta-sts.destination.example and https://mta-sts.destination.example/.well-known/mta-sts.txt as needed). If an active enforce policy exists, the daemon returns a policy map instruction forcing Postfix to require TLS authentication (secure match=...).
There is a catch if you also enable DANE. RFC 8461 section 2 says MTA-STS validation MUST NOT override a failing DANE validation. The resolver’s README warns that, because of how Postfix policy tables work, a resolved MTA-STS policy does override Postfix’s built-in DANE for that destination (the map answers secure, which replaces dane). If you run both, read that section of the README and decide which destinations get which policy.
Other MTAs differ: some implement MTA-STS natively, some need a helper like this one. Check your MTA’s documentation.

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
Gotchas

MX Record Switch Before Policy Update: Adding a new MX host to DNS before adding it to the HTTPS policy file causes delivery deferrals for all senders with cached policies. Send retries will fail until those external caches reach their max_age expiration.
A TXT record without a working policy host protects nothing. If mta-sts.<domain> does not resolve, returns 404 or 403, or presents an expired or wrong certificate, senders with no cached policy treat the domain as having no MTA-STS. Nothing fails visibly, so this can go unnoticed for years. Check the HTTPS endpoint from outside after every web or certificate change.
HTTP Redirect Misconfigurations: Redirecting https://mta-sts.example.com to https://www.example.com or forcing HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects breaks compliance. Senders MUST NOT follow redirects when fetching /.well-known/mta-sts.txt.
Wrong Content-Type: Serve the file as text/plain. Senders that follow the SHOULD in section 3.2 reject text/html or application/octet-stream.
Updating DNS TXT ID Before HTTPS Policy Body: If the DNS TXT id is updated before the new policy body is uploaded to the HTTPS server, senders immediately fetch the old policy body under the new ID, caching obsolete rules under the new ID handle.
Short max_age Weakening TOFU Protection: Setting max_age to 86400 (1 day) reduces operational risk during changes, but drastically weakens TOFU security against active network interdictions occurring between sending attempts.
Indefinite testing Mode: Domains leaving MTA-STS in mode: testing indefinitely receive diagnostic reporting data but gain zero active protection against downgrade or interception attacks.
Single-Label Wildcard Match Limitations: A policy listing mx: *.example.com matches mail.example.com, but will fail to match multi-label hosts such as region1.smtp.example.com or base domains like example.com.
Lack of MX-Specific TLSRPT Failure Codes: RFC 8460 lacks a dedicated error string for “MX host not listed in MTA-STS policy.” Operators must look for generic validation-failure codes paired with custom failure-reason-code strings.
Running DANE and MTA-STS through a Postfix helper: see the sending-side note above; the helper’s policy can replace Postfix’s DANE check.
Backup MX Misconfigurations Hidden Until Primary Failure: Backup MX servers that present invalid certificates or fail policy matches remain undetected during normal operations, failing only when primary MX servers go offline (RFC 8461 Section 8.4).

title: MTA-STS and TLSRPT: Enforcing TLS for Mail Without DNSSEC
text:
Exercises

DNS TXT Parser Edge Cases: Modify mtasts.py to process a DNS TXT payload containing trailing spaces or multiple semi-colons (e.g., v=STSv1; id=abc123;;). Verify whether your parser rejects the record or normalizes it in compliance with RFC 8461 Section 3.1.
Wildcard Boundaries: Feed mx_match() the pattern *.*.example.com. The policy ABNF allows only one leading *. followed by a domain. What does the lab’s matcher do with it, and should parse_policy() reject the line instead?
HTTP Body Size Limit Enforcement: Update fetch_policy() in mtasts.py to stream the HTTP response body and abort the request immediately if the payload exceeds 65,536 bytes (64 KiB). Test this against a mock server returning a 1 MB policy payload.
TLSRPT Aggregator Engine: Extend sender.py to generate an aggregate report JSON combining delivery results across three distinct destination domains (good.example, testing.example, and invalid.example). Validate the output format against the RFC 8460 JSON Schema.
Proactive refresh: Give Sender a daily background refresh that refetches the policy even when the TXT id is unchanged, as section 10.2 suggests. Rerun section 4 with HTTPS available on day 10. What happens on day 17 now?

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
text:
Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
At Layer 4 (L4), a network load balancer forwards incoming TCP and UDP packets to a pool of backend servers. To prevent breaking active connections, all packets belonging to a single TCP stream or UDP flow must land on the exact same backend server for the entire duration of that session.
Every serious L4 load balancer keeps a per-flow table, but that table is local to one LB instance. Behind Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing there are several instances, and an instance can restart, be drained, or stop receiving a flow because the router’s ECMP set changed. A flow that arrives at an instance with no state for it must still reach the same backend. So the backend choice has to be a deterministic function of the packet, the same on every instance, and it has to stay mostly the same when the set of backends changes. That function is a hash, and which hash you use decides how many connections break when you add or remove one server.
This chapter explores how L4 load balancing hashing operates, evaluates four key algorithms—Modulo, Consistent Hashing Rings, Rendezvous Hashing (HRW), and Maglev Hashing—and measures their balance, disruption, and computational complexity.

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
text:
Learning goals

Understand why stateless Layer 4 load balancing requires deterministic 5-tuple hashing to maintain flow stickiness across ECMP router fabrics.
Compare four major load balancing hash algorithms: Modulo, Consistent Hashing Ring with virtual nodes, Rendezvous (HRW), and Maglev.
Analyze how backend pool membership churn affects existing flows across each hashing strategy.
Measure build overhead, lookup latency, and hash distribution balance through practical Python benchmarking.
Examine real-world production implementations including Linux IPVS mh, Meta Katran, Cilium eBPF, and Envoy Proxy.

Version note. The three scripts ran on 2026-11-13 with Python 3.13.5 (stdlib only, blake2b as the hash) on Linux 6.12.94+. No IPVS, XDP, Katran or Cilium on the writing host (no root, no installs), so the production sections are written from their documentation and marked not run.

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
section: The problem: per-flow stickiness without per-flow state
text:
The problem: per-flow stickiness without per-flow state
When a client communicates with a load-balanced service, IP routing delivers the client’s packets to a L4 load balancer cluster sharing a virtual IP address (VIP). Routers typically distribute incoming traffic across the load balancer instances using Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing based on a 5-tuple hash of the packet headers:
5-tuple = (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol)
Because ECMP operates statelessly, any packet of a given flow will always hash to the same L4 load balancer instance, provided the network topology and active router paths remain stable.
                               +-------------------+
                               |   Border Router   |
                               |    (ECMP Hashing) |
                               +---------+---------+
                                         |
                +------------------------+------------------------+
                |                        |                        |
        +-------v-------+        +-------v-------+        +-------v-------+
        |  LB Instance  |        |  LB Instance  |        |  LB Instance  |
        |     LB-01     |        |     LB-02     |        |     LB-03     |
        +-------+-------+        +-------+-------+        +-------+-------+
                |                        |                        |
  ==============+========================+========================+==============
  (Every LB instance must map the same 5-tuple to the same Backend Server)
  ==============+========================+========================+==============
                |                        |                        |
        +-------v-------+        +-------v-------+        +-------v-------+
        | Backend be01  |        | Backend be02  | ...    | Backend be10  |
        +---------------+        +---------------+        +---------------+
For this architecture to work: 1. Consistency across LBs: Every LB instance must reach the exact same mapping decision for any given 5-tuple without communicating with other LB instances. 2. Per-flow stickiness: A flow’s packets must consistently route to the target backend server. If a packet lands on a different backend mid-stream, the receiving backend will not recognize the TCP sequence numbers or connection state and will respond with a TCP Reset (RST), tearing down the connection. 3. Resilience to churn: When a load balancer dies, or when a backend server is added or removed, the hash mapping must minimize disruption to unrelated flows.
While connection tracking (conntrack) tables can remember flow assignments locally, relying solely on connection tracking fails when an LB instance dies or when an ECMP topology change causes an existing flow to land on a different LB instance. If the new LB instance lacks state for that flow, its hash must pick the original backend for as many flows as possible. If connection IDs are present (e.g. QUIC traffic), specific routing mechanisms can be used instead; see QUIC load balancing with nftables.

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
text:
Four algorithms
To solve the stickiness problem statelessly, network software engineers use one of four primary hashing techniques.

1. Modulo Hashing (hash % N)
Modulo hashing computes a 5-tuple hash and takes the remainder when divided by the number of active backends N: backend = backends[hash(5-tuple) % N].
While simple and fast (O(1) lookup), modulo hashing suffers from catastrophic disruption when the pool size N changes. Removing or adding a single backend changes the divisor for every lookup. Consequently, almost all active flows are reassigned to different backends, triggering massive connection resets across the fleet.


2. Consistent Hashing Ring (Karger et al., 1997)
Consistent hashing maps both backend servers and client flows onto the same circular hash space (here 64 bits).
To avoid hot spots caused by uneven spacing, each physical backend is given V “virtual nodes” (vnodes) spread around the ring. 1. Each virtual node key (e.g., be01#0, be01#1) is hashed to a position on the ring. The ring maintains a sorted array of all virtual node hash values. 2. When a flow packet arrives, its 5-tuple is hashed to a position on the ring. 3. The load balancer performs a binary search (O(log(N·V))) to find the first virtual node key greater than or equal to the flow’s hash.
When a backend is removed, only the flows assigned to its virtual nodes are reassigned to adjacent downstream nodes. All other flows remain untouched.


3. Rendezvous Hashing / Highest Random Weight (Thaler & Ravishankar, 1998)
Rendezvous hashing (also called Highest Random Weight, or HRW) scores every backend for the flow key K, score(K, b) = hash(K || b), and picks the backend with the highest score.
HRW has optimal disruption: when a backend is removed, only the flows that were on it move; when one is added, only the flows it now wins move. But finding the maximum means scoring all N backends for every new flow, so lookups are O(N).


4. Maglev Hashing (Eisenbud et al., NSDI 2016)
Maglev is Google’s software load balancer, and its paper’s hashing scheme has become the default for L4 load balancers. It builds a lookup table of fixed prime size M, much larger than N. The lookup table is populated ahead of time using a deterministic permutation generation step for each backend.

Step 1: Permutation Generation
For each backend i, Maglev computes an offset and a skip from two independent hashes of the backend’s name: offset = h1(name) % M and skip = h2(name) % (M - 1) + 1. Backend i’s preference list of table slots is then perm[j] = (offset + j * skip) % M for j = 0, 1, 2, …
Because M is prime and skip is between 1 and M−1, skip and M share no factor, so each backend’s permutation visits every slot exactly once.


Step 2: Table Population Loop
Maglev fills the M-entry table by letting the backends take turns:

Maintain an array nxt[i] tracking the next position in backend i’s permutation.
Iterate through backends in round-robin order (i = 0, 1, …, N−1).
Backend i looks at its next preferred slot c = perm_i[nxt[i]].
If slot c is empty (entry[c] == -1), backend i claims it (entry[c] = i), advances its pointer nxt[i] += 1, and increments filled.
If slot c is already taken, backend i increments nxt[i] and checks the next candidate slot in its permutation until it finds an unassigned slot.
The process repeats until all M entries are assigned (filled == M).

Because every backend gets one slot per round, each ends up with M/N slots, give or take one. Because each backend’s preferences depend only on its own name, removing one backend mostly just hands its slots to others; the other backends’ early choices are unchanged.


Step 3: O(1) flow lookup
Once built, picking a backend is one hash and one array read: backend = table[hash(K) % M].

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
text:
Lab: measure balance and disruption
The following Python benchmarks compare Modulo, Consistent Ring (100 vnodes per backend), Rendezvous, and Maglev (M = 65537) across 200,000 synthetic flows.
Here is lbhash.py:
# lbhash.py: four ways to map a flow key to a backend.
import bisect, hashlib

def h(data, seed=0):
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.blake2b(data, digest_size=8, salt=seed.to_bytes(16, "little")).digest(), "big")

class Modulo:
    def __init__(self, backends): self.b = list(backends)
    def pick(self, key): return self.b[h(key) % len(self.b)]

class Ring:                                    # consistent hashing with virtual nodes
    def __init__(self, backends, vnodes=100):
        self.points = sorted((h(f"{b}#{i}".encode()), b) for b in backends for i in range(vnodes))
        self.keys = [p for p, _ in self.points]
    def pick(self, key):
        i = bisect.bisect(self.keys, h(key)) % len(self.keys)
        return self.points[i][1]

class Rendezvous:                              # highest random weight (HRW)
    def __init__(self, backends): self.b = list(backends)
    def pick(self, key): return max(self.b, key=lambda b: h(key + b.encode()))

class Maglev:                                  # Eisenbud et al., NSDI 2016, Pseudocode 1
    def __init__(self, backends, M=65537):
        self.b = sorted(backends); n = len(self.b); self.M = M
        offset = [h(b.encode(), 1) % M for b in self.b]
        skip = [h(b.encode(), 2) % (M - 1) + 1 for b in self.b]
        nxt = [0] * n; entry = [-1] * M; filled = 0
        while True:
            for i in range(n):
                c = (offset[i] + nxt[i] * skip[i]) % M
                while entry[c] >= 0:
                    nxt[i] += 1; c = (offset[i] + nxt[i] * skip[i]) % M
                entry[c] = i; nxt[i] += 1; filled += 1
                if filled == M:
                    self.table = entry; return
    def pick(self, key): return self.b[self.table[h(key) % self.M]]
Here is compare.py:
# compare.py: modulo vs ring vs rendezvous vs Maglev on the same 200k flows.
import random, statistics, time
from lbhash import Maglev, Modulo, Rendezvous, Ring

random.seed(7)
flows = [f"198.51.{random.randrange(256)}.{random.randrange(256)}:{random.randrange(1024, 65536)}"
         f"->203.0.113.10:443/tcp".encode() for _ in range(200_000)]
B = [f"be{i:02}" for i in range(1, 11)]
print(f"{len(flows)} flows, {len(B)} backends; remove be05, then add be11\n")
print(f"{'algorithm':12} {'build ms':>9} {'max/mean':>9} {'stdev %':>8} {'moved -be05':>12} {'moved +be11':>12} {'ideal':>9}")
for name, cls in [("modulo", Modulo), ("ring x100", Ring), ("rendezvous", Rendezvous), ("maglev", Maglev)]:
    t = time.perf_counter(); lb = cls(B); build = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000
    before = [lb.pick(f) for f in flows]
    counts = [before.count(b) for b in B]
    mean = len(flows) / len(B)
    lb_rm, lb_add = cls([b for b in B if b != "be05"]), cls(B + ["be11"])
    after_rm = [lb_rm.pick(f) for f in flows]
    moved_rm = sum(a != b for a, b in zip(before, after_rm)) / len(flows)
    after_add = [lb_add.pick(f) for f in flows]
    moved_add = sum(a != b for a, b in zip(before, after_add)) / len(flows)
    print(f"{name:12} {build:9.1f} {max(counts) / mean:9.3f} {statistics.pstdev(counts) / mean * 100:8.2f} "
          f"{moved_rm:12.2%} {moved_add:12.2%} {'10% / 9%':>9}")

print("\nflows that moved off a *surviving* backend when be05 was removed:")
for name, cls in [("modulo", Modulo), ("ring x100", Ring), ("rendezvous", Rendezvous), ("maglev", Maglev)]:
    lb, lb2 = cls(B), cls([b for b in B if b != "be05"])
    sample = flows[:50_000]
    bad = 0
    for f in sample:
        a = lb.pick(f)
        if a != "be05" and a != lb2.pick(f):
            bad += 1
    print(f"  {name:12} {bad / len(sample):7.2%}")
Running python3 compare.py produces the following exact output:
200000 flows, 10 backends; remove be05, then add be11

algorithm     build ms  max/mean  stdev %  moved -be05  moved +be11     ideal
modulo             0.0     1.013     0.86       89.98%       91.03%  10% / 9%
ring x100          1.0     1.172     9.71       10.11%        9.25%  10% / 9%
rendezvous         0.1     1.011     0.70       10.02%        9.12%  10% / 9%
maglev            43.7     1.007     0.52       10.33%        9.29%  10% / 9%

flows that moved off a *surviving* backend when be05 was removed:
  modulo        79.96%
  ring x100      0.00%
  rendezvous     0.00%
  maglev         0.25%

Analyzing the results

Build Time (build ms): Modulo and Rendezvous build instantly because they perform no pre-computation. The Ring algorithm takes 1.0 ms to hash 1,000 vnodes and sort them. Maglev takes 43.7 ms in Python to compute permutations and execute its round-robin filling loop across M = 65537 table entries. That build happens only when the backend set changes, not per packet.
Load Distribution (max/mean and stdev %):

Ideal balance yields a max/mean ratio of 1.000.
Modulo, Rendezvous, and Maglev provide near-perfect load balance (max/mean 1.007 to 1.013, stdev % < 1%).
The Consistent Hashing Ring with 100 vnodes displays significant variance (max/mean of 1.172 and standard deviation of 9.71%). Achieving tight balance on a Ring requires thousands of virtual nodes per backend, which increases memory footprint and binary search lookup overhead.

Total Disruption on Churn (moved -be05 and moved +be11):

When removing 1 backend out of 10, the theoretical ideal number of affected flows is 1/10 = 10.00%. When adding an 11th backend, the ideal is 1/11 = 9.09%.
Modulo hashing fails completely: removing be05 shifts 89.98% of all flows, and adding be11 shifts 91.03% of flows.
Ring, Rendezvous, and Maglev closely track the minimum (about 10% on removal, about 9% on addition).

Surviving Backend Disruption:

The critical metric for L4 stability is whether flows assigned to a surviving backend (e.g., be01..be04, be06..be10) are disturbed when be05 is removed.
Modulo shifts 79.96% of surviving flows to different backends.
Consistent Ring and Rendezvous move 0.00% of surviving flows.
Maglev moves 0.25% of surviving flows. This minor disruption happens because filling the lookup table relies on relative permutation races; removing one backend allows remaining backends to claim permutation slots slightly earlier in the round-robin process. As documented in the NSDI 2016 paper, Maglev deliberately trades this small extra disruption for O(1) lookups and near-perfect balance.

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
section: Lab: lookup cost and table size
text:
Lab: lookup cost and table size
Here is scale.py, which measures how lookup cost scales with the backend count N, and how Maglev’s table size M affects balance:
# scale.py: lookup cost vs backend count, and Maglev table size vs balance.
import random, statistics, time
from lbhash import Maglev, Rendezvous, Ring

random.seed(7)
flows = [random.randbytes(13) for _ in range(50_000)]
print("lookup cost per flow (pure Python, so compare ratios, not absolute ns)")
for n in (10, 100, 1000):
    B = [f"be{i:04}" for i in range(n)]
    row = []
    for cls in (Ring, Rendezvous, Maglev):
        lb = cls(B) if cls is not Maglev else cls(B, M=65537)
        t = time.perf_counter()
        for f in flows: lb.pick(f)
        row.append((time.perf_counter() - t) / len(flows) * 1e9)
    print(f"  {n:5} backends: ring {row[0]:7.0f} ns  rendezvous {row[1]:9.0f} ns  maglev {row[2]:6.0f} ns")

print("\nMaglev table size M vs balance, 100 backends")
B = [f"be{i:03}" for i in range(100)]
for M in (251, 1021, 16381, 65537):
    lb = Maglev(B, M=M)
    share = [lb.table.count(i) for i in range(len(B))]
    print(f"  M={M:6}  entries/backend min {min(share):4} max {max(share):4}  "
          f"(max/min {max(share) / min(share):.2f})")
Running python3 scale.py produces the following exact output:
lookup cost per flow (pure Python, so compare ratios, not absolute ns)
     10 backends: ring    1452 ns  rendezvous      7503 ns  maglev    640 ns
    100 backends: ring     946 ns  rendezvous     69499 ns  maglev    634 ns
   1000 backends: ring    1248 ns  rendezvous    660033 ns  maglev    693 ns

Maglev table size M vs balance, 100 backends
  M=   251  entries/backend min    2 max    3  (max/min 1.50)
  M=  1021  entries/backend min   10 max   11  (max/min 1.10)
  M= 16381  entries/backend min  163 max  164  (max/min 1.01)
  M= 65537  entries/backend min  655 max  656  (max/min 1.00)

Key takeaways from lookup scaling
Note that pure-Python timing nanoseconds are useful only for comparing relative performance ratios, not absolute performance in compiled C/eBPF environments.

Rendezvous (O(N)): Lookup cost grows linearly with the backend count. At 10 backends, Rendezvous requires 7,503 ns per lookup; at 1,000 backends, lookup cost scales up to 660,033 ns (a ~88x slowdown). This makes Rendezvous unsuitable for large backend pools at high packet rates.
Ring (O(log(N·V))): Binary search over all virtual nodes. Cost stays roughly flat here (about 950–1450 ns, with noise), but the ring grows with N·V entries, which costs memory and cache locality.
Maglev (O(1)): Lookup cost stays flat (about 630–690 ns) regardless of whether there are 10 or 1,000 backends. It consists solely of a single hash operation, a modulo by M, and an array index lookup.



Table size M vs load balance
The Maglev paper picks M larger than 100 × N, so that backends’ shares of the hash space differ by at most about 1%: - At N = 100 and M = 251 (about 2.5 × N), each backend gets 2 or 3 slots: some backends receive 50% more new flows than others (max/min 1.50). - At M = 1021 (about 10 × N), the ratio improves to 1.10. - At M = 16381 (about 160 × N), allocation is virtually uniform (max/min 1.01). This is Cilium’s default table size. - At M = 65537 (about 655 × N), 655 or 656 slots each: 1.00. This is the default in Katran and Envoy.

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
section: Why disruption still matters: connection tracking on top
text:
Why disruption still matters: connection tracking on top
In production L4 load balancers like Meta’s Katran or Google’s Maglev, consistent hashing does not operate alone; it works in tandem with a fast connection tracking (conntrack) table:
  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | Incoming Flow Packet (5-tuple)                                    |
  +----------------------------------+--------------------------------+
                                     |
                                     v
                  +----------------------------------+
                  |  LRU Connection Tracking Table   |
                  +------------------+---------------+
                                     |
                     +---------------+---------------+
                     | Hit                           | Miss / Expired
                     v                               v
         +-----------------------+       +-----------------------+
         | Route to Recorded     |       | Compute Hash Pick     |
         | Backend Destination   |       | (Maglev / HRW / Ring) |
         +-----------------------+       +-----------+-----------+
                                                     |
                                                     v
                                         +-----------------------+
                                         | Populate LRU Table &  |
                                         | Forward Packet        |
                                         +-----------------------+

Established Flows: Packets matching an entry in the local LRU connection tracking table are forwarded directly to the designated backend server, ignoring the consistent hash lookup completely.
New Flows or Missing State: When a packet arrives with no active conntrack entry (such as a new SYN packet, or any flow arriving after an LB restart or ECMP route update), the load balancer executes the consistent hash function to choose a backend, then stores that mapping in its LRU table.

Under this two-tier model: - The 0.25% extra disruption measured for Maglev only hits established flows that also lost their connection-table entry: the LB instance restarted, or an ECMP change moved the flow to an instance that never saw it. Everyone else stays put because of the table, whatever the hash says. - Graceful Backend Draining: When taking a backend offline for maintenance, operators mark its weight as 0 or remove it from the active hash pool while preserving its existing entries in the connection tracking table. New connections hash to alternative healthy backends, while established connections continue uninterrupted until they complete naturally.

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
text:
In production (from docs, not run)
Production operating systems, kernel frameworks, and service proxies provide built-in support for consistent load balancing hash algorithms.

1. Linux IPVS (mh Scheduler)
Linux IPVS has had a Maglev hashing scheduler, mh, since kernel 4.18. By default it hashes the source address only. Two scheduler flags change that: - mh-fallback: if the chosen real server is unavailable (weight 0 or overloaded), try another instead of dropping. - mh-port: include the source port in the hash, so different connections from one client spread across servers.
# Set up a Virtual IP using the Maglev Hashing (mh) scheduler
ipvsadm -A -t 203.0.113.10:443 -s mh -b mh-port

# Add real backend servers to the virtual service pool
ipvsadm -a -t 203.0.113.10:443 -r 10.0.0.11:443 -m
ipvsadm -a -t 203.0.113.10:443 -r 10.0.0.12:443 -m
Not run. Written from ipvsadm(8); it needs root, the ip_vs and ip_vs_mh modules and the ipvsadm tool, none of which are available on the writing host.


2. Meta Katran
Meta’s open-source XDP/eBPF load balancer, Katran, uses Maglev consistent hashing as its primary forwarding algorithm. - Default Maglev ring size 65537. - Encapsulates routed packets using Generic UDP Encapsulation (GUE) or IPIP tunnels to pass packets to backends across Layer 3 boundaries. - Operates in Direct Server Return (DSR) mode, allowing backend servers to respond directly to clients, bypassing the load balancer on return paths.


3. Cilium eBPF Load Balancer
Cilium can replace kube-proxy in Kubernetes clusters using eBPF-based load balancing. Cilium supports Maglev hashing for service traffic distribution:
# Helm values excerpt for Cilium Maglev configuration
kubeProxyReplacement: true
loadBalancer:
  algorithm: maglev
maglev:
  tableSize: 16381 # bpf-lb-maglev-table-size


4. Envoy Proxy
Envoy implements MAGLEV and RING_HASH for upstream clusters. Both only make sense with a hash policy on the route (for example a header, a cookie or the source IP): without one, Envoy has no key to hash and the choice is effectively random. The Katran, Cilium and Envoy snippets are written from their documentation and were not run here.
# Envoy Cluster Configuration snippet using Maglev
clusters:
  - name: backend_service
    connect_timeout: 0.25s
    type: STRICT_DNS
    lb_policy: MAGLEV
    maglev_lb_config:
      table_size: 65537
    load_assignment:
      cluster_name: backend_service
      endpoints:
        - lb_endpoints:
            - endpoint:
                address:
                  socket_address:
                    address: 10.0.0.11
                    port_value: 8080

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
text:
Gotchas

Hashing Inappropriate Header Fields: Ensure the hash key contains only immutable 5-tuple fields. Never include TTL, TCP Window size, TCP Flags, or IP TOS/DSCP bits, as these change hop-by-hop or packet-by-packet within the same flow.
ICMP Messages and Packet Fragments: Path MTU Discovery ICMP packets and fragmented IP packets lack L4 TCP/UDP port headers. If an L4 load balancer cannot extract ports, it falls back to a 2-tuple (Source IP, Dest IP) hash, which can cause fragments to land on a different backend unless handled by specialized reassembly or ICMP payload parsing.
IPv6 flow label: RFC 7098 describes hashing the 20-bit IPv6 flow label (with the addresses) so LBs need not parse extension headers to find ports. But Linux deliberately changes a socket’s flow label after retransmission timeouts to try a different ECMP path (net.core.txrehash). An LB that hashes on the flow label without a connection table can therefore move exactly the connections that are already struggling.
Instances out of sync: For LB instances behind ECMP to pick the same backend, they need the same backend list (names, not just counts), the same hash seeds and the same M. Roll configuration changes to all instances together, or keep the old and new tables both available during the change.
Rebuild cost under churn: Lookups are O(1), but filling the table takes expected O(M log M) work and gets slower as the table fills. A flapping health check that rebuilds the table every second wastes CPU and reshuffles that small fraction of flows each time. Dampen health-check flaps and build new tables off the packet path.
Weight Adjustments in Maglev: Supporting weighted backends in Maglev requires larger backends to claim extra entries during the round-robin allocation phase, which increases lookup table fill times and slightly degrades disruption properties.
Non-prime M: If M is not prime, a backend’s skip can share a factor with M, its permutation then cycles through only part of the table, and the fill loop can spin forever once those slots are taken.

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
text:
Boring rule
For an L4 load balancer: Maglev with a prime table larger than 100 × the backend count, a per-flow connection table on top, identical configuration on every instance, and backend removal done by draining (weight 0, keep existing entries) rather than deleting. Use rendezvous hashing when the pool is small or the selection happens in clients, and never use plain modulo for anything whose membership changes.

title: Load Balancer Hashing: Modulo, Rings, Rendezvous and Maglev
text:
Try this

Modify lbhash.py to implement weighted backend support in Maglev by allowing backends with higher weights to claim multiple contiguous turns in the round-robin lookup table build loop.
Run compare.py with different random seeds. Observe whether Maglev’s surviving-backend disruption stays around 0.25%.
Change the table size M in scale.py to a composite number (for example 65536) and run it under timeout 60. Does the build finish? Print each backend’s skip and its greatest common divisor with M to explain what you see.
Increase the number of virtual nodes in lbhash.py’s Ring class from 100 to 1000. Benchmark how the standard deviation percentage improves in compare.py versus the increased lookup time in scale.py.
Implement a simple LRU cache wrapper around Rendezvous in Python. Measure the cache hit rate required for Rendezvous to match Maglev’s lookup cost at 1000 backends.

text: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
text:
Learning goals

Count the signatures a TLS server sends today to prove its identity, and work out why post-quantum signature sizes make that number a problem
Explain the core inversion in Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs): the CA does not sign a certificate and then log it; it logs the certificate and signs the log
Describe issuance logs, checkpoints, subtrees, inclusion proofs, cosigners and landmarks well enough to read the IETF draft
Implement the draft’s subtree and inclusion-proof algorithms, check them against the draft’s own test vectors, and run a toy CA that issues and verifies certificates
Compare the authentication bytes in a handshake for classical, post-quantum X.509 and both MTC forms
Know what is deployable now (nothing in production yet), what is planned, and what to watch as an operator

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
text:
Thesis
A TLS 1.3 server authenticates with a chain of signatures. The server’s own CertificateVerify signature proves it holds the key. The CA’s signature on the leaf proves the CA vouched for the name. And because browsers require Certificate Transparency, each certificate carries two or more Signed Certificate Timestamps (SCTs), each another signature. With Ed25519 or ECDSA each of those signatures is 64 bytes, so nobody counts them. With ML-DSA-44, the smallest standard lattice signature in FIPS 204, each one is 2,420 bytes and each public key is 1,312 bytes. The draft computes that two SCTs plus a leaf signature alone add 7,260 bytes to every handshake. That pushes the server’s first flight past the TCP initial congestion window and the QUIC anti-amplification limit, so the handshake costs an extra round trip.
Merkle Tree Certificates, being standardized in the IETF PLANTS working group (draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs, revision -08 of 2 November 2026), take most of those signatures out of the handshake. The CA appends what it certifies to an append-only Merkle tree, the issuance log. It signs the tree, not each certificate, and other parties cosign the same tree. A certificate then carries a short inclusion proof, a few hundred bytes of hashes, instead of signatures. For clients that already received the tree heads in advance, no CA or log signature crosses the wire at all. Transparency stops being an extra system bolted onto issuance. In Cloudflare’s words: “don’t log what you issue, issue by logging.”

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
text:
Mental model
  Today (X.509 + CT)                          Merkle Tree Certificates
  ------------------                          ------------------------
  CA signs leaf        ── sig #1              CA appends entry to its issuance log
  log A returns SCT    ── sig #2              CA signs a checkpoint / subtree   ┐ once per
  log B returns SCT    ── sig #3              cosigners (mirrors) cosign it     ┘ batch, not
  server signs handshake ── sig #4 (always)   per certificate
                                              certificate = entry + inclusion proof
  handshake carries: sig #1..#4                 + (standalone) subtree cosignatures
                                                + (landmark-relative) nothing more
                                              server signs handshake ── still 1 sig

            ┌──────────── subtree [8,13) ─────────────┐
            │      ┌─── [8,12) ───┐                    │   inclusion proof for entry 10:
            │   [8,10)       [10,12)                   │     d[11], [8,10), d[12]
            │   8    9     (10)   11          12       │   = 3 hashes = 96 bytes
            └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
text:
How the system fits together
The draft defines five roles. Most of them map onto parts of today’s Web PKI:








Role
Job
Today’s analogue




Certification authority
Validates requests (for example over ACME), appends a TBSCertificateLogEntry to its issuance log, signs checkpoints and subtrees with its CA cosigner key
CA


Issuance log
Append-only Merkle tree (RFC 9162 hashing) of everything the CA certified. Up to 2^48−1 entries per log. Only the CA adds entries; there is no public submission
CT log, but operated by the CA and holding only its own entries


Cosigner
Follows the log, checks it is append-only, signs subtrees. A mirror cosigner also keeps a full copy
CT log operators, witnesses


Monitor
Watches logs for certificates of interest
CT monitors


Relying party
Trusts a set of cosigners and, optionally, receives landmark subtrees ahead of time
Browser root store + CT policy



Three details are worth knowing because they change how certificates look:

The log entry does not contain the public key. TBSCertificateLogEntry holds subjectPublicKeyInfoHash, a hash of the key, and no signature. Post-quantum key and signature sizes therefore do not grow the log.
The serial number is the log position. serialNumber = (log_number << 48) | index. Revocation can then be done by ranges of serial numbers (section 7.5): “everything before index N” retires expired history in bulk, and “everything after index N” distrusts a CA from a point onward without breaking existing certificates.
The signature algorithm is a proof. An MTC is still an X.509 certificate. Its signatureAlgorithm is id-alg-mtcProof, and the signatureValue holds an MTCProof: the subtree [start, end), the inclusion proof, and zero or more cosignatures.


Subtrees and the two-subtree cover
The CA issues continuously. Every so often (the draft’s size estimate assumes every 2 seconds) it takes a checkpoint and must sign “everything since the previous checkpoint”, an arbitrary interval [prev, size). An arbitrary interval is not a node of the Merkle tree, and building a separate tree over it would not be provably consistent with the main log. The draft therefore defines a subtree as an interval [start, end) where start is a multiple of BIT_CEIL(end − start). That alignment guarantees a consistency proof against the full tree exists. It then shows (section 4.5.1) that any interval can be covered by two subtrees, each at most BIT_CEIL(end − start) in size. The CA signs those two subtrees. Each new certificate gets an inclusion proof into whichever of the two contains it.


Standalone vs landmark-relative

A standalone certificate carries the inclusion proof and the cosignatures on the subtree: the CA’s own, plus as many external cosigners as relying-party policy demands. It is usable immediately after issuance, by any client that trusts those cosigners.
A landmark-relative certificate carries only the inclusion proof. Periodically, for example hourly, the CA designates the current tree size as a landmark, and the subtrees between consecutive landmarks are distributed to relying parties out of band (a browser update channel). A client that already holds that landmark subtree needs no signature at all. The server learns whether the client is up to date through the TLS Trust Anchor IDs mechanism (draft-ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids). If the client is not, the server falls back to the standalone certificate.

The draft’s example sizing: with a 7-day maximum certificate lifetime and a landmark every hour, a relying party holds at most 169 active landmarks (338 subtree hashes), about 10.8 KB per CA.

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
section: Lab: the draft’s tree algorithms, checked against its test vectors
text:
Lab: the draft’s tree algorithms, checked against its test vectors
Everything here uses the Python 3 standard library only. Nothing touches the network.

The primitives
mtc.py implements, in order: the RFC 9162 Merkle Tree Hash, the subtree validity rule (draft section 4.1), subtree inclusion proofs (4.3), the relying party’s proof evaluation step by step as written in 4.3.2, and the two-subtree cover from 4.5.1.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Merkle Tree Certificate building blocks from draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs-08:
RFC 9162 Merkle Tree Hash, subtree validity (4.1), subtree inclusion proofs (4.3),
proof evaluation (4.3.2) and the two-subtree cover (4.5.1).  Standard library only."""
import hashlib

def H(b: bytes) -> bytes:
    return hashlib.sha256(b).digest()

def mth(d: list[bytes]) -> bytes:                       # RFC 9162 2.1.1
    n = len(d)
    if n == 0:
        return H(b"")
    if n == 1:
        return H(b"\x00" + d[0])
    k = 1 << ((n - 1).bit_length() - 1)                 # largest power of 2 < n
    return H(b"\x01" + mth(d[:k]) + mth(d[k:]))

def bit_ceil(n: int) -> int:
    return 1 if n <= 1 else 1 << (n - 1).bit_length()

def valid_subtree(start: int, end: int) -> bool:        # draft 4.1
    return start <= end and start % bit_ceil(end - start) == 0

def path(m: int, d: list[bytes]) -> list[bytes]:        # RFC 9162 2.1.3.1 PATH(m, D_n)
    n = len(d)
    if n <= 1:
        return []
    k = 1 << ((n - 1).bit_length() - 1)
    if m < k:
        return path(m, d[:k]) + [mth(d[k:])]
    return path(m - k, d[k:]) + [mth(d[:k])]

def inclusion_proof(d, start, end, index):              # draft 4.3
    return path(index - start, d[start:end])

def evaluate(proof, start, end, index, entry_hash):     # draft 4.3.2, step by step
    if not (valid_subtree(start, end) and start <= index < end):
        raise ValueError("bad subtree or index")
    fn, sn, r = index - start, end - start - 1, entry_hash
    for p in proof:
        if sn == 0:
            raise ValueError("proof too long")
        if fn & 1 or fn == sn:
            r = H(b"\x01" + p + r)
            while not fn & 1:
                fn >>= 1; sn >>= 1
        else:
            r = H(b"\x01" + r + p)
        fn >>= 1; sn >>= 1
    if sn != 0:
        raise ValueError("proof too short")
    return r

def find_subtrees(start, end):                          # draft 4.5.1, verbatim logic
    if end - start <= 1:
        return (start, end), (end, end)
    last = end - 1
    split = (start ^ last).bit_length() - 1
    mask = (1 << split) - 1
    mid = last & ~mask
    left_split = (~start & mask).bit_length()
    left_start = start & ~((1 << left_split) - 1)
    return (left_start, mid), (mid, end)


Checking against Appendix C
The draft ships “accumulated” test vectors. You hash every valid subtree of trees up to size 130, and every inclusion proof in them, into one rolling SHA-256, and compare with a published value. vectors.py does both and also runs every proof through the relying-party evaluate() function:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check mtc.py against the accumulated test vectors in Appendix C.1.1 and C.1.2
of draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs-08, then evaluate every proof (relying-party side)."""
import hashlib
from mtc import H, mth, valid_subtree, inclusion_proof, evaluate

D = [bytes([i]) for i in range(130)]
h1, h2, checked = hashlib.sha256(), hashlib.sha256(), 0
for end in range(0, 131):
    for start in range(end + 1):
        if not valid_subtree(start, end):
            continue
        st = mth(D[start:end])
        h1.update(f"[{start}, {end}) {st.hex()}\n".encode())
        for index in range(start, end):
            proof = inclusion_proof(D, start, end, index)
            h2.update((f"{index} [{start}, {end})" + "".join(" " + p.hex() for p in proof) + "\n").encode())
            assert evaluate(proof, start, end, index, H(b"\x00" + D[index])) == st
            checked += 1
print("C.1.1 subtree hashes   ", h1.hexdigest() == "b82806ad4265bb151c1119c0f4db437bb4d1a1f887b3a7fba1cd4ebf552e3e81")
print("C.1.2 inclusion proofs ", h2.hexdigest() == "ac2a8f989e44d99e399db448050ff5f19757df53cfb716aa81015d3955d8163f")
print("proofs evaluated by the relying-party code:", checked)
C.1.1 subtree hashes    True
C.1.2 inclusion proofs  True
proofs evaluated by the relying-party code: 12807
Both published digests match. That is strong evidence the implementation follows the draft exactly: a single wrong bit in any of 12,807 proofs would change the digest.


A toy CA
toyca.py issues four batches of a few hundred entries, cuts a checkpoint after each, covers each new interval with two subtrees, and gives every entry a certificate (subtree, inclusion proof, signed subtree hash). A relying party then checks one honest certificate, one where the entry was swapped, and one with a truncated proof. Finally it prints the authentication-byte budget.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""A toy Merkle Tree CA: append entries, cut a checkpoint every BATCH entries,
cover each new interval with two subtrees (4.5.1), hand out proofs, and let a
relying party check them.  Then print the authentication-byte budget."""
import random
from mtc import H, mth, find_subtrees, inclusion_proof, evaluate

random.seed(7)
log, checkpoints, certs = [], [0], {}
for batch in range(4):
    for _ in range(random.randint(250, 400)):           # one checkpoint's worth of issuance
        log.append(b"tbs-entry:%d:example-%d.test" % (len(log), random.randrange(10**6)))
    prev, size = checkpoints[-1], len(log)
    left, right = find_subtrees(prev, size)
    print(f"checkpoint {batch + 1}: entries [{prev}, {size}) covered by subtrees {left} and {right}")
    for idx in range(prev, size):                       # "sign" each subtree once, issue many certs
        st = left if idx < left[1] else right
        certs[idx] = (st, inclusion_proof(log, st[0], st[1], idx), mth(log[st[0]:st[1]]))
    checkpoints.append(size)

idx = 1000
(start, end), proof, signed_hash = certs[idx]
leaf = H(b"\x00" + log[idx])
print(f"\ncert for entry {idx}: subtree [{start}, {end}), proof = {len(proof)} hashes = {32 * len(proof)} bytes")
print("relying party, honest entry  :", evaluate(proof, start, end, idx, leaf) == signed_hash)
forged = H(b"\x00" + log[idx].replace(b"example", b"evil---"))
print("relying party, swapped entry :", evaluate(proof, start, end, idx, forged) == signed_hash)
try:
    evaluate(proof[:-1], start, end, idx, leaf)
except ValueError as e:
    print("relying party, truncated proof:", "rejected:", e)

print("\nauthentication bytes a TLS server sends besides its own key and CertificateVerify")
MLDSA44, ED = 2420, 64
def proof_bytes(span): return 32 * (span - 1).bit_length()
rows = [
    ("classic X.509, Ed25519/ECDSA, 2 SCTs", 3 * ED),
    ("classic X.509, ML-DSA-44, 2 SCTs", 3 * MLDSA44),
    ("MTC standalone, ~3,000-cert subtree, CA + 1 cosigner", proof_bytes(3000) + 2 * MLDSA44),
    ("MTC landmark-relative, ~5.4M-cert subtree", proof_bytes(5_400_000)),
    ("MTC landmark-relative, 2^32-cert subtree", proof_bytes(2**32)),
]
for name, b in rows:
    print(f"  {name:<55}{b:>7,} bytes")
checkpoint 1: entries [0, 332) covered by subtrees (0, 256) and (256, 332)
checkpoint 2: entries [332, 631) covered by subtrees (256, 512) and (512, 631)
checkpoint 3: entries [631, 950) covered by subtrees (512, 768) and (768, 950)
checkpoint 4: entries [950, 1277) covered by subtrees (896, 1024) and (1024, 1277)

cert for entry 1000: subtree [896, 1024), proof = 7 hashes = 224 bytes
relying party, honest entry  : True
relying party, swapped entry : False
relying party, truncated proof: rejected: proof too short

authentication bytes a TLS server sends besides its own key and CertificateVerify
  classic X.509, Ed25519/ECDSA, 2 SCTs                       192 bytes
  classic X.509, ML-DSA-44, 2 SCTs                         7,260 bytes
  MTC standalone, ~3,000-cert subtree, CA + 1 cosigner     5,224 bytes
  MTC landmark-relative, ~5.4M-cert subtree                  736 bytes
  MTC landmark-relative, 2^32-cert subtree                 1,024 bytes


Reading the output

The two-subtree cover. Checkpoint 2 had to sign entries [332, 631). The cover is [256, 512) and [512, 631). The left subtree reaches back to 256, before the interval starts, because [332, 512) is not aligned. The draft allows that: the left subtree may contain extra, already-certified entries, and the right one ends exactly at the checkpoint. Each subtree is at most BIT_CEIL(299) = 512 entries.
Proof size is logarithmic. Entry 1000 sits in subtree [896, 1024), 128 entries, so its proof is log2(128) = 7 hashes, or 224 bytes.
Tampering fails closed. Changing one name in the entry gives a different leaf hash, the recomputed root no longer matches the signed subtree hash, and the relying party rejects it. A shortened proof is rejected before any comparison, because the bit-walk in 4.3.2 ends with sn != 0.
The budget. These are the bytes beyond the server’s own public key and CertificateVerify signature, which every scheme still sends:









Scheme
Extra bytes
Where the number comes from




Classical X.509, Ed25519/ECDSA, 2 SCTs
192
3 × 64


X.509 with ML-DSA-44, 2 SCTs
7,260
3 × 2,420 (matches the draft’s own figure)


MTC standalone, ~3,000-entry subtree, CA + 1 cosigner
5,224
12 hashes + 2 × 2,420 (toy assumption: two ML-DSA-44 cosignatures, ignoring IDs)


MTC landmark-relative, ~5.4 M-entry subtree
736
23 hashes (matches the draft’s section 6.5 estimate)


MTC landmark-relative, 2^32-entry subtree
1,024
32 hashes, the upper bound the draft gives



The standalone form saves a little; the landmark-relative form is where the win is. That is why the design depends on clients receiving landmarks in the background and on servers holding both certificates.

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
section: What this means for people who run networks
text:
What this means for people who run networks

Nothing to deploy yet, but the timeline is short. The draft is a working-group document, not an RFC. Cloudflare announced on 29 September 2026 that it is becoming a public CA, with production MTC issuance planned for the first quarter of 2027 and inclusion targeted in Chrome’s new quantum-resistant root store, after an experimental deployment with Chrome. Plan for MTCs arriving over ACME for sites behind large CDNs first.
Servers will hold more than one certificate per name. A classical chain for old clients, a standalone MTC, and one or more landmark-relative MTCs, chosen per handshake from the client’s trust_anchors extension. Tooling that assumes “one cert file per vhost” (config management, expiry monitors, certificate inventories) needs to cope with that.
Middleboxes that parse certificates will see an unknown signature algorithm (id-alg-mtcProof). TLS inspection boxes and any “validate the chain on the wire” IDS rule must either learn MTCs or stop inspecting. The same class of devices already broke on large post-quantum key shares in the ClientHello.
Monitoring moves to issuance logs. If you watch CT for your domains today, you will eventually watch CA issuance logs too. They contain hashes of public keys, not the keys, so match on names and the key hashes you expect.
Handshake size is a network property. Whatever certificate form wins, measure the server’s first flight in bytes and compare it with the initial congestion window (commonly 10 segments, about 14 KB) and QUIC’s 3× anti-amplification limit. Crossing either one costs a round trip on every new connection.

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
text:
Case
A platform team running TLS termination for a few hundred internal services tested an ML-DSA-44 chain from a private PKI with one intermediate and two SCT-like signed timestamps from an internal log. The server’s first flight grew from about 4 KB to about 17 KB. QUIC handshakes from mobile clients gained a full round trip because the server hit the anti-amplification limit before the client’s second flight arrived. Moving the intermediate into the clients’ trust store as a directly trusted anchor removed one signature and one public key but not the round trip. The team concluded that for an internal PKI the useful parts of MTCs are the issuance-log design (one log, one CA cosigner, internal mirrors) and landmark-relative certificates pushed with their existing client configuration channel. They are tracking the draft rather than inventing their own.

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
text:
Trap
“MTCs remove signatures from TLS.” They remove the CA and transparency signatures. The server still proves possession of its key with a CertificateVerify signature, and with a post-quantum key that is still about 2.4 KB plus a 1.3 KB public key.
“An inclusion proof is a signature.” It proves only that an entry is in a tree with a given root. Trust comes from the cosignatures on that root, or from the relying party already holding it as a landmark. An inclusion proof into an unsigned, unknown subtree proves nothing.
“Any interval can be a subtree.” Only aligned intervals can. If you write your own log tooling and sign [332, 631) directly, you produce a tree that cannot be proven consistent with the log. Use the two-subtree cover.
“Landmark-relative is always used.” Only when the client signals it holds the landmark. Servers must keep a standalone certificate (or a classical chain) for everyone else, and the fallback path needs testing as much as the fast path.

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
text:
Boring rule
Count the signatures and bytes in your handshake before and after any certificate change. Treat the issuance log as the source of truth and the certificate as a pointer into it.

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
text:
Try this

Change toyca.py to cut a checkpoint every 3,000 entries and confirm that no standalone proof is longer than 12 hashes, as the draft’s section 6.5 estimates.
Implement subtree consistency proof verification (draft section 4.4.3) and check it against the Appendix C.1.3 accumulated vector.
Add serial = (1 << 48) | index to each toy certificate and write a relying-party check that rejects any serial below a minSerial you choose. That is the bulk revocation of section 7.5.
Using the landmark rule in section 6.4.2, compute the relying-party state for a 47-day certificate lifetime with landmarks every hour, and every six hours.

title: Merkle Tree Certificates: Keeping Post-Quantum TLS Handshakes Small
text:
Verification

vectors.py and toyca.py were run on this box with Python 3.13.5 (standard library only). Output is pasted verbatim. Both Appendix C.1.1 and C.1.2 accumulated digests from draft-08 matched.
The byte budget uses ML-DSA-44 sizes (1,312-byte public key, 2,420-byte signature) as quoted in the draft from FIPS 204. The standalone row is a stated toy assumption, not a measurement of a real deployment.
Not run: real MTC issuance, ACME, TLS trust-anchor negotiation and any browser. No public implementation was used. Deployment status comes from the Cloudflare announcements cited below and may change.
