title: X.509 Path Building Traps: Intermediates, nameConstraints and pathlen
text:
Reading the Output

Section 1: Valid Chain Verification
In Section 1 of the lab output, the OpenSSL path validation engine processes a fully compliant path:
== 1  Valid chain (leaf + intermediate, trust root)
   lab-x509/pki/leaf-ok.pem: OK
   exit=0
The execution command supplied the root trust anchor via -CAfile and the untrusted intermediate certificate via -untrusted. The path building engine successfully linked leaf-ok.pem \(\rightarrow\) Lab Intermediate A \(\rightarrow\) Lab Root CA. OpenSSL returns status code 0, indicating successful validation.


Section 2: Omitted Intermediate and OpenSSL AIA Behavior
Section 2 demonstrates what occurs when an intermediate CA certificate is omitted from the validation execution:
== 2  Leaf alone, no intermediate in -untrusted (AIA not fetched by openssl verify)
   C=US, O=Lab Example, CN=www.example.com
   error 20 at 0 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer certificate
   error lab-x509/pki/leaf-ok.pem: verification failed
   exit=2

Error Code 20 (X509_V_ERR_UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY): The path validation engine inspected the target leaf certificate at depth 0 (CN=www.example.com). It attempted to locate an issuer certificate matching the leaf’s AuthorityKeyIdentifier and Issuer DN. Because the intermediate certificate was not present in the local trust store (-CAfile) nor supplied as an untrusted candidate (-untrusted), lookup failed at depth 0.
AIA Non-Fetching: Despite leaf-ok.pem containing an Authority Information Access extension pointing to http://pki.lab/root.pem, openssl verify does not perform network I/O to retrieve missing certificates. The process returns exit code 2.



Section 3: Name Constraint Enforcement
Section 3 demonstrates the evaluation of nameConstraints enforced by Lab Intermediate A:
== 3  Name constraint violation: www.evil.test under .example.com intermediate
   C=US, O=Lab Example, CN=www.evil.test
   error 47 at 0 depth lookup: permitted subtree violation
   error lab-x509/pki/leaf-bad-dns.pem: verification failed
   exit=2

Error Code 47 (X509_V_ERR_PERMITTED_VIOLATION): The target leaf certificate (leaf-bad-dns.pem) contains a SAN/CN of www.evil.test. Lab Intermediate A asserts a critical nameConstraints extension with Permitted: DNS:.example.com.
During the constraint propagation pass at depth 0, the engine compares www.evil.test against the permitted DNS domain .example.com. Because www.evil.test does not match the suffix .example.com, the engine triggers error 47 and aborts verification with exit code 2.



Section 4 & 4b: Path Length Constraint Violations
Sections 4 and 4b illustrate how OpenSSL handles pathLenConstraint violations under different candidate pool configurations.
In Section 4, an illegal intermediate certificate (Lab Intermediate A2) was issued by Lab Intermediate A. Note that Lab Intermediate A carries pathlen:0:
== 4  pathlen violation: intermediate under a pathlen:0 CA
   C=US, O=Lab Example, CN=Lab Intermediate A2 (illegal)
   error 20 at 1 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer certificate
   error lab-x509/pki/leaf-via-a2.pem: verification failed
   exit=2

Error Code 20 at Depth 1: In this initial invocation, leaf-via-a2.pem was presented, but Lab Intermediate A2 was not explicitly supplied in the -untrusted set. The path building engine reached depth 1 and failed to locate the issuer of A2.

In Section 4b, all intermediate certificates (Lab Intermediate A and Lab Intermediate A2) were supplied in the -untrusted pool:
== 4b  pathlen violation with full chain in -untrusted
   C=US, O=Lab Example, CN=Lab Intermediate A
   error 25 at 2 depth lookup: path length constraint exceeded
   C=US, O=Lab Root, CN=Lab Root CA
   error 25 at 3 depth lookup: path length constraint exceeded
   error lab-x509/pki/leaf-via-a2.pem: verification failed
   exit=2

Error Code 25 (X509_V_ERR_PATH_LENGTH_EXCEEDED): With all candidates available, the engine successfully constructs the candidate chain: leaf-via-a2.pem (depth 0) \(\rightarrow\) Lab Intermediate A2 (depth 1) \(\rightarrow\) Lab Intermediate A (depth 2) \(\rightarrow\) Lab Root CA (depth 3).
Depth Analysis: Lab Intermediate A is at depth 2 in this candidate path. Its extension specifies pathlen:0, meaning zero intermediate CA certificates may follow it. However, Lab Intermediate A2 sits between Lab Intermediate A and the leaf. The path validation engine detects that 1 intermediate CA follows Lab Intermediate A, violating the pathlen:0 constraint. Error 25 is logged, and path validation fails.



Section 5: Unconstrained Intermediate Control
Section 5 presents a control test using Lab Intermediate B:
== 5  Same leaf DNS via unconstrained intermediate B (control)
   lab-x509/pki/leaf-via-b.pem: OK
   exit=0
Lab Intermediate B was issued without restrictive nameConstraints or pathLenConstraint limits. A leaf certificate issued under Intermediate B for www.example.com passes validation with exit code 0.


Section 6: Intermediate A Extension Analysis
Section 6 outputs the decoded text representation of Lab Intermediate A:
== 6  Intermediate A extensions (openssl x509 -text)
   X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical
                   CA:TRUE, pathlen:0
               X509v3 Subject Key Identifier:
                   19:F9:CD:88:B7:A5:D3:7A:BC:69:52:D9:1E:F4:56:E5:F1:10:33:2A
   

   X509v3 Name Constraints: critical
                   Permitted:
                     DNS:.example.com
               Authority Information Access:
                   CA Issuers - URI:http://pki.lab/root.pem
The output confirms two critical constraints that triggered the earlier validation failures: 1. Basic Constraints: Marked critical, specifying CA:TRUE and pathlen:0. Any child CA certificate signed by this key will fail path validation with error 25. 2. Name Constraints: Marked critical, specifying Permitted: DNS:.example.com. Any leaf certificate signed by this key containing hostnames outside .example.com will fail path validation with error 47.

title: X.509 Path Building Traps: Intermediates, nameConstraints and pathlen
text:
In Production

Correct Server Chain Assembly for Web Servers
To prevent client path building failures caused by missing intermediates, production web servers must serve the full certificate chain (leaf certificate followed immediately by intermediate CAs, excluding the self-signed root).

Nginx Configuration
In Nginx, the ssl_certificate directive must point to a file containing the concatenated leaf and intermediate certificates in proper order.
# (not run here)
# Combine leaf certificate and intermediate CA into a unified bundle
cat /etc/ssl/certs/example.com.crt /etc/ssl/certs/intermediate.crt > /etc/ssl/certs/fullchain.pem
# (not run here)
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/tls.conf
server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name www.example.com;

    # fullchain.pem must contain leaf first, then intermediates
    ssl_certificate /etc/ssl/certs/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/private/example.com.key;

    # ssl_trusted_certificate is used for OCSP stapling verification
    ssl_trusted_certificate /etc/ssl/certs/trust_anchor_root.pem;
}


HAProxy Configuration
HAProxy requires the leaf certificate, any intermediate CAs, and the unencrypted private key to be combined into a single file payload.
# (not run here)
# Assemble HAProxy combined PEM file
cat /etc/ssl/certs/example.com.crt \
    /etc/ssl/certs/intermediate.crt \
    /etc/ssl/private/example.com.key \
    > /etc/haproxy/certs/example.com.pem
# (not run here)
# /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
frontend tls_in
    bind *:443 ssl crt /etc/haproxy/certs/example.com.pem
    default_backend web_servers



Inspecting Remote Server Chains with OpenSSL
To diagnose TLS handshake chain issues on a live network interface, use openssl s_client with the -showcerts flag.
# (not run here)
# Connect to target TLS server and print all presented certificates
openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com -showcerts < /dev/null
To verify whether a local host can successfully build an X.509 path using system trust anchors:
# (not run here)
# Verify remote server path using default system trust store
openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com -verify_return_error < /dev/null


Simulating Non-Browser Handshakes with Python
To test path building in Python (which uses OpenSSL bindings without AIA fetching support):
# (not run here)
import socket
import ssl

hostname = 'www.example.com'
context = ssl.create_default_context()

with socket.create_connection((hostname, 443)) as sock:
    try:
        with context.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=hostname) as ssock:
            print(f"Successfully negotiated TLS with {hostname}")
            cert = ssock.getpeercert()
            print(f"Subject: {cert['subject']}")
    except ssl.SSLCertVerificationError as e:
        print(f"Path validation failed: {e.verify_code} - {e.verify_message}")

title: X.509 Path Building Traps: Intermediates, nameConstraints and pathlen
text:
Gotchas

Including Root CAs in the Server Handshake: Transmitting the self-signed root certificate in the TLS handshake wastes network bandwidth (adding 1-2 KB to initial packet sizes) and provides no trust value, as the client must already possess the root anchor in its local store.
Out-of-Order Intermediate Bundles: Placing intermediate certificates out of sequential order (e.g., intermediate 2 before intermediate 1) causes non-browser clients (Go, Java) to fail path building, even if all required certificates are present in the PEM file.
Trust Anchor Mismatch During CA Reissuance: When a Certificate Authority updates its root or intermediate signing key pair, servers serving newly issued leaf certificates alongside legacy intermediate files will cause clients to throw error 20 (unable to get local issuer certificate).
Case Sensitivity in nameConstraints: While DNS domain matching in X.509 is generally case-insensitive per RFC 5280, certain legacy TLS implementations treat dNSName entries in nameConstraints as case-sensitive byte strings, leading to unexpected verification failures for mixed-case hostnames.
Ignoring Criticality Flags: Custom PKI tooling that sets critical on custom or non-standard extensions will cause standard compliant verifiers (such as OpenSSL or BoringSSL) to reject the entire path with unhandled critical extension.
AIA Chasing Latency Spikes: Relying on web browser AIA fetching to resolve missing intermediates introduces unpredictable handshake latency spikes (100 ms to several seconds) if the CA’s HTTP AIA repository is slow or unreachable.
Stale Intermediate Caching in Browsers: Web browsers cache intermediate certificates encountered during previous browsing sessions. A broken server configuration missing an intermediate may pass validation on an operator’s browser due to cache state while failing completely for fresh client installs or API callers.
Cross-Signed Certificates and Loop Detection: Cross-signed intermediate certificates (used during root migration) create multiple valid candidate paths. Naive path building algorithms without loop detection can enter infinite recursion or hit path depth limits.

title: X.509 Path Building Traps: Intermediates, nameConstraints and pathlen
text:
Exercises

Diagnose a Missing Intermediate: Use openssl s_client -connect against an internal TLS endpoint. Extract the presented certificates into individual files and verify them using openssl verify -CAfile root.pem leaf.pem. Record the exact OpenSSL error code returned when the intermediate is omitted.
Construct a Constrained Sub-CA: Using OpenSSL CLI or Python cryptography, create a Root CA and issue a subordinate CA certificate with nameConstraints restricting dNSName to .internal.net. Issue two leaf certificates under this subordinate CA: one for host.internal.net and one for host.public.com. Execute openssl verify against both and document the diagnostic output.
Enforce pathLenConstraint Limits: Generate a three-tier CA hierarchy (Root CA \(\rightarrow\) Intermediate CA 1 [pathlen:0] \(\rightarrow\) Intermediate CA 2). Attempt to issue and verify a leaf certificate under Intermediate CA 2. Verify that OpenSSL throws error 25 (path length constraint exceeded).
Inspect System Trust Stores: Locate the default system CA bundle on your host Linux distribution (e.g., /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt or /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt). Use openssl x509 -text -noout to search for intermediate CAs that contain nameConstraints or pathLenConstraint extensions.
Simulate AIA Fetching Failure: Write a Python script using requests or urllib that retrieves a leaf certificate from a server known to omit its intermediate. Extract the AIA caIssuers URI from the certificate’s extension, download the intermediate payload manually, write it to a temporary directory, and execute an OpenSSL validation pass using the downloaded intermediate.

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
NIST published Special Publication 800-81 Revision 3, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide, as a final document on 19 March 2026, replacing the 2013 revision. It is written for enterprise DNS operators and is now the reference many security teams will audit you against. Most of it is sound operational practice you already know in outline. The useful part for an operator is the concrete numbers and the specific “do this, not that” statements: TTL ranges, SOA timer ranges, RRSIG validity, which record types to drop, NSEC versus NSEC3, how to stop clients bypassing your resolvers. This chapter pulls those recommendations out by section number, turns the zone-file ones into a small auditor you can run in CI, and gives resolver and firewall snippets for the rest. Other chapters in this part cover how DNSSEC, encrypted DNS and the stub resolver work; here we only check configurations against the guide.

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
Learning goals

Find the concrete, checkable recommendations in SP 800-81r3 and map each to its section.
Audit a zone file for TTL, SOA timer, information-leakage and DNSSEC parameter problems with a script.
Lock down zone transfers, dynamic updates and NOTIFY with ACLs, TSIG and ZONEMD.
Configure a recursive resolver for validation, automated trust-anchor rollover, QNAME minimisation and internal-only access.
Block resolver bypass (Do53, DoT, DoQ and DoH) at the network edge.
Score query names for possible DNS exfiltration, and know the limits of that score.

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
Version note
Everything here is checked against the final SP 800-81r3 PDF (DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-81r3, March 2026). Section numbers refer to that document. The auditor and the entropy scorer are Python 3.13.5 standard-library scripts and were run on the book’s build box. The BIND, Unbound and nftables snippets are written from those projects’ documentation and are not run here (no DNS server or nft binary on the box, and no root).

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
How the guide is organised
The guide has three layers:

DNS as a security tool (§2.1). Protective DNS: resolvers that filter by threat intelligence, log for forensics and act as a zero-trust policy enforcement point.
Protecting the protocol (§2.2). Integrity through DNSSEC, confidentiality through encrypted DNS, and general hygiene.
Protecting the service (§2.3, §3, §4, §5). Dedicated servers per role, hidden primaries, redundancy, then detailed sections for authoritative servers (§3), recursive servers (§4) and stub resolvers (§5).

The rest of this chapter follows §3 to §5, because that is where the checkable statements are.

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
Authoritative servers (§3)

Zone transfers, updates and NOTIFY (§3.1 to §3.4)







Topic
What the guide says




Who may transfer (§3.1.1)
ACL on the primary allowing only its secondaries. Disable transfers on secondaries unless they feed other secondaries, and then ACL those too.


Authenticating transfers (§3.1)
IP ACLs alone can be spoofed. Use TSIG (shared secret, RFC 8945) between servers in one administration; SIG(0) is the public-key alternative but costlier.


Integrity of the zone (§3.1)
ZONEMD (RFC 8976) lets a secondary check the transferred zone against a digest published in the zone, with no shared secret.


Confidentiality (§3.1)
TSIG and SIG(0) give integrity only. Use zone transfer over TLS (XoT, RFC 9103) or a protected network path.


Dynamic updates (§3.3)
Accept only from authorised senders (TSIG or ACL); TSIG’s signed timestamp also limits replay. Updates go only to the primary, and zones with dynamic updates should sit on a dedicated hidden primary, because update processing is expensive.


NOTIFY (§3.4)
Low risk, but secondaries should accept NOTIFY only from their primary (or the secondary they transfer from).





Zone content (§3.2, §3.5, §3.6)

Lame delegations (§3.2.1, §3.6.2). Check delegations regularly, both your parent’s view of you and your delegations to children. A delegation to a hosting provider whose contract has lapsed is a hijack risk: someone else can sign up with that provider and serve your subdomain. When you retire a zone, remove the delegation and the zone data.
SOA timers (§3.2.2). Refresh too high gives zone drift (secondaries serve stale data); too low gives zone thrash (constant transfers). Set refresh from the zone’s rate of change, suggested range 1200 s to 432000 s, with retry a fraction of refresh.
Information leakage (§3.5.1). Leave HINFO, RP and LOC out of internet-facing zones. Decide on TXT records case by case; SPF, DKIM and DMARC are legitimate.
Dangling CNAMEs (§3.6.1). A CNAME to a name in someone else’s domain (a cloud app, a SaaS page) becomes a takeover if that name or its domain is released. Monitor them and delete the ones you no longer need.
Look-alike domains (§3.6.3). Watch new registrations that resemble yours, register the obvious ones defensively, and keep retired delegations parked for a while.



TTLs (§3.7.1)

Default TTLs should be in the range 1800 s to 86400 s (30 minutes to a day).
Lower TTLs are fine for specific records you expect to change soon, and some load-balancing setups use 60 s or less.
On DNSSEC-signed RRsets avoid 30 s or less; very short TTLs cause trouble in validating caches.
Never use a TTL of 0. The guide is explicit: even 5 to 30 s is significantly better than 0.
TTLs must be shorter than the RRSIG validity period covering the RRset.



DNSSEC signing (§3.8)







Topic
Recommendation




Algorithms (§3.8.1, Table 1)
RSA/SHA-256 (8, keys of 2048 bits or more), ECDSA P-256 (13), ECDSA P-384 (14), Ed25519 (15), Ed448 (16). Prefer the elliptic-curve algorithms because they keep responses small. 112-bit security is acceptable until 2030, then 128-bit. No post-quantum algorithm is specified yet.


Key lifetime (§3.8.1)
Signing keys: maximum 1 to 3 years. Automate ZSK rollovers; for KSK rollovers know how your parent zone handles DS updates (for example CDS/CDNSKEY). Keep the KSK in an HSM where practical.


Signature validity (§3.8.2)
Keep the RRSIG validity on the DNSKEY RRset short, for example 5 to 7 days, but significantly longer than the TTL. Short validity limits how long a stolen key is useful.


Denial of existence (§3.8.3, §3.8.4)
NSEC3 makes zone walking harder but not impossible, and costs CPU on both sides. The guide calls NSEC the more prudent approach. If you must use NSEC3, set parameters to minimise DoS risk (RFC 9276: zero extra iterations, empty salt). Compact denial of existence is an alternative.


Algorithm rollover (§3.8.5)
Follow RFC 6781: add new signatures before the new DNSKEY and DS; when removing the old algorithm, remove its DNSKEY before its signatures. Expect larger responses during the rollover.


Internal zones (§3.8.6)
Do not sign internal zones unless a policy requires it. If required, prefer a separate delegation from the external parent so no extra trust anchors are needed.


Time (§3.8.7)
Signers need an authoritative, secured time source.

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
Recursive servers (§4)

Encrypted DNS (§4.2.1). Offer DoT, DoH or DoQ to clients; restrict server TLS settings to the ciphers allowed by SP 800-52.
Stop resolver bypass (§4.2.2). Block outbound DNS (UDP and TCP 53) except from authorised resolvers or forwarders; block DoT (TCP 853) and DoQ (UDP 853); handle DoH (TCP 443) with an RPZ for known DoH hostnames plus firewall rules for DoH services on dedicated addresses; use MDM to stop users configuring their own encrypted DNS.
QNAME minimisation (§4.2.3, RFC 9156). Enable it; the extra queries are negligible once the cache is warm.
Exfiltration (§4.2.4). Detect DNS tunnelling by unusual query volume per host, changing patterns, high-entropy query names and known-bad domains from threat intelligence.
Validation (§4.2.5, §4.2.6). Validate DNSSEC with the root key as the trust anchor, enable automated trust-anchor rollover (RFC 5011) and watch the logs.
Access (§4.3). Recursive servers answer only internal clients; block inbound 53 from the internet. Give them a primary and backup authoritative time source (§4.3.1).
Stubs and mobile hosts (§5). Point stubs only at enterprise resolvers; mobile hosts either validate with the same trust anchors and policy or tunnel back to the enterprise resolvers.

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
Lab
The lab checks a deliberately bad zone, then a fixed one, against the numeric §3 recommendations, and scores a short query log for exfiltration. audit.py is a small single-purpose parser (one record per line, parenthesised SOA), not a replacement for named-checkzone or a full DNS library.

The auditor
audit.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""audit.py ZONE [RRSIG-VALIDITY-DAYS]: check a zone file against the numeric
and hygiene recommendations of NIST SP 800-81r3 (March 2026) and RFC 9276.
Small parser: one RR per line, no multi-line records except a parenthesised SOA."""
import sys, re

zone = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
validity_days = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
zone = re.sub(r"\(([^)]*)\)", lambda m: " ".join(m.group(1).split()), zone)
origin, default_ttl, rrs = ".", None, []
for line in zone.splitlines():
    line = line.split(";")[0].rstrip()
    if not line.strip():
        continue
    if line.startswith("$ORIGIN"):
        origin = line.split()[1]; continue
    if line.startswith("$TTL"):
        default_ttl = int(line.split()[1]); continue
    f = line.split()
    owner = f.pop(0)
    ttl = int(f.pop(0)) if f[0].isdigit() else default_ttl
    if f[0] == "IN":
        f.pop(0)
    rtype, rdata = f[0], f[1:]
    name = origin if owner == "@" else owner + "." + origin
    rrs.append((name, ttl, rtype, rdata))

findings = []
def flag(level, sec, msg):
    findings.append((level, sec, msg))

signed = any(t in ("DNSKEY", "RRSIG", "NSEC3PARAM") for _, _, t, _ in rrs)
for name, ttl, rtype, rdata in rrs:
    rr = f"{name} {ttl} {rtype}"
    if ttl == 0:
        flag("FAIL", "3.7.1", f"{rr}: TTL 0 must never be used")
    elif signed and ttl <= 30:
        flag("FAIL", "3.7.1", f"{rr}: TTL <= 30 s on a signed zone breaks validating caches")
    elif ttl < 1800 and rtype not in ("DS", "DNSKEY"):
        flag("WARN", "3.7.1", f"{rr}: below the 1800-86400 s range; fine only for records you are about to change")
    elif ttl > 86400:
        flag("WARN", "3.7.1", f"{rr}: above 1 day")
    if validity_days is not None and ttl >= validity_days * 86400:
        flag("FAIL", "3.7.1", f"{rr}: TTL not below RRSIG validity ({validity_days:g} d)")
    if rtype in ("HINFO", "RP", "LOC"):
        flag("FAIL", "3.5.1", f"{rr}: exclude {rtype} from internet-facing zones")
    if rtype == "TXT":
        flag("INFO", "3.5.1", f"{rr}: TXT kept? decide case by case (SPF/DKIM/DMARC are fine)")
    if rtype == "CNAME" and not rdata[0].endswith(origin):
        flag("CHECK", "3.6.1", f"{rr} -> {rdata[0]}: off-zone target, confirm it is still registered and yours")
    if rtype == "NS" and not rdata[0].endswith(origin):
        flag("CHECK", "3.6.2", f"{rr} -> {rdata[0]}: provider-hosted NS, confirm the contract and zone still exist")
    if rtype == "SOA":
        refresh, retry = int(rdata[3]), int(rdata[4])
        if not 1200 <= refresh <= 432000:
            flag("WARN", "3.2.2", f"SOA refresh {refresh}: outside 1200-432000 s, risk of zone thrash or drift")
        if retry >= refresh:
            flag("FAIL", "3.2.2", f"SOA retry {retry} >= refresh {refresh}: retry should be a fraction of refresh")
    if rtype == "DNSKEY":
        alg = int(rdata[2])
        if alg in (5, 7, 8, 10):
            flag("WARN", "3.8.1", f"DNSKEY algorithm {alg} is RSA: prefer 13 (ECDSA P-256) for smaller responses")
    if rtype == "NSEC3PARAM":
        _, _, iters, salt = rdata
        flag("WARN", "3.8.3", "NSEC3 in use: SP 800-81r3 calls NSEC the more prudent default")
        if int(iters) != 0 or salt != "-":
            flag("FAIL", "3.8.3", f"NSEC3 iterations={iters} salt={salt}: RFC 9276 says 0 and empty ('-')")
if validity_days is not None and not 5 <= validity_days <= 7:
    flag("WARN", "3.8.2", f"DNSKEY RRSIG validity {validity_days:g} d: guide suggests about 5-7 days")

order = {"FAIL": 0, "WARN": 1, "CHECK": 2, "INFO": 3}
for level, sec, msg in sorted(findings, key=lambda x: (order[x[0]], x[1])):
    print(f"{level:5} §{sec:6} {msg}")
counts = {k: sum(1 for f in findings if f[0] == k) for k in order}
print(f"\n{len(rrs)} RRs, signed={signed}: " + ", ".join(f"{v} {k}" for k, v in counts.items()))
sys.exit(1 if counts["FAIL"] else 0)

$TTL 3600

Scoring query names (§4.2.4)
qname-entropy.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""qname_entropy.py: score query names the way SP 800-81r3 §4.2.4 suggests
(entropy of the leftmost labels, label length, query volume per host)."""
import math
from collections import Counter

def entropy(s):
    c = Counter(s)
    return abs(-sum(n / len(s) * math.log2(n / len(s)) for n in c.values()))

log = [("10.0.0.21", "www.example.net"), ("10.0.0.21", "mail.example.net"),
       ("10.0.0.34", "login.microsoftonline.com"), ("10.0.0.34", "fonts.gstatic.com")]
log += [("10.0.0.77", f"{chunk}.t.exfil-test.example") for chunk in (
    "mzxw6ytboi2dqnrrgq3tkmzwgy", "nbswy3dpeb3w64tmmqqgc3tz", "on2hgzltoq2dcnbqgyztqmjq",
    "gezdgnbvgy3tqojqgezdgnbv", "kruge2lbnvqw4ylcmvzw2ylu", "mfrggzdfmztwq2lknnwg23tp")]

per_host = Counter(h for h, _ in log)
print(f"{'host':10} {'qname':48} {'left':>4} {'H':>5}  verdict")
for host, q in log:
    left = q.split(".")[0]
    h = entropy(left)
    suspicious = len(left) >= 20 and h >= 3.5
    print(f"{host:10} {q:48} {len(left):4} {h:5.2f}  {'SUSPECT' if suspicious else 'ok'}")
print("\nqueries per host:", dict(per_host))

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
Reading the output
One line causes most of the failures. $TTL 0 applies to every record without an explicit TTL, so the SOA, both NS records, ns1, the HINFO, RP and LOC records and the NSEC3PARAM all fail the “never TTL 0” rule: 8 of the 14 failures. api has an explicit TTL of 20 s, which fails the separate rule for signed zones (30 s or less). www at 300 s is only a warning, because a short TTL is acceptable for a record you are about to change.
The SOA is upside down. Refresh 300 s is below the 1200 s floor, and retry 600 s is longer than refresh. A secondary would poll every five minutes and wait longer after a failure than between successes.
Leakage and DNSSEC parameters. HINFO, RP and LOC fail §3.5.1. The DNSKEY uses algorithm 8 (RSA), which is allowed but produces larger responses than 13. NSEC3 with 10 iterations and a salt fails RFC 9276, and NSEC3 itself is flagged because §3.8.3 prefers NSEC. A 30-day DNSKEY RRSIG validity is outside the 5 to 7 day suggestion.
CHECK means a human must look. The script cannot know whether shop-example.azurewebsites.net is still your app or whether your contract with dnshost-old.example is still active; those are the dangling-CNAME and lame-delegation checks from §3.6. Feed this list into whoever owns the registrations.
The fixed zone exits 0. It has a sane $TTL 3600, refresh 7200 s with retry 1800 s, two in-zone name servers, algorithm 13 and no NSEC3, and is checked against a 7-day validity. One warning (the 300 s AAAA) and one CHECK (the GitHub Pages CNAME) remain, both deliberate and documented. Because the exit code is 0 only when there are no FAILs, the script can gate a zone repository in CI.
Entropy. The six test queries from 10.0.0.77 have leftmost labels of 24 to 26 characters with 3.52 to 4.09 bits of entropy per character, which is typical of base32-encoded data. Normal names stay at 2.32 or below. That host also sent 6 of the 10 queries. Entropy alone produces false positives (CDN and tracking hostnames are often random-looking), so, as §4.2.4 says, combine it with per-host volume, pattern changes and threat intelligence before alerting.

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
Gotchas

“864000 seconds (1 day)” in §3.2.2 is a typo. 864000 s is 10 days; one day is 86400 s. The auditor uses the 1200 to 432000 s range the same sentence gives.
Table 1 prints “Ed225516”. It means Ed25519, DNSSEC algorithm 15.
$TTL is inherited. One bad $TTL line poisons every record without an explicit TTL, as the lab showed. Check it first.
TTL and RRSIG validity interact. A long TTL with a short signature validity means caches hold records whose signatures expire; validating resolvers cut the TTL, but non-validating caches may serve them anyway (§3.7.1).
NSEC3 does not hide your zone. Hashed names can usually be cracked offline; the guide prefers NSEC. If policy forces NSEC3, use zero iterations and no salt.
Blocking port 53 does not stop DoH. DoH looks like HTTPS. You need RPZ entries for known DoH names, address blocks for dedicated DoH services, and endpoint management.
Encrypted DNS blinds passive monitoring. §4.2.4 notes that network taps cannot see query names in DoT, DoH or DoQ; do exfiltration detection on the resolver, not on the wire.
Do not sign internal zones by reflex. On combined authoritative and recursive servers the server would only validate its own data (§3.8.6).

title: Auditing DNS Against NIST SP 800-81r3
text:
Exercises

Add a check to audit.py that flags TXT records other than SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and run it on both zones.
Extend audit.py to warn when a DNSKEY or DS TTL is longer than one day, since §3.7.1 explains why those benefit from shorter TTLs during emergency key changes.
Write a script that resolves every off-zone CNAME target in a zone and reports NXDOMAIN or a target domain that no longer has NS records (§3.6.1). Run it against one of your own zones.
Lower the entropy threshold in qname-entropy.py until a normal name becomes SUSPECT. What does that tell you about using entropy alone?
In a lab with Unbound and the nftables policy above, try dig @1.1.1.1, kdig +tls @1.1.1.1 and a DoH query from a client, and record which ones the policy stops and which need the RPZ.

title: The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
text:
The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
Put a TCP proxy in front of a service and the service loses something it used to have for free: the client’s address. Every connection now comes from the proxy. Logs show one IP, rate limits throttle everybody at once, allow-lists stop working, and an abuse report becomes impossible to answer. HTTP proxies paper over this with X-Forwarded-For or Forwarded, but a layer 4 proxy cannot edit headers it does not understand, and SMTP, IMAP, SSH, MySQL and TLS-passthrough traffic have no such header anyway.
The PROXY protocol is the common fix. The proxy writes one small header at the very start of the backend connection: “this connection was really from 203.0.113.7:51514 to 198.51.100.10:443”. The backend reads it, strips it, and carries on as if the client had connected directly. HAProxy, nginx, Envoy, Traefik, Caddy, Postfix, Dovecot, Exim and most cloud load balancers speak it. It is also an easy way to let anybody on the Internet choose their own source address, if you configure it wrong.
This chapter builds both header versions from the specification, runs a proxy and five kinds of backend in a private network namespace, and shows the failures you will meet in production: spoofing through a backend that “accepts PROXY if present”, headers that arrive in pieces, backends that were not told about the header, and health checks.

title: The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
text:
Learning goals

Encode and decode PROXY protocol v1 (text) and v2 (binary) headers, including TLVs and the CRC32C checksum.
Explain why a receiver must require the header on a listener and must not guess whether it is present.
Restrict who may send the header, and say what that restriction does and does not protect.
Read the header correctly from a byte stream, without over-reading and without assuming one recv() is enough.
Configure the sending and receiving side in HAProxy, nginx and Postfix, and recognise the symptoms of a mismatch.
Decide when the PROXY protocol is the right tool and when Forwarded, TLS client certificates or direct server return are better.

No packages were installed. The specification is the HAProxy document “The PROXY protocol, Versions 1 & 2” (revision 2020/03/05), fetched from haproxy.org on 2026-11-14. The HAProxy, nginx, Postfix and AWS snippets in the production section come from their current documentation and are not run here.

title: The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
text:
Where the address goes
   client 203.0.113.7:51514
        |
        |  TCP to 198.51.100.10:443
        v
   L4 proxy (HAProxy, NLB, ...)                         backend 10.0.0.2:443
        |  new TCP connection from 10.0.0.1:40122 -------->  getpeername() = 10.0.0.1
        |
        |  with PROXY protocol, the first bytes on that connection are:
        |  "PROXY TCP4 203.0.113.7 198.51.100.10 51514 443\r\n"  (v1)
        |  or a 16+ byte binary block                             (v2)
        |  followed by the client's bytes, untouched
Two properties make it work for every protocol:

It is sent once, first, by the connection initiator. The proxy writes the header before any client byte. The backend reads it before handing the socket to the application protocol. Nothing is ever sent back.
It describes the connection, not a request. One header per TCP connection. That is why the specification says a proxy that multiplexes several clients’ requests over one backend connection “MUST NOT” use it (section 2): the backend would attribute every request to the first client.


Version 1
One line of US-ASCII:
PROXY TCP4 192.168.0.1 192.168.0.11 56324 443\r\n
PROXY TCP6 2001:db8::50 2001:db8::2 40000 443\r\n
PROXY UNKNOWN\r\n
Fields are separated by exactly one space, ports and IPv4 octets have no leading zeros, and the line ends with CRLF (a bare LF is invalid). The longest legal line is 107 bytes (PROXY UNKNOWN with two full IPv6 addresses and two five-digit ports), so a receiver that has not seen CRLF in the first 107 bytes must give up. UNKNOWN means “I speak the protocol but cannot describe this connection”; the receiver then uses the real socket addresses.


Version 2
Version 2 is binary, fixed-offset and extensible:
offset  size  field
0       12    signature 0D 0A 0D 0A 00 0D 0A 51 55 49 54 0A   ("\r\n\r\n\0\r\nQUIT\n")
12      1     version (high nibble, always 2) | command (low nibble: 0 LOCAL, 1 PROXY)
13      1     address family (high nibble) | transport (low nibble)
                0x11 TCP/IPv4  0x12 UDP/IPv4  0x21 TCP/IPv6  0x22 UDP/IPv6
                0x31 UNIX stream  0x32 UNIX dgram  0x00 UNSPEC
14      2     length of everything that follows (network order)
16      12    IPv4: src addr, dst addr, src port, dst port    (36 for IPv6, 216 for UNIX)
...     ...   TLVs: type (1 byte), length (2 bytes), value
The signature is deliberately hostile to other protocols. It starts with an empty line, contains a NUL, and spells QUIT, so an HTTP, SMTP, FTP or TLS server that receives it by mistake fails at once instead of half-working (section 5 of the spec).
The LOCAL command means “this connection is the proxy’s own, for example a health check”: the receiver must accept it and use the real endpoints. The length field lets a receiver skip address blocks and TLVs it does not understand. The receiver must always honour it, even for LOCAL.
Registered TLVs (section 2.2):








Type
Name
Carries




0x01
ALPN
the ALPN protocol the client negotiated, e.g. h2


0x02
AUTHORITY
the host name the client asked for, normally the TLS SNI


0x03
CRC32C
checksum of the whole header, computed with this field zeroed


0x04
NOOP
padding, ignored


0x05
UNIQUE_ID
an opaque ID of up to 128 bytes for correlating logs across proxies


0x20
SSL
client-side TLS facts: version, cipher, client-certificate CN, verify result


0x30
NETNS
the network namespace name the connection arrived in


0xE0–0xEF
custom
application specific; AWS uses 0xEA for the VPC endpoint ID

title: The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
text:
The lab
Three files: the codec, the lab and a shell wrapper.
proxyproto.py builds v1 and v2 headers and reads exactly one header from a socket. The reader is the interesting part. It reads 5 bytes to tell PROXY (v1) from the v2 signature, then reads exactly as many bytes as the format says, never more, so the application data that follows stays in the socket for whoever handles the connection next.


proxyproto.py

"""PROXY protocol v1 and v2 (haproxy.org proxy-protocol.txt), standard library only."""
import ipaddress, socket, struct

SIG = b"\r\n\r\n\x00\r\nQUIT\n"            # 12-byte v2 signature
LOCAL, PROXY = 0x0, 0x1
TLV_NAMES = {0x01: "ALPN", 0x02: "AUTHORITY", 0x03: "CRC32C", 0x04: "NOOP", 0x05: "UNIQUE_ID",
             0x20: "SSL", 0x30: "NETNS"}

def _crc_table():
    poly, table = 0x82F63B78, []            # CRC-32C (Castagnoli), reflected
    for i in range(256):
        c = i
        for _ in range(8):
            c = (c >> 1) ^ poly if c & 1 else c >> 1
        table.append(c)
    return table
_T = _crc_table()

def crc32c(data):
    c = 0xFFFFFFFF
    for b in data:
        c = _T[(c ^ b) & 0xFF] ^ (c >> 8)
    return c ^ 0xFFFFFFFF

def v1(src, dst):
    (sip, sport), (dip, dport) = src, dst
    fam = "TCP6" if ipaddress.ip_address(sip).version == 6 else "TCP4"
    return f"PROXY {fam} {sip} {dip} {sport} {dport}\r\n".encode()

def v2(src=None, dst=None, command=PROXY, tlvs=(), with_crc=False):
    if command == LOCAL:
        fam, addr = 0x00, b""
    else:
        (sip, sport), (dip, dport) = src, dst
        s, d = ipaddress.ip_address(sip), ipaddress.ip_address(dip)
        fam = 0x11 if s.version == 4 else 0x21            # TCP over IPv4 / IPv6
        addr = s.packed + d.packed + struct.pack("!HH", sport, dport)
    body = addr + b"".join(struct.pack("!BH", t, len(v)) + v for t, v in tlvs)
    if with_crc:
        body += struct.pack("!BHI", 0x03, 4, 0)
    hdr = SIG + bytes([0x20 | command, fam]) + struct.pack("!H", len(body)) + body
    if with_crc:
        hdr = hdr[:-4] + struct.pack("!I", crc32c(hdr))
    return hdr

class ProxyError(Exception):
    pass

def recv_exact(sock, n):
    buf = b""
    while len(buf) < n:
        chunk = sock.recv(n - len(buf))
        if not chunk:
            raise ProxyError(f"connection closed after {len(buf)} of {n} header bytes")
        buf += chunk
    return buf

def read_header(sock):
    """Read exactly one PROXY header from a stream socket, never a byte more.
    Returns dict(version, command, src, dst, tlvs). Raises ProxyError on anything else."""
    first = recv_exact(sock, 5)
    if first == b"PROXY":                                  # v1: read up to CRLF, max 107 bytes
        line = first
        while not line.endswith(b"\r\n"):
            if len(line) >= 107:
                raise ProxyError("v1 line longer than 107 bytes")
            line += recv_exact(sock, 1)
        parts = line[:-2].decode("ascii").split(" ")
        if parts[1] == "UNKNOWN":
            return {"version": 1, "command": "UNKNOWN", "src": None, "dst": None, "tlvs": {}}
        if len(parts) != 6 or parts[1] not in ("TCP4", "TCP6"):
            raise ProxyError(f"bad v1 line {line!r}")
        for p in parts[4:]:
            if not p.isdigit() or (p != "0" and p.startswith("0")) or int(p) > 65535:
                raise ProxyError(f"bad v1 port {p!r}")
        src = (str(ipaddress.ip_address(parts[2])), int(parts[4]))
        dst = (str(ipaddress.ip_address(parts[3])), int(parts[5]))
        return {"version": 1, "command": "PROXY", "src": src, "dst": dst, "tlvs": {}}
    rest = recv_exact(sock, 7)
    head = first + rest
    if head != SIG:
        raise ProxyError(f"no PROXY header (first bytes {head[:8]!r})")
    ver_cmd, fam, length = struct.unpack("!BBH", recv_exact(sock, 4))
    if ver_cmd >> 4 != 2 or ver_cmd & 0xF not in (LOCAL, PROXY):
        raise ProxyError(f"bad version/command 0x{ver_cmd:02x}")
    body = recv_exact(sock, length)
    raw = SIG + bytes([ver_cmd, fam]) + struct.pack("!H", length) + body
    out = {"version": 2, "command": "LOCAL" if ver_cmd & 0xF == LOCAL else "PROXY",
           "src": None, "dst": None, "tlvs": {}}
    alen = {0x11: 12, 0x12: 12, 0x21: 36, 0x22: 36, 0x31: 216, 0x32: 216}.get(fam, 0)
    if fam in (0x11, 0x12, 0x21, 0x22) and length >= alen:
        n = 4 if fam >> 4 == 1 else 16
        a = body[:alen]
        sport, dport = struct.unpack("!HH", a[2 * n:])
        out["src"] = (str(ipaddress.ip_address(a[:n])), sport)
        out["dst"] = (str(ipaddress.ip_address(a[n:2 * n])), dport)
    p, off = body[alen:], 16 + alen
    while p:
        if len(p) < 3:
            raise ProxyError("truncated TLV")
        t, l = struct.unpack("!BH", p[:3])
        v = p[3:3 + l]
        if len(v) != l:
            raise ProxyError("TLV overruns header length")
        if t == 0x03:
            zeroed = raw[:off + 3] + b"\x00\x00\x00\x00" + raw[off + 7:]
            if crc32c(zeroed) != struct.unpack("!I", v)[0]:
                raise ProxyError("CRC32C mismatch")
            out["tlvs"]["CRC32C"] = "ok"
        elif t != 0x04:
            out["tlvs"][TLV_NAMES.get(t, f"0x{t:02x}")] = v.decode(errors="replace") if t in (1, 2) else v.hex()
        p, off = p[3 + l:], off + 3 + l
    if out["command"] == "LOCAL":                          # health check: use the real endpoints
        out["src"] = out["dst"] = None
    return out

lab.py puts four addresses on lo and runs, all as threads in one process:

an L4 proxy on 10.0.0.1 with one listening port per experiment, each configured to send a different header (or none) to a different backend;
five backends on 10.0.0.2: strict (port 9000, header required, only from the proxy’s address), plain (9001, no PROXY support), guessing (9002, “parses PROXY if the bytes look like one”, reachable by anyone), naive (9003, assumes the header arrives in one recv()), and Python’s real http.server (9004), which was never told about the header;
a client on 10.0.0.50 and an attacker on 10.0.0.66.



lab.py

"""PROXY protocol lab. Run inside `unshare -urn` (see lab.sh): 10.0.0.1 = L4 proxy,
10.0.0.2 = backends, 10.0.0.50 = real client, 10.0.0.66 = attacker."""
import http.server, ipaddress, socket, threading, time
import proxyproto as pp

PROXY_IP, BACKEND_IP, CLIENT_IP, ATTACKER_IP = "10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2", "10.0.0.50", "10.0.0.66"
TRUSTED = [ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.0.1/32")]          # only the proxy may send PROXY headers
log = []

def listen(ip, port, handler):
    s = socket.socket()
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind((ip, port))
    s.listen()
    def loop():
        while True:
            c, peer = s.accept()
            threading.Thread(target=handler, args=(c, peer), daemon=True).start()
    threading.Thread(target=loop, daemon=True).start()

def reply(c, who):
    data = c.recv(4096)
    c.sendall(f"hello {who[0]}:{who[1]} you sent {data[:24]!r}\n".encode())
    c.close()

# ---- backends ----
def strict(c, peer):              # port 9000: header REQUIRED, and only from trusted sources
    if not any(ipaddress.ip_address(peer[0]) in n for n in TRUSTED):
        log.append(f"strict : refused {peer[0]} (not a trusted proxy)")
        return c.close()
    c.settimeout(3)
    try:
        h = pp.read_header(c)
    except (pp.ProxyError, socket.timeout, UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError) as e:
        log.append(f"strict : dropped {peer[0]}: {e}")
        return c.close()
    who = h["src"] or peer
    log.append(f"strict : v{h['version']} {h['command']} client={who[0]}:{who[1]} tlvs={h['tlvs']}")
    reply(c, who)

def plain(c, peer):               # port 9001: no PROXY support at all
    log.append(f"plain  : client={peer[0]}:{peer[1]}")
    reply(c, peer)

def guessing(c, peer):            # port 9002: WRONG, "accepts PROXY if present", open to all
    first = c.recv(5, socket.MSG_PEEK)
    who = peer
    if first == b"PROXY" or first == pp.SIG[:5]:
        who = pp.read_header(c)["src"]
    log.append(f"guess  : connection from {peer[0]} logged as client={who[0]}:{who[1]}")
    reply(c, who)

def naive_once(c, peer):          # port 9003: WRONG, assumes the header arrives in one recv()
    data = c.recv(232)
    ok = data.startswith(pp.SIG) and len(data) >= 16 + int.from_bytes(data[14:16], "big")
    log.append(f"naive  : first recv() returned {len(data)} bytes -> "
               + ("header complete" if ok else "partial header, connection rejected"))
    c.close()

class Quiet(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):  # port 9004: a real HTTP server, not told about PROXY
    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):
        log.append("http   : " + (fmt % args))
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b"ok\n")

# ---- the L4 proxy ----
def make_proxy(backend_port, header, bytewise=False):
    def handle(c, peer):
        try:
            relay(c, peer)
        except OSError:          # backend hung up on us: the client just sees the close
            c.close()
    def relay(c, peer):
        data = c.recv(4096)
        b = socket.socket()
        b.bind((PROXY_IP, 0))
        b.connect((BACKEND_IP, backend_port))
        hdr = header(peer, c.getsockname())
        if bytewise:                        # TCP may deliver the header in pieces: simulate it
            for i in range(len(hdr)):
                b.send(hdr[i:i + 1]); time.sleep(0.002)
        else:
            b.sendall(hdr)
        b.sendall(data)
        resp = b""
        while chunk := b.recv(4096):
            resp += chunk
        c.sendall(resp)
        c.close(); b.close()
    return handle

def client(src, dst, payload=b"GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n"):
    s = socket.socket()
    s.bind((src, 0))
    s.settimeout(3)
    s.connect(dst)
    s.sendall(payload)
    out = b""
    try:
        while chunk := s.recv(4096):
            out += chunk
    except (ConnectionResetError, socket.timeout):
        pass
    s.close()
    return out.decode(errors="replace").splitlines()[0] if out else "(connection closed, no reply)"

def run(title, src, dst, payload=b"GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n"):
    log.clear()
    answer = client(src, dst, payload)
    time.sleep(0.05)
    print(f"\n--- {title}")
    for line in log:
        print("  " + line)
    print(f"  client got: {answer}")

def main():
    listen(BACKEND_IP, 9000, strict)
    listen(BACKEND_IP, 9001, plain)
    listen(BACKEND_IP, 9002, guessing)
    listen(BACKEND_IP, 9003, naive_once)
    srv = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer((BACKEND_IP, 9004), Quiet)
    threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
    tlvs = [(0x01, b"h2"), (0x02, b"app.example.net"), (0x05, b"req-7f3a91")]
    v2 = lambda peer, local: pp.v2(peer, local, tlvs=tlvs, with_crc=True)
    v1 = lambda peer, local: pp.v1(peer, local)
    none = lambda peer, local: b""
    local = lambda peer, local: pp.v2(command=pp.LOCAL)
    def tampered(peer, local):     # flip one bit of the source address after the CRC was computed
        h = bytearray(pp.v2(peer, local, tlvs=tlvs, with_crc=True)); h[19] ^= 0x01
        return bytes(h)
    proxies = {8001: (9001, none, False), 8002: (9000, v2, False), 8003: (9000, v1, False),
               8004: (9000, local, False), 8005: (9003, v2, True), 8006: (9000, v2, True),
               8007: (9004, v2, False), 8008: (9000, tampered, False)}
    for port, (bport, hdr, bw) in proxies.items():
        listen(PROXY_IP, port, make_proxy(bport, hdr, bw))
    time.sleep(0.1)
    print("CRC-32C check value of '123456789':", hex(pp.crc32c(b"123456789")), "(expected 0xe3069283)")
    h = v2((CLIENT_IP, 40000), (PROXY_IP, 8002))
    print(f"v2 header with ALPN, AUTHORITY, UNIQUE_ID, CRC32C: {len(h)} bytes")
    print("  " + h[:16].hex(" ") + "  <- signature, ver/cmd 0x21, fam 0x11, len")
    print("  " + h[16:28].hex(" ") + "  <- src 10.0.0.50, dst 10.0.0.1, ports 40000, 8002")
    run("1. L4 proxy, no PROXY protocol", CLIENT_IP, (PROXY_IP, 8001))
    run("2. proxy sends v2 (+TLVs, CRC32C) to the strict backend", CLIENT_IP, (PROXY_IP, 8002))
    run("3. proxy sends v1 to the strict backend", CLIENT_IP, (PROXY_IP, 8003))
    run("4. proxy health check with a LOCAL command", PROXY_IP, (PROXY_IP, 8004))
    forged = b"PROXY TCP4 203.0.113.7 10.0.0.2 4444 9002\r\nGET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n"
    run("5. attacker connects straight to the 'PROXY if present' backend", ATTACKER_IP, (BACKEND_IP, 9002), forged)
    run("6. attacker connects straight to the strict backend", ATTACKER_IP, (BACKEND_IP, 9000), forged)
    run("7. attacker goes through the proxy and smuggles a header in the payload", ATTACKER_IP,
        (PROXY_IP, 8002), forged)
    run("8. header delivered one byte per segment, backend reads once", CLIENT_IP, (PROXY_IP, 8005))
    run("9. header delivered one byte per segment, backend reads exactly", CLIENT_IP, (PROXY_IP, 8006))
    run("10. proxy sends v2 to an HTTP server that was not told about it", CLIENT_IP, (PROXY_IP, 8007))
    run("11. one bit of the header flipped in transit", CLIENT_IP, (PROXY_IP, 8008))

main()



lab.sh

#!/bin/sh
# Rootless: a private network namespace where we are "root" only inside it.
exec unshare -urn sh -c '
  ip link set lo up
  for a in 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2 10.0.0.50 10.0.0.66; do ip addr add $a/32 dev lo; done
  python3 lab.py
'

title: The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
text:
Reading the results
The header dump. 71 bytes: the 16-byte fixed part (signature, 0x21 = version 2 + PROXY, 0x11 = TCP over IPv4, length 0x0037 = 55), the 12-byte IPv4 address block (0a000032 is 10.0.0.50, 9c40 is port 40000, 1f42 is 8002), then four TLVs: ALPN (5 bytes), AUTHORITY (18), UNIQUE_ID (13) and CRC32C (7). The CRC-32C implementation is checked against the standard check value for 123456789, 0xE3069283, before it is trusted with anything else.
1, 2 and 3: the point of the protocol. Without a header the backend sees the proxy (10.0.0.1). With v2 or v1 it sees the real client (10.0.0.50) and, with v2, what the proxy learned on the client side: the negotiated ALPN, the requested host name and a connection ID it can put in its own logs.
4: health checks. The proxy connects on its own behalf with LOCAL. The strict backend accepts it and reports the real peer, 10.0.0.1. A backend that rejects LOCAL, or a proxy that sends no header at all on health checks to a backend that requires one, produces the classic “every backend is down but they are all fine” outage. AWS documents the same thing from the other side: after you enable proxy protocol on a Network Load Balancer target group, health-check connections carry a header too, and targets that cannot parse it fail their health checks.
5: spoofing through a guessing backend. This is the misconfiguration the specification forbids in so many words: the receiver “MUST not try to guess whether the protocol header is present or not … Otherwise it would open a major security breach by allowing untrusted parties to spoof their connection addresses” (section 2). The attacker at 10.0.0.66 connected straight to the backend, wrote its own PROXY TCP4 203.0.113.7 ... line, and was logged as 203.0.113.7. Any allow-list, rate limit or audit trail keyed on the client address is now under the attacker’s control. This is not a lab curiosity. CVE-2026-53791 is exactly this bug in the rsync daemon before 3.5.0: an attacker who could connect straight to rsyncd sent a crafted PROXY header with a forged source address and walked past hosts allow / hosts deny (NVD; fixed in rsync 3.5.0).
6: the two rules that close it. The strict backend requires the header on that listener and only accepts connections from the proxy’s address. The attacker is refused before a byte is parsed. The second rule matters even when the first holds: a backend that requires the header but accepts it from anybody can still be fed any address by anybody who can reach it.
7: smuggling through the trusted proxy fails. The attacker sends a forged PROXY line as its first bytes through the proxy. The proxy prepends its own, real header, and the strict backend reads exactly one header, so the forged line arrives as application data (you sent b'PROXY TCP4 203.0.113.7 1'). This only works because the reader stops at the end of the first header. A receiver that loops “while the next bytes look like a PROXY header” reopens hole 5.
8 and 9: TCP is a byte stream. The proxy wrote the header one byte per segment. The naive backend’s first recv() returned 1 byte and it gave up. The strict reader asks for exactly what the format needs and loops until it has it. The specification allows a receiver to be impatient (it “may reject an incomplete line which does not contain the CRLF sequence in the first atomic read operation”) but recommends tolerance. Real proxies send the header in one write, so this rarely shows up until something in the path splits segments, a userspace TCP stack is involved, or a test harness writes slowly.
10: a backend that was not told. Python’s http.server received the v2 signature, which begins with \r\n, read an empty request line and closed the connection without answering. Other servers answer 400 Bad Request or log a TLS “unknown protocol” error. That is the signature doing its job: fail fast and visibly rather than parse garbage as a request.
11: CRC32C. One bit of the source address was flipped after the checksum was computed, and the strict backend dropped the connection. The checksum protects against corruption and buggy intermediaries, not attackers: anyone who can forge a header can compute a CRC.

title: The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
text:
Production configuration (not run here)

Sending side: HAProxy
# haproxy.cfg (not run here)
frontend smtp_in
    mode tcp
    bind :25
    default_backend mta

backend mta
    mode tcp
    # v2 header on every connection; add the TLVs you will actually log
    server mx1 10.0.0.2:25 send-proxy-v2 proxy-v2-options crc32c,unique-id check
send-proxy sends v1, send-proxy-v2 sends v2, and proxy-v2-options adds TLVs: ssl, cert-cn, ssl-cipher, cert-sig, cert-key, authority, crc32c and unique-id (HAProxy configuration manual, “proxy-v2-options”). By default HAProxy also sends the header on health checks when the server uses it for normal traffic, unless the check has its own port or addr; check-send-proxy forces it in that case.


Receiving side: HAProxy behind another proxy
frontend public
    bind :443 accept-proxy           # header REQUIRED on this bind line
    # or, when only some sources are proxies:
    # tcp-request connection expect-proxy layer4 if { src -f /etc/haproxy/proxies.lst }
accept-proxy on a bind line makes the header mandatory for that listener. tcp-request connection expect-proxy layer4 makes it mandatory only for the listed sources, which is the safe form of “some clients come through a proxy and some do not”: the decision is taken from the real source address, not from the bytes the client sends.


Receiving side: nginx
# nginx (not run here); requires the realip module for set_real_ip_from
server {
    listen 443 ssl proxy_protocol;    # every connection on this listener must start with a header
    set_real_ip_from 10.0.0.1;        # trust the header's address only from this proxy...
    real_ip_header   proxy_protocol;  # ...and then use it as $remote_addr
    allow 10.0.0.1;                   # ...and refuse everyone else outright
    deny  all;
}
The trap here is that set_real_ip_from does not stop anybody from sending a header. It only controls whether nginx replaces $remote_addr with it. $proxy_protocol_addr is still whatever the connecting host wrote, so anything that logs or acts on $proxy_protocol_addr directly must sit behind a firewall or allow/deny that limits the listener to the proxies. An nginx listener with proxy_protocol rejects connections that lack the header and logs “broken header”. That message is the first thing to look for when a new proxy is put in front.


Receiving side: Postfix
# main.cf (not run here)
postscreen_upstream_proxy_protocol = haproxy   # when postscreen is the listener
# or, without postscreen:
# smtpd_upstream_proxy_protocol = haproxy
Mail servers are where the PROXY protocol earns its keep, because SPF, DNSBL lookups, greylisting and rate limits all depend on the real client address. They are also where a parsing bug hurts most, because the parser runs before any authentication. Treat PROXY-protocol parsers as an exposed attack surface and keep them patched. Exim 4.100.1 (September 2026) fixed an out-of-bounds write in its PROXY protocol v1 parsing (CVE-2026-94054) and a read of uninitialised stack memory (CVE-2026-94056), both reachable when an attacker controls what arrives as the proxy header. Both are another argument for the source-address restriction in scenario 6: a parser that only trusted proxies can reach is a much smaller target.


Cloud load balancers

AWS Network Load Balancer: proxy protocol v2 is a target-group attribute. Through a VPC endpoint service the header carries a custom TLV PP2_TYPE_AWS (0xEA) whose first value byte is the subtype PP2_SUBTYPE_AWS_VPCE_ID (0x01), followed by the endpoint ID (AWS NLB documentation, “Proxy protocol”).
Other providers have similar switches and custom TLVs. Before you rely on one, check which TLV types the provider documents and test that your parser skips the types it does not know.

title: The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
text:
When not to use it

HTTP through an HTTP-aware proxy. If the proxy terminates HTTP, use Forwarded (RFC 7239) or X-Forwarded-For and strip any copies that arrive from clients. The PROXY protocol describes the TCP connection and would attribute every request on a reused upstream connection to the first client.
Direct server return or transparent proxying. If the load balancer preserves the client source address (DSR, IPVS in DR mode, NLB with client IP preservation, Linux IP_TRANSPARENT), there is nothing to restore and adding a header only adds a failure mode.
Identity. The header says where a connection came from, as claimed by a proxy you trust. It is not authentication. If the backend needs to know who the client is, use TLS client certificates (and the SSL TLV, or terminate mTLS at the backend).
UDP. v2 has UDP families, but a header on every datagram, or on the first datagram of a flow, is something sender and receiver have to agree on outside the specification. Check what your proxy actually does before you depend on it.

title: The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
text:
Gotchas

Turning it on at one end only. Enabling send-proxy-v2 before the backend accepts it breaks every connection. Enabling accept-proxy before the proxy sends it breaks them too. Roll out with a dedicated listener (a second port that requires the header), move traffic to it, then remove the old one.
Health checks. Check that health-check connections carry a header (or LOCAL) when the backend requires one, and that the backend accepts LOCAL.
Mixing proxied and direct clients on one listener. That is exactly the “guess” the specification forbids. Use two listeners, or decide by source address as in expect-proxy layer4 if { src ... }.
Trusting the header from anybody. Firewall the backend so only proxies can reach PROXY-enabled listeners. nginx’s set_real_ip_from is not a firewall.
Chained proxies. Each hop must consume the incoming header and produce a new one carrying the original client. A middle proxy that forwards bytes without parsing hands the backend two headers, and a strict backend treats the second as application data.
Server-speaks-first protocols. SMTP, FTP, IMAP and SSH servers must not send their banner before the header has been read (section 2). A backend that greets first and then reads the header times out against a proxy that waits for the banner.
TLS passthrough. With TLS passing through the proxy, the header comes before the ClientHello. The backend’s TLS stack must be told to strip it first, otherwise the first TLS record looks corrupt.
Logging the wrong field. After the header is parsed, keep logging the proxy’s address as well as the client’s. When the proxy itself misbehaves you will need to know which one it was.

title: The PROXY Protocol: Keeping the Client Address Through an L4 Proxy
text:
Exercises

Extend proxyproto.py with the IPv6 family and run scenario 2 with 2001:db8::50 as the client. Check that the address block is 36 bytes and the length field changes accordingly.
Add a backend that accepts the header from anybody but requires it. Show that the attacker can still choose an address, and write down which firewall rule fixes it.
Make the proxy in scenario 7 forward the client’s bytes without adding its own header (a non-parsing middle hop). What does the strict backend log now? What rule should a middle hop follow?
Add the 0xEA AWS TLV with a fake vpce-0123456789abcdef0 ID and teach the reader to decode it, while still skipping custom types it does not know.
Time how long the strict backend waits for a header from a client that connects and sends nothing, and add the “at least 3 seconds” timeout the specification suggests. What does a missing timeout cost you under a connection flood?
Replace the lab proxy with HAProxy on a machine where you can install it, configure send-proxy-v2 proxy-v2-options crc32c,authority, and decode the real header with proxyproto.read_header.

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
For network operators and system engineers, forward proxies are a fundamental mechanism for controlling outbound traffic, enforcing security policies, and bridging distinct network segments. Unlike reverse proxies—which sit in front of servers to perform load balancing or SSL termination—forward proxies sit in front of clients. They act as intermediaries for requests directed to external origins, providing a central point where outbound traffic can be filtered, audited, logged, or authenticated.
Understanding client-side forward proxy behavior is essential for troubleshooting connectivity failures in enterprise networks, containerized environments, and CI/CD pipelines. When an application fails to connect to an external API, the root cause often traces back to subtle differences in how client HTTP libraries handle proxy environment variables, how domain name resolution is delegated, or how HTTP CONNECT tunnels interact with TLS handshakes. A misconfiguration can lead to security risks such as credential leaks over unencrypted proxy links or privacy breaches via DNS leaks.
This chapter covers the mechanisms of client-side forward proxies. We examine plain HTTP proxying using absolute-form URLs, transport-layer tunneling using the HTTP CONNECT method, and SOCKS protocol proxying. We also analyze the environment variables standard across Unix environments (http_proxy, https_proxy, no_proxy), detailing implementation differences between common clients like curl, Python’s standard urllib, and the requests library. Note that this chapter focuses exclusively on client-side forward proxies; server-side mechanisms such as the PROXY protocol (HAProxy headers passed from load balancers to backend servers) are out of scope.

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
Learning goals

Differentiate between plain HTTP proxying (absolute-form requests), HTTP CONNECT tunneling, and SOCKS4/5 proxying.
Explain how domain name resolution differs between local client resolution and proxy-side resolution across HTTP and SOCKS protocols.
Analyze the HTTP CONNECT method, including proxy port restriction ACLs and the visibility of TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) to intermediary proxies.
Evaluate security implications of proxy authentication headers (Proxy-Authorization) and transport security (http:// vs https:// proxy endpoints).
Identify and mitigate environment variable edge cases, including HTTP_PROXY security considerations (CGI/httpoxy) and implementation inconsistencies in NO_PROXY pattern matching.
Troubleshoot forward proxy connection failures using command-line diagnostic tools and standard logging patterns.

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
Concepts and Architecture

Protocol Comparison
Client-side forward proxies operate at different layers of the network stack depending on the proxy type requested by the client.









Proxy Protocol / Mode
Name Resolution
What the Proxy Sees

None at Proxy Layer (Unless payload is encrypted)



                  +-----------------------------------+
                  |        Client Environment         |
                  |                                   |
                  |  +-----------------------------+  |
                  |  |  dns.py (127.0.0.53:53)     |  |
                  |  |  (Local Client Resolver)    |  |
                  |  +--------------^--------------+  |
                  +-----------------|-----------------+
                                    | DNS (socks5://)
                                    |
   +--------------------------------+---------------------------------+
   |                                                                  |
+--+-------+     Absolute / CONNECT / SOCKS5h      +------------------+--+
| Client   |-------------------------------------->| proxy.py            |
+----------+                                       | (127.0.0.20:3128/1080) |
                                                   +---------+--------+
                                                             |
                                                             | Proxy Resolves
                                                             | & Forwards
                                                             v
                                                   +------------------+
                                                   | origin.py        |
                                                   | (127.0.0.10:8080)|
                                                   +------------------+


Absolute-Form HTTP Requests
When an HTTP client connects directly to an origin server, it opens a TCP connection to the origin’s IP address and issues an origin-form request:
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: origin.lab:8080
When configured to use an unencrypted HTTP forward proxy for HTTP traffic, the client opens a TCP connection to the proxy server instead of the origin server. The client then issues an absolute-form request containing the complete scheme, host, port, and path, as specified in RFC 9112 section 3.2.2:
GET http://origin.lab:8080/index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: origin.lab:8080
Upon receiving an absolute-form request, the proxy: 1. Performs DNS resolution for origin.lab if necessary. 2. Opens a TCP connection to origin.lab:8080. 3. Rewrites the request line to origin-form (GET /index.html HTTP/1.1). 4. Appends or updates the Via HTTP header field (RFC 9110 section 7.6.3) to track request routing and prevent loops (e.g., Via: 1.1 labproxy). 5. Forwards the request to the origin server.
Because the client sends the destination hostname in the absolute-form URI directly to the proxy, the client does not need to perform a local DNS query.


The HTTP CONNECT Method
Plain absolute-form HTTP proxying cannot handle TLS-encrypted traffic (https://) without breaking the end-to-end security model, as the proxy would need to read and rewrite HTTP headers in cleartext. To proxy encrypted traffic or arbitrary binary protocols, HTTP clients use the CONNECT method (RFC 9110 section 9.3.6).
The CONNECT process works as follows:
Client                         Proxy                         Origin
  |                              |                             |
  |--- CONNECT origin.lab:8443 ->|                             |
  |    HTTP/1.1                  |                             |
  |                              |--- TCP Connect ------------>|
  |                              |<-- Connected ---------------|
  |<-- HTTP/1.1 200 ------------ |                             |
  |    Connection Established    |                             |
  |                              |                             |
  |================ TLS Handshake / Ciphertext ===============|
  |================ Transferred Intact via Tunnel =============|

Tunnel Request: The client connects to the proxy and sends a CONNECT request using authority-form targeting the desired destination host and port:
CONNECT origin.lab:8443 HTTP/1.1
Host: origin.lab:8443
Proxy Setup: The proxy establishes a TCP connection to origin.lab on port 8443.
Tunnel Confirmation: If the connection succeeds, the proxy returns an HTTP 2xx status code (typically 200 Connection Established).
Opaque Data Transfer: From this point forward, the proxy stops parsing HTTP data. It functions as a bi-directional TCP stream relay, forwarding raw bytes back and forth between the client and origin.


SNI Visibility and ECH
Even though payload data within a CONNECT tunnel is encrypted via TLS, standard TLS 1.3 handshakes send the Server Name Indication (SNI) extension inside the ClientHello message in cleartext. An intermediary HTTP proxy parsing initial bytes after a CONNECT 200 response can inspect the ClientHello to extract the target SNI domain name (origin.lab). Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) encrypts the SNI payload, preventing the proxy from identifying the destination hostname beyond what was requested in the CONNECT target string.


Port Restriction ACLs
Because an unrestricted CONNECT proxy can be abused as an open TCP relay to attack internal network services (such as SSH, SMTP, or database ports), production proxies enforce strict access control lists (ACLs). For example, Squid proxies restrict CONNECT targets using rules like http_access deny CONNECT !SSL_ports, limiting connections to approved ports (typically 443). If a client issues a CONNECT request for an unauthorized port (such as port 22), the proxy rejects the request with an HTTP 403 Forbidden status line, and the client aborts with a tunnel failure error.
Once the tunnel is established, the origin server receives a standard TCP connection from the proxy’s IP address. The origin server cannot inspect the HTTP headers to determine if the connection passed through a CONNECT tunnel, because no Via or forwarding headers are injected into the encrypted TLS stream.



Proxy Authentication
Proxies can enforce authentication before forwarding traffic or establishing tunnels (RFC 9110 sections 11.7.1 and 11.7.2).

Challenge: When an unauthenticated request reaches an authenticating proxy, the proxy responds with HTTP status 407 Proxy Authentication Required and includes a Proxy-Authenticate header specifying supported schemes (e.g., Basic realm="Proxy").
Credentials: The client re-issues the request, adding a Proxy-Authorization header containing credentials (e.g., Proxy-Authorization: Basic bGFiOnNlY3JldA== for RFC 7617 HTTP Basic authentication).
Consumed by the proxy: Proxy-Authorization is meant for the proxy that asked for it (RFC 9110 section 11.7.2). The proxy checks the credentials and does not pass them on; in the lab the origin’s header dump in scenario 5 contains no Proxy-Authorization.


Transport Security of Proxy Credentials
When contacting an HTTP proxy URL (http://proxy.lab:3128), proxy authentication headers are transmitted over an unencrypted TCP connection to the proxy. Anyone with network access to the path between client and proxy can capture these base64-encoded credentials.
To protect proxy credentials, modern environments use HTTPS proxies (https://proxy.lab:8443), where the client establishes a TLS session with the proxy server itself before transmitting HTTP commands or Proxy-Authorization headers. Support for secure HTTPS proxy endpoints was added in curl 7.52.0.



SOCKS Protocol and DNS Resolution (SOCKS5 vs SOCKS5h)
SOCKS (RFC 1928) operates at a lower networking layer than HTTP proxying, relaying raw TCP/UDP streams without interpreting application-layer protocols.
During a SOCKS5 handshake: 1. The client sends a version and authentication method selection message. 2. The proxy responds with the selected method (0x00 for no authentication, 0x02 for username/password as defined in RFC 1929). 3. The client sends a connection request specifying the Address Type (ATYP): - ATYP 0x01: IPv4 address (4 bytes) - ATYP 0x03: Domain name (1-byte length followed by domain string) - ATYP 0x04: IPv6 address (16 bytes)

Local vs Remote DNS Resolution
The distinction between socks5:// and socks5h:// in client configuration defines where DNS resolution occurs:

socks5:// (Local Resolution): The client resolves the origin domain name to an IP address using its local DNS resolver before communicating with the proxy. It then sends an ATYP 0x01 (IPv4) or ATYP 0x04 (IPv6) request to the SOCKS proxy.

Risk: If the destination domain is on an isolated internal network accessible only by the proxy, local resolution fails (returning NXDOMAIN). Additionally, sending local DNS queries for destination domains can cause DNS leaks, exposing intent to local network observers.

socks5h:// (Remote Resolution): The client defers domain resolution to the proxy by sending an ATYP 0x03 request containing the unresolved hostname string. The proxy resolves the name on its own network interface and establishes the TCP connection.

A similar distinction exists between socks4:// (IPv4 address only) and socks4a:// (supports domain strings).



Proxy Environment Variables
Command-line applications and standard software libraries rely on environment variables to configure proxy routing behavior dynamically:

http_proxy / HTTP_PROXY: Specifies the proxy server for plain HTTP requests.
https_proxy / HTTPS_PROXY: Specifies the proxy server for HTTPS requests (via CONNECT).
all_proxy / ALL_PROXY: Specifies a fallback proxy for all traffic schemes (commonly used for SOCKS proxies, e.g., socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080).
no_proxy / NO_PROXY: Specifies comma-separated patterns for hosts that must bypass the proxy and connect directly.


Lowercase vs Uppercase (httpoxy Security)
A security vulnerability known as httpoxy (CVE-2016-5385 family) affects Web server software running in CGI or CGI-like environments. In standard CGI specifications, incoming HTTP request headers are converted into environment variables prefixed with HTTP_. An attacker sending an HTTP header named Proxy: http://attacker.com causes the web server to set HTTP_PROXY=http://attacker.com within the execution context of the script.
If the underlying application library automatically reads HTTP_PROXY, outgoing HTTP requests made by the server application are hijacked and redirected to the attacker’s proxy.
To mitigate this risk: - curl: for plain HTTP it reads only lowercase http_proxy and ignores uppercase HTTP_PROXY, for exactly this reason. The other variables (HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY, NO_PROXY) are accepted in either case. - Python (urllib / requests): Reads uppercase HTTP_PROXY, but includes a runtime safety check: if the REQUEST_METHOD environment variable is present (indicating execution within a CGI process), Python ignores HTTP_PROXY.


NO_PROXY Implementation Inconsistencies
There is no formal RFC defining the syntax for no_proxy. As a result, parsing rules differ across HTTP implementations:

Suffix Matching: Most implementations perform suffix matching. A rule such as origin.lab matches origin.lab and subdomains such as www.origin.lab.
Leading Dots: Leading dots (e.g., .origin.lab) are supported across implementations to match subdomains, though behavior regarding the exact apex domain can vary.
Wildcards: The wildcard string * is supported as a global bypass flag by curl, urllib, and requests. However, partial domain wildcards such as *.origin.lab are not supported standard syntax in curl or standard Python libraries; they fail to match target hosts and result in requests being proxied.
IP Literals vs Hostnames: Matching is strictly string-based in most libraries. An entry of 127.0.0.10 in NO_PROXY bypasses the proxy when connecting to http://127.0.0.10:8080/, but does not bypass the proxy when connecting to http://origin.lab:8080/, even if origin.lab resolves to 127.0.0.10.
CIDR Block Support: CIDR notation (e.g., 127.0.0.0/8) is supported in curl (since version 7.86.0) and Python’s requests library (via urllib3), but is not supported by standard Python urllib.request.
Port Matching: Specifying host:port (e.g., origin.lab:8080) is supported in Python’s urllib and requests, but is unsupported in curl 8.14.1 (where port specifiers cause matching failures).




PAC Files and WPAD
In modern desktop operating systems and web browsers, proxy settings are often managed dynamically via Proxy Auto-Configuration (PAC) and Web Proxy Auto-Discovery Protocol (WPAD):

PAC Files: JavaScript files defining a function FindProxyForURL(url, host) that returns a string indicating which proxy to use (e.g., "PROXY proxy1.lab:3128; DIRECT").
WPAD Protocol: Discovers the PAC file URL automatically via DHCP Option 252 or local DNS queries targeting wpad.domain.lab.

Command-line utilities such as curl and standard runtime libraries for languages like Python, Go, and Rust do not embed JavaScript execution engines and do not process PAC files or perform WPAD resolution natively. Operating system settings relying on PAC/WPAD must be manually translated into static environment variables for command-line tool compatibility.
