#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Tiny authoritative-only DNS server on 127.0.0.53:53 for the lab.
Answers A queries from a fixed table and logs every question it receives,
so we can see which names a client resolved itself."""
import socket, struct, sys

TABLE = {"origin.lab": "127.0.0.10", "www.origin.lab": "127.0.0.10"}   # intranet.lab is NOT here

s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(("127.0.0.53", 53))
log = open(sys.argv[1], "a", buffering=1)
while True:
    q, peer = s.recvfrom(512)
    qid, flags, qd = struct.unpack("!HHH", q[:6])
    i, labels = 12, []
    while q[i]:
        labels.append(q[i + 1:i + 1 + q[i]].decode()); i += 1 + q[i]
    qtype = struct.unpack("!H", q[i + 1:i + 3])[0]
    name = ".".join(labels).lower()
    log.write(f"dns: query {name} type {qtype}\n")
    question = q[12:i + 5]
    if name in TABLE and qtype == 1:
        ans = b"\xc0\x0c" + struct.pack("!HHIH", 1, 1, 60, 4) + socket.inet_aton(TABLE[name])
        s.sendto(struct.pack("!HHHHHH", qid, 0x8180, 1, 1, 0, 0) + question + ans, peer)
    elif name in TABLE:
        s.sendto(struct.pack("!HHHHHH", qid, 0x8180, 1, 0, 0, 0) + question, peer)   # NOERROR, no data
    else:
        s.sendto(struct.pack("!HHHHHH", qid, 0x8183, 1, 0, 0, 0) + question, peer)   # NXDOMAIN

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Origin web server on 127.0.0.10: HTTP on 8080, HTTPS on 8443 (cert for
origin.lab). Logs the request line and the headers that tell us how the
request arrived."""
import http.server, ssl, sys, threading

class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        seen = {k: self.headers.get(k) for k in ("Host", "Via", "Proxy-Authorization", "X-Forwarded-For") if self.headers.get(k)}
        self.server.log.write(f"origin:{self.server.server_port}: {self.requestline!r} from {self.client_address[0]} {seen}\n")
        body = (b"via-proxy" if self.headers.get("Via") else b"direct") + b"\n"
        self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body))); self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)
    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

def serve(port, tls):
    srv = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.10", port), H)
    srv.log = open(sys.argv[1], "a", buffering=1)
    if tls:
        ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER); ctx.load_cert_chain("origin.crt", "origin.key")
        srv.socket = ctx.wrap_socket(srv.socket, server_side=True)
    srv.serve_forever()

threading.Thread(target=serve, args=(8443, True), daemon=True).start()
serve(8080, False)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""A small forward proxy that logs what it is told.

127.0.0.20:3128  HTTP proxy: absolute-form requests and CONNECT (no auth)
127.0.0.20:3129  same, but requires Proxy-Authorization: Basic (lab:secret)
127.0.0.20:1080  SOCKS5 (RFC 1928), no auth

The proxy resolves names from its own table (it sits in "another network"),
so intranet.lab resolves here even though the client's DNS has no record.
CONNECT is only allowed to ports 443 and 8443, like Squid's SSL_ports ACL.
"""
import base64, socket, struct, sys, threading

PROXY_DNS = {"origin.lab": "127.0.0.10", "www.origin.lab": "127.0.0.10", "intranet.lab": "127.0.0.10"}
CONNECT_PORTS = {443, 8443}
log = open(sys.argv[1], "a", buffering=1)

def resolve(host):
    return PROXY_DNS.get(host.lower(), host)

def pipe(a, b):
    def one(x, y):
        try:
            while (d := x.recv(65536)):
                y.sendall(d)
        except OSError:
            pass
        for s in (x, y):
            try: s.shutdown(socket.SHUT_RDWR)
            except OSError: pass
    t = threading.Thread(target=one, args=(b, a), daemon=True); t.start()
    one(a, b); t.join()

def sni(hello):
    """Server name from a TLS ClientHello (RFC 8446 4.1.2, RFC 6066 3)."""
    try:
        if hello[0] != 0x16 or hello[5] != 1:
            return None
        i = 9 + 2 + 32
        i += 1 + hello[i]                                   # session id
        i += 2 + struct.unpack("!H", hello[i:i + 2])[0]     # cipher suites
        i += 1 + hello[i]                                   # compression
        end = i + 2 + struct.unpack("!H", hello[i:i + 2])[0]; i += 2
        while i < end:
            et, el = struct.unpack("!HH", hello[i:i + 4])
            if et == 0:
                n = struct.unpack("!H", hello[i + 7:i + 9])[0]
                return hello[i + 9:i + 9 + n].decode()
            i += 4 + el
    except (IndexError, struct.error):
        return None

def read_head(c):
    data = b""
    while b"\r\n\r\n" not in data:
        d = c.recv(4096)
        if not d:
            return None, b""
        data += d
    head, rest = data.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)
    return head.decode("latin-1").split("\r\n"), rest

def http_proxy(c, need_auth, port):
    lines, rest = read_head(c)
    if not lines:
        return c.close()
    method, target, ver = lines[0].split(" ")
    hdrs = [l for l in lines[1:]]
    auth = next((l.split(":", 1)[1].strip() for l in hdrs if l.lower().startswith("proxy-authorization:")), None)
    who = ""
    if auth and auth.lower().startswith("basic "):
        who = " user=" + base64.b64decode(auth[6:]).decode().split(":")[0] + " (password visible to anyone on the path to the proxy)"
    log.write(f"proxy:{port}: {lines[0]!r}{who}\n")
    if need_auth and auth != "Basic " + base64.b64encode(b"lab:secret").decode():
        c.sendall(b'HTTP/1.1 407 Proxy Authentication Required\r\nProxy-Authenticate: Basic realm="lab"\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n')
        log.write(f"proxy:{port}: -> 407\n"); return c.close()
    if method == "CONNECT":
        host, p = target.rsplit(":", 1)
        if int(p) not in CONNECT_PORTS:
            c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n")
            log.write(f"proxy:{port}: -> 403 (CONNECT to port {p} not allowed)\n"); return c.close()
        u = socket.create_connection((resolve(host), int(p)))
        c.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established\r\n\r\n")
        first = c.recv(4096)
        log.write(f"proxy:{port}: tunnel to {host}:{p} opened; ClientHello SNI={sni(first)!r}; everything after this is opaque TLS\n")
        u.sendall(first); return pipe(c, u)
    # absolute-form: http://host[:port]/path (RFC 9112 3.2.2)
    assert target.startswith("http://"), target
    hostport, _, path = target[7:].partition("/")
    host, _, p = hostport.partition(":")
    u = socket.create_connection((resolve(host), int(p or 80)))
    keep = [l for l in hdrs if l.split(":")[0].lower() not in ("proxy-authorization", "proxy-connection", "connection")]
    req = [f"{method} /{path} {ver}"] + keep + ["Via: 1.1 labproxy", "Connection: close"]
    u.sendall(("\r\n".join(req) + "\r\n\r\n").encode() + rest)
    pipe(c, u)

def socks5(c):
    ver, n = c.recv(2); c.recv(n); c.sendall(b"\x05\x00")             # no authentication
    req = c.recv(4)
    if len(req) < 4:
        log.write("socks:1080: client sent the greeting, then closed without a CONNECT request\n")
        return c.close()
    ver, cmd, _, atyp = req
    if atyp == 1:
        host = socket.inet_ntoa(c.recv(4)); kind = "IPv4 address (client resolved the name itself)"
    elif atyp == 3:
        host = c.recv(c.recv(1)[0]).decode(); kind = "domain name (proxy resolves)"
    else:
        host = socket.inet_ntop(socket.AF_INET6, c.recv(16)); kind = "IPv6 address"
    port = struct.unpack("!H", c.recv(2))[0]
    log.write(f"socks:1080: CONNECT ATYP={atyp} {kind}: {host}:{port}\n")
    u = socket.create_connection((resolve(host), port))
    c.sendall(b"\x05\x00\x00\x01" + socket.inet_aton("127.0.0.20") + struct.pack("!H", 1080))
    pipe(c, u)

def listen(port, handler):
    l = socket.socket(); l.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    l.bind(("127.0.0.20", port)); l.listen(16)
    while True:
        c, _ = l.accept()
        threading.Thread(target=handler, args=(c,), daemon=True).start()

threading.Thread(target=listen, args=(3128, lambda c: http_proxy(c, False, 3128)), daemon=True).start()
threading.Thread(target=listen, args=(3129, lambda c: http_proxy(c, True, 3129)), daemon=True).start()
listen(1080, socks5)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fetch URL with Python's urllib and with requests, both reading the
proxy environment variables, and print what each one did."""
import sys, urllib.request
import requests

url = sys.argv[1]
for name, fetch in (("urllib", lambda: urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=3).read()),
                    ("requests", lambda: requests.get(url, timeout=3, verify="origin.crt").content)):
    try:
        print(f"{name:8s} {fetch().decode().strip()}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{name:8s} error: {type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:90]}")

#!/bin/sh
# Forward proxy lab. Run as: unshare -urnm sh lab.sh   (no root, no installs)
set -e
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
ip link set lo up
L=$(mktemp); B=$(mktemp)
# client-side name resolution: only the lab DNS server, no hosts entries
printf 'nameserver 127.0.0.53\noptions timeout:1 attempts:1\n' > /tmp/lab-resolv.conf
printf '127.0.0.1 localhost\n' > /tmp/lab-hosts
mount --bind /tmp/lab-resolv.conf /etc/resolv.conf
mount --bind /tmp/lab-hosts /etc/hosts
[ -f origin.crt ] || openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes \
  -keyout origin.key -out origin.crt -days 3650 -subj /CN=origin.lab \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:origin.lab,DNS:intranet.lab" 2>/dev/null
python3 dns.py $L & P1=$!; python3 origin.py $L & P2=$!; python3 proxy.py $L & P3=$!
sleep 0.7; : > $L     # drop start-up noise (http.server looks up its own name at bind time)
C="env -i PATH=$PATH HOME=$HOME"            # every client starts with an empty environment
show() { sleep 0.2; sed 's/^/    | /' $L; : > $L; }
cu() { # cu VAR=value... URL [curl options]: one line of curl's view, then the server logs
  rc=0; info=$($C "$@" -s -S -o $B -w 'HTTP %{http_code} %{http_connect}, connected to %{remote_ip}:%{remote_port}' 2>$B.err) || rc=$?
  echo "  curl: $info, body=$(cat $B 2>/dev/null)$( [ $rc -ne 0 ] && echo ", exit $rc: $(cat $B.err)")"
  : > $B; show
}
echo "== 1. plain HTTP through the proxy (http_proxy)"
cu http_proxy=http://127.0.0.20:3128 curl http://origin.lab:8080/a
echo "== 2. uppercase HTTP_PROXY only: curl ignores it, Python honours it"
cu HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.20:3128 curl http://origin.lab:8080/b
$C HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.20:3128 python3 pyclient.py http://origin.lab:8080/b | sed 's/^/  /'; show
echo "   ...and with REQUEST_METHOD set (a CGI environment), Python ignores HTTP_PROXY"
$C HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.20:3128 REQUEST_METHOD=GET python3 pyclient.py http://origin.lab:8080/c | sed 's/^/  /'; show
echo "== 3. HTTPS through the proxy: CONNECT, then an opaque TLS tunnel"
cu https_proxy=http://127.0.0.20:3128 curl --cacert origin.crt https://origin.lab:8443/d
echo "== 4. CONNECT to a port outside the allow-list"
cu https_proxy=http://127.0.0.20:3128 curl https://origin.lab:22/
echo "== 5. proxy authentication (Basic)"
cu http_proxy=http://127.0.0.20:3129 curl http://origin.lab:8080/e
cu http_proxy=http://lab:secret@127.0.0.20:3129 curl http://origin.lab:8080/f
echo "== 6. SOCKS5: who resolves the name? (socks5:// vs socks5h://)"
for scheme in socks5 socks5h; do
  echo "-- $scheme://, origin.lab (in the client's DNS)"
  cu ALL_PROXY=$scheme://127.0.0.20:1080 curl http://origin.lab:8080/g
  echo "-- $scheme://, intranet.lab (only the proxy can resolve it)"
  cu ALL_PROXY=$scheme://127.0.0.20:1080 curl http://intranet.lab:8080/h
done
echo "== 7. no_proxy matching: direct or proxied? (curl, urllib, requests)"
printf '   %-16s %-28s %-10s %-10s %-10s\n' no_proxy URL curl urllib requests
for np in origin.lab .origin.lab '*.origin.lab' 127.0.0.10 127.0.0.0/8 origin.lab:8080 '*'; do
  for u in http://origin.lab:8080/ http://www.origin.lab:8080/ http://127.0.0.10:8080/; do
    c=$($C http_proxy=http://127.0.0.20:3128 no_proxy="$np" curl -s $u)
    py=$($C http_proxy=http://127.0.0.20:3128 no_proxy="$np" python3 pyclient.py $u | awk '{print $2}' | tr '\n' ' ')
    printf '   %-16s %-28s %-10s %-10s %-10s\n' "$np" "$u" "$c" $py
  done
done
: > $L
kill $P1 $P2 $P3 2>/dev/null || true
rm -f $L $B $B.err

   127.0.0.0/8      http://www.origin.lab:8080/  via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   127.0.0.0/8      http://127.0.0.10:8080/      direct     via-proxy  direct    
   origin.lab:8080  http://origin.lab:8080/      via-proxy  direct     direct    
   origin.lab:8080  http://www.origin.lab:8080/  via-proxy  direct     direct    
   origin.lab:8080  http://127.0.0.10:8080/      via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   *                http://origin.lab:8080/      direct     direct     direct    
   *                http://www.origin.lab:8080/  direct     direct     direct    
   *                http://127.0.0.10:8080/      direct     direct     direct

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
Reading the output

Scenario 1: Plain HTTP Through the Proxy
In Scenario 1, curl executes an HTTP request with http_proxy=http://127.0.0.20:3128:
== 1. plain HTTP through the proxy (http_proxy)
  curl: HTTP 200 000, connected to 127.0.0.20:3128, body=via-proxy
    | proxy:3128: 'GET http://origin.lab:8080/a HTTP/1.1'
    | origin:8080: 'GET /a HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8080', 'Via': '1.1 labproxy'}

curl connects to the proxy address 127.0.0.20:3128 rather than resolving origin.lab.
Notice that no DNS log entries (dns: query...) appear in the trace for this scenario. curl relies on the proxy to resolve the target destination.
curl issues an absolute-form request line to the proxy: GET http://origin.lab:8080/a HTTP/1.1.
The proxy rewrites the request to origin-form (GET /a HTTP/1.1), injects the header 'Via': '1.1 labproxy', and forwards the request to origin.py.
origin.py detects the Via header and returns body=via-proxy.



Scenario 2: Uppercase HTTP_PROXY and CGI Environment Detection
Scenario 2 evaluates client behaviors when only uppercase HTTP_PROXY is defined:
== 2. uppercase HTTP_PROXY only: curl ignores it, Python honours it
  curl: HTTP 200 000, connected to 127.0.0.10:8080, body=direct
    | dns: query origin.lab type 1
    | dns: query origin.lab type 28
    | origin:8080: 'GET /b HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8080'}
  urllib   via-proxy
  requests via-proxy
    | proxy:3128: 'GET http://origin.lab:8080/b HTTP/1.1'
    | origin:8080: 'GET /b HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8080', 'Via': '1.1 labproxy'}
    | proxy:3128: 'GET http://origin.lab:8080/b HTTP/1.1'
    | origin:8080: 'GET /b HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8080', 'Via': '1.1 labproxy'}
   ...and with REQUEST_METHOD set (a CGI environment), Python ignores HTTP_PROXY
  urllib   direct
  requests direct
    | dns: query origin.lab type 1
    | dns: query origin.lab type 28
    | origin:8080: 'GET /c HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8080'}
    | dns: query origin.lab type 1
    | dns: query origin.lab type 28
    | origin:8080: 'GET /c HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8080'}

curl completely ignores HTTP_PROXY. It performs local DNS queries for origin.lab (type 1 for IPv4 A, type 28 for IPv6 AAAA) via dns.py (127.0.0.53) and connects directly to 127.0.0.10:8080, receiving body=direct.
Python’s urllib and requests honor uppercase HTTP_PROXY by default, routing the request through proxy.py:3128 (returning via-proxy).
When REQUEST_METHOD=GET is set in the process environment (simulating a CGI environment susceptible to httpoxy), both urllib and requests detect the CGI variable, disable HTTP_PROXY processing, perform local DNS resolution, and connect directly to the origin.



Scenario 3: HTTPS Through Proxy via CONNECT Tunnel
Scenario 3 tests encrypted TLS tunneling using https_proxy:
== 3. HTTPS through the proxy: CONNECT, then an opaque TLS tunnel
  curl: HTTP 200 200, connected to 127.0.0.20:3128, body=direct
    | proxy:3128: 'CONNECT origin.lab:8443 HTTP/1.1'
    | proxy:3128: tunnel to origin.lab:8443 opened; ClientHello SNI='origin.lab'; everything after this is opaque TLS
    | origin:8443: 'GET /d HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8443'}

curl issues a CONNECT origin.lab:8443 HTTP/1.1 request to the proxy on port 3128.
The proxy opens a TCP connection to 127.0.0.10:8443 and responds to curl with HTTP 200 Connection Established.
curl initiates the TLS handshake through the tunnel. proxy.py inspects the initial byte payload, logs the cleartext SNI value (origin.lab), and relays the encrypted stream.
origin.py receives the decrypted TLS stream. Because CONNECT tunnels prevent proxy header injection, no Via header is present. origin.py returns body=direct.



Scenario 4: CONNECT ACL Port Restrictions
Scenario 4 attempts a CONNECT tunnel to port 22:
== 4. CONNECT to a port outside the allow-list
  curl: HTTP 000 403, connected to :-1, body=, exit 56: curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403
    | proxy:3128: 'CONNECT origin.lab:22 HTTP/1.1'
    | proxy:3128: -> 403 (CONNECT to port 22 not allowed)

curl requests a tunnel to origin.lab:22.
proxy.py checks its port ACL, rejects port 22, and returns HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden.
curl catches the 403 status from the proxy, aborts the request, and exits with error code 56 (CURLE_RECV_ERROR, reported as CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403).



Scenario 5: Proxy Authentication
Scenario 5 tests basic authentication challenges on port 3129:
== 5. proxy authentication (Basic)
  curl: HTTP 407 000, connected to 127.0.0.20:3129, body=
    | proxy:3129: 'GET http://origin.lab:8080/e HTTP/1.1'
    | proxy:3129: -> 407
  curl: HTTP 200 000, connected to 127.0.0.20:3129, body=via-proxy
    | proxy:3129: 'GET http://origin.lab:8080/f HTTP/1.1' user=lab (password visible to anyone on the path to the proxy)
    | origin:8080: 'GET /f HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8080', 'Via': '1.1 labproxy'}

The initial request without credentials triggers an HTTP/1.1 407 Proxy Authentication Required response from proxy.py.
Re-running curl with proxy credentials (http://lab:secret@127.0.0.20:3129) succeeds.
proxy.py logs the authenticated user (user=lab). Because the proxy URL is http://, the Proxy-Authorization: Basic bGFiOnNlY3JldA== header was sent unencrypted over the network to the proxy.
The proxy strips Proxy-Authorization before forwarding to origin.py. origin.py sees only standard HTTP headers and the Via proxy tag.



Scenario 6: SOCKS5 vs SOCKS5h DNS Resolution
Scenario 6 contrasts client-side vs proxy-side name resolution:
== 6. SOCKS5: who resolves the name? (socks5:// vs socks5h://)
-- socks5://, origin.lab (in the client's DNS)
  curl: HTTP 200 000, connected to 127.0.0.20:1080, body=direct
    | dns: query origin.lab type 1
    | dns: query origin.lab type 28
    | socks:1080: CONNECT ATYP=1 IPv4 address (client resolved the name itself): 127.0.0.10:8080
    | origin:8080: 'GET /g HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8080'}
-- socks5://, intranet.lab (only the proxy can resolve it)
  curl: HTTP 000 000, connected to :-1, body=, exit 97: curl: (97) Could not resolve proxy: 127.0.0.20
    | dns: query intranet.lab type 1
    | dns: query intranet.lab type 28
    | socks:1080: client sent the greeting, then closed without a CONNECT request
-- socks5h://, origin.lab (in the client's DNS)
  curl: HTTP 200 000, connected to 127.0.0.20:1080, body=direct
    | socks:1080: CONNECT ATYP=3 domain name (proxy resolves): origin.lab:8080
    | origin:8080: 'GET /g HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'origin.lab:8080'}
-- socks5h://, intranet.lab (only the proxy can resolve it)
  curl: HTTP 200 000, connected to 127.0.0.20:1080, body=direct
    | socks:1080: CONNECT ATYP=3 domain name (proxy resolves): intranet.lab:8080
    | origin:8080: 'GET /h HTTP/1.1' from 127.0.0.1 {'Host': 'intranet.lab:8080'}

With --proxy socks5://... and the URL http://origin.lab:8080/, curl performs local DNS lookups for origin.lab, resolves 127.0.0.10, and sends a SOCKS5 request with ATYP=1 (IPv4).
With socks5:// and the URL http://intranet.lab:8080/, curl attempts local DNS queries for intranet.lab. Because dns.py does not know intranet.lab, the local lookup returns NXDOMAIN. curl fails and exits with error code 97.

Misleading error message: curl 8.14.1 prints Could not resolve proxy: 127.0.0.20, although the proxy address is an IP literal and never needed resolving. The DNS log shows what really failed: the client’s own lookup of intranet.lab. The proxy log confirms that curl sent the SOCKS greeting and then hung up without a CONNECT request.

With socks5h://, curl makes no local DNS query for either name. It sends a SOCKS5 request with ATYP=3 (domain string). proxy.py resolves intranet.lab using its internal mapping, establishing a successful connection.



Scenario 7: NO_PROXY Matching Matrix Analysis
Scenario 7 evaluates no_proxy rules across curl, urllib, and requests:
== 7. no_proxy matching: direct or proxied? (curl, urllib, requests)
   no_proxy         URL                          curl       urllib     requests  
   origin.lab       http://origin.lab:8080/      direct     direct     direct    
   origin.lab       http://www.origin.lab:8080/  direct     direct     direct    
   origin.lab       http://127.0.0.10:8080/      via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   .origin.lab      http://origin.lab:8080/      direct     direct     direct    
   .origin.lab      http://www.origin.lab:8080/  direct     direct     direct    
   .origin.lab      http://127.0.0.10:8080/      via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   *.origin.lab     http://origin.lab:8080/      via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   *.origin.lab     http://www.origin.lab:8080/  via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   *.origin.lab     http://127.0.0.10:8080/      via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   127.0.0.10       http://origin.lab:8080/      via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   127.0.0.10       http://www.origin.lab:8080/  via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   127.0.0.10       http://127.0.0.10:8080/      direct     direct     direct    
   127.0.0.0/8      http://origin.lab:8080/      via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   127.0.0.0/8      http://www.origin.lab:8080/  via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   127.0.0.0/8      http://127.0.0.10:8080/      direct     via-proxy  direct    
   origin.lab:8080  http://origin.lab:8080/      via-proxy  direct     direct    
   origin.lab:8080  http://www.origin.lab:8080/  via-proxy  direct     direct    
   origin.lab:8080  http://127.0.0.10:8080/      via-proxy  via-proxy  via-proxy 
   *                http://origin.lab:8080/      direct     direct     direct    
   *                http://www.origin.lab:8080/  direct     direct     direct    
   *                http://127.0.0.10:8080/      direct     direct     direct    
Key takeaways from the test matrix:

Domain Suffix Matching (origin.lab, .origin.lab): All three clients match domain suffixes consistently. Setting no_proxy=origin.lab or no_proxy=.origin.lab bypasses the proxy for both origin.lab and www.origin.lab.
IP Matching vs Hostname Matching (127.0.0.10): If no_proxy=127.0.0.10, requests to http://127.0.0.10:8080/ go direct. However, requests to http://origin.lab:8080/ go via-proxy across all clients. Matching is strictly string-based; clients do not resolve origin.lab to check if its IP matches NO_PROXY.
Wildcard Prefixes (*.origin.lab): Glob wildcard prefixes fail across all clients. When no_proxy=*.origin.lab, all requests go via-proxy. Wildcard globs are invalid syntax in standard NO_PROXY parsing implementations.
CIDR Notation (127.0.0.0/8): When targeting http://127.0.0.10:8080/, curl and requests evaluate the CIDR range and go direct. Python’s urllib fails to parse CIDR notation, treating it as a literal string mismatch, and routes the request via-proxy.
Port Specificity (origin.lab:8080): Python’s urllib and requests parse host-port combinations in NO_PROXY, successfully routing requests to origin.lab:8080 direct. curl 8.14.1 does not support port specifiers in no_proxy; it fails to match origin.lab:8080 and routes the request via-proxy.
Catch-All Wildcard (*): Setting no_proxy=* acts as a universal bypass flag across all three implementations.

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
In production

Squid Configuration (Production HTTP/CONNECT Proxy)
The snippet below demonstrates a minimal production /etc/squid/squid.conf restricting CONNECT tunnels to SSL ports and setting up Basic authentication.
# (not run here)
# Define target ACL ports
acl SSL_ports port 443 8443
acl Safe_ports port 80 8080 443 8443

# Deny requests to unsafe ports
http_access deny !Safe_ports

# Deny CONNECT requests to non-SSL ports
http_access deny CONNECT !SSL_ports

# Configure Basic Authentication
auth_param basic program /usr/lib/squid/basic_ncsa_auth /etc/squid/passwords
auth_param basic realm Production Forward Proxy
acl authenticated_users proxy_auth REQUIRED

# Allow authenticated users
http_access allow authenticated_users
http_access deny all

# Listen on port 3128
http_port 3128


Dante Configuration (Production SOCKS5 Proxy)
The configuration below demonstrates a basic Dante /etc/sockd.conf server configuration enforcing remote DNS resolution and authenticated client access.
# (not run here)
logoutput: /var/log/sockd.log
internal: 10.0.0.1 port = 1080
external: eth0

socksmethod: username

user.privileged: root
user.unprivileged: sockd

client pass {
    from: 10.0.0.0/8 to: 0.0.0.0/0
    log: connect disconnect error
}

socks pass {
    from: 10.0.0.0/8 to: 0.0.0.0/0
    command: bind connect udpassociate
    log: connect disconnect error
}


SSH Dynamic Port Forwarding (On-Demand SOCKS5)
Engineers can create an ad-hoc local SOCKS5 proxy routed through a remote SSH jump host:
# (not run here)
# Establish local SOCKS5 proxy on port 1080 via remote-bastion
ssh -ND 1080 user@remote-bastion.example.com

# Route application traffic through the SSH SOCKS5 proxy using remote DNS
curl --proxy socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 https://internal.service.local/


System Configuration Integrations
Different system tools require specific configurations to respect forward proxies:

Git Client Configuration
# (not run here)
# Set global HTTP and HTTPS proxy
git config --global http.proxy http://proxy.example.com:3128
git config --global https.proxy http://proxy.example.com:3128

# Set SOCKS5h proxy for Git over HTTP/HTTPS
git config --global http.proxy socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080


APT Package Manager (/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/80proxy)
// (not run here)
Acquire::http::Proxy "http://proxy.example.com:3128/";
Acquire::https::Proxy "http://proxy.example.com:3128/";


Systemd Service Environment (/etc/systemd/system/my-service.service.d/override.conf)
# (not run here)
[Service]
Environment="http_proxy=http://proxy.example.com:3128"
Environment="https_proxy=http://proxy.example.com:3128"
Environment="no_proxy=localhost,127.0.0.1,.internal.example.com"


Docker Daemon Proxy Configuration (/etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/http-proxy.conf)
# (not run here)
[Service]
Environment="HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:3128"
Environment="HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:3128"
Environment="NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,docker-registry.example.com"

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
Operational notes

Long-Lived Connections (WebSockets & gRPC): HTTP CONNECT tunnels support persistent bi-directional protocols like WebSockets and gRPC. However, network operators must ensure intermediary proxy idle timeouts (timeout tunnel in HAProxy or read_timeout in NGINX) are tuned appropriately or TCP keepalives are enabled to prevent silent session termination.
Proxy Idle Timeouts: Intermediary proxies enforce read/write idle timeouts on inactive TCP connections. Applications utilizing long-lived HTTP/1.1 connections or TCP tunnels must transmit periodic application-layer pings or transport keepalives to prevent proxies from dropping idle sockets.
Proxy Visibility Limits:

For plain HTTP, the proxy can inspect full URLs, request headers, query parameters, and payload bodies.
For HTTPS via CONNECT, the proxy can inspect only the destination target IP/port and cleartext TLS SNI domain names during setup. Payload content and path parameters remain end-to-end encrypted.

TLS Interception Proxies (SSL Bumping): Forward proxies configured to perform deep packet inspection (DPI) on HTTPS traffic break the TLS connection by acting as a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM). The proxy terminates TLS with the client using a dynamically generated certificate signed by a custom internal Certificate Authority (CA).

Operational Impact: Clients must install the internal proxy CA root into their system and runtime trust stores. TLS interception breaks applications that pin certificates or ship their own CA bundle (many language runtimes and container images do).

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
Gotchas

DNS Leaks via socks5://: Configuring socks5:// instead of socks5h:// causes clients to resolve domain names using local DNS. This can leak private internal hostnames to local DNS servers and fail when resolving internal-only domain names.
Invalid NO_PROXY Wildcards: Placing wildcard domain patterns like *.example.com in no_proxy fails across curl, urllib, and requests. Standard implementations treat the asterisk as a literal character, causing bypass rules to fail. Use domain suffixes (e.g., .example.com or example.com) instead.
Case Sensitivity in http_proxy: curl ignores uppercase HTTP_PROXY to mitigate httpoxy security risks. Scripts relying only on uppercase HTTP_PROXY work in Python but go direct under curl. Use lowercase http_proxy, which every client reads; for the other variables, setting both cases is harmless.
CIDR Incompatibility in Python urllib: Standard Python urllib.request does not support CIDR ranges (such as 192.168.0.0/16) in NO_PROXY. It evaluates CIDR entries as literal string comparisons, causing connections to bypass rules and route through the proxy.
Hostname vs IP Mismatch in NO_PROXY: NO_PROXY string matching does not perform DNS resolution. If NO_PROXY contains 10.0.0.5, connecting to http://10.0.0.5 bypasses the proxy, but connecting to http://internal.lab (which resolves to 10.0.0.5) routes through the proxy.
Port Specifiers in curl no_proxy: Adding port numbers to no_proxy entries (e.g., example.com:8080) works in Python libraries but fails in curl, causing curl to ignore the rule and forward requests through the proxy.
Unencrypted Proxy Credentials: Passing proxy credentials in an http:// proxy URL (http://user:pass@proxy:3128) transmits credentials in base64-encoded cleartext. Protecting them needs an https:// proxy URL (TLS to the proxy itself), supported by curl since 7.52.0.
Silent change of route under CGI: Running Python HTTP applications in CGI environments automatically disables uppercase HTTP_PROXY processing. If environment configuration relies solely on uppercase HTTP_PROXY, outgoing requests switch from proxied to direct connections without warning.

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
Exercises

Fix a SOCKS DNS Leak: Configure curl to fetch an internal domain through a SOCKS5 proxy on 127.0.0.1:1080. Compare packet captures or DNS server logs when running curl --proxy socks5://... vs curl --proxy socks5h://.... Verify which mode emits local DNS queries.
Audit Application NO_PROXY Behavior: Write a test script in Python using urllib and requests to query an internal IP endpoint. Test NO_PROXY set to 127.0.0.0/8 vs 127.0.0.10. Document which client library correctly bypasses the proxy under each setting.
Inspect HTTP CONNECT SNI Leaks: Run tcpdump or tshark on a local interface while making an HTTPS request through an unencrypted CONNECT proxy (curl --proxy http://127.0.0.1:3128 https://example.com). Extract the TLS ClientHello packet from the capture and locate the cleartext SNI hostname extension.
Simulate httpoxy Environment Safeguards: Create a Python script using urllib.request that prints whether it routes a request through a proxy defined in HTTP_PROXY. Execute the script normally, then execute it with REQUEST_METHOD=GET python script.py. Observe and explain the change in proxy routing behavior.
Configure Strict Squid Port Restrictions: Modify a local Squid proxy configuration to allow CONNECT requests only to port 443. Attempt to issue a curl --proxy HTTPS request to origin port 8443. Analyze the HTTP response status code and curl exit code returned.

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
Verification
The tests and output documented in this chapter were executed in an isolated Linux environment.

Executed in Lab:

Rootless Linux network namespace execution (unshare -urnm).
Python-based local DNS server (dns.py) listening on 127.0.0.53:53.
Python-based dual HTTP/HTTPS origin server (origin.py) listening on 127.0.0.10:8080 and 127.0.0.10:8443.
Python-based proxy server (proxy.py) implementing HTTP absolute-form proxying, HTTPS CONNECT tunneling, HTTP Basic authentication, and SOCKS5 handling across ports 3128, 3129, and 1080.
Execution of curl (8.14.1) and Python client harnesses (urllib, requests 2.34.2) across 7 scenario suites.

Not Run (Production Reference Examples):

External Squid (squid.conf), Dante (sockd.conf), SSH daemon (ssh -ND), APT, Git, systemd, and Docker daemon proxy configuration blocks under the “In production” section are included for reference.

title: Forward Proxies: HTTP CONNECT, SOCKS5 and the Proxy Environment Variables
text:
Sources

RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics (Sections 7.6.3 Via, 9.3.6 CONNECT, 11.7 Proxy Authentication). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1 (Section 3.2.2 absolute-form). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html
RFC 1928: SOCKS Protocol Version 5. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1928.html
RFC 1929: Username/Password Authentication for SOCKS V5. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1929.html
RFC 7617: The ‘Basic’ HTTP Authentication Scheme. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617.html
curl Manual Page: ENVIRONMENT and --noproxy documentation. https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html
Everything curl: Proxy usage and protocol documentation. https://everything.curl.dev/usingcurl/proxies
Python urllib.request Documentation: Environment variable handling. https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.request.html

title: Workbook Guide and Learning Paths
text:
Workbook Guide and Learning Paths
This workbook is a collection of experiments, not a requirement to install every network operating system. Start with the concepts and exercises that match your current knowledge and lab environment. Each path below moves from foundations toward more complex failures; repeat a prerequisite whenever its evidence is unclear. The book is vendor-neutral: platform-specific commands are examples of a concept, and their defaults and supported features must be checked on the chosen version.

title: Workbook Guide and Learning Paths
text:
Before every lab
Read the topology, addressing, software prerequisites and cleanup instructions. Predict the expected path and outcome, capture a baseline, introduce one fault at a time, then verify the repair. Record device versions, timestamps, the observation point, route or VLAN state, counter deltas and the result in both directions. Treat simulated output or a written procedure as a hypothesis until you run it on the stated platform. Some exercises require licensed or separately obtained images; the individual chapter identifies these requirements.
Linux namespace labs can run without network-device images when the host permits unprivileged user/network namespaces and has the listed kernel features and tools. They alter only the isolated lab namespace when run exactly as instructed; do not copy their firewall, DHCP or interface commands into the host namespace. Containerlab and multi-NOS exercises need their specified images and a working container runtime. Hardware, wireless and managed-switch exercises require appropriate equipment or feature-capable simulation.

title: Workbook Guide and Learning Paths
text:
Foundation path



Order
Learn and practice
Evidence to retain




1
IPv4 addressing and address planning
Prefix, range, overlap and summary checks


2
Ethernet and frames, then access VLAN membership
Port VLAN table, ARP behavior and restored connectivity


3
Tagged trunk failure
Affected VLAN, unaffected control VLAN and both trunk memberships


4
IP forwarding and return path
Forward and reverse routes, loss and recovery


5
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery
Route, neighbor state, filter counter and recovery


6
DHCPv4 exchange
Message types and transaction correlation; distinguish the teaching code from a production lease


7
Stateful filtering, source NAT and destination NAT
Policy counters, observed original/translated addresses and return path



The namespace-based examples above were run on the writing host as documented in their chapters. Kernel, tool and permission differences can change the result; check the prerequisites and record your own observations.

title: Workbook Guide and Learning Paths
text:
Switching and campus path
Study VLANs and trunks, spanning-tree elections and link aggregation. Then build the workbook’s VLAN, spanning tree, aggregation and Linux LACP member failure, inter-VLAN and DHCP, and first-hop redundancy labs. Extend the campus project with the failure-domain matrix.
Checkpoint: for a chosen VLAN, identify the access port, trunk membership, active spanning-tree path, virtual gateway owner and route to the destination. Explain what changes when an uplink, gateway or access switch fails. Verify software support and exact topology before assuming a guard or redundancy behavior from another implementation.

title: Workbook Guide and Learning Paths
text:
Routing and policy path
Begin with static routes and the policy-table lookup exercise and VRF overlap and fallback. Continue through single-area OSPF, areas and BFD, IS-IS, eBGP or eBGP with GoBGP followed by import policy, route reflectors and BGP policy. For advanced troubleshooting, use OSPF adjacency diagnostics, redistribution design, route tags and MED, prepend and ECMP, and ECMP real flows.
Checkpoint: given a prefix, identify its origin, advertisement, import decision, eligible paths, selected RIB route, forwarding next hop and return path. Explain why a full adjacency or established session does not prove that a particular route is usable. Compare behavior against the actual NOS and version rather than a universal preference table.

title: Workbook Guide and Learning Paths
text:
Services, security and operations path
Use DHCP relay diagnostics, MTU and MSS, IPv6 operations, IPv6 first-hop security, QoS queues, and API conditional updates. Add ACL and NAT, uRPF, control-plane ACL, NTP and syslog and DSCP and delay where supported.
Checkpoint: correlate a client symptom with an observation at the access edge, control plane and destination; distinguish an address-configuration failure from DNS, routing, firewall and application failures. For every proposed change, name the trust boundary, expected counter and rollback condition.

title: Workbook Guide and Learning Paths
text:
Advanced overlay and integration path
After underlay routing works, progress through VXLAN bridge, EVPN/VXLAN, GRE, VRF-lite and the dual-home project. Use multicast distribution and its failure exercises when the design needs multicast. Validate underlay next-hop reachability, encapsulation MTU, overlay control-plane state and tenant forwarding separately.
The paths are learning aids, not a guarantee of complete certification coverage. Consult the current objectives for the specific certification and platform, and practice any platform-specific tasks using their current documentation.

title: Lab Host and the Image Set
text:
Lab Host and the Image Set
This part is the hands-on track for the lab machine that already has Arista cEOS, Nokia SR Linux, and FRR loaded. The earlier chapters teach the same protocols on free images. Here the point is to see one behaviour in three command languages, on hardware you can actually start.

title: Lab Host and the Image Set
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Reach the lab host and see which images are loaded
Stay inside the memory budget of a 4-vCPU, 15 GB machine
Deploy and destroy a Containerlab topology without leaving it running
Push a config into cEOS, SR Linux, and FRR after the node is actually ready

cEOS is not a free image. This book does not tell you how to download it and does not ship the image. The labs assume the tag is already present, which it is on this host.

Reach the host

title: Lab Host and the Image Set
text:
Push a config
Wait, then send the CLI. Example for a lab named forward:
until docker exec clab-forward-r-ceos Cli -c "show hostname" >/dev/null 2>&1
do sleep 5; done

docker exec clab-forward-r-ceos Cli -p 15 -c "
enable
configure terminal
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.12.2/30
end
write memory
"
SR Linux, one candidate commit:
docker exec -i clab-forward-r-srl sr_cli <<'EOF'
enter candidate
set interface ethernet-1/1 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/1 subinterface 0 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/1 subinterface 0 ipv4 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/1 subinterface 0 ipv4 address 10.1.13.2/30
commit now
quit
EOF
If a set path is rejected, stop and tab-complete that leaf on this image. The SR Linux tag is latest. The command shape is stable. A leaf name can move.
FRR takes a startup-config file. The frr kind writes it to frr.conf and starts the daemons you list. zebra always starts.
r-frr:
  kind: frr
  image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  startup-config: r-frr.frr.conf
  daemons: [ospfd]

Kind defaults used in every lab
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:

    nokia_srlinux:
      image: ghcr.io/nokia/srlinux:latest
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
Data interfaces are eth1, eth2, and so on in the topology file for cEOS and FRR. Inside EOS those are Ethernet1, Ethernet2. Inside SR Linux the topology name ethernet-1/1 is the port. eth0 is management on all three. Do not put a lab prefix on eth0.
Link addresses on a cEOS ipv4: field make Containerlab configure no switchport and the address after boot. Use that only on routed labs. A VLAN lab must not set ipv4 on a switchport.

title: Lab Host and the Image Set
text:
What this track covers
The spread matches the work of an associate-level track and a professional-level track: switching, IPv4 and IPv6, first hop, OSPF, IS-IS, BGP, policy, ACLs, NAT, DHCP, VXLAN, EVPN, and a management API. Later chapters add path MTU, STP edge guards, DHCP snooping, MLAG, VRF-lite, stub areas, redistribution, MED, policy routing, uRPF, SPAN, GRE, a control-plane ACL, SLAAC, NTP, and delay. It is not an exam blueprint, and it does not use exam question banks.

title: Lab Host and the Image Set
text:
Rule for every later chapter

One lab directory under /data/labs.
containerlab deploy -t topology.clab.yml from that directory.
Wait until the CLI answers.
Check the table in the chapter before you call the lab done.
containerlab destroy -t topology.clab.yml --cleanup before the next lab.

None of the labs in this part were left running on the host. The topologies match Containerlab 0.83 and the image tags above. Boot them yourself and keep the show output.

title: Three-Router Forwarding
text:
Three-Router Forwarding
One IPv4 triangle, three operating systems. Each router has a loopback. OSPF is not in this lab. Static routes are, so a missing route is your fault and not a protocol’s.

title: Three-Router Forwarding
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Wire FRR, cEOS, and SR Linux in one Containerlab file
Put an IPv4 address on the data interface in each CLI
Install the one static route each router needs for the far loopback
Prove the path with ping sourced from the loopback

title: Three-Router Forwarding
text:
Addressing



Node
Loopback
eth1
eth2




r-frr
10.0.0.1/32
10.1.12.1/30 to r-ceos
10.1.13.1/30 to r-srl


r-ceos
10.0.0.2/32
10.1.12.2/30 to r-frr
10.1.23.1/30 to r-srl


r-srl
10.0.0.3/32
10.1.13.2/30 to r-frr
10.1.23.2/30 to r-ceos

title: Three-Router Forwarding
text:
Topology
name: forward
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    nokia_srlinux:
      image: ghcr.io/nokia/srlinux:latest
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    r-frr:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-frr.frr.conf
      daemons: [staticd]
    r-ceos:
      kind: arista_ceos
    r-srl:
      kind: nokia_srlinux
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r-frr:eth1", "r-ceos:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r-frr:eth2", "r-srl:ethernet-1/1"]
    - endpoints: ["r-ceos:eth2", "r-srl:ethernet-1/2"]
r-frr.frr.conf:
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.0.0.1/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.1.12.1/30
!
interface eth2
 ip address 10.1.13.1/30
!
ip route 10.0.0.2/32 10.1.12.2
ip route 10.0.0.3/32 10.1.13.2
!

title: Three-Router Forwarding
text:
cEOS
interface Loopback0
   ip address 10.0.0.2/32
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.12.2/30
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.23.1/30
ip route 10.0.0.1/32 10.1.12.1
ip route 10.0.0.3/32 10.1.23.2

title: Three-Router Forwarding
text:
SR Linux
enter candidate
set interface ethernet-1/1 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/1 subinterface 0 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/1 subinterface 0 ipv4 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/1 subinterface 0 ipv4 address 10.1.13.2/30
set interface ethernet-1/2 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/2 subinterface 0 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/2 subinterface 0 ipv4 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/2 subinterface 0 ipv4 address 10.1.23.2/30
set interface lo0 admin-state enable
set interface lo0 subinterface 0 admin-state enable
set interface lo0 subinterface 0 ipv4 admin-state enable
set interface lo0 subinterface 0 ipv4 address 10.0.0.3/32
set network-instance default type default
set network-instance default admin-state enable
set network-instance default interface ethernet-1/1.0
set network-instance default interface ethernet-1/2.0
set network-instance default interface lo0.0
set network-instance default static-routes route 10.0.0.1/32 admin-state enable
set network-instance default static-routes route 10.0.0.1/32 next-hop-group to-frr
set network-instance default next-hop-groups group to-frr admin-state enable
set network-instance default next-hop-groups group to-frr nexthop 1 ip-address 10.1.13.1
set network-instance default next-hop-groups group to-frr nexthop 1 admin-state enable
set network-instance default static-routes route 10.0.0.2/32 admin-state enable
set network-instance default static-routes route 10.0.0.2/32 next-hop-group to-ceos
set network-instance default next-hop-groups group to-ceos admin-state enable
set network-instance default next-hop-groups group to-ceos nexthop 1 ip-address 10.1.23.1
set network-instance default next-hop-groups group to-ceos nexthop 1 admin-state enable

title: Three-Router Forwarding
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-forward-r-frr vtysh -c "ping 10.0.0.2 source 10.0.0.1"
docker exec clab-forward-r-frr vtysh -c "ping 10.0.0.3 source 10.0.0.1"
docker exec clab-forward-r-ceos Cli -c "ping 10.0.0.1 source 10.0.0.2"
docker exec clab-forward-r-srl sr_cli "ping 10.0.0.1 network-instance default -I 10.0.0.3"
The SR Linux ping flag may be -I or a source leaf. Read the help on the node if the flag is refused.

Predict

Each loopback answers only after the static route exists. Connected pings succeed first.
A ping from r-frr to 10.0.0.2 leaves via 10.1.12.2. It does not hairpin through r-srl.
Shutting r-ceos Ethernet2 does not break r-frr to r-ceos. It does break r-srl to 10.0.0.2.

title: Three-Router Forwarding
text:
Drill
Delete the static route for 10.0.0.3 on r-frr. Ping 10.0.0.3 and confirm the failure. Put the route back. Then shut r-ceos Ethernet2 and confirm which pings die.

title: cEOS Interfaces and LLDP
text:
cEOS Interfaces and LLDP
Before VLANs, learn the port names. Containerlab’s eth1 is EOS Ethernet1. LLDP is how you prove the cable you think you built is the cable the switch sees.

title: cEOS Interfaces and LLDP
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Map eth names to EOS and SR Linux names
Read LLDP neighbours on cEOS and SR Linux
Tell a management port from a data port
Explain why an interface can be up in Linux and down in the NOS

title: cEOS Interfaces and LLDP
text:
Topology
Two nodes and one link are enough. Reuse the kind block from the lab host chapter.
name: lldp
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    nokia_srlinux:
      image: ghcr.io/nokia/srlinux:latest
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    srl:
      kind: nokia_srlinux
  links:
    - endpoints: ["sw:eth1", "srl:ethernet-1/1"]

title: cEOS Interfaces and LLDP
text:
Config
cEOS, after Cli answers:
interface Ethernet1
   description to-srl
   no shutdown
lldp run
SR Linux:
enter candidate
set system lldp admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/1 admin-state enable
set interface ethernet-1/1 description to-ceos
commit now
Leave the port as a switchport on cEOS. LLDP does not need an IP address.

title: cEOS Interfaces and LLDP
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-lldp-sw Cli -c "show lldp neighbors"
docker exec clab-lldp-sw Cli -c "show interfaces Ethernet1 status"
docker exec clab-lldp-srl sr_cli "show system lldp neighbor"
containerlab inspect interfaces -t topology.clab.yml

Predict

show lldp neighbors on cEOS names the SR Linux chassis on Ethernet1.
Ethernet1 is connected. Management0 has the Docker address and is not in the LLDP table for this link.
show interfaces Ethernet2 is down. Nothing is cabled there.

title: cEOS Interfaces and LLDP
text:
Drill
Add a second link, sw:eth2 to srl:ethernet-1/2, deploy with --reconfigure only if you destroyed the lab first, and confirm LLDP shows two neighbours. Then shut Ethernet2 and watch that neighbour disappear within one LLDP hold time.

title: VLANs and Trunks on cEOS
text:
VLANs and Trunks on cEOS
Two switches, two VLANs, one trunk. Hosts in the same VLAN ping. Hosts in different VLANs do not, because nothing here routes.

title: VLANs and Trunks on cEOS
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Create VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on cEOS
Set an access port and a trunk
See a tag with tcpdump on the trunk
Show that a missing allowed VLAN is a blackhole, not a routing problem

title: VLANs and Trunks on cEOS
text:
Addressing



Host
Switch port
VLAN
Address




h1
sw1 Ethernet1
10
172.16.10.11/24


h2
sw1 Ethernet2
20
172.16.20.11/24


h3
sw2 Ethernet1
10
172.16.10.12/24


h4
sw2 Ethernet2
20
172.16.20.12/24



The trunk is sw1 Ethernet3 to sw2 Ethernet3. No IP on the switches.

title: VLANs and Trunks on cEOS
text:
Topology
name: vlan
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw1:
      kind: arista_ceos
    sw2:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.20.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    h3:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.12/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    h4:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.20.12/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sw1:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "sw1:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["h3:eth1", "sw2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h4:eth1", "sw2:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["sw1:eth3", "sw2:eth3"]
Do not put ipv4 on these links. That would turn the ports into routed ports.

title: VLANs and Trunks on cEOS
text:
Both switches
vlan 10
   name users
vlan 20
   name servers
interface Ethernet1
   switchport mode access
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Ethernet2
   switchport mode access
   switchport access vlan 20
interface Ethernet3
   switchport mode trunk
   switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
On sw2, Ethernet1 is still VLAN 10 and Ethernet2 is still VLAN 20. The trunk is the same list on both ends.

title: VLANs and Trunks on cEOS
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-vlan-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.10.12
docker exec clab-vlan-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.20.11
docker exec clab-vlan-sw1 Cli -c "show vlan"
docker exec clab-vlan-sw1 Cli -c "show interfaces trunk"
Capture on the trunk from the host namespace if you want the tag:
containerlab inspect interfaces -t topology.clab.yml
Find the veth for sw1 Ethernet3 and run tcpdump -eni <veth> vlan on the lab host. VLAN 10 frames between h1 and h3 carry tag 10.

Predict

h1 reaches h3. h2 reaches h4.
h1 does not reach h2. There is no SVI and no router.
Remove VLAN 20 from sw2’s allowed list. h2 stops reaching h4. h1 still reaches h3.

title: VLANs and Trunks on cEOS
text:
Drill
Change sw2 Ethernet2 to VLAN 10 by mistake. h2 and h4 stop talking, and h2 starts seeing h1’s subnet. Put it back. Then remove VLAN 10 from the trunk and write down which pings fail.

title: Spanning Tree on cEOS
text:
Spanning Tree on cEOS
Three switches and three links are a loop. Rapid PVST picks a root and blocks one port. This lab makes that choice obvious, then moves the root on purpose.

title: Spanning Tree on cEOS
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Turn on rapid PVST and set a root
Read root, designated, and alternate ports
Predict which link blocks when all costs are equal
Move the root and watch the blocked port move

title: Spanning Tree on cEOS
text:
Topology
name: stp
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw1:
      kind: arista_ceos
    sw2:
      kind: arista_ceos
    sw3:
      kind: arista_ceos
  links:
    - endpoints: ["sw1:eth1", "sw2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["sw1:eth2", "sw3:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["sw2:eth2", "sw3:eth2"]
Three cEOS nodes is the heavy lab on this host. Destroy anything else first.

title: Spanning Tree on cEOS
text:
All three switches
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
vlan 10
   name users
interface Ethernet1
   switchport mode access
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Ethernet2
   switchport mode access
   switchport access vlan 10
Access mode is enough. The VLAN is the same on every port, so the triangle is one broadcast domain. On sw1 only:
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096

title: Spanning Tree on cEOS
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-stp-sw1 Cli -c "show spanning-tree vlan 10"
docker exec clab-stp-sw2 Cli -c "show spanning-tree vlan 10"
docker exec clab-stp-sw3 Cli -c "show spanning-tree vlan 10"

Predict

sw1 is root. Its bridge id contains priority 4096.
sw1’s Ethernet1 and Ethernet2 are designated forwarding.
Either sw2 Ethernet2 or sw3 Ethernet2 is alternate discarding. The other is designated or a root port. Write down which one blocked. With equal costs the tie break is the bridge id, so it is stable across reboots of this topology.

title: Spanning Tree on cEOS
text:
Drill
Set sw2’s VLAN 10 priority to 0 and sw1 back to the default 32768. The root moves to sw2. The blocked port is no longer the same link. Put sw1 back at 4096 before you destroy the lab, so the next run matches this chapter.
Do not add a fourth switch on this host.

title: Link Aggregation on cEOS
text:
Link Aggregation on cEOS
Two physical links, one port-channel, LACP on both ends. The host still has one VLAN. Pulling one member must not move that VLAN to down.

title: Link Aggregation on cEOS
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Build a port-channel with LACP active mode
Put the port-channel in a VLAN and leave the members out of VLAN config
Read which members are collecting and distributing
Shut one member and keep the VLAN up

title: Link Aggregation on cEOS
text:
Topology
name: lag
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw1:
      kind: arista_ceos
    sw2:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.12/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sw1:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "sw2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["sw1:eth2", "sw2:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["sw1:eth3", "sw2:eth3"]

title: Link Aggregation on cEOS
text:
Both switches
vlan 10
   name users
interface Ethernet1
   switchport mode access
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Ethernet2
   channel-group 1 mode active
interface Ethernet3
   channel-group 1 mode active
interface Port-Channel1
   switchport mode access
   switchport access vlan 10
mode active sends LACP. mode on would bundle without negotiation and is the wrong default for this lab. Do not also set a VLAN on Ethernet2. The port-channel owns the switchport config.

title: Link Aggregation on cEOS
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-lag-sw1 Cli -c "show port-channel"
docker exec clab-lag-sw1 Cli -c "show lacp neighbor"
docker exec clab-lag-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.10.12

Predict

Port-Channel1 is up with two members.
h1 pings h2.
interface Ethernet2 then shutdown on sw1. The port-channel stays up on one member. The ping still works.
Shut Ethernet3 as well. The ping stops.

title: Link Aggregation on cEOS
text:
Drill
Change sw2 Ethernet3 to mode passive. The bundle still forms, because active plus passive negotiates. Change both ends of Ethernet3 to mode on while Ethernet2 stays active. That member will not join. Put both ends back to active and confirm two members again.

title: Inter-VLAN Routing and DHCP
text:
Inter-VLAN Routing and DHCP
The VLAN lab stopped at layer 2. This one adds switched virtual interfaces so VLAN 10 can reach VLAN 20, then turns the same switch into the DHCP server for VLAN 10.

title: Inter-VLAN Routing and DHCP
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Route between two VLANs on one cEOS switch
Point a host default at the SVI
Serve DHCP for one VLAN from EOS
See that a host with no route still cannot leave its subnet

title: Inter-VLAN Routing and DHCP
text:
Topology
One cEOS switch and three Alpine hosts. h1 and h3 are VLAN 10. h2 is VLAN 20. h3 starts with no address and asks DHCP.
name: svi
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.10.1
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.20.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.20.1
    h3:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sw:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "sw:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["h3:eth1", "sw:eth3"]

title: Inter-VLAN Routing and DHCP
text:
Switch
vlan 10
   name users
vlan 20
   name servers
interface Ethernet1
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Ethernet2
   switchport access vlan 20
interface Ethernet3
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Vlan10
   ip address 172.16.10.1/24
interface Vlan20
   ip address 172.16.20.1/24
ip routing
ip dhcp server
ip dhcp pool USERS
   network 172.16.10.0/24
   range 172.16.10.50 172.16.10.80
   default-gateway 172.16.10.1
   lease 0 0 10
ip routing is required. Without it the SVIs exist and do not forward.
On h3, after the switch is configured:
docker exec clab-svi-h3 udhcpc -i eth1 -n -q
docker exec clab-svi-h3 ip addr show eth1

title: Inter-VLAN Routing and DHCP
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-svi-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.20.11
docker exec clab-svi-sw Cli -c "show ip route"
docker exec clab-svi-sw Cli -c "show ip dhcp binding"

Predict

h1 reaches h2 through the switch. The first hop is 172.16.10.1.
h3 has an address inside 172.16.10.50–80 and a default route.
Remove ip routing. The SVIs stay up and the ping between VLANs fails. Put it back.

title: Inter-VLAN Routing and DHCP
text:
Drill
Add a static host route nowhere: on h1, ip route del default. The ping to h2 fails. The ping to 172.16.10.12, if you give h3 a moment, still works if you ping inside the VLAN. Restore the default.

title: First Hop: VRRP and VARP
text:
First Hop: VRRP and VARP
Two distribution switches, one virtual IP. VRRP elects a master. VARP does not elect anyone. Both are on cEOS. This lab runs VRRP first, because that is the protocol the earlier first-hop chapter used, then shows VARP as the anycast form you will see on an EOS leaf.

title: First Hop: VRRP and VARP
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Build one VLAN across two cEOS switches with a host attached
Configure VRRP so sw1 is master
Fail the master and watch the virtual IP move
Replace the election with VARP and explain what you gave up

title: First Hop: VRRP and VARP
text:
Topology
name: fhrp
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw1:
      kind: arista_ceos
    sw2:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip link add br0 type bridge
        - ip link set eth1 master br0
        - ip link set eth2 master br0
        - ip link set br0 up
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev br0
        - ip route add default via 172.16.10.254
  links:
    - endpoints: ["sw1:eth1", "sw2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sw1:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth2", "sw2:eth2"]
h1 has two links. A bridge on the host makes both ports one LAN, so the virtual IP is reachable whichever switch is answering.

title: First Hop: VRRP and VARP
text:
VRRP
On both switches:
vlan 10
   name users
interface Ethernet1
   switchport mode trunk
   switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
interface Ethernet2
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Vlan10
   ip address 172.16.10.2/24
ip routing
sw2 uses 172.16.10.3/24 on Vlan10. Then sw1:
interface Vlan10
   vrrp 10 ipv4 172.16.10.254
   vrrp 10 priority-level 110
sw2, same virtual address, priority-level 100.

title: First Hop: VRRP and VARP
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-fhrp-sw1 Cli -c "show vrrp"
docker exec clab-fhrp-sw2 Cli -c "show vrrp"
docker exec clab-fhrp-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.10.254

Predict

sw1 is master. sw2 is backup.
Shut Vlan10 on sw1. sw2 becomes master. The ping to .254 returns after a short gap. h1’s route does not change.
No shut on Vlan10. sw1 preempts because its priority is higher.

title: First Hop: VRRP and VARP
text:
VARP, after VRRP works
Remove the vrrp lines. On both switches:
ip virtual-router mac-address 00:1c:73:00:00:0a
interface Vlan10
   ip virtual-router address 172.16.10.254
There is no master. Both switches answer for .254 using the shared MAC. Shutting one SVI still leaves .254 on the other, without an election. You lose the single-owner property. You gain a gateway that does not wait for hellos. Write down which behaviour you want on a campus distribution pair and which you want on a leaf pair that already has ECMP underneath.

title: Static Routes across Three NOSes
text:
Static Routes across Three NOSes
The forwarding chapter used loopbacks and two statics each. This chapter adds a host LAN behind each router and a default on the host, which is the shape you actually operate.
Use the same triangle as Three-Router Forwarding. Add one Alpine host on a third data port of each router.

title: Static Routes across Three NOSes
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Number a LAN on FRR, cEOS, and SR Linux
Point each host at its router
Install the two remote LAN routes on each router
Find which static is missing when one direction fails

title: Static Routes across Three NOSes
text:
Prefixes



Router
LAN
Host




r-frr eth3
172.16.1.1/24
h-frr 172.16.1.10 via .1


r-ceos Ethernet3
172.16.2.1/24
h-ceos 172.16.2.10 via .1


r-srl ethernet-1/3
172.16.3.1/24
h-srl 172.16.3.10 via .1



Transit links stay 10.1.12.0/30, 10.1.13.0/30, and 10.1.23.0/30.
Each router needs a static for the two LANs it does not own. r-frr:
ip route 172.16.2.0/24 10.1.12.2
ip route 172.16.3.0/24 10.1.13.2
r-ceos uses EOS syntax (ip route 172.16.1.0/24 10.1.12.1). r-srl uses a next-hop-group per prefix, the same shape as the forwarding chapter.
cEOS Ethernet3 is no switchport before the address. SR Linux must bind ethernet-1/3.0 into network-instance default.

title: Static Routes across Three NOSes
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-static-h-frr ping -c 2 172.16.2.10
docker exec clab-static-h-frr ping -c 2 172.16.3.10
docker exec clab-static-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip route"

Predict

h-frr reaches both remote hosts.
Delete only 172.16.3.0/24 on r-ceos. h-frr still reaches h-srl if the path is r-frr to r-srl direct. h-ceos stops reaching h-srl.
A missing host default looks like a router failure and is not. Check ip route on the host first.

title: Static Routes across Three NOSes
text:
Drill
Add a floating static on r-frr for 172.16.2.0/24 via r-srl (10.1.13.2) with distance 50, and keep the primary via r-ceos at distance 1. Shut r-ceos Ethernet1. The LAN moves to the long path. Confirm with traceroute from h-frr.

title: OSPF in One Area
text:
OSPF in One Area
Take the triangle from Three-Router Forwarding and delete the static routes. OSPF area 0 replaces them. Loopbacks are the prefixes you want to see in every table.

title: OSPF in One Area
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Start OSPF on FRR, cEOS, and SR Linux on the same links
Recognize a Full adjacency on each CLI
See the remote loopback as an OSPF route
Tell a dead adjacency from a missing network statement

title: OSPF in One Area
text:
FRR
daemons: [ospfd] on the node. In frr.conf, keep the interface addresses and replace the static routes with:
router ospf
 ospf router-id 10.0.0.1
 network 10.1.12.0/30 area 0
 network 10.1.13.0/30 area 0
 network 10.0.0.1/32 area 0

title: OSPF in One Area
text:
cEOS
interface Loopback0
   ip address 10.0.0.2/32
   ip ospf area 0.0.0.0
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.12.2/30
   ip ospf area 0.0.0.0
   ip ospf network point-to-point
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.23.1/30
   ip ospf area 0.0.0.0
   ip ospf network point-to-point
router ospf 1
   router-id 10.0.0.2

title: OSPF in One Area
text:
SR Linux
Put the interface addresses in as in the forwarding chapter, including lo0 10.0.0.3/32. Then:
set network-instance default protocols ospf admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 version ospf-v2
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 router-id 10.0.0.3
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 area 0.0.0.0 admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet-1/1.0 admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet-1/1.0 interface-type point-to-point
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet-1/2.0 admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet-1/2.0 interface-type point-to-point
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 area 0.0.0.0 interface lo0.0 admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols ospf instance 1 area 0.0.0.0 interface lo0.0 passive true

title: OSPF in One Area
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-ospf-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec clab-ospf-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec clab-ospf-r-srl sr_cli "show network-instance default protocols ospf neighbor"
docker exec clab-ospf-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip route ospf"

Predict

Two Full neighbours on every router.
10.0.0.2/32 and 10.0.0.3/32 are OSPF routes on r-frr.
A missing ip ospf area on one cEOS interface leaves that link with no adjacency and the rest of the triangle up.

title: OSPF in One Area
text:
Drill
Set ip ospf cost 50 on r-ceos Ethernet1. The path from r-frr to 10.0.0.2 may stay direct because the other way is two links. The path from r-frr to a prefix that can use either side will prefer the cheaper side. Record the route before and after.

title: OSPF Areas, Cost, and BFD
text:
OSPF Areas, Cost, and BFD
Area 0 is the triangle’s left link. Area 1 is the right link. The cEOS router is the ABR. BFD on the area 0 link is the failure detector. You are not trying to build a large OSPF domain. You are trying to see an ABR and a fast hello in the table.

title: OSPF Areas, Cost, and BFD
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Put two areas on one cEOS router
See a type-3 inter-area route on FRR
Raise a cost and watch the route stay, because there is no alternate area 0 path
Turn on BFD and read the session

title: OSPF Areas, Cost, and BFD
text:
Links



Link
Prefix
Area




r-frr eth1 — r-ceos Ethernet1
10.1.12.0/30
0


r-ceos Ethernet2 — r-srl ethernet-1/1
10.1.23.0/30
1



Loopbacks: 10.0.0.1 on FRR in area 0, 10.0.0.2 on cEOS in area 0, 10.0.0.3 on SR Linux in area 1.
There is no r-frr to r-srl link in this lab. One path is the point.

title: OSPF Areas, Cost, and BFD
text:
cEOS ABR
interface Loopback0
   ip address 10.0.0.2/32
   ip ospf area 0.0.0.0
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.12.2/30
   ip ospf area 0.0.0.0
   ip ospf network point-to-point
   ip ospf cost 10
   bfd interval 300 min-rx 300 multiplier 3
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.23.1/30
   ip ospf area 0.0.0.1
   ip ospf network point-to-point
router ospf 1
   router-id 10.0.0.2
   bfd all-interfaces
If bfd all-interfaces is refused, set BFD under the Ethernet1 OSPF interface only. Check show bfd peers.
FRR side of the same link, in frr.conf, with daemons: [ospfd, bfdd]:
interface eth1
 ip address 10.1.12.1/30
 ip ospf area 0
 ip ospf network point-to-point
 ip ospf bfd
SR Linux stays in area 0.0.0.1 on ethernet-1/1.0. Copy the single-area OSPF block and change the area id. Do not enable BFD on SR Linux until the EOS and FRR session is up. Add it only if info from state bfd on this image shows a peer. The lab is done when EOS and FRR show a BFD up session. SR Linux in area 1 without BFD is still a valid ABR lab.

title: OSPF Areas, Cost, and BFD
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-areas-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec clab-areas-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip route ospf"
docker exec clab-areas-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec clab-areas-r-ceos Cli -c "show bfd peers"

Predict

r-frr has one neighbour, the ABR.
10.0.0.3/32 on r-frr is an inter-area route, not intra-area.
Changing the area 0 cost changes the metric of every area 1 prefix on r-frr. There is no other path to switch to.

title: OSPF Areas, Cost, and BFD
text:
Drill
Put SR Linux’s loopback in area 0 by mistake (advertise it from cEOS Loopback0’s area, or set the SR Linux interface to area 0 while the ABR interface stays in area 1). The adjacency on that link drops or never forms. Put the area ids back until both neighbours are Full.

title: IS-IS across FRR and cEOS
text:
IS-IS across FRR and cEOS
IS-IS is the other link-state IGP you will meet in a professional design. This lab is two routers and one link so the NET, the level, and the adjacency are the whole story. SR Linux can join as a third node once the pair is up.

title: IS-IS across FRR and cEOS
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Assign an ISO NET on FRR and on cEOS
Form a level-2 point-to-point adjacency
Advertise a loopback without a network statement
Read the difference between an OSPF area and an IS-IS level

title: IS-IS across FRR and cEOS
text:
Topology
name: isis
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    r-frr:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-frr.frr.conf
      daemons: [isisd]
    r-ceos:
      kind: arista_ceos
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r-frr:eth1", "r-ceos:eth1"]

title: IS-IS across FRR and cEOS
text:
FRR
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.0.0.1/32
 ip router isis CORE
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.1.0.1/30
 ip router isis CORE
 isis network point-to-point
!
router isis CORE
 is-type level-2-only
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
!

title: IS-IS across FRR and cEOS
text:
cEOS
interface Loopback0
   ip address 10.0.0.2/32
   isis enable CORE
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.0.2/30
   isis enable CORE
   isis network point-to-point
router isis CORE
   net 49.0001.0000.0000.0002.00
   is-type level-2
Both NETs share area 49.0001. The system id is the unique part. A duplicated system id will not form a healthy adjacency.

title: IS-IS across FRR and cEOS
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-isis-r-frr vtysh -c "show isis neighbor"
docker exec clab-isis-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip route isis"
docker exec clab-isis-r-ceos Cli -c "show isis neighbors"

Predict

One adjacency, level 2, point-to-point.
Each loopback is in the other router’s IS-IS table.
Changing FRR to is-type level-1 while cEOS stays level-2 drops the adjacency. Matching levels brings it back.

title: IS-IS across FRR and cEOS
text:
SR Linux, optional third
Add r-srl on 10.1.0.4/30 only after the pair is up, on a new link, with NET 49.0001.0000.0000.0003.00 and level 2. The instance path is under network-instance default protocols isis. Tab-complete net and level-capability on this image. If the leaf names differ, the FRR and cEOS pair is still the lab.

title: eBGP between Three Autonomous Systems
text:
eBGP between Three Autonomous Systems
Each corner of the triangle is its own autonomous system and originates one LAN. No router is allowed to become transit for a prefix it does not own unless you decide it should. That decision is the next chapter. This one is reachability only.

title: eBGP between Three Autonomous Systems
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Number three private ASNs and three LANs
Bring up eBGP on FRR, cEOS, and SR Linux
See a prefix with a two-AS path
Spot a session stuck in Active because the neighbour address is wrong

title: eBGP between Three Autonomous Systems
text:
Plan



Node
ASN
LAN
Router-id




r-frr
65001
172.16.1.0/24 on lo as 172.16.1.1/32
10.0.0.1


r-ceos
65002
172.16.2.1/32
10.0.0.2


r-srl
65003
172.16.3.1/32
10.0.0.3



Transit links are the same /30s as the forwarding triangle. Use loopbacks as the originated prefixes so you do not need hosts yet.

title: eBGP between Three Autonomous Systems
text:
FRR
daemons: [bgpd]
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.0.0.1
 neighbor 10.1.12.2 remote-as 65002
 neighbor 10.1.13.2 remote-as 65003
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 172.16.1.1/32
The loopback must exist or network will not advertise it.

title: eBGP between Three Autonomous Systems
text:
cEOS
interface Loopback0
   ip address 172.16.2.1/32
router bgp 65002
   router-id 10.0.0.2
   neighbor 10.1.12.1 remote-as 65001
   neighbor 10.1.23.2 remote-as 65003
   network 172.16.2.1/32
Ethernet addresses stay no switchport as in the forwarding lab. BGP does not turn a switchport into a routed port for you.

title: eBGP between Three Autonomous Systems
text:
SR Linux
After the interfaces and network-instance default exist:
set routing-policy policy accept-all default-action policy-result accept
set network-instance default protocols bgp admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols bgp autonomous-system 65003
set network-instance default protocols bgp router-id 10.0.0.3
set network-instance default protocols bgp afi-safi ipv4-unicast admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols bgp group ebgp admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols bgp group ebgp export-policy [ accept-all ]
set network-instance default protocols bgp group ebgp import-policy [ accept-all ]
set network-instance default protocols bgp neighbor 10.1.13.1 peer-as 65001
set network-instance default protocols bgp neighbor 10.1.13.1 peer-group ebgp
set network-instance default protocols bgp neighbor 10.1.13.1 admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols bgp neighbor 10.1.23.1 peer-as 65002
set network-instance default protocols bgp neighbor 10.1.23.1 peer-group ebgp
set network-instance default protocols bgp neighbor 10.1.23.1 admin-state enable
set network-instance default protocols bgp afi-safi ipv4-unicast ipv4-unicast admin-state enable
Originate 172.16.3.1/32 from the loopback. On this image the leaf may be under the ipv4-unicast family as a route or under a local-rib export. If network is not a leaf, add a static route to the loopback prefix and an export policy that matches it. The session itself is the part that must be Established before you fight origination.

title: eBGP between Three Autonomous Systems
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-ebgp-r-frr vtysh -c "show bgp summary"
docker exec clab-ebgp-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip bgp"
docker exec clab-ebgp-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip bgp summary"
docker exec clab-ebgp-r-srl sr_cli "show network-instance default protocols bgp neighbor"

Predict

Two Established sessions on each router.
172.16.2.1/32 on r-frr has AS path 65002.
172.16.2.1/32 on r-srl may arrive via 65001 65002 and via 65002. Two paths means the triangle is transitive. That is normal eBGP. The policy chapter is where you stop one of them.

title: eBGP between Three Autonomous Systems
text:
Drill
Set r-ceos’s neighbour toward r-frr to remote-as 65009. The session goes Active or Idle. The other session stays up. Fix the ASN.

title: iBGP and a Route Reflector
text:
iBGP and a Route Reflector
One autonomous system. Two FRR clients. One cEOS reflector. The clients do not peer with each other. A prefix learned by the reflector from client A must reach client B, which is the rule a full mesh would have covered and a reflector covers with less sessions.

title: iBGP and a Route Reflector
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Build two iBGP sessions to a reflector and none between clients
Advertise a distinct loopback from each client
See the reflector’s cluster list on the far client
Break the lab by forgetting next-hop-self, and fix it

title: iBGP and a Route Reflector
text:
Topology
name: rr
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    rr:
      kind: arista_ceos
    client-a:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: client-a.frr.conf
      daemons: [bgpd]
    client-b:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: client-b.frr.conf
      daemons: [bgpd]
  links:
    - endpoints: ["rr:eth1", "client-a:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["rr:eth2", "client-b:eth1"]









Node
Link address
Loopback
BGP




rr
10.1.1.1/30 and 10.1.2.1/30
10.0.0.1/32
AS 65000, route-reflector-client on both neighbours


client-a
10.1.1.2/30
10.0.0.2/32 and prefix 172.16.10.1/32
AS 65000


client-b
10.1.2.2/30
10.0.0.3/32 and prefix 172.16.20.1/32
AS 65000
