The sessions peer on the physical /30. A missing IGP does not take the session down. Each client originates a loopback that is connected on lo. next-hop-self on the reflector rewrites the next hop to the reflector’s interface address, which both clients already have as a connected route.

title: iBGP and a Route Reflector
text:
cEOS reflector
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.1.1/30
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.2.1/30
router bgp 65000
   router-id 10.0.0.1
   neighbor 10.1.1.2 remote-as 65000
   neighbor 10.1.1.2 route-reflector-client
   neighbor 10.1.1.2 next-hop-self
   neighbor 10.1.2.2 remote-as 65000
   neighbor 10.1.2.2 route-reflector-client
   neighbor 10.1.2.2 next-hop-self

title: iBGP and a Route Reflector
text:
FRR client A
client-a.frr.conf:
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.0.0.2/32
 ip address 172.16.10.1/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.1.1.2/30
!
router bgp 65000
 bgp router-id 10.0.0.2
 neighbor 10.1.1.1 remote-as 65000
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 172.16.10.1/32
 exit-address-family
!
client-b.frr.conf is the same shape: lo is 10.0.0.3/32 and 172.16.20.1/32, eth1 is 10.1.2.2/30, the neighbour is 10.1.2.1, and the network statement is 172.16.20.1/32. The address you network has to exist on lo or BGP will not originate it.

title: iBGP and a Route Reflector
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-rr-client-b vtysh -c "show ip bgp 172.16.10.1/32"
docker exec clab-rr-rr Cli -c "show ip bgp summary"

Predict

client-b has 172.16.10.1/32. The next hop is 10.1.2.1 because of next-hop-self.
The path shows the reflector as the point it was reflected. show ip bgp on FRR includes the cluster list.
Remove route-reflector-client on both neighbours. client-b loses the prefix. The sessions stay Established. Put the knob back.

title: iBGP and a Route Reflector
text:
Drill
Peer a third FRR client the same way and originate 172.16.30.1/32. You add one session, not a new mesh. That is the operational reason the reflector exists. Remove it before you leave the lab so the host is not holding three FRR nodes plus cEOS overnight.

title: BGP Policy
text:
BGP Policy
The eBGP triangle accepts every prefix on every session. This chapter keeps the triangle and adds three controls: a prefix-list that drops a leak, a local preference that picks an exit, and a community that tells the far AS not to readvertise.
Use the eBGP lab’s ASNs and links, shown in its topology diagram. Originate one extra prefix on r-frr, 203.0.113.0/24, which is documentation space and stands in for a prefix you do not own.

title: BGP Policy
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Drop a prefix on the way into cEOS
Prefer one exit with local preference on FRR
Tag a prefix with no-export and watch it stop at the next AS
Read the policy and the route, not just the session state

title: BGP Policy
text:
cEOS, inbound filter toward FRR
ip prefix-list FROM-FRR seq 10 deny 203.0.113.0/24
ip prefix-list FROM-FRR seq 20 permit 0.0.0.0/0 le 32
router bgp 65002
   neighbor 10.1.12.1 prefix-list FROM-FRR in
203.0.113.0/24 must be on an interface or a static on r-frr or BGP will not originate it. A blackhole static is enough:
ip route 203.0.113.0/24 Null0
router bgp 65001
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 203.0.113.0/24

title: BGP Policy
section: FRR, prefer the direct cEOS exit
text:
FRR, prefer the direct cEOS exit
You have two ways to reach 172.16.2.1/32: direct from 65002, and via 65003. Set local preference on the cEOS neighbour:
route-map PREFER-CEOS permit 10
 set local-preference 200
router bgp 65001
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  neighbor 10.1.12.2 route-map PREFER-CEOS in

title: BGP Policy
text:
no-export
On r-ceos, toward r-srl only, attach the well-known community to its own LAN:
route-map TAG-NO-EXPORT permit 10
   match ip address prefix-list OWN
   set community no-export
ip prefix-list OWN seq 10 permit 172.16.2.1/32
router bgp 65002
   neighbor 10.1.23.2 route-map TAG-NO-EXPORT out
   neighbor 10.1.23.2 send-community
r-srl may install the prefix. r-srl must not send it on to r-frr. Confirm on r-frr that the only path for 172.16.2.1/32 is the direct session, not 65003 65002.

title: BGP Policy
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-ebgp-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip bgp 203.0.113.0/24"
docker exec clab-ebgp-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip bgp 172.16.2.1/32"
docker exec clab-ebgp-r-srl sr_cli "show network-instance default route-table ipv4-unicast prefix 172.16.2.1/32"

Predict

cEOS has no path for 203.0.113.0/24.
FRR’s best path to 172.16.2.1/32 has local preference 200 and neighbour 10.1.12.2.
After no-export, r-frr does not learn 172.16.2.1/32 from r-srl.

title: BGP Policy
text:
Drill
Change the prefix-list to permit 203.0.113.0/24 and deny everything else by deleting sequence 20. You just blackholed the legitimate LAN. Put sequence 20 back. Write one sentence on why a prefix-list without a later permit is a lockout.

title: ACLs and Edge NAT
text:
ACLs and Edge NAT
Two small labs. The first is an ACL on the cEOS switch that already routes between VLANs. The second is source NAT on a Linux node in front of one server. They teach different tools. Do not run them as one topology.

title: ACLs and Edge NAT
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Write an extended ACL that denies one host and permits the rest
Apply it inbound on an SVI and prove the direction
Masquerade a LAN behind one address on a Linux gateway
Undo both without locking yourself out of management

title: ACLs and Edge NAT
text:
Lab A — ACL
Reuse Inter-VLAN Routing and its topology. h1 is 172.16.10.11. h2 is 172.16.20.11. Add:
ip access-list BLOCK-H1
   10 deny ip host 172.16.10.11 host 172.16.20.11
   20 permit ip any any
interface Vlan10
   ip access-group BLOCK-H1 in
Management0 is not in VLAN 10. The ACL cannot cut your CLI session. That is deliberate. An ACL on the management interface is how people lock a lab.
docker exec clab-svi-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.20.11
docker exec clab-svi-sw Cli -c "show ip access-lists BLOCK-H1"
The ping fails and the deny counter moves. A second host in VLAN 10, if you add one at .12, still reaches h2 because the permit matches.

Drill
Move the ACL to Vlan10 out. The counter stops moving and the ping works, because traffic from h1 arrives inbound on Vlan10. Put it back to in.

title: ACLs and Edge NAT
text:
Lab B — NAT
name: nat
topology:
  nodes:
    gw:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iptables
        - sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.1/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip addr add 203.0.113.1/24 dev eth2
        - ip link set eth2 up
        - iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth2 -j MASQUERADE
    inside:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.10.1
    outside:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 203.0.113.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["inside:eth1", "gw:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["gw:eth2", "outside:eth1"]
apk needs a path to the internet from the management interface while the container starts. If apk fails, the image has no iptables and the lab stops there. Do not invent a second NAT tool.
docker exec clab-nat-inside ping -c 2 203.0.113.10
docker exec clab-nat-gw iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -v

Predict

The ping works.
On outside, a tcpdump -ni eth1 icmp shows the echo request from 203.0.113.1, not from 172.16.10.10.
Delete the MASQUERADE rule. The ping fails because outside has no route back to 172.16.10.0/24. Add the rule again.

title: IPv6 on the Same Triangle
text:
IPv6 on the Same Triangle
Same three routers as the forwarding lab. IPv6 only, so a missing ipv6 line cannot hide behind a working IPv4 ping.

title: IPv6 on the Same Triangle
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Address a /127 point-to-point and a /128 loopback
Forward IPv6 on FRR and on cEOS
Install one static IPv6 route on each
Ping a loopback with an explicit source

title: IPv6 on the Same Triangle
text:
Plan








Node
Loopback
Toward the next router




r-frr
2001:db8:0::1/128
2001:db8:12::0/127 to cEOS, 2001:db8:13::0/127 to SR Linux


r-ceos
2001:db8:0::2/128
2001:db8:12::1/127 and 2001:db8:23::0/127


r-srl
2001:db8:0::3/128
2001:db8:13::1/127 and 2001:db8:23::1/127



A /127 has two addresses, ::0 and ::1. Use them as written.

title: IPv6 on the Same Triangle
text:
FRR
interface lo
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:0::1/128
!
interface eth1
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::/127
!
interface eth2
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:13::/127
!
ipv6 route 2001:db8:0::2/128 2001:db8:12::1
ipv6 route 2001:db8:0::3/128 2001:db8:13::1
2001:db8:12::/127 is the same as 2001:db8:12::0/127.

title: IPv6 on the Same Triangle
text:
cEOS
ipv6 unicast-routing
interface Loopback0
   ipv6 address 2001:db8:0::2/128
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::1/127
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ipv6 address 2001:db8:23::/127
ipv6 route 2001:db8:0::1/128 2001:db8:12::
ipv6 route 2001:db8:0::3/128 2001:db8:23::1
Without ipv6 unicast-routing the addresses exist and the router does not forward.

title: IPv6 on the Same Triangle
text:
SR Linux
Enable ipv6 admin-state on each subinterface and add the address beside the IPv4 block from the forwarding chapter, or instead of it. Static routes use the same next-hop-group shape with an IPv6 next hop. Bind lo0.0 into the default network-instance.

title: IPv6 on the Same Triangle
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-ip6-r-frr vtysh -c "ping 2001:db8:0::2 source 2001:db8:0::1"
docker exec clab-ip6-r-ceos Cli -c "ping ipv6 2001:db8:0::1 source 2001:db8:0::2"

Predict

Both pings work after the statics exist.
A neighbour ping of 2001:db8:12::1 from FRR works before any static route does.
Removing ipv6 unicast-routing kills the far loopback ping and leaves the connected ping up.

title: IPv6 on the Same Triangle
text:
Drill
Add OSPFv3 on the FRR and cEOS link only (ipv6 ospf6 area 0 on FRR, ipv6 ospf area 0 on EOS) and delete the statics between those two. Leave SR Linux on statics. You should see one OSPFv3 neighbour and a remaining static for the SR Linux loopback.

title: VXLAN Bridging
text:
VXLAN Bridging
Two leaves, one VLAN, one VNI. The underlay is a routed link with OSPF so the loopbacks can reach each other. The hosts think they are on one LAN. There is no trunk between the leaves.
This chapter is the data plane with static flood lists. The next chapter replaces the flood list with EVPN. Do the static lab first so a broken BGP session is not your only theory.

title: VXLAN Bridging
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Number an underlay and a loopback per leaf
Bind VLAN 10 to VNI 10010
Flood to the other VTEP with a static list
Show that the host MAC is learned on the VXLAN interface

title: VXLAN Bridging
text:
Topology
name: vxlan
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    leaf1:
      kind: arista_ceos
    leaf2:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.12/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "leaf1:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "leaf2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["leaf1:eth2", "leaf2:eth2"]

title: VXLAN Bridging
text:
Both leaves
leaf1 is shown. leaf2 swaps the /30 ends and uses loopback 10.0.0.2/32. The flood target on leaf2 is 10.0.0.1.
vlan 10
   name users
interface Ethernet1
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.0.1/30
   ip ospf area 0.0.0.0
   ip ospf network point-to-point
interface Loopback0
   ip address 10.0.0.1/32
   ip ospf area 0.0.0.0
interface Vxlan1
   vxlan source-interface Loopback0
   vxlan udp-port 4789
   vxlan vlan 10 vni 10010
   vxlan vlan 10 flood vtep 10.0.0.2
router ospf 1
   router-id 10.0.0.1
leaf2 Ethernet2 is 10.1.0.2/30.

title: VXLAN Bridging
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-vxlan-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.10.12
docker exec clab-vxlan-leaf1 Cli -c "show interface Vxlan1"
docker exec clab-vxlan-leaf1 Cli -c "show vxlan vtep"
docker exec clab-vxlan-leaf1 Cli -c "show mac address-table"

Predict

h1 reaches h2.
The MAC of h2 is learned on Vxlan1, not on Ethernet2.
OSPF is Full on the underlay. If OSPF is down, the flood VTEP is unreachable and the ping fails even though VLAN 10 is up locally.

title: VXLAN Bridging
text:
Drill
Remove the flood line on leaf1 only. h1’s ARP for h2 fails. h2 can still ARP for h1 if leaf2 still floods. One-way flood lists are a classic broken overlay. Put the line back.

title: EVPN Control Plane for VXLAN
text:
EVPN Control Plane for VXLAN
Start from the VXLAN lab and delete the static flood lines. BGP EVPN in one AS tells each leaf about the other’s MAC. The VNI does not change. The underlay OSPF does not change.
Use the VXLAN lab diagram for this topology. The link is still the underlay; the control plane is now BGP.

title: EVPN Control Plane for VXLAN
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Remove a static flood list without losing host reachability
Configure EVPN on cEOS for one VLAN
See a type-2 route for the remote host MAC
Tell an underlay failure from an EVPN failure

title: EVPN Control Plane for VXLAN
text:
BGP on leaf1
interface Vxlan1
   vxlan source-interface Loopback0
   vxlan udp-port 4789
   vxlan vlan 10 vni 10010
router bgp 65000
   router-id 10.0.0.1
   neighbor 10.0.0.2 remote-as 65000
   neighbor 10.0.0.2 update-source Loopback0
   !
   vlan 10
      rd 10.0.0.1:10
      route-target import 65000:10
      route-target export 65000:10
      redistribute learned
   !
   address-family evpn
      neighbor 10.0.0.2 activate
These are iBGP speakers in the same AS. The neighbour address is the other loopback. OSPF on the underlay is what makes that address reachable, so there is no multihop knob.
leaf2 uses router-id and rd 10.0.0.2, neighbour 10.0.0.1, and the same route-target.
No vxlan vlan 10 flood vtep line. If you leave it, you will not know whether EVPN is doing the work.

title: EVPN Control Plane for VXLAN
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-vxlan-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.10.12
docker exec clab-vxlan-leaf1 Cli -c "show bgp evpn summary"
docker exec clab-vxlan-leaf1 Cli -c "show bgp evpn route-type mac-ip"
docker exec clab-vxlan-leaf1 Cli -c "show vxlan address-table"

Predict

The EVPN session is Established.
A MAC-IP route for h2’s MAC exists on leaf1 after h2 has talked.
Shutting Ethernet2 (the underlay) drops both OSPF and the ping. The VLAN on Ethernet1 stays up. That split is the operational lesson: the host link is fine and the overlay is not.

title: EVPN Control Plane for VXLAN
text:
Drill
Change leaf2’s route-target import to 65000:99. The session stays up. The MAC route is received and not imported. The ping fails. Put the route-target back. Session state is not forwarding state.

title: Reading SR Linux with gNMI
text:
Reading SR Linux with gNMI
The CLI shows the same data the box will give a controller. This lab reads one interface over gNMI with the gnmic image already on the host, then changes the description and reads it again.

title: Reading SR Linux with gNMI
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Find the SR Linux management address from containerlab inspect
Get one YANG path with gnmic
Change a leaf from the CLI and see the get change
Keep the gNMI client off the data-plane links

title: Reading SR Linux with gNMI
text:
Topology
Use the LLDP lab, or a single SR Linux node with no links. A single node is enough.
name: gnmi
topology:
  kinds:
    nokia_srlinux:
      image: ghcr.io/nokia/srlinux:latest
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    srl:
      kind: nokia_srlinux
Set a description so the get has something to return:
enter candidate
set interface ethernet-1/1 description lab-host-track
set interface ethernet-1/1 admin-state enable
commit now

title: Reading SR Linux with gNMI
text:
Get
containerlab inspect -t topology.clab.yml
Take the IPv4 address of clab-gnmi-srl. The management network Containerlab creates is reachable from a container on that network. gnmic is not installed on the host. Run the image:
docker run --rm --network clab ghcr.io/openconfig/gnmic:latest \
  --address <mgmt-ip>:57400 \
  --username admin \
  --password 'NokiaSrl1!' \
  --insecure \
  get --path /interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/description
The Docker network name is clab unless you set another management network. If the run cannot resolve the node, use the address from inspect rather than the container name.

Predict

The get returns lab-host-track.
Change the description to changed and commit. The next get returns changed.
A wrong password fails before any path is read. Fix the password. Do not open the port to anything but the lab.

title: Reading SR Linux with gNMI
text:
Drill
Subscribe for 30 seconds instead of get:
docker run --rm --network clab ghcr.io/openconfig/gnmic:latest \
  --address <mgmt-ip>:57400 \
  --username admin \
  --password 'NokiaSrl1!' \
  --insecure \
  subscribe --path /interface[name=ethernet-1/1]/admin-state \
  --mode once
--mode once is a single sample. If you have time, use stream mode, shut the interface from sr_cli, and watch the update. Cancel the client when you have seen it. Do not leave a subscribe running.

title: Production Failure Drills
text:
Production Failure Drills
This is the lab you keep. One cEOS pair does VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF toward one FRR core. Four hosts sit on two VLANs. You break one piece at a time and write down what still works. That is the production habit. The protocols are the ones this track already built.

title: Production Failure Drills
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Draw the failure domain of a trunk, a VRRP master, and an OSPF link before you touch them
Run three drills and record evidence
Restore the lab to the starting state
Say which failures this image set still cannot show

title: Production Failure Drills
text:
Shape
        r-frr
        /   \
     sw1     sw2      VRRP .254 on VLAN 10 and VLAN 20
      | \   / |
      |  \ /  |
     h1  h2  h3 h4    h1,h3 VLAN 10 · h2,h4 VLAN 20
sw1 and sw2 are cEOS. r-frr is FRR. Hosts are Alpine. Two cEOS plus one FRR fits the host. There is no SR Linux in this lab so the failure notes stay about one design.



VLAN
Subnet
Gateway
Master




10
172.16.10.0/24
172.16.10.254
sw1 priority 110


20
172.16.20.0/24
172.16.20.254
sw2 priority 110



OSPF area 0 on sw1 Ethernet3 — r-frr eth1 (10.1.1.0/30) and sw2 Ethernet3 — r-frr eth2 (10.1.2.0/30). Each switch advertises its VLAN prefixes. The trunk between sw1 Ethernet4 and sw2 Ethernet4 carries VLAN 10 and 20 so VRRP hellos have a path.
Build it from the VLAN, VRRP, and OSPF chapters. Do not add a fourth heavy node.
Hosts:



Host
Address
Default




h1, on sw1
172.16.10.11/24
172.16.10.254


h3, on sw2
172.16.10.12/24
172.16.10.254


h2, on sw1
172.16.20.11/24
172.16.20.254


h4, on sw2
172.16.20.12/24
172.16.20.254

title: Production Failure Drills
text:
Baseline, before any drill
docker exec clab-drill-sw1 Cli -c "show vrrp brief"
docker exec clab-drill-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec clab-drill-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.10.12
docker exec clab-drill-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.20.11
docker exec clab-drill-h1 ping -c 2 10.0.0.1
Give r-frr a loopback 10.0.0.1/32 in OSPF so the third ping has a target that is not on the campus VLANs.
All three pings work. sw1 is master for VLAN 10. sw2 is master for VLAN 20. Two OSPF neighbours are Full.

title: Production Failure Drills
text:
Drill 1 — trunk VLAN missing
On sw2, remove VLAN 20 from the trunk allowed list.

h2 stops reaching h4.
h1 still reaches h3.
VRRP for VLAN 20 may go dual-master because hellos died. Write down show vrrp on both switches.
Put VLAN 20 back. Masters return to one each. Do not start drill 2 until they have.

title: Production Failure Drills
text:
Drill 2 — VRRP master down
Shut Vlan10 on sw1.

sw2 becomes master for VLAN 10.
h1 still pings 172.16.10.254 and h3.
OSPF on sw1 may drop if you shut the whole box instead of the SVI. Shut only Vlan10 so the underlay stays. That is the point: first-hop failure and core adjacency are different layers.
No shut Vlan10. sw1 preempts.

title: Production Failure Drills
text:
Drill 3 — one OSPF uplink
Shut r-frr eth1.

The neighbour to sw1 goes down. The neighbour to sw2 stays Full.
h1 still pings h2. Campus traffic does not need r-frr.
h1’s ping to 10.0.0.1 fails if sw1 was the only way and sw1 has no other route. If sw1 still has VLAN OSPF to sw2, the ping may take the long path. Record which one you built. A passive VLAN interface, as in the open-image campus lab, makes the ping fail. An active VLAN OSPF adjacency hides the failure. Choose passive on the SVIs so this drill means something.

title: Production Failure Drills
text:
Restore
Unshut every interface. Allowed VLAN list is 10 and 20 on both ends. VRRP masters match the table. Two OSPF neighbours are Full. Then:
containerlab destroy -t topology.clab.yml --cleanup

title: Production Failure Drills
section: What these images still will not show
text:
What these images still will not show
A wireless client roam, a phone registration, an SD-WAN policy on a controller, and a carrier MPLS VPN are not in this image set. Do not fake them with a static route and call it the same thing. The drills above are the production set this host can prove: broadcast domain, first hop, and IGP, broken one at a time, with the show command written down.

title: Path MTU and TCP MSS
text:
Path MTU and TCP MSS
A link in the middle of the path is smaller than the links at the edges. A ping that sets the Don’t Fragment bit dies there. A TCP session can survive the same path when the SYN carries a smaller maximum segment size.

title: Path MTU and TCP MSS
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Build a path whose middle hop is smaller than the edges
Show that a large ICMP echo with DF set fails, and a smaller one passes
Clamp TCP MSS on the router that owns the small link
Explain why a black hole remains when ICMP “fragmentation needed” is filtered

title: Path MTU and TCP MSS
text:
Topology
name: mtu
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    r-frr:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-frr.frr.conf
    r-ceos:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.1.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.1.1
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.2.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.2.1
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "r-frr:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r-frr:eth2", "r-ceos:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r-ceos:eth2", "h2:eth1"]
r-frr.frr.conf carries the addresses and the routes. Leave daemons unset so only zebra starts. No dynamic protocol.
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface eth1
 ip address 172.16.1.1/24
!
interface eth2
 ip address 10.1.0.1/30
!
ip route 172.16.2.0/24 10.1.0.2
!
On r-ceos:
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.0.2/30
   mtu 1400
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 172.16.2.1/24
ip route 172.16.1.0/24 10.1.0.1
ip routing
Shrink the FRR side of the same link from the host, after the lab is up:
docker exec clab-mtu-r-frr ip link set eth2 mtu 1400

title: Path MTU and TCP MSS
text:
Verify
ICMP payload plus 28 bytes of IP and ICMP header is the packet size. A 1372-byte payload is a 1400-byte packet. A 1472-byte payload is a 1500-byte packet.
docker exec clab-mtu-h1 ping -c 2 -M do -s 1372 172.16.2.10
docker exec clab-mtu-h1 ping -c 2 -M do -s 1472 172.16.2.10
Busybox ping on Alpine may spell the DF flag differently. If -M do is rejected, run ping --help inside the container and use the option that forbids fragmentation. Record the spelling you used.

Predict

The 1372-byte echo returns.
The 1472-byte echo does not. The interfaces on h1 and h2 are still up.
ip link show eth2 inside r-frr reports 1400.

title: Path MTU and TCP MSS
text:
TCP MSS
On r-ceos Ethernet1:
interface Ethernet1
   tcp mss ceiling ipv4 1360 egress
From h1, open a TCP session to a listener on h2:
docker exec -d clab-mtu-h2 nc -lk -p 8080
docker exec clab-mtu-h1 sh -c "echo hi | nc -w 2 172.16.2.10 8080"
Capture on h2:
docker exec clab-mtu-h2 tcpdump -ni eth1 -c 4 'tcp port 8080'
The SYN from h1, after it has crossed the router, should advertise an MSS no larger than 1360. If nc is missing, apk add busybox-extras on that Alpine node. Stop the chapter there if apk cannot reach a mirror. Do not invent a second path around the missing package.

title: Path MTU and TCP MSS
text:
Drill
Put an ACL on r-ceos that denies ICMP unreachable and still permits everything else, inbound on Ethernet1. Repeat the 1472-byte ping. The failure is now silent: no “fragmentation needed” comes back. Remove the ACL when you are done. That silent failure is the production black hole people chase for a day. containerlab destroy -t topology.clab.yml --cleanup before the next chapter.

title: STP Edge Guards
text:
STP Edge Guards
Rapid PVST already picked a root in the spanning-tree chapter. This lab adds the two guards that keep an edge port from joining the topology by accident. Root guard refuses a better root. BPDU guard shuts a port that was supposed to face a host.
Destroy every other lab first. Three cEOS nodes at 2 GB each need the host to themselves.

title: STP Edge Guards
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Mark an access port edge and turn on BPDU guard
Watch that port go errdisabled when a switch is attached
Put root guard on the port that faces the current root
Recover an errdisabled port without reloading the switch

title: STP Edge Guards
text:
Topology
name: guards
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw-root:
      kind: arista_ceos
    sw-access:
      kind: arista_ceos
    sw-rogue:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["sw-root:eth1", "sw-access:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["sw-access:eth2", "h1:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["sw-access:eth3", "sw-rogue:eth1"]
Leave sw-rogue unconfigured until the BPDU-guard test. An unconfigured cEOS still speaks spanning tree on its ports.

title: STP Edge Guards
text:
Base STP
On sw-root and sw-access:
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
vlan 10
   name users
interface Ethernet1
   switchport mode trunk
   switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
On sw-root only:
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096
On sw-access Ethernet2, the host port:
interface Ethernet2
   switchport access vlan 10
   spanning-tree portfast
   spanning-tree bpduguard enable
Ethernet3 on sw-access stays default until the drill. Do not put the host and the rogue on the same port.

title: STP Edge Guards
text:
Verify root guard
On sw-access Ethernet1:
interface Ethernet1
   spanning-tree guard root
Then on sw-root, make it a worse root:
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 61440
docker exec clab-guards-sw-access Cli -c "show spanning-tree vlan 10"

Predict

Ethernet1 on sw-access moves to a root-inconsistent state. It stops forwarding VLAN 10.
sw-access does not accept sw-root as root while the guard is on, and it also does not become a stable root through that port.
Remove the guard, or put sw-root’s priority back to 4096. The port forwards again. Put the priority back before the next test.

title: STP Edge Guards
text:
Verify BPDU guard
Shut Ethernet3 is not required. Configure it as an access port in VLAN 10 with the same edge commands as Ethernet2, then watch it die because sw-rogue sends BPDUs:
interface Ethernet3
   switchport access vlan 10
   spanning-tree portfast
   spanning-tree bpduguard enable
docker exec clab-guards-sw-access Cli -c "show spanning-tree bpduguard"
docker exec clab-guards-sw-access Cli -c "show interfaces Ethernet3 status"

Predict

Ethernet3 is errdisabled. Ethernet2, where h1 sits, stays up. h1 can still ARP if you give the switch an SVI, but you do not need the SVI for this test.
shutdown then no shutdown on Ethernet3 clears the errdisable only until the next BPDU. The rogue is still there.
Remove BPDU guard from Ethernet3 and the port forwards. That is the wrong fix on a real access port. The right fix is to disconnect the rogue. Shut sw-rogue Ethernet1 and then recover Ethernet3.

title: STP Edge Guards
text:
Drill
Enable errdisable recovery cause bpduguard and errdisable recovery interval 30 on sw-access. The port returns by itself and falls over again. Write down why a 30-second recovery on a host port is a loop you do not want in production. Destroy the lab before you leave.

title: DHCP Snooping and ARP Inspection
text:
DHCP Snooping and ARP Inspection
The switch already hands out addresses in the DHCP chapter. This lab changes the question. Which port is allowed to answer, and which ARP messages are allowed to stick. Snooping builds a binding table. Dynamic ARP inspection drops ARP that is not in that table.

title: DHCP Snooping and ARP Inspection
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Turn on DHCP snooping for one VLAN and trust only the server port
Read a binding learned from a real lease
Drop ARP from a static host until you add a source binding
Point at the port a rogue DHCP server used

title: DHCP Snooping and ARP Inspection
text:
Topology
name: snoop
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    srv:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
    rogue:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.9/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["srv:eth1", "sw:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sw:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["rogue:eth1", "sw:eth3"]
h1 starts with no address. It will ask.

title: DHCP Snooping and ARP Inspection
text:
Switch
vlan 10
   name users
interface Ethernet1
   switchport access vlan 10
   ip dhcp snooping trust
interface Ethernet2
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Ethernet3
   switchport access vlan 10
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping information option
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
ip dhcp snooping bridging
Bridging mode is what makes snooping work when the server is in the same VLAN as the client. The trust command belongs on Ethernet1 only.

title: DHCP Snooping and ARP Inspection
text:
Server
apk has to work for this chapter. If it does not, stop and destroy the lab.
docker exec clab-snoop-srv apk add dnsmasq
docker exec clab-snoop-srv sh -c 'printf "%s\n" \
  "interface=eth1" \
  "bind-interfaces" \
  "dhcp-range=172.16.10.50,172.16.10.80,255.255.255.0,2m" \
  > /etc/dnsmasq.conf'
docker exec clab-snoop-srv dnsmasq
Do not start dnsmasq on rogue yet.

title: DHCP Snooping and ARP Inspection
text:
Verify snooping
docker exec clab-snoop-h1 udhcpc -i eth1 -n -q
docker exec clab-snoop-sw Cli -c "show ip dhcp snooping"
docker exec clab-snoop-sw Cli -c "show ip dhcp snooping binding"

Predict

h1 has an address in 172.16.10.50–80.
The binding names Ethernet2, VLAN 10, and h1’s MAC.
Start dnsmasq on rogue with a different range, 172.16.10.200,172.16.10.210, then release and renew on h1. The new lease still comes from 172.16.10.10. Offers that enter Ethernet3 are dropped.

title: DHCP Snooping and ARP Inspection
text:
ARP inspection
Add a second host address by hand on h1 after the lease test, or use rogue as the static host. This example uses rogue, which already has 172.16.10.9.
ip arp inspection vlan 10
interface Ethernet1
   ip arp inspection trust
Ethernet2 and Ethernet3 stay untrusted. Read rogue’s MAC:
docker exec clab-snoop-rogue cat /sys/class/net/eth1/address
EOS wants that MAC as dotted groups of four hex digits. aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff becomes aabb.ccdd.eeff. Then:
ip source binding 172.16.10.9 aabb.ccdd.eeff vlan 10 interface Ethernet3
Use the MAC you read, not the placeholder.
docker exec clab-snoop-rogue ping -c 2 172.16.10.10
docker exec clab-snoop-sw Cli -c "show ip arp inspection statistics"
docker exec clab-snoop-sw Cli -c "show ip source binding"

Predict

Before the binding, the ping fails and the drop counter moves.
After the binding, the ping to the server works.
Ethernet1 did not need a binding. It is trusted.

title: DHCP Snooping and ARP Inspection
text:
Drill
Delete the source binding and watch the ping fail again. A binding on the wrong interface is the same failure. Destroy the lab when the counters make sense.

title: MLAG on cEOS
text:
MLAG on cEOS
Two switches, one port-channel from the downstream switch’s point of view. MLAG keeps that bundle up when one upstream member fails. The peer link is not the host path. It is how the two leaves agree.
Destroy every other lab first. This topology is three cEOS nodes.

title: MLAG on cEOS
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Build a peer link in its own VLAN and keep spanning tree off that VLAN
Form an MLAG domain and read active state
Attach a downstream port-channel as MLAG 20
Shut one member and keep the two hosts in the same VLAN talking

title: MLAG on cEOS
text:
Topology
name: mlag
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    leaf1:
      kind: arista_ceos
    leaf2:
      kind: arista_ceos
    hostsw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.12/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["leaf1:eth1", "leaf2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["leaf1:eth2", "leaf2:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["leaf1:eth3", "hostsw:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["leaf2:eth3", "hostsw:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "hostsw:eth3"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "hostsw:eth4"]

title: MLAG on cEOS
text:
Leaves
leaf1 is shown. leaf2 uses 10.255.255.2/30 and peer-address 10.255.255.1. Everything else matches.
vlan 10
   name users
vlan 4094
   name mlag-peer
   trunk group mlagpeer
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
no spanning-tree vlan 4094
interface Port-Channel10
   switchport mode trunk
   switchport trunk group mlagpeer
interface Ethernet1
   channel-group 10 mode active
interface Ethernet2
   channel-group 10 mode active
interface Port-Channel20
   switchport mode trunk
   switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
   mlag 20
interface Ethernet3
   channel-group 20 mode active
interface Vlan4094
   ip address 10.255.255.1/30
   no autostate
mlag configuration
   domain-id lab-mlag
   local-interface Vlan4094
   peer-address 10.255.255.2
   peer-link Port-Channel10
If mlag configuration is rejected, the mode command on this image is mlag. The subcommands are the same. The prompt you want is (config-mlag).

title: MLAG on cEOS
text:
Downstream switch
vlan 10
   name users
interface Port-Channel20
   switchport mode trunk
   switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
interface Ethernet1
   channel-group 20 mode active
interface Ethernet2
   channel-group 20 mode active
interface Ethernet3
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Ethernet4
   switchport access vlan 10

title: MLAG on cEOS
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-mlag-leaf1 Cli -c "show mlag"
docker exec clab-mlag-leaf1 Cli -c "show port-channel dense"
docker exec clab-mlag-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.10.12

Predict

show mlag reports the domain lab-mlag, local-interface Vlan4094, and a peer that is active.
Port-Channel20 on leaf1 has one member, Ethernet3. The other member lives on leaf2. hostsw sees both members in Port-Channel20.
The ping between h1 and h2 works.
Shut leaf1 Ethernet3. The ping still works. It now uses leaf2 only. no shutdown brings the member back.

title: MLAG on cEOS
text:
Drill
Shut Port-Channel10 on leaf1. That is the peer link, not a host link. Record what show mlag says and whether the ping survives. A split peer with both host members still up is the failure MLAG is specifically bad at. Restore the peer link, confirm active, then destroy the lab.

title: VRF-Lite
text:
VRF-Lite
One switch, two routing tables, the same addresses in both. VRF-lite is how a campus or a lab router keeps two customers apart without a second chassis. Nothing here is an MPLS VPN. The routes never leave the box.

title: VRF-Lite
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Create two VRFs and put routed ports in them
Use the same subnet in both VRFs on purpose
Prove that each host reaches only its own VRF
Read a route in one VRF and see that the other VRF does not have it

title: VRF-Lite
text:
Topology
name: vrf
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h-a1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 10.1.1.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 10.1.1.1
    h-a2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 10.2.2.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 10.2.2.1
    h-b1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 10.1.1.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 10.1.1.1
    h-b2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 10.2.2.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 10.2.2.1
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h-a1:eth1", "sw:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h-a2:eth1", "sw:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["h-b1:eth1", "sw:eth3"]
    - endpoints: ["h-b2:eth1", "sw:eth4"]
The hosts share addresses. They do not share a link, so ARP is not confused. The switch is what keeps the tables apart.

title: VRF-Lite
text:
Switch
vrf on an interface clears addresses already configured there. Set the VRF first, then the address.
vrf instance CUSTA
vrf instance CUSTB
ip routing
ip routing vrf CUSTA
ip routing vrf CUSTB
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   vrf CUSTA
   ip address 10.1.1.1/24
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   vrf CUSTA
   ip address 10.2.2.1/24
interface Ethernet3
   no switchport
   vrf CUSTB
   ip address 10.1.1.1/24
interface Ethernet4
   no switchport
   vrf CUSTB
   ip address 10.2.2.1/24
There is no static route and no leak. Each VRF only knows the two connected subnets you just typed.

title: VRF-Lite
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-vrf-h-a1 ping -c 2 10.2.2.10
docker exec clab-vrf-h-b1 ping -c 2 10.2.2.10
docker exec clab-vrf-sw Cli -c "show ip route vrf CUSTA"
docker exec clab-vrf-sw Cli -c "show ip route vrf CUSTB"
docker exec clab-vrf-sw Cli -c "show vrf"

Predict

h-a1 reaches 10.2.2.10. That answer is h-a2.
h-b1 reaches 10.2.2.10. That answer is h-b2, not h-a2.
Each VRF table shows 10.1.1.0/24 and 10.2.2.0/24 as connected. The default VRF table does not.
A ping from h-a1 to h-b1’s address is a ping to the local gateway’s other customer, and it stays inside CUSTA. You cannot aim it at CUSTB from the host.

title: VRF-Lite
text:
Drill
Leak one prefix on purpose:
ip route vrf CUSTA 10.9.9.9/32 egress-vrf CUSTB 10.2.2.10
If egress-vrf is rejected, check ip route ? and use the inter-VRF form it prints. Then ping 10.9.9.9 from h-a1. The return path does not exist until CUSTB has a route back, so the ping fails in one direction. Add the opposite static, confirm one echo, then delete both statics. An accidental leak is how two customers become one. Destroy the lab after the routes are gone.

title: OSPF Stub, NSSA, and Summary
text:
OSPF Stub, NSSA, and Summary
Area 0 and one other area were enough to see an inter-area route. A stub area is the next decision. The spoke does not need every external prefix in the network. It needs a default, and it needs the summaries you meant to send.

title: OSPF Stub, NSSA, and Summary
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Make area 1 a stub and watch external routes disappear on the spoke
Make it totally stubby and watch inter-area routes disappear too
Turn the same area into an NSSA and originate one external from the spoke
Replace two spoke prefixes with one summary on the ABR

title: OSPF Stub, NSSA, and Summary
text:
Topology
name: stub
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    r-frr:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-frr.frr.conf
      daemons: [ospfd]
    r-ceos:
      kind: arista_ceos
    r-spoke:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-spoke.frr.conf
      daemons: [ospfd]
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r-frr:eth1", "r-ceos:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r-ceos:eth2", "r-spoke:eth1"]
There is no link between r-frr and r-spoke. The ABR is the only way through.

title: OSPF Stub, NSSA, and Summary
text:
Area 0 and a normal area 1
r-frr.frr.conf:
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.0.0.1/32
 ip address 172.16.1.1/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.1.0.1/30
 ip ospf area 0
 ip ospf network point-to-point
!
router ospf
 ospf router-id 10.0.0.1
 network 10.0.0.1/32 area 0
 network 172.16.1.1/32 area 0
!
Leave redistribute connected and redistribute static off until the stub test. Area 1 should start with inter-area routes only.
r-spoke.frr.conf:
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.0.0.3/32
 ip address 172.16.30.1/32
 ip address 172.16.30.2/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.2.0.2/30
 ip ospf area 1
 ip ospf network point-to-point
!
router ospf
 ospf router-id 10.0.0.3
 network 10.0.0.3/32 area 1
 network 172.16.30.1/32 area 1
 network 172.16.30.2/32 area 1
!
r-ceos:
interface Loopback0
   ip address 10.0.0.2/32
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.0.2/30
   ip ospf network point-to-point
   ip ospf area 0
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 10.2.0.1/30
   ip ospf network point-to-point
   ip ospf area 1
router ospf 1
   router-id 10.0.0.2
   network 10.0.0.2/32 area 0
ip routing
docker exec clab-stub-r-spoke vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec clab-stub-r-spoke vtysh -c "show ip route ospf"

Predict

r-spoke has inter-area routes for 10.0.0.1/32 and 172.16.1.1/32.
No external routes exist yet.

title: OSPF Stub, NSSA, and Summary
text:
Stub, then totally stubby
On r-ceos and on r-spoke, area 1 becomes a stub. Both sides must agree or the adjacency drops.
r-ceos:
router ospf 1
   area 1 stub
r-spoke, inside router ospf:
area 1 stub

Predict

The adjacency returns after both sides match.
r-spoke gains a default route from the ABR.
Add redistribute connected on r-frr only if those loopbacks were not already in OSPF. Then add a static on r-frr, ip route 198.51.100.0/24 Null0, and redistribute static. r-spoke does not learn 198.51.100.0/24. r-ceos does, as an external, on the area 0 side.

Totally stubby is an ABR setting. On r-ceos only:
router ospf 1
   area 1 stub no-summary
r-spoke stays area 1 stub without no-summary.


Predict

172.16.1.1/32 disappears from r-spoke.
The default route remains. A ping from r-spoke to 172.16.1.1 still works if the ABR has the route.

title: OSPF Stub, NSSA, and Summary
text:
NSSA
Remove the stub commands on both sides. Replace them with NSSA.
r-ceos:
router ospf 1
   no area 1 stub
   area 1 nssa
r-spoke:
no area 1 stub
area 1 nssa
ip route 203.0.113.0/24 Null0
router ospf
 redistribute static

Predict

r-ceos learns 203.0.113.0/24 as an NSSA external.
r-frr learns it as an external only after the ABR translates it. If r-frr stays empty, set area 1 nssa translate type7 always on r-ceos and check again.

title: OSPF Stub, NSSA, and Summary
text:
Summary
On the ABR, while area 1 is a normal area or an NSSA (a stub will not flood the components you are summarizing into the stub):
router ospf 1
   area 1 range 172.16.30.0/24

Predict

r-frr sees 172.16.30.0/24 and does not see both /32s.
Shut the command and both /32s return.

Destroy the lab. The spoke should not be left redistributing a static into area 0 by accident.

title: Redistribution and Route Tags
text:
Redistribution and Route Tags
A prefix may cross from OSPF into BGP once. If it crosses back, the two protocols advertise each other’s copies and the preference flips. A tag is a mark the route carries so the return trip can refuse it.

title: Redistribution and Route Tags
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Redistribute an OSPF prefix into BGP and see it on the far router
Redistribute a BGP prefix into OSPF and see it on the near router
Tag the BGP-into-OSPF copy
Refuse that tag when OSPF is redistributed back into BGP

title: Redistribution and Route Tags
text:
Topology
name: redist
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    r-ospf:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-ospf.frr.conf
      daemons: [ospfd]
    r-ceos:
      kind: arista_ceos
    r-bgp:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-bgp.frr.conf
      daemons: [bgpd]
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r-ospf:eth1", "r-ceos:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r-ceos:eth2", "r-bgp:eth1"]

title: Redistribution and Route Tags
text:
Starting configs
r-ospf.frr.conf:
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.0.0.1/32
 ip address 172.16.10.1/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.1.0.1/30
 ip ospf area 0
 ip ospf network point-to-point
!
router ospf
 ospf router-id 10.0.0.1
 network 10.0.0.1/32 area 0
 network 172.16.10.1/32 area 0
!
r-bgp.frr.conf:
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.0.0.3/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.2.0.2/30
!
ip route 198.51.100.0/24 Null0
!
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.0.0.3
 neighbor 10.2.0.1 remote-as 65000
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 198.51.100.0/24
 exit-address-family
!
r-ceos, before any redistribute:
interface Loopback0
   ip address 10.0.0.2/32
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.0.2/30
   ip ospf network point-to-point
   ip ospf area 0
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 10.2.0.1/30
router ospf 1
   router-id 10.0.0.2
   network 10.0.0.2/32 area 0
router bgp 65000
   router-id 10.0.0.2
   neighbor 10.2.0.2 remote-as 65001
ip routing
Confirm OSPF is Full and BGP is Established before you redistribute anything.

title: Redistribution and Route Tags
text:
One direction, then the other
router bgp 65000
   redistribute ospf
docker exec clab-redist-r-bgp vtysh -c "show ip bgp 172.16.10.1/32"

Predict

r-bgp has 172.16.10.1/32 from AS 65000.

Now the other direction, still with no tag:
router ospf 1
   redistribute bgp
docker exec clab-redist-r-ospf vtysh -c "show ip route 198.51.100.0/24"
docker exec clab-redist-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip bgp 198.51.100.0/24"


Predict

r-ospf has 198.51.100.0/24 as an OSPF external.
On r-ceos the BGP table may also grow a local path for that prefix, learned from OSPF and fed back. If you see two paths, you are looking at the loop this chapter exists to stop. If you see one path, the feedback is still one redistribute command away. Either way, put the tag on before you call it done.

title: Redistribution and Route Tags
text:
Tag and deny
route-map FROM-BGP permit 10
   set tag 100
route-map BACK-TO-BGP deny 10
   match tag 100
route-map BACK-TO-BGP permit 20
router ospf 1
   redistribute bgp route-map FROM-BGP
router bgp 65000
   redistribute ospf route-map BACK-TO-BGP
If OSPF external routes stop being eligible, the BGP line needs match internal external on the same redistribute command. Add those two words only if show ip ospf database external has the prefix and BGP does not consider it.
docker exec clab-redist-r-ospf vtysh -c "show ip ospf database external 198.51.100.0"
docker exec clab-redist-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip bgp 198.51.100.0/24"

Predict

The external LSA on r-ospf carries tag 100.
r-ceos still has the eBGP path from r-bgp for 198.51.100.0/24.
It does not install a second path that came from OSPF. 172.16.10.1/32 is still on r-bgp, because that prefix was never tagged.

title: Redistribution and Route Tags
text:
Drill
Remove BACK-TO-BGP from the BGP redistribute line. Watch the second path appear. Put the route-map back. Destroy the lab after a single path remains.

title: BGP MED, Prepend, and ECMP
text:
BGP MED, Prepend, and ECMP
Two links to the same neighbor AS. MED can prefer one of them. AS-path length is compared earlier, so a prepend beats a better MED. When the two paths are equal, maximum-paths installs both.

title: BGP MED, Prepend, and ECMP
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Prefer the low-MED link when both paths come from the same AS
Overturn that choice with AS-path prepending
Install both links as ECMP once the metrics match

title: BGP MED, Prepend, and ECMP
text:
Topology
name: med
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    r-frr:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-frr.frr.conf
      daemons: [bgpd]
    r-ceos:
      kind: arista_ceos
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r-frr:eth1", "r-ceos:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r-frr:eth2", "r-ceos:eth2"]
r-frr.frr.conf:
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 172.16.1.1/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.1.12.1/30
!
interface eth2
 ip address 10.1.13.1/30
!
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.0.0.1
 neighbor 10.1.12.2 remote-as 65002
 neighbor 10.1.13.2 remote-as 65002
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 172.16.1.1/32
  neighbor 10.1.12.2 route-map MED-LOW out
  neighbor 10.1.13.2 route-map MED-HIGH out
 exit-address-family
!
route-map MED-LOW permit 10
 set metric 50
!
route-map MED-HIGH permit 10
 set metric 200
!
r-ceos:
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.12.2/30
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.13.2/30
router bgp 65002
   router-id 10.0.0.2
   neighbor 10.1.12.1 remote-as 65001
   neighbor 10.1.13.1 remote-as 65001
ip routing

title: BGP MED, Prepend, and ECMP
text:
Verify MED
docker exec clab-med-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip bgp 172.16.1.1/32"

Predict

Both neighbors are Established.
The best path is 10.1.12.1, metric 50.
10.1.13.1 is valid and not best, metric 200.
MED is only compared here because both paths are from AS 65001. A path from a third AS would not lose on MED alone.

title: BGP MED, Prepend, and ECMP
text:
Prepend beats MED
Change MED-LOW on r-frr. Edit the file or vtysh:
route-map MED-LOW permit 10
 set metric 50
 set as-path prepend 65001 65001 65001
clear ip bgp * soft out on r-frr, or the EOS side clear ip bgp 65001 soft.

Predict

The best path flips to 10.1.13.1 even though its MED is worse.
The AS path via 10.1.12.1 is longer. Length is compared before MED.

Take the prepend off before the next step. Soft-clear again. The low MED must be best again.

title: BGP MED, Prepend, and ECMP
text:
ECMP
On r-frr set both route-maps to metric 50. On r-ceos:
router bgp 65002
   maximum-paths 2
Soft-clear.

Predict

show ip route 172.16.1.1/32 on r-ceos lists two next hops.
Shut Ethernet2. One next hop remains and the prefix stays. no shutdown restores both.

Destroy the lab.

title: Policy-Based Routing
text:
Policy-Based Routing
The routing table has one best path for a prefix. Policy routing picks a next hop from the packet that arrived, before that lookup. Here only h1 is steered. h2 uses the default route. Both hosts share a subnet, so the difference is the match, not the destination.

title: Policy-Based Routing
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Match one source address in a PBR class
Send that traffic to a next hop that is not the default route
Show that a second host in the same subnet is unaffected
Remove the policy and watch h1 follow the table again

title: Policy-Based Routing
text:
Topology
name: pbr
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    sw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    r-a:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-a.frr.conf
    r-b:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-b.frr.conf
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.10.1
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.12/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.10.1
  links:
    - endpoints: ["sw:eth1", "r-a:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["sw:eth2", "r-b:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sw:eth3"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "sw:eth4"]
r-a.frr.conf:
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.9.0.1/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.1.1.2/30
!
ip route 172.16.10.0/24 10.1.1.1
!
r-b.frr.conf is the same shape with lo 10.9.0.2/32, eth1 10.1.2.2/30, and the same return route via 10.1.2.1.

title: Policy-Based Routing
text:
Switch
vlan 10
   name users
interface Ethernet3
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Ethernet4
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Vlan10
   ip address 172.16.10.1/24
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.1.1/30
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.2.1/30
ip routing
ip route 10.9.0.1/32 10.1.1.2
ip route 10.9.0.2/32 10.1.2.2
Both loopbacks are reachable before you add a policy. h1 and h2 both use r-a for 10.9.0.1 and r-b for 10.9.0.2. That is the table. Remember it.
EOS applies PBR with a class and a policy, not with ip policy route-map.
ip access-list PBR-H1
   10 permit ip host 172.16.10.11 any
class-map type pbr match-any CM-H1
   match ip access-group PBR-H1
policy-map type pbr PM-H1
   class CM-H1
      set nexthop 10.1.2.2
interface Vlan10
   service-policy type pbr input PM-H1
If set nexthop is rejected, stop and read class CM-H1 ?. Use the set form the help prints. Do not fall back to a routing-table static that would move h2 as well.

title: Policy-Based Routing
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-pbr-h1 traceroute -n 10.9.0.1
docker exec clab-pbr-h2 traceroute -n 10.9.0.1
docker exec clab-pbr-sw Cli -c "show policy-map type pbr interface Vlan10"
Alpine may need apk add traceroute. If apk fails, use ping and tcpdump -ni eth1 on r-a and r-b instead. h1’s echo request should arrive on r-b. h2’s echo request for the same destination should arrive on r-a.

Predict

h1 reaches 10.9.0.1 via 10.1.2.2 even though the routing table says 10.1.1.2.
h2 still uses 10.1.1.2.
The policy counters increment only for h1.

title: Policy-Based Routing
text:
Drill
Remove the service-policy from Vlan10. h1’s next hop returns to 10.1.1.2. Put the policy back, then shut Ethernet2. h1’s ping to 10.9.0.1 fails or falls back, depending on whether this image drops the set next hop when it is unreachable. Record which one you saw. A policy whose next hop is down is a black hole unless the platform falls back. Destroy the lab after you know which it did.

title: Unicast RPF
text:
Unicast RPF
An ACL names the sources you typed. Unicast reverse-path forwarding asks a different question: is the source reachable out the interface the packet arrived on. Strict mode says the interface must be the best path back to that source. A spoofed address fails that test. The real host address does not.

title: Unicast RPF
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Turn on strict uRPF on the port that faces the hosts
Pass a packet whose source is in the connected subnet
Drop a packet whose source is not reachable back out that port
Tell a uRPF drop from an ACL drop

title: Unicast RPF
text:
Topology
name: urpf
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    r-ceos:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.10.1
    srv:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.20.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.20.1
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "r-ceos:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["srv:eth1", "r-ceos:eth2"]

title: Unicast RPF
text:
Router
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 172.16.10.1/24
   ip verify unicast source reachable-via rx
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 172.16.20.1/24
ip routing
Strict mode is rx. Loose mode would be any, which only asks whether the source exists somewhere in the table. This lab uses strict.

title: Unicast RPF
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-urpf-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.20.10
docker exec clab-urpf-h1 ip addr add 203.0.113.50/32 dev eth1
docker exec clab-urpf-h1 ping -c 2 -I 203.0.113.50 172.16.20.10
docker exec clab-urpf-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip interface Ethernet1"
If busybox ping rejects -I, install nothing yet. Add the address and run ping from a network namespace, or use nping only if you already added it. The check that matters is on the server:
docker exec clab-urpf-srv tcpdump -ni eth1 -c 4 icmp
Run the spoofed ping again while tcpdump listens.

Predict

The ping from 172.16.10.11 is captured on srv and returns.
The ping from 203.0.113.50 is not captured on srv. The source is not reachable out Ethernet1. The best route for 203.0.113.50 does not exist, so strict mode drops it.
show ip interface Ethernet1 shows unicast reverse-path verification.

title: Unicast RPF
text:
Drill
Add a static on r-ceos:
ip route 203.0.113.50/32 Ethernet1 172.16.10.11
The spoofed source is now reachable out the arrival port, so strict mode passes it. That is why uRPF is not a substitute for an ACL on a network that has loose routes back to the edge. Delete the static and confirm the spoof is dropped again. Then delete the extra address on h1 and destroy the lab.

title: SPAN
text:
SPAN
A troubleshooting port should see a copy of traffic without being in the forwarding path. SPAN does that. The source is the host port. The destination is a tap that is not a member of the VLAN.

title: SPAN
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Mirror one access port to a destination port
See the host’s frames on a tap that has no address in the VLAN
Confirm the tap does not answer ARP for the hosts
Remove the session and watch the copies stop

title: SPAN
text:
Topology
name: span
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.12/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
    tap:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sw:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "sw:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["tap:eth1", "sw:eth3"]
The tap has no address. Give it a link that is up:
docker exec clab-span-tap ip link set eth1 up

title: SPAN
text:
Switch
vlan 10
   name users
interface Ethernet1
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Ethernet2
   switchport access vlan 10
monitor session 1 source Ethernet1 both
monitor session 1 destination Ethernet3
Do not put Ethernet3 in VLAN 10. Do not give it an IP address.
docker exec clab-span-sw Cli -c "show monitor session"
If the session is refused, read the reason and stop. cEOS accepts this configuration in the 4.37 manual’s command set. A platform note in the error is the result. Do not invent a second mirror syntax.

title: SPAN
text:
Verify
In one terminal:
docker exec clab-span-tap tcpdump -ni eth1 -c 6 icmp
In another:
docker exec clab-span-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.10.12

Predict

The ping works. h1 and h2 are in VLAN 10.
tcpdump on the tap prints the ICMP echo and the echo reply, or at least the echo if the direction came up as rx only. both should show both.
The tap does not appear in the switch MAC table as a normal host of VLAN 10. show mac address-table vlan 10 lists h1 and h2.
no monitor session 1 stops the copies. The ping still works.

title: SPAN
text:
Drill
Change the source to Ethernet2. The tap now sees h2’s port and goes quiet when only h1 is idle and h2 is the one pinging. Put the source back to Ethernet1 before you destroy the lab so the last show monitor session matches the figure.

title: GRE over the Underlay
text:
GRE over the Underlay
The tunnel is an interface. The underlay is how the tunnel endpoints reach each other. If the route to the tunnel destination points back into the tunnel, the tunnel never comes up. This lab keeps those two tables apart on purpose.

title: GRE over the Underlay
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Number a GRE tunnel between two loopbacks
Keep the loopback route on the physical link
Ping a far LAN through the tunnel
Break the tunnel by pointing the underlay route at the tunnel, then fix it

title: GRE over the Underlay
text:
Topology
name: gre
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    r1:
      kind: arista_ceos
    r2:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.1.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.1.1
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.2.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.2.1
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth1", "r2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "r1:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "r2:eth2"]
Two cEOS nodes. Destroy anything else heavy first.

title: GRE over the Underlay
text:
Routers
r1:
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.0.1/30
   mtu 1500
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 172.16.1.1/24
interface Loopback0
   ip address 10.0.0.1/32
interface Tunnel0
   mtu 1476
   ip address 172.31.0.1/30
   tunnel mode gre
   tunnel source Loopback0
   tunnel destination 10.0.0.2
ip route 10.0.0.2/32 10.1.0.2
ip route 172.16.2.0/24 172.31.0.2
ip routing
r2 swaps the ends. Ethernet1 is 10.1.0.2/30. Loopback0 is 10.0.0.2/32. Tunnel0 is 172.31.0.2/30, destination 10.0.0.1. The underlay static is ip route 10.0.0.1/32 10.1.0.1. The LAN route is ip route 172.16.1.0/24 172.31.0.1. Ethernet2 is 172.16.2.1/24.
The underlay static points at the physical next hop. The LAN static points at the tunnel. Those are different routes. Do not summarize them into one default that recurses.
GRE adds 24 bytes. The tunnel MTU is 1476 so a 1500-byte host packet is not asked to fit inside a 1500-byte underlay packet.

title: GRE over the Underlay
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-gre-r1 Cli -c "show interface Tunnel0"
docker exec clab-gre-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.2.10
docker exec clab-gre-r1 Cli -c "ping 10.0.0.2 source 10.0.0.1"

Predict

Tunnel0 is up.
The host ping works. The path for 172.16.2.0/24 is the tunnel address, not Ethernet1’s peer.
A ping from loopback to loopback uses the underlay static and does not need the tunnel. If that ping fails, fix it before you debug the tunnel. The tunnel cannot find its destination otherwise.

Capture on r2 Ethernet1 while h1 pings h2:
docker exec clab-gre-r2 tcpdump -ni eth1 -c 2 proto 47
cEOS may not have tcpdump. If the command is missing, skip the capture. Protocol 47 is GRE. The host ping is still the test that matters.

title: GRE over the Underlay
text:
Drill
Replace the underlay static on r1 with ip route 10.0.0.2/32 172.31.0.2. The tunnel destination is now reached through the tunnel. Tunnel0 drops or the host ping dies. Put the physical next hop back. Confirm Tunnel0 and the host ping. Destroy the lab.

title: Control-Plane ACL
text:
Control-Plane ACL
A transit packet is forwarded. A packet addressed to the router is punted. The control-plane ACL sees the second kind. This lab denies ICMP to the router from one host and leaves forwarding to a server alone.

title: Control-Plane ACL
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

See the read-only default control-plane ACL
Replace it with a lab ACL that denies one ICMP flow
Prove transit traffic still flows
Put the default ACL back

title: Control-Plane ACL
text:
Topology
name: cp
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    r-ceos:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.50.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.50.1
    srv:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.60.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.60.1
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "r-ceos:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["srv:eth1", "r-ceos:eth2"]
You configure this switch with docker exec and Cli. That path does not cross the control-plane ACL. A real SSH session from h1 would. Do not lock a management port you still need.

title: Control-Plane ACL
text:
Router, before the ACL
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 172.16.50.1/24
interface Ethernet2
   no switchport
   ip address 172.16.60.1/24
ip routing
docker exec clab-cp-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.50.1
docker exec clab-cp-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.60.10
docker exec clab-cp-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip access-lists default-control-plane-acl"

Predict

Both pings work.
The default ACL is present and marked readonly. It permits ICMP and the routing protocols. You cannot edit it in place.

title: Control-Plane ACL
text:
Lab ACL
This list is a lab stand-in. It is not a production control-plane policy. A production list starts as a copy of default-control-plane-acl and then tightens the management sources. The short list below is safe here because the CLI arrives through docker exec, and because the last line still permits transit-facing protocols you might add later.
ip access-list CP-LAB
   10 deny icmp host 172.16.50.10 host 172.16.50.1
   20 permit ip any any
system control-plane
   ip access-group CP-LAB in
docker exec clab-cp-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.50.1
docker exec clab-cp-h1 ping -c 2 172.16.60.10
docker exec clab-cp-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip access-lists CP-LAB"

Predict

The ping to 172.16.50.1 fails. The deny counter moves.
The ping to 172.16.60.10 works. That packet is forwarded, not punted.
A ping from srv to 172.16.50.1 still works. The deny names h1 only.

title: Control-Plane ACL
text:
Drill
Change line 10 to deny icmp any any. Both the for-us ping from h1 and the for-us ping from srv fail. The host-to-server ping still works. Put line 10 back to the host-specific deny.
When you are finished, remove the lab ACL so the default one returns:
system control-plane
   no ip access-group CP-LAB in
Confirm show ip access-lists lists the default ACL on the control plane again. Then destroy the lab.

title: IPv6 SLAAC
text:
IPv6 SLAAC
The IPv6 chapter put addresses on both ends by hand. SLAAC is the other way. The router advertises a prefix. The host builds an address and a default route from that advertisement. You do not type an address on the host.

title: IPv6 SLAAC
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Send router advertisements on one VLAN
Watch an Alpine host address itself from the prefix
Ping the router’s link-local and global addresses
Stop the advertisements and watch the host keep the address until it expires

title: IPv6 SLAAC
text:
Topology
name: slaac
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sw:eth1"]
Bring the host link up and allow router advertisements even if the container has forwarding on:
docker exec clab-slaac-h1 ip link set eth1 up
docker exec clab-slaac-h1 sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.eth1.accept_ra=2
docker exec clab-slaac-h1 sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.eth1.autoconf=1
Do not add an address.

title: IPv6 SLAAC
text:
Switch
ipv6 unicast-routing
vlan 10
   name users
interface Ethernet1
   switchport access vlan 10
interface Vlan10
   ipv6 enable
   ipv6 address 2001:db8:10::1/64
   ipv6 nd ra interval 4
ipv6 nd ra disabled is the off switch, used in the drill. If that command is rejected, ipv6 nd ? prints the disable form. Use that form and no other.

title: IPv6 SLAAC
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-slaac-sw Cli -c "show ipv6 interface Vlan10"
docker exec clab-slaac-h1 ip -6 addr show dev eth1
docker exec clab-slaac-h1 ip -6 route

Predict

Vlan10 has 2001:db8:10::1/64 and a link-local in fe80::/10.
eth1 on h1 grows a global address inside 2001:db8:10::/64. It also has a link-local. You did not type either one.
The host has a default route via the router’s link-local.
docker exec clab-slaac-h1 ping -c 2 2001:db8:10::1 returns.

title: IPv6 SLAAC
text:
Drill
On Vlan10, disable router advertisements with the command from the help. Delete the global address on h1 (ip -6 addr flush scope global dev eth1) and wait. It should not come back. Enable advertisements again. The address returns without a reboot. Destroy the lab.

title: NTP and Syslog
text:
NTP and Syslog
Logs without a clock are hard to line up with a packet capture. This lab makes one Alpine node the NTP server and the syslog server. The switch is the client of both. apk has to work. If it does not, stop and destroy the lab.

title: NTP and Syslog
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Serve NTP from Alpine with a local stratum
Point cEOS at that server and read the association
Send switch logs to UDP 514 and read one message you caused
Stop both services and see the switch report the loss

title: NTP and Syslog
text:
Topology
name: obs
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    log:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.90.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["sw:eth1", "log:eth1"]

title: NTP and Syslog
text:
Alpine
docker exec clab-obs-log apk add chrony rsyslog
docker exec clab-obs-log sh -c 'printf "%s\n" "allow 172.16.90.0/24" "local stratum 8" >> /etc/chrony/chrony.conf'
docker exec clab-obs-log chronyd
docker exec clab-obs-log sh -c 'printf "%s\n" \
  "module(load=\"imudp\")" \
  "input(type=\"imudp\" port=\"514\")" \
  >> /etc/rsyslog.conf'
docker exec clab-obs-log rsyslogd
Chrony on Alpine reads /etc/chrony/chrony.conf. If that path is missing, chronyd -h or the package’s sample file names the real one. Append the two lines there.

title: NTP and Syslog
text:
Switch
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 172.16.90.1/24
ntp server 172.16.90.10
logging host 172.16.90.10
logging trap informational
ip routing

title: NTP and Syslog
text:
Verify
docker exec clab-obs-sw Cli -c "show ntp status"
docker exec clab-obs-sw Cli -c "show logging"
docker exec clab-obs-log sh -c "grep -n . /var/log/messages | tail -n 20"
Make a message you can find:
docker exec clab-obs-sw Cli -c "configure
interface Ethernet1
   description lab-log-test"

Predict

NTP reports the server 172.16.90.10. The stratum follows the server. The clock does not have to be a real reference. It has to move, and it has to match between the two nodes closely enough that new log lines are not minutes off.
/var/log/messages on the Alpine node gains a line that mentions lab-log-test or Ethernet1. If rsyslog wrote somewhere else, find /var/log -type f shows the file that just grew.

title: NTP and Syslog
text:
Drill
kill rsyslogd inside the log node. Change the description again. The switch still accepts the command. The file on the log node does not grow. Start rsyslogd again and change the description a third time. The line appears. A logging host that is down does not block configuration. It drops the history. Destroy the lab.

title: DSCP Trust and Measured Delay
text:
DSCP Trust and Measured Delay
cEOS will take a QoS configuration. It will not show you the queues of a hardware switch. This chapter keeps those two facts apart. The EOS half is the trust command you would keep on a real box. The Linux half is a delay you can measure with ping.

title: DSCP Trust and Measured Delay
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Trust DSCP on a cEOS ingress port and read it back
Add a fixed delay with tc netem on Linux
Measure that delay with ping before and after
Remove the qdisc and watch the RTT fall

title: DSCP Trust and Measured Delay
text:
Lab A — trust on cEOS
One switch, one host. This lab does not share a topology with Lab B.
name: trust
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
  nodes:
    sw:
      kind: arista_ceos
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.10.11/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "sw:eth1"]
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 172.16.10.1/24
   qos trust dscp
ip routing
docker exec clab-trust-sw Cli -c "show qos interface Ethernet1"

Predict

The interface reports DSCP trust.
A ping still works. Nothing in this lab drops or reorders. cEOS in a container has no forwarding ASIC queues to starve. Do not treat a successful ping as proof of a hardware scheduler.

Destroy trust before Lab B.

title: DSCP Trust and Measured Delay
section: Lab B — delay you can measure
text:
Lab B — delay you can measure
name: delay
topology:
  nodes:
    gw:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.1.1/24 dev eth1
        - ip addr add 172.16.2.1/24 dev eth2
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip link set eth2 up
        - sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.1.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.1.1
    h2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:latest
      exec:
        - ip addr add 172.16.2.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 172.16.2.1
  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "gw:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["h2:eth1", "gw:eth2"]
docker exec clab-delay-h1 ping -c 5 172.16.2.10
docker exec clab-delay-gw tc qdisc add dev eth2 root netem delay 80ms
docker exec clab-delay-h1 ping -c 5 172.16.2.10
docker exec clab-delay-gw tc qdisc del dev eth2 root
docker exec clab-delay-h1 ping -c 5 172.16.2.10

Predict

The first five echoes are well under 80 ms. Container scheduling adds a little. It does not add 80.
The middle five sit near 80 ms one way, so the RTT sits near 80 ms or a bit over. netem on one interface delays one direction.
After tc qdisc del, the RTT falls again.

title: DSCP Trust and Measured Delay
text:
Drill
Add loss 10% to the same netem line (tc qdisc change dev eth2 root netem delay 80ms loss 10%). Some echoes vanish. That is the difference between a policy that marks packets and a path that actually drops them. Delete the qdisc and destroy the lab.

title: OSPF Authentication
text:
OSPF Authentication
A neighbor that forms with anyone on the link will form with the wrong router. Message-digest authentication requires the same key id and the same key on both ends. The lab key below is the string lab-md5-key. It is a classroom value. Do not reuse it on a network you care about.

title: OSPF Authentication
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Bring up OSPF with no authentication and record the neighbor
Require MD5 on both ends and watch the neighbor return
Change one key and watch the adjacency drop while the interfaces stay up
Put the key back without restarting the containers

title: OSPF Authentication
text:
Topology
name: ospfauth
topology:
  kinds:
    arista_ceos:
      image: ceos:4.37.0F
      memory: 2G
    frr:
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:containerlab-10.7.1
  nodes:
    r-frr:
      kind: frr
      startup-config: r-frr.frr.conf
      daemons: [ospfd]
    r-ceos:
      kind: arista_ceos
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r-frr:eth1", "r-ceos:eth1"]
r-frr.frr.conf starts with no authentication:
frr defaults traditional
service integrated-vtysh-config
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.0.0.1/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 10.1.0.1/30
 ip ospf area 0
 ip ospf network point-to-point
!
router ospf
 ospf router-id 10.0.0.1
 network 10.0.0.1/32 area 0
!
r-ceos:
interface Loopback0
   ip address 10.0.0.2/32
interface Ethernet1
   no switchport
   ip address 10.1.0.2/30
   ip ospf network point-to-point
   ip ospf area 0
router ospf 1
   router-id 10.0.0.2
   network 10.0.0.2/32 area 0
ip routing
docker exec clab-ospfauth-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
The neighbor reaches Full. Interfaces are up. That is the baseline.

title: OSPF Authentication
text:
Matching keys
On r-frr interface eth1:
interface eth1
 ip ospf authentication message-digest
 ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 lab-md5-key
On r-ceos Ethernet1:
interface Ethernet1
   ip ospf authentication message-digest
   ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 lab-md5-key
Apply both sides before you decide the lab is broken. A one-sided key looks the same as a wrong key.
docker exec clab-ospfauth-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec clab-ospfauth-r-frr vtysh -c "show ip ospf interface eth1"

Predict

The neighbor returns to Full.
The interface still shows 10.1.0.1/30 and 10.1.0.2/30. Authentication did not change the subnet.
The FRR interface output names message-digest.

title: OSPF Authentication
text:
A wrong key
On r-ceos only, replace the key:
interface Ethernet1
   no ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 lab-md5-key
   ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 lab-md5-WRONG
docker exec clab-ospfauth-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec clab-ospfauth-r-ceos Cli -c "show ip interface Ethernet1 brief"

Predict

The neighbor is gone or stuck below Full.
Ethernet1 is still up and still has 10.1.0.2/30. A routing-protocol failure is not a link failure.
Ping from r-ceos to 10.1.0.1 still works. OSPF is not required for a connected ping.

Put lab-md5-key back on r-ceos. Remove the WRONG key. The neighbor returns without a reboot.

title: OSPF Authentication
text:
Drill
Change the key id on one side to 2 and leave the other side on id 1, with the same string. The adjacency drops. Key id is part of the match. Restore id 1 on both sides, confirm Full, and destroy the lab.

title: Multicast Distribution Failure Exercises
text:
Multicast Distribution Failure Exercises
