These vendor-neutral exercises use forwarding evidence rather than a particular CLI. Use a simulator or isolated lab with IGMPv3, PIM-SM, packet capture, and multicast forwarding. Record a baseline and restore each change before introducing the next fault.
source S -- R1 -- R2 -- R3 -- VLAN 20 -- switch -- receiver H1
                   \        /                  \-- receiver H2
                    -- R4 --
S is 192.0.2.10; its group is 239.1.1.1 for ASM or 232.1.1.1 for SSM. R1 is the ASM RP at 192.0.2.1. R2 prefers the direct path to R1 for RPF; R4 provides an alternate path. Assign transit addresses and configure an IGP and PIM on all transit links, multicast routing, IGMP on the receiver LAN, VLAN 20 snooping and a querier, and consistent RP mapping for ASM. Send a numbered UDP stream with TTL 16. H1 joins the ASM group; H2 initially does not.
Verify PIM neighbors, routes to the source and RP, H1 membership, switch VLAN and multicast table, and router (*,G) and (S,G) state. Depending on the platform’s SPT policy, source-tree forwarding may begin quickly. Check H1’s sequence numbers. A capture on H2 can still see multicast depending on unknown multicast handling and hardware behavior; absence of an application join does not prove port isolation.

Membership: stop H1. Observe the membership change, queries, and eventual state removal. Repeat with H2 also joined: H1 leaving must not remove remaining LAN interest. Allow for timers and capture IGMP.
Snooping and VLANs: restore H1, then remove its port from VLAN 20. The router may retain membership until timers expire, but H1 loses traffic immediately. Restore the VLAN and renew membership if needed. Compare switch table, counters and capture.
RPF: change R2’s route toward S so its selected upstream points through R4 while traffic still arrives directly from R1. If that route controls multicast RPF, wrong-interface drops increase and delivery fails. A separate multicast RIB or automatic reconvergence can change the outcome; inspect actual RPF and tree state. Restore the route and verify recovery.
TTL: set sender TTL to 1. Local reception on the source LAN can work, but the packet cannot cross the routed path to H1. Capture at source and first router; restore TTL 16.
SSM: join (192.0.2.10, 232.1.1.1) with an IGMPv3-capable application and send to that group. Verify (S,G) state toward S without an RP. Joining the group with a different source does not request the original source’s stream. Check application and platform support if the source-specific join fails.

For each fault document timestamps, observations at two points, a hypothesis, the repair, and restored baseline. If the IIF and OIL are correct but traffic is missing, inspect TTL, ACLs, MTU, egress counters and receiver socket state. Remove the stream and revert lab configuration afterward.

title: Policy Routing: Table Order, Throw and Blackhole
text:
Policy Routing: Table Order, Throw and Blackhole
A router can have the correct specific route and still choose a different path because a policy rule looks up another table first. This lab separates rule order from longest-prefix matching within a table. Linux commands provide a reproducible example; other platforms implement policy differently.

title: Policy Routing: Table Order, Throw and Blackhole
text:
Objectives and requirements
Predict a lookup with two tables, make an exception using a throw route, compare it with a blackhole, and explain why neither a route lookup nor a dummy interface proves end-to-end delivery. You need Linux, iproute2, unshare, and permission to create user and network namespaces. No external interfaces or installed routing daemons are used. Systems that disable unprivileged user namespaces or lack the dummy driver cannot run this form. Do not execute the setup in your normal host namespace.
The following commands were checked on Linux with iproute2 7.3.0 inside unshare -rn; exact output and UID vary. The addresses are documentation addresses. Dummy interfaces discard transmitted packets: these are route lookup tests, not connectivity tests.

title: Policy Routing: Table Order, Throw and Blackhole
text:
Build an isolated router
Start a shell inside a new user and network namespace; all subsequent commands in this lab run inside that shell. Exit it to remove these temporary interfaces and routes. A new namespace has its own routing tables and loopback; it does not carry your host’s interfaces or routes.
unshare -rn bash
ip link set lo up
ip link add name uplinkA type dummy
ip link add name uplinkB type dummy
ip link set uplinkA up
ip link set uplinkB up
ip addr add 192.0.2.10/32 dev lo

# Main table: a specific destination via B.
ip route add 203.0.113.0/24 dev uplinkB
# Policy table: a default via A for packets with this source.
ip route add default dev uplinkA table 100
ip rule add priority 100 from 192.0.2.10/32 lookup 100

ip rule show
ip route show table 100
ip route show table main
The built-in local rule normally has priority 0, the new rule has priority 100, and the main-table rule normally has priority 32766. Lower numbers are evaluated first. Local-address handling can therefore take precedence over the new rule. 192.0.2.10 is assigned to loopback to give the lookup a valid local source; the destination is not local.

title: Policy Routing: Table Order, Throw and Blackhole
text:
Predict before looking
Will a packet from 192.0.2.10 to 203.0.113.7 select A’s default or B’s /24? Run:
ip route get 203.0.113.7 from 192.0.2.10
On the test host the result contained dev uplinkA table 100. The source rule reaches table 100 first; its default is a successful lookup, so the main table’s more-specific route is not compared with it. Longest-prefix match applies inside the table consulted, not across every table in the system.

title: Policy Routing: Table Order, Throw and Blackhole
text:
Add a controlled exception
ip route add throw 203.0.113.0/24 table 100
ip route get 203.0.113.7 from 192.0.2.10
ip route get 198.51.100.7 from 192.0.2.10
For 203.0.113.7, the /24 throw route beats table 100’s default and makes that table’s lookup behave as if no route was found. Rule processing continues to the main table, which selects uplinkB. The unrelated destination still selects uplinkA through table 100’s default. A throw does not send traffic out an interface, and fallback works only if a later rule finds a usable route.

title: Policy Routing: Table Order, Throw and Blackhole
text:
Replace throw with a blackhole
ip route replace blackhole 203.0.113.0/24 table 100
ip route get 203.0.113.7 from 192.0.2.10
The test host reported RTNETLINK answers: Invalid argument. The selected blackhole is a terminal discard, not a request to continue to the main table. Error text and behavior exposed to local applications depend on route type and tools; do not treat this message as proof of remote packet delivery. A prohibit or unreachable route is also a terminal decision with different error behavior.
Restore the lookup and remove the policy rule:
ip route del blackhole 203.0.113.0/24 table 100
ip rule del priority 100
ip route get 203.0.113.7 from 192.0.2.10
exit
The final lookup selects uplinkB in the main table. Exiting the namespace shell cleans up the lab, provided no other process remains in it.

title: Policy Routing: Table Order, Throw and Blackhole
text:
Troubleshoot and extend

A lookup selects A when B has the more-specific route: inspect ip rule show and each table in priority order, not only ip route show without a table argument.
A throw does not reach B: check for later matching rules, a main-table route and the lookup’s actual source. A throw with no later usable route ends in failure.
ip route get reports the selected route for the supplied lookup keys; it does not transmit a test packet, prove neighbor resolution, test filtering, or validate a return path. For forwarded traffic, include the appropriate input interface and other policy selectors when modeling a lookup, and validate with real endpoints and captures.
Add a more-specific route in table 100 and predict which entry wins there. Remove it before exiting. Repeat with another source address assigned to loopback and explain why the source rule does not match it.

Sources: Linux ip-rule manual and ip-route manual. For the broader model, see Policy Routing and VRF.

title: Address Planning, VLSM and Summary Failure
text:
Address Planning, VLSM and Summary Failure
Design an address plan before configuring devices. This exercise uses only paper and Python’s standard library; no network privileges or device image are required. It covers allocation, overlap, summarization and the difference between address ownership and actual reachability. The plan is an arithmetic example, not an allocation for deployment.

title: Address Planning, VLSM and Summary Failure
text:
Requirements
A site receives IPv4 192.0.2.0/23 and IPv6 2001:db8:abcd:1200::/56 for this exercise. The site needs four IPv4 LANs with space for 100, 50, 25 and 10 assigned addresses, including gateways, plus a numbered point-to-point link with two endpoints. Leave the remaining space unallocated. Give each LAN an IPv6 /64; reserve room for growth. Assume ordinary IPv4 subnet addressing for LANs and /31 support at both ends of the point-to-point link. In a real deployment, use space allocated to the organization: the IPv4 parent includes 192.0.3.0/24, which is not reserved for documentation; do not use this parent in a network without authorization.
For the IPv4 LANs, select the smallest subnet with enough usable addresses. Allocate larger blocks first on valid boundaries. Identify network, first and last usable address and broadcast; do not reserve the first host automatically for a gateway unless your design says so. For /31, both addresses are point-to-point endpoints under RFC 3021; there is no directed subnet broadcast.

title: Address Planning, VLSM and Summary Failure
text:
One valid answer



Use
IPv4 prefix
Usable range or endpoints
Broadcast




LAN A, 100
192.0.2.0/25
.1–.126
.127


LAN B, 50
192.0.2.128/26
.129–.190
.191


LAN C, 25
192.0.2.192/27
.193–.222
.223


LAN D, 10
192.0.2.224/28
.225–.238
.239


Point-to-point
192.0.2.240/31
.240 and .241
none



A /25 contains 128 addresses, 126 conventionally usable; /26, /27, and /28 have 62, 30, and 14. The parent /23 runs from 192.0.2.0 through 192.0.3.255. The unallocated space includes .242–.255 in 192.0.2.0/24 and all of 192.0.3.0/24; its exact representation as aligned prefixes takes more than one block. Do not equate spare capacity with an already configured subnet.
For IPv6, the /56 fixes the first three hextets and the first two hexadecimal digits of the fourth. Its 256 /64s run from 2001:db8:abcd:1200::/64 through 2001:db8:abcd:12ff::/64. Allocate 1200, 1201, 1202, and 1203 to the LANs; leave the rest reserved for growth. IPv6 has no broadcast address. A /64 is a normal choice for LANs using SLAAC; do not assume an end site is always assigned a /48 or that every link type uses /64.

title: Address Planning, VLSM and Summary Failure
text:
Verify the plan
Save as check-plan.py and run python3 check-plan.py. The assertions check parent membership, capacity, pairwise overlap, and IPv6 subnet boundaries. They do not prove address ownership or that a device is reachable.
from ipaddress import ip_address, ip_network
from itertools import combinations

parent4 = ip_network('192.0.2.0/23')
allocations = {
    'A': ('192.0.2.0/25', 100),
    'B': ('192.0.2.128/26', 50),
    'C': ('192.0.2.192/27', 25),
    'D': ('192.0.2.224/28', 10),
    'link': ('192.0.2.240/31', 2),
}
blocks = {name: ip_network(prefix) for name, (prefix, _) in allocations.items()}
for name, net in blocks.items():
    required = allocations[name][1]
    usable = net.num_addresses if net.prefixlen == 31 else net.num_addresses - 2
    assert net.subnet_of(parent4) and usable >= required, name
    print(name, net, 'usable:', usable)
for (a, x), (b, y) in combinations(blocks.items(), 2):
    assert not x.overlaps(y), (a, b)

parent6 = ip_network('2001:db8:abcd:1200::/56')
lans6 = [ip_network(f'2001:db8:abcd:{0x1200+i:x}::/64') for i in range(4)]
assert parent6.num_addresses // lans6[0].num_addresses == 256
assert all(net.subnet_of(parent6) for net in lans6)
assert all(not x.overlaps(y) for x, y in combinations(lans6, 2))
print('IPv6 LANs:', ', '.join(map(str, lans6)))
assert ip_address('192.0.2.240') in blocks['link']
assert ip_address('192.0.2.241') in blocks['link']
print('Plan checks passed')
Fault injection: change B to 192.0.2.64/26. It overlaps A and the pairwise check fails. Restore B. Try 192.0.2.128/27: it has only 30 conventionally usable addresses and the capacity check fails. Restore the original plan before proceeding.

title: Address Planning, VLSM and Summary Failure
text:
Summary and failure drill
Suppose the site advertises 192.0.2.0/23 upstream and has specific internal routes for the five allocated blocks. Traffic to 192.0.2.25 can reach LAN A if its internal path and return path are working. Traffic to unallocated 192.0.3.8 still matches the summary upstream. A discard route for the aggregate at the site boundary can stop traffic for uncovered space from looping back to an upstream default, but deliberately drops that traffic; it does not make the destination reachable. More-specific active routes override that discard route in the same forwarding table.
Now remove LAN B’s specific route while keeping the summary and aggregate discard. Traffic to B falls into the discard unless another more-specific matching route exists. The upstream summary alone cannot signal this partial failure. If a summary is withdrawn only when its last component disappears, test both partial and complete failure and confirm the implementation’s actual behavior. If an address in the aggregate belongs behind another site, advertising the summary without a correct exception can attract traffic to the wrong place. Use a different allocation or coordinate specific routing and failure behavior.

title: Address Planning, VLSM and Summary Failure
text:
Check yourself

Why does 192.0.2.64/26 overlap A, even though it has a different prefix length?
What are the two endpoints of 192.0.2.240/31 and why is this exception unsuitable to assume for a shared LAN?
How many /64s fit in a /56? What is the final /64 in this exercise?
Why can a summary be present upstream while one component is unreachable?
What evidence besides the script is needed before assigning production addresses?

References: CIDR, RFC 4632, IPv4 /31 point-to-point links, RFC 3021, and IPv6 end-site assignment, RFC 6177.

title: Build a Router and Break the Return Path
text:
Build a Router and Break the Return Path
A successful forward lookup does not prove that a reply can return. Build two hosts and a router from isolated Linux network namespaces, then deliberately remove the receiver’s route back. This lab uses Linux as an implementation of vendor-neutral forwarding concepts.

title: Build a Router and Break the Return Path
text:
Prerequisites and topology
You need Linux with user and network namespaces enabled, veth support, Bash, ip, nsenter, unshare, sysctl, and ping. Some systems disable unprivileged user namespaces. Run the script only through the unshare -rn command shown below: it enables forwarding in the new router network namespace, not on your host. The script was tested with Linux and iproute2 7.3.0; timings and ping output vary.



Node
Interface
Address
Gateway




H1
c1
10.10.1.10/24
10.10.1.1


Router
r1
10.10.1.1/24
directly connected


Router
r2
10.10.2.1/24
directly connected


H2
c2
10.10.2.10/24
10.10.2.1



A veth pair acts like a virtual cable. The shell’s isolated network namespace is the router; two background processes hold the host namespaces open. The router’s connected routes are created by assigning its interface addresses. The host default routes send remote traffic to the router; they do not describe the return direction on the other host.

title: Build a Router and Break the Return Path
text:
Run the experiment
Save the following as forwarding-lab.sh and execute exactly unshare -rn bash forwarding-lab.sh. The trap terminates the background namespace holders on normal exit or error. This uses disposable namespaces, not persistent named namespaces. Avoid killing the outer process with SIGKILL, which cannot run the cleanup trap; if interrupted abnormally, terminate any remaining sleep 300 children belonging to your lab.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 300 & h1=$!
unshare -n sleep 300 & h2=$!
trap 'kill "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2

ip link add r1 type veth peer name c1
ip link add r2 type veth peer name c2
ip link set c1 netns "$h1"
ip link set c2 netns "$h2"
ip link set lo up
ip addr add 10.10.1.1/24 dev r1
ip addr add 10.10.2.1/24 dev r2
ip link set r1 up
ip link set r2 up

nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip addr add 10.10.1.10/24 dev c1
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set c1 up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip route add default via 10.10.1.1
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip addr add 10.10.2.10/24 dev c2
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set c2 up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip route add default via 10.10.2.1

sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
printf '\nBaseline routes and ping\n'
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip route get 10.10.2.10
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip route get 10.10.1.10
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.10.2.10

printf '\nRemove H2 return route; ping should fail\n'
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip route del default
if nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip route get 10.10.1.10; then
  echo 'Unexpected return route' >&2; exit 1
fi
if nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.10.2.10; then
  echo 'Unexpected ping success' >&2; exit 1
fi

printf '\nRestore H2 return route\n'
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip route add default via 10.10.2.1
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.10.2.10
printf 'Baseline restored.\n'
A normal run shows a successful ping, a missing H2 route and failed ping, then a successful ping after restoration. On the test host the first response had TTL 63: one router decremented the reply’s initial TTL of 64. Initial TTL is a host setting, not a universal constant. The fault deliberately removes only H2’s default; the router still has both directly connected routes.

title: Build a Router and Break the Return Path
text:
Trace the packet

H1 sees 10.10.2.10 is outside 10.10.1.0/24; it selects the default via 10.10.1.1 and resolves the gateway’s Ethernet address with ARP.
The router receives the IP packet, decrements TTL and selects the connected 10.10.2.0/24 route. It resolves H2 on r2 and sends a new Ethernet frame. Source and destination IP addresses remain H1 and H2; link-layer addresses change at the router.
H2 receives the echo request. With its default removed, it has no route to 10.10.1.10, so it cannot send the echo reply. The failed ping alone does not prove the exact loss location: the H2 route lookup provides separate evidence of this fault.
Restoring the gateway gives H2 a route for the reply. H1 can receive the reply because its address is on its directly connected LAN.

A route lookup alone does not prove that ARP, a firewall or a remote application works. To confirm actual packet arrival at H2 in a larger lab, capture ICMP on its ingress interface or compare interface/ICMP counters, then inspect the return route and egress traffic. Check both directions when diagnosing a real network.

title: Build a Router and Break the Return Path
text:
Further drills
Modify a copy of the script to set net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 after the successful baseline, verify that forwarding fails while the router’s interface addresses remain present, then re-enable it and retest. Changing ip_forward resets several IPv4 parameters to host/router defaults, so apply any custom sysctls after the change. As a separate experiment, break H1’s default route and distinguish a local route lookup failure from the missing return path. Predict each outcome before running it, and keep the cleanup trap.
References: Linux network namespaces, veth, and Linux IPv4 sysctls.

title: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and an ICMPv6 Filter Failure
text:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and an ICMPv6 Filter Failure
IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery (ND) to resolve a next hop’s link-layer address and maintain reachability. Blocking Neighbor Solicitations can make a directly connected destination unreachable even when both interfaces have IPv6 addresses and the route is present. This isolated Linux lab demonstrates the failure and the evidence needed to distinguish it from a missing route.

title: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and an ICMPv6 Filter Failure
text:
Prerequisites and topology
You need Linux, Bash, ip, nft, nsenter, unshare, ping, veth support and permission to create user/network namespaces and nftables rules. Some hosts restrict these capabilities. The first shell becomes node A; a child namespace is node B. a0 and b0 are opposite ends of a veth cable. A is fd42:1::1/64, B is fd42:1::2/64. These ULA addresses are for this isolated experiment; generate a suitable unique prefix for a real site.
Run the script through unshare -rn as shown. Its firewall rule exists only in A’s new network namespace. Do not run the script directly on the host, where it would create interfaces and alter host firewall state. The lab was tested on Linux with iproute2 7.3.0; packet counts and neighbor states vary with timing.

title: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and an ICMPv6 Filter Failure
text:
Run the fault and repair
Save the script as nd-lab.sh, then run unshare -rn bash nd-lab.sh. The trap stops the namespace holder on exit; avoid SIGKILL, which cannot execute the trap. The two nodad flags keep setup brief and deterministic here; they disable Duplicate Address Detection for these lab addresses and are not a general operational recommendation.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 60 & h=$!
trap 'kill "$h" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$h" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link add name a0 type veth peer name b0
ip link set b0 netns "$h"
ip link set lo up
ip link set a0 up
ip -6 addr add fd42:1::1/64 dev a0 nodad
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip link set b0 up
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip -6 addr add fd42:1::2/64 dev b0 nodad

printf '\nBaseline route and ping\n'
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip -6 route get fd42:1::1
nsenter -t "$h" -n ping -6 -c 1 -W 1 fd42:1::1
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip -6 neigh show dev b0

printf '\nDrop solicitations arriving at A and clear B cache\n'
nft add table ip6 ndlab
nft 'add chain ip6 ndlab input { type filter hook input priority 0; policy accept; }'
nft add rule ip6 ndlab input icmpv6 type nd-neighbor-solicit counter drop
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip -6 neigh flush dev b0
if nsenter -t "$h" -n ping -6 -c 1 -W 2 fd42:1::1; then
  echo 'Unexpected ping success' >&2; exit 1
fi
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip -6 route get fd42:1::1
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip -6 neigh show dev b0
nft list chain ip6 ndlab input

printf '\nRemove the fault and retry\n'
nft delete table ip6 ndlab
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip -6 neigh flush dev b0
nsenter -t "$h" -n ping -6 -c 1 -W 2 fd42:1::1
nsenter -t "$h" -n ip -6 neigh show dev b0
printf 'Connectivity restored.\n'
Baseline ping succeeds. With the rule in place and B’s cached entry cleared, B still has an on-link route, but its Neighbor Solicitations arriving at A are dropped. The test host showed an unsuccessful ping and a positive nftables drop counter; the neighbor entry can show INCOMPLETE or FAILED depending on observation time. Removing the rule and flushing the failed entry permits a fresh resolution and the ping succeeds. A successful send or a route lookup does not prove neighbor resolution or packet delivery.

title: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and an ICMPv6 Filter Failure
text:
Explain what happened
B determines that A is on link, then sends a Neighbor Solicitation to A’s solicited-node multicast group to learn its link-layer address. A normally replies with a Neighbor Advertisement. With the fault, A’s input chain discards the solicitation before normal ND processing. A cached neighbor entry can temporarily mask the problem, which is why the lab clears B’s entry after installing the filter. Neighbor entries normally move through states as traffic and reachability confirmation change; STALE alone is not evidence of failure.
This rule intentionally blocks only incoming Neighbor Solicitations at A. It does not demonstrate every ICMPv6 failure and should not be copied into a real firewall. ICMPv6 also carries essential errors such as Packet Too Big for path MTU discovery; blanket blocking can cause failures that look like broken applications or large-packet black holes. Filter according to role and scope, preserving necessary control traffic; see the ICMPv6 recommendations below.

title: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and an ICMPv6 Filter Failure
text:
Extend and investigate

Repeat without clearing the cache immediately after adding the rule. Does traffic continue temporarily? Compare B’s neighbor state and rule counter; cache timers and upper-layer reachability confirmation influence the result.
Use an authorized packet capture on a0 or b0 to compare the solicitation and advertisement before and during the fault. Record interfaces and direction: an ingress capture can observe a packet that the firewall later drops.
Repeat the lab without nodad, allow tentative addresses time to complete DAD, and inspect the address state before testing. Compare with the DAD exercise.
Explain why an installed connected route, an up interface and a successful local address assignment are each insufficient to prove that a remote application is reachable.

References: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, RFC 4861, ICMPv6 filtering recommendations, RFC 4890, and IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration, RFC 4862.

title: VLAN Access Membership: Build, Break and Repair
text:
VLAN Access Membership: Build, Break and Repair
Two hosts can have addresses in the same IPv4 subnet and still be unable to exchange frames if their access ports belong to different VLANs. In this lab a Linux VLAN-aware bridge models an Ethernet switch. You will inspect membership and MAC learning, move a port to another VLAN, and restore it. The concepts apply broadly; configuration and hardware counters vary by switch.

title: VLAN Access Membership: Build, Break and Repair
text:
Prerequisites and plan
You need Linux, Bash, unshare, nsenter, ip, bridge, ping, and permission to create user/network namespaces and veth interfaces. The kernel must support VLAN-filtering bridges. Some hosts disable unprivileged user namespaces. Run only through unshare -rn, so the bridge and interfaces are isolated from the host network. The lab was tested with iproute2 7.3.0; MAC addresses, timings and neighbor states vary.



Endpoint
Address
Bridge port
Baseline access VLAN




H1
10.44.10.1/24
p1
10


H2
10.44.10.2/24
p2
10



Each host connects to a bridge port through a veth pair. The host sends untagged frames. The port VLAN ID (PVID) classifies untagged ingress into a VLAN; the untagged flag removes the VLAN tag on egress for that membership. The bridge uses VLAN and destination MAC when forwarding. This is an access-port lab, not a tagged trunk; it does not run STP or model a hardware ASIC.

title: VLAN Access Membership: Build, Break and Repair
text:
Run the lab
Save as vlan-lab.sh and run unshare -rn bash vlan-lab.sh. The shell’s network namespace contains the bridge; two short-lived background processes hold the host namespaces. The trap cleans up on normal exit or error. Avoid SIGKILL, which cannot run the trap; after an abnormal termination, stop any remaining lab sleep 60 children.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 60 & h1=$!
unshare -n sleep 60 & h2=$!
trap 'kill "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2

ip link add name br0 type bridge vlan_filtering 1 vlan_default_pvid 0
ip link add name p1 type veth peer name h1e
ip link add name p2 type veth peer name h2e
ip link set h1e netns "$h1"
ip link set h2e netns "$h2"
ip link set p1 master br0
ip link set p2 master br0
bridge vlan add dev p1 vid 10 pvid untagged
bridge vlan add dev p2 vid 10 pvid untagged
ip link set br0 up
ip link set p1 up
ip link set p2 up

nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip addr add 10.44.10.1/24 dev h1e
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set h1e up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip addr add 10.44.10.2/24 dev h2e
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set h2e up

printf '\nBaseline: both access ports in VLAN 10\n'
bridge vlan show
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.44.10.2
bridge fdb show br br0

printf '\nFault: move p2 to VLAN 20\n'
bridge vlan del dev p2 vid 10
bridge vlan add dev p2 vid 20 pvid untagged
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip neigh flush dev h1e
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip neigh flush dev h2e
bridge vlan show
if nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 2 10.44.10.2; then
  echo 'Unexpected connectivity across separate VLANs' >&2; exit 1
fi
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip neigh show dev h1e

printf '\nRepair: restore p2 to VLAN 10\n'
bridge vlan del dev p2 vid 20
bridge vlan add dev p2 vid 10 pvid untagged
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip neigh flush dev h1e
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip neigh flush dev h2e
bridge vlan show
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 2 10.44.10.2
printf 'Baseline restored.\n'
The baseline and repaired pings succeed on the test host. During the fault, the port listing shows p1 in VLAN 10 and p2 in VLAN 20, and the ping fails. H1 considers H2 on-link and sends ARP requests, but the bridge does not flood VLAN 10 frames out a port that belongs only to VLAN 20. A neighbor can appear INCOMPLETE or FAILED depending on timing. A failed ping alone cannot prove a VLAN mismatch; the membership listing is separate evidence.
vlan_default_pvid 0 prevents an implicit default PVID from admitting untagged traffic before the explicit assignments. The FDB includes learned and permanent entries; inspect the device, VLAN and entry type rather than counting every entry as a learned host. The host neighbor cache is deliberately flushed to make the ARP failure visible; in a real network cache state can affect timing and symptoms.

title: VLAN Access Membership: Build, Break and Repair
text:
Extend the experiment

Remove p2’s VLAN membership without assigning a replacement PVID. Predict what happens to its untagged ingress traffic, inspect bridge vlan show, then restore VLAN 10.
Put both ports into VLAN 20 without changing IP addresses. They can again communicate at Layer 2 because they share a VLAN; the IP subnet number does not automatically select a VLAN. Restore the baseline afterward.
Add a third host in VLAN 20, with an appropriate separate subnet, and prove isolation. Routing between VLANs requires a router or Layer 3 switch and explicit addressing and policy; it is not provided by the bridge here.
Compare this access-port failure with the tagged trunk lab. A mismatched native/PVID configuration across switches can also leak traffic into an unintended VLAN; loss is not the only possible symptom.

Record the topology, expected result, VLAN table, FDB, neighbor state, fault and repair. End-to-end connectivity after repair is necessary evidence; it does not prove every VLAN, trunk or security policy is correct.
References: Linux bridge documentation and bridge(8) VLAN options.

title: Tagged Trunk: A Missing VLAN and an Unaffected Control
text:
Tagged Trunk: A Missing VLAN and an Unaffected Control
An inter-switch link can remain physically up and carry one VLAN while silently excluding another. Build two VLAN-aware Linux bridges, put a host in each of VLANs 10 and 20 at each end, then remove VLAN 10 from one trunk endpoint. This extends VLAN Access Membership from one bridge to two. The concepts are vendor-neutral; the commands demonstrate one Linux implementation.

title: Tagged Trunk: A Missing VLAN and an Unaffected Control
text:
Plan and prerequisites



Host
Bridge / port
VLAN
Address




H1
br1 / p1
10
10.44.10.1/24


H2
br2 / p2
10
10.44.10.2/24


H3
br1 / p3
20
10.44.20.1/24


H4
br2 / p4
20
10.44.20.2/24



br1:t1 and br2:t2 are the two ends of one veth cable. Both carry VLANs 10 and 20 as tagged members. Each host-facing bridge port uses its VLAN as PVID and emits untagged frames. The bridges have no default PVID and do not route between VLANs. The topology has a single inter-bridge link; no redundant loop or spanning-tree exercise is implied.
You need Linux, Bash, unshare, nsenter, ip, bridge, ping, user/network namespace permission, veth support and VLAN-aware Linux bridges. Some hosts restrict these capabilities. Run only in the isolated user and network namespace below; do not create this bridge or modify interfaces on a production host. The script was tested with iproute2 7.3.0; timings and MAC addresses vary.

title: Tagged Trunk: A Missing VLAN and an Unaffected Control
text:
Build, break and restore
Save as trunk-lab.sh and run unshare -rn bash trunk-lab.sh. Four background processes hold host namespaces; the trap stops them on exit. Avoid SIGKILL, which cannot run cleanup. If the parent terminates abnormally, stop any remaining lab sleep 90 children. The experiment does not rely on Docker or hardware switch images.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 90 & h1=$!
unshare -n sleep 90 & h2=$!
unshare -n sleep 90 & h3=$!
unshare -n sleep 90 & h4=$!
trap 'kill "$h1" "$h2" "$h3" "$h4" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$h1" "$h2" "$h3" "$h4" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link add br1 type bridge vlan_filtering 1 vlan_default_pvid 0
ip link add br2 type bridge vlan_filtering 1 vlan_default_pvid 0
ip link add t1 type veth peer name t2
ip link set t1 master br1
ip link set t2 master br2
bridge vlan add dev t1 vid 10
bridge vlan add dev t1 vid 20
bridge vlan add dev t2 vid 10
bridge vlan add dev t2 vid 20
ip link set br1 up
ip link set br2 up
ip link set t1 up
ip link set t2 up
setup_host() {
  pid=$1; port=$2; hostif=$3; br=$4; vid=$5; addr=$6
  ip link add "$port" type veth peer name "$hostif"
  ip link set "$hostif" netns "$pid"
  ip link set "$port" master "$br"
  bridge vlan add dev "$port" vid "$vid" pvid untagged
  ip link set "$port" up
  nsenter -t "$pid" -n ip link set lo up
  nsenter -t "$pid" -n ip addr add "$addr" dev "$hostif"
  nsenter -t "$pid" -n ip link set "$hostif" up
}
setup_host "$h1" p1 h1e br1 10 10.44.10.1/24
setup_host "$h2" p2 h2e br2 10 10.44.10.2/24
setup_host "$h3" p3 h3e br1 20 10.44.20.1/24
setup_host "$h4" p4 h4e br2 20 10.44.20.2/24
bridge vlan show
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.44.10.2
nsenter -t "$h3" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.44.20.2
bridge vlan del dev t2 vid 10
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip neigh flush dev h1e
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip neigh flush dev h2e
bridge vlan show dev t2
if nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 2 10.44.10.2; then exit 1; fi
nsenter -t "$h3" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.44.20.2
bridge vlan add dev t2 vid 10
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip neigh flush dev h1e
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip neigh flush dev h2e
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 2 10.44.10.2
The baseline membership listing shows both VLANs on t1 and t2 without the Egress Untagged flag, and the access ports with PVID Egress Untagged. Both test pings succeed. After VLAN 10 is removed from t2, its listing shows VLAN 20 but no VLAN 10: H1 to H2 fails while H3 to H4 still works. Restoring VLAN 10 restores H1-to-H2 connectivity. Flushes of H1 and H2 neighbor entries make the ARP phase observable rather than depending on cache timing. A ping loss proves a symptom, not its cause; compare membership, counters, FDB and captures at both ends.

title: Tagged Trunk: A Missing VLAN and an Unaffected Control
text:
Follow the frame
H1 sends an untagged ARP request. p1 classifies it into VLAN 10; br1 can forward it out t1 with an 802.1Q VLAN 10 tag. br2 accepts it on t2 only while t2 permits VLAN 10, then sends it untagged out p2. H2 replies through the reverse path. When t2 no longer permits VLAN 10, that VLAN cannot traverse this link even though t1, t2 and VLAN 20 remain operational. The test does not simulate a physical cable break.
If supported, capture on t1 and t2 with a VLAN-aware packet analyzer to observe the tag. Interface offload and capture location can alter how tags appear; a capture on a host access interface generally sees untagged traffic. Inspect bridge fdb show br br1 and bridge fdb show br br2 after traffic to relate learned source MACs to ports and VLANs. Stale entries can persist after a change; do not infer current reachability from an old FDB entry alone.

title: Tagged Trunk: A Missing VLAN and an Unaffected Control
text:
Practice

Remove VLAN 20 from t1 instead, leaving VLAN 10 present. Predict and verify which flow fails; restore it.
Remove VLAN 10 from both trunk ends and compare the listings with the one-sided fault. Do not confuse the absence of a VLAN with a down physical link.
Examine the PVID/untagged configuration before designing a native-VLAN test. A mismatch can put untagged traffic into the wrong VLAN and cause leakage as well as loss. Test it only in an isolated topology and document intended versus observed VLAN at each end.
Explain why this lab needs a router to exchange IP traffic between the two VLANs. Add that routing in a separate topology and verify policy and the reverse path.

References: Linux bridge documentation and bridge VLAN options.

title: Stateful Filtering: Direction, Counters and Return Traffic
text:
Stateful Filtering: Direction, Counters and Return Traffic
A firewall rule must identify where packets enter and leave, not merely the service name. In this lab H1 may initiate IPv4 echo requests to H2; H2 may reply but may not initiate a new echo request to H1. Removing the return-state rule demonstrates why permitting only the forward packet is insufficient. Linux nftables implements the exercise; the reasoning applies to stateful firewalls generally.

title: Stateful Filtering: Direction, Counters and Return Traffic
text:
Prerequisites and policy
Complete Build a Router and Break the Return Path first. This self-contained script recreates that topology: H1 10.10.1.10/24, router r1 10.10.1.1/24, router r2 10.10.2.1/24, H2 10.10.2.10/24. Both hosts have default routes through the router. The forward chain filters packets passing through the router; traffic addressed to the router itself traverses a different hook and is not protected by this lab’s forward chain.
You need Linux, Bash, unshare, nsenter, ip, nft, sysctl, ping, veth and conntrack/nftables kernel support, and permission to create user/network namespaces. Some environments prohibit these operations. Run the script only using unshare -rn: it creates a firewall table and enables forwarding inside a new isolated network namespace. Never run it directly against host interfaces or a production ruleset. The cleanup trap stops the namespace holders; avoid SIGKILL, which bypasses the trap. The example was tested with iproute2 7.3.0; counters and timing vary.
The policy is deliberately narrow: permit H1’s ICMP echo request to H2, allow established/related traffic, and drop other forwarded IPv4 traffic. This is a demonstration, not a complete firewall policy. In particular, a general established/related rule can allow traffic beyond this one echo reply; a production policy needs an explicit design for its zones, protocols, IPv6, management plane and state handling.

title: Stateful Filtering: Direction, Counters and Return Traffic
text:
Run the experiment
Save as acl-lab.sh and run unshare -rn bash acl-lab.sh:
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 300 & h1=$!
unshare -n sleep 300 & h2=$!
trap 'kill "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link add r1 type veth peer name c1
ip link add r2 type veth peer name c2
ip link set c1 netns "$h1"
ip link set c2 netns "$h2"
ip link set lo up
ip addr add 10.10.1.1/24 dev r1
ip addr add 10.10.2.1/24 dev r2
ip link set r1 up
ip link set r2 up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip addr add 10.10.1.10/24 dev c1
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set c1 up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip route add default via 10.10.1.1
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip addr add 10.10.2.10/24 dev c2
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set c2 up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip route add default via 10.10.2.1
sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
nft add table ip acllab
nft 'add chain ip acllab forward { type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop; }'
nft add rule ip acllab forward ct state established,related counter accept
nft add rule ip acllab forward iifname r1 oifname r2 ip saddr 10.10.1.10 ip daddr 10.10.2.10 icmp type echo-request counter accept
nft add rule ip acllab forward counter drop
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.10.2.10
if nsenter -t "$h2" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.10.1.10; then echo unexpected; exit 1; fi
nft -a list chain ip acllab forward
nft flush chain ip acllab forward
nft add rule ip acllab forward iifname r1 oifname r2 ip saddr 10.10.1.10 ip daddr 10.10.2.10 icmp type echo-request counter accept
nft add rule ip acllab forward counter drop
if nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.10.2.10; then echo unexpected; exit 1; fi
nft list chain ip acllab forward
nft insert rule ip acllab forward ct state established,related counter accept
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 1 10.10.2.10
nft delete table ip acllab
Expected sequence: H1’s first ping succeeds; H2’s new reverse ping fails. The first counter shows a reply matched established/related, the second shows an H1 request accepted, and the final counter shows a dropped packet. After the chain is replaced with only the request permit and a drop, H1’s next ping fails: the request counter rises, but the reply has no matching permit and reaches the drop counter. Inserting the state rule at the beginning restores H1’s ping. Exact counts depend on other traffic and timing.
The test removes only its own ip acllab table. No NAT is configured. The isolated router still needs working routes and IPv4 forwarding; a stateful firewall cannot repair a missing return route. Conntrack associates the ICMP reply with the request in this experiment. Do not assume that every related flow, fragment or ICMP error is treated identically by all implementations.

title: Stateful Filtering: Direction, Counters and Return Traffic
text:
Interpret and extend

Trace an H1 request through iif r1 and oif r2, then its reply in the reverse direction. Why would a rule permitting only an echo request not admit the echo reply?
Compare the first nft -a list counters with the listing after the chain is replaced. Rule handles and counters change when rules are recreated; they are not a permanent audit history.
Move a broad drop above the permit in a disposable copy and predict the result. Rules in this chain are evaluated in order; a terminal verdict stops evaluation. Restore the original order and retest.
Add an explicit stateless echo-reply permit instead of the state rule in a separate isolated run. Specify source, destination and interface direction carefully. Explain why a broad reverse permit is not equivalent to allowing only replies to legitimate initiated flows.
Compare forward traffic with a probe addressed to the router itself. The latter does not traverse this forward chain. Design and test a separate management-plane policy rather than assuming this lab’s rules protect it.

A rule counter identifies a matching packet, not a successful end-to-end transaction. Capture at the relevant interfaces, check routing and neighbor resolution, observe both directions, and test representative application traffic. The lab’s expected denial of H2 initiation is not proof that all unsolicited protocols are blocked on a real firewall.
References: nftables manual, connection tracking sysctls, and ACL Thinking.

title: Source NAT: Observe the Translation and Return Path
text:
Source NAT: Observe the Translation and Return Path
Source NAT changes the source address seen by a remote endpoint. Stateful NAT also maps matching reply packets back to the initiating host. Neither translation nor a successful rule counter proves that routing, filtering or the application is correct. This lab measures what the server actually sees, then repeats with a new flow after removing the translation rule.

title: Source NAT: Observe the Translation and Return Path
text:
Plan and prerequisites
H1 is 10.10.1.10/24, the router is 10.10.1.1/24 on r1 and 10.10.2.1/24 on r2, and H2 is 10.10.2.10/24. Each host uses its local router address as default gateway. H2 runs a UDP echo-like server that replies with the source IP it observed. The “outside” address is private here because both networks are isolated; this is a translation demonstration, not an Internet connection.
You need Linux, Bash, unshare, nsenter, ip, nft, sysctl, Python 3, veth and nftables NAT/connection-tracking support, plus permission to create user and network namespaces. Some systems restrict these capabilities. Run only with unshare -rn: the router, interfaces, forwarding setting and NAT rule are created in a disposable network namespace. Never run the script directly on the host. The script was tested on Linux with iproute2 7.3.0; port translation and counters vary.

title: Source NAT: Observe the Translation and Return Path
text:
Build and test
Save as nat-lab.sh and run unshare -rn bash nat-lab.sh. The child processes hold the host namespaces; the trap stops them and the temporary server on exit. Avoid SIGKILL, which cannot run the trap; after abnormal termination, stop any remaining lab sleep 300 or server children. The receiver uses a ten-second timeout; if the machine is heavily loaded, extend it and the namespace-holder duration in an isolated copy.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 300 & h1=$!
unshare -n sleep 300 & h2=$!
trap 'kill "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link add r1 type veth peer name c1
ip link add r2 type veth peer name c2
ip link set c1 netns "$h1"
ip link set c2 netns "$h2"
ip link set lo up
ip addr add 10.10.1.1/24 dev r1
ip addr add 10.10.2.1/24 dev r2
ip link set r1 up
ip link set r2 up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip addr add 10.10.1.10/24 dev c1
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set c1 up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip route add default via 10.10.1.1
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip addr add 10.10.2.10/24 dev c2
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set c2 up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip route add default via 10.10.2.1
sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
nsenter -t "$h2" -n python3 -u - <<'SERVER' &
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(('10.10.2.10', 9999))
s.settimeout(10)
for _ in range(2):
    data, peer = s.recvfrom(1024)
    s.sendto(peer[0].encode(), peer)
s.close()
SERVER
server=$!
trap 'kill "$server" "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$server" "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
nft add table ip natlab
nft 'add chain ip natlab post { type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; }'
nft add rule ip natlab post ip saddr 10.10.1.10 oifname r2 counter masquerade
nsenter -t "$h1" -n python3 - <<'CLIENT'
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(('10.10.1.10', 40001))
s.settimeout(3)
s.sendto(b'first', ('10.10.2.10', 9999))
seen = s.recv(1024).decode()
print('Server saw with NAT:', seen)
assert seen == '10.10.2.1'
CLIENT
nft list chain ip natlab post
nft delete table ip natlab
nsenter -t "$h1" -n python3 - <<'CLIENT'
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(('10.10.1.10', 40002))
s.settimeout(3)
s.sendto(b'second', ('10.10.2.10', 9999))
seen = s.recv(1024).decode()
print('Server saw without NAT:', seen)
assert seen == '10.10.1.10'
CLIENT
wait "$server"
The first assertion requires H2 to report 10.10.2.1: the router’s r2 address replaced H1’s source. H2 replies to that address and the connection-tracking NAT mapping delivers the reply to H1. The nftables rule counter should increment for the new flow; the exact packet count is not an end-to-end delivery counter.
After the NAT table is removed, the second client uses a different UDP source port to create a new flow. H2 reports 10.10.1.10 and can still reply because its default route points to the router. Stateful NAT chooses a binding for the first packet of a flow; later packets can continue using that binding even after a rule changes. A new tuple prevents an old mapping from misleading the comparison. Do not assume a rule edit immediately changes every existing session.

title: Source NAT: Observe the Translation and Return Path
text:
Trace and investigate

H1 routes the packet to 10.10.1.1. The router chooses r2 as the outgoing interface. Its postrouting rule matches H1’s source and masquerades it to r2’s address.
H2 sees the translated source. It replies to that source, and the router uses the connection mapping to reverse the translation before forwarding to H1. Source-port translation can also occur to avoid collisions; this lab asserts only the source address.
Without NAT, H2 sees H1’s original address. Its default route supplies the return path. If that route is removed, the unmodified reply fails even though the forward packet can arrive.
NAT is not a firewall policy. A separate filter can deny a translated or untranslated flow, and an accept rule in one chain does not necessarily override a later drop elsewhere. Inspect the relevant hooks, rules and counters.

Extend the isolated script with a third client flow after removing H2’s default route. Predict the difference between translated and untranslated traffic, verify the server’s observation and reply outcome, then restore the route. Use packet capture on both router interfaces or a connection-tracking tool if available to correlate original and translated tuples; do not rely on one counter or a single ping. Never flush a production connection table to make a test convenient.
References: Traditional NAT, RFC 3022, nftables NAT behavior, and nftables manual.

title: Destination NAT: Map a Service and Verify the Backend
text:
Destination NAT: Map a Service and Verify the Backend
A destination NAT (DNAT) rule can map a service address and port to a backend. The translated destination still needs a route, the forwarding policy must permit it, and replies must traverse the translation state. This lab compares a mapped UDP request, a new request after removing the mapping, and a direct backend control.

title: Destination NAT: Map a Service and Verify the Backend
text:
Plan and prerequisites
H1 10.10.1.10/24 is the client, router r1 is 10.10.1.1/24, router r2 is 10.10.2.1/24, and H2 10.10.2.10/24 runs a UDP service on port 9999. Hosts use their local router interface as default gateway. A rule on packets arriving at r1 maps 10.10.1.1:8080/UDP to 10.10.2.10:9999/UDP. Both addresses are private and exist only inside the lab; no public service is exposed.
You need Linux, Bash, unshare, nsenter, ip, nft, sysctl, Python 3, veth and nftables NAT/connection-tracking support, and permission to create user and network namespaces. Run the script only as unshare -rn bash dnat-lab.sh, never directly on the host: all interfaces, forwarding settings and firewall rules belong to the disposable namespace. Some environments restrict namespaces or kernel modules. The script was tested on Linux with iproute2 7.3.0; timing and counters vary.

title: Destination NAT: Map a Service and Verify the Backend
text:
Build and test
Save as dnat-lab.sh and run unshare -rn bash dnat-lab.sh. The trap stops the host-namespace holders and backend on normal exit or error. Avoid SIGKILL, which bypasses cleanup; after abnormal termination, stop any remaining lab sleep 300 or server children. The server waits at most ten seconds; on a heavily loaded machine increase the timeout in an isolated copy.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 300 & h1=$!
unshare -n sleep 300 & h2=$!
trap 'kill "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link add r1 type veth peer name c1
ip link add r2 type veth peer name c2
ip link set c1 netns "$h1"
ip link set c2 netns "$h2"
ip link set lo up
ip addr add 10.10.1.1/24 dev r1
ip addr add 10.10.2.1/24 dev r2
ip link set r1 up
ip link set r2 up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip addr add 10.10.1.10/24 dev c1
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set c1 up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip route add default via 10.10.1.1
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip addr add 10.10.2.10/24 dev c2
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set c2 up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip route add default via 10.10.2.1
sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
nsenter -t "$h2" -n python3 -u - <<'SERVER' &
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(('10.10.2.10', 9999))
s.settimeout(10)
for _ in range(2):
    data, peer = s.recvfrom(1024)
    s.sendto(b'backend-response', peer)
s.close()
SERVER
server=$!
trap 'kill "$server" "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$server" "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
nft add table ip dnatlab
nft 'add chain ip dnatlab pre { type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; }'
nft add rule ip dnatlab pre iifname r1 ip daddr 10.10.1.1 udp dport 8080 counter dnat to 10.10.2.10:9999
nsenter -t "$h1" -n python3 - <<'CLIENT'
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(('10.10.1.10', 40001))
s.settimeout(3)
s.sendto(b'hello', ('10.10.1.1', 8080))
data, peer = s.recvfrom(1024)
print('Received:', data.decode(), 'from', peer)
assert data == b'backend-response' and peer == ('10.10.1.1', 8080)
CLIENT
nft list chain ip dnatlab pre
nft delete table ip dnatlab
nsenter -t "$h1" -n python3 - <<'CLIENT'
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(('10.10.1.10', 40002))
s.settimeout(1)
s.sendto(b'no mapping', ('10.10.1.1', 8080))
try:
    data, peer = s.recvfrom(1024)
    raise AssertionError(f'unexpected response: {data!r} from {peer}')
except socket.timeout:
    print('New flow without mapping: timed out as expected')
CLIENT
kill -0 "$server"
nsenter -t "$h1" -n python3 - <<'CLIENT'
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.settimeout(3)
s.sendto(b'direct control', ('10.10.2.10', 9999))
data, peer = s.recvfrom(1024)
print('Direct backend control:', data.decode(), 'from', peer)
assert data == b'backend-response' and peer == ('10.10.2.10', 9999)
CLIENT
wait "$server"
First, H1 receives backend-response from the apparent service tuple 10.10.1.1:8080. The DNAT counter shows the initial request matched. After the NAT table is deleted, a new client tuple sent to the same address and port times out: the gateway has no listener at that port. The direct control then reaches 10.10.2.10:9999 while the backend is still running, proving basic backend reachability in this topology. The local unconnected UDP client observes a timeout; other clients or platforms may report an ICMP-derived error instead.

title: Destination NAT: Map a Service and Verify the Backend
text:
Follow both directions
The client sends toward the router’s r1 address. In the router’s prerouting NAT hook, the destination becomes 10.10.2.10:9999; the subsequent route lookup selects r2. The backend receives a packet from H1 and replies through its default gateway. Connection tracking applies the reverse translation so H1 sees the reply as coming from 10.10.1.1:8080. This result depends on the backend’s return route crossing the same translation state; asymmetric forwarding can break it.
Without the mapping, the destination remains the router’s local address and is not forwarded to H2. A different client source port makes the second request a new flow: existing state can retain a translation after a rule change. The direct-control request uses the backend address, and is possible here because H1 has a route through the lab router; Internet clients would require appropriate routing and policy to reach such an address.
DNAT does not by itself authorize the forwarded packet. A firewall may need an explicit permit and can evaluate original or translated tuples depending on hook and platform. Conversely, adding the mapping can make a service reachable when forwarding policy allows it. Validate the actual service, source restrictions, both directions and exposure before making any real change.

title: Destination NAT: Map a Service and Verify the Backend
text:
Failure drills

In an isolated copy, block forwarding to the backend while keeping the DNAT rule. Compare NAT and filter counters and backend capture: a NAT hit alone is not delivery.
Remove H2’s return route and repeat a fresh mapped flow. Observe the backend receiving the request and the client failing to get a reply; restore the route.
Change the mapped backend port to a non-listening port. Distinguish a correct mapping to the wrong service from a missing mapping using captures or counters.
Document the original and translated five-tuples, hook, rule counter, selected route, backend listener and return path. Do not flush a production connection table to perform these tests.

References: Traditional NAT, RFC 3022, nftables NAT, and the source NAT lab.

title: DHCPv4 on the Wire: A Minimal Isolated Exchange
text:
DHCPv4 on the Wire: A Minimal Isolated Exchange
Observe DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPOFFER, DHCPREQUEST and DHCPACK as actual UDP packets without installing a DHCP server. The deliberately small Python endpoints below demonstrate message layout and correlation on one isolated link. They are teaching code, not compliant general-purpose DHCP implementations: they do not configure the client address, maintain a real lease database, retransmit, renew, rebind, implement relay handling, or authenticate peers.

title: DHCPv4 on the Wire: A Minimal Isolated Exchange
text:
Lab boundary
You need Linux, Bash, Python 3, ip, unshare, nsenter, veth support and permission to create user and network namespaces. Some systems restrict these features or binding UDP ports 67 and 68. The test was run in an unprivileged user/network namespace; run only through unshare -rn, never on a shared LAN. Broadcast DHCP replies from a test server can disrupt real clients. A default route is added inside the isolated client namespace solely to select the veth interface for broadcasting; it is not a DHCP-installed route.
The server is 10.55.0.1/24 on s0, and the client connects through c0 with no configured IPv4 address. The server offers 10.55.0.100 with a 600-second lease value. The fixed transaction ID and client hardware field are synthetic, so captures are easy to correlate; they are not a unique identity or a security mechanism. Both endpoints use broadcast for this simplified exchange.

title: DHCPv4 on the Wire: A Minimal Isolated Exchange
text:
Save the protocol code
Save this file as dhcp_wire.py in a new working directory:
import socket, struct, sys
MAGIC = b'\x63\x82\x53\x63'
XID = 0x12345678
MAC = bytes.fromhex('020000000001')
SERVER = '10.55.0.1'
OFFER = '10.55.0.100'

def option(code, value):
    return bytes((code, len(value))) + value

def packet(op, msg_type, extra=b''):
    yiaddr = socket.inet_aton(OFFER if op == 2 else '0.0.0.0')
    hdr = struct.pack('!BBBBIHH4s4s4s4s16s64s128s', op, 1, 6, 0, XID, 0, 0x8000,
                      bytes(4), yiaddr, bytes(4), bytes(4), MAC.ljust(16, b'\0'), bytes(64), bytes(128))
    return hdr + MAGIC + option(53, bytes([msg_type])) + extra + b'\xff'

def parse(data):
    if len(data) < 240 or data[236:240] != MAGIC:
        raise ValueError('bad BOOTP header or cookie')
    xid = struct.unpack_from('!I', data, 4)[0]
    if xid != XID or data[28:34] != MAC:
        raise ValueError('unexpected client transaction')
    opts = {}; i = 240
    while i < len(data):
        code = data[i]; i += 1
        if code == 255: break
        if code == 0: continue
        if i >= len(data): raise ValueError('missing option length')
        n = data[i]; i += 1
        if i+n > len(data): raise ValueError('truncated option')
        opts[code] = data[i:i+n]; i += n
    return data[0], socket.inet_ntoa(data[16:20]), opts

s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BROADCAST, 1)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BINDTODEVICE, (sys.argv[2]+'\0').encode())
s.settimeout(5)
if sys.argv[1] == 'server':
    s.bind(('', 67))
    for expected, reply in ((1, 2), (3, 5)):
        data, peer = s.recvfrom(2048)
        op, yiaddr, opts = parse(data)
        assert op == 1 and opts[53] == bytes([expected])
        if expected == 3:
            assert opts[50] == socket.inet_aton(OFFER) and opts[54] == socket.inet_aton(SERVER)
        extra = option(54, socket.inet_aton(SERVER)) + option(51, struct.pack('!I', 600))
        s.sendto(packet(2, reply, extra), ('255.255.255.255', 68))
        print('server received', expected, 'sent', reply, flush=True)
else:
    s.bind(('', 68))
    for sent, expected in ((1, 2), (3, 5)):
        extra = b'' if sent == 1 else option(50, socket.inet_aton(OFFER)) + option(54, socket.inet_aton(SERVER))
        s.sendto(packet(1, sent, extra), ('255.255.255.255', 67))
        data, peer = s.recvfrom(2048)
        op, yiaddr, opts = parse(data)
        assert op == 2 and opts[53] == bytes([expected]) and yiaddr == OFFER
        assert opts[54] == socket.inet_aton(SERVER)
        print('client sent', sent, 'received', expected, 'yiaddr', yiaddr, flush=True)
s.close()
A BOOTP header is 236 bytes; the DHCP magic cookie follows, then length-delimited options. Here option 53 contains message type, option 54 identifies the selected server, option 50 names the requested address and option 51 carries a lease value. The parser validates lengths, transaction ID and the synthetic client field. It does not implement full RFC validation, option overload, relay information, address conflict detection or production security. Code 1/2/3/5 represents Discover/Offer/Request/Ack respectively.
Save the next block as dhcp-lab.sh in the same directory, then run unshare -rn bash dhcp-lab.sh. The background process holds the server namespace and the trap cleans it up on normal exit or error. Avoid SIGKILL; if the parent is killed abnormally, stop any remaining lab sleep 60 or server child. The server times out rather than waiting indefinitely.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 60 & serverns=$!
trap 'kill "$serverns" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$serverns" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link add c0 type veth peer name s0
ip link set s0 netns "$serverns"
ip link set lo up
ip link set c0 up
ip route add default dev c0
nsenter -t "$serverns" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$serverns" -n ip addr add 10.55.0.1/24 dev s0
nsenter -t "$serverns" -n ip link set s0 up
nsenter -t "$serverns" -n python3 ./dhcp_wire.py server s0 & srv=$!
trap 'kill "$srv" "$serverns" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$srv" "$serverns" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
python3 ./dhcp_wire.py client c0
wait "$srv"
A successful run prints that the server received 1 and sent 2, then received 3 and sent 5; the client reports the same message sequence and yiaddr 10.55.0.100. Output ordering across processes may vary. No client address is applied and no traffic to that address is tested. A real client must validate the ACK, manage lease state and configure its interface and options according to its implementation and applicable standards.

title: DHCPv4 on the Wire: A Minimal Isolated Exchange
text:
Investigate and extend

Compare the request’s transaction ID and client field with both responses. Why does this client reject a reply for a different transaction?
Change the client’s requested-address option in a disposable copy. The teaching server’s assertion rejects it; real servers have more complex selection, authorization and error behavior.
If packet capture is available, observe UDP 67/68 on c0 and s0 inside their respective namespaces. Confirm broadcast destinations, DHCP message types and option values. A capture at one point is not evidence of processing by the other endpoint.
Explain why the server offers the address but ip addr show dev c0 would not show it installed. Then use the DHCP relay diagnostics exercise to trace the extra relay and return-path requirements.
Restore all modified files and clean up the namespace processes. Do not attach this toy server to a real network.

References: DHCPv4, RFC 2131, DHCP options, RFC 2132, and BOOTP, RFC 951.

title: Linux VRFs: Overlapping Addresses and Lookup Fallback
text:
Linux VRFs: Overlapping Addresses and Lookup Fallback
Two routing domains can use the same addresses but reach different endpoints. A missing VRF route, however, can fall through to a later Linux policy rule and select the main table. This lab demonstrates both facts and a terminal unreachable default. It complements the multi-NOS VRF-lite lab with an executable Linux example.

title: Linux VRFs: Overlapping Addresses and Lookup Fallback
text:
Topology and prerequisites
The router namespace contains VRF red (table 100) and blue (table 200). Interfaces rred and rblue each have 10.55.0.1/24; each connects to a separate host namespace using 10.55.0.2/24. Both hosts run a UDP server on port 9999, returning their domain name. The addresses intentionally overlap in isolated domains; they must not be bridged together.
You need Linux with VRF, veth, network/user namespaces, Bash, ip, nsenter, unshare, and Python 3. Run only as unshare -rn bash vrf-lab.sh, never on the host network. Some kernels or environments do not support VRF creation or the needed permissions. This exercise uses SO_BINDTODEVICE in Python rather than ip vrf exec, avoiding that helper’s separate cgroup/BPF prerequisites. It was executed with iproute2 7.3.0; output and interface details vary.

title: Linux VRFs: Overlapping Addresses and Lookup Fallback
text:
Run the test
Save the following as vrf-lab.sh and run unshare -rn bash vrf-lab.sh. Background processes keep the two host namespaces and UDP servers alive. The trap stops them on normal exit or error; SIGKILL bypasses cleanup, so stop remaining lab children after abnormal termination.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 60 & redhost=$!
unshare -n sleep 60 & bluehost=$!
trap 'kill "$redhost" "$bluehost" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$redhost" "$bluehost" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link set lo up
ip link add red type vrf table 100
ip link add blue type vrf table 200
ip link set red up
ip link set blue up
ip link add rred type veth peer name hred
ip link add rblue type veth peer name hblue
ip link set hred netns "$redhost"
ip link set hblue netns "$bluehost"
ip link set rred master red
ip link set rblue master blue
ip addr add 10.55.0.1/24 dev rred
ip addr add 10.55.0.1/24 dev rblue
ip link set rred up
ip link set rblue up
nsenter -t "$redhost" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$redhost" -n ip addr add 10.55.0.2/24 dev hred
nsenter -t "$redhost" -n ip link set hred up
nsenter -t "$bluehost" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$bluehost" -n ip addr add 10.55.0.2/24 dev hblue
nsenter -t "$bluehost" -n ip link set hblue up
ip route get vrf red 10.55.0.2
ip route get vrf blue 10.55.0.2
nsenter -t "$redhost" -n python3 -u - <<'SERVER' &
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(('10.55.0.2', 9999)); s.settimeout(10)
d, p = s.recvfrom(100); s.sendto(b'red', p)
SERVER
sr=$!
nsenter -t "$bluehost" -n python3 -u - <<'SERVER' &
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(('10.55.0.2', 9999)); s.settimeout(10)
for _ in range(2):
    d, p = s.recvfrom(100); s.sendto(b'blue', p)
SERVER
sb=$!
trap 'kill "$sr" "$sb" "$redhost" "$bluehost" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$sr" "$sb" "$redhost" "$bluehost" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
python3 - <<'CLIENT'
import socket
for vrf in ('red', 'blue'):
    s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BINDTODEVICE, vrf.encode()+b'\0')
    s.settimeout(3)
    s.sendto(b'query', ('10.55.0.2', 9999))
    value = s.recv(100).decode()
    print(vrf, 'received', value)
    assert value == vrf
    s.close()
CLIENT
ip link set rred down
if ip route get vrf red 10.55.0.2; then echo 'Unexpected red route' >&2; exit 1; fi
ip link add name leak0 type dummy
ip link set leak0 up
ip route add default dev leak0
ip route get vrf red 10.55.0.2
ip route add table 100 unreachable default metric 4278198272
if ip route get vrf red 10.55.0.2; then echo 'Unexpected fallback' >&2; exit 1; fi
ip route del default dev leak0
python3 - <<'CLIENT'
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BINDTODEVICE, b'blue\0')
s.settimeout(3)
s.sendto(b'query', ('10.55.0.2', 9999))
value = s.recv(100).decode()
print('blue after red link down:', value)
assert value == 'blue'
CLIENT
ip link set rred up
ip route get vrf red 10.55.0.2
wait "$sr" "$sb"
The two route lookups select rred/table 100 and rblue/table 200 for the same destination. The UDP client binds its socket to each VRF device; it receives red and blue respectively. This proves which test server responded, not that all applications or every traffic class are isolated.
After rred is brought down, the first red lookup fails because there is no usable route in this isolated setup. The script then creates a dummy default route in main: a red lookup falls through the l3mdev rule and selects leak0. This is evidence of route selection, not evidence that the dummy device delivered traffic. Adding unreachable default to table 100 makes the next red lookup fail instead of continuing to main. The high metric follows the Linux VRF documentation’s example and permits more-specific routes and suitable lower-metric defaults to take precedence; dynamic-routing daemons may interpret that metric differently. The blue server continues to answer while the red link is down, then the red connected route returns when rred comes up.

title: Linux VRFs: Overlapping Addresses and Lookup Fallback
text:
Understand the boundary
A VRF associates interfaces and a routing table, and the Linux l3mdev policy rule selects the relevant table. Policy rules are evaluated by priority: a higher-priority rule can direct traffic elsewhere, and a table lookup with no route can continue to later rules. A terminal unreachable route stops this particular fallback; it is not a substitute for auditing other policy rules, socket bindings, route leaks, firewall policy or management access. Check ip rule show and all relevant tables on the target system.
A process must select the intended VRF for its sockets. Here SO_BINDTODEVICE does that explicitly. ip vrf exec can be useful on supported systems but has cgroup/BPF requirements. Services bound in the default VRF and Linux’s *_l3mdev_accept settings can change which sockets accept traffic; inspect the configuration instead of assuming a VRF is a complete security boundary. Capture on real ingress/egress interfaces where needed: forwarded packets are not necessarily visible on the VRF device itself.

title: Linux VRFs: Overlapping Addresses and Lookup Fallback
text:
Extend

Inspect ip rule show, ip route show table 100, ip route show table 200 and ip route show table main at each stage in a disposable copy. Identify the rule that permits fallback.
Remove the unreachable default, repeat the main-table fallback, then restore it. Explain why an installed unreachable default is different from an absent route.
Use a longer-running pair of servers to repeat the red traffic test after restoring rred; this script verifies the red route after restoration but has already stopped the red server.
Design an intentional route leak with a non-overlapping test prefix and both forward and return paths. Define source validation and policy first; the same destination prefix in both VRFs is ambiguous without the lookup context.

References: Linux VRF documentation, ip-vrf(8), and Policy Routing and VRF.

title: ECMP: Observe Real Flows and Remove a Path
text:
ECMP: Observe Real Flows and Remove a Path
Equal-cost multipath (ECMP) can distribute different flows across next hops. It does not normally combine two links into twice the bandwidth for a single flow, nor does a route listing prove that data arrived. This lab sends UDP to two isolated responders behind distinct next hops, then explicitly removes one path and tests new flows. It complements the Linux ECMP lookup and resilient groups chapter.

title: ECMP: Observe Real Flows and Remove a Path
text:
Topology and prerequisites
The sending namespace has r1 10.1.0.1/30 and r2 10.2.0.1/30. Each link leads to a separate host namespace: A uses 10.1.0.2/30, B uses 10.2.0.2/30. Both hosts deliberately have 192.0.2.1/32 on loopback and listen on UDP 9999, but reply with distinct labels A or B. This models two equivalent destinations for an experiment; it is not a routing-protocol advertisement or a complete anycast design. Each host has a return route via its own link.
You need Linux with IPv4 multipath routing, Bash, Python 3, ip, sysctl, unshare, nsenter, veth support and permission to create user/network namespaces. Run only using unshare -rn bash ecmp-lab.sh; the routes, sysctl and interfaces are isolated from the host. Some systems restrict namespace operations or lack multipath support. Tested on Linux with iproute2 7.3.0. The trap stops the host and server processes on normal exit or error; SIGKILL bypasses cleanup, so stop remaining lab children after abnormal termination.

title: ECMP: Observe Real Flows and Remove a Path
text:
Build and observe
Save as ecmp-lab.sh and run unshare -rn bash ecmp-lab.sh:
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 60 & ha=$!
unshare -n sleep 60 & hb=$!
trap 'kill "$ha" "$hb" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$ha" "$hb" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link set lo up
ip link add r1 type veth peer name h1
ip link add r2 type veth peer name h2
ip link set h1 netns "$ha"
ip link set h2 netns "$hb"
ip addr add 10.1.0.1/30 dev r1
ip addr add 10.2.0.1/30 dev r2
ip link set r1 up
ip link set r2 up
nsenter -t "$ha" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$ha" -n ip addr add 192.0.2.1/32 dev lo
nsenter -t "$ha" -n ip addr add 10.1.0.2/30 dev h1
nsenter -t "$ha" -n ip link set h1 up
nsenter -t "$ha" -n ip route add default via 10.1.0.1
nsenter -t "$hb" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$hb" -n ip addr add 192.0.2.1/32 dev lo
nsenter -t "$hb" -n ip addr add 10.2.0.2/30 dev h2
nsenter -t "$hb" -n ip link set h2 up
nsenter -t "$hb" -n ip route add default via 10.2.0.1
sysctl -qw net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy=1
ip route add 192.0.2.1/32 nexthop via 10.1.0.2 dev r1 weight 1 nexthop via 10.2.0.2 dev r2 weight 1
nsenter -t "$ha" -n python3 -u -c 'import socket;s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_DGRAM);s.bind(("192.0.2.1",9999));exec("while True:\n d,p=s.recvfrom(100)\n s.sendto(b\"A\",p)")' & sa=$!
nsenter -t "$hb" -n python3 -u -c 'import socket;s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_DGRAM);s.bind(("192.0.2.1",9999));exec("while True:\n d,p=s.recvfrom(100)\n s.sendto(b\"B\",p)")' & sb=$!
trap 'kill "$sa" "$sb" "$ha" "$hb" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$sa" "$sb" "$ha" "$hb" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
python3 - <<'PY'
import socket,collections
counts=collections.Counter()
for i in range(40):
 s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_DGRAM);s.settimeout(1);s.sendto(b'q',('192.0.2.1',9999));counts[s.recv(10).decode()]+=1;s.close()
print('ECMP responses:',dict(counts))
assert set(counts)=={'A','B'}
PY
ip route replace 192.0.2.1/32 via 10.2.0.2 dev r2
python3 - <<'PY'
import socket
for i in range(5):
 s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_DGRAM);s.settimeout(1);s.sendto(b'q',('192.0.2.1',9999));value=s.recv(10).decode();s.close();assert value=='B'
print('After removing path A: all responses B')
PY
The script sets the Linux IPv4 multipath hash policy to include transport fields in the isolated sender namespace. Each new UDP socket normally receives a different ephemeral source port, yielding multiple flow keys. On the test host, 40 requests produced 21 A responses and 19 B responses; the exact split is not guaranteed. The assertion checks that this sample reached both paths, not a particular ratio. Hash seeds, kernel versions, socket port selection and sample size can change the distribution; if only one path appears, inspect route and policy state and repeat with more distinct flows before diagnosing an error.
After ip route replace, only the B next hop remains and five new requests return B. This is an explicit routing change, not automatic link failure detection or dynamic routing convergence. The servers run until the trap stops them. The client creates a new socket per request; it does not measure a long-lived session or packet reordering.

title: ECMP: Observe Real Flows and Remove a Path
text:
Analyze the result
For each request, the sender selects a next hop from the ECMP route, sends a frame to that next hop, and receives the selected server’s label. The reply follows the server’s return route. Different five-tuples can hash differently, but a fixed flow key normally stays on one path while the topology and hash inputs remain unchanged. Implementations may rehash on topology changes or other events; they need not provide the same hash or exact distribution. A sampled route lookup and a successful response are different evidence: here the response confirms the application reached one of the test endpoints.
A physical link can stay up while a downstream service fails. A static ECMP route does not automatically prove a next hop is healthy; detection and route withdrawal depend on the implementation and configured routing or tracking mechanisms. A single successful probe can exercise only one selected path. Test multiple independent flows, both directions, and failure scenarios; account for asymmetric paths and stateful devices.

title: ECMP: Observe Real Flows and Remove a Path
text:
Extend

Keep a UDP socket open and send several packets with the same tuple. Record the response labels, then change the route and observe whether the flow is remapped. Do not assume an existing stateful session survives a path change.
Use ip route get with the relevant source, protocol and port fields to compare predicted next hops with actual packets. Confirm tool and kernel support; route get is a lookup, not a packet transmission.
Test a silent failure by stopping one responder while retaining both next hops. Some flows can time out even though the route still lists both. Restore the server, then remove the route as the script does. The exercise needs a server that remains active for the extra requests; adjust the disposable script and cleanup accordingly.
Read the resilient groups chapter before comparing flow remapping. Bucket assignment, weights, timers and offload behavior differ from this simple multipath route.

References: Linux IP sysctls, Linux resilient next-hop groups, and IPv4 ECMP analysis, RFC 2992.

title: Classic STP: Observe a Triangle Reconfigure
text:
Classic STP: Observe a Triangle Reconfigure
Three bridges in a triangle have a Layer 2 loop unless a control mechanism prevents it. This isolated lab uses Linux kernel classic STP, not RSTP or MSTP, to observe a blocked port, a link failure and recovery. It complements the spanning-tree election walkthrough, whose RSTP example uses different costs and roles.

title: Classic STP: Observe a Triangle Reconfigure
text:
Topology and prerequisites
Bridges bra, brb and brc form a triangle. Ports ab/ba, ac/ca and bc/cb are veth pairs; the first letter denotes the local bridge. H1 10.66.0.1/24 attaches to brb through bp; H2 10.66.0.2/24 attaches to brc through cp. Bridge priorities 4096, 8192 and 12288 make bra the intended root.
