Veth port costs on the test host were 2; check actual values rather than assuming the arithmetic in the RSTP chapter applies here.
You need Linux with bridge STP and veth support, Bash, ip, bridge, unshare, nsenter, ping, and permission to create user and network namespaces. This script requires an iproute2/kernel combination supporting stp_mode kernel. Run only with unshare -rn bash stp-lab.sh: it creates an intentionally redundant Layer 2 topology inside a disposable namespace. Never attach it to a real network. The test host used iproute2 7.3.0. Timer values in this example use the Linux bridge netlink clock-tick units used by that system (USER_HZ 100): 400, 100 and 600 correspond to 4, 1 and 6 seconds. Confirm supported syntax and units for your version; these shortened lab timers are not production recommendations.

title: Classic STP: Observe a Triangle Reconfigure
text:
Run and inspect
Save as stp-lab.sh, then run unshare -rn bash stp-lab.sh. It waits at least 12 seconds at each of three stages and takes over 40 seconds including probes. Two background processes hold the host namespaces; the trap stops them on normal exit or error. SIGKILL bypasses cleanup, so stop remaining lab sleep 90 children after abnormal termination.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 90 & h1=$!
unshare -n sleep 90 & h2=$!
trap 'kill "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$h1" "$h2" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
for b in a b c; do
  ip link add name "br$b" type bridge stp_mode kernel stp_state 1 forward_delay 400 hello_time 100 max_age 600
  ip link set "br$b" up
done
ip link set bra type bridge priority 4096
ip link set brb type bridge priority 8192
ip link set brc type bridge priority 12288
ip link add ab type veth peer name ba
ip link add ac type veth peer name ca
ip link add bc type veth peer name cb
ip link set ab master bra
ip link set ac master bra
ip link set ba master brb
ip link set bc master brb
ip link set ca master brc
ip link set cb master brc
for p in ab ba ac ca bc cb; do ip link set "$p" up; done
ip link add bp type veth peer name h1e
ip link add cp type veth peer name h2e
ip link set h1e netns "$h1"
ip link set h2e netns "$h2"
ip link set bp master brb
ip link set cp master brc
ip link set bp up
ip link set cp up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip addr add 10.66.0.1/24 dev h1e
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip link set h1e up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip addr add 10.66.0.2/24 dev h2e
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip link set h2e up
sleep 12
printf 'Baseline port states:\n'
bridge link show
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 1 -W 2 10.66.0.2
ip link set ac down
sleep 12
printf 'After A-C failure:\n'
bridge link show
bridge fdb show br brb
bridge fdb show br brc
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip neigh flush dev h1e
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip neigh flush dev h2e
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 3 -W 2 10.66.0.2
ip link set ac up
sleep 12
printf 'After restoring A-C:\n'
bridge link show
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ip neigh flush dev h1e
nsenter -t "$h2" -n ip neigh flush dev h2e
nsenter -t "$h1" -n ping -c 3 -W 2 10.66.0.2
On the test host, before the failure cb on brc was blocking, while bc on brb and the A-facing ports were forwarding; the hosts communicated through brb–bra–brc. After ac was disabled, ca became disabled and cb transitioned to forwarding, providing a brb–brc path. After ac returned and the tree settled, cb blocked again. The three host probes after each change succeeded in the checked run. MAC addresses, costs, timing and output vary with implementation.
The script shows FDB entries and flushes each host’s neighbor cache before post-change probes so ARP is exercised again. A flush changes the experiment: this is a connectivity and state check, not a measurement of uninterrupted production convergence. In a preliminary run, a single ping failed after the port showed forwarding; multiple factors, including cached forwarding and neighbor state, can affect that observation. Record MAC tables and capture packets before attributing a specific cause. The 12-second waits are lab allowances rather than guaranteed convergence limits; on a slow system inspect the states and repeat after the tree stabilizes.

title: Classic STP: Observe a Triangle Reconfigure
text:
Practice

Before running, calculate the expected root and blocked side from bridge IDs and actual equal port costs. Compare bridge link show with ip -d link show bra, brb, and brc while the lab is running. The root_port field is a bridge port number, not necessarily the interface’s Linux ifindex.
Run a timestamped continuous probe during failure and restoration, without manually flushing neighbor state. Record the last successful, failed and recovered probes, FDB changes and port transitions. Probe interval bounds measurement precision.
Change the priority of brb in a disposable copy and predict the resulting root before observing it. Different root or port costs can change which side blocks.
Compare with RSTP elections. Classic STP’s timer-based transitions do not demonstrate RSTP proposal/agreement, edge behavior, MST instances or vendor guard features.

References: Linux bridge documentation and ip-link bridge options.

title: LACP Bond: Member Failure and Recovery
text:
LACP Bond: Member Failure and Recovery
Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) lets two systems negotiate a group of links as one logical connection. A configured member is not necessarily selected and forwarding: inspect partner and aggregator state as well as traffic. In this isolated Linux exercise, two bonds negotiate across two veth pairs, then one member is taken down and restored.

title: LACP Bond: Member Failure and Recovery
text:
Topology and prerequisites
The first namespace has bondA with members a1 and a2; the second has bondB with members b1 and b2. The links are a1–b1 and a2–b2. The logical interfaces use 10.88.0.1/24 and 10.88.0.2/24. There is no physical switch, STP domain or multi-chassis system in this test. Veth-reported speed and observed latency are not physical-link performance measurements.
You need Linux with bonding and veth support, Bash, ip, unshare, nsenter, ping, access to /proc/net/bonding and permission to create user/network namespaces. Some systems prohibit these operations or cannot load the bonding module. Run only as unshare -rn bash lacp-lab.sh: never enslave or reconfigure host interfaces for this exercise. Tested on Linux with iproute2 7.3.0; field availability, timing and negotiation behavior vary.

title: LACP Bond: Member Failure and Recovery
text:
Build and test
Save as lacp-lab.sh and run unshare -rn bash lacp-lab.sh. It enables LACP on both ends, waits for negotiation, records state, takes a1 down, tests the remaining path and brings a1 back. It takes roughly half a minute. The trap stops the namespace holder on normal exit or error; SIGKILL bypasses cleanup, so stop any remaining lab sleep 90 child after abnormal termination.
set -eu
unshare -n sleep 90 & peer=$!
trap 'kill "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link set lo up
ip link add name bondA type bond mode 802.3ad miimon 100 lacp_rate fast
ip link add name a1 type veth peer name b1
ip link add name a2 type veth peer name b2
ip link set b1 netns "$peer"
ip link set b2 netns "$peer"
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link add name bondB type bond mode 802.3ad miimon 100 lacp_rate fast
ip link set a1 master bondA
ip link set a2 master bondA
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set b1 master bondB
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set b2 master bondB
ip link set a1 up
ip link set a2 up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set b1 up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set b2 up
ip addr add 10.88.0.1/24 dev bondA
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip addr add 10.88.0.2/24 dev bondB
ip link set bondA up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set bondB up
sleep 12
printf '\nBond state (baseline or restored):\n'
ip -d link show bondA
cat /proc/net/bonding/bondA
nsenter -t "$peer" -n cat /proc/net/bonding/bondB
ping -c 2 -W 1 10.88.0.2
ip link set a1 down
sleep 3
printf '\nBond state with a1 down:\n'
ip -d link show bondA
cat /proc/net/bonding/bondA
ping -c 2 -W 1 10.88.0.2
ip link set a1 up
sleep 12
printf '\nBond state (baseline or restored):\n'
ip -d link show bondA
cat /proc/net/bonding/bondA
ping -c 2 -W 1 10.88.0.2
On the test host, ip -d link show bondA reported ad_num_ports 2 after baseline negotiation, 1 after a1 was disabled and 2 after restoration. The partner key and MAC were present, both member statuses were initially up, a1 became down during the fault, and pings succeeded at each recorded stage. The exact state fields and convergence time vary; inspect both ends and wait for negotiation rather than relying only on these fixed sleeps. A ping after a wait does not measure packet loss during the transition or prove both links carry data.
The setting lacp_rate fast requests a fast LACPDU rate from the partner; it is not an end-to-end failure detector. miimon 100 polls link carrier approximately every 100 ms. Carrier detection, LACP negotiation, the selected aggregator, neighbor updates and application retries can all influence actual recovery. If a member remains electrically up while a downstream path fails, carrier monitoring alone may not detect the fault.

title: LACP Bond: Member Failure and Recovery
text:
Investigate

Compare actor and partner information, aggregator ID, member link states, selected port count and logical interface state on both ends. An up bond alone does not prove two members are synchronized and usable.
Run a timestamped continuous probe while changing a1, and record loss and recovery separately from the fixed-wait test. The probe interval bounds measurement precision; a successful final ping is not proof of zero interruption.
Inspect member TX/RX counters before and after traffic. With the default Layer 2 hash, one peer’s traffic can remain on one member. Different flows and hash policies may use links differently; two members do not guarantee one flow receives twice the bandwidth or that traffic splits evenly.
In an isolated copy change one side’s mode or disconnect one link and observe the partner state and data behavior. Some implementations allow a temporary fallback when no partner is established; verify the actual platform’s configuration instead of assuming a mismatch must immediately drop everything.
Consider a minimum-links policy and the capacity needed after a failure. Test actual platform behavior before using it to trigger routing failover. Restore the baseline and verify the member and application states.

References: Linux bonding driver documentation, IEEE 802.1AX link aggregation, and Link Aggregation.

title: eBGP Without Containers: Advertise and Withdraw a Route
text:
eBGP Without Containers: Advertise and Withdraw a Route
Two BGP speakers can exchange a prefix while the underlying data plane remains a separate concern. This lab runs the open-source GoBGP daemon in isolated Linux network namespaces, establishes eBGP, advertises a documentation prefix and withdraws it. It needs no container runtime or vendor image. It tests the BGP control plane only; a route in GoBGP’s RIB is not proof of kernel installation or packet forwarding.

title: eBGP Without Containers: Advertise and Withdraw a Route
text:
Requirements and topology
The first speaker is AS 65001, router ID 10.0.0.1, interface 10.99.0.1/30. The second is AS 65002, router ID 10.0.0.2, interface 10.99.0.2/30. A veth pair connects the two network namespaces. The advertised prefix is 192.0.2.0/24, used only as documentation data inside the isolated lab.
You need Linux, Bash, ip, unshare, nsenter, grep, seq, standard core utilities, namespace permission and the gobgp and gobgpd executables. The lab was tested with upstream GoBGP v4.11.0, Linux and iproute2 7.3.0. Binaries and command behavior can differ by release and architecture. Keep the BGP and gRPC API listeners in the isolated namespaces: the example’s API is unauthenticated and is bound to namespace loopback. Do not attach this lab to a shared or production network.
For Linux x86-64, obtain the v4.11.0 release and verify its published checksums before extracting the two executables. The following digest identifies the Linux AMD64 archive observed for this release; verify it against the publisher’s release metadata and checksum file as well:
b45eefb6f8cb662740efa99631f14bac23c9ea8cca158843293a3ecb5cbc72b6  gobgp_4.11.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz
Set GOBGP_DIR to the absolute path of the directory containing the verified executables and export it. Check both versions and executable permissions. Other architectures need their own matching upstream asset and checksum. Avoid installing unverified binaries or exposing the API outside the lab.

title: eBGP Without Containers: Advertise and Withdraw a Route
text:
Build, advertise, withdraw
Save as bgp-lab.sh; with GOBGP_DIR exported, run unshare -rn bash bgp-lab.sh. The second namespace is held by a background process. The trap stops both daemons and the namespace holder, removes the temporary configuration files and removes their directory on normal exit or error. SIGKILL bypasses cleanup; after abnormal termination stop remaining lab children and remove the specific temporary directory. Daemon logs are suppressed to keep the example readable; for diagnosis in a disposable copy, capture each daemon’s logs in its own temporary file and protect them as operational data.
set -eu
: "${GOBGP_DIR:?Set GOBGP_DIR to the directory containing gobgp and gobgpd}"
work=$(mktemp -d)
unshare -n sleep 90 & peer=$!
trap 'kill "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; unlink "$work/r1.toml" 2>/dev/null || true; unlink "$work/r2.toml" 2>/dev/null || true; rmdir "$work" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link set lo up
ip link add r1 type veth peer name r2
ip link set r2 netns "$peer"
ip addr add 10.99.0.1/30 dev r1
ip link set r1 up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip addr add 10.99.0.2/30 dev r2
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set r2 up
cat > "$work/r1.toml" <<'CONFIG'
[global.config]
  as = 65001
  router-id = "10.0.0.1"
[[neighbors]]
  [neighbors.config]
    neighbor-address = "10.99.0.2"
    peer-as = 65002
CONFIG
cat > "$work/r2.toml" <<'CONFIG'
[global.config]
  as = 65002
  router-id = "10.0.0.2"
[[neighbors]]
  [neighbors.config]
    neighbor-address = "10.99.0.1"
    peer-as = 65001
CONFIG
"$GOBGP_DIR/gobgpd" -f "$work/r1.toml" --api-hosts 127.0.0.1:50051 --pprof-disable > /dev/null 2>&1 & d1=$!
nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgpd" -f "$work/r2.toml" --api-hosts 127.0.0.1:50051 --pprof-disable > /dev/null 2>&1 & d2=$!
trap 'kill "$d1" "$d2" "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$d1" "$d2" "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; unlink "$work/r1.toml" 2>/dev/null || true; unlink "$work/r2.toml" 2>/dev/null || true; rmdir "$work" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
ready=0
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
  if "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" neighbor 2>/dev/null | grep -q Establ; then ready=1; break; fi
  sleep 1
done
[ "$ready" -eq 1 ] || { echo 'BGP session did not establish' >&2; exit 1; }
"$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" neighbor
nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" neighbor
"$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib add 192.0.2.0/24 nexthop 10.99.0.1
seen=0
for _ in $(seq 1 20); do
  if nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib 2>/dev/null | grep -q '192.0.2.0/24'; then seen=1; break; fi
  sleep 1
done
[ "$seen" -eq 1 ] || { echo 'Route was not received' >&2; exit 1; }
nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib
"$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib del 192.0.2.0/24 nexthop 10.99.0.1
gone=0
for _ in $(seq 1 20); do
  view=$(nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib) || { echo 'Cannot query peer RIB' >&2; exit 1; }
  if ! printf '%s\n' "$view" | grep -q '192.0.2.0/24'; then gone=1; break; fi
  sleep 1
done
[ "$gone" -eq 1 ] || { echo 'Route was not withdrawn' >&2; exit 1; }
nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib
The script polls for Establ rather than assuming a fixed establishment time, then prints each neighbor table. It injects 192.0.2.0/24 with next hop 10.99.0.1, waits for the second speaker’s RIB to show it, and withdraws it. On the test host the remote RIB showed the prefix, next hop and AS path 65001, then Network not in table. The withdrawal check requires the RIB query itself to succeed; a failed API query is not treated as proof of withdrawal. Timings and text formatting can vary across versions.

title: eBGP Without Containers: Advertise and Withdraw a Route
text:
Understand what was proved
The two processes exchanged a BGP advertisement and withdrawal over a TCP session. The injected prefix is a control-plane test object; there is no destination host behind it in this topology. GoBGP’s displayed best path is not equivalent to an operating-system FIB entry or an end-to-end data-plane test. Next-hop resolution and BGP-to-kernel integration depend on the routing stack and configuration. For a forwarding lab, create an actual destination, explicitly configure the routing installation mechanism and return path, and verify packets at both ends.
AS 65001 appears in the eBGP advertisement’s AS path; the prefix and AS numbers are examples, not public announcements. The lab uses a simple permissive policy suitable only for isolated testing. Real external peering requires explicit import/export policy, route-origin and prefix controls, session protection, monitoring and agreement with the peer.

title: eBGP Without Containers: Advertise and Withdraw a Route
text:
Failure drills

In a disposable copy, configure the wrong peer AS on one side. Record the session state and daemon logs; fix the AS and wait for Established. Do not interpret a TCP connection alone as a working BGP session.
Withdraw the prefix while keeping the session up, as the script does. Explain why session state and route presence must be checked separately.
Add a second documentation prefix and withdraw only one. Verify the other stays in the remote RIB. Record the exact commands and the selected address family.
Continue with eBGP Import Policy to compare incoming paths with the selected RIB and change the permitted prefix length.

References: GoBGP getting started, GoBGP v4.11.0 release, and BGP-4, RFC 4271.

title: eBGP Import Policy: Exact Prefixes and More-Specifics
text:
eBGP Import Policy: Exact Prefixes and More-Specifics
An Established BGP session can carry routes that the receiver deliberately refuses to select. This lab uses two isolated GoBGP speakers to distinguish a neighbor’s incoming advertisements from the receiver’s selected RIB, then changes an allowlist to admit a more-specific prefix. It builds directly on eBGP Without Containers.

title: eBGP Import Policy: Exact Prefixes and More-Specifics
text:
Prerequisites and policy
Use the verified GoBGP v4.11.0 executables and Linux namespace prerequisites from the preceding lab. Export GOBGP_DIR as their absolute directory. The script creates AS 65001 at 10.99.0.1/30 and AS 65002 at 10.99.0.2/30; both API listeners are unauthenticated and bound to the loopback interface of their isolated namespaces. Run only as unshare -rn bash bgp-policy-lab.sh and do not connect this test to a shared or production network. It was executed with GoBGP v4.11.0 and iproute2 7.3.0; configuration semantics, output and capabilities can differ by version.
The receiver’s global import policy permits exactly 192.0.2.0/24 and rejects unmatched routes. The sender announces that prefix, its more-specific 192.0.2.128/25, and unrelated 198.51.100.0/24. These documentation prefixes are control-plane examples only. Before running, predict which appear in the receiver’s Adj-RIB-In and selected RIB. A policy scoped globally can affect more than one peer: this lab has only one, and it is not a production policy template.

title: eBGP Import Policy: Exact Prefixes and More-Specifics
text:
Run the experiment
Save as bgp-policy-lab.sh and run unshare -rn bash bgp-policy-lab.sh. The script creates temporary configuration files, two daemons and a namespace holder. Its trap terminates the processes and removes those temporary files on normal exit or error; SIGKILL bypasses cleanup. Daemon logs are suppressed; in a disposable debugging copy capture and protect separate logs. Polling loops have bounded waits and treat a failed RIB query as an error, not as evidence of absence.
set -eu
: "${GOBGP_DIR:?Set GOBGP_DIR to the directory containing gobgp and gobgpd}"
work=$(mktemp -d)
unshare -n sleep 90 & peer=$!
trap 'kill "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; unlink "$work/r1.toml" 2>/dev/null || true; unlink "$work/r2.toml" 2>/dev/null || true; rmdir "$work" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
sleep 0.2
ip link set lo up
ip link add r1 type veth peer name r2
ip link set r2 netns "$peer"
ip addr add 10.99.0.1/30 dev r1
ip link set r1 up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set lo up
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip addr add 10.99.0.2/30 dev r2
nsenter -t "$peer" -n ip link set r2 up
cat > "$work/r1.toml" <<'CONFIG'
[global.config]
  as = 65001
  router-id = "10.0.0.1"
[[neighbors]]
  [neighbors.config]
    neighbor-address = "10.99.0.2"
    peer-as = 65002
CONFIG
cat > "$work/r2.toml" <<'CONFIG'
[global.config]
  as = 65002
  router-id = "10.0.0.2"
[global.apply-policy.config]
  import-policy-list = ["allow-exact"]
  default-import-policy = "reject-route"
[[defined-sets.prefix-sets]]
  prefix-set-name = "approved"
  [[defined-sets.prefix-sets.prefix-list]]
    ip-prefix = "192.0.2.0/24"
    masklength-range = "24..24"
[[policy-definitions]]
  name = "allow-exact"
  [[policy-definitions.statements]]
    name = "permit-approved"
    [policy-definitions.statements.conditions.match-prefix-set]
      prefix-set = "approved"
    [policy-definitions.statements.actions]
      route-disposition = "accept-route"
[[neighbors]]
  [neighbors.config]
    neighbor-address = "10.99.0.1"
    peer-as = 65001
CONFIG
"$GOBGP_DIR/gobgpd" -f "$work/r1.toml" --api-hosts 127.0.0.1:50051 --pprof-disable > /dev/null 2>&1 & d1=$!
nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgpd" -f "$work/r2.toml" --api-hosts 127.0.0.1:50051 --pprof-disable > /dev/null 2>&1 & d2=$!
trap 'kill "$d1" "$d2" "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; wait "$d1" "$d2" "$peer" 2>/dev/null || true; unlink "$work/r1.toml" 2>/dev/null || true; unlink "$work/r2.toml" 2>/dev/null || true; rmdir "$work" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
ready=0
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
  if "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" neighbor 2>/dev/null | grep -q Establ; then ready=1; break; fi
  sleep 1
done
[ "$ready" -eq 1 ] || { echo 'BGP session did not establish' >&2; exit 1; }
"$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" neighbor
nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" neighbor
"$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib add 192.0.2.0/24 nexthop 10.99.0.1
"$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib add 192.0.2.128/25 nexthop 10.99.0.1
"$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib add 198.51.100.0/24 nexthop 10.99.0.1
seen=0
for _ in $(seq 1 20); do
  received=$(nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" neighbor 10.99.0.1 adj-in) || exit 1
  if printf '%s\n' "$received" | grep -q '192.0.2.0/24' && printf '%s\n' "$received" | grep -q '192.0.2.128/25' && printf '%s\n' "$received" | grep -q '198.51.100.0/24'; then seen=1; break; fi
  sleep 1
done
[ "$seen" -eq 1 ] || { echo 'Not all routes observed in Adj-RIB-In' >&2; exit 1; }
printf '\nReceiver Adj-RIB-In:\n%s\n' "$received"
accepted=$(nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib) || exit 1
printf '\nReceiver selected RIB:\n%s\n' "$accepted"
printf '%s\n' "$accepted" | grep -q '192.0.2.0/24'
if printf '%s\n' "$accepted" | grep -Eq '192.0.2.128/25|198.51.100.0/24'; then echo 'Unexpected accepted prefix' >&2; exit 1; fi
nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" policy prefix add approved 192.0.2.0/24 24..25
nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" neighbor 10.99.0.1 softresetin
changed=0
for _ in $(seq 1 20); do
  accepted=$(nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" global rib) || exit 1
  if printf '%s\n' "$accepted" | grep -q '192.0.2.128/25'; then changed=1; break; fi
  sleep 1
done
[ "$changed" -eq 1 ] || { echo 'More-specific not accepted after refresh' >&2; exit 1; }
printf '\nReceiver selected RIB after policy change:\n%s\n' "$accepted"
printf '%s\n' "$accepted" | grep -q '192.0.2.0/24'
if printf '%s\n' "$accepted" | grep -q '198.51.100.0/24'; then echo 'Unexpected unrelated prefix' >&2; exit 1; fi
nsenter -t "$peer" -n "$GOBGP_DIR/gobgp" neighbor
In the tested run, the receiver’s Adj-RIB-In showed all three advertisements while its selected RIB contained only 192.0.2.0/24. The exact /24 prefix-set entry does not accept the /25, even though the /25 lies inside its address range. The unrelated prefix is rejected by the default action.
The script then adds a second prefix-set entry with length range 24..25 and requests an inbound soft reset. The selected RIB now contains both 192.0.2.0/24 and 192.0.2.128/25; 198.51.100.0/24 remains absent, and the neighbor table remains Established in the observed run. A soft reset or route refresh re-evaluates or requests routes according to the implementation and negotiated capabilities; it is not a guarantee that a peer exports everything. Check the version-specific behavior before making a real change.

title: eBGP Import Policy: Exact Prefixes and More-Specifics
text:
Interpret the evidence
In this GoBGP version, neighbor ... adj-in exposes the three received paths, while the global selected RIB shows the result after this global import policy. Counters and “received”/“accepted” labels can refer to different stages of the implementation: do not infer a policy result from a single summary number. Inspect policy attachment, the relevant input view and the selected route together. RIB presence still does not prove kernel FIB installation or application reachability.
If both routes were actually installed in the same forwarding table, packets matching the /25 would use it over the /24 by longest-prefix match. This script does not install them into a kernel FIB or send traffic, so it does not itself demonstrate that forwarding outcome. More-specific routes can have large traffic and security effects: allow only the prefix lengths and origins authorized by the design.

title: eBGP Import Policy: Exact Prefixes and More-Specifics
text:
Extend

Change the length range to 24..24 in a fresh isolated run and verify that the /25 remains rejected. Compare the input and selected views, not just session state.
Add an explicitly permitted unrelated test prefix, reprocess routes using the version’s documented mechanism, and verify exactly what changed. Then restore the original policy.
Add an export filter on the sending side and compare the sender’s advertised view with the receiver’s input view. This extension is not implemented or tested here.
Explain how prefix filters, origin validation and AS-path policy address different risks, and why an accept decision in this lab does not authenticate a route’s origin.

References: GoBGP v4.11.0 policy documentation, GoBGP CLI syntax, and BGP-4, RFC 4271.

title: Campus Lab: VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF
text:
Campus Lab: VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF
A campus is three jobs at once. Access ports keep user and server broadcast domains apart. Two distribution routers share a virtual gateway so a host still has a first hop when one router stops. A core router learns those prefixes with OSPF so the path beyond the closet is dynamic. This chapter builds that shape as one netlab file on FRR and Linux.

title: Campus Lab: VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Read a campus as access bridges, distribution SVIs, and a routed core
Express VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF in one topology.yml
Predict which router owns each virtual IP
Check same-VLAN reachability and inter-VLAN reachability separately
Explain why this lab does not trunk both VLANs around a square

title: Campus Lab: VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF
text:
What the design is doing
        R1          OSPF core
       /  \
     D1    D2        IRB, VRRP, OSPF
     | \  / |
     |  \/  |
    S1      S2       S1 VLAN 10, S2 VLAN 20
   H1 H4   H2 H3








Layer
Nodes
Forwarding




Core
R1
OSPF only. Two point-to-point links.


Distribution
D1, D2
One SVI per VLAN, VRRP on each SVI, OSPF toward R1.


Access
S1, S2
Bridge only. S1 is VLAN 10. S2 is VLAN 20.


Hosts
H1–H4
Linux. Default route is the VLAN’s VRRP address.



VRRP is split on purpose. D1 is master for VLAN 10 (priority 110) and backup for VLAN 20 (priority 100). D2 is the opposite. A failure of one distribution router moves only one virtual IP. The other VLAN stays on its master.
Hosts in one VLAN talk at layer 2 through their access bridge. A packet from H1 (VLAN 10) to H2 (VLAN 20) hits the VLAN 10 virtual IP, is routed by whichever router owns it, and leaves on the VLAN 20 SVI. Both distribution routers have both SVIs, so that hop does not need the core. OSPF still matters: R1 must learn 172.16.10.0/24 and 172.16.20.0/24, and the core links must come up Full.
The VLAN SVIs are OSPF passive. They are advertised, and they do not send hellos onto the access bridges.

title: Campus Lab: VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF
section: Why this is not a trunk square
text:
Why this is not a trunk square
A common drawing connects both access switches to both distribution switches with trunks that carry every VLAN. That is a layer-2 loop. Cisco layer-2 images break the loop with spanning tree. FRR’s STP does not run on VLAN trunks (BPDUs go out tagged). Linux in netlab has no STP module. This lab keeps each VLAN in its own bridge, so D1 and D2 can both sit on that VLAN for VRRP, and the two VLANs never form a cycle.
On these Linux bridges an access VLAN is untagged. The VLAN id is the bridge (vlan10, vlan20), not an 802.1Q tag on the wire. Tagged trunks are the subject of the VLANs and trunks chapter. Use them when you want to see tags, on a topology that is still loop-free.

title: Campus Lab: VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF
text:
Topology
Checked with netlab 26.10 (networklab on PyPI). netlab create plans addresses and writes FRR and Linux config. It does not start containers.
# topology.yml
---
name: campus
provider: clab
defaults.device: frr

vlans:
  users:
    id: 10
    mode: irb
    prefix.ipv4: 172.16.10.0/24
    gateway.protocol: vrrp
    gateway.id: 254
    gateway.vrrp.group: 10
    links: [ H1-S1, H4-S1, D1-S1, D2-S1 ]
  servers:
    id: 20
    mode: irb
    prefix.ipv4: 172.16.20.0/24
    gateway.protocol: vrrp
    gateway.id: 254
    gateway.vrrp.group: 20
    links: [ H2-S2, H3-S2, D1-S2, D2-S2 ]

groups:
  dist:
    members: [ D1, D2 ]
    module: [ vlan, ospf, gateway ]
    vlans:
      users:
        ospf.passive: true
      servers:
        ospf.passive: true
  access:
    members: [ S1, S2 ]
    device: linux
    module: [ vlan ]
    vlan.mode: bridge
  hosts:
    members: [ H1, H2, H3, H4 ]
    device: linux
    role: host
    module: [ routing ]
    routing.static:
      - ipv4: 0.0.0.0/0
        nexthop.gateway: true

nodes:
  R1:
    module: [ ospf ]
  D1:
    vlans.users.gateway.vrrp.priority: 110
    vlans.servers.gateway.vrrp.priority: 100
  D2:
    vlans.users.gateway.vrrp.priority: 100
    vlans.servers.gateway.vrrp.priority: 110
  S1:
  S2:
  H1:
  H2:
  H3:
  H4:

links:
  - R1-D1
  - R1-D2

validate:
  r1_sees_d1:
    description: R1 is Full with D1
    nodes: [ R1 ]
    devices: [ frr ]
    plugin: ospf_neighbor('10.0.0.2')
  r1_sees_d2:
    description: R1 is Full with D2
    nodes: [ R1 ]
    devices: [ frr ]
    plugin: ospf_neighbor('10.0.0.3')
  same_vlan:
    description: H1 reaches H4 inside VLAN 10
    nodes: [ H1 ]
    devices: [ linux ]
    plugin: ping('172.16.10.9')
  other_vlan:
    description: H1 reaches H2 across VLANs
    nodes: [ H1 ]
    devices: [ linux ]
    plugin: ping('172.16.20.7')
gateway.id: 254 is the last usable host in the /24, so the virtual IPs are 172.16.10.254 and 172.16.20.254. nexthop.gateway: true tells each host to use the gateway on its own VLAN. Node order fixes the other host addresses. Insert a node above H1 and those addresses move. Read node_files/ after netlab create if you change the file.

S1 and S2 get no IP. Their startup scripts create a bridge and enslave the access ports. D1’s rendered VRRP stanza is the same idea as a hand-written interface block, generated from the YAML priorities:
interface vlan10
 vrrp 10 priority 110
 vrrp 10 preempt
 vrrp 10 ip 172.16.10.254
interface vlan20
 vrrp 20 priority 100
 vrrp 20 preempt
 vrrp 20 ip 172.16.20.254
D2 swaps the priorities. Both SVIs on D1 also contain ip ospf passive.

title: Campus Lab: VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF
text:
Bring it up
netlab up needs root and a container runtime. This chapter’s create step was run here. The up, connect, and validate steps were not.
python3 -m venv netlab-venv
netlab-venv/bin/pip install networklab==26.10
netlab-venv/bin/netlab create
netlab-venv/bin/netlab up
netlab-venv/bin/netlab validate
Read state from the devices:
netlab connect D1 vtysh -c "show vrrp"
netlab connect D2 vtysh -c "show vrrp"
netlab connect R1 vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
netlab connect R1 vtysh -c "show ip route"
netlab connect H1 ip route
netlab connect H1 ping -c 3 172.16.10.9
netlab connect H1 ping -c 3 172.16.20.7

Predict

D1 is Master on VRRP group 10 and Backup on group 20. D2 is the reverse.
R1 has two Full neighbors, 10.0.0.2 and 10.0.0.3, and both VLAN prefixes in the OSPF table.
H1 pings H4 without leaving VLAN 10. The path does not use a router.
H1 pings H2. The first hop is 172.16.10.254 on D1, then D1 routes onto VLAN 20.
S1 has no route to 172.16.20.0/24. It is a bridge.



Drill — move VLAN 10
On D1, shut VRRP group 10 and watch D2 take 172.16.10.254. H1’s default route does not change. netlab connect H1 ping -c 3 172.16.20.7 should work again once D2 is Master. Bring the group back and D1 should preempt, because preempt is on.
Tear the lab down with netlab down --cleanup when you also want the generated files removed. Without --cleanup, containers stop and topology.yml stays.

title: Campus Lab: VLANs, VRRP, and OSPF
text:

title: Campus Design: Failure Domains and Verification
text:
Campus Design: Failure Domains and Verification
A redundant drawing is not yet a resilient network. A useful design identifies which traffic must survive each failure, what detects that failure, which component changes forwarding, and how the result will be measured. This project extends the campus VLAN, VRRP and OSPF lab; use its addressing and topology rather than assuming the abstract design below already has two of everything.

title: Campus Design: Failure Domains and Verification
text:
Translate requirements into tests
Assume the lab has user and server VLANs, two distribution routers D1 and D2, and one core R1. A host uses a virtual first-hop address; OSPF advertises connected VLANs toward the core. Define success for specific source and destination pairs, not just “the network stays up.” For example: same-VLAN traffic, inter-VLAN traffic, and traffic from each VLAN to a core-side test endpoint. Agree on an allowed interruption for each service and measure it; a routing adjacency timer is not an application recovery objective.
The design intentionally has a single R1 and single access switch per VLAN. Duplicating D1 and D2 does not eliminate those common failure points. Likewise, two uplinks in the same conduit, two power supplies on the same feed, or both controllers dependent on the same service can fail together. Inventory physical and logical dependencies: power, management, DNS, addressing, authentication, software, configuration and cabling paths. Availability math that multiplies independent probabilities is misleading when failures share a cause.








Failure
Intended effect to verify
Evidence




D1 stops
D2 can take over the affected gateway and carry the specified flows
VRRP state, host neighbor entry, switch MAC table, loss interval, return route


D1–R1 link fails
Core-bound traffic uses an available alternate path if the design provides one
Link and OSPF state, route/FIB on D1 and R1, bidirectional traffic


R1 fails
Core-side service is unavailable in this single-core lab
Endpoint probes and topology inventory; do not claim core redundancy


One access switch fails
Its attached hosts lose that access path
Switch/port state and host reachability; a second distribution router cannot repair an absent access switch


VRRP advertisements are filtered but data links remain
Both routers may believe they should be active after timers expire
State and captures at both routers, duplicate ownership and MAC movement; test only in isolation


Client VLAN is absent from a trunk
Physical link may remain up while the affected VLAN fails
VLAN membership, STP state, counters and endpoint probes



The exact effect of a failed uplink depends on routes and physical topology. If D1 still owns the virtual gateway and retains a usable path through another router, gateway movement may be unnecessary. If it remains active but has no usable onward path, hosts can send traffic to a black hole. VRRP by itself tracks the virtual-router election, not arbitrary remote application health. A platform may track a link, route or probe and alter priority; validate what the chosen tracking signal actually covers, how quickly it changes, and whether the backup can forward the affected destinations.

title: Campus Design: Failure Domains and Verification
text:
Convergence is a chain
A fault is detected, communicated to a control process, translated into route and forwarding changes, and finally noticed by the application. These stages can overlap. VRRP advertisement timers, routing convergence, FIB programming, MAC learning, ARP/ND state and application retries all contribute to observed interruption. Faster failure detection is useful only if it measures the right path and does not cause unstable flapping. BFD reports the health of its configured session path; it is not an end-to-end application test.
On failover, inspect the virtual IP and MAC, switch forwarding table and host neighbor state rather than assuming all hosts immediately use the correct path. The resulting forward and return paths need not be symmetric. A stateful firewall or NAT device between them can have additional state-sharing requirements; a successful routing failover does not prove existing sessions survive.

title: Campus Design: Failure Domains and Verification
text:
Controlled lab matrix
Deploy the linked campus lab using the versions and prerequisites in that chapter. Its netlab create evidence is configuration generation, not proof that the topology was deployed successfully. For each test below, run a timestamped, low-rate probe for every traffic pair and a representative application transaction if available. Capture baseline for at least a short stable interval, inject one fault, record recovery, restore the fault, and check the original baseline. Device syntax and convergence times differ; do not copy production configurations into the lab.

Whole distribution failure: stop D1. On D2 verify virtual-router state and VLAN interfaces; on R1 verify the selected routes. On the hosts check neighbor entries and both directions of traffic. Restart D1 and observe whether preemption changes the gateway again. Record both failure and restoration interruptions.
Uplink failure: disable D1’s core-facing link while leaving its access-facing interface and VRRP running. Before doing so, predict whether D1 has an alternate route for the core-side destination. Compare its RIB/FIB, D2’s route, VRRP state and traffic. If using a tracked priority, verify the trigger and the effective priority; do not assume it is configured by default.
Core failure: stop R1 and verify the reachability lost. Test local same-VLAN and inter-VLAN traffic separately; their survival depends on the remaining access and distribution paths, not on the core endpoint’s reachability.
Return path: in the isolated lab remove or filter the route on R1 back to one VLAN. Observe whether the forward probe reaches the remote endpoint and whether replies return. Restore the route and verify the selected FIB and application traffic.
Control-plane partition: filter VRRP advertisements only between D1 and D2 in an isolated variant with packet captures. Record the possibility of simultaneous active states, MAC movement and disruption; the outcome depends on timing and topology. Remove the filter, verify a single active router and confirm traffic recovery.
VLAN fault: remove one test VLAN from the relevant lab link or bridge. Verify which traffic is affected while physical link remains up, then restore membership. If the chosen lab uses separate untagged bridges rather than trunks, alter the appropriate bridge membership instead of inventing trunk commands.

For every drill save a timeline containing fault start, detection, protocol transition, route/FIB changes, last failed and first successful probe, plus the observation point. Probe interval bounds measurement precision: one-second probes cannot prove a 100 ms outage. Packet capture or higher-frequency controlled probes can improve resolution but add overhead. The drills are a vendor-neutral test plan; they have not been executed as a complete deployment in this chapter.

title: Campus Design: Failure Domains and Verification
text:
Review the design
Which components remain single points of failure? What happens if the active first hop loses only its upstream link? What does the chosen tracking probe verify, and what can it miss? Could a partial failure preserve VRRP while breaking an application? Which direction and which VLAN did each test actually cover? Record risks and proposed changes, then repeat the matrix after every material design change.
References: VRRPv3, RFC 9568, BFD, RFC 5880, and loop-free convergence framework, RFC 5715.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
Edge Dual-Home Lab
This chapter is a full edge workout: one customer site, two uplinks to two providers, first-hop redundancy on the LAN, filtered eBGP, and failure drills. Stack: Containerlab + FRR + Alpine (mid-2026 free path). Optional SR Linux as a PE substitute for CLI diversity.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Design dual-homed CE addressing and AS layout

Prefer one uplink with local-preference; backup with AS-path prepend

Combine VRRP VIP for hosts with dual CE or single CE dual-uplink patterns

Prove failover with ping bursts, BGP tables, and traceroute

Ship a lab folder that meets the book’s definition of done

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
Design choices (pick one primary)

Pattern A — Single CE, two eBGP uplinks (simpler)
        pe1 (AS65010)
       /
   ce (AS65001) ---- LAN ---- hosts (GW = ce LAN IP or VIP if HA pair)
       \
        pe2 (AS65020)


Pattern B — Dual CE + VRRP (more realistic campus edge)
        pe1
       /
   ce1 === VRRP VIP === LAN --- hosts
       \   /
        ce2
         \
          pe2
This chapter implements Pattern B as the main lab and notes how to simplify to A.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
Topology YAML
name: dualhome

topology:
  nodes:
    ce1:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/ce1:/etc/frr
    ce2:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/ce2:/etc/frr
    pe1:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/pe1:/etc/frr
    pe2:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.2.1
      binds:
        - ./config/pe2:/etc/frr
    h1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2 iputils
        - ip addr add 192.168.50.10/24 dev eth1
        - ip link set eth1 up
        - ip route add default via 192.168.50.254
    lan:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3.20
      exec:
        - apk add --no-cache iproute2
        - ip link add br0 type bridge
        - ip link set br0 up

  links:
    - endpoints: ["h1:eth1", "lan:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["ce1:eth1", "lan:eth2"]
    - endpoints: ["ce2:eth1", "lan:eth3"]
    - endpoints: ["ce1:eth2", "pe1:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["ce2:eth2", "pe2:eth1"]
Enslave LAN ports to br0 in a deploy hook:
for n in eth1 eth2 eth3; do
  docker exec clab-dualhome-lan ip link set $n master br0
  docker exec clab-dualhome-lan ip link set $n up
done

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
CE1 config sketch
frr version 10.2.1
frr defaults traditional
hostname ce1
!
interface lo
 ip address 10.0.0.1/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 192.168.50.2/24
 vrrp 1 ip 192.168.50.254
 vrrp 1 priority 200
!
interface eth2
 ip address 172.16.10.1/30
!
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.0.0.1
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor 172.16.10.2 remote-as 65010
 !
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 192.168.50.0/24
  neighbor 172.16.10.2 route-map FROM-PE in
  neighbor 172.16.10.2 route-map TO-PE out
 exit-address-family
!
ip prefix-list SITE seq 5 permit 192.168.50.0/24
ip prefix-list SITE seq 10 deny any
!
ip prefix-list DEFAULT-OK seq 5 permit 0.0.0.0/0
ip prefix-list DEFAULT-OK seq 10 deny any
!
route-map TO-PE permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list SITE
route-map TO-PE deny 20
!
route-map FROM-PE permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list DEFAULT-OK
 set local-preference 200
route-map FROM-PE deny 20
!
line vty
no bgp ebgp-requires-policy is a lab convenience on some FRR versions—prefer explicit policies always in “production-shaped” labs.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
CE2 config differences

LAN IP .3, VRRP priority 100

Uplink 172.16.20.1/30 to pe2

Outbound prepend so pe2 is less preferred by others if both advertise:

route-map TO-PE permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list SITE
 set as-path prepend 65001 65001

Inbound local-pref 100 (lower than ce1’s 200) if both learn default:

route-map FROM-PE permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list DEFAULT-OK
 set local-preference 100
For dual-CE, each CE may only have one uplink—VRRP chooses which CE hosts use; each CE’s BGP prefers its own default. Advanced: iBGP between ce1/ce2—optional stretch goal.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
PE1 / PE2 sketch
hostname pe1
!
interface lo
 ip address 1.1.1.1/32
!
interface eth1
 ip address 172.16.10.2/30
!
router bgp 65010
 bgp router-id 1.1.1.1
 neighbor 172.16.10.1 remote-as 65001
 !
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 0.0.0.0/0
  network 1.1.1.1/32
  neighbor 172.16.10.1 route-map FROM-CE in
  neighbor 172.16.10.1 route-map TO-CE out
 exit-address-family
!
ip prefix-list CE-ALLOW seq 5 permit 192.168.50.0/24
ip prefix-list CE-ALLOW seq 10 deny any
!
route-map FROM-CE permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list CE-ALLOW
route-map FROM-CE deny 20
!
ip prefix-list ORIGINATE seq 5 permit 0.0.0.0/0
ip prefix-list ORIGINATE seq 10 permit 1.1.1.1/32
route-map TO-CE permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list ORIGINATE
!
line vty
pe2 mirrors with AS 65020, 2.2.2.2, 172.16.20.2.
Hijack drill: temporarily add network 203.0.113.0/24 on CE—PE must not install it.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
Drill 1 — Primary PE session loss
docker exec clab-dualhome-ce1 ip link set eth2 down
sleep 2
docker exec clab-dualhome-ce1 vtysh -c 'show bgp summary'
docker exec clab-dualhome-h1 ping -c 20 2.2.2.2
docker exec clab-dualhome-h1 traceroute -n 2.2.2.2

Predict → observe → fix







Predict
If false




Host still uses ce1 VIP (VRRP unchanged)
—


ce1 loses default → traffic blackholes unless ce2 takes VIP or ce1 has alternate
Add static floating / iBGP / kill VRRP master



Important teaching moment: if only ce1 is master and its uplink dies, VRRP does not care unless you track the uplink (BFD/link tracking) or lower priority. Options:

Shut ce1 LAN to force VRRP failover (crude).

Configure track/priority decrement when eth2 down (if supported).

Run dual default via both CEs with host-side multipath (rare).

Document which design you chose. Professional edges tie FHRP priority to uplink health.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
Drill 2 — Force VRRP failover
docker exec clab-dualhome-ce1 ip link set eth1 down
sleep 3
docker exec clab-dualhome-ce2 vtysh -c 'show vrrp'
docker exec clab-dualhome-h1 ip neigh flush dev eth1
docker exec clab-dualhome-h1 ping -c 10 2.2.2.2
docker exec clab-dualhome-h1 traceroute -n 2.2.2.2

Predict
ce2 Master; path via pe2; short disruption.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
Drill 3 — Policy rejection
# on ce1 temporarily
docker exec -it clab-dualhome-ce1 vtysh
# network 203.0.113.0/24 under bgp + dummy interface address if needed
docker exec clab-dualhome-pe1 vtysh -c 'show bgp ipv4 uni 203.0.113.0/24'

Predict
Empty / not best—filter works. If accepted, fix FROM-CE prefix-list.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
Drill 4 — Name/time smoke (hygiene)
Optional: add dnsmasq A record vip.site.lab → 192.168.50.254 and dig from h1; confirm date -u roughly matches host.

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
verify.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
fail() { echo "FAIL: $*" >&2; exit 1; }

docker exec clab-dualhome-h1 ping -c 2 -W 1 192.168.50.254 || fail "vip"
docker exec clab-dualhome-pe1 vtysh -c 'show bgp ipv4 uni' | grep -q '192.168.50.0' \
  || fail "pe1 missing site"
# hijack should be absent
if docker exec clab-dualhome-pe1 vtysh -c 'show bgp ipv4 uni' | grep -q '203.0.113.0'; then
  fail "hijack accepted"
fi
echo OK

title: Edge Dual-Home Lab
text:
Summary

Dual-home labs combine multihoming policy and first-hop HA—design their interaction

FRR eBGP + prefix-lists + VRRP are enough for a portfolio-quality edge

Always test policy negatives (hijack) and uplink vs VIP failures separately

Prefer link tracking or clear runbooks when master loses upstream

This lab maps to capstone C2 in the ops part

Next part: policy, QoS vocabulary, and hardening—filters beyond BGP, control-plane protection, and checklists.

title: FRRouting Cheat Sheet
text:
FRRouting Cheat Sheet
FRR runs on Linux; host interfaces and addresses are visible through ip, while routing daemons are managed through vtysh. Daemons must be enabled in the image or lab configuration. Replace the node and interfaces with those in your topology.

title: FRRouting Cheat Sheet
text:
Connect and inspect
docker exec -it clab-LAB-r-frr vtysh
docker exec clab-LAB-r-frr ip -br address
docker exec clab-LAB-r-frr ip route show
At the vtysh prompt:
show running-config
show interface
show ip route
show ipv6 route
show ip ospf neighbor
show bgp summary
show bgp ipv4 unicast
show bgp ipv4 unicast 203.0.113.0/24

title: FRRouting Cheat Sheet
section: Configure and verify a static route
text:
Configure and verify a static route
configure terminal
ip route 192.0.2.0/24 10.1.12.2
end
show ip route 192.0.2.0/24
Remove it with no ip route 192.0.2.0/24 10.1.12.2 in configuration mode. A route requires a reachable next hop. FRR configuration persistence depends on the container image and its mounted configuration; write memory writes the configured FRR files, but lab recreation can replace them. Save changes in the lab’s source configuration.

title: FRRouting Cheat Sheet
text:
Troubleshoot
Compare FRR’s route with Linux ip route get 192.0.2.1; check interfaces, neighbor state, and captures with tcpdump -ni eth1. BGP and OSPF show commands require their corresponding daemons and configuration.
